title: Ticket #3721: update curl external
description: NOTE This would appear to be a security problem, but in reality is mitigated by a number of factors. (CVE-2013-2174) https://rhn.redhat.com/errata/RHSA-2013-0983.html curl has a buffer overflow attack that could allow arbitrary code execution, and since file transfer plugins do run with privilege, this could allow a submitter to escalate their own privilege on an execute machine. However, because HTCondor dynamically links curl, it is up to the machine owner to provide an updated curl library. This is true for the Linux and MacOS platforms we currently support. On Windows, the curl_plugin is not currently included in the distribution (it should be, but that's a separate issue). We should still upgrade the external for people who are compiling from scratch on systems without libcurl. However, this issue will not cause a special security release.

title: Ticket #3371: Create authorization ping tool
description: It's quite useful to be able to invoke an "echo" command on a remote condor daemon to see which authorizations the current user has. This suggestion is from experience - this has been extraordinarily useful in the Globus world, as it allows sysadmins to test the functionality of their site's authorization setup. We've had many folks complain about the complexity of configuring Condor authorization - a mechanism like this will help people test their own sites. title: Ticket #683: Job can be in neither job_queue.log nor history
description: When a job finishes, the schedd first removed it from the job_queue.log, then writes it into the history. This creates a window during which condor_q and condor_history can report that the job doesn't exist at all. (This has been erratically seen in the test suite.) It also means that if the schedd crashes at exactly the wrong moment, the job disappears. We can't just swap the order of operations, or we risk duplicate copies appearing in the history, or both condor_q and condor_history reporting the job. The correct solution is to make the edit to both files atomic. This might be an argument for moving both files over to SQLite, which I believe can guarantee an atomic commit for multi-file situations.

title: Ticket #7332: GSI bug with newer OpenSSL
description: A bug in GSI causes client and server to get out-of-sync with newer versions of OpenSSL (first noticed in Ubuntu 18). A patch has been applied to our Globus external and submitted to the gridcf GitHub project (https://github.com/gridcf/gct/pull/136). It's unknown if this can be worked around at the Condor layer. Original Ticket Description The GSI auth tests started failing on Ubuntu 18. Investigate why. To reproduce, create empty directory and place attached Dockerfile in it. From within that directory: docker build . docker run -t -i <imagehash> /bin/bash #inside docker container: su - condor condor_master sh run_this If you do this on dumbo.chtc.wisc.edu likely everything is cached. Image id is 0ef6c9db9803
remarks: 2019-Dec-16 11:20:49 by tim: Zach tried this test on the build machine and it worked there in env matching the build. Still investigating 2020-Apr-10 07:42:27 by tim: Bulk change of target version from v080808 to v080809 using ticket-target-mover. 2020-Aug-20 22:38:27 by jfrey: There's a bug in GSI in function gss_init_sec_context(). When the client side finishes the SSL handshake, if there's a payload to be sent to the server, it indicates that the full authentication protocol is complete. The client then skips the post-handshake data exchange, putting the two sides out of sync. In older versions of openssl, the client SSL code appears to wait for a reply from the server before indicating the SSL handshake is done. On Ubuntu 18, the client SSL code indicates the handshake is done while providing a payload to send to the server. Fixing the bug causes the GSI authentication to succeed on Ubuntu 18. But the GSI test still fails on Ubuntu 20, Debian 10, and CentOS 8. Additionally, there's a bug in the Condor layer when there's a network error when receiving the post-handshake message from the server about whether it's happy about the handshake. This can cause the client to think the server is happy when it is not. 2020-Oct-19 13:05:59 by zmiller: CODE REVIEW: The changes to the Condor code look good. I did not review the proposed changes to GSI, and am leaving that for their development team. Resolving.

title: Ticket #6935: Unexpected exceptions in Python bindings
description: The Python bindings often raise Python exceptions which are not consistent with the way the rest of the community uses them. Here are the patterns I saw: - usage of RuntimeError (or sometimes ValueError!) when unable to do stuff with another host/process/daemon Any sort of communication error is an IOError. It would be even better to make one or more subclasses of IOError for different categories of problems so people can distinguish them without having to parse text. - usage of SyntaxError or RuntimeError when there is a problem parsing a classad SyntaxError is reserved for Python syntax errors. For classad parsing errors, make a new classad.ParseError exception. - usage of TypeError or ValueError (often inconsistently) when failing to evaluate expressions Better to make an EvaluateError (classad.EvaluateError?) instead so people can tell it's a problem with their classad. - usage of ValueError when an object is not iterable This is pretty clearly a TypeError. - usage of RuntimeError at all RuntimeError is too generic; it leads to people parsing the error message to figure out what the actual problem is, which we don't want. A couple of other problems (files and line numbers are from src/python-bindings in master (8a4c7f9ad6)): bulk_query_iterator.cpp lines 122-125: if (m_selector.failed()) { THROW_EX(RuntimeError, "select() failed."); } select() failing is probably an OSError especially if it has an errno associated with it. classad.cpp line 526: if (!PyObject_HasAttrString(source.ptr(), "__iter__")) THROW_EX(ValueError, "Must provide a dictionary-like object to update()"); Use TypeError. config.cpp lines 245, 580: if (!py_hasattr(source, "__iter__")) { THROW_EX(ValueError, "Must provide a dictionary-like object to update()"); } TypeError. JobEventLog.cpp line 53: THROW_EX( RuntimeError, "deadline must be an integer" ); TypeError.
remarks: 2019-Mar-02 20:34:35 by tlmiller: > Here are the patterns I saw: > > - usage of RuntimeError (or sometimes ValueError!) when unable to do stuff with > another host/process/daemon > > Any sort of communication error is an IOError. Just to be certain: it's an IOError to specify a host which doesn't exist? > It would be even better to make one or more subclasses of IOError for > different categories of problems so people can distinguish them without > having to parse text. .... > - usage of ValueError when an object is not iterable > > This is pretty clearly a TypeError. Implying that when object.__iter()__ returns an object which doesn't have an iterator, it's also a TypeError? Does code like the following make sense? if (m_claim.empty()) {THROW_EX(ValueError, "No claim set for object.");} Would it make more sense to return a failure, instead? Likewise, claim.cpp is lousy with: // FIXME: Should at least be IOError THROW_EX(RuntimeError, "Startd failed to activate claim."); but IOError seems a little ill-fitting -- the IO succeeded, but the command in question did not. That seems like maybe the function should return success or failure and only throw IOError if something actually happened to the I/O? 2019-Mar-03 13:09:17 by tlmiller: Is there a reason that _classad_module.cpp and _htcondor_module.cpp exist? (Can we really not bully CMake into making different libraries out of the same source file?) Is there a reason that they aren't symlinks? (It would seem to violate the principle of least astonishment for the wheel-built modules to be different.) 2019-Mar-04 11:42:47 by matyas: > Just to be certain: it's an IOError to specify a host which doesn't exist? Yes. title: Ticket #4908: EventLog lock contention
description: CMS has noticed a high level of contention for the EventLog lock (we had one schedd which stalled for >5 minutes, which led to the master nuking the process), which led me to poke at the schedd via strace. A few things that could be cleaned up: The event and the corresponding "job ad information" are written under separate locks - meaning that a separate event entry could be logged between the two. Under high contention, the lock deletion code becomes a mess as it tries to obtain the lock in order to delete it. I observed multiple processes racing in the deletion code - meaning a given process may recreate the lock several times in order to obtain (and delete) it. :( I can't see any reason why O_APPEND can't be used here. The FILE * buffers the events so only one write() call is done on fflush. I wouldn't want to depend on that for correctness in all cases, but it would be nice to be able to make the tradeoff. Perhaps O_APPEND is used if EVENT_LOG_LOCKING=false. We really don't care about job ad updates - we wanted to use the EventLog for forensics (what got run where). I don't see a mechanism for doing that - would be useful.
remarks: 2015-Feb-23 11:09:10 by tannenba: At first blush, I very much like the idea of giving the event log writing code the "dprintf" treatment such that a lock is only required on rotation iff the config file disables event log writing, and then set the param table to disable event log locking by default. This change should be at the lower level of the event writing code so we impact not only the schedd event log, but all event log writes (i.e. job event log, dagman event log). We should be sure that any daemon (except perhaps dagman itself? ie limit it to schedd/shadows that have condor access?) that gets the lock is able to do the rotation, and also investigate the mess surrounding removing the lock file. Setting to v080304 and assigning to Jaime (since he did the coding for the dprintf log treatment). Not directly related, and should be a separate ticket, but also thinking about the event logs, I am thinking about disabling fsync by default on job and schedd event logs (but keeping it enabled by default on dagman event logs), and also about a way to keep the dagman event logs on an ssd. Ie a knobs like SPOOL=path and SPOOL_HIGH_SPEED=path, and SPOOL_HIGH_SPEED would store just the job_queue.log and DAGMan event log files by default. 2015-Mar-04 14:03:35 by jfrey: I have implemented the following changes for 8.3.5: Each event is written with a single write() syscall. This makes it safe to turn off locking of the user log and event log. This doesn't affect the rotation lock for the event log. For rotation of the event log, the lock file is always a long-lived, explicitly named file, in the LOCK directory by default. This eliminates the need for the schedd to acquire the lock and delete the file every time it writes an event. In a future release, we will make non-locked writing the default. 2015-Apr-07 08:54:17 by bbockelm: Re-opening due to noticing a bug (before 8.3.5 release). This fails because DAGMan does not have permission to lock the file. This behavior is the same in previous versions of Condor. 2015-Apr-08 08:11:37 by bbockelm: For gittrac history - follow-up work is being done in #4989. I disagree that this is the same behavior as before. Previously, this message was only seen if there actually was log contention on startup - probably fairly rare. Now, this warning will be printed for every single DAG. Further, won't this cause the same lock to be used for all user logs? 2015-Apr-08 10:17:59 by jfrey: In previous versions of Condor, if you set EVENT_LOG_ROTATION_LOCK in the config file, then you would see those same errors messages in the same situations. title: Ticket #1823: management of many child heartbeat timers doesn't scale well
description: When the schedd has 40k-50k running jobs, we observe that it spends a large fraction of its time handling heartbeats from the shadows. A typical call stack looks like this: #0 0x000000000059b35c in TimerManager::InsertTimer(tagTimer*) () #1 0x000000000059bd90 in TimerManager::ResetTimer(int, unsigned int, unsigned int, bool, Timeslice const*) () #2 0x0000000000585ac1 in DaemonCore::HandleChildAliveCommand(int, Stream*) () #3 0x00000000005803e2 in DaemonCore::CallCommandHandler(int, Stream*, bool) () #4 0x000000000058df57 in DaemonCore::HandleReq(Stream*, Stream*) () #5 0x0000000000590740 in DaemonCore::HandleReqSocketHandler(Stream*) () #6 0x0000000000590235 in DaemonCore::CallSocketHandler_worker(int, bool, Stream*) () #7 0x00000000005906da in DaemonCore::CallSocketHandler_worker_demarshall(void*) () #8 0x0000000000651458 in CondorThreads::pool_add(void (*)(void*), void*, int*, char const*) () #9 0x00000000005897b9 in DaemonCore::CallSocketHandler(int&, bool) () #10 0x000000000058b6b5 in DaemonCore::Driver() () #11 0x000000000057e860 in main () The problem is that InsertTimer() is expensive because it does a linear search through existing timers to find the appropriate place to insert the timer that enforces NOT_RESPONDING_TIMEOUT for the shadow that has just sent a heartbeat. The workaround is to set SHADOW_NOT_RESPONDING_TIMEOUT higher. Proposed Solution The timers could be stored in a std::multimap with the firing time as the key. This would allow efficient insertion. However, removal or resetting of a timer would still be expensive, because it involves a linear search for a timer with the specified id. This could be solved by having a map of id to timer. When there are many timers registered to fire at the same time, removal or resetting of a timer from the multimap would still be expensive. This would need to be studied. If it is a problem, we could use std::map instead and create our own doubly linked list to handle collisions. Removal of timer objects (given a pointer) from the doubly linked list would be fast. An alternative solution is to not have one timer per child. Instead, periodically do a sweep over all children to see if any have stalled. This would sacrifice accuracy of enforcement of NOT_RESPONDING_TIMEOUT. The parent process could be late by as much as the sweeping interval to notice that a child is not responding. That seems perfectly acceptable. Making timer management scale has the advantage that it could benefit other situations in condor where there are large numbers of timers. However, it is a more complicated change than simply having a single timer to check for hung children.

title: Ticket #5163: Buffer received messages from ReliSock
description: Currently, there's no buffering on the ReliSock for receiving data (unlike sending data, which is buffered until 4KB or EOM). Each thing coded on the socket (string, integer) is a separate call to recv() (and two fcntl and a poll). This is especially obvious when receiving ClassAd updates (NOTE: during later investigation, it was revealed that the problematic case is qmgmt updates, not ClassAds). Each attribute in an ad requires two recv()'s, meaning each attribute is about 10 syscalls. I think RcvMsg should do a non-blocking read into a buffer; if there's insufficient bytes immediately available, then repeat the blocking read with precisely the number of bytes required.
remarks: 2015-Jul-22 22:03:14 by bbockelm: Chatting with Jaime, there might be something more subtle here (we think that it does "the right thing" in many cases). Maybe this only occurs when in non-blocking mode? 2015-Aug-03 08:55:39 by bbockelm: Found some time to poke around at this one - ClassAds didn't seem to be the problem in the end. Instead, it was a lot of the QMGMT commands (for example, condor_submit results in two recvfrom() syscalls per attribute; condor_shadow updates have a similar cost). Enabling buffering in the ReliSock isn't too tricky - will push a branch soon. The tricky part is the interplay between ReliSock and the Selector object; as the file descriptor no longer has bytes to read, it is no longer marked as ready by select. Hence, any code touching ReliSock's must explicitly understand the buffered mode. Accordingly, I left buffering off by default and only enabled it for DaemonCore-managed sockets and places where the socket has a short managed lifetime. This will prevent such buffered sockets from leaking to places like the python bindings.
check_ins: 2015-Aug-03 08:42 Check-in [45451]: Allow ReliSock to buffer incoming data. #5163 This adds a buffered mode to the ReliSock (off by default) which keeps a 4KB buffer internal to the socket object itself. As the buffer mode will screw up polling of the underlying FD, it is only enabled for sockets registered for read in DC. (By Brian Bockelman )
creator: bbockelm

title: Ticket #5499: shadow can hang while rotating log when max log > 1
description: Via rust, we have a report that a shadow was seen spinning in cleanUpOldLogFiles and other shadows locked waiting for it to release the rotation lock. The customer used a debugger to determine that the problem is that the current directory is not the condor log directory, and that the rotate_file(oldname,newname) call in cleanUpOldLogFiles was being passed a simple filename as oldname, and a fully qualified filename as newname. This is equivalent to calling rotate_file(pwd+oldname,newname), which is not what this code is supposed to do, but which would work if the pwd is the log directory. If it isn't, then the while loop in cleanUpOldLogFiles will never exit, and that shadow will never give up the rotation lock.

title: Ticket #115: Scrub download data
description: In the download logs, from roughly April to May 2008, if the user used reload, bookmarks, or back/forward, they could be listed as downloading the same file repeatedly. This has since been corrected. (It’s still possible, but much, much more unlikely.) However, the old downloads are still in the logs. This data should be expunged. The logs are in /p/condor/public/license/sendfile-* A tool to copy the file from stdin to stdout, expunging the duplicates can be found in /p/condor/workspaces/adesmet/graphs/downloads/scrub-sendfile. I’ll attach a copy as well. If the version in /p/condor/workspaces is still around, it’s probably newer and should be preferred. The tool just looks for multiple downloads of the same file by the same email address inside of $WINDOW, which is a number of seconds. We might use a value of somewhere between 60*60*1 and 60*60*24 inclusive depending on how aggresive we want to be. To purge any duplicate downloads, you could use 60*60*24*365. The tool relies on a quirk of the new system to identify potentially wrong records. (The old system provided an ID number that was the pid. The new system uses a pid and an additional number, seperated by an underscore.) Old records should be passed through unmodified. As a result, no matter how aggressively you set the tool, it won’t purge duplicate downloads from the old system. Be wary when making this adjustment; the condor-admin mail filter is appending to these files frequently; done wrong you could lose some data. (Imported from 1627 (backup) 1627 (public))

title: Ticket #4637: Support scope-id specification for link-local IPv6 addresses.
description: When you configure HTCondor to use IPv6 only on a machine that does not have a global IPv6 address, HTCondor (rightly) prefers the link-local address. However, Linux (et alia?) requires a link-local IPv6 address to be specified with a trailing %<scope-id>. Problems: HTCondor appears to blithely ignores non-numerics after an IPv6 address. HTCondor address discovery doesn't supply interface information. HTCondor probably discards interface information when writing to its .address file. HTCondor probably discards interface information when writing a sinful and/or to a classad. I don't imagine this is important to fix any time soon (who actually uses link-local addresses?), but it might be wise to temporarily suppress their generation until they actually work. inet_pton should be doing the correct thing. condor_sockaddr should be correctly holding on to the scope id in v6.sin6_scope_id. Conversion into Sinful almost certainly loses it! A scope ID can always be an integer (it's an index of the interface). Linux, at least, allows an interface name; inet_pton will find the matching integer. It's okay if we throw away the interface name and only use the integer internally. Observation: the only way to determine the correct scope-id is to get it off an active connection to the host in question. The server cannot know what scope-id you'll need, nor can the negotiator. Is there any point to trying to support them at all? It seems like it might be useful for setting up a pool quickly (just slap some machines on a switch and rely on the link local addresses), but we're literally down to guessing which interface to use. We could potentially support binding to a single IPv6 link local interface and assuming that all link-local connections should use it. Ideally we should always support specifications on the command line.
remarks: 2018-Jan-16 14:25:57 by jfrey: Ticket #6518 includes improvements so that scope-ids are handled correctly in the following situations: There's a single link-local IPv6 address on the local machine. A single link-local IPv6 address is specified by the NETWORK_INTERFACE config param. This should handle a lot of use cases, including "just slap some machines on a switch".

title: Ticket #400: Feature: Set NUM_CPUS and MEMORY based on default value
description: It would be nice if one could specify NUM_CPUS and MEMORY as an expression relative to the default value. Why? To take a real example based on CS architecture group needs, maybe you want to add a "whole-machine" slot that can hog all of the CPUs and the RAM. You use a clever combination of START, SUSPEND, PREEMPT, and KILL to ensure that the whole-machine slot and the remaining slots are mutually exclusive. Now you could say (assuming a 2 CPU machine with 2 GB of ram) NUM_SLOTS=3 RAM=4*1024 NUM_CPUS=4 SLOT_TYPE_1 = cpus=50%, ram=50% NUM_SLOTS_TYPE_1 = 1 However, this fails if you add memory to the machine, or try to use this policy for a pool with mixed numbers of CPUs per machine. A policy would be: NUM_SLOTS=3 RAM=$(ACTUAL_RAM)*2 NUM_CPUS=$(ACTUAL_CPUS)*2 SLOT_TYPE_1 = cpus=50%, ram=50% NUM_SLOTS_TYPE_1 = 1 Assuming ACTUAL_RAM and ACTUAL_CPUS existed and worked, this would Just Work even on a mixed pool. Policy expressions based on Memory would work correctly. It may be worth considering #246, which calls for DetectedCPUs to be added to Machine ClassAds
remarks: 2009-Apr-21 16:37:11 by adesmet: Another option would be to allow the following: SLOT_TYPE_1 = cpus=100%, ram=100% SLOT_TYPE_2 = cpus=100%/($(NUM_SLOTS)-1), ram=100%/($(NUM_SLOTS)-1) NUM_SLOTS_TYPE_1 = 1 NUM_SLOTS_TYPE_2 = $(NUM_SLOTS)-1 You'd need to teach the SLOT_TYPE code to accept expressions in SLOT_TYPE_* and NUM_SLOTS_TYPE_*. You would also need to allow overcommiting resources. Currently it doesn't, and this is a useful error for debugging bad configurations. We can issue a warning of overcommision on startup, but in reality no one will ever notice. Currently Condor does EXCEPT. # Currently Condor detects this mistake with a fatal error. NUM_CPUS=2 SLOT_TYPE_1 = cpus=2 SLOT_TYPE_2 = cpus=2 2009-Dec-17 17:10:30 by matt: As of 7.4.0, DETECTED_CORES/MEMORY is available, and many config param values are evaluated ClassAd expressions. This gets you RAM=$(DETECTED_MEMORY)*2, but not SLOT_TYPE1=cpus=$(DETECTED_CORES). I'd consider this resolved. If you agree, please resolve it. 2009-Dec-17 17:37:10 by adesmet: Works for me!

title: Ticket #2219: RFE: check for deferred jobs that missed their window in the scheduler
description: There are certain conditions where a deferred job that misses its window can fail to enter the 'held' state. For example, it may fail to be matched with a slot in time, or (more rarely) the startd might fail after matching. These conditions can arise because deferred jobs are only checked for holding in the startd. A similar check could be added to the scheduler: the count() routine could include a scan for jobs with deferral, and if they have missed their window and are still idle, the scheduler can put them on hold. Adding this check would increase the consistency of the behavior for deferred jobs missing their window.

title: Ticket #2167: Propagate DAG node priorities down to job priorities
description: This resulted from today's meeting with the Spalding lab people. Anyhow, they basically want node priorities to propagate down through sub-DAGs, and then to the actual Condor priorities of the node jobs within the sub-DAGs. Since you can specify node priorities in each DAG, there would have to be some kind of concatenation of priorities at each level, and then DAGMan would eventually pass the result when it submitted a job. Also, the user would be able to set priorities for the top-level DAGs (maybe we'd need a new condor_submit_dag command-line flag for this, because we don't want to encourage people to edit the .condor.sub files). A DAG would get its priority from its Condor priority, so that way priorities could get propagated down through sub-DAGs. So, for example, if a top-level DAG itself had a priority of 5, and then it had a subdag external node with a priority of 3, and that sub-DAG had a node with a priority of 6, the job might end up getting submitted with a priority of 50306. (Obviously, this would only work right for a certain range of priority values; and we'd have to think about how to handle negative priorities, since they are allowed.) Hmm -- and we'd have to really think about this, because in that example, "deeper" nodes with have better priorities, which might not be what we want... There should probably be a flag to turn this on or off -- the implication if it's on is that DAGMan would override any Condor priorities set in node job submit files.

If anything, I think it makes what we want to do more complicated, because which priority do we set? I wish they'd have given a more detailed scenario of how this is supposed to be used -- I'm not totally sure what it gains us over just having one priority value. 2011-Jun-15 10:56:41 by nwp: My plan now is to sum the priorities of the dag harmonically from the root to a node, then multiply the user priority by that sum to give a priority for that job. Then insert the priority in the node job file. Negative priorities will be set to 1 for the first round, until we see what is the correct thing to do. Another idea is to sum exponentially. Here I mean Harmonic sum: s-1=x1-1+...+xn-1 Exponential sum: 2-s=2-x1+... 2-xn The point here is to preserve order. 2011-Jun-15 12:53:41 by psilord: How do you handle diamond-style dag structures with your priority propagation math? Suppose you have a user priority and job priorities and this dag: a -> b, c b -> d -> e -> f c, f -> g What's the priority of g? 2011-Jun-15 13:10:25 by nwp: Good question. I am thinking I will initially take max_prio(S), where S is the set of parent dag nodes. 2011-Jun-15 16:17:34 by psilord: There are different choices for the mixing of the contributions of the priorities from parental paths: max, min, average, statistical variance, choose one only, and [infinite set of functions].... Why are any of them better than any other? In practice, which one would be what the user wants to do? I could see something like a priority of a node dominating all nodes below it. A high priority node would contaminate the future nodes with the same priority. This is your max_prio(S) solution. It seems to makes sense, but I could see other functions that would be just as useful, like take the priority of the first parental node after being lexographically sorted. Is it possible for the user to supply a function which acts as a selector for an arbitrary number of contributing priorities and have it default to max() unless otherwise specified? My intuition tell me no, since Condor isn't that flexible in this context.... but if you could do it cheaply in your time, that might be the way to go. 2011-Jun-15 16:19:36 by psilord: Also, see my remark on ticket #1482 about priority calculations between jobs. That can represent a DAG as well. 2011-Jun-15 16:23:06 by psilord: Hrm, wrong ticket, lemme find the right one... 2011-Jun-15 16:27:24 by psilord: Ah ok, here it is: #1992. It might not be directly applicable here, but it would be good to have in your mind. 2011-Jun-30 09:31:21 by nwp: Currently, we want to avoid starving high-priority children that have low-priority parents, so the priorities get copied up, to the parents. But then if a user declares a toplevel low priority DAG node, the priority gets overwritten. If you have a library of DAGs, you may want the toplevel priority to take precedence. Of course then a solution is to have a policy that a library DAG node can only have a priority in a certain range, say, (0,100), and the toplevel DAG node policy would then be to have priority in the range of, say, (101,200). (Currently here means the patch as it is on 30 June 2011). 2011-Jun-30 12:53:14 by nwp: OK, here is a use case where I am not sure what to do: A->B, C->D. Here A is high priority, B is low. C is low, D is high. This dag gets submitted. A runs first, finishes, and then B starts. C runs, and starts up D. Does D then preempt B? My intuition is that the sequence A,C,D,B is better. 2011-Sep-14 15:13:46 by psilord: Ok I reviewed it. Looks good. 2011-Sep-14 15:26:05 by nwp: Merged to master at 2853cb6. title: Ticket #791: Reduce shadow memory usage
description: Of all of the daemons, the memory size for the shadow is the most important. A user might have hundreds or thousands running simultaneously. Over the years we've gotten lax about what creeps in, and the shadow's non-sharable heap is pretty big. We should find out where the memory is going and try to cut down on it, either eliminating it or only using the memory when we use the feature requiring the memory (eg #786).
remarks: 2010-Oct-20 15:59:08 by jfrey: Bulk change of target version from v070504 to v070505 using ./ticket-target-mover. 2011-Jan-27 14:46:04 by danb: Bulk change of target version from v070505 to v070506 using ./ticket-target-mover. 2011-Feb-01 14:49:30 by tannenba: Bulk change of target version from v070506 to NULL using ./ticket-target-mover. 2012-Jul-19 14:57:09 by adesmet: One of the potential paths that has been repeatedly considered is the "multi-shadow," where we have a single shadow serving multiple starters, sharing the overhead. 2012-Jul-19 15:05:06 by adesmet: See also Ticket #3137: Reduce memory usage of libcondor_utils 2012-Jul-19 15:12:36 by adesmet: Brian Bockelman did an in depth investigation and posted his results on condor-devel https://lists.cs.wisc.edu/archive/condor-devel/2012-July/msg00014.shtml The key bits are here: When I last talked to Miron about multi-shadow, he suggested first wringing every last byte out of the current one before even proposing the multi-shadow. So, I spent about an hour with igprof and staring at smaps. I measured a shadow as having 360KB of heap, about 550KB total unshared space, and 274KB of data live on the heap (so about 25% waste due to fragmentation). Here's what I found that we could save. List is in ascending order of difficulty to implement. 055 kB 0) Turn off classad caching: 55KB. 008 kB 1) Copy of job's classad inside the file transfer object: 8KB 005 kB 2) gethostbyaddr -> gethostbyaddr_r (including all callsites, even in the logging code! See ExecuteEvent::writeEvent): 5KB. 002 kB 3) getpwnam, getpwuid to reentrant versions: 2KB 007 kB 4) Remove stats object from DaemonCore for shadow: 7KB 100 kB(?) 5) libcondor_utils has 156KB of dirty writable memory (non-const statics?) that can't be shared: 100KB? This part was not included in my heap calculations, but is indeed non-shared. 005-015 kB 6) Cleanup of auth code to reduce heap fragmentation: 5-15KB 009 kB 7) Un-loading the IpVerify table after usage: 9KB. 070 kB 8) The configuration subsystem. This would be one tough nugget to crack (note: would all be shared with the multi-shadow), but is very lightly used after the shadow fires up. 70KB. Lessons learned: Classad caching does more harm than good for a single shadow (20% of heap) If we squeeze really hard at odds-n-ends in the heap, we can shrink the heap by 10%. I don't think all the items listed above are plausible (especially 8). Non-const globals in libcondor_utils consist of 25% of the total memory footprint. There are 332 source files in libcondor_utils - whack-a-mole time? Similarly, there are a few things sitting around in the other Condor libraries, but nothing as sizable. Obviously sharable resources for the multi-shadow (parameter subsystem, auth hash maps and tables, daemon core object) make up 50% of the heap. It's not immediately obvious how much the ClassAd cache will affect the multi-shadow, but I would expect a bit of sharing. Let's estimate 50% of the current cache is sharable, or 10% of the total heap. So, we can squeeze about 15% of the shadow size by continuing to shave things and turning off caching. Assuming 10 jobs per 1 shadow, we could realize a 60% memory gain. Both numbers become more dramatic if we can figure out who's hanging out in the data segment. after 5 minutes with 'nm', it appears the data segment consists primarily of the parameter table. From digging around, all of the param table and all the ATTR_* symbols are in the not-shared data segment, and hence become unique memory. The simplest way forward seems to be: Change ATTR_* to const char [] and inline the symbols. Right now, we keep N+1 copies of the symbol name and one copy of the symbol contents in memory (the symbol name and contents are about the same size; N is the number of uses of the ATTR_*). Inlining would reduce this to just N. Change the param table to be based on macros (plain symbols can be in the read-only section; structs have to be initialized), and load it on the first use. Having the attribute names and the param table non-shared are a rather embarrassing way to spend 25% of the shadow's memory budget! Updated estimates after playing with the shadow for more than an hour: All the linked libraries add up a bit more drastically than I originally thought (I had ignored all the small ones and just looked at the big ones in my first estimates). Adding in all my optimizations, there are 888KB of Private_Dirty memory. I squeezed things down to 96KB for libcondor_utils's data segment from 156KB. The savings are more drastic on more recent versions of GCC (where LTO is available). There's not much more left to squeeze out due to vtables, got, and plt. There's probably 150KB of unique data per shadow, once you subtract out the things I mention above. Hence, 738KB can be thought of as "overhead". So, running 10 jobs per shadow would result in an 75% memory savings. In all, it indicates that multi-shadow would be beneficial and "shadow squeezing" is going to continue to have diminishing returns.

title: Ticket #3799: USE_SHARED_PORT should automatically add SHARED_PORT to DAEMON_LIST
description: If one sets USE_SHARED_PORT=True but SHARED_PORT is not added to DAEMON_LIST, and shared_port daemon is not run by some other means, then only local communication is possible. The daemons complain in their logs SharedPortEndpoint: failed to open /path/to/shared_port_ad: No such file or directory SharedPortEndpoint: did not successfully find SharedPortServer address. Will retry in 60s. It may not be obvious to users why this happens and what to do about it. Proposed Change When USE_SHARED_PORT=true in the master, SHARED_PORT should be automatically added to DAEMON_LIST. There are very unusual situations where one might not want this. In those cases, there should be a way to override the default behavior: AUTO_INCLUDE_SHARED_PORT_IN_DAEMON_LIST=False. Under this proposal, in the unusual situation where the master does not have USE_SHARED_PORT=true, but some other daemons do, SHARED_PORT will not be automatically added to DAEMON_LIST. The goal is just to make the common case easier, so we will not try to solve this unusual case. This change is a prerequisite for making USE_SHARED_PORT=true by default. However, it is compatible with either default.

title: Ticket #6061: fd_set bounds checking can cause abort in Selector class
description: In recent versions of linux, the FORTIFY_SOURCE compiler flag adds a run-time array bounds check that causes an abort if a call to FD_SET() and friends would index past the end of a single fd_set. This is causing problems in our Selector class, which uses an array of fd_sets with FD_SET() to support file descriptor values too large to fit in a single fd_set (default limit of 1024). In HTCondor 8.2, we removed the FORTIFY_SOURCE flag for the Selector class's source file. We want a better fix that lets us keep the flag enabled. We can define a modified form of FD_SET() (and related macros) that calculates the address of the desired fd_set within the array of fd_sets and the offset within that fd_set, and invokes the real FD_SET() with those values.

title: Ticket #2472: Increase precision of classad::Value::integerValue to 64 bits
description: There have been at least a couple cases where there's a growing use-case for obtaining values from config files and/or classads that are > 2GB. One particular example is #2471 The "right" answer would be supporting something like param_integer_64bit(), however this in turn would require the classad library to support integer values of 64 bit precision. I think this could be accomplished with reasonable effort by changing the type of classad::Value::integerValue from "int" to "long long" (or however we choose to denote a 64 bit integer type). With an internal integer representation of 64 bits, we can then also provide accessor methods like EvaluateAttrInt64(), or EvaluateAttrLongLong, whichever seems most appropriate. I might also propose an accessor like EvaluateAttrOffT, for off_t values that may be 4 bytes on older systems.
remarks: 2011-Nov-09 13:59:47 by matt: Once this is done, param("MAX_..._LOG") code needs to be updated to use a param_int64_t (or similar) that does ClassAd evaluation. 2011-Dec-22 17:52:44 by eje: Developing on branch V7_7-gt2472-classad-64-bit-int-publicbranch 2012-Jan-20 11:05:13 by eje: There are some new unit tests associated with testing the 64-bit support, which you can run like this: # now includes testing classad support for 64-bit vals: $ ./src/condor_tests/condor_unit_tests -t OTEST_Old_Classads -f ======== SUMMARY: ======== Total Tested Objects: 1 Total Unit Tests: 282 Passed Unit Tests: 282 Failed Unit Tests: 0 Aborted Unit Tests: 0 Skipped Unit Tests: 0 Total Time Taken: 0 seconds Test suite has passed. # test param_integer and friends: $ ./src/condor_tests/condor_unit_tests -t FTEST_config -f ======== SUMMARY: ======== Total Tested Objects: 0 Total Unit Tests: 4 Passed Unit Tests: 4 Failed Unit Tests: 0 Aborted Unit Tests: 0 Skipped Unit Tests: 0 Total Time Taken: 0 seconds Test suite has passed. 2012-Jan-23 16:35:30 by eje: Design princpiples for the proposed changes: The internal integer member used to store integer values in the classad lib (Value::integerValue) changed from 'int' to 'long long', which has guaranteed precision of >= 64 bits. The data type for integer values is abstracted to a named type IntType, which is defined in the "classad" namespace and so is accessible to all code in the classad library. IntType is ideally intended to be internal to the classad lib. Calling code would get integer values as 'int' or 'long' or 'long long', etc. In practice, this ideal is violated in various places. The IntType data type is also defined in the ClassAd class definition, so that customer code using the classad libs can refer to "ClassAd::IntType" as a convenient synonym for "classad::IntType" classad API functions that currently return 'int&' on the parameter list, e.g. ClassAd::EvaluateAttrInt(), now support an additional 'long long' overloading. the same is true for int-returning functions at the compat_classad layer, e.g. Assign(... long long&), LookupInteger(... long long&) and EvalInteger(long long&). param_integer() from the config library has new friends param_long() and param_long_long() If calling code asks for 'int&' from a classad, and the evaluated value exceeds min/max 'int' value, the current proposed semantic is to return error condition if the function does this, or EXCEPT if no error return code is possible. Other proposed semantics were to cap the values at min/max value for return type. The new functionality is currently unit tested in OTEST_Old_Classad.cpp and the new FTEST_config.cpp There are cases in the condor code where the interface layer with compat_classad and/or classad is bypassed - that is, where a direct reference to IntType is required, even though that type was ideally going to be internal. I changed required declarations to IntType in those places. Ideally, those places are candidates for rewriting in the future to adhere to classad or compat_classad functions instead, but I considered that out of the scope for this ticket. Some of my working assumptions regarding mixed pools: there are two likely cases (imo): the case where a 64-bit value is configured in config file, in which case I expect such values to be mostly used locally to machines. If you configure 64 bit values, and the code can handle 64 bit values, and the environment supports them, then this will work. Otherwise it will fail, however that is already true, so I don't see this as loss of functionality. The other case is values residing on various classads. Here, the main potential problem I see is that somehow a value on a 64-bit machine grows to > 2 gig, and then goes over the wire to a 32 bit machine, where it is likely to cause problems. I don't see any way for this to not cause problems, however I also see these as likely to be rare, since pools today appear to be running fine and not generating such large values. If they were, we'd already be seeing bad behavior. What our overflow policy is will need to be considered. the proposed policy is described above, however perhaps an "all EXCEPT" policy is even better to avoid any code that ignores return values, and fail early and informatively. I think that mixed pool related problems are best dealt with via educating the user community via any needed documentation and other support. 2012-Jan-24 11:15:29 by eje: Matt recommended auditing for classad attributes and config params that are most at-risk for causing overflow problems in a mixed pool. Running list: attributes or params related to filesystem sizes, file sizes attributes related to RAM/mem schedd cumulative statistics

title: Ticket #6718: Fix spooling of late materialization itemdata
description: Just before releasing 8.7.9, we discovered that the new item data spooling feature (qmgmt command SendMaterializeData) was leaking memory by creating a new JobFactory object but not adding it to JobFactoriesSubmitPending. The item data was being stored in the JobFactory object and written into the spool directory. When the subsequent SetJobFactory qmgmt command was processed, a second JobFactory object was created (and added to JobFactoriesSubmitPending). Lacking an in-memory copy of the item data, it read the data from disk. The handler for SendMaterializeData should be adding its JobFactory to JobFactoriesSubmitPending and the handler for SetJobFactory should be using that object instead of creating a new one. But the code for reading the item data from the network directly into the JobFactory object hadn't been tested and it was too close to the release of 8.7.9, so we fixed the leak by deleting the first JobFactory object after the item data was received. Now, we should replace that quick fix with the real fix and test that it works.

title: Ticket #4375: VM universe should better handle failures to launch (guest VM)
description: In a team meeting a while back, Miron made it clear that HTCondor itself should better handle the case in which a VM universe job fails to launch due to a broken hypervisor state. With KVM, at least, what happens now is that the failure-to-launch causes a Shadow Exception and the job goes on hold. It seems sensible to me that (a) HTCondor should better report the problem to the user, and perhaps to a log, and (b) the job should go back into the queue to be rerun. Put another way, it is not the user's fault that the job failed to launch, so HTCondor should take responsibility for it. This ticket is related to other VM universe ones that are about monitoring the health of the underlying hypervisor, but it is not a duplicate.
remarks: ToddT, TimC, and ToddM discussed this. If I (and TimC) recall correctly, we agreed to the following as the immediate plan. The VM universe will be improved to identify failures to launch. On a failure to launch, the job will be rescheduled. The startd will maintain one or more machine-ad attributes indicating which "subsystem" failed to launch. (A subsystem might just be a job universe, to start.) More detail needs to be determined here. We suggested at least a single attribute listing all failed subsystems; subsystems would be removed from this list if and only if a job succeeded to launch (subject to administrative action). We could potentially add additional attributes (e.g., HasWorkingVM), to simplify writing requirements expressions; or additonal information (e.g., WhyIsTheVMBroken), for the convenience of the administrator. Bonus features: add a flag (like -vm or -java) to condor_status to filter by BrokenSubsystem and display it. This proposal may obviate the need for #4524. We agreed that follow-up work should include #4542 (EvictReason). Additional follow-up work may include setting the default requirements and/or start expressions to use these attributes. Additional follow-up work will include detecting failures to launch in other job universe (#4543). 2014-Sep-04 13:54:23 by tlmiller: Issues for Review Is there a less-dramatic way to all of the following? Force the job to be rescheduled. Write a message to the log (set by the user in the submit file). (Required, but only for future work.) Force an update to the job ad (in the schedd). [#4542] Would it make more sense to add a new event type? Is adding a new CA_* command OK? ToddT thinks job updates should go through the starter's pipe to the startd, but that only seems to apply if we happen to know that the JIC is an instance of JICShadow. I would also need to know more about the semantics and persistence of those updates. The idea of having a LastBrokenReason was stolen from other attributes like HoldReason. However, the analogy is flawed in two major ways: primus, a broken universe may be "fixed" by running some other job (that is, without any specific human intervention); secondus, as a consequence, the BrokenReason may change without the machine leaving the broken state. Does this suggest we should reconsider allowing the machine to run jobs while broken? See https://docs.google.com/a/wisc.edu/document/d/1BJ8_xh1ywGKu_xFZBkNOqQruugfyOhwERi01RmMWqRQ for a brain-dump on attribute naming. What can we do, in the message from the first point, to help the administrator locate the corresponding, and hopefully more-helpful, messages in the VM GAHP and/or starter log(s)? Is condor_update_machine_ad the appropriate approach for a command-line tool for telling HTCondor to try running VM universe jobs (or whatever) again? If we can use the pipe from the starter, do we need to keep the current mechanism for the admin anyway? 2014-Sep-04 14:11:02 by tlmiller: A brief overview of the current implementation: As our concern is with failures to launch VM jobs, we begin in VMProc::StartJob(). We inspect the return and error codes from the call to the VM GAHP. For those which are not determined to be the user's fault, we call jic->notifyStarterError() to propagate a status message back to the user, and in such a way that doing so causes the job to be rescheduled. We then notify the startd that the VM universe is broken. The mechanism for doing so is a new daemon core command. It's another in the CA_AUTH_* series, chosen because that series of commands already handles ClassAd transport, and I thought it would be wise not to attempt to enumerate all possible failure cases and/or attribute schemas. The mechanics of the implementation therefore required fewer than fifty lines of code, comments included. The business logic is quite a bit larger. By using a new daemon core command, we also expose this interface to the administrator is a natural way. That logic takes care of updating the ClassAd list of universes known to be broken and rolling/updating the Reason variables. Doing these operations in the startd (a) ensures consistency and (b) obviates the need for a round-trip so the starter can acquire the information it requires to merge the ads itself. I added a -broken flag to condor_status which is generally uninteresting. It presently doesn't print the reason(s) for the broken universe(s), because doing that right would really require either regex projections or a second round-trip. 2014-Sep-09 21:02:30 by tlmiller: Discussed the current implementaton briefly with TJ. I will investigate extending the ulog pseudo-op, if necessary with a new event (rescheduled) to write a message to the log and force a job-ad update to the schedd. This may be less incorrect than dying with a shadow exception, which causes some unnecessary log-spam. (Additonal code may be necessary; I'm not sure what the starter code does after you return false from StartJob().) He also seemed to think that adding a CA_AUTH_* command was a reasonable way to handle updating the machine (rather than job) ads. I wrote a design document after our discussion: https://docs.google.com/a/wisc.edu/document/d/1RVXLXzHI73YuQfvmGyidLFzs1jTaGcIzPrPo6_x7fs0/edit 2014-Sep-17 14:47:29 by tlmiller: The design doc is a little light on implementation specifics, but I think it captures the points that have come up in discussion, and if the abstract design is good, I don't think we're talking about anything complicated anyway. 2014-Sep-17 14:48:40 by tlmiller: Updated existing code to reflect updated design doc, except with respect to the proposed alternative for the rescheduling mechanism. Additionally, the 'U?' errors should probably be treated as 'U' errors and tickets generated appropriately. The errors should also be documented to the greatest extent reasonable, especially the 'U' errors.

title: Ticket #7109: Provide reasonable overloads for Undefined / Error in python
description: One constant irritation in the python bindings is that the Value.Undefined evaluates to true. This is because boost python, when creating the Value class, utilizes the default integer overloads. Since, in ClassAds, Undefined is represented by the integer 1, Undefined becomes coerced to 1 which becomes coerced to True. Thus, both Undefined and Error are true! Thus, because a + 1 evaluates to undefined, the following two statements have different behaviors: if classad.ExprTree("a + 1"): print "ta-da!" if classad.ExprTree("a + 1").eval(): print "ta-da!" The second will print ta-da while the first does not. Surprise! When discussing other surprising behaviors in #7107, I realized that we can, of course, overload the boost-provided operators for the classad.Value class. It's a bit awkward and not a first-class operation -- but not crazy either.

title: Ticket #841: New test: Does process X exceed allowable memory usage Y?
description: New test: Check actual memory usage of various Condor daemons. If the usage is more than X (which would be determined by OS/Arch combination, and would have to be identified by examination of existing usage), that is a failure. As new libraries are added, the test value would likely need to increase, but this test would let us catch quickly if we accidentally grew our in memory usage. This might work by simply starting up the daemons, waiting 30 seconds, and measuring usage, but that may not exercise leaky or bloated parts. Ideally the daemons would be run through some basic paces. It would also be good to set a minimum memory usage, below which results are implausible. This will potentially detect bugs in the test itself, or cases where a daemon is wildly malfunctioning but tests that test it are erroneously passing.

title: Ticket #5972: Starter crash during exit()
description: A post to the htcondor-users list reports a seg-faulting starter. The problem appears to be due to an attempt to send a ClassAd over a socket inside a global destructor, after the global destructors for some internal ClassAd data structures have already been called. I can reproduce the crash on linux by having the shadow EXCEPT() immediately after creating its child process for moving the input sandbox. The crash doesn't happen consistently, as there's a race between the starter reaping its child process (and calling EXCEPT() due to the failed transfer) and the starter receiving a SIGTERM from the startd. Here is the sequence of events in the starter: File transfer of the input sandbox is started (child process created) Network connections to the shadow are closed on the remote side SIGTERM received, starter begins a graceful shutdown With no jobs running, starter calls DC_Exit(), which deletes DaemonCore and then calls exit() Destructor for classad::specialAttrNames is called Destructor for CStarter object is called, which causes the following events Destructor for JICShadow is called Destructor for FileTransfer is called, which tries to cancel the active transfer FileTransfer::abortActiveTransfer() ASSERT()s because daemonCore is NULL The starter's custom exception cleanup function tries to write a log entry and send a ClassAd message to the shadow Sending the ClassAd message seg-faults because it tries to evaluate TargetType, which accesses classad::specialAttrNames, which is already deleted. A simple fix for this problem would be for the starter to disable its custom exception cleanup routine (set _EXCEPT_Cleanup to NULL) before calling DC_Exit(). A better fix would be do most of the tear-down of CStarter and its member objects before calling DC_Exit(), probably by making the CStarter object not be a global object, but one that's deleted before DC_Exit().
remarks: 2016-Oct-18 16:16:33 by jfrey: Setting _EXCEPT_Cleanup to NULL in CStarter::StarterExit() does prevent this crash. But we're still blundering through a minefield of potential crashes. The FileTransfer destructor called under exit() still causes an EXCEPT() due to daemonCore being NULL. There are surely other pitfalls waiting for us. 2016-Oct-18 16:39:24 by jfrey: The original post to htcondor-users was made on October 17, 2016, by Antontio Dorta <adorta@iac.es> with the subject line condor_starter... kernel: NMI watchdog: BUG: soft lockup - CPU stuck for.... 2016-Oct-21 10:09:11 by jfrey: I initially committed this fix to the master branch, when I had intended it to go into the 8.4 stable series. title: Ticket #4660: Add sub-second accurate timestamps to dprintf logs
description: It would be very helpful when analyzing logs to have the option for sub-second accurate dprintfs. Also, less important but still valuable would be the ability to drop a stacktrace at into the dprintf log. This will implemented by adding two new flags for the dprintf logs. D_SUB_SECOND will cause fraction values to be printed after the seconds field in the timestamp. D_TIMESTAMP will cause unix epoch time to b printed instead of human readable time. The old LOG_USE_TIMESTAMPS config knob will turn this flag on for all log files. D_BACKTRACE will cause "(bt:hash:depth)" to be printed before the dprintf message, and the first time that the "hash" value occurs, a stack backtrace will follow the current message.

title: Ticket #457: NETWORK_INTERFACE should trump IP rewriting
description: When Condor transmits its contact address, it rewrites the IP address to match the IP address of the interface upon which it is talking. This messed up something Todd Miller was doing because the interface upon which it was talking happened to be NATed. In his case, NETWORK_INTERFACE was set to the public IP address and if Condor had just sent that without any rewriting, everything would have worked. He was able to work around the problem by changing the default route. From this case we concluded that if the admin explicitly sets NETWORK_INTERFACE, then Condor should just send that without any rewriting.

title: Ticket #292: Ensure ProcD named pipe uniqueness on Windows
description: The ProcD uses named pipes for its communication. On Windows, named pipes do not exist in the file system namespace but rather have names of the form \\.\pipe\name. The default in Condor for Windows is to use the name \\.\pipe\procd_pipe. If two Condor instances attempt to run on the same machine without at least one of them overriding the default (using PROCD_ADDRESS), one of the two instances will fail. This is not a problem on UNIX because named pipes use file system names and we default to a path relative to $(LOCK), which must be different for different Condor instances.

title: Ticket #768: JobRouter does not see buffered job ad updates
description: When the schedd makes changes to job ads using the NONDURABLE flag, it sometimes happens that data remains in memory buffers and is not written to disk indefinitely or until some further commit causes the buffer to be flushed. JobRouter and Quill cannot see the changes until they are flushed. A specific example where this caused trouble was JobFinishedHookDone not being visible to JobRouter a long time after a routed job had actually finished. This caused JobRouter not to mark the source job finished until the schedd flushed its buffers due to other activity. Flushing after each transaction could negatively impact performance. Therefore, for 7.4.0, I have added a timer to the schedd that flushes after some configurable maximum time when a NONDURABLE commit happens. The configuration parameter name is SCHEDD_JOB_QUEUE_LOG_FLUSH_DELAY, which defaults to 5 seconds.

Without this, JobRouter and Quill do not see some updates to job ads for an unbound amount of time. The upper bound is now controlled with SCHEDD_JOB_QUEUE_LOG_FLUSH_DELAY (default 5s). #768 (By Dan Bradley )

title: Ticket #3330: ENABLE_ADDRESS_REWRITING not applied to claim request protocol
description: The schedd address is sent to the startd in the claim request protocol. Since it is sent as a CEDAR string rather than a classad address attribute, the CEDAR address rewriting rules have not been automatically applied. The result is that a schedd on a multi-homed machine will send the same address to all startds it claims, regardless of which network interface the schedd uses to contact them. The startds may not be able to reach the schedd at the given address. If so, claim lease renewals will fail if using the startd-sends-alive protocol. The workaround for this problem is to use PRIVATE_NETWORK_INTERFACE and PRIVATE_NETWORK_NAME. This is good enough to handle one private network. If there are multiple disjoint private networks, it is not flexible enough. This problem goes back much further than 7.8.0, but I have not bothered to do the archaeology to trace it back to a precise version.

title: Ticket #7236: Allow maxjobs per workflow to be changed for running workflows
description: Stuart wants the ability to edit maxjobs per workflow for running workflows. Stuart wants jobs to be aggressively evicted in LIFO (last in, first out) order to get below the specified max.
remarks: 2019-Sep-04 14:35:46 by anderson: I would also like users (or cluster admins) to be able to change -maxidle for a running DAG as well. 2019-Sep-19 14:58:26 by coatsworth: We've been discussing for some time about how to edit the properties of an in-progress DAG. The ideal solution would be to make a new tool called condor_dagedit, which opens a socket connection to the condor_dagman process and sends it commands. So you could tell it to change MaxJobs, MaxIdle or really anything else this way. Unfortunately this also requires significant engineering effort, meaning it's is unlikely to happen anytime soon, if ever. Another approach is for condor_dagedit to write a new event to the dagman event log, indicating that the value of an attribute has changed. Then when dagman scans the log, it takes action upon seeing the event. One advantage is that the change is persistent, it will be replayed in the event of dagman abort/recovery. A disadvantage is this must be run from the machine that submitted the job, it cannot be done remotely. A third approach (which we like the best) is to skip making a new tool entirely. Instead we can just set these attributes via the condor_dagman job ad, then use condor_qedit to change the values. Every time that dagman updates its job ad with information about nodes completed, nodes ready, etc., it also checks if the other attributes (MaxJobs, MaxIdle, etc) have changed. If so, it updates its internal attributes. This approach is probably the easiest and fastest. The biggest problem is that dagman doesn't check in with the schedd very often, so it could take several minutes for the update to kick in (this can be tweaked, at the cost of heavier impact on the schedd). Any thoughts on these? 2019-Sep-19 15:03:44 by pfc: The third approach sounds great to me, and has the advantage that the current value is easy to inspect. As for the frequency with which DAGMan checks, can't it be asked/forced to do so via another command if the user is impatient? (I.e. condor_reconfig -dagman, or if that isn't sensible, a custom condor_dag_refresh akin to condor_reschedule?) 2019-Oct-24 17:45:11 by coatsworth: This finished now and checked into our master branch, it will ship in the v8.9.5 release. I'm going to set this ticket to docpending so I can add documentation to the manual before closing it. For a quick reference, you can now edit a running condor_dagman instance by setting values for any of the following attributes in the job ad: DAGMan_MaxJobs DAGMan_MaxIdle DAGMan_MaxPreScripts DAGMan_MaxPostScripts When DAGMan notices that any of these attributes has a changed value, it will update its internal setting accordingly. 2019-Nov-12 15:52:20 by coatsworth: Marking as complete for now, some follow up work happening in #7368

title: Ticket #7666: condor_ssh_to_job should fully work with singularity
description: When a job running inside singularity is connected to with condor_ssh_to_job, several things don't quite work today. Because we never want to assume anything about what might be inside the container, we launch the sshd outside the container, and have it run nsenter to launch a shell inside the container, with stdin/out/error magically connected to the ssh session. However, the stock nsenter doesn't allocate a pty for the session, and the pty that ssh allocates gets lost when we enter the container, because singularity remounts /dev/pts on the inside. Also, the environment variables set by the job are not reset inside the interactive shell. While we could set the ones that the starter knows about, singularity itself sets several extra environment variables which we don't know about, and may be of particular important when gpus are in play. Also, we need to give nsneter a different set of command line options if we are entering a singularity container that was started by a non-setuid singularity. This is annoying, as we can't tell really if singularity is configured to be setuid or not. So, we will write a replacement nsenter that fixes all these problems.

title: Ticket #3625: Statically compiled gsoap functions cause segfault in GSI plugins
description: The UW compile of HTCondor statically links what RHEL refers to as libgsoap++. This causes SEGFAULTs on the HTCondor-CE. When the GSI plugin is invoked, LCMAPS is loaded and an libxacml callout (which uses libgsoap++) is performed. libxacml is compiled against gsoap 2.7.16 but gets the gsoap 2.7.10 symbol from the one in the condor daemon. Mixing symbols from different versions of gsoap is probably what causes the SEGFAULT. You can see the soap symbols exported by doing this: [bbockelm@brian-test ~]$ nm -D /usr/sbin/condor_collector | grep soap | grep -v _Z | grep ' T ' | wc -l 283 I propose we hide or link these symbols. Because of gsoap's somewhat-notorious ABI issues, I'd propose hiding the symbols.
remarks: 2013-May-15 11:01:11 by tstclair: Why isn't gsoap treated like the other externals yet? Platform where possible? 2013-May-15 12:19:02 by bbockelm: Personally, I'd be worried about ABI compatibilities. gsoap upstream does not really maintain ABI compatibility - even if they retain linking capability. Here, the system and Condor had versions of gsoap that could link but still blew up when mixed. On top of this, the code generator reuses function names - we need to patch our arguments to the code generator to use different function names, even if we dynamically link. 2013-May-16 20:29:35 by bbockelm: It was a tough fix, but with a few gsoap flags and linking tricks, I can avoid the overlapping definitions. Passes the SOAP tests, so I'm closing the ticket.

description: Todd Tannenbaum wrote: Can someone explain why the code doesn't simply call get_random_uint() from the util lib instead of these bizarre platform dependent attempts to generate a random number? There's probably not a good reason (other than to provide the minimal fix). We need the initial port number to be (a) different in different simultaneously-existing processes and (b) different from bind to bind within the same process. Using a PRNG after seeding it with our PID should meet both requirements. If get_random_uint() doesn't do that, we should understand why (and rewrite the port-choosing code to do that unless our understanding of why says we should do something else).
creator: tlmiller

title: Ticket #4699: Allow user prio preemption to work on partitionable slots
description: In 8.2 we added support to allow RANK to preempt multiple pslots via setting knob ALLOW_PSLOT_PREEMPTION=True in the config of the central manager. We now need to add similar support for user prio preemption. So now with the code added in this ticket ALLOW_PSLOT_PREEMPTION=True works with startd RANK and also PREEMPTION_REQUIREMENTS for user priority preemption. However, even in v8.7.10, some mechanisms that are known to currently not work as expected in conjunction with pslot preemption are: PREEMPTION_RANK MaxVacateTime, so jobs that take a long time to vacate could cause problems on the machine. concurrency limits consumption policies non-fungible custom resources, i.e. resources that cannot be expressed as a number, like GPU device IDs. So dealing with CPU cores, Memory, and Disk should all work, but not GPUs. Consider early preemption may be an issue?
remarks: 2016-May-03 11:32:42 by tim: More work needs to be done here. 2016-Oct-17 16:58:25 by tannenba: So putting a finer point on what more work still remains - The issue is PREEMPTION_REQUIREMENTS and PREEMPTION_RANK are still both evaluated in the context of the pslot, not the dslot, so they don't work as expected if they reference attributes about the user who would be preempted. In addition, the special attributes that the negotiator normally adds about the current user/group aren't added for the pslot preemption evaluations. In the case of PREEMPTION_REQUIREMENTS, the commits already made to this ticket get us part way there, in that it is evaluated once for each dslot, with an attribute CandidateSlot set so that the expression can consult rolled-up dslot attributes in the pslot. But this requires that the admin write their PREEMPTION_REQUIREMENTS in a special way that is different for pslots vs static slots, and also requires that the startd does rollup for anything referenced in PREEMPTION_REQUIREMENTS. I admit I am wondering if ignoring the rollup info for now, and simply referencing the dslot in the negotiator, would be better for the time being until we think through the rollup mechanism more. Effort estimate to resolve this ticket is O(2weeks). 2018-May-07 15:22:47 by jfrey: Code Review (for the most recent changes by Todd Tannenbaum) The map of slot name to ClassAd* can be built once at the start of the negotiation cycle. Setting a bogus RemoteUser attribute should be done for all forms of pslot preemption, not just for user priority. 2018-May-07 16:30:40 by jfrey: I've pushed changes that address my code review. 2018-May-10 13:52:53 by jfrey: Code Review Greg's changes look good. Todd's changes to clear the MatchList cache look good. Todd's changes to remove the hard-coded check on priority for user priority preemption has a couple issues: The rejPreemptForPrio count is now meaningless. If a claim takes a while to be preempted (e.g. long retirement time), nothing prevents the negotiator from giving the slot to a different preempting job every negotiation cycle. It could even ping-poing between the same two preempting jobs (or sets of jobs).

title: Ticket #1531: Manual section on the dedicated scheduler is really misleading
description: In Section 3.13.10 of the Manual, "Condor's Dedicated Scheduling", the big picture/intro is really misleading. The only reason one needs to bother setting up a dedicated scheduler is to support the execution of parallel universe jobs. Instead of simply stating this, the manual has a bunch of text implying that you need to setup a dedicated scheduler if you have dedicated resources (as opposed to opportunistic resources). That's nuts, if you have dedicated resources, just set START=True, SUSPEND=FALSE, and PREEMPT=FALSE on your cluster machines, and you're done. Seems like this book chapter does a better job of explaining all this, maybe the Manual should lift some text/examples from it. Behold the misleading Manual text: Applications that require multiple resources, yet must not be preempted, are handled gracefully by Condor. Condor combines opportunistic scheduling and dedicated scheduling within a single system. Opportunistic scheduling involves placing a job on a non-dedicated resource under the assumption that the resource may not be available for the entire duration of the job. Dedicated scheduling assumes the constant availability of resources; it is assumed that the job will run to completion, without interruption. To support applications needing dedicated resources, an administrator configures resources to be dedicated. These resources are controlled by a dedicated scheduler, a single machine within the pool that runs a condor_schedd daemon.

title: Ticket #1024: Only link gSOAP into daemons with a SOAP interface
description: SOAP support for daemons is provided by DaemonCore. The details of how gSOAP handles method dispatching are exposed to DaemonCore. The result is all programs that link with daemoncore.a must also provide gSOAP stubs, e.g. must have a SOAP interface. Historically, all daemons were given a default interface (GetVersion, GetPlatform). The only daemons with a meaningful interface beyond the default are condor_schedd, condor_collector and condor_soapshell. In so much as the gSOAP dependency: is unnecessary for most deamons, introduces a linking dependency for all daemons (overhead), and complicates the creation of new daemons; it is proposed that the dependency be broken. The proposal to break the dependency is: Insulate DaemonCore from gSOAP [DONE] Create a dc_soap interface encapsulating the gSOAP logic: soap_core.cpp [DONE] Provide an implementation of dc_soap for daemons with no SOAP interface: no_soap_core.cpp [DONE] Include the no_soap_core.o in daemoncore.a [DONE] Remove all default SOAP interfaces [DONE] Introduce SOAP_LIB for linking into daemons with a SOAP interface [DONE] Remove all gsoap_*.h default interfaces [DONE] Remove all soap_*Stub.cpp default interfaces [DONE] Update condor_schedd/collector/soapshell to use SOAP_LIB [DONE] Provide a solution for Windows [DONE] Either, figure out equivalent of ELF/a.out __attribute__((weak)) support for Windows [N/A on windows] Or, setup Windows targets to link against soap_core.cpp,mimetypes.cpp and no_soap_core.cpp where appropriate [DONE]

title: Ticket #1474: job ad schema - schedd tolerance w/o reliance on condor_submit
description: What is a Job Ad's Schema? There is one. It is a combination of the expectations from all the components that operate on a job. For instance, the Schedd expects an Owner, JobStatus, JobUniverse, Requirements etc. condor_q also wants CpuTime etc. The shadow wants an Iwd. Startd expects Requirements, etc. The starter wants a Cmd. Etc... The Schedd currently ignores jobs that are missing an Owner, a JobStatus or a JobUniverse. The Schedd is thus relying on condor_submit to provide all these attributes. This reliance isn't even safe because of qedit, ex. $ condor_qedit 514.0 JobUniverse UNDEFINED Set attribute "JobUniverse". $ condor_q -l | grep Uni JobUniverse = UNDEFINED ScheddLog after restart: Job 514.0 has no JobUniverse attribute. Removing.... Preventing qedit from changing attributes is not a proper solution. Preventing the schedd from allowing these attributes to be changed is not proper either. Value validation is proper, and making the components that deal with job ads to have sane and consistent defaults.

title: Ticket #5964: Inconsistencies in credential filenames when using accounting groups
description: Iain reported that credentials were being swept prematurely. Everything worked fine until he started playing with accounting groups. Some very preliminary investigation showed that there is some disagreement on the names of the files between various entities, where some assume that the name is simply the unix username (e.g. "zmiller") and some are including the accounting group information (e.g. "physics.zmiller"). The correct behavior here should be to ignore accounting groups and always use the "Owner" of the job when dealing with credentials in the SEC_CREDENTIAL_DIRECTORY. A more thorough investigation would be needed to determine how exactly the mismatch is manifesting itself, but clearly it's wrong and can just be fixed.
remarks: 2016-Oct-13 11:54:50 by zmiller: Iain, any other remarks or wisdom you would like to add to this ticket would be helpful. Thanks! 2016-Oct-13 12:01:32 by iain.steers: So, at the moment we're working round this by using SEC_CREDENTIAL_SWEEP_TIME set to 2 weeks. For the most part this seems okay. However there is a slight snag in that the afs tokens seem to go "stale" or disappear even with renewal. For example: 1. I submit a job or set of jobs which run fine. 2. As per the work-around my credential is left in the cred dir. 3. Some hours-day later I come back and submit some more jobs. 4. Get file warnings from condor_submit as the schedd is unable to access afs. There will have been other users, potentially in the same accounting group in the meantime. I'm thinking either the PAG was eaten by something or the schedd is attempting to use the wrong PAG, potentially as a side-effect of this bug. Unfortunately given where the PAGs sit and their interaction with kernel space its basically impossible barring some information from keyctl to tell where the PAG is and what happens to it. Note: This doesn't appear to be a problem on the worker-node side as the aklog is done under the EUID of the user. This doesn't work for the schedd, presumably due to the single-process nature. 2016-Nov-28 13:23:43 by zmiller: CODE REVIEW: Looks good.

title: Ticket #2608: Keep track of startd ads that disappear, aka absent ads
description: Similar to how the collector can persistently store ads where offline=true, the idea is to allow the collector to remember ads for resources that simply disappear. (aka ads that go absent) Initial steps: Admin can specify a classad constraint in the config of the collector, eg COLLECTOR_RECORD_AS_ABSENT. if this knob is not present, then all behavior is as before. If the collector is about to remove an ad from its hashtables because the lease on this ad has expired, then the above constraint is evaluated against this ad evaluates to True, then Absent=True is implicitly inserted into the ad and the collector records this ad to disk in the offline log. This handles the case of marking a startd absent if it disappeared unexcused, aka if it disappeared without first invalidating its ad (e.g. the execute machine crashed). Just like offline ads, when an update is received at the collector, the ad is no longer considered absent and the persistent absent ad is removed. By default, the collector will append "&& (Absent = ! = True)" to the query constraint unless the constraint already references the Absent attribute (similar to how condor_submit inserts OpSys unless specified). After the above is done, the following future work could happen: In addition to marking an ad as absent when the lease expires, the collector could persistently write a resource ad to disk the first time it sees it, aka on insertion (not on update). Then the persistent ad is only removed from disk upon an receipt of an invalidation. This could handle the scenario where the collector is dead at the time the resource ad lease expires. Initially, only startd ads will be supported as absent ads. The reason is for this initial limitation is for the implementation we will leverage the collector code already present for offline ads, and that code only stores startd ads persistently. If the absent ad feature proves to be popular we can expand it to support other types of ads (master, schedd, etc) in the future. For years, the BaTLab had a number of jobs that could never run clogging up our queues. Some of these jobs couldn't run because of bad requirements; other because they were targeted at platforms that didn't exist (because we didn't have them or because of typos). These jobs became a problem when, for unrelated reasons, it became a real problem for other users to have these pointless jobs in the queue. We addressed the majority of the problem by implementing a Metronome-level whitelist of permissible platforms. This had the benefit of allowing us to give the user a good error message at submission time, rather than an obsure one a week later, when their job timed out. However, this solution has a few obvious problems, centering around the fact that we have to manually maintain the whitelist, which thus gets out of date easily. Historically, checking to see if the target platform is in the pool at submission time hasn't been especially useful, because platforms drift in and out of our pool constantly -- we would reject submissions only to accept the same one a few minutes later. We looked into a few solutions, but at heart they all involved polling the collector and acting as its memory, which none of us were really interested in doing. When we heard about offline ads, we thought they were just the thing for us: a way for Condor to keep track of what "should be" in the pool for us. They turned out not to work in that capacity; hence absent ads. We will be using them as (a) a platform whitelist that's always up-to-date (to within however long we decide to keep ads) and (b) a data source for reporting platform availability to our users.
