title: Ticket #912: Static buffer in cream_gahp command processing
description: When the cream_gahp processes a command, it allocates a static buffer of 500 entries to hold the arguments to that command. If the command has more than 500 arguments, the gahp will blithely run past the end of the array. Currently, this only affects the CREAM_PROXY_RENEW command when there are 500 or more jobs associated with the renewed proxy. Other commands can have more than 500 arguments, but the gridmanager doesn't use them in that way currently. The static buffer needs to be resized when the available data will overflow it.

title: Ticket #5437: starter induced holds cause output sandbox xfer
description: When the starter initiates a job hold, like with a cgroup OOM event, output files are transfered back to the submit machine. When a user runs condor_hold, the output sandbox is not brought back. These should be consistent.
remarks: 2016-Jun-18 14:58:31 by tlmiller: Code Review Starter->Hold() primarily sends the job the hold signal. Starter->allJobsDone() calls CStarter::TransferOutput() if JIC::allJobsDone() returned true (which it usually will for vanilla universe); this function will in turn call JIC::TransferOutput(), which will do file transfer. Starter->shutdownFast() kills a bunch of processes. It will also call Starter->allJobsDone() if all the jobs were already done (or were killed immediately as a result of shutting down fast). So the second two removals appear to be necessary. The call to Starter->Hold() may have been superfluous, but I'm not sure about the implications, one way or the other, for someone using ssh-to-job (as far as I know, the only way to get a second Proc object in a single job). It seems like somebody who's logged in shouldn't be kicked out (in case they want to do a post-mortem, which this patch makes harder to do because they won't get intermediate files back). This may be another ticket. The other concern would then be what this does to the starter log (we already have too many cases where the normal course of action is the abnormal termination of the starter), but that's probably another ticket as well.

title: Ticket #6866: scitokens: Skip credd redirect to webpage
description: The TOKENS/OAuth mode assumes a very specific behavior of the CREDMON - particularly that the user needs to go to a corresponding URL run on the schedd. This is not true in the case of the OSG-Connect hosts, where the CREDMON has the private key needed to issue its own tokens. I propose adding a new flag, CREDMON_WEB_REDIRECT=[true||false] (naming should be parallel with #6862) that allows the credd to skip any web requests and just wait for the CREDMON_COMPLETE file. With this, I think we can migrate the OSG-Connect setup to use the new TOKENS mode. [Note: this ticket might be deeper than expected as we might need the jobs to start life on hold until the corresponding credential appears... Needs to be investigated by the implementer]
remarks: 2019-Feb-07 21:17:36 by bbockelm: It seems that the credd redirect to webpage can be done for a single provider if SEC_CREDENTIAL_PRODUCER is set (provided you don't mind it's called "scitokens"; see #6909). It appears that SEC_CREDENTIAL_PRODUCER has undocumented magic values such as CREDENTIAL_ALREADY_STORED (see #6091); I'd like to add more semantics: If SEC_CREDENTIAL_PRODUCER is set to SEND_CREDENTIAL_REQUEST, instead of fork/exec'ing the credential producer, it will send the job's blocking credential requests as a list of base64-encoded classads to the credd. These "credential requests" will have the same contents as the OAuth credential requests (that may end up requesting the user to go to the web UI). If the admin sets <SERVICENAME>_BLOCKING = True in the configuration file, then we assume that any credential requests for this particular service are sent as above and not as part of the requests sent for "oauth mode" that might result in a web URL being generated. This will allow the credmon to get all the requests that do not require a full OAuth2 workflow at once and process them before the job is queued. 2020-Apr-10 07:46:13 by tim: Bulk change of target version from v080906 to v080907 using ticket-target-mover.

title: Ticket #5749: Pegasus problems with DAG priorities
description: Pegasus has run into problems with the current DAG node priority scheme (which I'd like to simplify anyhow). This is from Mats: I would like to see: if defined(explicit node prio): // user provided a priority to use effective node prio = explicit node prio else: // no priority specified, use the default strategy effective node prio = max(parents' effective prios, DAG prio) ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~ Stuff after this is from Kent: I'd actually like to simplify things even more, maybe this: if defined(explicit node prio): // user provided a priority to use effective node prio = explicit node prio else: // no priority specified, use the default strategy effective node prio = DAG prio Or, maybe what I'd really like is this: if defined(explicit node prio): // user provided a priority to use effective node prio = explicit node prio + DAG prio else: // no priority specified, use the default strategy effective node prio = DAG prio That would get rid of the problem of increasing your DAG priority erasing priority differences between the nodes. I'm okay with either of the last two, though. At any rate, I'd really like to get rid of the feature of a parent node's priority "trickling down" to its children -- I think that's complicated and hard to understand. Unless someone really needs that, I'd like to simplify things in that regard... (Having the max() function in there causes problems if we ever implement having DAGMan respond to priority changes while it's running -- I'm sure there was a ticket about that somewhere, but I can't find it now.) Anyhow, one issue with this is how much people are using DAG priorities right now, and whether this will goof things up for them.

title: Ticket #7324: Make job event log parser less fragile
description: In #7191, we changed the message that follows the event log type number, job id, and timestamp for one of the event types. This change is backwards-compatible (later versions of the reader can read earlier versions) but not forwards-compatible (earlier version of the reader cannot read later versions). This kind of change is frustrating. It would be nice if the reader itself was less fragile to these kinds of changes. In particular, it would be nice to always get the event number, job id, and timestamp out, even if the rest of the message can't be parsed as expected. This is hard right now, but should become easier in the future if event parsing becomes lazy. So, defer until that happens.
creator: karpel

title: Ticket #5319: Fix argument parsing for jobs
description: Both of our argument parsing systems are weird messes a bit unlike everything else. Both systems are confusing. Proposed: There is a new argument entry in the submit file. Maybe args or newarguments. The new entry's value is preserved exactly in the job's ClassAd On the execute side, the string is passed... on Linux/Unix via execv("/bin/sh", "-c", escaped_executable + " " + arguments, null) (Bonus optimization: If the arguments contain no "interesting" characters that a shell might interpret, including but not limited to the set ["'\$], break the string on whitespace and call execve(executable,arglist); on Windows the arguments as passed in as the single argument passed to winmain. Thus on Linux/Unix the escaping syntax is "Whatever Bourne shell uses" (the defacto standard and what system() does). On Windows the escaping syntax is "Whatever your program does (which is probably the default C library's behavior)" which is the native behavior. Thus, we are (mostly) out of the escaping/argument parsing business and users get to use escaping they are likely already familiar with. Potential problem: does the bash -c linger between the parent and the real job? Will it end up catching signals we intend for the real job? How do we select the new, non-backward compatible behavior? New keyword (arguments3?)? Clever attempt to detect the need? (Not technically backward compatible, but may work in practice.) A Perl-style "require=8.12" to use all sorts of new behavior?
creator: adesmet

title: Ticket #695: Race condition can cause crash in collector and schedd
description: The collector and schedd are susceptible to a race condition that can cause a core dump. If a shut down request is sent to the collector or schedd while they are processing a command that forces them to fork a subprocess (condor_q/condor_status), then the termination signal is processed first before cleaning up the child process. When the child processes information is cleaned up, a core will result. This can be reproduced on the collector by issuing: condor_status -any & sleep 1 & killall -TERM condor_collector

title: Ticket #3367: Condor thinks VMs in OpenStack's "SHUTOFF" state are running
description: OpenStack has VM states in addition to the Amazon EC2 states. One of them is a "SHUTOFF" state. The VMs are still in the system and can be restarted, but they are not running. Condor thinks VMs in this state are running when in reality they are not (condor_q reports them running). Per Jaime: Should be easy to fix. The tricky part is what should Condor do? Two options spring to mind: 1) Consider the job complete, destroy the instance, and let the job leave the queue. 2) Mark the job as Idle with GridJobStatus set to SHUTOFF and let the user set PeriodicRemove to destroy the instance if they want to. For my use case in glideinWMS I'd choose 1), however, I could see where 2) would be preferable.

title: Ticket #3672: Never try to start held EC2 jobs.
description: Presently, the grid manager attempts to (re)start any (non-spot) job with a client token but not an instance ID. For held jobs, this is at best extra work; for OpenStack (and possibly other services), it's positively dangerous, because RunInstances() isn't idempotent. However, doing so is unnecessary. We could adapt GM_SEEK_INSTANCE_ID to locate (or not) the instance ID of every (non-spot) held job, moving the conditional for REMOVED jobs from GM_INIT to GM_SEEK_INSTANCE_ID. This would prevent the gridmanager from attempting to restart held jobs, which should be more efficient.

title: Ticket #3388: GridJobStatus not updated by SIRs.
description: Although the job is idle, HTCondor is checking the status of the Spot Instance Request. We should be copying it into the job ad when we do. In particular, if we report the status-code field in addition to the status field, our users will be better-able to tune their bidding stategy (e.g., from seeing states like 'price-too-low'). This will probably require updating the API date field in the EC2 GAHP.
remarks: 2013-Jan-02 16:41:27 by tlmiller: Because the set of status values for spot and dedicated instances are (currently) disjoint, it will be unambiguous to combine the two into the job ad attribute GridJobStatus, and I have a patch ready to so do. Jaime and I feel that the simplicity and consistency of this approach recommend it over adding a new job ad attribute especially for spot instance request statuses. The 'status-code' values are also disjoint, and provide more detail than the 'status'. In particular, "instance-terminated-by-price", "price-too-low", and "capacity-not-available" look potentially valuable for tuning bids. Given that we don't currently report the SIR 'status', I'd be OK with skipping it entirely, and just sing the 'status-code'. However, it looks like obtaining 'status-code's will require using a new(er) API version. In practice, I think this will have minimal effect on using the EC2 GAHP with Amazon (which, of course, supports the new API version); but it's unclear what effect (if any) it will have on other services or software, like OpenStack. Creating a binary which specifies the newer version (for testing) won't be time-consuming, but the testing could be. So, Tony: just how interested are you in the bidding information? :) 2013-Jan-11 17:11:04 by tiradani: I am very interested in the bidding information as long as it doesn't break compatibility with OpenStack or Eucalyptus. Eucalyptus has recently renewed their focus on being API compatible with EC2, so that may not be as big of a worry. Then again, according to http://www.stackgeek.com/blog/kordless/post/comparison-of-open-source-cloud-support-for-ec2, Spot Instances aren't supported on OpenStack or Eucalyptus, so the issue may be moot. Additionally, OpenStack Folsom supports the API version up to 2009-04-04. http://docs.openstack.org/folsom/openstack-compute/admin/content/metadata-service.html What version is needed to get the 'status-code'? 2013-Jan-15 15:52:09 by tlmiller: The second-to-most-recent, 2012-10-01. title: Ticket #6923: Python Bindings: streamlined submit semantics
description: When you condor_submit from the command line, you don't need to explicitly provide a schedd or transaction if you don't want to. So why do you need to from the bindings? This ticket changes the signatures of Submit.queue and Submit.queue_with_itemdata so that all of the arguments are keyword arguments, changes the meaning of one of the existing arguments, and adds a new optional argument. The argument ordering is the same, so this will not break existing users. Semantics change of old argument: txn (transaction) will be now be optional. If it is None, a Transaction will be created and used internally. if a Transaction is given, it is used to submit the job, just like it is now. New optional argument: schedd. If None, submits to the local Schedd. txn and schedd cannot both be non-=None=, because if you have a Transaction you should just pass it in. If they are both passed, we throw a ValueError. Combined, this means you don't need to do the "get a Schedd, get a Transaction, then submit" rigmarole if you're doing what most users do: submit to the local schedd. You just create your Submit and queue it, which mirrors the behavior on the command line (create a submit file, then submit it). All of this will be implemented via pure-Python wrappers over the existing C++ bindings code. No changes are necessary to the underlying bindings.
remarks: 2019-Feb-20 20:33:12 by bbockelm: > When you condor_submit from the command line, you don't need to explicitly provide a schedd or transaction if you don't want to. So why do you need to from the bindings? Because the transaction model - and the relation between submission and the proxy object (the Schedd) - is very important? The analogy is teaching someone about SQL without teaching them about transactions. Sure, your SQL client probably has an autocommit mode, but at some point the concept of a transaction is pretty important to the model. So, I see this as "help people get going to the point they realize you simplified away a core concept they need to know". With that in mind, still think the approach is correct here? 2019-Feb-20 20:41:39 by karpel: > So, I see this as "help people get going to the point they realize you simplified away a core concept they need to know". I am unconvinced that most users ever need to know about transactions at all. Admins should, but admins will be digging deeper into the API anyway. 2019-Feb-20 20:50:22 by bbockelm: > I am unconvinced that most users ever need to know about transactions at all. I think that's still compatible with my analogy and statement. The majority of DB users are a-OK with autocommit mode, hence the fact its default in most (all?) SQL clients I am aware of! However, it's still a core concept! Hence my question is whether there should be some explicit space put between the "streamlined" mode and the existing syntax. Another case to pull from is libcurl, whose C API has an "easy" mode -- and the corresponding function names are all called easy_*. Should this be submit or easy_submit? A class method or a module-level method? 2019-Feb-20 21:57:14 by karpel: I guess that, as a user, I don't consider submitting jobs without a transaction to be "unsafe" in the same way that autocommiting partial changes to a DB is, because (at least from my perspective) a single queue command is atomic. I think a better analogy from DB-world would be that this aims to be the equivalent of making a blog post through your Wordpress web interface instead of writing the text and metadata into the DB yourself. Power-users and admins might need that for maximum whatever, but most people just want to get their blog post up. An example from Python-world would be how Requests' sessions work (http://docs.python-requests.org/en/master/user/advanced/#session-objects). You create a Session and then make multiple requests from it, as if it were the main library API. They let you shoot yourself in the foot by doing a lot of requests to the same place without making a Session, but it is the first major "advanced" topic, and I imagine if you google "help my requests are slow", the first thing you'll find is that. It seems like the equivalent for us would be being able to do Schedd.submit(submit_obj), or do txn = Schedd.transaction(); txn.submit(submit_obj). But it seems that the bindings have been moving away from that kind of API. 2019-Feb-20 22:55:32 by bbockelm: > I don't consider submitting jobs without a transaction to be "unsafe" in the same way that autocommiting partial changes to a DB is I don't see autocommit as unsafe: rather, it's a significant simplification. In terms of the bindings -- what about a module-level function of htcondor.submit? htcondor.ez_submit? 2019-Feb-21 14:37:45 by karpel: Abandoned in favor of #6926

title: Ticket #7261: Late materialization submit fails when +key used itemdata dict
description: When submitting a job using queue_with_itemdata() and using max_materialize (with the python bindings), it fails with. Traceback (most recent call last): File "submit_min.py", line 39, in <module> submitRes = sub.queue_with_itemdata(txn, 1, iter(jobAds)) RuntimeError: Failed to send job factory for max_materilize. This doesn't seem to happen if e.g.: setQArgs is used instead for a similar purpose. Also, note the typo ( "materilize" rather than "materialize") in the schedd message. For reference, here is a python example that fails (unless I comment the "max_materialize" line): import classad import htcondor sub = htcondor.Submit(""" universe = vanilla executable = test.sh arguments = 3 max_materialize = 1 Output = out.$(Cluster)-$(Process) Log = log.$(Cluster).log """) jobAds = [] ad = {} for name in ("Job1", "Job2"): ad['+JobName'] = classad.quote(name) jobAds.append(ad) with schedd.transaction() as txn: submitRes = sub.queue_with_itemdata(txn, 1, iter(jobAds)) Also for reference, here is a python example using setQArgs that does work: import classad import htcondor sub = htcondor.Submit(""" universe = vanilla executable = test.sh arguments = 3 max_materialize = 1 Output = out.$(Cluster)-$(Process) Log = log.$(Cluster) """) sub['+JobName'] = '$(Name)' sub.setQArgs('Name in ("Job1" "Job2")') schedd = htcondor.Schedd() with schedd.transaction() as txn: cluster = sub.queue(txn)
remarks: 2019-Sep-16 10:22:05 by johnkn: The problem is that +JobName is not a valid key for the itemdata dictionary. We should be catching that in the python bindings, but we aren't so it gets over to the schedd and then fails to parse. The schedd sees this Queue +JobName from <file> which isn't valid. When you use QArgs, you also change this to use name on the queue line, so the Schedd sees this Queue name from <file> which is valid and so it works. you could also have used My.JobName instead of +JobName 2019-Sep-16 10:22:29 by karpel: The below works. Incidentally, in your first example, you re-use the same dictionary in the itemdata. This will result in a list of itemdata containing the same dictionary over and over, so they'll all have the last name you gave. Each item must be its own dictionary for what you want to do to work. import classad import htcondor sub = htcondor.Submit(""" universe = vanilla executable = test.sh arguments = 3 max_idle = 1 output = out.$(Cluster)-$(Process) log = log.$(Cluster).log """) itemdata = [] for name in ("Job1", "Job2"): itemdata.append({"My.JobName": classad.quote(name)}) schedd = htcondor.Schedd() with schedd.transaction() as txn: submitRes = sub.queue_with_itemdata(txn, 1, iter(itemdata)) 2019-Sep-17 08:14:57 by khurtado: johnkn: Thanks, I can confirm using My.JobName rather than +JobName works. karper: Indeed, thanks. That was a quick example to isolate the problem, where I ended up making that mistake. Question though: While John's answer makes sense to me, why does +JobName works (after moving "ad = {}" inside the loop for example, when there is no "max_materialize/max_idle" line? Shouldn't it give the same error? $ cat submit_items.py import classad import htcondor sub = htcondor.Submit(""" universe = vanilla executable = test.sh arguments = 3 Output = out.$(Cluster)-$(Process) Log = log.$(Cluster) """) schedd = htcondor.Schedd() jobAds = [] for name in ("Job1", "Job2"): ad = {} ad['+JobName'] = classad.quote(name) jobAds.append(ad) with schedd.transaction() as txn: submitRes = sub.queue_with_itemdata(txn, 1, iter(jobAds)) print("ClusterId: {}".format(submitRes.cluster())) $ python submit_items.py ClusterId: 2551 $ condor_q 2551 -af:h ProcId JobName ProcId JobName 0 Job1 1 Job2 $ 2019-Sep-17 14:01:14 by johnkn: yes, it should give the same error (in theory). but it doesn't because it goes through a different code path that happens to automatically convert +JobName to My.JobName. late materialization actually sends the schedd a QUEUE statement to be parsed, while the old form of submit sends job classad to the schedd. 2019-Sep-18 07:07:14 by khurtado: John: Understood. Thank you! I will replace all of my +Attribute lines to use My.Attribute instead and move on. 2019-Sep-18 07:22:09 by khurtado: Wait, while for my case, I'm just going to replace things to use My.Attribute, should this ticket remain with the "defect" label, where the bug fix would be to make submission with and without "max_idle/max_materialize" behave the same (with respect to how it handles +A -> My.A) to avoid confusion? 2019-Sep-24 16:10:37 by johnkn: I believe this fix here it to aggressively convert +Attr in to My.Attr at the time members are added to the submit "dictionary" This means that when you do this sub = new Submit() sub['+Foo'] = 'bar' what actually happens is this sub = new Submit() sub['My.Foo'] = 'bar' We will also change the get method to do only-the-fly conversion of +Foo to My.Foo, so that if you try and lookup '+Foo' you will get what you expect. But + prefixed keys will never appear when you enumerate keys in the submit "dictionary"

title: Ticket #6759: Improve new JobEventLog API before release
description: The current JobEventLog interface is not very Pythonic, and on further reflection, way more complicated than it needs to be. Instead: class JobEventLog: # Raises IOError if we can't initialize the log reader for filename. __init__(filename) # Returns the next event in the log, if any become available before the deadline. __next__() # Returns self, so that this class functions like file iterators (where # iterators don't maintain their own seek pointer). __iter__() # Sets self's deadline and then returns self. events(deadline=None) This is the interface we actually wanted, more or less, eliminates a lot of functions, and is more Pythonic than the previous API. Example usage: import os import htcondor from htcondor import JobEventType jel = htcondor.JobEventLog("logfile") # Stop waiting for events sixty seconds from now. for event in jel.events(deadline=+60): if event.type == JobEventType.EXECUTE: break; else: print("Failed to find execute event before deadline, aborting.") sys.exit(-1) # Do something else. # Stop waiting for events ninety seconds from now. for event in jel.events(deadline=+90): if event.type == JobEventType.JOB_TERMINATED: break; else: print("Failed to find terminated event before deadline, aborting.") sys.exit(-1)
remarks: 2018-Sep-13 13:29:40 by tlmiller: None of us (TJ, ToddM, or Mark) are super happy about 'events()' and 'deadline', but we also can't come up with anything better. (The main argument in favor of deadline is that -- despite it not being an absolute value for coding convenience reasons -- is (a) it sounds more like (if not quite enough) it applies to the whole sequence of events and (b) "a deadline of None" pretty clearly means "no deadline".) 2018-Sep-13 13:30:19 by tlmiller: The above example should probably go into the documentation (for #6736). 2018-Sep-13 16:40:15 by tlmiller: Since this API is new for 8.7.10, no further documentation is necessary.

title: Ticket #1136: Eliminate "static" releases of Condor
description: We ship static binaries on the theory that they are widely portable. This was true once, but at least on Linux our static binaries are less portable because libc insists on loading other libraries at runtime, hitting versioning problems. Our dynamic binaries have proven to be more portable. We recommend the dynamic binaries and have for some time. We believe almost no one uses the static binaries, and people who are can probably use the dynamic binaries. Conclusion: stop building and shipping static binaries. Benefits: Less user confusion about which version to build. Fewer Rust tickets helping people having problems with the static binaries. Less disk space for us. (Disk usage causes NMI disk and network grief, fills our quotas in AFS, means we need to burn a pile of DVDs for backups which is a nuisance.) See also #1135 ("Real" dynamic binary releases) which proposes changes to how we build our dynamic binaries. User feedback See the "User feedback" on #1135. The two overlap so much that I'm just collecting it there.

title: Ticket #5175: Have condor_dagman condor_rm jobs on SIGUSR1 (revert #4618)
description: In #4618, the assumption was made that SIGUSR1 implies the schedd is removing the DAGMan job, hence DAGMan no longer needs to do the 'condor_rm' itself. It seems that we have taken off our suspenders and are living dangerously with only a belt! For CMS, we use SIGUSR1 as the hold signal also (we do this so users can return later and restart the dagman job). Hence, after upgrading to 8.3.2, DAGMan started leaking jobs. Can we either revert #4618 outright or restore the prior behavior as a config option?
remarks: 2015-Jul-27 09:24:45 by wenger: I'll think about doing this as a config option -- I don't think we want to go back as the default. I can't remember how completely the code is torn out -- it may not be too hard to put in a config option for this... One question, though: is there a reason you can't do condor_rm instead of condor_hold on the DAG, as a workaround? Is the DAG you're holding a sub-DAG? If not, as far as I can tell, you could accomplish pretty much the same thing by condor_rm'ing your DAGMan, and then re-submitting it and having it run the rescue DAG when you want to continue. (I assume that you'd also want to kill running PRE and POST scripts if this option is enabled...) 2015-Jul-27 15:57:21 by bbockelm: Hi Kent, The reason we use condor_hold here is that the DAG and all its related files live in $SPOOL. If we do a condor_rm, all our state goes away. Brian 2015-Jul-30 11:13:41 by tannenba: Hi Brian, How are jobs being leaked ? My definition of leak is there are jobs in the queue submitted by DAGMan, and yet the DAGMan job has been removed. In the current code, if you did a condor_hold of the dagman job, the dagman goes on hold and thus no further progress is made in the workflow, but jobs submitted by dagman up to that point can continue and finish. If you remove the held DAGMan job, all workflow jobs are removed (covering this case this was a major reason we adopted #4618 and one of the reasons we do not want to revert it). So I don't see how any jobs are leaked... Sounds like what you want is condor_hold of a dag should not only pause submission of new jobs, but also cancel the already submitted jobs. Seems like pretty specific behavior. As such, on your end would it be easy to do the following to get the behavior you want: condor_hold <DAG job> (assuming SIGUSR1 set as hold signal) condor_rm -cons 'DAGManJobId=?=<DAG job>' We don't want to revert #4618, but perhaps we could put in a knob that if True it tells DAGMan to remove its own children via the same condor_rm -cons command above (knob would default to false). Also, should this be a child ticket of #5162 and thus, as a priority 2 ticket, is this something that must be resolved for v8.3.8? Thanks 2015-Jul-30 15:12:31 by bbockelm: Hi Todd, The HoldKillSig for CMS dag jobs is SIGUSR1. Hence, we expect all jobs are removed when we do condor_hold of the dag job. The problem with #4618 is that, before, SIGUSR1 meant "cleanup jobs and exit with no rescue DAG". Now it means simply "cleanup jobs", and it assumes someone else will perform the cleanup (where the assumption certainly does not hold for us!). Having a knob to return to the old behavior is certainly acceptable. I realize we're not the most common use case. I moved this down to a priority 3 ticket because we have a workaround in place (basically what you suggested, except we do it within the python bindings. Hence, it's not necessary for 8.3.8. Brian 2016-Feb-01 15:23:45 by wenger: Also see discussion in #4209. 2016-Apr-12 16:38:43 by wenger: Note: The way to test DAGMan removing its own child jobs is to essentially make a copy of the job_dagman_rm test, except with config to turn on the remove option, and a -append line to condor_submit_dag that unsets the OtherJobRemoveRequirements attribute.

title: Ticket #1835: ArgList displaying very odd behavior on Windows
description: There exists a very odd bug inside ArgList that is being exposed in condor_hdfs on Windows. The bug manifests in the Hadoop::startService( NodeType type) function, when we try calling arglist.RemoveArg(0) on around line 512. This causes a crash on Windows. If however one calls arglist.Count() or even arglist.GetArgsStringForDisplay before calling arglist.RemoveArg(0), the problem goes away and condor_hdfs goes merrily on its way. This behavior was not exhibited in 7.5.4. The only changes made to the arglist class was done over a year ago before the 7.5 series and the code in hadoop.cpp that calls on RemoveArg was written by Faisal during his original work on hadoop for Condor. The only change between 7.5.4 and 7.5.5 are the switch over to the new Windows libraries in the Windows 7 SDK and the possible changes in compiler optimization switches being used. No code changes are present around the relevant blocks of code.

title: Ticket #4621: Help CMS use a very small condor_shadow_s
description: CMS has started to use the condor_shadow_s on its pools. In 8.3.1, this shrinks the per-shadow RAM usage to 640kb. We can do better: krb5 is not used and (looking at the smaps, could be a big consumer of RAM). The 32-bit shadow_s would be much smaller than the 64-bit one. So, here's an idea: Remove KRB5 linkage from condor_shadow_s daemon. If you need to use KRB5, then you're stuck with condor_shadow. Move condor_master_s from condor-static-shadow to the base condor RPM. I do not believe we can mix the 32-bit condor_master with the 64-bit condor_procd without further work. Binary datastructs (such as struct ProcFamilyUsage, which differs in size between the 32-bit and 64-bit build) are in the procd protocol and written directly across the Unix socket. Do not ship the 64-bit condor-static-shadow RPM. Place the 32-bit condor-static-shadow RPM in the 64-bit release repo. This would allow us to cleanly install the 32-bit static via puppet using RPMs. All the other mechanisms so far require hackery of the RPM DB or installing from tarballs.

title: Ticket #4271: Implement a knob to limit total time for a negotiation cycle
description: The negotiator has a knob to limit the negotiation cycle time per user and per pie spin. We want to add a knob NEGOTIATOR_MAX_TIME_PER_CYCLE which places an upper time limit on the total negotiation cycle across all users/spins.
remarks: 2014-Mar-21 14:24:40 by tannenba: TESTING Place the following into condor_config of a personal condor: # Negotiation cycle should quit after 5 seconds NEGOTIATOR_MAX_TIME_PER_CYCLE = 5 # For testing, tell negotiator to pause 1 second after considering # each request NEG_SLEEP = 1 Next, submit a bunch of jobs: executable = c:\utils\sleep.exe arguments = 6000 requirements = GlobalJobId =!= UNDEFINED && NotThere =?= True queue 20 Note the requirements expression used above will a) cause the jobs to never match, and b) cause all the jobs to end up in their own autocluster. This, combined with the NEG_SLEEP setting in the config file, will ensure that negotiation will take longer than 5 seconds, assuming we submit more than 5 jobs. title: Ticket #1589: some CCB connection failures are not detected
description: A schedd at UCSD that submits jobs to a glidien pool using CCB stopped functioning properly because the number of registered sockets exceeded the internal limit set by DaemonCore. This is an expected condition when there are bursts of activity, but we would expect the number of registered sockets to decrease after the burst subsides. This never happened to the schedd at UCSD. The schedd did not in fact have very many file descriptors allocated. The "registered sockets" were entries in the socket table for reverse connection requests via CCB, and, as such, do not consume a file descriptor. These requests were for RELEASE_CLAIM and INVALIDATE_KEY commands (to startds). Some of these pending commands had been issued weeks ago and appeared to have built up gradually over time. What appears to have happened is this: No deadline is set when creating the DCMessage object to send the command, so when the CCB client starts up, it does not set a timer to eventually expire the request. After initiating the non-blocking CCB request, startCommand() does set a deadline on the socket via SEC_TCP_SESSION_DEADLINE, so the sockets have a deadline set, but since they are in a reverse-connecting state, the CCB client is in charge of enforcing the deadline, and this deadline was set too late for the CCB client to know about it. If we get a response back from the CCB server indicating failure, then there is no problem, because we abort the reverse-connect. However, the problem is if we get back a 'success' response from the CCB server, but we never establish the reversed connection (i.e. ReverseConnectCallback() is never called). This could happen if the remote daemon successfully connected to us but then a communication error (e.g. timeout) prevents the reverse connect command from being successfully processed on our end. In this case, the only thing preventing us from waiting forever is a deadline on the socket, but since there is no deadline, we end up waiting forever, consuming a slot in the DaemonCore socket table. The problem can be addressed by always setting a deadline for reverse connection attempts. We thought we had solved all problems such as this with TCP_SESSION_DEADLINE, but that is applied too late in the game for CCB connections. It would be nice if we could propagate the error processing the reverse connect command rather than propagating back 'success' immediately when connect() succeeds. However, this would require an ACK in the reverse-connect command protocol. There is currently no ACK. It was designed that way to avoid latency.

(By Dan Bradley )

title: Ticket #5899: Job router UPDATE_JOB_INFO hook output bugs
description: If the Job Router's UPDATE_JOB_INFO hook prints out attributes to be applied to the routed job, they aren't always handled properly. First, UpdateRoutedJobStatus() assumes that the routed job is visible in the mirror of the job queue log, which is not true for a newly-submitted job. It's very likely not to be there the first time the UPDATE_JOB_INFO hook is called. In FinishCheckSubmittedJobStatus(), we handle this situation, with an upper limit on how long the job can absent from the job queue mirror set by MAX_JOB_MIRROR_UPDATE_LAG. Second, UpdateRoutedJobStatus() attempts to modify the routed job ad in the queue of the source schedd. If routed jobs go to a separate schedd, this will fail. Both of these situations lead to the routed job being aborted. The router can easily end up in a loop of routing the same job repeatedly.

description: If you run the the full set of tests repeatedly (say, because you're bisecting a bug, or just doing incremental development), the tests will eventually get unusably slow, going from taking a few hours to taking a day or more. title: Ticket #2448: RPM should ship with empty condor-config.local
description: The Problem The Condor RPM is pretty nice. It includes a local_config_dir (/etc/condor/config.d). I want to use this in OSG: I want to install the default Condor RPM with no changes, then customize it by dropping files into the config.d directory. This would be sweet. Unfortunately, two things collide: The Condor RPM has a condor_config.local that defines several parameters including daemon_list. The rules for reading configuration files are that the config.d directory is read first, then the condor_config.local file: http://www.cs.wisc.edu/condor/manual/v7.6/3_3Configuration.html#param:LocalConfigDir This means that without being tricky (see workaround below), users cannot override anything in the condor_config.local by dropping files into the config.d directory. I think that Condor should encourage people to use this method of configuration and should make it as easy as possible outside of the box. It's nice for users to leave the Condor configuration files unchanged (and only add to config.d) because "rpm -q --verify condor" will tell you that the Condor files haven't been changed. Proposed Change Specifically, I recommend: You should ship an empty condor_config.local file. If you think you need any of the configuration that exists in the condor_config.local file, you should push it into the condor_config that ships with the RPM. You should make this change in the stable series. Workaround There is a workaround, but it's ugly. A user like me can put the following into a file in the config.d directory: LOCAL_CONFIG_FILE = REQUIRE_LOCAL_CONFIG_FILE = FALSE DAEMON_LIST = MASTER, SCHEDD
remarks: 2011-Sep-09 08:11:10 by matt: You should look at how the Red Hat RPMs handle this, it has evolved since your first snapshot of our spec and default config. 2015-Feb-11 16:01:51 by bbockelm: I believe this is already done in a different ticket. Marking as abandoned.

title: Ticket #6958: Param CHIRP_DELAYED_UPDATE_PREFIX is broken
description: Contrary to its name and vague documentation, the config param CHIRP_DELAYED_UPDATE_PREFIX is a list of the full names of attributes that can be set via Chirp's set_job_attr_delayed command. A single asterisk, which can appear anywhere in each entry, can be used for wildcard matching. The default value was originally Chirp*. In 8.6.10, the shadow was changed to treat the items in CHIRP_DELAYED_UPDATE_PREFIX as prefixes of attribute names with no wildcard option, and the default value was changed to Chirp (#6557). The code in the starter wasn't changed. Thus, Chirp is now the only attribute that can be set in the default configuration. To be useable, CHIRP_DELAYED_UPDATE_PREFIX must be set differently for the shadow and starter. The values for the starter need a trailing asterisk and the values for the shadow can't have one.

title: Ticket #2018: RequestMemory should be configurable with a default in condor_config
description: Some folks at LIGO work on dynamic slot provisioning. For that they use hard memory limits for each executing job, as advertised via RequestMemory. RequestMemory is typically a user-defined value or approximately the size of the job's binary as a default. The later is a rather poor value in practice as it is usually too small. For that reason, LIGO asked whether it is possible to set a default in the condor_config that will be used if users don't specify RequestMemory in their submit files. title: Ticket #5732: Allow more flexible command order within DAG files
description: Just had a discussion about #5729 with Lauren, and in the course of this she mentioned that she didn't realize that most commands that reference a node must come after the node is defined. For example, the following is not legal: SCRIPT PRE A ... JOB A ... We think this should probably be changed, to allow a "natural" ordering of certain commands: JOB A PARENT A CHILD B SCRIPT PRE B ... JOB B ... SCRIPT POST B ... I think the way to do this would be to go to a "two pass" parsing, where we parse JOB, SUBDAG EXTERNAL, and FINAL commands in the first pass, and everything else in the second pass.

title: Ticket #5698: Add GAHP statistics to grid ads
description: Add some statistics about GAHP commands to the Grid ads advertised by the gridmanager. The stats will be collected by the GahpServer object and reported by each Resource object. Since multiple Resource objects may share the same GAHP server, multiple Grid ads may have stats for the same GAHP. The stats are for all commands handled by that GAHP server, not just commands involving a specific Resource's service. Detecting which Grid ads share a GAHP can be done by examining the new GahpPid attribute. Some GAHPs are not represented, because no Resource object uses them. For example, the nordugrid_gahp used to do file transfers for cream jobs. These are the new statistics GahpCommandsIssued Total number of commands issued, plus a Recent count GahpCommandsTimedOut Total number of commands that the gridmanager timed out, plus a Recent count. GahpCommandsInFlight Current number of commands issued, plus a Peak count. This is commands issued for which the gridmanager is awaiting a result (does not include timed out commands). GahpCommandsQueued Current number of commands waiting to be issued (not issued yet due to throttles), plus a Peak count. GahpCommandRuntime Stats on time it took for commands to complete in the GAHP, including average, min, max, std.dev., and sum. Both lifetime and Recent. If the gridmanager times out a command (due to GRIDMANAGER_GAHP_CALL_TIMEOUT), the runtime of the command is GRIDMANAGER_GAHP_CALL_TIMEOUT. Timed out commands do not count in GahpCommandsIssued. We may want to change this behavior.

title: Ticket #744: Node job abnormal term + recovery mode + node retries -> DAGMan error
description: LIGO just ran into the problem that, when DAGMan goes into recovery mode, and hits a node job that terminated abnormally and has retries, DAGMan hits a fatal error (this is from the dagman.out file): 9/11 23:55:23 Event: ULOG_JOB_TERMINATED for Condor Node6cc7c3f0914d5f352145006fcf860a4d (762838.0) 9/11 23:55:23 Node 6cc7c3f0914d5f352145006fcf860a4d job proc (762838.0) failed with signal 11. 9/11 23:55:23 Retrying node 6cc7c3f0914d5f352145006fcf860a4d (retry #1 of 1)... 9/11 23:55:23 Number of idle job procs: 0 9/11 23:55:23 ERROR "Searched for node for cluster 762838; got -1!!" at line 1151 in file dag.cpp Note that if the node job fails but exits normally (e.g., returns a non-zero exit code rather than gets killed by a signal), DAGMan handles things correctly. Here are the relevant parts of the node job log: 000 (762838.000.000) 09/11 00:54:30 Job submitted from host: <10.20.30.1:34870> DAG Node: 6cc7c3f0914d5f352145006fcf860a4d ... <lots of unimportant stuff cut> 005 (762838.000.000) 09/11 16:58:05 Job terminated. (0) Abnormal termination (signal 11) (0) No core file Usr 0 00:00:00, Sys 0 00:00:00 - Run Remote Usage Usr 0 00:00:00, Sys 0 00:00:00 - Run Local Usage Usr 0 09:48:20, Sys 0 00:00:39 - Total Remote Usage Usr 0 00:00:00, Sys 0 00:00:00 - Total Local Usage 329 - Run Bytes Sent By Job 743770368 - Run Bytes Received By Job 0 - Total Bytes Sent By Job 0 - Total Bytes Received By Job ... 009 (762838.000.000) 09/11 16:58:05 Job was aborted by the user. ...
remarks: Hmm -- now I'm not sure whether recovery mode has anything to do with it. title: Ticket #4089: errno trashed by threading code for some IO operations
description: Blocking I/O operations in condor_read(), condor_write(), and Selector are surrounded by thread calls that allow other threads to run while the I/O blocks. After the operation completes, errno (or WSAGetLastError() on win32) is checked on failure. However, stop_thread_safe() makes calls that can overwrite that error code. The callers need to save errno/WSAGetLastError() before calling stop_thread_safe().
remarks: 2013-Nov-22 13:16:20 by tannenba: Are you sure this code is needed? My aging memory seems to recall that on with glibc, when using pthreads, errno is stored in thread local storage automagically. And on Windows, WSAGetLastError info is also stored in thread local storage iirc. I guess I never knew anything about MacOS... 2013-Nov-22 13:24:45 by tannenba: Oh, maybe you are saying that system calls inside of stop_thread_safe() can trash the errno sitting in TLS? Maybe it would be better to protect errno inside of stop_thread_safe()... 2013-Dec-06 13:35:25 by jfrey: I don't think it matters much whether errno is saved inside or outside of stop_thread_safe(). I did it outside because in the future, there could be callers that don't care about errno. 2013-Dec-09 15:10:25 by gthain: CODE REVIEW Approved.
check_ins: 2013-Nov-20 15:39 Check-in [38779]: error trashed by threading code for some IO operations. #4089 Save errno (or WSAGetLastError() on win32) before calls to stop_thread_safe() if we're interested in the value. stop_thread_safe() makes calls (like dprintf()) that may overwrite the error value. title: Ticket #5948: Permissions on subdirectories not properly preserved by file transfer
description: At least on Linux/Mac platforms, for non-directory files, the output transfer process preserves the file permissions while ignoring the umask. Unfortunately, the code to preserve file permissions on subdirectories applies the umask of the HTCondor daemon (which is typically 022). There does not appear to be a knob to override this. This is surprising; permissions on transferred subdirectories should work the same way as transferred files. In addition, if file transfer is occurring from a Windows machine to a Linux machine, the subdirectory will end up with permission 000 on the Linux machine. Reported by Michael Pelletier on htcondor-users in this post.
remarks: 2016-Oct-19 11:14:27 by mvpelletier: Sorry I didn't flag this to you guys sooner, I first puzzled over it a couple of years ago, and didn't look closely enough at it to realize it wasn't my own fault. In my current project, it would be very helpful to have a patched binary for 8.4.9 on RHEL6 if possible, to avoid the need for a post-output-transfer chmod in a DAG node or some such. 2016-Nov-03 11:20:26 by tannenba: Testing Notes Given a job and submit file that look like this - [tannenba@localhost mkd]$ cat mkd.sh #!/bin/sh mkdir outdir touch outdir/smell chmod 777 outdir chmod 777 outdir/smell [tannenba@localhost mkd]$ cat mkd.sub executable = mkd.sh should_transfer_files = YES transfer_output_files = outdir queue Here are the results submitting the job before the patches in this ticket; note the permissions on directory outdir are not 0777: [tannenba@localhost mkd]$ condor_submit mkd.sub Submitting job(s). 1 job(s) submitted to cluster 2. [tannenba@localhost mkd]$ umask 0002 [tannenba@localhost mkd]$ ls -ld outdir/ drwxr-xr-x. 2 tannenba tannenba 4096 Oct 19 19:14 outdir/ [tannenba@localhost mkd]$ ls -l outdir/ total 0 -rwxrwxrwx. 1 tannenba tannenba 0 Oct 19 19:14 smell And here are the results submitting the job after the patches in this ticket; note the permissions on directory outdir are now 0777 as expected: [tannenba@localhost mkd]$ condor_submit mkd.sub Submitting job(s). 1 job(s) submitted to cluster 3. [tannenba@localhost mkd]$ umask 0002 [tannenba@localhost mkd]$ ls -ld outdir/ drwxrwxrwx. 2 tannenba tannenba 4096 Nov 3 10:32 outdir/ [tannenba@localhost mkd]$ ls -l outdir/ total 0 -rwxrwxrwx. 1 tannenba tannenba 0 Nov 3 10:32 smell 2016-Nov-23 11:18:18 by jfrey: Code Review Shouldn't the default permissons for a directory be 0700? With 0600, the user can't access the files inside the directory. 2016-Dec-01 17:19:21 by tannenba: Indeed, changed default perm to 0700.

title: Ticket #197: Reduce frequency of DAGMan sleeps for log file consistency
description: Right now, if there are multiple log files, we sleep for one second before every submit (so that we can be sure to get events in the right order in recovery mode, because the timestamps are only precise to 1s). I'm pretty sure that we can relax this to just doing a sleep before each cycle of submits, because I don't think it really matters if we get the submit events for sibling jobs in the exact right order, as long as we don't get a submit event for a job before the terminated event of its parent.

title: Ticket #3465: Remote IO in Vanilla Universe
description: POSIX Remote IO (the ability to access the submitter's filesystem) is one of the features in standard universe and missing from the vanilla universe. However, most of the ingredients are there. We have WantIOProxy and chirp IO which can provide POSIX remote IO when the job is run under parrot. I propose wrapping chirp IO in a FUSE filesystem, allowing us to mount the submitter's filesystem. We can then use filesystem namespaces to make this mount private to the job and have lifetime equal to the job's processes. Design document incoming. Will post this to UW git as branch "V7_9-vanilla_remote_io-branch".
remarks: 2013-Jan-28 08:31:05 by bbockelm: dthain pointed out the following: http://www.cse.nd.edu/~ccl/software/manuals/man/chirp_fuse.html It is based on the CCL chirp client implementation and provides a far richer set of error handling, timeouts, and retries. We ought to add integrating with that FUSE implementation (if present) to the TODO list in the design document. Ideally, we would have only one Chirp client implementation, based on the CCL one. This may be out-of-scope for this ticket. 2013-Apr-04 10:13:59 by gthain: Comments on the design document: 1) If the filesystem is always mounted under /condor, that means that nested condors (personal condors or glideins) only see the most-nested condor. 2) The knob to turn this on or off is on the execute side or on the submit side? 3) The knob "WantIOProxy" is not new, and already has some semantics. I'm a little leery of making it also enable the fuse mount. Should we have another job attributes that turns on fuse mounting independently of chirp? 4) The new knobs don't appear in the param table. 5) When I try to run the code on Fedora 18, my job just goes on hold with errno 13: permission denied

title: Ticket #528: BNL schedd periodic expression eval excessively infrequent
description: The ATLAS group at BNL submit large numbers of Panda pilot jobs with the following job policy: LeaveJobInQueue = JobStatus == 4 PeriodicRemove = (JobStatus == 4 && (CurrentTime - EnteredCurrentStatus) > 300) They report that occasionally, large numbers of jobs in Completed state pile up despite this policy. When I looked at the latest pileup today, they had 29000 jobs in the queue, with roughly 28000 that should have been removed by the PeriodicRemove expression. Some of the jobs had been in Completed state for over 12 hours. I suspect the Timeslice code is causing the time between periodic expression evaluations to grow excessively when the number of jobs in the queue becomes large.
remarks: 2009-May-27 16:49:41 by jfrey: As a workaround, I've asked BNL if they can remove the LeaveJobInQueue expression from their jobs. 2009-May-27 16:56:03 by jfrey: I looked at some BNL logs from yesterday, where the periodic expression evaluation took at least 6.5 minutes to run. The logs rolled, so I don't know when it started. At the default PERIODIC_EXPR_TIMESLICE setting of 0.01, that means the expressions won't be re-evaluated for 650 minutes (11 hours). 2009-May-27 20:17:13 by xzhao: I asked Torre, and he agrees to remove these policies from the ATLAS panda pilot condor-g submit file. Xin 2009-May-27 21:18:47 by jfrey: One reason the evaluation of the periodic expressions took so long at BNL was that PeriodicRemove evaluated to true for many of the jobs. The subsequent removal of the jobs counts as part of the time to evaluate the expressions. 2009-May-29 02:06:47 by danb: We definitely need to add an upper bound to the periodic expression timeslice interval to prevent insane things like this. I'll do that. 2009-May-29 07:51:52 by tannenba: Excellent, thanks Dan. Patch committed into the master, gonna resolve this ticket. Note to Jaime - BNL won't get this until we merge the BNL branch back to the master..

title: Ticket #482: Thread Local storage breaks cross tests from 32b rhel 3->64 bit rhel3
description: When thread support was merged, the cross test failed from 32 bit rhel 3 to 64 bit rhel3. All other combinations seem to work. The tests fail early, in remote_pre, because condor_config_val (and all the tools) core dump on startup when trying to initialize dprintf. Running condor_config_val under gdb shows the following: Program received signal SIGSEGV, Segmentation fault. _condor_dprintf_va (flags=4096, fmt=0x82c3ba0 "config: using subsystem '%s', local '%s'\n",args=0xffff96a8 "\200u7\b\231;,\b\bu7\bN\032@�\002@\"\016\b\bu7\b\bu7\b\034\026 @\bu7\b\bu7\b�@�\a@\"\016\bps7\b\bu7\b>I\a@�\001@�020\002") at dprintf.c:201 201 CurrentTid = 0; and gdb seems confused about TLS: (gdb) p CurrentTid Cannot find thread-local variables on this target I've disabled this cross test for the moment, when this test is resolved the 32 bit rhel3 -> 64 bit rhel3 test should be re-enabled.
remarks: 2009-May-15 06:32:01 by tannenba: It seems more serious than just x86_64_rhas. We observed very strange behavior (gdb crashing, master just stopping) on SL4.6. For v7.3.1, going to disable linking in of pthreads/TLS all together, and then get rid of TLS for 7.3.2. 2009-May-15 09:25:29 by gthain: We need to read the drepper white paper at http://people.redhat.com/drepper/tls.pdf Note that C98 adds support for the __thread storage specifier, perhaps that would be a better implementation? There's gcc options that might help: -mtls-direct-seg-refs -mno-tls-direct-seg-refs Controls whether TLS variables may be accessed with offsets from the TLS segment register (%gs for 32-bit, %fs for 64-bit), or whether the thread base pointer must be added. Whether or not this is legal depends on the operating system, and whether it maps the segment to cover the entire TLS area. For systems that use GNU libc, the default is on. -ftls-model=model Alter the thread-local storage model to be used (see Thread-Local). The model argument should be one of global-dynamic, local-dynamic, initial-exec or local-exec. The default without -fpic is initial-exec; with -fpic the default is global-dynamic. 2009-Aug-17 08:34:06 by tannenba: Re the remark above - good thinking, and looks promising, but I have to say having been burned on TLS once I am shy to try another iteration of it again. 2009-Aug-17 08:41:01 by tannenba: So one of the more subtle and annoying aspects of getting rid of the thread local storage is dealing w/ the recursive nature of dprintf(). dprintfs() happens all over Condor, including in the hashtable template etc. And yet dprintf() wants to display the tid. So we are left with some choices: Deal w/ the recursive nature of the above by being able to detect a re-entrancy into dprintf and making it a no-op, or Use pthread keys to give us the same mechanism as TLS, and stash the tid in the key.

title: Ticket #3170: Fixed length buffers
description: From Florian Weimer - ClassAd:: LookupString(const char *, char *) cannot be used securely This variant of ClassAd::LookupString() copies a string of undetermined length (whose contents is potentially controlled by an attacker) into a buffer with a fixed, but unknown size. Such an interface cannot be used in a secure fashion, much like the stdio function gets(). This LookupString() variant must be removed. On a related note, ClassAd::LookupString(const char *, char *, int) fails to NUL-terminate long strings and should probably take a size_t argument, not an int.

title: Ticket #6372: "first-class" names for "+pre" or "+post" and company
description: The naming for pre- and post- scripts is consistent but something of a mess, and we kind of think that "pre" and "post" are misleading in the vanilla universe anyway, since they aren't the first and last tasks in the shishkebab DAG (they won't be running in the same environment as the job proper). We should consult with an RCF to see if we can do better. pseudo-BNF {Pre,Post}{Cmd,Args|Arguments,Env|Environment} {Pre,Post}[Success]Exit{Code,BySignal,Signal} Possibilities for new prefixes include: transfer_input_files[_cmd], but that could easily be misunderstood prepare_sandbox[_cmd] / check_sandbox[_cmd] are ambiguously ordered PostSandboxPreJob[_cmd] and PostJobPreSandbox[_cmd] are unambiguous but hard to say easy to confuse ValidateInputFiles[_cmd] and CheckOutputFiles[_cmd] post_input[_cmd] and pre_output[_cmd] It would be most consistent if all we did was change the prefix (and it would be easy to code).
remarks: 2017-Sep-12 10:59:33 by tlmiller: The RCFs point out that what most of their users would want is actually a vanilla-universe pre- or post- script, not the horrible hack that we have now. There wasn't any particular consensus on what to call what we have now, but there was consensus on it not sounding particularly useful. The consensus was that the shish-kebab/multiple command idea would be hard to explain.

title: Ticket #7563: Add missing mapping methods to Python bindings classad objects
description: Our Python bindings ClassAd object implements most of the Python dictionary interface, but is missing pop popitem (if possible with the same LIFO guarantee, but an arbitrary order is fine if not) copy clear fromkeys We should add these methods to the ClassAd object. See https://docs.python.org/3/library/stdtypes.html?highlight=pop#dict for the behavior of these methods. For all but clear() it may be more useful to add a method to ClassAd that creates a dict from the classad using evaluated values. [[anonymous: I don't think it is possible to implement these (reasons in bold)]] classmethod fromkeys(iterable[, value]) Create a new dictionary with keys from iterable and values set to value. fromkeys() is a class method that returns a new dictionary. value defaults to None. All of the values refer to just a single instance, so it generally doesn’t make sense for value to be a mutable object such as an empty list. To get distinct values, use a dict comprehension instead. copy() Return a shallow copy of the dictionary. pop(key[, default]) If key is in the dictionary, remove it and return its value, else return default. If default is not given and key is not in the dictionary, a KeyError is raised. [[anonymous: this will always be a copy of the value. if value is an ExprTree it may not be possible to evaluate it anymore]] popitem() Remove and return a (key, value) pair from the dictionary. Pairs are returned in LIFO order. Changed in version 3.7: LIFO order is now guaranteed. In prior versions, popitem() would return an arbitrary key/value pair.

title: Ticket #5270: jobs on hold after upgrading condor on htcondor-ce
description: Dan at US CMS T2 reported via RUST: The UW CMS T2 upgraded its condor from 8.2.7 to 8.2.9 yesterday. After that, many jobs have gone on hold on one of our three HTCondor-CEs. I believe all these jobs were running at the time of the upgrade. The problem shows up as a permission problem in the job's spool directory. The files are owned by condor rather than the owner of the job, so the shadow fails to write to the spool when the job finishes. I have a hypothesis about what went wrong. There are two schedds on an HTCondor-CE: the batch system schedd and the CE schedd. The jobs in the CE schedd are copied into the batch system schedd by JobRouter. The JobRouter is being used in the mode where the two jobs share the same spool. We have three HTCondor-CEs. The one that had this problem happens to have had the upgraded batch system schedd restart before the CE schedd restarted. The other two HTCondor-CEs that did not have the problem both had the batch system schedd restart after the CE schedd. My hypothesis is that the batch system schedd restarts and creates a shadow to reconnect to the job. Then the CE schedd restarts and chowns the job's spool to condor ownership. Then when the shadow tries to write to the spool on behalf of the user, it fails. See attached RUST for additional info including logs.
remarks: 2015-Sep-22 14:42:54 by bbockelm: Ah, nifty find! I think OSG has been hit this by a few times at other sites but haven't been able to figure out the underlying problem. The way Dan reports it makes it sound quite easy to reproduce. Has Jaime's patch for not chown'ing user directories landed yet? Is that something we could test out here? 2015-Sep-22 16:05:36 by jfrey: Not chowning user spool directories (#5226) is in 8.5.0, so we still need a fix for 8.2/8.4. 2015-Sep-22 16:08:35 by bbockelm: Is the only potential case where this fires the HTCondor-CE? If so, one approach is backporting the patch and hiding it behind a config var along the line of IS_CONDOR_CE=true. 2015-Oct-06 10:41:17 by jfrey: I've identified the source of this problem. It's a combination of behaviors in the schedd and the job router. The non-CE schedd is writing bogus entries in its job queue log, and the job router is choking on them, causing it to not see the full log and falsely believe jobs have disappeared. With the newer negotiation protocols that allow a resource request to result in multiple matches returned by the negotiator, the schedd can end up with more matches than it can use. Particularly, the schedd asks for more matches than it ends up being able to use. We saw some of the effects in #4554. One effect is that the schedd starts using a job id of -1.-1 as the target job for the extra matches. If the negotiator sends a REJECTED message, then the schedd will happily set attributes LastRejMatchTime and LastRejMatchReason for job -1.-1. This results in entries in the job queue log, even though this is an invalid job id. On restart, the schedd will skip over these nonsense log entries. But the job router chokes on these entries. On startup, it will stop reading the log at this point. So it does not see any activity after this point, like job submissions it performed. Thus, on restart, the job router may conclude that jobs it had previously routed have been orphaned (due to the destination job appearing to be missing), so it yields the source jobs back to the CE schedd. This includes chowning the spool files back to the condor user. If the destination job was already running, then the non-CE schedd/shadow will experience permissions problems. Also, the job router may later claim the job again and submit a new destination job. Then, there can be two jobs running that are using the same sandbox of files. The fix will consist of two changes: Add a guard to prevent the schedd from writing these specific nonsense job queue entries. Change the job router to ignore nonsense log entries and continue reading the log. We should also consider adding guards in the ClassAd log code to prevent all bad entries, but that's outside the scope of this bug fix. 2015-Oct-07 10:50:08 by tannenba: Thinking about the providence of this bug has raises a few questions - What should the router do if the incoming schedd says the job was routed, and the source schedd says it does not exist? Currently it gets cleaned up and starts over from scratch (re-run). But if the job is a pilot job, would it be better to simply throw it away? A key observation is the root of the problem is that the schedd and job router ended up with a different view of the system state because the router treated an anomaly in the log as a terminal error and the schedd just ignored it. This begs the implementation question - Do the sched and the job router share the same code to read the job_queue.log on recovery?? They should... How does the router know when the job got routed? What happens when the job_queue.log rotates in destination B? To get around this, does the router submit to destination schedd with leave_in_queue or? 2015-Oct-07 11:29:06 by danb: Re question 2: The router uses the quill code for reading and following the job queue log. If I recall correctly, that code is an independent implementation; it does not share code with the schedd's log reader. Re question 3: The router knows a job got routed when the job's "RoutedBy" attribute is equal to the name of the job router daemon. Re question 4: leave_in_queue is used in the routed copy of the job. In the original copy of the job the router uses the "Managed" attribute, similarly to how the gridmanager uses it. 2015-Oct-21 14:52:01 by tannenba: CODE REVIEW Patch looks good, thanks, resolving this ticket and associated RUST ticket.

title: Ticket #4898: SUBMIT_REQUIREMENTS and/or COMMIT_R... and/or JOB_INVARIANTS
description: Many of the SUBMIT_REQUIREMENTS use cases would also seem to benefit from setting COMMIT_REQUIREMENTS and/or JOB_INVARIANTS. For example, rejecting a submission with an unknown accounting group is all well and good, but is arguably useless without also prevent condor_qedit from changing it later. There may also be other attributes that should not be changed after job creation; the job's universe comes to mind. The most efficient way to implement something like COMMIT_REQUIREMENTS may be to mark job attributes mentioned in (the transitive closure of) SUBMIT_REQUIREMENTS as immutable. Actually performing the checks on each commit may be difficult to make sufficiently efficient, and (as TJ pointed out) may also require changes to condor_qedit (which allows multiple attributes to be changed on the same command-line, but may not create a single transaction for all of them). It may be generally wiser to allow queue super users to bypass the kind of immutability (which would make it different than the immutability for JobUniverse?). Also, it would be convenient and wise to list immutable attributes in the job ad itself. Other possibilities including scanning the commit (either explicitly or via a ClassAd log plugin) for attributes "of interest" and only evaluating the requirements for those job ads for which at least one of those attributes changed. On the other hand, it's not entirely clear what the semantic meaning of rejecting an update from the starter would be.

If #0 is mandatory, then all the others aren't really necessary, as things that violate the condition will never actually run. #2 may be too expensive. #3, #4, and #5 are "niceties" to inform the user early. #4 and #5 are slightly different because #4 comes from the user, and #5 comes from "condor" (i.e. the starter), although the starter does this at the request of the user so maybe differentiating between them isn't useful.

title: Ticket #4461: IPv6 used by default if enabled
description: One statement in the RFCs is that IPv6 should be used by default if available. Right now, if ENABLE_IPV6 and ENABLE_IPV4 are set to true, no IPV6 communication is ever done. In fact, it's impossible (due to a bug, outlined below) to use IPv6 to talk to daemons in at least one corner case. All my findings below are, except where noted, on this branch: https://github.com/bbockelm/htcondor/tree/ipv6_default We currently advertise whatever socket is created first. So, to make IPv6 preferred, we must create an IPv6 socket first. An even smarter idea is to make publicNetworkIpAddr protocol-aware. Right now, we just guess the first public socket is the correct one. This way if the connection to the collector goes over IPv6, we advertise IPv6. If the connection is IPv4, we advertise IPv4. I leave this for later If a socket is listening on [::], we return the local IP address instead when we generate the condor_sockaddr. The local IP address (usually, IPv4) is not protocol dependent; i.e., when converting an IPv6 command socket to a sinful string, a IPv4 address is returned. We should have a local IP address per IP protocol. In particular, we probably should assert that if we Sock::assign an IPv6 socket, the resulting address is actually IPv6. Not true in the current code. TODO for the future. I need to lookup some IPv6 texts, but I think doing this is very wrong - we should rely on some invocation of getaddrinfo to convert from [::] or 0.0.0.0 to something we can advertise to clients to bind against. TODO for the future. I mean, in general, this is fundamentally wrong according to Internet experts (one should use DNS / getaddrinfo on the client side to do the sorting of appropriate addresses to use). However, we disagree with said Internet experts... At least as far as I can tell, _condor_is_ipv6() always returns false because it is invoked before the param table is configured (at least, before config.d is read). We shouldn't cache things before param table is invoked. We should initialize both IPv4 and IPv6 in the hostname detection and just throw away the IPv6 one if it wasn't used; I didn't implement this part. In the future, we should convert this to ternary logic - default ENABLE_IPV6 to "auto" and use getaddrinfo to determine whether IPv6 should be used. TODO for the future. Initializing hostnames involves several steps that are IPv4 only (look at the TODOs in the code). I didn't fix this. ConvertDefaultIPToSocketIP may change a IPv6 address to an IPv4 one (incorrectly too, as it leaves the []) via string substitution. This function should be protocol aware. This prevents IPv6-only daemons from being found by mixed-mode clients (as they currently communicate via IPv4 by default). Moved to #4513: IPv6: ConvertDefaultIPToSocketIP always sets IPv4 address. Not fixed in this branch. If a daemon advertises an IPv6 sinful string and an IPv4-only daemon tries to talk to it via the Daemon() class, an IPv4 socket will be created but we attempt to call connect() with an IPv6 sockaddr. This results in a EPROTOTYPE but the do_connect function continues to block for about 6 minutes. EPROTOTYPE should be caught and no retries should be attempted. I did not fix this. There's enough sticky issues - especially in hostname resolution - that I think we should have a separate milestone of "use IPv6 by default if enabled" on the IPv6 roadmap.

title: Ticket #206: timeslice timers delay scheduling of local/scheduler universe jobs
description: The schedd uses a timeslice timer to aid in scheduling of Scheduler::timeout(), the main house-keeping function of the schedd, responsible for many things including scanning the job queue and counting idle jobs. The timeslice timer is used for scalability reasons. For very large queues, scanning the queue is expensive, so we schedule it less frequently. The result is that we maintain high throughput when dealing with large queues of reasonably long-running jobs. However, when our task is to run jobs with minimal delay after they enter the queue, the delays introduced by the timeslice timer tend to reduce response-time. This has been observed for scheduler/local universe jobs on highly loaded submit machines. Setting SCHEDD_INTERVAL_TIMESLICE close to 1.0 can be done to increase responsiveness, but this may sacrifice scalability quite a bit. The question is whether we can be more efficient about scanning for new jobs to run without all the expense that is currently implied by Scheduler::timeout(). A related worry is that occasional load spikes may cause the timeslice timer to overreact and introduce undesirable delays. I will make the timeslice calculation use an exponential moving average in its estimate of the expected runtime for the task, rather than just using the most recent runtime. This will smooth out temporary spikes.

title: Ticket #4031: Add simple meta-params to enable complex features with default
description: A meta-param is a single knob that when set, changes the value of multiple config params. Meta-knobs will be defined in the default param table like this [$FLAVOR.CHOCOLATE] friendly_name=Enable the chocolate daemon default = @end DAEMON_LIST=$(DAEMON_LIST) CHOCOLATE CHOCOLATE_DEBUG=D_FULLDEBUG CHOCOLATE_LOG=$(LOG)/ChocolateLog @end [$FLAVOR.LEMON] friendly_name=Enable the lemon daemon default = @end DAEMON_LIST=$(DAEMON_LIST) LEMON LEMON_LOG=$(LOG)/LemonLog @end Meta-params are used by adding the following to the config file. use flavor : lemon chocolate This will behave exactly the same as if the config file contains the following at the point where the use flavor line is. DAEMON_LIST=$(DAEMON_LIST) LEMON LEMON_LOG=$(LOG)/LemonLog DAEMON_LIST=$(DAEMON_LIST) CHOCOLATE CHOCOLATE_DEBUG=D_FULLDEBUG CHOCOLATE_LOG=$(LOG)/ChocolateLog As part of this change, attempts to use : to do simple parameter assignments in the config file will generate a warning that : is reserved for meta operations. Initially the only meta operation will be "use", later we may add "include" and other meta operations. The syntax for use will be [@]use <category> : <option-in-category> where @ is an optional character that makes the line not valid for earlier versions of HTCondor, but otherwise has no effect on the result. use is the case-insensitive keyword that indicates a meta knob reference <category> is one of a small number of meta knob categories. ROLE, POLICY, SECURITY, and FEATURE are the current categories. <option-in-category> is the name of the metaknob in the given <category>, for instance VMWARE is one of the metaknobs in the FEATURE category.

title: Ticket #1233: batch_test.pl shouldn't rely on /bin/sh redirection.
description: batch_test.pl starts tests with a line something like this: system("perl $test_program > $workdir/$test_program.out 2>&1") Problems: Assumes bourne shell-like shell (Probably not true under Windows, unless Perl is engaging in magic. While is possible.) Run into problems if $test_program ever includes "special" characters like whitespace, > or similar. Ideal solution: have perl itself capture the child's error and output, allowing the start command to be system('perl', $test_program), which solves both problems above.

title: Ticket #2809: Rogue condor_shadows after condor_rm -forcex
description: From the thread "[CondorLIGO] LIGO: condor_status out of sync". $CondorVersion: 7.6.6 Jan 17 2012 BuildID: 401976 $ $CondorPlatform: x86_64_rhap_6.1-updated $ 150 jobs were running under a DAG. The DAG was condor_rmed. Many (all?) of the jobs lingered in X. The user eventually noticed this after an unknown delay and ran condor_rm -forcex on them. The jobs left the queue, but the condor_shadows lingered. The corresponding condor_starters are believed gone. The condor_schedd no longer reported the jobs in condor_q, but the command "condor_status -submitters -total | grep USERNAME" includes the rogue shadows in the RunningJobs total. Currently gathering more information.
remarks: 2012-Feb-09 22:51:09 by pfc: This may be related to #556. 2012-Feb-10 14:30:50 by pfc: Updated priority to match Todd's new scheme (1=fire, 2=soon, 3=time permitting, 4=not yet prioritized, 5=wishlist/ideas). 2012-Feb-10 16:34:01 by adesmet: After some discussion, here are the problems and our current plan: PROBLEM: Jobs hang out in X far too long. SOLUTION: As of 7.6.6, Condor will kill shadows when the lease expires. This should cause the job to leave the queue. We hope this will resolve most, if not all, of the jobs hanging around in X. PROBLEM: condor_rm -forcex doesn't necessarily remove the job from the queue. SOLUTION: We will change -forcex to be more aggressive. -forcex should mean, "I don't care about this job in any way, tear it out of the queue by any means necessary." The shadow will be promptly killed and the job yanked from the queue. Some final cleanup may not happen. PROBLEM: Jobs hang out in X. SOLUTION: There isn't a clear cause for the problem. Multiple different problems may lead to this. Some are out of our control (e.g. a process stuck in uninterruptable sleep). Others may be bugs in Condor. So despite all of the above, we ask that any jobs that end up in X still be investigated and reported to us so we can identify the biggest problems and improve our handling. 2012-Feb-20 13:01:54 by adesmet: "We will change -forcex to be more aggressive" - Goal: 2012-02-25 2012-Feb-27 14:37:03 by adesmet: Seeking reviewer for the code. 2012-Mar-12 13:59:07 by adesmet: Closed #556: MAX_JOBS_RUNNING inconsistent with queue after condor_rm -force as a duplicate. It was associated with condor-admin 19245. 2012-Mar-21 15:48:50 by jfrey: CODE REVIEW The changes in actOnJobMyselfHandler() to aggressively kill a shadow on an rm -forcex look good.

title: Ticket #713: CCB does not honor TCP_FORWARDING_HOST
description: Matt noticed that if a CCB client has TCP_FORWARDING_HOST that the reversed connection attempt to the client goes to the client's private address, not its TCP_FORWARDING_HOST address. While working with Marquette, we also found that the CCB server's TCP_FORWARDING_HOST is not propagated to the CCB listener's advertised CCB address.
remarks: 2009-Sep-15 05:36:28 by matt: Looks like CCB doesn't honor TCP_FORWARDING_HOST... Seems CCB will ask an exec node on a private network to connect to a private IP. 08/19 19:42:02 CCBListener: received request to connect to NEGOTIATOR <24.90.251.184:40012> on <192.168.77.42:40163> with reverse connect address <192.168.77.42:40012>, request id 204. Negotiator is on private 77.42 and has TCP_FORWARDING_HOST set to 24.90.251.184, which does port forwarding so anyone can connect to it. CCB should ask the exec node to connect to the TCP_FORWARDING_HOST. 2009-Nov-18 11:05:31 by danb: I put a fix for this in 7.4.1.
