title: Ticket #6519: Add Managed Instance Group Support to GCE GAHP
description: Adding managed group instances to GCE GAHP server. This patch will add two new GAHP commands: GCE_GROUP_INSERT : create an instance template and a managed instance group GCE_GROUP_DELETE : delete aforementioned template and group Specifications are based on previously submitted design doc (ping me for access): https://docs.google.com/document/d/1B2V03lXR9YCgodRsUKdU1hHmbGbiQZAjSqt4rjV-bHY/edit Note that groups created this way last "forever". Functionality to automatically delete the group after a set number of hours is not yet supported. Can be tested by running gce_gahp and then sending the followng text: GCE_GROUP_INSERT 1234 https://www.googleapis.com/compute/v1 /<CRED_FILE> <PROJECT> us-central1-a gahp-test n1-highcpu-8 <IMAGE_NAME> NULL NULL true NULL 4 1 GCE_GROUP_DELETE 1234 https://www.googleapis.com/compute/v1 <CRED_FILE> <PROJECT> us-central1-a gahp-test
remarks: 2018-Jan-24 09:33:15 by jfrey: Code Review I have not read the design document yet. Some of my concerns below may be addressed there. Each of the new gahp commands performs two operations with the server, the creation/deletion of an instanceTemplate and an instanceGroupManager. Some thought needs to go into properly handling this 1-to-2 mapping of operations, particularly with regards to failure. The most immediate problem is that it appears that each gahp command will generate two RESULTS lines, which violates the standard gahp protocol outline. There should only be one RESULTS line that encompasses all of the actions performed for a given gahp command. There's also the issue of what happens when one of the operations fails. The client needs a well-defined recovery path, which can be as simple as make sure everything is deleted and tell the user there was a problem. For example, in GCE_GROUP_INSERT, if the second creation operation fails (instanceGroupManager), can the client retry the gahp command? If so, then the first creation operation (instanceTemplate) on the second attempt shouldn't fail when the resource already exists. If the client instead uses GCE_GROUP_DELETE to clean up the instanceTemplate, the command shouldn't fail because the instanceGroupManager doesn't exist. If these issues are too difficult to work out, one solution is to break these commands apart so that each GCE operation is a separate gahp command. Some of the comments in GceGroupDelete::workerFunction() refer to creation of resources instead of deletion. 2018-Feb-04 16:20:22 by dstrain: Here is a new version. I have changed the result string to concatenate the two results if there were two operations. For failure modes, if the first insert succeeds and the second succeeds, the client will need to send a delete to clean up the template. I believe I have modified the delete to continue if the first delete fails. i.e. It will attempt to delete both. Is this what you are looking for? If not, can you clarify the procedure you'd like to implement? (I don't know if splitting the operations is the best idea. It will become more complicated in the future, since you will need to create 2 templates [one for instances, and one for timekeeper]). 2018-Feb-04 16:20:47 by dstrain: Here is a new version. I have changed the result string to concatenate the two results if there were two operations. For failure modes, if the first insert succeeds and the second succeeds, the client will need to send a delete to clean up the template. I believe I have modified the delete to continue if the first delete fails. i.e. It will attempt to delete both. Is this what you are looking for? If not, can you clarify the procedure you'd like to implement? (I don't know if splitting the operations is the best idea. It will become more complicated in the future, since you will need to create 2 templates [one for instances, and one for timekeeper]). 2018-Mar-28 16:09:53 by jfrey: Rather than stapling two result messages together with a semicolon, I like something along these lines: When a GAHP command consists of multiple requests to the service, try each request in sequence. If a request fails, stop and return a failure result with the error message for that request. If all requests succeed, return a success result. In the case of a deletion request, treat an "object doesn't exist" error as a success. This gives the client of the gahp a simple recourse for failures: call GCE_GROUP_DELETE until it reports success, optionally ask for intervention from the user. 2018-Apr-05 18:33:28 by dstrain: I have submitted a new patch. I think this is the error message semantics you want? If not, please let me know what should be modified. 2018-Apr-19 16:49:58 by jfrey: The latest patch is close to the error semantics I have in mind. I'll commit it and then make the changes I think are needed.

title: Ticket #343: condor_master -pidfile will stomp pidfile of running master
description: If you run "condor_master -pidfile /tmp/master.pid" twice in a row, /tmp/master.pid will contain the PID of the second condor_master, the one that exited immediately because because it failed to get the InstanceLock. To reproduce: Install and configure Condor so it can run. condor_master -pidfile /tmp/master.pid cat /tmp/master.pid - Note the PID. condor_master -pidfile /tmp/master.pid cat /tmp/master.pid - Note the PID. Check MasterLog. Note that the second instance exited immediately, but that its PID matches the PID from step 5. Observed behavior: /tmp/master.pid contains the PID of the second, exited condor_master. Expected behavior: /tmp/master.pid contains the PID of the first, still running condor_master.

title: Ticket #5765: condor_history should honor SCHEDD_HOST if it is defined
description: condor_history should default to a remote query to the schedd defined in SCHEDD_HOST when SCHEDD_HOST is defined. Since you may still want to query the local history files explicitly even when SCHEDD_HOST is defined, a new argument -local will be added that will force the old behaviour of condor_history. i.e it will force it to will read from the configured history file(s) As a part of this change, remote condor history will supply a projection for the default output, and a new option for streaming results will be added to condor_history and to the remote history query. We should consider adding support for streaming into the 8.4 release as well.
remarks: 2016-Jun-30 11:17:08 by johnkn: The reason for the new streaming option is that the current remote condor_history wire protocol puts an End-of-Message only at the end of the entire response. This causes the client side to buffer the results and to only hand them back to the condor_history code once all of the results have been recieved. Thus the current wire protocol results in condor_history not printing any output until all of the results have been recieved - and the entire result stream must fit into memory on the client side or the operation will fail and print nothing.

title: Ticket #7888: Document how X509 user proxy type determines delegated proxy type
description: It has now happened enough times in LIGO that we think it would be useful to document that if a user specifies to use a proxy, and the indicated proxy is NOT of type "RFC 3820 compliant impersonation proxy", then the delegated proxy that condor will create for each such job will be of type "Proxy draft (pre-RFC) compliant limited proxy." For an increasing number of consumers of proxies, this will not be accepted. In such a case, the original proxy needs to be created as an RFC 3820 compliant proxy. Given the limited remaining usefulness of proxies we are not requesting a change in behavior, but just that this behavior be documented, since otherwise it has proven time-consuming to track down anew on multiple occasions.
creator: jlwillis

title: Ticket #3961: VM universe should support an exit status code
description: Construct some well-known mechanism which would allow a VM universe job to provide an exit status. This exit status should become the job's ExitStatus (and ExitBySignal/ExitCode/ExitSignal), and as such, reflected (recorded?) in the job ad.
remarks: 2013-Oct-04 14:48:22 by cat: Todd Miller and I discussed a user interface for this feature. The basic idea is to introduce a new command on all VM-universe execute nodes and have it be responsible for setting up the magic on the VM guest to communicate back an exit status code. Usage: condor_vm_exit EXITCODE This command accepts a single integer exit code, intended to parallel Linux shell exit codes but really just an integer value that is open to interpretation. HTCondor validates the argument and arranges for it to be set in the job classad in the ExitCode attribute; if the argument is missing or not valid, the job ExitCode is set to 0; extra arguments are silently ignored. At this time, we do not have a clear proposal for how this command will be implemented, but hey. (For future reference: We purposefully left the name of the command slightly generic. Someday, we may decide to extend the command to shut down the VM guest properly. However, this is hard to get right (highly system dependent) and not terribly high value (once we have documented the proper shutdown command per platform, it is easy to copy and use), so we decided to focus on getting totally right the first use case of condor_vm_exit.)
creator: tlmiller

title: Ticket #2389: Dynamically link Globus and VOMS libraries in UW builds
description: In the UW builds of Condor on linux, dynamically link against the Globus and VOMS libraries we build. We also want to distribute a copy of those libraries. We also need to make Condor more amenable to varying versions of Globus when others (including distro maintainers) build Condor. The gahp_server and nordugrid_gahp replace some object files in the Globus libraries they use with modified versions. This can cause undefined behavior (including crashes) if a different version of the library is used. Milestones Dynamically link Globus and VOMS libraries in UW builds [DONE] If/when distributing Globus/VOMS libraries, make sure they're stripped when appropriate [DONE] If distributing Globus/VOMS libraries in native packages, ensure we set RPATH correctly (lib vs lib64). This can get tricky when linking binaries as part of an external (gridftp_server, blahp). I added explicit calls to strip as an installation step, but my calls don't know what temporary directory CPack will use to assemble a native package. title: Ticket #7021: Declare build products from external projects
description: Suppose we have this setup: We have an external project, foo, in the Condor build, The foo target produces as part of the build a library libfoo.so, and There is a condor executable condor_foo that links against libfoo.so. In this case, some build generators (particularly, ninja) fail. This is because ninja will analyze the entire build dependency graph prior to starting the build and bail out if there are unmet dependencies. make, on the other hand, is lazy. It does not compute dependencies until it tries to build a given target. So if there's an undeclared side-product (as is the situation above), make won't notice unless the external project build is not complete by time it tries to build condor_foo. This is why make is "normally happy" but, on large machines with lots of parallelism, we have to do make externals followed by make: we have missing dependencies and the build system doesn't get the ordering correct. We are simply lucky that, for example, all the CREAM dependencies are normally done by time the cream_gahp is linked. CMake 3.x fixes this by adding a BUILD_BYPRODUCTS attribute - you can declare what files the external project will generate and CMake can generate the dependencies accordingly. We can't assume CMake 3.x however; we are stuck on 2.x. I propose adding a custom target in condor_post_external that has the same side-effect as what CMake 3.x does internally.

title: Ticket #1819: SubmitInfo.pm needs some cmake love
description: I went looking in the SubmitInfo.pm on the master branch and found things that look like this: my @minimal_build_configure_args = ( '-DPROPER:BOOL=OFF' => undef, '-DCLIPPED:BOOL=ON' => undef, '-DWITH_BLAHP:BOOL=OFF' => undef, '-DWITH_BOOST:BOOL=OFF' => undef, '-DWITH_COREDUMPER:BOOL=OFF' => undef, '-DWITH_CREAM:BOOL=OFF' => undef, '-DWITH_CURL:BOOL=OFF' => undef, '-DWITH_DRMAA:BOOL=OFF' => undef, '-DWITH_EXPAT:BOOL=OFF' => undef, '-DWITH_GCB:BOOL=OFF' => undef, '-DWITH_GLOBUS:BOOL=OFF' => undef, '-DWITH_GSOAP:BOOL=OFF' => undef, '-DWITH_HADOOP:BOOL=OFF' => undef, '-DWITH_KRB5:BOOL=OFF' => undef, '-DWITH_LIBVIRT:BOOL=OFF' => undef, '-DWITH_LIBXML2:BOOL=OFF' => undef, '-DWITH_UNICOREGAHP:BOOL=OFF' => undef, '-DWITH_VOMS:BOOL=OFF' => undef, ); That's wrong since the arguments are key/value pairs but here the whole thing being represented as only the key value. Instead it should be (at the minimum) this: my @minimal_build_configure_args = ( '-DPROPER:BOOL' => 'OFF', '-DCLIPPED:BOOL' => 'ON', '-DWITH_BLAHP:BOOL' => 'OFF', '-DWITH_BOOST:BOOL' => 'OFF', '-DWITH_COREDUMPER:BOOL' => 'OFF', '-DWITH_CREAM:BOOL' => 'OFF', '-DWITH_CURL:BOOL' => 'OFF', '-DWITH_DRMAA:BOOL' => 'OFF', '-DWITH_EXPAT:BOOL' => 'OFF', '-DWITH_GCB:BOOL' => 'OFF', '-DWITH_GLOBUS:BOOL' => 'OFF', '-DWITH_GSOAP:BOOL' => 'OFF', '-DWITH_HADOOP:BOOL' => 'OFF', '-DWITH_KRB5:BOOL' => 'OFF', '-DWITH_LIBVIRT:BOOL' => 'OFF', '-DWITH_LIBXML2:BOOL' => 'OFF', '-DWITH_UNICOREGAHP:BOOL' => 'OFF', '-DWITH_VOMS:BOOL' => 'OFF', ); Then I noticed that Z added something like this (note the -G usage): 'x86_64_winnt_5.1' => { 'build' => { 'configure_args' => { '-G \"Visual Studio 9 2008\"' }, 'prereqs' => undef, 'xtests' => undef, }, 'test' => { 'configure_args' => { @default_test_configure_args }, 'prereqs' => undef, 'testclass' => [ @default_testclass ], }, }, Which is wrong because it is an odd number of keys in the configure_args hash table. To make it a legal hash table definition, but following the wrong rendering above, it would be: 'configure_args' => { '-G \"Visual Studio 9 2008' => undef }, However, it really should be: 'configure_args' => { '-G' => 'Visual Studio 9 2008' }, Then I noticed the larger problem that the SubmitInfo system was never taught properly about how the cmake argument syntax differed from the configure syntax. For example, currently when '-DFOOBAR:BOOL' => 'OFF' is assembled, the = sign is mandatorily enforced to form "-DFOOBAR:BOOL=OFF" and passed as a command line argument. This is the same thing when the -G flag to cmake is used. However, in that case the = sign is forbidden. The method of option construction currently in SubmitInfo is a direct result of how configure processes its arguments. In the configure flavor of SubmitInfo, the difference between a key with an undef value and a key with a defined value is whether or not a = gets used when the final option to configure is generated. This is not true in the cmake system for all arguments one can pass to cmake. So, the right way to fix this is to construct two namespaces: cmake_args => { '-G' => '\"Visual Studio 9 2008\"', etc, etc, etc }, cmake_cache_entries => { 'WITH_VOMS:BOOL' => 'OFF', etc, etc, etc }, where cmake_args are not assembled with an =, but cmake_cache_entries are and the -D added when they are assembled. I don't have time for this work at the moment, but this is what should be done to bring the SubmitInfo system in sync with the cmake changes.

If the argument definition is "-DFoo" => "Bar" then you get the form -DFoo='Bar' If the argument definition is "-DFoo Bar" => undef then you get the form -DFoo Bar This allows the funky Windows style arguments to be expressed with minimal effort. 2011-Apr-13 16:19:24 by psilord: Ok, I looked at the patch. title: Ticket #7164: Busy Loop in CEDAR auth on windows on connection closure
description: condor_read() is supposed to return -2 when attempting to read from a socket that's been closed by the peer. But it only does this if recv() returns 0 (normal connection shutdown). If the connection closes abnormally (e.g. recv() returns -1, errno=ECONNRESET), condor_read() doesn't return the special "closed" value. When this happens to a ReliSock, the underlying socket will be ready for read, but ReliSock::readReady() will return false. For readers attempting to do non-blocking operations, this can lead to a busy loop of checking but not reading from the ReliSock until the timeout is hit. SecManStartCommand::receiveAuthInfo_inner() is one location where this can occur. On unix, after recv() fails once with ECONNRESET, subsequent calls return 0. This limits us to one pass through the loop. On Windows, recv() will fail with WSAECONNABORTED on every call, resulting in looping bounded only by the ReliSock's timeout. We should add a check in condor_read() for the common "connection died" errno values and return -2 when they occur.

title: Ticket #2366: Remove version from OpSys and add OpSysVer and Distro attributes
description: We should gather some of the accumulated wisdom from the Batlab and do a better job of identifying the operating system, distro and version in execute nodes. OPSYS on Windows machines should be WINDOWS See OPSYS_NAME comment below. Most Windows programs don't care what version of the Windows OS they run on. But Condor sets the OPSYS attribute for Windows execute nodes to a value that contains the version number (WINNT50, WINNT51, etc). So it requires effort on the part of the user to specify that their program will run on most versions of windows. The default behavior for Condor is that programs will execute only on the nodes that have the same version of Windows as the submit node. The {Quote: OpSys} attribute should just be WINDOWS by default. And there should be a parameter ENABLE_VERSIONED_OPSYS that enables the old behavior of appending the OS version number to the OPSYS attribute. This will default to false A new attribute OpSysVer will contain an integer value representing the version number of the OS. Win2k = 500, WinXP = 501, Win2003 = 502, Vista = 600, Server2008 = 600 or 601, Win7 = 601. A new attibute OpSysAndVer will have the legacy OpSys value, where WinXP = "WINNT51", etc. changes for unixen Most of the commercial Unix flavors also have OS version appended to OpSys. But support for non Linux flavors of unix is mostly legacy, so we will not change the way these machines publish OpSys. OpSysVer and OpSysAndVer will be added to these machines, but ENABLE_VERSIONED_OPSYS will default to true so OpSys and OpSysAndVer will be the same. changes for Linux For linux variants, {Quote: OpSys} carries no meaning, we need to publish additional attributes: DISTRO and DISTROVER with values to be set using techniques from the batlab's hawkeye scripts. OpSys "WINDOWS" "RedHat" "FreeBSD" OpSysVer (Major * 100 + Minor) OpSysMajorVer 5 OpSysAndVer "WINNT51" "REDHAT5" "SOLARIS23" OpSysName "Windows XP" "Red Hat 5.11" "Ubuntu 10.04" "Suse 10.2"

This should be a reasonably portable way of learning at run time the distro and version on Linux, as well as some of the capabilities promised by the LSB. # Capabilities list, colon seperated # :core-3.0-amd64:core-3.0-ia32:core-3.0-noarch:graphics-3.0-amd64:graphics-3.0-ia32:graphics-3.0-noarch LSB_VERSION=`/usr/bin/lsb_release -v -s` # Distribution name (Ubuntu, ScientificCERNSLC, RedHatEnterpriseServer) LSB_ID=`/usr/bin/lsb_release -i -s` # Distribution version (10.04, 4.8, 5.6) LSB_RELEASE=`/usr/bin/lsb_release -r -s` 2011-Sep-14 10:26:14 by dthain: I would like to add some thoughts about the user experience that might be used to guide the technical discussion. Most users (that I work with) are not knowledgable about the distinctions between different kinds of Linux. The local sysadmins worry about installing and managing the machines, and the users often don't even know what distro is in use. They see a machine listed as LINUX in condor_status and assume a program compiled on one Linux machine will run on another Linux machine. They are astonished and disappointed to find this is not the case. This happens a lot at universities where multiple IT operations are contributing to the same Condor pool. Thus, I think that the default system configuration should be very conservative about choosing execution machines that are likely to be compatible with the submitting machine. This gives the highest probability of success for the beginning user, but still allows the expert user to choose whatever resources they like. In the case of Linux, jobs should only run on machines with the same distribution and the same version, to some number of significant digits. Further, the system should make some effort to show the user that machines are significantly different, through condor_status and other displays, so that they understand why things don't match. There are multiple ways to accomplish this. Approach A - The prevailing Condor philosophy seems to be to define as many properties as possible, and let the knowledgable user pick from them. (OpSys, Distro, MajorVersion, MinorVersion, etc...) However, this has two downsides. (1) The default SUBMIT_EXPRS become rather complicated and difficult to override. For example, if the user defines Distro in their Requirements expression, should that cause MajorVersion to be dropped from the default SUBMIT_EXPRS? (2) A lot more information needs to be presented in condor_status and frieds to make it clear to users what is going on. Approach B - The opposite approach would be to put define OpSys to be something very specific like "REDHAT" or even "REDHAT5". This has the advantage of requiring no change to the existing default submit expressions logic, and also makes it abundantly clear to the user that one Linux distribution is incompatible with the other. They will have to go out of their way to try to run a code on multiple operating systems. Note that approach B does not prevent the use of additional machine attributes for the expert user, but it is simply emphasizing the use of OpSys as the common case. I favor the latter approach, but whatever approach is taken, I think it is important that the default submit expression be much more conservative than just selecting OpSys=="LINUX". 2012-Mar-26 17:37:26 by bgietzel: See http://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~bgietzel/opsys.html for opsys param values for each machine in new BaTLab.

title: Ticket #6325: late materialization expands $(Process) early when list has http: file
description: The creation of the late materialization digest file is supposed to skip expanding $(Process) in the digest file, and instead expand it only when materializing each job. This code is confused when the same line as a : later on, such as when a transfer input files line has an http:// file on it. Thus the following submit line submit fragment transfer_input_files = ./$(Process).dat, http://example.com/data incorrectly becomes this line in the digest incorrect submit digest fragment transfer_input_files = ./0.dat, http://example.com/data

title: Ticket #4318: Nordugrid_gahp crashes on failed CWD command
description: As part of submitting a job to a NorduGrid ARC server, the gahp issues a CWD command to learn the job's id. It's expecting a response like 250 "jobs/#######". But in some cases, it gets 226 Abort finished. When this happens, the gridftp client library returns a NULL pointer for the results buffer, which the nordugrid_gahp unconditionally dereferences.

We believe the crashes are due to the blahp's multi-threaded nature. Before the caching code, there was little to no data shared between threads that weren't explicitly sharing ClassAd data structures. Now, they share the cache and cached ExprTrees. title: Ticket #4748: Have non-zero default for DAGMAN_MAX_JOBS_IDLE
description: Stuart at LIGO suggested that we have an out-of-the-box non-zero setting for DAGMAN_MAX_JOBS_IDLE. I figure this is not a bad idea -- most users would probably never notice, and the ones that do notice are the ones that need it. And a user or site can always override the default if they need to. title: Ticket #7867: condor_submit_as_dag should use Python API
description: Currently, condor_submit_as_dag calls the condor_submit command-line tool. It would be nice to use the Python API instead. This proved too tricky to do in timer for 8.9.9, but may prove possible with further investigation. Obtaining the itemdata is straightforward, but useless without the queue count and the variable names. Some experimentation will be necessary to determine if the queue count in the original submit file is always preserved (through simplification); if the itemdata specifies the variable names and/or they can be reliably obtained through parsing the queue statment; and if the itemdata returned by the API implicitly includes the queue count or not. Deferring until condor_submit_as_dag sees enough usage to warrant the further work.
creator: tlmiller

title: Ticket #3577: ExitCode is not propagated from Shadow to Schedd
description: For some reason, on a subset of my local jobs, the ExitCode is not propagated to the schedd. I've included the ShadowLog. Look at job 20142.0. You see the following line: 04/16/13 20:53:08 (20142.0) (16846): Inside RemoteResource::updateFromStarter() which shows the updated classad includes ExitCode. However, there's no corresponding SetAttribute(ExitCode = 195) logged. A quick perusal of the code doesn't show any reason why this would be. If I look at the user log, it has the correct status.
remarks: 2013-Apr-17 07:11:40 by bbockelm: I narrowed this down a bit. The ExitCode is only missing if output is transferred by the Shadow. I'm assigning this to Dan as it appears he's the last one to touch this particular area of the code. The propagation of the status is a bit twisted. 2013-Apr-17 16:54:48 by danb: The problem appears to be caused by an old bug that was tickled by new code in 7.9.4. The old bug is this: In QmgrJobUpdater::updateJob(), it pushes attributes to the schedd --- possibly a subset of the dirty attributes. If the transaction succeeds, it clears the dirty flag on all attributes, not just the ones that were pushed. New code in 7.9.4 updates an attribute to indicate whether file transfer is in progress. Depending on a race between reaping the file transfer process and receiving the final update from the starter, this could result in attributes in the final update to the schedd not being pushed. When the race condition strikes, the following appears in the shadow log: Delaying shutdown of shadow, because file transfer is still active. 2014-Jun-12 14:25:58 by tannenba: Note that besides causing ExitCode to be incorrect in condor_history (as mentioned in the version history blurb), this bug also causes Condor-C grid jobs to always report a zero ExitCode.

title: Ticket #3218: Support JobPrio scope across multiple schedulers
description: Given a set of jobs across all Schedds in a pool owned by the same user that are competing for the same set of resources, we would like to decrease the number of jobs that begin execution ahead of higher priority jobs. E.g. decrease the instances of job priority inversions. See the below attached design document for details re motivation, goals, and design. This mechanism is controlled via the config knob USE_GLOBAL_JOB_PRIOS, which will default to false. The work for this design is complete, thus resolving; however, more work needs to be done before documentation. See #3691. Milestones Modify the Schedd to report JobPrioArray and JobPrioArrayOverflow attributes. [2 days] Modify the Schedd to support the Negotiator-Schedd protocol extension. [2 days] Modify the Negotiator to implement the new procedure. [3 days] Testing [4 days] EMBED: Status Table of Derived Tickets TN: Developer # Status Type Pri Created Changed Target Due Date Days left Title tannenba 3255 resolved enhance 2 2012 Oct 2012 Oct v070902 2012-10-05 -3288.9 Implement JobPrioArray and JobPrioArrayOverflow attrs in submitter ad tannenba 3256 resolved enhance 2 2012 Oct 2012 Oct v070902 2012-10-08 -3285.9 Implement Negotiator-Schedd protocol extension for global jobprios gthain 3257 resolved enhance 2 2012 Oct 2013 Jan v070903 2012-10-10 -3283.9 Implement USE_GLOBAL_JOB_PRIOS mechanism in the negotiator
remarks: 2012-Sep-05 12:34:29 by bbockelm: Here's the basic problem description (contributions from both sfiligoi and bbockelm): CMS would like to assign global priorities to jobs. Each job can potentially have a different priority, in a range spanning O(100k) different values. In practice, we envision having O(100) different priority levels at any point in time. The need for O(100k) levels is so that it is possible at any given moment to pick a priority number between two existing ones. From a currently running instance, the ratio of (# of unique priorities) : (# of jobs) is 1:100. In the current implementation, each workflow gets a priority, and the jobs share that priority. A subset of the jobs can be boosted (so, there's not precisely 1 priority per workflow). There is no current plan to have more than two priorities per workflow, but that doesn't imply there won't be further changes in the future. These job priorities should be global for a user/group. Job X from user1@domain1@scheddA should be run before job Y from user1@domain1@scheddA if the X.JobPrio > Y.JobPrio. We are targeting the system to scale to at least 100k running jobs. There is no way to run this from a single schedd host; and it is not only a Condor schedd scalability issue, other resource intensive processes have to run alongside Condor as well. The stage-in / stage-out can take a large amount of resources. We can peg a 1Gbps line at a modest level of runningjobs (10k). This will provide another barrier to single-schedd solutions; not insurmountable, but considerable. Right now, all jobs share the same submitter (user@domain), and are multiples schedds. That might not be true in the future, so the solution should respect group priorities. CMS isn't interested in preemption-based solutions (but definitely kudos to Erik for figuring out one!) 2012-Sep-05 12:35:35 by bbockelm: Here is my proposal. I understand Todd and Igor are working on an alternate one. My proposal is to, during each spin of the pie, only negotiate with jobs whose priority is equal to the maximum job prio of all submitters in the group. The max job prio is known from the submitter ads (and assumed to be INT_MIN if not present). If there's only one submitter in the group, do not apply this rule. As an example, let's say we have: user1@domain1@ScheddA Job 4, Prio 9 Job 5, Prio 8 user1@domain1@ScheddB Job 1, Prio 10 Job 2, Prio 8 Job 3, Prio 10 Suppose further the sort order is scheddA, then scheddB. The max job prio is 10, so the negotiation will look like: Connect to ScheddA, get job 4, spin. Update submitter ad to have max job prio to 9 Connect to ScheddB, get job 1 - assign. Get job 3 - assign. Get job 3 - assign. Get job 2 - spin. Update submitters's max job prio to 8. Connect to ScheddA, get job 4, assign. Get job 5 - spin. Update submitter ad to have max job prio 8. Connect to ScheddB, get job 2 - spin. Connect to ScheddA, get job 5 - assign. Get NO_MORE_JOBS. Done. Connect to ScheddB, get job 2 - assign. Get NO_MORE_JOBS. Done. Example implementation attached (don't be fooled by the fact it compiles - it likely doesn't work, but hopefully shows that the implementation is simple). Another approach is Igor's idea to include all the possible job prios in the submitter ad (I'd think you need to add a limit to the number of job prios posted, but that's a fairly small tweak). I believe this approach keeps the logic simpler, at a cost of spinning more often. This patch is a no-op except when there are multiple schedds with the same submitter who is using multiple job priorities. The effects are theoretically pretty small assuming there's a large number of jobs per priority. 2012-Sep-05 12:51:17 by sfiligoi: Any solution will likely need changes in core Condor components (e.g. Negotiator and Schedd), so it will need sign off by the highest level of Condor management (i.e Miron, and possibly others). We thus need a comprehensive study of the problem and of any proposed solution(s). 2012-Sep-05 20:36:53 by bbockelm: We had a quick phone call about this. I wasn't able to stay for the full thing (so I don't know the conclusion). One very solid point ToddT and others made was to consider the case where we have 30k job slots, a single schedd can run 20k jobs at a time, and all the "high priority" jobs are in one schedd. In such a case, you will have at least 10k low-priority jobs running. This RFE would not handle such a case well. CMS mostly avoids this because the difference between "global running jobs" and "maximum running jobs in a schedd" is fairly close and the distribution of high priority jobs is "not that bad" (but still bad enough that this is an issue!). This likely changes in the future if we want to go up to 100k jobs - as stated previously, we will never be able to support all of CMS in a single schedd. CMS will still need to load-balance somewhat between multiple schedds. We will take this input back to CMS to see if this won't upset the whole idea. 2012-Sep-06 11:53:52 by eje: A few other points from the 9/5 phone call: the condor schedulers are fed by a potentially much larger wmagent "pre-queue" : https://twiki.cern.ch/twiki/bin/view/CMSPublic/CompOpsWorkflowOperationsWMAgentToolkit one part of the wmagent's job is to do balancing of JobPrio across available schedulers ("manure spreading") balancing can fail in various ways (e.g. if one schedd goes down temporarily and fails to get its share of high prio jobs). Totally eliminating these failure modes is not possible because it is not possible to guarantee prevention of all failure modes in JobPrio balancing, some kind of metric is desired to at least measure if any changes to condor yielded an improvement whether the wmagent's behavior can be improved is an open question for inquiry whether the wmagent can adaptively respond to a job being removed from a condor scheduler (or if it fails, etc) is another important question. If it can adaptively reschedule jobs, that would allow significant ability to correct JobPrio imbalances when the occur 2012-Sep-06 12:58:52 by bbockelm: Another failure mode is that there is a minimum granularity of number of jobs the WMAgent can pull off the global queue. Depending on the dataset, the minimum might be 100 or 10,000 (there's been cases of up to 500k minimum granularity, but I think those are considered mistakes). ...I will CC some additional folks so they can check the accuracy of this statement... However, some of this is inherent to the workflow and cannot be removed. I don't think I understand the question about jobs being removed. Do you mean removed from one schedd and added to another one? For a metric, I would suggest the percent of jobs in the system that are priority starved - i.e., what percentage of jobs have higher priority than the lowest-priority running job. Note this metric can only be zero in the degenerate case where any job can run at any site. This is not true. Steve Foulkes provided us with a table of job priority distribution. title: Ticket #4027: config should allow # inside of multi-line declarations
description: Users generally expect in config files that the line comment character # can be used at the start of lines that follow a line continuation to comment them out. like this ALLOW_WRITE = $(MARY) \ $(JOE) \ # $(FRED) \ $(SALLY) Users expect that the result of parsing this will be ALLOW_WRITE = $(MARY) $(JOE) $(SALLY) But instead, the config parsing code give us this ALLOW_WRITE = $(MARY) $(JOE) # $(FRED) $(SALLY) A different but related problem is that comment lines that end in a continuation character will 'eat' the next line, which is probably not what the user intended. Thus # this is the allow list\ ALLOW_WRITE = $(MARY) $(JOE) $(SALLY) will result in undefined ALLOW_WRITE, this can be surprising also. The config parsing code should be modified so that both of these cases behave in the expected ways. In effect lines that are comments should end at the newline, ignoring any continuation characters that may exist. But lines that are not comments should treat a # after the continuation character as if the line following the # did not exist EXCEPT to notice whether that line has a continuation character of it's own.

title: Ticket #6919: On recycle, shadow can log new job's events under old job's id
description: IN2P3 reported an issue where the DAGMan event log occasionally shows a certain job ID executing twice, although the shadow and schedd logs clearly show the same job ID only running once. This happens when the shadow is recycled. The BaseShadow object is deleted and a new one created. But the WriteUserLog data member (named uLog) is static, so it's left in place. If the new job doesn't require any event logging, then the initialization code for the new BaseShadow object also leaves WriteUserLog object alone. This results in events for the new job being written to the old job's event logs under the old job's id. A comment says that the WriteUserLog object is static so that the exception handler can use it to write a ShadowException event. We can make the object non-static and have the exception logging code use the existing pointer myshadow_ptr to find the object. If myshadow_ptr is NULL, then it could write an error to the daemon log instead (there would be no current job to log an event for).

title: Ticket #355: Event Log reader library ASSERTS upon log rotation
description:
Sergy M at CERN reports the following: I've been working tightly with Sergey Belov on Condor's user log reader client for Dashboard. He said that i should write to you about encountered problems with read user log condor library. Currently I've faced with my log reader exiting with current assertion fault: 3/24 09:45:58 ERROR "Assertion ERROR on (m_lock->isLocked())" at line 1274 in file read_user_log.cpp (in one line; my email client wraps the line). The error is caused by log rotation. The same behavior is encountered with test_log_reader from the condor_src package. The condor version is 7.2.1, but i believe that the same may be true for 7.2.0. After strace-ing my logreader's process, I've got this output (for readability, without opening&closing "/dev/null" by dprintf and with my comments): // at this point of execution, a check for rotation log is being made // this line prints some debug info // (descriptor 6 is the "/dev/null") write(6, "readEvent: checking to see if file (/home/condor/local.vtb-generic-99/log/EventLog) matches: NOMATCH
", 101) = 101 // this closes the log file (descriptor 4 is the log file) close(4) = 0 // and now it tries to lock the closed file fcntl64(4, F_SETLKW, {type=F_WRLCK, whence=SEEK_SET, start=0, len=0}) = -1 EBADF (Bad file descriptor) // dprint write(6, "FileLock::obtain(1) failed - errno 9 (Bad file descriptor)
", 59) = 59 // prints to stderr write(2, "ERROR "Assertion ERROR on (m_lock->isLocked())" at line 1274 in file read_user_log.cpp
", 87) = 87 exit_group(4) = ? Process 9247 detached After examining the source code in read_user_log.cpp, i've found out that on line 865 logreader calls CloseLogFile( ), which closes the logfile descriptor without closing it's FILE*. After that, of course, the ReopenLogFile() is called, which does not reopen the file because of FILE* pointer being not null. The consequences are obvious. A possible fix is in the diff below, but i dont know what consequences may be caused by this modification. Through, with this fix it does not exit with assertion fault on log rotation anymore. :) -- Sergey Mitsyn. diff -U0 ~/src/cond_x/condor-7.2.1/src/condor_c++_util/read_user_log.cpp read_user_log.cpp --- /root/src/cond_x/condor-7.2.1/src/condor_c++_util/read_user_log.cpp 2009-02-16 17:44:05.000000000 +0100 +++ read_user_log.cpp 2009-03-23 17:19:13.000000000 +0100 @@ -865 +865 @@ - CloseLogFile( ); + CloseLogFile( true );
remarks: Waiting for confirmation from Sergey that this is fixed.

title: Ticket #705: GCB causes daemons to hang
description: Two users found their GCBized schedds hanging when they upgraded. Disabling GCB fixes the problem. The problem: GCB assumes that read (and a _bunch_ of other functions) return int (32 bits on Linux 32 and Linux 64). read returns ssize_t, and on 64-bit Linux that is a 64-bit quantity. (Returning int is the old POSIX standard.) User information Both users are using 64-bit systems Ticket 19542 19623 GCB 7.0.5 7.2.1 Working 7.2.0 Bad 7.2.1 7.2.3, 7.2.4 condor-admin #19542 Backtrace #0 0x00000030c68c4360 in __read_nocancel () from /lib64/libc.so.6 #1 0x000000000083f182 in GCB_read () #2 0x0000000000831036 in __wrap_read () #3 0x000000000059aad7 in DaemonCore::Driver () #4 0x00000000005a46d1 in main () strace: read(4, 0x7fff80e4fe10, 8) = -1 EAGAIN (Resource temporarily unavailable) read(4, 0x7fff80e4fe10, 8) = -1 EAGAIN (Resource temporarily unavailable) read(4, 0x7fff80e4fe10, 8) = -1 EAGAIN (Resource temporarily unavailable) read(4, 0x7fff80e4fe10, 8) = -1 EAGAIN (Resource temporarily unavailable) read(4, 0x7fff80e4fe10, 8) = -1 EAGAIN (Resource temporarily unavailable) read(4, 0x7fff80e4fe10, 8) = -1 EAGAIN (Resource temporarily unavailable) Investigation Reproduced. Requires an x86-64 machine. In DaemonCore::Driver at daemon_core.cpp:2605 is code like this: #ifndef WIN32 // Drain our async_pipe; we must do this before we unblock unix signals. // Just keep reading while something is there. async_pipe is set to // non-blocking mode via fcntl, so the read below will not block. while( read(async_pipe[0],asyncpipe_buf,8) > 0 ); #endif This loop loops forever. Of course read() is being transformed into __wrap_read(), which itself is a thin wrapper for GCB_read(). GCB_read() correctly detects that this is not a GCB managed FD and hands the call off to the system read(). Why this constantly returns a positive value is not yet known. With much assistance from psilord, the next layer of the problem has been cracked. The generated assembly is testing the return code from __wrap_read() as a 64-bit value, but __wrap_read() is returning a 32-bit value. __wrap_read is returning a 32-bit -1 (0xffffffff) to indicate an error. This is interpreted as 0x00000000ffffffff, which is 4294967295, which is positive. Assuming that about 4 billion bytes have been successfully read(), the loop tries again. The problem: GCB assumes that read (and a _bunch_ of other functions) return int (32 bits on Linux 32 and Linux 64). read returns ssize_t, and on 64-bit Linux that is a 64-bit quantity. The relevant code: 0x00000000004e3e0a <_ZN10DaemonCore6DriverEv+2048>: callq 0x7265b0 <__wrap_read> 0x00000000004e3e0f <_ZN10DaemonCore6DriverEv+2053>: test %rax,%rax 0x00000000004e3e12 <_ZN10DaemonCore6DriverEv+2056>: setg %al - Set if ZF=0 and SF=OF 0x00000000004e3e15 <_ZN10DaemonCore6DriverEv+2059>: test %al,%al 0x00000000004e3e17 <_ZN10DaemonCore6DriverEv+2061>: jne 0x4e3df4 <_ZN10DaemonCore6DriverEv+2026> Annotated: callq __wrap_read - Call __wrap_read. %rax is 0x00000000ffffffff. The lower 32 bits are eax, and represent -1, but rax as a whole is 4294967295 test %rax,%rax - Set eflags/rflags. OF is 0. If rax>0: SF=0, ZF=0. if rax<0: SF=1, ZF=0. if rax==0: SF=0, ZF=1. Because rax is 4294967295, SF=0, ZF=0 setg %al - if ZF=0 and SF=OF: al=1, otherwise al=0. Given het above: al=1. test %al,%al - Set eflags/rflags. OF is 0. If al==0: ZF=1, otherwise ZF=0. Because al=1 is ZF=0 jne <_ZN10DaemonCore6DriverEv+2026> - if ZF==0: jump backward (redo loop), otherwise continue. Because ZF==0, the loop continues. Useful Links AMD64 Architecture Tech Docs - In particular, book 1 for registers and flags, book 3 for assembly.

Looking at the assembly might be helpful there too. If the wrapper is manually using eax instead of rax, then that is what you need to figure out why it is doing that. Look for something forcing the return value to be hard coded to 32 bits. 2009-Sep-01 18:16:05 by psilord: Oh just now I noticed the bolded text. Ok, that's the error. read returns size_t, not int. That be be the totality of the problem. Now you just have to fix gcb to choose the right return types for the right platforms. 2009-Sep-02 15:14:08 by adesmet: GCB itself has been updated with a fix, but it hasn't been tested against Condor yet. 2011-Nov-09 16:49:19 by adesmet: GCB is dead.

title: Ticket #6626: Final job ad updates missing from history file
description: When a job completes, there is a race condition that can cause the final changes to the job ad performed by the schedd to be missing from the copy of the ad written to the history file. The most noticeable missing change is updating RemoteWallClockTime to include the time from the execution interval just concluded. For many jobs, this can result in a RemoteWallClockTime value of 0. The cause is a race condition when attempting to recycle a shadow when there's no new job available. The schedd sets the job's status to COMPLETED and tells the shadow to exit. The final updates to the job ad (done in delete_shadow_rec()) are deferred until the reaper for the shadow process is called. If the periodic job policy evaluation occurs in between these events, it will call DestroyProc(), triggering the retirement of the job from the queue and into the history file. This probably also affects jobs that the shadow puts on hold. This problem was first reported by the CMS group. It has happened a couple times a day recently in CHTC. A simple fix is to change ResponsibleForPeriodicExprs() to look for a shadow_rec for HELD and COMPLETED jobs and skip policy evaluation if there is one. It already does this for REMOVED jobs. A more robust fix would be to always do the ad modifications of delete_shadow_rec() in RecycleShadow(). This would require more changes to allow a shadow_rec to not have a job associated with it, or an alternate data structure for shadows that don't have a job. These changes are probably not suitable for the stable series.

This attribute also measures total wallclock time but is updated by the shadow and sent to the schedd before the shadow reports that it's done with the job. 2018-May-10 10:10:57 by gthain: CODE REVIEW Looks good.

title: Ticket #569: Expand Executable/Cmd in condor_starter, not condor_submit
description: Assuming a job is submitted from /home/adesmet... Submit file Job ad Executable = /foo Cmd = "/foo" Executable = foo Cmd = "/home/adesmet/foo" Executable = $$(EXE) Cmd = "/home/adesmet/$$(EXE)" Executable = /$$(EXE) Cmd = "/$$(EXE)" This makes sense if instead of $$(EXE) we say something like Executable = $$(OpSys)/$$(Arch)/myjob.exe which turns into Cmd = "/home/adesmet/$$(OpSys)/$$(Arch)/myjob.exe" In which case the path is relative to our submit point. However, if you're using the machine attribute to find the absolute path to a binary, it's surprising: Executable = $$(PATH_TO_MATLAB) turning into Cmd = "/home/adesmet/$$(PATH_TO_MATLAB)" Since PATH_TO_MATLAB will be things like "/opt/matlab/bin/matlab", prepending the submit point would be very wrong, generating silliness like "/home/adesmet/opt/matlab/bin/matlab". The manual says, "If no path or a relative path is used, then the executable file is presumed to be relative to the current working directory of the user as the condor_submit command is issued." While the current behavior arguably conforms, it seems reasonable that a user would expect the relative path to be checked after $$ expansion. The current situation is surprising. This is all a side effect of the absolute-or-relative resolution happening at condor_submit time. Proposal 1: delay the absolute-or-relative resolution until the last possible moment, just before the condor_startd/starter needs it. At this point $$WHATEVER is known and can be expanded, and the resulting expanded Cmd tested for absoluteness. If it's a relative path, prepend Iwd (already in the job ad) to it. Complications: not all paths go via the startd/starter. The grid and schedule universes are the most obvious examples. They would either need to be taught to handle Iwd themselves, or condor_submit would need to conditionally do absolute-or-relative resolution. Proposal 2: If Executable contains "$$", defer expansion until "later". Pretty much all of the work in Proposal 1 still needs to be done, but for the default case where there is no $$ in the submit file nothing changes nor needs to change.

title: Ticket #3131: investigate security issue
description: THIS IS A SECURITY ISSUE and is NOT FOR PUBLIC DISCUSSION everything that follows is referencing a pool that uses only host-based authorization with no authentication. when conodor receives a connection, it decides if the connection is authorized by looking at an ALLOW_X list (for example, ALLOW_ADMINISTRATOR). this list can contain IP addresses, hostnames, and wildcards in either. if the IP address has a reverse DNS entry that maps the IP to, for example, "condor.cs.wisc.edu", then an attacker may connect from that IP address and actually be authorized as if they were coming from a different IP address. proposed fix: after doing a reverse lookup, also do a forward lookup to verify that the IP that initiated the connection is a valid IP for that DNS hostname.
remarks: 2012-Jul-17 13:54:37 by zmiller: CONFIRMED i actually tested this by setting up a "naughty" reverse DNS for exec-1.batlab.org: % host exec-1.batlab.org exec-1.batlab.org has address 128.104.103.1 % host 128.104.103.1 1.103.104.128.in-addr.arpa domain name pointer exec-1.batlab.org. 1.103.104.128.in-addr.arpa domain name pointer astro.cs.wisc.edu. and here is the authorization list on bio.cs.wisc.edu: % condor_config_val hostallow_administrator tonic.cs.wisc.edu, chopin.cs.wisc.edu, astro.cs.wisc.edu, stork.cs.wisc.edu, pinguino.cs.wisc.edu, cobalt.cs.wisc.edu nation.cs.wisc.edu i then logged in to exec-1.batlab.org and was able to issue a condor_off command to bio.cs.wisc.edu. here is the master log (notice the IP/hostname correlation): 07/17/12 13:49:07 Calling Handler <DaemonCommandProtocol::WaitForSocketData> (2) 07/17/12 13:49:07 DC_AUTHENTICATE: received DC_AUTHENTICATE from <128.104.103.1:49786> 07/17/12 13:49:07 DC_AUTHENTICATE: added incoming session id bio:4051:1342550947:7 to cache for 80 seconds (lease is 3620s, return address is unknown). 07/17/12 13:49:07 DC_AUTHENTICATE: Success. 07/17/12 13:49:07 IPVERIFY: matched user unauthenticated@unmapped from astro.cs.wisc.edu to allow list 07/17/12 13:49:07 Adding to resolved authorization table: unauthenticated@unmapped/128.104.103.1: ADMINISTRATOR 07/17/12 13:49:07 PERMISSION GRANTED to unauthenticated@unmapped from host 128.104.103.1 for command 60005 (DC_OFF_GRACEFUL), access level ADMINISTRATOR: reason: ADMINISTRATOR authorization policy allows hostname astro.cs.wisc.edu; identifiers used for this remote host: 128.104.103.1,astro.cs.wisc.edu 07/17/12 13:49:07 Received TCP command 60005 (DC_OFF_GRACEFUL) from unauthenticated@unmapped <128.104.103.1:49786>, access level ADMINISTRATOR 07/17/12 13:49:07 Calling HandleReq <handle_off_graceful()> (0) for command 60005 (DC_OFF_GRACEFUL) from unauthenticated@unmapped <128.104.103.1:49786> 07/17/12 13:49:07 Return from HandleReq <handle_off_graceful()> (handler: 0.000s, sec: 0.004s, payload: 0.000s) 07/17/12 13:49:07 Return from Handler <DaemonCommandProtocol::WaitForSocketData> 0.0041s 07/17/12 13:49:07 Got SIGTERM. Performing graceful shutdown. 2012-Jul-17 14:48:05 by tannenba: Thoughts on a patch: When Condor does the reverse dns for host based authentication, it needs to implement forward-confirmed reverse dns. At a high level, when the server receives a connection from the client, Condor should do an inverse lookup to get a list of hostnames associated with that address. For each hostname, it should do a forward lookup, and discard any entry in the list where a forward lookup does not return the same address. This should be a simple patch, but things are more complicated now with the IPv6 code. With the addition of IPv6, it is not clear the host alias functionality is intact, and also not clear that all code paths funnel through condor_gethostbyaddr() anymore like they did before IPv6. 2012-Jul-18 11:56:33 by tannenba: Thoughts on a workaround: Until folks upgrade their binaries, I folks would be safe if they changed their host allow/deny settings to only reference IP addresses (no hostnames). For instance, instead of hostallow_write = *.cs.wisc.edu instead do hostallow_write = 128.105.* ---- _2012-Aug-23 13:52:45 by zmiller:_ Bulk change of target version from v070802 to v070803 using ./ticket-target-mover. ---- _2012-Aug-23 14:11:43 by zmiller:_ Bulk change of target version from v070802 to v070803 using ./ticket-target-mover.

title: Ticket #7488: Dataflow jobs should also check executables and standard input
description: In #7231 we introduced dataflow jobs to HTCondor, defined as a job with declared input files and output files where the output files are more recent than the inputs. This implies that the job has already been run. When the condor_shadow detects a dataflow job, it has the option of skipping it rather than running it again. We now want to extend the definition of a dataflow job, so it not only compares the timestamps of input and output files, but also executables and shared libraries. Before we start, an important question for the LIGO team: do we want to compare the executables + shared libraries on the submit machine, or on the execute machines? We're assuming it's on the submit side because we don't know where the jobs are going to land. If you want to compare with files on the execute machines, how are we going to find them? Are they in a shared file system somewhere?
remarks: After further thought, any shared libraries would either be part of transfer_input_files, or pre-installed on the execute machines, so we don't need to check them. We do need to check the standard input, if specified in the job ad. 2020-Feb-18 11:36:05 by coatsworth: I'm looking through my notes now and seeing a few more requirements for this ticket which are not indicated here. These will make it unlikely to complete in time for the 8.9.6 release. Details as follows: Currently, the decision to skip dataflow jobs is controlled by the SHADOW_SKIP_DATAFLOW_JOBS configuration knob. We don't want this to be a system-wide option, rather it should be set in the job submit file. I'll add a new submit attribute called skip_dataflow which defaults to false. This will be called SkipIfDataflow in the job ad. We also want the job ad to indicate if it was skipped due to being a dataflow job, such that this information appears in condor_history. I'll call this attribute to DataflowJobSkipped, it will have possible values true or false, and will only appear if SkipIfDataflow is set to true. We want to add a new event that appears in the log, indicating if a dataflow job was skipped. I'll plan to call this ULOG_JOB_DATAFLOW_SKIPPED. In addition to checking the timestamp of the executable file, we also want to check the timestamp of a standard input file if this was specified. One final clarification. We're comparing the timestamps of the input files to 1) output files, 2) executable file, 3) standard input file. In order for this to be considered a dataflow job (and hence skipped) do these all need to be newer than the input files? Or does it suffice for any of them to be newer? Please let me know if I'm confused about any of the above items. Also, as always naming things is a challenge, so if anybody has better suggestions for attribute names feel free to share them here. 2020-Mar-10 10:17:28 by pfc: The ball is in Condor's court to release in 8.9.7 (ETA mid/late April), then it will be in LIGO's court to test.

title: Ticket #990: Address new ClassAds performance concerns
description: Summary of new ClassAds Optimization Task This is one of the identified flightworthy development activities for 7.5. Current people assigned to work on this: Jim Hill and Dan Bradley As shown in #227, new classads performs about 5x slower matchmaking and 1-2x slower in instantiating real job and machine ads. Our job is to figure out why and if possible fix it. Tasks and Due Dates 2009-12-4 [DONE]: Profile the benchmarks and understand where the CPU time is being spent. 2009-12-18 [DONE]: Optimize algorithms identified as problematic. 2010-01-08: (Jim) Add tests of FlattenAndInline to classad_functional_tester. Once integration of new classads into Condor is done, run performance tests of full Condor system (e.g. submit 100k jobs, drain 100k queue) and see if there are any performance issues relating to the new classad integration. Optimize again if needed. Matchmaking Optimizations How much slower new ClassAds is than old ClassAds is reported here for each optimization. The comparison was done using the loop times for cabench_query-newlist. How much difference each optimization makes depends on the order in which they are applied in some cases. I'm just reporting what I observed when applying optimizations in the following order: 4.8x: no optimization 3.9x: using hash_map for AttrList 1.8x: compiling with -O2 (1.7x for -O3, which doesn't seem worth it). It is interesting to note that old classads is not helped much by compiler optimization. I think it is the STL code in new classads that benefits so much from optimization. 1.4x: using max depth instead of EvalState cache. 0.72x: FlattenAndInline machine requirements before matchmaking. Without special attention to references to "MY" this was 0.84x in my tests. 0.62x: Optimize structure of the match ad and flatten references to TARGET to a single global-scope lookup. 0.39x: Add short-circuiting in && and || operators. Conclusion: It seems a good idea to "flatten" the requirements expressions before matchmaking, since they will usually be evaluated multiple times. This, in combination with the other optimizations allows us to do matchmaking at a faster rate than with old ClassAds. TODO: I noticed that flattening does not simplify some expressions such as (true && X --> X where X is some boolean expression). It may be worth making it smarter. Ideally, the flattening would happen before the ads are sent to the collector, saving a little cpu time in the central manager. However, it doesn't appear to make a big difference. Inlining might bloat memory usage a bit (6% in our test), but further simplification could help counter that. To reduce memory usage, it might be worth flattening (but not inlining) all attributes other than requirements. Parser Optimizations How much slower new ClassAds is than old ClassAds is reported here for each optimization. The comparison was done using the setup time for cabench_query-newlist. How much difference each optimization makes depends on the order in which they are applied in some cases. I'm just reporting what I observed when applying optimizations in the following order: 1.7x: no optimizations 1.4x: optimize ClassAd::Insert() to use single-lookup insertion method. 1.5x: using hash_map for AttrList. 0.85x: compiling with -O2 0.89x: FlattenAndInline machine requirements before matchmaking. Inlining caused 6% increase in memory usage. Conclusion: the optimizations we did to improve matchmaking did not hurt parsing speed. Individually, some of them slow down parsing slightly, but overall parsing is faster.
remarks: 2009-Dec-02 17:26:40 by danb: Observations We looked at the following using callgrind: cabench_query-newlist --enable-2way 3 collector.ads-new 10000 '[Requirements = (target.Arch == "X86_64"); JobUniverse = 5; MyType = "Job"; TargetType = "Machine"]' looking up attributes Matchmaking in new ClassAds spends about 30% of its time looking up attributes in ClassAds. In the 1.2 million calls to ClassAd::Lookup(), there are 6.4 million calls to strcasecmp(). The AttrList data structure is an stl map, which is implemented as a balanced tree, so I would expect O(log(N)) string comparisons per lookup. The machine ads in this sample have ~160 attributes, and log2(160)=7.3, which is close to the observed ratio of 5.3 string compares/lookup calls. Question: would it be better to use a hash table here? Old classads uses a hash table. Matchmaking with new ClassAds is about 4.5x slower than old. In new ClassAds we observe 5x as many string compares as lookups in this benchmark. Since we only spend 30% of our time in lookups, I'm being sloppy to suggest that the 4.5x slowdown is due to the 5x string compares, but it is still a tempting comparison to make. Also: in some simple tests I did, strcasecmp() is ~60 times more expensive than strcmp(). If we could figure out how to canonicalize strings without hurting memory size too much, this could be a big win. state cache In AttributeReference::_Evaluate(), there is some stuff that looks things up and adds things to state.cache. This consumes ~30% of the matchmaking time. The intention is to prevent infinite recursion due to recursive references and to speed up evaluation when there are multiple references to the same thing. I suspect that the overhead of copying evaluation results into the cache is greater than the typical savings from reusing those results. If we get rid of the cache, we would just need some way of preventing infinite recursion. This could be done with a simple depth counter and a fixed maximum depth, or it could be done with something like the existing solution (using a set or hash data structure) but without the overhead of caching the evaluated results. insertion into map/hash The existing pattern for inserting attributes into ClassAds and the eval state cache is to first search for an existing entry using find(), remove it if there is one, and then insert. It should be more efficient to attempt to insert and if this fails due to an existing entry to modify the entry returned by insert() (i.e. only one lookup in all cases). 2009-Dec-10 17:37:42 by danb: I just found a big memory leak in the Flatten() code. This makes me less confident that this code has been rigorously tested. If we are to trust it, I think we need to create a suite of tests that check the validity of the flattened expressions.

title: Ticket #3998: condor-reuse-slotN can't logon locally on CSL windows nodes
description: The dynamic slot users on windows (condor-reuse-slotN) are added to the local group "Users". This is how they get the priviledges to run jobs. In the CSL the AD policy prohibits the local "Users" group from logging in, so the condor-reuse-slotN accounts can't login and thus fail to run jobs. Therefore we need a way to tell HTCondor to put the dynamic run accounts into local group other than "Users". A new knob DYNAMIC_RUN_ACCOUNT_LOCAL_GROUP will be used to configure this. If this knob is not set, the HTCondor will default to the behavior of adding dynamic run accounts to the local group called "Users".

title: Ticket #7172: submit_utils should not create custom resources with leading _ names
description: submit_utils treats any keyword starting with request_ as a custom resource request, and starting with 8.9.2, any attribute in the job add that starts with Request gets the same treatment. Thus, the following statement in submit request__ = 1 Will result in A job classad that contains this Request_ = 1 Requirements = . && (TARGET._ >= Request_) This is clearly nonsense. Submit utils should ignore any custom resource name that begins with _, and should also require that custom resource names be at least 2 characters long.

title: Ticket #2720: condor_submit creating files with $$([])
description: condor_submit is helpful and checks to see if output, error, log, etc files can be written to by pre-creating them. However, this is the wrong thing to do if a file name is evaluated with $$([]). In the general case, it is impossible to guess the file name. Instead of trying, condor_submit should skip the file and assume it will be ok later. Example - $ cat test.sub cmd = /bin/echo args = $$([$(Process)+100]) output = test.out.$$([$(Process)+100]) queue 10 $ cat test.out.* 100 101 102 103 104 105 106 107 108 109 However, $ ls test.out.* 0 test.out.$$([0+100]) 0 test.out.$$([5+100]) 4 test.out.100 4 test.out.105 0 test.out.$$([1+100]) 0 test.out.$$([6+100]) 4 test.out.101 4 test.out.106 0 test.out.$$([2+100]) 0 test.out.$$([7+100]) 4 test.out.102 4 test.out.107 0 test.out.$$([3+100]) 0 test.out.$$([8+100]) 4 test.out.103 4 test.out.108 0 test.out.$$([4+100]) 0 test.out.$$([9+100]) 4 test.out.104 4 test.out.109 The expected result does not have the "test.out.$$([#+100])" files.

title: Ticket #4973: Make consumption policies and matchlist caching work together
description: Consumption policies and matchlist caching don't work well together in the negotiator. When a partitionable slot ad with a consumption policy is matched to a job, it is removed (or is not added) to the matchlist cache. Thus, the pslot ad is only matched to a single job of a schedd's resource request, instead of to multiple jobs.
remarks: 2015-Apr-29 15:22:53 by bbockelm: Per phone call - This is likely a regression - can be backported to stable. Given timelines, most likely target is 8.5.0. Brian 2015-May-28 17:11:05 by tannenba: Brian, I don't think [44903] does quite the right thing. Recall that the MatchList is sorted according to all the various negotiator and job rank expressions. When you put the modified pslot back into the MatchList, it should be inserted into the proper place (ie insertion sort). The way things stand now, if any rank expressions refer to attributes that are modified when a pslot is split, things will break. For instance, think about a policy where rank expressions refer to the Cpus attribute of the pslot (eg a best-fit type policy like jobad Rank=RequestedCpus-Cpus). 2015-May-28 19:31:08 by bbockelm: Ah, good catch! I was worried about the approach but couldn't construct a clear counter-example. I wanted to avoid re-sorting the match list, but that appears unavoidable. If I add a sort in, can you see other potential problems? 2015-May-29 08:58:55 by bbockelm: Pushed a fix to re-sort the match list. This patch was tested by setting up a personal HTCondor instance with 4 partitionable slots, each containing 4 cores, and NEGOTIATOR_PRE_JOB_RANK=Cpus (breadth-first-filling). A cluster of 8 jobs was submitted; with this patch, each p-slot received two matches (instead of 2 p-slots receiving 4 matches). I additionally used the same setup with NEGOTIATOR_PRE_JOB_RANK=-Cpus to validate that depth-first-filling also works. 2015-Jun-12 10:50:59 by jfrey: Code Review Consumption policies, matchlist caching, and pslot preemption can't all be used together. Each pslot will only have one preempting claim handed out per cached match list. This can be considered future work. Your sorting code in insert_candidate() is overly complex. You only need one loop to move entries up in the list until the space for the new entry is in the right spot. Using size_t in insert_candidate() is only adding extra casts.

title: Ticket #4070: Sock::serialize() fills fixed size buffer
description: Sock::serialize() (/src/condor_io/sock.pp around line 1713) blindly allocated a 500 byte buffer, fills, and returns it. ReliSock::serialize() and SafeSock::serialize (/src/condor_io/reli_sock.cpp around line 830 and /src/condor_io/safe_sock.cpp around line 780 respectively) call Sock::serialize(), append more information onto the buffer, and return it. Problem 1: The caller needs to know that all of these serialize functions return memory that must be delete[]ed. I believe it's used safely today, but it would be easy to overlook if someone added a new call to serialize. It also makes the caller's code a little more complicated, adding that call to delete[]. Problem 2: 500 bytes is a bit arbitrary. I believe it's safe today, but easy to overlook if someone adds information to the strings. Proposed: Add a dependency on MyString or std::string, and return that.

title: Ticket #1788: Opening /dev/null for write with O_CREATE fails on solaris 11
description: On x86-64 Solaris 11, attempts to open /dev/null for writing with O_CREAT via safe_open_wrapper() fails with errno 6 (ENXIO). This is because safe_open_wrapper() first tries to open the file with O_EXCL and bombs out if that fails with an error other than EEXIST. On Solaris 11, the open returns ENXIO instead. On Solaris, /dev/null is a sym-link to /devices/pseudo/mm@0:null, a character special file. Attempts to open the character special file with O_EXCL work as expected (fail with EEXIST). Attempts to open a file that sym-links to the character special file with O_EXCL work as expected (fail with EEXIST). But on Solaris 11, opening /dev/null with O_EXCL fails with ENXIO. This goes against the man-page for open(), which says opening a sym-link with O_EXCL always fails with EEXIST. This came up in the test suite, where the Condor-C test jobs have their stdout and stderr set to /dev/null.

title: Ticket #1272: Dead connection not noticed by shadow for two hours
description: The user reports jobs randomly restarting. Examination of the starter and shadow logs for one such jobs shows that 5 hours after the job starts, the starter gets a read error on the connection with the shadow. The errno is 10054 (An existing connection was forcibly closed by the remote host). The starter proceeds to attempt to write to the socket every 5 minutes, getting the same error each time, until it's killed. The shadow log shows no activity, just that it's no longer receiving job updates from the starter. Two hours after the first failure in the starter, the shadow finally gets a read error, with the same errno of 10054. It goes into reconnect mode, immediately decides that the job lease duration of 20 minutes has expired, and exits signaling failure. The schedd presumably then aborts the claim, resulting in the startd killing the starter. The 2-hour interval between the starter and shadow noticing the broken connection sounds suspiciously like the default TCP keep-alive interval. The 5-hour interval between job start and first failure is also a little suspicious. Will need to see if other failures have the same interval. The submit and execute machines are both Windows. The execute machine is running 7.2.4 and the submit machine is running 7.0.1. I see several problems in the communications between shadow and starter that contribute to this problem: The shadow doesn't notice if it stops receiving job update messages from the starter. The shadow could go into reconnect mode when it misses updates. If it's not there, we can add an upper bound on the interval between messages from the starter, known by the shadow. This upper bound should be less than the job lease duration. The starter doesn't close the connection on failure. If it did, that could cause the shadow to notice the problem sooner. The shadow bases the job lease duration on the last message it received from the starter, not when it noticed the broken connection. Thus, in this case, it never tried to reconnect.

title: Ticket #5724: Avoid DAGMan confusion caused by node jobs going on hold
description: Miron feels that node jobs going on hold doesn't really fit the model of DAGMan controlling a workflow (and this is also causing problems for Pegasus). Several ideas: DAGMan passes a flag to the schedd that says, "Never put this job on hold". If a job goes on hold DAGMan considers this a failure and removes the job (which is then considered a failure). Each hold event counts as a retry towards the node's allowed retry count. If DAGMan gets to a point where all queued node jobs are on hold, it should generate a DAG abort. If DAGMan gets to a point where all queued node jobs are on hold, it should put itself on hold. Note that, in the default case of having no retries, option 3 would be the same as option 2. Also, option 3 could be combined with option 4 or 5. There seems to be agreement that whatever behavior we decide on should be optional; but not sure whether it should be opt-in or opt-out. Also note that we already have the config knob DAGMAN_MAX_JOB_HOLDS, which defaults to 100. Setting that to 1 would be the same thing as option 2. (DAGMan already logs the hold reason to the dagman.out file, although maybe it should also log the reason code and reason sub-code.)
remarks: 2016-Jun-14 15:13:15 by wenger: Just talked to Miron about this, and (to start with, at least) he wants to implement option number 4 (once the DAG gets to a point where it can't make any progress unless jobs are released, the DAG will abort). I need to think a little more about this, but initially I think that if all jobs in the queue are on hold, and there are no ready jobs we are in that state. (Hmm -- what about throttles? I need to think about whether there's some way throttles could goof up the calculation of whether we're "stuck".) Also, multi-proc node jobs may make this a little tricky. Probably have a new config knob to opt out of this behavior. 2016-Jun-20 10:43:31 by wenger: I asked for responses to the "abort DAG if stuck" idea on htcondor-users, and the response was mixed. Some people really liked it, but some people thought it would be too "hair-trigger". So I proposed that we have a timeout: abort the DAG if it's been stuck for more than N seconds, where N is configurable. Still waiting for responses on that... 2016-Jun-28 13:24:53 by wenger: The really important thing with this is that we avoid "false alarms". The part of that that's going to be the trickiest is making sure we have a correct count of the total number of job procs (belonging to the DAG) in the queue. (We don't count that now.) Anyhow, I'm thinking that we should have some tests that try to hit the trickiest boundary conditions for this, like having a multi-proc cluster where some procs are running, some go on hold, and then one fails and the cluster gets removed. (I'm thinking that we could pass the CondorID to the actual test executable, and have it behave differently depending on the proc ID.) I guess we should also have a test to make sure that throttled and deferred scripts don't trigger a "stuck" alarm. 2016-Jul-21 09:13:42 by wenger: Just did a build/test of what I have so far, and a bunch of tests have failed. These failed across all platforms: jobstate_log noop_node rescue_recov This failed on some platforms: job_held 2016-Jul-24 14:54:35 by wenger: For test, have both single- and multiple-proc clusters. Have some jobs put themselves on hold (pass $(JOB) as an argument), check that non-held jobs finish before DAG is aborted. (For multi-proc clusters, one proc should be held, others should be expected to finish.) 2017-Apr-12 14:30:55 by wenger: A note from an old email from Miron: he wants the timeout to be specified in minutes, not seconds... 2017-Jun-01 13:22:10 by wenger: My recollection is that this pretty much works, except if you have a final node.

title: Ticket #6221: Allow alternate spool locations for job sandbox directories
description: There are situations where we'd like the job sandbox directories to reside somewhere other than the SPOOL directory, and that location can vary based on attributes in the job ad. One case is Argonne National Lab, where all jobs belong to a project allocation and files (of any notable size) should reside under a project-specific directory tree. Another case is the HTCondor-CE in OSG. When submitting into a batch system that doesn't support file transfer, the CE's SPOOL directory must reside on a shared filesystem that either doesn't have root-squash or is hosted on the CE machine. Having the job sandbox live under the user's home directory and never chowned to/from the condor user could relax this restriction. For an initial implementation, we'll focus on the Argonne case, which is a little simpler. Only the job sandbox directories will be relocatable. The alternate location will be determined by a ClassAd expression evaluated against the job ad, provided via the config file. If the expression evaluates to a string, then the result is used as an alternate SPOOL base directory. Otherwise, the regular SPOOL directory is used as normal. The alternate spool location is assumed to exist and have the same owner and permissions as the regular spool directory. The usual directory hierarchy is created in the alternate location for the job sandbox directories. Standard universe checkpoint files will reside in the alternate location, but the ickpt file (the spooled executable when copy_to_spool=true) will remain in the regular spool directory. Other job-specific files, like the MyProxy password file, will also remain in the regular spool directory. Concerns with the current implementation: Undefined behavior if alternate spool value for a job changes over the job's lifetime. Setting config knob to a plain pathname (without quotes) will fail, an easy mistake to make Alternate spool location must exist and have same owner/permissions as main spool directory. getJobSpoolPath() now does two param() calls and one expression parse (if knob is set) on every invocation.

title: Ticket #3473: Gridmanager ignores Arguments2 for Cream jobs
description: When the gridmanager constructs a CREAM job request, it only looks at the Arguments1 attribute in the job ad, ignoring Arguments2. This means that if the user quotes the job's arguments in the submit file, then the job is submitted to CREAM without any arguments. Unfortunately, the CREAM Job Description Language (JDL) document (https://edms.cern.ch/file/592336/1/CREAM-JDL.pdf) is vague on how to properly encode the job's arguments. The arguments are represented by a single string, and it sounds like that the string will be processed verbatim by the shell on the execute machine.

title: Ticket #3920: Running the same Dag Test in parallel say N instances at once
description: Many of the current dag tests can only have one instance running at once because of either node log files or dag lock files clashing with siblings.
remarks: 2013-Sep-16 12:15:04 by wenger: As Bill notes above, I think there are two (at least) issues with running more than one instance of a given DAG test at the same time: Node job log file(s). DAG lock files. For the majority of the tests that use the default node job log file, the log file issue could be overcome by specifying a unique default log file name (maybe based on the test job's PID). For the tests that still use the old-style (individually-specified) node job log files, we'd have to take a different approach. The only thing I can think of offhand is to have the test script create a unique subdirectory for each instance, and actually run the test in that subdirectory (and have all of the node job log files in the per-test subdirectory). (Note that you can't use macros in the log file names in this case.) The lock file is currently specified as an argument in the .condor.sub file, but you can't change it via condor_submit_dag. It wouldn't be hard to add a -lockfile argument to condor_submit_dag to allow this. (We also could set DAGMAN_ABORT_DUPLICATES to false, but I think that would goof up a second or third instance of almost all of the tests.)
