title: Ticket #2632: Condor ignores memory usage by processes that fork without exec
description: In days of old when Linux threads were new, Condor over-reported memory usage by threaded programs, because it didn't know the processes were sharing memory. To work around this, Condor was made to ignore memory usage by processes with the FORKNOEXEC process flag, because this flag was set for threads. The down side, of course, is that it does not see memory usage by real processes that fork and do not exec. This was deemed a small enough disadvantage, because it is common for forked sub-processes to share a lot of their memory with the parent anyway, so the same over-reporting problem applied. Now that Linux threads no longer have the problem of being confused for processes, and we have PSS to avoid over-reporting memory usage by forked sub-processes, the FORKNOEXEC workaround should be removed. To underscore this, an incident in GLOW occurred today in which an ATLAS job used too much memory in a forked sub-process. Debugging the problem was made harder by the confusing fact that Condor was not seeing the bulk of the memory usage.

title: Ticket #882: DAGMan should use flex/yacc and have a real AST
description: Currently, dagman does a one pass adhoc compilation of dagfiles into an in memory dag. This makes maintaining and extending the dagman language harder than it needs to be. What we should do is use standard tools like flex/bison and rewrite the front end to parse the dagfiles into an in memory AST, run various type checking and splice coalescing passes over it, then convert the AST into the in memory dag. Regularizing the tokenization of the dag language would allow us to use C style string literals in many places we don't now like #725. The current lexer doesn't allow spaces in file names, job names,or in arguments to SCRIPTs. The current design of the lexer means each place where we handle those lines we must code an independent solution. Also, having an AST which could act as an intermediate language for the dag allows us to plug in different front end lexer/parsers, such as for the Pegasus dax language. As a proof of concept, I wrote a new lexer in 4 hours which not only tokenizes a reasonable interpretation of the current tokens in the dag language, but accepts string literals in all locations where we'd like. I'd predict maybe 40 more hours of work to write the bison file and get a complete AST in memory with the same multi-dag parsing functionality that dagman currently has.

title: Ticket #7060: Easy way to do "condor_submit_dag" from Python
description: Based on discussions at HTCondor week, it'd be useful if there was a "simple" way to submit DAGs to HTCondor, via the python bindings, based on an existing DAG file. remarks: 2019-May-21 14:31:46 by coatsworth: I already have a Python binding for DAGMan ready to go. The API for using it looks something like this: dag = htcondor.Dag() dag.LoadFromFile("sleep.dag") dag_args = { "maxidle" : 10, "maxpost": 5 } submit = dag.Submit(dag_args) schedd = htcondor.Schedd() with schedd.transaction() as txn: cluster_id = submit.queue(txn, 1) print("Submit.queue returned cluster_id = " + str(cluster_id)) This effort stalled a few months ago and there were two main reasons for this: The binding fundamentally depends on a .dag file and always will. There was a lot of opposition to this. Josh was looking into an interface to programatically generate DAGs, and we were colliding on the API namespace. The second problem is easily solved. The first one is not. Removing the dependency on the .dag file is a massive engineering effort that is not realistic. I think we need to accept this in order to move forward. 2019-May-21 14:46:04 by bbockelm: Can we simplify this slightly? How about: with open("sleep.dag", "r") as fp: dag = htcondor.Dag(fp.read()) schedd = htcondor.Schedd() with schedd.transaction() as txn: handle = dag.queue(maxidle = 10, maxpost = 5) print("Submit.queue returned cluster_id = {}".format(handle.cluster())) 2019-May-21 14:50:52 by karpel: dag = htcondor.Dag.from_file(path_to_file) is much saner. Users should not have to read the file in themselves. Having a single htcondor.Dag (htcondor.DAG?) object without needing another htcondor.Submit makes more sense to me. The actual submission seems sensible, but I don't know enough about DAGs to say which arguments should be part of the htcondor.Dag object and which should be arguments to the queue command. 2019-May-21 14:56:57 by bbockelm: dag = htcondor.Dag.from_file(path_to_file) is much saner. Users should not have to read the file in themselves. Sounds good to me. I went with the constructor-based approach for symmetry with Submit. Having a single htcondor.Dag (htcondor.DAG?) object without needing another htcondor.Submit makes more sense to me. I like DAG. I think of Submit as meaning "submit file" object, not "submit to queue". Hence, since DAG is separate file format, I thought it made a lot of sense to have a separate object. The actual submission seems sensible, but I don't know enough about DAGs to say which arguments should be part of the htcondor.Dag object and which should be arguments to the queue command. Given I want the DAG object to represent a DAG file, I think of queue as the instantiation of the DAG -- hence I put the arguments in the queue method. 2019-May-21 14:59:32 by coatsworth: This is shorter but not simpler. Also there are some things that just won't work, ie. passing file pointers as function parameters won't work in Windows. We should discuss the API offline. I also want to get some feedback from Collin and other users so we make these decisions based on what they need, not what we think is best. 2019-May-21 15:21:33 by karpel: Related question, now that I'm actually reading the ticket: do the bindings themselves need an in-memory DAG representation if there's no way to use it except to write out actual files? Or do we just need a high-level tool (htcondor-jobs or whatever) that helps users make those files in a sensible way? 2019-May-22 07:43:27 by bbockelm: Right - that's a good point. So, the syntax becomes: dag = htcondor.Dag(filename="sleep.dag") schedd = htcondor.Schedd() with schedd.transaction() as txn: handle = dag.queue(maxidle = 10, maxpost = 5) print("Submit.queue returned cluster_id = {}".format(handle.cluster())) 2019-Jun-01 15:54:35 by karpel: Given that there's currently no plan to let you do anything but submit an existing DAG file, why not import htcondor schedd = htcondor.Schedd() with schedd.transaction() as txn: handle = htcondor.submit_dag(path_to_dagfile, maxidle = 10, maxpost = 5) print("cluster_id = {}".format(handle.cluster())) Doubly-so given that even if we added an API for building DAG files, we would want to keep that in-memory representation quite separate from the submission process to emphasize that the file on disk is the source of truth for DAGMan. 2019-Aug-06 11:29:36 by coatsworth: This ticket is a duplicate of #6275, and since I was referencing that ticket in my commits I'm going to make it the "official" ticket for the condor_submit_dag python binding. title: Ticket #6734: Need a python binding for sending a credential like condor_submit does
description: In order to submit jobs that use the SEC_CREDENTIAL_PRODUCER mechanism via the python bindings, we need a python binding that can send a ticket to the CREDD in the same that that condor_submit currently does. What condor_submit currently does is 3 things run the script specified by SEC_CREDENTIAL_PRODUCER, the output of this script is treated as a binary blob and called an uber-ticket. send the uber-ticket to the condor_credd along with the full name of the current user. This is essentially condor_store_cred add <user> <uber-ticket>, but since the credd expects the ADD command as a string, the uber-ticket is first base64 encoded. add the SendCredential attribute to the job being submitted. Ultimately, we want it to be easy for users of the python-bindings to submit jobs in a way that gives all of the functionality of condor_submit without a lot of special code in the python script to deal with side issues like spooling of files and SEC_CREDENTIAL_PRODUCER. But we also want python scripts not to be forced to use hacks to disable or defer these side issues - for instance, there is no need to call SEC_CREDENTIAL_PRODUCER each time we submit a job, a much lower cadence would be better and it should be possible for a sophisticated script writer to choose to do that. So for ease of implementation and flexibility of use, we will start by writing the low-lever worker functions that give script writers access to the individual steps. This will NOT be part of the submit class, but rather a new CREDD class with at least three methods. A method that sends an uber-ticket to the CREDD and returns success or failure; A method that checks to see if the CREDD already has an uber-ticket for that user, and a method that invokes SEC_CREDENTIAL_PRODUCER and returns a object containing the uber-ticket. === CREDD binding API There will be a new object, Credd that represents a connection to a specific condor_credd in much the same way the the Schedd and Collector objects do. The Credd object can be constructed from an optional location_ad. It will have methods to add , delete , and query various kinds of credentials. Each of these functions will take an optional username, if no username is supplied, the name of the current user will be used. class htcondor.Credd([ location-ad ]) A command interface to a condor_credd daemon, if no location-ad is supplied then the default credd is used. method add_password( password [, user= None ]) -> None add a password for the given user. If no user is supplied, the current user is used. In most cases, only administrators can add passwords for users other than themselves. method delete_password([user= None ]) -> None delete the password for the given user. If no user is supplied, the current user is used. In most cases, only administrators can delete passwords for users other than themselves. method query_password([user= None ]) -> Bool ask if the given user has a stored password. returns True or False. method add_user_cred( credtype, [credential= None ] [, user= None ]) -> None add a credential of type credtype for the given user. If no user is supplied, the current user is used. If no credential is supplied, one for the given credtype will be generated if possible. credential is treated as a hunk of binary data and sent verbatim to the credd. The expected contents of credential will depend on the credtype, so if the credtype is krb the credential should be a Kerberos ticket, or whatever the condor_credmon for krb expects to consume. If the credtype is krb and no credential is provided, the output of the SEC_CREDENTIAL_PRODUCER script will be used. method delete_user_cred( credtype [, user= None ]) -> None delete the credential of the credtype for the given user. If no user is supplied, the current user is used. method query_user_cred( credtype [, user= None ]) -> DateTime ask if the given user has a credential of the given credtype. If no user is supplied, the current user is used. If a credential exists, the time the credential was stored is returned. (if the credtype is password, the current time will be returned, as the storage time may not be available) method add_user_service_cred( credtype, credential, meta, [, user= None ]) -> None add a service credential of type credtype for the given user. If no user is supplied, the current user is used. Currently, the credtype must be OAuth. The service name, handle, and other metadata must be specified as a ClassAd, schema TBD. method delete_user_service_cred( credtype , meta_,[, user= _None ]) -> None delete a service credential of the credtype for the given user. If no user is supplied, the current user is used. Currently, the credtype must be of type OAuth. The service name, handle, and other metadata must be specified as a ClassAd, schema TBD. method query_user_service_cred( credtype, meta [, user= None ]) -> CredStatus ask if the given user has a service credential of the given credtype. If no user is supplied, the current user is used. Currently, credtype must be of type OAuth. The service name and optional handle is specified in the meta argument, schema TBD. Information about stored credentials for that service are returned as a CredStatus object. method check_user_service_creds( credtype, ClassAdList, [, user= None ]) -> CredCheck ask if the given user has all of the permissions indicated by the list of classads in ClassAdList for the given credtype. This is intended for use with OAuth, and there will be a method on Submit that will return a ClassAdList of permissions that the job will be needing. credtype enum { password, krb, oauth } class htcondor.CredStatus a class that holds the return value of Credd.query_user_service_creds(). it will contain information about what service credentials are stored, whether there are refresh or use tokens, and timestamps for the various tokens, schema TBD. class htcondor.CredCheck a class that holds the return value of Credd.check_user_service_creds(). It may contain a URL that the user should visit in order to acquire the needed OAuth tokens. where password should be a string, and blob is a binary hunk of data, usually the contents of a file. condor_store_cred equivalency New arguments will be added to condor_store_cred so that the underlying c++ credd communication can be accessible on the command line as well as python bindings. In particular, the add, delete, and query commands will be extended to allow a - credtype modifier, and arguments will be added to allow the credential itself to be supplied by filename. For example # run the credential producer to make a ticket and then store it in the credd ./sec_credential_producer > tmpfile condor_store_credd add-krb -i tmpfile # ask the credd if the user has OAuth tokens for box condor_store_cred query-oauth -s box

title: Ticket #3536: Create cedar session between gridmanager and ft-gahp
description: In order for file transfers between the gridmanager and ft-gahp to work, the ft-gahp must be authenticated and authorized at WRITE level by the gridmanager when it connects to perform the transfers. This requires the proper security configuration in the config files of both daemons. In BOSCO, this is done by using a pool password, and distributing the password file to all remote cluster submit nodes. This setup has some drawbacks, particularly if the ft-gahp is to be used outside of the default BOSCO configuration: Configuring the proper security settings and distributing the credentials (whether a pool password or some other credential) adds complications to a blahp+ft-gahp installation on each cluster submit node. The credential on the cluster submit nodes is vulnerable to compromise. An attacker could use it to attack the home HTCondor installation. These problems are unnecessary, as we already have a trusted channel between the gridmanager and ft-gahp: the ssh connection that securely communicates the gahp's stdio. It would be difficult and inefficient to use the gahp's stdio streams to perform the actual transfers. But we could use them to establish a CEDAR security session that can be used when the gahp makes its additional connections to the gridmanager. We would define a new gahp command to do this. The gridmanager and gahp would then insert this security session into their CEDAR layers.

title: Ticket #4284: Improve synchronization of the job log.
description: For updates, there's no reason to use fsync (which sync's data and metadata) on the job_queue.log; only fdatasync (which only sync's data) is really needed. The metadata probably only needs to be synchronized on rotation... ...speaking of which, our current code for job_queue.log rotation is not safe. We use rename() to rotate the file; there's no guarantee which copy of the data is in which file after a crash. To make sure the rename persists, we need to call fsync on the directory to make sure the directory metadata is on disk.

description: It's trying to spool non-existent output files...? $ condor_submit -debug -remote grid0.lab.bos.redhat.com y.sub 03/18/11 13:36:44 Locale: English_United States.1252 Submitting job(s). 1 job(s) submitted to cluster 13395. 03/18/11 13:36:57 ReliSock: put_file: Failed to open file c:\temp\mrg_13395.0.lo g, errno = 2. 03/18/11 13:36:57 DoUpload: (Condor error code 13, subcode 2) SUBMIT at 10.11.9. 224 failed to send file(s) to <10.16.43.33:39820>: error reading from c:\temp\mr g_13395.0.log: (errno 2) No such file or directory; SCHEDD failed to receive fil e(s) from <10.11.9.224:52438> DCSchedd::spoolJobFiles:7002:File transfer failed for target job 13395.0: SUBMIT at 10.11.9.224 failed to send file(s) to <10.16.43.33:39820>: error reading fro m c:\temp\mrg_13395.0.log: (errno 2) No such file or directory; SCHEDD failed to receive file(s) from <10.11.9.224:52438> ERROR: Failed to spool job files.
remarks: 2011-Mar-18 16:02:04 by tstclair: I've traced it through to file_transfer.cpp: if ( Ad->LookupString(ATTR_ULOG_FILE, buf) == 1 ) { UserLogFile = strdup(condor_basename(buf)); // add to input files if sending from submit to the schedd if ( (simple_init) && (!nullFile(buf)) ) { if ( !InputFiles->file_contains(buf) ) InputFiles->append(buf); } } but this makes no sense to me at all, why would you transfer in an output file? especially one == $(Cluster).$(Process).log 2011-Mar-21 15:53:36 by zmiller: i believe this problem is a result of changing who writes the submit event, which happened in 7.5.4. previously, condor_submit wrote the event, and so the log file existed and was able to be transferred. as of 7.5.4, the schedd writes the event, so the log file is missing, resulting in this error. 1) this appears to be a windows-only problem. on unix, condor_submit touches all output files (including the log file) to test for permission to write. hence, the log file does still exist on unix. 2) on unix this exposed another bug, documented in ticket #1991. 2011-Mar-22 15:38:31 by jfrey: Here's the sequence of events during a remote submit that causes the problem: Condor_submit sends the job ad to the schedd, containing paths local to condor_submit. The transaction for the submission is committed, which triggers the schedd to write the submit event to the user log. Files are spooled from condor_submit to the schedd, including the user log (this is a new network connection). When the spooling is complete, the schedd rewrites paths in the job ad to point at its spool directory. Since the writing of the submit event occurs before the job ad is rewritten, the schedd attempts to write the submit event using the path that's local to condor_submit. If condor_submit and the schedd are on the same machine, that write and the subsequent spooling of the user log will be successful. Otherwise, both actions will fail. 2011-Mar-22 16:46:09 by jfrey: For a simple fix for 7.6.0, we can either delay the writing of the submit event until after the job ad is rewritten or move up the ad rewriting to just before the submit event is written. Either way, the schedd needs to know at transaction commit time whether files will be spooled. It can figure this out by looking at the JobStatus (5, Held) and HoldReasonCode (16, SpoolingInput). Also, condor_submit should not spool the user log (unless it's writing the submit event because it's talking to an old schedd). Some additional work that should be considered: The schedd should never attempt to run a remote job with unspooled files. Condor_release should not work on such jobs. Should there be a new job status for these jobs? Or should spooling be part of the job submission? I.e., the job doesn't appear in the queue until spooling is complete. 2011-Mar-23 15:08:45 by jfrey: One minor problem with the proposed solution: if the user log has events from previous jobs, then those events will be lost when condor_transfer_data is run. If we want to retain those events, we would have to delay the submit event logging until after the job's input files are spooled and have condor_submit send the user log as an input file if it exists. 2011-Mar-25 10:28:09 by jfrey: New proposed patch for 7.6.0: Delay logging of submit event until after input files are spooled, if spooling input files. Prevent jobs waiting for input files to be spooled from being released. Suppress logging of abort event when a job waiting for input files to be spooled is removed. Automatically remove jobs which spend too much time waiting for input files to be spooled. This prevents loss of previous events in the user log when a remote job is submitted. It makes it more likely to have jobs in the queue which don't have any presence in the event log, but now those jobs can't be accidentally released. 2011-Mar-28 09:28:40 by tstclair: so for a user which exits on the schedd it works fine. But if submitted from a user which does not exist on that schedd you get a shadow error (didn't used to) 03/28/11 09:27:09 (180.0) (31122): WriteUserLog::initialize: init_user_ids() failed! 03/28/11 09:27:09 (180.0) (31122): ERROR "Failed to initialize user log to /home/tstclair/work/personal-condor/spool/180/0/cluster180.proc0.subproc0/mrg_180.0.log" at line 777 in file /home/tstclair/work/spaces/ref/git/src/condor_shadow.V6.1/baseshadow.cpp 03/28/11 09:27:09 (180.0) (31122): WriteUserLog: not initialized @ writeEvent() 2011-Mar-28 11:59:32 by tstclair: I also found c:\temp\mrg_179.0.log in my log directory on my linux schedd. 8o/ 2011-Mar-28 18:15:45 by jfrey: After talking with Dan and Zach, I've changed the proposed fix to the following: Prevent jobs waiting for input files to be spooled from being released. Do job ad rewriting in CommitTransaction(). Don't transfer userlog as input file. I have a patch that does these three items, which I will attach. Here are some additional changes that would allow sharing of user logs between multiple spooled jobs and better cleanup of jobs when spooling fails: Add new file transfer mode for userlog (append with file locking) For spooled jobs, rename userlog on schedd to _condor_userlog. Do output remap of userlog from _condor_userlog to original path. Automatically remove jobs which spend too much time waiting for input files to be spooled. I consider this second set of changes optional for 7.6.0. 2011-Mar-28 18:48:33 by jfrey: The log file named c:\temp\mrg_179.0.log appears to be the fault of getPathToUserLog() and is_relative_to_cwd() in a new callsite I added. They assume the filename in the UserLog attribute in the job ad is formatted for the local architecture. With my new patch, UserLog should have path information stripped before any calls to InitializeUserLog(). As for the shadow error, I found a comment in condor_submit() that says Owner should always be set by the schedd rather than submit. But with the current code, what user is the shadow using as the job owner in this case? Hopefully, my new patch won't break in the same way. 2011-Mar-29 09:54:00 by tstclair: so there doesn't appear to be any error with users that exist, but the afore mentioned error still exists with unrecognized users 2011-Mar-30 13:14:03 by cweiss: Patch looks good to me. I didn't see anything that worried me.

title: Ticket #7152: Further decrease annex node AWS query limit usage
description: Chris Paul has reason to believe that writing more efficient queries, contrary to the documentation, causes fewer request rate caps to be hit. The default scripts should be updated again to leverage this. Hence the three aws describe-instances commands now appear as: aws ec2 describe-instances --region ${region} --query \ 'Reservations[*].Instances[*].Tags[?Key==`aws:ec2spot:fleet-request-id`].Value' \ --instance-id ${EC2InstanceID} aws ec2 describe-instances --region ${region} --query \ 'Reservations[*].Instances[*].ClientToken' \ --instance-id ${EC2InstanceID} aws ec2 describe-spot-fleet-requests --region ${region} --query \ 'SpotFleetRequestConfigs[*].SpotFleetRequestConfig.ClientToken' \ --spot-fleet-request-id ${sfrID}

title: Ticket #2700: Centralize tool functionality into a tool core
description: Several tools share initialization steps and have duplicate code across all of them as a result. Creating a single location for this code will reduce duplication and also help reduce tedious changes when the functions called by all the tools end up changing. V7_7-tool_core-branch Steps: Unify debug, version, help, address, and pool options. The debug option at least needs to be unified before attempting to do further work on the dprintf code, as changing dprintf_config currently entails changing over a dozen callsites all doing the same thing. Identify what else is shared amongst tools.

title: Ticket #2645: Maintain DAGMan state in a better way
description: Todd T and I just had a discussion about improving the way DAGMan maintains its internal state and re-creates it in recovery mode. Right now it basically does this by modifying the node job user log files (truncating them and writing POST script terminated events to them). That really isn't such a great idea, and we still run into problems if jobs from separate DAGs share log files (and this is why you currently can't use macros in log file names for DAG node jobs). We came up with a couple of different ways of dealing with this: DAGMan no longer reads the user log files -- instead, it passes a "node status file" name to the schedd via condor_submit, and the schedd writes the current job status into that file (in addition to writing to the normal user log, if one is specified). DAGMan still reads the user log files, but it writes its own file that maps node names to log file names and cluster IDs. (This would require a two-phase condor_submit, where it writes the log file name and cluster ID to stdout; DAGMan would then write these to its own file, and then tell condor_submit to continue and actually submit the job.) So in recovery mode, DAGMan would first read this "side" file, and then use that information to read the correct events from the correct log files. (Also see #445.)

title: Ticket #6606: Don't overwrite OMP_NUM_THREADS env variable if user has set it
description: Condor sets OMP_NUM_THREADS isn't primarily to ensure that cpu usage doesn't exceed the requested usage -- the cgroup cpu shares option we set enforces that. And, there's nothing condor can do to prevent a job from changing this environment variable after condor has spawned the job. However, we see a large number of applications linked with open mp, often, in the case of 3rd party code, without the user knowing open mp is under the hood. The default for openmp is to spawn as many threads as cores detected, and this, combined with the cpu limiting, causes massive code slowdowns. The machine wasn't overloaded, and neighboring jobs on the same machine weren't effected, but when there are 32 threads competing for one core, we could see orders of magnitude performance impacts. But, if the user explicitly sets OMP_NUM_THREADS in their job ad, we should honor that, and trust that they know best.

title: Ticket #1069: Schedd shows no responsiveness during negotiation
description: The current negotiation cycle involves a single connection from the Negotiator to the Schedd, on which all jobs and matches are communicated. During the lifetime of the connection, the Schedd and Negotiator are unresponsive to user commands and other operations. For the Negotiator, this is not a huge issue. It's primary function is to perform negotiation cycles. User commands requiring the Negotiator are condor_q -better-analyze and condor_userprio. For the Schedd, this is a significant issue. The primary function for the Schedd is to accept and manage jobs. User commands effected are condor_submit (critical) and condor_q (less critical). Normal operation includes communication with Shadow processes and Startds. Loss of condor_submit functionality is a hindrance to user experience and burden to automated systems submitting to the Schedd. Loss of communication with Shadow processes and Startds can result in failures that effect throughput and overall system health. For the Schedd, this issue can be resolved by allowing the Schedd to re-enter select during negotiation. Also, the negotiation protocol could be modified to become more asynchronous in general. Plan Miron wants just the following: Schedd's negotiation loop is changed to be asynchronous. Schedd must support receiving matches "out of the blue", not just a match for the most recent job that was sent to the matchmaker. Miron wants to see numbers showing the effect of this change before considering further changes, such as batching of job requests. As we discussed, this plan is expected to reduce time spent by the schedd in negotiation, but it will likely increase time spent by the negotiator, since the negotiator may have to wait longer to get the next job from the schedd. Results I made the schedd's negotiation loop asynchronous. I then ran simple tests against the ghost pool (7k slots) timing how much time is consumed in the schedd and the negotiator when matching 1000 jobs. Async Matches Jobs/Cluster Schedd Time Negotiator Time no 1000 1000 10s 30s yes 1000 1000 10s 70s no 1000 10 330s 350s yes 1000 10 10s 390s Jobs/Cluster: number of jobs in each auto cluster Schedd Time: time in which schedd was solely engaged in negotiation Negotiator Time: time from start to stop of a negotiation cycle (in all cases, about 20s of this was spent pulling ads from the collector) Additional tests were run with the schedd having to work harder. However, due to the need for more memory, I had to switch schedd machines. The previous tests were done with the schedd running on my laptop. The following tests were done with the schedd running on a server-class machine (c158.chtc.wisc.edu). In conducting the following tests, I also discovered a scaling problem in auto clustering #1665. The following results are with the patch for that problem applied in both the sync and async cases. jobs in queue: 100k MAX_JOBS_RUNNING: 1000 condor_q activity: 10/min Async Matches Jobs/Cluster Schedd Time Negotiator Time no 1000 10 260s 280s yes 1000 10 11s 300s no 1000 1 3100s 3100s yes 1000 1 16s 3000s Although condor_q queries were attempted at the same rate in both tests, the synchronous schedd was entirely unresponsive to these queries during negotiation, whereas the asynchronous schedd remained responsive during all but 9s of time when it was building the list of prioritized jobs. Alternate Plan After talking with Miron, the following plan of action was shelved for the time being. Planned fix: Move towards an asynch negotiation cycle as described in attached paper below. Milestones Dan becomes familiar w/ the proof-of-concept implementation. (1 day) Merge proof-of-concept code into the master branch. (2 days) Circuit Breakers (2 days) Make certain the negotiator max negotation time breaker continues to work. Add a breaker about the max number of resource requests per user, and a useful notification when this breaker trips. Backwards compatibility. Be able to talk old synchronous schedd and new asynch schedds. (1 day) Regression tests for circuit breakers (2 days) Honor job priorities (3+ days? Depends how we want to implement, currently unknown) Fix match rejection reason, perhaps by asynchronously sending out "failed match" ads. Not certain if this is important to fix immediately or not - may slow down flocking if we don't, since flock levels increment when we receive a negative match response from a negotiator. (3 days) Test (3 days)

If yes, perhaps we should think twice? If no, can glexec be fixed? I'm not trying to be lazy here (yet). I'm just still hoping it's not necessary. 2011-May-23 16:00:00 by danb (for Igor): I would be surprised if it was a glexec problem. glexec already destroys all the environment. Condor then reconstructs it. The question is: Why it reconstructes everything but PATH? 2011-Jul-19 17:07:50 by danb: I discovered today that when condor reconstructs the job environment, it overrides all variables in the job environment with any variables set by glexec. PATH is one of the variables set by glexec. That explains the behavior you observed. I am inclined to reverse the order of precedence. If there is a conflict between intended job environment and environment set by glexec, we should use the job environment. I am a little unsure about whether to make this change in the stable series or not. It could be considered a behavioral change or a bug fix. I have to make this change at least for X509_USER_PROXY in the stable series in order to be able to have proxy updates take effect when using glexec 0.7+. I suppose we could be conservative and just treat PATH specially as well, rather than changing the precedence of all variables. With glexec 0.6.8-3, I see the following environment from within a process launched by glexec: PATH=/usr/local/bin:/usr/bin:/bin GLEXEC_CLIENT_CERT=/tmp/x509up_u275 HOME=/osghome/osg_cmsuser01 LCMAPS_LOG_LEVEL=1 LCMAPS_DEBUG_LEVEL=0 LCMAPS_DB_FILE=/etc/glexec/lcmaps/lcmaps-suexec.db LCMAPS_LOG_FILE=/var/log/glexec/lcas_lcmaps.log LCAS_LOG_LEVEL=1 LCAS_DEBUG_LEVEL=0 LCAS_DB_FILE=/etc/glexec/lcas/lcas-suexec.db LCAS_LOG_FILE=/var/log/glexec/lcas_lcmaps.log JOB_REPOSITORY_ID=2011-07-19.16:35:00-22437 LCMAPS_VERIFY_TYPE=uid_pgid LCMAPS_POLICY_NAME=glexec_get_account LCMAPS_LOG_STRING=2011-07-19.16:35:00-22437-glexec_get_accounts LCAS_LOG_STRING=2011-07-19.16:35:00-22437-glexec_get_accounts I believe newer versions of glexec also set LOGNAME, USER, and X509_USER_PROXY. The only problem that I can think of if any of these environment variables were overwritten by variables set by Condor or by the job ClassAd, is that nested invocations of glexec would not overwrite the LCAS/LCMAPS/JOB_REPOSITORY_ID variables. After the first invocation, these variables would all be frozen. 2011-Aug-18 15:01:26 by danb: I talked with both Jim Kupsch and Zach. They agreed to the plan. In the stable series (7.6.4), we make a special case to preserve the job's PATH. In the development series (7.7.2), whenever there is any conflict, job environment trumps environment inherited from glexec. 2011-Aug-22 12:01:26 by zmiller: Didn't get to the review yet, will have it done by this wednesday. The resulting job will run every minute. Replacing "cron_hour=* " with "cron_minute=0" will accomplish what is desired.

title: Ticket #1710: Change 'retval &=' idiom in unit test suite
description:
Some problems were found with a particular idiom used in the unit test suite. The context of use is that a pile of setup functions need to be called and if any of them fail, the setup fails. The problem is that the first failure leaves the process state in a bad way and subsequent calls use wrong information, creating problems. Here's an example (all in the same function): OTEST_TmpDir.cpp: ret_val &= condor_getcwd(original_dir); OTEST_TmpDir.cpp: ret_val &= !chdir(".."); OTEST_TmpDir.cpp: ret_val &= condor_getcwd(parent_dir); OTEST_TmpDir.cpp: ret_val &= !chdir(original_dir.Value()); OTEST_TmpDir.cpp: ret_val &= !mkdir("tmp", 0700); OTEST_TmpDir.cpp: ret_val &= !chdir("tmp"); OTEST_TmpDir.cpp: ret_val &= !chdir(original_dir.Value()); OTEST_TmpDir.cpp: ret_val &= !mkdir(long_dir, 0700); OTEST_TmpDir.cpp: ret_val &= !chdir(long_dir); OTEST_TmpDir.cpp: ret_val &= !chdir(original_dir.Value()); OTEST_TmpDir.cpp: ret_val &= !chdir(deep_dir.Value()); OTEST_TmpDir.cpp: ret_val &= !chdir(".."); OTEST_TmpDir.cpp: ret_val &= !rmdir("tmp"); OTEST_TmpDir.cpp: ret_val &= !chdir(long_dir); OTEST_TmpDir.cpp: ret_val &= !chdir(".."); OTEST_TmpDir.cpp: ret_val &= !rmdir(long_dir); Suppose the last chdir fails and then we rmdir a valid directory--except not the one we expected, which could impact a different test. I see this particular idiom was done in: OTEST_Directory.cpp OTEST_StatInfo.cpp OTEST_TmpDir.cpp The method I'd like to fix this with is a hybrid combination of macros and implementation functions. The "cut_" is an abbreviated for condor_unit test and puts the macros and functions into a "namespace". The macro signatures are: cut_assert_z(expression) cut_assert_nz(expression) cut_assert_gz(expression) cut_assert_lz(expression) cut_assert_gez(expression) cut_assert_lez(expression) cut_assert_true(expression) cut_assert_false(expression) Most of these functions are transitive in nature, meaning they take the result of the value and return it after checking it. This allows both of these idioms to exist: int fd; fd = cut_assert_gez( open("foobar", O_RDONLY) ); cut_assert_gez( fd = open("foobar", O_RDONLY) ); The macros/functions would be defined like this: #define cut_assert_z(expr) \ cut_assert_z_impl(expr, #expr, __FILE_, __LINE__); #define cut_assert_nz(expr) \ cut_assert_nz_impl(expr, #expr, __FILE_, __LINE__); /* don't return anything: the process will die if value not zero */ void cut_assert_z_impl(int value, char *expr, char *file, int line) { int tmp_errno = errno; if (value != 0) { dprintf(D_ALWAYS, "Failed cut_assert_z(%s) at line %d in file %s.
", expr, line, file); dprintf(D_ALWAYS, "A possibly useful errno is %d(%s).
", tmp_errno, strerror(tmp_errno)); exit(EXIT_FAILURE); } } int cut_assert_nz_impl(int value, char *expr, char *file, int line) { int tmp_errno = errno; if (value == 0) { dprintf(D_ALWAYS, "Failed cut_assert_nz(%s) at %d in %s.
", expr, line, file); dprintf(D_ALWAYS, "A possibly useful errno is %d(%s).
", tmp_errno, strerror(tmp_errno)); exit(EXIT_FAILURE); } return value; } and so on. The result of doing the above, is when an assertion fails on a line like this: cut_assert_z( unlink("foobar") ); You get this as output from the program if unlink doesn't return zero: Failed cut_assert_z(unlink("thingy")) at line 123 in file foo.c. A possibly useful errno is 2(No such file or directory). After this is done, change lines like this: ret_val &= !chdir(deep_dir.Value()); to cut_assert_z( chdir(deep_dir.Value()) ); For any unix call which doesn't fit into this model, write a new cut_assert_* function or just open code the check. These assertion functions should in general be used for "glue" code that the condor unit tester program needs in order for correct operation while providing the environment for the tests. The actual unit tests themselves should continue to be written to the style currently used.
remarks: 2010-Oct-13 17:40:45 by slauson: I attached a diff of the changes. Let me know if it's good to commit. 2010-Oct-13 18:40:04 by psilord: There are some things you need to fix: Add in the rest of the functions/macros like cut_assert_gez/lez, etc. I like symmetry. The return value of safe_open_wrapper is not an int, but a FILE*. So in this case I'd make a cut_assert_not_null(void *value) macro and function pair and use that. Check value != NULL. Also make a symmetric call of cut_assert_null(void *value). It appears that you need to touch files and do so by calling safe_open_wrapper(). However, you ignore the returned file pointer which leaves the file open in the process space. If you want to just create a zero length file do this instead: void create_empty_file(char *file, char *mode) { FILE *f = NULL; cut_assert_not_null( f = safe_fopen_wrapper(file, mode) ); cut_assert_z( fclose(f) ); } And then call create_empty_file("whatever", "w+"); when you need to make a file. This way all of the file handles are properly cleaned up. Leaving file handles open complicates debugging when using tools like lsof or strace. 2010-Oct-13 18:41:29 by psilord: Delete the current patch and attach a new one when you have it ready and I'll review it. Thanks! 2010-Oct-14 09:40:20 by psilord: Small correction, you can just have the signature for create_empty_file be the path, and not the mode. The mode is implicit in the action the function wants to do. 2010-Oct-14 11:39:13 by slauson: I made the fixes you listed and attached an updated diff of the changes. 2010-Oct-14 14:01:24 by psilord: I did another review, and suggested some additional changes to him out of band. Hopefully, it'll be checked in today or tomorrow.

description: Currently the job router matches jobs to routes in a round-robin fashion, which results in non-deterministic behavior unless admins write JOB_ROUTER_ENTRIES requirements statements that are mutually exclusive. title: Ticket #3668: resource monitoring of ssh_to_job is not as advertised
description: The condor manual says, "Resource consumption of the sshd process and all processes spawned by it are monitored by the condor_starter as though these processes belong to the job, so any policies such as PREEMPT that enforce a limit on resource consumption also take into account resources consumed by the ssh session." But in fact, the resource consumption of the sshd and processes it spawns are not reported in the job ad. The way the starter collects resource usage is to call each UserProc:PublishUpdateAd() in turn and then send the resulting ad to the shadow and the startd. The problem with this is that each UserProc overwrites the attributes in the ad. To prevent the sshd process resource usage from overwriting the job's usage, SSHDProc::PublishUpdateAd() is a no-op. The startd handles ImageSize specially. It updates this attribute in its copy of the job ad based on its own monitoring (see Claim::publish()). Therefore, the combined memory usage by the job and sshd tree is seen by policy expressions such as PREEMPT. This is arguably better than adding the sshd tree usage into the attributes reported in the job ad. It does feel a little sneaky though. If this is the behavior we want, it needs to be better documented in the code and the manual.

title: Ticket #3392: Update DAGMan documentation for RETRY + SPLICE
description: I had the following exchange with Igor: Date: Wed, 19 Dec 2012 08:35:33 -0600 From: Nathan Panike <nwp@cs.wisc.edu> To: Igor Sfiligoi <sfiligoi@fnal.gov> Cc: wenger@cs.wisc.edu Subject: Re: Q about mixing retry with splices On Tue, Dec 18, 2012 at 05:55:18PM -0800, Igor Sfiligoi wrote: > Hi Nathan. > > Quick question about mixing RETRY statements and splices in dagman. > (I could not find an explicit reference in the manual) > > If I have a DAG like this: > JOB A a.sub > SPLICE B b.dag > SPLICE C c.dag > JOB D d.sub > PARENT A CHILD B C > PAREND B C CHILD D > RETRY A 3 > RETRY B 3 > RETRY C 3 > RETRY D 3 > > Will it work? > What will be the semantics if B fails? Will it re-run the whole b.dag? Only the failed nodes? Igor, It won't work. Internally, SPLICE expands into a bunch of nodes, and RETRY only works on a node at a time. If you want to retry the whole b.dag, you must change to SUBDAG EXTERNAL. What I expect to happen: SPLICE expands to a bunch of nodes, named (say): B+A, B+B, B+C. DAGMan will look at the RETRY statement and not find a node B that matches. So the complaint would be something akin to "No node B found". I have not tried it. Hopefully DAGMan will give a helpful error message, and not silently fail. This is something I have been working on (eliminating the differences between SPLICE and SUBDAG EXTERNAL), but my changes break rescue and recovery and I have not worked all that out. > > Thanks, > Igor Probably would be helpful to clarify this in the manual...

title: Ticket #6939: 8.8 Python bindings not compatible with 8.6 Python bindings
description: In HTCondor 8.7.10, we replaced the old log reader API in the python bindings with a new API, due to several several major bugs in the old implementation. CMS's CRAB software uses the old API in a way that can't be replicated with the new API. Their use of the old API isn't affected by its bugs. As a short term solution (8.8.x), we should re-introduce the old API, marked as deprecated. For a long term solution (8.9.x), we may need to expand the new API to handle CMS's use case. CMS's report on the problem is available here: https://github.com/dmwm/CRABServer/issues/5829 API Replacement The event reader API in 8.6 and 8.7 has several major flaws, which would take major work to fix. These were revealed when trying to use the API in the HTCondor test suite (#6736). The API was considered fundamentally broken to the point that no one could be using it. So a new API was defined and the old one removed in 8.7.10. One of the principle differences is that the old API takes a file handle from the user and the new API takes a filename for the file to read events from. The major flaws in the old API are as follows: Taking a file handle created in Python code and operating on it in C/C++ code doesn't work in Python 3 on Windows. The code to block waiting for new events to be appended to the file doesn't work. CMS CRAB's Event Reading The CRAB service processes large workflows for CMS. It uses DAGMan to manage the execution of the workflows that it creates. To monitor the status of a workflow, it periodically runs a script that opens the user job event log, reads all new events, and updates the workflow state in a file on disk. The script also records on disk its position in the event log file after reading all events. On the next execution, it reads in the file position and seeks to that point in the file before reading events, thus skipping events already processed. This setup can't be done with the new event reader API, which takes a filename for the event file and always reads from the beginning of the file. The CRAB software could be rewritten so that all of the log reading is done in a long-lived process that keeps a single JobEventLog object and checks it periodically for new events. If the long-lived process had to restart, then it would be forced to re-read the entire event log and recompute the workflow state from scratch. CRAB only uses the read_events() function in the event reading API.
remarks: 2019-Mar-06 14:48:07 by tlmiller: Another good reason not to accept file handles is that the inotify interface takes filenames, not fds (because, of course, not all fds are files). I guess we could work around that and fall back on polling if the file handle didn't correspond to an actual file. Aside from that, I'm OK with having an API where the constructor has an optional seek-this-far-before-parsing value and the object has a tell() function, whose return value is suitable for use there. The user would be responsible for ensuring the log in question hadn't rotated since it was first opened, but that's easy for the use cases we've heard about (and this API doesn't have to be duplicated for the eventual rewrite of the job queue log). 2019-Mar-06 16:20:49 by jfrey: I think the optional file position constructor argument and tell() function is the best solution for what CMS needs. 2019-Mar-26 13:43:51 by tlmiller: Code Review Looks good. (Including the not-for-Python-3 commit.) 2019-Mar-26 13:46:05 by tlmiller: Doc Review We should probably mention in the release notes that the bindings were only brought back for Python 2.

title: Ticket #7781: Add a SCRIPT HOLD feature to DAGMan
description: A couple different people have been asking about adding a mechanism into DAGMan that will execute a script when jobs go on hold. Initially we talked about executing the POST script when jobs go on hold, but this results in really ugly semantics and conditions in the code that can only lead to pain and sorrow. Instead, we propose adding a brand new HOLD script into condor_dagman that can be defined in a .dag file as follows: SCRIPT HOLD [JobName | ALL_NODES] ExecutableName [arguments] This script will execute using similar mechanics to the pre and post scripts. One major difference is it will have no bearing on the final status of the node; whether or not a hold script succeeds, the dag will continue processing as per usual. A design doc is available here: https://docs.google.com/document/d/1HkdeFP-yrYUEEPHoSqGzJFc-lZy_Nf1Qqi3NMJ4rc8I/edit#

title: Ticket #5568: Enable policy to limit active DAGs per user
description: In order to fairly share the SCHEDULER universe slots on the SCHEDD, the CMS global pool would like to have a way to limit the number of active Scheduler universe jobs a given user can have. There are a variety of ways this could be implemented. Each having significant tradeoffs in ease of development, flexibility, and runtime cost. The options are Make a new knob that explicitly sets a per-user limit of active dags. Something like MAX_RUNNING_SCHEDULER_JOBS_PER_OWNER. This is both the easiest to implement, and the least costly in terms of SCHEDD runtime, but it the least flexible. Put counters for the active submitter into the SCHEDD ad when evaluating START_SCHEDULER_UNIVERSE and START_LOCAL_UNIVERSE. This is the most work, the mostly costly in runtime (by quite a lot ). But it is also the most flexible and consistent with the current design. Add an additional START expression for scheduler and local universe jobs that is evaluated in the context of the submitter ad rather than the schedd ad. Something like START_SCHEDULER_UNIVERSE_BY_OWNER. This option is relatively easy to do, and about as flexible as option 2). Unlike option 2) it adds no overhead to the SCHEDD when the knob is not set, but the runtime cost when the knob is set is about equal to option 2. A rather significant wrinkle to this work is that the SCHEDD currently doesn't actually keep job counters by owner. It keeps them by submitter, where the contents of the job itself can be used to either set the submitter name or to decorate the owner name to produce a new submitter name. For instance, a job that has NiceUser = true Will produce a second submitter record for a user and thus give them an entirely new set of counters and limits. The submit keywords Accounting_Group and Accounting_Group_User can also be used to create a new submitter record. Consequently, as a part of this work. I am proposing that we change the SCHEDD so that the counters for Scheduler and Local universe jobs will always be applied to the submitter whose name is the same as the jobs's Owner attribute. (Thus ignoring NiceUser and Accounting_xxx keywords in the job).
remarks: 2016-Mar-22 15:26:02 by johnkn: Incidently, the SCHEDD currently creates a new SCHEDD ad for each idle scheduler or local universe job every time it goes looking for scheduler or local universe jobs to start. There is significant room to optimize this code, but at the risk of having attributes of the SCHEDD ad not be refreshed when a scheduler or local universe job is started. The current code is wasteful, but does guarantee freshness. 2016-Jun-21 15:09:45 by johnkn: We will be implementing option 1 above for the 8.5.6 release.

title: Ticket #1878: HEP jobs make CS desktops dependent on the HEP AFS cell
description: Joe Meehean just ran into a problem (and I think I ran into the same problem) where his desktop hung for several minutes because of AFS problems (see condor-admin #21589). It turns out that the problem is this: CS machines have an AFS token on them that allows Condor jobs to access the HEP AFS cell. Once a job has done this, the AFS cache on the machine contains files from HEP, even after the job is no longer running on the machine. As long as those files are in the cache, the machine periodically needs to contact HEP, so if any kind of network problem happens, your machine hangs... Joe pointed out that there is actually a more general problem that a Condor job could do something like download illegal music into /tmp or something like that...

title: Ticket #6344: Cross-protocol CCB should not cause schedd or shadow to EXCEPT
description: Yutaro Iiyama (among others) reported a problem where an IPv4-only schedd would crash when matched with a startd which was only advertising IPv6. The problem was that the IPv4-only schedd was contacting the CCB over IPv4, which correctly causes CCB to tell the startd to call back over IPv4. Since the startd was not actually IPv6-only, it was able to do so. Everything actually worked until we attempted to assign the newly-accept()d (reverse) connection's socket to the (unopened) outbound socket object, which EXCEPT()d because the outbound connection was to an IPv6 startd, but the reverse connection was IPv4. After speaking with ToddT, we agreed that this fix has two pieces: (1), prevent the schedd from EXCEPT()ing in this situation and (2) add a protocol-matching hack into the negotiator, which is now ticket #6351.

The rest is all ADA to me. 2017-Jul-19 11:10:39 by tlmiller: Added what should fix the problem for Windows, but don't have time right at the moment to test on a Windows machine (the repro I have at the moment requires three machines and I don't know that there's a Windows machine I can break in the same network). Otherwise, assuming approval from another reviewer, I'm going to say that skipping the protocol checks for other assignments won't be problem, since this check has been in place for quite some time and this is the first we've heard of it causing problems; or, it'll be OK to make a new ticket for the next release about only doing this for CCB (if we can). 2017-Jul-31 16:30:53 by gthain: CODE REVIEW There are a lot of edge cases here, but I think we're strictly better for 8.6

title: Ticket #3003: cgroup reuse does not reset accounting statistics
description: We recently changed the cgroups implementation (#2734) to increase the likelihood of cgroup reuse (we now name the cgroup after the slot, not after the job running in it). This way, if a starter doesn't clean things up correctly, the job likely will reuse the cgroup (and hopefully clean it up properly afterward!). As an unfortunate side-effect, activity from the previous job (such as CPU usage, max memory usage) will be added to the subsequent job. If job 1 has 20 seconds of user CPU and job 2 has 1 second of user CPU (and reuses job 1's cgroup), the procd will report 21 seconds of user CPU for job 2. We need to reset statistics for: CPU usage. Max memory usage. Note: I've come to the conclusion that the max memory usage statistics the kernel keeps is useless for us, as it includes filesystem cache. Ouch. Block I/O. #2734 isn't in any current release, so we should do this before 7.9.0.

title: Ticket #3453: improve scheduling of condor_q processing in the schedd
description: The schedd responds to condor_q queries in the same stream of requests as all other queue management commands. It does not prioritize or schedule how it processes this stream. It just responds to each command in the order they are received. A burst of condor_q queries can therefore interfere with the processing of other commands, and can even cause the processing of running and completed jobs to fail. We propose that if the schedd has been configured to fork sub-processes to handle read-only queries (i.e. condor_q), then when the maximum number of sub-processes has been reached, it should not process further read-only commands in the main process. It should queue them, up to some limit. During this time, it should continue to process other commands (such as queue management write commands). This will have the effect of smoothing out bursts of condor_q queries or even chopping off the peak of the burst if it exceeds the request queue depth. Some changes to the client may be needed to avoid timing out too quickly while in the request queue. Some workarounds that may help in the current situation: increase the time between updates of running jobs (SHADOW_QUEUE_UPDATE_INTERVAL and job_lease_duration). This should reduce the rate at which copy-on-write causes pages to be unshared between the main schedd process and forked children. increase SCHEDD_QUERY_WORKERS if there is enough memory (if not, get more memory) find alternatives to condor_q, such as reading the user log to track job state A longer-term solution would involve responding to queries without blocking the main process and without forking a sub-process, but we do not propose implementing that at this time. This plan came out of a discussion with Todd, Jaime, Greg, TJ, and me (Dan).

Or will it also affect shadow reporting on job state changes? 2013-Jan-23 18:29:55 by bbockelm: Maybe the idea is too wild, but what about handing local condor_q instances a read-only file descriptor to the job log via unix domain sockets? That way, the processing is done in the condor_q process (like Igor's user log patch) instead of in the schedd. 2013-Jan-25 09:12:31 by sfiligoi: @Brian: Would not help... we still have condor_q from remote to deal with. 2013-Jan-25 09:35:06 by sfiligoi: One more request: Can we prioritize authenticated requests ahead of unauthenticated ones? We like to allow unauthenticated read access for debugging purposes, but this should not impact the main functionality of the system. 2015-Aug-01 21:09:16 by bbockelm: I believe the V3 protocol implements most of the goals of this ticket (except it doesn't have a queued query limit). Marking as resolved for now.

title: Ticket #1194: Build new ClassAds only as an external
description: Currently, we build two versions of new ClassAds when building Condor. One is an external and is used to build the Blahp and Cream externals. The other is in src/classad and is used to build the Condor daemons and tools. There should be one version of new ClassAds, built as an external, used to build Condor. Issues libcondorapi The main complicating factor in building ClassAds just as an external is libcondorapi, the library we provide to users to read and write user logs. Currently, it directly includes the new ClassAds object files and has no dependencies other than system libraries. With new ClassAds built only as an external, we'll need to provide libclassad in the release as an additional library for users to link against. New ClassAds themselves depend on PCRE, though libcondorapi's usage of ClassAds should never result in PCRE being called. Currently, libcondorapi includes stubs for the PCRE functions which call abort(). With an external-only ClassAds, we'll need to provide libpcre in the release or figure out how to make stubs work. We provide both static and dynamic versions of libcondorapi. For the dynamic version, we may have to set up relative rpaths for libcondorapi and libclassad in order for them to find libclassad and libpcre, respectively. Also, creating a shared version of libclassad currently fails on Solaris. Windows We would also need to change the Windows build to build ClassAds as an external.

title: Ticket #7040: Allow preemption of one dslot using additional resources from pslot
description: LIGO is running a large pool with pslots. They have observed that when there is a mix of single core jobs with different memory requirements, often preemption of a single small dslot can't happen because the preempting job requires more memory than the dslot has. Often in this case, the pslot is holding enough unused memory to "give" to the dslot to run. To get this to work today, we would need to enable multiple dslot preemption, which has a host of caveats. LIGO would like a simpler, more correct solution that would just use resources from the pslot.

title: Ticket #288: Port collision not noticed by condor daemons in windows
description: Under windows, two collectors are able to bind to 9618 at the same time (no errors reported), but only one of them receives anything on that port. Ben is able to reproduce this in a simple standalone test program. If he turns on SO_REUSEADDR, two programs can bind to the same port (in windows). Without SO_REUSEADDR, they cannot bind.
remarks: 2009-Feb-28 15:57:56 by burnett: It seems that this may be a DNS problem (or how we seem to break whilst using it): 02/27 23:14:02 Looking for matching Collector on 'nmi-0226.batlab.cs.wisc.edu'... 02/27 23:14:02 Found 'nmi-0226.cs.wisc.edu:0' Somehow, in this instance, on Windows, the master decides it is called nmi-0226.batlab.cs.wisc.edu but when it goes looking for a collector by the same name, the only one it finds is nmi-0226.cs.wisc.edu. You'll of course note the missing batman reference in the second host name. 2009-Feb-28 16:06:34 by burnett: This, of course, does not excuse the horribly broken Windows implementation of the SO_REUSEADDR socket option. Contrary to popular belief, it does not mean it is ok to re-bind to the socket if a connection is broken, instead of waiting for a time-out; it means bind as times as you like to this socket so long as you set the SO_REUSEADDR options. 2009-Mar-03 12:00:49 by burnett: The behavior exhibited on *nix machines cannot be duplicated on Windows. We expect to be able to re-bind to an address, if for some reason we crash. Windows provides another option SO_EXCLUSIVEADDRUSE, but it stops any re-binding until the original socket has been closed. And even then, the address is not guaranteed to be accessible. From MSDN: "In the case where the first bind sets no options or SO_REUSEADDR, and the second bind performs a SO_REUSEADDR, the second socket has overtaken the port and behavior regarding which socket will receive packets is undetermined. SO_EXCLUSIVEADDRUSE was introduced to address this situation." ... "A socket with SO_EXCLUSIVEADDRUSE set cannot always be reused immediately after socket closure. For example, if a listening socket with the exclusive flag set accepts a connection after which the listening socket is closed, another socket cannot bind to the same port as the first listening socket with the exclusive flag until the accepted connection is no longer active. This situation can be quite complicated; even though the socket has been closed, the underlying transport may not terminate its connection. Even after the socket is closed, the system must send all of the buffered data, transmit a graceful disconnect to the peer, and wait for a graceful disconnect from the peer. It is therefore possible that the underlying transport may never release the connection, such as when the peer advertises a zero-size window, or other such attacks. In the previous example, the listening socket was closed after a client connection was accepted. Now even if the client connection is closed, the port still may not be reused if the client connection remains in an active state because of unacknowledged data, and so forth." 2009-Mar-03 12:29:13 by danb: If I understand correctly, it sounds to me like SO_EXCLUSIVEADDRUSE has the semantics that we want. We only need to be able to rebind to the socket after stopping and restarting the collector (or other daemon), so the socket should have always been closed by the time we want to rebind. So the behavior we want is: 1. restart of the condor daemon can reuse the same port number immediately without any timeout between last use and next use 2. while we are bound to the port, nobody else should be able to bind to it --Dan 2009-Mar-03 13:10:07 by burnett: I think the problem is that since we won't actually be closing the port explicitly, we may not be able to bind to it again. We may need to wait until some time-out period has passed. 2009-Mar-05 11:30:48 by burnett: Looks as if, in practice, the Collector will come back up immediately after a crash, despite the warnings put forth by the MSDN documetation.

title: Ticket #6082: Remove whitespace after open parens in classads
description: The standard unparsing style for classads puts a space after every open paren, and before every close paren. This is unlike every programming language style guide in existence. It looks funny, and it is somewhat more expensive to parse and put on the wire. We should tighten up the parens, to improve performance, and make expressions with parens easier to read. That is, go from ( ( ( expr ) ) ) to (((expr)))

title: Ticket #4545: condor_submit permits syntatically invalid Requirements
description: It appears that condor_submit doesn't check the validity of the Requirements expression until __after__ it modifies it. Thus, the following submit-file line requirements = True ) && Machine == "e432.chtc.wisc.edu" || ( False is accepted and has the effect of disabling all of the automatically-added requirements. (The modified requirement is: ( True ) && Machine == "e432.chtc.wisc.edu" || ( False ) && (auto-generated) && (auto-generated) which is syntactically valid but mostly ignored because && binds tighter than ||.) While this is useful for system administrators debugging machines, it would be at best confusing for users who happen to make a similar typo and shouldn't be allowed. So when adding the check before the modifications, also add a new command or flag (DoNotModifyRequirements for either?). (Or, if +Requirements doesn't bypass the requirements modifications, should it?)
creator: tlmiller

title: Ticket #3280: glexec jobs go on hold after x509 update
description: When the shadow delegates an updated x509 proxy to the execute side, the job goes on hold soon after with the hold reason, "Proxy about to expire", even though the updated proxy is not about to expire and nor was the old proxy that was replaced. One workaround is to use long-duration proxies and (if using DELEGATE_JOB_GSI_CREDENTIALS=True) to disable the shadow's shortening of the lifetime of the proxies it delegates: DELEGATE_JOB_GSI_CREDENTIALS_LIFETIME = 0 I believe the cause of this problem is the following line in the starter: time_t expiration = x509_proxy_expiration_time(path.Value()); The path that the starter is passing into the function x509_proxy_expiration_time() is the value of X509UserProxy in the job ad. That is probably not the correct path on the execute node. Nothing is logged to tell us if there is an error reading the proxy, because there is no error checking to see if the call to x509_proxy_expiration_time() failed. The -1 in the following message gives us a hint that it is indeed failing to read the proxy: Attempt to refresh X509 proxy succeeded. Set timer 12 for PROXY_EXPIRING to -1

The proxy expires and no action is taken by the starter to put the job on hold. 2012-Oct-19 14:58:01 by danb: I have created a new ticket #3283 to track the separate problem of the initial proxy expiring.

title: Ticket #772: proxy refresh notification ineffcient in gridmanager
description: When the gridmanager notices that an x509 proxy file has been refreshed, it triggers the state evaluation timer for all Job objects that are using that file. In stress testing with BNL using 65,000 jobs, triggering the timers takes up to 8 minutes. Calling of the daemon-core handlers takes even longer. And in the vast majority of cases, the job objects decide they don't need to do anything. The proxy management code should be changed to use a callback function rather than a daemon-core timer to notify jobs of proxy changes. The callback function can quickly examine a couple variables and determine if the job's full state evaluation function needs to be invoked.

title: Ticket #6128: Job Router defaults sensitive to leading whitespace
description: The Job Router will not route any jobs if the JOB_ROUTER_DEFAULTS config parameter has any leading whitespace. The param system usually strips leading whitespace, but it can appear if an undefined macro is used, like so: JOB_ROUTER_DEFAULTS = $(JOB_ROUTER_DEFAULTS) [ MaxJobs = 10000; ] If JOB_ROUTER_DEFAULTS is unset before this, then the resulting value will start with a space. This trips up the feature added in #4433 that makes the square brackets in JOB_ROUTER_DEFAULTS optional. It ends up adding square brackets when a set is already present, resulting in a parse error from the new ClassAds parser. The code for #4433 needs to skip leading whitespace when checking whether the param value starts with an open square bracket.

title: Ticket #7693: Support oauth tokens and krb/kerberos credentials in local universe
description: Currently, LOCAL and SCHEDULER universe jobs do not have the ability to run with a user's OAuth tokens or Kerberos credentials. Adding this support for LOCAL universe would involve having the Starter process know to do the work that the shadow does when OAuth credentials ar erequested (as opposed to using a shadow syscall, since there is no shadow in this case). This is essentially reading files while root and then writing them into the sandbox while impersonating the user. Once that is in place, it should be fairly straightforward since there IS a job sandbox for the job so the credentials can be placed there and managed normally by the Starter. For SCHEDULER universe this would be much more work because there is no Starter process to manage credentials and no job sandbox in which to place them.

title: Ticket #2491: schedd crash after failed $$ expansion
description: There is a problem when $$ substitution fails. This causes the job to go on hold. In 7.7.1, this causes an immediate search for a new job to run on the claim associated with the held job (#1314). If no job is found, the claim is relinquished. When we eventually pop up the stack to the caller of GetJobAd(), this dereferences the deleted match rec, which causes the schedd to crash. All callers of GetJobAd() with the "expand $$ macros" option set to true must therefore be prepared for the match rec to be deleted.

title: Ticket #5704: Bosco file transfer broken by bad sinful string
description: For Bosco, file transfers are done between the gridmanager the ft-gahp, tunneled through an ssh connection. When the gridmanager issues transfer commands to the ft-gahp, it rewrites the initial ip:port in its sinful string to point at the tunnel endpoint. But in 8.5, this part of the sinful is ignored, and the address(es) in the addrs field is used. Thus, the ft-gahp attempts to connect to the wrong address and fails. The gridmanager needs to do a more intelligent rewrite of its sinful string, including both the initial ip:port and the addrs field.

title: Ticket #4816: Prevent changes to job id of queued jobs
description: The schedd does some simple checking to prevent a job's ClusterId and ProcId attributes from being modified. However, the check code in SetAttribute() assumes the value to be verified will be an integer literal. A client can bypass this by setting a value that's a ClassAd expression that begins with the job's valid ClusterId or ProcId. For example, to change a job's job id from 16.0 to 15.0, a user can do this: condor_qedit 16.0 clusterid '16 - 1' This example also bypasses a check in condor_qedit that does a case-senstive comparison on the attribute name when it should do a case-insensitive comparison. Doing this doesn't change the job's key in the job_queue.log maintained by the schedd.

title: Ticket #4050: detect and attempt to avoid problems caused by DNS lookup delays
description: There have been several instances where doing a DNS lookup blocks for several seconds, causing trouble for a busy HTCondor machine such as cascading timeouts. See ticket #3097 for one such example. Also, resolving the DNS names in ALLOW_ lists is done "lazily" which means it often happens while in the process of sending or receiving a command. If an entry is in mutliple ALLOW_ lists, it is looked up several times, which is inefficient. Also, the logging of failures is only done to D_FULLDEBUG, making the problem difficult to diagnose. This ticket exists to improve the situation. Design doc here: 4050 Design Doc: Improve DNS resolution in ALLOW_* and DENY_* lists

title: Ticket #6597: Slots can become stuck in Claimed/Busy forever after a job completes
description: If the shadow and schedd can't talk to the startd after job completion, then the slot can end up in Claimed/Busy state forever. After changes in #4491, the startd doesn't communicate with the schedd about the health of its claim while the starter is running. It assumes the starter is performing that function with the shadow. But after a job completes, the TCP connection between starter and shadow closes and the starter waits around to be told to exit by the startd. Normally, the shadow sends a deactivate claim message to the startd, and the schedd may send a release claim message. Either of these will cause the startd to tell the starter to exit. But if these messages can't be delivered, the startd and starter end up in a live-lock with each waiting for the other to tell it something about the current active claim. Killing the starter is sufficient to clear up the condition once it arises. The problem detailed in #6596 makes this condition very likely to occur. One way to avoid this situation is to have the starter exit once it has no further work to do. This could be after its last RPC to the shadow, or after the connection with the shadow closes.

title: Ticket #1252: rate limit wakeups in condor_rooster
description: Currently, the condor_rooster cycle consists of two phases: 1) query the collector for all machines for which ROOSTER_UNHIBERNATE is true 2) iterate through that list and wake up those machines. Ian Smith found that when users submitted a large number of short-running jobs, rooster would wake up a lot of machines in a short amount of time, which overloaded a power management service and which was more than necessary anyway, since the jobs were so short. It was suggested that the rate of wakeups could be limited along these lines: ROOSTER_WAKEUP_CMD = "/path/to/sleep_exec 30 $(BIN)/condor_power -d -i" And then create sleep_exec: #!/bin/sh sleep $1 shift exec "$@" However, the problem with this is that if there is significant time delay while iterating through the machines to wake up, they may no longer be in demand by the time we get to them. For example, if the user's jobs are quite short, they may all have finished on the machines which were already woken up. One idea would be to make the UNHIBERNATE expression expire so that the delay introduced by the rate limiting will not result in an indefinitely long wake-up loop. However, this doesn't quite work, because we only evaluate UNHIBERNATE once before iterating over the machines to wake up. If we did double-check this expression immediately before waking up a machine, then the following sort of expression could be used in combination with the sleep_exec strategy: UNHIBERNATE = MachineLastMatchTime > CurrentTime - 600 In addition, it would be nice to have a simple configuration setting to limit the number of machines woken up per cycle.

title: Ticket #6702: Allow NETWORK_HOSTNAME to be an alias hostname
description: When NETWORK_HOSTNAME is set, we pass the value through getaddrinfo() to get a full canonical name. If the call fails, then get_local_hostname() is set to return the configured value and the value returned by get_local_fqdn() is uninitialized. If the call succeeds, then the values returned by get_local_hostname() and get_local_fqdn() are set based on the canonical name in the results. This makes it impossible to use NETWORK_HOSTNAME to set a hostname that's a DNS CNAME (i.e. an alias hostname). The OSG wants to do precisely this to to ease relocation of glideinwms factory servers. If NETWORK_HOSTNAME is set, then getaddrinfo() shouldn't be called at all. Instead, the short and full hostnames should be set based on the value of the parameter (using DEFAULT_DOMAIN_NAME if available and needed).

title: Ticket #6352: Improve condor_top
description: The current condor_top is more or less a straight port of condor_top.pl to Python except that it uses the Python bindings to query the Collector directly for ClassAds rather than reading them from files passed via command-line. While helpful, there are many improvements that could be made to condor_top: Allow for ClassAds to be queried directly (current behavior) or supplied from the command-line (enhancement). Add a "non-live" mode where stdout can be redirected or piped. Default to monitoring whatever the role of the current machine is. If multiple roles are defined, default to monitoring the Schedd. Focus the columnar output on ClassAd-to-ClassAd changes (in runtimes, counts, rates, etc.) rather than totals since daemon start. Minor fixes and changes to condor_top (see below). These changes will make condor_top a more flexible tool that will allow admins to quickly find what subprocesses are spinning their wheels as well as help us to provide quicker support by analyzing emailed (i.e. offline) ClassAds or condor_top output. Minor fixes: Decrease the display width by one to avoid wrap in some terminal emulators. Fix the RAM suffixes, they are off by one. Display the daemon name and query time(s). Discard some specific attributes (e.g. SCGetAutocluster_cchit).

Continual live updates requires use of a flag (-l), otherwise condor_top prints once and quits. condor_top defaults to monitoring the local Schedd if run on a submit node. (Startd on execute node.) When running in "live" mode, condor_top prints out the recent duty cycle as a placeholder. Added/modified a bunch of columns. Their descriptions are in the man page. Added an option (-c) to choose which set of columns to display. "-c all" is fun with a wide terminal screen. When stdout is piped, columns/lines are not fit to the terminal window. All the "Updating" and "Warning" info now goes through stderr. 2017-Sep-07 17:21:09 by johnkn: CODE_REVIEW this looks very good. A lot of good improvements here.

title: Ticket #2741: condor_q -global produces inconsistent exit status
description: Parag noticed that condor_q exits with status 0 if there are no ads in the queue, but condor_q -global exits with status 1. I suspect it has been this way into the distant past, much longer ago than 7.6.0. I propose making condor_q -global exit with status 0 when all queues are empty. I'm finding out from Parag if it would be helpful to him for this to be fixed in 7.6. If he doesn't care, I'll do it in 7.7.
remarks: 2014-Jul-18 09:57:39 by jfrey: condor_q -global queries the collector for schedd ads with a filter that omits schedds with no jobs queued. If the query returns no ads, then condor_q prints All queues are empty and exits with status 1. Otherwise, it queries the schedds it's told about and exits with status 0. If none of those schedds have jobs queued, then the output will be empty. This can happen if the the queue emptied in the past several minutes and the schedd hasn't sent an update to the collector since.

description: Condor tools are a critical analysis technique in the test suite. These results are frequently our only validation that the scenario we establish is met. We have a robust system call which is very flexible called "runcmd". However if "runcmd" is not told it is ok for the command to fail, our test dies instantly! We have another command "runCondorTool" which allows for failure of any condor tool and attempts again up to some fixed number of times. Analysis recently showed that we never told "runcmd" that these "runCondorTool" calls could fail. Now we get critical followup attempts allowing us the results we need to judge the run of the test. However we have many places in intermittent test failures where we do not call condor tools in this safe way. Another routine "runToolNTimes" can be used where we just want the output or not which behaves like a system call substitution, These tools mean we will be fixing tests to use these methods to resolve many "random" failing tests.
