title: Ticket #1028: CCB and DC_NOP not happy under Windows
description: In Windows, when pidWatcherThread tries to wake up the main select, it tries to send a DC_NOP command to the daemon's command socket. When the daemon has a CCB address, this causes the check for UDP-to-self to get the wrong answer, which causes the command to try to do security negotiation, which results in blocking until a timeout occurs. This has been observed to make the schedd performance fall to pieces. Several things should be fixed: Register DC_NOP as ALLOW instead of READ and send it using the raw command protocol (never do security negotiation). There is no point in security for this command because all it does it wake up select. Anybody can wake up select, regardless of how we register this command. Always use the daemon's private address when sending DC_NOP. Fix the check for UDP-to-self so that it can correctly detect connections to the private and public addresses. Since from now on we are forcing the use of the raw command protocol, this should check will not be important for DC_NOP, but it could be important for other things. If the daemon does not have a UDP command port, send DC_NOP via TCP. This still should not block since we are using the raw command protocol.

title: Ticket #4800: Offload authorization to a separate process
description: Along with #189, one remaining reason we need a collector hierarchy is the cost of authentication. In #4137, authentication (for FS and GSI) was made non-blocking, allowing multiple authentication attempts to proceed at once. However, GSI itself is a costly operation in terms of CPU usage - in the case of a collector restart, there is simply no CPU fast enough to establish new connections for all startds in a large glidein pool. I propose introducing a new daemon - condor_auth_server - which will receive the remote TCP socket, perform authentication only, and then send the socket back to the parent. This will allow multiple CPUs to be utilized for GSI authentication.

title: Ticket #6997: condor_q gives false errors when using the -attributes flag
description: If condor_q is invoked with the -attributes command line flag in conjunction with -long, -json, or -xml flags, and the attributes ClusterId and ProcId are not both included, condor_q reports scary errors like Error: Two results with the same ID This is because condor_q code to assign jobs into collections really wants to see the job id attributes in order to sort the results by job id. A simple, (but wrong) one line code fix would be to automatically add those two attributes to the list provided with the -attributes flag, but this will then result in these attributes showing up uninvited in the user's output. Work-around for users running versions older than v8.8.3 is to add -stream-results flag, which will bypass the code that tries to sort ads by job id. If sort of the ads is important, then they could use -af:r rather than -long condor_q -af:lrng produces output that is the same as -long except that -af will not skip a missing attribute, but will always print something at that position. An alternate work around is to add ClusterId and ProcId to the list of attributes provided with the -attributes flag, although this will also alter the output.
remarks: The right fix here is to not try and sort the results when ClusterId and ProcId are not part of the projection. Or use the ad return order as a final sort key. Perhaps, stream-results should be turned on automatically when the output is -long and the projection does not include cluster and proc. . This is a bad idea, because it would potentially result in a connection being held to the schedd for a long time if the user pauses the output of condor_q somehow. 2019-May-13 15:50:11 by jfrey: Code Review This code looks good.

title: Ticket #334: Meaning of MAX_JOBS_RUNNING inconsistent
description: The type of jobs constrained by the config parameter MAX_JOBS_RUNNING is inconsistent. The manual says it applies to all job universes except the grid universe. The negotiation code in the schedd follows this policy. However, the code in Scheduler::timeout() to preempt shadows if over the limit does not count scheduler or local universe jobs. Thus, the schedd will let up to MAX_JOBS_RUNNING shadows run (i.e. not counting scheduler/local universe), but it will negotiate for fewer jobs (i.e. counting scheduler/local universe). We need to pick one meaning and make all of the relevant code honor it.

title: Ticket #6094: Profile collector UPDATE_STARTD_AD handler
description: Profiling results of the UPDATE_STARTD_AD handler for the Collector - with an eye toward finding areas that we can improve. The strategy will be to have several processes running long-lived condor_advertise that will read ads from stdin and send them on to the Collector. The processes pushing to stdin will send a burst of ads periodically then sleep for a few milliseconds and send some more ads. This will result in ads arriving in the collector on multiple sockets in a bursty way, which should be a pretty good simulation of actual operation. The UPDATE_STARTD_AD command handler will be instrumented to that it keeps track of calls and time for itself and various subtasks. That will guide modifications that will in turn be measured until we have a clear set of optimization tasks to choose from. The performance tables below were captured using 5 condor_advertise processes, each simulating 20 machines that each have 11 slots (1 partitional & 10 dynamic). 300 updates were sent for each ad for a total of 330,0000 updates See below for the raw data. Executive summary The clear implcation of the data is that the Classad parser is very slow, and a new parser optimized for speed could achieve significant gains - I believe the performance of Classad parsing could easily be doubled. Of lesser importance, but still significant would to speed up or avoid allocation and freeing of the exprtree nodes during updates in the Collector. Findings When handling STARTD Updates, the Collector spends 75% of the time in the function that gets a classad from a Cedar socket. Most of the remaining time is spent deleting the old ad. If we change the getAd function so that it doesn't parse the lines of the classad as it reads them off the Cedar socket, but instead stores them for later parsing (if needed), we can save about 1/2 of the time for that function and speed up handling of updates about 40%. Athough this strategy will make -constraint queries more expensive. This is evident in the fact that this strategy doubles the cost of generating the hashkey for the ad - it goes from 1% of the overall time to about 3%. If we instead change getad to do its own parsing of all of the simple values (numeric and string literals), and pass only the complex expressions to the normal Classad parser, we can achieve most of the same performance speedup (roughly 35%) while avoiding the increased cost of -constraint queries. title: Ticket #6581: condor_submit should not always read from stdin if no submit file
description: Michael Pelletier points out that it is possible to provide a valid submit hash on the command line of condor_submit, but that there is no way to tell condor_submit not to read from stdin in that case. For example condor_submit executable=/bin/sleep arguments=300 -queue 1 Is a complete and valid submit description, but if you run this command, condor_submit will wait forever trying to read the "submit file" from stdin. we need to rethink this behavior. The proposed fix is to add a new (optional) command line argument for explicitly specifying a submit file. This argument will allow - as the filename, and read from stdin in that case. change the behavior of the -queue command line argument so that condor_submit will only read from explicitly specified submit files when it is used. So, for example condor_submit executable=/bin/sleep arguments=300 -queue 1 Will submit a 300 second sleep job, and not read from stdin. condor_submit executable=/bin/sleep arguments=300 -submit foo -queue 1 Will read submit statements from foo, insert executable and args from the command line, and the submit a single job. And condor_submit -submit - -queue 1 Will read submit statements from stdin, and queue a single job using those statements. As is currently the case, it will be an error to have a queue statement in the submit file/stdin and also on the command line.

title: Ticket #4945: Partitionable slots stuck in Matched state forever
description: When using consumption policies and startd notification of matches with partitionable slots, it's possible for the partitionable to end up in Matched state forever. The problem is that when the startd looks up a Resource using a consumption policy claim id, there's a side-effect that makes that Claim object the primary claim for the Resource, and the previous current Claim is deleted. This happens when a MATCH_INFO message is received from the negotiator. So if the negotiator matches the pslot multiple times and sends MATCH_INFO messages, each Claim is displaced (and deleted) by the next Claim, and only the last one can be used to start a job. Worse, the timer to leave Matched state lives and dies with the first Claim. Once a second MATCH_INFO arrives, the timer is no more. The pslot will stay in Matched state forever unless the schedd attempts to use the last Claim handed out by the negotiator. Proposed Fix Pslots never enter Matched state when using consumption policies. When a MATCH_INFO message arrives for a pslot, the startd leaves the Resource in Unclaimed state. The function ResMgr::get_by_cur_id() ignores r_claims. The function ResMgr::get_by_any_id() does not juggle Claim objects unless explicitly requested by the caller. Only request_claim() will do so.

Behold : [tannenba@submit-4 ~]$ cat /proc/sys/kernel/keys/root_maxkeys 200 [tannenba@submit-4 ~]$ cat /proc/sys/kernel/keys/root_maxbytes 20000 [tannenba@submit-5 ~]$ cat /proc/sys/kernel/keys/root_maxkeys 1000000 [tannenba@submit-5 ~]$ cat /proc/sys/kernel/keys/root_maxbytes 25000000 ingwe.cs.wisc.edu{tannenba}54: cat /proc/sys/kernel/keys/root_maxkeys 1000000 ingwe.cs.wisc.edu{tannenba}55: cat /proc/sys/kernel/keys/root_maxbytes 25000000 Looks like submit-4 is currently running with 199 of its allowable 200 keys in use!! Also it is using almost a third of its key bytes quota... behold: [tannenba@submit-4 ~]$ cat /proc/key-users | head -1 0: 204 203/203 199/200 5867/20000 BTW, the fields for /proc/key-users is (from http://is.gd/mXp2M3 ) <UID> User ID <usage> Usage count <inst>/<keys> Total number of keys and number instantiated <keys>/<max> Key count quota <bytes><max> Key size quota I strongly suggest submit-4 have the same amount of root_maxkeys and root_maxbytes as apparently all other RHEL6 machine have... Another idea would be for HTCondor kernel tuning script to set these.

title: Ticket #2038: Long file paths corrupt memory in file locking code
description: If the FileLock class is given a file with path longer than 255 characters, it will corrupt memory, leading to a crash. FileLock::CreateHashName() creates a buffer of size _POSIX_PATH_MAX and passes it to the libc function realpath(). realpath() is expecting a buffer of size PATH_MAX. On our platforms, _POSIX_PATH_MAX is 256 with PATH_MAX is 1024 or 4096. We saw this crash the schedd on submit.chtc.wisc.edu when jobs were submitted with a user log path of 256 characters. We should review any other code that uses _POSIX_PATH_MAX.

title: Ticket #2716: Code review new Gratia Condor probe
description: The Condor Team owns the Gratia Condor Probe. Historically, the probe has been wacky: it's written in Python and it generates and runs Python code so that it can interact with the Python libraries. There has been one security flaw due to that (since it runs as root), and it's just icky. Brian Bockelman <bbockelm@cse.unl.edu> needed to make some changes to the probe and ended up rewriting it all in Python. As part of rewriting it, he got rid of code that deals with web services GRAM because it is no longer needed. Brian has tested the code fairly heavily, including: Running the probe by hand on 10 jobs and comparing the XML output with the old probe. They produced identical output. Running the probe on a backlog of data (two million jobs) for one site that wasn't running Gratia for a long time (two years?) No problems were found. Gratia is a critical part of the OSG infrastructure: people rely on the Gratia accounting on a daily basis. While we think the probe probably works well, we would like a thoughtful code review by a Condor developer who can think about the corner-edge-fringe-brink cases and suggest possible problems in the code. We'd like this review by early January so we can release an update in mid to late January. Todd suggests that perhaps Nathan is the right person to do the review, so I've assigned the ticket to him. Please reassign if needed.
remarks: 2011-Dec-14 17:37:46 by bbockelm: Not sure how much background Nathan has in Gratia, so I'll leave a few breadcrumbs. Specifically, we are reviewing condor_meter.pl versus condor_meter. You want to create a ProbeConfig file and send records to the test collector, gratia-osg-itb.opensciencegrid.org:80. For comparing outputs, I find it useful to set Debug to 6, which causes the raw XML used to be printed to stdout. To have the probe parse files, put a classad in the directory pointed to by DataFolder in the ProbeConfig file and run "condor_meter". The code has initial - but fairly untested - support for multiple classads per file. You might be able to just drop in the output of "condor_history -l" to generate test data (if that doesn't work, let's fix it). Note that condor_meter is meant to be a logic copy of that found in condor_meter.pl. title: Ticket #57: Improve execute directory names (Contain slot number, eliminate PID)
description: Currently execute directories are in the form $EXECUTE/dir_$(PID). It's not obvious how to correlate a slot to a directory. If you're debugging a job that you know is in slot 3, you don't immediately know if you want to look in dir_11220, dir_17755, dir_29229, or dir_6141. The directories could be more helpfully named. We might be able to go entirely to $EXECUTE/dir_$(SLOT) or $EXECUTE/slot_$(SLOT), though there are concerns that we're relying on PID collisions be unlikely (a risky assumption) to handle certain race conditions. For example, is it possible that the startd will fail to clean up dead execute directory on a starter crash or system reboot before a new starter starts using an identically named directory? Even if this is a concern, it's likely a problem today because PIDs aren't very unique. If it is a concern, we should solve it more thoroughly, perhaps using PID and Timestamp, or a GUID. So we might use $EXECUTE/dir_$(SLOT)_$(PID)_$(TIMESTAMP) or $EXECUTE/dir_$(SLOT)_$(PID)_$(GUID)

remarks: 2011-Aug-15 17:10:50 by bbockelm: Just FYI - this appears to still be an issue in the latest GT5.2 pre-release code. 2011-Aug-15 17:37:42 by bbockelm: To reproduce, try the submit file and test script I list below. Submit the first hundred jobs, and wait until a few start running on the remote CE. Then, "kill -9" the client's gahp_server. Let a few of the running jobs on the remote CE finish up. Submit a new Condor-G job to get it to fire up gahp_server again. The second gahp_server will be unable to restart the jobs. The hold reason would be that files could not be transferred out. On the remote host, one can verify that GRAM doesn't log destroying the job directory (even at TRACE), but indeed the files have been deleted. [bbockelm@brian-test gratia-probe]$ cat ~/tmp/testjob/test_g.submit universe = grid executable = test.sh output = test_g.out error = test_g.err log = test_g.log grid_resource = gt5 host.example.com:/jobmanager-condor remote_universe = vanilla ShouldTransferFiles = YES WhenToTransferOutput = ON_EXIT +remote_ShouldTransferFiles = "YES" +remote_WhenToTransferOutput = "ON_EXIT" queue 100 [bbockelm@brian-test gratia-probe]$ cat ~/tmp/testjob/test.sh #!/bin/sh env hostname date sleep 1 grid-proxy-info
attachments: gt5_failure.txt 54530 bytes added by bbockelm on 2011-Aug-16 03:08:15 UTC. I was able to capture the failure. I think the basic sequence is: gahp_server dies. Remote job completes, tries to stage out to dead gahp_server (and fails). This puts the job-manager into state GLOBUS_GRAM_JOB_MANAGER_STATE_FAILED_TWO_PHASE. gahp_server restarts, sends the STOP signal to the job-manager, and then instructs the job-manager to restart the job. The job-manager restart code internally transitions the job from GLOBUS_GRAM_JOB_MANAGER_STATE_FAILED_TWO_PHASE to GLOBUS_GRAM_JOB_MANAGER_STATE_FAILED_CLOSE_OUTPUT. The job-manager restarts the commit of the stageout failure error message. The failure message is successfully committed, then transitions to GLOBUS_GRAM_JOB_MANAGER_STATE_FAILED_FILE_CLEAN_UP, which deletes the output files. So, if the gahp_server is dead (or temporarily inaccessible) when the remote job-manager decides to stage out, the job will eventually be held and the output files will be deleted remotely upon restart. What actions are in the transaction covered by the two-phase commit? Is the transfer itself covered? I'm starting to think it should be. If a job fails and the gridmanager is inaccessible, upon restart the job-manager should reset to the DONE/POLL1 state. restart_on_failure.patch 6469 bytes added by bbockelm on 2011-Aug-17 17:22:16 UTC. The attached patch, for globus-gram-job-manager, clears up this issue. There were actually two issues: Once a file transfer fails, it will never be retried (noted in the previous comment). Now, if a file transfer fails and GRAM is unable to notify the remote client of the failure, a restart of the job-manager will place it back into a POLL1 state. stdio_updates basically don't work in GT5 because Condor-G will update GRIDMANAGER_GASS_URL in the RSL, while the merge is done against the expanded RSL. The merging is done against the in-memory RSL data structure, not rsl_spec which is written to disk. Further, stakeout is done based on the todo list, not the RSL. The patch fixes all of these things. On the phone, Jaime and I decided that restarting the job-manager is no longer necessary in GT5 if the stdio_update works. He'll be updating the gridmanager accordingly.

title: Ticket #7847: DAGMan inline submit descriptions declared independent of jobs
description: In #7352 we added the ability for DAGMan jobs to be described inline in a .dag file without requiring a separate submit file. As a result, you can now write an inline job description like in the following example: JOB MyJob { executable = /bin/echo arguments = Hello, world! output = helloworld.out } While this is a nice convenience for users, it isn't that helpful at the moment because different jobs cannot share the same submit description. We want to add a new condor_dagman command, SUBMIT-DESCRIPTION, that allows submit descriptions to be defined independently of jobs and referenced by name. For example: SUBMIT-DESCRIPTION MyInlineDescription { executable = /bin/echo arguments = Hello, world! output = helloworld.out } JOB MyJob MyInlineDescription As an implementation detail, we'll make a new data structure in condor_dagman (probably a std::map) that maps description names to SubmitHash objects. Description names must be unique. If a submit description is defined as part of a JOB command, it gets the name of the job. If defined independently as a SUBMIT-DESCRIPTION, the user is expected to provide a name. Any naming collision will cause condor_dagman to abort at parse time with an error in the log. Another implementation challenge is parsing: does a SUBMIT-DESCRIPTION need to be defined before a JOB can reference it? On the first pass, we'll expect these to be defined in order. Later, we should look into how we could pre-parse these descriptions so that order doesn't matter.

title: Ticket #4292: Allow output from evictions to be not-spooled
description: Here's the setup: Running jobs as part of a DAG node. We use periodic_remove to evict jobs that go over their memory limit. Users want to retrieve stdout / err from these cases in order to figure out what the heck went wrong with their jobs. Right now, if we set: WhenToTransferOutput = "ON_EXIT_OR_EVICT" then the stdout is copied to the schedd into the spool and the spool is deleted. AFAICT, there's no way to get access to the job's incomplete output from a DAGMan post-script. Traditionally, CMS has used a separate monitoring thread in its wrapper script to kill the job and make sure the output is returned; this drives me nuts because it replicates the procd. I'd like to have a new job attribute, SpoolOnEvict (defaults to true if not set) which controls whether job output is moved to the spool on an eviction. For CMS to be able to use this and not re-implement the current approach, this knob would need to go into 8.1.6. The implementation is fairly trivial if we can get agreement on the approach. Brian
remarks: 2014-Apr-16 11:42:49 by bbockelm: Discussed this on the phone 2 weeks ago with Todd. No objections were raised to the approach, although he asked me to verify that repeated condor_hold/condor_release on such jobs had predictable behavior. Just did the testing this morning; there are no apparent issues in evicting the jobs multiple times. The output files from the second eviction overwrites the files from the first. 2014-Apr-16 14:04:56 by tannenba: CODE REVIEW Only feedback is to edit condor_submit to that folks can enter either +SpoolOnEvict = True or spool_on_evict = True or SpoolOnEvict = True just like all the other submit knobs. Once this is done this ticket can go to docpending state. Thanks for the patch! 2014-Apr-16 14:13:40 by bbockelm: Hi Todd, I'd be happy to do that - however, it makes the SpoolOnEvict knob relatively prominent (where I was thinking of it being a somewhat hidden knob for a specific use case). Are you OK with making this a first-class config knob? I assume that I somehow should add this to the manpage too. Brian 2014-Apr-16 14:33:26 by tannenba: Brian, re your first remark above: my concern wasn't about output files being overwritten, it was with intermediate (checkpoint) files. Imagine a job that writes out a self-checkpoint and has transfer files ON_EXIT_OR_EVICT. If SpoolOnEvict is True (as it always has been), then checkpoint file is written to spool and the job will resume where it left off upon restart because files in spool are a) written atomically, and b) sent to the execute node on restart. If a self-checkpointing job has SpoolOnEvict set to False, what happens on restart? This is what I wanted you to test... my guess is the job will restart from the beginning, right? If true, at the very least, the documentation should note that setting SpoolOnEvict will prevent user level checkpoint/resume and is only intended for debugging purposes? Re the question about keeping SpoolOnEvict hidden or not - I'd vote for documenting it, but doing so in a way that clearly states the use case for this knob and what breaks/surprises are in store if you use it. 2014-Nov-04 13:36:07 by tannenba: See #4679 for follow-on work to this. As an aside, I am confused about why this ticket was moved (by TimT) from active to docpending without any of the code review changes being addressed, and then moved (by brian) from docpending to resolved without any documentation being added.

title: Ticket #6240: Setting x509 attributes on file transfer corrupts job queue log
description: In 8.5.8, we had the schedd start managing the X.509 attributes in the job ad (#5064). Part of this change was setting the attributes based on the job proxy that's received when the job's input sandbox is spooled to the schedd over the network. The code to modify the job ad in the queue is run in a child process of the schedd, which is a big No-No. The changes won't appear in the schedd's in-memory copy of the job queue. Worse, they can corrupt the on-disk job_queue.log file, due to competing writes from the two processes. Ben Jones at CERN has reported multiple occurrences of this when attempting to upgrade from 8.5.5 to 8.6 or 8.7. It should be easy to move the problematic code into the main schedd process, in the reaper for the child process doing the file transfer.

title: Ticket #949: CronJobBase::StartJob and RunJob return codes need review
description: CronJobBase::StartJob and RunJob are registered as timers, which means their return code is entirely ignored. StartJob returns 0 if the job is not idle, else RunProcess's return value. It is used by Reaper and Schedule. Its return code is ignored by Reaper. RunJob returns -1 if killing the job is not allowed, else KillJob's return value; else, RunProcess's return value. It is used by Reaper and Schedule. Its return code is ignored by Reaper. KillJob's return code is 0 if job is idle/dead or if a SIGKILL was attempted (even if it failed), 1 if job is sent a SIGTERM (note: a SIGKILL is registered), and -1 if the job is not running. The code is ignored when returned to KillHandler. RunProcess's return code is -1 on failure and 0 on success. Schedule's return code is 0 if uninitialized, or the return value of StartJob, SetTimer or RunJob. It is called by Initialize and SetPeriod, which return its code. SetTimer's return code is -1 if timer creation fails, otherwise 0. It is called by Reaper, where the code is ignored, and by Schedule. Initialize is called by InitializeAll where the return code is ignored. It is also called from the startd, where the return code is ignored. SetPeriod is called from CronMgrBase::ParseJobList and ParseOldJobList where the return code is ignored. Conclusion: StartJob and RunJob's return code is entirely unused, give the impression that it is used, and may be masking unhandled error conditions.
creator: matt

title: Ticket #1706: too many links in spool directory
description: The following appears in the shadow log when spool is on an ext3 filesystem and there are more than 16k jobs running: 10/08/10 22:31:52 (51652.0) (35391): FileTransfer::Init(): mkdir(/home/sfiligoi/glidecondor/condor_local/spool/cluster51652.proc0.subproc0) failed, Too many links (errno: 31) 10/08/10 22:31:52 (51652.0) (35391): FileTransfer::Init(): mkdir(/home/sfiligoi/glidecondor/condor_local/spool/cluster51652.proc0.subproc0.tmp) failed, Too many links (errno: 31) 10/08/10 22:31:52 (51652.0) (35391): Can't open directory "/home/sfiligoi/glidecondor/condor_local/spool/cluster51652.proc0.subproc0.tmp" as PRIV_USER, errno: 2 (No such file or directory) 10/08/10 22:31:52 (51652.0) (35391): Can't open directory "/home/sfiligoi/glidecondor/condor_local/spool/cluster51652.proc0.subproc0" as PRIV_USER, errno: 2 (No such file or directory) In the case where spooling is not needed, this is mostly harmless, because we never use these directories. Proposed Fix Create a hierarchy of directories: $(SPOOL)/<cluster mod 10000>/<proc mod 10000>/cluster<cluster>.proc<proc>.subproc<subproc>. This avoids exhausting the ext3 link limit at scales of up to 320M spooled clusters or 320M procs. The hash could be more clever, but this one has the advantage of being easy to reproduce in case some user has need to find the spool directory for a job. On startup, the schedd will need to move spool file/directories around and adjust the references to these paths in the job classads. This needs to be done carefully so that if the process is interrupted part way through it will get completed when the schedd is restarted. As part of the fix, I am also adding a spool version stamp so that we can improve the upgrade/downgrade process. Incompatibilities can be detected and conversion to a new format can be more efficiently triggered by simply looking at the version of the existing spool.

title: Ticket #6539: scheduler universe and dagman jobs leaked if condor_master dies
description: HTCondor is supposed to have a "belt and suspenders" approach to ensure it does not leave a mess of orphaned processes. Even in the event of the condor_master blowing up, the condor_schedd (and all other condor daemons under the master) should notice that the master went away (daemons poll to see if the master is still alive every 2 minutes) and proceed to shutdown if the master disappears. Unfortunately the schedd has a bug where on shutdown it only sends a sigterm to ONE scheduler universe job. The issue is when the master died the procd committed suicide, then the schedd would commmit suicide the first time it tried to reap a child. So if you have 50 dagmans in the queue, only one of them will be killed by the schedd upon shut down. In the normal case where the condor_master is still alive, this bug isn't a big deal because the condor_master will kill any/all pids left behind by the schedd. But if the condor_master is dead, this schedd bug is really bad. Recipe to reproduce the bug Submit 2 scheduler universe jobs. Do a ps auxw | grep condor_scheduniv_exec and observe the two scheduler universe jobs running. Now kill -9 the condor_master Within two minutes the condor_schedd will notice the master is gone, and will shutdown and exit. However, after the condor_schedd is gone, ps auxw | grep condor_scheduniv_exec will show one of the two scheduler universe processes was left behind. Plan to fix the bug One way to fix the bug would require the procd to hang around for some period of time after the condor_master has died in order to honor requests from the schedd (or startd, or starter, etc). This approach has been deemed to complicated for the stable series. Instead, we will configure systemd to cleanup any processes left behind after the condor_master exits. Although not directly related, we will also modify daemon core to do a shutdown fast instead of a shutdown graceful whenever an HTCondor daemon notices its parent has died. p.s. The approach in check-in [54166] was deemed to risky upon code review, and was reverted.
remarks: 2018-Jan-24 15:45:37 by johnkn: CODE_REVIEW of check-in [54166] (was reverted) - with this change, the schedd now sends a sigterm to ALL shadows, as well as all scheduler and local universe jobs before it reaps any children when it is doing a graceful shutdown. Prior to this change, the schedd would only sigterm ONE shadow OR ONE scheduler universe job or ONE local universe job each time the attempt_shutdown() timer ticked. it would then (likely) reap that child, wait a second and tick the timer again. The reason that the condor_dagman processes leaked when the master died was because the procd committed suicide, then the schedd would commmit suicide the first time it tried to reap a child. 2018-Feb-27 11:56:52 by matyas: CODE REVIEW This is fine as a last resort but if the schedd and other daemons are smart enough to notice that the master has gone away, we should give them a chance to do so. https://www.freedesktop.org/software/systemd/man/systemd.kill.html says that the default timeout for SIGKILLing a process is 90 seconds. Thank you. 2018-Mar-09 11:32:25 by tim: DOC REVIEW: Looks good

title: Ticket #4504: Concurrency test extension - sequential job submition
description: We suspect a bug with static concurrency limits. The idea was to submit slower towards a configured limit. However SimpleJob::RunCheck does not return until all the queue request complete and with sleep forever jobs, how do you submit additional jobs slowly, and with the same submit file and callbacks? The solution was to provide a callback so RunCheck can give you the name of the submit file it is creating. Then for each extra job you fork a child to call RunTest passing the testname and the submit file which gets you the same callbacks. Note this means you can not do things in callbacks with counters! In these tests we examine run queue for running and idle tests. The is a main callback in the parent which repeats evry 10 seconds as things change. We configure a hash and a taskname for each part of the tests adding as the value the number of additional jobs desired and the parents callback kicks them off, one per callback. ToDo All six tests are currently in slow submit mode due to a suspected bug with static slots and currency greater then one when jobs are submitted queue N. Once resolved, we'l do queue N submits and sequental(current mode) At this point job_concurrency_limitsS.run displays the issue fairly quickly in queue mode. Set $burst == 1 near top to flip to queue N submits.

title: Ticket #1356: Event log reader doesn't initialize properly with XML logs
description: Brian Bockelman has discovered that the user log reader doesn't initialize properly for reading the eventlog if the eventlog is in XML.
remarks: 2010-Apr-18 18:38:23 by bbockelm: Hey Nick, Actually, I uncovered two problems: 1) The initialize() method (no arguments) doesn't work like it should. Running things through a debugger, I could see that something failed when Condor was trying to figure out where the Event log was. Using strace, I was able to confirm the class never attempted to open any files, so it's not a permissions issue. 2) (More severe) The XML log parser does not handle log growths. That is, if you read all the events in the file and the file grows, then the event parser will always claim there are no more events in the file. To reproduce: 1) Create the log parser with an XML EventLog 2) Read all the events until readEvent returns ULOG_NO_EVENT. 3) Sleep until a new event is written to the log 4) Call readEvent again; it returns ULOG_NO_EVENT

title: Ticket #2983: RFE: Allow Collector to discard queries where client has given up
description: At high scale and high query rates, the condor_collector can become backed up responding to queries. Clients querying the collector will only wait for QUERY_TIMEOUT seconds, and may retry. Currently, the collector has no way to know it has fallen behind and will be responding to queries where the client has given up. Proposal, have the client provide a hint to the collector and allow the collector to disregard queries for which the client has likely given up. Note: When clients retry with large queries (output is large), the collector will not gracefully recover.

title: Ticket #3691: Remove hard-coded policies on how schedd can reuse claims
description: Currently, the Claim that is given out by the Negotiator to the Schedd is very open ended. As long as it matches the Startd requirements, the only additional restrictions on the Claim are hard-coded : it cannot be used for a different user, and it must be used for a job with the same set of concurrency limits. This situation has shown to be a problem when implementing the “Global Priority” feature. While the Negotiator will pick the globally higher priority job for a user, all bets are off once that job finishes, since the Schedd will pick the next job using local criteria. Other policies based on the global state of the system would equally be impossible to implement. The proposal is thus to remove the hard-coded claim reuse logic and for the negotiator to explicitly embed the restrictions on jobs that can reuse the claim in the requirements that are sent back to the Schedd. See Design Document for details.

That seems like a problem. 2013-Jul-08 16:28:36 by sfiligoi: Good catch... and shame on me for not thinking about it. I have added an explicit requirement that will prevent a job with a ClaimLimit to recycle a claim issues to a job without one (patch_1.1). 2013-Jul-09 09:25:48 by tannenba: Thanks for the patches! I pushed step_1.patch and step_1.1.patch into the repo onto git branch V8_1-gt3691. Also the NMI build and test pool is configured to run builds and regression tests on all platforms with every push to this branch, so we can see the regression tests. I did not push step_1b.patch. I was hoping for an (undocumented?) knob to conditionally to enable/disable this code, and this patch does not accomplish this because the offer from the negotiator is still unconditionally rewritten. I want the knob to be at the negotiator level to control if machine requirements are rewritten at all. The schedd then should look to see if _condor_match_requirements_claim is present in the offer to determine if it should use old hard-coded logic or not for concurrency and owner limits. I know some developer testing was performed, but there are no transcripts testing session remarks yet in the ticket and bugs still being found on code review day before the freeze, so changing this to be targeted for v8.1.1. I think next step for development on this branch is a bypass knob as described above, and then code in the schedd to conditionally bypass hard-coded owner checks if _condor_match_requirements_claim is present. For testing, we need to demonstrate claims are reused when they should and also NOT reused when they should not. Testing may be made easier if we had a way via config file to append a clause to the _condor_match_requirements_claim. 2013-Jul-09 09:59:03 by sfiligoi: The check is on ENFORCE_CONCURRENCY_LIMITS, instead of _condor_match_requirements_claim. It is disabled by default, and when enabled, only changes the behavior if ENFORCE_CONCURRENCY_LIMITS is set to False. 2013-Jul-10 18:00:16 by sfiligoi: Added a new patch that makes the new negotiator semantics optional. Also included the test I used to validate it.

title: Ticket #5250: Make meta knobs for exceeding cpu and memory limits
description: Define meta-knobs to have the startd immediately preempt and/or put on hold jobs that either exceed memory or cpu provisioned in the slot, ignoring any job retirement time or suspend rules. In the event the job is put on hold, a reasonable default hold reason and subcode should be provided, but there should also be a way for the admin to customize these. The meta-knobs should be written in a way that they can conflate with any pre-existing startd policy settings. Suggested names for these meta-knobs are - use policy: preempt_if_cpus_exceeded use policy: hold_if_cpus_exceeded use policy: preempt_if_memory_exceeded use policy: hold_if_memory_exceeded Behold Todd's awesome config knob prowess; suggested values for these knobs are - use policy: preempt_if_cpus_exceeded # # Publish the number of CPU cores being used by the job into # to slot ad as attribute "CpusUsage". This value will # be the average number of cores used by the job over the # past minute, sampling every 5 seconds, and rounded to two digits. # CpusUsage = ifthenelse( \ TotalLoadAvg > 0.0 && Activity!="Idle", \ int(CondorLoadAvg / TotalLoadAvg * \ ifthenelse(TotalLoadAvg < $(DETECTED_CORES), TotalLoadAvg, $(DETECTED_CORES)) \ * 100) / 100.0, \ 0) STARTD_EXPRS = $(STARTD_EXPRS) CpusUsage # # If the startd sees the number of CPU cores used by the job exceed the # number of cores in the slot by more than 0.8, preempt the job # immediately ignoring any retirement time. # CPU_EXCEEDED = (CpusUsage > Cpus + 0.8) PREEMPT = ($(PREEMPT:False)) || $(CPU_EXCEEDED) MAXJOBRETIREMENTTIME = ifthenelse($(CPU_EXCEEDED),0,$(MAXJOBRETIREMENTTIME:0)) WANT_SUSPEND = ($(WANT_SUSPEND:False)) && $(CPU_EXCEEDED) =!= TRUE use policy: hold_if_cpus_exceeded use policy: preempt_if_cpus_exceeded # # If the startd preempted a job because CPU usage exceeded the number # of cores in the slot, put the job on hold. # WANT_HOLD = ($(WANT_HOLD:False)) || $(CPU_EXCEEDED) WANT_HOLD_REASON = ifThenElse($(CPU_EXCEEDED), \ $(HOLD_REASON_CPU_EXCEEDED:"cpu usage exceeded request_cpus"), \ $(WANT_HOLD_REASON:UNDEFINED)) WANT_HOLD_SUBCODE = ifThenElse($(CPU_EXCEEDED), \ $(HOLD_SUBCODE_CPU_EXCEEDED:101), \ $(WANT_HOLD_SUBCODE:UNDEFINED)) use policy: preempt_if_memory_exceeded # # If the startd sees the memory usage of the job exceed the # memory in the slot, preempt the job immediately ignoring any retirement time. # MEMORY_EXCEEDED = (MemoryUsage =!= UNDEFINED && MemoryUsage > Memory) PREEMPT = ($(PREEMPT:False)) || $(MEMORY_EXCEEDED) MAXJOBRETIREMENTTIME = ifthenelse($(MEMORY_EXCEEDED),0,$(MAXJOBRETIREMENTTIME:0)) WANT_SUSPEND = ($(WANT_SUSPEND:False)) && $(MEMORY_EXCEEDED) =!= TRUE use policy: hold_if_memory_exceeded use policy: preempt_if_memory_exceeded # # If the startd preempted a job because memory usage exceeded the amount # of memory in the slot, put the job on hold. # WANT_HOLD = ($(WANT_HOLD:False)) || $(MEMORY_EXCEEDED) WANT_HOLD_REASON = ifThenElse($(MEMORY_EXCEEDED), \ $(HOLD_REASON_MEMORY_EXCEEDED:"memory usage exceeded request_memory"), \ $(WANT_HOLD_REASON:UNDEFINED)) WANT_HOLD_SUBCODE = ifThenElse($(MEMORY_EXCEEDED), \ $(HOLD_SUBCODE_MEMORY_EXCEEDED:102), \ $(WANT_HOLD_SUBCODE:UNDEFINED))

title: Ticket #6885: Allow multifile uploads
description: The multi-file transfer plugins provide a richer communication mechanism between the file transfer object and the plugins; we have declared in #6859 that we want this to replace the single-file plugin as the default mechanism. The biggest missing piece in the multifile setup in terms of functionality is the ability to upload (e.g., stageout for the condor_starter) using multifile plugins. This is the ticket to track that work. I propose to keep the existing wire protocol. Instead of doing the transfers in the order provided by the user, we will first sort transfers to group all the files using the same plugin. As we loop through files, instead of immediately performing the transfer, we will build up a TODO list of "deferred" transfers. Each time we hit a transfer incompatible with the current set of deferred transfers (or make it through the complete transfer list), we will execute the multifile plugin and send all the corresponding communication to the DoDownload-side. Here, "transfer incompatible" is any time where we change the protocol (http to https) or if the binary protocol requires us to do a round-trip and synchronize (see #6884; we have been recently surprised that for the last 9 years we always do a round-trip per file and plan to fix this).

title: Ticket #5600: Keep supplemental groups in my_popen()
description: When my_popen() or my_spawnv() is invoked and told that the child process should have no root privileges, it also removes all supplemental groups in the child process. Nowhere else in HTCondor do we do this. When acting as a non-privileged user, we always ensure that user's supplemental groups are in place. We should do the same for my_popen()/my_spawnv(). This bit the SWAMP folks, who tried to configure a filetransfer plugin that needed to run a binary accessible only via a supplemental group of the user. The fix for this consists of removing the call to setgroups() in my_popen() and my_spawnv(). These functions require that the process already has the desired UID set as the effective UID. This change assumes that Condor's privilege switching code always sets the user groups properly and no callers bypass Condor's privilege switching code to call seteuid() directly.

This won't be able to make it into the 7.3.2 release, but we can add code allowing the user to tell the gridmanager whether a server is GRAM5. They can do this by setting the grid-type to 'gt5' in the GridResource job attribute.
remarks: 2009-Aug-19 16:07:31 by jfrey: The 'gt5' grid-type is intended as a temporary solution to distinguishing between GRAM2 and GRAM5 servers. Currently, the GridResource or GridJobId attribute of the first job seen by the gridmanager for a given server determines whether it treats the server as GRAM2 or GRAM5. So mixing the two grid-types for a given server results in undefined behavior. If a server is ID'd as GRAM5, the gridmanager's behavior towards that server is changed as follows: Grid Monitor is disabled. Jobmanagers aren't stopped. GRIDMANAGER_MAX_JOBMANAGERS_PER_RESOURCE isn't applied.

title: Ticket #4441: condor_install can be used for an initial configuration for testing
description: We want any personal condor created for testing to use valid ports for the collector. "condor_install" which is really "condor_configure" in git would setup condor_collector == condor_host with no dynamic port request. So I modified it to use MetaKNobs for the local config file and they get dropped first in the file. This is only for the option --make-personal-condor. For this option, "use role : personal" comes out first. We still allow condor_host to get the machine name(full) and we delete the daemon list which would have hidden the one set up by the role:personal. So this means if you have a man folder in your release_dir you can go there and enter "./condor_install --make-personal-condor", set your path to those bins and CONDOR_CONFIG to release_dir/etc/condor_config, start condor_master and be ready to test.

title: Ticket #226: Account charges only for number of cpus
description: In 7.2 and 7.3, Condor looks at the Cpus attribute in the machine classad when deciding how much to charge the customer. It would be useful to have it evaluate an arbitrary expression (ideally floating point, but not critical). I know that Ian was working on a patch to do this some time in the past, but I haven't heard anything for quite a while. (( Note: this is #331, which is similar to this ticket but currently limited to accounting group quotas -Todd )) If the expression depended on job attributes as well as machine attributes, this would be most flexible. For example, it would allow a slot to play dual roles as a normal slot or a whole-machine slot, depending on the desires of the job. However, this would likely complicate the spinning pie algorithm quite a bit and so may not be worth it. I should also point out that the existing implementation that looks at "Cpus" does not take this into account during the spinning pie phase. It only takes it into account when charging the user.

title: Ticket #1004: Condor-C and Nordugrid grid jobs should share job status polling loop
description: The Condor-C and Nordugrid grid types have nearly identical code for handling batch queries of job statuses. For Condor-C jobs, condorresource.cpp's CondorResource::DoScheddPoll implements this on a timer setup in the constructor. Nordugrid jobs use nordugridresource.cpp's NordugridResource::DoJobStatus, again, set up in a timer in the constructor. The new CREAM grid type needed to do the same thing, but instead of copying the code again, I factored a bunch of it out into BaseResource. Ideally Condor-C and Nordugrid would be refactored to use this code as well, cutting down on duplicate code. You can see the changes in question in #939. The interface is documented in /src/condor_gridmanager/baseresource.h, but in short: Call BaseResource::StartBatchStatusTimer in The FooResource constructor Implement FooResource::BatchStatusInterval to return the interval the batch query should fire on. Implement FooResource::StartBatchStatus to initiate a batch query. It will probably launch the request via the gahp, then return BSR_PENDING Implement FooResource::FinishBatchStatus to continue and optionally complete a batch query. Typically should return BSR_PENDING repeatedly until the gahp replies, in which case it should process the results and return BSR_DONE Implement FooResource::BatchGahp to return the Gahp* used for your batch status queries. The batch status code will ensure that it's isStarted(), possibly calling Startup(), before calling into your other functions.

title: Ticket #4206: Reduce unused memory in DaemonCore data structures
description: The DaemonCore code wastes some memory in its data structures for callback handlers registered for various events. It uses unnecessarily large static arrays of structs with noticeable internal fragmentation. The amount of wasted memory is minor in most cases, but adds up quickly on a submit machine with a large number of shadow processes. Code for this ticket is committed on the branch V8_1-gt4206-daemoncore_diet. Most of event handler structs (CommandEnt, SignalEnt, SockEnt, PipeEnt, ReapEnt) are laid out inefficiently, leading to a lot of internal fragmentation. Their elements can be reordered to decrease the overall size of the struct. The event handler arrays comTable, sigTable, and reapTable are statically allocated with many more entries than required. They can be changed to dynamically-extendable arrays that start at a small size. Some additional changes to consider: Use StringSpace to store handler description strings. These are usually strdup()'d from static strings and many handlers may have the same description. Collapse the handler and handlercpp elements into a union, since both aren't used at the same time. Control the size of the ExtArrays more tightly. The default is to double the size when they need to be expanded. Trade-off of space vs. process startup time. Keep the arrays comTable, sigTable, and reapTable sorted by the num element, allowing faster lookup.

title: Ticket #3193: support evaluated expressions in xml query output
description: Currently there is no way to specify that you want an expression to be evaluated when generating -xml or -long output from condor_q and condor_status. This seems an arbitrary limitation, since one can get evaluated output when using -format in non-xml mode. Currently, the list of attributes to include in the long/xml output is specified via the -attributes argument. One possible solution would be to add a new option -expressions that lists expressions to be evaluated. Perhaps the following syntax would make sense, where each expression is assigned a name that will be used as the attribute name in the output: -expressions name1=expr1;name2=expr2;... If multiple -expressions are specified, they will be appended to the list of expressions.

title: Ticket #932: Bad string escaping in gahps
description: Many of the GAHPs don't escape strings in the GAHP protocol correctly. Many don't escape backslash. Some convert \r and \n to a space in addition to escaping them with a backslash. The GAHP escaping rules are as follows: Backslash, space, carriage-return ('\r') and new-line ('\n') characters that occur within a GAHP argument (in either a request or a result) are preceded by a backslash. All functions that escape GAHP arguments need to be changed to follow this rule.

title: Ticket #5417: Erratic startup ASSERTs with shared port on Windows
description: Sometimes on Windows a daemon (master?) will fail to start up. The system is using shared ports. Failure is probably in DaemonCore::InfoCommandSinfulStringMyself; one of the ASSERT(X.hasAddrs()) is failing. Probably because the shared port daemon wrote a sinful to file that lacks the addrs field. However, the sinful the shared port daemon writes is itself from DaemonCore::InfoCommandSinfulStringMyself. All exit paths from DC:ICSSM ASSERT(X.hasAddrs) or return NULL. The only path that doesn't is inside of if(shared_port_endpoint), which should never run on the shared port daemon itself. title: Ticket #7095: Schedd crash when removing scheduler universe jobs
description: When a scheduler or local universe job is removed, if the periodic job policy is evaluated immediately after the initial change in JobStatus, the job ad can leave the queue without the job or starter process being signaled that it should exit. The job will be allowed to continue running, and no final job event will be logged. For scheduler universe jobs, this could result in the schedd exiting with status 4 when the job exits with a ScheddLog entry similar to 06/21/19 11:41:35 (pid:3918818) (D_ALWAYS) scheduler universe job (7648644.0) pid 2163102 exited with status 1 06/21/19 11:41:35 (pid:3918818) (D_ALWAYS|D_FAILURE) ERROR "Assertion ERROR on (job_ad)" When a job is removed, its ad is updated and it's added to the stop_job_queue self-draining queue, which will send a signal to the job or starter process at a future date. The delay before the signal is sent is usually small, but can become large if a lot of jobs are removed at once. If the PeriodicExprHandler timer fires before stop_job_queue gets to the job, PeriodicExprHandler will call DestroyProc() on the job. This first call to DestroyProc() will add the job to the job_is_finished_queue self-draining queue, which does final cleanup on jobs ready to leave the queue. If job_is_finished_queue gets to the job before stop_job_queue, then DestroyProc() is called again, this time leading to the job leaving the queue. When stop_job_queue finally gets to the job, it can't find the job ad, so it doesn't signal the job or starter process. Once the job does exit, the reaper for scheduler universe looks up the job ad and calls ASSERT() if it doesn't find it. This bug was introduced in a bug fix in 8.8.0 (#6808). The fix allowed removed jobs whose LeaveJobInQueue expression changed from True to False to leave the queue. Prior to that, PeriodicExprHandler didn't call DestroyProc() on removed jobs.
remarks: 2019-Jun-05 09:12:05 by jfrey: Another fun detail: DestroyProc() can be called at any point during a job's lifetime, and the schedd will take the job out of the queue. Clients can do this for jobs they have rights on. 2019-Jun-05 12:45:22 by jfrey: I propose three changes to fix this bug: The schedule universe reaper logs an error and returns early if it can't get the job ad. DestroyProc() returns failure if the job isn't in COMPLETED or REMOVED status. PeriodicExprEval() doesn't call DestroyProc() if the job has a shadow_rec. I planned to have DestroyProc() make the shadow_rec check, but in the normal course of events, check_zombie() calls DestroyProc() just before the shadow_rec is deleted. Having that call to DestroyProc() succeed involved a larger change than I wanted for a stable release. 2019-Jun-19 12:28:35 by johnkn: CODE_REVIEW changes look good. I should note that the changes to not allow external qmgmt clients to destroy procs that are not in COMPLETED or REMOVED state seems reasonable, but I don't really understand the consequences here.

title: Ticket #174: condor_reconfig and friends should report security problems
description: For many client tools (including condor_reconfig, and almost certainly on, off, and restart), they simply report "Sent "Reconfig" command to daemon at <128.105.185.14:52759>". They don't report if the daemon accepted it. Indeed, if the security layer rejects it with 01/30 14:00:22 PERMISSION DENIED to unauthenticated user from host 128.105.121.21 for command 60004 (DC_RECONFIG), access level WRITE: reason: WRITE authorization policy contains no matching ALLOW entry for this request; identifiers used for this host: 128.105.121.21,chopin.cs.wisc.edu you'll have no idea. This confounds users all the time. A core problem is that the tools "fire and forget", this will require revising the protocol, potentially switching to TCP, and other work. Of course, failing for this reason deserves a non-0 exit code. (#172)

title: Ticket #5801: Master crashes after shared_port restart
description: The master will crash immediately after it restarts the shared port daemon. Immediately after restarting a daemon, the master sends an update of its ad to the collector. As part of the sinful rewriting code in ConvertDefaultIPToSocketIP(), it calls daemonCore->InfoCommandSinfulString() to fetch its sinful string. This method returns NULL for a short time after the shared port restarts, which the caller isn't expecting. We can change ConvertDefaultIPToSocketIP() to skip rewriting in this case. With this fix, the master no longer crashes. But for a short period after the shared port restart, if the master gets a reconfig, its ad in the collector and its address file will have no useful sinful strings. Within a minute, it recovers from this state.

title: Ticket #2014: Allow PrivSep to work with PID namespaces
description: We need to make sure PrivSep can work with PID namespaces. The "final" solution to #1959 was twofold: (Most of the code) Move registration of child with ProcD to the parent. (Simple flag) Ask for a PID namespace when clone'ing Talking with ZKM and Todd, we decided that we wanted to get (1) into testing ASAP (as there is a high likelihood of breakage because we're changing some pretty core control flow of daemon_core). Next up, we need to add support for PrivSep. The basic thought is we will introduce some new communication channel (perhaps a pipe) that is opened between the switchboard and the starter. The switchboard will clone/exec, but the child will be created with the CLONE_PARENT flag so the user job will become a child of the starter at birth (as opposed to the switchboard, its "natural" parent). Then, the switchboard will communicate back the PID of the child (again, perhaps through the pipe), and Create_Process will tell the starter to watch the "real child", not the switchboard. So, the task list is something like this: Commit #1959 to change the daemon_core control flow. Teach Create_Process to know about PrivSep and pass the switchboard an extra pipe for communication. Teach the switchboard how to correctly clone a new PID namespace. As part of the last item, we now have a more feature-rich means of communicating with daemon_core from the switchboard: it might be worth it to follow up in another ticket and improve error handling of exec failures.
remarks: Note: made some changes to the ticket, as it mixed cgroups and PID namespaces. I did some initial investigation into this. The basic problem with this approach is that daemon_core has no knowledge of PrivSep. This covered by a conditional when launching the process in the starter. This seems wrong. Why not make PrivSep something done by daemon_core? In such a case, this ticket would be rather straightforward. Without it, I'd have to sprinkle special PrivSep knowledge throughout the system.

title: Ticket #6954: add regression tests for submit utils.
description: Add a test that sends a variety of submit files / dictionaries to submit_utils and verifies the cluster and proc ads that are generated as a result. In support of this test. A hidden argument will be added to the -dry-run option of condor_submit so that the cluster id used for the dry run can be specified. condor_submit -dry-run:cluster=<id> <ads-file> <submit-file> will read from <submit-file> and generate cluster and proc ads and write them into <ads-file> using cluster id <id>. In this mode of operation condor_submit will assume the schedd is the same version as condor_submit, so that the test can be run without starting up a personal condor. A new perl test called cmd_submit_regress_dry will be written to make use of this option. It will use a collection of submit files specified by cmd_submit_regress_dry.subs and verify the ads using information in cmd_submit_regress_dry.expect. A similar python script will use these same files to test submit_utils through the python bindings. This is intended to be a regression test, so that in the future changes/additions to the submit language, late materialization, and/or refactoring of submit_utils can be verified without a lot of new testing effort. If possible, in the future we will compare the output of stable and development branches to insure that we don't break anything as we add new features. Another new hidden argument will be added to condor_submit to support late materialization testing. -digest <digest-file> will cause the submit digest to be written to <digest-file> in addition to being sent to the schedd. When used with -dry-run then the digest file will only be written to the file, and not sent to the schedd. This argument could be made public if users request it, but the RCFs have indicated that so far no-one has indicated an interest.

description: I think it would be really good if we could make DAGMan warnings more visible. I'm not sure what the right way is to do this -- probably needs some brainstorming. An obvious idea is emailing the user each time there's a warning, but in some circumstances that could result in them getting thousands of emails, which we don't want. Maybe we could batch emails together? Or maybe that's totally the wrong approach. Maybe we could create an html file that has error and warning messages, and encourage them to point their web browser at it? Anyhow, something I'd like to think about.

title: Ticket #6057: startd cron does not update startd policy ad
description: Gideon Juve wrote: I am having an issue where my startds reject valid claims, and I believe it is due to a bug somewhere in the startd. My startds are configured with one slot that is not partitionable. Each startd also runs a startd cron job that determines the value of the START expression that looks something like this: STARTD_CRON_JOBLIST = $(STARTD_CRON_JOBLIST) POLICY STARTD_CRON_POLICY_MODE = Periodic STARTD_CRON_POLICY_RECONFIG_RERUN = True STARTD_CRON_POLICY_PERIOD = 15m STARTD_CRON_POLICY_EXECUTABLE = get_policy_from_service Including: STARTD_CRON_AUTOPUBLISH = Always And the START expression is set like this: START = Policy And the value of Policy is updated by the cron job. When the policy needs to change, I reconfig the machine to get it to pull down its new policy from a central service. Occasionally, the policy change will cause the START expression to evaluate to TRUE when it was previously FALSE. When that happens, the collector (almost) immediately gets a new ad for the machine and it gets matched with a job. However, the startd rejects the claim for the remainder of UPDATE_INTERVAL (set to 300 seconds) until the startd reevaluates and republishes its ad again. In the rejection message in the log it prints the previous machine ad (not the one that it just sent to the collector). This leads me to believe that there is some internal state that is not getting updated when the cron job causes a new ad to be published. Eventually that state is updated the next time the startd publishes its ad. This is using 8.4.2 on Ubuntu 16.04. Preliminary investigation reveals the following problem: the startd cron job calls ResMgr::update_all() when STARTD_CRON_AUTOPUBLISH is set. ResMgr::update_all() ends up calling Resource::publish_for_update(), which calls Resource::publish() with the mask A_ALL_PUB, which calls RsMgr::adlist_publish() with the same mask. However ResMgr::adlist_publish() publishes ads (including the cron job ad) if and only if the mask has the public and update bits sets, and A_ALL_PUB does not set the update bit.
remarks: 2016-Dec-19 16:17:42 by tlmiller: It remains to be seen if this causes the reported problem, which on the surface appears to be the opposite issue. 2016-Dec-20 14:47:56 by tlmiller: Turns out that A_ALL_PUB does include A_UPDATE -- just indirectly. The actual problem is that update_all() doesn't actually update everything. title: Ticket #1287: optimize handling of shadow failure (reduce fsyncs)
description: When a shadow exits with an exception code, the schedd performs a number of updates to the job ad that are each committed as a separate durable transaction (one fsync per transaction). The result is that a fairly low rate of shadow failures can cause the schedd to become unresponsive, which causes more shadow failures. This can lead to an endless cycle of shadow failure. Eight transactions happen in _mark_job_stopped(). Additionally, there is a transaction in jobExitCode() to increment the shadow exception count. None of these transactions need to be durable.
remarks: 2010-Mar-17 11:19:25 by danb: Note that even job eviction causes mark_job_stopped() to be called, so one way to get into the cycle of failure was to start with a bunch of jobs being evicted. Then the schedd became unresponsive and the shadow failure cycle ensued.

title: Ticket #2501: clean up glexec job proxy
description: When glexec is invoked, it creates a copy of the job proxy. This proxy is not used by Condor, because we go out of our way to override X509_USER_PROXY so that the job uses the copy of the proxy managed by Condor. It is important to use the copy managed by Condor in order to make sure the job gets updates to the proxy. Condor should try to make sure the copy of the job proxy made by glexec is cleaned up. Perhaps the condor glexec job wrapper could just delete it. In versions of glexec that support disabling its creation, that could be done instead. Here is some more information from an email by Mischa: The create_target_proxy was indeed added after 0.6.8, in the 0.8 to be precise. We realized that the proxy creation behaviour in version 0.6 and below was arbitrary and indeterministic: sometimes the payload would be trying to use the pilot proxy, often there just wasn't a proxy due to internal errors. We then decided to fix this and decided how to do it. That's described on https://www.nikhef.nl/pub/projects/grid/gridwiki/index.php/Proxy_file_handling_in_gLExec This was implemented in 0.7, but we realized that the target proxy should be made optional. In the 0.8 it is still written by default but now made optional. If you are sure the payload doesn't need a proxy (no data access etc.) you can switch it off. The default proxy is a copy of the payload proxy (GLEXEC_CLIENT_CERT) owned by the target user in /tmp with a random name. The X509_USER_PROXY in the payload environment is explicitly set to that location. You have a point that if gLExec itself determined the target proxy name it probably could safely remove it (in linger mode). When the target filename is explicitly set (via GLEXEC_TARGET_PROXY) it might not be good, since the proxy might be reused by a next payload job. That was originally the motivation not to remove it, we probably should reconsider that. Once the epilogue-functionality is there (should be in the next release, before the end of this calendar year) I think that would be the right place to clean it.
remarks: 2011-Oct-05 16:07:59 by danb: Brian found that setting GLEXEC_TARGET_PROXY to the path of the proxy managed by Condor was an effective way to avoid a leaked proxy. Since glexec just copies the proxy rather than delegating it, this results in the proxy being overwritten with an identical copy, which should be harmless. Since this issue applies to both the case where the job is launched and the case where various other helper scripts are run, the solution needed to apply to both GLExecPrivSepHelper::run_script() and GLExecPrivSepHelper::create_process(). Since there was no convenient way to modify the environment in run_script() I chose to do all the environment manipulation in the glexec helper scripts, including the helper script used to launch the job.

title: Ticket #94: gridmanager mishandles gram error 156
description: Gram error 156 (JOB_CONTACT_NOT_FOUND) occurs when a client tries to contact a jobmanager but their job ids don’t match. This can happen when the jobmanager the client was talking to exits and a jobmanager for a different job is started and binds to the same port. When the gridmanage sees this error, it treats it like most other errors, first sending a STOP_JM message, then sending a cancel command, then putting the job on hold in the schedd. Instead, it should try to restart the jobmanager.
creator: jfrey

title: Ticket #5913: Consider ClaimId in collector forward filter
description: When a collector is filtering ads that it forwards to a parent collector, it should always forward a startd ad when the ClaimId changes. Otherwise, a negotiator pulling ads from the parent collector will give out stale claims that can't be used by the schedds. The ClaimId is in the private startd ad, which is not currently checked by the forwarding code. PublicClaimId, in the public startd ad, could be checked, but it's only published for Claimed slots.

title: Ticket #1403: Eliminate file transfer services started by Condor for grid universe
description: Condor starts up file transfers services under the gridmanager to perform file staging for several types of grid universe jobs: a GASS server for gt2, and a gridftp server for gt4 and cream. A remote user with a copy of the job owner's proxy can connect to these servers to read or write any file of the job owner, not just files related to their jobs. These servers also require a range of ports be opened for incoming connections, which some site admins may be reluctant to configure in their firewalls. For these reasons, we want to eliminate these file transfer services and have Condor act in a purely client mode for these job types. Milestones Build proof-of-concept file transfer code for Cream jobs [DONE] Write gridftp file transfer management code for gridmanager [DONE] Use active file transfers for Cream jobs [DONE] Use active file transfers for GRAM4 jobs [WON'T DO] Use active file transfers for GRAM2/5 jobs Add rate-limiting [DONE] Improve connection caching in nordugrid_gahp [DONE] Cream Jobs A Cream client can submit a job with a mixture of client- and server-initiated file transfers. Here is an example job description snippet: InputSandbox = { "gsiftp://remote.edu/foo/in" }; OutputSandbox = { "out1", "out2" }; OutputSandboxDestURI = { "gsiftp://localhost/out1", "gsiftp://remote.edu/foo/out2" }; When the job is first submitted, the client is given gridftp URLs for an Input Sandbox (ISB) and an Output Sandbox (OSB). These are directories used to hold input and output files transferred by the client. In this example, the server will transfer the files in and out2 between itself and remote.edu. In addition, the client can transfer additional input files to the ISB before signaling that the job should be started (i.e. submitted to the batch system behind the Cream server). Once the job completes, out1 will be available in the OSB for the client to retrieve. If the client wants to retrieve all output files itself, it can use wildcards to say that all output files should be saved. This removes the need to name all output files using transfer_output_files in the Condor submit file.

title: Ticket #4251: Eviction while ssh_to_job is active crashes the starter
description: When the starter spawns an sshd to handle condor_ssh_to_job, it creates an SSHDProc object and gives it a pointer to a ClassAd allocated on the stack. After the current call returns, the SSHDProc object has a pointer to an invalid area of memory in the stack. Any attempts to access it are likely to cause a crash. One way this happens is if the starter is told to shutdown while the ssh_to_job session is still active. The shutdown code looks at the SSHDProc's job ad to see what signal should be sent to kill the sshd process. title: Ticket #1116: Queue-management constraints shouldn't use TARGET scoping
description: The schedd's queue-management interface takes ClassAd expressions to constrain the set of job ads that a command will act upon. Although most expressions provided by clients use no scoping for their attribute references, some do use the 'target' scope, and the schedd (using EvalBool()), evaluates the expressions with the job ad as the target scope and using no local scope. When we switch to new ClassAds, this means most expressions won't evaluate properly. The changes to EvalBool() for new ClassAds (#1115) provides a temporary solution by stripping off the 'target' scopes in the expressions. For the long term, clients should stop using 'target' scopes in their constraint expressions. Then eventually, the code to strip off 'target' scopes can be removed. The CondorQ object should ensure that all expressions it sends to the schedd don't have any 'target' scoping in their attribute references.

title: Ticket #123: Grand unified param() system: Phase 1
description: Problems with configuring Condor: Documentation of features, the actual implementation, and the sample configuration files are separated, making it easy for them to drift apart. Condor is hard pressed to provide useful error messages or context when a setting is invalid. If a single setting is used (param()ed) in multiple places in the code, it's possible for them to drift and end up with different acceptable values or defaults. condor_config_val cannot report default values Creating a tool to present settings in a more user friendly way isn't terribly practical. Solution: A Grand Unified Configuration Table. The code would contain a single file that listed all configuration options, defaults, acceptable format (integer, floating point number, expression, string, etc), the acceptable range, acceptable length, which daemons or tools it impacts, the "category" and the documentation marked up in some simple to parse way. The documentation would not need to specifically mention the defaults or acceptable ranges as it's available in the other fields. There would also be a new tool, probably not distributed to users, which spits out the data in structured form on demand. It would use the category and daemon name to organize the entries. It could emit condor_config.generic (using the description stripped of all formatting as a comment). It could emit LaTeX for inclusion in the manual, this time using reformatting description. A flag day isn't really reasonable, but the old and new systems can exist side by side, with new code using the new system and old code converted as its convenient. If we integrate documentation into the system, it needs to be available for Karen to edit. Karen doesn't generally check out the code, and requiring both the code and the documentation would complicate just building the manual. And if we do the obvious: cramming the documentation in as C strings, we've added yet another escaping system to worry about. So this needs consideration. A possibility: Instead of going code to documentation, we might be able to go documentation to code: keep the documentation in LaTeX in CONDOR_DOC, and suck it into the code as part of the build process. Or keep the documentation and settings in a third file and pull it into both the documentation and the code. Benefits The act of adding a new configuration variable could automatically create at least a minimal configuration example and documentation entry. condor_config_val could automatically write out a default condor_config configuration file. condor_config_val can report defaults with something like, "EXAMPLE_SETTING not found. Using default of 42." condor_config_val can also provide on-demand documentation. When EXCEPTing because an invalid configuration setting was found, the description and acceptable limits could be shown to guide the user in fixing it. Testing for invalid configuration would be in a single shared location, simplifying code elsewhere that already validates input. With this single repository of data, various tools to present different, specialized views of the configuration file become practical. For example, if categorization is implemented or supplemented with tags, you could tag settings by which daemon they impact, and if they are security, performance, scalability, or something else. Then a user with a slow schedd can ask to see all setting tagged "schedd" and "scalability". (This is based on various previous suggestions, including psilord's message "ccv -dump" sent to condor-staff on Janury 26th, 2007, GNATS 716: and GNATS 819. It was imported from 1712 (backup) 1712 (public)) Milestones Hack upon the perl script for table generation [DONE] Debugging, submission to NMI, documenting. [Monday July 15th, 2009]

title: Ticket #4314: Shared port blocking
description: Since shared port no longer forks, any blocking behavior is very painful. I think I found a case where things currently block. It goes like this: Client requests daemon X from shared port. Shared port does socket passing to daemon X Shared port returns to DC and registers the socket for callback, setting a deadline. Daemon X does not respond. Deadline for client socket passes. Shared port fires command handler, which calls get() on the socket. This may block completely or for some amount of time set by the socket's timeout. We should call get() non-blocking regardless (in case if the daemon has a partial response, then goes to sleep) and we should make sure that if get() times out we fail the request if the socket's deadline has passed.
remarks: 2014-Apr-15 20:57:48 by bbockelm: Pushed a fix. To test: Setup a personal condor instance with shared port enabled and D_FULLDEBUG for shared port. Submit a handful of fake jobs. SIGSTOP the startd. Observe the shared port logs. The schedd should start shadows that try to talk to the startd. These will have a deadline of 20s. After 20s, look for log lines of the form "SharedPortClient - server response deadline has passed for..." referencing the SHADOW communication. Verify that it is indeed about 20s since the shadow tried to initiate contact.
