title: Ticket #3828: HA schedd frequently blocks on dead collector
description: When the first collector in an HA setup is on a dead machine, the schedd frequently blocks for a minute while trying to connect to it. 07/29/13 22:47:30 Sending RESCHEDULE command to negotiator(s) 07/29/13 22:47:30 Will use UDP to update collector condor01 <IP1:9618> 07/29/13 22:47:30 Will use UDP to update collector condor02 <IP2:9618> 07/29/13 22:47:30 Trying to query collector <IP1:9618> 07/29/13 22:47:31 attempt to connect to <IP1:9618> failed: No route to host (connect errno = 113). Will keep trying for 60 total seconds (59 to go). 07/29/13 22:48:30 attempt to connect to <IP1:9618> failed: No route to host (connect errno = 113). 07/29/13 22:48:30 Will avoid querying collector condor02 <IP2:9618> for 3540s if an alternative succeeds. 07/29/13 22:48:30 Trying to query collector <IP2:9618> Despite the message about avoiding the dead collector for an hour, it hits it again the next time it tries to send the RESCHEDULE command. The collector list is not being reused in this code. At a lower level, it is not a good idea to keep retrying and blocking on the connection after getting "No route to host".
remarks: I should note that the origin of this buggy behavior is much older than 8.0. It may even be older than 7.0. 2013-Jul-31 16:53:40 by danb: I have submitted a patch that fixes the low-level problem of trying in a blocking loop to connect to a host that is dead. The high-level problem still needs to be fixed, because each attempt to connect to a dead host still typically takes a second or two to fail (as opposed to the minimum of one minute it took to fail prior to the low-level fix). The problem is that each time sendReschedule() is called, a new query is performed to look up the address of the negotiator. Inside Daemon::getDaemonInfo(), we instantiate a new CollectorList. Inside there is some code to remember that a particular collector wasted a bunch of our time when we tried to connect to it. But this knowledge is not preserved, because it is chucked out when the CollectorList is destructed. 2013-Aug-01 10:01:27 by smoler: Note: Commit on Aug 1 by Karen is cherry pick of 8.0.2 version history item that got committed on master branch. Cherry pick is into V8_0-branch. 2013-Aug-07 20:28:23 by sfiligoi: How about the use case where the Collector is simply not running? E.g. due to the fact that it is undergoing software maintenance? And what about the use case of completely lost packets? No ICMP reply? Will the HA code switch fast to the next collector in these cases? 2013-Aug-08 10:01:33 by danb: The low-level fix is indeed still vulnerable to a lengthy connection delay. It is therefore important to have the higher-level code remember this and failover to the next collector for a while. That does happen in some parts of condor, but not in the schedd when sending a RESCHEDULE command. 2013-Aug-12 17:20:00 by danb: I created a patch for the higher-level problem. Now the record of painfully long collector queries is kept globally in each daemon, rather than only surviving as long as the CollectorList object. I have committed this to the master branch. It could be cherry picked back into V8_0-branch if there is strong enough need for it, and it is deemed safe enough. 2013-Aug-20 11:30:17 by tlmiller: CODE REVIEW This review is for the 8.0.2 patch only (37056), which looks good.

title: Ticket #4197: NUM_CPUS should have a default value in the config system
description: the configuration value NUM_CPUS, can be used to override the number of CPUS that the STARTD uses for provisioning the slots, but it has no default value in the config system. This causes a great deal of user confusion, and in fact even developer confusion. For instance VM_MAX_NUMBER is set to $(NUM_CPUS) by default, but by default NUM_CPUS has no value! The STARTD behaves as if NUM_CPUS was set by default to either DECTECTED_CORES (which includes hyperthreads) or to the actual number of physical cores depending on the configuration value of COUNT_HYPERTHREAD_CPUS. Unfortunately, this cannot be the default value of of NUM_CPUS since we don't know the state of COUNT_HYPERTHREAD_CPUS until after config has already been parsed. So the solution seems to be to have a new detected config variable DETECTED_CPUS. This is initially set to the number of hyperthreaded cores, then config is parsed. Then it is set to the number of physical, or hyperthreaded cores depending on the final state of COUNT_HYPERTHREAD_CPUS. The new config variable DETECTED_CPUS cannot be modified by the user (we just set it again after config is done). As a user convenience, there will also be a new detected config variable DETECTED_PHYSICAL_CPUS which is the count of only physical cpus, and will not include hyperthreads. NUM_CPUS will be set to $(DETECTED_CPUS) in the param table, but can still be overridden by the startd. the implementation of sysapi_ncpus should be changed to always return the count of actual physical and actual hyperthreaded cores, so that queries of sysapi get back real values. The STARTD should be changed to param NUM_CPUS when provisioning rather than using sysapi_ncpus.

title: Ticket #6903: GPU utilization can use different device index than GPU discovery
description: There was a report on condor_users that the device indexes reported by condor_gpu_utilization don't match the indexes reported by condor_gpu_discovery on the same machine. A close reading of the NVIDIA header files for the nvml library seem to confirm that this is a possibility. The nvml library may enumerate the GPUs in a different order than the driver and runtime library do. Apparently we are supposed to use the nvml functions nvmlDeviceGetHandleByPciBusId or nvmlDeviceGetHandleDeviceByUuid rather than nvmlDeviceGetHandleByIndex as we currently do. This means that condor_gpu_utilization will have to replicate at least some of the device enumeration code in condor_gpu_discovery so that it will know what Uuid or PciID had been assigned to each CUDA index, and then adjust its SlotMergeConstraint to tie utilization values to the correct CUDA devices In the long run, it might be less work to move the functionality of condor_gpu_utilization into condor_gpu_discovery, perhaps by making it part of the -dynamic output.

title: Ticket #4894: Report memory usage of VMs incorrect.
description: From #4338: Broken in testing on CHTC. Sometimes a VMU job will report correctly: 006 (171360.000.000) 12/16 13:25:37 Image size of job updated: 2097152 2097152 - ResidentSetSize of job (KB) ... sometimes it will get 006 (171404.000.000) 12/16 13:28:47 Image size of job updated: 8029125568646952238 959329332 - ResidentSetSize of job (KB) ... which is wrong in at least two ways. I see two things worth investigating: the conversion from unsigned long to long long when adding the memory value to the string before sending it to the starter, and the starter converting that value into a signed long int, instead. Second, the data structure in question is never zeroed; perhaps in certain cases the memory usage field is never filled out and we're picking arbitrary garbage off the stack? Was only able to reproduce once; analysis indicated the problem was probably occurring in shadow or the schedd, and may be the result of a race condition (although that doesn't make a whole lot of sense, since neither of those have VMU-specific code; maybe the unmasking factor is that the VMU doesn't send a memory size update until well after the initial execution report?).

title: Ticket #5769: Fix HAD|REPLICATION configuration incompability.
description: In 8.5.5, working HAD configurations looked something like this: HAD_PORT = 12345 HAD_ARGS = -p $(HAD_PORT) HAD_LIST = $(CM1):$(HAD_PORT), $(CM2):$(HAD_PORT) The REPLICATION daemon had the same set-up. In 8.5.6, this configuration needed to change to the following because we wanted shared port to be the default: HAD_PORT = 12345 HAD_ARGS = -p $(HAD_PORT) HAD_LIST = $(CM1):$(HAD_PORT), $(CM2):$(HAD_PORT) REPLICATION_SOCKET_NAME = HAD.USE_SHARED_PORT = FALSE We should work around the need to unset REPLICATION_SOCKET_NAME by changing the relevant HAD code to assume that the replication daemon(s) are using shared port if and only if HAD itself is; it would then become harmless to leave REPLICATION_SOCKET_NAME set to its default ("REPLICATION"). However, setting a subsystem knob in the param table is generally frowned upon as being, at best, counter-intuitive. TJ recommends, instead, that we make HAD_USE_SHARED_PORT and REPLICATION_USE_SHARED_PORT (possibly the latter should default to the former, given the assumption above) first-class configuration knobs respected by the master (for any daemon who shares the HAD or REPLICATION daemon binary) and the HAD and REPLICATION daemons themselves. We would still have some counter-intuitive behaviour, because USE_SHARED_PORT would no longer control all daemons, but since it currently doesn't control HAD or REPLICATION, this might actually be less confusing than the current set-up.

title: Ticket #5293: Clarify DAG priority documentation
description: From htcondor-users today: I would like to raise something which is unclear in the documentation, and that's around the idea of "priority". At first glance it seems that there are two distinct and unrelated priorities. (1) The job priority, which is set in the submit file with "priority = XXX" or using the condor_prio command line tool, and is reflected in the JobPrio ClassAd attribute. When there is a choice of jobs in the queue to be run next, for the same user/accounting group, then the negotiator will pick the one with the highest priority. http://research.cs.wisc.edu/htcondor/manual/current/condor_submit.html "priority = <integer> An HTCondor job priority can be any integer, with 0 being the default. Jobs with higher numerical priority will run before jobs with lower numerical priority. Note that this priority is on a per user basis. One user with many jobs may use this command to order his/her own jobs, and this will have no effect on whether or not these jobs will run ahead of another user's jobs." (2) The DAG node priority, which is set using the "PRIORITY <node> <value>" statement in the DAG file. When condor_dagman has a choice of which jobs to submit next into the queue, it chooses the one with the highest priority. http://research.cs.wisc.edu/htcondor/manual/current/2_10DAGMan_Applications.html#SECTION003108300000000000000 "The node priority affects the order in which nodes that are ready at the same time will be submitted. Note that node priority does not override the DAG dependencies. Node priority is mainly relevant if node submission is throttled via the -maxjobs or -maxidle command-line arguments or the DAGMAN_MAX_JOBS_SUBMITTED or DAGMAN_MAX_JOBS_IDLE configuration variables." Now, the documentation doesn't say at this point if the DAG node priority is related to the job priority. However, testing shows that it is (see end of message). What appears to happen is that the DAG node priority is also being used as the job priority. Not only that, but the DAG node priority overrides any job priority set explicitly in the submit file. On reading the documentation again, there is a hint of this behaviour where it says later on: "There is no way to change the priority in the submit description file for a job, as DAGMan will override any priority command placed in a submit description file." But until that point, I couldn't find any indication that the DAG node priority was in any way related to the job priority. Where this becomes important is where I've made a DAG with explicit node priorities - influencing the order in which things are run to optimise throughput - but then I decide that I want one DAG to take priority over another. It seems now that I have to apply offsets to all the DAG node priorities. I don't really have a problem with this behaviour - indeed it would probably be confusing to have two distinct priorities - but I think it could be made a lot clearer in the documentation for condor_dagman. The following would do the trick: "The PRIORITY keyword assigns a priority to a DAG node. The syntax for PRIORITY is PRIORITY JobName PriorityValue The node priority affects the order in which nodes that are ready at the same time will be submitted, and it also sets the job's priority in the queue, i.e. its JobPrio attribute. Note that node priority does not override the DAG dependencies."

title: Ticket #2556: File transfer attributes ignored for vm universe
description: The submit attributes should_transfer_files and when_to_transfer_output are ignored in many situations for vm universe jobs. The assumption is that the user always wants file transfer. The user should be able to request that files should never be transferred. Also, if the user tries to set these attributes to enable file transfer, condor_submit prints a warning that they may be typos.
remarks: 2013-Jul-17 13:01:07 by tlmiller: It is at best rather disconcerting for the manual (http://research.cs.wisc.edu/htcondor/manual/v8.0/2_11Virtual_Machine.html) to say For Xen and KVM jobs, if any files need to be transferred from the submit machine to the machine where the vm universe job will execute, HTCondor must be explicitly told to do so with the standard file transfer attributes: should_transfer_files = YES when_to_transfer_output = ON_EXIT transfer_input_files = /myxen/diskfile.img,/myxen/swap.img Any and all needed files on a system without a shared file system (between the submit machine and the machine where the job will execute) must be listed. WARNING: the line `when_to_transfer_output = ON_EXIT' was unused by condor_submit. Is it a typo? WARNING: the line `should_transfer_files = TRUE' was unused by condor_submit. Is it a typo? especially since it implies that you can't pre-stage KVM images, or load them from a shared filesystem. That is, if it is possible for when_to_transfer_output or should_transfer_files to be meaningful, condor_submit should never complain about them -- it's not wrong to specify the default. (This can be useful for self-documenting submit files, or if the default changes.) The interaction between vm_no_output_vm and transfer_output_files is also confusing, because vm_no_output_vm doesn't just prevent disk images from being transferred by default, but actually deletes them before file transfer occurs -- making what seems to be the obvious way of getting only one of the disk images back an inefficient way of putting the job on hold. It would be nice if condor_submit warned when both were set, since vm_no_output_vm is superflous when transfer_output_files is set. (If the VM disks aren't listed, they aren't coming back, and if they are, you specifically said you wanted them.)
creator: jfrey

title: Ticket #5339: TCP_FORWARDING_HOST disregarded.
description: Because TCP_FORWARDING_HOST is present only in the original Sinful, and not in the addrs parameter, recent versions of HTCondor will correctly advertise the forwarding host but completely ignore it. This causes us grief in the cloud, where it's fairly common for instances to have public IP addresses that aren't actually present on any interface in the instance. (This applies to EC2, where we recommend using TCP_FORWARDING_HOST rather than CCB; but Jan Balewski was having trouble using TCP_FORWARDING_HOST as early as 8.3.6 in an OpenStack VM setup, where the internal[ly-reported] IP is different than the external IP.)
remarks: 2015-Oct-26 11:18:18 by tlmiller: The patch permits TCP_FORWARDING_HOST to be either an IPv4 or an IPv6 address, but preserves the other protocol in the addrs entry. This is arguably a semantic change, given the manual definition, but since the manual's definition can be obtained by turning off the offending protocol, Alan and I decided that the flexibility was probably worth it. This patch does not support setting TCP_FORWARDING_HOST with a hostname (unless from_ip_string() is more ambitious than is probably wise). (The existing, backwards-compability code however, will; on the other hand, it could also return an IPv6 address, so who knows.) Do we want to support this moving forward? 2015-Oct-26 13:45:52 by adesmet: Code Review Needs change to documentation and an entry in the version history gotcha if we're going to change behavior to no longer accept hostnames. if fa.from_ip_string fails (that is, fa.is_valid() == false), we should log a warning that we're ignoring TCP_FORWARDING_HOST. 2015-Oct-26 14:17:16 by tlmiller: Duplicated the existing bad logic for hostname resolution, as this was easier than (a) documenting the change or (b) figuring out something sane and documenting /that/. 2015-Oct-26 17:18:37 by adesmet: Code Review Approved.

title: Ticket #1680: Job should be able to emit heartbeat to the starter
description: We are currently hosting some services for NEOS by running them as jobs under Condor. From time to time, these services hang. We have control over the source of these python-based services. It would be very useful to define a heartbeat protocol between the job and the starter. This way, condor could restart the job when it hangs, and clean up the sandbox. There are many possible implementations. I think if the job somehow sent a cedar CHILD_ALIVE message to the starter periodically, everything would just work. Obviously, that's tight coupling, and authentication might be a bit of a trick. Maybe the job could touch a file in the sandbox, and use that as a keepalive. Or SOAP, or ... ?

We currently tell people that they can do the same for their job by making it a script that executes their job and monitors it. However, turning cmd = /usr/bin/matlab args = ... queue into cmd = matlab_plus.sh args = ... queue is actually a non-trivial task, in any number of ways - from file-transfer semantics changing to the complexity of properly spawning (not exec'ing) and managing the actual job to identically model the life-cycle. What about a parallel management process that shares the execution environment of the job itself, e.g. cmd = /usr/bin/matlab args = ... monitor = my_monitor.sh queue my_monitor.sh can chirp and squawk. Semantics of monitor - o spawned after job (controlled by monitor_start_lag in seconds, provided job parent pid) o terminated after job completion (controlled by monitor_exit_lag in seconds) . possibly signaled about job termination, or not, make it just wait . possibly provided access to exit information of job o policy for termination during job execution . possibly just say no effect (like monitor_exit_fatal = false) . possibly monitor_exit_fatal = bool + true = terminate job and follow WANT_HOLD policy - NOTE: This is a place where we pick semantics + false = allow job to continue o resource consumption of monitor charged to job 2010-Sep-28 13:38:35 by matt: Re: "a job" as in not under the Master - All DaemonCore processes should be able to handle CHILD_ALIVE, including the Starter. 2011-Jan-27 14:50:47 by danb: Bulk change of target version from v070505 to v070506 using ./ticket-target-mover. 2011-Feb-01 16:20:02 by tannenba: Bulk change of target version from v070506 to NULL using ./ticket-target-mover.

title: Ticket #2805: KBDD broken on Windows, again
description: The kbdd was broken yet again very, very early in the 7.6 series and remains broken in the 7.7 series. How no one else seems to have noticed is completely beyond me at this point. The issue is roughly the same. The kbdd has its own main function, specifically, a WinMain function so that it creates a windowless "Window" application so that the user does not see anything visible. In 7.6, somehow the daemon_core main overrode it even though in 7.4 and 7.5 the WinMain was functioning as expected, especially since I had to implement passing on of command line arguments through it to the daemon_core main. In 7.7, the daemon_core main was moved into each specific daemon, including kbdd. This new main again overrode the WinMain and in both cases kbdd ended up being built as a command line application instead of a Windows application. Short term fix: In 7.6, override daemon_core's main with WinMain again. In 7.7, just move the relevant code in the kbdd crt main into WinMain and delete the crt main. Long term fix: Replace kbdd with something that does not carry all of daemon_core's baggage and dependencies. We do not need something so complicated just to watch and notify the startd of keyboard and mouse activity.

title: Ticket #2669: race condition in hibernation
description: In linux, after initiating hibernation, the startd sleeps for 10 seconds and then resumes normal operation. If hibernation completes within the sleep, all is well. If hibernation does not complete until after the end of the sleep, the startd will likely send a new ad to the collector, which has the side-effect of removing its persistent offline ad. Then when hibernation happens, the startd will have no offline ad to represent it. Therefore, the machine will never be woken by rooster and must be revived by some other means. It is not clear to me if a similar problem affects windows. The sleep(10) does not happen, but the issue is clouded by a confusing comment in the code that suggests hibernation is still asynchronous. I can think of two possible lines of attack: make the switch to hibernation block until complete revamp the concept of offline ads so that they are not lost when the machine advertises its online status The second option sounds more fault-tolerant, but will require more thought.
creator: danb

title: Ticket #2393: Job attribute "Arguments" appears as "Args" for Negotiator
description: Job classad attribute "Arguments" is seen as such by the Startd. The Negotiator however receives this attribute under the title "Args". Therefore, if policy decisions should be made on the Startd side based on "Arguments" the same expression also needs to be added for "Args" such that the Negotiator is able to handle it correctly. Example: Jobs with argument "force" should run immediately and preempt other jobs. This could lead to a RANK expression in the Startd of RANK = (Arguments =?= "force") However, this RANK will never be honored by the Negotiator as "Arguments" is undefined there. A workaround would be RANK = ( (Arguments =?= "force") || (Args =?= "force") ) To me this seems like either a consistency that should be documented or a bug.

title: Ticket #82: Review log timestamp format
description: The current timestamp format is strftime("%m/%d %H:%M:%S "...) in the upcoming 7.3.0. We should review it, and perhaps enhance it. (In 7.2.x and earlier, it's "%d/%d %02d:%02d:%02d " (month, day, hour, minute, second).) Possible enhancements: Add the year as the first element. Disk is cheap, and 5 extra bytes per line isn't going to break the bank. Pro: It's occasionally useful when facing very long log files that span 3 or more years. I've run into this in Rust occasionally. It's useful when you run into antique log files. Eliminates confusion if "12/1" is "Jan 12" (European style) or "Dec 1" (US style). 2009/12/01 is pretty unambiguously yyyy/mm/dd. This also helps US readers near the beginning of the year, where they may be expecting 1/12, see 12/1, and accidentally swap them. You can more easily pass the log through sort, even when the log spans a year, and get useful results. This can be useful if you're merging multiple files. (Of course, this necessitates the "pad dates" enhancement listed below.) Con: 99% of the time, it's deadweight. Done Pad month and date to 2 digits. (02/09 instead of 2/9) Disk is cheap, 0-2 bytes per line is negligable. Implemented in the master (7.3.0) as a side effect of switching to strftime("%m/%d...") Pro: You can more easily pass the log through sort and get useful results. This can be useful if you're merging multiple files. Con: 90% of the time, it's deadweight.

title: Ticket #5006: Dynamic Concurrency Limits
description: Enhancement Request Currently, the concurrency limits applied to a given job are evaluated before matchmaking starts. This prevents us from using machine attributes to determine the concurrency limit to apply. For example, we could do a partial evaluation of the concurrency limits in the current place; if that results in a ClassAd value, we apply concurrency limits immediately. Otherwise, we re-evaluate the attribute in the context of the potential match. Use Case CMS has a certain class (high-IO jobs) of jobs that can easily overwhelm site storage systems if too many such jobs are run on a single site. When there are several potential sites to chose from for running the job, we do not know the correct concurrency limit to apply unless we have a startd ad. I'm thinking our ConcurrencyLimit attribute will look like: ConcurrencyLimit = strcat("IO.", target.GLIDEIN_CMSSite) Currently, our "manure spreader" enforces this limit by limiting the number of high-IO jobs for a given site in the queue. This is very problematic; if the limit is 100 and there are N manure spreaders, then we have to set the limit to 100/N per schedd. If we have a non-random distribution of jobs between schedds (and we do), then we typically end up running 100/N high-IO jobs instead of the desired 100.

I like how the code does exactly what it did before if the concurrency limit is just a string. Jaime is going to do a more complete code review, but after a quick look-over: 1. In method rejectForConcurrencyLimits() this line looks suspicious: if (lastRejectedConcurrencyString == limits) {return false;} Seems at first blush like we want to return true here in order to reject, not false, right? 2. Patch should have a regression test; given item 1 above, not sure how much this patch was smoke tested. A regression test should be pretty simple to do in a personal condor. 3. Not excited about the call to EXCEPT if a limit drops below zero. I know that this patch is not responsible for this issue (i.e. it existed before this patch), but still seems very extreme to shutdown the entire matchmaker -vs- just logging something and refusing the match. 2015-Jun-15 22:28:47 by bbockelm: For the record, here's the submit file I used to test: executable = foo.sh log = test.log output = foo/test.out error = foo/test.err +ConcurrencyLimits=OpSys queue 20 I setup a 6 static slots and set the linux concurrency limit to 3. I then verified: From an empty cluster, a single negotiation cycle matched three slots. *: Additional slots in the match list were rejected. I uncommented the debug statement to make sure the rejection information was being cached. As claims were released (set CLAIM_WORKLIFE=0), concurrency limits were respected. I'll need help with a regression test here. 2015-Jun-16 11:10:40 by jfrey: More Code Review In addition to the items Todd mentioned before, I have one concern: In matchmakingAlgorithm(), when you try to pull a candidate from a populated MatchList, you return failure (no machines matched) if the top candidate exceeded a concurrency limit. Since different candidates can result in different limits, you need to keep looking at additional candidates. Your concurrency limit check should be moved into the preceding loop that pops candidates and checks for going over the submitter limit. 2015-Jun-16 12:19:14 by bbockelm: Good catch! Fix pushed. To validate, I used the same setup as before, but verified via inspecting the debug logs that the match list was utilized for each job (not rebuilt) and each entry inspected, even if there's a rejection. Brian 2015-Jun-19 16:20:14 by tannenba: Moving this ticket back to docpending status. We need more than just a version history blurb in the manual for this change. The section on Concurrency Limits, the condor_submit manpage, the Job Classad attributes section... they should all mention that the concurrency limits attribute in the job ad can either be a string (like it always has been) or a classad expression evaluated in the context of the candidate slot ad that should evaluate to a string. An example in the Concurrency Limits section of the manual (explaining the motivation/scenario and showing both a sample job submit similar to how this ticket does) would also be desirable.

title: Ticket #1803: vm_gahp xen/kvm script callouts as wrong user
description: Due to a bug in a code refactoring for 7.4.4, script callouts from the vm_gahp that should happen as root instead happen as the executing user. However, none of the callouts need to happen as root, since all interactions with libvirt occur via the client library now. Condor 7.5.4 is also affected. We'll do the following changes now. Additional changes can wait for later. Fix systemCommand() to perform callouts as root when requested. Remove check for uid root from condor_vm_xen.sh. Remove call to virsh from check routine in condor_vm_xen.sh.

title: Ticket #3994: Require DAGMan to run in workflow log mode?
description: I'm wondering whether, at some point, we should transition to requiring DAGMan to run in workflow log mode, disallowing the monitoring of individual log files specified in the node job submit files. This would simplify a bunch of other things, especially #3993 and #3889). The main down side I can think of with this is that such a DAGMan could not run on a pre-7.9 schedd. I guess as we get further past 7.9 this will eventually, at least, not be much of an issue. (Also see #3889, #3843.)
remarks: 2013-Oct-18 14:37:02 by wenger: I wonder if we should switch over to this fairly soon and see if anyone screams (in 8.1, not 8.0 obviously). Doing this would actually clear up a lot of #3334, and I think we could cut a fair amount of code out of DAGMan once we were sure we didn't need to backtrack. 2013-Oct-21 14:14:50 by wenger: Hmm -- the more I think about this, the more I think we should do it. We could disable non-workflow log mode and do a release, and then if nobody screams after a while, remove the code needed to deal with non-workflow log mode. 2013-Oct-21 14:31:42 by wenger: Peter and Stuart, do you see any problem with this from the LIGO end? Are you ever forcing DAGMan to run in non-workflow log mode? The change would take effect in the 8.1 series, so if you're staying with stable series only you wouldn't see it for quite a while. 2013-Oct-21 15:38:06 by pfc: I don't see any reason we would need to run 7.9 or earlier DAGMan jobs on 8.2 or later schedds, so if I correctly understand that to be the only real issue, then I think we have no problem with this. 2013-Oct-21 16:56:58 by wenger: If we actually do this, this ticket should just refer to disabling non-workflow log mode and updating the manual. There should be a derived ticket for taking all of the non-workflow log code out of DAGMan. 2014-Jan-24 10:52:22 by wenger: One note -- I just remembered that workflow log mode doesn't work for Stork nodes, so if we still support Stork nodes we have to leave some of the old-style code in place. 2014-May-12 10:30:55 by pfc: I don't think anyone has used Stork in forever. I would deprecate support for it if I were you. 2014-Aug-11 11:42:06 by wenger: Hmm -- something to think about here: should we completely remove the -dont_use_default_node_log command line flag and DAGMAN_ALWAYS_USE_NODE_LOG config code, or should we leave them in place but report errors if they're used? If we completely remove them, using the command-line flag would generate an error, but using the config macro would be silently ignored. Also, if we leave the code in place, should these options still be documented, but noted as no longer allowed? Or should we take them totally out of the documentation? 2014-Aug-12 10:20:09 by pfc: I think that if you remove them, (a) specifying them should produce a warning or error (lest people get confused); and (b) they should remain in the documentation (for a few years, if not forever) with a note saying that the feature has been removed as of version x.y.z (and if possible, a concise explanation of why or a link to the ticket) so that anyone who is bitten by it (or searches for it based on an old email) can easily understand what happened... 2014-Aug-12 11:05:11 by wenger: Yes, I talked with Karen Miller about this yesterday, and that's pretty much the plan we came up with... 2014-Aug-12 12:20:34 by wenger: Note: Documentation can't get fully updated until #2218 (Add a command-line option to put DAGMan into recovery mode?) is merged into the master. 2014-Aug-12 14:43:31 by wenger: This has been committed to master; I'm going to assign it to Zach for a retroactive review. 2015-Oct-21 11:54:51 by wenger: I'm going to resolve this, since it's been in the code for over a year now...

title: Ticket #2686: PSS doesn't work reliably
description: Proportional Set Size detection doesn't appear to work reliably. At Nebraska, it appears to work for only about 40% of the slots. root@red-man /etc/puppet/modules/condor/files/config.d> condor_q -pool red-condor.unl.edu -g -const 'ProportionalSetSizeKb is null && JobStatus == 2' -run | grep slot | wc -l 1069 root@red-man /etc/puppet/modules/condor/files/config.d> condor_q -pool red-condor.unl.edu -g -const 'ProportionalSetSizeKb isnt null && JobStatus == 2' -run | grep slot | wc -l 723 In fact, if I query a specific host, it appears that it only sporadicly works for different slots on a host: root@red-man /etc/puppet/modules/condor/files/config.d> condor_q -pool red-condor.unl.edu -g -const 'ProportionalSetSizeKb is null && JobStatus == 2' -run | grep node166.red.hcc.unl.edu 2016333.0 uscmsPool1026 11/29 12:32 0+08:20:58 slot6@node166.red.hcc.unl.edu 2049759.0 cmsprio051 12/3 12:24 0+03:26:52 slot4@node166.red.hcc.unl.edu 2049780.0 cmsprio050 12/3 12:24 0+03:24:43 slot2@node166.red.hcc.unl.edu 2049786.0 cmsprio050 12/3 12:24 0+03:24:43 slot8@node166.red.hcc.unl.edu 2050682.0 hcc 12/3 12:53 0+02:49:41 slot7@node166.red.hcc.unl.edu 2051810.0 cmsprio062 12/3 13:08 0+02:42:47 slot3@node166.red.hcc.unl.edu root@red-man /etc/puppet/modules/condor/files/config.d> condor_q -pool red-condor.unl.edu -g -const 'ProportionalSetSizeKb isnt null && JobStatus == 2' -run | grep node166.red.hcc.unl.edu 106558.0 cmsprio049 12/3 12:29 0+03:19:28 slot1@node166.red.hcc.unl.edu 107463.0 uscmsPool1355 12/3 13:40 0+02:07:51 slot5@node166.red.hcc.unl.edu I'm not able to discern any patterns as to why this might be happening.
remarks: 2011-Dec-06 14:01:18 by danb: Just to be clear: it is expected for ProportionalSetSizeKb to be missing for running jobs that have run for less than the shadow update interval (default 15 minutes). I can query your schedd and confirm that there are many jobs older than this which exhibit the problem. Strangely, I do not see this problem in CHTC, which is running 7.7.4. There have been no recent code changes relevant to this, as far as I know. Do you find any error messages matching 'smaps' or 'Pss' in ProcLog and/or ProcLog.STARTD? If so, could you please get a copy of /proc/<pid>/smaps for one of the job processes? 2011-Dec-09 11:26:11 by gthain: There is a bug in the pss code, in that we read the /proc/pid/smaps files in 512 byte chunks, and if the "Pss: xxx Kb" line crosses the boundary, we won't read it. 2011-Dec-12 10:36:38 by danb: Greg, I don't see the bug you mentioned. We read lines in 512 bytes chunks. Am I missing something? 2012-Jan-06 19:43:28 by bbockelm: Dan and I spent some time looking at this. There weren't any error messages in the ProcdLog when the procd was run by hand. 2012-Jan-07 11:21:20 by bbockelm: Some more mysterious behavior: root@red-man ~> condor_q -g -const '(ProportionalSetSizeKb_RAW > 0) && (ResidentSetSize > 0) && ProportionalSetSizeKb_RAW > ResidentSetSize' -format '%d ' ClusterId -format '%d ' ProportionalSetSizeKb_RAW -format '%d\n' ResidentSetSize | wc -l 846 This shows that there are 846 jobs where PSS > RSS; by definition, PSS <= RSS. I did take a look at a few random jobs, and does not appear to be startup effects. 2012-Jan-07 14:36:58 by bbockelm: Scratch that last update: it appears some startd's run code that predates #2632. 2014-Jul-28 13:02:03 by bbockelm: Closing old ticket. Reopen as necessary.

title: Ticket #7484: oauth credentials are swept too quickly
description: When a user has no jobs in the queue, the schedd may write a <username>.mark file in the SEC_CREDENTIAL_DIRECTORY, which tells the credd (I think?) that all of the user's tokens should be deleted. This causes a race between when a user obtains tokens and when the user submits a job that uses said tokens. If the schedd notices too quickly, writes the mark file, and the files are swept, the user is again prompted to obtain tokens. Writing the mark file is fine, but I propose that we leave it up the credmon to decide when to sweep tokens. The credmon has a better idea of the expiration date of the tokens and can make intelligent cleanup decisions depending upon the mtimes of the mark file, the refresh and access token files, and the tokens' expirations.

Please bump in priority. 2020-Jun-29 10:48:46 by zmiller: I changed the code (to be released in 8.9.8) to look at config SEC_CREDENTIAL_SWEEP_DELAY and wait until the .mark file is at least that many seconds old before sweeping. This of course stops HTCondor from deleting the creds out from under you, but there is still the open question: Should the CREDD or the CREDMON be responsible for deleting these? The answer shouldn't be "neither" but I guess it could be "both", which I think is what we have now. 2020-Jun-29 11:09:10 by tannenba: When is all the credmon / credd OAUTh stuff going to get documented? We need a ticket for this if we don't have one already. title: Ticket #4302: Paired slots should cross-advertise some of each others attributes
description: Since one member of a slot pair may be hidden (see #4280), in order to have useful displays from condor_status, the visible member of the pair should show state and activity and other attributes of it's partner. To simplify configuration, they should each advertise some of each others attributes. The set of attributes likely to be cross-advertised would include State, Activity, EnteredCurrentActivity, JobId, GlobalJobId, <?> The set of cross-advertised attributes should be settable by config knob. Two possible representations of the cross-advertised attributes are proposed. use a nested classad encode as a string The implementation of this should be such that switching between these two representations should be easy, possibly just by using a config knob.

title: Ticket #3097: fix vulnerability to DNS-lookup delays
description: Ben Cotton observed a case where a schedd melted down (i.e. failed to keep up with shadows) because an entry in the flocking list was not a valid DNS name. Presumably, the failing lookup kept taking a lot of time, but the schedd just kept doing it anyway. The death spiral began when a lot of these delays happened in a row. We saw this in the logs: 06/28/12 16:50:02 (pid:18733) Failed to start non-blocking update to unknown. 06/28/12 16:50:51 (pid:18733) Failed to start non-blocking update to unknown. 06/28/12 16:51:44 (pid:18733) Failed to start non-blocking update to unknown. 06/28/12 16:52:39 (pid:18733) Failed to start non-blocking update to unknown. 06/28/12 16:53:29 (pid:18733) Failed to start non-blocking update to unknown. 06/28/12 16:54:23 (pid:18733) Failed to start non-blocking update to unknown. 06/28/12 16:55:06 (pid:18733) Failed to start non-blocking update to unknown. 06/28/12 16:56:02 (pid:18733) Failed to start non-blocking update to unknown. Condor daemons already do some blacklisting of collectors that take a long time to fail. That is when querying. Perhaps the same needs to happen when publishing. A deeper fix would be to never block on DNS lookups.
remarks: 2012-Jun-29 09:52:48 by bcotton: I would also add that it would be beneficial if the log message were more clear about what's going wrong (e.g. which host name is failing to resolve). title: Ticket #1550: add set operators to ClassAds
description: Igor requests the ability to compute the intersection of two lists. For example, a job has a list of storage elements that it wants and a machine has a list of storage elements that it provides. In the requirements expression, we want to specify that these two lists must intersect. The best I could come up with was stringList_RegexpMember(), which requires that one of the lists be formatted as a regular expression.
remarks: 2011-Feb-25 14:33:53 by danb: When using new-classads, another idea is to use a nested ClassAd to represent one of the sets. The members of the set would be encoded as attribute names. The values would just bet set to true. To test for intersection of two sets, one would need to encode the other set as a boolean expression that looks for attributes in the ad. Example: In the machine ad: software = [ CMSSW_2 = true; CMSSW_3 = true; ] In the job ad: SoftwareMatches = TARGET.software.CMSSW_1 || TARGET.software.CMSSW_2 2011-Mar-02 17:23:53 by danb: After discussion with Igor, we agreed that the following would satisfy the use-cases that he has encountered so far: stringListsIntersect(A,B,[delimiter]) It returns true if string-lists A and B intersect. In the initial implementation, it will do all required inspection and digestion of the strings describing the sets on-the-fly in every call to the function, so it will be O(N log(N)).

title: Ticket #4928: Schedd<->negotiator protocol timeouts in CMS pool
description: We're seeing persistent issues with negotiator<->schedd timeouts during matchmaking. Historically, we've always ignored this as we figured "the schedd is really busy". However, spending some time staring at this, I think there's an underlying problem. Here's the setup: Users A and B have a lot of idle jobs in queue in a schedd. Negotiator sends many matches (~500) to User A. Negotiator sends END_NEGOTIATE to schedd. Negotiator starts negotiation with user B. Negotiator times out reading response from schedd. From the negotiator log: 03/05/15 16:55:15 condor_read(): timeout reading 21 bytes from schedd analysis.jbalcas@cms. 03/05/15 16:55:16 IO: Failed to read packet header 03/05/15 16:55:16 Failed to get reply from schedd From the schedd log: 03/05/15 07:55:32 Lost priority - 1350 jobs matched 03/05/15 07:55:32 Finished negotiating for analysis.jbalcas in local pool: 1350 matched, 0 rejected 03/05/15 07:55:32 Activity on stashed negotiator socket: <128.142.141.24:37159> 03/05/15 07:55:32 Using negotiation protocol: NEGOTIATE 03/05/15 07:55:32 Negotiating for owner: analysis.mmascher@cms 03/05/15 07:55:32 condor_write(): Socket closed when trying to write 2624 bytes to <128.142.141.24:37159>, fd is 19 03/05/15 07:55:32 Buf::write(): condor_write() failed (don't mind the timezone differences) It took about 16 seconds for the schedd to get to the END_NEGOTIATE. Perusing the logs, it seems the schedd has plenty of activity. Here's what I think is going on: The negotiator fills up the socket buffer with matches. The buffer is large, meaning this is non-blocking. It takes 16s to process all the matches in the schedd. From what I can tell, it takes 1 daemon cycle per match. So, if the buffer contained 500 matches then the END_NEGOTIATE, it takes 500 cycles to process all of them. By the time we get to the last message on the TCP socket, even though the schedd responds promptly, the negotiator has closed the socket. It's not entirely clear where all the time goes. In at least one case, I've observed this triggering FindRunnable - rebuilding the prio table took 5s in itself.

Ticket #1383: ldap dependencies in nordugrid_gahp cause portability headaches
description: The nordugrid_gahp is linked against the system OpenLDAP library. On many of our linux platforms, OpenLDAP is dependent on SASL or SASL2. For static linking, the SASL/SASL2 library needs to be included on the link line. With the way our build scripts are structured, the same link options are used for dynamic and static. It turns out that explicitly naming SASL/SASL2 on the link line makes the binary less portable between linux flavors. The WMS group discovered that a dynamic nordugrid_gahp built on rhel3 seg-faults on scientific linux 4. This is because rhel3's ldap uses sasl, while sl4's ldap uses sasl2. Both sasl libraries end up in the running process and butt heads. Removing the sasl library from the link line fixes the problem, but then the static link fails. For now, I'm going to hack the makefile to use different lists of libraries for the dynamic and static links of nordugrid_gahp. This requires manually expanding an imake macro, which is ugly and wrong. If we can dump the building of static binaries (#1136), this mess will go away.

title: Ticket #1679: UserLog reader will get stuck due to sticky feof
description: We have encountered many problems related to the UserLog reader, i.e. condor_wait getting stuck (see #1457), assorted DAGMan anomalies, etc. There are now many ways of monitoring the state of the reader's file pointer in order to make sure it will read events even after ending up in feof. Turns out, this can be solved internally by adding a check for foef(file_ptr) and a following call to clearerr(file_ptr) for every initiated event read. We have assorted checks for that, but there exist code paths (i.e. w/o rotation) that will never even get there. If we make sure for every event read,that we get rid of the sticky feof, we will encounter far less problems with the reader API. An additional aspect of that is that we - most likely - can get rid of the WRITE lock in the reader. So far the encountered failure looked a lot like a race condition -- and it is possible that the WRITE lock does something different to the file pointer (i.e. removing the sticky bit) than the READ lock. Since in 7.5 we mostly will have separate lock files anyway, this won't matter - but it revealed this bug yet another time.
check_ins: 2010-Sep-27 12:37 Check-in [19058]: This commit fixes a problem with the user log reader when its file pointer gets stuck in feof state. By checking for feof in every readEvent call and clearing the sticky bit, we prevent this from happening (see #1679) . (cherry picked from commit 9c0cd2f12a888f61af8540df35f0a2c35cc6d48e) (By Cathrin Weiss ) 2010-Sep-27 12:34 Check-in [19057]: This commit fixes a problem with the user log reader when its file pointer gets stuck in feof state. title: Ticket #2956: Cannot use "/" as a named chroot
description: #2822 introduced a bug where Condor tries to create the execute directory twice if the target chroot is "/". This is because the starter creates the execute directory, then the chroot code tries to create "$CHROOT/$EXECUTE_DIR" - and, if CHROOT=/, it tries to create //$EXECUTE_DIR, which already exists. The use case for us is having a cluster where "SL5" refers to a chroot-on-SL6 for some hosts, while it is the real-root on other hosts. Hence, all jobs ask for "SL5" (fwiw, we worked through this by simply turning off all SL5 nodes :). Patch incoming - the simple way to fix this is not invoke any of the chroot business if the target chroot is "/".
remarks: 2012-Apr-27 10:58:46 by tstclair: What is the use case for chrooting to "/", you could give full control to a non-priv user? 2012-Apr-27 11:18:40 by bbockelm: Chroot'ing doesn't provide any additional privileges, but it provides new environments. The use case is a heterogeneous cluster where the "SL5" environment is mapped to "/chroot/sl5" on some hosts and "/" on others. You want to just have to instruct users to add: RequestChroot="SL5" and have Condor "do the right thing", even if the right thing is to use "/" (i.e., a no-op). 2012-Apr-27 11:26:00 by tstclair: reviewed and pushed

title: Ticket #3214: No easy way to extract forensic info from User/Event Log
description: We are trying to prepare ourself to react to the event of one of our users turning malicious. One of the basic things we would need to determine in such event is where the jobs of such a user have been running. condor_history is of course not enough, since the job may have started several time due to preemption. We are thus planning to rely on the EventLog. Since we have a portal Condor installation, we fully control user submission. So the submit node can be considered un-compromised. The problem now is how to parse the information out of the EventLog. condor_userlog seems the natural choice, but lacks two important features: No support for -constraint It only shows the hostname. Since we are a glidein shop, this information is not really useful; we would need to print out other information, like the GLIDEIN_Identity. I thus propose to extend condor_userlog to give us the information we need.

title: Ticket #3701: Gridmanager can crash on certain replies from EC2 GAHP
description: Normally, when a command issued to the EC2 GAHP fails, it returns two strings explaining the nature of the failure. title: Ticket #2813: negotiator rejecting jobs because of insufficient priority
description: The problems encountered below at a site running Condor v7.6.6 were apparently resolved by downgrading the negotiator to v7.6.4. Incident Description All head and compute nodes at LHO, as well as the Condor central manager, were rebooted this morning to apply a kernel security patch. Jobs are being rejected by the negotiatior: [root@condor ~]# tail -f /var/log/condor/NegotiatorLog 01/27/12 15:39:30 (fd:7) Got NO_MORE_JOBS; done negotiating 01/27/12 15:39:30 (fd:7) Negotiating with magathos@xxx.xxx.xxx.xxx at <y.y.y.y:45385> 01/27/12 15:39:30 (fd:7) 0 seconds so far 01/27/12 15:39:30 (fd:7) Request 12907655.00000: 01/27/12 15:39:31 (fd:7) Rejected 12907655.0 magathos@xxx.xxx.xxx.xxx <y.y.y.y:45385>: insufficient priority 01/27/12 15:39:31 (fd:7) Request 12908931.00000: 01/27/12 15:39:31 (fd:7) Rejected 12908931.0 magathos@xxx.xxx.xxx.xxx <y.y.y.y:45385>: insufficient priority 01/27/12 15:39:31 (fd:7) Got NO_MORE_JOBS; done negotiating 01/27/12 15:39:31 (fd:7) negotiateWithGroup resources used scheddAds length 0 01/27/12 15:39:31 (fd:7) ---------- Finished Negotiation Cycle ---------- Resetting a user's priority to 0 using condor_userprio -setprio did not help; neither did clearing /var/lib/condor/spool/Accountantnew.log on the central manager and restarting Condor, or setting 'NEGOTIATOR_IGNORE_USER_PRIORITIES = True'. title: Ticket #6153: Fix corruption of job queue log when write fails
description: The code that writes the job queue log is very careful to detect write failures and refrain from writing any additional data. This makes it easy to recover after a restart, as any incomplete record occurs only at the end of the file and can be ignored. We have seen several cases where this is not the case. A log record is truncated in the middle of a line, and is followed by other log records. Recovery fails, as the single line containing parts of two log records is invalid, but is followed by other data. The truncated record appeared to be caused by a full disk, with the additional entries occurring after some space became available. But the schedd should have aborted on the truncated write. We have found a bug in Transaction::Commit() that explains this behavior. The function detects write failures, but doesn't act on them immediately. It continues playing the transaction, optionally writing all of the log records to a backup file. If the transaction is flagged as durable, it then tries to force the data to disk, and calls EXCEPT() if any of the I/O operations fail. If the transaction is non-durable, it silently ignores any failures.
remarks: 2017-Feb-22 15:04:35 by tannenba: Readers of this ticket may also be interested in the Remarks on #6131 2017-Mar-01 10:13:58 by gthain: CODE REVIEW Looks good. Pet peeve: I added a strerror to the message. It is unfortunate that we don't have the file name of the transaction log at this point, and the error message presumes that it is a job log.

title: Ticket #5285: Security hostname of SELF for portable localhost definition
description: Problem An administrator may want to say "trust everyone on this local computer" for a given operation. This is desired as the default behavior for a personal HTCondor. However, we can't easily express this. You can try something like ALLOW_READ=*/127.0.0.1,*/1::1,*/$(IP_ADDRESS) but that doesn't cover everything. Some Linux distributions have 127.0.0.2 set up to also mean loopback. (Or on Ubuntu or Debian, sometimes 127.0.1.1.) Every IPv6 enabled computer will have an arbitrary link-local address. Many computers will have multiple IP addresses. Some computers IP addresses will change at runtime. We'd like to catch all of these cases, at least most of the time, with a particular focus on having use role:personal Just Work almost all of the time. Goal It should be possible to write a security policy allowing any connection from the local computer without needing to enumerate specific interfaces. The result might look something like: ALLOW_READ=*/SELF Proposal Someone familiar with the networking code (probably tlmiller or adesmet) creates a new function bool Sock::connection_is_to_self() or similar. The function operates on an active connection and compares the local IP address to the remote IP address. If they are exactly the same, return true, otherwise return false. Someone familiar with the security code (probably zmiller) adds logic to test all connections against the above function. If true, the "IP address" used in security tests becomes the string "SELF". Thus ALLOW_READ=*/SELF becomes meaningful. [Edit: zmiller] We should look at the string first, and if it is equal to SELF, then call Sock::connection_is_to_self() to determine the answer, rather than call it on every connection. This also aids in backwards campatability, since existing config files will either have $(IP_ADDRESS) or an actual hard-coded IP address, and we can't go swapping that out from under them. Someone (probably johnkn) modifies role:personal to use this new syntax. Limitations and concerns Won't work if a system connects to itself from a different address than the destination. This is deemed silly, unlikely, and not worth worrying about. We're not certain about the risks of spoofing. Will our various supported operating systems accept external packets that purport to be from itself? Worst case this is no more dangerous than ALLOW_READ=*/$(IP_ADDRESS) , but may be perceived as being safer and lead to less security. Rejected ideas We considered a new authentication method, "ANONYMOUS_LOCAL" that would map to the user "ANONYMOUS_LOCAL" (or perhaps something else via the map file). This was rejected as adding complexity and noise to the log files. We could have special cased the method to not add noise to the log files, but that adds further complexity. The proposal above is believed to be a smaller change.

It turns out that by inspection of a running 7.6.3 condor pool, that the negotiator and schedd believe they are speaking a 7.5.4 or earlier protocol. This is very wrong. I'm checking with the original author of that compatibility code path to find out why it is horked. 2011-Oct-13 11:55:50 by psilord: This one is complicated, but I figured it out. It turns out that we added a new attribute to the submitter ads called "SubmitterTag". When this attribute is present, the negotiator (when negotiating for that submitter) would use a new protocol to the schedd which was created at the 7.5.4 release of condor. If this was not present it would use the pre 7.5.4 negotiation protocol. So, what happens is this: The negotiator pulls the submitter ads from the collector, grinds on them, and then contacts the schedd. While there is only one connection from the negotiator to the schedd, each submitter ad gets its own "conversation" on the socket. Each conversation is prefixed by a number which identifies the protocol version of the conversation. For non-dedicated scheduler submitter ads, the "SubmitterTag" attribute was present, and hence used the new 7.5.4+ protocol. For dedicated scheduler submitter ads, the "SubmitterTag" was not present due to coding error, and so it used the pre 7.5.4 protocol. What exacerbated the bug was that the schedlog only printed out the FIRST conversation protocol identifier that it was presented. So, we never saw it change in the schedd log during each negotiation conversation and so assumed that the shcedd was using the newer 7.5.4+ protocol for ALL conversations. This assumption was false. So, Dan Bradley is fixing the dedicated scheduler to add the SubmitterTag attribute, and I'm fixing the schedlog output to be far more clear about what it is doing for each submitterad. 2011-Oct-13 16:03:18 by psilord: Dan and I wrote the code, it is checked in and documented. Resolving.

title: Ticket #7742: make having a credential optional when using krb/kerberos and credmon
description: Currently, if the administrator sets up their pool to use kerberos credentials and a kerberos credmon, it is expected that all users on the system will in fact have a kerberos credential to use. This might not always be the case, and it should be possible to operated in a mode where kerberos credentials are sent with the job if they exists, or if desired, but also allow for submissions without. Probably this means we'll need a couple settings to express admin and user requirements and preferences. The below model mimics the security model (N ever, O ptional, P referred, R equired). However, this model has been known to be confusing for many, so suggestions are welcome for a better mechanism for both admins and users alike to describe this. config setting settings would be: N ever send cred, O ptionally send cred but don't by default, P refer to send cred by default but no error if no cred is sent, R equire that krb cred is sent. submit file settings would be: N ever allow my credential to be sent, O ptionally send cred if needed but don't request that behavior, P refer to send my cred but submit my job even if its not sent, R equire my cred be sent for this job. A user can already specify which OAuth creds they need, by OAuth type, so maybe we should just make krb another "type". However, krb creds might need special treatment because HTCondor does do special handling for krb creds in order to obtain AFS tokens. (More preceisly, the shipped krb credmon does the handling using a convention for keyring names that HTCondor can follow) For example: unlike their OAuth tokens, users might not even know about krb/afs, and they shouldn't have to do anything special in their submit file for their jobs to use have those creds/tokens.

title: Ticket #5401: Server should not retry failed authentication methods
description: If an authentication method fails for any reason, the client side removes the failed method from the list of methods it is willing to try and attempts to authenticate again. Why is the removal of a failed method only done on the client side? Seems like it would be good design for the server to also remove the failed method from the list of methods it is willing to serve, so that a faulty client does not waste a lot of the server's precious time. Also in the event of a bug or path, it is a lot easier to upgrade just a server than upgrade every client.... In Authentication:authenticate_continue() we have the following code errstack->pushf("AUTHENTICATE", AUTHENTICATE_ERR_METHOD_FAILED, "Failed to authenticate using %s", m_method_name.c_str() ); //if authentication failed, try again after removing from client tries if ( mySock->isClient() ) { Seems like the conditional for isClient() should be removed, so the failed method is removed from both the client and server side. (also see #5101)

title: Ticket #1911: Use precompiled headers during the build in the post cmake world
description: Before the switch over to cmake, the build on Windows leveraged MSVC compiler's precompiled headers capabilities to increase the speed of the build approx 4x. Before cmake, our Windows build made one precompiled header based on condor_common.h (actually, two - one for C and one for C++), and then used this precompiled header for all targets. This was easy enough to do because our old build system deposited all results (.obj object files, .pch precompiled header files, etc) into one flat subdirectory. Nowadays, Cmake deposits generated results for each target in its own sub-directory which makes sharing a pre-compiled header across multiple targets challenging - several folks on the web have discussed this and ways to get around it. As a generated precompiled header file is ~18MB, until precompiled headers shared across the entire solution, we want to limit the number of generated precompiled header files so the space required for a build does not explode in size by hundreds of megs. Propose the following milestones: Use precompiled headers only targets with a lot of source files (more than 90 - essentially just the utils and condorapi targets) to get the most bang for the buck - e.g. fastest compilation without using tons of extra disk. DONE Future Work Potential future work on this could include: Have a Cmake optional switch to enable/disable precompiled headers. Enable one precompiled header to be used across multiple targets. This would speed up the build on Windows even more, but the complexity involved makes me wonder if it is worth the trouble. What we have currently, but using precompiled headers w/ the really large targets like utils, already gives a nice speedup w/o the dangers of trying to force MSVC to do something it wasn't intended to do (sigh). Use precompiled headers of w/ g++ as well?

title: Ticket #5952: condor_submit -prepend - helpful given "include command" capability
description: If an "include:" or "include command:" directive uses any macros in its arguments list, then the "-append" command line option will not influence the operation of that include since those lines are added immediately before the "queue" command, after the include has already been evaluated. By offering a "-prepend" command line option, macros used by includes can take on the desired values. It may be necessary to make prepended macros immutable, so that a later entry in the submit description doesn't override what was supplied on the command line.

title: This attachment is private.
Ticket #4210: Fear the reaper a bit. Don't reap while selecting
description: In ticket #3992, we changed the DaemonCore event loop to invoke reaper handlers for all reaped child processes each time through the loop. We also moved where the reaper handlers are invoked, to between calling select() and examining the FDs that come up as ready (and calling handlers for them). The second change fouled up work fetch, and can probably cause other problems. The problem with work fetch is that its reaper closes an FD that select indicated is ready and opens a new FD that gets the same FD number and registers it for selection. Then the main driver calls the handler for the new FD, which isn't ready. The startd ends up doing a blocking read on an FD with no data. Here is a more detailed sequence of events: Child process created for work fetch, pipes for stdout/err registered for read in select Child exits and full data read from stdout/err pipes select() called, indicates that stdout/err pipes are ready for read (because write ends are closed) Reaper handling for child process occurs Stdout/err pipes are closed Create connected socket for starter to send updates to startd Starter process created, inherits one end of socket Other end of socket is registered for select (this has the same FD number as the stdout pipe closed above) Handlers for FDs select indicated as ready are looked up Read handler for socket to starter is called handler does blocking read on socket, but no data is available Before the starter will send any data on the update socket, it tries to connect to the startd's command port to send a DC_CHILDALIVE message. This results in a deadlock. But it's only temporary, as the starter will timeout on its connection to the startd and eventually exit because it can't send the message. That that point, the startd's blocking read returns failure due to the other end of the socket closing. But this takes many minutes. In ticket #4008, we added a timeout to the blocking read in the startd. This treated the symptom of this problem, but not the cause. The fix is to undo the change of when reaper handlers are invoked.

title: Ticket #1012: Schedd putting cluster ads on hold
description: Schedd sent email stating the following: Condor failed to start your job 9090.-1 because job attribute Args contains $$(VirtualMachineID). Note the procid of -1 !!! Submitting box is Windows XPSP3, execute nodes are all Windows 2003 Server SP2 x64, everything is running Condor 7.2.4 Jun 15 2009 BuildID: 159529.
remarks: 2010-Jun-01 15:46:59 by tannenba: There is a bug, and it can be reproduced as follows: submit a job that uses $$() macros in the job ad in an attribute other than executable, for instance Arguments = $$(Opsys) have copy_to_spool=true in the submit file (this is the default in v7.2.x, but not in v7.4.x), which means the executable will be copied into the SPOOL directory as file clusterXXX.ickpt.subproc0. Once a job is submitted as above, the job will go on hold when condor_preen runs because the ickpt file in SPOOL does not contain the string ".proc", which preen looks for. If preen does not find ".proc", it wants to know if any jobs exist w/ the cluster number found in the filename. Preen does this by trying to fetch the cluster ad from the schedd (job number XXX,-1), which should exist if and only if there is one or more jobs submitted into this cluster number. The problem is the schedd's rpc handler for GetJobAd in /src/condor_schedd.V6/qmgmt_receivers.cpp will always try to expand $$() macros, because the GridManager relies on this behavior. But cluster ads will never successfully expand, thus the problem. The fix should do the following: GetJobAd() in qmgmt_receivers should check for valid ranges of cluster and proc, and should invoke GetJobAd without expansion if and only if the proc requested is -1. This will still allow preen to quickly check for the existence of a any job in a cluster and yet not setoff this bug. holdJobRaw() in the schedd should do sanity checking on cluster and proc ids, and disallow proc values of -1. As a tangent, preen is inefficient if the job queue is large - need a subticket to address this. 2010-Jun-24 11:41:53 by tannenba: Note: before the patches created in this ticket, in addition to the bugs above, folks running a CCB broker (collector) on the same machine with a schedd will see all their standard universe jobs and/or spooled jobs go on hold with the same crazy -1 jobid email message.

title: Ticket #1507: Problem with gidd_alloc from procd
description: Burt Holzman (OSG & Fermilab) recently reported a problem. The problem is with the procd that the Condor Project ships to the VDT. This is a separate procd than ships with Condor. Greg Quinn used to maintain it, and I believe it's on a separate branch, but I'm not sure where. You can see the complete description of the problem at: http://crt.cs.wisc.edu/Ticket/Display.html?id=7280 (Used guest/guest to log in). Here are the interesting parts, in Burt's words. Note that gidd_alloc comes from this special distribution of the procd. There is an interaction between the GID tracking option of the Condor batch system on the Tier 1 and the glexec tracking GIDs. Essentially, the gidd_alloc process reparents itself to init, and sets its GID to one of the glexec tracking GIDs (discarding the Condor tracking GID). If the job exits normally, the glexec monitor terminates the gidd_alloc process; otherwise the job is terminated via condor_rm or condor_hold, Condor doesn't realize that gidd_alloc is part of the process tree and it lingers forever. This could be obviated if gidd_alloc added the glexec tracking GID as another supplemental GID (although that might be a privilege leak if the VO and user jobs rely on GID-based file permissions); or to maintain the PPID to the condor_exec process. and Dave Dykstra is modifying the glexec_monitor to catch signals and try to kill gidd_alloc. It would be nice if gidd_alloc made itself more trackable to the underlying Condor as well, which I think is where the VDT comes in. I don't know where gidd_alloc comes from or where the source is. I hope this is enough to go on. Let me and Burt know if you need more information.

title: Ticket #4705: use proper kibi and Ki abbreviations for powers of 2
description: Sprinkled throughout the manual are old style references to powers of 2, which are now ambiguous. Time to follow the NIST standard at http://physics.nist.gov/cuu/Units/binary.html For 1024 bytes, proper use is kibibytes, or KiB. Capitalization is significant for the abbreviated form KiB. (A lower case 'b' indicates bits.) For 2^20 bytes, proper use is mebibyte, or MiB. Capitalization is significant for the abbreviated form MiB. (A lower case 'b' indicates bits.) This ticket's task is to find all instances of things like Kbytes and Mbytes that are supposed to refer to powers of 2, and change them to follow the standard.

title: Ticket #6692: Improve wheel packaging of python bindings

remarks: 2018-May-29 13:23:14 by jpatton: Also, the docker image that we're using to base the packaging on needs to be updated so that wheels are built against more recent crytpo libs. See issue on bbockelm's docs GitHub repo: https://github.com/bbockelm/htcondor-python/issues/2 2018-Jun-13 14:36:05 by jpatton: Link to github version of [55050] for easier viewing: https://github.com/htcondor/htcondor/commit/bea10ec8e0142d0d4b23c4a8070546db4b4fb08c The changes to the actual codebase are pretty small. What I've done here is consolidated all the wheel packaging setup (not the packaging itself) in /src/python-bindings/CMakeLists.txt . I've also created a new target, _pyclassad, which builds as libpyclassad<py-ver>_<pkg-ver>_clean.so, that does not link against libpython. libpython does not exist in the manylinux1 docker image (except for libpython2.4... yuck). (Note: We should have a discussion about whether libpython should even be used in our normal python bindings build.) Finally, I added a way to append to the package version that is used for building the wheels so that we can release hotfixes between official HTCondor releases on PyPI. What I've done "behind-the-scenes" (though this will go into a github repo soon) is redo the manylinux1 docker image that we are using when actually building and packaging the wheels. Previously, we "burnt" a modified docker container to an image. This time, I took careful note of the changes I had to make to get condor to compile and to get correct manylinux1 wheels built (including patching the auditwheel utility), and then stored that in a build script which is called by a Dockerfile. This way when manylinux2010 (or whatever it ends up being called) comes out that updates the underlying manylinux image's OS, it's (hopefully) a one line change in the Dockerfile to update to the new image. I've also changed the name of the image to htcondor_manylinux1, which will help us be more clear when new manylinux images are released. There are a few changes I've made to the htcondor_manylinux1 docker image compared to the "original" condor_pypi_container image that was graciously provided by bbockelm: Compiled and installed a newer version of OpenSSL (i.e. libcrypto) than is shipped with the CentOS 5-based image. (The auditwheel utility packs this with the wheel!) The auditwheel patch is now smarter about how the condor_libs/ libraries are handled such that fewer errors are ignored (in fact, only when libclassad is not found at the beginning...) and their RPATHs are corrected (so libclassad is found at the end). 2018-Jun-22 09:22:43 by jpatton: Some more changes: Instead of copying libclassad and libcondor_utils to the wheel directly, I am now letting auditwheel take care of copying them. CMake now looks at WANT_PYTHON_WHEELS when deciding whether or not to use dlopen() with security and globus libs. These libs are now explicitly linked when building for Python wheels, so auditwheel puts copies of them into the wheel at repair time. title: Ticket #7129: Late materialization may not generate correct requirements
description: The fix for #7044 introduced a bug where when a user specifies Requirements in their submit file, and is also using late materialization, the code in submit_utils to generate a requirements expression automatically may do the wrong thing. This happens because in 8.9.2 the submit digest is pruned, but requirements generation needs access to unpruned file transfer lists (and possibly other things.) It was intended that pruned submit digests have a flag that prevent requirements from being generated at all (so all procs will share the clusters requirements), but when the user has a requirements statement, this check is being skipped. The fix is to always prune the requirements statement from the digest that is sent for a late materialization job. But this will introduce a new bug whereby requirements statements what have $() expansions will not work correctly. We consider this a less serious bug, and will work on a fix for that later. (see #7130)

title: Ticket #1854: Stack corruption in condor_hdfs due to writing beyond an array's bound
description: In condor_hdfs, an array of three integers (arrIO) is used to hold the pipe endpoints used for redirecting standard in/out/error. The Create_Pipe function accepts as a parameter an array of two integers to store the index values for the two endpoints of the pipe it creates. Whether the original coder was trying to be clever or something, arrIO is being reused while creating the pipes we want to use for output/error redirection. One mistake in this cleverness is the passing of the address of the last element in the arrIO array to the Create_Pipe function to serve as the pointer to the array for storing the two endpoints it is supposed to give back. This corrupts the stack when Create_Pipe writes outside the bounds of arrIO and may be the cause of the crash inside argList when condor_hdfs is compiled using O2 optimization on Windows. O1 optimization does not detect it but when full debug is run inside Visual Studio, VS detects the stack corruption. Solution: rewrite the way that the pipe endpoints are stored inside the initialization code for condor_hdfs. The logic of that block of code is a bit convoluted and could use some simplification.
remarks: 2011-Jan-18 14:25:16 by ziliang: Cause confirmed. The logic for creating and registering the pipes for stdout/err redirection was massively broken in condor_hdfs and I am not sure how, if it ever, worked, with the previous revision. Not only were we overwriting the FD of the write end of the first pipe we created with the FD of the read end of the second pipe we created, we also were saving the FD of the write end of the second pipe outside the bounds of the array we had set up to hold the FDs. We were also not saving the write ends and passing the read ends to the new process we were creating, so attempts to communicate back to the parent by writing out to stdout or stderr by the child probably was not working, or at the very least should not have worked, unless the pipes were full duplex. We were also not closing the write ends of the two pipes created so were leaking resources every time we created a new instance of hadoop. Something tells me we are not cleaning up the read ends either if we start up a new instance of hadoop and recreate the pipes for redirection. With Dan's permission, this is going into the 7.5.5 branch. Whether it makes it into the release will depend on if he needs to retag for the release, again. 2011-Feb-01 16:20:02 by tannenba: Bulk change of target version from v070506 to NULL using ./ticket-target-mover.

title: Ticket #7083: Job attribute CommittedTime can over-count job runtime
description: When a job completes, the shadow updates CommittedTime and CommittedSlotTime in the job ad to include the most recent interval of execution and pushes the changes to the schedd. This happens in the function BaseShadow::terminateJob(). If the shadow fails to connect to the schedd, it will retry later. The retry includes running BaseShadow::terminateJob() again, which will add more time to CommittedTime and CommittedSlotTime. This results in double- or triple-counting the job's most recent execution time. We need to add a flag that ensures the updating of these attributes is only done once in BaseShadow::terminateJob().
