title: Ticket #4586: Google cloud type doesn't work as documented
description: By following the documentation (HTCondor Version 8.3.0 Manual), I discovered that it is no more possible to use the GCE (Google Compute Engine) Grid. The reason is that Google modified his APIs. In particular, the 'gcutil' tool described in HTCondor manual is now deprecated and, with the current tools, I have not been able to find a way to generate an authentication file that can replace the .gcutil_auth. This problem affects all the released HTCondor versions, of course.
remarks: 2014-Sep-22 13:10:47 by timm: Here are some notes of how our student was able to use a combination of a python script as found on the google site plus the ReST apI to do authentication. I discovered an issue with the GCE's OAuth2 authentication method through the REST API. The issue has been accepted, but not yet solved, so, the only way of using the REST API with GCE is by authenticating with other approaches. In the next steps I will use the Python API to authenticate, obtaining the access token needed by the REST API. ######################## # PREREQUISITES # ######################## Python 2.5, 2.6, or 2.7 is required. Install the pip tool: Download https://bootstrap.pypa.io/get-pip.py And execute it, as superuser. Install Google API Python client # pip install --upgrade google-api-python-client (http://github.com/google/google-api-python-client) Install OAuth2 Python client pip install --upgrade oauth2client (https://github.com/google/oauth2client) ######################## # AUTHENTICATION # ######################## As described in "https://developers.google.com/compute/docs/api/python-guide", it is possible to get authenticated with the Python API. First of all, from the Google Cloud Console (https://console.developers.google.com), note your project id (next, will be called "MY_PROJECT_ID") access the project and, on the left column, reach "APIs & auth -> Credentials" create credentials and download the "Compute Engine and App Engine"'s JSON file. Save the JSON file as "client_secrets.json" in the folder you'll place the next script. The following Python script returns the access token needed by the GCE REST API. #!/usr/bin/env python import json from pprint import pprint import logging import sys import argparse import httplib2 from oauth2client.client import flow_from_clientsecrets from oauth2client.file import Storage from oauth2client import tools from oauth2client.tools import run_flow from apiclient.discovery import build DEFAULT_ZONE = 'us-central1-a' API_VERSION = 'v1' GCE_URL = 'https://www.googleapis.com/compute/%s/projects/' % (API_VERSION) PROJECT_ID = 'MY_PROJECT_ID' CLIENT_SECRETS = 'client_secrets.json' OAUTH2_STORAGE = 'oauth2auth.dat' GCE_SCOPE = 'https://www.googleapis.com/auth/compute' def main(argv): logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO) parser = argparse.ArgumentParser( description=__doc__, formatter_class=argparse.RawDescriptionHelpFormatter, parents=[tools.argparser]) # Parse the command-line flags. flags = parser.parse_args(argv[1:]) # Perform OAuth 2.0 authorization. flow = flow_from_clientsecrets(CLIENT_SECRETS, scope=GCE_SCOPE) storage = Storage(OAUTH2_STORAGE) credentials = storage.get() if credentials is None or credentials.invalid: credentials = run_flow(flow, storage, flags) http = httplib2.Http() auth_http = credentials.authorize(http) storage_data = open(OAUTH2_STORAGE) storageData = json.load(storage_data) storage_data.close() print storageData["access_token"] if __name__ == '__main__': main(sys.argv) ######################## # REST API # ######################## A simple REST call that returns the project's instances info contains is a GET request to: https://www.googleapis.com/compute/v1/projects/MY_PROJECT_ID/zones/us-central1-a/instances That contains in the header the following access token: Authorization: Bearer ACCESS_TOKEN_RETURNED_BY_PYTHON_SCRIPT In Curl, it's the foollowing: $ curl -H "Authorization: Bearer ACCESS_TOKEN_RETURNED_BY_PYTHON_SCRIPT" -X GET "https://www.googleapis.com/compute/v1/projects/MY_PROJECT_ID/zones/us-central1-a/instances" I believe it should be possible following this approach to get something that can work with HTCondor again. 2015-Jan-14 13:29:15 by jfrey: With the new Google Cloud SDK, I can get a credential file that HTCondor can use by running gcloud auth login. The credentials are written to ~/.config/gcloud/credentials. That's the only change in authentication that I see. The syntax for creating a new instance has changed in the v1 API, and the v1beta16 API we developed against is no longer available. I now have a patched HTCondor that can submit instances to the current GCE servers. I'll do a quick check to see if anything else in the API has changed that would affect HTCondor. 2015-Jan-23 10:24:18 by tlmiller: Code Review Changes look good to me.

title: Ticket #6041: Simplify how the Daemon client object locates the daemon
description: When the Daemon client object attempts to obtain the contact information for its daemon, it tries to be clever. If it determines that the requested daemon is the "local" one, it attempts to read the daemon's address file on the local filesystem to avoid a query to the collector. The daemon is considered local if the Daemon is constructed with a NULL name argument. If the Daemon is constructed with a non-NULL name or <subsys>_HOST is set in the config file, it may decide that the daemon is local if it determines that a daemon using the same configuration as itself would choose that name. It does this by looking up <subsys>_NAME in the config file. This has caused problems, specifically at Fermilab, where they have multiple schedds on a single machine. If <subsys>_NAME and the address file params aren't set to the same schedd's values in a tool's configuration, then it can end up talking to the wrong schedd when using -name or <subsys>_HOST. We propose changing the Daemon object so that when the daemon has an explicit name (either via the constructor or <subsys>_HOST), the Daemon object always queries the collector, and doesn't attempt to access the address files.

title: Ticket #2901: advertised checkpoint platform string is inconsistent
description: Dan Forrest noticed in numerous instances that a std univ job that had previously saved a checkpoint matched to a machine and wrote a new checkpoint with a different checkpoint signature than the one advertised by the startd on that machine. The job therefore no longer matched to the same machine that it just ran on. The part of the platform string that had changed was the vdso address. How is this possible? He observed that condor_ckpt_probe is dynamically linked, and that ld-linux.so gets (sometimes?) loaded before the vdso object. We found that ld-linux.so had been recently updated on the machine. This could explain why the vdso address changed: the size of ld-linux.so may have changed. Restarting condor caused the advertised checkpoint platform string to change, presumably making it consistent with the string associated with new checkpoints, until the next time something causes condor_ckpt_probe to generate a different value. Suggested workaround: statically link condor_ckpt_probe. The std univ jobs are statically linked, so it seems that condor_ckpt_probe should also be statically linked, so that it sees the same memory layout. I assume that this problem affects all previous 7.6 releases of Condor, but I don't know that for sure. The problem has been observed under 7.6.6 in GLOW. It has also been observed in CHTC (7.7.5) and CS (7.6.6).
remarks: 2012-Apr-13 14:41:58 by tannenba: additional wisdom from Dan Forest on this issue The basic problem is that recent OS upgrades have updated the file /lib/ld-linux.so.2 (now a symlink to /lib/ld-2.5.so on many machines) and this has changed the memory layout (regardless of setarch -R -L) and hence the VDSO location has changed. I have experimented with this a bit and it appears that statically linked binaries do not have this problem (because /lib/ld-linux.so.2 is not mapped to the process address space). It is also the case that all Condor checkpointable binaries are statically linked. So I am proposing that /usr/libexec/condor/condor_ckpt_probe should be statically linked for two reasons: 1.) The VDSO in the CheckpointPlatform attribute will match the actual VDSO address of the running program. 2.) The VDSO in the CheckpointPlatform attribute will hopefully not possibly change again after another OS upgrade. It should be fairly easy to statically link this program. Once this is done it should be pushed out to the various pools (GLOW, CHTC, and hopefully the CS Condor pool too) and the condor_startd's should be restarted to advertise the correct CheckpointPlatform. People with checkpointed jobs would probably then want to edit the LastCheckpointPlatform attribute: "LINUX X86_64 2.6.x normal 0x2aaaaaac7000" -> "LINUX X86_64 2.6.x normal 0x2aaaaaaab000" "LINUX INTEL 2.6.x normal 0x4001d000" -> "LINUX INTEL 2.6.x normal 0x40000000" Etc. Alternatively, the condor_startd's could all be restarted just to make sure the advertised CheckpointPlatform matches the CheckpointPlatform attribute returned by /usr/libexec/condor/condor_ckpt_probe (it looks like a reconfigure alone will not do this). Right now there are a lot of machines where this mismatch keeps checkpointed jobs from running again on the machine where the checkpoint originated! 2012-May-22 15:27:36 by tlmiller: The changes to CMake were made straightforward by playing games with the source to reduce the number of random things to which it needed to link. 2012-May-22 16:15:05 by tlmiller: Approved by GregT.

TJ, please follow up if I got any of this wrong. The result you get here is a consequence of how dictionary-style itemdata works. When submit sees an "extra" key (i.e., one that wasn't in the first itemdatum), it ignores it. When it sees a "missing" key (i.e., this itemdatum doesn't have a key that the first one did), it uses the most recent value for that key. Itemdata fundamentally forms a table, not a flexible schema. Each row of the table inherits the previous row's values. This is submit's normal behavior, but you can't access it using the CLI condor_submit tool because of how you specify itemdata. This behavior is only visible when using dictionary-style itemdata through the Python bindings. title: Ticket #5728: Sinful::addressPointsToMe() can't just compare the primary address.
description: It is possible for a Sinful to end up with an IPv6 primary address for a host with both addresses. Between two machines, this is possible based on configuration differences, e.g., PREFER_IPV4 or not; however, it is possible even on the same machine if one of the Sinfuls was not constructed by the DaemonCore classes. For instance, HAD constructs Sinfuls by hand after resolving a hostname. The hostname's first address is IPv6, but the HAD daemon's primary address is IPv4 because DaemonCore tries really hard to make that true. Thus, addressPointsToMe() needs to compare not just its primary address, but its addrs as well. In particular, if the other Sinful's primary address is my primary address, or is any of my addrs addresses, the other sinful points to me. (It may be wise to check, if the other Sinful has them, each address in its addrs, as well.) (Also, it appears to be valid to construct a Sinful out of the string, e.g., "hostname:9618"; this does not resolve hostname, opening the possibility that the either side of the comparison could have a hostname rather than an IP address as the primary address. It seems like the hostname should be resolved and the whole list of results used to compare.)

title: Ticket #6807: late materialization digest should support $RANDOM() expansions
description: Currently, $RANDOM_INTEGER() and $RANDOM_CHOICE() cannot be used with late materialization because these macros are expanded when the submit digest is created. To make these useful, these should not be expanded until the jobs are materialized. This is complicated by the fact that failure to expand a $RANDOM_* macro will abort the process that attempts it. This is unacceptable when it is the schedd doing the expansion. Also not expanding $RANDOM_CHOICE(foo) implies that foo cannot be pruned from the submit digest. This will only be a problem if foo is one of the prunable attributes, such as fetch_files. This is unlikely to be the case, but we should guard against it anyway. This will require that the code that builds the submit digest know the names of submit keywords that are referenced by $RANDOM_CHOICE() macros - which will require some refactoring of the macro expansion code.
remarks: This was likely fixed by #7044, but a test is needed.

title: Ticket #2517: Move GRAM4 and HDFS support into separate release.
description: The working on having Condor use dynamic libraries (#1135) is showing that we can make much smaller Condor releases. jfrey's current branch on this work reveals that of the 158 MB installed on an x86-64 RHEL4 release of Condor, 34 MB is GRAM4 support and 48MB is HDFS support. Over half of the install is support for two features that most users don't use. Given that the files in question are largely .jar files, and thus compressed, it's likely that more well over half of the Condor tar.gz is this support. Proposed: Move GRAM4 and HDFS support into separate release for the users that need the functionality. This will benefit the users who don't need that support, speeding downloads and reducing installation size.

title: Ticket #5378: Add regression test for required files in S3.
description: The condor_annex tool depends on a few files in S3 (because it can't upload everything inline). While we could upload a copy of each of those files as it was distributed to the same bucket where we upload the pool password, it seems like it might be less troublesome to version those files (and/or buckets) instead. In particular, we should add a --bucket option which identifies the bucket which holds the files (presently the template and two functions), and default it to some bucket name that includes the version (e.g., htcondor-annex-8.5.3). If the tool fails to find the bucket (or the files it needs in the bucket), it should error out with a message saying that you could try to use the --bucket option. To help ensure that the user never sees that message, add a regression test which checks for appropriately named bucket (subtest 1), that it contains the necessary files (subtest 2), that it can download the required files without any credentials (subtest 3), and that the downloaded files match the files in the source tree (subtest 4).

title: Ticket #2147: Optionally encode date/time in rotated log file names
description: Some users like having the date and possibly time included in the filenames of rotated log. So instead of having history, history.1, history.2, history.3 you might have history, history.2011-05-05, history.2011-05-04, history.2011-05-03 (This particular example assumes ROTATE_HISTORY_DAILY=TRUE.) It would be nice if this was an option for some or all log files that we rotate. The user who requested the feature was interested in the schedd's HISTORY log. Benefits: A given log file, once "aged", never moves, providing consistency for the user. Instead of having to rename all of the old files and delete the oldest, you just delete the oldest. Drawbacks: Identifying the oldest log file is trickier, especially if the mtime isn't reliable. If you let the user specify the format (probably using something like a strftime formatting string), it becomes possible for two filenames to collide.

While as an option this idea remains appealing for the reasons above, demand seems low and the benefits small.

title: Ticket #5682: Some real values printed incorrectly in ClassAds
description: In 8.1.2, we changed how floating point values are printed in ClassAds to be more human readable. title: Ticket #6104: condor_update_machine_ad
description: I noticed a few things about condor_update_machine_ad as a result of recent posts to condor-users. We begin with a bug report about a pair of command-line flags that I'm not at all sure condor_update_machine_ad was supposed to have: -name and -pool. The intent of the tool, as recorded in its man page, is to allow an administrator, after fixing an offline universe, to inform the startd about that universe being online. In this role, there's no need for -name or -pool, because the admin is already running commands locally (probably). Of course, the server-side code is transport-agnostic, so limiting the client only delays any abuse of the protocol. That would be sufficient reason to convert condor_update_machine_ad to require an authenticated ADMIN-level connection. Adding the ability to directly adjust the startd ad from another machine is probably not a concern at this level of privilege. Conversely, the indirect ability to modify the startd ad, via condor_config_val -set and condor_config_val -rset can be specifically rejected or granularly constrained by the configuration of the startd (and this more limited form of administrator privilege granted to a remote connection). Since the change is supposed to persist -- that is, survive across update cycles -- until changed equally persistently, e.g., by the failure of a VM universe job to launch, condor_config_val -rset may be the better example. Additionally, we need to investigate what protections, if any, are provided or necessary (e.g., not changing the Activity). Since we face the same problem with startd cron, that seems like a good place to hook in. However, we have to be careful to ensure that updates from condor_update_machine_ad both (a) still persist and (b) are run last, so that they can't be changed by the startd cron jobs. (Under the argument that the admin who runs condor_update_machine_ad by hand does not want the automatic background tasks of the startd cron jobs undoing her good work.) It would be consistent with other HTCondor tools but still surprising and disappointing if $ condor_update_machine_ad -name slot3@exec-13.batlab.org update.ad changed every slot on exec-13.batlab.org. Since the start cron jobs can already update individual slots (or, more usefully, each slot of a specific slot type, or each slot matching a constraint), this surprise shouldn't be too hard to avoid; it would also make the tool more powerful. A prospective usage scenario for running condor_update_machine_ad remotely is one in which a centralized resource (e.g., a fileserver) is being used to different time-varying degrees by a subset of the jobs. Rather than update the attempting to compute the usage of each job, it may be easier to query the fileserver (or the quota system) to determine how much space is left. By propagating this information to the startds, better scheduling decisions could be made (without having to query the centralized resource from every execute node).

title: Ticket #3306: NETWORK_INTERFACE ignored on some outbound connections.
description: In _condor_local_bind(), in condor_utils/internet.cpp, the outgoing port is unconditionally bound to all interfaces. This is called by do_connect_with_timeout(), which is called by do_connect() (both in do_connect.unix.cpp), which is called by part_send_job() (in the shadow), the source of the error message reported in condor-admin #24349. The error message report in condor-admin #23824 is from the starter, probably in open_file_stream() (condor_syscall_lib/file_stream.c), called from get_file (in condor_syscall_lib/xfer_file.c). open_file_stream() calls open_tcp_stream(), which calls _condor_local_bind(). In either case, it appears that it's possible for the OS to pick the wrong interface to send from, causing packets to be dropped. The solution would appear to be to fix _condor_local_bind() to respect NETWORK_INTERFACE, but it's presently unclear if (a) the starter/standard universe binary know about it and (b) if the checkpoint server, which also uses this code, knows about it.

title: Ticket #4569: Debugging tools for JobRouter.
description: We've received strong feedback from OSG site admins that the job router is quite difficult to debug. We'd like to see some client tools to help analyze setups. Suggestions we've received: Have a tool which can print all the routes (with or without defaults) and warn about any syntax errors (people often forget line continuations). title: Ticket #3756: provide command to peacefully pause a DAG
description: Upon invocation of this command, DAGMan should: stop submitting new jobs stop running any new PRE/POST scripts checkpoint any running standard universe (or otherwise checkpointable, e.g., DMTCP) jobs allow any other running jobs to complete on their own allow any running PRE/POST scripts to complete on their own generate a rescue file (or equivalent recovery state) The DAG should be restartable with one command. Maybe call it dagman_hold -peaceful, and dagman_resume? (Note: as a separate ticket, the peaceful hold should be "escalatable" to a graceful one if the user gets impatient.) Design doc at: https://docs.google.com/a/wisc.edu/document/d/1XzT5uAY0A_AD1ub4J-y29Ner0DkZqlaWiA1M20J5rTw
remarks: 2013-Jul-23 14:47:09 by wenger: As per today's LIGO phone call, this command should just be something like: condor_pause_dag <dagman id> That means that the script needs to figure out from DAGMan's classad what the name of the halt file is, and so on. I think we can do that now, by parsing the arguments in the classad, but I'm thinking that maybe DAGMan should stick the name of the primary DAG file into the classad explicitly -- that would make the pause command's job a lot easier. On the other hand, changing DAGMan itself might push this more towards 8.1 rather than 8.0. It's a new feature, but it's mostly (or all) entirely new code, rather than changes to existing code, so the chance of it breaking something existing is pretty darn small. We'll have to think about this, I guess... 2013-Aug-07 16:03:01 by wenger: Okay, here's my initial proposal: condor_halt_dag [-graceful|-really-graceful|-peaceful] <cluster.process...>|<user> Four options: (default): creates halt file, kills all child jobs (pretty much like condor_rm of DAG job, but safer because DAGMan won't exit until child jobs have all exited). -graceful: creates halt file, checkpoints and holds all checkpointable jobs, removes non-checkpointable jobs, does condor_hold on DAGMan (see explanation below). -really-graceful: creates halt file, checkpoints and holds all checkpointable jobs, does condor_hold on DAGMan (see explanation below). Non-checkpointable jobs are allowed to finish. -peaceful: just creates halt file (allows jobs already in the queue to finish). I'm not sure whether the "most severe" option should be the default, or maybe whether the "peaceful" option should be the default and the others should require flags like -fast. At any rate, though, these are the variations of "severity" that I can see. Peter -- I'm not sure if you need all of these options, but it sounds to me like the -graceful or -really-graceful options are the most useful to LIGO. Unfortunately, they're also the most complicated to implement... (Default and -peaceful should be pretty easy, I think.) Note: In the case that standard universe jobs are checkpointed and remain in the queue, DAGMan has to be held. If it's just halted with a halt file, it won't ever exit because it will be waiting for the standard universe jobs to finish. And, if it did exit, a rescue DAG can't represent the state of a checkpointed standard universe job that could be continued. condor_resume_dag <cluster.process...>|<user> Removes halt file, re-submits DAG if DAGMan exited and generated a rescue DAG, does condor_release on DAGMan if it was held, does condor_release on held node jobs. Other notes: Both commands will do nothing but print an error message if the specified Condor ID is not a condor_dagman. BTW, I'm wondering whether DAGMan itself should remove the halt file if it exits because all jobs have drained from the queue. 2013-Aug-19 17:22:28 by wenger: Oh, yeah -- something I just thought of: in the case of nested DAGs, this command should do the creation of the halt file, etc., for the sub-DAGs, rather than just treating them as any other child process (down to however many levels of sub-DAGs exist). 2013-Aug-20 14:32:56 by pfc: Stuart says we need --really-graceful above. 2013-Oct-17 16:19:26 by wenger: GregT says that a heuristic for deciding that non-standard universe jobs are checkpointable is that when_to_transfer_output is set to "on_exit_or_evict". 2013-Oct-17 17:33:31 by pfc: I don't think that heuristic is reliable/safe. Why not use an explicit indicator (e.g., can_checkpoint = true)? If it's not present, assume no checkpointing. 2013-Oct-18 09:35:23 by wenger: The above is just kind of a note -- I don't plan to rely on that, but I wanted to record it somewhere. But, yeah, we probably need some kind of explicit "can checkpoint" attribute for stuff like DMTCP and other jobs than can self-checkpoint. (I'm not sure what happens right now to a job than can self-checkpoint.) 2013-Oct-18 12:13:25 by wenger: ToddT and I had a discussion about this today, and we're looking for a little more clarification from the LIGO end. I guess the basic question is why you need to do the peaceful or graceful shutdown on a per-workflow basis rather than a per-machine basis. In other words, why doesn't a condor_off -graceful or -peaceful do what you need? 2013-Oct-21 11:43:49 by wenger: This is from Stuart via email: The main motivation for pausing an entire workflow is to stop a set of resource abusing jobs from causing problems while leaving other well behaved jobs running in the pool. 2013-Dec-10 14:26:02 by wenger: Comments from Stuart Anderson via email: You design document looks good to me. However, I would add under the “My proposal:” section that condor_halt_dag -peaceful should checkpoint and stop non-sub-DAG jobs when possible (and the equivalent statements about picking up from checkpoint images if/when restarting). I am less sanguine on commenting on the architectural choices, however, I am agreeable to not allowing de-escalation, but I would like to see checkpointing of non-sub-DAG jobs there as well. 2015-Sep-22 11:01:50 by tpdownes: After discussion w/Kent, chose to lower priority of this ticket. Most features available with dag.halt file. TPD also questions utility of including "checkpoint stduniv" jobs in this command rather than "condor_rm_dag -graceful".

title: Ticket #3242: remove an interactive job if client interrrupted before it starts
description: When the user runs condor_submit -interactive, they may have to wait quite a while for the job to get scheduled. If the user hits ctrl-c or closes the window before the job starts, the job should be immediately removed from the queue. Implementation For now, handle this simply via an interrupt handler in ssh_to_job that catches ctrl-c (SIGINT), windows closing (SIGHUP), etc, and have the interrupt handler remove the job. This handler is installed via the command-line switch -remove-on-interrupt to ssh_to_job; this switch is used by condor_submit -i. Note this solution still leaves a window of vulnerability if the user hits ctrl-c after condor_submit completes but before ssh_to_job spawns. This could be handled in the future via a lease on the job that gets renewed every time ssh_to_job polls to check if the job is running.

title: Ticket #6040: Cedar should set SO_REUSEADDR on all sockets
description: LSST reports that running a large number of very short jobs, or running a lot of short tools can exhaust the number of local TCP ports, with a lot of sockets in TIME_WAIT state. TIME_WAIT is fundamentally part of TCP, but we can reuse these sockets by setting the SO_REUSEADDR socket option. Currently, condor does this on daemon core command ports listening on fixed addresses, but no others. Being late in the series, we will not enable SO_REUSEADDR on all tcp sockets by default, but only if a param ALWAYS_REUSEADD is set to true. Note that these needs to be set on client sockets the tools use as well as server sockets in order to avoid exhaustion.

title: Ticket #7651: OFFLINE_MACHINE_RESOURCE_<tag> should work on reconfig for d-slots
description: the configuration OFFLINE_MACHINE_RESOURCE_<tag> is currently only read on startup of the Startd. It would be more useful if it was also read on reconfig. This will require some special case code in the Startd because we cant reassign resources on reconfig, so the code will have to pick up the offline knob, and then Adjust the Offline<Tag> attribute in the p-slot and all unclaimed slots. It will then have to pay attention to the Offline<Tag> attribute when moving GPUs between d-slot and p-slot, and when reporting the number of resources through the <Tag> attribute and Total<Tag> attribute. this will have the effect of making it a restart pref for partitionable slots, and allow Static slots the opportunity to choose to not match jobs if their GPUs go offline. Resources that are marked offline at startup will still require a restart to put them online, because the offline resources will not be assigned to any slot. Resources that are marked offline after the Startd has assigned resources, will be added to the offline list, but will not removed from any of the slot resource assignments. Thus resources that are marked offline at runtime, can be put back online at runtime as well, with the original slot resource assignments preserved. GPUs example In the following example, GPU device indices are used to make the example easier to read, but If you use offline resources, and particularly if you use nvidia-smi to drain GPUs, you should add the -short-uuid or -uuid option to GPU_DISCOVERY_EXTRA in your configuration so that GPUS have stable identifiers such as GPU-af3457b1 instead of CUDA1. The following config config fragment MACHINE_RESOURCE_GPUs=CUDA0, CUDA1, CUDA2 OFFLINE_MACHINE_RESOURCE_GPUS=CUDA1 Could result in the following slot attributes Name = "slot1@bob" GPUs = 1 TotalGPUs = 2 AssignedGPUs = "CUDA0, CUDA2" OfflineGPUs = "CUDA1" Name "slot1_1@bob" GPUs = 1 TotalGPUs = 2 AssignedGPUs = "CUDA0" OfflineGPUS = "CUDA1" If you then change the config to this config fragment MACHINE_RESOURCE_GPUs=CUDA0, CUDA1, CUDA2 OFFLINE_MACHINE_RESOURCE_GPUS=CUDA0 And reconfig but not restart, the slot attributes should change to this until the job in the d-slot completes Name = "slot1@bob" GPUs = 1 TotalGPUs = 1 AssignedGPUs = "CUDA0, CUDA2" OfflineGPUs = "CUDA0,CUDA1" Name "slot1_1@bob" GPUs = 0 TotalGPUs = 1 AssignedGPUs = "CUDA0" OfflineGPUS = "CUDA0,CUDA1" Since CUDA1 was offline at startup, it remains offline. Also the count of GPUs in the d-slot is now 0. Because of this, when the current job completes, the d-slot will no longer match a GPU requesting job, and will likely be deleted. Any new d-slot will be assigned CUDA2 since that is the only non-offline GPU assigned to the p-slot.

This would clearly be easier to implement than regexes, and Miron thinks it might be more understandable for the average user. Also, it just occurred to me that if you specify this inside a splice, it would only apply to nodes within that splice -- that would give users a way to have a command apply to only a subset of the nodes of their entire workflow, which might make the regex less necessary. One note about this: whatever the "for each" string is, we'd have to disallow actually having that for a node name...

title: Ticket #2516: Add bandwidth/connection limits controls on submit side
description: Submit points are frequently constrained by bandwidth. This may lead to claiming a bunch of machines, then spending long periods dribbling data out to them. Furthermore, a lot of machines pulling at the same time, can crush the poor submit point, leaving it unresponsive. We've seen both behaviors on the primary submit point for CHTC. Condor should be more intelligent. Users should not have to modify their jobs to avoid rendering their submit point unresponsive. Step 1 is figuring out the right solution. Random thoughts: Limit the number of concurrent file transfers. New file transfers would block upon hitting the limit. Limit the bandwidth being used, blocking new transfers until bandwidth is free. Limit the number of jobs starting; if too much file transfer (bandwidth or number) is occurring refuse more matches.

title: Ticket #5379: Strange AddressV1
description: I noticed the following AddressV1 (I pretty-printed it below for readability) on a CMS glidein: { [ n = "Internet"; p = "primary"; port = 48709; a = "129.93.182.27"; noUDP = true ], [ n = "red-d9n7.unl.edu"; p = "IPv4"; port = 48709; a = "129.93.182.27"; noUDP = true ], [ brokerIndex = 0; n = "Internet"; p = "primary"; port = 9637; ccbid = "377523"; a = "128.142.141.24"; noUDP = true ], [ brokerIndex = 0; n = "Internet"; p = "IPv4"; port = 9637; ccbid = "377523"; a = "128.142.141.24"; noUDP = true ], [ n = "Internet"; p = "IPv4"; port = 48709; a = "129.93.182.27"; noUDP = true ] } The corresponding MyAddress is: MyAddress = "<129.93.182.27:48709?CCBID=128.142.141.24:9637%3faddrs%3d128.142.141.24-9637#377523&PrivNet=red-d9n7.unl.edu&addrs=129.93.182.27-48709&noUDP>" Does this smell funny to anyone else? Particularly, why are there 5 entries for what appears to be two distinct addresses?
remarks: 2015-Nov-10 11:50:20 by tlmiller: [ n = "Internet"; p = "primary"; port = 48709; a = "129.93.182.27"; noUDP = true ], The "primary" address is the one used to the left of the question mark in the original Sinful string. We need to know this address so we can reconstruct the original Sinful string for backwards compatibility. This also allows to us to round-trip between the original Sinful string, through AddressV1, and back to the original Sinful string. While you would expect that the primary address is always one of the addresses in the addrs parameter of the original Sinful string -- and thus readily representable in a more-compact way -- that's not always the case. (See #5339 and #5182.) [ n = "red-d9n7.unl.edu"; p = "IPv4"; port = 48709; a = "129.93.182.27"; noUDP = true ], This is the configured private network; you can tell because the network name is not "Internet". It doesn't look like a private address, but it unless they're using CCB unnecessarily, it actually is. We represent it as its own address because it could be. [ brokerIndex = 0; n = "Internet"; p = "primary"; port = 9637; ccbid = "377523"; a = "128.142.141.24"; noUDP = true ], This is the "primary" address of the first CCB broker. [ brokerIndex = 0; n = "Internet"; p = "IPv4"; port = 9637; ccbid = "377523"; a = "128.142.141.24"; noUDP = true ], The broker's public address. This information is in broker's Sinful string's addrs attribute. [ n = "Internet"; p = "IPv4"; port = 48709; a = "129.93.182.27"; noUDP = true ] } The host's public address, as listed in its addrs attribute. To summarize: the new address representation is larger because it's intended to allow us to describe more networking configurations than the original Sinful string. In most cases, the AddressV1 will contain redundant information, but we consider orthogonality more important than compactness. 2015-Nov-10 11:52:12 by tlmiller: Marking resolved; will reopen if you reply.

title: Ticket #2146: Reduce 7.6 shadow memory usage.
description: The following ticket is meant to track modifications made to reduce memory footprint of the condor shadow under the V7.6 stable series. In investigating the memory profile, I've noticed that pmap -d can be quite misleading when comparing memory usage across versioned executables. When decreasing heap usage on a modified 7.6 condor_shadow, pmap -d can yield data which flies against /proc/<pid>/status + top , /proc/<pid>/smaps, and valgrind. Ref1: http://www-archive.mozilla.org/projects/footprint/footprint-guide.html Ref2: http://xpt.sourceforge.net/techdocs/nix/general/gnl04-ProcessAndMemories/ar01s03.html Before: /proc/<pid>/status ----------------------------------------------- Name: condor_shadow State: S (sleeping) SleepAVG: 98% Tgid: 5719 Pid: 5719 PPid: 4752 TracerPid: 0 Uid: 0 14475 0 14475 Gid: 0 14475 64 14475 FDSize: 64 Groups: 1070 14475 *VmPeak: 59540 kB *VmSize: 59536 kB VmLck: 0 kB VmHWM: 4480 kB *VmRSS: 4480 kB *VmData: 988 kB VmStk: 84 kB VmExe: 2124 kB *VmLib: 6864 kB VmPTE: 216 kB StaBrk: 00d7a000 kB Brk: 00e32000 kB StaStk: 7fff135f4590 kB Threads: 1 SigQ: 1/397311 SigPnd: 0000000000000000 ShdPnd: 0000000000000000 SigBlk: 0000000000000000 SigIgn: 0000000000001000 SigCgt: 0000000180014eed CapInh: 0000000000000000 CapPrm: 00000000fffffeff CapEff: 0000000000000000 Cpus_allowed: 00000000,00000000,00000000,00000000,00000000,00000000,00000000,ffffffff Mems_allowed: 00000000,00000003 After:/proc/<pid>/status ----------------------------------------------- Name: condor_shadow State: S (sleeping) SleepAVG: 98% Tgid: 10295 Pid: 10295 PPid: 10281 TracerPid: 0 Uid: 0 14475 0 14475 Gid: 0 14475 64 14475 FDSize: 64 Groups: 1070 14475 *VmPeak: 59392 kB *VmSize: 59388 kB VmLck: 0 kB VmHWM: 4220 kB *VmRSS: 4220 kB *VmData: 840 kB VmStk: 84 kB VmExe: 2124 kB *VmLib: 6864 kB VmPTE: 212 kB StaBrk: 092d1000 kB Brk: 09364000 kB StaStk: 7fff81a5c590 kB Threads: 1 SigQ: 1/397311 SigPnd: 0000000000000000 ShdPnd: 0000000000000000 SigBlk: 0000000000000000 SigIgn: 0000000000001000 SigCgt: 0000000180014eed CapInh: 0000000000000000 CapPrm: 00000000fffffeff CapEff: 0000000000000000 Cpus_allowed: 00000000,00000000,00000000,00000000,00000000,00000000,00000000,ffffffff Mems_allowed: 00000000,00000003 ----------------------------------------------- You can clearly see that the total memory usage has gone down, yet when running pmap -d across this experiment private memory usage went from 1188 -> 1228 which runs contrary to the afore mentioned data. NOTE: This type of behavior has only been demonstrated on RHEL(5) machines From reading, pmap reports just virtual mem large parts of which are likely to be paged to disk forever for shared libs. More accurate results can be obtained from /proc/<pid>/smaps. The following script analyzes such data:(http://www.pixelbeat.org/scripts/ps_mem.py) Before: Private + Shared = RAM used Program 2.1 MiB + 214.5 KiB = 2.3 MiB condor_shadow After: Private + Shared = RAM used Program 2.0 MiB + 210.5 KiB = 2.2 MiB condor_shadow ~ 5% reduction in size. In summary: pmap -d alone can yield an inaccurate picture of the world. To get a better picture /proc/<pic>/smaps should be used to determine the per-process impact of the condor_shadow.

title: Ticket #6105: Make use of classad cache be more explicit and cheaper
description: When the classad cache is passed an expr-tree, it will unparse it. This is a fairly expensive operation and something that we never actually want to do in our code. so to insure that it isn't happening that capability will be removed from the classad cache. Since this will involve an ABI change to the Classad code, some other changes will be rolled into the same commit. In particular. The classad library version will be bumped Classad cache insertion will be via explicit call InsertViaCache Creation of common Literals will have optimized methods Splitting of a single line of -long (old form) classad will be moved out of the classad library and into the compat layer Trivial constructors and destructors for ExprTree, Literal and Value classes will be moved into the header files to insure that they are inlined. The number factor will be moved from the Literal into the Value, where it packs better, but it will still be exposed through the Literal methods and not the Value methods (they are already friends...) The parentScope will be moved from ExprTree into child classes other than Literal

title: Ticket #3307: Condor build using Visual Studio 2012
description: With VS2012 out and the express version including the runtime manifests, it's a good chance to work on support for building HTCondor in VS2012. So far problems encountered include the linker pulling in way more than it should, in part due to the merger of daemon core and the util library. This causes soap dependencies to throw linker errors in condor_setup, which have been worked around by stubbing the offending functions in condor_setup. One bonus to using VS2012 is not needing boost anymore. VS2012 includes all of the C++ 11 functionality that we use in the classad code. Installer also needs some minor updates. Specifically, the VC++2012 runtime uses Windows Installer 4.5, whereas we are still set to 3.0. This may not require anything beyond an update to WiX and setting the value appropriately in the wix files. We do need to check whether the VS2012 build will work correctly on XP. Microsoft has released an update to allow for XP targeting, just need to confirm that it works.

title: Ticket #5050: Attributes set using chirp set_job_attr_delayed never go to shadow
description: The new condor_chirp command set_job_attr_delayed is meant to allow relatively cheap setting of custom job attributes into the schedd by the job, by storing the changes and then sending them along with the normal job update. But because of the way it was coded, the stored changes are cleared after the attributes are sent into the job hook but before the update ad is built to send to the schedd. The chirped attributes might show up in the final update, depending on the timing of the chirp calls and the normal periodic job update. Inspection of the code also indicates that there is a bug in the code meant to limit the number of unique attributes that may be chirped. Once an attempt has been made to hit that limit, NO update will ever be allowed after that time, even if it is to one of the attributes that was originally allowed.

title: Ticket #2795: spawn glexec less by keeping a helper process around
description: As you well know, Condor calls glexec way too many times; if I remember correctly, it is 3 times at startup and 3 times at job termination. The job termination invocations are actually quite problematic, since glexec may deny the request (for multiple reasons), thus preventing Condor from controlling the job it started. If I understand correctly the reasoning behind this, it is due to the need for Condor to do operations on behalf of the user, while making (reasonably) sure the user does not interfere with this. However, I and the NIKHEF guys may have found the solution; it is quite easy to make a process protected from other processes of the same user, modulo getting signals from them. (see below) So a malicious user would not be able to attack anything Condor was to run alongside the job processes (with the job UID); at best, it could hard kill it. In which case, you either restart the companion process and continue as if nothing happened, or kill the job, as you are doing today. The only edge case is when you cannot call glexec anymore... but this should be rare and it is not under the attacker control. Said that, what I envision is for you to start this companion process as first thing after you get the user proxy to the WN, keep an open connection with it, and do everything you currently do when invoking glexec, with the exception of actually starting the user job (you need to create the env, want to know when it finishes, etc.) This would reduce the typical number of calls to glexec to exactly 2 per user job; this could rise a little bit in case the user attacks this companion process, but should not be worse than what we have today. Moreover, you are guaranteed to always be able to control the job you started. (modulo the edge case described above) when starting a unreadable executable, by default you cannot attach ptrace and /proc/<pid>/* is root-owned. see man 2 prctl, in particular PR_SET_DUMPABLE It claims to be there since 2.3.20...
remarks: 2012-Jan-30 15:16:55 by bbockelm: Hi Zach, How would this compare with, say, using linger mode? In glexec 0.9, linger mode allows you to pass files between pilot/payload as well as signals. Brian 2012-Jan-30 15:43:46 by zmiller: linger mode may well solve the problem, as long as it can do everything to the payload that condor needs. at the moment, i believe condor does not play well with linger mode, but of course that should be addressed.

title: Ticket #3184: Condor collector deadlock
description: Our primary collector deadlocked last night and the master was unable to recover it. When the collector forked, the child process hit the below deadlock: [root@red-condor ~]# pstack 8377 #0 0x0000003bea2df01e in __lll_lock_wait_private () from /lib64/libc.so.6 #1 0x0000003bea28be9d in _L_lock_1685 () from /lib64/libc.so.6 #2 0x0000003bea28bbe7 in __tz_convert () from /lib64/libc.so.6 #3 0x00002b00e633c1a4 in _condor_dprintf_va () from /usr/lib64/libcondor_utils_7_9_1.so #4 0x00002b00e634ccf8 in dprintf () from /usr/lib64/libcondor_utils_7_9_1.so #5 0x00002b00e63af55e in ForkWork::NewJob() () from /usr/lib64/libcondor_utils_7_9_1.so #6 0x0000000000420a42 in CollectorDaemon::receive_query_cedar(Service*, int, Stream*) () #7 0x00002b00e64880d9 in DaemonCore::CallCommandHandler(int, Stream*, bool, bool, float, float) () from /usr/lib64/libcondor_utils_7_9_1.so #8 0x00002b00e64884e9 in DaemonCore::HandleReqPayloadReady(Stream*) () from /usr/lib64/libcondor_utils_7_9_1.so #9 0x00002b00e648918a in DaemonCore::CallSocketHandler_worker(int, bool, Stream*) () from /usr/lib64/libcondor_utils_7_9_1.so #10 0x00002b00e648961d in DaemonCore::CallSocketHandler_worker_demarshall(void*) () from /usr/lib64/libcondor_utils_7_9_1.so #11 0x00002b00e633fd18 in CondorThreads::pool_add(void (*)(void*), void*, int*, char const*) () from /usr/lib64/libcondor_utils_7_9_1.so #12 0x00002b00e6486225 in DaemonCore::CallSocketHandler(int&, bool) () from /usr/lib64/libcondor_utils_7_9_1.so #13 0x00002b00e648bd3c in DaemonCore::Driver() () from /usr/lib64/libcondor_utils_7_9_1.so #14 0x00002b00e646e1d1 in dc_main(int, char**) () from /usr/lib64/libcondor_utils_7_9_1.so #15 0x0000003bea21d994 in __libc_start_main () from /lib64/libc.so.6 #16 0x000000000040dd49 in _start () Not sure how this one happened. Perhaps there was a rogue thread active in the parent when the fork occurred? Globus can launch threads... This caused the child to hang around forever. Because it lasted for quite some time, the copy-on-write semantics caused the memory to grow quite quickly. Eventually the OOM-killer selected the parent collector and shot it. [Side note: the code to limit the number of children does not appear to be functioning, as this daemon had up to 7 children, but the maximum should have been set to two.] However, the children still have a port open on 9618. This means the master cannot start up a new collector, as its port is already taken. Why didn't the procd kill off the children after the collector died? Because, right before the OOM-killer took out the collector, it killed the procd. The system remained in this state until admin intervention was taken. It's about the third time in the last two weeks that this occurred.
remarks: 2012-Aug-08 08:34:12 by bbockelm: Scratch the side note about the number of children. I fat-fingered the condor_config_val query, and failed to notice we had increased this setting locally. 2012-Aug-08 09:02:15 by bbockelm: After some discussion with tstclair in #distcomp, I realized what's happening here. This occurred after an upgrade. On upgrade of condor-qmf, as the QMF config file is not marked %config(noreplace), it overwrote our config file, and re-enabled the QMF plugin. The collector was then restarted. A few hours later, puppet came by and fixed the config file. So, when I restarted the condor_collector, there was no evidence of threads. Long story short, the collector was running with threads, and dprintf uses a thread-safe, but non-reentrant call (localtime). This caused the children to deadlock, and the rest of the behavior. So the lesson here (besides the fact we need to tweak our puppet config) - collector plugins and forked children cannot mix!

title: Ticket #4211: Add #ifdef-like mechanism to config file parser
description: We would like to be able improve the config file syntax, and add new features with clean and clear syntax. But we are also reluctant to make changes that make it impossible for lder versions of HTCondor to parse the config files. If there was a way to mark sections of the config file to be ignored by older versions of HTCondor, then it would be much safer and easier for users to opt-in to new features without having to worry about preventing older daemons or tools from starting. To support this the 8.1.x series (and thus the 8.2.x series) should have the ability to parse something like the C++ #ifdef/#endif to mark off sections of the config file. The config file will be able to parse if <condition1> <config_statements_1> elif <condition2> <config_statements_2> else <config_statements_3> endif where condition can be a Boolean value (e.g. 0,1,yes,no,true,false). Boolean, Integer and floating point values are allowed. 0 is treated as false, all other numeric values are true. Question: should crufty booleans (t,T,f,F) be allowed? version <compare_operator> <version_string> (e.g. version > [v]8.1). Version literal values must be 2 or 3 integers separated by . and optionally proceeded by v. The v prefix is to allow for version comparisons to migrate into classads at some point in the future. For the same reason, the keyword version is case-insensitive. Note: HTCondor currently doesn't permit version numbers starting with values < 6. defined <param_name> (e.g. defined SLOT_TYPE_1). Evaluates to true if <param_name> is defined and not empty. We treat empty as undefined because it isn't possible to undefine built-in params, but they can be overridden with empty values, and because the result of expanding $(param_name) is the same in both cases. In the example above, the config system will parse and insert statements in <config_statements_1> if <condition1> is true, and will ignore (and not parse!) those in <config_statements_2> and <config_statements_3>. Not parsing is a key requirement, as it allows new syntax to be used inside blocks where <condition> evaluates to false: if version >= 8.3 ...config statements not valid to 8.2.x config parser.... else ...config statements that 8.2.x can parse... endif The if/elif/else/endif capability will also be useful when defining meta knobs whose behavior is influenced by user-defined knobs. The <condition> of an if/elif will will first be macro-expanded. Then version and defined expressions will be evaluated and replaced with 0 or 1, and then the final result evaluated for truth. (in theory - the initial implementation will not actually have 3 passes). The initial version of this feature will not support complex conditional expressions, but it is important to get if <bool>, if version, and if defined into the 8.2 series to enable future improvements without breaking compatibility. Some examples: if 1 iftest=one else if 0 iftest=two else iftest=three endif endif # expected result is iftest=three if defined iftestb iftestbd=iftestb defined elif defined $(iftest) iftestbd=iftest defined elif ! defined $(iftestb) iftestbd=iftestb not defined else iftestbd=four endif # expected result is iftestbd=four # test version iftver_test=8.0.6 if version >= $(iftver_test) iftestver= version >= $(iftver_test) else iftestver= version < $(iftver_test) endif # expected result is iftestver=version < 8.0.6 # test version equality if version == 8.1.4 iftestveris= is 8.1.4 else iftestveris=is not 8.1.4 endif # expected result is iftestveris=is not 8.1.4 # test version fuzzy equality if version == 8.1 iftestveris= is 8.1 else iftestveris=is not 8.1 endif # expected result is iftestveris=is 8.1 # test undef==false for references if ! $(TESTING_UNDEF) UNDEF_VALUE = 1 endif # expected result is UNDEV_VALUE=1

title: Ticket #4704: ShadowLog spurious "Can't open directory"
description: The ShadowLog frequently has D_ALWAYS messages in the form 11/05/14 17:49:07 (2.0) (15133): Can't open directory "/tmp/a/condor-8.2.3-x86_64_RedHat6-stripped/local.puffin/spool/2/0/cluster2.proc0.subproc0.tmp" as PRIV_USER, errno: 2 (No such file or directory) 11/05/14 17:49:07 (2.0) (15133): Can't open directory "/tmp/a/condor-8.2.3-x86_64_RedHat6-stripped/local.puffin/spool/2/0/cluster2.proc0.subproc0" as PRIV_USER, errno: 2 (No such file or directory) This appears to be normal behavior, so logging this is misleading noise and a red-herring when tracking down unexpected behavior. The code emitting the message is in Directory::Rewind (/src/condor_utils/directory.cpp around line 750). Perhaps failure to find a file in Directory::Rewind isn't an error worth logging at D_ALWAYS. Or perhaps whenever code is calling this should preemptively check for the directory's existence before creating the Directory object. Reproduction: tar xzf /p/condor/public/binaries/v8.2/8.2.3/condor-8.2.3-x86_64_RedHat6-stripped.tar.gz cd condor-8.2.3-x86_64_RedHat6-stripped/ ./condor_install --make-personal-condor source condor.sh condor_master mkdir submit cd submit cat > submit <<END universe=vanilla executable=/bin/date log=log queue END condor_submit submit condor_wait log cat ../local.*/log/ShadowLog

title: Ticket #5115: Windows drops events when event log locking is disabled.
description: When EVENT_LOG_LOCKING or ENABLE_USERLOG_LOCKING are not set on Windows, the relevant event log can end up with truncated or missing events if there are multiple writers. This happens despite the fact that the files are open for append only. The problem is that the c-runtime on Windows, does not pass the 'append only' flag down into the underlying Windows API call that opens the file, instead the c-runtime is simulating append-only behavior by seeking inside the implementation of write(). (The VS11 runtime was examined to determine this). The fix is to call the underlying Windows open API with the correct arguments for append mode directly, and then shove the resulting handle into the c-runtime's handle table.

title: Ticket #7578: Fix Kerberos krb5_free_addresses issue
description: THIS BUG WAS FIXED BEFORE IT MADE IT INTO A RELEASE While fixing up a coverity-found potential issue, a new bug was introduced where we passed a pointer to something that was supposed to be a NULL-terminated array but had no terminator, and furthermore also tried to free() memory that was on the stack. Interestingly, the code before this bug was introduced was not correct to begin with. It is supposed to be passing in a NULL-terminated array to krb5_free_addresses() and most definitely was not. Perhaps by luck neighboring memory had a zero, or perhaps malloc() allocated a larger block of memory than needed and conveniently filled it with zeros, or something. Even more surprisingly, that function free() 's the addresses passed in the array AND THEN ALSO FREE()S THE ARRAY ITSELF. So the NULL-terminated array can't be on the stack either and must be explicitly malloc() 'ed.

title: Ticket #5791: Problem with default JOB_DEFAULT_REQUESTMEMORY
description: Reported by Stuart via Tom to Condor ticket system. The default setting of JOB_DEFAULT_REQUESTMEMORY, ifThenElse(MemoryUsage =!= UNDEFINED,MemoryUsage,(ImageSize+1023)/1024) appears to be problematic for jobs submitted without RequestMemory under HTCondor 8.4.7 and Partitionable slots if they are preempted and need to match/run again. In particular, I noticed that a number of jobs in the LIGO CIT SL7.2 pool that where relying on this default where being rejected by partitionable slot STARTD’s with, 07/09/16 15:07:44 slot1_3: New machine resource of type -1 allocated 07/09/16 15:07:44 Setting up slot pairings 07/09/16 15:07:44 slot1_3: Slot requirements not satisfied. 07/09/16 15:07:44 slot1_3: Job ad was ============================ However, if I condor_qedit RequestMemory to be quantize(ImageSize/1024,1) then jobs are not rejected and start in a dynamic slot. I believe there are a few problems: 0) Sec 3.5.1.19 states a different default default value, http://research.cs.wisc.edu/htcondor/manual/v8.4/3_5Policy_Configuration.html#37135 JOB_DEFAULT_REQUESTMEMORY = ifThenElse(MemoryUsage =!= UNDEFINED, MemoryUsage, 1) then what I observe and what is stated in Sec 3.3.13, http://research.cs.wisc.edu/htcondor/manual/v8.4/3_3Configuration.html#25623 ifThenElse(MemoryUsage =!= UNDEFINED,MemoryUsage,(ImageSize+1023)/1024) 1) It looks like RequestMemory must be an integer to be effective. I first tried manually calculating a reasonable RequestMemory value for a test job and entered that via condor_qedit as a real number. However, even when I seriously inflated the value STARTD for the partitionable slot would still reject the job until I rounded that to an integer. 2) Even with STARTD_DEBUG = D_ALL I was unable to find a mention in StartLog of what “Slot requirements” where not satisfied. I think it would be very helpful to log this and make it easy to access, e.g., from a submit machine I would love to see “condor_q -better-analyze JobId” report details on the last failed attempt to start a job (if there was a match that was rejected). 3) Attempting to use the ResidentSetSize directly (or via MemoryUsage) in RequestMemory did not work (even after rounding to an integer). I did not investigate this very much, but I believe startd is not happy if RequestMemory is less than ImageSize. At any rate, the following was successful in getting a number of otherwise idle jobs running, A) Make a list of idle jobs requesting less memory than ImageSize before and after running qedit, condor_q -constraint "(jobstatus == 1) && (RequestMemory < ImageSize/1024)" -af globaljobid RequestMemory ImageSize/1024 B) Set all of those jobs to track their ImageSize, condor_qedit -constraint "(jobstatus == 1) && (RequestMemory < ImageSize/1024)" RequestMemory "quantize(ImageSize/1024,1)" C) Change the default setting for new user jobs being submitted, [root@ldas-pcdev2 ~]# cat /etc/condor/config.d/memory JOB_DEFAULT_REQUESTMEMORY = quantize(ImageSize/1024,1)

title: Ticket #2054: hfs looping on "group quota exceeded"
description: In old code, the cleanup of usage values and "pruning" of a group from further negotiation was done immediately after negotiation of that group. Part of this was setting a flag that would halt negotiation. And part of this was setting groupArray[i].numsubmits == 0, which would then hit if ( groupArray[i].numsubmits == 0 ) { ... continue; } This would skip negotiation for this group in the next iteration. The group would be pruned from all subsequent negotiation. The flag was a defensive measure taken due to comparison of doubles. In new code, negotiation for all groups is done followed by a new loop that does the clean up. There is no flag and the groups are not pruned immediately. Repro: NUM_CPUS = 100 GROUP_NAMES = a, b GROUP_QUOTA_DYNAMIC_a = .4 GROUP_QUOTA_DYNAMIC_b = .6 GROUP_AUTOREGROUP_a = FALSE The create a number of different users for group a. Like 5 users ranging from a.a1 to a.a5. executable =./sleep.a1 arguments = 600 universe = vanilla should_transfer_files = YES when_to_transfer_output = ON_EXIT +AccountingGroup = "a.a1" queue 200 Let the jobs fill the 40 slots and then grep exceeded NegotiatorLog 04/05/11 11:56:55 Rejected 1444.8 a.a4@basin.redhat.com <166.217.160.21:41826>: group quota exceeded 04/05/11 11:56:55 Rejected 1443.8 a.a3@basin.redhat.com <166.217.160.21:41826>: group quota exceeded 04/05/11 11:56:55 Rejected 1442.8 a.a2@basin.redhat.com <166.217.160.21:41826>: group quota exceeded 04/05/11 11:56:55 Rejected 1445.8 a.a5@basin.redhat.com <166.217.160.21:41826>: group quota exceeded 04/05/11 11:56:56 Rejected 1441.7 a.a1@basin.redhat.com <166.217.160.21:41826>: group quota exceeded In scenarios with lots of users like 100, you will get 100 rejections for "group quota exceeded". These could all be pruned either before or immediately after the 1st rejection (the one for a.a4 in the example).
remarks: 2011-Apr-18 16:25:53 by danb: Code review: For a stable series patch, it would be better to refrain from so much cosmetic surgery. There are a number of changes in code flow, variable names, whitespace, comment style, variable declaration placement---all of which do not really seem fundamental to the patch. That said, "submitterAds" is a much better name than "scheddAds" :). I am concerned about the change in what happens when the submitter limit is reached. Previously, this resulted in result=MM_RESUME, which (if I understand things correctly), resulted in the submitter remaining in line for consideration in future spins of the pie. In the patch, this case is handled by removing the submitter from the list of submitters, so I think this means this user will not be considered in subsequent spins of the pie: if (!ignore_submitter_limit && ((submitterLimit <= 0) || (pieLeft < minSlotWeight))) { // If limit is 0, and we are respecting submitter limits, don't waste time with negotiate negotiation_cycle_stats[0]->submitters_share_limit.insert(submitterName.Value()); dprintf(D_FULLDEBUG, "Submitter %s is at its submitter limit %g\n", submitterName.Value(), submitterLimit); submitterAds.Remove(submitter); continue; } In general, this seems like a pretty aggressive patch for a stable series. This makes it hard to be confident that no surprises are introduced. I'd recommend splitting this into two patches: one suitable for the stable series that fixes the problem with minimal code disturbance, and another with all the other improvements to the code. 2011-Apr-18 17:44:07 by eje: Ouch, good catch -- shouldn't remove submitter on hitting submitter limit. 2011-Apr-25 14:02:42 by danb: Looks good! title: Ticket #4883: Python bindings for dprintf
description: Use Case See #4875 - use case duplicated below: The OSG is starting a new project to investigate management of Xrootd caches placed in strategic (in terms of networking) locations around the grid. One important aspect of this is to improve the management of the remote instances. We'd like the xrootd daemons to run underneath the HTCondor master. Thus, we would like to have a python script which sits between the master and the xrootd daemon that periodically advertises to the collector and sends heartbeats to the master. As a part of this, we'd like the python shim script to be able to act as a DC-like daemon. Particularly, we'd like to be able to control the logging via the normal HTCondor logging subsystem Proposal I propose we add a "log" method to the HTCondor module with the following log(level, msg) Log a message to the HTCondor logging subsystem. :param level: Log category and formatting indicator; use the LogLevel enum for a list of these (may be OR'd together). :param msg: String message to log. Unlike "dprintf" proper, This will automatically add "\n" to the end of the log string. This doesn't accept formatting characters; python lets you do this directly.

title: Ticket #6914: Terminate event can have data transfer numbers reversed
description: If the shadow crashes after sending its final update for a completed job to the schedd, the schedd will restart it to ensure that final tasks like writing the terminate event are performed. In this recovery code path, the shadow will reverse the bytes sent and bytes received numbers in the terminate event. The shadow has a separate code path for writing the terminate event in recovery mode, as many of the data structures it would normally use aren't available. It pulls the relevant numbers from the job ad, instead. The recovery code path was confused about whether the transfer numbers in the job ad are relative to the job or the shadow.

title: Ticket #4180: Report on tunneling/delegation/reversal
description: Miron requested a document enumerating the advantages and disadvantages of connection tunneling, delegation, and reversal. WORK IN PROGRESS Tunneling, delegation, and reversal solve slightly different problems. A given solution might include any subset of them, including possibly some multiple times. Network Address Translation is considered to be a special case of firewalls. "Connectivity from X to Y" means that X can initiate a two-way communications channel to Y. This may be thwarted by firewalls, network failures, and more. In the interest of not drowning the document is qualifiers, almost every claim that appears to be universal actually means "overwhelmingly in practice." For example, overwhelmingly in practice, a direct connection is the fastest connection to initialize. But in very unusual situations, connection tunneling can be faster. "Intermediary processes" refers to processes that handle the stream between the client and the server beyond the routers, switches, firewalls, and NATs encountered in normal network operations. Routers, switches, and firewalls are excluded from this definition. Direct Connection The client establishes a direct network connection to the server. Advantages: Connections are initialized quickly. The minimal amount of work is done by the client and server to establish the connection. There are no intermediary processes adding delays. Connections have minimal latency. There are no intermediary processes adding latency. Connections have maximum bandwidth. There is no diversion adding unnecessary links which may limit bandwidth, and no intermediary processes which may limit bandwidth as a result of limited processor, RAM, or other constraints. Most robust. All other options involve more processes. Disadvantages: Requires connectivity from the client to the server. Client and server cannot establish a "better" (lower latecy, higher bandwidth, lower price) connection based on local knowledge. Connection Tunneling Examples: SOCKS HTTP proxy with CONNECT support GCB (no longer available) Advantages: Can allow protocol jumping. For example, a client with IPv4-only access might connect to a mixed-mode tunnel which makes the connection to an IPv6-only server. Can potentially bypass firewalls. Disadvantages: Turns a single connection into two: a connection from the client to the tunnel provider, then a connection from the tunnel provider to the server. These connections are subject to any disadvantages for the techniques used to establish them (direct, reversed, delegated). Requires connectivity from the client to the tunnel provider. Requires some sort of collaboration from the server-side. (SOCKS, GCB) For some tunnel providers where the server registers an intent to use the tunnel, the server requires outbound connectivity to the tunnel. (HTTP CONNECT) For other tunnel providers where the server does not register with the tunnel provider, any firewall must be configured to allow inbound connections from the tunnel provider to the server. Connection Reversal Examples: CCB GCB (no longer available) Advantages: Connections generally have maximum bandwidth. There is no diversion adding unnecessary links which may limit bandwidth, and no intermediary processes which may limit bandwidth as a result of limited processor, RAM, or other constraints. Can potentially bypass firewalls. Disadvantages: Requires connectivity from the server to the connection reversal provider. Requires connectivity from the server to the client. Requires connectivity from the client to the connection reversal provider. Turns a single connection into three: server to reversal provider, client to reversal provider, server to client. These connections are subject to any disadvantages for the techniques used to establish them (direct, reversed, delegated). Connection Delegation Examples: condor_shared_port Advantages: Allows sharing of otherwise limited inbound IP ports. Disadvantages: Limited to a single host. Absent specialized hardware, there is no way to hand a TCP connection to a process on another computer. Requires connectivity from the client to the server. NOTES Minimizing port/fd usage.

title: Ticket #1228: CLASSAD_LIB_PATH for new ClassAds
description: So called Old ClassAds allow for loading new functions via shared libraries dropped into CLASSAD_LIB_PATH. New ClassAds appear to contain the same low-level functionality, see classad/fnCall.cpp and classad/extra_tests.cpp, but it is not exposed by Condor. It should be exposed, possibly via CLASSAD_LIB_PATH.
remarks: 2010-Feb-18 16:45:24 by jfrey: Old ClassAds can be given a single shared library that provides additional ClassAd functions (via CLASSAD_LIB_PATH). If the evaluation code encounters a function that's not implemented in the ClassAd library and CLASSAD_LIB_PATH is set, it tries to open the library and look for a function with the same name as the ClassAd function being evaluated. If it finds one, it invokes it. In new ClassAds, you can supply multiple shared libraries that provide additional ClassAd functions. You explicitly register each library, at which point ClassAds opens the library and attempts to invoke a function named 'Init'. Init is expected to return an array of structs that provides a function name and function pointer for each new ClassAd function. The signature of the functions in the shared library is different between new and old ClassAds. In new ClassAds, all new functions must be registered before they can be invoked. In order to transparently support the old ClassAd shared libraries, we'd have to modify the new ClassAds code to be willing to deal with just-in-time lookups of added functions or figure out how to scan a shared library for all additional functions. 2010-Feb-19 11:16:51 by matt: Allowing for CLASSAD_LIB_PATH with new ClassAds is probably sufficient. Making the DSO mechanism backward compatible is likely overkill. 2010-May-07 15:24:46 by jfrey: Given the difference between the ABIs of new and old ClassAds for user-defined functions, we will add a new config parameter for specifying libraries for new ClassAd functions. The old paramater (CLASSAD_LIB_PATH) will no longer work. Condor may send email to the administrator if the parameter is defined in the config file. 2010-May-11 15:42:48 by jfrey: Pushed a commit to master for 7.5.3. There's now a CLASSAD_USER_LIBS config param, a list of libraries containing user-defined new ClassAd functions.

title: Ticket #4495: IPv6: mixed-mode central manager
description: (This is very early notes!) Goal Support mixed pools where some nodes speak IPv4 only and some nodes speak IPv6 only. Matchmaking must avoid matches where the two hosts cannot communicate because one is IPv4 only and the other is IPv6 only. Acceptable Limitations The project can be considered complete even if the final work includes these limitations. Later projects may remove limitations. It is likely that some limitations will prove to be unnecessary. The condor_collector and condor_negotiator must be able to receive and establish connections over both IPv6 and IPv4. Other daemons will not support IPv6 and IPv4 simultaneously. Non-central manager nodes will not support IPv6 and IPv4 simultaneously. If IPv6 is enabled for a given daemon, that daemon can only listen to a single IPv6 address and a single IPv4 address. Only the vanilla universe is supported. NETWORK_INTERFACE only supports a single address, IPv4 or IPv6. Private and link local addresses are not supported. A node configured for IPv4 or IPv6 only cannot communicate with a node only using the other protocol. Versions of HTCondor post-mixed-mode cannot communicate with pre-mixed-mode versions. CCB cannot act as a tunnel between IPv4 and IPv6. There is a one-to-one mapping between a daemon (or other running process) and contact information for it. This contact information will have a unique serialization suitable for passing between processes and a unique internal data structure. All nodes must have a working IPv4 loopback at 127.0.0.1. This includes nodes otherwise configured to exclusively use IPv6. PrivAddr only supports a single address, IPv4 or IPv6.

title: Ticket #2541: Memory utilization of classads (revised)
description: Problem Description When running heap profiles experiments on the schedd, we've found that doubling the queue count == doubling of the classad count in the schedd even though most of the data is the same across ads. Also when doing performance calculations on the collector it was determined that most of the time inside of the collector was spent churning on redundant data. Proposed solution Keep a cache of the current in memory classads. Design Approach key [str_name] = key[str_value] = weak_ptr<~ExprTree> After several iterations on possible implementations I've settled on this implementation because it has optimal speed performance without sacrificing any space savings. One thing that becomes apart when analyzing the data is that there is a large % or redundant data and a small % of data which churns. We could easily save more memory by having meta information in classads (possibly through nested ads). m_Cache[name][value] = weak_ptr<Cache_Element> All caching code backs against the Insert function(s) in classads. It was optimized so the main path by which messages come across the wire will do a look-up using a single string based function in the classads layer: bool Insert(const std::string& serialized_nvp); Initial Results Space savings depends on a couple of variables: Very simple tests yield space savings ~10-15% with iLoc savings ~ 10%. This is very difficult to quantify until it's tested at scale what the actual difference will yield. The complexity of the ExprTree's in the Cache, more complex >> savings in both speed and perf. So it is "fluid" Debugging There are a couple of internal features which have been added to aid in the diagnostics of the behavior of caching. There is an internal only knob which is hooked through DAEMON_CORE which enables a daemon to dump it's cache to a <subsystem>_classad_cache file under LOG when DEBUG_CLASSAD_CACHE=TRUE . The file dumping is hooked through SIGUSR2 kill -s 12 <collector_pid> -> drops $LOG/COLLECTOR_classad_cache NOTES This works for all DAEMON_CORE based daemons.

title: Ticket #3429: Improve blahp querying of Condor job status
description: The blahp's querying of Condor for a job's status can take much longer than necessary. We have seen this result in the blahp timing out and returning failure to the gridmanager. The blahp attempts to reduce the number of times condor_q is called by caching the output for subsequent status queries. If the cached condor_q output doesn't include the desired job, then the blahp calls condor_history. If condor_history doesn't turn up the job, the blahp calls condor_q for the one job, in case the cached condor_q output is too stale. If Condor's history file is fairly large, the condor_history command can take a long time. We can reduce this time by using the -match option to tell condor_history to exit once it finds one matching job. In the Condor build of the blahp, the caching of condor_q output doesn't work properly. Thus, all job status queries end up calling condor_history. If the job is still in the queue, then the -match option of condor_history won't reduce the runtime of the command. We can solve this by calling condor_q explicitly before condor_history (duplicating the call made after condor_history). In a future release, we should try to fix the condor_q caching code, at which point we could remove the added call to condor_q.

title: Ticket #7190: Bad messages from condor_submit -i
description: Episode 3 HTCondor tells you you’re “rejected” if it’s still setting up your interactive job. (Could it, rather, say something like “setting up your job environment” ?) The starter already explicitly informs the client if it makes sense to retry a failed attempt; the client does retry if it's condor_submit -i or condor_ssh_to_job -auto-retry, but doesn't otherwise. I therefore propose that we only make changes on the client side, where HTCondor only prints an error message from the starter if it causes the tool to exit (or the debug flag is set). Polled the RCFs to determine if we should print something explicit on failure (not just the error message) and/or something explicit on retry (e.g., "please keep waiting"). Christina thought 'no' on retries (since the users are already expecting to wait for a while), but suggests either better failure messages or prefixing the failure messages with a good explanation about the result. Lauren thought that a single message -- e.g., 'HTCondor is still preparing the job environment, please wait' -- was better than suppressing all warnings, to reassure the user that the tool hadn't hung. Mat agreed. Jim pointed out that condor_ssh_to_job should have (and it might already) a -q option to make scripting easier. Lauren also doesn't want an explicit/extra failure message, but to make the existing ones more useful/readable.

title: Ticket #2668: improve my_popen
description: Currently, my_popen() provides the option to suppress stderr or to mix stderr with stdout. Neither of these options is very helpful for debugging. In some situations it would therefore be preferable to provide separate stdout and stderr pipes. In addition, a convenience function should be added that does all the work of running a command and reading all of the stderr + stdout output into strings. One case where this has come up is in the invocation of the hibernation plugin in startd_hibernation.cpp.
creator: danb

title: Ticket #972: Fault recovery during cream job submission broken
description: If the gridmanager crashes after saving the job id of a Cream job, but before sending the Cream Start command, recovery is handled improperly. On restart, the gridmanager will assume the job has already been started and proceed directly to the GM_SUBMITTED state. Subsequent job status checks will show that the job is in REGISTERED state on the Cream server, but the gridmanager doesn't do anything special when it sees this. When the gridmanager starts managing a job that has GridJobId already set, it should check the job's status on the Cream server and send a Start command if the status is REGISTERED.
remarks: Pushed a fix to V7_4-branch for 7.4.1. 2009-Nov-20 16:31:51 by jfrey: The first attempt to fix fault recovery during job submission tripped over a race condition in the Cream server. A Status command immediately following a Start command can return REGISTERED instead of PENDING or IDLE. REGISTERED means the job hasn't been started with a Start command yet. As a result, during normal job submission, the gridmanager would issue a second Start command for about 10% of jobs. The Start would fail and the jobs would end up on hold. I've pushed a new fix to V7_4-branch for 7.4.1 that works around the problem by introducing a separate state for doing a job status poll on recovery.
