title: Ticket #2392: Changes to shadow log file initialization routines have broken SOAP
description: Prior to 7.6.x it was commonplace for us to set: QUEUE_ALL_USERS_TRUSTED = True On our SOAP-enabled schedulers and then submit jobs with "Owner = AnyOwnerWeLikeEvenIfItDoesNotExist" through the SOAP API. The jobs were also set to not run as owner on the execute nodes. The execute nodes are set up to run as logged-in domain users. On Window we would have the scheduler daemons running as a domain account, on Linux it would be context-switched to a local account on the machine. Condor would simple initialize the log files for the job under the spool/ directory as the user the schedd and shadow processes were running as. This worked great. Starting with 7.6.2 this setup now fails. Condor keeps trying to initialize the log files as the user found in the Owner attribute on the job. Subsequently shadow start fails because this owner never exists on the local machine. I see in the ShadowLog: 08/15/11 16:10:48 Initializing a VANILLA shadow for job 1736.9 08/15/11 16:10:48 (1736.9) (530): passwd_cache::cache_uid(): getpwnam("Daily") failed: user not found 08/15/11 16:10:48 (1736.9) (530): Daily not in passwd file 08/15/11 16:10:48 (1736.9) (530): init_user_ids() failed as user Daily 08/15/11 16:10:48 (1736.9) (530): set_user_egid() called when UserIds not inited! 08/15/11 16:10:48 (1736.9) (530): set_user_euid() called when UserIds not inited! 08/15/11 16:10:48 (1736.9) (530): passwd_cache::cache_uid(): getpwnam("Daily") failed: user not found 08/15/11 16:10:48 (1736.9) (530): Daily not in passwd file 08/15/11 16:10:48 (1736.9) (530): WriteUserLog::initialize: init_user_ids() failed! 08/15/11 16:10:48 (1736.9) (530): Failed to initialize user log to /opt/condor/local/spool/1/1736/9/cluster1736.proc9.subproc0/5585-9.log 08/15/11 16:10:48 (1736.9) (530): Job 1736.9 going into Hold state (code 22,0): Failed to initialize user log to /opt/condor/local/spool/1/1736/9/cluster1736.proc9.subproc0/5585-9.log 08/15/11 16:10:48 (1736.9) (530): RemoteResource::killStarter(): DCStartd object NULL! This is true for both Windows and Linux schedulers. In order to make things work I have at least have local accounts on the schedulers that match the names found in any Owner attribute in jobs submitted. While I realize this is the slightly more secure way to go, it's a major hassel and big deviation from the behaviour in pre-7.6.x. I say slightly because really it's just an inconvenience. I can still queue as any user I want with QUEUE_ALL_USERS_TRUSTED. That I now need to use a user who exists on the machine is only a minor upgrade in security to this very open, but incredibly necessary when using SOAP, hole. Ideally I'd like pre-7.6.x behaviour back. If that can't happen can we work out some way to disable this context switching in the shadow so the spawned sub-processes just run and read/write those log files in the spool directory as the user they happen to be running as on startup. It looks like things are failing specifically because init_user_ids() returns false on account of the user the shadow is running as, on both Linux and Windows, does not have the ability to context switch (makes sense, it's not root).

title: Ticket #83: Daemons hang using SSL with encrypted key file
description: Our SSL authentication method requires that the AUTH_SSL_CLIENT_KEYFILE and AUTH_SSL_SERVER_KEYFILE parameters point to a file containing the private key(s) to use. We currently do not support encrypted private keys, as they would additionally require a passphrase to be specified. However, if a daemon is configured to use a private key that is encrypted, rather than the SSL authentication method failing with a log message to that effect, the daemon hangs. This has been observed for the Collector running on Windows. As mentioned, specifying an encrypted key is a misconfiguration; but failing in a more user-friendly way in this scenario would be a big improvement. The hang is likely the result of OpenSSL prompting (in some invisible window) for the private key’s passphrase. OpenSSL allows for the specification of a custom passphrase-getting callback; leveraging that may be the easiest way to resolve this issue.

title: Ticket #5007: Condor-C double-counts runtime when job restarts
description: If a Condor-C job is evicted and restarted quickly, such that the gridmanager doesn't see the job in idle status, then condor_q will double-count the runtime of the job's first execution in its report of total job runtime. This is because when the job is evicted, the remote schedd adds the runtime of the first execution to RemoteWallClockTime, and when the job is restarted, ShadowBday is set to the start time of the second execution. The gridmanager doesn't notice that the job restarted. It copies the new RemoteWallClockTime value into the local job ad, but keeps the old ShadowBday. Then, condor_q adds the time since the old ShadowBday to the new RemoteWallClockTime. This was observed by Argo Graphics, Inc. The gridmanager should always use the remote schedd's ShadowBday value, along with the other job execution stats.

title: Ticket #3995: Condor_rm'ed DAGMan waits for node jobs to exit
description: It might be a good idea for a condor_rm'ed condor_dagman job to not exit until all of its child jobs have exited. We could do this by putting DAGMan into halt mode (in a non-reversible way, rather than with the halt file), and then condor_rm'ing the node jobs. I guess one question is whether there should be a way to force DAGMan to bypass this mode.
remarks: 2014-Oct-30 10:16:04 by wenger: Note that if we do this, and we have implemented the quick-and-dirty fix for #4686, we should undo that fix... 2014-Oct-30 10:27:56 by bbockelm: Some thoughts on this: We would need to tell the DAGMan process how much time it should wait. Would this be appropriate for the DAGMan config? We can always use SIGUSR2 for "immediate vacate", right? I'd also have the semantics to be that, if DAGMan returns before all jobs exit (i.e., the timeout hits), it writes out node_status with as accurate information as possible. If the schedd removes the jobs 1 ms after DAGMan exits (invalidating the node status), that's fine - the node_status file includes the timestamp of when it was written out and the user needs to understand things happen afterward. 2014-Oct-30 15:27:31 by wenger: This should also apply in the case of an ABORT-DAG-ON firing, and other cases where node jobs get removed. 2015-Jan-25 19:16:15 by wenger: Hmm -- just thinking about this, I think we'd be at least pretty close to what we want if we go into halt mode when we get the signal because of condor_rm. (We'd have to make sure that we stayed halted, not looking for the halt file...)
creator: wenger

title: Ticket #564: condor_q -better-analyze can't handle functions
description: In certain cases, condor_q -better-analyze has trouble dealing with classad functions whose arguments include Machine ad attributes. If the sub-expression containing a classad function evaluates to Undefined in the context of just the job ad, the analysis code can report that that sub-expression matches 0 machines, even if the sub-expression evaluates to true in the context of both job and machine ads. To reproduce, submit a vanilla job with these requirements: "foo" != string(Machine) && Machine =?= "foo" condor_q -better-analyze will say the job's requirements reject all machines and the first sub-expression matches zero machines. If the second sub-expression is changed to match some machines (by changing 'foo' to a hostname in the pool), -better-analyze can still report that the first sub-expression matches zero machines, even though the job will be matched and run.
creator: jfrey

title: Ticket #4753: Daemon log rotation broken when using clone()
description: In #3106, we fixed a bug where a race between a daemon and its forked child process to rotate the daemon log can result in the daemon writing to the rotated log file. The solution was to have the child process not perform log rotation. This is indicated via a new flag, DebugRotateLog, which is set to false in the child process. This same code is used in Create_Process() when spawning a new child daemon. When clone() is used to create the child, changing the flag in the child also changes it in the parent, and it's never changed back. As a result, the schedd on linux will stop rotating its log after spawning a shadow/starter/gridmanager. As a workaround, you can set USE_CLONE_TO_CREATE_PROCESSES=False in the config file.

title: Ticket #2941: condor_status should have -autoformat like condor_q does
description: condor_q has a -autoformat option (added as part of #2656) that is easier to use than -format. it would be nice if condor_status had this feature as well. the -autoformat option behaves like a series of -format commands with an implied first parameter of "%V" with a space between each field and a "\n" at the end of each record. It is assumed that everything on the command line up to the next '-' part of the -autoformat command. Thus: condor_status -autoformat Name OpSys Arch -pool .... results in the same output as: condor_status -format "%v" Name -format " %v" OpSys -format " %v\n" Arch -pool .... -autoformat can be abbreviated -af, and can be followed by a : and optional formatting qualifiers. t add a tab character before each field (instead of the default space) n add a newline character after each field , add a comma after each field l label each field V use %V rather than %v for formatting h print headings before the first line output the 'n' and ',' options are mutually exclusive. -autoformat can be mixed with -format on the same command line, and -autoformat can be specified multiple times with different formatting qualifiers. The last specification of -autoformat will control the prefix (t), and suffix (n,) for the entire command. Thus condor_status -af:, Name -format "%.3f" LoadAvg -format "%.3f" TotalLoadAvg will result in output like slot1@crane.cs.wisc.edu, 0.000, 0.250 slot2@crane.cs.wisc.edu, 0.000, 0.250 slot3@crane.cs.wisc.edu, 0.250, 0.250 slot4@crane.cs.wisc.edu, 0.000, 0.250
remarks: 2012-Aug-13 17:43:58 by sfiligoi: Just saw this. Why do we need -autoformat? Doesn't -attributes do exactly the same thing, conceptually? 2012-Aug-14 16:00:47 by johnkn: sfiligoi: -attributes does not print out the values of the attributes, it merely controls which attributes are returned from a query.

title: Ticket #6902: Stop changing argv[0]
description: When Condor runs an executable it sets the argv[0] to "condor_exec.exe". Greg tells me this was for historical reasons, so people could easily spot rogue Condor jobs using resources on their desktops. This causes problems with programs that use argv[0] to make decisions -- for example, the Python interpreter looks at the path to figure out where to look for its libraries. (This doesn't bite most people because it only happens when the Executable is python, not if it's a script with #!python.) This causes more trouble than it's worth so we should stop doing it.

title: Ticket #4895: condor_q blacklisting sole collector
description: The OSG packaging group is seeing repeated test failures where condor_q blacklists the sole collector that it is trying to contact. The collector blacklisting feature is meant for pools that have multiple redundant collectors for high availability. If one of those collectors goes down, then daemons will avoid contacting it for queries, and instead use the other collectors. The triggering of blacklisting in OSG's testing is odd for two reasons. First, blacklisting is pointless when there's a single collector. Second, condor_q is blacklisting the collector before it contacts it for the first time. This appears to be a glitch in how the Timeslice object for blacklisting is initialized. So far, the only way I see for this to happen is if the system clock moves backwards while condor_q is running. We are doing some tests with additional debugging to learn more. It's easy to change the code so that blacklisting never happens when there's only one collector. I'm holding off on that change until we understand why this is triggering in OSG's tests.
remarks: 2015-Feb-18 10:24:10 by blin: Jaime, I don't believe this is happening when condor_q is contacting the collector for the first time. The condor_ce_run script submits the job with condor_submit and then runs condor_q repeatedly, with a one second delay, until the job completes and then runs condor_transfer_data. Looking at the CollectorLog for the failed tests, I see multiple 'Got QUERY_SCHEDD_ADS' on one second intervals while the script is supposed to be running, so it doesn't seem like it's failing on the intial condor_q. 2015-Feb-18 13:47:08 by jfrey: I mean that the blacklisting happens before that specific condor_q process contacts the collector. title: Ticket #5787: Create condor-ec2 package to simplify use of HTCondor in the cloud.
description: First pass will be an RPM. The package will install (and configure HTCondor to use) a master shutdown script that shuts down the whole machine. It will include example code to show users how to distinguish between voluntary exits and exits during a system shutdown. The package will install (into the preconfigured default location) a script which will (a) advertise the instance's ID, (b) advertise and set TCP_FORWARDING_HOST to the instance's public IP, and (c) if the instance's IAM profile allows reflection and includes a role which which permits the download of a specific file in S3, download it and unpack it in /etc/condor/config.d.

Thanks. 2016-Aug-15 13:26:50 by tlmiller: My proposed version history item follows. I'd rather append "See manual section X" for details than "see the ticket for details," so I won't commit it until somebody has a better idea or we actually get that manual section written. \item HTCondor now provides a 'condor-ec2' RPM, intended to assist our customers in preparing EC2 images for service in an HTCondor pool. Installing this RPM changes the default configuration of HTCondor in a number of ways. \Ticket{5787} The EC2 RPM contains three files: a master shutdown script, a configuration file, and a script that will be executed by the HTCondor configuration system once on start-up. We will describe these in reverse (that is, chronological) order. The configuration script is called by a new line in the default HTCondor configuration file (that does nothing if the script isn't installed). That script (49ec2-instance.sh) generates output which HTCondor writes to 49ec-instance.config. The script extracts the instance's public IP address and instance ID from the EC2 metadata server, and writes them in configuration file format to standard out. (The configuration file in the RPM, described below, makes use of this information.) The script then installs a firewall rule which prevents non-root users from accessing the metadata server. This protects the instance against jobs which might try to use one of the roles associated with the instance. The script will examine those roles; if one grants permission to read a specific S3 object (as opposed to from an S3 bucket), the script will download that file and (if it's a .tar.gz) untar it into the config.d directory. The configuration file (50ec2.config) sets the TCP_FORWARDING_HOST to the public IP address and has the startd advertise its instance ID. It also activates execute directory encryption. Finally, it configures the startd to shut down after being unclaimed for 15 minutes, the master to shut itself down when the startd shuts down, and the master to run a script when it shuts down. The master shutdown script (master_shutdown_script.sh) simply shuts the machine down when the master exits. It contains code to distinguish between the master shutting down because the instance was unclaimed for fifteen minutes, or because the instance itself is shutting down (usually because of being outbid on Spot), but only for example purposes. 2016-Sep-15 09:11:16 by tim: Code Review: This looks good to me. title: Ticket #6847: Design a load-balanced HTTP file service for CHTC
description: We want to design and implement a load-balanced HTTP file server which we'll deploy somewhere in the CHTC cluster. This will help solve several problems: Jobs with large file transfers can place a heavy load on the submit servers. We want to shift this burden onto dedicated infrastructure whose only job is to serve files. Some CHTC users are using offsite file services which are very slow to download/upload data from. Some external users have been asking for something similar, we want to gain experience in this area so we can better advise them. This ticket is largely a placeholder for a design document that will explain the architectural details for such a system. We'll look at many questions including the following: What does the hardware architecture look like? How many physical machines do we need to host the various components? What hardware will we need to purchase? What does the software architecture look like? Will the load-balanced HTTP nodes be hosted in VMs or containers? What does the file system look like? Assuming we use a shared file system, is it better to go with HDFS, CEPH or something different? Where on the UW campus network is the best place for this to live? How much file system redundancy do we want? How many load balanced nodes do we want? Design document and ticket updates to follow.

title: Ticket #2557: ssh_to_job test fails on deb 6.0 in new batlab
description: The ssh_to_job test fails on deb 6.0 in the new batlab (exec-14.batlab.org). I can reproduce the problem with a personal condor on the same machine with all default settings. The sshd server claims that tcp wrappers rejects the connection. If I instead configure the personal condor to use 127.0.0.1 as its IP address instead of 128.104.103.14, condor_ssh_to_job succeeds. If I ssh_to_job from submit-2 to a job running in the base condor on this machine, it succeeds. If I ssh to the IP address of this machine (128.104.103.14) from this machine, the connection is refused. If I ssh to 127.0.0.1 or 127.0.1.1 from this machine, it succeeds. I conclude that tcp wrappers does not like connections that originate from 128.104.103.14. I don't understand why. Dan R temporarily set tcp wrappers to accept from anywhere, but ssh_to_job still didn't work.
remarks: 2011-Oct-18 09:40:56 by gthain: $ cat /etc/hosts 127.0.0.1 localhost 127.0.1.1 exec-5.batlab.org exec-5 $ cat /etc/hosts.allow ALL: localhost, 127.0.0.1 sshd: .wisc.edu, .batlab.org, 128.104.153.132 So, the ssh is binding to 127.0.1.1, which isn't in the hosts.allow. I've changed hosts.allow to allos ALL: 127., and submitted a test run. I'll let you know. 2011-Oct-18 11:23:24 by danb: Greg discovered the following: Oct 18 10:30:28 exec-14 sshd[15967]: warning: /etc/hosts.allow, line 11: host name/address mismatch: 128.104.103.14 != exec-14.batlab.org Oct 18 10:30:28 exec-14 sshd[15967]: refused connect from 128.104.103.14 (128.104.103.14) If we comment out the 127.0.1.1 exec-4 exec-4.batlab.org It all works. 2011-Oct-18 11:32:23 by danb: Conclusion: some systems are set up in a way that reject ssh connections from the eth0 interface, due to the hostname being mapped to 127.0.1.1 in /etc/hosts. This prevents ssh_to_job from succeeding in a personal condor that uses eth0. The workaround is to either fix /etc/hosts or to run the personal condor on the localhost interface. It would have been nice if Condor or at least the ssh_to_job test reported this problem more clearly. sshd did not log anything in its sshd.log at the default debug level. When I added -d to the sshd command-line, it reported in sshd.log that tcp wrappers rejected the connection, but it did not say why. In the ssh_to_job test, we could add the -d option and we could print the contents of sshd.log in the test logs.

title: Ticket #2107: optimize globus gridmap calls

title: Ticket #1681: shared_port deadlocking
description: In Igor's large-scale tests of condor_shared_port, we observed that the schedd often failed to send a heartbeat to the master, resulting in the master thinking that the schedd was hung. This appears to be caused by a temporary deadlock between the schedd and condor_shared_port. If all of the shared_port workers (SHARED_PORT_MAX_WORKERS=50) are busy, the shared_port server will attempt to service the next incoming request in the main process. If, at the same time, the schedd is doing a blocking connect through the shared_port server, the two processes can deadlock. SchedLog: 09/28/10 12:21:37 (pid:28067) DaemonCore: in SendAliveToParent() 09/28/10 12:24:46 (pid:28067) attempt to connect to <131.225.206.93:9999> failed: Connection timed out (connect errno = 110). 09/28/10 12:24:46 (pid:28067) DaemonCore: Could not connect to parent <131.225.206.93:9999?sock=9580_059f>. SendAliveToParent() failed. 09/28/10 12:24:46 (pid:28067) DaemonCore: Leaving SendAliveToParent() - FAILED sending to <131.225.206.93:9999?sock=9580_059f> SharedPortLog: 09/28/10 12:21:23 SharedPortClient: failed to connect to /home/igorschedd /glidecondor/condor_local/log/daemon_sock/28067_7d8e_1454 as requested by STARTD <131.225.191.183:34504?CCBID=131.225.206.102:7665#4810> on <131.225.191.183:58965>: No such file or directory 09/28/10 12:24:56 condor_read() failed: recv() returned -1, errno = 104 Connection reset by peer, reading 5 bytes from <131.225.206.93:0>. 09/28/10 12:24:56 IO: Failed to read packet header 09/28/10 12:24:56 SharedPortClient: failed to receive result for SHARED_PORT_PASS_FD to /home/igorschedd/glidecondor/condor_local/log/daemon_sock /28067_7d8e_1074 as requested by STARTD <131.225.191.175:50593?CCBID=131.225.206.102:7704#3996> on <131.225.191.175:34026>: Connection reset by peer Workaround Set SHARED_PORT_MAX_WORKERS so large that it never runs out or set NOT_RESPONDING_TIMEOUT very large. How to Fix [DONE] Use a non-blocking connect in SendAliveToParent(), because blocking connects between daemons are always sources of trouble, even without shared_port. In the shared_port server, create a queue for each target and only process N at a time from each queue where N is small compared to SHARED_PORT_MAX_WORKERS. If daemon A needs to connect to daemon B, it will not be possible for all of the workers to be blocked on daemon A and thus deadlock is avoided.

title: Ticket #4483: Remove GSI libraries from the shadow
description: The GSI libraries add about 100kB of memory to every process that links to them. If any GSI functions are called, even more memory is used. This presents a scalability problem for the condor_shadow, which almost never needs to use GSI. To remove GSI memory overhead from the shadow on linux, we plan to do the following: Don't link the condor_utils library against the GSI and VOMS libraries. Instead, dlopen() those libraries whenever they're needed. When the shadow needs to do something with the job's proxy certificate, have it fork a child process, which does the work and reports the results. With these changes and setting SEC_ENABLE_MATCH_PASSWORD_AUTHENTICATION=True, the shadow will never have the GSI libraries loaded and can avoid the associated memory overhead.

title: Ticket #6514: Group quotas don't allow both surplus and oversubscription
description: CERN reports problems with allocation of group quotas in Condor. They would like to give the whole pool, when needed to the "highprio" group. That group rarely has jobs, though. When there are no "highprio" jobs, they would like to give out slots in a 3 to 1 ratio of analysis to production. To implement this policy, they have in their condor config GROUP_ACCEPT_SURPLUS = True GROUP_NAMES = production, analysis, highprio GROUP_QUOTA_DYNAMIC_production=0.0025 GROUP_QUOTA_DYNAMIC_analysis=0.0075 GROUP_QUOTA_DYNAMIC_highprio = 0.99 The 99% for highprio isn't quite what they'd like, but it is close. Assuming a pool with 20 slots, and no high prio jobs, they'd like to see 15 analysis job and 5 production jobs. What they do see is that analysis is allocated 30 (!) slots, and production 10: 12/15/17 14:28:57 group quotas: group= analysis quota= 0.15 requested= 100 allocated= 30 unallocated= 70 12/15/17 14:28:57 group quotas: group= production quota= 0.05 requested= 100 allocated= 10 unallocated= 90 Analysis is furthest from quota, so it negotiates first, and gets all of the pool. The root cause is a combination of problems. First, the knob NEGOTIATOR_ALLOW_QUOTA_OVERSUBSCRIPTION defaults to true. When false, the configured quotas are scaled so that their sum is the size of the pool. When true, they are left as is, to allow one group strict priority access to pool by setting a very large quota. The root of the quota tree, the "<none>" group cannot be given a quota administrative. When NEGOTIATOR_ALLOW_OVERSCRIPTION is true, the generated config quota for <none> is the whole pool. When false, it is the size of the pool, minus the sum of configured quotas for all children, recursively. That is, usualy 0 slots. Now, when ACCEPT_SURPLUS is true, the negotiation calculates any surplus for every group. This is defined as the difference (if any) between the configured quota and the demand at that node. So, if NEGOTIATOR_ALLOW_QUOTA_OVERSUBSCRIPTION is true, and the config quota of a node is 1,000,000 slots, and there is no demand, the surplus at that node is 1,000,000 slots (no matter how many slots are actually in the pool), which will get divided up, and break quotas mightily. Setting NEGOTIATOR_ALLOW_OVERSCRIPTION to false fixes the problem, if sites don't need oversubscription.

title: Ticket #5912: Condor_submit should have syntax for job retries
description: condor_submit should have first class keywords to describe job retries, and it should automatically generate the appropriate OnExitRemove expressions in the job ad based on those keywords. Use of one or more of the keywords below will cause an appropriate OnExitRemove expression to be added to the job ad, and possibly other attributes as well. keywords will be one or more of name type description max_retries integer values > 0 should cause the job to retry N times retry_until int or expr futility exit code, or expression that when true, causes retries to cease success_exit_code integer exit code that will be returned on success Retries will continue until the job exits with the value of success_exit_code or has exited more than max_retries times. If success_exit_code is not set, then 0 will be assumed to mean success. if retry_until is an integer, it is equivalent to DAGman's UNLESS-EXIT keyword. It should contain an exit code that indicates futility and retries will cease when the exit code is equal to it. If it is an expression retries will cease when it evaluates to true. Use of max_retries and/or success_exit_code without max_retries will use a configuration knob to control the default retry count. If an OnExitRemove expression is also defined in the submit file, that expression will be ||'ed with the expression generated for doing retries.

title: Ticket #1402: VM universe: issues with bridged networking
description: There are several issue with bridged networking in VM universe job: - when no XML helper is used, the generated configuration for KVM machines uses virbr0 but this interface, according to libvirt documentation (http://wiki.libvirt.org/page/Networking) can not be used for bridged networking; - when no XML helper is used, the generated configuration for Xen machines does not contain any reference to the bridged interface (<source bridge="">). - when the default XML helper is used, the configuration use 'br0', which does not exist by default
remarks: 2010-May-12 15:45:22 by rrati: The usefulness of VM_BRIDGE_SCRIPT is questionable, at best, at this point. According to the config file comments, and the usage in condor, the script is intended to be passed to libvirt as the 'source script' for bridged networking. However, the source script is not used by libvirt for bridged networking and in the cases where 'source script' would be used (generic networking), it will not be able to be used by libvirt when VMs are run in unprivileged mode. Additionally, VM_BRIDGE_SCRIPT provides a means to create a network interface, but not to tear it down. This seems of limited utility in a controlled environment. The libvirt docs talk about setting up the bridge interface on the host OS, and it seems a much more useful use case for the box admin to setup the bridged networking interfaces for a machine that will run VMs with bridged networking. It is likely that VM_BRIDGE_SCRIPT is a hold over from before the libvirt conversion, when condor used the xen API directly. Additionally, dynamic interface creation and destruction could be handled, much cleaner, via the startd hooks. Perhaps the job submit files should be allowed to specify which bridge interface to use, with the administrator able to define a default in condor's configuration, for a case where multiple bridge interfaces could exist on a startd. The creation of all the interfaces would be the responsibility of the admin (via hooks or explicit OS configuration). Given all the above, it seems removing/deprecating the VM_BRIDGE_SCRIPT is the route to take, along with providing documentation on how to configure a bridge networking on the host. 2010-May-13 14:38:38 by jfrey: The patch looks alright to me. 2010-May-14 11:41:51 by rrati: Changes to documentation in ticket #1407

title: Ticket #4250: ScheddIpAddr in submitter ads not updated on change of schedd's sinful
description: If the schedd is using a shared port daemon and the shared-port daemon's address changes, the resulting change in the schedd's sinful address isn't reflected in the ScheddIpAddr attribute of the submitter ads. This causes some other daemons to fail to contact the schedd, as they try to use an old address that no longer works. The ScheddIpAddr attribute in the scheduler ad is updated as expected. We've seen this happen when a submit machine is using both a shared-port daemon and CCB, and the CCB_ADDRESS is changed. The ScheddIpAddr attribute is updated in the scheduler ad every time an update is sent to the collector, but the ScheddIpAddr attribute in the submitter ads is only updated on a reconfig. If the shared-port daemon's address changes on a reconfig, the schedd doesn't learn about the change immediately. It only learns about the change on its next periodic poll of the shared-port daemon's address (done every 5 minutes).
remarks: 2014-Mar-07 16:22:24 by jfrey: A workaround for this bug is to send a reconfig to the affected schedd.

title: Ticket #7885: SciTokens local-issuer credmon support
description: To summarize the discussion from #7862 and from a Zoom meeting, we are going to make changes to enable the SciTokens "local issuer" mode used by OSG. This was working before but was a bit of a hack, and we overlooked this mode when separating the krb/oauth modes in the CredD. Milestones: [DONE] condor_submit doesn't really need to invoke any credential producer, since the contents in this case are meaningless anyway. So it can skip the popen() and just initiate the connection to the CredD. It will do this when LOCAL_CREDMON_PROVIDER_NAME is set. [DONE] condor_submit will now send a "magic value" that tells the CredD to just touch a file in the SEC_CREDENTIAL_DIRECTORY_OAUTH for that user, instead of going through the OAuth flow, and instead of doing anything in the *_KRB directory. The magic value looks like "LOCAL:scitokens" (where "scitokens" is whatever is specified by LOCAL_CREDMON_PROVIDER_NAME) [DONE] Test this locally on moria. Test this on OSG-Connect Create a test for this This probably won't be needed by anybody, but you can use an old version of condor_submit with the SEC_CREDENTIAL_PRODUCER set to a program that produces "LOCAL:scitokens" as output. If the CredD is 8.9.9 or later it will recognize this magic string and do the right thing.

title: Ticket #6778: RANK based preemption not working with ALLOW_PSLOT_PREEMPTION
description: I am trying to enable RANK preemption to allow jobs with a specific classad to take over the cluster more or less immediately and run forever. This tag is restricted using JOB_TRANSFORM and PROTECTED_JOB_ATTRS which are great and easy-to-use features. On my central manager condor_config_val NEGOTIATOR_CONSIDER_PREEMPTION reports true. I explicitly set ALLOW_PSLOT_PREEMPTION = True and run condor_reconfig (I've also restarted to be really sure during testing). My standard execute node policy is: use POLICY:Always_Run_Jobs use POLICY:Limit_Job_Runtimes($(DAY)) MaxJobRetirementTime = ifThenElse(online_cbc_gstlal_inspiral =?= True, 100000000, $(MaxJobRetirementTime)) The idea is that most jobs get killed after a day and these special jobs (which stream data live from the LIGO instruments) are allowed to run "forever." I want to extend this policy to also allow the jobs to take over the cluster rapidly, with the underlying reason being that we want to be able to failover from one analysis data center to another when, e.g., there's an earthquake in CA that takes Caltech (LIGO HQ) down but doesn't affect the instruments themselves in LA/WA. Because ALLOW_PSLOT_PREEMPTION does not respect NEGOTIATOR_CONSIDER_EARLY_PREEMPTION, I have to modify the policy above by hand: use POLICY:Always_Run_Jobs MaxJobRetirementTime = ifThenElse(online_cbc_gstlal_inspiral =?= True, 100000000, 0) PREEMPT = (JobState == "Running") && ((time() - JobCurrentStartDate) > $(DAY)) RANK = (rank_foo =?= True) * 10 Basically, I want the behavior of "kill jobs after a day unless online_cbc_gstlal_inspiral is set" while enabling RANK preemption. rank_foo will eventually be replaced by online_cbc_gstlal_inspiral but my account can't set online_cbc_gstlal_inspiral. Am I missing something? The manual and your presentations are all fairly clear that RANK preemption should work with partitionable slots.

title: Ticket #4745: CEDAR pollutes CondorError object on success
description: When a CondorError object is passed into CEDAR, the object can end up with entries when CEDAR returns success. For example, when one authentication method fails but another succeeds, an error stack entry about the failed method is left in the CondorError object. Most callers aren't expecting this, so the error ends up in the failure message of any subsequent error. It would be better if CEDAR cleared the CondorError object when it returns success. If we want to get fancy, CEDAR would leave the CondorError object in the same state it received it when returning success. See the attachment in #3379 for an example.
creator: jfrey

title: Ticket #572: Be able to force DAG nodes to run on the same machine
description: Users would often like to be able to force several consecutive DAG nodes to run on the same machine (data stage in/process/data stage out, for example). Currently there's no good way to do this. Todd T and I just talked about this -- we would need something on the Condor end to keep "foreign" jobs from coming in and grabbing the relevant machine between the DAG jobs. Todd suggested the idea of being able to set a claim to not immediately time out after a job runs, and adding claim requirements and claim timeouts. So then, when the first job runs, it could do something like setting the claim requirements to be that the next job's parent be the current job (since we stick parent node names into the job classads anyhow). Then the last job in the sequence could unset the claim requirements and the claim would go away. Maybe not for phase 1, we'd also propagate this from schedds to startds, so it can show up in condor_q -analyze, for instance. We could also add something to the DAG language so that the user would just mark certain nodes as having to run on the same machine, and DAGMan would take care of the rest of the stuff automatically.
remarks: 2009-Jun-17 16:59:59 by matt: This sounds interesting, but seems strange. Does this aim to change the notion of the startd treating jobs as individual units to treating claims as such, e.g. the startd can/could/should cleanup after a job but now it's after a claim? 2012-Feb-07 15:05:11 by nwp: DAGman reuses claims now, from #2673 2016-May-18 16:42:18 by wenger: Hmm -- now that we have DAGMAN_HOLD_CLAIM_TIME, could we just do something like have DAGMan read the machine from the execute event of a parent job, and then add that to the requirements of a child job? Maybe we could make a new command like SAME_MACHINE_PARENT ... CHILD ... that would cause DAGMan to do this? 2016-May-18 16:48:06 by wenger: Ah, yeah -- here's a use case for this: I just talked to a user who has jobs that start out by doing a large download from iPlant, and then a long computation phase. They want to limit the number of jobs doing downloads at any one time to avoid overloading the iRODs, but then they want the computation part to not be throttled. So the solution would be to break the download part and the computation part into separate jobs, and use category throttles on the download part. The problem with that, of course, is that they need to have the two jobs run on the same machine; otherwise the download is wasted.

title: Ticket #1117: Query ads to the collector should have proper TARGET scoping
description: Queries to the collector consist of a query ad with a requirements expression that matches the ads the client is interested in. The collector performs a one-way matching operation to find the desired ads. Some of the attribute references in the requirements expression lack a 'target' scope, though they want to refer to attributes in the target ads. This works fine in old ClassAds, but fails with new ClassAds. As part of the switch to new ClassAds, both the collector and its clients should ensure that the query ad's requirements expression has the proper scoping for its attribute references. After enough time, these checks could be removed from the collector. The collector daemon and the CondorQuery object should call AddExplicitTargetRefs() on the query ad.

title: Ticket #4315: Python bindings should expose locking API
description: We would like to have the locking API exposed via the python bindings (preferably through a python context manager, like we do with transaction). HTCondor uses a special locking protocol that is not POSIX, involving taking POSIX locks in a special directory instead of taking the lock on the file itself. If a python application needs to take a lock on a file (such as a read / write lock on a user log), we should add an API to do this in a straightforward manner to avoid racing with HTCondor. I propose the following API: fd = open("/tmp/foo") with htcondor.lock(fd, htcondor.LockType.WriteLock) as lock: fd.write("blah") By using a context manager and not exposing something mutex-like, we help users avoid shooting themselves. Not bullet-proof, but it's better than nothing. I would expect this is a highly-specialized feature, probably only used by CMS.

title: Ticket #122: Let admin and user set various rlimits for jobs
description: The admin (via the starter's configuration file) and the user (via the submit file or condor_qedit) should be able to set any of the available hard rlimits for a job about to start. If both the user and the admin set them, the smaller value should be used. This way the user or admin can reign in jobs that use excessive CPU, memory, disk in a single file, simultaneously open files, processes, or more. An admin might want to set limits to, say, keep a job from thrashing. A user might want to set limits because his programs occasionally go haywire, and he'd rather that haywire jobs be killed or limited than allowed to keep going. The advantage of this over just policy is... The hard limit is absolutely hard, while policy limits can be briefly overrun before the policy notices. There are rlimits that limit things Condor does not currently track and would be extremely difficult for Condor to track. It should be impossible for a process to sneak out from the limits, while it is possible for for a program to intentionally or accidentally evade Condor's policies. (Imported from 1708 (backup) 1708 (public))

title: Ticket #7169: Startd can't update starter when EncryptExecuteDirectory=true
description: The startd periodically sends slot ad updates to the starter by writing a file in the job's execute directory. It always tries to write to $(EXECUTE)/dir_<pid>/.update.ad. But when the execute directory is encrypted, it should write to $(EXECUTE)/encrypted##/dir_<pid>/.update.ad. There may be other places where the startd uses the wrong execute directory when encryption is enabled. In CHTC, this causes our policy to evict long running jobs to not fire, since it relies on attributes updated by the startd to the starter.

description: The configuration setting STARTD_CRON_AUTOPUBLISH = If_Changed causes updates to be sent to the collector every time the cron job runs in some cases, even when there are no changes to the attributes generated by any cron jobs. title: Ticket #3829: PREEMPT==Undefined should be treated as False, not a fatal error
description: I've probably been bitten by this a dozen times over the years (referenced an attr in my PREEMPT expression that turns out not to exist on one machine for some reason, sending it into the valley of death). I can't see any reason why PREEMPT==Undefined should be fatal unless you're trying to force admins to discover missing attrs or something, but that seems obnoxious when you could just write a helpful warning to the StartLog instead. With the current behavior, one typo can take a pool down.

title: Ticket #1814: parent process needs to remember if child has UDP port
description: Currently, unix shadows do not have a UDP command port. This is done to save memory. Currently, all messages sent from the schedd to the shadow are sent via unix signals, but if new DC signals were added (as proposed by Rob for pushing out changes from condor_q), DaemonCore::Send_Signal() doesn't know that the child lacks a UDP port, so it might not correctly send the message (depends on network settings, but definitely doesn't work in the default case). What is needed is a flag in the address of the child that indicates that it cannot receive UDP. This will be useful in other situations (such as when using TCP forwarding) where a daemon needs to advertise this fact.

title: Ticket #7539: Ignore FlockLevel from remote negotiator in schedd
description: When flocking to multiple pools, and especially with FLOCK_INCREMENT > 1, the schedd incorrectly lowers the per-submitter flock level from time to time. That bug will be fixed in a separate ticket. As a result of that bug, a flocking negotiator will frequently contact a schedd and ask for job requests for a submitter, and the schedd will send no jobs, because it thinks it shouldn't be flocking there. Let's remove this check. If an (older) submitter ad exists in the remote collector, we should just honor it, and send jobs there.

title: Ticket #7217: Singularity jobs need to detect singularity errors
description: When HTCondor is configured for the starter to run a job under singularity, it just returns the error code of the singularity exec as the job exit code. If there is a singularity error, this is returned as a job exit code, so a configuration or system error causes the job to leave the queue. Just like we do with java universe, we need to differentiate a system or environment error from a job error.

title: Ticket #2015: Take advantage of filesystem namespaces
description: This is another child of the namespaces work started in #1959: filesystem namespaces. Per request from Todd, this is being separated out into a new ticket. This patch: Adds USE_FS_NAMESPACES; if set to true, it will mask /tmp and /var/tmp with $_CONDOR_SCRATCH_DIR. Hence, "condor_run ls /tmp" will return blank. This works with any Linux 2.6 kernel. Adds SQUASH_DIRS: set this to a list of directories to "squash" them to point at $_CONDOR_SCRATCH_DIR. Useful for sites that have other world-writeable directories. SQUASH_DIRS should work on any 2.6 kernel. Due to overlap with the PID namespaces code, the patch is based off PID namespaces rather than master. We again return to the question of privsep: we'll probably need to teach the switchboard how to do this. Because this is the second patch today that has new code for privsep and non-privsep, I'm starting to dig Todd's idea of making switchboard used by default, even if privsep is not used. I don't have the evening/weekend time to tackle this, but would be willing to be more patient on integrating this patch if someone wants to make that change. Unlike the PID namespace patch, the majority of this patch will have to be rewritten (with approximately equivalent functionality) to implement with the switchboard.
remarks: 2011-Oct-10 10:36:20 by psilord: In separate discussions with Todd and Brian B., I found out that the patch containing the file system name spaces patch also contained the functionality of the PID name spaces patch. We at Condor are a little leery of the PID name space patch since there is some ancient code and decisions in the functionality of Condor that affect how it interacts with low pid numbers. It turns out the the two patches can be separated. The file system name space patch still requires PID name space plumbing, but the expression of the PID name space behavior can be in a separate patch. I mentioned to bbockelm that if he separates the patch in this manner we'd accept the file system patch. 2011-Oct-26 16:29:21 by eje: It might be useful to support the ability for users to submit additional directories to be "squashed" onto the working dir, via the job ad, for example" universe = vanilla ... +SquashDirs = /a/dir /another/dir /yet/another/dir Brian pointed out that this might open up security holes if a user squashed something like "/etc" and wrote configurations that allowed some kind of priv elevation." A way to avoid such a hole would be some kind of directory black-list, either hard coded or admin-supplied, that prevents sensitive directories like "/etc" from being squashed. 2011-Oct-27 12:31:56 by eje: Recommendations so far: Rename SQUASH_DIRS to MOUNT_UNDER_SCRATCH Remove hard-coded mounting of "/tmp" and "/var/tmp", such that all requested mounts live on "MOUNT_UNDER_SCRATCH" and are under admin control Remove use of "USE_FS_NAMESPACES", so that mountings are enabled iff MOUNT_UNDER_SCRATCH is non-empty Enhance mounting logic a bit so that if "/a/requested/dir" appears on MOUNT_UNDER_SCRATCH, then (a) create "$(EXECUTE)/dir_xxxx/a/requested/dir" and then (b) mount "/a/requested/dir" --> "$(EXECUTE)/dir_xxxx/a/requested/dir" '/' --> DIR_DELIM_CHAR, and/or "s[0]=='/'" --> "!is_relative_to_cwd(s)" cmake support for something like HAVE_BIND_MOUNT or HAVE_FS_NAMESPACES (like what was done for HAVE_EXT_LIBCGROUP) If feasible, a run-time check for bind-mount PS, Greg suggested possibility of SCRATCH_FSTAB instead of MOUNT_UNDER_SCRATCH. 2011-Oct-27 12:38:28 by eje: More thoughts about supporting "+MountUnderScratch" in a submit file: If a directory like "/etc" is on the mounting black list, then would need to consider how to handle accidental/malicious requests for non-canonical dirs such as "/etc/" or "/etc/../etc" or "/./etc/" ... There are algorithms for canonizing directories, or could simply ignore any requested dir containing "." or "..", or which is otherwise noncanonical in some way. 2011-Nov-02 08:14:38 by bbockelm: eje - For items (6) and (7), all versions of kernel 2.6 in use have fs namespaces. You'd have to go back to RHEL3 to find one that doesn't support this flag. How far back do we need support for? 2011-Nov-28 16:41:13 by gthain: Can we look at using unshare(2), instead of clone(NEWFS_NS). That way we can have one code path that works with both fork(2) and clone(2). Also, we would need to be root when we clone, which gives me hives. Also, are you sure we need to elevate privs when we stat the mount points? 2011-Nov-29 14:32:11 by eje: A question relating to fs namespace use cases: One use case that was specifically mentioned was installing a legacy OS (e.g. SL5) in /path/to/SL5/install and then mapping "/" to "/path/to/SL5/install" for jobs that want to run under SL5 packages. The current candidate patch does not seem to support the above use case, since it only maps various directories to /path/to/job/scratch/dir 2011-Nov-30 13:30:40 by eje: I wonder if we shouldn't just go ahead and support something like: +MountAs <namespaced-path> <real-path> on the job submission side. So, if a job wants to run under /path/to/SL5/install, you include this in the submission: +MountAs "/" "/path/to/SL5/install" An admin-controlled blacklist would supply directories that are considered security risks for <real-path> values. So, you could prevent something like +MountAs "/tmp" "/etc" My thinking so far is that only restrictions on <real-path> are needed to maintain security - I'd be interested in whether others agree. 2011-Nov-30 14:12:27 by eje: This seems a little creepy: Q: I wrote a small C program that simply does an unshare(CLONE_NEWNS) followed by system("bash"). The man page says that the process should have its own namespace. So, in the shell I tried unmount /cgroup (cgroup is mounted on the original machine). When I do a mount in a shell on the machine, /cgroup is unmounted there too. Am I missing something here? I thought that CLONE_NEWNS was to let me unmount a file system from the process without affecting the main system. A: (As an aside, you didn't need to write a program - you could just use the unshare(1) utility). It is unmounting the filesystem only in the new namespace, and leaving it mounted in the original - the problem is that mount uses /etc/mtab to produce the list of currently-mounted filesystems, and that's just an ordinary file that can be updated by the mount command in the new namespace. This means that /etc/mtab gets out of synch with what's really going on (since there's only one /etc/mtab, but two mount namespaces). Check /proc/mounts instead, to see what's actually mounted in the current namespace. http://stackoverflow.com/questions/6258696/understanding-the-behavior-of-unshare-clone-newns 2011-Nov-30 14:21:31 by gthain: WRT to the mounting a complete SL6 hierarchy, I believe Brian has a chroot patch coming that takes care of that. WRT having the job describe the mountings, it seems like that mixes in too much knowledge of the execute-side into the job. 2011-Nov-30 14:27:30 by gthain: And in the, "you learn something new every day" category, /etc/mtab isn't even guaranteed to be up to date even when not using CLONE_NEWNS -- from the mount man page: -n Mount without writing in /etc/mtab. This is necessary for example when /etc is on a read-only file system.

title: Ticket #2445: condor_userprio callbacks limit size of submitter names to 63 chars
description: If a submitter record in the accountant is longer than 63 characters, for example a very long group name, or a very long host name, or any combination thereof, the callbacks invoked by condor_userprio will currently fail with a log message in the NegotiatorLog, because they are reading from the stream with a hard limit of 64 characters. This tripped up a downstream test where the host-name happened to be very long, and the group name was also somewhat long.

title: Ticket #6406: Vanilla-universe multicommand jobs
description: Ticket #2746 details much of the desired user interface to this feature, with the exception that the exit code/exit signal should be specifiable as in ticket #6367, and that success_exit_code for the "main" job should be joined by success_exit_signal and success_exit_by_signal. Ticket #6372 alludes to the question of naming the submit file commands for this feature, particularly with respect to usability. The current plan is to restrict the interface to this feature to pre-, main-, and post-, since explaining parallel arrays is a pain. (This suggests an obvious way around the problem for the Python bindings, where we write a utility function that converts a list of command objects into a job ClassAd.) Ticket #5419 is a duplicate from LIGO. It makes explicit the requirement that the extra command's executables need to be transferred automatically, with the same semantics as the 'main' executable. The idea of this ticket is that we currently have an n = 1 case for executables started by the vanilla universe. User requests have wanted to make this n = 3, but the domain of n in software design is {0, 1, many}. The hoped-for advantage is two-fold: Move "shish kebab" (linear) DAG (subgraph)s out of DAGMan and (almost entirely) into the starter. Allow for automatic/programmatic job re/de-composition. This will be necessary to automatically convert from a linear DAG subgraph to a single job. The basic observation is that, since we have vanilla-universe checkpointing, we know that we can stop, do intermediate file transfer, and restart an executable entirely within the starter and not have anything too terrible happen. It seems like a conceptually straight-forward extension to change to stop, do final and first file-transfer, and start another executable. (Accounting is currently kind of terrible with vanilla-universe checkpointing, and will get harder with this idea. At the very least, since we can't autocompose jobs from different owners anyway -- who knows how file access would work -- we have a sane place to start.) Since we'd be transferring files (or not -- there's some obvious opportunities for optimizations here) between different executables, we'd have (coarse-grained) checkpoints for free; this could even allow the schedd to run multi-command jobs on older starters, if we wanted that to happen. (Write the 'current' executable in as the old-style single executable; if the job comes back without any new-style completion attributes, synthesize them and move the next executable in the list to the old-style.) I suppose a strictly "script" approach could be simplified by doing file transfer only once, and indeed this may be the expected behavior -- that the prescript will be run once for each job start. (Would that make application-level checkpointing harder or easier?) This implies the need to be able to specify if a command is check-pointed... but that isn't enough, because everybody will want the pre and post scripts to run after and before file transfer in and out. It would be possible (with new code) to transform the job such that the main command's i/o happens as the pre-script's input and the post-script's output -- which would simultaneously indicate that the pre- and post- scripts aren't checkpointable, since there's no filetransfer in between -- but then the question of what to do about vanilla universe checkpointing for the main command arises... the answer may be to ignore the problem, since the only thing your pre-script could do would be input validation (everything else is rolled into the checkpoint), and you'd need to modify your program or script to do that for checkpoints anyway. On the other hand, because of file transfer / checkpointing, maybe it would make more sense to have pre- and post- commands be their own first-class things, which would be a little disappointing. A first pass might then implement the #2746 interface (with the addition of the success_* commands as noted above) without backwards compatibility and without file transfer / checkpointing. The key task here would be to transform the friendly submit-file UI to a job-ad syntax that is designed to support all the features we want (even if it the implementation doesn't initially, it'd be nice for the implementation to recognize that and fail). As implied above, we can specify the Python UI in much the same way as necessary (that is, without any particular reference to the job ad attributes). If these commands ran in a fully spun-up vanilla universe environment, this first pass would meet real-world needs and have a lot of users. After a discussion with GregT and TJ, it appears that fine-grained control over whose file transfer in or out runs when has no use-cases aside from implementing pre- and post- scripts. However, there is a use case for multiple pre- and post- commands, including cases where an administrator wants to run a pre- or post- command without displacing the user's pre- and post- commands. Additionally, having multiple pre- and post- commands simplifies certain types of job construction or modification (because you can just provide an additional pre- or post- command, rather than incorporating it into an existing one or adding a(nother) wrapper).

title: Ticket #2916: Infinite loop in gridmanager for gram jobs
description: If the job-manager for a gt2 gram job ends up running on a different port than the gridmanager expects, then the gridmanager can end up in an infinite loop trying to recover. The gridmanager bounces between GM_START state trying to restart the jobmanager (getting an OLD_JM_ALIVE error) and GM_REGISTER state, registering for callbacks using the bad port (getting a connection failed error). When the restart command results in an OLD_JM_ALIVE error, it includes the port of the currently-running jobmanager. The gridmanager should use that address for further attempts to connect to the jobmanager.
remarks: 2012-Apr-03 16:22:29 by jfrey: The infinite loop doesn't consume much cpu and the gridmanager continues to manage other jobs normally.

title: Ticket #1639: condor_store_cred fails to read passwords with certain characters
description: When a user attempts to enter a character using the alt+#### method on Windows using the condor_store_cred utility, no input is actually passed onto the program. This is due to the read_from_keyboard function in store_cred.cpp inside the condor c++ util library using _getch(). This also fails when using a keyboard layout that has the specific character present, such as the British layout, which has the British pound character as the alternate to 3 and was the main reason it was noticed. Another potential hiccup is the Japanese yen character, since Japanese keyboard layouts appear to allow a way to enter it faster than typing alt+0165. The issue can be bypassed by passing in the password using the -p argument in condor_store_cred, but the issue with not being able to enter characters like pound still remains, especially for people with British keyboard layouts.

Granted we upconvert back to unicode to use the password, but this eliminates any potential issues with input getting mangled because we may be in the wrong code page.

title: Ticket #3604: DMTCP integration shim broken: hard coded paths; missing libraries
description: Our DMTCP integration package doesn't work. There are at least two open problems: Problem 1: Newer DMTCP releases include new/differently named libraries. 0.5 of the DMTCP integration package fixes the Makefile, but fails to update the submit files to include the new libraries. Should be an easy fix. Workaround: ensure the DMTCP libraries are in transfer_input_files. Problem 2: The checkpoint restart script DMTCP has has hard-coded paths. This breaks restart when the path may change. I don't know if this is new behavior or not. If it's old behavior, it doesn't seem like restarts should have ever worked. Also worth checking: do the binary checkpoint blobs potentially include hard-coded paths? That could doom us just as hard. Be sure to notify a25442 when fixed. Be sure to notify LIGO folks when fixed.
remarks: 2013-May-09 19:44:36 by adesmet: The hard coded paths to checkpoint files don't appear to be a problem. DMTCP is prepared to cope with them moving via --restartdir, -d or the environment variable DMTCP_RESTART_DIR. On testing, they appear to work as advertised. I successfully made a checkpoint, moved things to a new location, and restarted it. This doesn't mean that open files necessarily work. That needs to be checked. Periodic checkpoints don't actually appear to work; needs to be investigated. Random observation: if we end up using filesystem namespaces, it may be possible to give jobs the illusion that their working directory doesn't actually change, potentially coping with some fragile programs. 2013-May-09 19:44:58 by adesmet: Also, check into the admin ticket and double check what the reported problem is. 2013-May-20 16:31:17 by adesmet: The absolute paths in the restart script are fine; the script is doing the right thing and rewriting them when we restart. The restart problems I was seeing while trying to reproduce were a red herring. The real problem is restarting on a slightly different CPU. To take an example I ran into, a simple program started up on a computer with SSE 4 support. glibc wisely took advantage of the SSE 4 support to optimize some string routines, caching the result. I checkpointed. The job restarted on a computer without SSE 4 support. glibc used the cached knowledge and tried to use the optimized version: SIGILL, dead. This bit standard universe recently; the solution was to add several CPU feature flags known to be problematic to the checkpoint string. This provides some increased safety but increases pool fragmentation. (It's also not as safe as possible, as it is ignorant of future features and omits some flags that exist today.) The answer for DMTCP support is probably the same. Doing this entirely in the script is tricky, so we probably won't have anything until there are changes to the vanilla universe in suppport. Current workarounds: Use a homogenous pool. Self limit jobs to a homogenous pools. Ensure initial run and checkpoint are on CPU with minimal capabilities, limit jobs to machines with those or greater capabilities.
creator: adesmet

title: Ticket #1793: IpVerify::PunchHole() doesn't work without specific IP address
description: IpVerify::PunchHole() is used to make internal adjustments to the authorization policy that we think should be automatic. Currently, it supports authorization by IP or by fqu@IP. There are two cases where it is being used to authorize fqu (at any IP), but since this is not supported, these adjustments to the authorization policy have no effect and we instead rely on the authorization policy defined by the user to allow access. The two cases are: 1) DaemonCore::Inherit() authorizing the parent security session and 2) CStarter::createJobOwnerSecSession() used by ssh_to_job.

title: Ticket #749: Schedd creates unnecessary job spool dirs
description: This description is copied from Red Hat Bugzilla ( https://bugzilla.redhat.com/show_bug.cgi?id=523806 ) In cases that require no file transfer (e.g. in which the spool directory is on a shared filesystem or the local filesystem), the condor schedd will attempt to stat, chown, and delete the spool directory when the job completes or is removed. This poses a problem in environments using NFS spool directories, since these operations are between one and two orders of magnitude slower on NFS (and may also unacceptably load the NFS server). How reproducible: Submit a job with a spool directory on a shared filesystem. Expected results: The schedd should neither create nor delete job spool directories in this case.
remarks: 2009-Sep-25 11:06:50 by willb: There is a fix on branch 7_4-ticket-749 2009-Sep-25 11:47:16 by adesmet: The diff, for reference: ----------------------- src/condor_schedd.V6/schedd.cpp ----------------------- index e8f5afa..b73a6e5 100644 @@ -2133,13 +2133,22 @@ bool jobIsSandboxed( ClassAd * ad ) { ASSERT(ad); int stage_in_start = 0; + MyString should_xfer; + MyString cleanup_anyway; + ad->LookupInteger( ATTR_STAGE_IN_START, stage_in_start ); if( stage_in_start > 0 ) { return true; } + if( ad->LookupString( ATTR_SHOULD_TRANSFER_FILES, should_xfer ) && + (should_xfer.upper_case(), should_xfer == "NO" ) && + !(ad->LookupString( "CleanUpSpuriousJobSandboxes", cleanup_anyway ))) { + return false; + } + int univ = CONDOR_UNIVERSE_VANILLA; ad->LookupInteger( ATTR_JOB_UNIVERSE, univ ); switch( univ ) { case CONDOR_UNIVERSE_SCHEDULER: What's CleanUpSpuriousJobSandboxes doing in there? It doesn't appear anywhere else in the code, doesn't have an ATTR_ macro, and generally seems suspect. What does ATTR_SHOULD_TRANSFER_FILES have to do with a job having or not having a sandbox? Something as simple as "condor_submit -s myjob.submit" will leave you with a job with a sandbox, but ATTR_SHOULD_TRANSFER_FILES as NO. 2009-Sep-25 14:15:08 by adesmet: As is, the patch will likely cause problems for jobs that spool their input (condor_submit -s, Condor-C, etc). Also, the upgrade path (qediting) is messy. Further investigation by willb and I reveals deeper, more suspicious behavior. The directories in question are referred to as the "sandbox" in the code. The spooled input code path works as expected: Spooled jobs create the sandbox inside file_transfer.cpp around line 340 inside FileTransfer::SimpleInit. The sandbox is owned by PRIV_CONDOR. The sandbox must be owned by PRIV_USER when the job runs, so it's chowned in aboutToSpawnJobHandler (schedd.cpp:2323). The sandbox is chowned back to PRIV_CONDOR in jobIsFinished (schedd.cpp:2614). The sandbox is deleted when the job leaves the queue (location not currently known) However, just before step 2 above, there is a surprise. In aboutToSpawnJobHandler (schedd.cpp:2257) if the sandbox doesn't exist, it is created. I have no idea why. I can think of no cases where a sandbox might not exist before, but must exist when the job starts. This code dates back to 2006 and was written by wright, so it's likely part of the original sandbox work. So: Why does aboutToSpawnJobHandler create the sandbox? Can we remove this code entirely? (This would eliminate the mkdirs above and hopefully solve Red Hat's problem.) jobIsSandboxed used to be clever. But it was buggy, so now it's stupid and assumes that all vanilla jobs (among others) are sandboxed, even if they aren't. Is it possible to be clever and safe? The problem appears to be lack of a reliable job ad attribute indicating a sandboxed job. Getting this right would also solve the problem. 2009-Oct-15 11:11:42 by willb: I've pushed a more comprehensive fix to the V7_4_1-spurious-spool-elimination branch. This branch introduces a new attribute ("NeverCreateJobSandbox") for jobs that should not be sandboxed. The new attribute is respected by both the shadow and schedd and is set automatically by condor_submit for jobs that do not require file transfer (only if these jobs are not submitted via "condor_submit -s" or via remote submit). This fix does not introduce any upgrade issues; a condor_submit with the fix will not affect old schedds or shadows, and schedds or shadows that do not include the fix will simply continue to have the old sandboxing behavior when running jobs submitted with a new condor_submit. 2009-Oct-15 11:15:33 by willb: I should note that the fix mentioned in my previous comment is not unduly clever; it simply shortcircuits jobIsSandboxed if NeverCreateJobSandbox is set in the job ad. Refactoring this part of the schedd (specifically, verifying that it's OK to fix the behavior Alan mentions above in aboutToSpawnJobHandler) is still worth doing. 2010-Aug-23 17:42:37 by adesmet: Bulk change of target version from v070403 to v070404 using ./ticket_target_mover. 2010-Oct-27 16:39:01 by adesmet: Bulk change of target version from v070404 to v070405 using ./ticket-target-mover.

title: Ticket #1286: shadow born w/a security session to the schedd
description: When the schedd creates a shadow, that shadow then immediately has to turn around and negotiate a security session with the schedd, which can be a fair amount of work on a fully loaded schedd. Instead it may be better to pass the information to the shadow such that when it is born a security session already exists. This should alleviate some issues where the shadow will exit if is can not negotiate the session within a given time-frame.

title: Ticket #7352: Add DAGMan inline submit descriptions
description: DAGMan currently requires users to provide external submit files to describe jobs in their workflows. We'd like to extend the DAGMan syntax so that submit descriptions can be included inline. The first step will be modifying the JOB command. Our current syntax expects the user to provide the path to a submit file in the local file system. We'll change this so a user can optionally provide a submit description in an inline classad, preceded by the SUBMIT keyword. For example, to define a job which sleeps for 10 seconds: JOB Sleep SUBMIT-DESCRIPTION { executable = "/bin/sleep" arguments = 10 } We also need to provide backwards compatibility. So the following syntax will still be valid: JOB Sleep sleep.sub To avoid confusion between submit files and submit descriptions, we'll allow users to reference submit files with an optional FILE keyword: JOB Sleep FILE sleep.sub Lastly, we'll allow submit descriptions to be declared independently of jobs. They can then be associated to jobs by passing the name instead of a classad. For example: SUBMIT-DESCRIPTION SleepSubmitDesc = { executable = "/bin/sleep" arguments = 10 } JOB Sleep1 SUBMIT-DESCRIPTION SleepSubmitDesc JOB Sleep2 SUBMIT-DESCRIPTION SleepSubmitDesc Internally, we'll extend DAGMan's Job() class to store the description in a SubmitHash member variable called _submitDescription. At parse time, condor_dagman will translate the inline classad to a SubmitHash object which can later be handed off directly to the schedd. Some other rules and assumptions: We will not support clusters with multiple procs. All inline submits are assumed to be "queue 1". The DAGMAN_USE_CONDOR_SUBMIT configuration knob must be set to False. If not condor_dagman will fail at parse time. Inline submits can coexist with regular submit files in the same .dag file.

title: Ticket #6810: Tolerate full sinful string in claim ids
description: Currently, the claim ids used to claim a slot start with a sinful string that contains just an IP address and port number between angled brackets. This can make it impossible for match password authentication to work when there are multiple startds behind the same shared port daemon. This can be fixed by using the startd's full sinful string in the claim id. But this will break parsing of the claim id, as '#' is used to separate fields in the claim id and will appear in a sinful string when CCB is enabled. We can change the parsing code to tolerate full sinful strings in the claim id. If the first character of the claim id is '<', then the first occurrence of '>' denotes the end of first claim id field, rather than the first '#'. Generating claim ids with full sinful strings will want until Condor 8.9.0 (#5604).

title: Ticket #4207: Giving multiple names to The Tool can lead to incorrect failures
description: Ticket #3686 made changes to The Tool (a.k.a condor_on/off/...) to make it easier to identify daemons when their names aren't full DNS hostnames and when the names of the master and its child daemons are different. This introduced a bug when specifying multiple names on the command line. The tool would report "Can't find address for <daemon type> <daemon name>" for some of the daemons, even though it received ads for those daemons from the collector. One way to trigger this is to include an invalid daemon name. Then, all subsequent daemons named on the command line will not be found. The problem is that when the tool examines the daemon ads for ones that match a given name, it changed the Name attribute in all of the ads rather than in just the ads that match the given name.

title: Ticket #3468: Negotiator rank expressions don't work with boolean values
description: Starting in Condor 7.9.0, the various negotiator job and preemption rank expressions failed to sort properly if they evaluated to a boolean value. This includes the default NEGOTIATOR_PRE_JOB_RANK of RemoteOwner =?= UNDEFINED. The issue is that classad::Value::IsNumber() doesn't consider boolean values to be numbers, even though they are treated as numbers in arithmetic operations in a classad expression. We plan to change IsNumber() to treat boolean values as numbers (True is 1, False is 0). Callers who care about values that are specifically integers or reals can use Value::IsIntegerValue() and Value::IsRealValue().

title: Ticket #2629: User-creatable job prerequisites
description: Problem: My job has a bunch of initial setup that is required. The common case is that I might need some large software package, like R or the Matlab Compiler Runtime installed. I can bring it with me, but if I'm running a large number of jobs, you can end up wasting lots of bandwidth and time downloading and installing it. Current work arounds typically system administrator intervention, and remove Condor's ability to manage the system. Proposal: A job can specify a prerequisite. Something like "Matlab-MCR-2011b." It also has a path to another submit file associated with it. So job might say: PREREQUISITIES=Matlab_MCR_2011b gcc Matlab_MCR_2011b=/path/to/Mathlab.submit gcc=/different/path/to/gcc.submit RANK=PREREQ_adesmet_Matlab_mcr_2011b + PREREQ_adesmet_gcc When the startd/starter is about to start a job, the machine checks if the prereqs are satisified. They default to not. If they are not, the second submit file is used to immediately run the job that sets up the prereq. However, instead of being put into EXECUTE in a directory that is wiped out quickly, the job runs in a directory that will persist for "a while" and that Condor knows is associated with the prereq. Maybe $(PREREQ)/$(Owner)/$(prereq_name). Once all prereq jobs are finished, the real job is allowed to run. Once a prereq is installed, it will be advertised in the form PREREQ_$(Owner)_$(prereq_name), allowing preference by RANK to avoid unnecessary installs. Installed prereqs will be deleted based on space used; aging out probably based on least recently used, but more clever techniques are possible. However, if a running job requires a given prereq, it will not be removed.

title: Ticket #1906: Update documentation for new Hierarchical Acct Group Quotas (HGQ)
description: The accounting groups feature has been enhanced to support hierarchical accounting groups and group quotas, as of 7.5.6 -- The condor documentation should be updated to explain the enhanced capability. Could these uses be better described with scaled ? The example of static quotas chooses child quotas that add up to 2 times the integer defined for the parent. However "scaled" would also work. Regarding the static quotas example, quotas are actually floating point values at that particular stage. I used an example where the results were integers because it was easier, but if the results of normalization are non-integer that is how they will be stored until a later step. There should be a description in the doc I attached that describes the final step of recovering fractional slots. That happens after initial quota assignment and surplus quota distribution (which both treat quotas as floating point). What I'm getting at here is that I need to document a type for the configuration variable. Your doc states that it is an integer, but the entire description (and your answer to previous question) really implies that it actually is a fl pt that is eventually truncated to provide an integral number of slots. 2011-Mar-31 10:00:27 by eje: A static quota is currently read from the config as a floating point, and so in that respect it is probably most accurate to define its type as float/real, however: pragmatically, it is intended to represent some number of slots, and so it will be easiest to think of it as 'integer' from a user/admin point of view.
