If a quota is configured or defaulted to zero, then it will only be able to run jobs if there is surplus quota available from other groups (and if it has autoregroup enabled, so it can accept surplus quota). FYI: there is a new synonym for GROUP_AUTOREGROUP_<>, called GROUP_ACCEPT_SURPLUS_<>. Dan seemed to like it, however at this point it hasn't been documented, and could be left undocumented. 2011-Apr-13 15:15:02 by smoler: What is the point of having a job set its AccountingGroup attribute ending in the "username"? For example, if there are group/subgroups such as GROUP_QUOTA_group_physics = 12 GROUP_QUOTA_group_physics.lab1 = 3 GROUP_QUOTA_group_physics.lab2 = 4 why does my job need to set +AccountingGroup = "group_physics.lab1.marysunshine" To distinguish, why is my job not +AccountingGroup = "group_physics.lab1" Related question: is this "username" subject to any limitations or verification? If there were 2 Unix logins ("john" and "jane"), and John submits his job with a "username" of "jane," what happens? 2011-Apr-13 15:17:59 by smoler: The older, existing Condor documentation on group accounting specified a 40 character limit on group names. Has this limit changed? If so, to what? And, how does any limit apply to subgroups, sub subgroups, etc. ? 2011-Apr-13 16:01:42 by eje: The "grp.user" format predates the introduction of this hierarchical group feature -- I left it as-is for backward compatibility. The "user" portion of this name is not authenticated, and is not required to be correlated with actual OS user name: it is essentially honor system at this point. (there are certainly good arguments for supporting authenticated user names, and perhaps also authenticated group names, in the future) There is no fixed limit on group name length. I've tested it with group names up to 80 characters long. 2011-May-05 15:18:45 by smoler: Configuration variable not yet documented, and should not be forgotten: GROUP_DYNAMIC_MACH_CONSTRAINT 2011-May-11 11:44:18 by smoler: E-mail about errors in the 7.6.0 manual's calculations (for dynamic quotas) and subsequent e-mails about terminology refer to configuration variables that are not referred to in the "downstream documentation." Please help me out by giving me definitions for these 2, as well as identifying any others that I wouldn't know about: ACCEPT_SURPLUS GROUP_DYNAMIC_MACH_CONSTRAINT 2011-May-23 15:23:53 by danb: GROUP_ACCEPT_SURPLUS - a boolean value that specifies whether groups should be allowed to use more than their configured quota when there is not enough demand from other groups to use all of the available machines. The default is false. GROUP_ACCEPT_SURPLUS_<group_name> - this setting applies to the specific named group. If not specified, the default is controlled by GROUP_ACCEPT_SURPLUS. GROUP_DYNAMIC_MACH_CONSTRAINT - this is an expression that specifies the set of machines in the pool that should be used to determine the size of the pool for dynamic quotas, which are expressed as a fraction of the total. When there are extra rarely used slots in the pool (e.g. administrative slots), it may be desirable to filter these out by specifying an expression for GROUP_DYNAMIC_MACH_CONSTRAINT that matches only the "normal" slots and not the special slots. GROUP_QUOTA_ROUND_ROBIN_RATE - the maximum sum of weighted slots that should be handed out to an individual submitter in each iteration within a negotiation cycle. If slot weights are not being used by the negotiator (NEGOTIATOR_USE_SLOT_WEIGHTS=false), then this is just the (unweighted) number of slots. The default is a very big number---effectively infinite. Setting this to a number smaller than the size of the pool can help avoid starvation. An example of the starvation problem when there are a subset of machines in a pool with large memory and there are multiple job submitters who desire all of these machines. Normally, Condor will decide how much of the full pool each person should get and then attempt to hand out that number of resources to each person. Since the big memory machines are only a subset of pool, it may happen that they are all given to the first person contacted, and the rest of the people requiring large memory machines get nothing. Setting GROUP_QUOTA_ROUND_ROBIN_RATE to a value that is small compared to the size of subsets of machines will reduce starvation at the cost of possibly slowing down the rate at which resources are allocated. NEGOTIATOR_USE_SLOT_WEIGHTS - a boolean value that controls whether the negotiator pays attention to SlotWeight in machine ads. The default is true. When false, each slot effectively has a weight of 1. GROUP_QUOTA_MAX_ALLOCATION_ROUNDS - an integer that specifies the maximum number of times in one negotiation cycle the negotiator will calculate how many slots each group deserves and attempt to allocate them. The default is 3. The reason it may take more than one round is that some groups may not have jobs that match some of the available machines, so some of the slots that were withheld for those groups may not get allocated in any given round. 2012-Dec-17 16:43:08 by smoler: Dec 17, 2012: Documentation task of getting the manual up to date will be completed by explicitly telling folks that we don't recommend mixing static and dynamic quotas, and removing the waiting/empty subsection on how mixing would work. Examples are to be generated and placed into the htcondor wiki. 2012-Dec-18 15:53:59 by smoler: Changes have gone into many branches of the manual. Last one went into 7.8.8.

title: Ticket #5416: master should have a command to query (and wait for) child readiness
description: In support of #5340, and for testing. it would be nice to have a command that can be sent to the master and it would reply with the readiness states of each of it's children. It would also be nice if the master could delay responding to query until the children had reached a known readiness state or a timeout had expired. A new command would be added to the master DC_QUERY_READY The Master would reply to this query with a classad containing a single global readiness attribute and 2 attributes for each child in the daemon list. IsReady = bool: all non-held daemons are in "Alive" state NumDaemons = int: number of daemons in DAEMON_LIST NumAlive = int: number of daemons in "Alive" state NumStartup = int: number of daemons in "Startup" state NumHold = int: number of daemons in "Hold" state NumHung = int: number of daemons in "Hung" state NumDead = int: number of daemons in "Dead" state # 2 attributes for each daemon in DAEMON_LIST <Daemon>_PID = int: PID or 0 if no child process <Daemon> = string: one of the <readiness-state> values # 1 optional additional attribute for some daemons in DAEMON_LIST <Daemon>_State = string: state reported by the daemon using =DC_SET_READY= The <Daemon> values will be the names from DAEMON_LIST, The possible string values for <readiness-state> will be "Alive" - got a pid and at least 1 alive message from that pid "Hung" - got a pid and at least 1 alive message, but none recently "Startup" - started the child, but have not yet got an alive message or decided it hung "Dead" - no pid and not on hold "Hold" - no pid and daemon has been condor_off'd "WaitForStartup" - no pid and waiting before starting the daemon "WaitForStartupFile" - no pid and waiting before starting the daemon For daemons that send the master a DC_SET_READY message, the string value sent in this message will be written to a <Daemon>_State attribute, it will be reported as part of the DC_QUERY_READY reply until a change of the <readiness-state> of the daemon clears it. In general, do not expect a daemon that is not in "Alive" state to have a <Daemon>_State attribute. In addition to the basic query, the DC_QUERY_READY command will have a ClassAd payload, that can be used to specify that the reply should not occur until a desired readiness state has been achieved or a timeout has expired. The attributes to control this will be ReadyRequirements = <readiness-expr> WaitTimeout = <max-time-before-reply-in-sec> When a non-zero timeout is supplied the ReadyRequirements expression will be evaluated against the readiness ad once per second, and the reply will be sent once the WaitTimeout has expired, or ReadyRequirements evaluates to true. So for instance ReadyRequirements = (NumDead > 0) || (IsReady && (STARTD_State =?= "Ready")) WaitTimeout = 60 Will tell the master to reply only once all daemons have sent at least 1 heartbeat, and the Startd has sent "ready", or after 60 seconds have expired. condor_who -quick will be enhanced to use the new DC_QUERY_READY command, and (possibly?) a new flavor of condor_tool will be created to make it easy to use the query ready command in a script.

title: Ticket #933: PER_JOB_HISTORY_DIR semantics changed inappropriately in 7.4.0
description: Summary In 7.4.0 (or 7.3.x I suppose), the semantics of PER_JOB_HISTORY_DIR was inappropriately changed in a way that could easily result in all disk space on a worker node filling up, and it causes problems for OSG's Gratia accounting service. Details In Condor 7.2.x and 7.4.x, PER_JOB_HISTORY_DIR was defined specifically as affecting the schedd. From the manual in 7.4.0: PER_JOB_HISTORY_DIR If set to a directory writable by the Condor user, when a job leaves the condor_schedd's queue, a copy of its ClassAd will be written in that directory. The files are named ``history.'' with the job's cluster and process number appended. For example, job 35.2 will result in a file named ``history.35.2''. Condor does not rotate or delete the files, so without an external entity to clean the directory it can grow very large. This option defaults to being unset. When not set, no such files are written. It's reasonable to think that this could be in a configuration file shared across a site since it only affects the schedd--it has no effect on a startd. Unfortunately, when this is set in Condor 7.4.0, it will also make the startd leave job classads in the PER_JOB_HISTORY_DIR. A site is unlikely to expect this, and it will eventually fill up the disk on an execute node with job classads. This change in the semantics of PER_JOB_HISTORY_DIR is bad and undocumented. I'm not quite sure what should be done, but I think that when 7.4.1 is released, PER_JOB_HISTORY_DIR shouldn't affect the startd by default. That is, we should revert this change in semantics as soon as possible. Perhaps there should be a STARTD_PER_JOB_HISTORY_DIR instead? This affects OSG sites because we use PER_JOB_HISTORY_DIR to collect job accounting data for our Gratia accounting service, and we are now getting extra history files that are not cleaned up.

title: Ticket #7581: Fix need to invoke and depth of recursion for MAX_REMAP_RECURSIONS
description: A user in a real environment has a file that lives in a directory hierarchy more than 20 levels deep. This tripped the "probably has a cycle" circuit breaker for file transfer remaps, which uses a recursive function. First of all, it seems like there is no purpose in walking the directory hierarchy if there are no remaps to apply. So I propose to add a check for that at the top of the recursive function to short circuit that whole process. This will be addressed in #7619. Also, there is very little performance overhead in doing the remaps when needed, as it's just in-memory processing of a directory hierarchy using a recursive function. However, we do need to have some finite limit in case there is a cycle in the remap rules, so I propose for this ticket we change the default for MAX_REMAP_RECURSIONS to 128.

title: Ticket #2279: Condor-C Failure in the OSG Summer School
description: We observed a pretty severe failure of Condor-C in the OSG Summer School this morning. About 30 students submitted jobs from a schedd in Wisconsin to a pool/schedd at UCSD. Basically, we saw a huge number from the CGAHPWorkerThread in talking to the remote schedd. The remote schedd was very unresponsive to a hand-run "condor_q". When I did a few "pstack" on the remote schedd, it was always blocked in condor_read. The FD it was reading from could be tracked back to a CGAHP worker thread. Talking to danb, I believe the issue is the blocking qmgmt interface. Dan claims that each attribute in the classad of a submitted job is sent as a separate round trip. So, a job with 10 attributes and a 100msec RTT would block the schedd for 1 sec. I believe that we had enough threads trying to submit in parallel that the blocking behavior caused most of them to basically fail. This would not show up in usage where the latency is small, or if there's a small number of submitters (assuming the working theory is correct).
remarks: 2011-Jun-28 16:18:51 by jfrey: Job submission appears to be the main problem here. The c-gahp is pushing multiple full job ads to the remote schedd with a round-trip per attribute. We need a method in the schedd's qmgmt client interface that allows the sending of one or more full job ads in a single round-trip, essentially a complement to GetAllJobsByConstraint(). 2012-Sep-07 13:21:55 by jfrey: #2575 should solve this problem.

title: Ticket #5046: gridmanager/blahp should perform bulk queries against batch backend
description: Currently, the blahp queries jobs one-at-a-time for their status. This is very inefficient (each job query is going to spawn at least one process - usually tens). It's also hard on the batch systems - which are often optimized for bulk queries. We should add a new status command that retrieves all jobs for the given user. Any of the resulting jobs known to the gridmanager ought to have their status updated.

title: Ticket #2783: Add attributes to JobAd to show time spent in file transfer
description: In order to collect statistics for the amount of time spent in file transfer vs. time spent executing user jobs, the job ad needs to publish some attributes. JobCurrentStartExecutingDate int, time_t that the job actually began execution. the difference between this and JobCurrentStartDate is time spent transferring the input sandbox for the current run. JobCurrentStartTransferOutputDate int, time_t that the job began transferring output (actually the time that FileTransfer::DoDownload began). This should be the same as the time that the job stopped executing. The difference between CompletionDate and this attribute is the time to transfer the output sandbox. CumulativeTransferTime float, accumulated time in seconds spent transferring data as reported by the filetransfer object.

title: Ticket #3891: Get Pegasus to fix sub-DAG submit files
description: Pegasus currently doesn't generate sub-DAG (at least) submit files by running condor_submit_dag (so they lack information like -CsdVersion). We would like to move to a model where Pegasus always runs condor_submit_dag to generate the submit files. This may mean adding additional options to condor_submit_dag to add the information that Pegasus needs for sub-DAGs. Note: Version above isn't terribly useful, because it doesn't refer to a Pegasus version.
remarks: 2014-Mar-07 10:53:05 by wenger: Okay, the basic problem here is that Pegasus needs to change/add some stuff in the .condor.sub file. So there are three options: Pegasus writes the .condor.sub file directly. Pegasus calls condor_submit_dag -no_submit with some special arguments. Pegasus adds information to the DAG file or some other file, and DAGMan calls condor_submit_dag -no_submit. Number 1 is what we're currently doing, but that's not good. At this point I'm leaning towards number 3. My idea is that we'd have something like a condor_submit_dag template file (with a name based on the DAG file name) and that file would contain things that override and/or add to stuff in the normal .condor.sub file. I think we should have something like a -use_submit_templates flag to condor_submit_dag that gets passed down to sub-DAGs -- I'm kind of leery of people getting unexpected behaviour of if we always use the template files without the user explicitly asking for it. 2014-Mar-19 15:59:53 by wenger: I just had a phone conversation with Karan about this. Pegasus has several requirements: Be able to set/change initialdir, log, error, and output. Add various custom classad attribute/value pairs. Specify whether or not to do autorescue. Specify the path to the .condor.sub file that will be created. Item 1 should be pretty easy, except maybe for initialdir -- I'll have to think about whether that will cause complications. Item 2 should be very easy. Item 3 should also be pretty easy -- I think we could just add the capability to append to the arguments line in the .condor.sub file. (If we have to change something that already exists in the arguments line it would get trickier.) Item 4 is a little trickier -- right now DAGMan expects the .condor.sub file for a sub-DAG to be in the same directory as the DAG file. Pegasus doesn't want this for a number of reasons, including that they don't generate the directory that the sub-DAG lives in until the planning step. (Although that may not be as much of a problem if DAGMan itself runs condor_submit_dag.) At any rate, they currently put the sub-DAGs in subdirectories, but put the .condor.sub files in the parent directory. (Hmm -- maybe one solution could be to put the .dag file for the sub-DAG in the parent directory, but put all of the other stuff, such as the node job submit files, in a subdirectory.) The other thing is, if we go with the template file idea, my thought was that the template file name would be based on the DAG file name, for example foo.dag.sub.tmpl or something. (The template file name would have to be automatically derivable from the DAG file name so that condor_submit_dag could automatically apply it.) I guess Pegasus could generate the template file after creating the subdirectory for the sub-DAG, so maybe this isn't such a problem. 2015-Sep-22 11:21:11 by tpdownes: This is a general Pegasus/HTCondor problem rather than a specific LIGO problem. Removing LIGO tag from ticket. De-prioritizing ticket to 3 ("before next series release") since if it were still causing fires, we'd know about it. Nevertheless, I suggest that Karan and Kent talk to discuss whether this is still a problem in 8.2/8.4 series so that they can remove ticket if appropriate. Tom 2016-Apr-06 12:56:49 by wenger: I'm suspicious that this is causing the problem LIGO just reported with condor_rm not removing node jobs, so I cranked up the priority on this. 2016-Apr-26 09:12:25 by wenger: Created V8_5-gittrac_3891-branch for this. 2016-Apr-26 09:16:47 by wenger: Oh, yeah -- as per the April 6 remark, we did confirm that this was causing the problem that LIGO ran into. 2016-Apr-26 11:31:54 by wenger: Phone conference today about this with Karan -- basically we need an option to condor_submit_dag that allows the user to specify the full path of the .condor.sub file that we create; the main work, though, is that we need to modify all of the paths in the .condor.sub file so that when it is submitted from the directory it's in, the .out, .log, etc., files end up in the same directory as the .dag file. 2016-Apr-26 12:03:23 by wenger: Hmm -- check whether -usedagdir will fix up the paths the way we need... 2016-Jul-18 16:55:35 by wenger: Just trying to understand this a little more clearly. But I want to clarify: does this mean that all of the paths for the node jobs of foo/my.dag are relative to bar, not foo? Otherwise this shouldn't work. I think it would help if the Pegasus developers could give me a tarball of a small example, with the .dag file, .condor.sub file, node job submit files, etc., in various directories, with the paths all set up the way they want them. assuming there was something like a -out option to condor_submit_dag.

title: Ticket #5553: 1 minute startup block if DNS record missing
description: When any HTCondor program starts, be it daemon or command line tool, it does a DNS lookup on our best guess for a hostname. It's trying to find a fully qualified domain name as well as an IP address. However, if the lookup fails for any reason we will retry every 3 seconds for up to 1 minute. The program blocks during this period. This is particularly noticeable on command line tools. The code always run as it provides configuration variables like IP_ADDRESS, which may be necessary to correctly interpret the configuration file. The unwanted behavior appears in [37747] 8c1a0005e224738c5f1ee6beeacda17a7529cd1 as a fix for "#3956: some schedd ads have a blank Name attr, make malformed GlobalJobIds". The code in question has been completely rewritten, but the behavior was carefully preserved. It's in init_local_hostname_impl in /src/condor_utils/ipv6_hostname.cpp, around line 117. Look for "SLEEP_DUR = 3". The original commit (88c1a) was trying intended to retry only for EAI_AGAIN. That is likely correct behavior. However, it will retry even for permanent errors (say, EAI_NONAME). Proposed fix: immediately after this code: int ret = ipv6_getaddrinfo(test_hostname.Value(), NULL, ai, hint); if(ret == 0) { gai_success = true; break; } Add something like if(ret != EAI_AGAIN) { gai_success = false; dprintf(...) // Details about the error returned and note about failure. break; }

title: Ticket #4342: Can't distinguish normal and abnormal job exit for Nordugrid ARC
description: In NorduGrid ARC, we can't distinguish between normal job termination and termination via a signal. If a job exits via signal 9, some ARC systems will report an exit code of 9 and others will report an exit code of 137. Currently, the gridmanager assumes exit codes greater than 127 are probably exit-by-signal and reports job termination as such. In newer versions of ARC, these exit codes are likely to be normal job terminations. We should modify the gridmanager to always report a normal job termination with the exit code given the ARC LDAP interface. Details When NorduGrid ARC submits a job to the local batch system, it creates a Bourne wrapper script that does some setup and tear-down before and after running the user job. The script determines the job's exit status using the $? variable, saves that value, and uses it with the 'exit' command at the end of the script. In some situations, it runs the job via GNU's /usr/bin/time, and other times it runs the job directly. If the job exits via signal 9, the value reported by $? will be 9 in the former case and 137 in the latter. In ARC 4.0.0, the wrapper script always runs the job directly if the batch system is HTCondor. For other batch systems, GNU's 'time' is used if it's available, otherwise the job is run directly. Some testing by Andrew Lahiff suggests that in 4.1.0, the behavior for HTCondor has changed to match that for other batch systems.

title: Ticket #3487: implement fair sharing in transfer queue
description: Problem The new round robin scheduling in the file transfer queue suffers from unfairness. Consider Brian's scenario: User A has transfers that last 1s and User B has transfers that last 1hr. If the transfer limit is 10 transfers, then after 10s, User B will have all the transfer slots and User A will be starved. This happens because we are giving the next free transfer slot to the user with the least recently started transfer. Proposed Solution Give the next transfer to the user with the least number of active transfers. In case of tie, give it to the user with the least recently started transfer.

title: Ticket #2828: Persistent security session and collector health cache for tools
description: New connections between Condor daemons are optimized by caching of security sessions. When High-Availability is in use, daemons also avoid collectors that have been unreachable in the recent past. The command-line tools don't see any of these benefits, since the information is only stored in memory. Each invocation of a tool needs to establish a new security session with each daemon it talks to and can spend a long time trying to contact a primary collector that's currently unreachable. We give the command-line tools the same benefits the daemons have by writing out security session and collector health information to a persist cache file on disk. Subsequent invocations of the tools would read in this file and use any relevant information. Argo Graphics has had their primary collector go down for prolonged periods of time, during which each tool invocation will spend a minute trying to talk to the dead machine before querying the secondary collector.
remarks: 2012-Feb-20 14:27:24 by matt: FYI - https://bugzilla.redhat.com/show_bug.cgi?id=472320 2012-Feb-20 15:25:14 by bbockelm: How do the tools express context? Where does the session get persisted? For example, if I do the following: X509_USER_PROXY=/tmp/foo condor_status then X509_USER_PROXY=/tmp/bar condor_status how will the tool determine if the persisted security session is still valid? title: Ticket #1707: improve scalability of shadow logging
description: In large-scale tests of glideinWMS, we have had the submit node become unresponsive to the point where it needed to be rebooted after being in this state for hours. System load reported by uptime was over 8000. There were 32k jobs running around the time the problem happened. Some evidence suggests that a large part of the problem is caused by locking of the shadow log. During the time when the system was unresponsive, large time skew between different shadows was observed: 10/08/10 09:37:33 (59903.0) (17861): ... 10/08/10 13:00:30 (64161.0) (47394): ... 10/08/10 13:00:30 (59858.0) (4887): ... 10/08/10 09:37:33 (70813.0) (73967): ... We believe that time skew was caused by some shadows getting starved (for hours!) trying to get a lock to the log file. In a standalone test, I've reproduced high system load with 10k processes doing nothing but vying for a lock to the same file, using the same method the condor shadow does. Every time the lock is released, there are O(35k) context switches, and the system becomes very unresponsive. The processes are just making a blocking syscall to the kernel, so all the activity is happening down in the kernel itself, not in user-space. In my particular test, the 15min load average reported by uptime is ~600. The process that gets the lock sleeps for 10 seconds and then releases it. If I change the sleep from 10s to 1s, the 15min load average approaches ~1000. This is in Scientific Linux 5.3. I think it is likely that contention for the lock to the shadow log is responsible for the system melt-down that we experienced. There may be other problems as well, but we must solve this one either way. Proposed Solution Miron wants improved management of the lock. At the very least, Condor should try to detect this type of problem and report it. In addition, we all agreed that the semantics of O_APPEND are acceptable in environments that support it (i.e. POSIX file systems, not NFS). So we can avoid locking when appending to the file in these cases. Step One [DONE] Condor processes should keep track of locking delays. They can report this to their parent process in their heartbeat message and the parent can report a summary of problems when it sees them. [DONE] Each message to the log file must be written with a single call to write() rather than multiple calls to fprintf() as are currently being done. [DONE] A new boolean configuration variable should be added called LOCK_DEBUG_LOG_TO_APPEND. When true and a lock file is configured, locking will happen on every write, as it does now. When false, locking will only happen during rotation. In Windows, it is ignored, because we always need to lock when writing. Step Two After gaining experience with the above, we may decide that even having the shadows lock to rotate the shadow log is unacceptable. If it is unacceptable, then we could have some other process handle the rotation. It should rotate at a smaller size than the shadows do. We will need to decide if the shadows should still rotate when they hit the upper bound or whether they should just wait for the log to be rotated. It is not acceptable to just continue appending to the log.
remarks: 2010-Oct-12 19:42:49 by matt: Two things we do to scale here - Stop locking the ShadowLog altogether Place ShadowLog in /dev/shm Generally the write semantics for the ShadowLog means its structure is sufficiently maintained without a lock. Also, the information present in the ShadowLog is not especially useful for debugging. Typically the significant issues are propagated to the SchedLog. If there is critical information in the ShadowLog it should be considered for inclusion in the SchedLog. Additionally, a ShadowLog without D_PID is useless. If the ShadowLogs are of importance, it has been suggested that they should be available via multiple streams, such as per pid, e.g. ShadowLog.pid. 2010-Oct-13 08:01:51 by danb: Erik Paulson sent me a link to an interesting blog post related to this issue: http://bryanpendleton.blogspot.com/2010/07/unix-file-locking-does-not-implement.html 2010-Oct-18 11:53:31 by danb: I have tested writing with O_APPEND under a variety of circumstances. I tested with 1k-10k writers alternately sleeping for a second and then writing. I have tested with write sizes from 0.5k-10k. I have tried a few different filesystems: ext3, tmpfs, jfs, AFS, NFS. I have run tests in a few different OSes: SL4, SL5, OS X 10.5. I also tested in SL5 running under VMware Fusion. In no case did I observe messages getting garbled when using O_APPEND. When I tested without the O_APPEND flag, I observed garbled messages only under AFS and NFS. It is well known that NFS does not fully comply with POSIX O_APPEND behavior (says so right in the man page for open()). However, from my tests it seems that if the writers are all on the same machine, O_APPEND works quite well in practice for both NFS and AFS. I did not test with writers to the same file from different machines, because we don't care about that case for Condor logging. I suspect that writers from different machines will produce garbled messages. Based on all that, I think it is reasonable to make the default behavior in Condor under unix to be LOCK_DEBUG_LOG_TO_APPEND=false. 2010-Oct-18 18:01:52 by matt: Will you preserve the existing DC_CHILDALIVE command, i.e. no change in arguments, and instead introduce a DC_CHILDALIVE_WITH_AD for an extensible way to carry data such as lock delays. 2010-Nov-19 16:18:48 by matt: DC_CHILDALIVE_WITH_AD is a nice thought, but may not be worthwhile. Instead, a DC_CHILDALIVE that is tolerant of a 2 argument call instead of 3 (3rd is the dprintf_lock_delay) may be more realistic. 2010-Dec-02 10:55:26 by danb: Ok, the extra floating point dprintf_lock_delay part of the DC_CHILDALIVE message is now optional.

title: Ticket #4505: service condor stop emits syntax error after condor_off
description: A relatively minor problem in the init.d script for Condor causes errors to be incorrectly printed to the screen (unsure if stdout/err) upon stopping the HTCondor service after a graceful shutdown of the startd. Steps to reproduce on Debian 7: Run condor_off $nodename from central manager Wait for startd to shutdown leaving procd and condor_master On execute node, run "service condor stop". Get this output: root@execute1000:~# service condor stop Shutting down Condor (fast-shutdown mode)... /etc/init.d/condor: 1: kill: Usage: kill [-s sigspec | -signum | -sigspec] [pid | job]... or kill -l [exitstatus] done. Despite error, Condor has shutdown. Normal behavior: root@execute1000:~# service condor start Starting up Condor... done. root@execute1000:~# service condor stop Shutting down Condor (fast-shutdown mode)... done.
remarks: I'm assuming based on the age of this ticket, and the fact that (I think?) it's just an annoyance and UI issue and not a functional problem, that it's safe to demote to priority 5. If I'm wrong, please speak up. 2019-Apr-10 15:41:15 by tpdownes: I presume it's worth killing based on pre-systemd-ness. The main impact of this (going by memory) is that configuration management systems want to know the state of services and do so through commands like "systemctl status condor.service". If "service X stop" returns something other than code 0 then puppet borks and a chain of other configuration management problems can occur where a node stops properly updating its config. So it's important that systemctl/service commands be "clean" in their behavior. Relatedly: Condor is a giant problem in state management because (effectively) condor_master knows more state than systemd. I'd just close it but wanted to provide some context.

title: Ticket #6492: DAGMan inconsistently tracks job holds, aborts jobs too early
description: Some CHTC users were getting their DAGMan jobs aborted for exceeding DAGMAN_MAX_JOB_HOLDS, although these jobs clearly had far fewer held procs than the maximum limit. This turned out to be more than a simple bug; DAGMan is fundamentally confused about how it tracks job holds. The problem is fairly basic. Some parts of the DAGMan code track held procs on a per-job basis, whereas other parts of the code track holds across the entire DAG. From reading the code, it seems like DAGMan was originally tracking on a per-DAG basis, then someone started refactoring it to a per-job basis, but they stopped halfway through. We need to pick one or the other. Given that we seemed to be moving to per-job tracking, this seems like the obvious solution to me. Any objections?
remarks: 2017-Nov-30 17:15:31 by coatsworth: I've moved this from stable release to dev since it turned out to be more complex than a regular bug. Previously, we aborted a DAG node if it exceeded DAGMAN_MAX_JOB_HOLDS holds across its entire lifetime. I've changed this so now the holds need to be simultaneous. However, the previous behavior is still desirable in certain cases. We should plan to implement both of them, but we have to balance this out across per-node or per-DAG tracking. To be continued...

title: Ticket #3690: Remove hard-coded policies on how schedd can reuse claims
description: Currently, the Claim that is given out by the Negotiator to the Schedd is very open ended. As long as it matches the Startd requirements, the only additional restrictions on the Claim are hard-coded : it cannot be used for a different user, and it must be used for a job with the same set of concurrency limits. This situation has shown to be a problem when implementing the “Global Priority” feature. While the Negotiator will pick the globally higher priority job for a user, all bets are off once that job finishes, since the Schedd will pick the next job using local criteria. Other policies based on the global state of the system would equally be impossible to implement. The proposal is thus to remove the hard-coded claim reuse logic and for the negotiator to explicitly embed the restrictions on jobs that can reuse the claim in the requirements that are sent back to the Schedd.

title: Ticket #362: implement named slots or class of slot types
description: Example: I have a large cluster. The nodes have anywhere from 1 to 8 slots available. I'd like to add a slot to every node in the cluster. I'd like this slot to always run under a consistent user/uid, say "admin". My main reason for doing this doesn't really matter, but let's say it's so i can do administrative tasks, maybe run sudo processes or some setuid binaries. I'd like to describe this simple addition in my condor configuration. Maybe i want to make similar additions to my config in the future, as well. What would be the best way to add this slot? If i've done a good job with my configuration, at best i have factored the eight possible slot configurations into eight separate configs. It seems that i would have to tack an extra slot onto each of these configurations (so now i have anywhere from 2 to 9 slots), advertise an extra attribute declaring that this slot is my admin slot, and then just match on this extra attribute when it comes time to run my admin jobs. What if i want to add additional restrictions to this slot, such as only letting certain people in my uid domain run jobs on it? What if i have wildly different slot setups across my cluster (much more than 8)? Do i have to respecify this for each separate slot configuration? If the answer is yes, then maybe named slots would be helpful. I could say "i'd like a slot called "admin" that i can match against on every node, that runs under uid "admin" in some toplevel config, and by the way only let uids "griswold" and "bgietzel" start jobs on it. I could specify this exactly once. If the answer is "no, condor already provides an easy way to tack on slots like this", then you should probably not add this feature (and maybe let me know of a good way to specify this).
remarks: 2009-Apr-04 21:45:12 by gthain: There's no good way to add an extra slot in Condor that I can think of. However, do you really want an extra slot, or an extra startd? The extra startd might give you more isolation from the operational condor, and let you set per-startd settings that you might not want in the real condor. This admin startd could report to a completely different pool, with different startds, so us lowly users wouldn't ever see it, or accidentally match to it. 2009-Apr-04 23:29:41 by matt: Nick's local name configuration work may be useful, see 3.3.1.2. 2009-Apr-05 00:23:19 by griswold: This is likely what we will end up doing in NMI for this specific case.

title: Ticket #2594: Negative process ages on mac
description: On the mac machines in the batlab (both old and new), we occasionally see errors like this: ProcAPI sanity failure on pid 1317, age = -1901480712 This error is printed by ProcAPI::do_usage_sampling(), which is called by ProcAPI::getProcInfo(). The likely problem is that the sysctl() calls made by getProcInfoRaw() don't fail if the given pid doesn't exist. They return success and leave the structures meant to contain the process info untouched. getProcInfo() and getProcInfoRaw() then read values out of these uninitialized structures. ProcAPI::getProcInfo() could be called repeatedly with a non-existent pid by KillFamily::takesnapshot(), which remembers pids it saw in the past and checks if they're still alive. getProcInfo()/getProcInfoRaw() need to be modified on Darwin to properly detect when a pid doesn't exist. It appears we can detect this by checking whether the second call to sysctl() sets bufSize to 0 or non-0.

title: Ticket #6884: Do not perform a network turnaround for each file transfer
description: Turns out that HTCondor's file transfer performs a network turnaround (roundtrip communication between shadow and starter) for each file transferred by File Transfer. This is really unfortunate as it hurts network throughput due to i) latency (esp if submit and execute host are separated by the WAN), and ii) by preventing the TCP window from filling up, esp if many small files are being transferred. Prior to any command sent by the file transfer object, the object will check to see if it needs a go-ahead from its peer. The condor_starter gives a "go-ahead always", meaning that the shadow never again waits. The condor_shadow gives a "go-ahead once", meaning the transfers between the shadow and starter requires a round trip between peers to finish. If condor_shadow is configured to not limit transfers (MAX_CONCURRENT_UPLOADS=0 or MAX_CONCURRENT_DOWNLOADS=0), then it will always send a "go-ahead always" without acquiring a transfer token. Additionally, the condor_shadow will send a "go-ahead always" after it has acquired the token only if MAX_CONCURRENT_UPLOADS=0. This appears to be dead code as, in this case, the shadow never acquires the token! Currently, once a transfer token is received, the shadow never relinquishes it and it does not appear to expire. Accordingly, it appears the starter always requests a go-ahead and the shadow provides one unconditionally without contacting the schedd. This setup appears to serve no purpose. We should have the shadow send a "go-ahead always" once it gets the transfer token. I believe this change is of minimal risk: if, in the future, we decide the token should be a lease (or go back to the "go-ahead once" behavior), the change is shadow-side only.

I consider this a 9-year-old bug given that code exists to make this asynchronous already -- but the code was unreachable! Hence, it's a late-coming bugfix. 2019-Jan-31 16:40:44 by tannenba: CODE REVIEW Patch looks good. I confirmed it works as expected; in the ShadowLog immediately after receiving the transfer token from the schedd: Sending GoAhead for 127.0.0.1 to receive C:\condor\test\first_file.sub With the patch it now says: Sending GoAhead for 127.0.0.1 to receive C:\condor\test\first_file.sub and all further files. Also confirmed by inspecting shadowlog and starterlog with D_NETWORK enabled that there are no longer any network turnarounds between each file being sent. Woot! Only comments are: Needs an entry in the version history (I'll add that). For such a simple/small patch, suggest in the future just pushing to master branch in git instead of creating a topic branch. title: Ticket #4913: submit files should support if/else and include like config files
description: The submit file parser should support the same improved syntax as config files got in the v8.2 series. if/else and include syntax. We will get the improved behavior by having condor_submit use the config file parser to read in submit files. The config parser will have to be enhanced to support this. In particular it will need to handle the Queue statement, which right now is a syntax error to the config parser. The fix will be that lines that have no '=' or multiple words before the '=' will be handed to a callback supplied by condor_submit for parsing. this callback will parse queue statements and return -1 for all others, which will then be treated as errors. The other thing that the config parser cannot currently parse is +Attribute=value -Attribute=value These will be re-written in the config parser to and then parsed as MY.Attribute=value MY.Attribute= Then condor_submit will iterate the submit hashtable at Queue time and shove all attributes that begin with "MY." into the job ad. One advantage of this design is that these attributes will now also be available for substitution in $(MY.Attribute). One other advantage to having condor_submit use the config file parser is that it opens up the possibility of having a param table and metaknobs in submit files. The work to fully enable these two features will not be done until a use case for them is found.

title: Ticket #4440: cream_gahp fails at startup due to lt_dlopen() search path
description: When the Globus threading model is set to something other than "none", Globus uses lt_dlopen() to load a Globus library with relevant functions. In the cream_gahp, we set the threading model to "pthread" because we use Globus and OpenSSL functions in multiple threads and need the proper synchronization. Unlike the system dlopen() on linux, lt_dlopen() ignores the program's RPATH when searching the requested library. Therefore, it won't find the Globus libraries that we include with the UW release of HTCondor. Thus, the cream_gahp fails at startup with an error like this: dlopen libglobus_thread_pthread: file not found There are a couple workarounds for this problem: Install native Globus packages. lt_dlopen() will then find the library in the standard system location. Set LD_LIBRARY_PATH to "$ORIGIN/../lib/condor". One way to fix this is to use dlopen() to load the library at the top of main(), before Globus's call to lt_dlopen(). Setting LD_LIBRARY_PATH in the environment at the top of main() does not work. The ltdl library is probably checking the environment variables when it's loaded, before main().

description: When the glexec linger option is turned on, condor_starter hangs in feed_wrapper() while waiting for the pipe to the wrapper to close. When we observed this, the wrapper was no longer running. The user job was running, indicating that the wrapper must have successfully exec'ed the job. title: Ticket #5528: Document docker universe volume mounts
description: The docker universe volume mount code is documented in ticket #5308 but never made it into the manual.
remarks: 2016-Jun-30 13:59:19 by wenger: Greg, do you have any example config and submit files you could send me for this? (Oops -- put this in the wrong ticket first.) 2016-Sep-29 09:49:02 by gthain: Here is an example configuration snippet. This defines two docker volumes, directories from the host (outer) filesystem which we'd like to make visible to the inner docker container, named TMP and DATA. TMP comes from /tmp on the host, and DATA from /home/data. We'll mount DATA read-only within the container. In 8.5, we get the new knob DOCKER_VOLUME_DIR_TMP_MOUNT_IF for conditional mounting of volumes. DOCKER_VOLUMES = DATA TMP DOCKER_VOLUME_DIR_DATA = /home/data:/home/data:ro DOCKER_VOLUME_DIR_TMP = /tmp DOCKER_VOLUME_DIR_TMP_MOUNT_IF = WantTmp =?= true DOCKER_MOUNT_VOLUMES = GTHAIN, DATA 2016-Sep-29 09:50:35 by gthain: Note that this has been in the 8.4 manual for a while.

The new Prios can range from INT_MIX+1 to INT_MAX. Higher priorities run before lower priorities, e.g. 1 then 0 then -1. If job A has {Pre,Post}JobPrio{1,2} defined and job B does not, the code skips the comparison. Order of comparison: PreJobPrio1, PreJobPrio2, JobPrio, PostJobPrio1, PostJobPrio2 2011-Mar-31 15:54:08 by psilord: Pardon me if I am brash, but that's a crappy interface. Why not make JobPrio an array of integers and then stable sort them in a particular order on the columns going left to right, filling in anything you don't know about with zero when there is a length mismatch job1: JobPrio = 1, 0 job2: JobPrio = 2 job3: JobPrio = 1, 3 Now, the jobs sort left to right in descending order (with canonnicalized job prio arrays]: job2 [2 0] job3 [1 3] job1 [1 0] This is sufficient to produce any fine grained ordering you want with macro level behavior depending on how many columns you put into the ordering. Likely, we use a crappy strtol on the JobPrio attribute for versions of Condor which don't have this feature. This means that if you downgrade a pool with array based JobPrios, then it'll convert the first number upto the , and the jobprio and functions like how it is supposed to.

title: Ticket #3106: Rotation of shared daemon log can result in writing to old file
description: With the change to keep the daemon log file open across multiple calls to dprintf(), when multiple processes are writing to the same logfile, both processes can end up rotating the log. Afterwards, one of the processes will continue writing to a rotated file. The rotated files will not grow beyond the maximum log size. We observed an example of this with the collector log of the batlab central manager. The collector was writing to CollectorLog.old, and CollectorLog contained 4 lines from the time CollectorLog.old was rotated. We believe the collector and a child it spawned to answer a query rotated the log, parent first and child second. The child wrote 3 lines to the new file and exited. The parent continued to write to the file rotated by the child. This is undesirable, as the latest log entries are written to an old file, where they can be easily missed by an admin. This will also affect the schedd, shadow, and gridmanager, all of which can have multiple processes writing to the same logfile.
remarks: 2012-Jul-03 16:41:23 by bbockelm: My $0.02: The "most generic, completely race-free solution" requires nasty locking, using syslog (yay!), or basically re-implementing syslog inside the condor_master. The "cheapest" solution I can think of is OS-specific: use inotify and a watch fd to determine when a logfile rotates. The "very close to race free, but expensive in syscalls" way to do this is to poll the watch fd prior to every line of logging. The "quicker, but a bit racy" way is to have DaemonCore select loop poll the watch fd for you. Regardless, you'd want to still have a timer that manually checks the status of the log periodically, as there are some weirdo corner cases in inotify. 2012-Jul-10 13:47:19 by jfrey: Here's a change that should make this situation much rarer: When a daemon decides that it's time to rotate the log, it first closes the fd and stats the log file by filename. If that indicates that the file needs to be rotated, then the daemon performs the rotation. In either case, it then reopens the file. If there's a lock file configured for the log, it should be locked during this entire sequence of events. When there isn't a lock file, there's still a race condition between two processes statting the file and renaming it. But it's a very narrow window of time. 2012-Jul-10 14:04:36 by jfrey: TJ suggests having a single daemon log rotation lock file used by all daemons when doing log rotation. This guarantees all log rotations are done atomically. 2014-Sep-03 14:14:15 by tannenba: Abandoning this ticket, as this is no longer an issue. The log file of a shared daemon log (by default, the shadow and gridmanager) uses a lock file when rotating the log to prevent problems, as per Jaime's suggestion above. Unfortunately, when a lock file is specified (eg SHADOW_LOCK) it looks like the log file is still continuously opened/closed upon every call to dprintf, although flock() is only called when the file is rotated. But improving this is the subject of a different ticket. 2014-Sep-05 14:02:58 by jfrey: This is still a problem. Here is a new proposed fix (different than the one made before), that addresses the case where a daemon forks off a short-lived helper process (e.g. the collector or schedd creating a child process to handle a client query). In the child process, the dprintf() code is instructed to never rotate the debug log and to close the log file after every write (like the shadow and gridmanager do). With this change, the log can grow beyond the maximum size when a child writes to it, before being rotated by the main daemon. But if child processes are relatively short lived, then the excess size will be limited. 2014-Sep-05 14:05:07 by jfrey: DaemonCore::Create_Thread() and the ForkWork class are the two primary places where the altered dprintf() behavior in child processes would be triggered. 2014-Oct-06 14:01:34 by johnkn: CODE REVIEW: patch looks good.

description: The changes documented below involve versions of Condor that were never released. Customers do not need to worry about them. An incorrect rebase of V7_4-branch caused it to be updated to the head of the master. The following command was likely responsible: # bad command git rebase origin V7_4-branch # what was intended git rebase origin/V7_4-branch The sha1 of V7_4-branch before the bad rebase was c49eb913f7c8aee2b9fb97bd63655806ae759c80. The sha1 of V7_4-branch after the bad rebase was 80fc0a87a790657756aed97dd3d4bdc852e50081, which was incorrectly believed to be a bad merge into V7_4-branch. In #1084, 80fc0a back to but not including 584e2bb18f4e038066e44b53cddd9945e0b9dbbb was surgically removed, but this still left a bunch of undesired things from the master branch in V7_4-branch. The bad rebase has been undone, but it has ramifications for anyone working with our git repository. All developers will need to check to make sure they don't have the bad rebase lurking in their repositories. If you haven't done a "git pull" or fetch since December 20th, you're probably okay, but check anyway. To check, on any local branch you have that is based on V7_4-branch, do the following, repleacing V7_4-branch with your local branch name. Check if you have the bad rebase on the branch: git rev-list V7_4-branch | grep c36ba64711f227570c5d5d06924a558bed85e2af Check the output and return code ("echo $?") of the previous command: If there is no output and a non-zero return code, all is well. This branch is safe. Go back to the start and repeat for other branches based on V7_4-branch. If you're out of branches, you're done! If the return code is 0 and the output is "c36ba64711f227570c5d5d06924a558bed85e2af", then you have the bad rebase. If this is the case, you must destroy and recreate the branch, otherwise you could reinfect the central repository. Continue: You'll need to delete your infected V7_4-branch and recreate it. Do you have committed changes to V7_4-branch that you haven't pushed? No un-pushed changes: Just run the following to delete and recreate the local branch: git checkout master git branch -D V7_4-branch git branch V7_4-branch origin/V7_4-branch Un-pushed changes: You will want to store your good changes away and reapply them. Be careful to not accidentally drag in the bad merge! You can not use git stash for this, as git stash will just stash away the bad merge. You can do this by hand, or you can use "git format-patch" and "git am" to store them away and re-apply them. Use "gitk" or similar to find the ranges of SHAs that contain your changes. Be sure to not include c36ba64711f227570c5d5d06924a558bed85e2af in the range! If you have multiple ranges, simply call "git format-patch" repeatedly, appending to the same file. Once you have your ranges, use the following, or something similar: git format-patch --stdout EARLIEST_GOOD_SHA1..CURRENT_GOOD_SHA1 > v7.4-rescue git checkout master git branch -D V7_4-branch git branch V7_4-branch origin/V7_4-branch git checkout V7_4-branch git am v7.4-rescue How it was fixed # Save good work on V7_4-branch. git format-patch --stdout 584e2bb18f4e038066e44b53cddd9945e0b9dbbb..V7_4-branch > ~/v7.4-rescue # Back V7_4-branch to the commit immediately before the bad rebase happened. git reset --hard c49eb913f7c8aee2b9fb97bd63655806ae759c80 # Reapply the good work git am v7.4-rescue # Patches 1, 6, and 7 did not apply cleanly so I had to edit the files # manually, add them to the index, and run git am --resolved # Delete upstream version git push origin :V7_4-branch # Push corrected version git push origin +V7_4-branch # Merge to the master # Since all of the V7_4 work was already merged to the master # and since there were some conflicts in how the patches were # reapplied to V7_4, I used the 'ours' merge strategy # so the master is untouched by the merge git checkout master git merge -s ours V7_4-branch

title: Ticket #7846: Allow singularity to ignore invalid bind mounts
description: When the OSG glidein sets up singularity, it unconditionally tries to bind mount many directories which may not exist in the user-provided image. The default is like this to prevent the host networking from applying firewalls to the VM guests. The lark use case is different - we want the packets to pass through the firewall for network accounting and/or any firewalling the sysadmin wants to perform on the job. title: Ticket #2652: procd pegging cpu when running a lot of short lived jobs.
description: When submitting a series of sleep 1 jobs, in recent editions of condor (compiled w/libcgroups on F15) the procd can peg the cpu. It appears from strace that it's checking the full file list for a proc entry over and over.
remarks: 2011-Dec-08 09:34:54 by gthain: Are you sure this is a regression? I see the procd take about 20 cpus seconds on my rhel5 machine when running 100 1 seconds jobs, with or without cgroup support compiled in. 2011-Dec-08 09:39:53 by tstclair: Yes it's a regression I do not see this on 7.6 series. 2011-Dec-09 10:18:31 by gthain: So, the problem isn't with cgroups, it's with the PSS code. Can you try running a build with HAVE_PSS undefined? What's happening is that everytime we snapshot, we parse all the /proc/*/smaps files, which are large. We read this file for every process because the same pass is then used to discover the parent child relationships. So, we end up parsing /proc/pid/smaps for every process on the system, which is slow. Most of the smaps files are in the area of 50kbytes, so it adds up. I don't see an easy way around this, without rejiggering most of procapi. 2011-Dec-13 15:28:11 by gthain: After discussion in fw, the decision is to rewrite procapi to make two passes through the entire process table. This will not be done for 7.7
derived_tickets: #2710 Need a way to turn off pss grepping through /proc/pid/smaps

title: Ticket #948: DaemonCore::Reset_Timer code needs inspection
description: DaemonCore::Reset_Timer calls directly to TimerManager::ResetTimer. Documentation says ResetTimer returns 0 on success and -1 if the timer is unknown. The current code for ResetTimer returns -1 properly and 0 on success OR if the timer is registered with a timeslice in which case the reset attempt is ignored. NOTE: This special casing for timeslice suggests that time slices are implemented too low in the TimerManager. A time slice should be layered, and this test mostly serves as one way to protect against improper use of a time slice. A better approach would be a first class timer id and time slice, to prevent misuse of a time sliced timer id as if it were a regular timer id. The return value of Reset_Timer is ignored almost everywhere (157 total uses), exceptions: gahp-client.cpp - returned from reset_user_timer, mixed with TRUE/FALSE, and then ignored vm_gahp_request.cpp - returned from resetUserTimer, mixed with TRUE/FALSE, and then ignored daemon_core.cpp - checked for failure (ASSERT) in HandleChildAliveCommand when resetting timer for HungChildTimeout cronjob.cpp - returned from KillTimer and then ignored admin_event.cpp - used to set m_timeridDoShutdown, but buggy and not worth saving, e.g. return value is conflated with Register_Timer return value note: also in eventd[.V2], which doesn't count and is used improperly HandleChildAliveCommand is the only proper use of a Reset_Timer return value. The check serves as a sanity check against DaemonCore's implementation of Timers. It checks to see if it has registered a timer that DaemonCore still knows about it, e.g. DC has not lost it and no one has cancelled it without resetting the recorded timer id. The uses of Reset_Timer's return value should be reduced to only HandleChildAliveCommand's, and then the decision should be made as to if the return value should be removed entirely. NOTE: CancelTimer's return value is also suspect. It returns if the timer was found or not. CancelAllTimers returns nothing.
creator: matt

title: Ticket #7684: Easy way to get platform-specific config via client tool
description: The most recent idea batted around in #7669 was something like condor_config_val -write:platform. ToddM has some different ideas, maybe he can add them here. Let's agree on something and do it. My original proposal was to split the platform-specific /etc/condor_config into two pieces: the platform-specific piece that should probably only contain information about paths on disk, and everything else (e.g., 'use security: host_based'). Then it would be easy to copy the bits you need just to know where the binaries and libraries are, and ignored everything else. Josh pointed out that the number of different places that Metronome looks for condor_config.example -- which is how it solves this problem -- is kind of absurd, and so maybe it's better to let the installer solve the problem of getting HTCondor's executable into the PATH and instead supply an executable that just spits the platform-specific bits out when run. The key idea here is that executable != binary, or at least doesn't have to, which means we don't have to decide anything at compile time or at run-time; the platform-specific installer can write the platform-specific script at package or install -time, whichever is easier.
creator: karpel

title: Ticket #1300: JobRouter (quill) fails on platforms with unsigned char
description: The quill classad log parser fails on platforms with unsigned char. The problem is that the comparison to EOF was never true, because EOF is -1 but the value returned from fgetc() was being stored in a char buffer. This was causing JobRouter to hang and/or crash on ppc64_sles9, ppc_aix_5.2, and ps3_ydl_5.0. I am fixing this in 7.5 because I am not aware of a pressing need for it in 7.4.

title: Ticket #765: Scheduler universe jobs should not trigger a matchmaking cycle
description: Our visitor Hailong noticed a problem. I had a memory of it being fixed a while ago, but at least in 7.2.4 it's not fixed. I couldn't find anything in the release notes for 7.3.x that suggest it has been fixed. The problem is that when he submits a DAGMan job, the first job has to wait five minutes to run after DAGMan submits it. My understanding of the problem is that the schedd tells the negotiator to run a matchmaking cycle when the scheduler universe job for DAGMan is submitted. When DAGMan submits the next job in less than 20 seconds, the negotiator ignores the request to run a matchmaking cycles, and we have to wait five minutes for the next matchmaking cycle. I know that we can change the matchmaking cycle to be shorter (and that's what we've done for now), but it seems that two things should be true: Submitting a scheduler universe job shouldn't tell the negotiator to start a matchmaking cycle. That would avoid the whole problem. If something requests a matchmaking cycle, but we haven't exceeded NEGOTIATOR_CYCLE_DELAY, we should automatically start another matchmaking cycle when the NEGOTIATOR_CYCLE_DELAY has been exceeded. That is, we should delay a matchmaking cycle but not ignore it.
remarks: 2009-Oct-02 11:47:07 by tannenba: In testing, this looks to be much better in 7.3.2 - the dagman job went into the queue and a reschedule happened, but when dagman submitted the first job another negotiation cycle happened after 20 seconds. :) So I am resolving this ticket. However, thinking about this inspired me to create enhance ticket #810 that details how this all should really work.

title: Ticket #1750: disconnect during file transfer causes starter to abort
description: The changes in commit b3ef6289 [18897] #1587 to improve handling of file transfer failures have somewhat broken disconnected shadow/starter handling. The changes were intended to improve handling of the case where file transfer fails and wants to put the job on hold. However, there are other types of failures (such as network disconnect) where file transfer can fail without trying to put the job on hold. These cases used to be handled by the shadow/starter disconnect behavior. Now, the starter just blows up in an assert: 11/01 14:58:57 Sandbox transfer failed. 11/01 14:58:57 ERROR "Assertion ERROR on (m_ft_info.hold_code != 0)" at line 435 in file jic_shadow.cpp I see the following responsible code: if(!m_ft_info.success) { ASSERT(m_ft_info.hold_code != 0); } One way to test this code path is to SIGSTOP the shadow while the job is running. Then when the job finishes and the starter is blocked waiting for a response to its file transfer request, do condor_off -schedd. The desired behavior is that the starter sees the connection to the shadow go bad and enters disconnected mode. Turning the schedd back on should cause a new shadow to connect to the starter and successfully finish the file transfer. I have verified that this worked in 7.4.2.
remarks: 2010-Nov-02 11:34:45 by psilord: I reviewed it. I think some changes could happen to the return value of transferOutput() to make things a bit more precise with what kind of failures could have happened, but the change as it stands is good enough and passes review.

title: Ticket #3278: Condor_rm of recovered DAG sometimes leaves node jobs running
description: I just noticed this in testing with 7.8.4, but it goes back a long way before that. I know what's going on -- at some point we changed from having DAGMan explicitly condor_rm each child job to having it do a big condor_rm with a constraint of the parent DAGMan's CondorID. But you can sometimes end up with a parent DAGMan that has a different CondorID, and then a condor_rm of the DAGMan job doesn't affect the node jobs... Here's how to reproduce this (when running a personal Condor): submit a DAG do a condor_restart clear out the lock file re-submit the .condor.sub file condor_rm the resulting DAGMan job
remarks: 2013-Apr-10 16:47:35 by wenger: I was just thinking about this (and #463), and I was thinking that one solution would be to have DAGMan not actually exit until it sees the removed events for all of its jobs (we'd have to create a new "remove mode" or something where it would watch for events but not submit any new jobs or start any scripts -- I guess that would be kind of like halt mode, although halt mode will run POST scripts, which we wouldn't want in remove mode). Anyhow, after some (configurable) amount of time, if DAGMan hadn't seen all the right remove events, it could fall back on removing the jobs individually, as it used to do. (And maybe it could do that immediately if the first condor_rm fails.) If the "individual job" condor_rms fail, it might make sense to re-try them. And, obviously, at some point DAGMan should just exit, but it should log some error message if it doesn't think all of the jobs have been removed successfully. 2013-Jun-03 16:41:29 by wenger: A note as per discussion in today's flightworthy meeting: TJ says that it looks like condor_rm returns 0 if it removes any jobs (even if some removes fail). So DAGMan can't really assume that condor_rm returning 0 means that all of the jobs were removed...

title: Ticket #2890: BOSCO shell independent setup
description: After usability test by Alain became evident that users don't know which shell they use and need a single setup file. Users will type source ~/bosco/boscosetup This will use 3 files: boscosetup - shell independent script shellselector - detects the shell used and selects the appropriate setup file shell dependent setup file (sh/csh version provided) boscosetup will be something like: # shell independent setup # replace the installation directory (default is $HOME/bosco) source $HOME/bosco/bosco.`$HOME/bosco/shellselector -q` shellselector is: #!/bin/bash # shellselector by Marco Mambelli, marco@hep.uchciago.edu # Expects the parent process to be a shell and provides its name # Used to select a shell dependent setup from an insependent one: # source setup.`./shellselector -q` # Without "-q" it prints informations about the shell detected # # Test show that $SHELL is unreliable # Current shell is preferrable to the login shell # if [ "X${1}X" == "X-hX" ] then echo "$0 [-h|-q]" echo " detects a shell and shell family" echo " -h prints this help message" echo " -q quiet, prints only the shell family (sh or csh)" exit fi MYSHELL="`ps -o ppid= -p $$ | xargs ps -o comm= -p `" # change the case statement below to have different setup files for ksh or zsh case "$MYSHELL" in bash|sh) SHELLFAM="sh";; ksh) SHELLFAM="sh";; zsh) SHELLFAM="sh";; tcsh|csh) SHELLFAM="csh";; *) if [ "X${1}X" == "X-qX" ] then SHELLFAM="sh" else echo "Unknown shell $MYSHELL"; exit 1 fi;; esac if [ "X${1}X" == "X-qX" ] then echo "$SHELLFAM" else echo "Your shell is $MYSHELL, of type $SHELLFAM" fi bosco.sh and bosco.csh are generated at the installation This code has been tested. title: Ticket #4417: Condor does not support limiting swap space via cgroups
description: Many machines in CHTC are configure with much more physical memory than swap space. For example, one generation of 24 core machines has 96 Gb physical memory and 24 Gb of swap. When cgroups were enabled on these machine, several jobs ran that required 8 Gb total virtual address space, that specified the default of 1Gb Request_Memory. The cgroup-enabled starter correctly limited these jobs to 1 gb ram, and pushed the remaining 7 Gb to swap. This machine then quickly ran out of swap space (according to "free"), even though it had 16 Gb of free ram. In this state, odd things started happening. ps would hang hard, the procd would frequently lock up, and the machine was often unresponsive, even though there was significant free memory.
remarks: 2018-Aug-24 13:16:55 by tannenba: The version history blurb for this ticket sums it up: "If cgroups are enabled on Linux, the amount of swap space used by a job is now limited to the VirtualMemory (slot attriburte) size of the slot it is running on."

title: Ticket #4944: New $macro expansion functions for submit
description: The config/submit macro expander should be extended with functions to allow expanding only parts of a filename expanding an integer with a specified field with (optionally with leading zeros) expanding a substring evaluating integer/real expression at expansion time expanding a single item from a list new functions $CHOICE(index,listname) or $CHOICE(index,item1,item2,...) $SUBSTR(name,start) or $SUBSTR(name,start,length) $INT(name) or $INT(name,format-specifier) $REAL(name) or $REAL(name,format-specifier) $F[pdnxq](name) or $BASENAME(name) or $DIRNAME(name) $CHOICE(index,listname) Expands to the N'th item in $(listname). if $(index) is found, it is expanded and evaluated to determine N, otherwise "index" is evaluated to determine N. $CHOICE(index,item1,item2,...) Expands the the N+1'th item in the $CHOICE argument list. if $(index) is found, it is expanded and evaluated to determine N, otherwise "index" is evaluated to determine N. $SUBSTR(name,start[,length]) Expands $(name) and returns length characters from the string starting with start. if $(start) is found, it is expanded and evaluated otherwise "start" is evaluated. if $(length) is found it is expanded and evaluated, otherwise "length" is evaluated. If start < 0, then start is treated as and offset from the end of the string rather than from the beginning. if length is not specified, the everything from start to the end of the string is returned. if length < 0, then it is added to the actual string length to the the number of characters returned, so $SUBSTR(name,0,-2) returns all but the last 2 characters of the expanded name. $INT(name[,print-specifier]) If $(name) exists, it is expanded and evaluated, otherwise "name" is evaluated. The resulting long long value is converted to a string using the printf format specifier. If no format is specified "%d" is used. $REAL(name[,print-specifier]) If $(name) exists, it is expanded and evaluated, otherwise "name" is evaluated. The resulting double value is converted to a string using the printf format specifier. If no format is specified "%.16G" is used. ".0" is appended if the resulting string has no "." $F[pdnxq](name) $(name) is expanded, then parsed as a filename and parts are returned based on the characters specified after $F. $BASENAME is the same as $Fnx. $DIRNAME is the same is $Fp. But $Fp is more expressive because the letters can be combined in arbitrary ways. p - print the entire directory portion if any. with trailing / d - print the last segment of the directory if any, with trailing / n - print the filename without extension x - print the file extension including leading . q - print double quotes around the entire output.

title: Ticket #6703: Use JobPrio to prioritize scheduler universe jobs
description: We currently have no way to establish priorities between different scheduler universe jobs. If a user submits 5 different scheduler universe jobs at the same time, but MAX_RUNNING_SCHEDULER_JOBS_PER_OWNER is set to 3, there is no way for that user to prioritize which jobs run first. That user could use condor_qedit or condor_prio to set JobPrio on these jobs, but scheduler universe jobs are run directly from the schedd, which does not pay attention to the JobPrio attribute. To enable scheduler universe job prioritization, we'll need to do at least the following: Change the way schedd handles scheduler universe jobs, so it runs them in priority order, not in random order Update the schedd to write an event to the user log every time the JobPrio of a schedule universe job is changed Update DAGMan to read in these "priority changed" events, and update the priorities of any remaining jobs accordingly Update DAGMan to use the JobPrio of its condor_dagman parent job as another factor for internal node priority A design document is available here: https://docs.google.com/document/d/1s82rFMOcY-WwrSfM5qN9qMD_V7AaBtVse8KPcbw8Ud0
remarks: 2018-Jun-27 14:48:36 by coatsworth: I'm chopping anything DAGMan-related out of here, we'll deal with that in a future ticket. There is plenty to worry about here just with the schedd and scheduler universe job priority.

title: Ticket #6353: Remove signal sent to shadow can cause wrong job to be removed
description: When a running job is removed, the schedd sends a signal (SIGUSR1) to the shadow. The shadow cleans up and exits with status 102, which means the job should be removed (if not already held). There's a race condition with the shadow connecting to the schedd after job completion to fetch a new job (recycling the shadow). The schedd can send the signal before the recycling (intended for the job the shadow has finished), and the shadow not process the signal until after the recycling. This will cause the shadow to abort the newly-fetched job, causing the job to be removed from the queue inappropriately. A simple fix for this problem is for the schedd to mark the shadow as ineligible for recycling when it's about to send this signal for job removal.
remarks: 2017-Jul-20 13:48:58 by jfrey: Some notes about the current patch: I considered moving when shadow_rec::preempted is set to true to where the schedd is about to send the signal (instead of after the signal is successfully sent). As this is the stable series, I was wary of unintentional side effects, especially if the signal delivery fails (possible if it's sent via CEDAR TCP). But if that fails, we probably have other problems. To play it safe, I added a new flag in shadow_rec instead. There's still a race condition for suspend and continue, where a signal intended for a shadow's old job is processed after it fetches a new job. Disabling recycling any time a suspend/continue is issued seemed a little harsh, and the consequences of a bad race are less severe. Still, we should think about a better solution. 2017-Jul-31 15:00:27 by gthain: CODE REVIEW Looks good, but let's keep thinking about suspend/resume.

title: Ticket #2310: WHEN_TO_TRANSFER_OUTPUT=NEVER
description: Based on Ian Chesal's message https://lists.cs.wisc.edu/archive/condor-devel/2011-July/msg00011.shtml Proposal: Add NEVER as a valid option for WHEN_TO_TRANSFER_OUTPUT. When NEVER, no output files are transferred back ever. Useful if the job is a wrapper that handles input and output itself. For example, a job might pull a workload from a database or web service and write results back there. Any files created might be temporary. You can put them in a subdirectory, but that adds needless complication. If also returns standard output and error, which may also be unwanted. Ian specifically notes that he wants standard output and error on the execute note for debugging, but no to be returned, so setting them to NULL won't work. Note: If you want standard output and error, but not any other files, you can do so with +TransferOutput="" . It should work with transfer_output_files=, but doesn't (#2311)

title: Ticket #5085: Need std::string Sinful::human_friendly() const
description: There should be a function, perhaps part of class Sinful, that takes a Sinful and returns something "human friendly," with a particular eye toward terseness. Sacrifices can be made for the representation; it will lose information and it won't be parseable. It is not appropriate for log messages where important information for debugging may be lost. This is just for the convenience of a quick scan by users. knoeller is implementing a simple version for condor_q; it will just replace everything after the question mark with "...". We at least want to do things like ignoring the primary address/port in favor what we find in addrs if addrs is present. I suggest eliminating the <angle brackets>, as the result isn't really a Sinful. This is for things like condor_q, whose default output used to start with nice short things like -- Submitter: foo.example.com : <192.168.0.55:35706> : foo.example.com but now can look like (in a fairly complex but not extreme case) -- Submitter: foo.example.com : <192.168.0.55:35706?addrs=192.168.0.55:35706+[fe80::abcd:1234:0001:1010]:35706&sock=collector&PrivAddr=%3c10.0.0.1:35706%3e&PrivNet=ExampleLand> : foo.example.com and I propose to turn that into something like -- Submitter: foo.example.com : [fe80::abcd:1234:0001:1010]:35706 : foo.example.com

title: Ticket #7057: Improve the "process all files in a directory" use case
description: It is surprisingly hard to process all the files in a single directory. For example, see https://agenda.hep.wisc.edu/event/1325/session/3/contribution/40/material/slides/0.pptx This gets effectively impossible once one needs to start escaping the contents of the job Arguments and TransferInput; in TJ's example, it was ultimately impossible to do and these had to be re-parsed out of the ClassAd at runtime. We should: Provide an alternate mechanism for providing a list of arguments. Could even be a JSON-formatted structure in the submit file. Provide a mechanism for providing a list of files to transfer where filenames can be any arbitrary, valid platform filename. Both could most likely non-default or something optimized for integration with the Python bindings. The goal is that we get to the point where we can process arbitrary directories of files "without any tricks".

title: Ticket #1880: More flexible actions as the result of job state changes
description: Incorporating part of #1490, because I want to be able to resolve that ticket now that code is in place to deal with the issue (condor_hold/condor_rm of DAGs) that's causing problems for LIGO. The stuff below relates to a more general capability to take action as the result of job state changes. Pete and I just met and came up with a more general way of dealing with this: we'd have a bunch of "job state transition actions" (e.g., auto_action_remove, auto_action_hold, auto_action_checkpoint, etc.). Probably initially we'd just implement auto_action_remove to deal with LIGO's DAG issue. This would be an expression in a job's submit file that would act on other jobs when the first job is removed. The one for DAGMan would be something like this: auto_action_remove = target.DAGManJobId == my.ClusterId eventually this could be extended to something like: auto_action_remove = if (expression) job_hold(constraint) so that removing one job could do something to other jobs besides removing them. The auto_action_remove should be done when a job is removed via condor_rm (but not condor_rm -f), periodic_remove, on_exit_remove, etc. One important consideration is that the auto_action_remove processing must not start until the originally-removed job is in the X state, so that we don't get into cycles if job A's auto_action_remove removes job B, and job B's auto_action_remove removes job A.
creator: wenger

title: Ticket #1183: Comments in classad regexes aren't real useful; fix docs.
description: Our documentation for the regexp classad functions says: X or x Ignore both white space and comments within the pattern. A comment is defined by starting with the pound sign (#) character, and continuing until the newline character. However, you can't practically get a newline into a classad value in Condor. So the comments are useless. We can't simply omit the documentation, since users need to know that they need to escape #.
