title: Ticket #3188: Extract information from userlog with condor_history
description: CMS needs a way to efficiently monitor the status of the jobs they submit to Condor. They have a system in place that calls condor_q on a frequent basis + condor_history when the job finishes. While this works, it puts a very high load on the system. So, the proposal is to have them parse the userlog, instead. However, they want to preserve the condor_q interface, in order to minimize code changes in their stack. The proposal is to extend condor_q to be able to parse the userlog. The proposed syntax is {code}condor_q -userlog <fname> ...{endcode} condor_history extended to be able to parse the userlog instead of the history file. syntax is condor_history -userlog <fname> ... i.e. mimicking the existing -jobads syntax.
remarks: 2012-Aug-09 16:00:31 by sfiligoi: I will have a pre-release for CMS use soon; we really need it ASAP. Please comment ASAP is the proposed command line syntax is (not) acceptable, since changing that after CMS starts to use it would be a significant hassle. 2012-Aug-11 05:59:36 by matt: Igor, what information are they after (what queries are run, what are the call semantics)? It may be a better change to modify condor_wait. 2012-Aug-11 12:04:57 by sfiligoi: I need the attributes of the job. In all states, not just when they are completed. It is used for providing monitoring info to users. Typical (simplified) use would be: codor_q -userlog a.log -xml -format '%i.' ClusterId -format '%i ' ProcId -format '%i ' JobStatus -format '%s\n' JOB_Gatekeeper i.e. where are/were my jobs running? Plus, we have a working system that uses condor_q, and would like to preserve it with minimal changes. PS: Each userlog contains pretty much only the information we need. In practice: -userlog /basepath/datasetXYZ/condor.log replaces the current -constraint 'Dataset=="datasetXYZ"' 2012-Aug-13 09:13:21 by tstclair: It seem much more like you want feed forward information, for something like this why not hook into the plugin facility, and you could tailor that way. Any time you hit condor_q (doesn't matter what) you impact performance directly, but in the plugin you could feed forward to some central loc to access this information, much akin to cumin. 2012-Aug-13 10:53:25 by sfiligoi: That's certainly an option, but it is an orthogonal one, in my opinion. Forwarding the info to a (remote) database just moves the problem from the schedd to the database itself. Sure, it may be more scalable, but it is still a single/central service. Moreover, it is yet another service to run... not really thrilled at the idea. Others may of course like it. On the other hand, the userlog is already there... so I am proposing a tool to parse it to get the final classad out; and condor_q seems the best place for it. 2012-Aug-14 05:54:09 by matt: Igor, what is consuming this information? -jobads and -machineads are arguably hacks (currently labeled "for debugging") that should be on a condor_analyze tool. condor_q may already have some of the code needed for this, the AttrListPrintMask & others, but it is not the best tool to implement this feature. Instead the code should be reusable, as in fact AttrListPrintMask is. Another new tool, maybe condor_parse_and_format, should appear to handle this feature request. The condor_q tool should remain an interface to the condor_schedd. The new tool could consume non-xml userlogs, xml userlogs, history files, PER_JOB_HISTORY_DIRs, non-xml EVENT_LOGs and xml EVENT_LOGs. Maybe if you even have privileges it could read the job_queue.log directly. 2012-Aug-14 09:42:08 by sfiligoi: The information is consumed indirectly by users; we have essentially a wrapper that calls condor_q, extracts the needed information, formats it and shows it to the users. I don't care if it is called condor_q or something else; condor_q just seemed the natural place. If you guys can agree on a new name FAST, I can move the code there; I just need something done within a week or so. But the command lines arguments and the output should remain similar. As for what kind of files condor_q can read, we pretty much cover all the formats right now, since it uses the ReadUserLog class. As for where it is implemented, I would be happy to move it into the shared library, if this is something people are interested in. Was just trying to minimize changes to the share pieces. 2012-Aug-15 07:22:01 by matt: Any reasonable name will work. I just suggest not condor_q -- not combining this with the existing condor_q tool. Also, the patch looks like it replicates a lot of logic around event types and is specific to the information you are after. It will be difficult to keep the logic up to date with changes elsewhere in the code base. For instance, NumJobStarts, EnteredCurrentStatus, Last*, MyType, and NODE_*, EXECUTABLE_ERROR, POST_SCRIPT_TERMINATED. What about putting this new tool in src/condor_contrib while supporting functionality can be developed to make it simpler to maintain and more general purpose? One thing that could be done to assist is allowing for ad diffs to be output into events. Right now specific attributes can be output, but not to all event types. There is also an internal dirty list maintained on jobs that could be exposed to the user log writer. 2012-Aug-30 17:25:32 by sfiligoi: While for CMS automated purposes condor_history will work just as fine, I think it is a disservice to the Condor community to not implement it in condor_q (also). When analysing a log containing not-yet-finished jobs, condor_history does not really provide any useful info (without using -format or similar), while condor_q does. 2012-Oct-22 14:59:59 by zmiller: Bulk change of target version from v070901 to v070902 using ./ticket-target-mover.

title: Ticket #883: VM universe refactor
description: The following are open items for refactoring in the next series: What: Coding: (In general all the code is subject to review.) 1.) Nix VMPARAM_ and JobVM from classad attributes 2.) Call it vm_description_file or vm_config_file. 2.) Have Condor parse libvirt and vmware description files to get list of files to be transfered. All existing vm-universe bugs #45,#272,#302,#303,#387,#405,#515,#517,#523,#618,#625,#626,#740,#854,#858 3.) test and verify xen_type = vmx..? 4.) remove VM_SCRIPT && XEN_SCRIPT entirely? 5.) title: Ticket #37: Bad schedd cron argument causes schedd to EXCEPT
description: (This replaces Drupal 1440 (backup) 1440 (public)) An invalid schedd cron argument will cause the schedd to EXCEPT. Once in this state, the schedd will EXCEPT every time it starts. This could be used by a user with submit permissions as a denial of service attack. More likely it will just be an annoyance. Say that you have the following as part of a schedd cron job: CronMinute=#/4 The schedd will EXCEPT with: 3/31 13:45:52 (pid:13081) Invalid parameter value ‘#/4’ for CronMinute3/31 13:45:52 (pid:13081) Job 31.0 put on hold: Invalid cron schedule parameters: Invalid parameter value ‘#/4’ for CronMinute 3/31 13:45:52 (pid:13081) Refusing attempt to add ‘HoldReason’ = ‘“Invalid cron schedule parameters: Invalid parameter value ‘#/4’ for CronMinute “’ to record ’31.0’ as it contains a newline, which is not allowed. 3/31 13:45:52 (pid:13081) ERROR “write inside a transaction failed, errno = 25” at line 67 in file log_transaction.C The problem is that the code is trying to set HoldReason to a string including two newlines. ClassAd values can NEVER have newlines (at least in the schedd, because it will corrupt the job queue log file). So the schedd EXCEPTs. The change probably needs to be made around line 12701 in Scheduler::calculateCronTabSchedule in condor_schedd.V6/schedd.C. The lines in question read: MyString reason( “Invalid cron schedule parameters:\n” ); if ( cronTab != NULL ) { reason += cronTab->getError(); } else { reason += error; } There are two errant newlines, one in the initializer for “reason”, as well as one returned at the end of either “error” or “cronTab->getError()”. Both must be removed.

title: Ticket #6735: Delay between execution of jobs on Windows with shared_port enabled
description: On Windows, when using the default configuration of USE_SHARED_PORT = True there appears to be a significant delay between the execution successive of jobs on the same claim/slot. This can add a lot of overhead if the jobs are short-running. The problem appears to happen because the condor_starter takes a long time to exit after the job completes because the SIGTERM from the condor_startd to the condor_starter is not delivered. Behold the following clue from the StartLog: 08/10/18 13:38:36 Send_Signal: Warning: could not send signal 15 (SIGTERM) to pid 6488 (still alive) 08/10/18 13:38:36 slot3: Error sending signal to starter, errno = 42 (Illegal byte sequence) 08/10/18 13:38:36 slot3: State change: Error sending signals to starter 08/10/18 13:38:36 slot3: Changing state and activity: Preempting/Vacating -> Owner/Idle 08/10/18 13:38:36 slot3: State change: IS_OWNER is false 08/10/18 13:38:36 slot3: Changing state: Owner -> Unclaimed 08/10/18 13:38:36 Starter pid 6488 exited with status 0 08/10/18 13:38:36 Warning: Starter pid 6488 is not associated with a claim. A slot may fail to transition to Idle. followed by lots of StartLog messages like the following 08/10/18 13:38:22 slot3: Got activate claim while starter is still alive. 08/10/18 13:38:22 slot3: Telling shadow to try again later. 08/10/18 13:38:23 slot3: Got activate claim while starter is still alive. 08/10/18 13:38:23 slot3: Telling shadow to try again later. ... Immediate Workaround Until this bug is fixed, a suggested configuration based work around is to simply disable the shared_port daemon on Windows. So first stop the HTCondor service on Windows (net stop condor), then append USE_SHARED_PORT=False to the condor_config[.local] file, the restart the HTCondor service (net start condor). Note this workaround means that HTCondor will no longer use a single well-known TCP port, and thus you may need to adjust firewall rules at your site accordingly. Reproduce To reproduce the problem, simply start a personal condor on Windows with shared_port enabled and submit a cluster of short jobs, and time how it takes the cluster of jobs to complete. Now re-run the same test with shared_port disabled, and behold the difference. On my Windows 7 laptop with four cores running HTCondor v8.7.12, the job cluster below took 76 seconds (!!!) to complete with shared_port enabled and just 7 seconds with shared_port disabled : executable = c:\utils\sleep.exe arguments = 0 transfer_executable = false log = fast.log queue 20 Suggested Source Code Patch Suggest that we first get signals working again reliably on Windows, perhaps by always having DaemonCore enable the UDP command port (even if shared_port is enabled) and then having the parent UDP signal directly to the child without going through shared port. Longer term, we should also consider having the condor_starter simply exit when it is done instead of waiting around for the startd to tell it to exit. This would have performance benefits on Linux as well.

title: Ticket #3537: Use euidaccess() instead of manually checking file permissions
description: We provide our own replacement for the access() system call that uses the effective uid instead of the real uid. Our replacement is call access_euid(). One problem it has is that when checking for execute permission on a directory, it only compares the file's owner and group to the effective uid and gid of the process. This ignores ACLs and secondary groups. This can lead to access() calls returning failure when the process does have the requisite permissions. On many (all recent?) versions of linux, there is a function to do this check correctly, called euidaccess(). It behaviors the same as access(), but uses the current process's effective uid and gid.

title: Ticket #5660: Build full manual on Fedora.
description: I just spend twenty minutes discovering that somebody else had committed buggy TeX to the manual. It turned not to be so bad because it had happened to be committed recently, but I was thinking it'd be good software development practice to test building the manual regularly. Unfortunately, not all of execute nodes can do so. While we could build the manual on the submit node, instead, doing so for every build would be unnecessarily taxing; instead, it seems easier to limit the build to some particular platform('s execute nodes). title: Ticket #4972: Support non-periodic application-level checkpoints in vanilla universe
description: As long as we're allowing the user to specify a particular termination condition (signal or exit code) to signal a successful checkpoint, why not transfer the sandbox whenever the application exits that way (if it asks)? This would allow applications which checkpoint based on events (e.g., finished an iteration of the computation) to give themselves the best possible chance of preserving their work (because it would no longer depend on being evicted with a long-enough grace period). Will need to implement throttling, for obvious reasons.
remarks: 2015-Aug-26 13:43:08 by tlmiller: Note that we'd like to make this work without requiring ON_EXIT_OR_EVICT -- if the job is configured without periodic checkpoints, it likely can't take one on eviction, and its state may not be consistent at that time. This may be best-implemented as part of #5238. 2015-Aug-27 16:38:30 by tlmiller: It looks like this should have worked without OR_EVICT the whole time, and now tests indicate that it isn't broken. The thinking about throttling is, for now, that if a user wants to hurt themselves by checkpointing "every five seconds", let them. Being able to detect that they're doing that -- and more generally, monitoring -- is more important. 2019-Sep-18 14:40:07 by tlmiller: Marking a three-year-old "defer" ticket abandoned.

title: Ticket #1789: Contribution for QMF-based managment
description: The proposed contrib module would be for Condor management using a QMF interface. QMF (Qpid Management Framework) is based upon the AMQP messaging implementation in Apache Qpid (https://cwiki.apache.org/qpid/qpid-management-framework.html). We have developed and tested a set of pluggable management resources for Condor on RHEL and Windows (32 and 64-bit). The current functional features include: * start and stop of daemons * job submission and control (submit, set attribute, hold, release, remove) * queries of live and historical job data and output files * get/set of of stats, priorities and limits from the negotiator * collector stats for job counts (running, edle, etc.) * submitters stats * slot statistics and properties Currently, this code base has external dependencies on: * Apache Qpid 0.8 (pre-release) * Boost C++ libraries (1.39 or higher) The initial full implementation of this was provided to Red Hat customers in MRG Grid 1.3. We would like to contribute this code per the guidelines at https://condor-wiki.cs.wisc.edu/index.cgi/wiki?p=MakingContributions.

title: Ticket #1273: User log event timestamps are ambiguous at daylight savings-> std chg
description: Because the user log event timestamps are in local time, without any indication of timezone/DST, the one hour "overlap" when transitioning from daylight savings to standard time in the fall causes ambiguity in interpreting the timestamps. title: Ticket #1766: ARCH=INTEL even when running on x64 versions of Windows
description: Since Condor is running 32 bit binaries on all flavors of Windows, these binaries run in the WOW64 sandbox on x64 flavors of Windows. So when Condor asks for the system architecture, it gets back the arch of the WOW64 sandbox rather than the native arch. The fix is to call GetNativeSystemInfo but this API is not available on Windows 2000, so this problem was complex to fix before we dropped Win2k support. The workaround is simple, just add ARCH=X86_64 to condor_config.local for machines that are running a x64 Windows OS.

title: Ticket #1336: when_to_transfer_output=NEVER
description: A user is using file transfer, and his job creates a number of files during its run. He doesn't want the files back; output and error are plenty. Condor cannot directly help him. The current workarounds are: Create an empty file and ask for it back via transfer_output_files. /dev/null works well for this. Do work in a different directory Have the program itself erase the files. All seem like needless busywork. The obvious solution is to say transfer_output_files= but that is identical to not specifying transfer_output_files at all: all discovered files are retrieved. Proposed: when_to_transfer_output=NEVER (This is distinct from "NONE" and "NEVER" which both mean "User failed to specify: issue an error. If you bodge one of them into your ClassAd, anything that is not ON_EXIT_OR_EVICT is treated as ON_EXIT.)

title: Ticket #5725: Think about DAGMan "authorization" nodes
description: (As per discussion in CHTC team meeting today.) The assumption is that the "regular" node jobs (or at least some of them) in a DAG require a certificate that needs human intervention to be renewed (so the DAG would not try to renew the cert automatically). It sounds like there was some earlier discussion of this (which I don't remember being involved in). Anyhow, I guess this is kind of a special case of the "provisioning node" idea. One question is, if the cert expires when jobs are in the queue, what should happen? This would really depend on the characteristics of the jobs -- e.g., if you can't get your output back once your cert expires, we might as well just remove all of the jobs at that point. Maybe one way this could be addressed is by allowing ABORT_DAG_ON for the authorization nodes -- if you specified ABORT_DAG_ON, the authorization node failing would abort the DAG; otherwise, I guess it would just mean that no new node jobs would be submitted. (Also see #5622: Allow "provisioning" nodes in a DAG?)
remarks: 2016-Jun-14 15:45:26 by wenger: Talked with Miron about this today. There are really two parts: The provisioning node stuff. Having the authorization node write to its log file, and have DAGMan react to those events. The idea for phase 1 is that we'll just have one authorization file for the whole DAG. Before any of the other DAG nodes are submitted, the authorization node has to start, and has to write some kind of "GO" event to its log (probably with chirp). Things to think about: Making sure rescue DAGs work right. Making sure recovery mode works right (if the schedd restarts, for example, pre-restart GO events don't "count") For later phases, we may have other events that the authorization node can write, such as "ABORT" and "HOLD". 2016-Jul-01 12:35:47 by wenger: Working on design document here: https://docs.google.com/document/d/1ZdDbsBZVL6Bbb9ks4y9ZEMFLfKA6qe5ItFT6djY_eoo/edit#heading=h.mx9oufbyi9xl 2016-Jul-08 13:53:56 by wenger: Okay, design doc is ready for review, so I'm going to assign this to Miron. 2016-Dec-15 13:37:58 by wenger: Created V8_5-gittrac_5725-branch for this... 2016-Dec-15 15:50:43 by wenger: A few tricky things: Need to make sure provisioning and authorization nodes interact correctly with halt files. Need to make sure PRE scripts (and POST scripts?) work correctly on provisioning and authorization nodes. Need to make sure provisioning and authorization nodes work correctly with final nodes. What if a provisioning/authorization node exits with status 0 before other nodes are all submitted? It probably should be retried. Should we automatically have retries on provisioning/authorization nodes? (I think once I get the basic provisioning functionality implemented, I should probably temporarily add provisioning nodes to a bunch of the existing tests and make sure they still run correctly...)

Ticket #3976: Add support for measuring the health of a VM host
description: As it stands today, it seems to be very difficult if not impossible to gauge the health of an execute host that claims to support VM universe. There is a separate ticket about proactively trying to test VM guest availability, which is one way to measure health. But this ticket is about reporting on past events as a means of measuring health. Sometimes, when HTCondor asks the hypervisor to start a VM guest, that process fails. In my experience, the most common failure results in a "VMGAHP_ERR_INTERNAL" message and a hold code of 6 (this is with the CHTC kvm offering). I have come to learn that this means that libvirtd is broken and will fail to start any VM guest until manually fixed. When I see this happening, I email htcondor-inf with the hypervisor hostname(s), so that they can be fixed. But that is a very reactive means of keeping a pool healthy. So I propose that HTCondor keep track of recent successful and failed attempts to start VM guests, and that this information be available such that an administrator could get the information and use it to investigate potentially broken machines. In discussions with Jaime, he suggested that TJ's statistics system might work here, but that is an implementation detail.

title: Ticket #6277: Gridmanager submits jobs to wrong remote blahp with --rgahp args
description: When a user is submitting grid universe jobs to multiple remote batch systems via the remote_gahp, jobs can end up going to the wrong system. This happens when the grid_resource line contains command-line arguments for the remote_gahp that precede the user@hostname field. When using grid-type batch to submit jobs to a remote cluster via ssh (aka bosco), the user can supply arguments in the grid_resource line that modify how the remote machine is contacted (which ssh keys to use, where the blahp is installed on the remote machine). These can be provided before or after the user@hostname field. The following are equivalent: grid_resource = batch slurm me@submit.foo.edu --rgahp-key bosco.rsa grid_resource = batch slurm --rgahp-key bosco.rsa me@submit.foo.edu But the gridmanager assumes only the first form will be used. For batch jobs, it only looks at the first three fields of grid_resource to determine which jobs should share the same gahp server. Thus, if the second form is used, jobs destined for different machines can all end up using the same remote blahp, which goes to only one of those machines. The gridmanager should be changed so that the entire contents of grid_resource are used to determine if two jobs have the same destination (and can share a blahp instantiation).
remarks: 2017-Jun-15 10:30:06 by tlmiller: Code Review Code looks fine and will solve the problem. However, it will also create two GAHPs for the given example, which may be suboptimal. Would it make more sense to sort the argument array before stringifying it into the GAHP name? 2017-Jun-16 14:40:31 by jfrey: A naive sort of the fields in GridResource could cause the gridmanager to conclude two values are equivalent when they aren't. For example, a user could store their ssh keys in a file whose name looks matches the hostname of one of their remote cluster submit nodes. And I don't want write an intelligent sort algorithm, which must be kept in sync with changes to the remote_gahp's command line arguments. I believe it's acceptable if when a user submits two jobs with different but equivalent GridResource lines, they get two gahps.

title: Ticket #587: Possibly allow elimination of ProcessId sleep at DAGMan startup
description: I'm not sure if this is a good idea or not, but it's requested in the associated RUST ticket. If we do this, we'd have to decide what's the right thing to do if DAGMan sees a lock file at startup -- probably it needs to just continue, because that would be what we need to do in response to condor_hold/condor_release of DAGMan.
remarks: Hmm, I'm thinking about this in conjucntion with the problem that the job_dagman_retry_recovery test has been failing on MacOS, because the ProcAPI::isAlive() function is returning UNCERTAIN, and we're having DAGMan quit in that case. I'm thinking that a way to deal with this would be to also store the Condor ID of the DAGMan in the lock file, and if isAlive() returns UNCERTAIN, or if you haven't stored a ProcessID object in the lock file for speed, we could check whether our Condor ID is the same as the one in the lock file, and continue if it is (on the grounds that that most likely represents recovery mode). (But we do need to keep the default to be that we quit if the process whose ProcessID is in the lock file is alive, because that dates back to LIGO's problem of the schedd sometimes accidentally restarting an extra DAGMan.) 2015-Aug-05 11:56:34 by wenger: Maybe either just change the Unique PID code to do the minimum (one second) sleep, or else replace the "Unique PID" stuff with the plain old OS PID... 2015-Aug-05 11:58:48 by wenger: Note: Also fix the bug with the re-multiplying of DEFAULT_PRECISION_RANGE if the unique PID stuff gets called more than once. 2015-Aug-05 12:52:40 by wenger: Okay, I'm going to investigate making the sleep shorter for 8.3.8. ToddT says look into changing this to creating a file in /var/lock and then getting a file lock on that file -- the lock will go away when the process does. 2015-Aug-06 14:42:15 by wenger: Notes from Brian Candler: There seems to be legacy magic in there, or hooks to support systems which were planned but never implemented. For example: createProcessId has a loop which waits for the value from generateControlTime to stabilise. However both the Linux and non-Linux versions of generateControlTime do nothing except set ctl_time=0. Similarly, ProcessId::confirm just sets true. This is all something to do with process "birthdays". Perhaps the idea was to run on a system which can tell you when process IDs are being recycled? 2015-Aug-07 10:05:02 by wenger: I'm going to change this ticket to reflect the creation of child ticket #5206.

title: Ticket #7870: Read IDTOKENS files for daemons as root, not condor
description: The files containing daemon credentials are currently expected to be owned by the canonical 'condor' user in /etc/condor. This ticket proposes changing them to be owned by root. One advantage of having them owned by condor is that the admin is probably logged in as the condor user when if running condor_token_create and so it's natural to create a file as that same user. However, in almost all other cases (KERBEROS, GSI, SSL, MUNGE, and even PASSWORD) the daemon credentials are owned by root and not readable by the condor user. For security and consistency I think IDTOKENS should be the same. If the admin is relying on HTCondor's "bootstrap" mode to have daemons auto-generate token requests and then store the tokens, this can be done as root as well, so I don't believe the burden on the administrator is a problem. If there are other pros and cons please add them to this description.

title: Ticket #568: Condor on Windows Vista 7.2.1/7.2.3 is dead after power saving
description: After Vista is woken up from the power saved state Condor 7.2.1 and 7.2.3 are not re-starting correctly. In this spesific case, the configuration file is kept on a network share, which is not accessible imediatly after the machine is woken because the machine's IP is dynamic, and it sometimes takes upwards of 2 minutes to get a new IP. As a temporary solution, placing the configuration on the local disk seems to help the problem. The greater issuue here is that Condor is epecting to be able to have network access imediatly once it is started, which may not always be the case. Making Condor depend on various network service does not seem to aliviate the problem. What Condor really needs is a way to detect if there is network connectivety.

title: Ticket #6332: Help users deal with missing default VPCs/subnet IDs
description: Security groups are VPC-specific; the default stack creates the security group we need (implicitly) in the default VPC. Therefore: Add an option to condor_annex -setup to set the VPC and subnet IDs; check if your account has a default VPC early, so we print a good error message rather than just fail to construct the security group stack; pass the VPC ID through to the security group constructor somehow (use a different template?); pass both options through into the user-specific config file we write; pull them back out again for ODI instances. Also allow the subnet ID to be specified on the command-line (but not the VPC ID, since that entails regenerating the security group).

title: Ticket #138: Reorganize /src/condor_tests
description: /src/condor_tests is a mess. It's almost entirely flat, with a given test having anywhere from 1 to 5+ files. (foo.run, foo.pl, foo.cmd, foo.dag, foo.in, foo.data, etc). It's a mess to wade through, with 1,010 files at the moment. After running tests it's an even bigger mess as many test dump their contents in the same directory. The rest use subdirectories, which helps some, but we're still looking at a directory with 2,937 files and subdirectories after a test run (based on x86 RHAP 5 on master branch on 2009-01-28). As we add tests, it will just get worse. We need to rethink this. A strawman is proposed below, but it's intended as a starting point to find a good plan, not as a solid proposal: Each test gets it's own subdirectory named after itself. Enumerating the tests becomes as simple as enumerating the subdirectories minus a few exceptions (anything beginning with a ., potentially "output"). (Complication: Many tests share files, for example the entire x_* set of files, though there are others.) Output is placed either within a sub-subdirectory (so, src/condor_tests/lib_eventlog_rotation-no_rotations_1/output) or in a shared directory (src/condor_tests/output/lib_eventlog_rotation-no_rotations_1). They have different advantages. As much as possible this functionality should either be in the scripts driving the tests, or in CondorTest.pm. Asking individual tests to sort it out for themselves is a recipe for a mess, and is part of how we ended up here.
remarks: We got here because Derek designed it this way. 2010-Jun-30 15:08:13 by adesmet: This work has been moved into #1124 and particularly #1147. Resolving.

title: Ticket #991: Make condor_shared_port work on windows
description: Summary This is one of the identified flightworthy development tasks for 7.5. People assigned to work on this: Ziliang Guo (doing the work) and Dan Bradley (helping as he can). Under unix, we have a mechanism for passing incoming connections (TCP sockets) from condor_shared_port to other daemons running on the same machine. We need to come up with a similar mechanism that works in Windows. Milestones Dates are not yet filled in, because we need to consider the priority of this relative to other things on Z's plate. See if named pipes can be used in place of the named socket we are using in unix. Ideally, we would like it to provide the following: Ability to transmit LPWSAPROTOCOL_INFO structure produced by WSADuplicateSocket() in condor_shared_port to target daemon. The input to the function that does this is just a TCP socket and a string that identifies who to pass the connection to. I am assuming that the string will be the basename of the named pipe or something like that. ACL that limits who can create named pipes that condor_shared_port will forward to (by default this should be limited to just condor, but would be nice to be able to adjust ACL for broader access so user tools using CCB can receive connections if that is desired) Ability to create named pipe in parent and pass it down to child. Ability to clean up named pipe in parent in case child does not. Ability to create 10s of thousands of named pipes so that 10s of thousands of processes can operate in shared-port mode. Implement functions for windows that are currently only defined when HAVE_SHARED_PORT is defined. May need to change the interfaces a bit depending on how similar the windows case is to the SCM_RIGHTS case. Wisdom Quite a few things were uncovered in the process of implementing shared port on Windows, some related to issues Dan found on the Unix side and some Windows specific. The named pipe abstraction that Condor uses does not appear suitable for anything besides piping standard in/out/err from a process. There appears to be some kind of problem with how the daemon connects and listens to the server side of the named pipe. Further testing will be needed to pin this down. At the same time, the named pipe abstraction is inappropriate for this usage case as it is part of daemonCore and the shared port implementation is also used in the CCB client, which is not a daemon. The generic assign operation in the Sock class did not copy over the peer name from the underlying file descriptor/Berkeley socket on Unix or Windows. This was fixed by Dan in the generic assign function used on Unix. Fortunately everything the generic assign function did was also done by the Windows specific assign, so the Windows specific assign function now calls the generic assign after it is finished with the Windows specific operations. Dprintfs, excepts, and asserts cannot be used in the thread that the Windows implementation of shared port spins off to listen on the named pipe. If this is incorrect, please correct this. However, while testing condor_q with the -debug option, the output from the dprintfs and condor_q's own output seemed to trample over one another and froze condor_q. Errata The code for cleanly shutting down the named pipe listening thread needs some work. Right now it relies on giving a separate function outside the SharedPortEndpoint class access to an event object to signal the destructor that the thread has properly terminated. This is due to a class function running inside that thread and deleting the class instance before the shutdown is complete may cause problems. Better solution is likely to make that separate function a friend of SharedPortEndpoint. There are no dprintfs inside the named pipe listener thread due to dprintf and company being not thread safe. Conditions that produced the problem: dprintfs are uncommented inside SharedPortEndpoint::PipeListenerThread USE_SHARED_PORT = true CCB_ADDRESS = $(COLLECTOR_HOST) Run condor_q -debug after the CCB address is picked up by the schedd The named pipes have default security, meaning anything can connect to it. ACLs have not been created to specify who can and cannot connect. However, as only a single instance of the named pipe server endpoint is permitted with the current design, nothing should be able to masquerade as the shared port server. The named pipe directory is hardcoded in the code due to the param table not being able to support different defaults for different platforms.
remarks: 2010-May-10 16:11:20 by tannenba: > +*: There are no dprintfs inside the named pipe listener thread due to dprintf and company being not thread safe. > + Who said? dprintf() was designed to be thread safe, and last I looked at that code it was thread safe. Note very early on in the dprintf process, the dprintf code grabs a mutex - look for _condor_dprintf_critsec > +*: Security has not been implemented on the named pipes themselves so in theory anything could connect. > + Bummer, must be changed imho. Was there a technical/architecture hurdle in the way? > +*: The named pipe directory is hardcoded in the code due to the param table not being able to support different defaults for different platforms. > Could we do what we do everywhere else, and param() w/ a different default value? 2010-May-10 16:15:14 by danb: We observed a deadlock that appeared to be caused by dprintf in the thread. Removing calls to dprintf made the problem go away. It was fairly repeatable. 2010-May-10 16:32:07 by danb: Regarding security. What Z means is that no ACL has been applied to restrict who can open a named pipe in the namespace used by Condor. This does not mean that the security policy for incoming connections to condor daemons is circumvented. However, other processes on the machine could probably mess with the named sockets created by condor daemons or create their own named sockets and receive connections via shared port. So yeah, it does seem like this should be addressed, but it's not as bad as it might have sounded. 2010-May-10 18:06:48 by ziliang: Incidentally, and I'll need to double check this, my intention when I call CreateNamedPipe was to allow only a single instance. So anyone else trying to create a separate instance of that particular pipe will fail and won't be able to masquerade as the server. 2010-May-10 18:12:08 by ziliang: Incidentally, while the deadlock was highly repeatable, where condor_q ended up deadlocking changed. 2010-Jul-28 15:30:41 by danb: I am closing this ticket. The windows shared port code has been merged in for 7.5.4.

title: Ticket #7489: HTCondor can't annex Spot
description: On January 24, 2020, we received a user report that condor_annex could no longer use Spot instances. After reproducing the initial user report, and having made no changes to the code, we contacted the Head of AWS Research to see what was going on. He put us in contact with the Principal Developer Advocate for EC2 Spot, who was quickly able to tell us: The dev team tracked things down. A change was rolled out that flipped the parameters to UpperCamelCase (i.e. "tagSpecificationSet" to "TagSpecificationSet", "groupSet" to "GroupSet", "blockDeviceMapping" to "BlockDeviceMapping"). We made the obvious changes to the code, confirmed that they solved the problem, and had pre-releases ready for distribution the next day.
remarks: original description: Daniel Corbett wrote on 2020 January 24 to say that he was getting the following error when trying to use condor_annex with Spot Fleet: <?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>\n <Response> <Errors><Error>UnknownParameter <Message>The parameter groupSet is not recognized</Message> </Error></Errors> <RequestID>6e371b3b-bdd9-4df6-a0e1-a9c4b8d57d1e</RequestID> </Response> The problem was trivial to reproduce on our resources, but did not happen as a result of any code changes that we made or configuration changes made by Daniel. 2020-Feb-04 22:41:34 by tlmiller: After a brief phone call, the Principal Developer Advocate for EC2 Spot wrote: The dev team tracked things down. A change was rolled out that flipped the parameters to UpperCamelCase (i.e. "tagSpecificationSet" to "TagSpecificationSet", "groupSet" to "GroupSet", "blockDeviceMapping" to "BlockDeviceMapping"). A quick smoke-tests seems to verify this. Patches forthcoming. 2020-Feb-04 23:27:21 by tlmiller: Patches pushed, under the assumption that the additional testing tomorrow won't find any problems. Should mean that we can make pre-releases available tomorrow. 2020-Feb-05 14:03:58 by tlmiller: Additional testing looks good. 2020-Feb-06 15:39:58 by tlmiller: Because the protocol change was only from a lower to an upper case letter, it may be possible to fix older binaries by editing the string constants in place. The following pair of commands did the trick on a binary built from the top of the 8.9.5 release branch (assuming ec2_gahp is in your PATH): perl -p -i -e 's/groupSet\./GroupSet./' `which ec2_gahp` perl -p -i -e 's/tagSpecificationSet\.1\./TagSpecificationSet.1./' `which ec2_gahp` These commands (or the equivalent invocations of sed, if you don't have perl installed) may work on other version of the ec2_gahp as well; it's not particularly likely that the bytes of those two strings collide with any binary code. However, you should certainly make a back-up copy of the ec2_gahp first. You can check to make sure that only two bytes were change by running hexdump on the ec2_gahp before and after and comparing them: cp `which ec2_gahp` ec2_gahp.backup hexdump `which ec2_gahp` > unmodified.dump perl -p -i -e 's/groupSet\./GroupSet./' `which ec2_gahp` perl -p -i -e 's/tagSpecificationSet\.1\./TagSpecificationSet.1./' `which ec2_gahp` hexdump `which ec2_gahp` > modified.dump diff -u unmodified.dump modified.dump The diff should show only two changed lines. 2020-Apr-10 07:43:03 by tim: Bulk change of target version from v080808 to v080809 using ticket-target-mover.

title: Ticket #7523: Add for_each_with_index() function to ClassAds?
description: TJ may have other good, or better, examples. Motivating example Determining how many of a p-slot's GPUs have been assigned to interactive jobs. The config knobbery to add an attribute to each slot which is true for interactive jobs and to then "roll up" that attribute for the p-slot is straightforward. However, the expression that computes how many slots are both assigned a GPU and are interactive is not simple. (It may become simpler in the future, because we should be able to roll up expressions, e.g., how many interactive GPUs this slot has.) Each component looks something like igv0 = child_gpus[0] * child_interactive[0] which wouldn't be so bad except that indexing off the end of a list is an error, not undefined, so you need to write a list for each possible length: igl2 = { $(igv0), $(igv1) } and choose the correct-length list: ifthenelse( size(child_gpus) == 1, sum(igl1), ifthenelse( size(child_gpus) == 2, sum(igl2), ... up to as many child slots the pslot is willing to make (in this case, limited by the number of GPUs). This, of course, is absurd. Proposal InteractiveGPUs = for_each_with_index( count_if_interactive, child_gpus ) for_each_with_index = ifthenelse( MY.child_interactive[TARGET.index], TARGET.value, 0 ) The function for_each_with_index() takes an attribute reference and a list. For each item in the list, the attribute referenced is evaluated in the context of its own ad (MY) and a context ad (TARGET) which has two attributes: index, which is the position of the item in the list, and value, which is the corresponding value. The result of the evaluation is stored at the corresponding index of the list which is the return value. IIRC, we generally disallow self-referencing attributes, so that shouldn't be a problem. We may also, however, may wish to make it invalid (an error) to call for_each_with_index() from inside an evaluation of for_each_with_index(). For usability reasons, it may be nice to immediately investigate the possibility of allowing the attribute reference to be an expression, with "its own" ad being the ad in which the function call is being made. Further extensions are fairly obvious (and include things like making the evaluation more function-call like by including argument references), but we don't shouldn't let this ticket get bogged down by them. Further discussion, however, may be valuable if simple semantic changes would simplify implementation and/or performance.

title: Ticket #4026: my_popen() doesn't reap child process on failure
description: In normal usage, my_popen() creates a child process and my_pclose() reaps it (by calling waitpid()). Thus, the child process is not seen by daemon-core's reaping code. But if my_popen() creates the child process and fails to exec() the desired program, it returns NULL but doesn't reap the child. The child process is later reaped by daemon-core, which calls the daemon's main reaper, which won't know what to do with the pid. The startd thinks it's a rogue starter and prints a big warning to the log, which can cause needless concern for the admin. When my_popen() is going to return NULL after creating the child process, it should call waitpid() first.
remarks: 2014-Feb-28 11:33:28 by tlmiller: Code Review The first conditional could fire without the child process terminating, and we probably don't want to block if we can avoid it. It wouldn't hurt to kill -9 the child process in the second conditional as well, even though that process is "on its way out the door". The code is otherwise clean, and since we want to make sure the child process is dead if we say it is, kill -9'ing it makes more sense than playing games with timing out in the waitpid() loops.
attachments: popen_reap.patch 764 bytes added by jfrey on 2013-Oct-31 21:19:15 UTC. Fix my_popen() to always reap the child process.

title: Ticket #6918: multicore jobs via python API scheduled onto single core static slots
description: CMS reported that multicore jobs can end up matched to single core static slots. There are two issues at work here: When submitting jobs via the Python API schedd.submit() or schedd.submitMany(), HTCondor fails to modify the job's requirements expression to contain the clause TARGET.Cpus >= RequestCpus. Unlike partitionable or dynamic slots, static slots do not have a clause in the slot requirement expression that checks that the slot has enough resources to satisfy the job. Static slots apparently rely on the job ad requirements to enforce this. In some sense, issue (1) above is expected, because the schedd.submit() methods are supposed to be handed a complete job classad from the user, which should already include a satisfactory Requirements expression. If the Python user wants HTCondor to construct a job classad (including the Requirements expression) from a job submit description in the same manner as the condor_submit command line tool, the Python API Submit class should be used. In fact, 99.99% of the time seems like users should use the Submit class and not the primitive/low-level Schedd.submit() method. To address this, in the v8.8.1 stable series we will patch the Python methods noted in issue (1) above to add restriction clauses for CPU and GPU resources. In the v8.9.x developer series in child ticket XXX, the Schedd.submit() methods will be renamed to be submit_raw_jobad() (or some such) to highlight the fact that no processing will be performed on the given job classad, and to encourage new development to use the Submit class instead. Also in the v8.9.x series, we will address issue (2) above so that static slot requirement expressions will ensure the job fits.

title: Ticket #4163: Schedd crashes when using PeriodicRemove for parallel jobs
description: If you submit a parallel job with a periodic remove expression this crashes the scheduler when it tries to remove the job. I experienced this problem in the following scenario: I'm submitting jobs via -remote to a remote dedicated scheduler. The job itself copies the result data to a central place on a file server and, thus, I don't need to transfer any data back using condor_transfer_data. Therefore, I want the scheduler to remove the job automatically and defined a "PeriodicRemove" expression in my submit script. If I do this for a parallel job the scheduler crashes when removing the job. Looking at the code I found the problematic part. It seems that during the remove operation of a job cluster the schedd tries to access data structures which have been deleted before. I don't understand the code completely but as I only submit jobs which have a single job per cluster the attached patch helped me to solve the issue for my version of condor. It will be problematic probably if you have multiple clusters in a job, so someone with a better understanding of the code should have a look...

But can be cases where it's called on another proc_id in the cluster first. In some places, DestroyProc() will be called on jobs in hashtable order as part of WalkJobQueue(). 2014-Feb-10 13:26:01 by gthain: Note that the above are all for parallel jobs with multiple procs, which are conceptually one job, so we want one history file entry, and one Completion time for them.

description: Coverity correctly points out that InitCommandSockets (/src/condor_daemon_core.V6/daemon_core.cpp around line 9676) implies that it's valid to pass in a sock_pair with a null ReliSock. If that's the case, later code dereferences it in unsafe ways. There are no known cases where this actively happens, but it is a landmine that could surprise future code. 9734 // Ensure we have a socket, setsockopt doesn't work otherwise. At conditional (1): "rsock" taking the false branch. CID 10511: Dereference after null check (FORWARD_NULL) Comparing "rsock" to null implies that "rsock" might be null. 9735 if(rsock) { 9736 if(!assign_sock(proto, rsock, fatal)) { return false; } 9737 } At conditional (2): "ssock" taking the true branch. 9738 if(ssock) { At conditional (3): "!assign_sock(proto, ssock, fatal)" taking the false branch. 9739 if(!assign_sock(proto, ssock, fatal)) { return false; } 9740 } 9741 9742#if defined ( WIN32 ) 9743 /** To better match the *nix semantics of SO_REUSEADDR we 9744 enable MSs SO_EXCLUSIVEADDRUSE option, which prohibits 9745 multiple process/identities/etc. from binding to the 9746 same address (which is just crazy behaviour!). 9747 9748 For further details refer to ticket #288. */ 9749 so_option = SO_EXCLUSIVEADDRUSE; 9750#endif 9751 9752 // Set options on this socket, SO_REUSEADDR, so that 9753 // if we are binding to a well known port, and we 9754 // crash, we can be restarted and still bind ok back 9755 // to this same port. -Todd T, 11/97 Passing null variable "rsock" to function "Sock::setsockopt(int, int, void const *, int)", which dereferences it. [show details] 9756 if( !rsock->setsockopt(SOL_SOCKET, so_option, 9757 (char*)&on, sizeof(on)) ) { 9758 if (fatal) { Proposed fix: restructure the code so that all interactions with rsock occur inside of the "if(rsock)" test. For symmetry, do so for ssock as well.

title: Ticket #3599: Concurrency Limits Regression Test
description: HTCondor Concurrency Limits Regression Tests job_concurrency_limits.run The concurrency test uses the SimpleJob::RunCheck. To do this it was extended to allow on abort function over-ride, allow a way to specify queue size and fix passing duration of zero(for a test job which runs forever). Concurrency tests have an expected number of jobs running and at least one job expected to be idle. We desired a way to delay for a bit when handling the last expected call back for a job running. In this case we wanted to wait a couple negotiation cycles. So we created third test in Check/CondorLog.pm{RunCheckMultiple}. This searches logs related to daemons and we can specify either the number of patterns seen(which it waits for with a timeout) or the number of new patterns we want to wait for(with a timeout). So while we delay a couple negotiation cycles, if we then see an idle job start to run, we fail the test as the concurrency controlled jobs are run forever so the idle jobs should not start if the concurrency limits are working.

title: Ticket #968: daemon ads contain many copies of sinful string
description: Daemon ads contain four copies of the address: SubsysIpAddr, MyAddress, PublicNetworkIpAddr, and PrivateNetworkIpAddr. This is overly complicated and we have begun to accumulate potential compatibility complexity where bits of condor pay attention to different attributes. Since 7.3.0, PrivateNetworkIpAddr is redundant, because the private address and network name are attributes of the full contact string advertised in all of the other attributes. Furthermore, when private network attributes are set, we chose to break compatibility with releases prior to 7.3.0, due to the change in the format of the sinful string, so continuing to support PrivateNetworkIpAddr does not gain us any added backward compatibility. Prior to 7.2.0, the negotiator depends on startds advertising the same StartdIpAddr or MyAddress in the public and private ads. Beginning in 7.2.0, the collector copies over MyAddress from the public to the private ad. The collector creates a hash key using SubsysIpAddr. It does not pay attention to MyAddress when doing this, so for backwards compatibility with older collectors, we need to keep advertising SubsysIpAddr. The daemon client object does not pay attention to MyAddress. Ads written into a daemon ad file do not contain MyAddress. Only ads sent to the collector do.

I made the daemon client object pay attention to MyAddress if SubsysIpAddr is not there. Daemon ad files now contain MyAddress. The collector now uses MyAddress or SubsysIpAddr when creating hash keys. 2009-Nov-17 13:04:45 by matt: Can we get a ticket targeting 7.7 that says SubsysIpAddr should be removed before the release of 7.8? Otherwise we're going to forget. 2009-Nov-17 13:31:30 by danb: Good idea. I added #971 to remind us to remove SubsysIpAddr.

title: Ticket #7470: HTCondor broken on AWS Fargate as setrlimit EXCEPTS w/o cap_resource
description: When HTCondor starts as root, it tries to increase the number of file descriptors that various daemons have via the MAX_FILE_DESCRIPTORS, SCHEDD_MAX_FILE_DESCRIPTORS, SHARED_PORT_MAX_FILE_DESCRIPTORS and others. The defaults in the param table for these are 4096. If it fails to raise the limit, it EXCEPTs. However, containers started in AWS Fargate have a hard limit of 1024 fds, and do not have CAP_SYS_RESOURCE, which is needed to raise the limit, even though they have uid = 0. Because of this, most HTCondor daemons EXCEPT on startup on Fargate. We will fix this by making the failure to raise the limits non-fatal.

title: Ticket #7535: startd should allow slots to be assigned specific custom resources
description: When the Startd creates a slot of any type (p-slot, d-slot, or static slot) it does so by parsing a string of the form that the SLOT_TYPE_<N> configuration knob reads. This is a complicated, semi free-form request for resources that looks like this <resource_tag1>=<quantity>, <resource_tag2>=<quantity>, ... example: Cpus=1/4, Memory=4096, Gpus=1 <quantity> may be an integer, a fraction, or a percentage, or the special values auto and minimal At a minimum we need to extend this to allow a specific instance or instances of a non-fungible resource, (e.g. GPUS) to be specified; Possibly like this: Cpus=2, Memory=4000, Gpus="CUDA2,CUDA3" . If we make this change, then P-slots and static slots could be configured to have specific GPUs assigned to them. And with a small amount of additional code we could construct the provisioning string for d-slots to assign specific GPUs there also. The mechanism for indicating to the STARTD what GPU assignments are desired would be left to a future ticket. The above syntax, while sufficient, would be a bit of a PITA to use - So we should probably allow some sort of smart assignment here such as Cpus=2, Gpus=(DeviceName:*Tesla*) which would indicate that we want to assign a GPU that has a CUDA<n>DeviceName attribute that matches /Tesla*/ Some things we need to consider: currently the provisioning syntax splits on the usual string list characters and then treats each item as a resource assignment. This means specification of the <quantity> cannot contain either spaces or commas - we should probably change that we should probably pick a syntax that can survive being imbedded into a classad attribute value so that the schedd can make requests. as a part of this work, we should stop advertising attributes of GPUs that are not assigned to the slot in the slot, and should remove the GPU id prefix from the attributes that are assigned to the slot.

title: Ticket #5158: Shadow launch queue woes.
description: We've noticed the schedd has poor behavior when there is a long shadow launch queue. We found some CMS schedds with 5k shadows waiting to launch in the schedd. I think we should: Not negotiate when there's more than 100 shadows left to launch. For now, in CMS land, we've added (TotalRunningJobs > ShadowsRunning+500) to CURB_MATCHMAKING. Advertise the number of unlaunched shadows in the schedd ad. Consider allowing multiple shadow launches per duty-cycle (for busy schedds). Similar to what we did for DCMessage, we should allow ourselves X milliseconds of shadow launching per duty-cycle (or JOB_START_COUNT, whichever hits first). Oh - and the obvious one. Have the schedd release claims if the # of pending shadows is over a certain limit.
remarks: 2015-Aug-04 13:00:53 by tlmiller: Regarding point 2: the schedd maintains a queue (called RunnableJobQueue) of jobs for which it must start a process but hasn't. This queue includes all jobs requiring a shadow (vanilla, docker, vm, java, and standard universes), and all scheduler and local universe jobs. This queue can become lengthy if the schedd or its host are overloaded, or if JOB_START_COUNT / JOB_START_DELAY are set too low for the workload. Because each entry in the RunnableJobQueue delays each subsequent entry, we feel that advertising the size of this queue better-answers Brian's request for a count of pending shadows. (It also makes it a one-line patch.) Based on the names of the above config knobs, and its plain-English reading, ToddT proposes NumJobStartsDelayed as the name for this attribute, which is way better than my brain-dead default (RunnableJobs). Regarding point 1: when point 2 is implemented, point 1 could be supported via the policy expression CURB_MATCHMAKING. The new subticket (#5192) records our intention to figure out what a sane default for CURB_MATCHMAKING would be, as this seems a little cleaner than adding another knob to support point 1. JaimeF, ToddT, and ToddM agree that points 3 and 4 should be punted to 8.5.x. (This implies creating at least one new subticket.) title: Ticket #2367: performance issue - n^2 fsync()ing algorithm in dedicated scheduler
description: There are three issues here: The algorithm need not be n^2, could be n DEFERRED #2397 DURABLE SetAttributeString could be NONDURABLE to avoid the fsync DONE: [26688] The dedicates scheduler battles the scheduler over the correct value for ATTR_SCHEDULER value because of a mismatch in ds_name and correct_scheduler DONE: [26687] First, in the 7.6 timeframe, the following code was added to the DedicatedScheduler... commit 03c931773b7b3f6060f5e33e1896f602fc01a7f0 Author: gthain <gthain> Date: Thu Apr 20 19:43:16 2006 +0000 make sure SCHEDULER attribute is set for all procs in a cluster of parallel jobs diff --git a/src/condor_schedd.V6/dedicated_scheduler.C b/src/condor_schedd.V6/dedicated_scheduler.C index 9586559..e301411 100644 --- a/src/condor_schedd.V6/dedicated_scheduler.C +++ b/src/condor_schedd.V6/dedicated_scheduler.C @@ -1981,8 +1981,14 @@ DedicatedScheduler::sortJobs( void ) // so put it in our array. (*verified_clusters)[next_cluster++] = cluster; - // While we're at it, make sure ATTR_SCHEDULER is right - setScheduler( job ); + // While we're at it, make sure ATTR_SCHEDULER is right for all procs + ClassAd *jobIter = job; + int proc = 0; + do { + setScheduler( jobIter ); + proc++; + jobIter = GetJobAd(cluster, proc); + } while (jobIter != NULL); } // No matter what, we want to remove our old array and start @@ -3776,9 +3782,10 @@ DedicatedScheduler::setScheduler( ClassAd* job_ad ) if( ! job_ad->LookupInteger(ATTR_PROC_ID, proc) ) { return false; } - if( SetAttributeString(cluster, proc, ATTR_SCHEDULER, - ds_name) < 0 ) { - return false; + + while( SetAttributeString(cluster, proc, ATTR_SCHEDULER, + ds_name) == 0 ) { + proc++; } return true; } The result is for every parallel job in the queue, SetAttributeString is called (n^2-n)/2 times. Second, each SetAttributeString is DURABLE and results in an fsync, could be NONDURABLE. Third, commit b7ab1748d7115ea16025baa09be2e47f3d2d26d8 Author: wright <wright> Date: Mon Apr 9 23:17:26 2001 +0000 + Added dirtyJobQueue(), which allows parts of the schedd external to qmgmt.C to set the flag that says the queue is dirty. This is useful when we do things to the in-memory version of job classads that we'd like to be truncated on shutdown, but that we don't need persistently logged immediately (eg fixing ATTR_USER on a reconfig'ed UID_DOMAIN). + Added code to InitJobQueue() to check for the ATTR_SCHEDULER attribute for MPI jobs and insert one if it's not there (just like we do for ATTR_USER). + Fixed the code in InitJobQueue() for adding ATTR_USER (and the new code for ATTR_SCHEDULER) so that we set the JobQueueDirty flag to true when we do it, so that the changes get truncated (persistently logged) on shutdown. diff --git a/src/condor_schedd.V6/qmgmt.C b/src/condor_schedd.V6/qmgmt.C index 2bd1ae0..39b398f 100644 ... + sprintf( correct_scheduler, "DedicatedScheduler!%s", Name ); ... Disagrees with, commit 356bbf10564d9d3936a709a0f945c162f2e29967 Author: wright <wright> Date: Tue Apr 10 22:59:11 2001 +0000 + Removed ds_scheduler and schedulerName(), since we just want to use ds_name and name() to set ATTR_SCHEDULER. + Cleaned up the initialization of ds_owner and ds_name: ds_name is now always "DedicatedScheduler@schedd.name", even if schedd.name contains an '@' sign itself. If there's an '@' in the schedd name, ds_owner will be "DedicatedScheduler@everything_before_the_@", for example, "DedicatedScheduler@wright", if the schedd name is "wright@raven.cs.wisc.edu". diff --git a/src/condor_schedd.V6/dedicated_scheduler.C b/src/condor_schedd.V6/dedicated_scheduler.C index ed27ccf..08117ca 100644 ... - sprintf( buf, "DedicatedScheduler!%s", Name ); - ds_scheduler = strnewp( buf ); + sprintf( buf, "DedicatedScheduler@%s", Name ); + ds_name = strnewp( buf ); ...
remarks: 2011-Aug-09 11:01:31 by matt: Greg, why did you make the setting of ATTR_SCHEDULER operate this way? It seems like only one loop, either in sortJobs or setScheduler, would be sufficient. There's a case where PU job {1.0, 1.1, 1.2} might have 1.1 removed, but neither loops appears to protect against that (I'm assuming it is invalid state to begin with). Can we reduce this code to a single loop that handles the error cases of when setting fails (likely to ignore anyway)? 2011-Aug-15 09:17:57 by gthain: First, note this is looping over the "procs", not the ranks, and there is almost never more then 2 procs per parallel job. 2011-Aug-17 12:41:30 by matt: Ok, the algorithm may iterate more than is necessary, but does not perform expensive operations on each iteration anymore. Given that the wisdom as to why the algorithm is doubly cautious has been lost and no time to fully validate -- let's defer the n^2 -> n for now.

title: Ticket #4319: add #include like mechanism to config file parser
description: config files should support a way to declare that other files should also be parsed in much the same way that #include works for C/C++. This would be both more flexible and more powerful than the current LOCAL_CONFIG_FILE mechanism. To minimize changes in the parser, and to follow the current metaknob convention. the syntax will be include : _file_ or include : _cmd_ | where _file_ is the path to the file to read. the path may contain config macro references, but those references must be valid at the time the include statement is parsed. include statements are executed right away as if the contents of file was in the current file at the include line. In the second form, cmd is a command line to run, the output of which is read in and parsed as config. (the second form is basically available for free because the code will re-use the config file parsing code that LOCAL_CONFIG_FILE currently uses.)

title: Ticket #6324: Execute directory cannot be an ImDisk ramdrive on Windows
description: A user at HTCondor Hamburg and also on condor-users reported that when he puts his execute directory on a Windows ramdrive using the ImDisk virtual disk driver. The HTCondor STARTD will abort on startup, The Start log has the following messages The entries in the StartLog: 06/22/17 14:07:08 sysapi_partition_id: GetVolumeNameForVolumeMountPoint error: 4390 06/22/17 14:07:08 ERROR "Failed to get partition id for SLOT1_EXECUTE=X:\Execute" at line 81 in file C:\condor\execute\dir_14532\sources\src\condor_startd.V6\slot_builder.cpp This happens because the ImDisk driver doesn't pretend to be an actual disk and therefore, GetVolumeNameForMountPoint returns ERROR_NOT_A_REPARSE_POINT. The STARTD treats this as a fatal error, but it doesn't need to. The STARTD only needs to have a unique id for each 'partition' so it can avoid having to get the free disk individually for every slot. If we change the sysapi code to log this error but then treat the drive letter as if it were the partition id, then the rest of the STARTD code would work correctly.

title: Ticket #7866: Shared port socket-passing oddities on Mac OS X
description: The combination of #7502 and [60471] causes us grief. To quote from a remark on #7799: When the shared port daemon sends its first child-alive message to the master, the master sees no data on the passed socket. When the shared port daemon forwards a connection for the collector's child-alive, the master reads the data from the passed socket just fine. The failure to read data for the shared port's child-alive appears to be tied to the master sleeping and not immediately responding to the connection from the shared port daemon. Reverting the master's behavior on macOS mostly fixes the problem, but the underlying cause should still be investigated.
remarks: 2020-Sep-28 13:39:11 by tlmiller: Is this related to the Mac OS X -specific blocking? Is the data getting lost because the shared port daemon is closing the childalive socket before the sent data is read by the master? That's not totally consistent with the collector not having any problems, but maybe there's something subtle about the special handling of connections from the shared port daemon itself? 2020-Oct-07 16:09:18 by tlmiller: Turning the MacOS X -specific blocking hand-off protocol does seem to fix the problem, but I don't understand why. (It could just be an expensive way of avoiding a race condition.) The original comment indicated that the hand-off protocol without the acknowledgement resulted in handed-off sockets being closed; this problem is that they're open, but never receive any data. This may just be a result of a subtle kernel change, but doesn't answer the question as to why only the shared port daemon itself seems to have this problem. An oddity I noticed during my testing: after rebuilding, the initial test run succeeds but takes noticeably longer to do so than subsequent runs. This may just be a caching issue, moving the the code out of its current race condition. Attempts to duplicate the issue without the shared port daemon failed, which means this likely has to do with the special-case socket-handoff code (using connect_socketpair()). 2020-Oct-07 16:26:14 by tlmiller: Switching do_shared_port_local_connect() to pass the nonblocking flag to PassSocket() caused a segfault (?!). Working around that didn't change the master's behavior any. 2020-Oct-07 17:04:20 by tlmiller: I weep: dup()ing the socket passed to the master (and throwing away the result) seems to make everything work. 2020-Oct-08 09:59:43 by tlmiller: To clarify: dup()ing the socket and deliberately leaking it seems to help. Moving the dup() from connect_socketpair_impl() to do_shared_port_local_connect() also seems to work. Forcing all daemons to always bypass the shared port daemon results in the collector -- and only the collector -- failing in the same way as the shared port daemon. This is probably a reflection of a race condition, potentially related to the fact that the master waits for the shared port daemon and the collector to each start up before starting the next daemon(s) on its list. 2020-Oct-08 10:08:15 by tlmiller: Adding a Sleep(1000); to the master just after StartDaemonHere() caused all the daemons to fail when forced to bypass the shared port daemon. 2020-Oct-08 14:52:10 by jfrey: Code Review I do not like this ugly hack. I would not put it in a sack. But I cannot think of anything better.

title: Ticket #5271: condor_q should show only current owner's jobs by default
description: By default, condor_q should show only jobs owned by the current user (unless the user is a queue super-user). If one or more user argument is specifed for condor_q, then only those owners' jobs will be shown. If no user argument is specifed, then a special value will be passed in the query ad for new schedds that means "add Owner==Me to the constraint". For older schedds Owner==<user> will be explicitly added to the constraint, with condor_q attempting to determine what value to use for <user> Thus the condor_q results may be somewhat different when talking to older schedds. There are actually 3 cases. When talking to an 8.5.1 or later schedd, the V3 query protocol is used and it's the schedd who figures out what the value of <user> is. When Talking to an schedd that supports the V3 protocol but is older than 8.5.1, condor_q figures out what <user> is and adds an explicit constraint to the query. When talking to schedd that do not support the V3 protocol, condor_q adds an explicit constraint and figures out what <user> is.

title: Ticket #4460: Further improvements to negotiation over high latency links
description: Resource Request Lists In #3585, we added the concept of a resource request count. With resource request counts, when the schedd sends a request to the negotiator, it includes an attribute that says "I want X number of resources like this". This definitely improved the speed of negotiation over high latency links (i.e. the wide-area internet) when making a lot of matches. However, if the schedd has a large number of autoclusters that do not match, they still are sent to the negotiator one at a time with a round-trip in between. In CMS, there are schedds sprinkled around the world, and at times there are hundreds of autoclusters that do not match. The work in this ticket allows the negotiator to ask for a resource request list from the schedd. A resource request list is a list of sorted resource requests, perhaps each with a resource request count. The negotiation protocol has been enhanced so the negotiator can ask the schedd to send a request list with a specified maximum number of entries. This maximum is controlled by the negotiator knob NEGOTIATOR_RESOURCE_REQUEST_LIST_SIZE (default value is 20); if set to 1, or if talking to an older schedd that does not implement the enhanced protocol, then the old protocol is used. Currently, setting this knob to a value greater than 50 or so may result in the schedd blocking on network I/O while sending the requests to the negotiator. In addition, with the new protocol, the resource requests themselves are no longer the entire job classad - instead, they are just the significant attributes from the job ad plus a few extra attributes (like cluster, proc, etc) that are explicitly examined by the negotiator. This makes the resource requests themselves much smaller than a job ad, speeding their transfer and minimizing the memory footprint at the negotiator. Potential Future Work The code in the negotiator that communicates with the schedd has been refactored into its own class in order to enable a variety of options should we need to make further scalability improvements. Some ideas include: The schedd could perform non-blocking network I/O when sending the request list, allowing it to send hundreds (thousands?) of requests without worry of impacting schedd performance. Currently the resource request list in the negotiator is not kept between pie-spins, thereby requiring negotiation to "start over" at each pie spin. The code in the negotiator that communicates with the schedd has been refactored to enable potential caching of this list (keyed by a tuple of user/schedd) across pie spins. Note doing this safely would require i) knowing if autocluster id wrapping has occured in the schedd, and ii) knowing if a match has been refused due to no-match-found or due to priority limits, as in the case of the latter the request must be tried again after a pie spin. Request lists could be fetched from multiple schedds/submitters in parallel at the start of the cycle. This probably only makes sense if the negotiator must examine all queued jobs to honor the semantics of preemption or startd rank expressions, i.e. if NEGOTIATOR_CONSIDER_PREEMPTION=True (in CMS it is currently False).

title: Ticket #207: Remove GRIDMANAGER_ MAX_ PENDING_ SUBMITS_ PER_ RESOURCE
description: GRIDMANAGER_MAX_PENDING_SUBMITS_PER_RESOURCE has probably out-lived its usefulness. It was originally added for gt2 jobs, when too many simultaneous jobmanager startups caused inetd's DoS alarms to trigger. Now, most sane values of GRIDMANAGER_MAX_JOBMANAGERS_PER_RESOURCE will provide the same benefit. For non-gt2 jobs, it doesn't make sense to place a throttle on the number of simultaneous submit requests; throttling across all requests is what you want. With Igor Sfiligoi, we found that GRIDMANAGER_MAX_PENDING_SUBMITS_PER_RESOURCE can negate the benefit of splitting the GRIDMANAGER_MAX_JOBMANAGERS_PER_RESOURCE throttle between submits and restarts. Since the former throttle is checked first and it isn't split between submits and restarts, new job submissions can get stuck behind a large wave of job completions or removals waiting for the former throttle before reaching their guaranteed half set of slots for the latter throttle. The reverse is also true. We recommended that he set GRIDMANAGER_MAX_PENDING_SUBMITS_PER_RESOURCE to effectively infinity.

title: Ticket #4525: Child alive is registered without payload
description: I observed (thankfully infrequent) cases on a busy CMS schedd (20k shadows) where the payload for child alive takes multiple seconds to arrive. My theory is the child got preempted after the startCommand and before the payload makes it to the TCP socket; due to the very busy state of the machine, the shadow didn't get rescheduled by the kernel. This caused the schedd to block for a few seconds. The fix is relatively simple - change the child alive handler from Register_Command to Register_CommandWithPayload. The child alive protocol requires a payload. Completely internal changes - no documentation needed.
