title: Ticket #2961: Roadmap for v7.9 development series
description: Note: For each item, need to create/add links to design documents and subtickets Enhancement items on the radar from UW UW Mission-Critical Priority Streaming CE. Continue work on Partitionable Slots. (#3241) BOSCO File Transfer. Provide explicit job sandbox movement operations to move files in the event that a schedd does not share a file system with the head (submit) node of a cluster where the blahp is launched. (#2386) UW High Priority Remove barriers that prevent Condor-C from serving as a CE #1376 Ckpt in Vanilla Universe. #2007 Local Universe jobs managed via a Startd co-located alongside the Schedd. Essentially Local Universe as Vanilla Universe jobs with an additional requirement. #3019 Tool so admin can ask the local startd what is happening. Simple command-line tool geared towards a Condor-ignorant system administrator that would contact the local startd and report who is using the machine from where. Similar to Unix's who; maybe a condor_who anyone ? #3046 Glideins: Startd chirps back job starts and completions to the job log on submit node. Homogenize Condor-G error codes (hold reason codes) into categories. Offload File Transfer from submit machine, via either transferd (as described in bosco file transfer design document) and/or leveraging http proxies. UW Medium Priority Interactive Jobs. Leverage ssh_to_job functionality to provide a way for users to request for an interactive shell session to be scheduled on an execute machine. #3088 GPU Support. Have Condor auto-discover NVIDA CUDA GPU resources, publish operational information on these GPUs in machine ClassAd. Sandbox GPU devices so they are only accessible to the job in which they were allocated. Allow GPUs to work w/ partitionable slots. Overlap file transfer w/ computation. Allow another job to be launched on the same resource while a starter is busy sending back the output sandbox from a previous job. This work is 80%+ completed on a branch; Fermi is expecting this functionality to make it into v7.9.x as they contributed Parags time last year. In hindsight, I think we made a mistake when we made this work dependent upon hierarchical claims/resource bundles, and instead should pursue the relatively straightforward original idea of allowing the schedd to have multiple activations per claim. Job Sandboxing. Continue leveraging Linux kernel mechanisms to provide better isolation between slots on the same machine. In particular, in v7.9 interested in providing better Memory (RAM usage) isolation between slots. DAGMan will use its own event log file. We could avoid DAGMan problems with file descriptor throttles and more by changing the schedd, shadow, and condor_submit to allow a job to have more than one user log file. So the user could specify whatever log file they wanted in their submit file, but DAGMan wouldn't pay any attention to that file. Instead, DAGMan could specify its own event log file in addition to the user-specified files. That way, DAGMan would only need to read a single log file, and we could solve a bunch of problems at one shot. This would also avoid "polluting" the per-job user logs with POST SCRIPT TERMINATED events. (#2807) Secure by default. IPv6/IPv4 mixed pools. Minimize Code Paths. Support for Run as Root. Multiple jobs per Shadow. Operational Metrics for people who shower. CondorView is limited and very long in the tooth. Now that we have a mechanism for statistics, the idea is a basic way to present them via a web browser without the need for geeky command-line tools; similar to the usage graphs provided by glideinWMS. Potentially relevant: Red Hat's contrib module: Plumage - Collector ClassAd data into MongoDB #594: CondorView collector should track arbitrary fields - Presumably we'll want to see historic data, not just instantaneous. Someone needs to keep the old data. The collector does this today (in very limited ways!) #595: Store CondorView database in more generic format #596: Serve CondorView data via SOAP (or other HTTP) interface #597: New CondorView user interface Various statistics we might be interested in (noted as documentation hasn't entirely caught up): #2197: General statistics architecture for Condor - See derived tickets #2006: RFE: publish some additional performance-related stats in schedd ad Allow transfer_output_remaps to work with sub-directories. Better blackhole detection - we can do smarter things than this recipe by involving the startd (or matchmaker?) such that each job need not discover the blackhole on its own. Enhancement items on the radar from Red Hat Combine Collector/Negotiator #3007 Collector/Negotiator/ClassAd performance work #2541 DONE PSlots #2826 #3435 Delta Cloud Mods Move to standards #3096 (General cleanup, readability, and perf) Packaging/Testing items on the radar from UW #3154 Clear/reliable mechanism to invoke the test suite outside of NMI. title: Ticket #3389: DAGMan should honor prio changes
description: There is currently no easy way to change the relative priority of a DAG compared to another DAG. condor_prio on a dagman ID does not do anything. One can set the priorities at submit time. But what if a user decides after the fact that he wants to change the priority of a DAG (relative to other DAGs)? Sure, one can change the prios of nodes already in the Condor Queue. And for the others hold the DAG, rewrite the DAGMAN file and release the DAG. But this is hardly user friendly. Instead, DAGMan should honor any change in its own priority setting, and adjust the relative priority of all the nodes accordingly. As a corollary, DAGMan should adjust the priorities also if it itself was submitted with a non-zero prio value. Now, implementation wise, DAGMan should have no problems finding out that his own prio changed. condor_prio adds a dedicated event (033) to the DAGMan's event log. title: Ticket #2432: sizeof(off_t) simultaneously 4 and 8, causes much grief.
description: Some portions of Condor have been modified to handle large files This was done by setting #define _FILE_OFFSET_BITS 64 in the cpp files where it is needed: access_euid.unix.cpp, dprintf.cpp, and condor_open.cpp. This works okay, until some code using off_t exists in both files that do and don't set _FILE_OFFSET_BITS=64. If you do, the errors will likely be non-obvious, there is a good change of silent memory corruption as you write 8-byte values into a structure with space for 4. This very problem has happened. It's a landmine, and if you hit it, working around it is difficult and verbose as you need to carefully segregate the 4 and 8 byte code paths. Z has run into it while working on the dprintf code. Proposed fixes. #define _LARGEFILE64_SOURCE and $define _LARGEFILE_SOURCE everywhere. Existing code relying on _FILE_OFFSET_BITS=64 would need to be modified to use off64_t, fseeko64, and friends. Existing code would continue working and could be modified to use the 64-bit types and functions on an incremental basis. Windows has slightly different functions; we can create condor_off64_t, condor_fseek64, and friends and implement on each platform. The implementations should be quite brief. #define _FILE_OFFSET_BITS 64 everywhere. While the ideal goal as Condor would handle large files everywhere, it is very dangerous as there are almost certainly places where we put file sizes and offsets into an int or unsigned int. Handling this would requiring checking the entire life-span usage of every variable passed in out return from a function dealing in off_ts. Any variable those variables touched would similarly need to be checked, and so on. High risk, requires getting everything right. Don't change anything Very high risk. If someone bumps into the problem, it's very hard to identify. Fixing it involves moving functions and structures into different files and keeping them completely isolated. If someone later causes the files to interact, bugs will reappear.
remarks: 2011-Sep-01 11:14:25 by ziliang: This bug actually can break the splitting of debug output to multiple files since dprintf_config fills in the array of off_t assuming they are size 4. Then when dprintf uses that array, it believes they are 8 and will read in the combined two entries. This means if there are two debug levels next to each other in the array used to organize their information, we get the wrong values for the max log size and can even end up being zero. The current fix is to also define _FILE_OFFSET_BITS in dprintf_config.cpp since the off_t array elements are internal to the dprintf system.

title: Ticket #6922: Embed local, subsys, or config name in shared port socket name
description: It would help in debugging for daemons to include their local, subsystem, or configuration (as in DAEMON_LIST) name in their shared port socket names. The master already sets a daemon's local name to its configuration name if appropriate, but since the master also creates (or at least names) the shared point endpoints for its children, we can't just change the SharedPortEndpoint constructor. Instead, let's split the knowledge about magic names out of the constructor and have the master (or the constructor, if necessary) supply the daemon's local/subsystem/configuration name. title: Ticket #7260: LD_PRELOAD a fake getpwnam into sshd for condor_ssh_to_job
description: LIGO (and the rest of the world) would really like condor_ssh_to_job to work with glided-in startds. There are several reasons these don't work today. This ticket addresses one reason. When the condor_startds spawns sshd, sshd runs as the non-root user of the job. At sshd startup, it looks at /etc/passwd to determine the shell and login name of the user. If this doesn't exist, or the shell isn't in /etc/shells, sshd will exit, and condor_ssh_to_job will unceremoniously hang up. To fix this, we will LD_PRELOAD a fake getpwnam library call into sshd that returns a valid shell. If this terrifies and administrator, a knob CONDOR_SSH_TO_JOB_FAKE_PASSWD_ENTRY = false will turn off the behavior.

title: Ticket #1160: CkptWallClock timers stack up
description: Every time the schedd is reconfigured, a new timer is registered to call CkptWallClock(). The previous timer is not removed. The default period is 1h. Prior to 7.4.1, this function was very expensive, because it updated each job in its own transaction. The end result was that schedd performance would degrade the more times it was reconfigured. One possible workaround is to set WALL_CLOCK_CKPT_INTERVAL=0. This disables the registration of the timer altogether. The down side is that if the schedd dies it may under-report how much wall time was consumed by some jobs. Thanks to Burt Holzman for the perfect environment in which to observe this problem. The bug was 10 years old!

title: Ticket #505: onexit policy expression regression tests are bogus and broken
description: All of the various onexit hold and onexit remove tests in test suite seem broken. They always return green, when in fact onexit policy expressions are broken in v7.3.2. (and maybe many other versions as well!!!) Observe : [tannenba@nmi-s002 todd]$ cat smell.sh #!/bin/sh exit 3 [tannenba@nmi-s002 todd]$ cat smell.sub executable = smell.sh universe = vanilla log = smell.log on_exit_hold = ExitCode != 55 queue [tannenba@nmi-s002 todd]$ cat smell.log 000 (87577.000.000) 05/21 15:30:43 Job submitted from host: <192.168.0.69:65244> ... 001 (87577.000.000) 05/21 15:30:44 Job executing on host: <192.168.0.69:65219> ... 007 (87577.000.000) 05/21 15:30:44 Shadow exception! UserPolicy Error: No signal/exit codes in job ad! 0 - Run Bytes Sent By Job 0 - Run Bytes Received By Job ... 001 (87577.000.000) 05/21 15:35:44 Job executing on host: <192.168.0.69:65219> ... 007 (87577.000.000) 05/21 15:35:44 Shadow exception! UserPolicy Error: No signal/exit codes in job ad! 0 - Run Bytes Sent By Job 0 - Run Bytes Received By Job A quick visual inspection of the onexit tests leads to confusion; some problems immediately seen include: The output is not understandable. Looks like any shadow exceptions appearing in the log are completely ignored?!?!?! Various bits look like they were copied and pasted from unrelated tests. The logic in the tests is broken. For instance, the onexit_hold_true test wants to see the test go into hold state. Once in the hold state, the test is removed. If the user log reports the job as aborted, the test returns success... but the aborted event handler never makes any check to that the job ever entered the held state! This test would pass if the job was immediately aborted upon submission w/o ever entering the hold state. The tests sleep for multiple seconds. There is no need for tests to be sleeping --- it just makes our test suite run slow and non-deterministically (i.e. what if the load average on the execute machine is very high?). How about having the test submit a job that immediately exits with a well known (and uncommon) exit code, and then have the policy expressions test on that?

description: This is mostly psilord's thinking; I'm just submitting to get some initial thoughts in. I'll let him flesh this out. Census of existing dprintf level usage. In practice, you would call it like this: dprintf(D_INFO, t(D_TAG1, D_TAG2, D_TAG3, ...), "hello world\n"); t would be a C++ overloaded function which takes 1-10 tags and calls t1, t2, t3, etc, etc, etc which are the C API calls. The tags are enums, specified in a header file. Now, there could be only a flat set of tags, or a tag hierarchy. Pros and cons should be figured out for both. As for the output, we can decide wether or not to propagate the tag names to the output lines or not, depending upon how we want to slice the data. The current dprint() implementation can be changed to recast its bit flags into appropriate tags.

title: Ticket #1475: Gridmanager misidentifying gram2 servers as gram5
description: Igor Sfiligoi reports that when using Condor 7.5.2 to submit jobs to gram2 servers, the gridmanager identifies a few of them as gram5. This causes it to disable its throttle on running jobmanagers, making it easy to swamps those servers. I've looked at some of Igor's log files, which show the gridmanager misidentifying osg-east.hms.harvard.edu as gram5. The grid monitor code disables itself before the gram version command is run. The version command properly indicates that the server is gram2. The jobs are submitted with a grid-type of 'gt2'. I can't figure out why the GlobusResource object has the server marked as being gram5. Here are the relevant lines from the gridmanager log: 06/23/10 14:40:52 [20899] gahp server not up yet, delaying ping ... 06/23/10 14:40:52 [20899] grid_monitor for osg-east.hms.harvard.edu:2119 entering CheckMonitor 06/23/10 14:40:52 [20899] Disabling grid_monitor for GRAM5 server osg-east.hms.arvard.edu:2119 ... 06/23/10 14:40:57 [20899] GAHP[21092] <- 'GRAM_GET_JOBMANAGER_VERSION 4 osg-east.hms.harvard.edu:2119' 06/23/10 14:40:57 [20899] GAHP[21092] -> 'S' 06/23/10 14:40:58 [20899] GAHP[21092] <- 'RESULTS' 06/23/10 14:40:58 [20899] GAHP[21092] -> 'R' 06/23/10 14:40:58 [20899] GAHP[21092] -> 'S' '1' 06/23/10 14:40:58 [20899] GAHP[21092] -> '4' '91' 06/23/10 14:40:58 [20899] resource osg-east.hms.harvard.edu:2119 is now up I've failed to reproduce this on my machine submitting to the same server. Making the grid monitor code delay until the version check is done before deciding anything would fix the bad behavior, but that doesn't resolve the source of the problem (why the GlobusResource object thinks the server is gram5 before the version check in some situations).

title: Ticket #1926: RFE: option for condor_userprio to report acctgrp stats hierarchically
description: With the new hierarchical accounting group support (#1393), users may find it useful to have condor_userprio report stats such that stats for a group include stats for its children (subtree). For example, if the usage for groups "a","a.b","a.c" are 1, 2, 3 respectively, the usage reported for "a" would be 6. (Currently, condor_userprio reports statistics for accounting groups independently of any children). Proposal is to provide condor_userprio with an option to report stats rolled up by accounting group hierarchy.
remarks: 2011-Sep-22 13:22:00 by eje: The attached patch implements an option to roll up accounting group attributes by hierarchy. The following attributes are rolled up by sum: ResourcesUsed<N> WeightedResourcesUsed<N> AccumulatedUsage<N> WeightedAccumulatedUsage<N> BeginUsageTime<N> is rolled up by min(). LastUsageTime<N> is rolled up by max(). Priority<N> and PriorityFactor<N> are set to 0.0 when rollup is in effect. This is because they no longer correspond to rolled up usage values, and there isn't a very meaningful way to roll priority or factor. 2011-Sep-22 13:42:53 by eje: REPRO/TEST This is a new feature, and so there is no repro condition. Consider the following accounting group configuration, with a simple hierarchy: NEGOTIATOR_DEBUG = D_FULLDEBUG NEGOTIATOR_INTERVAL = 30 SCHEDD_INTERVAL = 15 NEGOTIATOR_USE_SLOT_WEIGHTS = FALSE GROUP_QUOTA_MAX_ALLOCATION_ROUNDS = 1 NUM_CPUS = 10 GROUP_NAMES = a, a.b, a.c GROUP_QUOTA_a = 10 GROUP_QUOTA_a.b = 5 GROUP_QUOTA_a.c = 5 GROUP_ACCEPT_SURPLUS = TRUE Submit the following to populate the acct groups with some jobs: universe = vanilla cmd = /bin/sleep args = 6000 should_transfer_files = if_needed when_to_transfer_output = on_exit +AccountingGroup="a.c.u3" queue 1 +AccountingGroup="a.b.u1" queue 1 +AccountingGroup="a.b.u2" queue 1 Wait for the jobs to spin up, and test output of condor_userprio. The updated usage statement shows two new options "-grouporder" and "-grouprollup" $ condor_userprio -h usage: condor_userprio [ -pool hostname ] [ -all | -usage | { -setprio | -setfactor | -setaccum | -setbegin | -setlast } user value | -resetusage user | -resetall | -getreslist user | -delete user ] [-allusers | -activefrom month day year] [-l] [-grouprollup] [-grouporder] Legacy default behavior is preserved (sorting by prio, no rollup, etc): $ condor_userprio -all -allusers Last Priority Update: 9/22 11:36 Effective Real Priority Res Total Usage Usage Last User Name Priority Priority Factor Used (wghted-hrs) Start Time Usage Time ------------------------------ --------- -------- ------------ ---- ----------- ---------------- ---------------- <none> 0.50 0.50 1.00 0 0.00 12/31/1969 17:00 ??? a 0.50 0.50 1.00 0 0.00 12/31/1969 17:00 ??? a.c 0.50 0.50 1.00 1 0.02 9/22/2011 11:35 9/22/2011 11:36 a.c.u3@localdomain 0.50 0.50 1.00 1 0.02 9/22/2011 11:35 9/22/2011 11:36 a.b.u2@localdomain 0.50 0.50 1.00 1 0.02 9/22/2011 11:35 9/22/2011 11:36 a.b.u1@localdomain 0.50 0.50 1.00 1 0.02 9/22/2011 11:35 9/22/2011 11:36 a.b 0.50 0.50 1.00 2 0.03 9/22/2011 11:35 9/22/2011 11:36 ------------------------------ --------- -------- ------------ ---- ----------- ---------------- ---------------- Number of users: 3 3 0.05 9/22/2011 11:35 ??? Using the new "-grouporder" will place acct groups at top of output, in breadthfirst order (no rollup). Individual submitters are still sorted by priority as usual: $ condor_userprio -all -allusers -grouporder Last Priority Update: 9/22 11:37 Effective Real Priority Res Total Usage Usage Last User Name Priority Priority Factor Used (wghted-hrs) Start Time Usage Time ------------------------------ --------- -------- ------------ ---- ----------- ---------------- ---------------- <none> 0.50 0.50 1.00 0 0.00 12/31/1969 17:00 ??? a 0.50 0.50 1.00 0 0.00 12/31/1969 17:00 ??? a.b 0.50 0.50 1.00 2 0.09 9/22/2011 11:35 9/22/2011 11:37 a.c 0.50 0.50 1.00 1 0.04 9/22/2011 11:35 9/22/2011 11:37 a.c.u3@localdomain 0.50 0.50 1.00 1 0.04 9/22/2011 11:35 9/22/2011 11:37 a.b.u2@localdomain 0.50 0.50 1.00 1 0.04 9/22/2011 11:35 9/22/2011 11:37 a.b.u1@localdomain 0.50 0.50 1.00 1 0.04 9/22/2011 11:35 9/22/2011 11:37 ------------------------------ --------- -------- ------------ ---- ----------- ---------------- ---------------- Number of users: 3 3 0.13 9/22/2011 11:35 ??? With the "-grouprollup" option, acct group stats are rolled up the hierarchy (note that priority values are zeroed out for groups as rolled up priorities are meaningless). Non-group submitters are ordered as usual. $ condor_userprio -all -allusers -grouporder -grouprollup Last Priority Update: 9/22 11:41 Effective Real Priority Res Total Usage Usage Last User Name Priority Priority Factor Used (wghted-hrs) Start Time Usage Time ------------------------------ --------- -------- ------------ ---- ----------- ---------------- ---------------- <none> 0.00 0.00 0.00 3 0.30 12/31/1969 17:00 9/22/2011 11:41 a 0.00 0.00 0.00 3 0.30 12/31/1969 17:00 9/22/2011 11:41 a.b 0.00 0.00 0.00 2 0.20 9/22/2011 11:35 9/22/2011 11:41 a.c 0.00 0.00 0.00 1 0.10 9/22/2011 11:35 9/22/2011 11:41 a.c.u3@localdomain 0.50 0.50 1.00 1 0.10 9/22/2011 11:35 9/22/2011 11:41 a.b.u2@localdomain 0.50 0.50 1.00 1 0.10 9/22/2011 11:35 9/22/2011 11:41 a.b.u1@localdomain 0.50 0.50 1.00 1 0.10 9/22/2011 11:35 9/22/2011 11:41 ------------------------------ --------- -------- ------------ ---- ----------- ---------------- ---------------- Number of users: 3 3 0.30 9/22/2011 11:35 ??? 2011-Dec-16 15:22:08 by danb: Code review: This patch looks good to me. It's already in and documented, so I am marking this ticket resolved.

title: Ticket #2259: glideins fail to use glexec at lcg grid sites
description: When glideinWMS attempts to use glexec at various European grid sites, the starter fails in the following way: GLEXEC: error reading message from wrapper: Connection reset by peer Simple command-line tests of glexec succeed. Burt set up a glite CE at Fermilab and was unable to reproduce the problem. He and Igor got the following results in their tests: FNAL factory + FNAL gLite WN + glite-GLEXEC 0.8.0 = success FNAL factory + FNAL gLite WN + glite-GLEXEC 0.7.0-1 = success UCSD factory + RAL gLite WN + glite-GLEXEC 0.7.0-1 = fail FNAL factory + RAL gLite WN + glite-GLEXEC 0.7.0-1 = fail UCSD factory + CSCS gLite WN + glite-GLEXEC 0.8.1-1 = fail All those tests have linger=on.
remarks: 2011-Jun-21 17:56:40 by danb: I found that the problem is caused by restrictive permissions on a parent directory of the directory in which the glidein binaries are installed. $ ls -ld /home/cmspilot016 drwx------ 5 cmspilot016 cmspilot 4096 Jun 21 23:33 /home/cmspilot016 $ ls -ld /home/cmspilot016/globus-tmp.t2wn60.5546.0 drwx------ 5 cmspilot016 cmspilot 4096 Jun 21 23:33 /home/cmspilot016/globus-tmp.t2wn60.5546.0 The problem is that condor tries to run condor_glexec_job_wrapper via glexec, but condor_glexec_job_wrapper is installed in a sub-directory of a directory that the target user does not have permission to access. The target user in my test is cms140 and the user running the glidein is cmspilot016. On this same grid node, if I install glidein in /tmp, which does not have restrictive permissions, condor is able to use glexec successfully. Here is what happens if I try to run a program by hand via glexec in a directory that the target user does not have access to: $ /opt/glite/sbin/glexec /home/cmspilot016/test_job [gLExec]: Error while examining the executable that is about to be executed. It is unfortunate that this error message did not get reported by Condor, since lack of this made the debugging effort much more difficult. Before this ticket is closed, we should attempt fixing that or flag it as a bug to be fixed in the future. What can we do about the permission problem? One idea would be to have glidein install condor's glexec job wrapper (if not the rest of condor) in a location such as /tmp that is accessible to the target user. The down-side of this is that if the glidein gets kicked off the code without having an opportunity to clean up after itself, we may leave droppings behind in /tmp that are not immediately cleaned up by the batchsystem. In addition to the job wrapper needing to be accessible to the target user, the glidein's condor execute directory would also need to be accessible. Another idea would be to say that if sites support glexec, they must also have directory permissions set up to allow all possible target users to access all parent directories in which pilot jobs run. 2011-Jun-23 12:27:32 by danb: I have submitted a patch to 7.7.0 to capture and propagate diagnostic messages from glexec when it fails to run the job. 2011-Jun-23 12:40:07 by danb: The issue of parent directory permissions is, for now, considered to be a problem to be addressed outside of condor, so I am closing this ticket.

title: Ticket #2873: Document new arguments syntax in manual
description: "Job ClassAd Attributes" in "Appendix A: ClassAd Attributes" documents Args, but not the new Arguments. Furthermore, given that the two are subtly different, we should flesh out the description. Args: String representing the arguments passed to the job. This is used when the "old syntax" for "arguments" is used in the submit file. The string is space separated. Backslashes escaping double quotation marks are no longer present. Arguments: String representing the arguments passed to the job. This is used when the "new syntax" for "arguments" is used in the submit file. The string is formatted and escaped using the same rules as the new syntax in the submit file, although the exact representation may change to a different but equivalent one. For example "1 '2 2' 3" might become "1 2' '2 3".

A daemon or agent launched by launchd SHOULD NOT do the following as a part of their startup initialization: o Setup the user ID or group ID. o Setup the working directory. o chroot(2) o setsid(2) o Close "stray" file descriptors. o Change stdio(3) to /dev/null. o Setup resource limits with setrusage(2). o Setup priority with setpriority(2). o Ignore the SIGTERM signal. title: Ticket #769: Gridmanager jobs stuck in endless loop updating schedd
description: At several points during a Job object's life in the gridmanager, it needs to wait for changes to the job ad to be made persistent on disk (via the schedd). Currently, the job object triggers a connection to the schedd to update all dirty attributes in the job ad, verifies that the ad has no dirty attributes, then continues operation. If the ad still has dirty attributes, the job object triggers another connection to the schedd and waits. The connection to the schedd and the return of control to the job object occur in separate daemon-core handlers. In between these handlers, other code can make unrelated changes to the job ad, causing the job object to request a subsequent, unnecessary, update to the schedd. Under a heavy load of gt2 jobs, we have observed jobs get stuck in an endless loop trying to push the GridJobId attribute to the schedd, due to regular changes to LastRemoteStatusUpdate triggered by grid monitor status updates. The job objects need to check for the clean/dirty status of the specific attribute(s) they want pushed to the schedd.

title: Ticket #339: GCB: Don't pass useless gcb-inherit file to child process.
description: GCB always hands a gcb-inherit file to the next process whenever an exec() occurs. This is pointless and a bit wasteful if GCB isn't currently tracking any open sockets. In the case of the condor_starter starting a job, every single socket should be closed before calling exec(). As such, the gcb-inherit file is logically empty (although it probably contains some overhead). This wastes an FD and a few kiB on disk. (In addition, the unexpectedly open FD can confuse executables which grovel around in stuff they shouldn't. This happens to bork DMTCP, which may officially supported under Condor in the future.) Fix: If GCB is managing no sockets, it should not try to pass socket information to the exec()ed process. It should not set CB_INHERIT$PID, it should not write to /tmp/gcb-inherit-XXXXXX.

title: Ticket #7688: don't probe filetransfer plugins if not using them
description: There is a branch: V8_9-gt7688-branch There is a method in the FileTransfer object called InitializePlugins(). This invokes each plugin handler with the "-classad" option to see which methods are supported. This is called explicitly in the starter when it prints its classad so that we can advertise the support methods. However, InitializePlugins() is also called inside the SimpleInit() method. This seems helpful, but the end result is that almost every time we are instantiating FileTransfer object, we are probing all the plugins. The list of supported plugins has now growb to include box, gdrive, and likely more. Additionally, some of these plugins are written in scripted languages which needs to fire up an interpreter as well. The overhead of invoking all these plugins when every Shadow starts up is significant at scale. Currently, the only place that actually USES the plugins is the starter. We should therefor skip the probing by default in all other places where it is not needed. This means: Don't do it in the shadow at all Do it in the starter if plugins are actually used Do it in the starter when explicitly asked (By calling FileTransfer::GetSupportedMethods())

title: Ticket #7722: NonNegotiated Security Sessions have bad Subsystem attribute
description: When creating a non-negotiated security session, the local process fills in its own subsystem for the Subsystem attribute of the security policy. For a negotiated security session, Subsystem is normally set to the the subsystem of the client in the initial security negotiation. This inconsistency is observable with the family security session when the negotiator connects to the collector to fetch ads. The collector queries its peer's subsystem from the ReliSock (taken from the security session policy) and gets Collector. It then gives the connection a low priority for responding. If there's no family session, the peer's subsystem is negotiator and the query is given high priority. Proposed solution: When a client is resuming an existing security session, it should include its subsystem in the request to the server. The server should use that value for the peer's subsystem for the connection.

title: Ticket #3274: Priv-sep can't track all job disk usage

To fix this, we would have to add a new command to priv-sep.

title: Ticket #1249: CONDOR_VIEW_HOST doesn't support multiple destinations
description: CONDOR_VIEW_HOST is used to configure one collector to forward ads to another collector. (Incidentally, only some types of ads are forwarded--just what the view server and negotiator are interested in. Perhaps this should be generalized, see #1901.) It would be nice to be able to forward to multiple destinations. One use-case is an HA version of the multi-tier collector described in HowToConfigCollectors. Another use-case is more flexible aggregation of condor view results from various pools. Similarly, startd-flocking (e.g. super-pools) could be flexibly implemented by forwarding ads between collectors rather than directly from the startds themselves, since this would cut down quite a bit on the authentication load of the collectors that aggregate large numbers of startds. The same sort of logic to avoid forwarding to one's self should probably be retained for convenience.

title: Ticket #6719: Submitting multiple clusters broken in condor_submit
description: For arcane reasons, all jobs within a cluster must have the same executable. If the executable attribute changes in a submit description file, condor_submit will start a new cluster of job ads. Thus, one invocation of condor_submit can result in multiple clusters of new jobs. Starting with v8.7.9, this doesn't work correctly. For each cluster of jobs after the first, no attributes are set in the cluster ad (they all go into ProcId 0's ad) and the ClusterId attribute isn't set at all. The submission usually succeeds, but the schedd ends up getting confused. Also starting with v8.7.9, if there is a schedd job transform, the condor_submit may fail and end up reporting an error similar to ERROR: Failed to commit job submission into the queue. ERROR: Failed to apply a required job transform.

title: Ticket #7108: Allow DAGMan to untangle dense graphs with join nodes
description: LIGO approached us with a problem where some dags were executing very slowly. On inspection, we realized their graph structure was enormous with 660,000,000+ edges. The reason it got so dense was because of PARENT ... CHILD ... statements with large numbers of both parents are children. Default behavior in DAGMan is to put an edge between every parent and every child. However if there are 10,000 of each (as was the case with some of LIGO's statements) this results in 100,000,000 edges. In #7054 we provided a simple script to reorganize their .dag files by introducing a "join node": a single node in the middle which all parents and all children connect to. This reduces the number of edges from m*n to m+n. In LIGO's case it reduced the number of edges from ~660M to ~1.5M and improved the parse time, submit time and memory footprint by two orders of magnitude. Now we want to implement join nodes as a feature directly in DAGMan, to be added at parse time while condor_dagman is building the graph. They will be disabled by default, can be enabled by setting the DAGMAN_USE_JOIN_NODES configuration knob to true.

title: Ticket #1875: condor_master gets into busy-waiting state and starves jobs
description: While trying to get 7.5.5. out the door, it was noticed that the windows build machine wasn't making progress on build jobs. It turned out that the condor_master had gotten into a state where the main daemon-core loop was spinning without ever giving up the CPU. The "async_pipe" was returning true from select(), but the daemon core main loop was never trying to read from the handle, so the state was never cleared. Since the condor_master runs at higher priority than the jobs, all of the jobs were starving. The daemon core loop handles the async_pipe differently between windows and unix - it appears that in windows if two or more signals came in in a short enough period of time, any windows daemon-core based daemon could be put into this busy-waiting state.

title: Ticket #5565: submit or config self reference using $F() expansion results in hang
description: In the submit/config expansion code, self references are detected and expanded at parse time to prevent infinite recursion when expanding at runtime. So lines like this are detected and expanded at parse time. ENVIRONMENT = $(ENVIRONMENT) FOO=BAR But this detection of self reference doesn't recognize the new $F() 'fileparts' expansion added in the 8.4 series. Since it doesn't statements like this ENVIRONMENT = " $F(ENVIRONMENT) FOO=BAR " end up causing infinite recursion and a hang (and eventually a crash) when the submit/param code is asked to expand ENVIRONMENT. The code that detects self reference should be enhanced to recognize the $F() macro expansions, and possibly other $ function macro expansions as well.

title: Ticket #5070: condor_ssh_to_job fails with "Failed to get address of starter"
description: CHTC is reporting intermittent problems running condor_submit -i The tool fails with the error message "Failed to get address of starter for this job". Looking at the code, the tool polls the schedd until the job is in the "R"unning state. Once it is, the schedd immediately queries the address of the starter from the appropriate startd. If the starter cannot be found, the schedd returns a fatal error. However, there is a race here -- the shadow may not have activated the claim. If there is JOB_START_DELAY in place, the shadow may not even be running yet. We will change this so that this error isn't an immediate fatal error, but will allow for a retry.

title: Ticket #5420: HTCondor incorrectly preempting jobs
description: On both the LIGO and CMS glidein pools, we see consistent issue with slots being preempted despite the fact preemption is disabled. I suspect there's a lack of transaction safety here - the negotiator has a private ad corresponding to a preempting claim but a public ad corresponding to when the slot was unclaimed. Two suggestions: In the private ad, record the current state/activity. If it does not match the state/activity of the public ad, do not hand out a claim. Add a counter to the private and public ad; reject the private ad if the counters do not match in the negotiator. In other words, we try to make sure the private ad reasonably matches the public ad. The latter is more foolproof (consider what happens if a slot goes unclaimed->claimed->unclaimed between the two ad queries), the first would likely have a smaller performance impact.
remarks: 2015-Nov-30 17:08:02 by tannenba: Hi Brian, First a few questions: Are the slots you observe being preempted static slots or dynamic slots? (my guess is dynamic slots) Are both pools using a "collector tree"? How did you observe the situation where "the negotiator has a private ad corresponding to a preempting claim but a public ad corresponding to when the slot was unclaimed" ? Now some brainstorming: I cannot see how this would happen with static slots, but I imagine it could potentially happen with dynamic slots. In addition to your suggestions above, a third option would be to do away with private ads all together and instead have the startd put the claim right into the public ad as a private attribute. This would fix any transaction safety issue, potentially make the central manager more scalable (not sure about this, as we'd save the time by not creating a new classad but potentially take up time encrypting/decrypting the private attribute), always encrypt the capability between the startd and collector, and simplify the collector code moving forward. If you come back and say that this unwanted preemption is happening on static slots, then I would be baffled because of how things are supposed to be implemented (according to the design) with respect to static slots: The startd is supposed to always generate fresh new claim ids (both public and private) whenever a slot enters back into unclaimed. Updates sent to the collector from the startd should contain both the public and private ads in the same message, thus the updates should arrive atomically. The collector does do two separate queries, but it should query the private ads first and then subsequently fetch all the public ads. Given the above three design rules, it is hard to see how the matchmaker could end up with a preempting claim in the private ad and an unclaimed public ad when using static slots. Unless of course there is an implementation bug or regression. :O.
creator: bbockelm

title: Ticket #1930: Add support for advertising .NET on Windows
description: With the increasing use of the .NET framework for Windows application development, providing an out of the box solution for detecting which version of .NET is present on a machine becomes more useful. There are however a couple of caveats on how .NET versions are detected. The latest .NET runtime has no problems executing the bytecode of earlier versions. However, the runtime library that includes all of the classes and functionality are different from version to version. To be absolute certain that a .NET 3.5 application will run, the .NET 3.5 libraries must be installed even if .NET 4.0 has been installed. Further complicating this is how .NET 4.0 has been split into a "Client" and "Full" install. Thus merely advertising just the latest version of .NET installed on a Windows sytem is insufficient. Every version of .NET installed must be advertised. This page lists the differences between Client and Full: http://msdn.microsoft.com/en-us/library/cc656912.aspx The current design for advertising .NET involves using a single classad attribute, DotNetVersions, that holds a comma delimited list of .NET versions as follows: 1.1: .Net 1.1 2.0: .Net 2.0 3.0: .Net 3.0 3.5: .Net 3.5 4.0Client: .Net 4.0 Client Profile 4.0Full: .Net 4.0 Full Thus an end user who requires a specific version of .NET can add this expression to their submit file: requirement = stringListMember("3.5", "DotNetVersions")

title: Ticket #2536: make upper bound on time spent in Preempting/Vacate explicit
description: For adding support for draining partitionable slots (#2330), it is desired to make the upper bound on time spent in Preempting/Vacate explicit. Currently, the boolean KILL expression is used to terminate the Preempting/Vacating state. This makes it awkward to compute how long it could take to drain a slot, because the upper bound on time, if any, is embedded in the boolean expression. Also, there is no standard way for the job to express its requirements or preferences. The following is proposed: Add MachineMaxVacateTime: this is the maximum time in seconds that the machine will wait before escalating from a graceful shutdown of the job to a fast shutdown. This is evaluated when the job starts. This configuration setting is required. It defaults to 10 minutes, like the default for KILL used to be. In addition, the timing of the beginning of eviction will be changed. Previously, eviction was initiated at the end of the promised MaxJobRetirementTime. Now, if there is sufficient retirement time left, the goal is to begin evicting the job before the end of retirement so that if the job uses the full eviction time, it will finish by the end of retirement. If there is not sufficient retirement time left, eviction will be initiated without delay. Add JobMaxVacateTime: this is an optional expression supplied by the job. If it yields a number smaller than MachineMaxVacateTime, the job's value is used in place of the machine's. Alternatively, if there is sufficient retirement time to accommodate it, JobMaxVacateTime may increase the effective vacate time so that eviction is initiated earlier during retirement than it would have otherwise been. JobMaxVacateTime deprecates KillSigTimeout. WANT_VACATE will still work as it does today. This means that even if MachineMaxVacateTime is non-zero, if WANT_VACATE evaluates to false when the job is being evicted, the graceful shutdown stage will be skipped. KILL will still work as it does today, except that it cannot be used to grant more time than offered by MachineMaxVacateTime. Normally, KILL should just be set to false, and MachineMaxVacateTime should be used to control how long to wait. However, in unusual cases, KILL could be used to abort the graceful shutdown of a job. The new default will be false. In addition, a change to the job attributes RmKillSig and KillSig is proposed. Currently, in unix for vanilla jobs, the fast shutdown mode of the starter will send RmKillSig if it is defined, and if not, falling back to KillSig, and if that is not defined, falling back to SIGKILL (see #1198). This means it is possible for a job to ignore the fast shutdown signal, so the starter has some logic to escalate to SIGKILL if a custom signal was defined. One issue with this implementation is that the starter doesn't really know that the job is being removed; it only knows that fast shutdown is ensuing, so the semantics of RmKillSig and KillSig are a bit muddy. Another issue is that the signal escalation seems to duplicate functionality of graceful shutdown mode, so there is added complexity that may not really be necessary. Another issue is that the feature is tied to unix and to vanilla jobs. What if one wants graceful removal of windows jobs? We are still gathering requirements to find out what exactly is needed. Based on the feedback we get, we plan to select from one of the following options. [We have not received any indication that the second option is needed, so we have implemented just the first option. The second option can be added later if needed.] [DONE] Make fast shutdown of the job always use a hard kill. When requested by the user, have the shadow initiate a graceful shutdown of the job rather than a fast one. For condor_rm, the user could request this behavior by putting WantGracefulRemoval=True in the job ad. This is platform and job universe independent. This is the preferred option unless users need the greater flexibility provided by the second option. [NOT DONE] Everything as in the first option but additionally, when the shadow requests graceful shutdown of the job, it specifies a reason. The reason is used to select a custom kill signal, which may be specific to the cause of the shutdown: job removal, hold, condor_vacate, condor_vacate_job, PREEMPT, and so on.

title: Ticket #6125: default condor_q behavior in 8.6.0 has issues (-global)
description: condor_q by default now uses a new command int, QUERY_JOB_ADS_WITH_AUTH, instead of QUERY_JOB_ADS. This is because the default is to show the jobs only for the user doing the query, and one way to do this is to authenticate the user so the schedd knows exactly who is making the query. The new command int is registered with "authentication required". However, this breaks in a couple scenarios: 1) The administrator has disabled security negotiation (SEC_DEFAULT_NEGOTIATION=NEVER) or authentication (SEC_DEFAULT_AUTHENTICATION=NEVER). In this case, even a query against a local schedd will not work, because authentication is required but cannot happen. 2) Doing 'condor_q -global' will fail when querying remote schedds if the admin has not set up authentication methods that work across machines. This is quite common, as by default FS is used, which only works locally, and other mechanisms require some additional configuration. As such, we propose to use CLAIMTOBE as a last resort. This satisfies the requirement that the user authenticate, and although it's potentially imperfect, this is not a security issue as the schedd is just trying to do a "best effort" guess at which jobs to send. The user can always include the -alljobs flag to condor_q in which case the old command int is used. However, it's not quite as simple as just adding CLAIMTOBE into the auth methods list, since the administrator may have explicitly configured their pool's DEFAULT or READ authentication methods, and we don't want to make their configuration less secure than they intended. As such, we should only add CLAIMTOBE to the list of methods for READ access if neither DEFAULT nor READ methods have been set by the admin. This needs to be done in code, not just in the param table.
remarks: 2017-Feb-03 12:42:15 by tannenba: Also, something should be done with regards to sites that have set SEC_DEFAULT_AUTHENTICATION = NEVER As it is now, for sites that have done this, they are understandably very confused when condor_q fails to work. For instance, see this post in htcondor-users. 2017-Feb-03 13:26:19 by zmiller: For people that have negotiation and/or authentication set to "NEVER", the only option that will work for them is to use the old behavior of using the command int QUERY_JOB_ADS instead of QUERY_JOB_ADS_WITH_AUTH. This means essentially that they need to set CONDOR_Q_ONLY_MY_JOBS to false. We can do the following: If SEC_WHATEVER_NEGOTIATION or SEC_WHATEVER_AUTHENTICATION is set to NEVER, then condor_q should disregard the setting of CONDOR_Q_ONLY_MY_JOBS and always assume it is false. 2017-Feb-15 16:56:26 by tannenba: Config-based work-around for those running v8.6.0: Summary: Make sure your SEC_READ_AUTHENTICATION_METHODS and SEC_CLIENT_AUTHENTICATION_METHODS both include CLAIMTOBE in addition to any other methods you had set up. If you have already set them explicitly, you can just append to condor_config.local: SEC_CLIENT_AUTHENTICATION_METHODS = $(SEC_CLIENT_AUTHENTICATION_METHODS) CLAIMTOBE SEC_READ_AUTHENTICATION_METHODS = $(SEC_READ_AUTHENTICATION_METHODS) CLAIMTOBE If you have not set those, but have set SEC_DEFAULT_AUTHENTICATION_METHODS, then you can append this to condor_config.local: SEC_CLIENT_AUTHENTICATION_METHODS = $(SEC_DEFAULT_AUTHENTICATION_METHODS) CLAIMTOBE SEC_READ_AUTHENTICATION_METHODS = $(SEC_DEFAULT_AUTHENTICATION_METHODS) CLAIMTOBE If you have not set anything at all regarding authentication methods, then you should append this to condor_config.local: SEC_CLIENT_AUTHENTICATION_METHODS = CLAIMTOBE, FS, PASSWORD, SSL, GSI, KERBEROS SEC_READ_AUTHENTICATION_METHODS = CLAIMTOBE, FS 2017-Feb-15 16:58:40 by tannenba: CODE REVIEW Zach, is commit [50127] sufficient? I.e. if CERTIFICATE_MAPFILE is defined, won't it still not work without explicit (and non-obvious) intervention on the part of the poor sysadmin? 2017-Feb-16 12:56:15 by zmiller: Todd, yes there is still an issue there, but it's a pretty gnarly one. It's unfortunate, but here's the saga: First, Most CERTIFICATE_MAPFILE examples (At least, the one in manual section 3.8.4 talking about the map file) do include the dummy rule for CLAIMTOBE. So I'd say there's a pretty good chance people won't hit this case. Second, that logic would need to go in the SchedD, since that's who is doing the mapping. condor_q could attempt to infer that it should use the old command, but that would mean loading and parsing the mapfile, hoping that it's the same one the (local) schedd is using (and can't be done for querying a remote SchedD). Then, we need to see if there are any existing entries for CLAIMTOBE, in which case the admin has explicitly set something up and we don't know if CLAIMTOBE will work or not... (maybe they set it up to go to a dummy user, for example). In short, it's a lot of complicated and hacky logic. I would much prefer that the (poor, unsuspecting sysadmin) explicitly add the rule to their mapfile than add such convoluted code for this case. Consistency, and all that. 2017-Feb-16 13:54:12 by tannenba: How about the idea of in the simply having some default rules in a map files, such as if and only if there are no CLAIMTOBE rules explicitly listed, then you get CLAIMTOBE (.*) \1 ? 2017-Feb-16 14:20:05 by zmiller: Ah, gotcha. I was focused on the client trying to detect which command to send. But I think adding the default rule(s) make sense and is small enough we can do it in the stable series. People shouldn't be relying on the mapfile for access control (like in the old days of gridmap files) so I think no one will be suprised in that sense by this change. 2017-Feb-22 14:26:59 by zmiller: Upon further review, we already do the "right thing" for CLAIMTOBE. If no entry exists in the map file the canonical name is assumed to be whatever user was claimed. So I believe this ticket can now be resolved.

description: When multiple shadows are writing to the same log file, the attached failure to lock is observed. It looks like locks are not being obtained or respected between shadows.
remarks: 2009-Oct-01 06:39:20 by matt: How reproducible is there? What is the recipe for reproducing this? 2009-Oct-01 09:48:55 by dharris: The setup we are using in an all windows (XP/vista/server 2008) setup. About 28 CPU's. The problem occurs when we submit a series of jobs (about 30) that all take the same amount of time to execute (about 10 minutes each). Each jobs writes to a shared log file so that we can utilize condor_wait for our automation purposes. What appears to happen is that sometimes a shadow ignores the lock (or fails to lock) the log file and the file gets garbled and condor_wait will wait forever. This happens with "job executing on host" and "job completed" messages occur at the same time as well as "job size updated", or so it seems. Unfortunately we cannot consistently recreate this issue as it seems to be luck of the draw when messages get written to the log file. 2009-Oct-02 06:42:20 by matt: I wouldn't be surprised if this also broke DAGMan on Windows. 2009-Oct-02 06:53:03 by dharris: I will DAGMan today and see if it has an issue as well 2009-Oct-02 08:57:46 by nleroy: Do you have a ShadowLog and ScheddLog from a window in which this occurred? If the issue happens again I will have be able to produce some logs. Sorry for the delay. 2009-Oct-19 16:42:13 by zmiller: i believe the problem is now understood. on windows, files are locked using a kernel mutex where the filename is name of the mutex. however, if relative paths are involved, this can lead to two different names for the same file. example partial submit file: initial_dir = c:\path\to\subdir_foo log = ..\common.log queue initial_dir = c:\path\to\subdir_bar queue in both cases, the actual log file is c:\path\to\common.log. however, two differently named mutexes are used to "lock" the file because condor simply takes initial_dir and concats a forward slash and the log filename (in classad_helpers.cpp:getPathToUserLog). suggested fix: call realdir(), GetFullPathName(), or something along those lines before grabbing the mutex to ensure that different references to the same file end up using the same mutex. 2009-Oct-19 16:44:58 by dharris: That explanation makes sense with regards to our setup. 2009-Oct-20 15:45:47 by psilord: Patch afc161be5e4564b1bafc5f82bb6c6fffcfeeacd4 causes the test suite to fail to build. title: Ticket #7671: File Transfer mechanism for URL transfers from multiple data sources
description: We want to change how the File Transfer mechanism deals with url transfers. Currently, when a user includes a url under transfer_input_files, we simply transfer the file indicated by the url. LIGO has asked us to expand the File Transfer object with some intelligent decision-making, such that if the same file is available at a better url, we transfer it from there instead. For example, maybe the file is available from a closer/faster data source than the one indicated. Or, maybe the url is not accessible to the execute host, but there is another copy of the file that is available somewhere else. Beyond this high level description, however, we've been unable to make any progress for almost a year now (as of July 2020). One fundamental issue is we've failed to clearly describe the problem. The above description is just my latest attempt (of many) and will likely get changed again. We have also not established who is responsible for the intelligent decision-making. Who is responsible for providing a "better" url to get the file from? The user? The system administrator? The condor_shadow? The file transfer plugin itself? Other? How does this entity know where a "better" copy of the file is available? There are many more implementation details to be ironed out, but until we understand what we are actually building we can't move this forward.
remarks: 2020-Jul-08 16:08:01 by coatsworth: We discussed using pre job hooks as a possible mechanism to implement this. Although we can use these hooks to update job ad attributes, these updates never make it back to the shadow which ultimately is responsible for which files to transfer. So this doesn't seem like a viable option. 2020-Jul-27 18:01:11 by tlmiller: As I understand it, we can think about two major ways of optimizing file transfers when multiple sources of the file are available. EXTERNAL APPROACH The external approach starts with the idea that HTCondor should not be involved in the process of deciding from which source to download a file -- that the decision depends too heavily on client-specific factors and client-specific code for HTCondor to do anything sane. So consider a URL-based scheme, because that's the easiest way to gain control during the file-transfer process. From HTCondor's POV, the contents of the URL are irrelevant, as long as calling basename() on it gives a reasonable file name. This means a client could construct URLs like so: multi://file_//cvmfs/foo,http_//squid.local/foo,chirp_//foo And write a pretty simple Python script to check the local filesystem, and then the SQUID cache, and then fall back on a chirp transfer from the submit node. We (the HTCondor designers) ignore the difficulty of generating such URLs, at least for now. Or the client could write a plugin that -- somehow -- determined what the different URLs might be, and then went down the list, or a combination of the two (e.g., a symbolic representation like gwdata and a fall-back location on the submit node). In this approach, our immediate responsibility as HTCondor designers is to make sure that chirp during file transfer works, or provide an equivalent tool, and that the tool schedules transfers (in the schedd transfer token sense) appropriately. INTERNAL APPROACH The external approach suffers from a number of problems. Some of them can be addressed incrementally -- e.g., adding multi:// or an equivalent as a first-class HTCondor feature would dramatically reduce code duplication between the client's custom plug-in and our existing plug-ins -- but I see two that can not: (a) getting "the tool" to work is going to be a pain, and one that will add load the schedd (unless we finally move the transfer queue out of the schedd) and (b) it's against the HTCondor religion to let code on the execute side decide what to transfer. (An aside about efficiency: it would obviously be more efficient for both the schedd and "the tool" to batch the token requests and transfers. Invoking "the tool" as a multifile plug-in should allow it to do its own batching; obviously, HTCondor would have to batch transfers if it handled multi:// natively.) With respect to the religion, I boldly claim that rephrasing the problem in terms of multiple, explicitly-specified sources changes what's going on from heresy to a new form of retries, which we already permit the plug-ins to do with no further direction from the starter or the shadow. This may mean that there's a follow-up ticket for a feature to transform transfer_input_files via an external script (whether at submit time or at transfer time), but it seems reasonable and prudent to me to leave that as a follow-up ticket for now. Of the implementation ideas I've heard, a first-class execute-side transform of transfer_input_files sounds like the easiest for us to implement and the most like a hack (because keeping the implementation easy implies doing the transfers during the rewrite step). It has all of the disadvantages of the external approach, excepting only that we probably don't have to change anything to get falling back to "normal" file transfer to work. It also seems like fewer clients would be able to take advantage of this approach than making multiple sources for the same file a first-class concept. 2021-May-10 20:10:53 by pfc: The ball is in Peter's court to move this forward: https://github.com/lscsoft/osg-igwn/issues/268

title: Ticket #6963: Clean up argument names in the Python bindings
description: Argument naming via Boost's API is wildly inconsistent in the bindings. Some functions have named arguments, some don't, some do but they don't agree with the docs. This is not a nothingburger, because those names are exposed in the Boost signatures that sphinx-autodoc reads. Making clean, consistent docs with sphinx-autodoc therefore requires doing a pass to make sure the argument names are clean and consistent. This should not break any existing users unless they are using introspection to fill in arguments by name, which we consider very unlikely. And if they were, the existing argument names should be considered long-term bugs, not stable behavior. Nevertheless, this should probably only go into the dev series.

title: Ticket #7221: Client tools use local daemon instead of failing for nonhostnames
description: Mat asks: $ condor_submit -remote foo foo4.sub Submitting job(s). 1 job(s) submitted to cluster 69. shouldn't that have failed since there's no schedd named foo? condor_submit -remote calls get_daemon_name() and checks the return value for NULL. What get_daemon_name() actually returns if its argument does not contain an '@' or a '.', and is not resolvable, is the empty string. This is only checked for correctly in condor_config_val and condor_status. This unconventional arrangement arises because get_fqdn_from_hostname() returns an empty MyString on failure. (The no-DNS case also only works if we assume that the argument will never accidentally contain an FQDN.) This function, luckily, is only called from get_daemon_name() and build_valid_daemon_name(), so this can readily be changed. The smallest workable patch for stable would be add a check in get_daemon_name() for empty FQDNs. For the dev series, I'd like to remove both functions entirely (to make sure I didn't miss any calls) and replace them with functions with saner calling conventions.

title: Ticket #817: Return value of Parse() misused
description: The return value of Parse() is being used incorrectly in a number of places. This isn't surprising, as it isn't documented anywhere. If the parsing is successful, 0 is returned and the second argument is modified to point at the resulting ExprTree. If the parsing fails, the second argument is set to NULL and the position in the string at which parsing failed is returned. That position may be 0. So the success of the function call is given by by the value of the second argument, not the return value. But many callers assume that a return value of 0 means success and that the second argument subsequently points to a valid ExprTree. Condor_submit is the only caller that cares where the parsing failed. So to simplify the fix and avoid future errors, Parse() should be modified to always return non-zero on failure and accept a new optional int* argument, which will be modified to contain the location of the parsing failure.

title: Ticket #1822: enforce maximum stage-out size
description: There should be an option to limit the total size of output files staged out from each job. The user should be able to specify a limit on a per-job basis and the schedd admin should be able to specify a limit that applies schedd-wide. If the admin's limit is less than the user's specified limit, then the admin's limit should win. The scenario that motivated this proposal was a case encountered at Nebraska in which a user ran 100 jobs that each staged out 5GB of data, filling up the home partition, and interfering with other work. It would be nice to also limit the total volume of output in some way, but it is more straightforward to limit things on a per-job basis, and even if we had some sort of cross-job quota, it would still make sense to be able to limit output on a per-job basis, so this seems like a good place to start.

title: Ticket #1988: quill fails due to duplicate key
description: Steve Timm reports seeing the following error in the quill log: 03/17 15:01:54 SQL COMMAND: INSERT INTO ClusterAds_Horizontal (scheddname, cluster_id) VALUES ('hostname.edited', '2726591') 03/17 15:01:54 [SQL EXECUTION ERROR2] ERROR: duplicate key value violates unique constraint "clusterads_horizontal_pkey" The job in question has already finished. Updates fail until job_queue.log rotates. Steve notes that this error happened in conjunction with a reboot of the machines. In this case the condor_schedd/condor_quill machine rebooted and came back up before the postgres server was rebooted. Theory: perhaps an update to the db succeeded to modify the db but failed to consume this entry from the sql log, leaving behind a record that causes all subsequent updates to fail. Suggested workaround: manually remove conflicting entries from the db.

title: Ticket #544: Allow all the Condor daemons to the traverse the Windows Firewall
description: Have each Condor daemon register with the Windows Firewall. This will make it easier for administrators, as they will no longer need to open global port ranges on each Windows machine that has the Windows Firewall enabled. New implementation: The Condor Master will check if the Windows Firewall is enabled and keep a record of its state (possibly updated at some interval?). Then, calls to Create_Process(), with a priv state of either condor or root, will be added to the Windows Firewall as a "safe" application. The Create_Process() call will take the following steps: Check that we are at the correct priv state; if we are not, then we are done; Check that we are a daemon; if we're not, then we're done; Do a quick local table look-up to see if we have already added this application; if so, we're done; Otherwise, the daemon doing the executing will ping the Master and ask if the Windows Firewall is enabled (and cache the results); if it is not on, we're done; If the Windows Firewall is on, then request that the given executable be added to the Firewall's exception list.

title: Ticket #4773: CLASSAD_USER_LIBS for python
description: The CLASSAD_USER_LIBS configuration knob allows sysadmins to implement and expose their own C++ functions to the ClassAd library. This is a powerful tool for implementing functions that represent expressions impractical to write within ClassAds. Unfortunately, implementing a C++ function is difficult for the average sysadmin and somewhat underdocumented. I propose exposing python modules as an alternate mechanism for site-specific ClassAd functions. Proposal: If CLASSAD_USER_PYTHON_MODULES is set, it is a string list of python modules allowed to be invoked from ClassAds. Introduce the python_invoke ClassAd function; the first argument is a module name (whitelisted above) and the second a function name (anything starting with "_" is forbidden). Do not add this functionality to ClassAds proper, but as part of a C++ shared library. Note that we must whitelist modules to prevent remote users from invoking something from the "os" module. Also note that, as part of #4598, the python module may register functions within the top-level namespace of ClassAds as part of the module loading process.

title: Ticket #4266: Matchmaker should avoid matching startds about to leave a glidein
description: Especially in a glidein pool setting, it is a waste of time for the negotiator to make matches to startds that are likely to shutdown before the schedd is able to claim it. As the DaemonShutdown attribute is advertised in the machine classad, a simple patch could allow the negotiator to ignore ads that are going to go away soon. The thinking is to accomplish this via a new negotiator knob, NEGOTIATOR_TRIM_SHUTDOWN_THRESHOLD, an expression evaluated to an integer value within the context of the negotiator classad, with a default value of 0. When this expression evaluates to an integer X, and X is greater than 0, the negotiator will not make matches to machine ads that contain a DaemonShutdown attribute that evalutes to true when attribute CurrentTime is set to be X seconds into the future.
remarks: 2014-Mar-18 13:32:07 by tannenba: The assumption here is that DaemonShutdown contains logic like Activity=="Unclaimed" && (CurrentTime - EnteredCurrentActivity > GLIDEIN_Max_Idle) Unfortunately this is not currently true of glideInWMS, which actually contains logic like TotalTimeUnclaimedIdle > GLIDEIN_Max_Idle which is incorrect as it will result in the startd shutting down once it has hit a total of 20 minutes of idle time across its entire lifetime, ie. perhaps the slot is continuously being used, but there is 5 minutes of idle time between jobs. After four jobs, the startd will shutdown, which is not the desired behavior. Parag and I talked about this - I suggest that glideInWMS make the change above to reference CurrentTime, and then set NEGOTIATOR_TRIM_SHUTDOWN_THRESHOLD to whatever value Igor suggests. Note it could be set to be a function of the length of the previous negotiation cycle, which may have a nice self-limiting property.

title: Ticket #3409: stdout/stderr names are modified in execute sandbox
description: In 7.7.2, a change was made to the naming of stdout/stderr in the execute sandbox. When using file transfer, these files are now always given the names _condor_stdout and _condor_stderr. Previously, these special names were only used when the names specified by the user contained path information. The change in 7.7.2 was made so that the final filename saved on the submit machine would match the name specified by the user, but CMS also expects the name in the execute sandbox to match the name specified by the user (when just a bare basename was specified). After discussion with Jaime, we concluded that this was a dangerous area to touch in the middle of a stable series, so we were reluctant to restore the old behavior in the 7.8 series, unless the patch turned out to be very simple and easily verified.
remarks: 2013-Jan-02 17:38:19 by danb: I have attached a patch that provides the old behavior. It is simpler than I expected. Jaime, what do you think? 2013-Jan-03 10:08:06 by danb: I thought of one issue related to this patch. Suppose a job was evicted and spooled by a version of condor between 7.7.2 and the version containing this patch. Further suppose that this job was submitted with output and error as basenames, not paths. When resumed, this job would not append to the existing _condor_stdout and _condor_stderr files spooled by 7.7.2+. Instead, it would append to files with the names specified by the user. If instead the job had been spooled by a version prior to 7.7.2, there should be no problem. The same sort of problem was introduced in 7.7.2. Jobs with spooled output from prior to 7.7.2 when restarting under 7.7.2 and newer (without the proposed patch) will start appending to _condor_stdout and _condor_stderr rather than the existing output files with the names specified by the user. Bottom line: for people with spooled output who have not upgraded from 7.6 yet, the proposed patch will make life better. For people with spooled output who have already upgraded to 7.8, the proposed patch could make life worse. To address this, additional logic would be needed in the starter to check for the existence of _condor_stdout/err and to behave accordingly. 2013-Jan-03 12:10:55 by danb: I have prepared a second patch that resumes using the previously spooled output files. However, this detail turns out to be inconsequential. Why? Because the starter opens the output files with the O_TRUNC flag, so previously spooled stdout/stderr is always lost anyway. That seems wrong to me, but it does make our job easier in this instance. There is no need to complicate the patch to deal with previously spooled stdout/stderr files. 2013-Jan-03 12:29:03 by sfiligoi: Just an update from CMS AnaOps. We accept that the filename of stdout/err on the worker node is an undocumented feature, and thus cannot be relied upon. So we are making changes in our code to not rely on a specific file name. Bottom line, we are not pushing for this "bug" to be fixed in the stable 7.8 series anymore. Said that, we would still like a consistent behavior between Condor versions. Please settle on one naming convention, document it, and stick with it. Thanks, Igor for CMS AnaOps
attachments: stdio_names.patch 999 bytes added by danb on 2013-Jan-02 23:39:20 UTC. Restore pre-7.7.2 behavior in how stdout/stderr are named in the execute sandbox. stdio_names_resume_fix.patch 2963 bytes added by danb on 2013-Jan-03 18:20:11 UTC. For the record, here is the more complicated patch that (needlessly) handles the case of previously spool output files from 7.7.2+. Since the starter truncates the output files anyway, I don't think the extra complexity of this patch is worth it.

title: Ticket #1434: Quill Error_Sqllogs table lossage causes disk fill up
description: In file src/condor_tt/ttmanager.cpp, in function void TTManager::handleErrorSqlLog() something stupid happens. Suppose we have a situation where an insertion in the horizontal table fails due to a type mistake on the value (e.g., coresize = "eleventy-billion" instead of coresize = 11000000). At this point, the erroneous query AND the entire schedd_sql.log file is inserted into new a row in the Error_Sqllogs table. So, if you have a 1 Meg schedd_sql.log file, and have 1000 errors in it, you will consume 1GB of storage in the DB by having 1000 new rows inserted in the Error_Sqllogs table with each row having one copy of the schedd_sql.log file. condor_dbmsd will eventually get around to dropping and resetting that table. However, if it isn't running, or there are more errors with a large enough schedd_sql.log file that in one bulk load you fill the disk, you get screwed. The fix we're thinking of at this time is to simply stop appending the log file into the table and fill that entry with a "N/A" string or some such thing when it happens. We need to rethink why that code was storing the entire log like this.

title: Ticket #2832: Parallel collector queries
description: In a high-availability pool, when the primary collector is down, daemons and tools will attempt to query the unreachable machine for 60 seconds before trying one of the secondary collectors. Daemons will avoid the unreachable machine for an hour, then spend a minute in a blocking connection to the primary collector in case it's back up. Tools will spend a minute trying to connect to the dead machine every time. One way to minimize these delays is to query the multiple collectors in parallel. To minimize extra load, a single collector is contacted first. If an initial reply isn't received after several seconds, then connections to the other collectors are begun. Once a collector starts replying, connections to the other collectors are closed.
remarks: 2012-Feb-20 12:30:19 by matt: This could result in expensive query processing that is thrown away. Many TOOL generated collector queries are full dumps of memory. Closing a connection does not preempt the generation of a query response, only the sending of it. Instead, the timeout could be reduced and tools could be allowed to randomly choose between HA collectors. There may be a conflation of timeout for the connection and timeout for the query result. The suggestion is to have a short connection timeout and long response timeout. 2012-Feb-20 14:27:46 by matt: FYI - https://bugzilla.redhat.com/show_bug.cgi?id=472320
creator: jfrey

title: Ticket #6522: Remove cedar "internal" and "ASCII" coding methods

This leads to excess confusion for static analyzers, confusion for humans readers of the code, and slows down execution. We will remove these unsued serialization formats.

title: Ticket #682: Reduce port usage of gass server hack
description: We have a hack to the globus gass server library used in the gt2 gahp to improve parallelism. The globus libraries will only authenticate one connection at a time for a given globus_io handle. For the hack, we create 20 globus_io handles for listening, then copy the file descriptor from the first handle to the other 19 (and close the other fds). We end up with 20 globus_io handles for 1 listening port. This allows us to authenticate 20 incoming connections in parallel. The drawback to this is we need 20 ports at startup, though only one is retained. Igor Sfiligoi is dealing with sites that want to place severe limits on the number of open ports in their firewalls. The hack can be modified to close each additional fd as the additional globus_io handles are created. Then, only 1 additional port is necessary, rather than 19.

title: Ticket #7333: Develop an EC2 provisioner job based on condor_annex
description: We want the ability to provision remote compute resources (for example on Amazon EC2) and then run condor jobs on these resources as part of a workflow. In #5622 we discuss how to integrate a "resource provisioner" into condor_dagman. However that ticket only deals with how a provisioning step fits into a condor workflow. It does not deal with the actual provision logic: how does a running job communicate with Amazon EC2 to allocate resources? How does this job know when resources are ready? How does this job terminate these resources when no longer needed? Now we want to look at the actual logic for the provisioning job. Some important points to think about: How does this job communicate with an external compute service? What are the various states of a provisioning job? How does this job advertise its state to the outside world, such that other forces can act on it? How do we react to failure in a provisioning job? We'll develop such a provisioning job that runs on the CHTC pool for now. A design doc will become available below once I get a ticket number and create it.
remarks: 2020-Apr-15 16:21:50 by tlmiller: How does this job communicate with an external compute service? Why does DAGMan care? Or to put it another way, the next three questions are integration issues, but this one does not appear to be. What are the various states of a provisioning job? Again looking at this from DAGMan's PoV, I think the major question is if we care about submitting the provisioned-for jobs before the provisioner indicates that the resources are ready. If we don't, I'm not sure what DAGMan needs to know. For the user whose credit card is being charged, I don't know. Maybe the job ad, maybe just condor_annex status (or the equivalent tool). How does this job advertise its state to the outside world, such that other forces can act on it? What does DAGMan currently look at? Just the event log, IIRC. The provisioner can probably just chirp whatever it needs into the event log (assuming it needs anything at all). For the user whose credit card is being charged, that's a good question. How do we react to failure in a provisioning job? Since they are nodes, we have a lot of tools already, particularly in managing retries. What we may not have is a good idea of how to handle the need to run a clean-up step. This may be a good reason to presume that most provisioning nodes will actually be sub-dags, if I recall how a FINAL nodes works properly. This has the side-benefit of allowing people to pass around complicated provisioning scripts/workflows while keeping them easy to integrate.

remarks: 2011-Nov-28 10:44:43 by danb: Thanks for the patch, Lukas! In the manual, the behavior of HIBERNATION_PLUGIN_ARGS is explicitly defined: "Used only when the condor_startd is not initially invoking the plug-in to determine the low power states supported." So this patch would alter the defined behavior. Unfortunately, I don't know why the behavior is defined the way it is. Perhaps instead of changing it, we could add a new configuration variable HIBERNATION_PLUGIN_INIT_ARGS? I agree that suppression of stderr is bad, because it makes debugging impossible. However, I am concerned that by mixing stderr with stdout, we would introduce an implicit constraint on the behavior of the hibernation plugin: it must never emit any stderr output except in case of failure. (And in case of failure, only the first line of stderr output is logged.) I think to better handle this case, Condor should provide a popen-like implementation that provides separate stdout and stderr pipes. In addition, it should provide a convenience function that correctly handles reading the full stdout and stderr output into strings and returning the status of the program. title: Ticket #7763: notification = error doesn't send email when shadow holds the job
description: The condor documentation claims that notification = error should send email when the system (but not the user) puts the job on hold). This is reproducible by submitting a job with an input file to be xferred that doesn't exist, and condor_submit'ing it with -disable. Note the lack of email. The root problem here is the code in condor_utils in the shadow is checking to see if the shadow exit_code is set to JOB_SHOULD_HOLD, but this variable isn't passed in, and we just hard code -1.
