title: Ticket #4909: Make tear-down methods safe to call after DaemonCore is deleted
description: We have code that executes at process exit (like destructors for global objects) that may try to cancel things registered with DaemonCore. If DC_Exit() has been called, then DaemonCore has been deleted at this point, which can lead to a crash. To avoid this, we can make DaemonCore cancel methods return immediately if 'this' is NULL. Changes for #4773 exposed an instance of this in the starter. The CStarter object there is a global object that ends up calling daemonCore->Cancel_Timer() upon destruction (via JICLocalSchedd and BaseUserPolicy) when running a local universe job. At present, this only affects Windows, since we call _exit() on all unix platforms, which skips exit-time cleanup code (to be fixed). Prior to #4773, the TimerManager object was a static member of DaemonCore, so Cancel_Timer() didn't look at 'this'. Now, the DaemonCore object has a reference to the singleton TimerManager, and Cancel_Timer() references it through 'this'.

title: Ticket #2424: windows startd does not scale beyond 12 slots
description: Ian Chesal reports scaling problems when the startd is managing more than 12 slots. The system is a 40-core Dell server running Win2k8 Enterprise Server with SP2. The problem appears when many shadows try to activate claims to the startd around the same time. The first few succeed. The rest fail. After some investigation, we determined that the reason for failure is that the startd is spending lots of time (and burning CPU) in Starter::percentCpuUsage(). This led us to discover that USE_PROCD was set to FALSE in the Condor configuration. Ian turned on the procd and there was a noticeable improvement, but the problem is still not completely solved. He is able to get simple sleep jobs running on all the slots, but if he runs a real workflow that uses CPU, many slots spend a lot of time in Claimed/Idle. The procd is spending 100% of its time burning CPU. Looking at the logs, I see some starters exiting with status 1. No starter log exists in these cases, so whatever is causing the starter to fail is happening very early in the process, before logging is initialized. I notice that ProcFamilyMonitor::register_subfamily() starts by taking a snapshot. Since this operation is so expensive in this environment, this likely explains the procd being so busy. However, I do not see why this would cause the starter to fail. Ian tried tests with the following, but he reports no improvement: PID_SNAPSHOT_INTERVAL = 90 JOB_START_COUNT = 1 JOB_START_DELAY = 1

title: Ticket #1208: Dataflow with Files using Dagman
description: This ticket sketches a description of a possible enhancement to the DAGMan functionality. The enhancement is that if you have two nodes in this relationship A->B, when node A produces, and completes, a file Af that B solely requires to run, then B may immediately start, even though A is still running possibly producing other files for other nodes. This mimics much more of a dataflow dependency instead of a job completion dependency. Additionally, when Af is noticed and moved to where ever it needs to go so B can run, an event is written into the event log associated with the node such that we don't try to move the file again in other circumstances. Milestones The branch holding this work is V7_5-dataflow-2-branch. [condor_starter change]: Periodically bring closed output files back to spool [DONE] Implement a means to get the open files of a running process. [DONE] Implement: user turns on dataflow semantics with jobad attr, timer in starter to perform checks. transfer-dataflow-output-files [DONE enough] Modify the FileTransfer object to: Get all pids for job's process tree and get list of open files. #1515 [DONE] Using the filetransfer api, get the list: (filter (closed-file-in-pids-p job-pids) (filter output-file-p (enumerate-sandbox-files job-pids))) Transfer that list back as if ON_EVICT_OR_EXIT. [DONE] [file-transfer object change]: Make it so closed dataflow files are only brought back ONCE. Currently, even though the dataflow file is closed, it is brought back multiple times. If the file is repoened and closed again, maybe it can be brought back again (which would actually violate our assumptions so it needs to be seriously considered), but also only ONCE until the next time. This should be implemented by augmenting the file atalog to allow dynamic insertion of files into it after it has been created. I also need to check at final upload time that if there are dataflow files in the file catalog to NOT transfer them. Assumptions The files that are to be created by an executing node and used in the dataflow must have these semantics. This is more restrictive than how the filetransfer object decides a file is considered an output file or an intermediate file. The created file must not exist in the sandbox manifest. The file is atomically created and opened for use, once. Once the file is closed, it stays closed. There is a way on Linux/Unix to determine the open files a process is using. Condor knows a manifest of the sandbox, to determine when these files are present. There is a means by which the files can be moved asynchronously out of the job execution directory while the job is still running. Feasibility Determination of open files by a process on Linux. If one looks in the directory /proc/<pid>/fd you will find a list of fds opened by the process and the files to which they point. Using the command stat we can see that the read/write status of the fd is available for that file. This information is thusly available. If one knows the manifest of the sandbox, then any file added to the sandbox that is not referenced by an open fd would be considered a candidate for execution interleaving of a future node. Feasible to find files in the correct state on Linux: YES Condor today knows the sandbox manifest. Condor would need functionality to implement asynchronous file transfer while job is still running. Problems Idempotency of output files under retry/eviction/crash conditions. In this scenario: job A starts up file Af is produced. file Af is asynchronously transfered back and committed. execute node crashes/evicts/etc/fails. Job A restarts (also could with RETRY) on potentially different node. What will happen is file Af will appear as an input file in the sandbox when the job restarts. If the job is unware of the previous state it had written, it will regenerate Af, as which point the FileTransfer object will see it as an output file, and transfer it back again--overwriting the first transfer, causing a duplicate dataflow message, and making the entire dataflow possibly inconsistent unless care is taken. If the job is aware of the previous state and does not regenerate Af, then Af will never be transferred back and all is well. Dataflow connections between nodes do not have infinite capacity to store tokens. Example: if in the dataflow A->B, B consumes data tokens at a slower rate than A produces them, we would run out of disk space. So, when we're getting close to our allotment of space denoted for that specific stream, how do we signal A to stop? Suspend the process? other? If a job creates large temporary files, closes them, and reads them as for a table lookup or something similar, then they could be incorrectly flagged as a dataflow file (if the program opens and closes it now and then, but only reads it) and moved back, potentially causing space issues on the submit node or network bandwidth issues. NOTE: This can be fixed by allowing the user to specify via regex a list of files that should be considered to have dataflow semantics. Real world Jobs Some real world jobs don't fall under workflow model. Jobs which do things like: compute result open file with append write result close file repeat Jobs which overwrite their previous output files on restart. Real world examples of jobs that could benefit Craig Struble had a workflow where an image generation phase of N processes generated N images (where N is 200,000 or so) and then an accumulation phase summed the image into a single image. His main problem was that if you rendered workflow this as a DAG, you'd need storage space for 200,000 images--which were individually large and he didn't have that much space. Since DAGMan can't run a job until all of their parents complete, we are forced to store all 200,000 images before the accumulator process is run. The solution we came up with was there is a DAG producing the N images and the space needed for returning images is controlled by DAG throttling. Then, the post scripts on the image nodes copy the resultant image into a directory using unix rename()--which is atomic, where a seperate scheduler universe process is polling every X seconds and accumulating the partial results into the final image. When the DAG finishes, the final node writes a 'done' messge into the directory which completes the dataflow. This real world job is the exact type of dataflow job that the feature of this ticket could solve. References Flow Based Programming Flow Based Programming - Book Advances in Dataflow Programming Languages - This is particularly good. A data-driven workflow language for grids based on array programming principles - Interesting.

title: Ticket #7504: Expose version comparison in ClassAds
description: Doing version comparisons in ClassAds is a pain (see #2395 for examples), so let's provide some functions to make them easier: versioncmp(left, right) for consistency with strcmp() versionXY(left, right) for LT, LE, EQ, GE, and GT, for completeness version_in_range(version, min, max) for convenience These will be implemented with our existing natural_cmp() function. original description We should add one or more version comparison function(s) to ClassAds. We have a C function, natural_cmp, which does the job, so it's only a question of determining the right function names. Attached to this ticket is a first-pass implementation. It implements versioncmp() for consistency with strcmp(). It implements versionXY() for LT, LE, EQ, GE, and GT, for completeness. It has been suggested that we add a range-comparison function, for additional convenience. Something like version_in_range( low, version, high ) seems reasonable to me (assuming the other functions exist). The first-pass implementation is in ClassAds proper, rather than compat classads, so that the function is universally available. However, since libclassad should not depend on libcondor_utils, the natural_cmp() function is -- in this patch -- simply copied into fnCall.cpp, which is kind of evil. We should either move the new function(s) into compat classads, or do something saner than code duplication.

title: Ticket #2706: Schedd should kill claim when lease expires
description: When the claim lease between the schedd and startd expires, the startd kills the job and leaves the claimed state. The schedd doesn't do anything. In some cases, the shadow will notice that its connection to the starter has closed and exit with an error code. But if the startd machine drops off the network without a trace, the shadow may not notice the dead connection for 2 hours. To avoid this situation, the schedd should check for expired claim leases and abort the claim (and the shadow) when it sees an expired lease. Note: Having the schedd detect expired claim leases depends on the new startd-sends-alives protocol. Since this has been the default for a while and we want to remove the old schedd-sends-alives protocol, this dependency shouldn't be a problem.
remarks: 2011-Dec-13 06:26:38 by matt: Is this a bug in the Schedd's handling of STARTD_SENDS_ALIVES=TRUE? When do you plan to remove STARTD_SENDS_ALIVE=FALSE? 2011-Dec-13 10:06:10 by jfrey: I'd say it's a bug in STARTD_SENDS_ALIVES=TRUE. We want to put the fix into 7.6 if it's simple, which I believe it will be. As for removing STARTD_SENDS_ALIVES=FALSE, I think we'll need to wait for 7.9. It was only in 7.5.4 that we changed the default from False to True and had the schedd alone decide which value to use. 2011-Dec-13 12:56:30 by jfrey: I've attached a patch that makes the schedd relinquish a claim and kill the shadow if the claim lease expires. It works for claim that are running non-parallel jobs. The patch also fixes a bug when the schedd has a mixture of startd-sends-alive and schedd-sends-alive jobs. 2011-Dec-15 14:05:28 by tannenba: CODE REVIEW Looks good, just some minor changes - add comment at inserted time(NULL) to explain it is to deal w/ mixed startd and schedd send alive pools. get time(NULL) out of the while loop; can just use "now" remove extraneous lease_duration > 0 check in last conditional, it is gratuitous make sure srec isn't NULL before de-refing it don't try and send vacate to the startd - the lease expired on that side as well, so it isn't needed, and further more the schedd prolly cannot talk to the startd now anyhow, so it is just a waste of precious bodily fluids... i mean schedd resources... 2011-Dec-15 15:12:04 by jfrey: Patch committed and pushed with Todd's recommended changes.

title: Ticket #4328: Failed file transfers can be treated as successful by schedd/shadow
description: When the schedd and shadow transfer a job's files, they create a child process to handle the actual transfer. The exit status of the child process is examined to determine whether the transfer succeeded. The child will use exit code 0 to indicate failure and exit code 1 to indicate success. But the parent process considers any non-zero exit code a success (exiting via a signal is a failure, see #3104). The child process can have a non-zero exit status in several failure cases. Any call to ASSERT() or EXCEPT() results in an exit code of 4. A dprintf() failure results in an exit code of 44. The parent process must consider any exit condition other than an exit code of 1 as a failure. The parent process also expects to read a status update over a pipe from the child after the child exits (in FileTransfer::ReadTransferPipeMsg()). Failure to read this message will cause the transfer to be flagged as failed. But the final call to ReadTransferPipeMsg() could read an IN_PROGRESS message and not the FINAL_UPDATE message, in which case the transfer won't be flagged as failed. After the final call to ReadTransferPipeMsg(), FileTransfer::Reaper() should verify that Info.status==XFER_STATUS_DONE.
remarks: 2014-Apr-22 15:56:22 by jfrey: This could explain the behavior described in #4300. 2014-Apr-23 14:34:11 by tlmiller: Code Review Approved.

title: Ticket #3117: Why is Condor slow when hostname != FQDN?
description: It appears (see parent ticket) that when Condor runs with DNS enabled, but the hostname != FQDN, that it runs very slowly. Since this is arguably the correct configuration for many execute nodes (e.g., the collector or submit nodes exist in DNS but the execute node does not), this should be investigated and corrected.
remarks: 2012-Jul-11 11:17:36 by kronenfe: I don't think there is slowness due to a non-fqdn. I think that the delays can be attributed to a bug in the test suite. Here is the high level summary of that bug: a) The machine was advertising things without an FQDN b) The "start Condor up" code was expecting the startd to advertise with an FQDN c) The "start Condor up" code would timeout after roughly 3 minutes and say it hadn't properly started - even though it had. The bug here is that even though it timed out it would continue on to run the test d) Most of the tests would succeed. Except with an additional 3 minutes tacked on. These delays would accumulate and eventually trigger the global timeout. Note: the tests that did fail were mostly (all?) because they were looking for an FQDN in some manner. For example, we would query "condor_q -sub exec-13.batlab.org" but that would return false because the schedd had submitted itself with just exec-13 and no domain. I didn't check every failing test - only about 2 or 3 out of 7 - but since they all started succeeding when we fixed the domain I think this is a reasonable conclusion. TJ thinks there might have been a delay so I will assign this ticket to him in case he can find some further proof.

title: Ticket #3402: file transfer race condition in parallel universe
description: When using parallel universe, it is possible for the job to be marked as finished without transferring the output from some nodes in the job. There is a race between node 0 reporting its exit status and output being transferred from all the other nodes. When file transfer in the shadow uses blocking mode, the race is between initiation of transfer and processing the exit status of node 0. When non-blocking file transfer is used in the shadow (as in #3333), the race is between completion of file transfer and processing the exit status of node 0. In both cases, some nodes may not get a chance to transfer any files at all. In the non-blocking case, the transfers for some nodes may be halted midway.
remarks: 2012-Dec-28 15:02:43 by danb: The race condition goes away if the attribute ParallelShutdownPolicy is set to "WAIT_FOR_ALL". The default is "WAIT_FOR_NODE0". Therefore, I think the race condition is actually expected behavior.
creator: danb

title: Ticket #6600: net use command in a job on Windows leaks consoles
description: From one of our Windows condor users I had an interesting problem that we ran into using condor and the net use command that I wanted to sure with you. Basically what was happening is a set of condor jobs would always run the command net use W: \\path\to\share After some amount of job runs we noticed the W:\ was no longer available and jobs would just fail. After some investigating we discovered the following: Condor uses individual lsa logon sessions for each set of processes spawned off of the startd. The condor daemons use the native windows lsa functions to store credentials and launch new processes in session 0 (logon session). aka the services desktop. When you launch a process in session 0, you get a new lsa session id for each process. This creates separation so that one process you launch into session 0 doesn't impact other processes in the same session running as the same user. In a normal lsa session within session 0, you will see a new DosDevice created in \Sessions\0\DosDevices\<lsa session id> with only a Global symlink (which points to \Global??, the global devices mapped at \Device such as Harddisk0). This is fine, and you see the device go away when the session gets cleaned up. The problem occurs when you run the net use command within one of these lsa sessions running in session 0. When you do this, the DfsClient will create a new symlink object per lsa session in each lsa session DosDevice directory. (the symlink points to something like \Device\Mup\DfsClient\;W:<lsa session id>\Bala01\World). Looking through the condor source, it seems that in the daemon_core_main and condor_starter code a console is created for each starter. This is used to handle stdin/stdout as well as console commands to soft-kill processes (ctrl-c, etc.). In a normal scenario, this is fine, but I believe that when the DfsClient creates the symlink object, it connects to the console in your session and tests connectivity to the share you're mapping. Condor will run freeConsole, which will normally release objects and free up the lsa sessions that were created; however, since the =DfsClient= now has a connection to the console, the console won't actually be freed. The starter exits out, and your sessions and connections are left behind. This is why we have so many connections. This can only be reproduced in session 0, You can't reproduce this on an RDP or WinRM session because you will always get the same lsa session, and will only ever create one symlink object. The root of the problem seems to be that the DfsClient creates this mapping, and leaves the connection open for a long time. I'm not certain how long the DfsClient will keep these sessions open

title: Ticket #5885: enable the schedd to perform job classad transforms upon submission
description: [ Note: this ticket hopefully replaces #4804 and satisfies #5613 ] We want the schedd to be able to transform an incoming job classad upon submission. Transformations can be configured via either job_router style route classads, or via the tranform scripting language created for #5805. The schedd will attempt to apply all job transforms specified by new knob JOB_TRANSFORM_NAMES in order. A job transform should be skipped if a) the transform specified in the config file is not a syntactically valid classad, or b) a requirements expression in the transform ad evaluates to false. Transforms are applied to each newly submitted job in a transaction before the transaction is committed and also before SUBMIT_REQUIREMENTS are checked. Thus, a transform can edit values for either protected or immutable attributes, but an attempt to edit a protected attribute (such as ProcId or Owner) will cause the transform to fail thereby aborting the entire transaction. See the Remark below for examples and a simple smoke-test.

title: Ticket #5186: Starter should log by default allowed CPU, Mem, Disk
description: Glideinwms uses the information logged into the starter log to gather useful stats like, number of jobs ran by a glidein, good-put, bad-put etc. Starter does not log in its log by default max allowed resources like CPU, MEMORY and DISK to job. In case of single core glideins the info could be reliably extracted/assumed but not in case of the multicore glideins. This info is important in case of multicore glideins and without this, it is not possible to reliably compute the good-put/efficiency of jobs. A single line logging this info by default after the job starts will be good enough.

title: Ticket #2643: Win32 Condor tries to use user from the submit host on remote host
description: Discovered this when trying to use condor-c between two Windows submit machines, but the problem problem crops up in other areas. The basic problem is that condor tries to switch to a user@machine account on the remote submit machine using the originating submit machine's machine name. In my test the originating submit machine is called CRANE and the user is johnkn. johnkn has local-machine accounts on both machines The ScheddLog on the remote submit machine shows the following error: 11/17/11 10:05:49 (pid:3668) perm::init: Lookup Account Name johnkn failed (err=1332), trying Everyone This fails because the remote machine (VM-CRANE) is actually looking up account CRANE\johnkn which does not exist on VM-CRANE. What it should be doing to make Windows consitent with the way Linux works it be checking for the a johnkn account without a domain name.

title: Ticket #959: Linking both old and new ClassAds on AIX
description: Building V7_3-new_classads-branch on AIX is failing due to this error: ld: 0711-781 ERROR: TOC overflow. title: Ticket #3681: OpenStack scaling woes.
description: (Adapted from Tony's summary of 2013-06-06.) This incident ticket will serve as a parent ticket for the individual actionable tickets related to this incident. Environment RHEL5, 32-bit HTCondor 7.9.6 (On SLC5) OpenStack Essex The HTCondor queue is full of held EC2 jobs. These jobs are generally held because of a RunInstances() failure. None are spot instances, so we'll ignore that code path for the remainder of this report. HTCondor Problems When the grid manager restarts, each EC2 job in the queue looks for two attributes: the client token and the instance ID. Because of the environment (the third point above), almost all of the jobs have a client token but not an instance ID. Because of a bug in HTCondor (for which I believe I have a fix), even jobs which actually have instance IDs will appear as if they don't. Therefore, (effectively) every (held) job in the queue will cause the grid manager to issue a RunInstances() command. Since we have and use a client token, this operation should be idempotent; should therefore never accidentally start more than one instance per job. However, OpenStack neither supports idempotent RunInstances() nor complains when you supply a client token, which it then ignores. We must therefore return to using SSH keypair IDs for our two-phase commit; see ticket #3682. Since this RunInstance() command fails, the jobs will eventually go back on hold. However, a thousand RunInstances() calls on the OpenStack controller cause it grief. We should therefore batch RunInstances() commands; see ticket #3606. It would, however, be even better to skip the RunInstances() call entirely: see ticket #3672. In addition, on each startup, the grid manager issues two DescribeInstances() command, each of which also cause the controller grief. The first is used to ping the controller, to see if it's up. We should try to find some other, cheaper, no-op; see ticket #FIXME; the second is the batch status update. In addition, on each start up, the grid manager issue a DescribeInstances() command for each removed job, to determine if the removed job corresponds to instance which began running without the grid manager noticing. This calls must also be batched, or more likely, rendered redundant by trusting the results of the batched status update. This path is fraught with race condition peril; see ticket #3683. Finally, if a the batch status update's call to DescribeInstances() succeeds, it will most likely result in a large number of jobs changing state. This results in each changed job shifting from GM_SUBMITTED to GM_PROBE_JOB, where we ask the controller for more details about the job. This call could probably be made more efficient by filtering by the instance ID on the controller rather than the client. This call could probably be made redundant by expanding the amount of information returned from the EC2 GAHP from the EC2_VM_STATUS_ALL command; see ticket #3683. Other Problems Since these problems occur (mostly) when the grid manager restarts, other factors must have been causing the ongoing problems: HTCondor eventually finishes (if necessary, by timing out requests) and the jobs all go back on hold, at which point the grid manager dies with its work complete. We found three reasons why the grid manager was restarting frequently: A bug in glideinWMS was discovered where it was releasing held jobs, even though it was configured not to. (Releasing a job when the queue is entirely held causes the grid manager to start.) A work-around has been put in place and a permanent fix had already been checked into the source code repository. A bug in the grid manager was causing it to segfault with great frequency: 191 times between the fourth and fifth of June. Although these events resulted in core dumps, their stacks appear to have been smashed and rendered useless for debugging. The crashes seem to correlate well with the number of EC2 jobs, of which there were roughly a thousand (as opposed to the previous level of several hundred) between the fourth and fifth of June. Manually running condor_rm also restarts the grid manager. The problem is compounded because the grid manager checks, for each job in this situation (a client token but no instance ID), if an instance started before removing the job; doing so causes another call to DescribeInstances(). Conclusions We have three main tasks: (#3682) Reintroducing the SSH keypair ID style of two-phase commits. This will probably require that the user specify that they're using a service which doesn't support client tokens, since we can't readily tell. (#3683) We need to minimize the number of calls we make to DescribeInstances(), especially when starting up and removing jobs. (#3701) Determine and correct the cause of the segfaults.

title: Ticket #6179: There should be a metaknob for mapping users to groups
description: It will be a common use case of the classad usermap function to map users into accounting groups, so there should be a metaknob that makes that easy. We will base this (loosely) on the transform that LIGO created to map users into some custom attributes that behave much like the accounting group attributes. The transforms use the following config config suggested by ToddT to Ligo # # LIGO JOB TRANSFORM AND VALIDATE RULES # 1) converting the classads for AcctGroup,AcctGroupUser into LigoSearchTag,LigoSearchUser. # 2) Deleting AcctGroup,AcctGroupUser,AccountingGroup # 3) Asserting that LigoSearchTag is a member of a valid list or matches a regex # 4) Assert that LigoSearchUser is equal to "Owner" or their "LIGO name". # # Make a map representing valid LigoSearchTag values; in # this example, valid string values are "val1", "val2", or # any string value that begins with the character 'a' (to # demonstrate use of a regex in the list). SCHEDD_CLASSAD_USER_MAP_NAMES = $(SCHEDD_CLASSAD_USER_MAP_NAMES) ValidSearchTags # Note: You can put this map into a seperate file via using knob # CLASSAD_USER_MAPFILE_ValidSearchTags = /some/file/path CLASSAD_USER_MAPDATA_ValidSearchTags @=end * val1 found * val2 found * /^a/ found @end # Make a map where the Owner attribute is the key, and then the # value is a set of legit LigoSearchUser values. SCHEDD_CLASSAD_USER_MAP_NAMES = $(SCHEDD_CLASSAD_USER_MAP_NAMES) ValidSearchUsers # Note: You can put this map into a seperate file via using knob # CLASSAD_USER_MAPFILE_ValidSearchUsers = /some/file/path CLASSAD_USER_MAPDATA_ValidSearchUsers @=end * tpdownes thomas.downes * mathguys peter.couvares,thomas.downs,kent.wenger * tannenba todd.tannenbaum,mr.condor @end # Here we take care of # 1) converting the classads for AcctGroup,AcctGroupUser into LigoSearchTag,LigoSearchUser. # 2) Deleting AcctGroup,AcctGroupUser,AccountingGroup # If AcctGroup not defined, set LigoSearchTag to "None". # If AcctGroupUser not defined, set LigoSearchUser to the Owner. JOB_TRANSFORM_NAMES = $(JOB_TRANSFORM_NAMES) InsertLigoTags JOB_TRANSFORM_InsertLigoTags @=end [ COPY_AcctGroup = "LigoSearchTag"; COPY_AcctGroupUser = "LigoSearchUser"; DELETE_AcctGroup = true; DELETE_AcctGroupUser = true; DELETE_AccountingGroup = true; EVAL_SET_LigoSearchTag = LigoSearchTag ?: "None"; EVAL_SET_LigoSearchUser = LigoSearchUser ?: Owner; ] @end # Here we take care of # 3) Asserting that LigoSearchTag is a member of a valid list or matches a regex # Add a submit requirement that LigoSearchTag is set to something unrecognized. SUBMIT_REQUIREMENT_NAMES = $(SUBMIT_REQUIREMENT_NAMES) ValidateSearchTag SUBMIT_REQUIREMENT_ValidateSearchTag = \ userMap("ValidSearchTags",LigoSearchTag) isnt undefined SUBMIT_REQUIREMENT_ValidateSearchTag_REASON = \ strcat("Invalid value for LigoSearchTag: ",LigoSearchTag ?: "<undefined>") # Here we take care of # 4) Assert that LigoSearchUser is equal to "Owner" or their "LIGO name". # Add submit requirement that LigoSearchUser must be # set to be the same as Owner or as a valid "LIGO name" according to our map. SUBMIT_REQUIREMENT_NAMES = $(SUBMIT_REQUIREMENT_NAMES) ValidateSearchUser SUBMIT_REQUIREMENT_ValidateSearchUser = \ Owner =?= LigoSearchUser || \ userMap("ValidSearchUsers",Owner,LigoSearchUser) is LigoSearchUser SUBMIT_REQUIREMENT_ValidateSearchUser_REASON = \ strcat("Invalid value for LigoSearchUser: ", LigoSearchUser ?: "<undefined>", ".\n", \ " Valid values are: ",userMap("ValidSearchUsers",Owner)) # Finally, make sure nobody can change any attributes we set above IMMUTABLE_JOB_ATTRS = $(IMMUTABLE_JOB_ATTRS) \ AcctGroup AcctGroupUser AccountingGroup \ LigoSearchTag LigoSearchUser

title: Ticket #4144: Improve systemd support
description: There are a few features in systemd that we can utilize to improve the user experience. In particular, the following come to mind: Socket activation: systemd can reserve one or more sockets for HTCondor at boot time and pass them to the master (this would solve a very annoying problem if the HTCondor socket overlaps with the ephemeral port range and someone steals the socket on restart). This would require shared_port to be used, but would even allow us to have systemd control the precise sockets (IPv4 / IPv6 / unix) and network interfaces used by HTCondor. This is something HTCondor does by itself, but would now be done in a way consistent with the rest of the system. Watchdog: systemd has a well-defined heartbeat protocol we can utilize. This would allow systemd to restart the master if it ever hard-hangs. Status message: The condor_master can push an arbitrary string which is included as a part of the output of "systemctl status condor.service". I think it'd be useful to list all of the daemons which are currently down. If the master calls EXCEPT(), we should record it here. journald logging: We can send log messages directly to journald which can do fancy indexing by default (as well as forwarding on to syslog). See http://cgit.freedesktop.org/systemd/systemd/tree/src/systemd/sd-daemon.h for more info.

title: Ticket #2993: Allow draining to be cancelled
description: Currently, condor_defrag will not drain a machine if DEFRAG_WHOLE_MACHINE_EXPR evaluates to True for one or more p-slots in the startd. I propose that if a machine is already draining and DEFRAG_WHOLE_MACHINE_EXPR evaluates to True for one or more p-slots, that the draining will then be cancelled if a new condor_defrag knob DEFRAG_CAN_CANCEL is set to true. This is a very important change for HCC, as we have a stream of 8-core jobs and do not want to wait for an entire 64-core node to free up. Patch incoming.
remarks: 2012-May-15 11:45:31 by tannenba: Could you get what you want today without any patches by configuring your 64-way machines with eight 8-core pslots? 2012-May-15 11:46:30 by bbockelm: I wish. I already asked danb: condor_defrag works at the startd level, not at the p-slot level. 2012-May-15 15:47:47 by danb: Draining partitionable slots rather than machines was rejected during the design phase. In a possible future version, Miron wanted the interface between defrag and startd to be a request for a quantity of drained resources, not a request for a specific subset of the resources to be drained. Statically partitioning the resources across multiple startds is one way to achieve draining of partial machines in the current system. This would not work if you have policies that require the slots to all be under the management of a single startd (e.g. slot attributes). 2012-May-15 17:40:07 by tannenba: Patch 2 below being tested out on a cluster at HCC... 2012-May-16 10:58:51 by danb: Hi Brian, Review of patch 2: The intermingling of the stop-draining-early logic with the existing start-draining logic in Defrag::poll() seems to have a few quirks. For example, the following pre-existing optimization in Defrag::poll() could now cause the stop-early logic not to happen when it should: if( num_draining >= m_max_draining ) { dprintf(D_ALWAYS,"Doing nothing, because DEFRAG_MAX_CONCURRENT_DRAINING=%d and there are %d draining machines.\n", m_max_draining, num_draining); return; } else if( num_draining < 0 ) { dprintf(D_ALWAYS,"Doing nothing, because DEFRAG_MAX_CONCURRENT_DRAINING=%d and the query to count draining machines failed.\n", m_max_draining); return; } There are a few other similar cases. More fundamentally, the stop-early logic is using the same loop over candidates as the start-draining logic. Therefore, drain cancelation will only happen for draining machines that still happen to match DEFRAG_REQUIREMENTS. This works with the default requirements expression, and I can imagine that it would happen to work in most cases where the expression is customized, but at the very least, this quirk would need to be documented. As a user, I might not have expected DEFRAG_REQUIREMENTS to affect which draining machines would be chosen to stop early. If, on the other hand, we detangled the stop-early logic from the draining logic, then the question is whether a new configuration variable should be added to constrain which machines are considered. I think the answer is yes. In that case, perhaps the boolean DEFRAG_CAN_CANCEL could be eliminated in favor of an expression that matches machines for which draining should be stopped. Example: DEFRAG_CANCEL_REQUIREMENTS = $(DEFRAG_WHOLE_MACHINE_EXPR). One last minor concern is that cancellation of draining by defrag could undo draining that was initiated by condor_drain. That could be desired or not. There is not currently anything advertised in the draining startd ad that indicates why the draining was initiated. If there were, this could be used in the stop-early policy to avoid conflicting with administrator-initiated activity. I think this concern is minor, because the administrator has several workarounds available. 2012-Jul-02 14:39:22 by tannenba: Brian, will you be able to create a patch 3 to address the issues in the code review above on patch 2 ? 2012-Jul-16 13:37:27 by danb: Brian's new patch looks great to me. I have committed it.

Slightly cleaned up patch. condor_partial_defrag_v3.patch 9052 bytes added by bbockelm on 2012-Jul-16 17:28:59 UTC. Revised patch to address Dan's comments. The biggest change is to separate out the cancellation into a separate function call, preventing the two sets of functionality from interfering with each other. Added a new parameter, DEFRAG_CANCEL_REQUIREMENTS (defaults to $(DEFRAG_WHOLE_MACHINE_EXPR) ); when this evaluates to True for a node in the draining state, cancellation will be attempted. title: Ticket #1716: condor_getcwd() foiled by getcwd() libc bug on solaris
description: getcwd() has a bug under solaris as described here: getcwd() bug This affects Condor because condor_getcwd() manually allocates memory trying to find a big enough buffer such that it can hold the path in question. However, when getcwd() is called in a directory whose real path is > PATH_MAX, it will NEVER return anything other than NULL and ERANGE, even if the passed in buffer and size is plenty big enough to hold the path. The fix should be in the if (errno == ERANGE) code block in condor_getcwd() function to check that if buflen is > 20 Megs, it is probably an error and the function should bail. I think we can survive with < 20 Meg paths for a good long time.... :) This bug was found by our unit tests.

title: Ticket #6529: condor_q should have a mode showing idle jobs that will never match
description: There should be a mode of condor_q (actually variation of condor_q -analyze) where the output is the list of jobs that do not match any resources. This new output will be enabled by a new command line flag: -unmatchable When -unmatchable is used with the -analyze flag, it will cause the output to be lists of job id's with one of two headings. either "No slots match" which indicates that the job(s) do not match any slots, and "All slots reject" which indicates that the jobs match one or more slots, but that none of those slots match the jobs in return. condor_q -unmatchable -analyze -- Schedd: user@schedd.domain : <xxx.xxx.xxx.xxx:xxxx?... No slots match autocluster 1, jobs : 10784.0 10785.0 10785.1 All slots reject autocluster 2, jobs : 10786.0 The other way that -unmatchable can be used is as an additional constraint to any of the normal condor_q queries (other than -batch). In this mode, the output of condor_q is normal, but only jobs that are unmatchable are displayed. In particular, -unmatchable can be used with -total and with -af condor_q -unmatchable -tot -- Schedd: user@schedd.domain : <xxx.xxx.xxx.xxx:xxxx?... Total for query: 4 jobs; 0 completed, 0 removed, 4 idle, 0 running, 0 held, 0 suspended condor_q -unmatch -tot -af Jobs 4 The -unmatchable argument can be used with -machine, -mconst or -slotads although this may give results that are misleading since it will not be matchmaking with all of the slot in your pool. Also, Like everything else condor_q does, only the current user's jobs will be considered unless the -allusers argument is used. WARNING. On a large pool, condor_q -unmatchable is quite expensive because it fetchs all of the machine ads from the Collector in long form. It also fetches jobs from the Schedd in long form, although any constraint, username, or jobid list will reduce the amount of data the schedd returns somewhat.

title: Ticket #723: leave_in_queue documentation changes for -spool option
description: leave_in_queue (AKA LeaveJobInQueue in the job classad) is documented as defaulting to false. This is true... unless you're using the -spool option to condor_submit. In that case it defaults to leave_in_queue = JobStatus == 4 && (CompletionDate =?= UNDEFINED ||\ CompletionDate == 0 || ((CurrentTime - CompletionDate) < 864000)) That policy will keep the job in the queue for 10 days after completing. A user might instead prefer to have the job removed once the output is retrieved with condor_transfer_data. It might look something like this: leave_in_queue = (JobStatus == 4) && ((StageOutFinish =?= UNDEFINED) ||\ (StageOutFinish == 0)) (Note: above was changed from StageOutStart to StageOutFinish, as it more logically matches the intent.) If the user doesn't want his output (say, because the job itself will upload the results somewhere), they might want to set it explicitly to FALSE. This is only necessary if using -spool, as this is normally the default. leave_in_queue = FALSE Documentation on StageOutStart and StageOutFinish: When a job is spooled to the remote site (using condor_submit -spool or Condor-C), Condor will hold onto the output in the spool while the job waits Completed in the queue. condor_transfer_data can be used to retrieve the output, and Condor-C will do so automatically. When retrieval begins StageOutStart will be added to the job's ClassAd, set to the current time in Unix epoch time. When retrieval ends, StageOutFinish will be set to the current time in Unix epoch time. While it is possible to set these with +StageOutStart=something or +StageOutFinish=something in a submit file, it is not recommended.

title: Ticket #4847: Collector doesn't listen on UDP 9618 with shared_port, IPv6, and IPv4
description: (This ticket was split off from #4833.) If shared_port, IPv6, and IPv4 are enabled, then the collector does not listen on IPv6 UDP 9618. This is because DaemonCore::InitCommandSockets assumes that TCP and UDP sockets are on the same port. In the case of the collector using shared port, the collector listens on UDP port 9618 and the shared_port listens on TCP 9618 - breaking the code's assumption.
remarks:
2015-Jan-16 11:21 by tlmiller: As far as I can tell, it's a bug that the collector is trying to bind to a UDP port when shared port is enabled at all. The port should never be used. (Who would the collector ever tell about it? I guess maybe a collector tree, but it seems like this shouldn't generally be happening.) That being said, I think you've misidentified the code's assumption. The target ports can only differ from the requested ports if the requested ports were dynamically assigned. If they are, then we assume that InitCommandSocket() (singular) will do what it's supposed to and fail if it can't bind both the TCP and the UDP port. In point of actual fact, I don't think it does -- neither TJ nor I could find where, if InitCommandSocket() were given fixed port numbers, it actually binds the TCP port. Our best guess as to why it actually works right now is that the master uses a different method when it creates sockets for people to inherit, and nobody ever actually asks for an extra command socket on a specified port. This would tend to imply the master isn't doing the right thing here, but I need to investigate further. 2015-Jan-17 07:48:35 by bbockelm: When the collector and shared_port are enabled (and if COLLECTOR_USES_SHARED_PORT is left to the default of true), then the shared_port will listen on TCP 9618 (forwarding non-shared-port requests to the collector). Then, the collector will bind to UDP 9618 and a dynamic TCP port (this is because the remote daemons will still try to update via UDP). Hence, for the case where the collector host is using shared port, port=-1 and udp_port=9618. However, the code targetTCPPort = targetUDPPort = rs->get_port(); make an invalid assumption that port = udp_port. This causes the collector to break when shared_port is enabled in master. 2015-Jan-26 10:56:25 by adesmet: Based on discussion with ToddM, I believe this is how InitCommandSockets should work: If udp_port==1: Bind to a v4 TCP port as specified by port, all other ports (v4 UDP, v6 TCP, v6 UDP) should match the v4 TCP. If udp_port==port: As if udp_port==1 If udp_port!=1 && udp_port !=port: v4 TCP should get same port as v6 TCP, v4 UD should get same port as v6 UDP, but TCP and UDP don't need to match. 2015-Jan-26 13:29:26 by tlmiller: Provisional patch. title: Ticket #7338: Input file transfer should preserve relative paths
description: If the input directory contains ten thousand files, but any particular job needs only (say) two of them, then the following submit file will (should) work, but is amazingly inefficient: arguments = input/$(PROC).h input/$(PROC).f transfer_input_files = input The obvious fix is to instead say arguments = input/$(PROC).h input/$(PROC).f transfer_input_files = input/$(PROC).h input/$(PROC).f but this does not work, because transfer_input_files transfers all individually-named files to the root of the sandbox. Although the work-around in this example is easy (strip the leading input/ from each element of arguments), some jobs may really need a particular directory structure to function properly. Rather than make users with such jobs write a wrapper script, we should allow them to specify that they'd like to keep the relative paths they specify in their inputs. This work should be considered in combination with #7269 and #7270.
remarks: 2019-Oct-24 13:31:01 by anderson: It is also important that the directory structure be preserved when it is transferred, and for bonus points allow a white list and/or black list regexp() for what should or shouldn't be transferred--think /bin/rsync --recursive with and without --include and --exclude rules. 2019-Oct-24 14:17:48 by tlmiller: Maybe I'm misunderstanding the ticket, but I think HTCondor already does this. Does the following not do what you want when 'caches' is a directory? transfer_input_files = injection.xml, caches 2019-Oct-29 15:39:08 by tlmiller: Based on the call today, the issue is that transfer_input_files = input transfers too many files (to the point of causing problems), but transfer_inptut_files = input/a/1 input/b/2 input/a/3 results in the sandbox (partial listing): dir_1234: 1 2 3 which is not OK. I looked for transfer_input_remaps; we have an internal function with a similar name, but it's presently not available for end-users. Sorry any confusion. The general consensus of the call was that the HTCondor approach would probably be to integrate with #7269 and #7270, so that the new file transfer attributes would preserve directory structure. In the short term, you might be able to play games with symlinks (or hardlinks, if necessary) and create a directory structure for each job that has only the relevant files in it, and then transfer the whole thing. original ticket body follows This has become a major obstacle to porting LIGO pipelines to grid resources. e.g. input files are injection.xml, caches/H1-frames.lcf, caches/L1-frames.lcf and the command line for the job is normally --inj injection.xml --H1-data caches/H1-frames.lcf --L1-data caches/L1-frames.lcf. title: Ticket #5610: windows debug build doesn't link to debug build of boost-python
description: When building on Windows in Debug mode, the python bindings are linked to the non-debug version of boost-python. There is some hackery involved in fooling the linker into resolving everything anyway, but the result is non-functional bindings. The correct solution is to link with the debug version of boost-python, and to prevent pyconfig.h from seeing the _DEBUG define so that we end up with debug boost but not the debug version of Python (python27_d.dll). the boost headers will insure that python doesn't see the _DEBUG flag, but for this to work, we must always include python headers via the boost/python headers rather than using them naked.

title: Ticket #5240: collector crashes on RHEL7 when more than 1023 fds active
description: The collector will SIGABRT on the cs pool's new RHEL7 machine when more than 1024 file descriptors are active. The collector fails a compiler-generated assertion in FD_SET in selector.cpp, because we compile with -D_FORTIFY_SOURCE=2, and fortify "knows" that fd_sets can only have 1024 fd's in them, even though we go out of our way to malloc up larger fd_sets. Technically, we're breaking the rules by not using fd_set explicitly, but this trick has works for many versions of unix. For 8.2.10, I'll turn off -D_FORTIFY_SOURCE for selector.cpp only, and we'll need to think of a better solution for 8.4 or 8.5. Going all the way to epoll would be nice, but a little disruptive for a stable series.

description: James pointed me to a dying CMS schedd and I found something interesting. There are multiple "gaps" in the log where there is no activity (this is on a schedd which averages many hundred log messages per minute). After the gaps, there is always this message: 10/21/13 22:00:10 (pid:5304) condor_write(): Socket closed when trying to write 29 bytes to <$IP_V4_ADDRESS:37107>, fd is 20 The message immediately before varies - always in a different part of the code. To me, this is strong evidence that we are seeing blocking in condor_write. The call to the selector in that function is approximately this sequence (stripping out error handling and other conditionals): selector.execute(); selector.has_ready(); selector.fd_ready( fd, Selector::IO_READ ) ; nro = recv(fd, tmpbuf, 1, MSG_PEEK); // this blocks If the recv blocks but eventually gets data, you can have this: 10/21/13 22:31:19 (pid:16982) condor_write() failed: send() 4096 bytes to <$IPV4_ADDRESS:43363> returned -1, timeout=20, errno=32 Broken pipe. In our case, the former error message occurred after the schedd blocked for 15 minutes; the latter, 25 minutes. Blocking here was deadly - a huge number of jobs failed out immediately afterwards and the schedd strangled itself to death (well, into swap...). Note that the Linux man page explicitly says that if select() returns a FD as ready to read, it DOES NOT mean that subsequent read/recv will be non-blocking, even for a single byte! If you want to have non-blocking IO, then you must mark the socket as non-blocking. The simplest solution is to add a non-blocking flag for the duration of this function. I'm not totally convinced we need to ever select on read. Why we do this is lost to history.
remarks: 2013-Oct-22 13:58:40 by tannenba: In HTCondor CEDAR, when the timeout(x) method is invoked on a tcp socket and x is greater than 0, the socket is put into non-blocking mode. In your above log snippet, note that condor_write states the timeout is 20 - and thus this socket should already have been placed into non-blocking mode. Thus either your guess about what is causing the blocking is incorrect, or somehow the socket ended up with a non-zero cedar timeout and escaped having it set to non-blocking (maybe some relatively 'new' code path involving the shared port service or?). Do you have full logs someplace? Hard to understand how the timeout could be 20 and yet the socket is not already in non-blocking state... 2013-Oct-24 10:56:55 by jfrey: In some of the instances where a large gap in time is followed by failure in condor_write(), the failure is in a forked child process. The main schedd's pid is 5304. In the logs that Brian sent to Todd out-of-band, I see two cases where a large gap in time is followed by a condor_write() failure in the main schedd process. In both cases, the socket is closed, detected by the read field from select(). I'm not convinced that the large gaps are caused by condor_write() blocking on a recv(). As Todd said, those fds should be be marked non-blocking. I suspect those writes were just the next thing the schedd tried to do after becoming unblocked. 2013-Oct-24 15:18:07 by bbockelm: Ah - any alternate theory then? Certainly something is causing the main schedd to be blocked for awhile. Brian 2013-Oct-24 15:45:10 by sfiligoi: My (possibly naive) interpretation of the incident is that it was due to Schedd's memory fragmentation, paired with heavy spwapping. The schedd was 3G in size, and my guess is that (almost) every single page of those 3G was needed by the schedd to do any work. So when 20 childs forked over the span of a few minutes, the updates made a large fraction of the pages dirty, triggering heavy swapping activity. At that point, it started to take forever for the schedd to do any work, resulting in long gaps in the logs until the swapping died out. (and here my theory is that it was due to the shadows dying after hitting the timeout in communication with the schedd) PS: Don't have detailed facts to back it up... just my interpretation of the situation from being logged in at that time. 2014-Feb-05 14:55:39 by jfrey: Igor reports that they limited MAX_JOBS_RUNNING to reduce memory usage and haven't seen this problem since then. I am resolving this ticket. It can be reopened if the problem recurs.

title: Ticket #236: Submit Requirements Expression Feature for Condor
description: Submit Requirements Expression This is a development proposal. As a Condor administrator, I'd like to control the kinds of jobs that are submitted into my pool. I'd like to ensure things like: In my pool, each job ad has attributes added with the + option, so I'd like to check they are there and contain valid values. The schedd can reject jobs based upon its internal state, such as not accepting a job if the spool directory doesn't have enough space to hold it. I'll accept submitted jobs from user X, but only if they are in one of three Accounting Groups. I have a schedd specifically for cron jobs. I would like the schedd to only accept scheduler universe jobs that have these N attributes defined with valid values. Two possible implementations Requirements Expression in the Schedd In this implementation, there is a new condor configuration attribute called SubmitRequirements which lives in the condor_config file. The schedd reads this expression, and evaluates it in terms of the schedd and and a submitting ad, and if true, accepts the job it its queue. If false, we could evaluate another expression called SubmitFailExpression, also detailed in the condor_config file, which returns a state the job should go to: HOLD, IDLE, or REJECT, in which case the job is rejected as if the submit had failed (cluster id consumed, etc, etc, etc). Symmetric Match of Schedd Ad and Job Ad In this implementation, the schedd contains a matchmaker which takes the schedd ad, which has in it a Requirements expression and the submitting job ad, which also has a Requirements expression. It tries to match them together and if both Requirements expression return true, the job is allowed to be submitted. In this model, there are two more details of implementation: Job ad uses one Requirements expression which must be able to tell the difference between types of ads it is being evaluated against. Job ad has different requirements expression for matching to schedd as opposed to a startd. If the match fails, we could still use the SubmitFailExpression to determine what to do with the job. Commentary How is this related to gang-matching? In gang matching, a set of ads has to simultaneously resolve with themselves for all of them to be joined. In this model, there is always an implicit order of matching, and being accepted by, one or more submit points in a chain, and then matching to a slot. This ordering may imply a relaxation so we don't need to implement gang matching. A schedd accepting submitting jobs has a strong analog to a startd accepting jobs and probably much more can be done with this proposal than the simple things described here.

remarks: 2010-Jul-06 11:29:11 by smoler: From a condor-users post by Tim St. Clair: MAX_ACCEPTS_PER_CYCLE is a daemon core event loop variable which gives priority to connecting sockets in the event loop within condor, which effect daemon-core based daemons. Out of the gate, the schedd can spawn more processes then it can handle in it's current architecture. Some of this can be partially mitigated with existing variables, but it does not address the crux of the matter. The primary culprit is that the event loop is rather naive about how/where it spends it's time, so when the schedd spawns a series of shadows it spends a copious amount of time handling internal timers but not enough time talking with it's children, who "give up" in trying to communicate with their parent. As a result during large job bursts we had seen, under certain conditions, condor would enter into a "death spiral" of spawning & reaping shadows. This variable gives priority to the initial socket accept which prevents shadow cycling, and helps communications issues in general. We've noticed a significant decrease in the number of shadows which are spawned/killed when one tunes this variable, whose sweet spot is between 3 & 5 depending on your pool. Not to mention it decreases the number of overall communications errors and job restarts which directly affects pool throughput. e.g. in a oversubscribed pool of 3000 nodes we had seen communications errors in the range of several thousand, go down to less then 50. 2010-Jul-07 10:22:07 by tstclair: I purposefully left it off the radar for 7.5.3 and was planning to set the default to 3 or for 7.5.4. title: Ticket #3510: synchronized CHILDALIVEs may get dropped by the master
description: An incident in the CMS glidein system resulted in the master killing a bunch of collector processes that it incorrectly believed were hung. No communication errors were logged in the collector or master logs. Less than an hour before the problem, all daemons were reconfigured. We believe this caused the CHILDALIVE timers to be closely synchronized, resulting in the master's UDP buffer overflowing and some messages getting dropped. The workaround is to stop using UDP (e.g. use shared_port, which gets rid of UDP as a side-effect) or to make the master less busy by having the master use the procd. One possible improvement to HTCondor would be to avoid synchronizing these timers during reconfig. This could be achieved by using Reset_Timer_Period() rather than Reset_Timer(). It may also be wise to introduce some random skew when the timers are initially created. Another question: Why do we use UDP at all for this message?
remarks: 2013-Feb-22 15:47:58 by bbockelm: +1 for introducing random jitter. I'd even suggest that Condor may want to do that automatically for all clocks. Isn't there a way to have these items go through a unix socket? Is it possible for the Master to keep track of the number of missed child updates and make this queryable (if you directly contact the Master, like we do with the schedd)? 2013-Feb-25 08:52:09 by tstclair: +1 re no UDP 2013-Mar-05 11:23:42 by danb: My thought that Reset_Timer_Period() was a good solution turned out to be too simple. If we increase the time until the next call to the timer, then our parent may conclude that we are hung. That is why the current code just blindly sets the timer to fire in 1 second after a reconfig --- to ensure that we inform our parent of the new heartbeat interval before the old one expires. I have committed a fix for the common case in which the interval does not change during a reconfig. I think that is good enough for the 7.8 series. 2013-Mar-05 11:28:14 by johnkn: The patch for 7.8 series looks like it handles the common case and is safe. 2013-Mar-05 14:53:53 by danb: In 7.9.5, I made a second patch that adds skew to the child alive timer. I consider the issue resolved well enough until we see evidence to the contrary.

title: Ticket #7800: condor_watch_q should be able to track DAGs
description: condor_watch_q does not correctly group jobs (by batch name) that are part of DAGS if those jobs are submitted after condor_watch_q begins running. If the job is submitted before it starts running, condor_watch_q will pick up their batch names and group them together in group-by-batch mode. Jobs submitted afterwards (if condor_watch_q finds them in an event log it is already reading) will just have the generic name given to jobs without batch names, and therefore will not be grouped properly. This ticket corresponds to this external PR by Eric Lin: https://github.com/JoshKarpel/condor_watch_q/pull/50 , which solves this problem by determining which jobs in the initial query are actual DAGMan scheduler universe jobs and constructing a mapping between those DAGs and the event log for their jobs. That mapping is then used to track which clusters belong to event logs used by DAGs and adjust their batch names appropriately.

title: Ticket #2751: procd communication protocol is not 32/64-bit safe
description: The condor_procd speaks a binary protocol over a named socket. The communication messages used are simply the in-memory data formats dumped to the socket. Something like: write(fd, &foo, sizeof(foo)); Unfortunately, the size of the data structures differs between 32- and 64-bit; for example, struct ProcFamilyUsage is 40 bytes on 32-bit and 72-bytes on 64-bit. This means that, best case, mixing binaries will cause errors. Worst case, mixing binaries will cause garbled messages to be passed back and forth. Assigning to Todd so he can make the call as to whether this is a bug or a feature.
remarks: 2012-Jan-09 12:49:30 by tannenba: Thanks for reporting this. While not ideal, we currently claim that all binaries running on the same machine must have the same version and platform string. E.g. mix and matching binaries w/ different versions or platform strings is allowed within a pool, but not upon one machine. Given the above, while it would be nice to fix this problem, I think it would be better to expend effort elsewhere. Thus marking this ticket as abandoned.
creator: bbockelm

title: Ticket #7553: Collector can hang when a port scanner probes it
description: When an arbitrary application opens port 9618 and sends bytes, those bytes will end up going to the collector unless the bytes happen to match a shared port command id. When that happens, if the number of bytes is less than the size of a CEDAR packet header (5 bytes normally, 5+16 if integrity is enabled), then the collector will block forever or until the other end of the socket is closed. For the most part, command delivery to a HTCondor daemon is non-blocking, but in the special case of reading the CEDAR header after at least 1 byte is on the wire, the read is blocking, and the timeout is infinite. We should change this code so that the timeout is small when the socket is in non-blocking mode, and we should first make sure that the bytes that are already available are consistent with there being a valid CEDAR header on the way.

title: Ticket #2614: restart of glidein master causes leaked glexec processes
description: The use of a different procd process for the master than in the startd means that if the startd dies without cleaning up its children, the master will fail to clean up jobs that were started via glexec. We observed this in a case where the master was suspended for a while. When it was unsuspended, it detected a large clock jump and restarted itself. It immediately hard-killed the startd (probably because the startd had not been sending keepalives while suspended) and then the master's procd failed to clean up the job processes that had been started via glexec. The startd had its own procd. The host condor (running as root) did not have any problem cleaning up the processes leaked by the glidein when the glidein finally exited.
remarks: 2011-Nov-18 18:02:01 by danb: The plot thickens! When the glidein starts for the first time, the master is starting a procd, which is used by the startd. (This happens because the use of glexec requires it.) So at that stage, there is only one procd. Therefore, the problem of the master not being able to kill jobs started via glexec does not yet apply. But (at least on my mac) when the master restarts itself, the master and startd each create their own procd. Therefore, after the first restart, the master can no longer kill processes started by glexec. Why does the behavior change after the master restarts itself? For some reason, in the restarted startd, CONDOR_PROCD_ADDRESS_BASE is not set. I haven't yet understood why. I have traced the master and determined that it calls setenv(), and getenv() does return the value that it set. However, when the master's environment is merged into the child's, this environment variable is not copied. Another thing I happened to notice is that the original procd is not reaped. It hangs around in the zombie state. 2011-Nov-18 21:19:12 by danb: I discovered why the environment behaves strangely after restart of the master. The problem is caused by the following code in the master: // Get rid of the CONDOR_INHERIT env variable. If it is there, // when the master restarts daemon core will think it's parent // is a daemon core process. but, its parent is gone ( we are doing // an exec, so we disappear), thus we must blank out the // CONDOR_INHERIT env variable. char tmps[256]; sprintf( tmps, "%s=", EnvGetName( ENV_INHERIT ) ); putenv( tmps ); The problem with that code is that it puts a string from the stack into the environment. Once we exit from that stack frame, the memory can become corrupted. The reason the Env object does not see some environment variables that getenv() does see is that in MergeFrom( char const * const *stringArray ), it stops on the first invalid environment entry (i.e. an entry missing an assignment), whereas getenv() must keep going. 2011-Nov-18 21:43:27 by danb: I made two patches. The patch for the master corrupting its environment is for 7.6.5. The patch for the Env object's treatment of invalid entries is for 7.7.5. 2012-Jan-09 12:36:29 by zmiller: REVIEWED by zmiller, found no problems.

title: Ticket #6657: Support new GCE credentials file format
description: The Google Cloud SDK has changed how it writes user credentials on disk. Before, they were written as plain-text JSON in the file ~/.config/gcloud/credentials. Now, they're stored in two sqlite database files: ~/.config/gcloud/credentials.db and ~/.config/gcloud/access_tokens.db. Both file formats can store credentials for multiple user accounts. The current gce_gahp code assumes the file will contain credentials for just one account. If the file has multiple credentials, the gce_gahp will retrieve the ones that appear last. If the file has a mix of user and service credentials, the gce_gahp can end up with a mix of data from both credential types. We should add an optional gce account attribute in the job ad and corresponding field to the gahp commands. If the user doesn't specify an account, the gahp can pick a random one, but should ensure it uses data for just one account. Google's client SDK (gcloud) has a well-defined location for the credentials file(s). We should make specifying the location of the credentials file in the job ad optional, defaulting to the well-known location.

title: Ticket #5702: condor_rm on scheduler universe job does not halt submission
description: If you condor_rm a large DAG (say, 5k jobs) by condor_rm'ing the scheduler universe job(s) it/them-selves, you will find that jobs continue to be submitted and execute. These jobs survive the final removal of DAGMan itself which can take several minutes as the thousands of jobs are stopped. Known to be true for as long as I've used condor. Poked here and there but it came up again today. Had to manually condor_rm the jobs that survived. Tom
remarks: 2016-Jul-06 12:58:56 by wenger: Hmm -- I just saw this ticket. Anyhow, it's interesting that you say you've seen this for a long time, because (some time around the 8.1 series, maybe) we changed how this works. Anyhow, I'd like to see the dagman.out and dagman.log files from a case where this happened. 2016-Jul-06 13:24:25 by wenger: I'm less surprised that this might happen now than that it apparently happened with the "old" remove mechanism (where DAGMan itself removed the node jobs). I could see something maybe happening with the current scheme, if there's a race condition where the schedd does its node job removal before DAGMan job itself has been killed. (In the LIGO call today, Tom said that he thinks this tends to happen when the filesystem is heavily loaded, which seems like it adds credence to the "race condition" idea.) Also, Tom says that he came on at around 8.0, so if the change to the removal mechanism was made before then, this behavior might not have been seen with the old mechanism. (Also see #5175: Have condor_dagman condor_rm jobs on SIGUSR1 (revert #4618).) (Hmm -- #4618 was only fixed in 8.3.2, so that's certainly since Tom was around.) (I'm wondering if this could be reliably reproduced by introducing an artificial delay at the right point in the schedd code, assuming the "race condition" idea is correct.) 2016-Jul-06 13:34:00 by tpdownes: I can state with reasonable certainty (by memory) that the condor_dagman job remains on the system after it has entered the 'X' state according to the queue. It is during this period that it submits new jobs that are later "orphaned." title: Ticket #774: VOMS verification problems cause job failures
description: When attempting to extract the DN and VOMS attributes from an x509 proxy, the VOMS function we call tries to verify the signature on the VOMS attributes. If the verification fails, then the whole call to extract the attributes fails. This causes condor_submit to fail, and causes the gridmanager to put jobs on hold. Failure to verify the VOMS signature doesn't mean attempts to use the proxy will fail. We should find a way to extract the information even when this error condition occurs.
remarks: 2009-Sep-30 22:33:41 by jfrey: Pushed fix to V7_4-branch.

creator: jfrey

title: Ticket #1741: detect error/except loops and break them
description: Pete and I were just discussing exceptions in DAGMan, and the possibility that things could get into a state where DAGMan excepts, gets re-started, goes into recovery mode, and excepts again because of the problem that caused the original exception. Right now, if that happens, the loop will never be broken without manual action from a user. I don't think we've seen this very often, but it's certainly possible. At any rate, we were thinking that we could do something, maybe with periodic_hold, to detect such loops and break them after some configurable number of times.
creator: wenger

title: Ticket #6084: Add ULOG_JOB_AD_INFORMATION to events allowed in nodes.log file
description: We should probably allow ULOG_JOB_AD_INFORMATION in the nodes log file (this would help with a minor issue LSST is having, and it will probably be good in general). (Most of the time, at least, you won't be getting any job_ad_information events unless you specifically generate them. Although I could see a case where you might want such events in the "regular" user log file but not the nodes.log file.) Hmm -- maybe we should add a knob to let the user specify "extra" event types that will be allowed in the nodes.log file (we shouldn't let them remove any event types, because that would goof up DAGMan).
creator: wenger

title: Ticket #4113: Add GLOBUS_GATEKEEPER_TIMEOUT -alike to EC2.
description: This feature request was prompted by a failure mode of the EC2 tests after implementing #4004, where an EC2 simulator failure delayed the test suite by an hour. Although we've since added a shorter time-out for this test, this incident still pointed out the need for a lease on down resources (to prevent us from retrying indefinitely). Putting the job on hold after this lease expires will cause the test to fail (almost) immediately thereafter. After implementing this feature, the test suite will need to be modified to set the configuration variable EC2_RESOURCE_TIMEOUT to a very small value.

title: Ticket #1311: Be able to configure DAGMan's actions when condor_rm'ed
description: (This is resulting from condor-users email today from Robert Mortensen. The problem is that there's really no way to do what he wants.) My idea is to have a config knob for DAGMan to tell it what you want it to do when it's condor_rm'ed. Right now it just kills everything off, but you might want to do something like let jobs in the queue finish, or remove jobs but still run POST scripts, etc. We need to think some about exactly what options we would want to allow, but this might be a really useful feature.

title: Ticket #3639: add Fedora-specific condor rpm features to unified rpm
description: Using the OSG condor spec as a baseline, add any features from the Fedora rpm into the unified spec
remarks: Attaching a summary of what's different between the OSG and Fedora versions of condor.spec, not counting differences that are encapsulated in conditional %define blocks. See also the config file location differences attached in #3644. 2013-Jun-12 09:55:11 by edquist: For reference, the working copy of the unified condor rpm (which was based off of the OSG condor 7.9.6 version from "upcoming") is currently living here: https://vdt.cs.wisc.edu/svn/native/redhat/upcoming/condor-unified/ I have merged in any items from the Fedora rpm spec that were missing from OSG's into the unified one, as well as rearrange a lot of things that were common to both to reduce the size of the diff between Fedora's version and the unified one. Additionally I made a few small changes based on differences from Brian B's HCC version. A few questions I ran into doing this: - There are a handful of patches specific to Fedora's version, not sure whether they should be incorporated into the unified one: hcc_config.patch condor_pid_namespaces_v7.patch 0001-Apply-the-user-s-condor_config-last-rather-than-firs.patch condor_oom_v3.patch - For upgrades, the Fedora version does not restart the condor service, relying on condor to notice the binaries have changed and restart based on its configuration; the OSG version does a condrestart. Not sure which of these behaviors is newer / preferable. This can also be dealt with in the upgrade issues. - There are some things specific to the OSG rpm like %qmf, which it looks like was in Fedora's at some point and got removed. OSG does not enable it either; are people likely to ever want to enable/use it?

title: Ticket #1604: Named schedd syntax doesn't support HISTORY
description: I'd like to be able to set up multiple schedulers on a single machine and have history collection for each scheduler to go that scheduler's unique spool directory. So for schedd1: $(SPOOL)/1/history And for schedd2: $(SPOOL)/2/history Except history doesn't seem to work with the new named scheduler syntax. title: Ticket #4406: cream_gahp crashes under load
description: We have reports from multiple sources that the cream_gahp crashes frequently when used to managed more than a handful of jobs. The GlideinWMS folks at UCSD say this has been a problem since at least 8.0.x, but didn't prevent them from running the number of jobs they needed because the cream_gahp is stateless and was automatically restarted by HTCondor whenever it crashed. The problem is that the cream_gahp creates multiple worker threads to perform CREAM commands in parallel. But the Globus libraries were never told that multiple threads are in use. title: Ticket #3269: Grid-type batch doesn't work on systems with glite installed
description: When Condor uses the blahp to submit jobs to other batch systems, it needs to set GLITE_LOCATION in the environment for the blahp to find its components. If the system has a root-installed glite, then the standard login scripts will set GLITE_LOCATION to point at that installation. The is a problem for the XXXX_submit.sh scripts in Condor's blahp, which invoke bash with the -l argument. This causes the script to source the login scripts, overwriting our GLITE_LOCATION setting. Consequently, job submissions fail. It appears we can just remove the -l from the first line of the XXXX_submit.sh scripts. Settings in the user-specific login scripts shouldn't affect the job's environment or the script's ability to submit into the batch system. If sourcing the login scripts ends up being necessary, it could be done explicitly in the submit scripts while taking care to maintain the existing value of GLITE_LOCATION. The following code will duplicate the sourcing of login scripts at startup triggered by -l: if -r /etc/profile; then . /etc/profile fi if -r ~/.bash_profile; then . ~/.bash_profile elif -r ~/.bash_login; then . ~/.bash_login elif -r ~/.profile; then . ~/.profile fi

title: Ticket #3793: missing build dependency for std_local_ref
description: When doing a uw-style build with a large make -jN number (eg, -j24), I consistently hit a build dependency where the rule to generate receivers.cpp gets run before stub_gen is built (which is the utility used to generate receivers.cpp). This doesn't usually come up with smaller -jN's, since an earlier rule ends up building stub_gen in time, but there is no explicit dependency on it. (There is a receivers target that depends on stub_gen, but there is also a std_local_ref target, which has a rule to build receivers.cpp, but this does not depend on stub_gen or the receivers target.) One way to address this is to add a cmake dependency for receivers (and senders) on stub_gen. This seems to work, but the result is receivers.cpp gets generated twice once stub_gen is built; once for the receivers target and once for std_local_ref. Another way (my preference) would be to add a cmake dependency for std_local_ref on receivers (and senders). This adds an implicit dependency on stub_gen and avoids regenerating the .cpp files. There are similar looking holes for switches.cpp, which I think should be addressed the same way. My suggestion is to patch src/condor_syscall_lib/CMakeLists.txt like this: --- a/src/condor_syscall_lib/CMakeLists.txt +++ b/src/condor_syscall_lib/CMakeLists.txt @@ -125,13 +125,14 @@ if( STD_UNIVERSE ) # part 2: # set dependencies to ensure build dep order for parallel builds ################################################## - add_dependencies( condorsyscall stub_gen ) + add_dependencies( condorsyscall senders switches ) if (DOES_COMPRESS_CKPT) - add_dependencies( condorzsyscall stub_gen ) + add_dependencies( condorzsyscall senders switches ) endif() add_dependencies( switches syscall_numbers stub_gen ) add_dependencies( senders syscall_numbers stub_gen ) add_dependencies( receivers syscall_numbers stub_gen ) + add_dependencies( std_local_ref senders receivers ) add_dependencies( sys-list syscall_numbers stub_gen ) ################################################# This fix worked for me, but I'd like to put this out here in case anyone thinks there's a better way to address it. Thanks!
remarks: 2013-Jul-24 14:29:36 by edquist: I checked in this change to master, as recommended by TJ.

[...] (By Carl Edquist )
