title: Ticket #6968: IpVerify initialization shouldn't happen in middle of new connection
description: The Condor security authorization tables maintained by the IpVerify class are initialized lazily the first time an authorization decision needs to be made. This happens in the middle of the first network connection that the process makes (as either client or server), as its peer is waiting. The IpVerify initialization can include numerous DNS queries for hostnames mentioned in the security configuration. If any of these queries end up blocking for a long time, the peer may timeout and close the connection. For a long-lived daemon, this is usually a minor inconvenience, as the IpVerify initialization is only done once. For the shadow, it becomes a major problem, as the shadow will exit with failure if the startd hangs up on it when trying to activate the claim. This was demonstrated this week in a thread on htcondor-users. The IpVerify initialization should be done before any network connections are established. For daemons, this could be explicitly as part of daemoncore's startup. For tools, this could be done somewhere inside SecMan::startCommand() before the socket is created.

title: Ticket #5128: Collector tries to authenticate with self
description: At startup, the collector currently tries to detect whether it is trying to update itself; it is doing this incorrectly (it compares its default sinful with the collectors to update sinful as a string comparison). This causes a 30-second 'hang' of the daemon when using default settings. I think the fix looks like this: --- a/src/condor_collector.V6/collector.cpp +++ b/src/condor_collector.V6/collector.cpp @@ -1350,10 +1350,12 @@ void CollectorDaemon::Config() if( myself == NULL ) { EXCEPT( "Unable to determine my own address, aborting rather than hang. You may need to make sure the shared port daemon is running first." ); } + Sinful mysinful(myself); while( collectorsToUpdate->next( daemon ) ) { const char * current = daemon->addr(); if( current == NULL ) { continue; } - if( strcmp( myself, current ) == 0 ) { + Sinful theirsinful(current); + if( mysinful.addressPointsToMe(theirsinful) ) { collectorsToUpdate->deleteCurrent(); } } The fix above just papers over the issue, as it still relies on the concept of a 'default' socket.

title: Ticket #2317: Parallel Universe jobs get preempted upon renewal of job lease
description: The telling lines from the startd log are: 07/12/11 21:08:54 Calling Handler <Alive to schedd <10.14.0.18:54531>> (4) 07/12/11 21:08:54 slot1: State change: claim no longer recognized by the schedd - removing claim 07/12/11 21:08:54 slot1: Changing state and activity: Claimed/Busy -> Preempting/Killing Condor's keep-alive protocol, which is used between a schedd and claimed startds so that a startd knows when a schedd disappears and vice versa, changed between v7.4.x and v7.6.x. Back in v7.4.x, the schedd sent alive packets via UDP to the startds. In v7.6.x, in order to improve scalability/reliability and to be nicer to firewalls, the startd sends alive data via a roundtrip TCP connection to the schedd. Unfortunately, it looks like this new alive protocol and parallel universe jobs do not play together nicely. :( . We have an immediate work-around available - we can explicitly tell the schedd to use the old-style protocol by putting the following in the condor_config file seen by all schedds that will be submitting parallel universe jobs: STARTD_SENDS_ALIVES = False This simple config entry should hold the fort until we get this bug fixed.

title: Ticket #5082: Package HTCondor as an AMI and/or Docker image.
description: It would be super cool (for lame values of cool) to be able to provide a(n "offical") Docker image for tutorial use. The image would contain a personal condor and example submit files, or whatever; the idea would be to be able to say "docker run centos6 htcondor" and more-or-less immediately arrive at a shell where 'condor_q', 'condor_status', and 'condor_submit' would do useful things. Creating the image would be part of the release process (so people could easily test to new features, and also to prevent it from bit-rotting), but we'd also need effort writing/narrating/etc the tutorials using Docker. It would also be super cool to have an "official" AMI or two. The first idea was to make it easy to spin up a single startd at a time, having it join an existing pool (using the instance information, ideally in a way that lets us point people at a CloudFormation widget for a GUI). The second idea was to have two AMIs, one a central manager/submit point and the other a startd. Ideally, creating a startd instance in the same VPN as the CM would automatically cause it to join the pool. This configuration could perhaps be turned into the startd-only pool extension by having the central manager do the forwarding (and CCB?). The key is to make sure everything Just Works as easily as possible, and make it easy to customize as necessary (e.g., to join your pool).

title: Ticket #3855: Condor on Win32 retries forever if executable is invalid
description: When the Windows version of the STARTER cannot execute the user's job, it will retry forever instead of putting the job on hold. To reproduce the problem. submit this job from a Linux submit machine to a windows execute node. The job will fail, and then retry forever. executable = /bin/sleep log = test.log output = test.out error = test.err Requirements = OpSys=="WINDOWS" && Arch!="" queue The fundamental problem is that the failure to start the executable is never passed out of DaemonCore::Create_Process in a form that the starter will turn into a hold request. errno is never set, and the returned error message string is empty.

The Ornithology test has the same two main sections as the existing test: the first checks that the materialization limits are behaving as expected, and the second makes sure that itemdata makes it into the job ads correctly. I'm not too worried about the second one (I think the new test is basically doing the same thing the old one does, though because it checks the job queue log it's a little more in the guts of the system). The Ornithology test makes assertions about max_idle and max_materialize (that they are never exceeded, and that the limit is reached at some point during the test, in both cases). title: Ticket #3506: Master should restart all daemons when network address changes
description: If a machine's IP address changes, all Condor daemons on that machine can no longer be contacted, even from tools or daemons on that same machine. This situation is very likely to occur on laptops, which frequently move between different wired and wireless networks. BOSCO is making Condor installations on laptops more common, so addressing this problem is becoming more important. The condor_master should periodically examine the IP addresses of the local machine and restart all of the daemons (including itself) if it detects a change. The master already does this for substantial jumps in the system clock.
remarks: 2013-Mar-13 14:12:02 by tlmiller: BaTLab is also having chronic problems with distributions lying (or being mistaken) about their network being ready during startup. This causes the master to start up on 127.0.0.1, and, among other problems, reject DC_CHILDALIVE because the daemon in question is using the execute node's public IP. Sequences like the following are particularly aggravating: 03/13/13 13:02:39 PERMISSION DENIED to unauthenticated@unmapped from host 127.0.0.1 for command 60008 (DC_CHILDALIVE), access level DAEMON: reason: cached result for DAEMON; see first case for the full reason 03/13/13 13:05:52 Got SIGHUP. Re-reading config files. 03/13/13 13:05:52 Enumerating interfaces: lo 127.0.0.1 up 03/13/13 13:05:52 Enumerating interfaces: em1 128.104.103.3 up 03/13/13 13:05:52 Enumerating interfaces: virbr0 192.168.122.1 up 03/13/13 13:05:52 Setting maximum accepts per cycle 8. 03/13/13 13:05:52 Reconfiguring all running daemons. 03/13/13 13:05:52 Sent SIGHUP to STARTD (pid 1465) 03/13/13 13:05:58 WARNING: forward resolution of localhost6 doesn't match 127.0.0.1! 03/13/13 13:05:58 WARNING: forward resolution of localhost6.localdomain6 doesn't match 127.0.0.1! 03/13/13 13:05:58 PERMISSION DENIED to unauthenticated@unmapped from host 127.0.0.1 for command 60008 (DC_CHILDALIVE), access level DAEMON: reason: DAEMON authorization policy contains no matching ALLOW entry for this request; identifiers used for this host: 127.0.0.1,localhost,localhost.localdomain,localhost4,localhost4.localdomain4, localhost.localdomain, hostname size = 5, original ip address = 127.0.0.1 My initial suggestion was then for a knob that would, after the interface enumeration on a SIGHUP is done, check if the what it would select for the 'main' interface is now different, and if so, restart. A periodic check would be even tastier. 2013-Mar-21 16:12:38 by tlmiller: Actually, tastiest would be to have a configuration option that cause the master to block until a 'real' interface became available. Defining 'real' is nontrivial, but for BaTLab, "non-private" would work just fine. 2014-Jul-10 14:27:39 by tlmiller: LIGO's been bit by this as well, although since they specify NETWORK_INTERFACE, the master exits (unable to find an interface). It seems like it should be easy to work around your particular situation -- if the master can't find an interface to bind to, it should sleep for a while and then restart. For the laptop case (and a few others), it would be convenient to have a blacklist (e.g., I know I /don't/ want loopback or any of the VM interfaces, but I could be using eth0 or wlan0, or maybe usb0, and I have no idea what the IP might be, and it could be a private address).

title: Ticket #4369: SubmitterUserPrio does not work in PREEMPTION_REQUIREMENTS|RANK
description: The Manual in section 3.4.3 lists attributes that can be used in PREEMPTION_REQUIREMENTS and PREEMPTION_RANK expressions. One such attribute documented is SubmitterUserPrio. From file /src/condor_includes/condor_attributes.h - behold the misspelling of the attribute: #define ATTR_SUBMITTER_USER_PRIO "SubmittorUserPrio" Looks safe to simply correct the spelling so HTCondor operates as documented, as the code still uses SubmittorPrio internally (for backwards compatibilities when SubmitterUserPrio was first introduced). title: Ticket #4693: Condor-C should be smarter about proxy refresh
description: The gridmanager's forwarding of refreshed proxies for Condor-C jobs is not very scalable. When the local proxy is refreshed, the gridmanager immediately generates c-gahp commands to delegate the proxy to all remote jobs. There is a separate command for each remote job and no prioritization of c-gahp commands, so all of the delegations have to happen before any subsequent gahp commands can happen. In an OSG scale test of the HTCondor-CE with 10k jobs, this became a major problem. Forwarding the refreshed proxy to all 10k remote jobs took 70 minutes. Here are several ways we can improve things: Only forward a refreshed proxy when the previously-delegated proxy's lifetime has mostly elapsed. Prioritize c-gahp commands, with proxy refresh receiving a low priority. Have the schedd support a single proxy delegation for multiple jobs.
creator: jfrey

title: Ticket #5981: Enable encryption by default for credd commands
description: The credential-movement commands STORE_CRED and CREDD_GET_PASSWD require encryption to be enabled, with certain exceptions. They assume the encryption will be enabled via security policy in the config file. To make the admin's job easier, we should make the code explicitly enable encryption (failing if it's not available). This requires forcing authentication to always happen for these commands, and always using encryption for the QUERY mode of STORE_CRED. This presents some possible backwards-compatibility issues on Windows when storing user passwords. They should be minimal, since version-skew within a single machine is unlikely.

title: Ticket #1184: fstat() fails in procapi for large inodes in /proc
description: We noticed 32-bit condor on 64-bit systems sometimes producing errors messages such as the following: ProcAPI: fstat failed in /proc! (errno=75) I tracked this down to entries in /proc with inode values too big to represent in the 32-bit stat structure. Example: $ stat /proc/249577/stat File: `/proc/249577/stat' Size: 0 Blocks: 0 IO Block: 4096 regular empty file Device: 3h/3d Inode: 18446744072885960717 Links: 1 Access: (0444/-r--r--r--) Uid: ( 0/ root) Gid: ( 0/ root) Access: 2010-02-04 12:22:36.023594484 -0600 Modify: 2010-02-04 12:22:36.023594484 -0600 Change: 2010-02-04 12:22:36.023594484 -0600 The solution is to use the LFS call fstat64() when available. The consequence of this problem would be a wrong uid associated with a tracked process (it assumes the process belongs to root). This could lead to leaked processes when using a dedicated execution account to do process tracking.
remarks: 2010-Feb-04 16:52:08 by matt: It almost seems like Condor should require fstat64's presence. Otherwise someone could compile, only get fstat and run into this bewildering problem, which would appear to be fixed.

title: Ticket #3013: Pslots prevent Condor from negotiating jobs on idle pool
description: It looks like the negotiator cannot hand pslots off to a schedd unless there's a sufficient number of jobs in the queue. Setup a pslot with 100 CPUs, and submit a single job. The negotiator will assign the submitter a pieslice of 1; because the smallest pslot has a slot weight of 100, you get something along the lines of: 05/28/12 14:52:13 matchmakingAlgorithm: limit 4.000000 used 0.000000 pieLeft 4.000000 05/28/12 14:52:13 Rejected 1.14 bbockelm@unl.edu <129.93.239.129:60246>: submitter limit exceeded In other words, a private Condor setup cannot run jobs unless there are a sufficient number in queue to fragment the pslot. I'm running from master, about 2 weeks old.
remarks: 2012-Jun-20 11:24:02 by eje: What we're seeing here is another symptom of partitionable slots causing a breakdown of the semantics of 'slot weight'. The original semantic of slot weights was 'cost (in fairshare units) that a submitter must pay for matching a slot' With p-slots, this semantic breaks down: the default weight (number of cpus) doesn't represent a true cost of matching, since a job in reality peels off only some fraction of the p-slot's resources, and so in general it should not be charged the entire weight. Another closely related model breakdown is that with the original static slots, only one job could match against a slot, where for p-slots, multiple jobs can match. I'm going to look into how cleanly I can augment the negotiation loop with the ability to manage the accounting of matching multiple jobs against against p-slots in a single cycle. More generally, we (or at least I) need to clarify the desired relationship between p-slots, p-slot multi-resource accounting, slot weights, fairshare and quotas. 2012-Jun-20 11:51:29 by tannenba: Above eje says: I am going to look into how cleanly I can augment the negotiation loop with the ability to manage the accounting of matching multiple jobs against against p-slots in a single cycle. No!!! This is the wrong approach!!! There is no need for the matchmaker to do anything "smart" re pslots to solve this problem. There is no need for the matchmaker to even know about pslots period. The last thing we need is yet more attempts for the negotiator to be "smart". The whole idea is we don't want the matchmaker to match individual jobs against a pslot, we want the schedd to handle this level of detail. 2012-Jun-20 11:59:16 by tannenba: eje above wrote: With p-slots, this semantic breaks down: the default weight (number of cpus) doesn't represent a true cost of matching, since a job in reality peels off only some fraction of the p-slot's resources, and so in general it should not be charged the entire weight. I also disagree with the above statement. If the matchmaker matches a pslot with 100cpus to a schedd, then 100 IS the true cost of the match - that entire pslot was delegated to that schedd, so it should pay. When the next negotiation cycle happens, the accountant will see that (perhaps) the schedd only is really using 1 cpu out of the initial 100, and the charging will automatically adjust - just as if the schedd had 1 long running job and 99 1 second jobs. Think of it this way: the matchmaker is not in the business of matching jobs to slots. It is in the business of matching resource requests coming from schedds to slots. The schedd says "gimme a resource like this", and the matchmaker gives it out. What job, and even how many concurrent jobs, the schedd decides to run on this resource is up to the schedd. The matchmaker should not know or care at this level. Perhaps we should talk before you do anything on this ticket.... 2012-Jun-20 12:00:42 by bbockelm: Is it possible for the negotiator to "gift" the submitter more resources than they ask? In this case, we could increase the pie slice. The tougher case is when there is contention for resources. If we have 10 submitters with 10 jobs each and one resource with slot weight 100, who gets the resource? This gets even stickier with respect to concurrency limits. 2012-Jun-20 12:11:56 by tannenba: If we have 10 submitters with 10 jobs each and one resource with slot weight 100... Answer: The submitter with the best user priority. Same as if there was one resource with slot weight 1. 2012-Jun-20 17:04:55 by eje: Brian, in your repro scenario, are there any accounting groups involved, or no acct groups? (if you can attach repro config file(s) that would help me) 2012-Jun-20 17:36:23 by bbockelm: Here's the relevant config file for our negotiator: https://github.com/bbockelm/hcc-config/blob/master/modules/condor/files/config.d/03-red-collector So, accounting groups are involved. Not sure if it's relevant to the issue. 2012-Jun-21 17:45:12 by eje: A simplified repro/test configuration: NEGOTIATOR_DEBUG = D_FULLDEBUG # schedd-side optimizations can obscure negotiator behaviors CLAIM_WORKLIFE = 0 # shouldn't matter here, but customer site uses it: NEGOTIATOR_CONSIDER_PREEMPTION = FALSE # Test whether turning this off fixes the described problem NEGOTIATOR_USE_SLOT_WEIGHTS = TRUE # a single p-slot which will have weight == 10 NUM_CPUS = 10 SLOT_TYPE_1 = cpus=10 SLOT_TYPE_1_PARTITIONABLE = TRUE NUM_SLOTS_TYPE_1 = 1 # simple group quota structure to bring 'allocated' logic into play GROUP_NAMES = a GROUP_QUOTA_a = 10 # This will cause matchmaker to use 'allocated' instead of whole quota, which can cause # starvation problems if all available slots cost more than 'allocated' GROUP_ACCEPT_SURPLUS = TRUE Running the above configuration, submit a job (to group "a"): universe = vanilla cmd = /bin/sleep args = 600 should_transfer_files = if_needed when_to_transfer_output = on_exit +AccountingGroup="a.user" queue 1 You should see the job fail to match, because 'accept surplus' induces the 'allocated' quota to be (1) which is sent to the negotiation loop. The only available slot is partitionable, but has weight 10 and so the submitter "a.user" can't afford it: 06/21/12 15:13:38 matchmakingAlgorithm: limit 1.000000 used 0.000000 pieLeft 1.000000 06/21/12 15:13:38 Sending SEND_JOB_INFO/eom 06/21/12 15:13:38 Getting reply from schedd ... 06/21/12 15:13:38 Got NO_MORE_JOBS; done negotiating 06/21/12 15:13:38 This submitter hit its submitterLimit. 06/21/12 15:13:38 resources used scheddUsed= 0.000000 If you turn off slot weights: NEGOTIATOR_USE_SLOT_WEIGHTS = FALSE and restart the negotiator, the job should match: 06/21/12 15:14:05 matchmakingAlgorithm: limit 1.000000 used 0.000000 pieLeft 1.000000 06/21/12 15:14:05 Connecting to startd slot1@rorschach at <192.168.1.2:57864> 06/21/12 15:14:05 File descriptor limits: max 1024, safe 820 06/21/12 15:14:05 Sending PERMISSION, claim id, startdAd to schedd 06/21/12 15:14:05 Notifying the accountant 06/21/12 15:14:05 Successfully matched with slot1@rorschach 06/21/12 15:14:05 Reached submitter resource limit: 1.000000 ... stopping 2012-Jun-28 13:29:10 by eje: Regarding the 'fencepost' concept of allowing a slot to negotiate regardless of weight/cost: we need to keep in mind that it enables scenarios such as: 1) all slots are p-slots of 100 cpus 2) an acct group "a" with quota of 10 3) submit 100 jobs against "a", and against a cc-limit of 10 4) the negotiator matches a 100-cpu p-slot 5) the schedd gets ahold of it, and uses its new logic to parsel it out to all 100 jobs. 6) "a"'s quota is violated, and so is cc-limit In a pool with a large number of smaller-quota acct groups, this scenario becomes more likely. In a pool with p-slots of large weight, this scenario becomes more likely. I consider this an argument for the notion that whatever object is doing the matching of jobs to resources needs to have access to centralized accounting of cc-limits and group quotas, and that same object needs to be responsible for parseling out p-slots. Currently that object is the negotiator. If that object ever becomes the scheduler, the current practice of supporting multiple schedulers on a pool raises issues of centralized accounting of quotas, cc-limits, resource usages, prios, etc. It also seems a lot like making the scheduler into something that is nearly isomorphic to what we now call the matchmaker. 2012-Aug-23 13:52:15 by zmiller: Bulk change of target version from v070802 to v070803 using ./ticket-target-mover. 2012-Sep-11 11:06:53 by johnkn: Bulk change of target version from v070803 to v070804 using ./ticket-target-mover. 2012-Sep-19 16:15:53 by zmiller: Bulk change of target version from v070804 to v070805 using ./ticket-target-mover. 2012-Oct-25 17:52:16 by johnkn: Bulk change of target version from v070806 to v070807 using ./ticket-target-mover. 2012-Dec-19 09:30:47 by johnkn: Bulk change of target version from v070807 to v070808 using ./ticket-target-mover. 2013-Mar-28 17:16:00 by johnkn: Bulk change of target version from v070808 to v070809 using ./ticket-target-mover.

description: If, for example, the permissions of the SEC_CREDENTIAL_DIRECTORY are set incorrectly which CREDD_OAUTH_MODE=true, then a failure to write the credential request file (the file the CredD writes and the CREDMON consumes) is not propagated to the user, and their job is succesfully submitted even thought the job will not have the requested tokens. title: Ticket #918: JOB_ROUTER_NAME default broken in 7.3.2
description: In 7.3.2, the default for JOB_ROUTER_NAME changed from the hostname to an empty string. This caused two problems: On restart of JobRouter, the new JobRouter did not automatically adopt jobs it was previously managing. The ManagedManager attribute in src jobs is set to an empty string, which causes JobRouter to mess up in AdoptOrphans() and think that jobs belonging to the gridmanager are src jobs of the JobRouter. This appears to not do any harm other than emitting the following confusing message: found orphan with no routed destination job; yielding management of it. The change was unintentionally introduced in 49ba8395.
remarks: 2009-Nov-06 18:13:46 by danb: I have fixed this for 7.4.1. I changed the default JOB_ROUTER_NAME to "jobrouter". This creates an incompatibility on upgrade from anything prior to 7.4.1, but it can be resolved with condor_qedit, as I will document in the release notes. I think having a fixed string rather than a hostname is better in the long run, because if the hostname changes (or the job queue is moved to a different host) jobrouter will continue owning the jobs that it created.

title: Ticket #1757: condor_rm -forcex should remove jobs held from removal problems
description: Burt Holzman reports: We've seen situations in the past where condor-g jobs error out remotely for some reason, become held, and become difficult to remove from the queue. We execute condor_rm locally, the gridmanager talks to (or tries to talk to) the remote grid monitor, and fails (maybe the remote job is missing, or the grid monitor was killed, .. or some other failure). The job continues to stay in the queue and are held again. The only way currently to kill the job is to issue both a condor_rm and then a condor_rm -forcex if you get lucky enough to catch the job in the 'X' state. I'd like -forcex to work on any job no matter what its status, so I don't have to try to time things. How to Fix It would be nice to somehow distinguish between jobs that are on hold for other reasons and jobs that are on hold because removal has failed for some reason. Perhaps the latter should be removed by -forcex but not the former.

If so, does cms actually do anything w/ these grid jobs that go on hold other than trying to remove them? If so, perhaps the best solution would be to flag the jobs as "Nonessential". As of Condor v7.3.x and above, there is a job attribute, Nonessential. When this attribute is set to True, Condor will attempt to nicely remove problematic grid universe jobs rather than put them on hold. If any problems are encountered during the process of removing, the job will automatically be removed forcefully (aka like condor_rm -force) and thus leave the queue immediately, potentially leaving debris on the remote gatekeeper. Add the following line to the submit file to mark a job as nonessential: +Nonessential = True Thoughts? Perhaps the above already implemented mechanism allows us to resolve this ticket? 2011-Feb-10 13:35:38 by danb: It would be nice if "Nonessential" were documented. 2011-Feb-10 14:04:07 by burt: This sounds like what I need. Looking at the code, it looks like it does two things: skips the held state and removes the job immediately from the queue; and if the job is in X state and the remote resource is down, it immediately removes it from the queue. title: Ticket #6092: Job Router job event writing bugs
description: The Job Router's handling of job event logs has several bugs. These don't affect typical usage of the HTCondor-CE, but do affect other users (any time jobs are submitted by an avenue other than Condor-C). Here are the issues: The Job Router assumes that the UserLog and DAGManNodesLog job attributes contain full pathnames to files. If a value is a relative filename, it attempts to open the wrong file. The Job Router copies the UserLog and DAGManNodesLog job attributes from the source job to the routed job. In non-sandbox mode, this means events for the routed job show up in the source job's event log files. In sandbox mode, this means that the source job's event log files are overwritten by event log files for the routed job when it completes. The Job Router writes Terminate, Abort, and Hold events for the source job, but nothing else. Execute and Evict events are desired by some CMS folks. If UserLog and DAGManNodesLog are undefined in the source job ad, then no events are written to the global event log. Generally, the Job Router should handle job event logging similar to how Condor-C does it. It should remove event log file attributes from the destination job ad, and write a fuller set of events for the source job.
remarks: 2017-Mar-01 15:20:21 by gthain: CODE REVIEW All is good. Can we get some notes in this ticket about why the job router should be responsible for logging, and the religion behind it?

If the answer happens to be both, then the definition of one is missing and the mapping of the other is missing. 2009-Nov-25 10:07:01 by tannenba: Karen, re question number 4 above, there is both HDFS_DATANODE_WEB and HDFS_NAMENODE_WEB. Both should be of the format x.x.x.x:0. I think only HDFS_NAMENODE_WEB must be defined, as HDFS_DATANODE_WEB will default to a reasonable value for must folks of 0.0.0.0:0 which means bind to the default interface on a dynamic port. As for mappings to the hdfs xml config file, HDFS_DATANODE_WEB maps to dfs.datanode.http.address, and HDFS_NAMENODE_WEB maps to dfs.http.address. You also find this link helpful. 2009-Nov-25 14:17:57 by faisal: Thanks for these questions: I tried to give more description of how access filters in HDFS are implemented. Please let me know if they make more sense then before. HDFS_ALLOW and HDFS_DENY are used to regulate access to HDFS cluster. Here is more detail on how the access control works in HDFS. HDFS provides very minimal access control mechanism (if at all). Specifically it lacks any regular expression based host or IP access filters which otherwise are used through-out Condor. I added a way to regulate access to HDFS cluster using a similar mechanism as we have for Condor. On startup HDFS daemon (DaemonCore daemon) looks for HDFS_ALLOW and HDFS_DENY in Condor's configuration files. If these knobs exist, their values are used to filter access. Otherwise allow and dney access is configured using Condor's existing knobs for access control. Below is this mapping: if HDFS_ALLOW is missing: Allow filter will be configured using union of values from these knobs: a) ALLOW_READ b) ALLOW_DENY c) HOSTALLOW_READ d) HOSTALLOW_DENY Similarly, if HDFS_DENY is missing: Deny filter will be configured using union of values from these knobs a) DENY_READ b) DENY_WRITE c) HOSTDENY_READ d) HOSTDENY_WRITE The mappings from Condor's access filter and HDFS access filter is not one-to-one. There are two major differences. First, In HDFS we don't make any distinction between read access or write access. It is either allow a host/IP or This explain why mappings involving allow and deny filters considers both read and write combinations of corresponding configuration in Condor. Second major difference is that Condor's configuration for above filters also includes user and host combination e.g user@*.cs.wisc.edu. When copying over values HDFS simply ignores any entry that specify a user-host combination. As these above filters are an additional feature by us, they will not work if someone tries to use version of Hadoop software not shipped by us. In that case these mappings from Condors configuration file to Hadoop's XML files will simply be ignored. Of course there won't be any access control in that case as well. 2009-Nov-25 14:19:40 by faisal: Few other things you asked. Pelease let me know if these need more detail as well. Thanks a lot! The default value of HDFS_LOG4J is INFO. The required value for HDFS_NAME node is a sinful string (a.b.c.d:port). 2009-Nov-30 14:11:41 by smoler: In the Word document, the table gives a mapping of the configuration variable HDFS_REPLICATION, but no configuration variable of this name is defined. So, if it is a Condor configuration variable, we need a definition of what it does, as well as a default value. 2009-Dec-10 12:01:41 by faisal: HDFS_REPLICATION: HDFS replicates blocks for each files for fault tolerance. This configuration knobs can be used to configure the replication factor for these blocks. We don't perform any extra steps for this knob in Condor just pass it to dfs.replication in HDFS configuration files. 2009-Dec-11 13:39:35 by smoler: Info from an e-mail, interpreted by Karen: HDFS_REPLICATION is a Condor configuration variable. It is optional, and no default value is passed on to the HDFS configuration if it is not set. HDFS has its own default value of 3 that it uses, which is why setting it in a Condor configuration is optional, with no default. If set, it is an integer, and represents the replication factor used by HDFS. If set, it maps to the HDFS configuration variable dfs.replication

title: Ticket #3290: condor_shadow doesn't play well with mulitple SPOOL dirs
description: The condor_shadow is hard coded to look at SPOOL, and provides no means to pass it the same of a schedd it should be associated with. The following config: SPOOL = dir1 SCHEDD.SPOOL = dir2 would result in the shadow looking in dir1 instead of the appropriate directory dir2. This is especially an issue if dir1 has never been setup with a schedd and is therefore missing the spool_version file. The shadow needs a better means to track with its associated schedd. A better solution might be to remove the reliance on the SPOOL directory all together. Currently the reliance on the SPOOL directory seems to be tied to the File Transfer object.

title: Ticket #6568: Startd always kills jobs after 40 minutes (job lease not renewed)
description: Normally, the startd will renew the job lease automatically while the starter is alive (see #4491). However, due to startd code refactoring to fix #6524, the startd will no longer do this by default. Seems like the startd is now confusing the activation ad for the claim ad? The result is the job gets killed after job_lease_duration seconds (which defaults to 40 minutes). To reproduce, submit a job like so (note short job_lease_duration): executable = /bin/sleep arguments = 300 job_lease_duration = 20 queue And then in the StarterLog you will see the following (note lease expires 20 seconds after going into activity Busy): 02/13/18 13:47:27 slot1: Changing activity: Idle -> Busy 02/13/18 13:47:47 slot1: State change: claim lease expired (condor_schedd gone?), evicting claim 02/13/18 13:47:47 slot1: Changing state and activity: Claimed/Busy -> Preempting/Killing 02/13/18 13:47:47 slot1: Got DEACTIVATE_CLAIM while in Preempting state, ignoring. 02/13/18 13:47:47 Starter pid 5612 exited with status 0 The problem here is that the changes in #6524 switched from using the job ad passed from schedd at claim time to using the job ad passed from the shadow at activation time when it was deciding how to setup the keepalive behavior. This is controlled by the SCHEDD via attributes ATTR_STARTD_SENDS_ALIVES and ATTR_STARTER_HANDLES_ALIVES, and these attributes are not set in the job ad that the shadow sees and subsequently sends to the startd at activation time.

title: Ticket #4806: condor_q should support "-limit" to control the number of results
description: When debugging a schedd, I often want to look at a single job out of a problematic task. Hence, I do something along the lines of: condor_q -const BLAH | head to get a job ID, then condor_q 12345.6 -l | sort to get the attributes I'm interested in. In some cases, BLAH may match a few 10k worth of jobs - and I throw out everything but the first. Then, I have to do a second query (meaning a second fork on busy schedds, etc). It'd be more convenient (and more efficient use of resources) if I could combine this into a single query: condor_q -const BLAH -l -limit 1 | sort Note that condor_history uses -match for this, it should be changed to also take -limit as a synonym.

title: Ticket #7729: Negotiator given low priority in collector when using family session
description: When the family security session is in use, the negotiator's queries are given low priority by the collector. They should be getting high priority. This is due to the collector consulting the Subsystem attribute of the security policy ad to get the client's subsystem. For non-negotiated security sessions, each daemon sets Subsystem to its own daemon type. So the collector thinks queries from the negotiator are coming from a collector. As a short-term fix, we will have the collector give high priority to queries that it thinks are coming from a collector. This will give high priority to queries for all daemons in the same family process tree, but no other daemons do queries that require a forked child. Also, if a central manager is also running a schedd or startd, then the admin is probably not too worried about scalability. Ticket #7722 outlines a better fix, but it will have to wait for a future release.

title: Ticket #6991: Singularity jobs don't set TEMPDIR properly
description: In singularity, we reset the environment variables TMP and TEMP to point to the scratch directory inside the container. Presumably, this is a bind mount, so that writes to tmp won't write to the contained filesystem, and are accounted for in DiskUsage. In vanilla universe we also set TMPDIR to this value, which is the "standard" environment variable, although many older programs use TMP or TEMP. This ticket adds TMPDIR to that list.

title: Ticket #7683: NonNegotiated Security Sessions have bad AuthMethods attribute
description: When two Condor processes do security negotiation, the AuthMethods attribute in the policy ad is initially set to the list of authentication methods each side is able to try. Once an authentication method succeeds, AuthMethods in the final security session policy ad is set to that method (yes, the plural form is deceiving). For a non-negotiated security session, AuthMethods in the policy ad is set to the initial list of configured authentication methods. This value should not be a list, and none of the individual authentication methods is a valid value. This nonsense value pops into public view when an ad is advertised in the collector using a non-negotiated security session. The collector sets AuthenticationMethod in the advertised ad based on the value of AuthMethods in the session policy ad for the connection with the advertiser. This will happen most commonly for daemons on the same machine as the collector, which will use the family security session to talk with the collector. We propose that non-negotiated sessions use one of a small number of special authentication method names that indicate the nature of the relationship (and how the trust of the security session was established. Below is a list of all existing non-negotiated sessions, grouped by the proposed authentication name. Each entry lists the participants of the session, followed by the authenticated names. FAMILY Parent/Child: condor@parent, condor@child Family: condor@family gridmanager/ft-gahp: condor@parent, condor@child MATCH Startd/Schedd: execute-side@matchsession, submit-side@matchsession Starter/Shadow file transfer: execute-side@matchsession, submit-side@matchsession SubmitTool/Startd: User job attribute or job-owner@submit-domain, execute-side@matchsession Schedd/Negotiator: submit-side@matchsession, negotiator-side@matchsession Schedd/Collector: submit-side@matchsession, collector-side@matchsession

title: Ticket #5344: condor_submit -i lacks default request_memory
description: condor_submit -interactive submits a job, whose template submit file lacks a request_memory. This leads to jobs matching to machines with too little memory, and when strict memory limits are enforced, the interactive job can go on hold suddenly. Picking a good default seems difficult, but we will arbitrarily make the default 512 megabytes. If the end user needs to override this, they can in a custom submit file, but the default should be big enough to at least allow for moderate interactive usage.

title: Ticket #5651: Consider using signals for atomic checkpoint transfer.
description: While forcing the user to ensure that restarting their job works is a nifty property of the current checkpointing in vanilla universe strategy, some jobs will have high start-up costs. Our current plan is to just checkpoint these jobs less often, amortizing that cost. In case that ends up not working out for our users, we should start contemplating a system where the job signals the starter that it's time to do file transfer, and the starter signals the job when it's time to resume. The correctness issue that the process terminating itself solves is the one of ensuring that the checkpoint doesn't change while it's being transferred.
remarks: 2019-Apr-17 19:42:10 by tlmiller: Also consider using chirp commands. (e.g., may I update my checkpoint file / please transfer my checkpoint file)

title: Ticket #2194: Filter "no idle jobs" submitters prior to phase 4.1
description: The calculation of submitter limits will take submitters into account who have no idle jobs, and will not use slots given to them. This results in extra "spins" in the negotiation loop that could be avoided. Pre-filtering submitters with no idle jobs can reduce unnecessary iterations.
remarks: 2011-May-26 16:18:22 by eje: repro/test: Configuration: $ more 95.bz706512.config NEGOTIATOR_CONSIDER_PREEMPTION = FALSE NUM_CPUS = 10 GROUP_NAMES = a, b GROUP_QUOTA_a = 5 GROUP_QUOTA_b = 5 Test uses two submissions. The first submits a single job under submitter "a.u1": $ more a.u1.jsub universe = vanilla cmd = /bin/sleep args = 300 should_transfer_files = if_needed when_to_transfer_output = on_exit +AccountingGroup="a.u1" queue 1 The second will submit 4 jobs for submitter "a.u2": $ more a.u2.jsub universe = vanilla cmd = /bin/sleep args = 300 should_transfer_files = if_needed when_to_transfer_output = on_exit +AccountingGroup="a.u2" queue 4 The test is to first submit "a.u1.jsub", and let it negotiate. After it has negotiated, submit "a.u2.jsub." Before the fix, you will see this: The first Phase-4.1 spin is "a.u1" negotiating. The next three spins (4.1,4.2,4.3) are "a.u2" negotiating. You can see that on the first spin, "a.u2" is given a submitter limit of 2.5, even though 4 slots are available, since it is also including submitter "a.u1" in its computation. (Note, the third spin 4.3 is an artifact of #2195) $ tail -f NegotiatorLog | grep -e 'Phase 4..:' -e 'Negotiating with.* at' -e 'submitterLimit *=' 05/26/11 11:22:01 Phase 4.1: Negotiating with schedds ... 05/26/11 11:22:01 Negotiating with a.u1@localdomain at <192.168.1.2:34321> 05/26/11 11:22:01 submitterLimit = 1.000000 05/26/11 11:22:21 Phase 4.1: Negotiating with schedds ... 05/26/11 11:22:21 Negotiating with a.u2@localdomain at <192.168.1.2:34321> 05/26/11 11:22:21 submitterLimit = 2.482556 05/26/11 11:22:22 Phase 4.2: Negotiating with schedds ... 05/26/11 11:22:22 Negotiating with a.u2@localdomain at <192.168.1.2:34321> 05/26/11 11:22:22 submitterLimit = 2.000000 05/26/11 11:22:22 Phase 4.3: Negotiating with schedds ... 05/26/11 11:22:22 Negotiating with a.u2@localdomain at <192.168.1.2:34321> 05/26/11 11:22:22 submitterLimit = 1.000000 After the fix, we see that "a.u2" gets 4 slots, and "a.u1" is filtered due to its having no idle jobs to negotiate (Note, here the second spin 4.2 is manifestation of ticket #2195 -- once that is fixed I would expect "a.u2" to negotiate in one spin) $ tail -f NegotiatorLog | grep -e 'Phase 4..:' -e 'Negotiating with.* at' -e 'submitterLimit *=' -e 'Filtering submitter' 05/26/11 12:03:31 Phase 4.1: Negotiating with schedds ... 05/26/11 12:03:31 Negotiating with a.u1@localdomain at <192.168.1.2:47753> 05/26/11 12:03:31 submitterLimit = 1.000000 05/26/11 12:03:51 Filtering submitter a.u1@localdomain with no idle jobs 05/26/11 12:03:51 Phase 4.1: Negotiating with schedds ... 05/26/11 12:03:51 Negotiating with a.u2@localdomain at <192.168.1.2:47753> 05/26/11 12:03:51 submitterLimit = 4.000000 05/26/11 12:03:51 Phase 4.2: Negotiating with schedds ... 05/26/11 12:03:51 Negotiating with a.u2@localdomain at <192.168.1.2:47753> 05/26/11 12:03:51 submitterLimit = 1.000000 2011-Jun-15 18:19:46 by eje: See also #2230 2011-Jun-27 10:28:14 by danb: Thanks for the patch! Perhaps the log message, "Filtering submitter %s with no idle jobs" would be clearer if it were "Ignoring submitter %s with no idle jobs". You are only applying this filter when consideration of preemption is disabled. I think that is prudent for now, but perhaps something we should revisit later. The reason I think it is prudent for now is described in #2270: the spinning pie algorithm does not converge to fair share allocations when preemption is allowed. I am worried that this problem could be exacerbated by dropping submitters earlier in the cycle than we do already. 2011-Jun-27 14:14:13 by tstclair: pushed patch with modified comment block per review

title: Ticket #277: Avoid unneeded evaluation of job policy in new shadow
description: This is part of the large patch set contributed by Dan Forrest. Dan's patch prevents the new Shadow from evaluating the job policy when it receives the job_exit RSC from the Starter. According to Dan, it is unneeded since the Starter will have just sent the final update which would have triggered an evaluation. In addition, Dan says that the job ad is in an inconsistent state when the job policy is evaluated as a result of the job_exit RSC (I don't know what the details are regarding the inconsistent state). Chunks from the annotated diff of Dan's changes (which Todd has) that are associated with this ticket are labeled with a (26).

title: Ticket #3785: schedd tries to send UPDATE_JOBAD to scheduler universe jobs
description: When a job ad attribute is updated in the schedd, it sends the UPDATE_JOBAD signal to the shadow to tell it to refetch the newly-dirty job ad attributes. This code is not conditionalized on universe. So, when dagman updates attributes in it's own job ad, it results in a ton of error messages in the SchedLog, wherein it tries to send signal number 71005 (!) to the dagman process itself.

title: Ticket #4040: Optimize condor UserLog IO, via batching
description: We ran into an issue where a user submitted 60K jobs (not an issue), but then reprioritized all 60K jobs (condor_qedit JobPrio). Condor handled the condor_qedit just fine, but didn't handle the logging of the attribute changes well. This IO backed up the schedd, caused SECMAN timeouts for clients, and caused matching failures from the negotiator to that schedd. If a user streams job changes, we need the schedd to better stream the log output when there are multiple queued entries instead of doing the normal per-entry lock/write/unlock. It was the repeated file locking per entry that caused the excessive slowness in this particular case today. Furthermore, the user was adjusting the priority of all of their jobs to be the same (lower) priority to give space to their fellow teammates. This mean that for some jobs the condor_edit was setting JobPrio to the same value it had been set to previously, but also logging that it set the value to the same value as previously. I'd like to see those condor_qedit's become noop's and to not log.
remarks: 2013-Nov-05 15:03:55 by tannenba: I think the root of the problem here is #1791, which added a userlog event for an job attribute changes via qedit and also job priority changes. I propose reverting #1791. The user event log is not a mirror of the job_queue log; it has a specific purpose. The motivation for #1791 is unknown. The behavior to write a userlog event upon every qedit already had to be effectively reverted in ticket #3827 - my guess is if your user was running v8.0.0.3 (you did not fill in the broken version field) the problem would have never happened. Lets finish the job and revert the userlog event logging on job prio changes. Any objections? 2013-Nov-05 16:43:46 by eje: I will discuss downstream. It looks like somebody wanted the event information for qedit, prio, and chirp changes, so I need to determine if just excising them is an acceptable answer. 2013-Nov-05 19:55:36 by eje: Downstream we need to output these events, and the output needs to be made more scalable to support very large volume operations. 2013-Nov-07 12:19:14 by tannenba: Well, note that #3827 already broke things downstream. Also note that batching syncs will not help if each job is logging to a different event log file... The job event log cannot and should not be a clone of the job_queue.log. It is supposed to just log events that change the job status, as needed for consumption by a meta-scheduler like dagman. Maybe we should have a call to discuss the motivations for why this is needed downstream, or perhaps it could be written down along with requirements. My point here is maybe the job event log is not the right mechanism to achieve the downstream requirement. 2013-Nov-12 09:14:42 by eje: Downstream customers consider this information to be important to their understanding of their workflow histories. Customer response to our inquiry was: #1791 provides essential audit logging for a job group - without that logging we would be unable to identify how jobs were being modified, and in a large oganization where there are many people (or automated processes) who could be performing such actions this is critical information. And yes, we've seen problematic IO patterns in the UserLog where people are doing large-scale job modifications - so we need 4040 also. Additionally, at least one upstream customer also would like to preserve the option to record these updates (from #3827): 2013-Aug-26 12:21:10 by pfc: Can this be made optional? There are definitely instances where we might want qedits to be logged. (In fact, anytime it's not needed for scalability I'd prefer to leave them logged, since classad changes can be important for understanding the life of a job after the fact. There needs to be a way to continue recording this data on customer request, and to increase the efficiency of output at scale. A default of not recording it is sensible. Requesting it via command line option, e.g. 'condor_qedit -record-xxx', has been proposed previously, and seems reasonable. 2013-Nov-12 14:24:56 by tannenba: If the motivation to keep #1791 is for audit logging, why not use the schedd audit log instead (see #3493)? It was designed for auditing, unlike the event log which was designed for use by meta-schedulers like dagman and thus has all sorts of overhead for that purpose (like file locking, aggressive flushing to support 2PC, etc). Compared to the event log, the audit log provides better auditing meta data (e.g. it actually logs who made the change, something the event log does not do), provides age-based time rotation, is designed to be easy to answer basic what/who/when questions via a simple grep (i.e. all important 'fields' for a record appear on the same line), is centralized so there is just one place to look and to make it easy to copy off to another server for safekeeping (security audit archiving), and logs more relevant "audit" information (see #3563). Take the simple example of the admin wants to know when attribute foo changed from X to Y. The schedd audit log can tell you no matter how that attribute got changed, be it via condor_qedit, or via non-obvious changes like condor_chirp or chirp updates from the job itself. If the audit log does not audit something important downstream, I'd like to hear about it! Especially given that a mechanism specifically designed for auditing exists, I am not convinced that auditing is a reason to keep around #1791. 2013-Nov-12 14:40:12 by pfc: I think the question is whether you're are a scientist or an admin -- the audit long is perfect for admin-centered questions involving everything that happens in the context a schedd, but a scientist wants to be able to keep a history of each of their individual workflows alongside the results -- i.e., exactly what the userlog does now. I.e., the information for them isn't attached to a schedd, it's attached to a workflow. 2013-Nov-13 14:47:04 by tannenba: Nothing concrete yet, but just a thought floating around in my head that is somewhat related to this discussion, so I thought I'd share -- I am thinking of perhaps getting rid of all the code in the schedd that writes to the event logs and consolidating it all into a separate daemon that would run alongside the schedd. This daemon would monitor the job_queue.log (just like the job_router daemon) and be responsible for updating all the various event logs. This would keep the schedd from blocking all the time on event log locks, syncs, etc, and the increased concurrency from event log writing and regular schedd operations happening in parallel would hopefully improve scalability. It would also simplify the code, enabling us to do more sophisticated/experimental event notification schemes without the worry/risk of breaking the already overly complicated schedd. Of course, all the event log semantics would have to be preserved, but a key here realizing that events in the log do not have to appear right away. I.e. it is fine if the event logging daemon is a little bit "behind" the schedd, assuming that on the average it is able to keep up. 2013-Nov-15 12:10:25 by pfc: I love that idea! 2013-Nov-15 13:44:58 by eje: Does the job queue log embody all the information needed to preserve semantics of user log, audit log, etc? 2014-Mar-25 17:42:15 by eje: I have a patch that gets rid of redundant opening and closing of logs, via caching the structures that keep log files and their locks: V8_1-gt4040-optimize-userlog 2014-Mar-28 10:35:09 by wenger: Just talked with ToddT about this -- we think we should have some numbers on how much this improves performance before deciding it's worthwhile to merge this. How about this for a simple test?: submit 100k jobs on hold, and then do some operation on them -- remove them, or change priority or something, and measure how long this takes with and without the caching. I think you should be able to do that without having much in the way of resources. 2014-Mar-28 20:14:46 by eje: I did some experiments where I submitted 10,000 jobs, all sharing a log file, on hold into the queue. Then I invoked condor_prio: $ condor_prio +1 eje I took 10 samples each for timings of condor_prio. My first experiments I ran on all-local disk. In this environment, the caching was about 2-3% faster. A measurable improvement, but not huge. Turning fsync on and off had a large effect on total time, but did not have much impact the improvements from the caching. My second experiments I configured log files on an NFS mount. In this case, the caching has a fairly large impact (although interestingly, turning fsync on and off had very little impact). For these experiments, the condor_prio command had a mean execution time of 19.5 seconds with caching, and 30.4 seconds without. So the mean performance is about 30% faster with caching. The standard deviation with caching was 1.0 seconds, and without caching it was 2.5, so the caching also improved the consistency of the results: without the caching, I measured some substantial outliers with larger run times. Turning off fsync made the times slightly better in favor of caching, but the difference was small enough to be not very significant. Overall, the log file caching patch seems like a worthwhile performance improvement, particularly when logging over NFS. I suspect that larger performance improvements might be possible on NFS mounts with higher latencies, or higher traffic. 2014-Mar-29 09:25:45 by eje: When testing on any rev where #4111 is present, it may be useful to set: CONDOR_Q_USE_V3_PROTOCOL = false in the event that the new protocol makes it harder to assess the time it takes for a queue operation to complete. 2014-Apr-01 17:47:51 by eje: As an aside, I noticed a lot of 'creating directory' operations that look redundant, because the lock files themselves should have still been open. title: Ticket #6587: proxy delegation without file transfer
description: If one submits a job in the vanilla universe that does not use the file transfer mechanism (e.g. jobs on a filesystem mounted on execute nodes), the behavior of use_x509userproxy is not what you might expect. Rather than delegating the proxy to the worker node, the proxy-related variables retain the value they had on the submit node. Therefore, this scheme only works if one also sets x509userproxy to a location on a filesystem shared between the submit and execute nodes (and create a proxy there). This isn't proxy "delegation" per se, just a shared file. LIGO would be able to make fairly immediate use of proper proxy delegation in the absence of file transfer mechanisms to access X509-protected data on CVMFS. We consider this one step along the way toward obviating the shared filesystem dependency in many of our workflows.

title: Ticket #109: "ProcD has failed" messages appear in daemon logs when machines halt
description: As part of the normal Linux shutdown procedure, shortly before powering down, all processes are sent a SIGTERM. If Condor is still running (perhaps because a job is taking a long time to checkpoint), the ProcD will exit since it has no special handling for SIGTERM. The daemon that started the ProcD is then notified via its reaper, and responds with an EXCEPT. This results in "ProcD has failed" messages in daemon logs, and also can cause false alarm obituaries to be sent out.
creator: gquinn

title: Ticket #7512: Prevent FileTransfer from publishing sensitive URL data
description: Currently our FileTransfer object publishes URLs it wants to access to the transfer_history log, job hold messages and in some cases to other log files. In many cases this is very useful for debugging while file transfers are not working. Unfortunately it's also a security concern, since many places where URLs get published are world readable. This is especially true for S3 file transfers, where we publish access token information into the URL. We want to sanitize URLs in the FileTransfer object before publishing them anywhere. One suggestion was to strip all the GET arguments (following the ? character) although I don't think this is a good idea, since very often that information is useful for debugging, also because it's possible for sensitive data to appear before it. I propose that we come up with a whitelist of expressions which we redact or remove completely from the URLs.

title: Ticket #5190: Heavyweight job polling in Condor-C
description: We've had sysadmins complain about slow response times from the HTCondor-CE (and indeed, we are seeing issues where various actions hit socket timeouts). Poking around, it seems the most common place where the CE schedd is blocking is when it is queried from the condor-c gahp on the server side. Instead of using the relatively-scalable query protocol (as in condor_q), we are using qmgmt. This means the schedd isn't forking to respond to requests - all IO stays in the main process.

title: Ticket #7007: Add Box multifile transfer plugin
description: Now that we have OAuth tokens and the multifile transfer plugin system, we should make a few file transfer plugins that use these features to give users an easy mechanism for transferring files from/to their varied storage providers. This ticket is for one of the first implementations using Box. It's hard to tell if this is a typical workflow for storage provider API, but here's how it works for Box: The user specifies in their transfer_input_files a URL that specifies the token and provider names in the scheme and then the path to a file in their Box account. For example, transfer_input_files = (foo+)box://htcondor_files/input.tar.gz would use my Box token (optionally named "foo") to pull the file input.tar.gz from the htcondor_files folder in my Box account. The Box file transfer plugin uses the specified Box token to query the Box folder and file API endpoints to find the file id for each file given by the user, then uses the file ids to download the files to the user's sandbox. Traversing the user's account to find the right file id does add time to how long the plugin has to run, especially if the user's file is many folders deep with many files in each folder to iterate over. Is this the case with most storage provider APIs? This first implementation is for download only, upload capability will be added later.

title: Ticket #1429: SUBMIT_EXPRS docs vs code: Not like +syntax.
description:
The documention for SUBMIT_EXPRS claims: A comma-separated list of ClassAd attributes to be inserted into all the job ClassAds that condor_submit creates. This is equivalent to the "+" syntax in a submit description file. Not necessarily. condor_submit may pull in SUBMIT_EXPRS directly as though they appeared in the submit. That can lead to slightly different parsing. It may ignore it entirely. I suspect that some submit file commands will be parsed from SUBMIT_EXPRS and others won't. We should determine which behavior we want, then make it sure it apples to all submit file commands. Here are some examples: notification/JobNotification For example, in my submit file, I can specify Notification=ALWAYS (JobNotification=1 in the job ClassAd) in my using two different syntax: executable=/bin/true Notification=ALWAYS queue or executable=/bin/true +JobNotification=1 queue You can test that they are identical with the following commands: % /bin/echo -e "executable=/bin/true
notification=always
queue
" | condor_submit -verbose -dump /dev/null | grep JobNotification JobNotification = 1 % /bin/echo -e "executable=/bin/true
+JobNotification=1
queue
" | condor_submit -verbose -dump /dev/null | grep JobNotification If the documentation is correct, to specify this with SUBMIT_EXPRS, I might say: JobNotification=1 SUBMIT_EXPRS=JobNotification Except it doesn't work. condor_submit loads the JobNotification and parses it: % /bin/echo -e "executable=/bin/true
queue
" | env _CONDOR_JobNotification=1 _CONDOR_SUBMIT_EXPRS=JobNotification condor_submit -verbose -dump /dev/null | grep JobNotification ERROR: Notification must be 'Never', 'Always', 'Complete', or 'Error' Sure enough, you can pass in a string: % /bin/echo -e "executable=/bin/true
queue
" | env _CONDOR_Notification=ALWAYS _CONDOR_SUBMIT_EXPRS=Notification condor_submit -verbose -dump /dev/null | grep JobNotification JobNotification = 1 priority/JobPrio My job can use the +syntax to set JobPrio: % /bin/echo -e "executable=/bin/true
+JobPrio=42
queue
" | condor_submit -verbose -dump /dev/null | grep JobPrio JobPrio = 42 % /bin/echo -e "executable=/bin/true
priority=42
queue
" | condor_submit -verbose -dump /dev/null | grep JobPrio JobPrio = 42 But SUBMIT_EXPRS cannot: % /bin/echo -e "executable=/bin/true
queue
" | env _CONDOR_JobPrio=42 _CONDOR_SUBMIT_EXPRS=JobPrio condor_submit -verbose -dump /dev/null | grep JobPrio JobPrio = 0

title: Ticket #7284: Job route order doesn't reflect configuration
description: Our friends at CIEMAT/PIC reported on htcondor-users that the job route ordering does not reflect what they've added to the configuration, which causes confusion with how jobs are routed. For example, the following configuration (note the lack of requirements): 8.8 configuration fragment JOB_ROUTER_ENTRIES @=jre [ TargetUniverse = 5; name = "Local_Condor"; ] [ TargetUniverse = 5; name = "Local_Condor2"; ] [ TargetUniverse = 5; name = "Local_Condor3"; ] @jre Results in the following ordering that is reflected in the job router log: Route Name Submitted/Max Idle/Max Throttle Recent: Started Succeeded Failed Local_Condor2 0/ 10000 0/ 2000 none 0 0 0 Local_Condor 0/ 10000 0/ 2000 none 0 0 0 Local_Condor3 0/ 10000 0/ 2000 none 0 0 0 And so any submitted jobs actually only match to the Local_Condor2 route when we would expect them to route to Local_Condor from our configuration. Unfortunately, the actual situation is more complicated. There is not a single declaration order that we can use. The job router reads 3 knobs: JOB_ROUTER_ENTRIES, JOB_ROUTER_ENTRIES_FILE, and JOB_ROUTER_ENTRIES_CMD and uses the set of all routes declared there after eliminating duplicates (by name, case sensitively). The case-sensitive comparison of names is a bug, it should be case insensitive. Routes are stored in a hashtable, and then applied in hashtable order, which is the source of the problem. If we fix the case-sensitivity bug, that will change the hashtable order; which will potentially break configurations that happen to work now because hashtable order is working for them. So we plan to fix this problem by adding a knob JOB_ROUTE_NAMES. This will default to empty. If it is empty, then routes will be compared in hashtable order using the current case-sensitive hash. If it is not empty, then only routes listed in this knob will be used, and they will be compared in the order specified in the knob. Names specified in this knob will be treated as case-*IN*sensitive. in 8.8 We will also change the job router to compare case-*IN*sensitively when eliminating routes with the same name, since this is necessary to make the new knob work correctly. In the 8.9 series, we will add a Schedd style method of declaring routes, where each route will be specified by a knob whose name ends with the route name, something like this 8.9 job router configuration fragment JOB_ROUTER_ROUTE_NAMES = Local_Condor2, Local_Condor JOB_ROUTER_ROUTE_Local_Condor @=end [ TargetUniverse = 5; name = "Local_Condor"; ] @end JOB_ROUTER_ROUTE_Local_Condor2 @=end [ TargetUniverse = 5; name = "Local_Condor2"; ] @end Additionally, in 8.9 we will also support the native transform syntax as an alternative to job router syntax for specifying routes. so this will also work 8.9 job router configuration fragment JOB_ROUTER_ROUTE_NAMES = Local_Condor Local_Condor2 JOB_ROUTER_ROUTE_Local_Condor @=end NAME Local_Condor Universe Vanilla SET Requirements ($(MY.Requirements)) && NeedMorePylons @end JOB_ROUTER_ROUTE_LocalCondor2 @=end Name Local_Condor2 TargetUniverse 5 Set routedTo "Local2" @end

title: Ticket #735: starter, shadow, and startd deadlock on job ad update --> hold
description: A 3-way deadlock is observed in the windows nightly job_core_perhold_van test. I have seen it in the 7.2 branch, but I am fixing it in 7.4. The problem is that the starter sends a job update to the shadow and then waits for a response. The shadow evaluates job policy and wants to put the job on hold. The shadow connects to the startd and tells it to deactivate the claim. The startd tries to connect to the starter to send it a DC signal, but the starter is unresponsive, because it is waiting for the shadow. The fix I am making is to simply do the job policy evaluation in a 0-second timer so we can send a response to the starter right away.
remarks: 2009-Sep-14 14:10:24 by danb: The 0-second timer approach caused job_core_perremove-van to fail, because periodic_remove did not fire at job removal time. Therefore I am reverting that patch. Anyway, a different instance of a similar deadlock was observed that was not addressed by this patch, so I have implemented a different approach. The new approach is to have the startd reply to deactivate_claim immediately, rather than replying after signaling the starter.

description: With the introduction of more aggressive dynamic linking, it's possible to execve a condor binary that can't launch due to dynamic linker errors (wrong version of libcondor_utils). title: Ticket #3382: Removing a spot instance before instantiation causes it to go on hold.
description: If you remove a spot job before it starts an instance, you go to GM_SPOT_CANCEL, which cancels the spot request and goes to GM_SUBMITTED (in case an instance needs to be stopped). GM_SUBMITTED immediately jumps to GM_CANCEL, because the condorState of the job is still REMOVED. GM_CANCEL tries to stop the instance, but fails -- there not being an instance -- which puts the job on hold. The fix is for GM_CANCEL to only try to stop the instance if we know about one.

title: Ticket #1215: job_queue.log can be corrupted in case of rotation failure
description: Caused by a recent Windows problem (see gittrac #1191 ), we inspected the behavior of job_queue.log rotation a bit more closely. Turns out, in case of rotation failure, the old rotation file will be reopened with O_RDWR flag but without O_APPEND. Thus, future writers will start in the beginning of the file and therefore may produce nonsense for the schedd. That is, if the amount of data to be written in a schedd uptime does not exceed the amount of data written during the last session, the file's tail still consists of the old data. This will cause any future schedd to terminate until the job_queue.log file is manually deleted. The responsible code is the following (in bool ClassAdLog::TruncLog() in condor_c++_util/classad_log.cpp ): if (rotate_file(tmp_log_filename.Value(), logFilename()) < 0) { dprintf(D_ALWAYS, "failed to rotate job queue log!\n"); // Beat a hasty retreat into the past. historical_sequence_number--; int log_fd = safe_open_wrapper(logFilename(), O_RDWR | O_LARGEFILE, 0600); if (log_fd < 0) { EXCEPT("failed to reopen log %s, errno = %d after failing to rotate log.",logFilename(),errno); } log_fp = fdopen(log_fd, "r+"); if (log_fp == NULL) { EXCEPT("failed to refdopen log %s, errno = %d after failing to rotate log.",logFilename(),errno); } return false; } Obviously, on Linux it happens extremely rarely that a file rotation (i.e. a rename) does not succeed. As for Windows, it will fail if either file has another file descriptor open. Now, when exactly would this cause bad things? The job queue will get corrupted if the following conditions are met: rotate_file(.. ) returns a negative integer, i.e. rename(..) fails on POSIX or MoveFileEx(..) on WIN32. rename(..) will only in very rare occasions fail. One scenario that comes to mind would be a disk failure. MoveFileEx(..) in this scenario will fail if either the renaming file or the to be renamed file have another file descriptor open (which might be caused by a file-scanning anti-virus program or backup tool, for example) The corresponding code block is executed, and job_queue.log therefore opened with O_RDWR flag only. As a result, the next write to the job queue will start in the beginning of the file without truncating it. In case the old data will eventually entirely overwritten before the schedd's next restart, everything is ok. If the schedd terminates before the old data is entirely overwritten, this means that the file tail constitutes garbage which therefore renders the whole file to nonsense to the schedd upon restart. As a result the schedd will immediately terminate until the job_queue.log is manually deleted. manual deletion of the job queue will cause a loss of job information, and therefore: jobs Another (WIN32-only) quirk is the not necessarily atomic nature of MoveFileEx(..), which potentially could leave the job queue in a corrupted state (for example in case of a sudden reboot while rotating) I would like to collect some comments about how to deal with this problem. Some suggestions: a) Reopen the old file with O_RDWR | O_APPPEND | O_LARGEFILE . This will leave the file intact. On the downside, if the rotation is caused by a clean-up due to a dirty job queue (see CleanJobQueue() in condor_schedd.V6/qmgmt.cpp ), then some written changes will be expected (done by the function void ClassAdLog::LogState(FILE *fp) ). Another problem with this is that, in theory, job_queue.log might never be rotated and grow indefinitely. This would be unacceptable. b) Truncating the old file by setting the flag O_TRUNC. This will lead to a correct reinitialization of the file for the schedd and also avoid indefinite growth. But it can cause problems if, for example, quill is currently reading the job_queue.log. Additionally, there may be third-party tools beyond Condor's control that regularly read this file and therefore could get into trouble with this solution. Thoughts, comments?
remarks: 2010-Feb-15 13:51:29 by matt: First thought is that this seems like a rather major issue, even if rare. Second, use of Quill (deprecated?) or the JobRouter (nice and new) will make this more likely to happen. Does (b) suggest there will be a window where the only copy of the queue will be in the Schedd's memory? If so that seems like a dangerous solution. The typical solution to problems like this is to EXCEPT, and it looks like the intent of the original code was to just continue on. That suggests (a) as a better solution. Though (a) has a downside of indefinite job_queue.log growth, since we can rank sins, that's a less serious one than losing the queue altogether. 2010-Feb-17 16:56:16 by danb: Cathrin, I looked at the patch. It looks good to me, except I am a little worried about an upper bound of 30 seconds of sleep time in rotate_file(). I would be more comfortable with an upper bound of ~2 seconds. Regarding the question you pose in the comment after reopening the file. No, we definitely do not want to call LogState() on the reopened file. We want to just continue appending to the file as if we had never attempted to rotate the file. That way we are assured that at all times, the contents of the log can be used to reconstruct the in-memory classad collection. In your description of the problem in this ticket, you say that the job queue is corrupted and therefore information is lost if the schedd does not write beyond the existing contents of the file. However, even if the schedd writes beyond the end, the information it has overwritten is lost, so the job queue might not be reconstructable from the contents of the log. 2010-Feb-17 17:09:22 by matt: I am seriously concerned about any sleep() placed in the code, doubly concerned in the Schedd. The Schedd is not a multi-threaded daemon, any sleep will completely block all functions, not limited to: responding to condor_q, participating in negotiation (actually may block the negotiator indirectly), responding to shadows, sending keep alives to its master. In all situations we should return to DC::Driver as fast as possible. A sleep() directly prevents that. Instead of sleep(), register a timer to try the rotation sometime in the near future. The best thing would be to have rotation happening on a timer and the failure of rename should be propagated up to that timer so it can re-register itself for a short delay instead of its normal delay. 2010-Feb-18 14:50:29 by cweiss: It is true that the schedd will be blocked entirely due to sleep(). However, the event of a failing rotation should be rare anyway. Having a timer (or separate process) deal with the rotation ties back to the whole plan to have a logd at some point. I am not sure, though, whether currently it would a good idea to detach this from the schedd entirely, since there are certainly situations when the job queue should rather not be rotated. title: Ticket #4017: HTCondor-G -> NorduGrid -> HTCondor gives scrambled output
description: When Condor-G is used to submit jobs to a NorduGrid ARC server that submits into a Condor pool, the job's stdout/err gets mixed up with ARC's internal logs. This because both the gridmanager and the starter/shadow name the stdout/err files _condor_stdout and _condor_stderr. If ARC submitted the job directly to Condor, this would work fine. This problem doesn't occur if Condor's file transfer isn't used. In that case, the starter doesn't change the filenames of the wrappers stdout/err. I believe the best fix for this is to change the filenames used by the gridmanager when submitting jobs to NorduGrid ARC.

title: Ticket #6883: condor_gpu_discovery doesn't work with CUDA 10
description: with CUDA version 10, NVIDIA has changed the cuda runtime API in a way that is incompatible with condor_gpu_discovery, so the wrong values get reported for some attributes of the GPU. The workaround for users for now is to use version 9 of the libraries. Michael Pelletier suggests: In the meantime, you can also install the 9.2 release, and then set up the library path for condor_gpu_discovery to refer to /usr/local/cuda-9.2 instead of /usr/local/cuda, and that should get you through until they come out with an update for CUDA 10 support. The main cause of the problem appears to be that NVIDIA changed the cudeDeviceProp structure, but did not change the name of the API that populates it - And the structure is not versioned in any way. The API that populates it will just assume it was passed a structure of the size and layout that it was built for. In the current condor_gpu_discovery, the NVIDIA CUDA 10 runtime is just writing past the end of the structure that we pass it. Example code from NVIDIA completely ignores this issue, so at present we do not know what to check before allocating the structure to pass to the API, we might have to do some sort of heuristic check of the populated structure to figure out what version the NVIDIA libararies think they populated. update We have decided to use the runtime version to decide whether to use the Cuda10 or pre-Cuda10 version of the structure. We have also decided to prefer the driver library over the runtime library, which is a reverse of the previous preference.

title: Ticket #2593: Issues when teaching Condor to students
description: Hi all, We teach a "Grid and Cluster Computing" course once every 3 semesters, and today was our first hands-on day with building Condor clusters. I'm opening this ticket to record all the issues students ran into, under the assumption that other new Condor admins will hit the same things. In no particular order: 1) Security is a nightmare to ease folks in on. See https://condor-wiki.cs.wisc.edu/index.cgi/tktview?tn=2320 #2320. You either tell folks to run things insecure until they understand it, or spend a huge amount of time going over auth policies. I really like the idea of a "permissive mode" where the collector will distribute security tokens to anyone that connects, then is later turned off. 2) We had an issue where a student got InstanceLock to exist, but the condor_master appeared to be dead. When he did "service condor restart", Condor failed because it couldn't get the instance lock. Is advisory locking not working correctly? If another daemon actually has the lock, we should print out the PID of the "other guy" so the sysadmin can go searching for it. 3) If there is unparseable garbage in the config file, "service condor start" fails with: "FATAL: Unable to locate LOG in /etc/condor/condor_config" (regardless of what file or line is unparseable; always references LOG). This is specific to the UW RPM. 4) ALLOW_WRITE=* does not imply ALLOW_NEGOTIATOR by default. We had an issue where the CONDOR_HOST mapped to the external interface name, and the negotiator would contact the startd on the internal interface. This was fine by ALLOW_WRITE, but ALLOW_NEGOTIATOR=$(CONDOR_HOST), and the $(CONDOR_HOST) interface was not used. 4b) In the permission denied message, we should at least print out who has permission to that access level. It took me quite awhile to figure it out. Overall, much better than last time we taught this course, as we switched to the RPM. Got 5 working student clusters in a class period.
