title: Ticket #6929: Errors in writing compacted job_queue.log can cause corruption
description: The schedd persistently records all changes to its job queue by appending records to the job_queue.log transaction log. At startup, shutdown, and periodically, it compacts the log by writing a new file that contains just the current state of the job queue. It then uses this new file as the transaction log. The way it does so can lead to corruption if there's an error in the compaction process. Compacting the log (also called truncation in the code) consists of the following steps: Open file job_queue.log.tmp Write current job queue state to job_queue.log.tmp Close file handles for both job_queue.log and job_queue.log.tmp Rename job_queue.log.tmp to job_queue.log Open file job_queue.log in O_APPEND mode The critical bug is that when job_queue.log.tmp is opened, the O_CREAT flag is used but O_EXCL is not, and the file is never truncated. If the file already exists and is larger than the data the schedd writes (say from a failed attempt to compact the log), then the transaction log will contain invalid data. If the log is read before another compact operation, the reader will likely see illegal record formatting and an incorrect state of the job queue. In many cases, the schedd will refuse to start. There are several contributing factors that make corruption more likely to occur and affect users: If a compact operation fails, the .tmp file isn't removed. We need to close and reopen the new log file around the rename operation to avoid errors on windows. This causes us to skip past any extra data in a pre-existing .tmp file, instead of eventually overwriting it with new records. We avoid writing some transient job attributes (e.g. AutoClusterAttrs) in log records, but they will still appear in a compact operation. Thus, a compact operation done at schedd shutdown is likely to result in a larger file than a compact operation of the same log at schedd startup. Solution The main change to fix this corruption bug is to ensure that no data in an existing .tmp file survives a compact operation. A simple way to do this is to change the safe_open_wrapper_follow() we currently use to open the .tmp file to safe_create_replace_if_exists(). There are a few additional minor improvements we should make: unlink() the .tmp file if the compact operation fails. Don't leak an fd when fdopen() fails. Always have the log file open in append mode during normal operation. Currently, it's sometimes in append mode and sometimes isn't. User report This bug was uncovered while investigating a report of log corruption on htcondor-users. Based on their logs, this is our best guess as to what happened: On shutdown, schedd attempts to compact log Writes .tmp file, but fails to rename it. On startup, schedd successfully compacts log. Overwrites .tmp left from shutdown. New contents are 368 bytes shorter, due to AutoClusterId and AutoClusterAttrs not being present. End of log now contains a partial line plus last 12 lines of previous compact attempt. Schedd starts normal operations, appending new records to the end of the log. Machine is hibernated This happens six hours after schedd startup, before the first periodic compact operation. Machine wakes from hibernation Master immediately hard-kills all daemons due to large jump in system clock. Schedd restarts, aborts due to corruption in log. Miscellaneous I noticed an odd bit of behavior in the ClassAd log reader code (InstantiateLogEntry() in classad_log.cpp). If a log record has a valid opcode but there's something wrong with the rest of the line, we scan the rest of the file. If we don't see any EndTransaction records, then we pretend the problematic record was a truncated final line of the file (i.e. ignore the record and the active transaction, if any, and proceed). If the opcode is invalid or there is an EndTransaction afterwards, then reading of the file fails due to unrecoverable corruption. This seems like a strange division between recoverable and unrecoverable errors.

title: Ticket #1002: remove fallback to non-negotiated command protocol
description: SecMan will fall back to the non-negotiated command protocol (aka raw command protocol) if the client fails to get a response to DC_AUTHENTICATE. The assumption is that if we don't get a response then our peer must be pre 6.3.3, which means it doesn't understand DC_AUTHENTICATE. The problem is that we may fail to get a response for reasons other than an old peer and by attempting to reconnect to the peer, we may block the current process and hurt performance. Since we no longer care about compatibility with pre 6.3.3, this risk no longer seems worth the benefit of backward compatibility.

title: Ticket #3195: Maximize use of shared fs in the blahp
description: The blahp has code to determine when it can rely on a shared filesystem and when it has to employ explicit file transfer requests in the underlying batch system. This is done in the function bls_test_shared_dir() in blah_common_submit_functions.sh. This function always says relative pathnames cannot be accessed via a shared filesystem. As a result, if the ad given to the blahp by Condor contains a relative path, explicit file transfers are used even when they aren't necessary. This is a problem for SGE and some flavors of PBS, where file transfers by the batch system aren't supported. To fix this, we can change bls_setup_all_files() in blah_common_submit_functions.sh to always use absolute paths when calling bls_test_shared_dir(). Relative filenames are relative to the job's Iwd.

title: Ticket #488: [RFE] $([])
description: Context: log = $$([$(Process)+100]).log There are some subtleties with $$(). It is only evaluated after the job is matched to a machine. That's too late for choosing the log file, but not too late for other things, such as the arguments (which is what I assumed you were trying to set). $$() is evaluated after matching and $() is evaluated at submit time. We are only using $$() in this case because it happens to support evaluation of arbitrary expressions via $$([expr]) syntax. We don't need access to attributes of the machine in this expression, so it is too bad that something like $([expr]) isn't supported. That would do the trick nicely. --Dan

title: Ticket #522: condor_chirp fails when querying the value of a non-existing attribute
description: When querying the value of a non-existing attribute the condor_chirp get_job_attr command aborts, returning "abnormal program termination" on Windows and a core from SIGABRT on non-Windows.
remarks:
2010-Jul-15 00:05:24 by matt: Here's the skinny... On the shadow side, A get_job_attr for an attribute that does not exist hits pseudo_ops.cpp:pseudo_get_job_attr(name, expr) and returns -1: e = ad->Lookup(name); if(e) { ... } else { ...; return -1; }" The -1 gets returned to the "case CONDOR_get_job_attr" in NTreceivers.cpp, which happily handles it by encoding a response of "code(-1); code(0);" -- the -1 is the return value and 0 is the default errno. On the starter side, The receiver in io_proxy_handler.cpp eventually calls IOProxyHandler::convert to translate the errno (remember it was 0) into a CHIRP_ERROR code to send to condor_chirp. However, errno is not a known code, resulting in CHIRP_ERROR_UNKNOWN and a dprintf of "Starter ioproxy server got unknown unix errno:0" On the condor_chirp side, Result of CHIRP_ERROR_UNKNOWN is received, which triggers an unceremonious fprintf to stderr of "chirp: couldn't get response from server: Success" followed swiftly by abort(). The "Success" is from strerror(errno) and is meaningless. This behavior is definitely broken. 2010-Jul-15 00:28:05 by matt: Options for resolving this broken behavior - condor_chirp/PROTOCOL equates get_job_attr with getenv, which returns NULL if the env name isn't present Stop aborting, return non-zero - however, abort() is a actually triggered by a problem in the protocol Make unix_errno=0 known to IOProxyHandler::convert - however, requires picking an error code for 0, maybe CHIRP_ERROR_DOESNT_EXIST, changing all chirp client implementations to handle the new code, results in breaking wire protocol between new starter and old chirp clients Change pseudo_get_job_attr to set errno, maybe to ENOENT - better than converting errno=0 to CHIRP_ERROR_DOESNT_EXIST in IOProxyHandler::convert, but has all the same drawbacks Change pseudo_get_job_attr to return UNDEFINED - requires no protocol changes and no client changes, aligns well with ClassAd semantics and getenv("DOESNT_EXIST") -> NULL (Lookup("DOESNT_EXIST") -> UNDEFINED) 2010-Jul-15 00:29:29 by matt: diff --git a/src/condor_shadow.V6.1/pseudo_ops.cpp b/src/condor_shadow.V6.1/pseudo_ops.cpp index c71e1c2..c80230f 100644 --- a/src/condor_shadow.V6.1/pseudo_ops.cpp +++ b/src/condor_shadow.V6.1/pseudo_ops.cpp @@ -705,8 +705,9 @@ pseudo_get_job_attr( const char *name, MyString &expr ) dprintf(D_SYSCALLS,"pseudo_get_job_attr(%s) = %s
",name,expr.Value()); return 0; } else { - dprintf(D_SYSCALLS,"pseudo_get_job_attr(%s) failed
",name); - return -1; + dprintf(D_SYSCALLS,"pseudo_get_job_attr(%s) is UNDEFINED
",name); + expr = "UNDEFINED"; + return 0; } }

title: Ticket #6728: Undefined job policy expression can put job in tight run/idle cycle
description: When a job policy expression evaluates to Undefined, HTCondor is supposed to put the job on hold. If this happens when input transfer is starting and when_to_transfer_output is ON_EXIT_OR_EVICT, the starter ends up trying to start output transfer at the same time as input transfer and EXCEPTs. This sends the job back into idle status instead of held. This error in the starter can be triggered by any graceful shutdown command that it receives during the input sandbox transfer. The fix is for the starter to skip output transfer if the job hasn't started yet. An undefined job policy expression only triggers this bug in 8.7 (due to #6549), but other causes of a graceful shutdown to the starter would affect 8.6. The CMS team discovered this bug when their periodic remove expression included the following: JobStatus=?=2 && MemoryUsage > RequestMemory Two things that merit attention (probably deserving their own tickets): Consensus in the hallway is that we should change Condor so that an Undefined result for a job policy expression should treated the same as having not set the expression. The shadow doesn't evaluate the job policy expressions periodically before the job starts executing. It will do so in reaction to a job ad update from the starter or schedd.

title: Ticket #7093: Refactor/merge Scheduler:: and ResMgr:: try_token_request()
description: It's unclear where the common code belongs, but the Scheduler::try_token_request() and ResMgre::try_token_request() functions are very similar and should probably be merged to reduce future technical burden. It seems like DaemonCore might be a good place to put this function (although the decision about when to call it and with which arguments will have to remain daemon-specific).
remarks: 2019-Jun-20 08:53:50 by bbockelm: Additional refactoring requested from #7094: Add a callback for failure so we can convert the detection of authorization failures to use non-blocking mechanisms. Right now, an empty identity indicates to use the default. We should add an explicit define so it is obvious in the future (as opposed to looking like a programmer oversight). 2019-Jun-20 09:29:18 by bbockelm: Another thing to investigate here -- Currently, DC_FINISH_TOKEN_REQUEST requires encryption as we're not going to send a token back in the clear! Auto-approval mode, where we trust the network explicitly, doesn't use this RPC. However, if we use DaemonCore's "force authentication" feature, it refuses to the RPC for users that are authenticated-but-unmapped. It seems we want a slight twist on this -- force authentication but do not require the user to be mapped. 2019-Jul-14 20:36:43 by bbockelm: Ok, with 3 days left to go before the code freeze... Here's the PR for the refactor: https://github.com/htcondor/htcondor/pull/63 It not only gives the startd and schedd a common implementation of the token request workflow (improvement: both now support collector lists correctly!) but also switches everything to non-blocking. The nonblocking piece is useful in itself, but it also solves some memory management issues (as the SecMan which invokes the callback knows the socket is still valid). 2019-Jul-15 16:34:09 by tlmiller: Code Review Added two-subtickets for future work. Otherwise, OK. 2019-Jul-15 16:48:37 by tlmiller: On second thought, this is all internal code-cleanup and should have no user-visible effects. Brian, if you agree, please just go ahead and mark the ticket resolved. 2019-Jul-15 16:50:33 by bbockelm: Yup, agreed! Thanks for the "review under pressure". Much appreciated!

title: Ticket #1844: shadow fails to replace output directories in spool
description: When a non-empty directory exists in the job's spool directory, and this directory is listed in transfer_output_files, and output is being spooled, the shadow fails to replace the existing directory with the new one. The shadow aborts in FileTransfer::CommitFiles() in the following code: if ( rotate_file(buf.Value(),newbuf.Value()) < 0 ) { EXCEPT("FileTransfer CommitFiles Failed -- What Now?!?!"); } The reason for failure is that rotate_file() does not support rotation of one directory onto another directory if the target directory is non-empty.

title: Ticket #871: condor_q -xml -format changed behavior
description: Upon upgrading to a pre-release of 7.4.0, CMS found that the behavior of the following query changed in a way that broke the prodAgent instance serving the OSG: condor_q -xml -format "%s" Attr1+Attr2+Attr3 Prior to 7.3.2, the behavior of the above query was to produce xml output including all of the specified attributes (plus a few others that were always there by mistake/default). In 7.3.2 and the current pre-release of 7.4.0, the effect was to output an empty ad. The workaround is to query in 7.4.0 using the new syntax: condor_q -xml -attributes Attr1,Attr2,Attr3 but this does no work with older condor versions. A different workaround is to use multiple -format specifications: condor_q -xml -format "%s" Attr1 -format "%s" Attr2 -format "%s" Attr3 However, this change in behavior was not intentional and could cause problems for more people. I am making a patch that fixes it. I would like to get this into 7.4.0 so that there is no stable series version with the changed behavior.
remarks: The decision was to push this patch in 7.4.1.

title: Ticket #5554: Have docker universe report wall, CPU, and memory usage
description: At the European HTCondor Workshop, Andrew Lahiff from RAL noted that they couldn't use the Docker universe more widely because it does not report wall or CPU usage - a requirement for WLCG reporting. Wall time is fairly straightforward to derive (if nothing else, from docker inspect). Further, docker stats will get all the cgroup statistics from the container (which is a lot easier than trying to find the cgroup in a portable manner!). I have copied a sample interaction below. NOTE: This query takes about 2 seconds to perform. If you shutdown the unix socket after the HTTP GET request is sent - but before the response is received from the Docker daemon - the daemon will immediately return a HTTP 200 response with 0 length content. Hence, if you're working with the raw API (which may be the only option as docker stats doesn't have a raw formatting option), you must not shutdown the client end of the Unix socket. This shutdown issue is why the following example does not work with modern docker: echo -ne 'GET /v1.20/containers/fervent_poincare/stats?stream=0 HTTP/1.1\r\n\r\n' | nc -U /var/run/docker.sock It does seem that very recent versions of `curl` (7.40 and later) can talk to a Unix socket directly; the version on RHEL7 appears to be too old. title: Ticket #5104: ENABLE_IPV6=true should be the default in 8.5 series
description: Early in the 8.5 series (8.5.1?) we should set ENABLE_IPV6 to true by default.
remarks: 2016-Mar-15 15:26:23 by adesmet: Code review of [47675] "DNS lookups respect PREFER_IPV4." Passed. Everything outside of ipv6_addrinfo.cpp is perfect. I believe the changes to ipv6_addrinfo.cpp are correct. I have some general style/readability/maintainability concerns, but they should not block deployment of this. I'd prefer direct structure assignment over memcpy. So *rv = *ai instead of memcpy(rv, ai, sizeof(addrinfo)). Direct assignment is clearer (and could theoretically be faster, although probably not). Why does struct shared_context have a constructor and destructor, but the implementation is using malloc/free (as opposed to new/delete)? addrinfo_iterator::addrinfo_iterator silently drops results that are neither IPv4 nor IPv6. We should at least warn that we did so. The fairly complex deep-copy-and-resort logic for an addrinfo chain seems misplaced in addrinfo_iterator::addrinfo_iterator. Perhaps it should be in shared_context::shared_context, or perhaps a new, separate global function. 2016-May-31 09:41:13 by tlmiller: Changed memcpy to direct assignment. I don't know, but since I didn't write the code I don't want to futz with it. Warning added. Done. Constructor looks a little cleaner now.

title: Ticket #2442: submitter records deleted when prio-factor set to DEFAULT_PRIO_FACTOR
description: The accountant has logic for detecting when a submitter record has an explicit priority factor set on it, to prevent record deletion. This is to preserve the explicit setting. However, this check currently is keyed off of whether the priority-factor == the default factor, which causes incorrect deletion if the user explicitly sets the factor to that default value. This is particularly evident if there is a group priority factor default set, which is different than DEFAULT_PRIO_FACTOR.

"a.u2" still exists. [eje@rorschach ~]$ condor_userprio -l | grep -e '^Name' -e '^PriorityFactor' Name1 = "a" Name2 = "<none>" Name3 = "a.u2@localdomain" PriorityFactor1 = 4.000000 PriorityFactor2 = 1.000000 PriorityFactor3 = 2.000000 After the fix, we see that the entry for "a.u1" does not get removed, which is the correct behavior # accountant entries before any submitters: [eje@rorschach ~]$ condor_userprio -l | grep -e '^Name' -e '^PriorityFactor' Name1 = "a" Name2 = "<none>" PriorityFactor1 = 4.000000 PriorityFactor2 = 1.000000 # set prio factor for "a.u1" and "a.u2" as before: [eje@rorschach ~]$ condor_userprio -setfactor a.u1@localdomain 1 The priority factor of a.u1@localdomain was set to 1.000000 [eje@rorschach ~]$ condor_userprio -setfactor a.u2@localdomain 2 The priority factor of a.u2@localdomain was set to 2.000000 # entries immediately after setting prio factors: [eje@rorschach ~]$ condor_userprio -l | grep -e '^Name' -e '^PriorityFactor' Name1 = "a" Name2 = "<none>" Name3 = "a.u2@localdomain" Name4 = "a.u1@localdomain" PriorityFactor1 = 4.000000 PriorityFactor2 = 1.000000 PriorityFactor3 = 2.000000 PriorityFactor4 = 1.000000 # Now we see that both "a.u1" and "a.u2" still exist after update, as expected: [eje@rorschach ~]$ condor_userprio -l | grep -e '^Name' -e '^PriorityFactor' Name1 = "a" Name2 = "<none>" Name3 = "a.u2@localdomain" Name4 = "a.u1@localdomain" PriorityFactor1 = 4.000000 PriorityFactor2 = 1.000000 PriorityFactor3 = 2.000000 PriorityFactor4 = 1.000000 2011-Sep-23 16:06:07 by danb: Code review: looks good. title: Ticket #7640: net stop condor should not fail because of ALLOW_ADMIN config
description: The Windows way to shut down a service is net stop condor. This will fail if the ALLOW_ADMINISTRATOR configuration does not authorize any user on the local machine to send admin commands to the master. This is because of this code in the condor_master VOID StopService() { if( daemonCore->Send_Signal(daemonCore->getpid(), SIGQUIT) ) { runningService=FALSE; } } Send_Signal actually ends up opening a socket and sending a command on Windows, since signals are not a thing. This command then goes through the whole security layer, so it can fail even though the origination of the command is known to be authorized There is code in Send_Signal to short circuit and call the signal handler directly when the destination is the current process and the caller is the main thread. But when the Windows service manager sends notifications, it does not guarantee to use the main thread for them, so the short circuit can be bypassed.
creator: johnkn

title: Ticket #7355: condor_submit should never set the Owner attribute of the job
description: condor_submit will normally set the Owner attribute of the cluster ad that it is submitting to the name of the current user unless it is submitting to a remote schedd. (for the python bindings it doesn't know that the submit is remote, so it always sets the Owner attribute) This can cause submission to fail, because the schedd will reject the submit if the Owner attribute does not match the name of the mapped authenticated user that submits the job. For remote submits, condor_submit sets the Owner attribute to undefined since it knows it cannot assume that the mapped authenticated name is the same as the name of the current user. But anytime there is a map file, there is a danger that the mapped authenticated user is not the same as the current username. This can apply even when submitting locally. So condor_submit should never set the Owner attribute of the job, relying instead on the Schedd to set it. The downside of this change is that the schedd will no longer reject submissions when the mapping is broken and it would be unable to copy files from the submit directory, the jobs will instead be submitted, but then go on hold when file transfer fails. a new knob SUBMIT_SHOULD_SET_LOCAL_OWNER will be added. It will default to false in the code (not in the param table). setting it to true will restore the pre 8.9.5 behavior.

title: Ticket #5368: condor_transfer_data fails and causes schedd to except
description: Due to same safeguards added in #4522, the SchedD will except when transferring data out to the condor_transfer_data tool. Gory details: the problem is in BuildFileCatalog in the file transfer object, which hard-codes a parameter to the instantiation of a Directory object as PRIV_USER. This causes the Directory object to attempt to switch to user priv when iterating the contents of spool, which we don't want since user_privs have not been initted and spool is owned by the condor user anyway. The reason this is a regression is that without this check, some warnings would get dprintf'ed into the log, but it was not fatal. The commits in #4522 change the failure semantics. I could simply change the one call site that I'm aware of, but am uncertain we wouldn't be bitten again by a different use case. As such, my preference for 8.4.2 is to revert the change, going back to the same behavior as 8.4.0, and leave this alone for the stable series. We should put the EXCEPT back in and fix call sites in the dev series.

title: Ticket #2157: condor_config_val -config mixes stderr/stdout output
description: Typical output from condor_config_val -config: Configuration source: /var/home/condor/condor_config Local configuration sources: /unsup/condor/etc/condor_config.hosts /unsup/condor/etc/condor_config.global /unsup/condor/etc/hosts/puffin.local The actual list of files is sent to stdout. The headers (ex. "Configuration source:") go to stderr. Problem 1: No guarantee that they'll arrive in the right order on an interactive terminal (but in practice it's fine). Problem 2: If you route the output through less or try to capture it in another program, by default the headers disappear. Problem 3: It's not really an "error" and doesn't belong in stderr. We should make it stdout, not stderr. The code in question is in /src/condor_tools/config_val.cpp PrintConfigSources, line 716-729. BUT... why is it this way? Is someone relying on this behavior, perhaps having a script capture stdout to find a list of filenames and ignoring stderr? This behavior dates back to pre-2007 and probably dates back to the initial work.

title: Ticket #6817: Invoking python bindings as root changes euid to condor
description: Bug description and reproduction If a process running as root invokes the HTCondor Python bindings, the effective user id might change to user 'condor' (or to whatever uid is specified in the environment variable CONDOR_IDS). While this behavior is not a security problem per-se, because the privilege is being reduced instead of escalated, it is certainly unexpected. Here is a simple way to demonstrate the problem... just run python as root, invoke a common API binding, and observe the change in euid: [root@localhost build_880]# python Python 2.7.5 (default, Jul 13 2018, 13:06:57) [GCC 4.8.5 20150623 (Red Hat 4.8.5-28)] on linux2 Type "help", "copyright", "credits" or "license" for more information. >>> import os >>> import htcondor >>> os.geteuid() 0 >>> htcondor.enable_log() >>> os.geteuid() 994 Mitigation in this ticket While we have discussed potential fixes that are more systemic, this ticket will implement a minimally obtrusive fix for the stable series in order to reduce the chance of regressions. Specifically, we will introduce a method that causes all set_priv calls to be ignored (just as if the process is running without root access), and the utility library will default to this state. HTCondor daemons will explicitly enable priv switching in the utility library when they start up, but other processes (python and tools) will run with it disabled. Possible immediate work-around If using a version of the HTCondor python bindings earlier v8.8.0 and unable to upgrade (realize only the bindings need to be upgraded, not the HTCondor daemons themselves), a potential workaround for this bug would be for the caller to set environment variable CONDOR_IDS='0.0', which tells the bindings that the euid of user 'condor' is 0. Behold: [root@localhost release_dir]# python Python 2.7.5 (default, Jul 13 2018, 13:06:57) [GCC 4.8.5 20150623 (Red Hat 4.8.5-28)] on linux2 Type "help", "copyright", "credits" or "license" for more information. >>> import htcondor >>> import os >>> os.environ['CONDOR_IDS']='0.0' >>> htcondor.enable_log() >>> os.geteuid() 0 >>> htcondor.version() '$CondorVersion: 8.7.9 Jul 31 2018 BuildID: 446081 $' >>>

title: Ticket #4579: isQueueSuperUser should use case-insensitive usernames on Windows
description: On windows, usernames are case-insensitive. but when the SCHEDD checks to see if a username is a member of the queue super users group, it uses a case-sensitive comparison. This problem is exacerbated by the fact that case is preserved in some parts of HTCondor but not in others, so that if a username is not defined to be all lowercase, in some places it will forced to all lowercase before comparing it to the superusers list. View the admin rust queue a user comments: At (roughly) line 1483 in the \condor-8.2.1\src\condor_schedd.V6\qmgmt.cpp file, there is a block of code (in OwnerCheck2) that compares the usernames of the job owner and the entity trying to connect to the queue. Here is the relevant code ... // Finally, compare the owner of the ad with the entity trying // to connect to the queue. #if defined(WIN32) // WIN32: user names are case-insensitive if (strcasecmp(job_owner, test_owner) =3D=3D 0) { #else if (strcmp(job_owner, test_owner) =3D=3D 0) { #endif return true; } if (isQueueSuperUser(test_owner)) { dprintf(D_FULLDEBUG, "OwnerCheck retval 1 (success), super_user\n"); return true; } Note that the first part of this block of code in OwnerCheck2 correctly compares the two usernames on Windows platforms using a case insensitive function (strcasecmp). However, the second part of this block of code invokes isQueueSuperUser() to test if test_owner is one of the users named in the QUEUE_SUPER_USERS macro - and, the corresponding comparison in isQueueSuperUser() is still using a case sensitive function - here is the code (in isQueueSuperUser) from (roughly) line 1306 of the same file. if( strcmp( user, super_users[i] ) =3D=3D 0 ) { return true; } This code should be changed so that it uses case-insensitive comparison logic also.

title: Ticket #6114: Generate and pass runtime configuration to annex instances
description: If the instances have the proper software/configuration installed (which we'll want to make an RPM, eventually), and they're running as a compatible IAM role (and we offer a CloudFormation template to create one), then they can securely obtain configuration (including security tokens) from an S3 bucket (which also must be properly configured). What we'd like to do is (for a certain limited set of situations) automate the process of generating that configuration and uploading it to the S3 bucket in question. Since we can assume we "own" the uploaded file, and S3 assures us that partial writes don't happen, we won't worry about rolling back file uploads like we do everything else if something terrible happens. (In a later version, with a persistent daemon, when the instance-joining delay has passed, we could delete the uploaded file at that point.) In addition to the security configuration, we must pass the annex name in such a way that it will be advertised by both the master and the startd; since the mechanism already handles arbitrary configuration files, this should not be difficult. If it's just as easy, and it probably will be, we'd like to allow the admin (or user) to specify a configuration directory into which we will write additional configuration and security token files. This will afford admins (or users) an easy way to adjust their condor configuration on a per-annex basis.

title: Ticket #3438: EC2: Be paranoid about executing and logging TerminateInstances().
description: Tony Tiradani has seen OpenStack acknowledge a TerminateInstances() command, but (because of network problems) subsequently fail to terminate the instance. HTCondor needs to do three things to minimize the damage from this failure case: (1) Issue an explicit TerminateInstances() command for each job before it leaves the queue. Because TerminateInstances() is idempotent, this will not have any ill effect. (2) Log, in the job ad, when it sent TerminateInstances() and what response it received and when. (3) Record, in the job ad, the reason for the job leaving the queue. title: Ticket #4607: Always update node status file
description: Right now, we have some code in dag.cpp (see Dag::DumpNodeStatus) that prints out: "Node status file not updated because it is not yet outdated" then skips the printing out the node file. However, there's a very important thing we miss by not writing out the update -- the last updated timestamp. Since querying the status of the DAGMan job in the condor_q is quite unreliable (schedds at scale... sigh), we'd be able to skip the query if DAGMan never skipped the node status file. We would look at the timestamp and, if it's more than N minutes old, then query the schedd for the DAGMan job status. Why not trust that DAGMan always writes out the node status file? This assumes there are no future bugs in DAGMan in the hold / remove path. This assumes that no sneaky admin did a "kill -9" on condor_dagman. Belt and suspenders! It's the HTCondor way. More seriously - we need something that emulates a job lease in a distributed system like this. It would be perfectly acceptable for this behavior to be a HTCondor config parameter.
remarks: 2014-Sep-25 10:39:36 by wenger: Actually, now that I think about it, I'd rather add it to the node status file specification in the DAG file, as opposed to making it a new config param. So it would be something like this: NODE_STATUS_FILE statusFileName [minimumUpdateTime] [ALWAYS_UPDATE]

title: Ticket #6790: Submit object in python bindings needs a spool flag
description: The Submit object in the python bindings has no support for spooling job files to the schedd. The old submit() function in the Schedd object does have a spool flag. The Schedd object already has spool() and retrieve() methods for doing the transfers of the job input and output sandboxes. You can make spooling of job files work with the the Submit object today by manually setting several attributes in the job ads. Here's an example: #!/usr/bin/python import htcondor import sys, os os.environ['X509_USER_PROXY'] = '/home/dcameron/dev/aCT/proxies/proxiesid2' coll = htcondor.Collector('ce513.cern.ch:9619') sch = coll.locate(htcondor.DaemonTypes.Schedd) schedd = htcondor.Schedd(sch) # Including paths in Output or Error requires some extra changes cad = {"Cmd": "/bin/ls", "Output": "job.$(ClusterId).$(ProcId).out", "Error": "job.$(ClusterId).$(ProcId).err", "Iwd": "/tmp/output", "+JobStatus": "5", "+HoldReason": "\"Spooling input data files\"", "+HoldReasonCode": "16", "+LeaveJobInQueue": "JobStatus == 4 && (CompletionDate =?= undefined || CompletionDate == 0 || ((time() - CompletionDate) < 864000))", "UserLog": "/tmp/output/job.$(ClusterId).$(ProcId).log"} sub = htcondor.Submit(cad) ad_list = [] with schedd.transaction() as txn: jobid = sub.queue(txn, ad_results=ad_list) for ad in ad_list: ad["ClusterId"]=jobid schedd.spool(ad_list) print (jobid) Note: If you want the output and error filenames to contain any path information, then you also need to set TransferOutputRemaps.

title: Ticket #7882: Spurious out of memory errors with cgroup_memory_policy = soft
description: Note: This is a dup of htcondor-17 The HTCondor starter can ask the cgroup memory controller to freeze all processes within a job's cgroup when the memory usage of all the processes in the cgroup hits some limit. That is, if the startd is runnning as root, and CGROUP_MEMORY_LIMIT_POLICY = hard. The starter does this by writing the memory size of the slot, in bytes to memory.memory_limit_in_bytes. When this happens, the starter is notified, and it has a decision to make. It can remove the job from the worker node and put it on hold. Or, it can ignore the message, sleep for a bit, and hope for the best. Early versions of HTCondor just did the former, but we ran into a problem – on machines running non-condor services that used significant amounts of memory, the starter could get the out-of-memory signal even when the job was using less than the amount allocated to the slot (because a non-condor process was hogging memory, and cgroups don't support memory reservations, just limits. It seemed unfair to put the job on hold (and this was something that the Nemo cluster tripped over a lot), so, we changed HTCondor to check how much memory the job was using, and if it was using less than the allocation, we'd continue, and usually the OOM signal eventually made it to the real offender. However, when we poll the procd to ask it how much memory the job is using, there are a lot of categories of memory: let's just consider the main two: user-space RSS, and the kernel page cache used by the job. The limit in memory.memory_limit_in_bytes, does not count just the user-space RSS, but it includes at least some amount of kernel page cache (this is, arguably a bug, but what are you going to do?). So, when the starter gets the OOM signal, if it just looks at the pure user space RSS, it will always be lower than the provisioned memory limit, and it will let the job go, and it will get into a tight loop, making no progress. CHTC got hit by this a lot. So, we changed the memory reported by the start to include the page cache. It seemed inconsistent to have one memory usage that was only used for the "what do I do when I get OOM'ed" vs. the job as a whole, so we only report the one. Now this becomes a problem if CGROUP_MEMORY_LIMIT_POLICY = soft, as the page cache can grow arbitrarily large. Note that the sum of all memory usage, including user + kernel space is capped to the limit when the policy is hard. Note that it is reflecting the true memory used, but it becomes not very useful if you have a PERIODIC_HOLD policy that looks at this value. LIGO has both a periodic hold policy that puts the job when it is using more than 1.5 times the provisioned amount and a SOFT memory policy. LIGO's goal is to only have a hard limit for the sum of all jobs on a machine – if there is just one job running (or one job using a significant amount of memory), LIGO is happy to let it use all of the memory on the machine, if none of the other jobs want it. (Or Maybe up to 1.5 times the provisioned amount, according to the SYSTEM_PERIODIC_REMOVE policy). A modest proposal: It was a mistake to support either a soft or hard memory limit policy. These are two separate limits in cgroups v1 (there are three in v2, grid help us all) I would suggest that we always set both, with the soft limit below the hard limit. 1) Add knobs that allow the startd (or is it starter?) CGROUP_MEMORY_LIMIT_HARD and CGROUP_MEMORY_LIMIT_SOFT to set the hard and soft limit to a classad expression referencing aspects of machine (MY) or job (TARGET). 2) When CGROUP_MEMORY_LIMIT_POLICY is set to HARD, that sets the following values to the knobs added in step 1: CGROUP_MEMORY_LIMIT_HARD = Memory CGROUP_MEMORY_LIMIT_SOFT = 0.9 * Memory 3) When CGROUP_MEMORY_LIMIT_POLICY is set to SOFT, that sets the following values to the knobs added in step 1: CGROUP_MEMORY_LIMIT_HARD = TotalMemory (...this attribute is startd DetectedMemory - ReservedMemory IIRC...) CGROUP_MEMORY_LIMIT_SOFT = 0.9 * Memory 4) We add a fourth "CUSTOM" option to CGROUP_MEMORY_LIMIT_POLICY. If CGROUP_MEMORY_LIMIT_POLICY=CUSTOM, then the startd will EXCEPT with an error if either CGROUP_MEMORY_LIMIT_HARD and CGROUP_MEMORY_LIMIT_SOFT are not explicitly set in the config file, and/or if CGROUP_MEMORY_LIMIT_HARD is not greater than CGROUP_MEMORY_LIMIT_SOFT. If CGROUP_MEMORY_LIMIT_POLICY is anything but CUSTOM, then CGROUP_MEMORY_LIMIT_* knobs are ignored. We can document the CUSTOM option as only for kernel tuning experts and is not recommended for general use. 5) Change the procd so that we only report RSS; specifically, we want to inspect the cgroup rss metric which we believe encapsulates the anonymous memory footprint of the set of processes in the group (but not cache pages). 6) When the starter catches the OOM signal, and we are using cgroups to monitor job usage, then we kill the job if all memory used by the cgroup (both RSS and active_file/cache) is greater than CGROUP_MEMORY_LIMIT_HARD. If this is too difficult to code because of the way we channel everything through the silly procd, then alternative kill the job if MemoryUsage (which default to RSS) > CGROUP_MEMORY_LIMIT_SOFT .

title: Ticket #1956: Move stduniv to new starter/shadow
description: What would it take to move stduniv to the new starter/shadow where WantRemoteIO would always be false? Remote system calls: The lifeline socket from the job to the stduniv shadow should instead be from the job to the new starter. All communication by the stduniv job does should be funneled through to the new starter. It needs a little more work to figure out how this socket lives in relation to daemoncore. The starter would only support those calls which the executable needs to start up, shut down, and find out where the checkpoint image is located or to where it should be written. All others are shunted to the local file system via WantRemoteIO = False. If we wanted to support the rest of Remote I/O, then the new starter can either handle the remote i/o requests itself or shunt them via a protocol over a daemoncore socket to the new shadow who will provide answers. This could be done over chirp as well. Checkpointing: A user job needs to locate the checkpoint when needing it, or a place to put it when creating it. Source checkpoints can live in these places: submit machine checkpoint server third party file server Destination checkpoints can live in these places: submit machine checkpoint server third party file server There is some leeway in how the job actually gets the checkpoint. For example, the shadow could use file transfer to transfer the checkpoint from the submit machine to the execute machine before the job starts up. When the starter starts the job it'll tell it the on disk location to restart from. If the checkpoint was always read/written from the local disk under the starter's control. Then file transfer plugins could be invoked to pull/push a checkpoint to wherever it needs to go. Starter: A new StdunivProc has to be derived from OSProc which encapsulates things like periodically checkpointing, handling the connection from the stduniv job, starting the job with the right exec personality, etc. I don't think this will be too hard. A mechanism for periodic checkpoints would have to be made. This could just be two attributed in the job ad, specified in the submit file, which contain the periodic signal to be sent, plus the time span between each sending. title: Ticket #92: Dynamic directory names appended on reconfig
description: If a daemon is given -d on the command line, it rewrites the values of LOG, SPOOL, and EXECUTE by appending its IP address and pid. It sets the appropriate environment variables so that its children will use the rewritten values. This is used for glide-in, so that multiple glide-ins to the same cluster can automatically have different log, spool, and execute directories. It appears each time the daemon receives a reconfig (via either condor_reconfig or SIGHUP), it will append another copy of the IP and pid to LOG, SPOOL, and EXECUTE, and start using the new values.
remarks: 2010-Mar-18 10:36:48 by jfrey: Pushed a fix to V7_4-branch. Now, the modified LOG, SPOOL, and EXECUTE values are left untouched on a reconfig. This means that a change of these parameters in the config file will be ignored. This keeps the daemon's handling of these parameters the same as its children, which never see changes of the values in the config file.

title: Ticket #5446: Condor-C jobs aborted when lease is less than one hour
description: When a Condor-C job's lease duration is less than three hours, the lease may not be renewed frequently enough. If the lease duration is less than one hour, then it may not be renewed before it expires, causing the job to be aborted. When all job leases are checked (and possibly renewed), a timer is set for the next time a renewal needs to happen (max 1 hour). If a new job shows up from the schedd or is submitted to the remote server, this timer isn't re-evaluated with the new job's lease. So if the new job has a shorter lease, it wouldn't get renewed when it should.
remarks: 2016-Jan-06 15:57:17 by jfrey: Also, in the job submitted to the remote schedd, the default lease duration should be 40 minutes, not 20 minutes. We changed this default in condor_submit in 8.3. 2016-Feb-01 10:50:14 by tlmiller: Code Review Looks good.

title: Ticket #5153: Add Travis CI yaml file
description: I'd like to add a .travis.yml file to the repository root. This provides support for http://travis-ci.org, a continuous integration product that's tightly integrated with Github. Wait - you ask - don't we already have a CI product? Travis CI itself is actually fairly limited - single platform, fairly limited amount of max build time, no separate testing phase from build. It is no batlab! However, it has one killer feature missing from batlab: ability for unauthenticated users to trigger builds for arbitrary code. The platform is container-based if sudo is unnecessary for building and VM-based otherwise. Relative to the number of people with github accounts, batlab users are rare. Allowing us to do clipped builds from arbitrary patches should help ease the pain of contribution (both for the contributors and the patch reviewers) from folks outside the core team. We could check the results of the build from any newcomer before we start taking a close look. This would be completely optional; I propose no changes to the contribution process. I propose adding a minimal clipped build to enable support. Other than adding a file to our repo, there's no other action needed.

title: Ticket #3087: DAGMan on NFS problems
description: Message on condor-staff: Hi, For the OSG User school, we wanted the students to work out of NFS. I remembered that DAGMan may not work well when the job log files are on NFS. I talked it over with Todd, and he reminded me that this problem has been addressed because of CREATE_LOCKS_ON_LOCAL_DISK. http://research.cs.wisc.edu/condor/manual/v7.8/3_3Configuration.html#param:NewLocking Rock on! We can use DAGMan when submitting from NFS. This is great, and it worked well for the school. Three things surprised me. Two are documentation issues (Karen) and one may be a problem with a d default configuration setting: 1. The documentation for CREATE_LOCKS_ON_LOCAL_DISK says: When True, job user logs and the global job event log are written to a directory named condorLocks That's not true, is it? The logs are still written where the user specified them, but the locks for those files are written on local disk, right? 2. The documentation for DAGMan says: http://research.cs.wisc.edu/condor/manual/v7.8/2_10DAGMan_Applications.html#4668 Log files for node jobs should not be placed on NFS. NFS file locking is not reliable, occasionally resulting in simultaneous acquisition of locks on a single log file by both the condor_schedd daemon and thecondor_dagman job. By default, this isn't true anymore, right? At least on Unix, it's only true if someone disables CREATE_LOCKS_ON_LOCAL_DISK. I think this should be clarified 3. The default for DAGMAN_LOG_ON_NFS_IS_ERROR is True which causes errors when I submit from NFS, even if CREATE_LOCKS_ON_LOCAL_DISK is True. This is broken, right? I shouldn't be getting an error if I'm putting locks on local disk, right? -alain

title: Ticket #125: Create a daemonCore skeleton for Java services
description: We currently have a source code "skeleton" for folks who want to create a daemon core service in C++; it is sitting in /src/condor_dcskel . We also have some pithy documentation. Now we want to do the same thing, but for services that will be implemented in Java. What inspired this? Well, we did or are doing a bunch of work to incorporate a Java service (see tickets #7, #209) as a Condor daemon including: run under the master w/ keep alives respond to condor_on, condor_off, condor_reconfig, etc. read config params out of the Condor config file and rewrite them as appropriate for the service in question. etc, etc. Since we did this, and we have been asked before by collaborators about incorporating Java-implemented services into Condor, we are trying out creating a Java-based daemon core skeleton. This ticket will hold thoughts/design/code on this effort.
remarks: 2009-Jan-29 21:16:30 by faisal: A java based daemon inside Condor can be a java process created using Create_Process call. In order to make launching of a desired java service slightly convenient, in terms of constructing command line arguments, we can require it to be packaged as a single jar file. This jar file should then contain all necessary components (java classes, third-party libraries and even some static resources e.g files etc). On interesting issue here is concerning the fact that main logic of our daemon is now running as a separate process. We might like to open a communication channel between java process and any other daemon and/or client. I think there is a way to open a command channel to a process created by Create_Process? 2009-Feb-24 12:00:02 by faisal: I created two version of skeletons: (a) One is based on creating a Java process (java -jar <jar-containing-main-class.jar>) that can run under the control of our Master daemon. Its life cycle (create, restart/re-config, destroy) is managed by Master. All the necessary parameters to start a jvm e.g classpath can be controlled using Condor's configuration file. Under this configuration only possible way for java/c++ communication, at this point, is to use sockets. (b) A JNI based skeleton that uses JNI to create jvm inside our C++ code and compiles with the Condor. I am writing an example JAVA program along with a README file for its usage. As it uses JNI, we can easily call methods inside jvm with some overheads.

title: Ticket #1110: cron-like jobs not re-executing with dynamic provisioning
description: See https://bugzilla.redhat.com/show_bug.cgi?id=505119 The job has a requirement that the Memory on the slot where it runs is larger than its ImageSize. After the job runs once the ImageSize is updated to a more reasonable value, and that value is likely greater than 1MB. The result is the job matches, but when it goes to run on the dynamically created slot its requirements prevent it.
remarks: 2011-Jan-03 12:54:51 by danb: I sometimes find myself wondering why RequestMemory gets compared to ImageSize in the job's default requirements. ( ( RequestMemory * 1024 ) >= ImageSize ) Doesn't the schedd adjust its copy of the slot ad so that the advertised memory of the slot is reduced to the amount requested? If so, then why doesn't the default memory requirement address the problem described in this ticket? ( ( TARGET.Memory * 1024 ) >= ImageSize ) 2011-Jan-03 14:14:40 by matt: The Schedd does. The Negotiator does not. Without the expression the Negotiator will hand out matches that cannot actually be used because during activation the Job's ImageSize will be larger than the Memory requested. Without having the RequestMemory:ImageSize comparison in the Requirements, there is no way of debugging this except for looking at StartLogs. The comparison allows for detection of the issue via condor_q -bet, and has the benefit of preventing the creation of matches that cannot be used. 2011-Jan-03 15:53:30 by danb: What about replacing this: ( ( TARGET.Memory * 1024 ) >= ImageSize ) && ( ( RequestMemory * 1024 ) >= ImageSize ) with this: TARGET.Memory >= RequestMemory 2011-Jan-04 10:34:09 by matt: In that case the Schedd will still receive a match from the Negotaitor, and it may prevent the Schedd from activating the claim. If it didn't the Startd will definitely prevent activation. The means to debug such a situation still requires hitting log files instead of the usual means of -bet, and will still result in the generation of unused matches.

title: Ticket #2415: add automatic retries to glexec
description: Igor requests that when a glexec operation fails, Condor should automatically retry X times with time-delayed backoff. This would help in situations where the new hold-on-failure behavior added in #2324 would cause jobs to go on hold due to transient failures of glexec (e.g. due to overload of the mapping service).
remarks: 2013-Jan-04 15:45:40 by danb: I have attached a patch that implements automatic retries in case of transient glexec failures. Two new configuration knobs are added: GLEXEC_RETRIES (default 3) specifies the maximum number of times to retry a failed glexec call. Random exponential backoff is used, with a minimum delay of GLEXEC_RETRY_DELAY and a maximum retry delay of 100*GLEXEC_RETRY_DELAY seconds. The starter is blocked during the retry loop, so it will not send daemon heartbeats or respond to any communication during that time, so it would be best to keep the upper bound reasonable small (say 10 minutes). I have tested this patch in 7.8.8. It is a fairly large patch for a stable series, but it should only impact installations using glexec. Igor has made a strong request for this feature in 7.8, because changes in 7.7 have caused useability problems in cases where glexec experiences transient failures. Prior to the 7.7 changes, transient glexec errors caused shadow exceptions but were otherwise not visible to users. After the 7.7 changes, transient glexec errors cause user jobs to go on hold. With automatic retries, the glidein administrators will be able to tune the error threshold at which glexec errors cause jobs to go on hold. 2013-Jan-07 12:33:29 by zmiller: CODE REVIEW by zmiller just gave it a first-pass review. at a high level, i have one question: why do the retry in shell code, where the code is duplicated several times between the scripts? because it needs to be done in C for condor_glexec_run anyways, what about having GLExecPrivSepHelper::run_script() function do the retries, since it wraps all the calls to the glexec helper scripts? perhaps then there could be one code path that does the retries via a function called by both GLExecPrivSepHelper::run_script() and GLExecPrivSepHelper::create_process(). i do recognize that condor_glexec_run is a bit different beast from the others. however, i was curious if you had considered that approach. it seems like it would eliminate a lot of changes to the helper function signatures and script argument passing code, as well as the scripts themselves. 2013-Jan-07 13:34:35 by danb: I think it would be reasonable to do the retries in the C code rather than the helper scripts. However, condor_glexec_kill is called by the procd, not the starter, so there are still several pretty different code paths where the retry loop needs to be implemented. Also, I hate sticking sleep() calls in Condor proper! But I'd be willing to submit an alternate patch if you like. 2013-Jan-09 11:21:46 by zmiller: given that, let's go with your first approach. however, that is a very interesting point about the procd. i am uncomfortable blocking for long periods of time in the procd vs in the starter. isn't the procd also used by all other daemons on the system? this could cause all of condor to become unresponsive. in the procd, the glexec_kill() function already does fork/exec. perhaps we could remove the waitpid() so it runs in the background. the only action performed after waitpid() is to dprintf() in the case of failure. and at the moment, neither of the two invocations of glexec_kill() check the return code anyways. thoughts on this? 2013-Jan-09 11:29:20 by danb: I like the idea of doing a non-blocking fork of condor_glexec_kill. For single-slot glideins, blocking in the procd is less worrisome than it would be in other situations, but we should be prepared for all cases. I'd vote for making this change in the dev branch. 2013-Jan-09 14:52:18 by zmiller: dan and i discussed in person, and are going to roll in the non-blocking "glexec_kill" into the stable version. 2013-Jan-10 12:41:59 by danb: I have a patch that avoids blocking the procd for the glexec kill operation. However, I am having second thoughts about it. The client who is requesting the kill (i.e. the starter) is expecting the job to be dead when the call returns. Is it acceptable to violate that assumption? 2013-Jan-10 13:59:38 by danb: Here is an example of what I think can happen when the job lingers after the starter calls Kill_Family(): Suppose there is a job that uses ON_EXIT_OR_EVICT file transfer. When the job is evicted, condor "chowns" the output to condor by tarring it as the user and untarring it as condor (over a pipe). If condor_glexec_kill loses the race, tar may start reading from files that are still being written to. This could result in a corrupted snapshot of the sandbox. We do wait for the top-level process in the job to exit, so the race is only between the killing of child processes and the return of Kill_Family(). As such, it is a fairly obscure corner case, but I still think it may be an important one to get right. If Kill_Family() in the client kept polling the procd to see if the processes were all gone, that would be one way to avoid blocking in the procd. However, that is a bit out of scope for the current ticket, I think. 2013-Jan-10 15:00:40 by zmiller: dan -- okay, i'm convinced. let's waitpid() for glexec_kill to finish for this round of code changes.

remarks: 2010-Mar-15 16:39:35 by psilord: psilord's review of the MyString Work: General style comments ---------------------- 1. In C, two strings next to each other get concatenated by the compiler automatically. This allows you to change something like this: e.emit_test("Does the = operator work correctly when an empty MyString gets assigned a non empty MyString?"); into the much more readable this: e.emit_test("Does the = operator work correctly when an empty MyString " "gets assigned a non empty MyString?"); You should use this idiom more and not have any strings of program text go beyond 80 characters. 2. When a unit test discovers a true bug, don't fix the bug, but write up a public ticket for it in git trac. Write the test how it is supposed to work, but leave it commented out in the setting of it into the function_driver. We may fix the function driver to notice "skipped" or "buggy" tests and emit them at the end. Be VERY CAREFUL to ensure that you don't enshrine bugs in the API you are testing into the test suite. If I do 1 + 2 and get "periwinkle" as an answer, that is not correct! Don't just assume it is correct because the system gave you that answer. Of course, we might be relying on that answer somewhere in Condor, but that is out of your scope for now. :) If it doesn't make sense, it is most likely wrong. Of course, if any tests cause segfault ot other horrible thing like that, that is in instant git trac ticket. Fixes ----- In function: copy_constructor Rename to copy_constructor_value_check. Add a new function called copy_constructor_pointer_check which does the same procedure as copy_constructor_value_check, but checks only that the pointers returns by one.Value() and two.Value() are in fact different. set_char_last This test doesn't test what the emit_test function states and due to that it passes with a false positive. Please fix. random_string_many_chars This test doesn't test that the randomly generated string only contained characters from the set in question. // put into the little utility file for the unit tests. int all_str_are_picks(MyString &str, char *picks) { int i; for(i = 0; i < str.Length(); i++) { if (strchr(picks, (int)str[i]) == NULL) return FALSE; } } return TRUE; } You'd call it like: all_set_is_picks(rnd, "0123456789"); Most of your random string tests and the function random_string_hex will benefit from it. random_string_negative_length User the e.emit_problem function for your Fails comment note. This allows it to showup in the resultant output. equals_operator_my_string_empty_non_empty The boolean test doesn't makes sense.dd concatenation_my_string_itself This test looks very wrong, are you stating that MyString a("foo") a += a; and then a is equal to "foo"? You expect "foo" in the expected_header and if a.Value() != "foo" it would be an error. I would expect a.Value() to be "foofoo" and so != "foo" and it would have been marked an error. So the output of your unit tests should have shown at least one error. If what I believe is not the case, then it seems MyString has a bad bug to me! I realize that unit testing is difficult, but ultimately, one must ask if the answer you are computing makes sense! concatenation_char_null The note of this test should be an e.emit_problem header. Also, this looks like a bug as well. :) concatenation_int_large For this test, use INT_MAX concatenation_int_small For this test, use INT_MIN concatenation_uint_large For this test, use UINT_MAX concatenation_long_large For this test, use LONG_MAX The test of this should do a strcmp against a.Value() and char buf[1024]; sprint(buf, "%s%d", "foo", LONG_MAX); if (a.Value() != buf) { ... } the reason is because LONG_MAX changes depending upon if you are on a 32-bit or 64-bit OS. I might propogate this sprintf idea to the similar functions above. concatenation_long_small For this test, use LONG_MIN hash_empty hash_non_empty This is hard to test because 0 to UINT_MAX are all valid numbers and the hash function is a black box. For example, the hash funciton could return 0 for *everything* asked of it. It'd be a pretty bad hash function to have, but it would be mathematically legal. These two are ok as they stands, but there should be a e.emit_comment for both of them explaining the situation. find_empty That test looks like it exposes a bug in MyString. Given the description of find, if find is passed a "", then it should return 0. But here it returns -1. I'd say this is another bug. vsprintf_empty vsprintf_non_empty vsprintf_return_true vsprintf_cat_empty vsprintf_cat_non_empty Memory is leaked in these tests. I might have missed some, so search for 'new' and similar things which allocate memory, like strdup, or Strdup, etc. vsprintfHelper vsprintf_catHelper Should go to the utils file. append_to_list_string_non_empty_empty append_to_list_mystring_non_empty_empty Appending an empty string to a mystring in reality appends a comma to it? I'd definitely mark that as a problem, and a probable bug. Especially since append_to_list_mystring_empty_empty or append_to_list_mystring_empty_non_empty didn't do the same behavior with an empty string. read_line_null_file sensitive_string_equality_default_constructor sensitive_string_hash_function_empty Yikes! That's a bad bug and a git trac ticket to say the least! 2010-Oct-20 16:03:30 by jfrey: Bulk change of target version from v070504 to v070505 using ./ticket-target-mover. 2010-Dec-07 09:26:45 by tstclair: With recent cmake modifications there exists the ability to perform correct unit testing. http://www.cmake.org/cmake/help/cmake-2-8-docs.html#command:add_test 2011-Jan-27 14:46:04 by danb: Bulk change of target version from v070505 to v070506 using ./ticket-target-mover. 2011-Feb-01 16:01:00 by tannenba: Bulk change of target version from v070506 to NULL using ./ticket-target-mover.

title: Ticket #1393: Implement tiered groups and hierarchical fairshare
description: There needs to be a a way to specify multiple levels of groups and a mechanism to provide proper fairshare accounting in negotiation.
remarks: 2010-May-05 09:58:47 by jrt: notes: Here is an example of a group config. As it stands the group/subgroup delimeter is "." It's the same as the group/user delimeter. The assumption is that accounting groups are specified as group.group.group.username. All groups in a list of subgroups must be declared in config. All groups must have a quota declaration. If a group does not have a quota declaration, it will effectively prune it's subgroups from the tree. One can use a dynamic or a static quota declaration. If one uses a static declaration and the subgroup quota>parent group quota, the subgroup quota will be set to be equal the parent. All groups can have submitters. The quota for these submitters is whatever is unclaimed by subgroups. See below a1 and b1 are top level groups and thier quota adds up to .8. That means 0.2 is left for users within no group. also see below that a1.a3.a1, a1.a3.a2, and a1.a3.a3 add up to 0.8. That means submitters in group a1.a3 will have 0.2 for quota. For autoregroup, it's a hierachy. Groups with the same parent get first chance at unused slots. In order for a group to get a chance at unused slots from some subgroup across the tree, autoregroup needs to be set from the common parent to the group that wants to grow. ------------------------------ GROUP_NAMES = a1, b1, a1.a2, a1.a1, a1.a3, a1.a3.a1, a1.a3.a2, a1.a3.a3, b1.b2, b1.b1 GROUP_QUOTA_DYNAMIC_a1 = .4 #GROUP_QUOTA_a1 = 40 GROUP_QUOTA_DYNAMIC_b1 = .4 GROUP_QUOTA_DYNAMIC_b1.b1 = .4 GROUP_QUOTA_DYNAMIC_b1.b2 = .6 GROUP_QUOTA_DYNAMIC_a1.a2 = .2 GROUP_QUOTA_DYNAMIC_a1.a1 = .2 GROUP_QUOTA_DYNAMIC_a1.a3 = .6 GROUP_QUOTA_DYNAMIC_a1.a3.a3 = .2 GROUP_QUOTA_DYNAMIC_a1.a3.a2 = .2 GROUP_QUOTA_DYNAMIC_a1.a3.a1= .4 GROUP_AUTOREGROUP_a1 = TRUE GROUP_AUTOREGROUP_a1.a3 = TRUE GROUP_AUTOREGROUP_a1.a3.a1 = TRUE GROUP_AUTOREGROUP_b1 = TRUE GROUP_AUTOREGROUP_b1.b2 = TRUE GROUP_AUTOREGROUP_b1.b1 = TRUE example job file: arguments = 600 universe = vanilla should_transfer_files = YES when_to_transfer_output = ON_EXIT +AccountingGroup = "a1.a3.a1.jrt" queue 100 note how the group and user is specified 2010-May-12 12:14:24 by eje: This list is in no particular order: 1) SimpleGroupEntry::staticquota should be type 'bool' 2) SimpleGroupEntry::groupName should be type 'MyString'. Will prevent malfunction if admin uses long group names (or deep hierarchy, etc). 2a) scheddName should be MyString. 3) Reorg for readability: handle short/easy case at top of function: if (NULL == groups) { // negotiate w/ all users who do not belong to a group. negotiateWithGroup(untrimmed_num_startds, untrimmedSlotWeightTotal, minSlotWeight, startdAds, claimIds, scheddAds); // ----- Done with the negotiation cycle dprintf( D_ALWAYS, "---------- Finished Negotiation Cycle ----------\n" ); completedLastCycleTime = time(NULL); return TRUE; } // rest of code for (groups != NULL) ... 4) can a dynamic group quota be set to zero by admin? (If they do, it will flag as error in current code). 5 Is this a bug? (should be groupName[0]?) //leave the name null for now so it doesn't trip up the sort groupArray[0].groupName[255]= '\0'; 6) Recommend groupArray be std::vector<SimpleGroupEntry> (can use .push_back(), .size(), etc) 7) Recommend a comment to annotate fact that sort() also induces the tree structure (left/right/parent, etc) (maybe rename to induce_tree()?) 8) Proposal: logic for tree structure induction may be cleaner if pre-process groupnames: "g1.sg2.sg3" ==> vector<string>: ["g1", "sg2", "sg3"] (so list of groups would become type vector<vector<string> >). Would be able to take strstr(), strchr(), etc out of tree induction logic. Length of vector directly gives depth of group, etc. Could just apply STL sort(groups.begin(),groups.end()), and then iterate down the list: Each time vector length increments, you just moved to new ply of tree. Each time you see length decrement, you just moved out of subtree. 9) using 'double' instead of 'float' would make sure quota roundoff accumulation is insignificant, although unlikely to be a major problem. 10. consider renaming '.left' and '.right' to something like '.prev' and '.next', (left and right frequently denote children in binary trees). Might be even better for clarity to have each node directly store vector of child indexes. e.g. (std::vector<int> children), instead of using linked list. I think this would also eliminate some of the inner loops over children used for counting over linked list. 11. copygroup() ===> operator=() ? 12. I think it would improve clarity to do the allocation of jobs to HFS slots as a tree-recursion algorithm. Probably depth-first recursion, since a given group gets jobs if there is any 'pie' left over after its children. Could either write recursive function directly, or use a node stack if that makes carryover of fractional quotas easier. 2010-Jun-10 15:35:56 by eje: Added an updated patch which is same as previous patch except for some added comments about significance of topological tree node sort, and the storage of children as linked list of indexes. 2010-Oct-20 16:03:30 by jfrey: Bulk change of target version from v070504 to v070505 using ./ticket-target-mover. 2011-Jan-27 14:46:04 by danb: Bulk change of target version from v070505 to v070506 using ./ticket-target-mover. 2011-Feb-01 16:08:44 by tannenba: Bulk change of target version from v070506 to NULL using ./ticket-target-mover. The latest patch needs to be rebounced. I will update and attach asap. --Erik 2011-Feb-02 17:39:55 by danb: This feature is being referred to as "Hierarchical Fair Share". The "Fair Share" calculation is different from Condor's other fair share algorithm, which relies on a running average of past usage, and a priority factor, to determine fair share. To avoid confusion, should we refer to this new feature as "Hierarchical Group Quotas"? From a user's point of view (i.e. in log messages), it may make sense to simply refer to it as "Group Quotas", since there may or may not actually be a hierarchy. Let me make sure I understand the implications of slot weights being unsupported in HFS. This changes behavior for existing configurations that use group quotas, right? As I recall, slot weights were added by Cycle specifically for group quotas. Now, if any groups are defined, it looks to me like slot weights are no longer supported, whether one is using the group hierarchy or not. In Accountant::AddMatch() you update the stats for the user's group. Should you also be updating the stats for parent groups? I think no, but I want to make sure you agree. The following comment is no longer accurate, because there is always a group record, yes? // Determine if we need to update a second customer record w/ the group name. New configuration variables NEGOTIATOR_USE_SLOT_WEIGHTS, HFS_MAX_ALLOCATION_ROUNDS, HFS_ROUND_ROBIN_RATE, and GROUP_ACCEPT_SURPLUS are referenced. These should be added to condor_utils/param_info.in so that they are known to the config system (e.g. the default values are visible to condor_config_val). By the way, condor standard coding style dictates that {}'s surround the inner block in cases such as this: while (ClassAd* ad = group->submitterAds->Next()) group->submitterAds->Remove(ad); There were a number of such cases. The HFS algorithm depends on IdleJobs and RunningJobs in the submitter ad to determine how many slots a submitter wants. Jobs which only match a subset of the machines (or none at all) may throw things off. Your solution to that is HFS_MAX_ALLOCATION_ROUNDS and HFS_ROUND_ROBIN_RATE, yes? I like "ACCEPT_SURPLUS" in place of "AUTOREGROUP"! 2011-Feb-03 09:20:09 by eje: Re: HFS vesus "HGQ" or "GQ" (stylish!), the "fair share" was referring to "fair share" of slots, and also fair-share of surplus quotas. I can substitute references of "HFS" to "HGQ", etc. Re: slot weights, our experience has been that they don't work well in an accounting-group environment, due to packing-problem kinds of issues. It just doesn't fill slots very well in general. However, it doesn't break the algorithm to allow weighted slots. I also suspect that the newer "allocation rounds" and "round robin" loops on top of the negotiation would mitigate that, but I haven't tested that theory. I'm willing to (re)enable weighted slots with HFS, although I'm dubious about how well they work together. Re: AddMatch(), I agree that not propagating to parent groups is the right policy. Each job runs against a particular group, and so for these purposes it would be inappropriate to count a group's usage against parent groups. Re: comment, in this new scheme every job has a group, so yes that comment no longer applies. Re: documentation of params, I'll update the docs asap. Re: "{}", I'll put them in whenever I next update the code. Re: max-allocation-rounds and round-robin-rate, yes those loops are designed to mitigate slot-filling problems. "Allocation-rounds" are a way to adapt to cases where a group's jobs cannot match slots, and so it can attempt to allocate to other groups if possible. "Round-robin" is for mitigating what we've been calling the "overlapping-effective-pool" problem, where multiple groups may be "competing" for the same subset of slots. It preserves relative allocation ratios in the "sub-pool", and minimizes starvation. There is a test-case attached to this ticket that exercises these loops. We've also been getting good feedback on these from customers. 2011-Feb-03 10:35:00 by danb: I should also point out that this patch depends on the configuration system handling configuration macros with names containing "." characters. In the current implementation, this works, despite the fact that "." has a special meaning. There has been talk about reimplementing the configuration system. I don't know if this use of "." would be problematic. It might be worth running this by Will Benton or Pete Keller to see how much noise they make. 2011-Feb-03 13:10:32 by willb: I can't think of any reason why dots-in-macro-names wouldn't continue to work in the design that Pete and I discussed. In any case, a rework of the configuration subsystem is probably pretty far off in the future at this point. 2011-Feb-04 09:08:47 by eje: Attached updated patch to address Dan's feedback -E 2011-Feb-04 09:27:30 by danb: Thanks for the quick patch! One thought: should HGQ_MAX_ALLOCATION_ROUNDS be named GROUP_QUOTA_MAX_ALLOCATION_ROUNDS? Similar suggestion for HGQ_ROUND_ROBIN_RATE. These settings apply to group quotas, whether there is a hierarchy or not, don't they? 2011-Feb-04 10:27:01 by eje: Everything is a hierarchy -- some are just flatter than others :-) (Attached a patch with HGQ_ -> GROUP_QUOTA_) 2011-Feb-04 12:17:50 by danb: As far as I am concerned, this patch can be pushed to the master branch for 7.5.6. Go ahead! Or if you would like me to do it, let me know. 2013-Jan-15 16:02:11 by gthain: Let's work on a design doc for this a HgqDesignDoc

title: Ticket #2946: Enforce strict FIFO of parallel jobs even with remote submission
description: The Dedicated Scheduler runs parallel jobs in a FIFO manner. However, when jobs are submitted remotely, and their input is spooled, the dedicated scheduler will only run the jobs that have finished spooling their input. Therefore, it is possible that a job with a later cluster id will be ready to run before a job with an earlier cluster ids. This will introduce a parameter that will cause very strict FIFO even in this case -- idle dedicated jobs will wait for earlier jobs to finish spooling before being considered to run.
remarks: 2012-Sep-26 13:40:51 by tstclair: commit here.. is this done? 2013-May-20 14:55:43 by tannenba: CODE REVIEW Logic of the patch seems flawed. Patch has ClassAd *spoolingInJob = GetJobByConstraint(fifoConstraint.c_str()); if (spoolingInJob) { spoolingInJob->LookupInteger(ATTR_CLUSTER_ID, cluster_causing_skippage); } The above code will find some cluster that meets the fifo constraint, but will not find the smallest cluster that meets the fifo constraint. Seem like as written, the patch will fail to work correctly if three jobs are submitted (job 1.0, 2.0, 3.0) and lets say 1.0 and 3.0 are still spooling. Isn't it possible that job 2.0 will be able to run if GetJobByConstraint() happens to return 3.0 ? Shouldn't the code patch iterate through all the jobs that match the constraint and store the one with the lowest cluster id? Also there are no documentation commits for this ticket. (or regression tests). 2013-May-20 17:24:43 by gthain: HOWTO reproduce: in the condor_config, set DEDICATED_SCHEDULER_WAIT_FOR_SPOOLER = true Spin up a personal condor, and submit several parallel jobs. Put them all on hold with a HoldReasonCode of 16 (HOLD_CODE_SpoolingInput) $condor_hold -a $condor_qedit gthain HoldReasonCode 16 Then, submit a new parallel job, and check for the following message in the SchedLog: 05/20/13 17:22:45 (pid:11678) Job 377.0 is spooling input files, will block all 381.0 until spooling completes 05/20/13 17:22:45 (pid:11678) Job 377.0 is spooling input files, will block all 379.0 until spooling completes 05/20/13 17:22:45 (pid:11678) Found no idle dedicated job(s) Release all the job, making sure to first set the hold code to something other than 16, so that condor_release will work, and watch the jobs match and run. 2013-May-21 11:38:07 by tannenba: CODE REVIEW #2 [35771] looks good, thanks. title: Ticket #4191: Abort DAG after a specified number of node failures
description: Brian Bockelman wants to be able to abort a DAG after a specified number of node failures, even if the DAG could make forward progress. This should be pretty easy, since we already keep a running count of the number of failed nodes. So we just have to add a knob for the user, and check that each time through the event/submission loop, I guess. My initial thought is to have something like this: DAGMAN_MAX_NODE_FAILURES = 5 If we used that terminology, I think that a value of 0 would mean that the DAG would be aborted on the first node failure, and a negative value would disable this setting.
remarks: 2014-Jun-12 14:18:31 by wenger: Maybe it would be better to have a macro like DAGMAN_ABORT_ON_FAILURE; then 0 would mean don't abort, 1 would mean abort on the first failure. We'd also have to define whether a node that fails and then succeeds on a retry counts as a failure -- my initial thought is to say no.
