title: Ticket #4484: Significant blocking in Schedd::count_jobs
description: On busy schedds (50k to 150k idle jobs), we noticed significant blocking in Schedd::count_jobs. Looking through the code: Do we have any profiling information available on where time is spent? Would it be possible to walk jobs in parallel? Can tasks in this function be split into separate callbacks? This would allow us to decrease the entire time spent blocking.
remarks: 2014-Aug-09 12:30:45 by bbockelm: I didn't really tackle the underlying issue (the time it takes to walk a queue of 100k jobs), but I did notice that there are three separate timeslices right now: qmgmt's priorecarray (5%, not configurable). Periodic expr (default 1%, configurable but undocumented). count_jobs and friends (default 5%, configurable and documented). The branch V8_3-gt4484 changes count_jobs and priorecarray to a 1% default and makes them both configurable with SCHEDD_INTERVAL_TIMESLICE. The overall affect is that these periodic tasks will now take up to 3% of the schedd's time by default, down from 11%. Since they can block for quite awhile (3s) each, I think this is more appropriate. 2014-Aug-09 14:53:55 by sfiligoi: Instead of throttling the housekeeping, could we do some things in parallel? E.g. counting jobs and advertising to the Collector could easily be done from a forked process. There is a reason we do these things, so I do not want to do them any less often than needed. 2014-Aug-11 13:33:09 by tannenba: Reducing the amount of time we can do count_jobs and recompute the prio rec array can have other issues, as Igor says. For instance, delaying the prio rec array timer could result in longer delays before changes in job priority take effect, i.e. jobs with worse job priority may be started ahead of jobs with better priority. Some other brainstorm ideas: Create an object in the schedd per owner that is kept throughput the lifetime of the existence of jobs in the queue from that owner. This is something Miron has long wanted to store accounting information in the schedd per owner. Assuming we do this, we could also keep a priority queue of job ids per owner. This would remove the need to periodically count jobs and resort prio rec arrays - instead we would amortize this cost at job submit and removal time. Of course, this is not a trivial change, and we may need to do something more clever than just a priority queue to enable insertion/removal of many thousands of jobs at once. Use an openmp merge sort to do the prio rec array heavy lifting, instead of doing a qsort in a single thread. This is less of a major change than the above, but also may not yield us very much... More ideas to follow... 2014-Aug-11 13:49:49 by bbockelm: To put it another way - what's the upper bound of the percentage of time the schedd should spend non-blocking? My claim is that 11% is too high. I have a hard time believing that, with a queue of 100k jobs, decreasing the frequency at which we update the . The prio rec array is similar - how bad is it if changes in priority take a few minutes to propagate when we never change priorities and are running 10-20k jobs? I'm not saying there's no effect of changing the default, just that it's out of balance. With respect to the frequency - the timeslice provides an upper and lower bound for the frequency. If decreasing the timeslice interval causes the frequency to go high for comfort, we should adjust the upper instead! I think the question of "how much time is spent doing this in the worst case" should be separated from "how quickly can we do this". I view the former question as more important. 2014-Aug-11 14:38:37 by sfiligoi: While I fully agree we should have good "worst case" emergency breaks, let's make sure we do not hit those limits on a regular basis on a busy system (like the one CMS is operating). 2015-Feb-05 19:35:58 by bbockelm: Deferring this for now. With the fixes to the keepalive protocol in 8.3.2, the small pauses are far less critical. We now can monitor this in the DC statistics; if it becomes a problem in the future, we'll re-open.

title: Ticket #6143: Improve errno values in queue-managment api
description: The schedd's remote queue management API (ConnectQ(), SetAttribute(), etc) includes an errno value anytime it returns a failure for a call. The schedd is very inconsistent about setting a useful value for this errno. For example, if SetAttribute() fails, the caller doesn't know whether the job in question isn't in the queue, the given attribute is protected, or the given attribute value is invalid (unparseable). I propose the following errno values, which build on the existing usage: EACCES: Requested action is privileged (e.g. modify job owned by another user, modify protected attribute). ENOENT: No job for given job id. EINVAL: All other errors, primarily bad parameters. Includes submission limits and non-existent attributes.

title: Ticket #2803: condor_status -state time comparison wrong in face of clock skew
description: condor_status -state will provide information about the amount of time a slot has been in its current state. On a machine with clock skew from the collector, this information will be inaccurate. This is because the duration calculation is based off LastHeardFrom (Collector's timestamp on the ad), when it should be based off MyCurrentTime (the node's timestamp). diff --git a/src/condor_status.V6/prettyPrint.cpp b/src/condor_status.V6/prettyPrint.cpp index 233d724..bc22771 100644 --- a/src/condor_status.V6/prettyPrint.cpp +++ b/src/condor_status.V6/prettyPrint.cpp @@ -814,7 +814,7 @@ formatElapsedTime( int t , AttrList *al ) { int now; - al->LookupInteger( ATTR_LAST_HEARD_FROM , now ); + al->LookupInteger( ATTR_MY_CURRENT_TIME , now ); t = now - t; return format_time( t ); } Originally the code (0a57fab4: Tue Mar 3 21:20:46 1998) compared against condor_status' local time, which was also wrong. It was later updated (8a589453: Tue Mar 10 16:57:20 1998), to compare against LastHeardFrom, which does not take skew into account.

title: Ticket #6513: SciTokens support and refactor of credential management code
description: Placeholder ticket. Design doc, derived tickets, and all that to coming ASAP. Git branch: V8_7-SciTokens-2-branch The current work plan is to work "backwards" from the execute machine to the submit machine, so that some concrete functionality can begin to exist sooner and be tested and used even if the whole system isn't completed end-to-end and appropriately polished. "Phase Zero" Milestones: [DONE] Store credentials within SEC_CREDENTIAL_DIRECTORY by UID/username. (One refresh token per module per user) [DONE] User manually obtains and supplies their access tokens using the SEC_CREDENTIAL_PRODUCER. Stored in SEC_CREDENTIAL_DIRECTORY with correct filenames. Access tokens received by execute machine on job startup using syscall socket. [DONE] User manually obtains and supplies their refresh tokens into the SEC_CREDENTIAL_PRODUCER. Stored in SEC_CREDENTIAL_DIRECTORY with correct filenames. CredD calls a hook or pings CREDMON to obtain access tokens from refresh tokens. Execute node receives only access tokens and also refreshes access tokens from shadow periodically. [DONE] SEC_CREDENTIAL_PRODUCER can specify type of credential produced, as well as produce multiple creds, all stored tidily in the SEC_CREDENTIAL_DIRECTORY. [4/2] Create module architecture. CredD now reads module configuration, starts CREDMONs as children (if needed) and uses correct CREDMON or hook to do refresh. Credmon capable of receiving redirects/tokens to store in SEC_CREDENTIAL_DIRECTORY condor_submit queries CredD to determine if all creds needed are present, advises user of services missing. During condor_submit, CredD creates request files with needed info for missing services, submit returns a URL to the CREDMON with request ID included Some rudimentary cleanup of unused tokens That will get us to a "working" although still clumsy system. Plenty more to be done after that, and I will create a new list of milestones at that time.

title: Ticket #5295: Add RPC in shadow for starter to fetch opaque credential from shadow.
description: Assuming that any job in the queue implies that an opaque credential has already been stored by the credd, the shadow can then grab that credential directly without talking to the schedd or credd. (It must exist on the local disk in SEC_CREDENTIAL_DIR/<user>.cred) Before running the job, the starter will get the credential from the shadow via daemoncore command CREDD_GET_PASSWD. See ticket #5296 for the starter side of things.
remarks: 2015-Oct-13 16:13:37 by tannenba: Why are we sending the uberticket from the shadow to the starter via a file transfer sub-command? That code is already so complicated.... plus the starter may end up simply discarding it if a .cc file already exists on the execute node. How about the alternate idea: The starter is born with a socket back to the shadow for remote system calls and a copy of the job classad. For remote system calls, the starter acts as the client and the shadow is the server. So instead of file transfer munging, how about if the job classad has an attribute saying the job needs an uberticket, and the .cc file does not already exist, the starter simply does a remote system call back to the shadow to securely (ie with cedar encryption enabled) pull the uberticket (and then store it, sighup, etc). This could be done very early in the lifetime of the starter, before any file transfer crap. Advantages: This works cleanly even if the user does not want any file transfer (which will be the common case at CERN) It is much simpler conceptually, and probably implementation wise as well vs expanding the file transfer stuff Because the starter simply pulls the uberticket (instead of the shadow pushing it), if the .cc file already exists at the execute node (also common), then nothing is unnecessarily transferred. Thoughts? 2015-Oct-14 12:01:42 by zmiller: I agree sending using file transfer is not a good idea, having initially gone down this road. I've abandoned that approach. A couple other ideas I had: Send uberticket as part of claim activation. This minimizes round trips perhaps but requires changing that protocol in a backwards compatible way which may also be complex. Have shadow send a new command to starter to store the credential before running the job. Have the starter pull the credential from the credd via RPC since the credd is managing those tokens. Have the starter pull the credential from the shadow via RPC (todd's suggestion). Given that the socket from starter to shadow already exists, ##4 seems like it is the most straightforward to implement, and I am going with that. 2015-Oct-14 18:45:19 by zmiller: The shadow currently supports this using a separate daemoncore command, CREDD_GET_PASSWD, using the same wire protocol as the CredD. The advantage of that is you could just as easily point it at a CredD instead of a shadow. However, it does mean an extra TCP connect, so I may switch this to a SYSCALL. For now, though, I am resolving this ticket.

title: Ticket #6840: Finish separation of read and write qmgmt commands
description: In HTCondor 7.5.0 (#930), we separated the QMGMT_CMD cedar command into two commands, one for read-only operations (QMGMT_READ_CMD) and one for operations that modify the job queue (QMGMT_WRITE_CMD). For backwards compatibility, clients can still start a QMGMT_READ_CMD command (which is just QMGMT_CMD renamed) and then promote it to a connection that will modify the queue. This is needless complexity at this point, and it makes it harder for us to change the schedd to not handle any read-only requests in-process. We should complete the separation of these two cedar commands. Most clients of the schedd now employ a version check and will use QMGMT_WRITE_CMD when wanting to modify the job queue. But a few don't do this. They always use QMGMT_READ_CMD for modification requests. They are condor_shadow.std, condor_prio, and condor_preen. We can assume that condor_shadow.std and condor_preen will be the same version as the schedd, but condor_prio with -name can have version skew. Thus, we need to be careful about when we make QMGMT_READ_CMD only work for read-only connections.

title: Ticket #2395: New ClassAd functions: versioncmp, versionokay
description: As people increasingly advertise version numbers for libraries, kernels, and the like, they'll want to do range comparisons. A current implementation might look something like: # Machine: LIBC_VERSION_MAJOR = 4 LIBC_VERSION_MINOR = 12 LIBC_VERSION_REVISION = 42 # Job MIN_LIBC_VERSION_MAJOR = 4 MIN_LIBC_VERSION_MINOR = 12 MIN_LIBC_VERSION_REVISION = 36 REQUIREMENTS = \ (MIN_LIBC_VERSION_MAJOR > LIBC_VERSION_MAJOR) || \ (MIN_LIBC_VERSION_MAJOR == LIBC_VERSION_MAJOR && \ MIN_LIBC_VERSION_MINOR > LIB_VERSION_MINOR) || \ (MIN_LIBC_VERSION_MAJOR == LIBC_VERSION_MAJOR && \ MIN_LIBC_VERSION_MINOR == LIB_VERSION_MINOR && \ MIN_LIBC_VERSION_REVISION >= LIBC_VERSION_REVISION) This is a mess to write and to read. It's easy to make a mistake. It gets even longer if you want to test for a maximum version. It grows especially confusion if you want to work with strings in the form "4.13.36" and end up playing with the string manipulation functions. Proposed: new ClassAd functions for comparing version numbers. (The proposal for comparing versions numbers below is based on a system I wrote for comparing version numbers of RPMs based strictly on the file name. While you can create pathological cases, I believe it will work for the overwhelming number of version number strings.) Proposed interface Integer versionCmp(String a, String b) Compare two version numbers in strings a and b. If version a is earlier than b, a negative number is returned. If b is earlier than a, a positive number is returned. If the versions are the same, 0 is returned. For comparisons, versions numbers are broken into chunks. Punctuation is removed and delimits chunks. Letters and digits are broken into discrete chunks. So 4.12.42a-ac would break into the chunks 4, 12, 42, a, and ac. To compare two versions (which is to say, series of chunks), go chunk by chunk. If the chunk consists of digits, it is converted to an integer and the two compared, returning -1 if a<b and 1 if a>b. If letters, the two are compared with strcmp, returning on a positive or negative number, continuing on a 0. If the two chunks are identical, move to the next chunk. If all chunks are identical, return 0. If one series of chunks runs out of chunks to compare but the other doesn't, the shorter series is "earlier" (so versionCmp("2","2.3") is -1). If a chunk consists of "*" (which is not considered punctuation), comparison immediately stops and 0 is returned (effectively making "*" a wildcard valid only once at the end of a version number) Boolean versionOkay(String test, String min, String max) Is the version test between min and max, inclusive? min or max can be UNDEFINED to indicate no-minimum or no-maximum. max can be omitted and will default to UNDEFINED. Functionally identical to: ((min =?= UNDEFINED) || (versionCmp(test,min)>=0)) && ((max =?= UNDEFINED) || (versionCmp(test,max)<=0)) Open questions Different data types: How do you compare "2.3-a" and "2.3.4"? Or , for Linux kernel's "2.4.21-32.EL" and "2.6.9-89.33.1.EL.cernsmp". If either side is alphabetic, strcmp. This is likely "wrong," but any answer is likely to be nonsensical. How often will we get to this point where earlier chunks won't resolve the problem? Declare digits to sort earlier than letters. (This is identical to using strcmp, but removes the ASCII assumption to ordering.) Different version lengths: For Red Hat versions, compare "5" to "5.1". Padding with zeros (so treat "5" as "5.0") sounds promising, but may the wrong answer for max in versionOkay. For example, how do you say, "anything 5.x"? versionOkay(ver, "5.0", "5.99999999") would work, but is ugly and may fail if 5.A follows 5.9. Stop comparison at shorter version: functionality equivalent to a wildcard. So versionOkay(ver, "5", "5") would successfully match anything that began with "5.x" (and a few other variations). This is problematic if your version really is 5 and is followed by 5.1 and you want exactly 5; workaround is to advertise "5" as "5.0". It also screws you if you want a very specific version number and you can't predict sub versions. So I want exactly "2.3.4" and "2.3.4a" comes out; I'll end up matching it. Specify length to compare in chunks, defaulting to 0 meaning "all". Puts additional burden of understanding on the user. Complicates interface to both versionCmp and versionOkay. Explicitly understand "*" as "wildcard." It can only be at the end (putting it in the middle is nonsensical). When comparing chunks, if we hit "*" on either side, we stop and return 0. So "2.3.4" will not match "2.3.4a", but "2.3.4.*" or "2.3.4*" will. This solution is currently documented in the proposed interface above.

title: Ticket #6786: notification on Error poorly documented
description: Page 909 of the HTCondor 8.7.9 manual states If defined by Error, the owner will only be notified if the job terminates abnormally, (as defined by JobSuccessExitCode, if defined) or if the job is placed on hold because of a failure, and not by user request This differs from from the HTCondor 8.6.12 manual by the inclusion of the text surrounding JobSuccessExitCode. The meaning of JobSuccessExitCode is not defined anywhere in the manual and is undefined for all jobs in my 8.7.9 queue and condor_history. Even when one uses the submit command success_exit_code it remains undefined. So, I think it's safe to say that there's a documentation bug here. But, it does more or less behave as we want it to. For HTCondor 8.7.9, the behavior of Error includes when jobs exit by a code other than 0 or by the explicit value set by success_exit_code. What is less clear (from the text above) is whether it will continue the behavior of notification on abnormal termination (e.g. a segfault). I'd much prefer to see text that was clearer ("this looks like a job for bulleted lists!") and relies only on classads / commands that exist. For example: If *set to* Error, the owner *will be notified* if the job terminates abnormally (e.g. segfault), or if the job exits with a code other than that set by success_exit_code (default value of 0), or if the job is placed on hold by HTCondor due to a failure / cgroups limit rather than through use of the command condor_hold. Obviously the documentation should reflect your intent and the actual behavior. So, please fix as you see fit. Thanks!

The code from shouldSend() dates back to 8.7.7, and the code for success_exit_code to at least as far back as 8.5.8 (?!), so I'm not sure why you're not seeing anything. 2018-Oct-01 14:50:41 by tlmiller: Based on a review of the code, the documentation should read something like the following: Owners of HTCondor jobs are notified by e-mail when certain events occur. title: Ticket #5903: Fix RESCHEDULE command sent to schedd after job submission
description: In order for the schedd to promptly handle a newly-submitted job, the submitter should send a RESCHEDULE command to the schedd. Otherwise, the job may sit idle for many minutes, even if there are resources available to run it immediately. We've found two issues that foil this way to have the schedd promptly handle a new job: The Job Router doesn't send a RESCHEDULE. The DCSchedd object always sends RESCHEDULE via UDP, even if the schedd can't accept UDP messages (e.g. it's using shared port).
remarks: 2016-Sep-29 10:39:00 by tannenba: CODE REVIEW Code review is good, as now the job router simply does the exact same thing as condor_submit. Only criticism of the patch is the version history entry is written like it is targeted to a developer (i.e. something appropriate for a git commit message), and not targeted for an end-user. A couple potential thoughts for the future (and for a separate tickets) come to mind: the schedd should automatically do a reschedule at controlled intervals whenever a job moves into the idle state, thus rescheduling whenever even with shared_port, seems like daemons other than the shadow and starter could have a UDP command socket enabled for intra-machine communication.

title: Ticket #1413: Condor Cron on Windows is no longer functioning
description: This problem was reported to Cycle Computing by Hartford Life. They have a more complicated setup but Doug was able to reproduce the failure with a pretty simple .bat file. Pre 7.0.5 everything was fine. This cron job caused no issues and ran successfully on Windows. With a switch to 7.4.2 Hartford is unable to run the cron job. Doug confirmed this was still working as of 7.2.x. Here are the details for recreating the problem using a simple .bat file: In your config file: STARTD_CRON_NAME = SYSCAPS SYSCAPS_JOBLIST = PRTDIAG SYSCAPS_PRTDIAG_EXECUTABLE = C:/Condor/test.bat SYSCAPS_PRTDIAG_PERIOD = 1m The file used is a simple batch file: echo %TIME% > c:\condor\test.out We get the following output in StartLog: 05/14 15:33:47 Create_Process(): executable: 'C:/Condor/test.bat' 05/14 15:33:47 Executable is a batch file, running: "C:\WINDOWS\system32\cmd.exe" /Q /C "C:/Condor/test.bat" PRTDIAG 05/14 15:33:47 GetBinaryType() returned 0 05/14 15:33:47 Create_Process: CreateProcess failed, errno=267 05/14 15:33:47 Cron: Error running job 'PRTDIAG' In 7.2 we got this output: 5/14 12:34:25 Executable is a batch script, so executing C:\WINDOWS\system32\cmd.exe /Q /C "C:/Condor/test.bat" PRTDIAG 5/14 12:34:25 GetBinaryType() returned 0 5/14 12:34:25 Cron: STDOUT closed for 'PRTDIAG' 5/14 12:34:25 Cron: STDERR closed for 'PRTDIAG' 5/14 12:34:25 Cron: 'PRTDIAG' (pid 448) exit_status=0
remarks: 2010-Jun-02 19:49:08 by ichesal: Hey guys: any updates on this? This is a feature used heavily in some enterprise client accounts. Thanks! - Ian C. 2010-Jun-08 16:17:05 by tannenba: Hmmmm... in the above log snippet, errno is 267 from Create_Process, which on Win32 means: "The directory name is invalid". I am going to assign this ticket to Pete, and he'll check and see if this problem is specific to Windows or also can be reproduced on Linux. If the latter, Pete will work on a patch; if the former, he'll reassign to Cathrin. 2010-Jun-09 11:15:47 by psilord: Using 7.4.2, I attempted to reproduce this on unix with this config file setup: STARTD_CRON_NAME = SYSCAPS SYSCAPS_JOBLIST = PRTDIAG SYSCAPS_PRTDIAG_EXECUTABLE = /tmp/foobar SYSCAPS_PRTDIAG_PERIOD = 1m It worked as expected. I found this forum thread which talks about unexpected conditions one may get an invalid directory when trying to exec a process under windows. Search for "invalid". It may be of help to Cathrin.

title: Ticket #6339: Don't EXCEPT() when setting NETWORK_INTERFACE to an IPv6 address.
description: When looking for the scope ID of an IPv6 address, HTCondor unconditionally attempts to create a condor_sockaddr from the interface's address. This will fail because condor_sockaddr refuses to create addresses of types we don't know how to use (everything except AF_INET, AF_INET6, and AF_UNIX). Instead, since we're looking for an IPv6-specific thing anyway, check to see if the interface is IPv6 before doing anything with.
remarks: 2017-Jul-11 12:31:15 by zmiller: CODE REVIEW: Why keep iterating ifa after finding a result? Or maybe a better question is, in what case would there be multiple matches between addr and the retreived ifaddrs, and do we always want to return the scope from the last match? 2017-Jul-11 13:47:39 by tlmiller: The code originally did return immediately after finding a result. A commit in 2014 fixed the resulting memory leak (ifaddr is dynamically allocated), but neglected to break out of the loop when it obtained the first result. I'll insert a break for clarity. 2017-Jul-11 16:16:03 by zmiller: Are you adding the break; in a separate ticket? 2017-Jul-11 16:33:50 by tlmiller: See [51584]. 2017-Jul-11 19:20:21 by zmiller: I was just following up... title: Ticket #4754: JobRouter doesn't set Managed to ScheddDone after the job completes
description: When a routed job completes, the JobRouter marks its source job as completed but doesn't do any other cleanup with DestroyProc(), which can lead to race conditions in file stageout. We would like the JobRouter's cleanup behavior to more closely match that of the GridManager. More information can be found in #4719 under "Jaime's comments".

title: Ticket #7528: startd doesn't advertise availability of avx512 instructions
description: Newer Intel cpus now support 512 bit vector instructions, the so-called avx512. However, there are several subsets of these, and Linux doesn't advertise in the /proc/cpuinfo flags field just avx512, as HTCondor had assumed, rather it advertises the subsets, like avx512f. Let's change HTCondor to correctly detect and advertise that a machine has avx512 instructions.

title: Ticket #830: Condor misbehaves with full disks
description: In general, we don't nicely handle the edge case of a disk filling up for most any Condor daemon or operation. title: Ticket #7482: Restrict remote files access to a whitelist of directories
description: Motivation Many batch systems assume a shared file system between the server where the job is submitted and the server where the job runs. To remove reliance upon the existence of a shared file system, HTCondor provides its own custom mechanisms for a job running on a remote server to access to the filesystem of the submit host: HTCondor File Transfer. Chirp. Remote System Calls. Streaming I/O of stdin, out, err. Read/write access in HTCondor is performed as the job's Owner (submitting user), and thus is restricted based on file system permissions. However, today this is the only restriction. For example, when Chirp is enabled today, a client on the execute node can write any file on the submit machine which the user owns. We should restrict this to only allow access to a certain set of predetermined files. Proposed Change Implement a configuration knob LIMIT_DIRECTORY_ACCESS that can contain a comma-separated list of sub-directories on the file system of the submit machine. If specified, this list will act as a whitelist for all read or write access by the condor_shadow for purposes of file transfer, chirp, or remote I/O. Any file access must happen in one of the listed sub-directories, or in a child sub-directory of the listed directories, or in the SPOOL sub-directory associated with the specific job. If file access is attempted to an unspecified location, an error message will be written to the ShadowLog, and it will be treated exactly as if the user attempted to access a file owned by a different user... e.g. for File Transfer the job will go on hold with a hold message containing the name of the file, for Chirp the client will receive an errno EACCES. If LIMIT_DIRECTORY_ACCESS is unspecified in the config file, then the job attribute LimitDirectoryAccess is consulted and will behave exactly like the config knob. This could be very useful in conjunction with a job transform to limit file access to the job's current working directory, for example. If neither is specified, then the current behavior is unchanged (i.e. no whitelist restriction). Note that this whitelist of directories should be canonical, and may optionally contain one asterisk character as a wild-card. For example: # Limit access to files by vanilla universe jobs to /export/htcondor_data folder, # or to any folder in a user's home directory that has the name htcondor_data, # or to files in the spool directory. LIMIT_DIRECTORY_ACCESS = /export/htcondor_data,/home/*/htcondor_data Another example: # Limit access to files by vanilla jobs solely to files in the jobs SPOOL. # We do this by putting only one entry into the whitelist: a directory that # does not exist on the system. LIMIT_DIRECTORY_ACCESS = /THIS_SUBDIR_DOES_NOT_EXIST

title: Ticket #3992: Don't fear the reaper! Reaper events are being starved
description: Plan Add knob MAX_REAPS_PER_CYCLE to control how many reaper handlers will get called per daemon core event loop. Default will be 0 - a value of 0 means call as many reapers as are waiting at the time we exit select(). Also, currently daemon core invokes reaper handlers very late in the event loop. Instead, it should invoke reapers early, esp before invoking new command handlers that may want to spawn new workers. Motivation and Reasoning In CHTC on a busy submit node, observed the shared_port_daemon getting into a state where it literally had 0 child worker processes on the system, and yet the log file claimed it could not spawn any additional workers because it was already at 1000 max worker. This happened over and over, and obviously greatly impacted the performance of the shared port daemon due to limited concurrency. The problem is the shared_port_daemon is spawning very short-lived workers at a much faster rate than it reaps them (note: this is exasperated by the default MAX_ACCEPTS_PER_CYCLE being 8). An exited child means completed work that needs to be committed (in the case of a shadow for instance), or a worker that is ready for more work once we reap (in the case of shared port, collector, etc). So assuming that a reaper handler will spawn either zero or one new processes at most (usually zero), we have an incentive to prioritize reapers to clean-out the system. In the words of Blue Oyster Cult, "Don't fear the reapers!" Yes, I'm old.

title: Ticket #7178: new materialization is not triggered when jobs begin to run
description: When a job that is part of a late materialization cluster changes to run state, the cluster should materialize new jobs up to the max_idle limit. This isn't happening unless the transaction that commits the change of state of the job also changes the cluster ad (which doesn't usually happen). In practice, new jobs only materialize when existing jobs in that cluster are removed from the queue, because job removal (completion) will change the cluster ad.

title: Ticket #5145: Handle TCP_FORWARDING_HOST in AddressV1
description: We don't currently handle TCP_FORWARDING_HOST in AddressV1. (See #5339 for our approach to handling it in the addrs parameter of the Sinful.) Arguably, we should simply add the forwarding host as a new inbound route, but maybe that's actually better left to AddressV2 (since it wouldn't be symmetric with the original Sinful). Also, get_sinful_public() should probably set noUDP when TCP_FORWARDING_HOST overwrites the primary address (and the DaemonCore code that does this not), in case anybody else actually ever calls get_sinful_public().
remarks: 2015-Oct-23 10:40:41 by tlmiller: From the original ticket description: The issue may be that TCP_FORWARDING_HOST is applied very late in the advertising process, and as such doesn't appear in the addrs parameter. TCP_FORWARDING_HOST not appearing in the addrs parameter is actually a serious bug now, because it will cause HTCondor to ignore TCP_FORWARDING_HOST when actually doing networking. (It's still advertised.) I therefore split this ticket into #5339 -- fix the addrs problem -- and rewrote this one to reflect its more speculative nature.

title: Ticket #2950: Have a condor_submit mechanism for dealing with random seeds
description: Miron suggested this in today's BMRB software meeting, when we were talking about CS-Rosetta... Anyhow, he wants some kind of provision in condor_submit to get a random seed and stuff it into the classad for a job (rather than having the job itself look at /dev/random at startup or something like this). The intent of this is that, for example, if a vanilla universe got preempted and restarted, it would restart with the same random seed that it ran with the first time -- so that you'd truly be re-doing the same calculation as opposed to a different calculation. This would also serve as a record of the random seed used, that could be helpful for debugging.
creator: wenger

title: Ticket #1385: improve information reported for multi-core jobs
description: Overview CPU usage by multi-core vanilla jobs on OSG (i.e. HTPC jobs) is under-reported at condor sites. Gratia records that the job ran on 1 core in all cases. The reason is that the user log and job history entry do not say how many cores the job ran on. The condor accountant, on the other hand, can take into account the number of cores via SlotWeight, which defaults to the number of cores associated with the slot. Miron does not want condor's job accounting to get overly tied to the specific concept of cores, but he does want us to report what the charge was for using the resource. For most purposes, we could consider the charge to be the SlotWeight times the wall clock time, summed over all the run attempts for the job. The sum of this charge across all jobs run by a user will not be exactly equal to the charge computed by the accountant, because the accountant deals in claims, not jobs, so any Unclaimed/Idle time will be charged by the accountant but will not show up in the charge associated with individual jobs. Furthermore, the time boundaries of claims observed by the accountant depend on the sampling interval in the negotiator, the staleness of information in the collector, and so on. It still seems useful to have a concept of a charge per job, as long as people realize that this is not identical to the accountant's view of things. Job suspension raises an additional question. Should the suspended time be counted towards the charge for using the resource? The accountant can be configured either way via NEGOTIATOR_DISCOUNT_SUSPENDED_RESOURCES (default false). So to really be correct when reporting the per-job charge, we would need to find out how the negotiator is configured. An easier but sloppier approach would be to assume that this configuration setting is the same on the submit machine as on the central manager. An even simpler approach, which is what I propose below, is to always discount suspended resources in what we report in the job and change the default in the negotiator to do likewise. I think that is a more useful default and it is not worth much effort supporting the other case until we have a need for it. Proposal Add the following attributes to the job ad: [DONE] CumulativeSlotTime: Sum of SlotWeight*(WallClockTime-SuspensionTime) over all run attempts for a job. [DONE] CommittedSlotTime: Sum of SlotWeight*(WallClockTime-SuspensionTime) over run attempts that contributed to goodput for this job. Analogous to CommittedTime. [DONE] CommittedSuspensionTime: Time the job spent suspended during run attempts that contributed to CommittedTime. This is just plain missing in the current system and needs to be added, irrespective of everything else here. [DONE] MachineAttrXXX: where XXX is a machine attribute listed in the configuration variable JOB_MACHINE_ATTRS. The value stored in this attribute is the evaluation of the corresponding machine attribute when the job started running (i.e. at the same time when $$ macros are evaluated). Why have JOB_MACHINE_ATTRS when we already have $$? The values of $$ expansions are only persisted in the job history ad as a sort of accident and this has never been formalized. $$ only works inside of a string, so if you are storing numeric data, any expressions that refer to it must convert string values to numeric values. By enforcing a naming scheme that ties the name of the attribute in the job ad to the name in the machine ad, it is easier to know how to interpret the values. For example, gratia could check for MachineAttrCpus and use it if it is there, without worrying about how the site is configured. If MachineAttrCpus is not available, how can gratia calculate the number of cores used by the job? For sites that use the default SlotWeight, the number of cores can be obtained from CumulativeSlotTime/(RemoteWallClockTime-CumulativeSuspensionTime). This works even for jobs that run on X cores in one run attempt and Y cores in another run attempt. The answer will be the time-weighted average of the number of cores, which seems like the most reasonable thing to report in this case. For sites that configure a different SlotWeight, it would be incumbent on the admin to make sure MachineAttrCpus is defined.

title: Ticket #4884: Starter should export OMP_NUM_THREADS to job environment
description: Programs built with OpenMP, including Matlab, gnu sort (!) and many others, look to the environment variable OMP_NUM_THREADS to determine how many threads to spawn. If not set, they default to spawning as many threads as the machine has cores. We are seeing a number of examples in CHTC and OSG where a user will submit a job with RequestCPUs = 1, and the openMP code will then spawn many cores. If every job that lands on a machine does this, we end up with n^2 threads running, and a very slow machine. By forcing OMP_NUM_THREADS to the number of cores provisioned on the machine, we should mitigate the damage this causes.

Ticket #2403: negotiator spends lots of time in addRemoteUserPrios()
description: I profiled the negotiator in GLOW and found that it was spending most of its time in addRemoteUserPrios(). I suspect this function is especially expensive in GLOW, because we have a lot of machines with O(100) slots, and this function loops over all slots. This function gets called to insert user priority and usage information into the machine ad before each match test. In days of old, this function only needed to be called once per startd per cycle, because the information did not change during the cycle, but now the usage of the user and group is included, and this can change during the cycle. The proposed solution is to replace the insertion of actual values with classad function calls. The function calls will call up custom functions that the negotiator registers with the classad library. Once this is done, we can return to the good old days of only calling addRemoteUserPrios() once per startd per cycle. We could go even further and not insert things into the machine ad at all. Instead, people would call functions to retrieve the desired values. However, I think the cost of calling this function once per startd per cycle is negligible, so for now I would just like to treat this as an internal optimization-only change.
remarks: I tested this patch on GLOW. The negotiation cycle went from 20-30 minutes to 4 minutes. It is now spending most of its time in IsAMatch(), as one would expect.

title: Ticket #2116: ENABLE_USERLOG_LOCKING is ignored when writing log events
description: The ENABLE_USERLOG_LOCKING parameter is ignored when writing log events, and locking is always performed. The problem is that class WriteUserLog's initialize() method first opens the log file (and sets up the FileLock object to perform locking), then checks ENABLE_USERLOG_LOCKING to see if it should disable locking (it calls internalInitialize(), which calls Configure(), which does the check). This can probably be fixed by calling internalInitialize() before openFile() in initialize(), but we need to check whether the reordering will introduce any new problems.

title: Ticket #5779: the MapFile class needs to handle literal keys
description: in support of #5751, if the usermap has hundreds or thousands of entries in the mapfile, the current MapFile class is fairly slow to do lookups in that case. Then the mapfile has keys that are essentially literals (i.e. not making using the regex substitution), we can do much better by implementing that as a hash lookup. So the MapFile class needs to be able to read input files and treat the second value each row of the file as either a regex or a simple literal key. It would store regex entries in the same way as before, but consecutive simple literal entries of the same method will be coalesced into a single hashtable. The MapFile class will take a flag to the function that parses a file that tells it whether this new method of parsing is available. If it is, and the second value in a row begins and ends with / (i.e. like a perl regex) then it will be treated as a regex entry. otherwise it will be treated as a simple literal entry. Regex entries can have one or more letters following the closing / to indicate regex options. The options are i case insensitive U ungreedy Awk style substitutions will be made on the value of the third field when it is returned. \0 will be substituted for the entire match, \1 for the first regex capture group, etc. When the second field is not a regex, only \0 will be substituted. so for example mapfile fragment * Bob security,csuser.\0 * Alice security,math * /^todd.*/i htcondor,chtc,csuser.\0 * /(*.).cs/ csuser.\1 * /*./ guest If the above map file is used, the following lookups would occur. Input Map result Bob security,csuser.Bob john guest ToddL htcondor,chtc,csuser.ToddL alice.cs.wisc.edu csuser.alice

title: Ticket #7744: checkpointing should allow incremental output transfer
description: HTCondor currently requires the job to copy its output to spool after every checkpoint, so that the complete set of output is available for copying to its final destination when the job completes. It is apparently common for the output of a job to be both large and unnecessary for resuming the application after a checkpoint; for instance, a log (perhaps in many different files) of simulation states, where only the most recent simulation state is necessary for continuing, but earlier entries in the log are of interest and are part of the output. In this scenario, transferring the partial output back to spool at each checkpoint is too inefficient an approach to be useful. Options: allow the user to specify that some files should be transferred on checkpoint, but stored as output instead of in spool the same, but mark those files as not to be transferred back from spool how do we deal with partial output files? (that is, ones that may get appended to between checkpoints) If we have to deal with those, and can do so without transferring the whole thing again, should we just apply that to storage in spool and not make the user have to worry about it? (Compute the hashes during the upload and store them so the submit node doesn't have to keep doing that.) issues -- doe we require the user to remove previous partial outputs between checkpoints? where would we store the list of files we've already transferred, if not? (if we don't, and instead transfer to spool but not back, we would need a list of files in spool from the shadow that match the don't-transfer list to avoid transferring them again)
remarks: 2020-Jul-20 14:02:05 by tlmiller: LaurenM expects that when jobs of this type voluntarily checkpoint, their timestep files will either be complete or missing entirely, which may simplify things for us, initially.

title: Ticket #5283: Shared port deadlock on Windows?
description: The test job_dagman_submit_parse fails pretty regularly on Windows when the default for USE_SHARED_PORT is changed to true. The symptom is a time-out. The last thing the test prints is "Good. We need the dag to run<1>". The next thing that's supposed to happen is the test noticing a DAGMan failure. DAGMan properly prints out 09/25/15 15:00:30 ERROR: node B: job ID in userlog submit event (3.0.0) doesn't match ID reported earlier by submit command (0.0.0)! Aborting DAG; set DAGMAN_A BORT_ON_SCARY_SUBMIT to false if you are *sure* this shouldn't cause an abort. but its log ends with 09/25/15 15:00:31 attempt to connect to <128.104.103.14:46247> failed: connect errno = 10048. Will keep trying for 10 total seconds (10 to go). rather than 09/25/15 13:16:54 Wrote metrics file job_dagman_submit_parse.dag.metrics. 09/25/15 13:16:54 Metrics reporting is not available on this platform. 09/25/15 13:16:54 SharedPortEndpoint: Destructor: Problem in thread shutdown notification: 0 09/25/15 13:16:54 **** condor_scheduniv_exec.1.0 (condor_DAGMAN) pid 21148 EXITING WITH STATUS 1 which would tend to indicate that the DAGMan process hung trying to contact a daemon (probably the schedd). In the schedd log, we see 09/25/15 15:00:31 (pid:11516) DaemonCore::Wake_up_select called from an unknown thread. windows tid = 7144 ... 09/25/15 15:01:36 (pid:11516) condor_read(): timeout reading 5 bytes from collector at <128.104.103.14:46247>. 09/25/15 15:01:36 (pid:11516) IO: Failed to read packet header 09/25/15 15:01:36 (pid:11516) Failed to send RESCHEDULE to unknown daemon: This makes me think that the shared port daemon locked up, since the collector does not record any connection attempts after 15:00:28 except for two negotiator ad updates. While investigating why job_dagman_submit_parse fails on Windows when shared port is turned on, I took a gander at the Windows socket-passing code, and discovered that it is full of scary blocking writes to and reads from a named pipe. Naturally, since it looked like the problem I was diagnosing was caused by or had a symptom of a daemon hanging, I went to look at what the passed-to side of the conversation was doing. The passed-to (daemon) side of the conversation creates a named pipe, and then creates a thread in SharedPortEndpoint::StartListener() that blocks in the Windows equivalent of accept(). This thread writes its process ID back to the pipe (so that the shared port daemon can duplicate the received FD into the daemon's process) and then does some magic to construct the socket. (Windows sockets aren't just FDs.) At this point, it grabs a lock, adds the new socket to the list of received sockets, and releases the lock. (As far as I know, the lock operations are all OK.) It then schedules an immediate timer so that the main daemon core thread will handle the rest of the communication. It calls Register_Timer_TS() to do so. (Which grabs a big mutex which I haven't examined.) This function calls Register_Timer, which calls TimerManager::NewTimer. TimerManager::NewTimer calls InsertTimer, which calls DaemonCore::Wake_up_select() if the next timer has changed. (Which it probably has, given that we're registering an immediate timer.) On Windows, if Wake_up_select() is called from anything other than the main thread, it does nothing. If the daemon is just waiting around for connections, it may never pick up the phone. On further review, there's a call to Do_Wake_up_select() in Register_Timer_TS(), inside the mutex, which should cause a write to the async pipe to occur.

title: This attachment is private.
Ticket #6155: Check collector connectivity before starting annex
description: We should also consider attempting to verify connectivity. The idea is here is that condor_annex -setup would create a Lambda function in the user's account, and then call it with the IP and port of the collector. The function would attempt to connect to that IP and port, and having done so, do whatever works best to generate an permission-denied error in the collector's log (e.g., issues a DC_NOP command without doing negotiation). The hope is that the connect-and-command sequence can be done for this particular command without involving CEDAR or the HTCondor libraries, keeping the Lambda function small and light. I think Lambda functions can't be called by anyone but the account owner by default, but as long as we make sure of that, the Lambda function can trust the caller, and we don't need to worry about security (e.g., rate-limiting and the like). condor_annex could then grovel the collector log to make sure the connection happened to the collector in question. (The trusted lambda function could say, yes or no, I connected, but couldn't verify that the address matched the collector in question.)
remarks: 2017-Feb-17 13:16:47 by tlmiller: Zach wrote: Okay, here's a string of 13 bytes you can use to send a legitimate DC_NOP: "\x01\x00\x00\x00\x08\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\xea\x6b" We'll need to make sure that D_COMMAND is set for the shared port daemon and/or the collector (the shared port daemon should forward DC_NOP to the collector but might not; we'll have to check), possibly depending on if shared port is enabled; but this shouldn't be hard to do in the context of either an automated set-up tool or assuming the default instructions. 2017-Feb-17 13:18:11 by tlmiller: Jason's assignment is to write the Lambda function, not for the rest of this ticket. 2017-Feb-17 13:25:47 by jpatton: As added motivation for using the AWS Lambda method, at least for now, "The [AWS] Lambda free tier includes 1M free requests per month and 400,000 GB-seconds of compute time per month." It would take a ridiculous amount of annex setups in a month to reach this limit, so this solution should be "free." 2017-Feb-23 12:12:49 by tlmiller: Jaime had a(t least one) clever idea yesterday. We'd been thinking the daemon could generate a random number on start-up and reply to a new (entirely unauthenticated) daemon core command with that, as a way of making sure the Lambda function and condor_annex were talking to the same collector. Jaime noted that this could be accomplished by condor_annex calling the same daemon core command from condor_annex, as well, and just comparing the result to the indirect (via Lambda) route's result. This neatly avoids any need to figure out another path for reporting the data (e.g., condor_config_val -direct).

title: Ticket #1690: Gridmanager assumes job not in queue if SetAttribute fails
description: When SetAttribute() fails when the gridmanager is connected to the schedd, and the failure is not caused by a network failure, the gridmanager assumes the job is no longer in the queue. As a result, it skips setting any subsequent dirty attributes. This can lead to a situation like #1689, where a job ends up not being held when it should be. To see if a job really has left the queue when SetAttribute() fails, the gridmanager could try a GetAttribute() on an attribute that exists in all job ads. If that succeeds, the job is still in the queue. It's unclear what the gridmanager should do in this case, but pretending the job isn't in the queue is certainly the wrong answer.

title: Ticket #4216: Grid jobs can leave local queue without canceling remote job
description: When the gridmanager encounters an error with a job, it may put the job on hold for user intervention and free all data structures related to the job. If the job is later removed but is still submitted to a remote server, the gridmanager receives the job again and cleans up all state on the remote server before letting the job leave the local job queue. We have found a case where the gridmanager takes the removed job out of the queue before attempting to clean up any state on the remote server. This has been observed with EC2 jobs, leaving ssh key pairs created by the gridmanager on the EC2 server. But it can affect any grid job. Each time the gridmanager connects to the schedd, there are two queries it may perform. The first query is for any jobs that it should be managing but currently isn't. This normally applies to jobs that have just been submitted or released. The gridmanager starts managing the jobs returned by the query. The second query is for jobs that it's managing whose status has changed to the Held, Removed, or Completed state. This usually indicates the user has held or removed a job and the gridmanager needs to cancel the job on the remote server. The first query is done at startup and whenever the schedd sends a signal to the gridmanager indicating there are new jobs for it to manage. The second query is performed on every connection to the schedd. If the second query returns a job in Removed state that the gridmanager isn't currently managing, the gridmanager immediately lets the job leave the queue. Normally, when a held job is removed, the schedd signals the gridmanager that it has new jobs to manager. The gridmanager then connects the schedd and issues the two queries described above. The remove job will be returned for both queries. The first query results in the gridmanager starting to manage the job. The second query tells it that the job is removed (redundant in this case, as the Removed status is part of the job ad returned for the first query). The problem occurs when the gridmanager connects to the schedd after a held job has been removed but before the schedd has sent the signal to the gridmanager about new jobs to manage. The gridmanager will skip the first query (about new jobs) but still issue the second query (about Removed/Held/Completed jobs). The removed job will be returned by the second query but the gridmanager isn't managing it, so the gridmanager lets it leave the queue immediately. Connecting to the schedd can be triggered by events other than the signal from the schedd. For example, the gridmanager may need to modify attributes for other jobs in the schedd's queue. Possible solutions: Combine the two queries, modifying the constraint depending whether the "new jobs" signal has been received. The gridmanager would start managing all jobs returned by the query that aren't been managed yet. This would be more efficient for the schedd, but is probably too large a change for the stable series. When the second query returns jobs that the gridmanager isn't managing, the gridmanager leaves the jobs in the queue, and optionally sends itself the "new jobs" signal. This is a small change suitable for the stable series.

title: Ticket #3880: RFE: Cooperative Scheduling
description: Awhile back, an OSG Blueprint discussion about cooperative scheduling between glideinWMS and the site batch system evolved into an HTCondor design document. See attached. Work on this is not currently active (I'm following up with some related-but-distinct ideas elsewhere), but I wanted to record the design for historical purposes. Some juicy nuggets within the document: A new condor_chirp verb so the pilot can inform the schedd about the last job commit and the next expected job commit (the site negotiator can rank preemptions accordingly). A condor_rooster-like mechanism for the negotiator to warn jobs when they are in danger of being preempted (the pilot could then avoid starting new jobs). A new condor_chirp verb so the pilot can query whether the site starter is in DRAIN state (so no new jobs are started while the slot is draining).

title: Ticket #2792: Make gram proxy refresh delay time configurable
description: When the gridmanager notices that the proxy for a gt2/gt5 job has been refreshed, it doesn't immediately forward the proxy to the gram jobmanager. It waits until the jobmanager's proxy has less than 6 hours of lifetime left. This is done to prevent excessive proxy delegations when the user updates their proxy frequently, since the gridmanager must delegate once per job. This is causing problems for glideinWMS, which requires that the job's proxy have at least 12 hours of lifetime remaining when the job starts executing. If the proxy's lifetime is less than 12 hours, the job aborts at startup. We should make the time at which the gridmanager forwards the refreshed proxy configurable.

title: Ticket #2638: MAX_<SUBSYS>_<LEVEL>_LOG not honored
description: Parameters of the form MAX_<SUBSYS>_<LEVEL>_LOG in the config file are not honored. Debug level-specific log files (those set via <SUBSYS>_<LEVEL>_LOG) grow without bound. This was reported by Igor Sfiligoi and confirmed by Jaime Frey. Igor's original email: Seems like MAX_<subsys>_<level>_LOG is not honored. We had set GRIDMANAGER_FULLDEBUG_LOG=$(GRIDMANAGER_LOG).fulldebug MAX_GRIDMANAGER_FULLDEBUG_LOG=1000000 GRIDMANAGER_DEBUG=$(GRIDMANGER_DEBUG) D_FULLDEBUG but the fulldebug files are now way too big! [gfactory@glidein:/tmp]$ ls -lrS ... -rw-r--r-- 1 condor condor 30272306 Nov 11 20:46 GridmanagerLog.schedd_glideins3.fecms.fulldebug -rw-r--r-- 1 condor condor 30819112 Nov 11 20:46 GridmanagerLog.schedd_glideins7.fecms.fulldebug -rw-r--r-- 1 condor condor 30862403 Nov 11 20:46 GridmanagerLog.schedd_glideins19.fecms.fulldebug -rw-r--r-- 1 condor condor 47644375 Nov 11 20:46 GridmanagerLog.schedd_glideins18.fecms.fulldebug -rw-r--r-- 1 condor condor 48050678 Nov 11 20:46 GridmanagerLog.schedd_glideins17.fecms.fulldebug -rw-r--r-- 1 condor condor 50295843 Nov 11 20:46 GridmanagerLog.schedd_glideins10.fecms.fulldebug -rw-r--r-- 1 condor condor 118487712 Nov 11 20:46 GridmanagerLog.schedd_glideins15.fecms.fulldebug Are we doing anything wrong? The maximum file size for the various daemon logs are stored in an array of off_t named MaxLog. Both dprintf.cpp and dprintf_config.cpp reference this array. The problem is that _FILE_OFFSET_BITS is #defined to 64 at the top of dprintf.cpp but not dprintf_config.cpp. Setting this macro this way causes off_t to change from a 32-bit value to a 64-bit value on 32-bit versions of linux. So the two source files think the elements in the array are different sizes.

title: Ticket #5542: Add priority to scheduler universe?
description: The Hubble Space Telescope people currently have a setup where they are running a lot of small DAGs (~10 nodes per DAG). They are also setting priorities at the per-DAG level, because they have three general priorities of runs (highest is calibration, medium is processing new data, and low is reprocessing old data). (I had a phone conversation with Mary Romelfanger about this on Tuesday.) Anyhow, DAG priorities work for them, except for the following problem: they often have more than 200 DAGs in the queue, so when the submit a new one, it goes to the back of the scheduler universe queue, even if it's higher priority than everything else in the queue. Mary was able to identify some changes she thinks they'll be able to make on their end to stay below 200 queued DAGs, which would solve their immediate problem. But I figure this is something that HTCondor should be able to handle itself. Their DAGs are relatively short-lived, so it sounds like adding priority to the scheduler universe would solve their problem (this meaning that a higher-priority job would immediately go to the front of the queue, but not that it would preempt running jobs). I'm not sure that this is the right way to solve the underlying problem -- another possible solution is to have the option to run the DAGMans themselves as vanilla universe jobs (although handling the file transfer issues could be a pain). Also, the Hubble people are in a single-user scenario -- it occurred to me that in a multi-user scenario, people could abuse the scheduler universe priority, so if we implement it maybe it should be off by default, with a config knob to turn it on. At any rate, I wanted to record this so we can do some thinking about how to better handle large numbers of small DAGs...

title: Ticket #5811: After shared_port restart, endpoint should quickly check for addr.
description: The function SharedPortEndpoint::RetryInitRemoteAddress() unconditionally waits for sixty seconds after it fails to find the shared port daemon's address file. Instead, on the initial startup and after each restart, we should try again after a (few) seconds(s) because with the exception of CCB, we're just waiting for the shared_port daemon to start and write out a file, which shouldn't take very long and unnecessarily delays start-up. Doing so minimizes the window where the master will not have an address after the shared_port daemon crashes. (A faster restart of the shared port daemon may also be wise.)
creator: tlmiller

title: Ticket #4703: Invalid COLLECTOR_HOST should cause condor_master ASSERT(0)
description: If COLLECTOR_HOST is invalid, say because CONDOR_HOST= COLLECTOR_HOST=$(CONDOR_HOST):0 the central manager's condor_master will complain 11/05/14 17:05:06 Warning: Configuration file sets 'COLLECTOR_HOST=:0'. This does not look like a valid host name with optional port. 11/05/14 17:05:06 Invalid address: :0 ... 11/05/14 17:05:06 Collector port not defined, will use default: 9618 and merrily launch the condor_collector on 9618. This can cause a lot of grief. Things seem like they're working, but aren't really. Tests might pass until two tests happen to run simultaneously and collide on 9618 when they're supposed to be using a dynamic port. This case is, sadly, not hypothetical. Proposed: If a node is the central manager (DAEMON_LIST includes condor_collector) and COLLECTOR_HOST is invalid, then things are Seriously Messed Up and drastic measures should be taken. Either the condor_master should just ASSERT(0), or it the condor_master should disable the collector. The error is detected in getCmHostFromConfig in /src/condor_daemon_client/daemon.cpp around line 2256, but it's not obvious that that is where it should be fixed.
creator: adesmet

title: Ticket #534: Problem running Cygwin jobs - keyboard activity detected?
description: The problem is not quite nailed down yet, but it looks like Windows jobs @ Monash are being suspended when they should not be. At first blush, it appears that Condor is detected keyboard activity when in fact there is not any. The only thing noticeably different about these errant jobs -vs- other Win32 jobs is the jobs are Cygwin jobs. David, if you have more information, please email condor-admin@cs.wisc.edu... this will give you a ticket number back as well.
remarks: 2009-Oct-21 15:21:21 by psilord: Ben Burnett has left the Condor project. This ticket being being unassigned. 2010-Feb-01 13:40:56 by adesmet: (From the user:) We here at [DELETED] have just noticed there has been some traffic with regards to the ticket #534. The actual problem really was that Condor was not tracking properly the process tree of Cygwin job where the child process was thought to be the PC load instead of Condor load. As you can imagine with the condor configured to suspend condor jobs if the local load is high, this would keep pausing our Cygwin jobs and as we were expecting heart-beats from them, we would eventually lose the whole process. So to us it seems that you have addressed this issue in some way between versions of 6.8 and 7.2 and probably can close this ticket. title: Ticket #3496: monitor file transfer i/o activity
description: We propose to have the file transfer queue manager collect monitoring information about i/o activity in the file transfer processes. The quantities to be monitored will be bytes transmitted per second, file read/write load, and network read/write load. By "load" we mean number of file transfer processes performing read/write calls. These quantities will be reported as exponential moving averages over various time scales, by default, 1 minute, 5 minute, 1 hour, and 1 day. The attached design document contains further details.

title: Ticket #6694: Extend condor_reassign_slot to accept multiple victims
description: We should be able, when specifying a victim job, to instead specify multiple victim jobs (at the same startd) whose resources will be coalesced to run the beneficiary job. To quote #6659: There is a startd command to vacate a set of claims and return a new claim ID which corresponds to the coalescensce we can use as the basis. (Would we (need to) construct a new match record? Where in the schedd would we hang the knowledge about which job should run on the new match while the command was in nonblocking flight?) We may need to modify the startd to accept claims rather than preempting claims. A brief of analysis of the startd reveals this command to be REQUEST_CLAIM. It does not appear to instrinsically require preempting claims to function, but it is currently coded to assume that those are the only ones it receives. After a brief discussion with ToddT, it seems plausible to move forward on the basis that whoever has the appropriate capability (knows the claim ID) should control how they're used, including whether or not to honor max retirement time. The code change for this policy change should be as simple as identifying if the extra claim IDs are for active claims (in which case the command is being issued on behalf of condor_reassign_slots); if they are, then don't require that their retirement time has expired, and also invalidate the preempting (and preempting preempting) claims, since the corresponding slot will shortly cease to exist. After a discussion with Jaime, our conclusions were: (a) our conclusions should be checked with TJ and GregT; (b) coalescing existing claims should be its own (new) startd command. I suggested (b) out of a concern that it would be too easy to accidentally alter the existing semantics of the REQUEST_CLAIM code when modifying it for this use case. Jaime concurred and immediately added that separating preparing the slots to coalesce from actually coalescing them would avoid a problem in the existing implementation of REQUEST_CLAIM, where resources are reassigned from the slots being coalesced before they've been deactivated. This implies that the schedd would deactivate each of the victim claims, and then send the coalesce command. This approach has the additional benefit that it's a straight extension of the existing one-for-one reassignment code. Since the schedd already waits asynchronously for deactivation, this removes complexity from the startd without much increasing it in the schedd. (The schedd would have to check, on each deactivation notice (shadow exit), if this deactivation completed a set, rather than if it were the single victim. This should not be difficult.) The startd would refuse to coalesce slots that weren't claimed/idle; each dslot in the set would also have to be a child of the same pslot (because we currently don't have a mechanism to reassign resources between pslots). The schedd could delay picking which match record was re-used by setting the 'next job' attribute on each match record in the set but ignoring it until the deactivation at hand completed the set. It's not clear if the startd's new COALESCE command would return a new claim ID or not. It would reduce potential confusion about stale claims if the startd invalidated all coalesced claims, which implies issuing a new claim ID for the coalesced claim. Additionally, this approach would allow for commonality with the potential use-case where the schedd wants to make an existing pslot claim larger: it would request the pslot claim and then deactivate the other claims and coalesce them; doing so in that order should minimize the number of times a claim is deactivated unnecessarily.

title: Ticket #7656: Tradeoffs between query and xquery should be made clear in the docs
description: The manual currently says, regarding query(): This returns a list of ClassAd objects, meaning all results must be buffered in memory. This may be memory-intensive for large responses; we strongly recommend to utilize the =xquery()= The first half of this is accurate, but the opinion at the end is just wrong: most people will not be doing a large enough query to warrant the need to use xquery, which has performance impacts on the submit machine. title: Ticket #5391: HTCondor View: Cross-graph caching
description: When multiple graphs are on the same page, they should share parsed JSON data as much as possible, similarly to how the table-linked-graph does now. Avoiding parsing a a big speed boost. The naive solution (there is a global cache), means we're keeping around a copy of the raw data even if we'll never use it again. Perhaps it doesn't matter and the memory cost is low enough to not be worth fixing. If it does matter, the "right" solution is to track usage; non-linked graphs would drop a claim when done rendering; table-linked-graphs would hold it indefinitely. Might want to lag deleting a cache entry for a second or two so that a later loading graph can find it. Either way, we'll need some clever to cope with multiple graphs issuing the load request "simultaneously." Rough plan: When I decide to load some data, I check the cache; if it's present, use it. If it's marked as "incoming", register our render function to be called when it arrives. If it's neither, mark it as incoming and handle the load; when we get the data, toss it into the cache and callback any registered functions that were waiting. Either way, probably want a "flush cache" option, perhaps both globally or for a single file. Useful for self-updating graphs.

title: Ticket #6047: Systemd stop command must block until condor_master exits
description: When HTCondor is running under systemd, the command used to stop HTCondor needs to block until the service is completely shut down (i.e. the condor_master has exited). Immediately after the stop command exits, systemd kills any lingering processes and logs an error for the service in its logs. The service's state is marked as 'failed'. The stop command is set in the systemd configuration file with the ExecStop parameter. We currently set condor_off -master, which returns immediately after signalling the condor_master. We also set TimeoutStopSec to 20 seconds, but it appears that affects how long systemd will wait for the stop command to finish.
remarks: 2016-Dec-09 08:03:04 by tim: Actually, the stop time is the 90 second system default in the 8.5.x series. 2019-Jun-07 10:23:56 by tim: Fixed by #6096 in version 8.6.7

title: Ticket #4580: Fix pslot startd RANK preemption
description: The commits made for #3667 have several shortcomings: Failure to include required schedd code patches, thus startd RANK simply cannot work properly on pslots. The changes in the negotiator only look at aggregation of cpu/memory/disk, and thus fail to consider extra user-defined resources. This could create very difficult to debug situations for the administrator. The design document needs to be enhanced to explicitly answer questions like how does the schedd know when all the preemptions of dynamic slots are complete such that a (larger) dynamic slot can now be created. title: Ticket #2907: glexec new default umask causes issues
description: Recent versions of glexec have changed the default umask to 077. This breaks Condor-glexec integration. The issue is that condor_glexec_setup will call "mkdir" to create the sandbox. This previously resulted in a sandbox with perms 0755; it now results in 0700 (owned by the payload). Condor will then attempt to chdir to the sandbox (as the pilot) and invoke glexec again. For the new behavior, the chdir fails due to EPERM and the job goes on hold. This can be fixed by using "install -m 755 -d" instead of "mkdir -p" in condor_glexec_setup.
remarks: 2012-Apr-02 14:54:42 by danb: Thanks for the suggested fix, Brian. I applied it. 2012-Apr-02 14:57:01 by bbockelm: For posterity's sake: it appears the umask change in glexec was a development bug. However, I still think it's appropriate future-proofing to explicitly set the mode.

title: Ticket #6102: Synchronize Job Router's polling functions
description: The Job Router has different daemoncore timers for two polling functions. One function snoops on the schedd's job_queue.log and maintains an in-memory copy of the queue state. The other function looks at all routed jobs and performs any required actions on them. This includes propagating attribute changes from the routed job ad to the source job ad. These have the same interval by default, but can get out of synch by configuration or due to runtime delays. I have observed frequent occasions where the Job Router will push attribute updates to the source job ad in the schedd twice, because its view of the schedd's queue isn't updated after the first push. We should merge these polling operations under a single daemoncore timer. It would first update the in-memory mirror of the job queue, then examine all of the routed jobs. The latter uses information from the former for much of its work.

title: Ticket #2842: revamp job attributes, requirements for needs of partitionable slots
description: In order to know how to partition slots for jobs, the job needs to specify requirements for CPU,Memory,Disk and other scalar resources in form that is explicit. And the Execute nodes need to measure the actual use of memory and disk and publish values into the Job Ad so that the user can learn what their job requirements actually are. The current system of using ImageSize a proxy for memory usage is too error prone. We need a better measure, and the execute node needs to able to choose what that better measure is. So we will define a new attribute in the job ad. MemoryUsage which will be set by the starter to the best measure available. It is anticipated that on most platforms this will result the starter setting MemoryUsed = ResidentSetSize. In addition, condor_submit needs to be changed so that it no longer automatically adds expressions testing ImageSize into the Requirements expression. See subtickets for details of the various parts of this task. title: Ticket #1297: Kbdd messages could be ignored due to bad authorization defaults
description: Somewhat related to #714. In order for keyboard/mouse activity to be detected on several important platforms (aka Windows Vista and above, or Linux w/ 2.6 kernel and USB keyboards), X_EVENT_NOTIFICATION messages from the kbdd must make it to the startd. Unfortunately, the startd currently registers the X_EVENT_NOTIFICATION command as authorization level DAEMON, which can be overly restrictive in some installations because the kbdd needs to run as the end-user and therefore may not have access to required credentials. The result is keyboard activity may not detected because the startd will dump notifications from the kbdd if the authorization check fails. Proposed fix: have the startd register X_EVENT_NOTIFICATION as level ALLOW, and then confirm (by inspecting the source address of the message) that the incoming message originated from the same machine.

title: Ticket #7343: Provide live-updating equivalent of condor_q: condor_watch_q
description: CHTC users are perpetually told to not run condor_q repeatedly, and also not to run it in any kind of automated loop. This is to prevent them from DOSing the schedd. Since we keep having to say it, this is clearly something people want. We should make a new tool using the Python bindings (and distributed as part of them) that reads event logs to reproduce the "job status" part of condor_q, but with live updates. It will not do everything that condor_q does, but it will do the thing that people who want to watch condor_q want: to know how their jobs are doing, live. Known issues at time of merge: Does not work well on DAGs. The best set of options at the moment is condor_watch_q -f dagfile.dag.nodes.log -groupby log, but the output is not very useful. condor_watch_q will need to learn more about DAGMan. #7800 Does not work well for late materialization. condor_watch_q will need to look at the cluster ad for additional information. We can't capture batch names for clusters that have entirely left the queue, which may lead to unexpected grouping/naming of rows. Perhaps we could look in the history? The active job ids table column will not display what is expected when grouping by batch name and two clusters end up in the same row.

title: Ticket #6876: Support output file remaps for URLs
description: On output, we can only specify an "output destination": if set, on the final transfer from the condor_starter, we copy each file in the output sandbox to: OutputDestination + "/" + filename This really means everything -- including stdout and stderr from the job. We believe this has been highly unpopular and that users actually want only specific transfers to go URLs. For now, I'd like to keep the OutputDestination semantic to preserve backward compatibility - but this might be removable in the future. Instead, we should use the existing transfer_output_remaps on the upload side. If the output file is to be remapped to a URL, then it should be transferred from the starter using a hook instead of CEDAR. By removing a limit on the existing remap mechanism, we have minimal user interface changes. In terms of when the hook is invoked, we should keep the existing logic for OutputDestination. This is only invoked when it is a "final transfer" (which is only true for Upload from the starter to the shadow). The hooks should not be invoked when the file transfer output is used by client tools (condor_transfer_data or the Python bindings).

title: Ticket #2566: race condition in condor_history
description: condor_history may skip over some jobs if rotation of the history file happens between the time condor_history builds a list of the history filenames and the time it opens "history". The problem is that "history" may get renamed in the interim. Igor suspects he encountered a case where condor_history skipped over a bunch of jobs. The above race condition may explain it, but we are not sure it is what really happened. How to fix: do not rename the main history file. When it is initially created, name it "history.<timestamp>", like the names of the rotated history files. Then "rotation" just means we delete one history file and open a new history file, but no files get renamed.

title: Ticket #6525: Remove all rewriting of sinful strings in ads going on the wire
description: In old versions of HTCondor, daemons would rewrite their sinful string in ads going on the wire to reflect the interface being used. As part of the IPv6 work in 8.3.x, this code was largely disabled (#5074). But a variant of it was kept for HTConndor-CE (#4849).
