title: Ticket #2835: revamp default job requirements esp given partitionable slots
description: The way condor_submit sets up default job requirements for memory, disk, etc, is pretty convoluted and typically does not do what users expect. Especially given our push towards partitionable slots, it is time to revisit this. So currently the default requirements looks like this: Requirements = ( TARGET.Disk >= DiskUsage ) && ( ( TARGET.Memory * 1024 ) >= ImageSize ) && ( ( RequestMemory * 1024 ) >= ImageSize ) RequestMemory = ceiling( ifThenElse(JobVMMemory =!= undefined, JobVMMemory, ImageSize / 1024.000000) ) Proposed to change such that default job requirements expression does not insert in any sub-expressions related to partitionable resources (currently memory, disk, cpu). no default (in condor_submit) for RequestMemory etc; of course submit exprs knob could set one Add XxxUsage for each partitionable resource, e.g. MemoryUsage, DiskUsage, that makes the units match up with RequestXxx units (e.g. everything based on Mbytes?) and references a 'best practice' attribute. So on Linux, MemoryUsage = ResidentSetSize * xxx So if and only the job ad specifies RequestDisk and RequestMemory, job requirements would look like Requirements = ( Disk >= RequestDisk ) && ( Memory >= RequestMemory ) NOTE: we either need to bite the bullet and make all units the same (bytes? Mbytes?) or include unit multipliers in the above
remarks: 2012-Feb-27 21:49:49 by tstclair: I think we need to add a warning on submission if no RequestMemory is given such that the user can make sense out of it, being silent is not an option imho given that I was completely trip'd by this. 2012-Apr-02 15:46:37 by tstclair: So this should be updated and kicked out of review per that last meeting as the defaults need to change. 2012-Apr-25 13:13:00 by johnkn: Given this submit file Executable = dummy Universe = Vanilla Queue 1 condor_submit will now produce Request* and Requirements expressions like this: RequestMemory = ifthenelse(MemoryUsage =!= undefined,MemoryUsage,1) RequestDisk = DiskUsage RequestCpus = 1 Requirements = <opsys_expr> && (TARGET.Disk >= RequestDisk) && (TARGET.Memory >= RequestMemory) By comparison, 7.6.6 would produce the following instead RequestMemory = ceiling(ifThenElse(JobVMMemory =!= undefined,JobVMMemory,ImageSize / 1024.000000)) RequestDisk = DiskUsage RequestCpus = 1 Requirements = <opsys_expr> && (TARGET.Disk >= DiskUsage) && ((TARGET.Memory * 1024) >= ImageSize) && ((RequestMemory * 1024) >= ImageSize)) 2012-Apr-27 15:38:18 by johnkn: Igor points out that we changed the policy between 7.7.5 and 7.7.6 to warn about using Memory and Disk in Requrements. He suggests that we should give users an entire series to transition to the new policy before having condor_submit warn about it. I propose that we do this. In particular I propose Create a new config knob ENABLE_SUBMIT_WARNINGS_ABOUT_UPCOMING_POLICY set the default value for this knob to FALSE. Have 7.8 check this knob before warning about Memory & Disk in requirements Have 7.9 NOT check this knob before warning about Memory & Disk. At about 7.8.5 either switch the default value for this knob to TRUE, or remove the code that checks the knob for Memory & Disk in requirements. Also we should support Igor's use case of having a way to disable Requirements checks against memory & disk entirely - Add code in condor_submit to check for a request_memory=undefined statement in the submit file, and have it NOT add a reference to RequestMemory into Requirements in that case.

title: Ticket #4148: Pass non-fungible slot resource IDs to the job via environment
description: User-defined slot resources that have resource IDs, (i.e. are non-fungible) must be published to the Starter and/or job in order to be useful. See #4141 There should be a way for the configurator to define what environment variable to publish a given resource id into. To take the particular case of GPU resources, the config # add this to your config file to define 4 non-fungible GPU resources MACHINE_RESOURCE_GPUs = CUDA0,CUDA1,CUDA2,CUDA3 Will result in slots being assigned GPUs resources, the specific IDs of which are published in the slot ad in the AssignedGPUs attribute. This will be a comma separated list, so a slot that is assigned 2 GPUs might have this attribute in it's machine ad. AssignedGPUs = "CUDA0,CUDA1" When a job lands on this slot, the assigned GPUs will be propagated into the job's environment as: _CONDOR_AssignedGPUs=CUDA0,CUDA1 But in order to work the NVIDIA's CUDA api, it also need to be published to the job's environment as CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES environment variable, with everything but the device numbers removed like this (see #2011) _CONDOR_AssignedGPUs=CUDA0,CUDA1 CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0,1 To get this behavior, you can add the optional configuration to specify an additional environment variable for assigned resources. HTCondor recognizes CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES and the OpenCL equivalent GPU_DEVICE_ORDINAL and will strip all but [0-9,] from AssignedGPU before assigning it to one of these # this config produces the above environment MACHINE_RESOURCE_GPUs = CUDA0,CUDA1,CUDA2,CUDA3 ENVIRONMENT_FOR_AssignedGPUs = CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES # this config is equivalent, but makes the transformation of IDs explicit MACHINE_RESOURCE_GPUs = CUDA0,CUDA1,CUDA2,CUDA3 ENVIRONMENT_FOR_AssignedGPUs = CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=/[ a-zA-Z]+// This is generalized so that for this configuration # config a tag resource MACHINE_RESOURCE_Tag = VINI, VICI, VIDI ENVIRONMENT_FOR_AssignedTag = WHAT_I_DID=/$/I_/ NUM_SLOTS_TYPE_1 = 1 SLOT_TYPE_1_PARTITIONABLE = true SLOT_TYPE_1 = Cpus=100%, Disk=90%, Memory=90%, Tag=100% A job that requests a Tag resource like this # this is in the jobs submit file request_tag = 1 Then the dynamic slot that is used to satisfy the job request will have these attributes TotalTag = 3 DetectedTag = 3 TotalSlotTag = 1 Tag = 1 AssignedTag = "VINI" And when the job starts on that slot, the job's environment will contain. _CONDOR_AssignedTag=VINI WHAT_I_DID=I_VINI
remarks: 2014-Jan-24 10:08:49 by johnkn: ENVIRONMENT_FOR_AssignedTag needs way to indicate string substitution operations on the right hand side, something like ENVIRONMENT_FOR_AssignedGPUs = CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=/CUDA// which would indicate that CUDA should be removed from the device ID before assigning it to the CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES environment variable. If the slot has AssignedGPUs = "CUDA2,CUDA3" Then the job environment will have _CONDOR_AssignedGPUs=CUDA1,CUDA2 CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=1,2 2014-Jan-30 10:19:10 by johnkn: [39261] added a new config knob for each non-fungible user defined resource FOO there is a config koob ENVIRONMENT_FOR_AssignedFOO which can contain a set of environment variables and associated perl style regex replacement rule for converting assigned FOO ids when setting that environment variable. If there is a user defined resource # configuration MACHINE_RESOURCE_FOO = "IDA,IDB,IDC" ENVIRONMENT_FOR_AssignedFOO = MYFOO=/ID([A-Z])/"$1"/ FOO2=/ID// FOO3 Then when a slot gets assigned a Foo, the machine ad will have # machine/slot ad FOO = 2 AssignedFOO = "IDA,IDB" And the job environment will have _CONDOR_AssignedFOO=IDA,IDB MYFOO="A","B" FOO2=A,B FOO3=IDA,IDB

title: Ticket #2970: CONDOR_INHERIT causes recursive glideins to misbehave
description: In a test of Igor's CrosOSG CE, there is a glidein within a glidein. The inner glidein failed shortly after being started, because the master was trying to send a CHILDALIVE message to the outer glidein. This failed due to authorization errors. The inner glidein should not be trying to send CHILDALIVE messages to the outer glidein. The reason it is trying to do so is that the CONDOR_INHERIT environment variable is being passed to the job executed by the outer glidein. Proposed fix: remove CONDOR_INHERIT from the environment as soon as it is read in DaemonCore. It should never be passed to a child process of a daemon.
remarks: 2012-May-03 14:34:45 by danb: I learned more: CONDOR_INHERIT is passed to the job when JOB_INHERITS_STARTER_ENVIRONMENT is true. Otherwise, it is not passed. Furthermore, the value is explicitly set by the starter in DaemonCore::CreateProcess(). It is not just a value left over from what the starter itself inherited. 2012-Oct-08 14:53:03 by tannenba: Code Review. I wonder if scheduler universe has a similar issue, and seems like it would be easy to write a regression test for this. But the code patch itself looks fine, so resolving.

title: Ticket #2423: FileTransfer shouldn't back-date file modification times
description: When the FileTransfer object is receiving files in the schedd or starter, it back-dates the modification times by 3 minutes. This doesn't appear to be necessary and can be confusing. This happens in FileTransfer::DoDownload(). Comments in the method say that it used to issue an fsync after writing each file to ensure that its modification time is older than when file transfer completes. This is to prevent unmodified input files from being transferred as output. But on some OS's, when using fsync, writes can still be delayed and the file modification time set to some time after the write and fsync. So the method manually sets the modification time to 180 seconds in the past. This back-dating is not needed in the starter, where we transfer as output any file whose size or modfication time changes during job execution. In the schedd, I don't see how back-dating solves the supposed problem. No matter what you set the modification time to, a delayed write would just set it to the undesired future time afterwards.

description: Create a command-line tool that pushes a new credential to the credd without actually submitting a job. Perhaps this can be implemented simply as a flag to condor_submit. title: Ticket #6749: Check CURB_MATCHMAKING before building RRLs for negotiator
description: The CURB_MATCHMAKING expression is a way to have the schedd stop soliciting new resources from the negotiator if it's getting too busy. Before sending each RRL (resource request list) ad to the negotiator, the schedd checks this expression. If it evaluates to True, then the schedd tells the negotiator it has no more jobs to give. Recently, schedds in CMS's global pool came under heavy load due to, in part, the number of autoclusters growing out of control (one job per autocluster). The CURB_MATCHMAKING expression evaluated to True, but the schedd still built the full set of RRLs it would send before telling the negotiator "I have no jobs for you". Building the RRL set in memory took so long that the negotiator timed out waiting for the schedd to respond. CMS has negotiation prefetch enabled, so long waits by the negotiator for multiple affected schedds went in parallel. But it was still a big waste of time for all daemons involved. When the negotiator sends a NEGOTIATE command to the schedd, the schedd should check CURB_MATCHMAKING before building the RRL sets and, if the expression evaluates to True, immediately tell the negotiator that it has no jobs for it.

title: Ticket #4774: OOM Management issues
description: RAL reported in htcondor-users they observed a signficant number of jobs going on hold with the following message in the ShadowLog: 10/08/14 14:26:26 (860002.0) (30272): ERROR "Error from slot1@xxxxxxxxxxxxxx: Close_Pipe error" at line .... After a long debugging session with RAL, we noticed a few OOM notification management issues: When the VanillaProc object is destroyed, the m_oom_efd pipe is not de-registered (also, the other end of the pipe is never closed). The handler is active, so it's possible to get a use-after-free. The probability of this issue greatly increased in #4435 where it became possible to have the OOM-killer enabled along with the OOM notification (previously, the OOM-killer was always disabled when the OOM notification was enabled). VanillaProc is a sub-class allocated on the heap with no virtual destructor. Oops. Because the OOM killer can fire along with the OOM notification, we should check for the notification in VanillaProc::JobReaper. This way, it's much more likely we put the job on hold when the OOM killer is enabled and sent the job a SIGKILL. On newer kernels, when memory.use_hierarchy is enabled in the memory controller, attempting to disable the OOM killer fails with EINVAL in a not-top-level cgroup; this is the underlying cause of #4435. Now that we understand this is the problem, we ought to make the log message less scary.

title: Ticket #1825: code optimization bug in x86 rhel3 build
description: The x86 rhel3 builds on V7_5_5-branch and trunk are failing tests in various ways. I spent some time looking into this and concluded that it is likely due to incorrect code generation by the compiler. I got a second opinion from Pete and he agreed. We would like to be proven wrong! The problem is that a call to std::string::c_str() returns a string lacking a null terminator. Previous calls to std::string::c_str() on this same string work correctly. In the debugger, we can see the string has a null terminator before the call to c_str() and lacks one after the call to c_str(). The value that is written where the null is desired comes from a location on the stack that is not initialized within Create_Process() but it is within that function's stack frame. It happens in the following code: /usr/include/c++/3.2.3/bits/basic_string.h:229 80fc648: 8b 85 c8 0f ff ff mov 0xffff0fc8(%ebp),%eax ; get address of string 80fc64e: 03 40 f4 add 0xfffffff4(%eax),%eax ; move to end of string /usr/include/c++/3.2.3/bits/char_traits.h:119 80fc651: 8a 8d 6f 0d ff ff mov 0xffff0d6f(%ebp),%cl ; read value from stack 80fc657: 88 08 mov %cl,(%eax) ; assign value to end of string Typically, in the first few calls to Create_Process, the address 0xffff0d6f(%ebp) points to a null byte. But eventually it is common for some other value to be in this location. We verified that we can set this value to something arbitrary at the top of the function, and it still has that value when it gets to the above code that references the address. This makes it seem unlikely that this value is being corrupted within Create_Process(). While stepping through the code up to the point where the value is referenced, we never observe this location getting modified. There are no explicit references to this stack offset anywhere else in the code. Other calls to c_str() read the null value from a static variable rather than from a location on the stack, and this makes sense given the C++ code in the STL header file. I have observed this same problem from binaries built on two different NMI build machines for this platform: nmi-0102 and nmi-0228, so it is not a problem specific to one machine. The compiler in both cases is gcc 3.2.3, but the specific version string differs: gcc (GCC) 3.2.3 20030502 (Red Hat Linux 3.2.3-24) gcc (GCC) 3.2.3 20030502 (Red Hat Linux 3.2.3-59) From all of the above, it seems that the compiler simply generated bad code. The end result is that the first argument to the following function call is an unterminated const char *. ClaimIdParser claimId(session_id.c_str(), session_info.Value(), session_key.c_str()); When the program reads from the bytes after the end of the string, valgrind correctly detects the read of uninitialized memory. This is the first complaint from valgrind, other than a complaint very early in the program within some ipv6 code, which Greg says is expected. In Condor, the problem is usually not detected until the child process tries to read from an environment variable inherited from its parent. The value of the environment variable contains some garbage characters which typically cause the child to EXCEPT like this: 12/22/10 04:19:57 ERROR "Assertion ERROR on (sesid)" at line 2834 in file /home/condor/execute/dir_5930/userdir/src/condor_io/condor_secman.cpp How to Fix We are not very happy with any of the options for fixing this: Turn off optimization for this file on this platform. Turn off optimization for the entire build on this platform. Perturb the affected code so that the problem appears to go away. (For example, call c_str() once and store the result for subsequent use.)

title: Ticket #5535: Partitionable slots can sometimes provision too little disk

Brian 2016-Mar-15 16:06:49 by gthain: My understanding is that CMS is seeing a problem where dslots are created correctly from the pslot on first use, but then claim reuse is failing in the startd when a second job tries to reuse the slot. Claim reuse fails because the dslot's Disk attribute is smaller than the Request_disk in the job ad, even though it matched in the schedd. This is because the "Disk" attribute in the pslot means "currently free kbytes of disk on the execute partition", for some value of "current". Unlike the Memory and Cpus attribute, the value of the Disk attribute changes constantly, although the collector's copy of the job ad may not have the most up-to-date version. The attribute TotalSlotDisk does not change, but it isn't used for anything. The Disk attribute in the dslots and static slot is based on the fraction of the pslot the job initially requested. So, if whatever the job requested for disk was 10% of the currently available disk in the pslot, the startd remembers that it was 10%, and gives it that fraction. The buggy thing is that as the free disk in the pslot grows or shrinks, the disk attribute in the dslot is updated to be 10% of the pslot value. I guess this thinking goes back to static slots, and assuming the execute directory is shared with non-condor uses. Also, although the startd support overriding MEMORY and NUM_CPUS in the config file, it doesn't support a DISK attribute. So, I propose that the Disk attribute for dslots be fixed over their lifetime, and that we add a DISK param, if only for testing and debugging. 2016-Mar-21 14:30:30 by johnkn: code_review this change is very subtle. but it looks good to me. It will round up disk requests from a Kbytes request to .1 % of current disk, thereby allowing up to 500 slots without running out of disk while also guaranteeing that the disk allocation has a slop of about .1% of disk and thus has a bit of room to decrease from the allocated amount without causing the slot activation to fail. 2016-Aug-10 13:41:11 by tannenba: For people who are hit by this bug, the best option is to upgrade to HTCondor v8.4.5 or newer. I say "possible" because I didn't test it, but I think it will work around the bug. Of course, the down side is you'd better be sure you don't have jobs that exhaust the disk space on these nodes since the startd will no longer examine the job's RequestDisk. title: Ticket #810: Schedd should be able to intelligently reschedule all on its own
description: I think the time has come to get rid of requiring condor_submit to issue a condor_reschedule. These days the schedd is smart enough to not blow itself up if it were to reschedule on every transaction commit (due to mechanisms like the Timeslice class) - and that is essentially what is happening (poorly) now anyhow. Furthermore, the schedd could even be smarter about it. I think we want the schedd to call StartLocalJobs() whenever it sees one or more scheduler or local universe jobs enter the queue, and timeout() whenever it sees jobs of any other universe. At first blush, this would seem a lot better to me than what we have now. For instance, this way we would have zero latency of the type described in #765.

title: Ticket #5470: TimerRemove attribute broken
description: TimerRemover is a job attribute that sets a lease on a job submission to the schedd. The value is interpreted as a unix epoch time after which the job should be removed. The submitter can update the time periodically. It is used by Condor-C when a JobLeaseDuration is set in the source job ad (the default for Condor-C jobs is no lease). TimerRemover is evaluated as part of the job policy expressions. If the schedd delegates evaluation of these expressions to another daemon (shadow, gridmanager, job router), it will need to forward subsequent updates of the TimerRemove expression. It appears this does not happen at the moment. As a result, jobs for which TimerRemove is being updated in the schedd will end up being removed by one of these other daemons if they are doing job policy evaluation. This involves several bug fixes, primarily to ensure that updates to TimerRemove are forwarded to any daemon that assumes responsibility for evaluating the job policy expressions.
remarks: This is a regression from version 8.2. In 8.2, any update of TimerRemove is propagated to the shadow or gridmanager. I suspect #4613 disrupted the dirty attribute tracking of the schedd's job queue. 2016-Jan-14 16:23:48 by jfrey: The introduction of the JobQueueJob object in #4613 caused this regression. The method LogNewClassAd::Play() enables dirty attribute tracking on each ClassAd created in the collection. Starting with #4613, this ad is then handed to ClassAdLogTable::insert() in the schedd code, which creates a JobQueueJob object, copies all attributes from the original ad into it, and deletes the original ad. It doesn't propagate the dirty tracking bit from the original ad. A fix for 8.4 would be for ClassAdLogTable::insert() to propagate the dirty tracking bit from the source ad, or always enable it in the new JobQueueJob ad. In 8.5, we should investigate leaving dirty tracking disabled and explicitly setting dirty flags where needed. Also, eliminate the ad copy in ClassAdLogTable::insert(), as the source ad should already be a JobQueueJob object. 2016-Feb-01 11:01:47 by tlmiller: Code Review Looks good, except for a quibble with check-in 47472. The code opts for simplicity by always forwarding the evaluated value, which is fine, but the conditional evaluates ATTR_TIMER_REMOVE_CHECK rather than looking it up. This probably further simplifies the code, but raises the question of what the semantics are when ATTR_TIMER_REMOVE_CHECK fails to evaluate. This should never occur in practice, but a comment saying "bad user, don't do that" might be appropriate.

title: Ticket #4631: Slow buffer growth antipattern in ProcAPI::GetSystemPerfData().
description: In ProcAPI::GetSystemPerfData() (condor_procapi/procapi.cpp:3212), we call RegQueryValueEx() with a 40K buffer. If that's not large enough, we realloc() the buffer and increase its size by 4K, and call RegQueryValueEx() again. We repeat this until the buffer is large enough. Conventional wisdom suggests that we should instead double the size of the buffer each time, thus reducing us from O(n) syscalls (and realloc()s) to O(log n). If we're hitting this potential problem as hard as we expect, it's possible that this bug explains the "performance cliff" we've notice on the BaTLab Windows machines.
creator: tlmiller

title: Ticket #406: Recursive $(macro) expansion causes condor_submit to hang
description: If a setting in the condor_submit submit file contains a recursive entry, condor_submit will hang. Now make a simple change and resubmit: requirements=false universe=vanilla arguments=foo arguments=$(arguments) bar cmd=/bin/date queue Observe that condor_submit hangs. It is chewing up as much processor as it can get, and its memory usage is slowly growing. My guess is that it's expanding the second arguments using the second arguments, so it becomes "$(arguments) bar bar", then "$(arguments) bar bar bar", and so on. Expected behavior: Ideally? This works like the condor configuration file, allow this sort of prepending and appending. It's useful for supporting users; I can say something like "Add requirements=($(requirements)) && NeedExtraBacon" after your existing requirements expression. title: Ticket #328: DAGMan lazily evaluates and opens node job log files
description: This is already in progress, but I figured I should make a ticket for it.
remarks: Basically, the idea is that we would deal with the log files as lazily as possible (at node submit time, rather than at DAGMan startup time). The big change is that the multi-log-file code would have to be able to have a dynamic, rather than static, list of log files to monitor. * Basic changes: - Current log-file-related code to parse a DAG goes away (which means that condor_submit_dag will not check for log file specifications; that will only happen in DAGMan itself). - We only monitor log files associated with active jobs in the DAG, rather than monitoring all relevant log files. - Have a command-line flag for whether to check for valid log file specifications when parsing the DAG (defaults to yes). * More details: Have an object for each log file; all LogFile objects go into a hash table indexed by canonicaled file name; there is a side list with pointers only to the active file objects (for better performance). struct LogFile { int refCount; int fd; long lastOffset; // maybe last timestamp of file // maybe other stuff } * Interface to multi-log-file code: MonitorLogFile(const char *logfile, bool recovery); - Make pathname canonical - Look for LogFile object in "main" list - If not found, create new LogFile object (includes file truncation if not in recovery mode) - If reference count is 0: - Open file - If file was previously used, seek to the proper location - Add to active list - Increment reference count UnmonitorLogFile(const char *logfile, bool recovery); - Make pathname canonical - Find LogFile object in "main" list - Decrement reference count - If reference count is now 0: - Get and save current location in file - Close file - Remove from active list ULogEventOutcome readEvent(ULogEvent * & event); - Go through all of the active log file objects and find the next unread event. DAGMan calls MonitorLogFile() just before submitting a job; calls UnmonitorLogFile() just after dealing with the TERMINATED event for a job. At submit time, DAGMan will also save the log file name in the Job object, in case the submit file gets modified during the job's lifetime. When we're finished with the job, we can free the log file name string to save memory. We need to save the list of inactive files in case one job uses a log file, then the log file becomes inactive, and later on another job uses it and it becomes active again -- we have to know to seek past the events we already saw when we re-open the file. * Recovery mode: In recovery mode, we'd have to register the log file for a job when it gets put into the ready queue. Hmm -- maybe we should just do it that way all the time to avoid having different cases in the code for "normal" mode and recovery mode. It would be less efficient, but simpler. Something to think about, anyhow. * Rescue DAGs: I don't think we'd have to do anything special when executing a rescue DAG. * Advantages: - Allows the possibility of lazy splice evaluation. - Reduces the number of file descriptors used by DAGMan. - Eliminates current duplicate DAG parsing code in the log file implementation. - Allows more flexible "on-the-fly" generation of submit files; but overwriting a submit file that was used earlier in the DAG can cause problems and shouldn't be done (this is also true with the current log file setup). * Possible future developments: Phase 2: limit fd use by not keeping open fds to all active log files (fds would be opened and closed each time we get an event). Phase 3: allow macros in log file names (but not $(JOB)) Phase 4: make node IDs unique across all DAGMan instances, so we don't need to truncate log files. * Suggestions from Miron, 2008-10-28: If a node job submit file doesn't specify a log file, DAGMan should specify a standard log file on the condor_submit command line. DAGMan could also delete that file at the end of the run (if successful), since the user presumably doesn't care about it. (Kent -- maybe there should be a config macro to turn off deleting the log file.) Do something like "SUBDAG INLINE" instead of "SPLICE". * Notes during implementation: The ReadMultipleUserLogs destructor should print a warning if there are any "active" log files. Hmm -- should the log code touch a non-existant log file when it's registered, so that we can open the file right away? 2009-06-25: plans from today's code review: * Make changes as per code review. * Push out with lazy log file code still disabled. * Make sure nightly tests still work. * Pete reads code in detail. * Turn on lazy log file code. * Make sure nightly tests still work. * Completely remove the old code. * Implement the "no log file required" feature. 2009-07-08: changes to plan for expediency: * Put it in with the existing Condor Hashtable code; switch to STL and keying on both st_dev and st_ino later. 2009-07-16: once final version is coded, test with symlink to log file across file system. 2009-07-24: this has been enabled on the trunk, and all tests were green last night. Still needs changes to use STL map instead of Condor HashTable, and also to index on devise as well as inode. 2009-Nov-17 11:51:35 by wenger: I've created two new tickets (#966: use STL map; #967: index on device) to capture the unfinished aspects of this ticket, so I'm resolving this ticket.

title: Ticket #2862: Schedd should collect statistics on sub-sets of completed jobs.
description: Now that we have statitics on completed/failed jobs in the SCHEDD. we would like to be able to collect the same sorts of statistics on subsets of the jobs. In particular we would like to have separate numbers for local vs. flocked jobs. or statistics for particular users. In order to accomplish this. I propose to add a new parameter that will enable the administrator to define a separate sets of schedd statistics with a prefix for each of the statistics values, and a ClassAd expression that will define whether a job should be counted in that set of statistics. a new set of params that match the pattern SCHEDD_COLLECT_STATS_FOR_(.+) will define the statistics set. the last part of the param name will be used as a prefix for the attributes published in that set. The value of the param will be a ClassAd expression that evaluates to a boolean value against a completed job ad. TRUE will cause that job to be counted in that set. So, for instance. SCHEDD_COLLECT_STATS_FOR_GLIDEIN = regexp("^glidein",RemoteHost) would define a statistics set having the prefix 'Glidein' that would include statistics for any job whose RemoteHost value begins with the text "glidein". As a future task, It might also be nice to create open-ended sets of stats pools - where the prefix would contain the string valued result of the class ad Expression. so SCHEDD_COLLECT_STATS_BY_USER = User would make a separate set of statistics prefixed with "User_???_" for each unique value of the class-ad attribute User.

title: Ticket #6572: qedit has unexpected behavior with late materialization
description: when you use condor_qedit <clusterid> to edit a late materialization job, the edits will be applied only to jobs that have already materialized. the way materialization works is to use the submit digest to make a full job ad for ProcId <N> compare each attribute of this job ad to the cluster ad, deleting attributes that match submit the remaining attributes from the pruned job ad into the queue. If condor_qedit is to have the desired effect when editing all of the jobs in a cluster, two changes have to happen the cluster ad must be modified along with all of the currently materialized jobs attributes in the cluster ad that were modified after submit time must be pruned from the job ad as part of step 2 above. This new behavior will be accomplished by having condor_qedit send a special flag along when it calls SetAttributeByConstrint to indicate that the cluster ad's should be considered when evaluating the constraint. condor_qedit will send this flag when it knows that the constraint will match all of the jobs in a cluster when it matches the cluster ad. The schedd will then also modify a new attribute in the cluster ad : EditedClusterAttrs which will be a list of attributes in the cluster ad that have been modified since the cluster was originally submitted. condor_qedit will only send this new flag when talking to a schedd that is 8.7.7 or later and only when the -constraint option has not been used.

title: Ticket #7733: Improve job id validation checks
description: The schedd has poor validation of job ids for SetAttribute() and DeleteAttribute() qmgmt calls. If the job id isn't a valid key in the committed job queue log, it assumes the ad has been created in the active transaction (if any). It rejects the attribute modification unless the cluster id matches active_cluster_num and the proc id is less than next_proc_num. When submitting a new cluster, this allows SetAttribute() of arbitrary negative proc ids. When not submitting a new cluster, this allows SetAttribute() of cluster id -1 with arbitrary negative proc ids. The actions are logged in job_queue.log, but don't appear to affect the in-memory queue (since the ads don't actually exist). When the log is compressed, the errant entries disappear (since they aren't in the in-memory version). The only practical effects appear to be that the SetAttribute() and DeleteAttribute() calls succeed, and the Job Router will report errors when reading the log. We are making the following changes to improve the code that validates SetAttribute() and DeleteAttribute() calls: Change TotalSubmitProcs from immutable to secure and remove the special exception for it. Reject all modification of nonexistent job ids by default, even for calls internal to the schedd. Use of the NONDURABLE flag is no longer required to detect an invalid job id, which the dedicated scheduler was relying on. Submit transforms and late materialization are exempted from this check. They may need to modify ads created in the active transaction that would be rejected by our heuristic for allowed in-transaction edits (examining active_cluster_num and next_proc_num). They are internal code and assumed trustworthy. We could remove this exemption if we had an efficient way to check a job id against all of the ids created in the active transaction.

title: Ticket #7363: SSL memory leak
description: It appears we have a memory leak in the SSL code. Greg says: It looks like guts inside an SSL CTX aren't getting free'd. I think the problem is near the end of condor_ssl_auth::authenticate, we do X509 *peer = (*SSL_get_peer_certificate_ptr)(ssl); X509_NAME_oneline(X509_get_subject_name(peer), subjectname, 1024); setAuthenticatedName( subjectname ); setRemoteUser( "ssl" ); setRemoteDomain( UNMAPPED_DOMAIN ); dprintf(D_SECURITY,"SSL authentication succeeded to %s\n", subjectname); (*SSL_CTX_free_ptr)(ctx); (*SSL_free_ptr)(ssl); free(buffer); return success; From my reading of the openssl docs, SSL_get_peer_certificate increments a reference count, and the cert inside the SSL CTX (named ssl in this case) won't free the cert inside it when CTX_free is called. I think we need an X509_free(peer) call, like we do elsewhere.

title: Ticket #4959: ClassAds is/isnt operators not strict enough
description: According to the ClassAd specification, the meta-comparison operators is and isnt (=?= and =!= in old ClassAd syntax) evaluate whether two values are exactly identical. They are stricter than == and != on equality. We've found two ways in which the implementation isn't strict enough: There should be no type conversion. So 3 is 3.0 should evaluate to False. With the current code, it evaluates to True. Two AbsTime values should match only if they represent the same moment in time and have the same timezone offset. In the current code, the timezone offsets are ignored. So the following expression should evaluate to False, but currently evaluates to True: abstime("2015-03-03 12:13:15+0000") =?= abstime("2015-03-03 13:13:15+0100")

title: Ticket #7226: config auto use metaknob
description: For the config system, it would be useful to be able to specify a metaknob that is always appended to the config, but only when some other knob is not defined. A new knob pattern will be used to enable this AUTO_USE_<category>_<tag> The value of this knob will be evaluated as a config if expression, and if it evaluates to true, then configuration will behave as if use <category> : <tag> Was appended to the configuration. So, for example, if condor_config contains condor_config fragment AUTO_USE_ROLE_SingleNodePool = ! defined DAEMON_LIST AUTO_USE_SECURITY_TrustLocalAdmin = ! defined ALLOW_WRITE Then once all of the config files had been parsed, the configuration would be check to see if DAEMON_LIST was defined, and if it not would load use ROLE:SingleNodePool, and it would check to see if ALLOW_WRITE was defined, and if not, it would load use SECURITY:TrustLocalAdmin Here are the example metaknobs for use in the above statements. Note that these are suggested metaknobs, they are not actually in param_info.in param_info.in fragment [$ROLE.SingleNodePool] description=Automatic default role when no DAEMON_LIST is specified default: @end DAEMON_LIST = COLLECTOR NEGOTIATOR SCHEDD STARTD CONDOR_HOST = $(IP_ADDRESS) if ! $(CondorIsAdmin) # use a dynamic port for non-rootly condor COLLECTOR_HOST = $(CONDOR_HOST):0 # Windows needs a unique name for the procd pipe PROCD_ADDRESS = \\.\pipe\condor_procd_pipe_$(USERNAME) endif @end [$SECURITY.TrustUser] description=Authorization policy based on user accounts - args(admin_username, condor_username) if ! $(2?) error : use SECURITY:TrustUser requires 2 arguments, an admin username, and a condor daemon username endif ALLOW_ADMINISTRATOR=$(1)@$(UID_DOMAIN) $(2)@$(UID_DOMAIN) ALLOW_OWNER=$(1)@$(UID_DOMAIN) $(2)@$(UID_DOMAIN) ALLOW_READ=* # allow_write used only by schedd for job submission ALLOW_WRITE=* ALLOW_DAEMON=$(2)@$(UID_DOMAIN) ALLOW_NEGOTIATOR=$(2)@$(UID_DOMAIN) ALLOW_NEGOTIATOR_SCHEDD=$(ALLOW_NEGOTIATOR) $(FLOCK_NEGOTIATOR_HOSTS) ALLOW_WRITE_COLLECTOR=$(ALLOW_WRITE) $(FLOCK_FROM) ALLOW_WRITE_STARTD=$(ALLOW_WRITE) $(FLOCK_FROM) ALLOW_READ_COLLECTOR=$(ALLOW_READ) $(FLOCK_FROM) ALLOW_READ_STARTD=$(ALLOW_READ) $(FLOCK_FROM) @end [$SECURITY.TrustLocalAdmin] description=Security policy to trust only local administrator and condor itself usage=Use for single node pool when HTCondor is running as a service that and can impersonate users default=use Security : TrustUser(root, condor) win32_default=use Security : TrustUser(Administrator, LOCAL_SYSTEM)

title: Ticket #2024: JAVA_MAXHEAP_ARGUMENT should be removed/deprecated/fixed
description: JAVA_MAXHEAP_ARGUMENT handling is problematic. According to the documentation it is supposed to indicate the flag users use to indicate the max heap argument to the JVM, not including the value we want it set to. This works in older versions of the JVM, or at least in IBM's version circa 1.4.x, but Sun/Oracle JVMs since at least the 1.6 series require a numerical value such as -Xmx100m. The code for passing a value to the JVM checks for the presence of a value in JAVA_MAXHEAP_ARGUMENT and checks to make sure it begins with -Xmx. The way this check is written seems to imply that users can add an actual value after "-Xmx", which contradicts what the comments above the config knob say. The comment is also incorrect in saying that passing just "-Xmx" works in the Sun JVM. If the check for "-Xmx" passes, Condor passes the value on without further modification without appending any additional values to it, again in contradiction to the comments above the configuration option. If the test fails, it will construct a -Xmx argument by appending the amount of memory divided by the number of slots to -Xmx before passing it onto the JVM. Users that remove "-Xmx" from the configuration file and using the JAVA_EXTRA_ARGUMENTS configuration knob to pass in their own -Xmx value are thus passing in two values, which the JVM accepts but I do not know what actually gets used. This is primarily causing Windows users a lot of grief as they tend to have newer versions of Java installed. Proposed Solution: Remove JAVA_MAXHEAP_ARGUMENT entirely. Users that need to pass a value in are often already doing so via JAVA_EXTRA_ARGUMENTS. The documentation for this configuration knob is incorrect as it is and the behavior makes assumptions that are no longer valid.

title: Ticket #2927: allow a standalone checkpoint to be submitted to the standard universe
description: We would like to be able to submit an existing standalone checkpoint image as a standard-universe executable. This is to support the following campus grid use-case: we have jobs with complex environmental dependencies, which read lots of input data and then compute for a long time, producing a small output we submit them as standard-universe jobs to our local condor pool, let them start up and read all their input data, and then checkpoint and exit we submit the standalone checkpoint to another remote condor pool (e.g., via Condor-C) this allows to job to run in that foreign environment without its software dependencies or input data With #2877, we can now do this, except we must submit the resulting remote job as a vanilla universe job and as a result it cannot continue to checkpoint. Since the considerable remote/foreign resources we have access to (1000's of cores) are opportunistic, checkpointing would unlock significant goodput for us.
remarks: 2012-May-22 15:03:25 by tannenba: Thinking we could/should spend a little bit of time looking at this to see how big a project it is.... But if it is significant, the effort should go into getting ckpt support into vanilla universe instead. 2012-Jul-02 14:09:15 by tlmiller: > With #2877, we can now do this, except we must submit the resulting remote job as a vanilla universe job and as a result it cannot continue to checkpoint. What prevents you from continuing to use stand-alone checkpointing? 2012-Jul-25 10:52:40 by tlmiller: I tried starting a stand-alone checkpoint up as standard-universe job, but with the command-line arguments necessary to resume from its checkpoint. The job started, but not from the checkpoint: the command FD over-rides the command-line argument(s) related to the checkpoint file. Fixing this would be suprisingly tricky because the syscall library startup routines presently assume that the command FD (that is, the standard universe) entails remote system calls. It may be possible to work around this by copying the stand-alone checkpoint to the appropriate place in the spool, but it turns out that the standard universe uses a "pseudo" remote system call to handle fetching the checkpoint at start-up. Distentangling the two seems like it would be difficult and time-consuming, at best.

title: Ticket #1872: Grid jobs never rematch after failed $$() substitution
description: When the gridmanager retrieves a job ad from the schedd, the schedd replaces occurrences of $$(Foo) with the value of Foo in the resource ad obtained via match-making. If the resource ad doesn't have a Foo attribute, the schedd immediately puts the job on hold. If the job is released, this same process repeats. There's no mechanism to rematch the job when this error occurs. The job is stuck in an unusable state. When this error occurs, either the schedd or the gridmanager should modify the job ad so that it will be rematched. This can be done in addition to or instead of holding the job. As a work-around, you can force the job to be rematched by munging some job attributes: condor_qedit <job.id> Matched False condor_qedit <job.id> CurrentHosts 0

title: Ticket #1521: auto-selected output files and spooling are problematic
description: When output is auto-selected rather than being explicitly listed with transfer_output_files, the behavior is not optimal when spooling is being used. The spooled output files are dumped into the spool directory along with the existing spooled input files. Then when a client such as condor_transfer_data attempts to fetch the spooled output, everything in the spool is transferred, including the user log, the spooled input, and the spooled output. I propose fixing this by recording in the job ad the list of output files that were copied from the execute node. Call it SpooledOutputFiles. This should override TransferOutputFiles when fetching the output from the spool. This also happens to be useful in the solution to one of the problems in #1520. The problem is that entries in the TransferOutputFile list that are paths are stored in the spool directory as basenames. Something analogous to the schedd's rewriting of the spooled input file list needs to happen for the output files after stage-out is complete. This could be accomplished by specifying the spooled (rather than origin) paths in SpooledOutputFiles.

title: Ticket #5974: Reread credmon's pid file periodically
description: Daemons that interact with the credmon read the credmon's pid file the first time they interact with it, and cache the value indefinitely. If the credmon exits and restarts, the daemons can no longer signal it, and may end up signalling some innocent process that gets the reused pid. The credmon client code should re-read the pid file periodically to avoid this problem.

title: Ticket #4236: CCB listener should disconnect
description: The CCB protocol has no explicit disconnect RPC - the CCB listener simply hangs up on the server and the daemon exits. This is very problematic for the glideinWMS use case; it's not possible to distinguish between "daemon shut down" and "transient network issue". We observe the following sequence of events: Negotiator queries collector for list of startds, which includes worker node foo. Negotiator matches foo to schedd bar. Foo shuts down and disconnects from the CCB. Schedd bar launches shadow, which attempts to activate claim for foo. Shadow blocks for several minutes trying to connect to startd which is already shut down. If the CCB was aware that the connection was hopeless, we could save a significant amount of time in the last step. More importantly, we could distinguish between a network issue with a glidein and a clean shutdown. Right now, if we see shadows failing to connect to a glidein-based startd, it's a long process to correlate logs across several machines (usually to discover it was a clean shutdown).
remarks: 2014-Apr-01 08:38:28 by bbockelm: I did some investigation here - Adding an explicit "disconnect" message appears to be feasible in a backward-compatible manner. The disconnect won't really buy us much efficiency in activating claims. Right now, it will try only one connection per CCB server (so, on the CMS CCB setup, it currently tries twice). So, the impact outside CMS will probably be fairly limited. Seems like the bigger impact is that we can log communication attempts after explicit disconnects (for example, trying to claim a dead startd) and the frequency of unexpected disconnects. 2015-Apr-29 15:12:27 by bbockelm: We agreed 2 weeks ago that we will put this off until 8.5 (and make it high priority then). Decreasing the priority for now.

title: Ticket #5077: Specify accounting_group, accounting_group_user at DAG level
description: LIGO is interested in specifying (at the DAG level) accounting_group and accounting_group_user for node jobs. It sounds like there are basically three use cases (as per discussion on the LIGO call today): All nodes in the workflow (including nodes of sub-DAGs) have the same accounting_group and accounting_group_user. Sub-DAGs may have different accounting_group and accounting_group_user values. Individual nodes may have different accounting_group and accounting_group_user values. For case 1, I guess if you specify values in a top-level DAG, they should "trickle down" to sub-DAGs unless they're overridden at the sub-DAG level. It also sounds like case 1 is the most important for LIGO, followed by case 2 and then case 3. My first thought is to make this a generic capability (e.g., "-append 'accounting_group = ligo5') rather than implementing accounting-group specific commands (e.g., "-accounting_group = ligo5"). We have to think about where these values should be set. Again, there are several possibilities: Actual DAG file commands. Configuration macros. Command-line arguments to condor_submit_dag. (Getting things to work correctly with sub-DAGs may require a combination of these.) Note: This could be done with a combination of VARS and submit file changes, but I'm assuming that the reason for LIGO's request is to be able to set things overall for a workflow with much less user work that the VARS/submit file changes method would require.

As we are unlikely to universally adopt 8.4 series, it should be a development target for 8.5. 2015-Nov-25 16:00:14 by wenger: Gittrac #5107: Set DAGMan ClassAd attributes directly in DAG file will do at least part of this. (I'm not sure about propagating to node jobs.) 2015-Dec-16 10:48:12 by wenger: Maybe we can just add a flag to the #5107 changes that says "propagate this to all children". 2016-Jan-04 17:00:47 by wenger: Note: Because of changes in #5107 requested by Miron, that feature can no longer be used to set accounting_group, etc. 2016-Jan-04 17:07:59 by wenger: There are four main questions for how to do this: How to specify the accounting_group, etc., at the top level. How to pass this to node jobs. How to pass this to sub-DAGs. How to override this for lower levels if we want to do that. I need to check with LIGO about whether they'd rather do something like specify accounting_group, etc., in a config file or the DAG file itself, or on the condor_submit_dag command line. Passing this to node jobs is pretty simple: we can just use the -append flag to condor_submit. Passing it to sub-DAGs is more complicated, because we have to both actually pass the relevant values to the sub-DAG, and tell the sub-DAG to pass the values to lower-level jobs. Overriding accounting_group, etc., for lower levels (sub-DAGs, for example), clearly can't be done on the command line. 2016-Jan-12 11:34:28 by wenger: Also see #5444 -- these will both need similar infrastructure. 2016-Jan-12 12:29:08 by wenger: I'm thinking that part of the infrastructure for this might be adding something like a -deepappend flag to condor_submit_dag. title: Ticket #6837: Schedd leaks memory when flocking to a non-existent pool
description: MWT2 reports that one of their schedds is leaking .5Gb memory a day, and has been since at least May. Inspection of the logs reveals that the schedd is trying to flock to several pools, one of which doesn't exist anymore, and the other two have security settings which are blocking the RESCHEDULE command. It turns out that the dc_collector object supports non-blocking connects. When an update is send to a collector that is not yet connected, or whose connection is in flight, we queue up the ads to be sent to the collector. If the non-blocking connect then fails to connect for any reason, we delete the pending ad. If there are any more outstanding updates, we initiate one new non-blocking connect and send the next ad in the queue. The problem is that updates happen with a much faster frequency than the non-blocking connect timeout. So, if the non-blocking timeout is set to 20 seconds, we can frequently have several updates in the interim. Thus, this pending update queue can grow without bounds. For 8.8, we'll fix this by clearing the queue of pending updates. For 8.9, there's no reason to keep more than one update for the same command and instance of ad.

title: Ticket #7725: clean up API to wrap / unwrap for encryption
description: Clean up the API to wrap() and unwrap() in authentication.cpp, sock.cpp, reli_sock.cpp. Created a new type of object Condor_Crypto_State that holds all state for a given encrypted connection: a KeyInfo object, which contains: algorithm key length key data duration iv length iv data method_key_data_length and method_key_data - data for use by each specific algorithm. e.g. 3des stores expanded "key schedules" for quicker operation. num - message number Calls to wrap()=/=unwrap() only use this object to keep state and nothing else. The socket object now keeps a Condor_Crypto_State object which it passes to each call for encryption and decryption. While working on this ticket, I discovered that MUNGE, PASSWORD, and SSL authentication methods also instantiate a Condor_Crypto_3des object (type hard-coded) to use for exchanging key data during authentication. So they also now contain their own private Condor_Crypto_State object for their own internal use. This state is separate from the state object used for passing encrypted payloads over the socket post-authentication. The iv length and data are now dynamically sized (used to be hard-coded to be 8 bytes) so each method can use whatever it needs. For serialization/deserialization the IV, method_key_data, and message num are NOT included. If that is needed a new ticket should be created and linked here.
remarks: 2020-Jul-08 19:12:45 by tannenba: Not sure if the above ticket description quite captures our discussion.... My understanding (without having looked at the code in a long time) is the wrap() and unwrap() functions need some read-only information from the session object (such as algorithm, key), and needs to write some state information into the socket object (as state like IV needs to be kept per socket / tcp connection). So the thinking was the wrap/unwrap would take read-only ref to the session, and a read/write ref to what amounts to a "void *" state buffer to be kept in the socket object. The socket object does not need to understand or interpret this state buffer, it just needs to pass it into calls to wrap/unwrap. 2020-Jul-08 20:48:11 by bbockelm: Additional thoughts: We will need to move the wrap/unwrap API to work at the message level as opposed to the byte level, at least for ReliSock. Something will need to mutate the session state - for non-shared sessions, we'll want to keep a connection counter. This doesn't have to be the wrap / unwrap API, but the session state may not necessarily be a black box to the ReliSock. You'll want to have an additional authenticated buffer passed to wrap / unwrap in order to add protection against modification of the pre-encryption handshake and header. See the AES PR for an example.

title: Ticket #6564: Report recent metrics for custom machine resources (GPUs)
description: IceCube would also like to have what we've called "recent" metrics about GPUs, ideally broken down by device, available in the same places and ways (excepting the user log's summary) as the job metrics. Primarily, that in addition to the ClassAd-based recording we already do, we associate one of the exiting recency code's ring buffers which each reported attribute; each time we get a new value to push, we can "tick" the clock or not appropriately, and then insert into the ClassAd the resulting recent value (via the probe's Publish() method?). We will need to record the last tick time and first sample times on our own, however, it appears; and monitoring jobs should write zeroes when they start up so that we can establish the first interval. title: Ticket #294: Launching Condor from the command-line on Mac OS X Launchinproblematic
description: Launching the Condor daemons from the command-line can be problematic due to Mach bootstrap namespaces and security contexts. These are tied to the session under which the daemons are spawned. When the session ends, the daemons lose the ability to access some system services. Most notable of these is the DirectoryService, which handles lookups of user account information among other things. In NMI, we observed getpwnam() returning NULL for user accounts defined in OpenLDAP and calls to the DirectoryService command-line client returning the error eServerNotRunning. If possible, the Condor daemons should attempt to put themselves in the proper Mach bootstrap namespace and security context when they daemonize themselves. This article has information about pitfalls with running daemons on Mac OS X: http://developer.apple.com/technotes/tn2005/tn2083.html
remarks: 2009-Sep-18 13:37:31 by cstruble: A hack to work around this limitation on OS X 10.5 is to launch condor_master using the command launchctl bsexec PID condor_master as the root user, where PID is the process id of a process running in the global bootstrap namespace. I tried this with the PID of /usr/sbin/DirectoryService and Condor was able to run jobs and restart even after logging out. Before, Condor behaved incorrectly and couldn't restart when started from the command line.
creator: jfrey

title: Ticket #2874: Batlab meltdown due to Condor testsuite on Mac and BSD
description: On March 7, Scot Kronenfeld attempted to make the Condor testsuite run faster by having the test harness hard-kill all of the daemons after each test, rather than soft-killing the master and waiting for the daemons to exit. On macosx and freebsd, the kernel tables for processes and/or file descriptors filled up, causing Condor to fail and leaving lots of processes orphaned after Condor restarted. Here's the chain of events we believe led to this situation: Process tracking via environment variables is only supported on linux. So each time the test harness hard-killed all of the daemons associated with a test, they didn't have a chance to clean up their children. Metronome's Condor wasn't aware of these children, since the condor_master started by the test daemonizes itself and the environment tracking can't be used to connect it to the test job. The batlab has dedicated slot users. So normally, these orphaned processes would be cleaned up by the root Condor once Metronome exits. But there were enough orphaned processes (possibly from several slots) to fill up the kernel's internal tables. Suddenly, nothing could open any more files. The procd failed and the startd and some starters exited. The master survived and restarted the startd. But there were still many orphaned processes, since only the starter cleans up all processes owned by the dedicated slot user. We rebooted the machines to clear everything up and Scot reverted his change. Here are improvements that could be made to Condor to prevent this from happening: Change test suite to run condor_master in the foreground, so that parent-child process tracking of Metronome's Condor can find orphaned children of test suite's Condor. Add process tracking via the environment on macosx and freebsd. This may or may no be possible depending on the OS APIs. When using a dedicated slot user, the starter should kill all processes owned by that user before starting the job. When using a dedicated slot user, the startd could kill all processes owned by that user when cleaning up after the starter. In KillFamily::hardkill(), iterate between takesnapshot() and spree() to catch processes created while we're trying to kill their parents.

title: Ticket #2931: Reconfig can cause negotiation cycle failure
description: Reconfigs can take a long time and in some cases cause a disruption in communication that causes failure in the negotiation cycle. The previous code only blocked the group tree building parts of the cycle and not the daemoncore part. Blocking in the cycle has to be selective due to: // Service any interactive commands on our command socket. // This keeps condor_userprio hanging to a minimum when // we are involved in a lot of schedd negotiating. // It also performs the important function of draining out // any reschedule requests queued up on our command socket, so // we do not negotiate over & over unnecesarily.

NEG_SLEEP = 30 Spin up a pool, and follow the negotiator log with the following grep: $ tail -f NegotiatorLog | grep -e ' Cycle ' -e 'GRANTED.*RECONFIG' -e 'GRANTED.*GetPriority' -e 'begin sleep' -e 'end sleep' -e 'Delaying reconfig' -e 'NEGOTIATOR_INTERVAL =' 04/10/12 09:49:10 ---------- Started Negotiation Cycle ---------- 04/10/12 09:49:10 ---------- Finished Negotiation Cycle ---------- In a second window, submit a few jobs, like so: universe = vanilla cmd = /bin/sleep args = 30 should_transfer_files = if_needed when_to_transfer_output = on_exit +AccountingGroup = "none.user0000" queue 4 Watch the negotiator log, until you see the first sleep delay: $ tail -f NegotiatorLog | grep -e ' Cycle ' -e 'GRANTED.*RECONFIG' -e 'GRANTED.*GetPriority' -e 'begin sleep' -e 'end sleep' -e 'Delaying reconfig' -e 'NEGOTIATOR_INTERVAL =' 04/10/12 09:49:10 ---------- Started Negotiation Cycle ---------- 04/10/12 09:49:10 ---------- Finished Negotiation Cycle ---------- 04/10/12 09:49:15 ---------- Started Negotiation Cycle ---------- 04/10/12 09:49:15 begin sleep: 30 seconds Now submit the following reconfig + userprio sequence. You should now see the following in your two windows: $ tail -f NegotiatorLog | grep -e ' Cycle ' -e 'GRANTED.*RECONFIG' -e 'GRANTED.*GetPriority' -e 'begin sleep' -e 'end sleep' -e 'Delaying reconfig' -e 'NEGOTIATOR_INTERVAL =' 04/10/12 09:49:10 ---------- Started Negotiation Cycle ---------- 04/10/12 09:49:10 ---------- Finished Negotiation Cycle ---------- 04/10/12 09:49:15 ---------- Started Negotiation Cycle ---------- 04/10/12 09:49:15 begin sleep: 30 seconds 04/10/12 09:49:45 end sleep: 30 seconds 04/10/12 09:49:45 PERMISSION GRANTED to unauthenticated@unmapped from host 192.168.1.2 for command 60012 (DC_RECONFIG_FULL), access level WRITE: reason: WRITE authorization policy allows access by anyone 04/10/12 09:49:45 Delaying reconfig. 04/10/12 09:49:45 begin sleep: 30 seconds $ condor_reconfig -neg ; condor_userprio Sent "Reconfig" command to negotiator eje@localhost.localdomain Next, the second sleep completes, and then the userprio is serviced. title: Ticket #6421: Improve transfer_output_remaps syntax
description: While we were pondering syntaxes for multi-step jobs (see #6406), Christina noted that the grouping syntaxes would be a big improvement over the current syntax for transfer_output_remaps, which is a big long string with significant characters and their escapes. Viz: transfer_output_remaps = "results$(proc) = output/results$(proc); params$(proc) = output/param$(proc)" would be more-easily written on multiple lines. Mat noted that it would also be clearer to explicit indicate the direction of remapping, viz: transfer_output_remaps @= { results$(proc) -> output/results$(proc) param$(proc) -> output/param$(proc) } Since transfer_output_remaps already includes a custom parser, this shouldn't be horribly difficult to implement, and "ASCII arrow right" seems even less likely to show up in a filename than equals or semicolon. It would still have to have an escape, though. The custom parsing code could detect if the string had newlines and start by converting them into semicolons and then stripping leading and trailing whitespace. Additionally, since this would turn into the old-style representation (whatever it might be) in the job ad, it would have to be careful about escaping semicolons and equal signs appropriately (however that might be; the manual specifies how to do it in the submit file language). The initial implementation could use the existing here file syntax -- transfer_output_remaps @= END_REMAPS ... @END_REMAPS initially, so this ticket doesn't need to be assigned to TJ until we're sure it's worth adding syntactic sugar for this feature.
creator: tlmiller

title: Ticket #781: Shadow dies with SIGILL
description: Sometimes in large batches or all the time, the condor shadow blows up with an illegal instruction. And the schedd records this fact like this: 8/15 04:37:51 (pid:25772) Shadow pid 5142 died with signal 4 (Illegal instruction) It could be the compiler is generating instructions that don't work across all 64-bit intel processors (both AMD64 and EM64T), but that is a guess. See ticket for more information.
remarks: 2009-Oct-09 16:03:07 by psilord: Ligo has stated this ticket is not urgent. It had only happened in a single block of time on a submit machine that before and after the event ran just fine. The machine uses ECC memory which hadn't caught a bit correction in the last two weeks. So bad stick of ram is unlikely. What is more likely is a particular user or set of jobs caused the shadow to take a weird code path leading to the SIGILL. The logs are available in the associated rust ticket and they need datamining to figure out the common condition of the faulting shadows. For example, were they all from the same user or cluster?

title: Ticket #6071: Change default thread count in cream_gahp
description: Some of our users have experienced problems when there's a large difference between the number of requests the gridmanager will issue to the cream_gahp (GRIDMANAGER_MAX_PENDING_REQUESTS, default 50) and the number of requests the cream_gahp can execute in parallel (CREAM_GAHP_WORKER_THREADS, default 6). This problem is worst when some of the requests take a long time to complete. When the gridmanager's timeout for a request is reached, the gridmanager will discard it and issue a new request in its place. But the cream_gahp will still execute the timed-out request as well as the new one. Thus, the cream_gahp may have a backlog of requests much larger than GRIDMANAGER_MAX_PENDING_REQUESTS queued up internally, with the gridmanager's timeout ticking away before the cream_gahp has started processing them. Setting these config params to the same value by default will help avoid this backlog from building. Better yet, the cream_gahp can start rejecting new requests if it has too many queued already. We do this already for the blahp (#5253).
remarks: 2017-Apr-15 08:51:01 by tim: CODE REVIEW: Nice change 2017-Apr-20 10:29:35 by tim: DOC REVIEW: OK

title: Ticket #6972: Add x509 proxy support with late materialized jobs
description: Late materialization doesn't work with jobs requiring x509 proxies at present. Some details: According to the logs, the factory fails with: Reason = "failed to create ClassAd for Job 1532.0 : Submit:-1:unable to read proxy file. Changing proxy permissions to 666 bypasses that issue, but all x509 related classads that are automatically filled on the client-side are not created (x509UserProxyFirstFQAN, x509userproxysubject, etc) and defining them by hand via e.g.: +x509userproxysubject doesn't work. According to TJ, the code that fills these classads in the Schedd is skipped for late materialization at the moment.
remarks: 2019-Mar-29 20:23:30 by bbockelm: Keny, what happens when you fill in +x509userproxysubject by hand? 2019-Mar-29 22:41:20 by khurtado: Hi Brian, Attempts to set +x509userproxysubject by hand are ignored, as opposed to random variables. In other words, +A = value set the classad as expected, but requests for appending +x509userproxysubject (or any of+x509UserProxyEmail, +x509UserProxyFirstFQAN, +x509UserProxyVOName, +x509UserProxyFQAN ) are simply ignored. Considering a minimal modification to the string like +x509userproxysubject2 does work, I assume there is some sort of protection mechanism in condor against those classads, (probably due to the issues allowing setting or editing x509userproxysubject would imply in terms of security while mapping grid jobs to users based on the subject?) 2019-Apr-01 09:59:16 by johnkn: x509userproxysubject is a secure attribute and cannot be set by the job. Only the Schedd can set it. The Schedd does not do this for late materialization jobs at present. The current code in the Schedd skips setting the proxy subject, and other proxy attributes when there is no external socket during commit, and it will not set these attributes into the cluster classad. Late materialization has no external connection when materializing the proc ads - so the x509 proxy code in the Schedd gets skipped. 2019-Apr-04 04:52:15 by bbockelm: We control the schedd configuration, correct? We should be able to set: SYSTEM_SECURE_JOB_ATTRS= and continue the testing. 2019-Apr-04 08:45:03 by khurtado: Hi Brian, Thanks! I didn't know that knob. So, if I set: use_x509userproxy = False SYSTEM_SECURE_JOB_ATTRS = in the schedd and pass the proxy with: +x509userproxy = /tmp/x509up_u... instead of x509userproxy = /tmp/x509up_u... so that the factory doesn't attempt to read the proxy file but just passes the classad (plus all the other x509 classads (+x509userproxysubject, +x509UserProxyVOName, +x509UserProxyFirstFQAN, etc)), then things work fine even without doing chmod 666 or 644 to the proxy anymore. I will go with that workaround until the relevant changes are eventually implemented in condor. Thanks for the help! 2019-Apr-12 13:43:06 by jfrey: I've pushed code to fix this in 8.9. 2019-Apr-14 13:52:07 by khurtado: Awesome! Thanks! Just to have an idea of when this will be included in a dev release, will this be eventually on v8.9.1 or v8.9.2? 2019-Apr-15 11:47:56 by jfrey: The changes will be in v8.9.2.

Ticket #7660: Python ExprTrees should be able to parenthesize themselves
description: classad.ExprTree should have a method that returns the same expression, but wrapped in parentheses. This would be helpful when building up complex expressions. In particular, the fact that these give the same result is a problem: >>> x = classad.ExprTree("x == 1") >>> y = classad.ExprTree("y == 2") >>> z = classad.ExprTree("z == 3") >>> (x & y) | z x == 1 & y == 2 | z == 3 >>> x & (y | z) x == 1 & y == 2 | z == 3 We can't fix that, but we can do (x & y).parenthesize() | z. I don't have any strong opinions on the name of the method. parenthesize is accurate but long and hard to type. Maybe wrap or group?
remarks: 2020-May-22 10:40:00 by tlmiller: I think the actual problem is with the operators used here. Python will evaluate (x & y) | z in the correct order -- calling __and__ followed by __or__. Both functions need to parenthesize their arguments: x & y -> (x) & (y) w | z -> (w) | (z) ------------------ (x & y) | z -> ((x) & (y)) | (z) An obvious optimization would be to not parenthesize 'simple' ExprTrees. 2020-May-22 10:50:44 by tlmiller: Actually, thinking about the C++ implementation, I realized it would be harder to implement this wrong behavior than the correct one. So I tried: >>> w = (x & y) | z >>> w.eval() 10 >>> q = x & (y | z) >>> q.eval() 2 which sure makes it look like the issue is just one of converting ExprTrees to strings. (Either we don't parenthesize subexpressions, or we do but have a bug in optimizing the extra ones away.)
creator: karpel

title: Ticket #1167: GSI leaks memory
description: We have several pieces of evidence that GSI authentication leaks memory. I found one leak that goes back to at least 7.1.4, probably earlier. There is another leak in the new VOMS stuff, first released in 7.3.2. Evidence: I took a look at one of the glidein 7.4.1 sub-collectors at UCSD. By analyzing strings in the core file, it is pretty obvious that there is a memory leak related to GSI or VOMS. There are less than a hundred security sessions and ads in the collector, but the count of how many times the same string appears in the core file comes up with some fairly big numbers: 14427 lcg-voms.cern.ch0 15590 DOEGrids 15593 DOEGrids1 0 15849 computers1 16020 cern1 17004 proxy 23306 ESnet 23568 ESnet1 0 23605 net1 24614 ]MH/ 25517 doegrids 25524 Services 27071 DOEGrids CA 1 34215 Services1+0) 34325 doegrids1 38820 Certificate Authorities 39241 Certificate Authorities1 40049 ESnet Root CA 1 51072 org1 A google heap profiler dump from a 7.4.1 condor_collector from glideinWMS in Nebraska showed that 60% of all memory was allocated in CRYPTO_malloc. Unfortunately, the lack of stack frames made it impossible to see where that was being called from. Running GSI-authenticated condor_q under valgrind shows a leak going back to at least 7.1.4, probably earlier. The leak is in Condor_Auth_X509::get_server_info(), which does not free memory allocated in a couple globus calls that it makes: definitely lost: 616 bytes in 7 blocks indirectly lost: 2,054 bytes in 100 blocks On a platform that supports VOMS (linux), I found another leak reported by valgrind when I run condor_q: ==3765== 16,736 (552 direct, 16,184 indirect) bytes in 6 blocks are definitely lost in loss record 116 of 122 ==3765== at 0x40213C0: malloc (vg_replace_malloc.c:149) ==3765== by 0x82D29DD: default_malloc_ex (in /scratch/dan/condor/peep/src/condor_q.V6/condor_q) ==3765== by 0x82D305E: CRYPTO_malloc (in /scratch/dan/condor/peep/src/condor_q.V6/condor_q) ==3765== by 0x830D046: asn1_item_ex_combine_new (in /scratch/dan/condor/peep/src/condor_q.V6/condor_q) ==3765== by 0x830FC5D: ASN1_item_ex_d2i (in /scratch/dan/condor/peep/src/condor_q.V6/condor_q) ==3765== by 0x8310400: ASN1_item_d2i (in /scratch/dan/condor/peep/src/condor_q.V6/condor_q) ==3765== by 0x8304A14: ASN1_item_dup (in /scratch/dan/condor/peep/src/condor_q.V6/condor_q) ==3765== by 0x8307BD6: X509_dup (in /scratch/dan/condor/peep/src/condor_q.V6/condor_q) ==3765== by 0x8280FF0: globus_gsi_cred_get_cert_chain (globus_gsi_cred_handle.c:996) ==3765== by 0x815DC09: extract_VOMS_info (globus_utils.c:313) ==3765== by 0x81FA039: Condor_Auth_X509::authenticate_client_gss(CondorError*) (condor_auth_x509.cpp:742) ==3765== by 0x81FAA06: Condor_Auth_X509::authenticate(char const*, CondorError*) (condor_auth_x509.cpp:159) ==3765== ==3765== LEAK SUMMARY: ==3765== definitely lost: 552 bytes in 6 blocks. ==3765== indirectly lost: 16,184 bytes in 690 blocks. I have confirmed that the daemon-side of the connection has the same leak. This leak goes away if I set USE_VOMS_ATTRIBUTES = False. The globus function globus_gsi_cred_get_cert_chain appears to be the cause of the leak, even though we are calling sk_x509_free on the allocated object. I found that calling sk_x509_pop_free() instead of sk_x509_free() solves the leak. This is consistent with other uses of globus_gsi_cred_get_cert_chain() in condor code.

title: Ticket #4735: Speed up V3 query protocol
description: When watching condor_q V3 queries go through a busy CMS schedd (10k running jobs, 20k in queue), I observed most of the wait time was due to #4594. [Basically, DC's driver isn't called enough to iterate through the entire queue before timeout.] I see two other things we can do: During "busy spikes", anecdotally, we returned to DC about once a second. While #4594 appears to speed up the V3 protocol for very selective queries, performance still suffers on large query results (as we're using the TCP buffer of usually 128KB, we return at most 128KB / second in this case). Proposal: We should use a fork worker to respond to the query from a child process. We only respond in-process if we are out of workers. This should be a nice balance of performance and memory usage - giving the admins something they can tune. (Outright bug) After any pipe or socket is serviced, DaemonCore will re-invoke select on further sockets to see if they are still ready to read (comment says this is done in case if a prior handler drained this socket and the current handler is blocking). Obviously, checking a write socket to see if there's a read ready will return false. Hence, on a busy schedd, it may be very difficult to ever get DC to respond past the first set of ads. Proposal: Only perform this re-check if the socket is registered read-only.
