title: Ticket #3859: RFE: support user group and netgroup in ALLOW_* and QUEUE_SUPER_USER
description: Specific use case for user lists would be for maintaining QUEUE_SUPER_USERS. ALLOW_* expressions should be able to use netgroups when referring to machines or people also. My working concept for this rfe: suppose you have this entry in /etc/group: que_su:x:1000:eje,dryan,mkudlej QUEUE_SUPER_USERS = %que_su then users eje, dryan and mkudlej would be allowed as queue super users, by virtue of checking group membership using the output of the standard C getgrnam() library function. Another example: ALLOW_ADMINISTRATOR = +admin_hosts Would allow any authenticated canonical user user@domain/host from the /etc/netgroup list 'admin_hosts' matching tuple (host,user,domain) (netgroup lookup using innetgr() library function) note, in a netgroup triple (host,user,domain) any or all of the three can be empty, signifying wildcard behavior. For example, the tuple (,eje,) would match user 'eje' for any host and any uid-domain. The plan for domains is to use condor's concept of uid-domain. This is condor-specific behavior, but the strings listed in a netgroup definition are arbitrary, and so there's no barrier to adopting a condor-specific convention.
remarks: 2013-Aug-19 12:41:25 by tannenba: You definitely need a design doc for this. Some questions to consider for your design (these questions and similar ones should be discussed in the design doc): Unlike QUEUE_SUPER_USER, the ALLOW_* settings do not take a list of local login names. They take a list of authorization principals that can include hostnames, subnets, and mapped user identities. When do these get expanded? Only on a condor_reconfig? Or if I change /etc/groups will that automatically change HTCondor's authorization without issuing a reconfig? If the latter, why, and how will it remain scalable? At what level of the code will this expansion happen - the config macro subsystem level, the authorization level, ??? What are the pros and cons to the different approaches, which do you recommend, and why? Thinking a bit about my own question above: Should this be in the low-level HTCondor libraries at all? Couldn't it be a tool that reads a condor_config and rewrites out the "expanded with group info" configs? Why should every daemon and tool (and shadow instance) carry around group expansion code, dependencies on netgroup code, etc, when the only time it is needed is when writing a config file? Could the tool look for group names to expand, read in the local logins associated with that group, run them through the condor mapping process to come up with mapped htcondor principals, and then rewrite out the ALLOW_* knobs? How about groups on Windows (e.g. don't group identifiers have a domain and group name etc)? While we may choose to not implement all features on all platforms, we should at least understand that the design is such that we can choose to implement it at a later date without changing the user interface. 2013-Aug-19 12:44:28 by tannenba: Added Zach to Notification list of this ticket as the changes involve security. Until such time as the design doc is written (in google docs, following the outline etc) and approved, please keep any implementation code on a topic branch. Gracias! 2013-Aug-19 16:57:03 by eje: My interpretation is that group and netgroup lookup happens on the fly, so it is the version where changing group or netgroup files alters htcondor's authorization without a reconfig. The potential drawback is increased cost of lookups. The advantage is that it provides more than just syntactic sugar for existing config. That is, if it was only expanded at config time, it behaves as just a shorthand for the already-existing functionality, although the shorthand would be more useful than nothing. A possible optimization would be to check the traditional-style entries on the list first, although I usually consider optimizations as best addressed on future refinement tickets, based on customer feedback. 2013-Aug-20 13:57:54 by eje: Another comment on expansion: netgroups can themselves be defined in terms of various wildcards, and other netgroups. So (1) pre-expanding a netgroup into some kind of extensional set of 'concrete' hosts/ips is not a well defined process: at best it could be done via generate-and-test, and (2) if you actually could accomplish (1), the size of the resulting list could easily be prohibitively large. Rather like attempting to pre-expand '*/*' in the existing htcondor security syntax. 2013-Aug-21 11:04:42 by tannenba: Going out and doing a netgroup lookup on every command across thousands of machines is a non-option in my mind. In HTCondor we have even had to cache results for supplemental groups, and also cache results for wildcard results in AUTHORIZE lists - this was not done as a refinement, it was done out of necessity to stop melting down NIS, OpenLDAP, etc at customer sites. 2013-Aug-22 10:05:00 by eje: The netgroup lookup is also governed by the caching and SEC_<access-level>_SESSION_DURATION machinery. 2013-Aug-27 00:02:00 by eje: DESIGN DOC: https://docs.google.com/document/d/10KEa1UIpAheCVYRZy7teTRF6qLe743LZ4EcLAoaqa8c/edit 2013-Aug-28 22:18:44 by eje: TESTING - netgroups on ALLOW_* and DENY_* To test netgroups, you need to have ypserv, ypbind and rpcbind installed and running on sandbox. I set my nis network to local: 127.0.0.1 Configure /etc/netgroup like so: $ cat /etc/netgroup test1 (localhost,eje,) test2 (localhost,test_user_1,) # (don't forget to issue 'make' in /var/yp) The test configuration is: ALL_DEBUG = $(ALL_DEBUG) | D_SECURITY # keeps everything local NETWORK_INTERFACE = lo SEC_DEFAULT_AUTHENTICATION_METHODS = CLAIMTOBE SEC_DEFAULT_AUTHENTICATION = REQUIRED # enable 'everything' for exactly the members of test1 and test2 netgroups ALLOW_ADMINISTRATOR = +test1, +test2 ALLOW_OWNER = $(ALLOW_ADMINISTRATOR) ALLOW_DAEMON = $(ALLOW_ADMINISTRATOR) ALLOW_NEGOTIATOR = $(ALLOW_ADMINISTRATOR) ALLOW_WRITE = $(ALLOW_ADMINISTRATOR) ALLOW_READ = $(ALLOW_ADMINISTRATOR) # if this is enabled, it overrides +test2 on allow #DENY_READ = +test2 # this has the 'default' mapfile expressions CERTIFICATE_MAPFILE = $(CONDOR_HOME)/certificate_mapfile.txt To test 'allow' for +test1 and +test2, spin up the pool and issue a condor_status command as yourself. You should see the command succeed by matching test1, and in the CollectorLog you should see a message like this: IPVERIFY: matched canonical user eje@uid_domain/localhost to netgroup test1 on allow list if you issue condor_status logged in as test_user_1, then it should also succeed by matching netgroup test2: IPVERIFY: matched canonical user test_user_1@uid_domain/localhost to netgroup test2 on allow list Now, if you also place +test2 on DENY_READ: DENY_READ = +test2 If you issue a condor_status as test_user_1 now, the command should fail, as DENY_* overrides ALLOW_*. 2013-Aug-28 22:35:58 by eje: TESTING - user groups on QUEUE_SUPER_USERS I tested by adding a user (test_user_1) to 'my' group: $ cat /etc/group eje:x:1000:test_user_1 Then add user group 'eje' to QUEUE_SUPER_USERS QUEUE_SUPER_USERS = %eje I tested by submitting a job as myself (eje), and then attempting to remove the job logged in as test_user_1. You should be able to remove the job because test_user_1 is a queue super user by virtue of being on user group 'eje' 2013-Aug-30 16:33:01 by eje: Notes on setting up NIS and netgroups Currently netgroups are only served via NIS (there is no file-based back end option, like user groups). So you have to set up an nis server to exercise the netgroup feature. I adapted the following from: http://www.server-world.info/en/note?os=Fedora_16&p=nis http://www.yolinux.com/TUTORIALS/NIS.html These were what I had to do on F18. Note, selinux may also need to be disabled. # Install rpcbind, ypbind, ypserv, ypcat $ yum install ypserv ypbind yp-tools rpcbind # configuring a local ypserv # add these lines to /etc/sysconfig/network NETWORKING=yes GATEWAY=127.0.0.1 NISDOMAIN=localdomain # configure ypbind # put this line in /etc/yp.conf: ypserver localhost # create a file /etc/netgroup (was not created by default) $ cat /etc/netgroup test1 (localhost,eje,) test2 (localhost,test_user_1,) # point netgroups at NIS, which is currently only working option # add this line to /etc/nsswitch.conf netgroup: nis # edit /var/yp/Makefile so 'netgrp' dep is present on "all:" target all: passwd group hosts rpc services netid protocols mail netgrp # start up rpcbind (note, this is 'portmap' daemon on some sytems) $ systemctl enable rpcbind.service # start up ypserv $ systemctl enable ypserv.service # initialize ypserv databases # /usr/lib64/yp/ypinit -m $ cd /var/yp; make # start up ypbind $ systemctl enable ypbind.service # at this point you should be able to dump yp databases: $ ypcat -k netgroup test1 (localhost,eje,) test2 (localhost,test_user_1,) # Whenever you edit /etc/netgroup, you should remake: $ cd /var/yp; make 2013-Sep-16 16:04:56 by eje: Design doc allegedly passed review, so I am going to flip this to code review. title: Ticket #7549: Negotiator prefetch breaks flocking
description: CHTC reports that the number of flocking out jobs has almost completely gone to zero. Investigation shows that with negotiator rrl prefetch on, (now the default), the negotiator sends an END NEGOTIATE command after the prefetch, as well as after the negotiation proper. When the schedd gets each one, it recalculates the flock level. After an END NEGOTIATE after prefetch, no jobs have been matched, and none have been sent. The schedd treats this as if the user has been completely satisfied, and then lowers the flock level. As a result, the flock level is frequently knocked back to zero, and no jobs flock out. To fix this, we will notice when the end of negotiation message really means end off rll fetch, and ignore the rest of the end of negotiation processing. This should also remove some load from the schedd.
remarks: 2020-Mar-11 13:32:54 by jfrey: Code Review m_num_resource_reqs_sent is the wrong trigger for this early out in scheduler_handleNegotiationFinished(). The negotiator can and will ask for more resource requests during the main negotiation conversation. The correct trigger is if getNumJobsMatched() and getNumJobsRejected() both return 0. That indicates that the negotiator hasn't sent any results, which should be true if and only if it's in prefetch. 2020-Apr-10 07:46:37 by tim: Bulk change of target version from v080906 to v080907 using ticket-target-mover. 2020-Sep-17 11:13:11 by jfrey: This code was back-ported to 8.8.10 (#7754).

title: Ticket #1921: JobUniverse is required attribute for fetch work hook
description: From Derek Weitzel: I was setting up job hooks for a startd today, and noticed a bug. Either the documentation is incorrect, or the startd. When first trying with the minimum required classad specified in: http://www.cs.wisc.edu/condor/manual/v7.4/4_3Computing_On.html#sec:cod-application-attributes with only Cmd and Owner, the job was always rejected. But when we added JobUniverse = 5, it was accepted. I believe this has to do with the default START statement. The default start statement is: Requirements = (START) && (IsValidCheckpointPlatform) Where IsValidCheckpointPlatform checks the universe of the job. Therefore, the required entries for a hook job are: Cmd Owner JobUniverse

title: Ticket #5962: Scale Testing the Grid Universe (with Clouds)
description: The grid universe consists of three pieces: the schedd, the grid manager, and the GAHP. When doing scale testing, we generally ignore GRIDMANAGER_SELECTION_EXPRESSION, and just test one user submitting jobs to one schedd, which starts one grid manager, which starts one GAHP. If a specific desired scale is required, it still desirable to determine the scaling limits (and performance curve, if possible) of a single GAHP, so we can predict how many a given scale will require. We generally do scale testing with sleep jobs. (It will be convenient for the duration of the sleep to be in the job arguments.) This eliminates a lot of awkwardness when getting starting; it also allows us to easily control job duration, which can help isolate different parts of the system for testing. It also minimizes (or, with a little cleverness, entirely eliminates) file transfer. Although file transfer may be a bottleneck in production, especially when testing across a WAN, for scale testing we assume that file transfer is a solved problem. At sufficiently large scale (more than 100,000 jobs?), the schedd itself may becomes a bottleneck. This largely depends on how frequently new jobs enter the queue, and how frequently old jobs leave the queue. The longer the sleep job, the lower both of these rates need to be obtain a particular scale. If you're testing using the grid universe for provisioning.... BEFORE YOU START You're really going to want some way to know if the weird state(s) reported by the job queue are real or a problem brought on by HTCondor getting overloaded. You're going to want a second source of information about your jobs on the target system, if at all possible. When you check to make sure things are working, you should also check with the second source of information. Note that the information in HTCondor's job queue could be several minutes old. The steady state of a job should usually be R(unnning). An I(dle) job may be in the process of starting up, but shouldn't stay that way for very long. (Many jobs staying idle for a long time may be a sign that the schedd is overloaded.) A job on H(old) indicates a problem. The occasional job may go on hold because of transient problems, but a lot of them going on hold may indicate a more serious (scaling) problem. INITIAL TESTING The first thing to test is a single, short, and basic sleep job, just to confirm that the whole cycle works with your testing set-up. SCALE-OUT TESTING For scale-out testing, set the duration of the sleep job to longer than you care to test for. We'll test the ability of the system to deal with job termination later. In this phase of testing, we're seeing how fast the system can start jobs, as well as how many simultaneous jobs it can handle. HTCondor's internal time-outs are fairly generous, but the schedd can't do anything else while a group of jobs is being submitted, so your queue statements should stay relatively small if you're doing provisioning with the grid universe jobs. (The negotiator assigns resources to the schedd, but the schedd claims those resources from the startds running on them.) Try submitting a 'queue 10' and making sure it works, then a 'queue 100', and then a 'queue 1000'; you may need to examine the GAHP or grid manager logs to determine if the GAHP is tripping on any rate-limiting (and if so, if it's responding properly). You can use DAGMan to manage job submission speed, instead, if you prefer, but 1000 sounds like a nice number of jobs for which to time the job start delay. Also, you can push on the rate-limiting code by submitting multiple large batches of jobs; just be sure to give the schedd "enough" time to work between batches. Generally, you don't need to let the system sit for more than about twenty minutes at whatever the desired size is to get a good idea of how it will hold up in the steady state over a longer period of time; I believe all of our timers / leases are shorter than that. UNSTEADY STATES Try removing jobs in small and then larger batches (keep an eye on how long each removal takes, for the same reason you did while submitting). Some grid universe jobs may take a considerable amount of time to remove (for instances: some services require that we poll the state of a job that's existing until it actually does, because they can go into a partially-exited error state; we therefore may have to wait a long time, considering the polling interval, for that job to exit). From a steady state, kill -9 the gahp; the gridmanager should shut itself it down and then be restarted by the schedd. Verify that the before and after states are the same, and remain so after the grid manager has exited recovery (check its log). This could take a while. Repeat this exercise -- although it should have exactly the same result -- for the grid manager itself. If both of those exercises result in an appropriate steady-state, kill -9 the schedd; the master will restart it, and all state should be recovered. DYNAMIC STATES Remove a large batch of jobs and replace it (by submitting again) with a batch of short-duration jobs. Make sure the system behaves while you're doing this. Once you've replaced all the long-duration jobs with short-duration jobs, the number of running jobs should start decrease naturally on its own. As it does, feed new short-duration jobs in to replace the lost ones. This better-represents the steady state of a busy pool. SCALE-IN TESTING Scale-out testing, but with condor_rm instead of condor_submit. PROVISIONING If you're using the grid universe to do provisioning, the concerns about schedd busy-ness become greater, since each job is adding a core (or more) for the schedd to claim. Also, you're probably concerned with making those jobs' VMs run a startd and report to a central manager. To address the first issue, you could -- and many sites do for other reasons -- run the provisioning jobs in one schedd and the sleep/test jobs out of another (most easily done on a different machine). The schedd (on a beefy enough machine with good networking) handle 100,000 jobs without too much trouble, so unless you're doing fairly large-scale testing, one will be enough. When you check the state of the HTCondor system, then, you'll also need to run condor_status. See https://htcondor-wiki.cs.wisc.edu/index.cgi/wiki?p=ChtcScaleTestSetup for wisdom on setting pools for large-scale testing. (The example happens to have used a lot of EC2 nodes to generate the scale, but the HTCondor configuration of the on-premises is independent of that.)

title: Ticket #693: rpmbuild mangling Globus jar files
description: On rhel5, when rpmbuild builds the rpms for the Condor release, it repacks all of the jar files. It does so in such a way that the gt4 gahp fails on startup in some situations. Earlier versions of Red Hat don't do this repacking. In later releases of Fedora Core, the jar repacking can be disabled by adding this macro to the rpm .spec file: %define __jar_repack %{nil} To disable the jar repacking on rhel5, the best solution I've found is to redefine the __os_install_post macro. The definition varies by platform, so we'd need to be explicit about where we redefine it. It's a hack, but it works. We would add the following to the .spec file when building on rhel5: %define __os_install_post \ /usr/lib/rpm/redhat/brp-compress ; \ %{!?__debug_package:/usr/lib/rpm/redhat/brp-strip %{__strip}} ; \ /usr/lib/rpm/redhat/brp-strip-static-archive %{__strip} ; \ /usr/lib/rpm/redhat/brp-strip-comment-note %{__strip} %{__objdump} ; \ /usr/lib/rpm/brp-python-bytecompile ; \ %{nil}
remarks: 2009-Aug-27 11:27:54 by willb: Try the following, which should work on RHEL. %global __jar_repack %{nil} 2009-Aug-27 14:49:46 by jfrey: The %global line didn't prevent the jar repacking. Using rpm --showrc on my RHEL 5 machine to see the value of __os_install_post, I see that brp-java-repack-jars is run unconditionally. On a Fedora Core 9 machine, the execution of brp-java-repack-jars is conditional on __jar_repack. 2009-Sep-01 15:27:24 by jfrey: I met with Will Benton today about this problem. Here is a summary of what we discovered: The version of rpm and redhat-rpm-config installed on the NMI x86-64 rhel 5 machine (nmi-0251) is almost 3 years old. Will thinks the jar repacking may be better in more recent versions, which are available for rhel 5. I will build rpm packages on a CSL x86-64 rhel 5 machine with the updated rpm packages and see if the resulting jars suffer the same problem as those produced in NMI. Interesting observation: jar tvf produces a different listing for the repacked jars. Original jar contents: 0 Thu Oct 14 17:57:34 CDT 2004 META-INF/ 106 Thu Oct 14 17:57:32 CDT 2004 META-INF/MANIFEST.MF 0 Thu Oct 14 17:57:30 CDT 2004 org/ 0 Thu Oct 14 17:57:34 CDT 2004 org/apache/ 0 Thu Oct 14 17:57:34 CDT 2004 org/apache/naming/ 0 Thu Oct 14 17:57:32 CDT 2004 org/apache/naming/java/ 1253 Thu Oct 14 17:57:30 CDT 2004 org/apache/naming/java/javaURLContextFactory.class 105 Thu Oct 14 17:57:32 CDT 2004 org/apache/naming/java/package.html 104 Thu Oct 14 17:57:32 CDT 2004 META-INF/INDEX.LIST Repacked jar contents: 104 Tue Jan 01 00:00:00 CST 1980 META-INF/INDEX.LIST 106 Tue Jan 01 00:00:00 CST 1980 META-INF/MANIFEST.MF 1253 Tue Jan 01 00:00:00 CST 1980 org/apache/naming/java/javaURLContextFactory.class 105 Tue Jan 01 00:00:00 CST 1980 org/apache/naming/java/package.html 2009-Sep-01 17:01:27 by jfrey: I built Condor 7.3.2 rpms on chevre.cs.wisc.edu, an x86-64 rhel 5 machine with newer rpm packages than the NMI build machine. title: Ticket #6499: Add multiple file transfer support to curl_plugin
description: Right now the curl_plugin can only transfer a single file at a time, which wastes TCP connections and context switches, among other things. Update the plugin to accept multiple files as input, then transfer them all at once. Instead of declaring the URLs to transfer on the command line, read them in via stdin using nested classad format. Similarly, we'll have to update the statistics output to send data for multiple files. Design document: https://docs.google.com/document/d/12v2FjSEJIkX0wxnuIBXlpsLOQwpaxxj0TZUxKBWJZ9g
remarks: 2017-Dec-07 16:43:31 by zmiller: Just to be clear, it's not just a matter of updating the plugin only, but also the file transfer object itself. In short: If the plugin advertises that it supports the new API (when invoked with the -classad flag), then the file transfer object needs to group all input files of one type together, cons up the nested classad describing what transfers to do, and supply that as the stdin to the plugin. And, as you already mentioned, if the plugin supports the new API, the code that processes the output will also need to be updated. 2018-Mar-02 06:57:16 by tannenba: Please add the URL to the design document for this ticket to ticket description. 2018-Aug-08 16:54:36 by coatsworth: I've finally added tests for this, so I'm going to mark the ticket as resolved. I suspect once it starts getting used in the real world we'll need to do more work on it, but for now it's working as described in the design doc.

title: Ticket #3361: MPI Parallel Universe jobs fail when USE_NFS=True
description: When running an OpenMPI job with USE_NFS=True, the job never runs and we have a shadow exception. 007 (030.000.000) 12/04 17:48:10 Shadow exception! Error from slot11@beaver.cs.wisc.edu: File /scratch/samf/personal-condor/spool/30/0/cluster30.proc0.subproc0/contact maps to url local:/scratch/samf/personal-condor/spool/30/0/cluster30.proc0.subproc0/contact, which I don't know how to open. ToddT described a workaround and Alan helped Sam get the workaround working: no_nfs.sh #!/bin/sh export _CONDOR_USE_NFS=False shadow_location=`condor_config_val real_shadow` exec $shadow_location $* where we have in condor_config.local REAL_SHADOW = $(SBIN)/condor_shadow SHADOW = $(SBIN)/no_nfs.sh and have placed no_nfs.sh in $(SBIN). The file pseudo_ops.cpp appears to be the culprit. The one in condor_shadow.V6.1 needs to be changed as a lot of is too similar to the one in condor_shadow.std.
remarks: 2012-Dec-07 11:21:42 by tannenba: The problem is a protocol mismatch: the remote I/O client in the vanilla starter does not understand all the potential file mappings that the remote I/O server in the shadow may return. Behold from /src/condor_starter.V6.1/io_proxy_handler.cpp : result = REMOTE_CONDOR_get_file_info_new(path,url); if(result==0) { dprintf(D_SYSCALLS,"Directed to use url %s\n",url); ASSERT( strlen(url) < CHIRP_LINE_MAX ); if(!strncmp(url,"remote:",7)) { strncpy(path,url+7,CHIRP_LINE_MAX); } else if(!strncmp(url,"buffer:remote:",14)) { strncpy(path,url+14,CHIRP_LINE_MAX); } else { EXCEPT("File %s maps to url %s, which I don't know how to open.\n",path,url); } So if USE_NFS=True, the remote I/O server in the shadow will return a mapping URL that starts with local:, and the remote I/O client in the starter only understands remote: and buffer:remote. Plan for stable series fix: in the vanilla shadow, insert USE_NFS=False and USE_AFS=False into the param table on shadow startup and after a reconfig. Given that the only remote I/O client in the world known to exist is the one in the starter, this seems like a safe/acceptable solution for the stable series. Plan for developer series fix: For the development branch moving forward, we should either teach the remote I/O client how to handle all the possible server responses such as local:, or rip out the possibility for local: responses from the server. 2012-Dec-14 09:42:38 by tstclair: This commit breaks compat in the stable series, && we depend. 2012-Dec-14 11:07:45 by tannenba: Tim, re the above, how do you "depend" ? Is my statement above about how the new starter is the only known remote I/O client incorrect, i.e. did you guys write your own remote i/o client? 2012-Dec-19 09:30:47 by johnkn: Bulk change of target version from v070807 to v070808 using ./ticket-target-mover. 2012-Dec-26 16:57:25 by samf: We tried using set_runtime_config in baseshadow.cpp:config(). We want to use param_insert instead as set_runtime_config sets values and waits for them to be read into the parameter hash table when the user runs condor_reconfig. param_insert does indeed work when setting param_insert("USE_NFS","False");

title: Ticket #369: anacron-like behavior in crondor (Intelligent windows with priorities)
description: This is a complex, unfinished idea based on a discussion Todd Miller and I had. I think there are good ideas in here, but it's a bit of a jumble, sorry. It will need to be made more concrete and probably broken into smaller pieces. Goals: Provide anacron-like behavior: "I don't care when you run this, but run it once per day/week/month" Mix this with other Condor policy, so I can avoid particular times of day. Use cases: A big submit machine (NMI) has a bunch of users with cron or crondor jobs that submit nightly builds. Everyone wants to run them "after hours", but early enough that the jobs will be done by the time they get into work. So everyone just picks an arbitrary time. 12:30 AM is popular for some reason. Jobs end up unnecessarily crushing the machine. It seems like Condor should have the ability to be more clever. A user might say "Start somewhere between 11:00 PM and 4:00 AM". Currently you could say "Start at 11:00 PM, and give up if 4:00 AM rolls around," but that's not quite equivalent. In practice if 100 jobs all are willing to start at 11:00 PM, the schedd will merrily start them (we're talking local universe here) all at the same time, crushing the poor machine for a bit. Limits on simultaneous running jobs will space them out, but the order will just be FIFO. Something more clever could be done, ideally in a way that is easy for the administrator and trivial or transparent for the users. You could use Requirements to not start if the load is too high, but there really isn't a ranking mechanism for local jobs so that jobs getting near the end of their window get to jump in front of the line.
remarks: 2009-Apr-08 15:40:37 by tlmiller: So for our particular use case, what we'd be doing is running a job (nmi_submit) in the local (or scheduler) universe that turns around and fires off DAGMan. (Two, actually, but the second is just to get automatic restarts of a single scheduler-universe job.) The DAG creates load on both the submit node on the execute nodes, but the submit node first. As noted, I'd like something a little more sophisticated than a load-based limit on the scheduler and local universes, both because I expect the submit node to have idle time outside of the "suggested" range, and because I need to avoid starvation. I want the logic to be something like, "If the submit node is idle, submit a once-a-day job that hasn't run yet for this day. If it's near the end of the day and all the once-a-day jobs haven't been submitted yet, submit them, regardless of load-based limits or throttling. If it's 'after hours', increase the load below which the machine is considered idle."

title: Ticket #2570: preemption does not work when group quotas are in effect
description: I previously put logic in place to limit the computation of pie-left and submitter-limit when group quotas are in effect, because otherwise negotiate() does not assign slots in a way that guarantees respect of other group quotas. However, a side effect of this logic is that it doesn't allow one submitter to preempt another as desired, when preemption is enabled. A complete solution will involve addressing these conditions: <eje> What we need is to allow preemption inside of accounting groups, but the inner negotiation loop does not respect accounting group boundaries -- it will grab slots in such a way that it steals slots that would need to be used by other groups to properly respect quotas <eje> my previous solution imposed limits on submitter-limit, which properly respected quotas, but does not allow a submitter to steal slots from already-running jobs inside that group <eje> we need a way to say "yes, you can preempt, but only preempt jobs that are running in the same acct group as you are" <eje> So, an added condition for preemption. in addition to having smaller priority value, and preemption-requirements evals to true, when HGQ is in effect we also have to have a match on accountinggroup(submitter) and accountinggroup(submitter-who-currently-has-slot-claim) <eje> we also need logic to express constraint: "if your group G quota is Q, and number of jobs running against G is N, then you can use up to (Q-N) new slots and after that you have to attempt to preempt jobs running against G"

title: Ticket #2120: Cgroup feature should be documented in manual for 7.7.x series.
description: The CGroup pid tracking functionality, which is about to go into Condor, should be documented in the manual.
remarks: 2011-Oct-12 11:10:48 by smoler: From Brian Bockelman: Hi Karen, We realized there was a significant feature - cgroups integration - that was added to 7.7.0 but never documented. Sorry about that - since I'm not on the Condor team, I didn't really know it was needed. Information: Cgroups is a mechanism in newer Linux kernels (2.6.24 or later) which provides kernel-level tracking for process trees and resource consumption. Starting in 7.7.0, the Condor can create and use cgroups for each job, offloading much of the procd's task to the kernel. This significantly improves the accuracy of Condor accounting (especially for short-lived processes) and improves the reliability of job killing. Cgroups integration is available on any kernel which supports it; it is in the stock 2.6.24 kernel or later. Related parameters: BASE_CGROUP: this controls the base directory name of the cgroup Condor will use; each job will be in a unique cgroup that is a subdirectory called job_XYZ, where XYZ is the job process/cluster. If BASE_CGROUP is "/", then job 123.45 will run in a cgroup called "/job_123.45". If BASE_CGROUP is "/condor", then job 123.45 will run in "/condor/job_123.45". This allows Condor to flexibly integrate in an existing cgroup setup. 2011-Oct-12 13:36:12 by matt: Brian, What groups need to be mounted in the BASE_CGROUP? What if they are mounted in independent places, can we have MEMORY_CGROUP_ROOT and CPUACCT_CGROUP_ROOT? What permissions are required on the mount point(s)? Do you have an example cgconfig.conf to include? 2011-Oct-14 15:01:08 by bbockelm: Hi Matt, I'll attach a cgconfig.conf separately. If you don't want to hand mount, you'll need one of these and to enable the cgconfig service. The sample cgconfig.conf is designed for BASE_CGROUP=/condor. To use the cgroups feature, Condor must be run as root. If the cgroups are mounted in independent places, there is no issue - but the same cgroup name will be used for all controllers. Condor will use freezer, cpuacct, memory, and blkio cgroups. If you don't have one of these mounted, it will log this in the procd and fallback to the standard procd accounting in such case. I think this answers all your questions? 2011-Dec-01 11:46:59 by smoler: Pete's leaving. Greg T. inherits this ticket. 2012-Feb-01 11:50:40 by smoler: Greg wrote section 3.13.13. Karen edited. Task complete.

title: Ticket #4918: Add network condition as an criterion into HTCondor matching process
description: Current HTCondor matchmaking process does not consider the network conditions between different cluster sites. Thus it is highly possible that the computing capacity satisfies the job's requirement, while the bad network throughput between the submission site and execution site results in a long time spent in file transfers. This will decrease the overall goodput of the HTC system. We propose to integrate network conditions into HTCondor matchmaking algorithm to improve the matchmaking decision, in which less overall time should be spent on file transfer and the overall system goodput could be improved.
creator: zzhang

title: Ticket #6026: RHEL 7.3 breaks standard-universe Fortran (et al.?) math
description: Andrew Feldt wrote: Has anyone else run into this issue? If a fortran code contains math functions (sin, cos, etc.), then, while it can be compiled just fine (even statically) without condor_compile but condor_compile fails at the link stage with: /usr/lib/gcc/x86_64-redhat-linux/4.8.5/../../../../lib64/libm.a(s_sin.o): In function `__cos': (.text+0x4682): undefined reference to `_dl_x86_cpu_features' /usr/lib/gcc/x86_64-redhat-linux/4.8.5/../../../../lib64/libm.a(s_sin.o): In function `__sin': (.text+0x46b2): undefined reference to `_dl_x86_cpu_features’ and so on for each math function. Fortran codes without math functions compile just fine with condor_compile. This worked without issue at RHEL 7.2. This is for: condor-8.4.9-1.el7.x86_64 gcc-gfortran-4.8.5-11.el7.x86_64 redhat-release-server-7.3-7.el7.x86_64 Is there a known solution? and replied to himself: Further debugging shows that I can force this to work by extracting dl-support.o from /lib64/libc.a and adding this explicitly to the condor_compile line. E.g. transform condor_compile gfortran mycode.f -o mycode to condor_compile gfortran mycode.f dl-support.o -o mycode This is a rather crude workaround. Is there a better permanent solution?
remarks: 2017-Mar-07 13:56:12 by tlmiller: We need to verify that we're still running the Fortran standard universe tests. 2017-Mar-08 14:21:11 by tlmiller: Rebuilding the standard universe glibc with an up-to-date copy of the sources (2.17-157, rather than 2.17-32) solves the problem. But what's our policy, with respect to which minor version(s) of a release we support? It seems likely that running a -157 condor_compile on a -32 machine would work, but I don't actually know. 2017-Mar-14 10:41:49 by tlmiller: Since we don't have an older (RHEL7.0) machine to test against, our plan is the following: (1) Upgrade the external on the 8.6.x branch. (2) Reactivate the standard universe fortran tests. (3) Verify that at least one of those tests employs double-precision floats and calls a function whose implementation uses the dl-* function(s). If the standard universe tests all pass after doing this, go ahead and push the commit for 8.6.2. 2017-Mar-16 11:42:07 by tlmiller: RHEL7 is displaying Fortran test problems that RHEL6 isn't, and which I have not yet been able to reproduce. Testing on all platforms is in progress; if the others generally pass, I'll disable the RHEL7 tests and push the commit. That leaves two thing undone: (1) fixing the RHEL7 tests and (2) adding a test for this specific problem. To that end, the following is an example which does not condor_compile without the fix; to change to a version which does, simply remove the *8 from the real in line 3. program atest implicit none real*8 arg,ans arg = 3.1419d0 ans = sin(arg) write(6,*) 'ans = ',ans end 2017-Apr-05 13:39:59 by tlmiller: See test run IDs 399964 and 399939. The following platforms fail the same five Fortran tests (job_ckpt_f-areauc_std, job_ckpt_f-floats_std, job_ckpt_f-integers_std, job_ckpt_f-reader_std, job_rsc_f-direct-write_std): Debian8 (glibc-2.19), RedHat7 (glibc-2.17), and Ubuntu 14 (glibc-2.19). Ubuntu 16 does not have (or at least does not test) standard universe; neither do the Fedoras. Debian7 is 2.13 (we don't build glibc-2.14, 15, or 16). 2017-Apr-10 10:23:54 by tlmiller: It turns out that libgfortran calls fstat() on the standard FDs to determine if they're safe to use; if they aren't, it caches that result on sets its FDs to -1. This check occurs at library (static) initialization time, which is to say, after the starter has mangled the FDs, but before our libsyscall has had a chance to activate (or not, if it's running in stand-alone mode) the FD mapping code. The fix (that FDs 0, 1, and 2 don't ever return EBAD, but instead if they would, return ENOENT) is more than a bit of a hack, but since we need to look at the command-line arguments to really decide if we should be doing FD mapping, it'd be very tricky to do anything better. 2017-Apr-11 15:29:54 by jfrey: Code Review ENOENT doesn't appear to be an errno value that fstat() can return normally. The other errno values it can return are probably no better for this purpose. I'd feel less itchy about this hack if FDs 0, 1, and 2 could be fstat()'d once main() has been called (and the syscall library's FD handling initialized). 2017-Apr-12 09:37:48 by jfrey: Code Review I misread the code. The intention is to return ENOENT only if the fstat() fails with EBADF. I'm ok with that behavior. The code will change the value of errno from EBADF to ENOENT even if the fstat() succeeds. But successful calls are allowed to change errno, so that's not a real issue. 2017-Apr-12 11:20:51 by tlmiller: I suppose we could document this somewhere in case it causes someone grief, but I don't think we really ever put technical details like this in the manual. 2017-Apr-17 17:05:05 by tim: DOC REVIEW: Looks good

title: Ticket #1219: ConcurrencyLimit problems with new ClassAds
description: I noticed that condor_q from the current 7.5.1 build is unable to run -better-analyze in CHTC (CM 7.5.0). The failure is caused by entries such as the following in the negotiator's classad response to GET_PRIORITY: ConcurrencyLimit.jmag = 0.0 This causes condor_q to report: Could not get priorities from negotiator The code that produces these entries appears to be this in Accountant.cpp: attr.sprintf("ConcurrencyLimit.%s = %f\n", limit.Value(), count); In new classads, "." is not a valid character in an attribute name, so condor_q cannot parse the classad. Presumably if the negotiator were using new classads, it would fail to insert these attributes into the ad, but it ignores the return value of Insert(), so this information would simply be missing.

title: Ticket #6476: Master self-exec messes up systemd integration
description: When the master detects a new condor_master binary or the admin runs condor_restart -master, the master will shutdown all of the daemons and then call exec() on its own binary. If the master is running under systemd, this can interfere with systemd services. At the moment, these consist of watchdog keep-alive messages and systemd binding the shared port command port. The primary problem is that the master doesn't preserve the environment variables needed for these functions, so the new master image won't use them properly. As a result, after a master restart, the master will stop sending watchdog alive messages, leading to systemd killing the master after 20 minutes. Also, the shared port daemon will attempt to bind the already-bound condor command port, which will fail. In these situations, the safest course of action is for the master to exit. Systemd will restart it shortly afterwards.
remarks: 2017-Nov-14 15:27:32 by jfrey: Some developers expressed concern about having the master exit if it isn't 100% certain that systemd will restart it. There's another solution: when the master wants to re-exec() itself, it can first restore the systemd-related environment variables and FDs so that the new image sees them. 2017-Dec-20 11:03:05 by tim: CODE REVIEW: Looks good

title: Ticket #386: BIND_ALL_INTERFACES always trumps NETWORK_INTERFACE
description: BIND_ALL_INTERFACES defaults to True, even if NETWORK_INTERFACE is set, which is strange behavior. I think that the correct behavior should be that if NETWORK_INTERFACE is set in the configuration file / environment, BIND_ALL_INTERFACES should default to False, unless explicitly set. Even better, I think that BIND_ALL_INTERFACES should be deprecated, and the following behavior should replace it: NETWORK_INTERFACE would default to '*', which is equivalent to to 'BIND_ALL_INTERFACES = True'. Otherwise, if NETWORK_INTERFACE is set to an IP address or interface name (i.e. "eth0") would be equivalent to " 'BIND_ALL_INTERFACES = False' and 'NETWORK_INTERFACE = <name|addr>' as specified.

title: Ticket #555: strptime() failure in stduniv with gnu extensions
description: The strptime() function in glibc apparently has some gnu extensions associated with its definition that cause it to fail when used in a condor_compile'd program. See rust ticket for many details.
remarks: 2009-Sep-30 15:10:25 by psilord: Ok, I've p reproduced the error in this setup: Linux nmi-v001 > uname -a Linux nmi-v001 2.6.9-55.EL.100hz #1 Tue Mar 31 20:07:07 CDT 2009 x86_64 x86_64 x86_64 GNU/Linux Linux nmi-v001 > condor_version $CondorVersion: 7.1.4 Nov 10 2008 BuildID: 113473 $ $CondorPlatform: X86_64-LINUX_RHEL3 $ 2009-Sep-30 15:41:19 by psilord: Ok, I figured it out. The bug is that the %z format option, which is a GNU Extension to the POSIX interface to strptime in order to support strftime(), isn't implemented in the revision of glibc (2.3.2, actually 2.3.2.27.9.7) used in RHEL3. I looked at the glibc code itself, and %z isn't in the cases of the switch statement. Since the RHEL3 full port of Condor uses that exact revision of glibc, any program condor_compiled on a RHEL3 port of Condor using strptime() and the %z format option is doomed to fail. I have in fact reproduced this problem outside of condor_compile all together, removing Condor from the equation (to be specific, on a real RHEL3 machine running the user's test case). It appears in my testing that the RHEL5 full port of Condor doesn't suffer from this problem and the glibc on that machine implements %z. 2009-Sep-30 15:45:58 by psilord: My advice, mentioned in the ticket, is to use the POSIX format specifiers instead of the GNU extensions and/or upgrade to the RHEL5 full port of Condor.

title: Ticket #1560: fix "unknown negotiator" problem
description: For better or worse, when flocking is enabled, the schedd needs to know which flocking level it is dealing with when negotiating. If it can't figure it out, the schedd refuses to negotiate, with the message "unknown negotiator". The schedd's algorithm for identifying the negotiator requires the admin to set NEGOTIATOR_HOST and/or FLOCK_NEGOTIATOR_HOSTS to something with a DNS entry matching the peer address observed by the schedd when receiving a connection from the negotiator. Proposal Have the schedd insert a "tag" into the submitter ad. When the negotiator connects to the schedd to negotiate, it should present this tag. By choosing a tag that uniquely identifies the flocking level (e.g. the collector name), the schedd can use it to identify which flocking level is being negotiated. Nothing special has to be done for multi-homed negotiators or negotiators that run on a different host from the collector. The algorithm doesn't even assume that there is only one negotiator per collector. This can also make FLOCK_NEGOTIATOR_HOSTS optional in the schedd. It's only use would be for identifying older negotiators and as a macro in the config file for authorization policy. By not setting it at all, the admin can have the schedd query the address of the negotiator (for sending RESCHEDULE) rather than relying on the config file for the address.

title: Ticket #4298: Move stuff out of DAGMan Job object
description: To do some of the stuff Brian is requesting for #4115, we'll need to keep quite a bit more information associated with each node (Job object). For example, each proc ID for multi-proc nodes, counts of job procs running, idle, etc. But at least most of that stuff we only care about while the node is queued -- once the node has finished we can probably forget about it. When I was thinking about this, it also occurred to me that we probably already have some information in the Job object that falls into this category. For example, CondorID -- I don't think we need that after the node is finished, unless maybe it failed, for the error message. Submit tries probably falls into this category, and maybe even node retries. So I'm proposing that we should create a new object that contains all of this temporary information, and just instantiate the object when the jobs for a node are submitted, and then delete the object after the node has finished. I just did a quick look through the Job object, and I think there's quite a bit there that we only care about while the node/job is in the queue, so this might give us a pretty good saving of memory for large DAGs.
creator: wenger

title: Ticket #105: PrivSep: disk usage can be underreported
description: When gathering disk usage information about a running job, the Starter recurses through the sandbox adding up file sizes. In PrivSep mode, this can result in some files not being accounted for since the Starter can only do this as Condor's UID and may not have permission to stat some of the files. Fixing this seems to require adding a "du" operation to the PrivSep Switchboard. The Switchboard already has code to safely walk the sandbox file tree, so this would be a pretty small change.

title: Ticket #4332: Don't terminate Create_Thread() children via exec()
description: When a daemon creates a child process using fork() without exec() (usually by calling Create_Thread()), we override the exit() function with our own version that calls exec("/bin/true") or exec("/bin/false") to terminate the process. This is avoid cleanup code that executes on exit, like destructors for static C++ objects, which may have effects external to the process. Unfortunately, this causes a lose of information in the child's exit status. Any non-zero exit code is translated into the exit code of /bin/false, which can vary by platform (1 on Linux an BSD, 255 on Solaris). In the FileTransfer object, a non-zero exit code indicates success. But a call to EXCEPT() or a dprintf() failure results in the same non-zero status observed by the parent process. We can preserve the full exit status by terminating the child process via a call to _exit(). This call skips exit-time cleanup code like C++ destructors.

title: Ticket #410: Collector bloat/leak
description: Two major users are seeing massive collector bloat/leaks. In both cases the startds reporting in are glideins and there is almost certainly regular churn and thus lots of new security sessions. Igor Sfiligoi's main CMS collector is tracking about 12,000 startd ads. These ads take about 80 MB ("condor_status -l | wc") It's fed by 75 subordinate collectors running on the same machine. Nothing else submits ads to the collector. There are regular queries. The subordinate collectors are running about 70 MB each. The main collector is 4.0 GB. Yesterday it was 3.9 GB, suggesting a growth rate of 0.1 GB/day. Given that the collector was started March 6th and is 4 GB on April 23rd, this rate seems about accurate. SEC_DEFAULT_SESSION_TIMEOUT is 50000 (about 14 hours). The collector has been running long enough that security sessions should be timing out and shouldn't be responsible for the bloat. Joe Boyd's CDF collector was born the afternoon of April 13 at about 2.4 GB. It was steady at that level for about a day, grew slowly for another day, then bloated up to about 3.0 GB over the next 24 hours. It stabilized for about half of a day, then jumped to 3.4 GB over about a day, another half-day of stability, then it shot up to 3.6 GB over another half-day. SEC_DEFAULT_SESSION_TIMEOUT is 288000 (about 3.3 days). We only have about 4.5 days of data, but this should still be long enough for security sessions to start rolling over. CDF had been restarting their collector regularly with 7.0 because of this exact reason. The above is with 7.2.1 and doesn't represent an improvement.

remarks: 2014-Mar-25 15:06:24 by gthain: Wouldn't it be simpler if Hashtable::remove just called operator++ on the victim iterator? 2014-Mar-25 21:26:30 by bbockelm: Good catch. I refactored that code into a common function. All unit tests for this feature still pass. I just pushed a build to NMI to look for obvious regressions. Hopefully that will lead to good news in the morning. 2014-Mar-26 10:16:08 by gthain: There's also the question of what the semantics should be in general for deleting the object an active iterator points to. The HashTable code in general doesn't know what the next action of the user of the code will do next after the deletion: will it increment the iterator, dereference it, or check for end()'ness? Seems like depending on what the user chooses to do, iteration over a hash table that has random deletions in it could lead to either repetition of an iterated item, or skipping one. We should be clear about what the semantics are. 2014-Mar-26 11:42:00 by bbockelm: Hi Greg, I think the semantics are this: Whenever a caller returns to DC, the iterator may be moved forward if the current item is deleted. So, to avoid skipping or duplication, the caller should: Not dereference the current iterator before returning to DC. I.e., they should do (*it)++. Be aware that the iterator may change position if it is returned to DC. The iterator may be equal to end() upon being called from DC, even if it wasn't before returning to DC. On being called from DC, consume the current iterator before incrementing it. Never cache the iterator value when returning to DC, as there is no guarantee the value hasn't been free()'d before the function is called again. So, never store (*it) into a class's member variable. A correct use would be: while (it != end()) { Foo *value = (*it)++; ... do something, such as writing value to the network ... if (some conditional) { return; } } where 'it' is a class member and this code is in a function that is a DC callback handler. Brian 2014-Mar-26 16:23:54 by bbockelm: Hi Greg, NMI build looks good. I have no further commits planned for this item. Accordingly, assigning this back to you for merge and backport. Brian

title: Ticket #5221: condor_q treats -name differently than other tools
description: condor_q and condor_rm handle their -name command-line argument differently, which can lead to them talking to difference schedds. condor_rm uses the -name argument value to create a DCSchedd object and uses that object to communicate with the schedd. condor_q uses the -name argument value to query the collector for the given schedd's ad, uses the sinful string from that ad to create a DCSchedd, and uses that object to communicate with the schedd. When the DCSchedd object is given a name but not an address or pool, it may decide that the named schedd is local and look for its information in a local address file instead of querying the collector. It will do this if the given name matches the SCHEDD_NAME parameter in the config file. If the address file can't read, it falls back to querying the collector. These divergent paths for locating the schedd are causing problems for Fermilab, which runs multiple schedds on a single machine. They have situations where condor_q -name and condor_rm -name contact different schedds, leading to confusion when condor_rm says jobs don't exist. One workaround is to disable the writing of the schedd address and ad files. This would require that all tools be used with -name and they would always query the collector to locate the schedd. Another workaround is to always use -pool, which forces a query of the collector.

But it's the wrong solution. If we're going to change how a client locates a schedd, that should occur in the Daemon client object (maybe specific to the DCSchedd object). 2016-Dec-07 11:32:30 by jfrey: No version history for this change. It is an incomplete fix intended for a specific user (Fermilab) that won't affect most other users. We will inform Fermi directly about the change.

title: Ticket #257: Track file sizes in checkpoints
description: This is part of the large patch set contributed by Dan Forrest. This patch includes information about the sizes of a stduniv application's files in the file table in its checkpoint. This avoided a problem that Dan often tripped over where an application would: run for a while produce a periodic checkoint run for while longer adding more data to its files get evicted without producing a checkpoint restore from the periodic checkpoint At this point, the data that was added after the periodic checkpoint was taken but before it was evicted is still in the files, and if the application appends to a file that data will remain there (and likely end up being duplicated). Tracking the file size in the file table allows files to be truncated to the size stored in the checkpoint when an application is resumed. I'm not certain, but the above scenario may only be a problem for compressed files. Chunks from the annotated diff of Dan's changes (which Todd has) that are associated with this ticket are labeled with a (8).

title: Ticket #312: Pipe read/write limitations
description: When communicating with children via pipes, condor is subject to an OS limitation in the amount of data it can send to the child and a built in limitation to the amount of data it can read from the child. When sending data to the child (stdin pipe), condor is subject to the Operating System's definition of the maximum pipe buffer size. In linux, this size of 4096 prior to 2.6.11 kernels, and 64k in 2.6.11+ kernels. This manifests itself with the Job Router hooks, where the finalize hook tries to send >4k of data to the hook. On Red Hat Enterprise Linux 4, only 4k of data will get to the child. When reading data from the child (stdout,stderr), condor has a number of built in limitations: 1) There's a hard coded limit of 10k of data. 2) Condor will close the stdout/err pipe once it reads all data. If a child writes data, then pauses for a period of time before outputting more data then it's likely not all data will make it to condor.

title: Ticket #742: Slots left Claimed Idle when there are no jobs
description:
https://bugzilla.redhat.com/show_bug.cgi?id=523482 Description of problem: It is possible to have slots left in the Claimed state with no running jobs, and no jobs to run!, until the claim lease expires. Version-Release number of selected component (if applicable): condor-7.4.0-0.4 How reproducible: 100% Steps to Reproduce: 1. start condor (make sure schedd start) 2. mv /usr/sbin/condor_shadow /usr/sbin/condor_shadow- 3. submit a job (echo -e 'executable=/bin/sleep
arguments=5
transfer_executable=false
notification=never
queue 1
' | condor_submit) 4. watch condor_status -total until there is a Claimed slot, can also check condor_status | grep Claimed, it should be Claimed Idle 5. remove the job (condor_rm -a will do it) Actual results: The Claimed slot will remain that way until the claim lease expires. This can be verified by watching the StartLog on the slot's machine. Expected results: The slot should be returned to the Unclaimed state. Additional info: Running a job on a slot is a multi-step process. Three steps the Schedd goes through are to 1) REQUEST_CLAIM on the Startd 2) start a Shadow for the job 3) let the Shadow ACTIVATE_CLAIM on the Startd. The Schedd will RELEASE_CLAIM on the Startd for all jobs that have an active Shadow. Anything that prevents step (2) from succeeding, such as the Shadow cannot be executed (induced above) or a condor_rm -a while the Schedd is loaded (original way of hitting this bug) and Shadow execution is cancelled, will demonstrate this bug. The Schedd keeps match_rec's for each job it is starting, the match_rec has a status field that can indicate M_STARTD_CONTACT_LIMBO (step 1 completed), M_CLAIMED (step 2 completed). The Schedd sends RELEASE_CLAIM on M_CLAIMED and should be changed to on M_STARTD_CONTACT_LIMBO as well.
remarks: I have tried to reproduce and understand this issue. My attempts to reproduce it are based on the master branch, but I am pretty sure the results apply to V7_4 as well. I think there was some confusion when testing the proposed solution ([15697]). It does not solve the problem, but the observed behavior is influenced by some race conditions, so it may be that while testing, the race made it appear that the behavior had improved. The status of the match goes from LIMBO to CLAIMED when the startd responds to the schedd's CLAIM_REQUEST. The schedd never tries to start a shadow while the match is still in the LIMBO state. Furthermore, the schedd should never send RELEASE_CLAIM while the match is in the LIMBO state, at least until better claim management exists that prevents one schedd from obliterating another schedd's prior claim with the same id. Here's what I observe when following the procedure specified in this ticket for reproducing the problem: after the job is removed, the next call to StartJobs() will cause the schedd to try to find a job to run on the claim. If it finds no more jobs to run on it, then the claim is deleted and RELEASE_CLAIM is sent to the startd. The delay before the call to StartJobs() can be quite short but it can be up to SCHEDD_INTERVAL seconds, possibly leaving one with the impression that the claim has been leaked. So I think the problem is really that if a job is removed while in the queue of jobs pending to start, the schedd does not quickly notice that the associated claim is idle. This could be easily solved in the master branch by making a call to ExpediteStartJobs() somewhere in the job removal code path. I recommend that we revert [15697] and [17675] in V7_4-branch. The latter patch basically tries to undo the effect of the former patch, but may not be catching all cases. 2010-Mar-26 18:27:21 by danb: After discussing with Matt, I went ahead and reverted [15697] and [17675] in V7_4_2-branch. In master branch (7.4.3), I added a call to ExpediteStartJobs() when jobs are removed to speed up discovery that a claim in CLAIMED state needs some attention (either picking a different job or removing the claim).

title: Ticket #4575: Daemons with a debug lock file should leave log open
description: When multiple daemons are writing to the same debug log file, we use a lock file during log rotation to avoid race conditions. To ensure that all daemons use the newly-rotated file, each daemon closes the file after every write and reopens it before the next write. This is needlessly inefficient. Instead, the daemons can leave the log file open, and use the following procedure to ensure rotation happens when necessary and daemons always write to the newest log file: Use lseek() to find the current file size. If it's not time to rotate, then write line as usual and skip remaining steps. Acquire lock. Fstat() the open file descriptor and stat() the log file using its filename. Close the file descriptor for the log file. If the two stat structs identify the same file, then perform rotation. Open log file. Release lock. Now we're ready to write the requested line. On windows (and if LOCK_DEBUG_LOG_TO_APPEND=True on unix), the lock is held the entire time the log file is open. We would need to change that.

title: Ticket #5734: Nonexistent owners cause problems in schedd
description: In most of HTCondor, authenticated usernames in CEDAR don't have to correspond to OS user accounts, although they frequently do. However, in the schedd, we usually map an authenticated username to a job's Owner attribute, and the Owner attribute must be a valid local OS user account. Job files will be owned by this account, and the schedd and its children with act as this account for file access and other possible activities. Currently, a job's Owner attribute is set to match the authenticated username of the submitting client without any check on its validity. This leads to various failures during and after job submission. Some actions are performed as the condor user or root instead of the job owner. The schedd repeatedly tries and fails to run the job. The schedd can EXCEPT when it can't become the non-existent user. Attempts to remove the job can fail. There a few fixes we should make: The job event writing code shouldn't attempt to switch to user privilege if it fails to initialize the user info. This leads to an EXCEPT of the schedd in 8.5. The schedd should refuse a job submission if the Owner attribute doesn't correspond to a valid OS user account.

title: Ticket #7359: Python bindings multi-thread programs crash talking to Schedd
description: There have been multi-threaded python programs that have multiple threads talking to the same Schedd. Even when these threads don't share a Schedd object, they can still crash because there is global state in condor library code that is not properly protected by a critical section.
remarks: We're taking a two-pronged approach to fixing this: TJ is working on breaking the dependence on global state in the bindings. This should make these problem that REANA observed not actually crash Python, although it will still cause exceptions due to deadlocking the schedd (https://github.com/reanahub/reana-job-controller/issues/190). Josh is working on applying a shared Python lock to every function call in the bindings, which should make it impossible for two threads to be in our code at the same time. We can slowly roll this protection back from individual functions if/when we clean up the underlying interfaces to be thread-safe. We can also make the lock be per-daemon, if we also add a way to uniquely identify daemons to the bindings. Unclear as of yet how much of this will go back into stable, but probably none of it, because TJ will likely break backwards compatibility for Schedd.edit. 2019-Dec-12 12:32:32 by jpatton: REVIEW: Looks good to me, the latest commits fix the "unhashable" problems in both 3.7 and 2.7, assuming that the other Python 3 versions will be fine. title: Ticket #3199: defrag draining rate is too small

title: Ticket #892: add support for a shared TCP listener port
description: Currently, each daemon has it's own TCP listener for its command socket. On a high-scale submit node, this adds up to a lot of ports, which caps scalability at around 23k running jobs. If you want to poke holes in a firewall for these ports, a large range must be opened, and there is not a very strong assurance that it is condor that is using these ports, since it dynamically opens and closes command sockets as daemons come and go, potentially leaving ports open to other processes that were not intended to be open through the firewall. The solution that I'm working on is to have an optional service that allows all the condor daemons on a machine to share the same TCP listener. Connections are accepted by the shared port service and the file descriptor is passed to the requested target daemon. It's pretty simple and doesn't require fundamental changes to Condor's networking or security layers. In unix, this passing of the file descriptor happens over a named socket. I believe windows has its own mechanism (see #991). There will be a protocol change, so daemons using the shared port service will not be reachable by older versions of condor. The protocol change is to send the id of the requested daemon immediately after connecting to the shared port. The id is the name of the shared socket, which is advertised, like CCB contact information, in the url-encoded key=value parameters in the contact string. The shared port service does not accept arbitrary paths to named sockets, because this might be a security problem. It only accepts base-names and it prepends the path to the daemon socket directory. This implies that only daemons with the ability to create named sockets in that directory will be able to accept connections through the shared port service. I'm currently planning on making this directory writable only by condor, so this will not allow daemons running in PRIV_USER_FINAL to accept connections through the shared port service unless the admin changes the permissions on this directory. I'm not aware of a case where this is a concern.
remarks: I have completed support for sharing a port between condor daemons on all of our unix platforms except for HPUX. This is going into 7.5.0. Standard universe daemons do not use the shared port. The code compiles on HPUX but fails at runtime in sendmsg() with "Bad file number".

title: Ticket #2272: Need command-line tool condor_checkpoint_job
description: The condor_checkpoint command needs a companion condor_checkpoint_job, similar to condor_vacate_job. Condor_checkpoint connects to a startd and tells it to checkpoint one of its running jobs. In a pool with strong security enabled, a user will typically not have the necessary authorization to issue this command (the startd will reject it). Condor_checkpoint_job would connect to the schedd and tell it to checkpoint one or more of the user's running jobs.

title: Ticket #7420: Collector.directQuery cannot return multiple ads
description: Collector.directQuery always returns exactly the first ad it gets, which is not the correct semantics for its nominal command line equivalent condor_status -direct <address>, which can return multiple ads. We probably can't directly fix Collector.directQuery for backwards compatibility right now, but we can add a new method that does the right thing. Wild thought: maybe add a flag to the signature that switches between the old bad behavior and the correct behavior, old behavior by default? Might be a better deprecation/transition path. Could do this in Python if it's tricky in C++, leveraging a new "private" method Collector._directQuery that we don't document but does implement the right behavior. Collector.directQuery has other flaws as well. There is no way to pass in a daemon address, this method always does a locate and then a direct query to the first locate result, but a direct query should be able to work even if the daemon isn't advertising to a collector. Both the Schedd and Startd can return ads of multiple types, some of which have no corresponding daemon_type There is no constraint argument The query command has a classad payload, and is thus extensible, but not all daemons accept the same options Thus the proper solution is probably to deprecate this method, and add methods on the various daemon objects that do the equivalent of direct query but without the locate. Users that want to be able to do a direct query and get multiple ads back will have to startd = htcondor.Startd(coll.locate(...)) startd.directQuery()

title: Ticket #938: Cream Gahp should batch requests
description: The cream api allows the client to provide a list of jobs upon which an action should be performed (submit, start, status, suspend, resume, cancel, purge). Condor currently invokes these commands repeatedly, once per job, which is inefficient. Condor should batch these requests when possible. Execution of a request could be delayed a couple of seconds to wait for additional requests that could be batched with it. This batching could be done in either the gridmanager or the cream_gahp. Note that the specific case of batching status is #939. That said, individual job statuses are still issued when a job is initially submitted, so there is still benefit to batching those. Plan as executed Batching commands on the gridmanager side provide too complex. The design was complex to start, and ignored that internally the gridmanager's queue is a list of strings. Collecting up relevant commands would haven necessitated rearchitecting the entire queue system to make commands some more complex object, and fixing every section of code that touched the queue. This turned into a rathole and was abandoned. Instead we're doing the batching in the cream_gahp, which has proven to the simplier. No waiting was implemented, but significant benefits are already being seen. The exact benefit will depend on the load; do the workers clear out the queue faster than batchable requests are added? Command status These are the commands that are run once (or more) per job: CREAM_JOB_CANCEL - DONE. condor_rming a 500 job run generated 500 calls batched into 142. Note: may never be called in the normal stream of events. CREAM_JOB_PURGE - DONE. Cut 500 job run from 500 calls to 78. CREAM_JOB_REGISTER CREAM_JOB_START - DONE. Cut 1000 job run from 1000 calls to 150ish, or 500 calls to 81 CREAM_SET_LEASE CREAM_JOB_STATUS - Called once per job after CREAM_JOB_REGISTER Abandoned Plan Both the condor_gridmanager and the cream_gahp are doing queuing of GAHP commands. The gridmanager does it for historic reasons. The gridmanager does so for historic reasons; the GT2 GAHP immediately turns commands into outbound requests. The gridmanager implements the queuing in GahpClient::now_pending (/src/condor_gridmanager/gahp-client.cpp 2128) and GahpServer::poll (/src/condor_gridmanager/gahp-client.cpp 2344). The cream_gahp implements queuing in enqueue_request (/src/cream_gahp/cream_gahp_server.cpp 291) and worker_main (/src/cream_gahp/cream_gahp_server.cpp 1891) The gridmanager has an timeouts on requests handed off to the GAHP. (TODO: Find it) This is again historic, as the GT GAHP wasn't trusted to not occasionally drop outstanding commands on the ground. This may cause problems if we batch commands in the gridmanager, and responses may take longer as we collect up commands, wait for the remote side to do more work, or simply waiting for longer output to be collected. Rationale Why the gridmanager instead of the GAHP? Since both the gridmanager and the gahp implement queues of commands, this could have been implemented in the GAHP. So why not? The pros and cons of each are: GAHP + Relatively isolated + All commands already go through the queue - Will need to explode single response into multiple responses for the multiple input commands; we'll need to carry around mapping information to associate them. - Complicates the relatively simple GAHP. GAHPs should be thin wrappers over grid specific APIs, smarts should be in the gridmanager. Gridmanager + Core logic could potentially be reused for other grid types, providing future benefits. + No need to disable the gridmanager's command timeout - Commands don't necessarily end up in the queue at all; only if too many commands are outstanding. Ultimately they are very simple. I was ultimately swayed by a desire to keeps GAHPs as simple as possible, and a hope that this logic might be reused directly for other grid types in the future. Plan Changes will all occur in the gridmanager, nothing will change in the GAHP. (This assumes that the necessary batch commands exist in the GAHP.) Change the gridmanager to always queue commands. This shouldn't necessarily increase latency, will simplify the code (reducing two paths (immediate and queued) into one), and will make the following more effective. Break GahpClient::now_pending into two commands: GahpClient::now_pending (always queues command) and GahpClient::run_pending (always sends the command) Pick a command to start with. start or purge seem like good candidates. Whichever we pick is hereby the batchable command. When we grab the front of the queue of outstanding commands, we'll check if it's a batchable command. If it is, we'll spin the queue looking for other commands of the same type, extract them, and merge the lot into a single command. At this point we start seeing benefits, but only if the gridmanager is so busy that commands are arriving in the queue faster than they're being dispatched. To items in the job queue, add an "arrived in queue" time. When pulling items out of the queue, check the arrival time. If the job is batchable, and (arrive_time + 5 seconds) < now_time, ignore it and move down to the next item in the queue. If you hit the end of the queue without finding a command, but there is at least one job in the queue, reset the GahpServer::poll_timer to the time of the next job. (The "5 seconds" is probably a user configurable knob, but should probably be small and aggressive, otherwise the system feels unresponsive.) At this point we should see the meat of our optimization benefit. work through the remaining command that we want to batch.
