title: Ticket #2337: Implement 64-bit support for file i/o in stduniv
description: LIGO would like that stduniv file i/o can break the 32-bit boundary. It is currently a hard restriction that this is true even on 64-bit machines. Milestones [DONE] Write a test to show 64-bit files not working. [DONE] Figure out why 64-bit file stduniv test fails. [DONE] Fix the FileTab to honor the off_t type instead of int for lseek(). [DONE] Fix the stub generator to produce stubs that are congnizant of the return types of syscalls instead of them just being all 'int' return types, which is provably wrong. Also, the fixing of the lseek() member function on the FileTab requires the stub generator to be fixed since the stub generator generates calls to members of the FileTab which have different return types. [DONE] Fix any ramifications from the previous step, things like fixing system call return value checks to be cognoscente of pointers, stopping handling undefined return values from system calls that returned void (but weren't handled properly), etc, etc, etc [DONE] Analyze the changes in the protocols from before my change to after my change to determine if I introduced protocol incompatibilities. I'm writing a document which records the steps I did and the problems found and solutions performed. (Two problems found which break compatibility.) [DONE] Run through the test suite on all machines, fix any missed problems. Unfortunately, the getdirentries syscall is fragile, and this feature breaks it the rest of the way in an unknown manner. It will be fixed after this feature gets checked in. [DONE] Polish the large file test and put it into the test suite. [IGNORING] Check and possibly fix the llseek() system call, since it was defined very poorly in the stduniv and needs some thinking to figure out. [DONE] Final check and committing into master.
remarks: 2011-Aug-01 14:35:43 by psilord: Ok, after some inspection, and some hacking. I have preliminary support working for a standalone stduniv job. I need to expand my test programs to be much more precise in what they check to ensure I can read, write, seek, get the seek position, etc properly over the 2, 4, and 8 (for good measure) GB range for files. I am now going to check to see if the support functions for remote I/O too. I know, though, that I need to fix the llseek() call since it seems to have been broken for a very long time wrt 32/64 bit file offsets. 2011-Aug-02 10:45:13 by psilord: After some more debugging, I found this: #undef lseek #if defined( SYS_lseek ) extern "C" int REMOTE_CONDOR_lseek( int , off_t , int ); off_t lseek ( int fd, off_t offset, int whence ) { int rval,do_local=0; errno = 0; sigset_t condor_omask = _condor_signals_disable(); if( MappingFileDescriptors() ) { _condor_file_table_init(); rval = FileTab -> lseek ( fd , offset , whence ); } else { if( LocalSysCalls() || do_local ) { rval = syscall( SYS_lseek, fd , offset , whence ); } else { rval = REMOTE_CONDOR_lseek( fd , offset , whence ); } } _condor_signals_enable( condor_omask ); return (off_t ) rval; } Notice how the return type of the lseek got squashed into an int and then expanded again. This means I need to edit the stub generator to use the same return type for rval as for the function being stubbed. 2011-Aug-04 14:10:42 by psilord: I beat the stub generator with a baseball bat. Now it emits the return types of the senders/switches/receivers to be the correct type associated with the syscall instead of just "int" all the time like it used to. I also fixed the stub generator to know when some return types are pointers and to use the correct check of the returned value from the syscall. More work needs to be done for return value verification, but it is a helluva lot better now than what it was. I went and found all (well, all that I found, at any rate) of the places we were dealing with an int that was supposed to be an off_t when dealing with file offsets and fixed them. No on a 64-bit machine, at least standalone mode will deal with file sizes larger than 32-bits now. This is a conspicuous improvement. 2011-Aug-10 16:31:30 by psilord: After much more serious work in the stub generator in order to fix random assumptions the original authors made because everything was an 'int' return type, it is now more type correct than ever. The stub for getwd() the hardest one to figure out. It already is a special switch, but the sender and receiver used a pseudo call. The pseudo call was of a different type than the function itself, which caused numerous problems. I fixed it by creating another system call which had the right prototype. The whole way we deal with pseudo_calls of real syscalls is pretty wrong. Also, the full prototype for getwd() is 'char* getwd(char *buf)' which is problematic since it means that the rval and the buf both have to proprocessed properly and memory accounted for in the rpc call. I avoided the issue with the new rpc call called getwd_special() which type correctly calls the pseudo call. 2011-Aug-11 14:53:52 by psilord: It seems that I seriously broke getdirentries() as a result of all of my changes. I am unsure why and at least the rest of the stduniv test suite passes. I checked the senders/switches/receivers for that call explicitly against a revision of condor which does not have my changes and, while there were some surface differences which were intended, the functionality was identical. I'm now testing to see how that call functions without my changes. Maybe it was broken before I started. Also, I need to fix another small interface in the CondorFileTable object to handle 64-bit file size properly. 2011-Aug-12 11:07:20 by psilord: It turns out getdirentries() is broken before any of my changes happened. If I revert all of my changes, getdirentries() works with remote i/o but fails in standalone mode. With my changes, it fails in both instances. So, I will continue my work on this ticket until it is finished, commit it, then fix getdirentries() to function properly again. 2011-Aug-15 12:28:13 by psilord: It had a couple rounds of failing to build in the NMI, but I fixed those. However, the test suite blew up in an undebuggable way (time out errors) for non stduniv tests. So I have to do some more iterations of pushing it through NMI to see what is going wrong. 2011-Aug-15 13:58:07 by tannenba: Test program needs to call ckpt(), e.g. we need to test that 64bit support works across a standalone checkpoint/restart cycle. 2011-Aug-22 12:15:03 by psilord: Today I'm meeting with nwp to help debug the failing getdirentries/getdents syscall. 2011-Aug-22 16:41:29 by psilord: Ok, it seems that the condor file buffer for stduniv uses an 'int' to record the size of the file, I need to explore this and figure out if this is where the type narrowing is happening for the lfs test in remote i/o mode to condor. 2011-Aug-24 14:46:30 by psilord: Ok, the condor file buffer code was indeed narrowing the offset values into large files. It did this because the "chunks" in the file buffer knew what offset into the file they represented--but the variable it kept it in was an int, not an off_t. I have now found and fixed this issue. The large file test now passes with a 7GB file in standalone mode and remote I/O mode. It turns out though, that the receiver code emits an %d for the file offset. This rolls over and outputs negative numbers in the shadow log for file sizes larger than 2GB. This is less than useful. So I have to fix up the code generator to be knowledgeable of this situation and use some other format conversion form instead. 2011-Aug-25 13:17:59 by psilord: Ok, I found a limitation in the codebase concerning the 64-bit file offsets. The crux of the issue is that Condor is (generally) compiled without _LARGEFILE_SOURCE and _FILE_OFFSET_BITS=64. This means that on 32 bit machines, by default, the syscall library's definition off off_t will be 4 bytes wide. So, if a user compiles a 32 bit application with those two things defined, intending to want >2GB files, the off_t in the application will be 8 bytes wide, but the off_t in the syscall library will be 4 bytes wide. There doesn't seem to be a good way to automatically figure out this binary incompatibility between the type sizes. So, we'll just document what works. It seems that on 64-bit machines, those two flags don't affect the size of off_t. I will call the compilations of Condor that do not use the two #defines as 32CN 64CN. This is the only way Condor is compiled today. Now, an application can be compiled 32-bit or 64 bit, and either have the above constants defined for it or not. I will call these 32AN 32AY 64AN 64AY. Then here is a chart which describes if an application doing 64-bit file offsets with remote i/o will work with a specific type of Condor: Application Type Condor Shadow 64-bit File Offsets Supported 32AN 32CN NO 32AN 64CN NO 32AY 32CN NO 32AY 64CN MAYBE 64AN 32CN NO 64AN 64CN YES 64AY 32CN NO 64AY 64CN YES So, tell users that 64-bit condor with 64-bit stduniv applications function wrt 64-bit file sizes--anything else doesn't work. 2011-Oct-10 14:59:21 by psilord: Documented, resolved.

title: Ticket #4719: JobRouter fails to write userlog due to bad permissions
description: Symptoms of the error: When submitting a remote job to a Condor instance with a job router, we will see error messages in the job log that the JobRouter has aborted the job after the job has terminated and output has been retrieved (see attached job log). There is a corresponding error in the JobRouterLog about being unable to write to the job log: 11/13/14 11:29:08 (395.0) Writing terminate record to user logfile 11/13/14 11:29:08 WriteUserLog::initialize: safe_open_wrapper("log") failed - errno 13 (Permission denied) 11/13/14 11:29:08 WriteUserLog::initialize: failed to open file log 11/13/14 11:29:08 (-1.-1) Unable to open user log (event 5) This does not appear to be an issue with grid universe jobs that are submitted to a client's local schedd. Cause of the error: After some discussion with Brian B. and Jaime, the issue appears to be that the JobRouter is setting the job status to COMPLETED and Managed to ScheddDone then letting the Schedd handle cleanup on some periodic check that chowns the user's files to the condor user. The JobRouter then tries to terminate the job as the user but can't write to the user log because of the previous chown. Since the cleanup/chown appears to be happening periodically, this results in a race condition. The GridManager has similar behavior except it actually calls DestroyProc(), which chowns the user's files. The JobRouter should probably just mirror the behavior of the GridManager. Reproducing the error: Submit a vanilla universe job to the remote CE's schedd: condor_submit -remote fermicloud133.fnal.gov -pool fermicloud133.fnal.gov:9619 test.sub When the job completes, retrieve your files: condor_transfer_data -name fermicloud133.fnal.gov -pool fermicloud133.fnal.gov:9619 <job id> Repeat as necessary since the error depends on the race condition. Jaime's comments The sequence of events for the gridmanager is as follows: Transfer output files to the spool directory Set job status to COMPLETED Write the terminate event as the user Set Managed to ScheddDone and call DestroyProc() Steps 2 and 4 are done in separate connections to the schedd. The DestroyProc() is what triggers the chowning of the spool directory to the condor user. COMPLETED should be a terminal state (no pun intended), so it should only be set after output files have been transferred back to the job’s spool directory and attributes about the job’s execution (like exit code) have been written to the job ad. Calling condor_transfer_data shouldn’t trigger chowning of the job spool directory. But trying the transfer before the DestroyProc() would explain a failure that Brian Lin has been seeing, where the transfer fails because it can’t read an output file with restricted permissions. As the gridmanager operates now, condor_ce_run should wait until JobStatus is COMPLETED and Managed is ScheddDone (or undefined, if for some reason the job runs directly under the CE schedd and isn’t routed). It would be easier on the client if step 2 were merged into step 4, with step 3 coming before it. Then, the client only has to consult the JobStatus attribute to see if it can retrieve the output files, and writing the terminate event won’t run into permissions problems. I don’t see a call to DestroyProc() in the job router for completed jobs. I assume it’s relying on the schedd to call it on some periodic check after Managed has been set to ScheddDone. That may be setting up a race condition between the spool directory being chowned and the client retrieving the output files.

title: Ticket #6724: condor_submit should determine spool files for late materialization
description: Currently, late materialization cannot be used when spooling input files because condor_submit never determines which files to spool, and thus never spools them. Currently condor_preen will delete spooled files for not-yet-materialized jobs. Also, there is no way to share a spooled file between jobs, so even if all of the jobs use the same input, the file would have to be spooled multiple times. We should probably fix the second problem before we add support for spooling to late-materialization. Possible spooling issues: user disk quota if there are shared input files, knowing NOT to update them when checkpointing. if there are shared input files and a checkpoint, knowing to use the checkpoint file We will most likely want to add to the cluster ad a special attribute that is the list of shared input files. This will probably be something we figure out by looking at the submit rather than requiring the user to tell us.

title: Ticket #3526: GRAM version detection fails if jobmanager service not defined
description: When the gridmanager receives gram jobs, it probes the remote resource to determine whether it's running GRAM2 or GRAM5. This affects how the gridmanager interacts with the remote system. The gridmanager (via the gahp) issues a globus_gram_client_register_get_jobmanager_version() request to the gatekeeper service 'jobmanager' on the remote system. A GRAM2 jobmanager will reply with gram error HTTP_UNPACK_FAILED. A GRAM5 jobmanager will reply with success and some version information. On most systems, gatekeeper service 'jobmanager' is an alias to one of the other service names (typically, 'jobmanager-fork'). We've now seen a system where 'jobmanager' is not a valid service name. When this happens, the gram code returns error SERVICE_NOT_FOUND. The gridmanager will mark the jobmanager as GRAM2 and periodically retry issuing the version request. Instead, the gridmanager should try the gatekeeper service names given by the Condor jobs in their GridResource attribute. Those should be valid service names, if the user hasn't screwed something up.

title: Ticket #3176: Schedd can't remove local universe execute directories
description: When the schedd starts up, it ensures the execute directory for local universe jobs exists and is empty. It uses Directory::Remove_Entire_Directory() to clean out any subdirectories. But when it instantiates the Directory object, it doesn't provide a privilege level. As a result, Remove_Entire_Directory() tries to remove files/directories only as the current privilege (i.e. condor). But the directories are owned by the owner job, so the removal fails. If we passed in PRIV_CONDOR to the Directory constructor, then Remove_Entire_Directory() would also try the removal as the file/directory owner. This all takes place in Scheduler::initLocalStarterDir().

title: Ticket #3208: File transfer with older starters can put stdout/err in wrong location
description: When a new shadow talks with an old starter (pre/post 7.7.2), file transfer is being used, and the job's stdout and stderr contain any path information, the shadow needs to rename the files in the ad sent to the starter and add remaps to their real destinations. Otherwise, the files will end up in the IWD. In some situations, the shadow doesn't know what version the starter is at the point it needs to do the renames. This can happen if security negotiation is disabled or SEC_ENABLE_MATCH_PASSWORD_AUTHENTICATION is set to True. GlideinWMS is running into this situation. The best fix we can do without a significant protocol change is to have the shadow always perform the stdout/err renames when it doesn't know the starter's version and it does know that file transfer will be used. This won't affect new starters. There is still the possibility for stdout/err to be written to incorrect locations when ShouldTransferFiles="IF_NEEDED" with a new shadow and old starter. There's no simple fix for this, as the shadow needs to know when sending the job ad to the starter whether file transfer will be used. The starter makes that decision after the shadow sends the job ad. If the shadow had the slot ad, it could figure out what the starter would decide. But this is a corner case that doesn't warrant a protocol change in a stable series.
remarks: 2012-Aug-24 17:31:06 by danb: Code Review: This patch looks okay to me. It is too bad that it doesn't work with the default file transfer mode IF_NEEDED. The workaround is for the user to use file transfer mode YES. 2012-Sep-06 18:20:52 by sfiligoi: Too bad ShouldTransferFiles="IF_NEEDED" is the default. So a lot of users are likely to be hit by this.

title: Ticket #200: standard universe is not compatible with spooling
description: if you submit a standard universe job with 'condor_submit -spool' or a remote submit (for example, via condor-c) the job will never run successfully. in particular, the old shadow does not know where to find the spooled executable to send to the starter, and tries to read a directory as if it were the executable. it probably doesn't make sense to use remote-submitted standard universe jobs for the purpose of remote I/O, since the shadow will be running under the remote schedd and that is probably not what users expect. however, the remote-submitted standard universe concept is still useful for checkpointing, which is why they want this to work.
remarks: 2010-Oct-27 12:11:24 by danb: I stumbled into this problem when testing my changes to the spool directory layout for #1706. My changes do not alter the fact that standard universe and spooling are incompatible, but my changes do alter the way it fails. Rather than failing late in the game and getting stuck in an infinite retry loop in the standard universe shadow, condor_submit fails to spool the files. This happens because the schedd is now smart enough to know not to create a per-job directory for standard universe jobs.

title: Ticket #2049: condor_procd crashes on SIGHUP
description: We recently encountered an issue where glideins were getting preempted. Before the preempting remote batch system sent a SIGTERM/SIGKILL combination, it first sent SIGHUP to the entire process tree. All the standard daemons that use DaemonCore re-read their config files, but the condor_procd crashed -- and then the other daemons shut themselves down. How to Fix Since condor_procd does not read any configuration files, just ignore SIGHUP.
creator: burt

title: Ticket #4934: Support IPv4 clients connecting to a mixed-mode pool.
description: Currently command line tools on an IPv4-only host will receive only IPv6 addresses from mixed-mode collectors for mixed-mode daemons. As a result, the command line tools cannot connect from an IPv4-only host. Goal: Command line tools running on IPv4-only hosts should to be able to contact mixed-mode daemons. New clients will choose an address based on protocol availability. Old clients will be given a best guess choice made by the collector. For proposed changes, see the design document. (Does PrivNet include a port) Sock::do_connect (/src/condor_io/sock.cpp line 1108) - First tries to use CCB (Sock::special_connect) . If that fails, tries a direct connection. title: Ticket #5333: Potential bug with DAGMan maxidle/DAGMAN_MAX_JOBS_IDLE
description: The DAGMan manual asserts that "maxidle" (and so, presumably, DAGMAN_MAX_JOBS_IDLE) limit jobs in the queue based upon the number of processes (not clusters). However, facilitators at CHTC have encountered many times when user jobs are submitted by dagman far beyond a point where the number of processes has exceeded the number specified for DAGMAN_MAX_JOBS_IDLE. When this happens, the queue can end up with too many jobs such that performance suffers (new jobs not matched readily, condor commands like "condor_q" don't return, etc.). Lauren Michael would be happy to provide a test case from a current user, and/or coordinate so that someone can do a full-scale test on one of our lesser-used submit servers.
remarks: 2015-Oct-22 15:51:09 by lmichael: FYI, Christina just tested the following case: DAG: Fifteen "JOB" lines, each with a submit file with "queue 3"; CONFIG dagman_config dagman_config: DAGMAN_MAX_JOBS_IDLE = 12 Result: all fifteen submit files of 3 processes were submitted Her test case can be viewed on submit-5.chtc.wisc.edu in /home/ckoch5/tests/dag_max_idle The JobID of her DAG was 5768099, and other Job IDs are in the log files (in the above path) Thanks, Lauren 2015-Oct-23 11:40:24 by wenger: Could you attach the relevant dagman.out file to this ticket? 2015-Oct-23 15:54:37 by wenger: Hmm -- I thought there was a maxidle test, but it looks like there isn't. Clearly there should be... 2015-Oct-26 13:05:23 by wenger: It looks like what's happening is that the maxidle limit is only being evaluated once per submit cycle. I'm thinking that maybe the easiest way to fix this is to set the max number of submits per cycle to 1 if you set maxidle, and then also increase the frequency of the submit cycles. (I guess if you set maxidle and also explicitly set the number of submits per cycle, your setting should be applied but probably with a warning if it's greater than 1...) 2015-Oct-26 13:12:00 by wenger: Hmm -- looks like that's not the whole problem. It looks like we are counting clusters, not procs... 2015-Oct-26 13:40:46 by wenger: Note that writing appropriate tests is now broken out into a separate tickets: #5345. 2015-Oct-27 16:54:10 by wenger: Created a branch for this: V8_4-gittrac_5333-branch 2015-Oct-28 09:36:50 by wenger: Okay, it looks like there are actually two problems here: First, we only check the maxidle count one time per submit cycle. So if your maximum number of submits per cycle is high relative to your maxidle setting, maxidle won't work very well. But the bigger problem is that, because of a bug in how we count idle job procs, we only count each cluster once, no matter how many idle procs it has. So maxidle doesn't really work right if you have multi-proc submit files for your node jobs. My current thought for the first one is to just force the cycle time and number of submits per cycle to small values if you have maxidle set. The second one is trickier -- I think we'll have to individually keep track of whether each proc in a cluster is idle or not. 2015-Nov-04 13:45:40 by wenger: There's also a third problem, that removing an idle job, for example, doesn't seem to reduce the idle count. 2015-Nov-04 13:47:21 by wenger: Oops, I'm wrong about removing idle jobs. At any rate, though, I need to check that the idle counts get updated correctly in a bunch of different cases... 2015-Nov-06 08:45:46 by wenger: Note: #5373 (Clean up DAGMan "node ending" code) is kind of related to this one, too... 2015-Nov-06 08:49:34 by wenger: There were actually three somewhat separate problems that I found that could goof up maxidle: We were just keeping track of the "is idle" state per node, not per proc. For multi-proc nodes, the node status gets set to STATUS_ERROR as soon as one proc fails; that was causing subsequent proc terminations to not update the idle count, even after the first problem was fixed. If you have a low maxidle setting (especially if you have multi-proc submit files), the number of submits per cycle can overwhelm maxidle, since the idle count only gets updated once per cycle. Part of the problem with fixing the first one was that Job::Cleanup() was getting called too soon for multi-proc nodes, which was goofing up the idle count. 2015-Nov-06 16:10:42 by wenger: Merged to V8_4-branch on verbal okay from Zach; ticket should be updated with code review note. 2015-Dec-22 16:29:53 by zmiller: CODE REVIEW: Had already reviewed and given verbal okay, forgot to update the remarks. Looks good.

title: Ticket #4871: Allow -notify_user to be set in condor_submit_dag
description: Tom Downes just pointed out that -notify_user is not available on the condor_submit_dag command line. I'm also wondering whether we should have config macros specific to DAGMan for -notification and -notify_user.
remarks: 2015-Sep-22 13:28:12 by tpdownes: I've setup Condor 8.2.6 according to the most recent suggestions from the Condor team and have notifications working again. I am curious about the behavior under DAGs, which is not obvious to me from the manual. Let's say a user submits a DAG with jobs each of which have this in its submit file: notification = Complete notify_user = thomas.downes@ligo.org Further suppose that DAGMAN_SUPPRESS_NOTIFICATION is not set globally or locally and reverts to its default value of True. The entry in the manual for this variable states "Defaults to True, implementing behavior in which the user receives one notification email when the condor_dagman job completes, rather than thousands of notifications from each of the jobs submitted by condor_dagman." This is suggestive that the DAG-handled submission of a job with notifications enabled will create a notification at the end of the DAG run irrespective of the settings used in condor_submit_dag or in the file.dag.condor.sub file created by condor_submit_dag. # RESPONSE FROM KENT #Hmm -- the language in the DAGMAN_SUPPRESS_NOTIFICATION documentation #is incorrect. The DAGMAN_SUPPRESS_NOTIFICATION setting doesn't have any effect #on whether you get a notification email for the DAGMan job itself, and that defaults to #never. However, empirically, I don't believe that a notification is generated unless . I do see the ability to manually set "-notification" to condor_submit_dag but I don't see a corresponding "-notify_user" setting. How is one supposed to set these values for the DAG? Is this the recommended path to generate a post-DAG notification to a user-specified e-mail address? 1. condor_submit_dag -no_submit file.dag 2. Add 2 lines noted above to job ClassAd in "file.dag.condor.sub" 3. condor_submit file.dag.condor.sub That works as it ought to, but it seems like there are 2 too many steps. # RESPONSE FROM KENT #Yes, you're right. There are two or three problems here: # #1) The language in the DAGMAN_SUPPRESS_NOTIFICATION section is misleading. #2) There should be a way to set notify_user in condor_submit_dag. Probably just adding a -notify_user argument is the way to go. #3) I wonder if -notification should default to always for DAGs. Or maybe there should be config macros for -notification and -notify_user? 2015-Sep-22 13:38:53 by tpdownes: In-person conversation with Kent suggest following actions: -notify_user argument to condor_submit_dag DAGMAN_NOTIFICATION DAG config entry DAGMAN_NOTIFY_USER DAG config entry Open questions: Should notification-related DAG config entries actually be keywords in .dag file so that they are more "user facing"? Should condor_dagman "inherit" the notification settings of its jobs following some rules? For example, if any job sets notification != Never, to inherit that value for the condor_dagman job?

title: Ticket #715: Make building clipped Condor very portable (NMI)
description: We want to make building clipped Condor very portable -- so portable that a native build can be easily performed on every platform in the BatLab. This would solve the problem of the NMI lab running RHEL3 binaries everywhere, and even worse, or running ancient versions of Condor on some of the more arcane platforms. Clipped Condor is already very portable, so this really isn't that big of a task. At first blush, what needs to happen is the following: configure.ac has to correctly detect the platform condor_sysapi needs to return the correct arch and opsys make_final_tarballs has to have the hash tables updates for the appropriate architectures If the externals all build, then this is <20 minutes of work [hee hee! that was a shockingly wrong estimate!]. If the externals don't build, then we probably want --with-proper to just use as externals what it finds on the machine. Milestones 03/24/2010 - Fix failing tests [DONE]. 03/09/2010 - Fix failing/pending builds [DONE] Fix Hpux gnu tar cannot make >2GB files. [DONE] Fix solaris 5.8 to not compile soapshell [DONE] Fix startd segfault on x86_suse_10.0 [DONE] Requires #1106 to complete. 02/01/2010 [DONE] Merge V7_4-submit_info-branch all the way into master. This may cause issues, but it should be dealt with by fixing them, not by reversion.

The work I've done so far involved altering the submit_info file format to allow specification of configure arguments to both the build and test glues. Here is some rationale behind it: The main problems concerning integrating Nick's work (which weren't caused by Nick, but something I ran into in the course of continuing his work) were: 1. You couldn't pass arbitrary configure arguments for either the builds or the tests that varied by platform. 2. The automatic building of a platform defined in submit_info was coupled to the presence of the platform description in submit_info. This meant a platform that normally wasn't built could be specified on the command line to condor_nmi_submit, but then couldn't have any prereqs associated with it, since associating prereqs with it would cause it to be built in the nightlies, etc, etc, etc. So, if you wanted to do a one off of a platform which required a prereq, you were out of luck. 3. Whitespace handling in submit_info was a complete joke and was never thought about in the parsing code. The parsing code was also pretty large pile of unmaintainable and confusing trash. 4. There was no good way to build/test condor on unknown platforms which needed arbitrary configure args, prereqs, or other things in an attempt to try to build a port noone has ever tried on before and noone knows anything about. As an example, suppose x86_64_fedora_12 comes out tomorrow and NMI finds that they can run some other port on it so it shows up in the pool. There is no good way to run a test build on that platform through NMI itself since number 1 and 2 from above opposed the action and you couldn't specify all of the configure flags to turn everything, or just a subset of features, off. So, I rewrote the horrible submit_info file to be a pure perl syntax SubmitInfo.pm file where we encode everything we care about the build and test of every platform into statically initialized data structures. It is nice to have ONE place in a file where everything for that platform is specified and it makes adjusting the build and test parameters for a platform hilariously easy and almost context free. Then I fixed condor_nmi_submit to load this module at run time (after checking it out of git if need be, etc), and write all of the build/test glue using it. One very nice feature I added was that you now specify build/test sets of platforms in SubmitInfo.pm and give them real names. for example, I can type this now: ./condor_nmi_submit <args> --platforms=official_ports and get all of the ports we natively compile and officially wish to distribute. Of course, it is smart, so you can do --platforms=official_ports,ia64_rhas_4 and it'll produce the union of the set and the platform, it even works when and if you supply multiple sets in addition to individual platforms. By default, if you don't specify any platforms, you get 'official_ports'. As a bonus, the SubmitInfo.pm file is actually also a perl executable which you can run. It will typecheck what you wrote to ensure that you typed in legal information, answer simple questions about the information, or generate interesting reports about the data--like which platforms use what prereq and stuff like that. 2009-Nov-04 16:05:42 by psilord: I have workspace build, tests, and builds with automatic tests working. I've found one kind of nasty problem, which I wrote into #974 as well. Basically, not only does the glue code expect to be identical across all branches (except for the SubmitInfo.pm file), it expects to be identical across all time as well. What this means is that we don't have the capability of easily rebuilding tags and branches previous to Feb 1, 2010 because the new glue code expects to see the new concepts it wants on past tags and branches. I vote we just say goodbye to the ability to build previous things and move on with our lives. 2010-Feb-10 10:24:42 by psilord: After several more days of watching. It appears there was one more issue which I've already fixed and seen work, but I'll describe here. The issues was in the nightly.pl build script, we call condor_nmi_submit with --nightly and that checks out each SubmitInfo.pm file associated with a branch, and submits a build. The problem was that once SubmitInfo.pm was loaded, if we tried to load it again (say for a different branch), perl's module idempotency check caused the module to not be loaded, but report as having loaded properly. Since the V7_4-branch and master SubmitInfo.pm files were so close together, I hadn't noticed this. The fix was to do some hackery with perl's module system and delete the knowledge of the loaded module from perl's global module state so when the load module happened again the module would actually load. In this scenario, the definitions of the exported symbols and whatnot override the previous definitions, which is what we want. title: Ticket #4522: priv-state code may unset supplemental groups
description: The priv-state code has some strange behavior. If call sites are not very careful, the supplemental groups may become unset. For instance, this could happen if the user uid/gid is reinitialized when already in user priv-state. This land-mine was stepped on in #4437. In #4437, we just did a minimal fix of the call-site in the shadow since it was in the stable series. With this ticket, we want a solution in the developer series that prevents a future developer from stepping on the same land mine: either the priv-sep code should deal with this sequence of invocations correctly, or if this is overly difficult to fix, at least it should assert/execept with a clear error message and comments in the code. But what is not acceptable is just leaving the code in a state whereby user priv info may be silently dropped like we observed in #4437.

title: Ticket #1370: condor_q and condor_status reports should use -format interface
description: condor_q and condor_status have a bunch of code internally to generate the various supported reports. They read the relevant ClassAds, and pass them through printf. A user can reproduce those reports from scratch using -format and -constant, to varying levels of accuracy. For example HowToWriteaCondorqWrapper documents how to almost reproduce the default condor_q report. Note that it's hard to read (it was hard to write) and it hard codes unsafe assumptions about the possible values of JobStatus. We have two very different code paths to accomplish the same result. This is bad because redundant code paths bloat our code and create opportunities for bugs to sneak in. The two code paths can drift so that one might include features not present in the other. (Today the C-code implements a number of features that are impossible to exactly reproduce in -format commands.) We can't offer users a starting template if they want to craft their own reports. Proposed: The core of all reports generated by condor_q and condor_status (that is, excluding the headers and footers) should be generated as though by using the -format and -constraint options. This will simplify the code. This will exercise our -format and ClassAd code to ensure they include functionality we ourselves would want. It would let us add a "-dump-command" option that would output the exact condor_q or condor_status command to replicate the core of the report, giving users a template to start from. This should be approached one report at a time. I suggest starting with "condor_status -master" which can be exactly replicated with condor_status -format '%s\n' Machine -master (It should be possible to replicate using condor_status -any -format '%s\n' Name -constraint "MyType=='DaemonMaster'" but limitations in how the constraint is done mean it doesn't work. It should. See #508 for details.) After creating the basic glue to make this work at all, then move from report to report, implementing them. If a given report can't be perfectly implemented, create a ticket documenting the additional functionality needed (ex. #1368), and move on to the next report.

title: Ticket #4488: Allow re-queue DAG POST jobs
description: (Kent and I discussed this in April, but I don't think I created a ticket.) The POST scripts for CMS can sometimes take a very long time to finish - however, they are idle 99% because they wait for an external service to acknowledge job completion. Because each POST script takes 20MB of RAM (they are python-based), we limit the number of concurrent running POSTs to 10. This causes blocking behavior - other jobs can't be processed if we have 10 jobs that are taking a long time to complete in the external system. I would like to see a new option for post scripts, "REQUEUE X TIME Y". If the POST job exits with code X, then the POST script is added to the end of the event queue after Y seconds.

title: Ticket #3967: ClassAd quantize() can fail when in a cached expression
description: During evaluation of the ClassAd quantize() function, if the second argument is a list, we evaluate each element of the list. We use a variant of ExprTree::Evaluate() that looks up the parent scope in the ExprTree of the list element. If the whole exprTree has been cached, this parent scope isn't set and the evaluation fails. We should be using the ExprTree::Evaluate() variant that takes an EvalState object, which contains the necessary scope information. The incorrect behavior can be observed with this command: condor_status -af '[a = quantize(3, {2})].a' This should print '4' for each machine ad in the collector. If ClassAd caching is enabled, blank lines are printed instead.

title: Ticket #3064: debug_wait should be volatile

title: Ticket #7498: Opt-in printing of job event log as JSON records
description: Proposal: it would be convenient if admins/users could opt-in to printing their job event logs as JSON records instead of as formatted text (the current behavior). JSON is a nice format for this because it balances human readability with much easier, more flexible, and backwards-compatible parsing. Plus, you don't need our library code to parse it! I am imagining a config knob JOB_EVENT_LOG_FORMAT (USER_JOB_EVENT_LOG_FORMAT?), as well as a submit-level override job_event_log_format (or perhaps log_format, to match the existing log command). The values for this knob would be VERBOSE (?) or JSON. Each record should contain two keys: one to hold "event" information, like the type of the event, the timestamp, a human-readable cause, etc; and one to hold a user-defined projection of the job ad at the time of event. It would be convenient if we supported both a whitelist and a blacklist mode for the projection, so that it's easy to specify a small, human-readable set, or to exclude certain things if you're just slurping them up into a database. This format is easily extensible to events that don't concern a single job. For example, a cluster or set-level event could produce a record with a "cluster_ad" key instead of a "job_ad" key (perhaps they should both just be "ad"; the point is that we can provide the right ad for the event type). To maintain a degree of human-readability, the JSON format should be reasonably verbose, something like { # one event "event": { "code": 7 "cause": "job was held", "holdReason": "you messed up real bad", "timestamp": 12345678, # any other details coming from the event architecture itself... }, "job_ad": { "ClusterId": 1234, "ProcId": 42, # user/admin-set projection of job ad follows... } } { # next event # contents... } The JSON output should just be the result of doing JSON conversion on the event classad (which is currently converted into formatted text). ToddM points out that not all the information is in the event ad; things like the timestamp may need to be injected before printing. (superseded by the paragraph above the example format) Note the above is not strictly valid JSON (it's not an array of records, it's just records stacked after each other). In Python (for example), parsing these is a little annoying (https://stackoverflow.com/questions/27907633/multiple-json-objects-in-one-file-extract-by-python/47958749), but not prohibitively so. We would need to point this out clearly in the docs and give strategies for parsing the event log correctly.
remarks: 2020-Feb-10 20:39:12 by bbockelm: Note the format proposed is basically JSON streaming: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/JSON_streaming Several libraries handle newline-delimited streams well. YMMV for the more complex example above. 2020-Feb-11 08:59:38 by tlmiller: In particular, I think we want "Concatenated JSON". Quoting Wikipedia: "The advantage of this format is that it can handle JSON objects that have been formatted with embedded newline characters, e.g., pretty-printed for human readability." In particular, it suggests -- and I think we want for readability anyway -- a newline after each object. On the other hand, it seems like it the reader might be easier to code and more resilient to pretty-printing changes if we keep our record separator intact (...\n): import json # Warning, terrible Python ahead text = "" blobs = [] with open("log") as file: while True: line = file.readline() if line == "": blobs.append(json.loads(text)) break elif line == "...\n": blobs.append(json.loads(text)) text = "" else: text = text + line for blob in blobs: print(blob)

title: Ticket #2360: CCB command handlers can block for 20s due to misbehaving client
description: We had an incident that we believe was caused by "misbehaving" daemons that made the CHTC collector block for 20s each time the collector tried to service CCB_REGISTER commands from those daemons. When the CCB server (collector) services the CCB_REGISTER command, and security negotiation is turned on, it is possible that the command payload (a small classad) has not arrived yet. If security negotiation is disabled, the command int and the payload are part of the same message, so by the time we get to the command handler, we know that the payload has already been sent. Security negotiation causes the command int and the payload to be sent in separate messages. The solution we would like to follow is to add an option when registering a command to tell DaemonCore to wait (non-blocking) for at least one byte of the payload to arrive. Then we can afford to use a very short timeout in the command handler, and the server will not be vulnerable to strangely behaving clients that do not send the payload for 20 seconds.
remarks: 2011-Aug-08 16:57:55 by danb: I should note that when a daemon first starts up, it does a blocking CCB_REQUEST, so this is unlikely to be the case that was causing trouble. If the initial request fails, or if the CCB connection ever goes bad, daemons then retry connecting periodically using asynchronous requests.

title: Ticket #3988: Support OpenNebula's "unknown" state.
description: Parag Mhashilkar writes: Glideinwms shutdown the VM from within the VM itself as a matter of cleanup when there is no work to be done for a while. When this happens in the VM launched by OpenNebula, OpenNebula puts the VM in the unknown state. Condor sees this state and thinks that the VM is done and puts the VM job in complete state. What we want is for condor to recognize this state and to explicitly issue a terminate on that VM if the vm stays in unknown state for a while. Or a solution on similar grounds so that the vms are not forgotten. ... Unknown state is a tricker business. From what I understand, if openenbula cannot get any info about he vm from the libvirtd, it puts the vm in unknown state. So the problem could be transient. However in our case, its almost always a vm shutdown from within the vm. I have also mentioned this issue on the opennebula mailing list that openebula should be able to get more info from the libvirt and put the vm in stopped state rather than unknown. Said that even if we get any fixes from openenbula, it will be a while and till then we have to manually (or rather cron) remove these vms periodically to free up the resource. ... Terminate (on stop or unknown) is indeed what we want. Since unknown could mean many things, will it be possible for htcondor to try few times before issuing a terminate? Also, if and when opennebula gives more concrete info on vm status, we may also have to take those changes into account.
remarks: 2013-Oct-18 10:20:06 by tlmiller: Parag's logs don't include the "unknown" state. Replied seeking more information. 2014-Jan-09 13:45:43 by tlmiller: Parag will look into this further; the "unknown" state was being reported by OpenNebula's tools, not its EC2 interface.
creator: tlmiller

title: Ticket #1673: request for coordinated exit among glideins
description: Dear Condor team. We want to submit a set of multiple-slot glideins that each starts X startds (on multiple nodes). The problem is how to shut them down. The current mechanism is to shut down individual glideins if not used for N minutes. This can mean that a fraction of the startds of a multi-slot request dies, but not all of them; but the Grid batch system still charges us for all X slots (MPI model). We need a better way to do this. An obvious solution would seem to be for the startds in the multi-slot request to know about each other, and only die if ALL of them are idle for more then N minutes. I don't think there is a way in Condor today to do this. Do you think this is something you could add? Thanks, Igor for the glidein/corral team
remarks: 2010-Sep-24 11:34:58 by psilord: Do we have any kind of a hook that when a startd decides to die it can fire off a script to condor_off -constraint the rest of them? 2010-Sep-24 11:38:04 by psilord: The responsibility of this is interesting. If it is the glidin factory's responsibility, then it can do a condor_status -const on a set of glidins and compute whether or not all of them should die. If so, in one fell swoop it could kill them. On the other hand, if the slots all had to communicate with each other, that smacks of distributed communication protocols, which will likely be more complex to get right and be harder to debug. 2011-Jan-27 14:50:47 by danb: Bulk change of target version from v070505 to v070506 using ./ticket-target-mover. 2011-Feb-01 16:20:02 by tannenba: Bulk change of target version from v070506 to NULL using ./ticket-target-mover.

Ticket #5775: OOM killed all jobs in htcondor cgroup rather than offending job
description: Below are a bunch of logs from Tom at LIGO showing strange behavior with cgroups, where jobs that are well below there memory limit were being targeted by the OOM and thus put on hold by HTCondor. After investigation, it turns out that if memory use_hierarchy is 1, then hitting the limit at the parent notifies all children, even if those children are below their usage. The upshot we think when LIGO put all of htcondor into a cgroup hierarchy, and some other process outside of the HTCondor hierarchy on the machine exhausted memory, the OOM typically picked a HTCondor job to be killed (because we set the OOM priorites that way, to ensure jobs get killed before HTConnor daemons). Obviously having HTCondor put jobs on hold due to memory when the jobs were not using anything close to their requested_memory is undesired. Our approach to improve this situation is to add a boolean config knob, IGNORE_LEAF_OOM. If set to True, upon notification from the OOM, the starter will check how much memory the job is using. If the job is using more memory than allocated, the job is killed and put on hold as before. But if the job us using less memory than allocated, the starter will then ignore the notification from the OOM and continue to let the job run. Hopefully, some other process will be killed, and when it does, the job will get unfrozen and continue to run. As a next step, if this approach works well in testing, we should a) set IGNORE_LEAF_OOM to True by default in the param table, and b) setup a more reasonable default for MEMORY that understands HTCondor cannot allocate all physical RAM - some must be set aside for the system OS and/or a few typical system services that are common on execute nodes(like monitoring, puppet, etc). Reported by Tom from LIGO: It looks to me like 1 job greatly exceeded its memory request and took down a number of other jobs that were respecting their memory request. Is this Condor-intended behavior? Is it a consequence of my use of memory.use_hierarchy - the only way I know of to cap total Condor consumption before it uses all of RAM? If so, do you know of a way of guiding the OOM killer to target offending jobs within a hierarchy first? title: Ticket #4867: Docker Universe should check command at submit time.
description: The following submit file currently causes us grief. universe = docker command = file-on-disk docker_image = ubuntu queue 1 {encode} condor_submit will set TransferExecutable to false, which will cause the starter to conclude that shouldn't prepend the full path to the command passed to Docker. Even if we actually did transfer the executable, the job still won't run because the sandbox is not in the PATH by default. condor_submit should check to see if the commmand exists on the submit disk in the usual way. If it does, do nothing special. (Let it be transferred, or not, according to the usual rules.) If it does not exist, then fail if transfer_executable is not false, explaining that setting transfer_executable to false in Docker universe is how you tell HTCondor that you want to run a command from the image, not from the sandbox. The starter will then prepend the sandbox('s mountpoint) to the command if and only if transfer_executable is not false (true or absent) and the path is relative. (This assumes that transfer executable is true or absent when running jobs off a shared file system.)
creator: tlmiller

title: Ticket #7318: Implement data reuse mechanism in the starter
description: We'd like to have a mechanism for the execute side to maintain files between job invocations. This data: Will be referred to by its contents (i.e., a checksum) Is allocated and managed. The execute side decides when it will reuse the data and the lifetime. The shadow is responsible to inform the execute side when the data potentially will be reused. Is guaranteed to not have the aggregate reused data go over some admin-defined threshold. Does not persist between startd restarts. That is, it's not permanent "state" the startd keeps (contrast with the job queue log the schedd maintains). Is private and belongs to the submitting user. See design doc: https://docs.google.com/document/d/1OoEJuh5URXMIrGDJp8QI9MfcbfsFy8XnnrJEY9Cvfuw/edit#heading=h.vmt7b4o3ffxu

title: Ticket #3422: Fix locking code
description: Locking code appears to not work under heavy load. Either rip it out and replace with something from condor_utils or fix the error handling.
remarks: 2013-Jan-09 19:03:20 by bbockelm: There are actually some deeper issues here - Properly done, we should use retries with exponential backoff. There's no guarantee the sysadmin isn't also invoking iptables. Alternately, the process with the lock may have gone to sleep indefinitely due to some unknown bug. Probably what we should do is some sort of opportunistic locking approach - try doing a lock. After 1s, switch to the exponential backoff algorithm. It's going to be fairly miserable to have a well-designed interface for the admin setup/cleanup scripts. Probably no sysadmin is ready for this sort of behavior - no one does concurrent iptables I suspect, so no one is ready for things to fail due to this reason. 2013-Jan-09 19:46:23 by bbockelm: The locking code seems to have been mostly a matter of a wrong locking flag (FD_SETLK versus FD_SETLKW). Once that's fixed, the next problem is the firewall cleanup code. Since the iptables rules for bridge mode are pretty trivial, that may not be such a big issue for the demo. Definitely an issue for the NAT code.

title: Ticket #3072: JobRouter should forcex jobs that can't be removed
description: I found a case where the JobRouter couldn't remove an orphaned jobs. The source job got removed by the user, cleaning up the spool directory. When restarting the JobRouter, it correctly identified the destination job as from the source job. It tried to remove the destination job (grid universe, batch gahp). The schedd passed the remove signal to the gridmanager; when the constructor of the infnbatch job fired, it failed to acquire the proxy, placing the job immediately on hold. Every JobRouter poll interval, this occurs. Minimal solution: if "JobStatusOnRelease = 3" in the job's classad, forcibly remove it. Thorough solution: when removing the job, set an attribute ("OrphanRemovedByRouter = TRUE"). If that is set on an orphan job, forcibly remove it.
remarks: 2012-Jun-21 09:41:12 by danb: Forcibly removing the orphan job may still leave behind an orphan in the "remote" batch system. Is there a lease or something that will eventually take care of that? 2012-Jun-21 09:44:51 by jfrey: There's no mechanism for a lease with the blahp, as most batch systems it submits into don't support leases. 2012-Jun-21 09:55:41 by bbockelm: Hi Dan, That's why my suggested solution is to only forcex after it has attempted to remove it once. I guess the safer alternate would be to ignore jobs it has already attempted to remove? Brian 2014-Nov-26 11:19:35 by jfrey: I've changed the gridmanager so that grid-type batch jobs can be removed after the job sandbox has been removed. There are some deeper issues with sandbox management between the job router and gridmanager, but that is beyond the scope of this ticket. 2014-Dec-01 09:26:06 by tim: CODE REVIEW: Looks good, I approve this change.

title: Ticket #7031: Make CheckpointExitCode a first-class submit command.
description: If we're claiming that support for self-checkpointing jobs in vanilla universe is no longer experimental, we should add it to the submit language as a first-class command. TJ proposes, and I concur, that the job ad attribute WantFTOnCheckpoint is effectively redundant with having +SuccessCheckpointExitCode set, and that the latter would be better without the 'Success' prefix. Thus: self-checkpointing.submit checkpoint_exit_code = 17 would: set the job ad attribute WantFTOnCheckpoint to TRUE. set the job ad attribute SuccessCheckpointExitCode to 17. (It turns out that when_to_transfer_output does not need to be set to ON_EXIT_OR_EVICT. This also means that checkpoint updates do not need to be atomic, which simplifies things for our users.) The document at HowToRunSelfCheckpointingJobs should updated to reflect the new syntax and that ON_EXIT_OR_EVICT is optional. This ticket renders #7014 obsolete. This ticket renders #7022 obsolete. This ticket renders #7003 part 1 obsolete.
remarks: 2019-Jun-11 18:35:27 by tlmiller: ... did this ever need ON_EXIT_OR_EVICT set? The old documentation doesn't think so. The code certainly supports the assertion that it's not presently necessary. Have I just been being confused? 2019-Jun-14 17:12:25 by tlmiller: Part 1, from #7013: Write (after the doc freeze thaws) a new page/section in the manual about self-checkpointing (in the vanilla universe, where it matters). Introduce/reinforce the ON_EXIT_OR_EVICT idea, best practices about atomic updates to checkpoint files, and the general sequence and tools used to test self-checkpointing. This does not necessarily need to mention ExperimentalSupportForPeriodicCheckpointingInVanillaUniverse, but it could. The use of chirp might also be discussed, if only to explain why its limitations. To be more specific, the condor_vacate_job / condor_transfer_data pairing pairing should be mentioned, not just in the self-checkpointing section, but also in their respective man pages. 2019-Jun-14 19:51:40 by tlmiller: Updated HowToRunSelfCheckpointingJobs; needs a polishing pass. 2019-Jun-20 11:56:46 by tlmiller: Reviewed in-person.

title: Ticket #88: PrivSep Switchboard should provide more detail in error messages
description: When the Switchboard fails to perform a requested operation, it sends an error string back to its calling Condor daemon. This feature is useful, but the error messages themselves are often too general. For example, you may get something like: "failure to chown sandbox". It would be more useful to get the exact system call errno or what safety check failed. Perhaps more useful would be something like an "error stack". It may also be useful to allow warning messages to be propagated up to the calling daemon in addition to errors. For example, "recursive chown complete, but some FS nodes left alone due to wrong ownership" (See #86). Of course, however this is improved we need to keep it simple since this is in the root-enabled portion of Condor's PrivSep architecture.

remarks: 2020-Feb-26 16:02:02 by tannenba: I tend to think of the bindings for negotiation and COD as experimental, and I am not aware of any existing (or planned) users. Not certain I want to commit to support these methods once 8.9 moves to a new stable series; we have other higher priority work to do. Thus my thinking is we should remove the negotiation and COD examples from the tutorials and documentation for now instead of spending development effort fixing/documenting them. 2020-Feb-27 09:01:29 by karpel: Done. Will downgrade priority, but leave the ticket open for now.

title: Ticket #3834: DAG hung at LIGO
description: See the "Socket between submit and execute hosts closed unexpectedly" emails on the LIGO list, starting July 24, 2013. Note: at first glance, I'm not sure whether this is really a DAGMan problem or a problem in some other part of HTCondor.
remarks: 2013-Aug-07 17:06:35 by wenger: Okay, here's the problem: 07/24/13 06:45:45 Number of idle job procs: 22 07/24/13 06:45:45 Of 2236 nodes total: 07/24/13 06:45:45 Done Pre Queued Post Ready Un-Ready Failed 07/24/13 06:45:45 === === === === === === === 07/24/13 06:45:45 1363 0 0 0 250 609 14 Note that 22 jobs procs are supposedly idle when there are no jobs in the queue!! The idle count clearly got goofed up somehow. I'll try to figure that out, but I'm also thinking that, as a failsafe, when the number of queued jobs hits 0, we should also set the number of idle job procs to 0. (Note that the idle count is job procs, not just jobs, so it is possible for the idle count to be greater than the "jobs in the queue" count.) 2013-Aug-07 17:36:22 by wenger: Ah, here's the problem: 07/23/13 11:02:17 Number of idle job procs: 16 07/23/13 11:02:17 Event: ULOG_JOB_TERMINATED for Condor Node 9565424f3cb7e9e7af84554e3e30f4a1 (3577562.0.0) 07/23/13 11:02:17 Number of idle job procs: 16 07/23/13 11:02:17 Event: ULOG_SHADOW_EXCEPTION for Condor Node 9565424f3cb7e9e7af84554e3e30f4a1 (3577562.0.0) 07/23/13 11:02:17 Number of idle job procs: 17 We get the shadow exception after the terminated event, which goofs things up because we still increment the idle count... So when we get an event that would normally mark a job as idle, we need to make sure the job hasn't already finished! 2013-Aug-13 10:22:36 by jfrey: Code Review This change looks good. 2013-Aug-13 13:31:11 by wenger: Fixes have been merged to V8_0-branch and master, so I'm going to resolve this.

remarks: 2014-May-12 10:15:52 by danb: The Wisconsin CMS T2 cluster was struck by this same error 666666 when attempting to execute jobs. In our case, many of the errors happened on machines that are not using partitionable slots. We also seem to see a bias towards higher error rates on newer beefier machines. We were running condor 8.0.5 at the time the error struck. 2015-Sep-21 13:03:50 by tpdownes: From Juan at Caltech: We managed to track this problem down to the multi-threaded processes running on the worker nodes and forking off enough processes to exceed the per user process limit (ulimit -u). At start-up (after a reboot), all jobs manage to make it to the nodes and finish. When a new job tries to occupy the vacated slot, the system won't allow it because the user, i.e. "gstlalcbc", has reached or exceeded the limitby then. The work-around is to set a really high limit in /etc/security/limits.d/90-nproc.conf (RHEL6) and /etc/security/limits.d/20-nproc.conf(RHEL7). For our purpose, we just set the nproc limit to unlimited for the gstlalcbc user since it's difficult to pin-point the exact ceiling for the multi-threaded jobs that run on the nodes. For reference the default limit for nproc is 1024 on RHEL6 and 4096 on RHEL7. 2015-Sep-21 13:05:46 by tpdownes: From LIGO's perspective the problem is resolved but Dan Bradley may wish to note our solution. (I realize this is an old ticket - I'm doing housecleaning)

title: Ticket #3137: Reduce memory usage of libcondor_utils
description: One of the things which really increases the shadow size is the non-shared portion of the data segment of libcondor_utils.so. It is currently 156KB in our releases. This is due to: Attributes being defined as global symbols. Parameter table is copied in the non-shared segment. TJ reports that MSVC handles "static const" correctly for the parameter table; GCC definitely does not. Boo! Excessively large PLT. 1 can be addressed by switching to defines. 2 can be fixed by forcing the parameter table into the text segment. 3 can be helped by LTO (although, honestly, there are just too many compilation units!). Patch is incoming - gets the data segment to 71KB. Hunting around, there are still some large statically-allocated arrays of size PATH_MAX (4KB) which almost certainly wastes memory, as well as a few other small sins. See posting to condor-dev.
remarks: Parameter table is copied in the non-shared segment. TJ reports that MSVC handles "static const" correctly for the parameter table; GCC definitely does not. Boo! I think this may have something to do with the shift to from static -> dynamic. Windows is still all static. This wouldn't violate the embedded packaging rules of Fedora, but it does bloat the shadow size (to the rest of the binaries combined!) to about 3MB. As much as I love small binaries, I think this particular case is worth it. 2012-Jul-19 08:38:23 by tstclair: buku nmi issues with patch: http://submit-2.batlab.org/results/run-details.php?runid=53984 I may have time later to run through. 2012-Jul-19 09:02:17 by tstclair: Now tracking in: master-shadow-memory 2012-Jul-19 21:10:03 by bbockelm: Latest build seems to have gone much smoother. That saves another 100KB. I've not heard strong opinions for or against, but I'm personally for it. Could you write such a patch? The one I have was a cop-out: I just created a new static library, condor_utils_static and linked the shadow to that. It works, but it ended up compiling condor_utils twice (felt like it was doubling the build time!). Another thing - the original patch had some changes to build/cmake/CondorConfigure.cmake that I was playing with: Enabling -flto. Can you do an NMI run on a platform with a more recent GCC? Disabling exceptions. We could disable exceptions everywhere in libcondor_utils. Enabling -Os. This decreases code size at the cost of optimizations... but maybe right for Condor? The latter two are commented out. Enabling LTO does seem to cause the compiler to find undefined references - some are in the schedd (easy fix), some are in CREAM (more difficult). Brian 2012-Jul-25 15:43:51 by tstclair: So I've added the check for compiler version, I think we'll revisit the static linkage when we address the multishadow till then I'll cop-out and wait for the other ticket. 2012-Jul-25 15:46:50 by tstclair: merged to master on 7/25 but imho requires a 2nd pass review, kicking to jfrey. 2012-Aug-01 15:32:03 by jfrey: I don't see any problems with the changes, but I have a few questions: Do your changes to the attribute names cause anything to move from non-shared memory to shared memory? Were the attribute names stored in non-shared memory before? I did a quick check on a couple binaries. Before your changes, there was one occurence of the string "ATTR_JOB_UNIVERSE" per reference in the souce code (both in binaries and libraries). After your changes, there was one occurence of the string "JobUniverse" per source file that mentioned ATTR_JOB_UNIVERSE (both in binaries and libraries). The primary benefit here seems to be shrinking the number of symbols that need to be resolved by libcondor_utils. I'm using rhel5. Do some of the copies of JobUniverse get coalesced with -flto? Do your changes to the param table cause anything to move from the data segment to the text segment? Were the parameter names and string values previously in non-shard memory, along with the the param_info_t structs? 2012-Aug-03 10:32:52 by bbockelm: Hi Jaime, Yes - attribute names were in non-shared memory before. They are shared now. Let's take "JobUniverse" as an example, a string of 11 characters. Previously, each reference to JobUniverse was an 8 byte pointer; it's now 11. Depending on the alignment, it's likely (but not guaranteed) many places will round this up to taking 16 bytes. Additionally, there was an entry in the library's and executable's hash map that contains the string "ATTR_JOB_UNIVERSE" (17 chars). Each reference to the job universe requires a fairly large jump in memory to the other library, thrashing the cache. So, for the 3 cases of ATTR_JOB_UNIVERSE in the shadow (don't forget to add the null byte), 2 * 18 + 3*8 = 60; 12+16+16 = 44 (looking at hexdump, in the condor_shadow, I see 3 cases of "JobUniverse", two of which are padded). In this case, repeating the string is a win. The bigger difference is that these strings were previously non-shared, and are now in the text section. In the case of LTO, all the "JobUniverse" strings are coalesced into one, saving a few more bytes (16, I think); above, I quote the non-LTO case. Brian

title: Ticket #241: File Transfer plugins
description: We want to allow URL-style file names for specifying the job's sandbox, e.g. transfer_input_files and transfer_output_files. Currently all files handled by the file transfer object are assumed to live on the submit machine, and are fetched by the starter via the shadow. For 7.4.0, URLs will only be supported for transfer_input_files. Supporting transfer_output_files will have to wait until the next series. Immediate Plan Allow job sandbox file names to have URLs that allow a file transfer plugin to be called (via a well-defined API) by the File Transfer Object to actually move the file in to the execute (or spool) directory. DONE Implement and demonstrate HTTP plugin. DONE Implement and demonstrate globus.org plug. DONE Implement and demonstrate HDFS (hadoop filesystem) plugin. DONE Add support for transfer_output_directory for using plugins to move job output. DONE Status The code is written and compiles and is checked into the V7_3_2-filetransfer_plugin-branch. Major changes are in condor_c++_util/file_transfer.[cpp|h] and the creation of the new directory condor_filetransfer_plugins. The code passed simple tests. More testing to come, and a test needs to be added to the test suite. Known and suspected problems documented below. Details The new file transfer command (5) will not be sent unless you set ENABLE_URL_TRANSFERS to True. When the FileTransfer object is instatiated, SimpleInit() now calls the function InitializePlugins(). This function params for FILETRANSFER_PLUGINS which should be a comma separated list of invokable plugins. These are invoked one at a time with the "-classad" option to find out their capabilities. See the API description below for details. The plugin is then entered into a hash table keyed on each of its supported methods. In FileTransfer::DoUpload(), if the file to be sent looks like a URL, according to the function isUrl(), then a different filetransfer command is sent. NOTE: this is not a different daemoncore command, it is a different integer as part of the DoUpload() protocol. (0 == still means "finished", 1 == normal,..., 4 == delagate proxy). now, 5 means "i'm sending you a URL, and you download it". The basename (filename to write on the DoDownload() side) is still decided by the sender, so filename remaps should still work even with URLs. In DoDownload(), if we received command 5, we then read the URL and attempt to retreive it. We find the type of the URL (up to the first ':'), look that up in the plugin_table hash table, and invoke the plugin. The current API to the plugin follows. NOTE: this format is going to change, as it has serious limitations. The limitations and suggested new format are below. invoking the plugin with the '-classad' should produce something like this: PluginVersion = "zkm! or maybe v0.1, or maybe a monotonically increasing int" PluginType = "FileTransfer" SupportedMethods = "http,ftp,file" otherwise, it is assumed that the first argument is the URL, and the second is the local filename to write the contents to. See the file src/condor_filetransfer_plugins/plugin-prototype for an example. PROBLEMS WITH THIS PLUGIN API: passing the URL on the command line sucks for a couple reasons: passwords for ftp and http can currently only be supplied by encoding them in the URL. they may be visible to other users by running 'ps'. example: http://zmiller:mypass@www.cs.wisc.edu/index.html there are limits on the length of command-line arguments (relatively small ones too if i remember), so the "data:" type becomes quite a bit less useful. so, i was thinking this would be better: command line options: <none> print usage? [-]-help print usage. -classad print classad (PluginType, PluginVersion, SupportedMethods) -get process stdin as a classad and do what it says with option '-get' (and eventually -put?) stdin will have a classad explaining what to do. SourceURL = url://to.the.place/and/directory/to/find/the_file DestFile = /full/path/to/local/filename then, the plugin dumps the contents to stdout. progress information is (optionally) reported on stderr. format of this is undefined for now. then, condor will select() on both stdout and stderr of the plugin. if both are inactive for some amount of time, it will be aborted. this way, simple plugins can simply dump the contents to stdout and be done with it. more advanced ones (robotic tape fetching plugins) can write progress information on stderr to keep the transfer alive if that data itself takes a while. OTHER PROBLEMS WITH THE NEW FILETRANSFER CODE: 1) this problem was resolved. move along. 2) i'm not sure if the shadow will timeout if for example, the starter is downloading a 2GB file. 3) i haven't tested remaps 4) this problem was resolved. move along. 5) when using remaps, the quoting is potentially messy. in transfer_input_files, things are separated with commas. URLs that contain commas should probably be encoded using the %2C method. also, in the remaps, equal signs and semicolons are special and need quoting. 6) the plugin API should be changed (see above) that's all for now.

title: Ticket #5688: Add JSON parsing/unparsing for ClassAds
description: JSON is a popular data format that's very similar to ClassAds, with lists and records of simple data values that can be nested arbitrarily. It would be very handy to parse JSON in ClassAds and vice versa. The main difference between ClassAds and JSON is that JSON doesn't support expressions with operators or functions. We can address this difference by representing expressions in JSON as decorated strings that can be recognized by the JSON-to-ClassAd parser. Differences between ClassAds and JSON Simple data types ClassAds have absolute and relative time types. ClassAds have the Error value. JSON does not make a strong distinction between integer and floating point numbers. Special values like Inf or NaN are not allowed. The ClassAds value Undefined can be mapped to JSON's null. JSON strings allow Unicode characters. In UTF-8 encoding (the default), most characters don't require an escape sequence. ClassAd strings are ASCII, with an escape notation for 8-bit non-ASCII values. Records (ClassAds vs JSON objects) The names in JSON objects are case-sensitive. Implementations can choose whether to preserve order and how to handle duplicate names. Expressions JSON doesn't support operators or functions. For all data types in ClassAds that cannot be directly represented in JSON, we will represent them as annotated strings that the JSON->ClassAd parser can recognize and restore to their original form. We are borrowing an idea that Microsoft used to represent dates as a special data types (http://weblogs.asp.net/bleroy/dates-and-json). In JSON, forward slash is one of the characters that can be escaped by a back slash inside a string, even though there's no need to do so. We can use this odd feature to represent an expression as a string in such a way that we can recognize it as something other than a simple string if we parse the JSON back into ClassAds. Here is how we'd represent the expression A + B in JSON: "\/Expr(A + B)\/" If our JSON-to-ClassAd parser sees this string, it will parse the text between the parentheses as normal ClassAd syntax. Other JSON parsers will treat it as a normal string. All ClassAd values should round-trip properly when rendered as JSON and read back directly. If the JSON text is parsed and unparsed by some other JSON library, then expressions may not be recognized, as they may no longer have the escaped slashes. Also, the distinction between integer and real numbers may be lost (integer becomes real or vice versa). JSON text can suffer some damage when round-tripped through ClassAds. Duplicate item names and ordering of items in an object are not preserved, but this is allowed by the JSON spec. If a JSON object contains multiple items whose names vary only in alphabetic case, then only one of the items will remain. This is not allowed by the spec.
remarks: 2016-May-31 14:54:54 by jfrey: The new -json option to condor_q and condor_status prints multiple JSON objects with only a newline for separation. The JSON parser for ClassAds will read this back properly, returning one ad each time it's invoked. But the output as a whole is not a valid JSON document. If that is a concern, we could insert a more-easily recognizable separator between objects or render the entire output as a list of objects (with list begin/end characters at the start and end).

title: Ticket #754: Option for jobs that run multiple times to append to output and error
description: Currently when a Condor job runs for the second or later times, it completely replaces the output and error files. While this is usually the correct behavior, it may not be what is desired in all cases. For example, the VDT is using Condor's cron behavior and would like the output and error to be appended to reflect an ongoing log file. Proposal: Add new options for condor_submit: "AppendError" and "AppendOutput". Both default to FALSE. If TRUE, these files will be appended to, not replaced, when a job runs a second or later time. This may lead to excessively large files for cron jobs that run over a long period or very frequently. In such a case automatic rotation and deletion might be nice; see #755. #326 suggests general shell-like control that might be used to implement this.

title: Ticket #1761: Local job slow to exit can kill schedd
description: The change made for ticket #699 uncovered a consistency problem in the value of Scheduler::LocalUniverseJobsRunning. It is recomputed periodically in Scheduler::count_jobs(). It is also updated when a local job is started (incremented) and when the job's starter exits (decremented). The counting of jobs marked for holding or removal which have yet to be killed is ambiguous. count_jobs() doesn't include these jobs, but between calls to count_jobs(), they are counted (due to when the decrement happens). If count_jobs() executes between when a job is marked for holding/removal and when its starter exits, LocalUniverseJobsRunning ends up under-counting and possibly going negative. Ticket #699 causes the schedd to EXCEPT when this happens. We're seeing this occasionally in the test suite with the job_core_perhold_local test. To remove ambiguity in LocalUniverseJobsRunning, count_jobs() (and count(), which it calls) can be changed to not ignore held and removed jobs. CurrentHosts in the job ad accurately reflects whether the job is running, so we could just remove the job status check. A similar change should be done for scheduler universe jobs.

title: Ticket #4133: Purged EC2 jobs may go on hold instead of being removed.
description: If a service purges its record of an instance before we attempt to terminate it (but after we've checked to see if it's still active), the attempt will fail, causing the job will go on hold. Instead, we should check the error, and if it fails because the instance we're trying to terminate doesn't exist, treat that as a success. This bug may be triggered by another bug, in which we neglect to wait for the status of the job to change before checking to see if it terminated.
