title: Ticket #304: Find a way to work around valid Layered Service Provider (LSP) on Win.
description: A common problem for Condor on Windows is improperly written Layered Service Providers (LSP). It would be nice to find a way to work around valid LSPs on Window, so that Condor could co-exist with them. From Wikipedia: "A Layered Service Provider (LSP) is a feature of the Microsoft Windows Winsock 2 Service Provider Interface (SPI). A Layered Service Provider is a DLL that uses Winsock APIs to insert itself into the TCP/IP stack. Once in the stack, a Layered Service Provider can intercept and modify inbound and outbound Internet traffic. It allows processing all the TCP/IP traffic taking place between the Internet and the applications that are accessing the Internet (such as a web browser, the email client, etc)." If possible, it would be nice if Condor could automatically bypass any of the installed LSPs and thus never fall victim to a broken one. Also, doing this would allow for applications that depend on the LSP to run in conjunction with, or as a job managed by Condor (currently, if the LSP "breaks" the socket, Condor will simply not work). For the Condor explanation of things, see: http://www.cs.wisc.edu/condor/manual/v7.2/7_4Condor_on.html#SECTION008414000000000000000
remarks: 2009-Mar-09 11:15:38 by burnett: Short of intercepting socket calls, or reverting to Winsock 1.x, there seem to be no way to disable LSPs across Windows flavours. The exception is Vista, which supports protecting process from malformed LSPs. Via the WSCSetApplicationCategory() API, Condor can select which layered service provider (LSP) categories are associated with its daemons. 2009-Oct-21 15:35:34 by psilord: Ben Burnett has left the Condor Project. This ticket is being unassigned. 2010-Oct-20 15:59:08 by jfrey: Bulk change of target version from v070504 to v070505 using ./ticket-target-mover. 2011-Jan-27 14:21:33 by danb: Bulk change of target version from v070505 to v070506 using ./ticket-target-mover. 2011-Feb-01 14:49:30 by tannenba: Bulk change of target version from v070506 to NULL using ./ticket-target-mover. 2015-Mar-07 15:44:49 by tannenba: Using newer Winsock APIs introduced since Vista, I think we finally can deal with LSPs by default. The problem is LSPs implementations may be sloppy and fail to implement socket inheritance features. So our algorithm is as follows - First, we get the real kernel handle, which can be obtained on recent Windows versions (Vista and newer) via an ioctl call. If it turns out that _sock is a real kernel handle, we can likely just call SetHandleInformation() which is Microsoft's current recommendation for changing the inheritance of a socket. But if _sock is from an LSP, of SetHandleInformation() fails for some reason, then we duplicate the kernel handle into a new socket that has the inheritance we want, and close the original _sock. As for documentation, besides the Version History blurb, I updated FAQ Wiki page WhyDaemonsExitThousandThirtyEight.

Ticket #7066: condor_q -current is wrong when schedd restarts and reconnects
description: currently condor_q -current calculates the current runtime by subtracting the shadow birthdate from the current time, and -run takes that value and adds RemoteWallClockTime to get the total runtime. When the Schedd restarts and reconnects to a running job, a new shadow is created and ShadowBDay is updated, and then RemoteWallClockTime is updated so that the runtime before the reconnect becomes 'historical' runtime. This means that after a reconnect condor_q -run is still correct. but condor_q -current only shows how long the current shadow has been alive rather than the actual current runtime of the job from the perspective of the job (and of the stater). We should change condor_q so that the calculation of current runtime uses JobCurrentStartDate, which does not get changed when a reconnect happens.

title: Ticket #6227: Memory leak in python bindings due to dprintf buffering
description: Jitendra in htcondor-users reports observing a memory leak when attempting to verify the memory leak fix in #5727. He used the snippet of python code from that ticket and saw the leak in both 8.4 and 8.6. I can reproduce the behavior on my own machine. Valgrind confirms that #5727 fixed a memory leak. It also revealed that the additional memory leak is due to dprintf() buffering all log messages in memory until a dprintf_config_*() function is called. The python bindings don't do this, but so expose a couple functions to let the user do so. The python bindings should call one of the dprintf config functions with reasonable defaults (e.g. subsystem TOOL and flags to drop all messages) during initialization, and allow the user to alter these via exported functions.

title: Ticket #1018: queue super user cannot drop privs
description: As of 7.2.0, the queue super user has the power to change the value of Owner to any owner who has a job in the queue or who has ever had a job in the queue during the life of the current running schedd. This was added for JobRouter. The problem with this is that condor_shadow authenticates to the schedd as the condor user (always a super user) when performing set_job_attr operations on behalf of chirp calls made by the job. Therefore, the job can change its own Owner attribute, requeue itself, and gain access to somebody else's account. It can only gain access to accounts that have submitted a job to condor or to the "condor" user, and it can not gain access to root, because condor will not run jobs as root. A pithy example of how to reproduce the problem appears in a remark from tannenba below. The solution we decided to pursue in 7.2.5 and 7.4.1 is to add a qmgmt command that allows the queue super user to reduce privileges to that of an ordinary user so that all subsequent operations in the qmgmt session are done as though by the other user (like seteuid() in unix). The job queue updater used by the shadow (and local starter) does this in all cases immediately after establishing a qmgmt session. This addresses the problem of chirp but also reduces risk of other operations being allowed that should not be. Changing the shadow to authenticate as the user instead of condor is another possible solution. This is problematic, because not all authentication methods support authenticating as the user from within a condor daemon. For those methods that do support authentication based on priv state (such as FS), the security session cache does not keep track of what priv state was used to create the session, so we would either need to fix that, or change all shadow --> schedd communication to be done as the user (including the daemon keepalive and possibly other things I am forgetting). Removing the power of the super user to directly change Owner is another option. In fact, with the "seteuid()" qmgmt operation, the JobRouter should no longer need the queue super user to have the power to directly set Owner. However, changing the JobRouter seems like a larger than necessary change in the stable series, so this should probably be done in the current development series, leaving the extra super user power as is in the stable series if not beyond.
remarks: 2009-Dec-02 18:41:01 by danb: Todd had an idea: just make Owner immutable. JobRouter does not need to change the owner. It just needs to be able to set it. I'm planning to make a patch that does that in 7.2 and forward. I already have a patch that implements qmgmt seteuid, and it's not very complex, but given the immutable Owner, I think the seteuid patch can be safely put in 7.5 instead of the stable series. 2009-Dec-03 10:18:58 by danb: The problem is slightly worse than we previously thought. Even before 7.2.0 chirp can set the owner to the condor user. This is possible because in all existing versions of condor, any user is allowed to set Owner to the authenticated name of the qmgmt connection, and the shadow authenticates as the condor user. So in all versions of condor that support chirp's set attribute operation (appears to be 6.5.4+), it is possible to become the condor user. In 7.2.0+, it is also possible to become other users who have previously submitted jobs. Since the condor user is always the queue super user (regardless of configuration), becoming the condor user gives one power to modify all other jobs in the queue, effectively allowing one to become those users as well. Therefore, the only additional exposure added in 7.2.0+ is the ability to become users who no longer have jobs in the queue but who submitted jobs to this schedd in the past (since the schedd was last started). 2009-Dec-03 15:18:11 by danb: I have attached two patches, one proposed for stable series 7.2 and 7.4 and the other for the development series 7.5. The stable series patch makes Owner immutable. The development series patch makes the job queue updater (used by shadow and local starter) set its effective qmgmt owner name to the user. 2009-Dec-04 13:16:03 by tannenba: Pithy example of how to reproduce this issue. When you first submit the below job, the Owner attribute will be that of the submitting user. However, after the job runs, the Owner attribute will change. Assuming that your are running bash and Condor is in your path. 1. First create file test.sub : universe = vanilla +WantIOProxy = True executable = $ENV(CONDOR_CHIRP) arguments = set_job_attr Owner \"$ENV(CONDOR_USER)\" when_to_transfer_output = ON_EXIT leave_in_queue = JobStatus==4 queue 2. Then enter the following commands: bash export CONDOR_USER=`condor_config_val schedd_log | xargs ls -l | awk '{print $3}'` export CONDOR_CHIRP=`condor_config_val libexec`/condor_chirp condor_submit test.sub 2009-Dec-04 14:56:35 by tannenba: Finished code review of stable series fix, and pushed it to V7_2-branch, then merged this into V7_4_1-branch, V7_4-branch, and master. 2009-Dec-07 13:25:59 by danb: The devel-series fix has been committed for 7.5.0 and both JobRouter and Gridmanager have been updated to use the new "set effective owner" qmgmt mode. title: Ticket #6698: Provide the ability to identify black hole slots
description: The GlideinWMS folks would like to have a way to identify when a slot is a black hole, i.e. some X number of jobs fail over a short Y minute time-span. Currently, the only way to do this is to to write a STARTD_CRON that polls the RecentNumJobStarts and if it's too high, set the START expression to False. The slot should be marked as a black hole if jobs are starting/finishing too quickly We will identify jobs that 'finish too quickly' by publishing statistics about the average/min/max lifetime of the starter that can be used to influence the START expression. So the IsBlackHole sub-expression of the START expression could be IsBlackHole = IfThenElse(JobBusyTimeAvg is undefined, false, JobBusyTimeAvg < $(EXPECTED_JOB_MINIMUM_RUNTIME))
remarks: I propose adding a new stat that will keep track of the average time that a job is on the slot. That is (execution time + transfer time) which corresponds to the time that the slot claimed/busy This new stat will publish total,min,max,average and std-deviation of claimed/busy time for all slots. These stats will be undefined until the first time a slot leaves the busy state. So your black hole expression could be IsBlackHole = IfThenElse(AvgJobBusyTime is undefined, false, AvgJobBusyTime < $(EXPECTED_JOB_MINIMUM_RUNTIME)) 2018-Jul-16 17:46:39 by marco: Lorena was mentioning about an AvgJobBusyTime over 20 min updated every 5min. If things go bad, jobs may fail in a few seconds, so 20 min would eat out > 100 jobs. On the other side, some jobs may last hours, so frequent updates of the value may use CPU for nothing. Updating on an event base (job completion) or letting the update frequency be a variable (we could have it in the config at condor startup - depending on the expected length of jobs) would be better. Other possibilities could be: an �average execution time on a moving window�. The avg execution time of the last N jobs, where N is configurable (better) or a fixed number, e.g. 10. The moving window is good because if the 1st job runs OK and then something breaks, a general avg would not help in finding the black hole (skewed heavily by the first long job). It could also be populated from the beginning (no preference about waiting the first N jobs or not), JobStarts would tell us if we reached the min number of jobs. Alternatively, an attribute like LastJobRunTime, the value of TotalJobRunTime when a job ends, would be good. There is a mechanism that I don�t remember now, that allows keeping the last N values of an attribute and we could use that to calculate the avg on the moving window. 2018-Jul-17 08:44:16 by johnkn: I'm thinking that the value is an average of job duration, and that it updates on job exit - and that there are 2 values. a value for the life of the startd, and another one that is the average only of the jobs that have exited in the last 20 minutes. 2018-Jul-17 11:27:28 by marco: I like the fact that the value is updated after the end of each job (better than periodically because jobs may have big variability in duration). What happens if 20 minutes have not gone yet? Would be possible to consider the last 10 jobs instead of the last 20 minutes for the average? The problem I see w/ 20mins is that if a job runs fine and then they start failing, we will not realize anything is wrong until the 20mins are gone (which may be many failed jobs). I'm trying to understand the values to see if I can evaluate that. I see JobStarts and RecentJobStarts (last 20 min) as counters for the number of jobs that started. Probably those are what you use but I don�t see a total running time in the machine attributes. TotalJobRunTime and TotalClaimRunTime for the total running times for a job and all jobs within a claim. Is it there a sum for all jobs that run under a startd (if 2 jobs ran at the same time in 2 partitionable slots, that time should count double)? Is TotalTimeClaimedBusy something that similar to that? 2018-Jul-24 11:22:00 by johnkn: The stats I am looking at don't appear in any permanent ClassAd right now. There would be a stat for the min, max & average lifetime of a Starter. This is a decent approximation of the lifetime of a job + the transfer time. I am also looking into having a stat for the average execution time of a job, but that's a bit more work right now. If The average lifetime of a Starter drops below some threshold and the Glide-in stops accepting jobs, then that average will never change again, and the Glide-in will stop accepting jobs forever until it dies (which will be 20 minutes later I understand) If the glide-in is working, and then stops working, then yes it will take a few jobs to go by for the average to drop down to the point where you detect the problem, but this is what you want - otherwise a single short job will have the potential to take down your whole pool - a single short job will only quickly kill off a startd that doesn't have a record of success. This is why the 20 minute windowed average is not as useful as the overall lifetime average. 2018-Jul-25 15:39:45 by johnkn: These two new probes will generate 16 attributes in each slot ad when enabled. Because that's a lot, they will not be published by default. You can enable them for publication by adding this STARTD.STATISTICS_TO_PUBLISH_LIST = $(STATISTICS_TO_PUBLISH_LIST) JobDuration, JobBusyTime To the configuration of your execute node. 2018-Jul-25 15:51:49 by johnkn: Due to the way the statistics probes work, the qualifier Avg will appear at the end of the attribute name, not at the beginning. So for 2, 2 minute jobs, you would see something like this. title: Ticket #3530: Allow groups of jobs to dynamically blacklist bad hosts or sites
description: Goal: make it easy for a set of similar jobs to blacklist a host or site that has proven to be problematic. Use case: I'm submitting a bunch of very similar jobs to the grid, perhaps OSG. As is the nature of the grid, I'm dealing with a very mixed environment. While I'm using my Requirements to filter machines I can't use as best I can, in practice I'm likely to run into machines or entire sites that seem like they'll work, but in practice cause my job to fail. So I want to avoid these machines and sites. Ideally I'd like this to be automatic, as the grid is constantly in flux and I have better things to do than checking my logs to identify bad machines and adjust things to avoid them. I am not the pool or grid administrator, so solutions that involve changing the configuration of Condor are not an option. Today's solution: Assuming I know my job usually works, and that restarting it on a different machine will usually fix the problem, I can: Set leave_in_queue to leave the job in the queue if it doesn't return a satisfactory exit code. Set match_list_length=5 Set requirements to reject any matches that appear in the list. Today's problems: This causes autocluster fragmentation as various jobs match lists change. There is no global understanding; if I have a black hole machine that causes jobs to reliably fail, potentially every single job will have to land there once before moving to a machine they can succeed on. What is desired: A user accessible way to say: These jobs are 'similar' If one of these similar jobs runs on a machine and is unhappy, add the machine to a blacklist. The blacklist might be maintained by the schedd, the negotiator, or someone else. (for varying definitions of unhappy, but based on something in the ClassAd is the obvious choice, especially the exit code) All of the similar jobs consult the blacklist and refuse those machines, perhaps via the requirements expression, but there are other possible solutions. Expire entries from the blacklist after X seconds. Short term solution: Create a new tool that monitors job logs to identify problematic sites. The tool maintains its own blacklist. When a new machine (or potentially site!) is identified as being problematic, add it to the blacklist, then condor_qedit the similar jobs to set Blacklist=foo.example.com,bar,example.com, etc. Then ensure that the jobs all have requirements=!stringListMember(Name,Blacklist) Questions: When do you expire entries from the blacklist? Can you send a solitary "probe" job to a new machine (or an old machine we're considering removing from the blacklist) before machine is deemed acceptable? What if to detect that a job failed, I need to check the output?
remarks: 2013-Mar-06 14:53:53 by bbockelm: Hi Alan, Can't the tool be the job_router? Dan and I recently have put in the ability for it to edit jobs that match a certain set of requirements. Combined with an arbitrary script callout, it seems we are fairly close. A few other thoughts: Keep the blacklist in the submitter ad, and have the negotiator automatically insert this list during the matchmaking cycle. Allow the schedd and job to provide a "minimum job time" and enforce this on the schedd side. Brian

title: Ticket #6732: speed up the schedd check for a change in an autoclustered attribute
description: Stats from a busy CMS Schedd show that we are spending quite a bit of time determining if a SetAttribute call is changing a significant attribute of a job. from Brian's email - We spend a good chunk of time reading off the next setAttribute command from the socket. Would be useful to be able to batch attribute updates. - A shocking amount of time is going to AutoCluster::preSetAttribute. Seems that we are re-parsing the list of significant attributes (allocating lists and strings galore) to see if the changed attribute is in the list of sigattrs. Could we not turn this into a hashmap lookup? String search? If we bulk-processed updates, we could at least re-parse the list only once. - To quantify, it seems we are paying 0.5ms per attribute. I'm seeing 13 - 45ms per shadow update -- seems small, but adds up to 1 week of processing time since the schedd was restarted a month ago. In the worst case, that implies the schedd could do nothing else but process shadow updates at somewhere between 20 and 100Hz. Roughly estimating from strace, I see up to 50Hz sometimes. This matches with the stats below. Brian Examination of this code shows that there is a lot of room for improvement here. The proposed solution is twofold optimize preSetAttribute by doing the check without allocating any memory Skip calling preSetAttribute entirely for running jobs, and instead always invalidate the autocluster id whenever a job goes back into idle state. title: Ticket #2321: Misconfigured collector straddling public and private networks
description: The OSG Grid School had trouble configuring a pool that spanned a private network and the public internet. Execute nodes sat on either the private network or the public network. The central manager and submit nodes were dual-homed machines that straddled the two networks. The public addresses of the dual-homed machines were routeable from the private network. Their schedd could not be reached by the startds on the public network. This was because the schedd was advertising its private address in its ads to the collector. The schedd was advertising its public address in its local address file. CONDOR_HOST was set to the public name of the central manager. When advertising themselves to the collector, daemons will advertise the interface they used to connect to the collector. So why was the schedd advertising its private address when it should be connecting to the collector via the public address? NETWORK_INTERFACE was set to the private address on the central manager. This meant that the collector was binding to all interfaces, but advertising the private address in the collector ad it advertises to itself. When the schedd wanted to send an ad to the collector, it contacted the collector via the address in COLLECTOR_HOST, retrieved the collector ad, looked up the collector's address there, then reconnected to the collector via that address. Since that address was the private one, the schedd advertised its private address. This non-obvious behavior appears to be caused by the way the DCCollector class works.

title: Ticket #7123: Remove std uni checks from start expression when no std uni in startd
description: Today, the startd unconditionally &&'s in a clause to the Requirements expression IsValidCheckpoint, which checks if the target job is standard universe, and if so, that the platform of any previous checkpoints the job has made matches this platform. As we remove standard universe, more and more startds don't support standard universe at all. The startd knows if it has a standard universe starter. Let's remove this check from start if the start has no standard universe. Doing so simplifies the start'd requirements expressions, removes a couple of significant attributes and makes matchmaking faster in the increasingly common case where a startd doesn't support standard universe.

title: Ticket #3927: how do I know if my collector is unable to keep up with incoming ads?
description: This issue should ultimately be resolved via a documentation update either in the manual or the wiki. The question is: what exactly can/should I monitor in the CollectorLog or collector ad to tell me if the collector is dropping updates, how many it's dropping, and at what rate? The reason I need to know is that I'm trying to ratchet down my CLASSAD_LIFETIME in order to deal with a very large pool of opportunistic resources that regularly come and go without warning (#3926). But I don't know how far I can ratchet down CLASSAD_LIFETIME and *_UPDATE_INTERVAL before the collector is unable to keep up and starts to drop incoming ads, because I don't know how to monitor that.

title: Ticket #885: condor_off is irreversible when daemon is already off
description: We ran the following commands in CHTC. Not only did HDFS not get started but we couldn't find any way to ever start it again without restarting the master. condor_off -subsys HDFS <hostname> condor_on -subsys HDFS <hostname> Resulted in the following MasterLog: 10/23 16:49:29 The HDFS (pid 19944) exited with status 4 10/23 16:49:29 restarting /usr/sbin/condor_hdfs in 3600 seconds 10/23 17:07:04 Got SIGHUP. Re-reading config files. 10/23 17:07:04 Reconfiguring all running daemons. 10/23 17:07:04 Sent SIGHUP to STARTD (pid 18703) 10/23 17:12:55 Handling daemon-specific command for "HDFS" 10/23 17:12:55 Canceling timer to re-start HDFS 10/23 17:13:05 Handling daemon-specific command for "HDFS" So HDFS was already off and was waiting to restart when we sent our condor_off. Then when we sent condor_on, it did not start. With increased debugging, we see this in MasterLog: 10/23 17:18:27 Handling daemon-specific command for "HDFS" 10/23 17:18:27 ::RealStart; HDFS on_hold=0 10/23 17:18:27 ::RealStart; HDFS stop_state=1, ignoring It appears to me that the following code is responsible. It seems that the stop state should be set after the check to see if we are running, not before. This same pattern repeats for other shutdown modes. stop_state = GRACEFUL; // Test for pid after setting state so HA daemons that aren't // running get notified that they are shutting down if( !pid ) { // We're not running, just return. return; }
remarks: 2009-Dec-21 12:46:57 by danb: The patch I submitted for this ([16742]) undoes some of the changes from commit 3924ee46, which was trying to fix a race condition in stop/start of HA daemons. Now we need to figure out how to solve that race condition without causing irreversible condor_off. One idea is to make use of the existing GotDaemonsOff global state in the master. It is currently not set when initiating shutdown of the master, but it would be appropriate to do so. When this flag is set, we could disallow startup of any daemons or at least HA daemons. 2009-Dec-23 13:50:54 by danb: I reverted my previous fix for this, which just undid parts of 3924ee46, which introduced the irreversible condor_off problem. I also reverted 3924ee46 and the accompanying patch 89697cc1. In place of all those reverted patches, I have created [16777] which fixes the race condition on master shutdown with HA daemons and also avoids the irreversible condor_off problem. The patch makes use of a flag that gets set when the master is shutting down. In shutdown mode, no new daemons are allowed to start (including both HA and non-HA daemons).

title: Ticket #2265: Machine ads/condor_startd should advertise no more Memory than ulimit
description: Condor may be running subject to memory limits set via ulimit/setrlimit. In particular the maximum virtual memory size (RLIMIT_AS) and the maximum data segment size (RLIMIT_DATA). (Also maybe the maximum resident set size. RLIMIT_RSS)) Condor should detect this (getrlimit), and if any such limit is smaller than the calculated Memory total, set Memory to the smallest relevant limit. Reasoning: We are encountering a site that is advertising memory of 4,096, but apparently hitting a lower limit of about 1,536. There is no point in advertising RAM we can't actually use. Worth considering: While individual processes may be limited 1,536 MB, what if my job needs 4,096 MB spread evenly across 4 or more processes? Then I could run on such a machine. However, such a case seems likely rare and not worth the complexity of coping with it. Worth being aware of: #2266: Condor should optionally enforce rlimits on RAM, file size
creator: adesmet

title: Ticket #6226: Use modern security encryption methods (AES supplied by openssl)
description: Current work is being committed to V8_9-gt6226-zkm-branch The V8_9-gt6226-zkm-branch will be squash-merged to V8_9-gt6226-branch after cleanup and then that branch will be merged to master. Summary This is the first draft of AES-GCM support in CEDAR. AES-GCM, being an AEAD approach, integrates both encryption and authentication into a single operation and utilizes modern algorithms compared to the existing options (e.g., BLOWFISH + MD5). By leveraging OpenSSL for these operations, we get access to hardware-based acceleration. Current Activity Updating the V8_9-gt6226-branch code to use the new wrap()/unwrap() API merged into master from V8_9-crypto-wrap-branch from #7725. Currently, AES crypto "works" when doing, for example, a condor_ping command to the SchedD. But I suspect socket inheritance of AES-enabled sockets is currently broken so you can't currently run an entire condor master/family requiring use of AES. Notes Because the AEAD encryption operations generate a message digest for each encryption call, we can't do an encryption call for each get_bytes (also, calls to get_bytes would no longer be associative). For AES-GCM, we have to switch to encrypting at the message level instead. I realized the above fact after a first draft of the code, resulting in a bit of a messy commit history. I would suggest squashing the PR. Most of the difficulty is in selection of the IV. Reuse of IVs is particularly problematic in AES-GCM and we have 12 bytes to work with. Here's the scheme: The IV starts off as a 12 byte random number. We need some randomness as non-negotiated sessions (such as the family session) are reused. The first 4 bytes are reused as a message counter. For negotiated sessions, the second 4 bytes are reused as a "connection counter". The connection counter is incremented for each new TCP connection. For non-negotiated sessions, we thus have at least 8 bytes (2^64)of randomness -- significantly more if the connections are short (e.g., if all connections are elss less than 65,536 messages then we have 2^80). From the birthday paradox, this implies we can safely reuse this billions of times with a fairly low probability of collision (10^-9). We can't have the "connection counter" for non-negotiated sessions because those sessions are reused across multiple daemons - there's no way to have a linear counter. This also assumes a negotiated session is not shared with multiple entities. This assumption probably needs to be more battle tested. The decryption and encryption side must agree on the connection counter and the message counter values for decryption to succeed. This prevents all replay attacks for negotiated sessions and replay attacks in the middle of a connection for non-negotiated sessions. This is the first encryption algorithm with the longer keylength (256 bits). This is fine except for negotiated sessions as those are currently fixed-size at 128 bits. Right now, we just repeat the key twice (meaning non-negotiate sessions are really 128-bit security). To Do [DONE] The relisock should calculate a message digest for the header handshake and include the digest in the AAD of the first encrypted packet. This ensures the relisock doesn't proceed if the header was tampered with. The SafeSock path is entirely untested and likely doesn't work. [DONE] We generate the symmetric key based on the first letter in the encryption algorithm list. We should parse the list and generate a key only if the encryption algorithm is needed (otherwise we'll have to ensure all future algorithm names have unique first letters - e.g., adding AES-GCM-128 wouldn't work). [DONE] I suspect the padding and padding byte is actually not necessary. It looks like AEAD is doing some internal management of the blocks. [DONE] When generating a non-negotiated session we should either always generate a 256-bit key or generate a longer key if AES-GCM is being considered. Move the V8_9-gt6226-branch code to use the new wrap()/unwrap() API merged into master from V8_9-crypto-wrap-branch from #7725 Merge V8_9-gt6226-branch into master

title: Ticket #1019: ssl and voms interaction breaks some uses of GSI authentication
description: jaime has been working on this and discovered much evilness in VOMS and how we link it. i'll let him comment on that.
remarks: 2009-Dec-02 23:38:43 by jfrey: As noted in #992, a patch I made to VOMS to delay a static initializer until the first use of VOMS (#786) caused GSI authentication to fail after the first authentication attempt. Tracking and down fixing the problem has been a string of problems that is hopefully at an end now. The static initializer modified in #786 (Initializer::Initializer() in src/api/ccapi/voms_api.cc) makes a number of changes in openssl, including registering several proxy-related OIDs and registering callbacks for thread-locking. All of this code is omitted if the macro NOGLOBUS is defined. Thus, the code is only meant to be included in the flavor of VOMS that assumes no GSI libraries will be present (GSI makes same equivalent calls into openssl). In Condor, we were using the no-GSI flavor of VOMS (called nog). The VOMS and GSI initializing calls into openssl seemed to stepping on each other if the VOMS ones occurred second. The best solution was to switch VOMS flavors to the appropriate GSI one and thus eliminate the VOMS calls into openssl. But the openssl initializing code in VOMS was still being called. I then found that in the version of VOMS we were using (1.8.9, roughly), NOGLOBUS was defined at the top of voms_api.cc, so the initializing code was called in all flavors. I noticed that the in version of VOMS used in the VDT (1.8.8_2), the openssl initializing calls are absent from the GSI flavors of the library. I found the source and confirmed that voms_api.cc had no definition of NOGLOBUS. Instead, NOGLOBUS is defined on the compile line when building just the nog flavor. I tried building Condor against version 1.8.8_2 of VOMS and ran into conflicting symbols. VOMS includes a copy of the oldgaa library from GSI, with slightly modified behavior but the same function names. When dynamically linking VOMS and GSI, the linker can apparently sort things out. But static linking fails miserably. Due to formatting differences between the two versions of oldgaa, it's difficult to determine how they differ in functionality. So rather than change VOMS to use the GSI version of oldgaa, I renamed all of the functions in the VOMS version, so that both versions could coexist. During testing, Zach and I discovered that the two oldgaas differ in how they treat Email/emailAddress fields in an X509 DN string. The GSI version will convert 'Email' to 'emailAddress', while the VOMS version won't. After a few other minor changes, VOMS 1.8.8_2 appears to work when linked with Condor. 2009-Dec-03 15:00:18 by jfrey: I just pushed a commit to V7_4-branch for 7.4.1 with the following changes: Switch the VOMS external to 1.8.8_2 (used by the VDT) Use the appropriate Globus flavor of the VOMS library, rather than the nog flavor.

This version doesn't have the memory bloat that #786 attempted to fix. It also doesn't have the GSI authentication problem introduced by #786, which is detailed in #992. (By Jaime Frey )

title: Ticket #6676: singularity should use --pwd argument when on shared filesystems
description: I'm working a bit with singularity and how to make it work on shared filesystems. I think I"ve got an easy one to fix. Here is my submit file. I'm working on Debian 9 with a backport of the 8.6.8 release from debian testing. I've got a specific execute node I'm working with whose relevant config is below. executable = /bin/ls Arguments = -lh +SingularityImage = "/cvmfs/ligo-containers.opensciencegrid.org/dockerhub/ligo/software:stretch" requirements = Machine == "execute3012.nemo.uwm.edu" initialdir = /home/tpdownes/singularity-testing Universe = vanilla Error = singularity-$(ClusterId).err Output = singularity-$(ClusterId).out Log = singularity-$(ClusterId).log accounting_group = cgca.condor Queue 1 I have singularity.conf configured on the execute node to bind mount /home but to make no attempt to bind mount the specific users directory. The point being that I want users to be able to traverse to other user's home directories (a common use case) and this combination is the one that is most predictable for both the Condor use case and the singularity shell use case at the command line. mount home = no bind path = /home On condor, I have to explicitly give it /home to bind: SINGULARITY_JOB = !isUndefined(TARGET.SingularityImage) SINGULARITY_IMAGE_EXPR = TARGET.SingularityImage SINGULARITY_BIND_EXPR = "/home:/home:rw" This causes the execution of 05/11/18 10:10:20 Attempting to run: '/usr/bin/singularity /usr/bin/singularity --version'. 05/11/18 10:10:20 [singularity version] 2.5.1-dist 05/11/18 10:10:20 Parsing bind mount specification for singularity: /home:/home:rw 05/11/18 10:10:20 Arguments updated for executing with singularity: /usr/bin/singularity exec -B /home:/home:rw -B /localscratch/condor/execute/dir_122520 -B /home/tpdownes/singularity-testing -C /cvmfs/ligo-containers.opensciencegrid.org/dockerhub/ligo/software:stretch /bin/ls -lh 05/11/18 10:10:20 Running job via singularity. But... the output is that of my home directory even though I've explicitly set initialdir above (just to be extra-certain). Manually running /usr/bin/singularity exec --pwd $(pwd) -B /home:/home:rw -B /localscratch/condor/execute/dir_122520 -B /home/tpdownes/singularity-testing -C /cvmfs/ligo-containers.opensciencegrid.org/dockerhub/ligo/software:stretch /bin/ls -lh Has the expected behavior. So does, of course, the same submit file without +SingularityImage. So I think the solution is to use the --pwd argument explicitly, at least on shared filesystems. It may be relevant even for the non-shared case, too.
remarks: 2018-May-11 10:25:21 by tpdownes: Setting SINGULARITY_TARGET_DIR = /srv only has the expected impact of properly bind mounting the scratch dir to /srv 05/11/18 10:23:34 Attempting to run: '/usr/bin/singularity /usr/bin/singularity --version'. 05/11/18 10:23:34 [singularity version] 2.5.1-dist 05/11/18 10:23:34 Parsing bind mount specification for singularity: /home:/home:rw 05/11/18 10:23:34 Arguments updated for executing with singularity: /usr/bin/singularity exec -B /home:/home:rw -B /localscratch/condor/execute/dir_123375:/srv -B /home/tpdownes/singularity-testing -C /cvmfs/ligo-containers.opensciencegrid.org/dockerhub/ligo/software:stretch /bin/ls -lh 05/11/18 10:23:34 Running job via singularity. It has no impact on the actual working directory of singularity. Which remains the user home directory. 2018-May-11 11:04:14 by tpdownes: Outwardly appears that you're explicitly ignoring this use case. 2019-Jun-05 09:59:36 by gthain: Singularity doesn't like to have bind mounts inside of other bind mounts. This happens with a condor shared filesystem often, because singularity, by default bind mounts home directories. To fix this, condor will disable this by default, with a knob SINGULARITY_MOUNT_HOME = true

title: Ticket #3474: DAGMan jobs and Condor-C
description: Igor reports that when using multiple logs with DAGMan and submitting to grid universe Condor, one gets: 012 (4326.000.000) 01/30 16:25:52 Job was held. Failed to initialize user log to /dev/null or <path to DAGManNodesLog> Code 22 Subcode 0 Igor also reports this reproduces 100% of the time. remarks: 2013-Feb-01 14:53:25 by sfiligoi: Just to be clear: The path of the dagmanlog is valid (and is not /dev/null). The message is just misleading. 2013-Feb-01 15:03:48 by nwp: Can you provide a JobAd where this is happening? It will help in debugging. 2013-Feb-01 15:19:50 by sfiligoi: Submit file with problems: universe = grid grid_resource = condor red.unl.edu red.unl.edu:9619 executable = a.sh output = a.out.$(Cluster).$(Process) error = a.err.$(Cluster).$(Process) log = a.log DAGManNodesLog=b.log ShouldTransferFiles = YES WhenToTransferOutput = ON_EXIT x509userproxy = /home/sfiligoi/.globus/x509_igor_cms queue 1 Submit file without problems: universe = grid grid_resource = condor red.unl.edu red.unl.edu:9619 executable = a.sh output = a.out.$(Cluster).$(Process) error = a.err.$(Cluster).$(Process) log = a.log ShouldTransferFiles = YES WhenToTransferOutput = ON_EXIT x509userproxy = /home/sfiligoi/.globus/x509_igor_cms queue 1 2013-Feb-01 15:46:03 by nwp: Question ought to be "What is Condor-C doing that it gives a hoot about DAGManNodesLog?" 2013-Feb-01 16:36:17 by wenger: Yeah, that's was I was wondering. I don't know why Condor-C should care about this... (I initially thought that an invalid path was goofing things up, but Igor says any path, even valid, for DAGManNodesLog causes problems.) 2013-Feb-01 17:20:23 by bbockelm: Isn't it as simple as just removing this attribute from the job by default when Condor-C is used? Igor, what happens if you add the following to the submit file: +remote_ DAGManNodesLog = /dev/null ? 2013-Feb-01 17:47:29 by bbockelm: Igor asked me to explain more thoroughly - Condor-C will copy all the attributes from the submit schedd to the remote schedd by default. In particular, DAGManNodesLog is copied to the remote side. In particular, if you have the htcondor-ce-client installed, you can do this: _condor_SUBMIT_EXPRS=DAGManNodesLog _condor_DAGManNodesLog="/tmp/baz/boo" condor_ce_run red.unl.edu:9619 echo "hello world" On the remote side: [root@red ~]# condor_ce_q uscmsPool018 -held -- Submitter: red.unl.edu : <129.93.239.129:9620?sock=8556_0571_4> : red.unl.edu ID OWNER HELD_SINCE HOLD_REASON 43851.0 uscmsPool018 2/1 17:40 Failed to initialize user log to /dev/null or /tmp/baz/boo 1 jobs; 0 completed, 0 removed, 0 idle, 0 running, 1 held, 0 suspended (I made it so the /tmp/baz/ directory was root-owned on the CE but the user could write into it on the submit node). Then, on the submit side: [bbockelm@hcc-briantest rpmbuild]$ condor_q -held -- Submitter: hcc-briantest.unl.edu : <129.93.244.208:33351> : hcc-briantest.unl.edu ID OWNER HELD_SINCE HOLD_REASON 132.0 bbockelm 2/1 17:41 Failed to initialize user log to /dev/null or /tmp/baz/boo 1 jobs; 0 completed, 0 removed, 0 idle, 0 running, 1 held, 0 suspended While we're at it, can we change the hold reason on the submit side to reflect where the hold is coming from? 2013-Feb-01 19:03:25 by nwp: If both the userlog and the DAGManNodesLog are /dev/null, DAGMan will not get the events that track the job's progress. DAGMan will never see a job be submitted, execute, and terminate. 2013-Feb-04 12:16:41 by nwp: From a discussion on #discomp: the plan should be to have Condor-C suppress the DAGManNodesLog attribute, verify that that works correctly, and write a job_dagman_condorc regression test to make sure it continues to work correctly. 2013-Feb-19 15:42:54 by wenger: I think the initial description is a bit unclear/incorrect -- if I remember correctly, the problem happens when DAGMan uses the single default log file for all of the node jobs; if you just have DAGMan use the log files specified in the submit files, things work okay. So it fails with the default log file, but works if you have multiple log files (it should also work if you specify the same log file in each submit file -- it's the "default log" specification that goofs things up. 2013-Feb-25 15:49:00 by nwp: Can Igor or Brian try condor-c with the attached patch? 2013-Mar-29 11:08:44 by jfrey: This problem was triggered by #2807 with the addition of the DAGManNodesLog job attribute. We need to strip this attribute when submitting a Condor-C job to a remote schedd. 2013-Mar-29 11:49:00 by nwp: This shows we need a DAGMAN/CondorC regression test. 2013-Mar-29 11:56:04 by wenger: Just a reminder, stripping off the attribute at the Condor-C level will goof up DAGMan, because it will still expect events to be written to the "workflow log". If DAGMan can correctly recognize a job as Condor-C, it can just turn off the "workflow log" option at the job level in the DAG, and that would solve the problem. My brain is still pretty spacey today -- can we do this just by looking for "universe = grid" in the submit file? If so, it's a pretty easy fix just in DAGMan... 2013-Mar-29 13:50:50 by jfrey: The job submitted by DAGMan would still have the DAGManNodesLog attribute and events for the job would still be written. It's only in the new job submitted by the gridmanager where DAGManNodesLog is omitted. The new job isn't being monitored by DAGMan. 2013-Mar-29 14:23:25 by wenger: Okay, that seems fine, then -- I thought the stripping off of the attribute would prevent DAGMan from seeing the events in the "workflow log". 2013-Apr-02 16:03:02 by jfrey: I verified that when a HTCondor-C job has dagman_log set, the DAGMan log contains entries only for the HTCondor-C job, and not the new job submitted by the c-gahp.

title: Ticket #7088: DAGMan inefficiencies with very large graphs
description: LIGO is reporting problems with one of their DAGs running horribly slowly. It turns out their DAG is extremely large: ~300,000 vertices ~660,000,000 edges ~350 MB .dag file ~90 GB in memory footprint Greg has done some additional profiling which reveals that fork/exec-ing condor_submit at this size takes ~3 seconds. We need to quickly figure out ways to reduce the in-memory footprint of this DAG while also speeding up the submission process. To speed up the submission process, we're modifying DAGMan to use the submit_utils library instead of forking condor_submit. TJ is currently working on this in #6974. We estimate this will reduce submit time from ~3 seconds per job to ~0.1 seconds. As for reducing the in-memory footprint, one initial obvious approach is to reduce the number of edges by optimizing many-PARENT-many-CHILD relationships using intermediate nodes. This would reduce the number of edges in these cases from m*n to m+n. For LIGO's graph, this would reduce the ~660M edges to ~1.5M edges. I'll continue updating this ticket with details about other metrics that DAGMan is producing.

title: Ticket #7572: getenv in submit should support a blacklist and whitelist
description: In order to integrate the jupyter batch spawner with HTCondor, it would be useful to have a way to use the condor_submit getenv keyword, but with a way to import less than all of the current environment. What is needed for jupyter spawner is probably a blacklist, but for most users, a whitelist might be better. We should add a mechanism that does both. Perhaps by allowing the argument of getenv to be a boolean or a list of patterns like this # get all but PATH or PYTHONPATH (case insensitive) getenv = !PATH, !PYTHONPATH # get any environment variables that start with PY or GO and don't end in ly (case insensitive) getenv = PY* GO* !*LY There will be no provision for case-sensitive matching for environment, we could possibly add it in the future if needed, but some platforms are case-insensitive for environment variables, so we should be case-preserving but case-insensitive. We should use Stringlist match semantics rather than regex, although we will have to separate this into two lists internally, a blacklist and a whitelist. If the whitelist is empty, then * will be presumed. if the blacklist is empty then nothing will be blacklisted.

description: People, including us, frequently have trouble correctly configuring Condor to use strong authentication. There are many parameters that must be set correctly. title: Ticket #3618: Procd failures can lead to fork-bomb of the system
description: When the procd fails (i.e. the other daemons can no longer communicate with it), the daemon that spawned it will attempt to restart it. It will retry spawning the procd until it can open the procd's named pipe and communicate with it. If the procd can't be restarted successfully due to a permanent error (like the directory to contain the named pipe doesn't exist), the daemon will continue spawning procd processes without reaping them, until fork() fails due to there being too many processes. The problematic code is in ProcFamilyProxy::recover_from_procd_error(). We have seen this happen on one of the macs in the batlab. It was caused by config param $(HOSTNAME) changing value after HTCondor first starts up, and it being used in the name of the LOCK directory. HOSTNAME changed from the fully-qualified hostname to the simple name of the machine (without domain). When HTCondor first started, something ensured that the LOCK directory existed. Later, after HOSTNAME changed, the procd failed and the startd attempted to restart it, but they were then trying to use a directory that didn't exist. There are several changes we could make to fix this problem: Put a limit on the number of times recover_from_procd_error() tries to restart the procd. The method would then either return failure or EXCEPT(). recover_from_procd_error() can kill and reap procd processes when they fail. Some additional items that need investigation: In the default HTCondor configuration, why do we include HOSTNAME in the name of the LOCK directory when it's place under /tmp? Why is HOSTNAME initially the full hostname on the batlab macs, then changing later on to not include the domain?

title: Ticket #5666: submit via python bindings should work like condor_submit
description: It should be possible to submit jobs to the SCHEDD via python bindings and get all of the same defaults and behavior as condor_submit without having to replicate all of that code in your python script. The way to do this is to move most of the code in the current condor_submit that builds up a job ad from a submit file into the condor_utils library. Then both condor_submit and python bindings could use that same library to make a job ad from a submit file/hashtable and get the same defaults and validiation behavior. the condor_submit source would still have all of the code to process command line arguments and talk to the schedd. But it would use shared library code to parse the submit file and make a job ad from it. The submit python bindings could expose the hashtable that results from parsing the submit file to python code, and then provide a python method to make a job ad from that submit hashtable, then the current python bindings chould be used to send that job ad along to the schedd. At that point, the python bindings code to manipulate the job ad just prior to sending it should be removed - because a much more correct manipulation would happen in the code that turns a submit file/hashtable into a job ad.
remarks: 2016-May-17 09:51:56 by bbockelm: Some notes from a whiteboard session between TJ and myself: We want to introduce a new class, Submit. This object behaves like a dictionary (unordered hash table of key-value pairs) and represents the text in a submit file up to a single "queue" statement. The object will have the following methods (in addition to the "standard dictionary protocol"): queue(N): submits N copies of the current job represented by the Submit object to the schedd. queueForEach("ColumnA", "ColumnB", [(0, 0), (1, 1), (2, 2), procs=N): Submits N jobs per entry in the list, where ColumnA and ColumnB are substituted with the values of the entry. queueFrom("ColumnA", "ColumnB", file, procs=N, separator=","): Submits N jobs per entry in the list, where ColumnA and ColumnB are substitute with fields form the file. queueAction: Queue the job given an Action object. See notes below on the Action object. gthain noted queueForEach and queueFrom are not particularly pythonic; however, they might be necessary once we start having factory jobs. Hence, we note them here but don't intend to implement them in this ticket. A future alternate might be to drop these and allow the equivalent to be constructed by the Action object. The queue* methods will only work if there's a currently active transaction. We will add a module-level function, parseSubmitFile, that parses a submit file and returns an iterator which produces Submit and Action objects. The Action class represents a queue statement parsed from a submit file. Users cannot construct these objects - they only come from parseSubmitFile. So, a few code examples: submit = htcondor.Submit() submit["executable"] = "my_great_script.sh" submit["output"] = "output.$(ProcId)" with schedd.transaction(): for filename in os.listdir(...): if filename.endswith(".mpeg"): submit["arguments"] = filename submit.queue(3) The above will submit 3 jobs per filename ending ".mpeg" in a given directory. with schedd.transaction(): for submit, action in parseSubmitFile(open("/tmp/foo.submit")): submit.queueAction(action) The above will be equivalent to calling condor_submit /tmp/foo.submit. 2016-May-17 10:49:21 by bbockelm: Note: we probably need an ad_result keyword argument on the queue* methods (just like we do with submit in order to support spooling jobs. 2016-May-17 13:38:12 by bbockelm: Talking further with TJ: Priority for 8.5 is the Submit object; parsing submit files can come in 8.7 as this seems esoteric to us. title: Ticket #5373: Clean up DAGMan "node ending" code
description: The code that deals with "node ending" events is getting more and more complicated and difficult to deal with. For example, if there's some action you need to perform when a node is finished (whether successfully or unsuccessfully) including all retries, if any, there is no clear place to do this. Things like testing whether we need to retry a node is done in a number of places, marking the node successful or unsuccessful is done in a number of places, etc. I think that a lot of this problem is caused by the fact that some of this code dates from when things were much simpler (e.g., no pre/post scripts, no retries, no multi-proc nodes, no noop nodes, no maxidle, no DAG abort, etc.). I'd like to see something like the following: A method that's called every time one "try" of a node is finished. A method that's called every time all "tries" of a node are finished. Maybe some of the code that's now in the Dag class should get moved into the Job class. Some of the methods that should get cleaned up: Dag::PreScriptReaper() Dag::TerminateJob() Dag::RestartNode() Dag::ProcessFailedSubmit() Dag::ProcessAbortEvent() Dag::ProcessTerminatedEvent() Dag::ProcessJobProcEnd() Dag::ProcessPostTermEvent() Dag::ProcessSubmitEvent()

title: Ticket #1330: Idle scheduler jobs can crash schedd when spooling input files
description: When a job's input files are transferred to the schedd over the network as part of a job submission, the job is submitted on hold, the files are transferred, then the job is released by the schedd. The function in the schedd that's called once the transfer is complete (Scheduler::spoolJobFilesReaper()) does the following: Start a queue transaction Modify some attributes in the job ad call releaseJob() Commit the transaction releaseJob() ends up calling Scheduler::timeout(), which will attempt to start any idle scheduler universe jobs, using a transaction to update the job ad. So if there are any idle scheduler universe jobs, the schedd attempts to start two transactions in parallel, which blows an ASSERT(). Here's a stack trace: #0 0xb7c5df84 in abort () from /lib/i686/cmov/libc.so.6 #1 0x081db092 in _EXCEPT_ (fmt=0x84e4475 "Assertion ERROR on (%s)") at except.c:89 #2 0x082378f9 in (this=0x85f1880, cluster=3770857, proc=0, srec=0x0) at schedd.cpp:2420 #7 0x0813722f in aboutToSpawnJobHandlerDone (cluster=3770857, proc=0, shadow_record=0x0) at schedd.cpp:2378 #8 0x081372cf in func=0x814000c <find_idle_local_jobs(ClassAd*)>) at qmgmt.cpp:3761 #11 0x0814086f in Scheduler::StartLocalJobs (this=0x85f1880) at schedd.cpp:6284 #12 0x081329ae in Scheduler::timeout (this=0x85f1880) at schedd.cpp:653 #13 0x0814be4f in Scheduler::needReschedule (this=0x85f1880) at schedd.cpp:11155 #14 0x081502f9 in releaseJob (cluster=3770907, proc=0, reason=0x84af8b5 "Data files spooled", use_transaction=false, email_user=false, email_admin=false, write_to_user_log=false) at schedd.cpp:12610 #15 0x08139715 in Scheduler::spoolJobFilesReaper (this=0x85f1880, tid=24272, exit_status=256) at schedd.cpp:3245 #16 0x081c71cd in DaemonCore::CallReaper (this=0x8682448, reaper_id=6, whatexited=0x84c974c "pid", pid=24272, exit_status=256) at daemon_core.cpp:8902 #17 0x081c7401 in DaemonCore::HandleProcessExit (this=0x8682448, pid=24272, exit_status=256) at daemon_core.cpp:9002 #18 0x081c7059 in DaemonCore::HandleDC_SERVICEWAITPIDS (this=0x8682448) at daemon_core.cpp:8573 #19 0x081bc265 in DaemonCore::Driver (this=0x8682448) at daemon_core.cpp:2868 #20 0x081d1110 in main (argc=1, argv=0xbf9fbe98) at daemon_core_main.cpp:2255 An easy solution would be to make Scheduler::needReschedule() trigger a call to Scheduler::timeout() by daemon-core immediately after the current handler, rather than calling it directly. timeout() can already decide to delay the next time it runs, so this change shouldn't break any assumptions made by callers to needReschedule().
remarks: 2010-Apr-05 13:57:22 by jfrey: This crash is being observed repeatedly by nanoHub. The cases examined, a scheduler universe job exits, but OnExitRemove evaluates to False, so the job returns to Idle. Immediately afterwards, input file spooling for another job completes. This results in a call to Scheduler::timeout() while the first job is idle, but a transaction is open for the second job. 2010-Apr-05 14:00:32 by jfrey: In the nanoHub case, the reaper for the first job should trigger a re-execution. title: Ticket #581: Dynamic startd slots lose SLOTx_STARTD_ATTRS
description: If a slot is partitionable (SLOT_TYPE_1_PARTITIONABLE=TRUE), the dynamic slots created will lack any attributes added using SLOTx_STARTD_ATTRS. Attributes added using STARTD_ATTRS will appear as expected. They will appear in the base partitionable ad, but they disappear when the dynamic slot is created. They don't show up in the classad emitted when STARTD_DEBUG=D_MACHINE. If a job requires one or more of these attributes, the startd will reject the job, citing, "6/18 17:45:10 slot1.1: Job requirements not satisfied." and "6/18 17:55:10 slot1.1: Request to claim resource refused." Expected behavior: the attributes in question appear in all dynamic slots derived from a base slow showing these attributes. To reproduce: Set up a simple condor install. "tar xvzf condor-*.tar.gz; cd condor-*; ./condor_install --install". Append the following to the generated condor_config. (This example assumes that the machine has two CPUs.) STARTD_DEBUG=D_MACHINE SLOT_TYPE_1 = cpus=2 NUM_SLOTS_TYPE_1 = 1 SLOT_TYPE_1_PARTITIONABLE=TRUE PATH_TO_DATE="/bin/date" STARTD_EXPRS=PATH_TO_DATE TEST1="number-one" TEST_SHOES=2 SLOT1_STARTD_ATTRS=TEST1, TEST_SHOES Start the install up. Using "condor_status -l", observe that PATH_TO_DATE, TEST1, and TEST_SHOES are present. Submit a simple job requiring TEST_SHOES. For example: executable=/bin/sleep arguments=300 output=eraseme.out error=eraseme.err log=eraseme.log requirements=TEST_SHOES > 0 request_cpus=1 request_disk=1 request_memory=1 queue Allow a matchmaking cycle to run. Observe that the job doesn't run. Check the StartLog and find something like: 6/18 17:45:10 slot1.1: Job requirements not satisfied. ... 6/18 17:55:10 slot1.1: Request to claim resource refused. Between those points is a dump of the dynamic class ad. Observe that PATH_TO_DATE is present, but TEST1 and TEST_SHOES are not. Matthew Farrellee hypothesizes that "the dynamic slot is missing a call to Resource::published when it is created in command.cpp."

title: Ticket #3589: Gridmanager doesn't use spooled executable for cream jobs
description: For CREAM jobs (and probably other job types), the gridmanager checks the Cmd job attribute to find the job's executable. If the user sets copy_to_spool to True in the submit file, then the executable is copied into the spool directory, but Cmd still contains the original filename. title: Ticket #6271: /var/run/condor not recreated on EL7
description: On EL7, /var/run is cleaned up on boot-time. This means /var/run/condor is deleted, which causes the master to not be able to create a FIFO in /var/run/condor and will start procds over and over. The proper way to fix this is to create a *.conf file in /etc/tmpfiles.d which describes the directory. Then, it will be recreated automatically by systemd-tempfiles. The process is documented at https://www.freedesktop.org/software/systemd/man/tmpfiles.d.html and the file should look something like this: #Type Path Mode UID GID Age Argument d /var/run/condor 0755 condor condor - - To test creation manually, run systemd-tmpfiles --create

title: Ticket #7030: SSL host verification
description: The SSL authentication, on the client side, does not perform any authorization for the server certificate. That is, any valid certificate is accepted as a server certificate. So, if your server certificate has /CN=htcondor.org and it is presented for a schedd at google.com, the client does not complain. Rather than introduce a dubious SSL_DAEMON_NAME as was originally done for GSI, I propose that we simple apply RFC 2818 rules to verify the host alias (as was done a few years back for GSI). This avoids any dependency on the security of reverse DNS, which matches modern security practices.

If not set, GSI will utilize reverse DNS to determine the hostname associated with an IP. Given this is widely considered a Bad Idea (even Globus stopped doing this as of last year), I would prefer to not introduce this undesired behavior into new functionality (as we have decided this isn't a security issue). 2019-May-07 04:32:53 by bbockelm: From an email: We don't see this as a security issue in the end given this is been the behavior since the start. One can always manage allowed server certs via ALLOW_CLIENT. We should follow the RFC and do the host check, and this should be the default behavior. There will be a knob to disable the check (= SSL_SKIP_HOST_CHECK=) in case anyone needs it. Ability to do unauthenticated SSL will be split out into #7032. This will go in 8.9 but not stable. I will make the changes.

title: Ticket #2662: Gridftp server in Condor broken
description: The gridftp server that we build and distribute with Condor fails at startup. It prints the following error and exits -1: Error: Failed to initialize: an unknown error occurred The failure occurs when globus_l_gsc_activate() calls globus_xio_driver_load() to load the "pipe" xio driver. Xio drivers "gssapi_ftp", "telnet", and "tcp" were loaded successfully immediately beforehand. The problem started in Condor 7.5.1, when we switched from Globus 4.2.1 to 5.0.0. Globus's xio module supports drivers that can be dlopen'ed. Since we statically link all Globus libraries in Condor 7.6 and before, we patch our Globus build to turn the xio drivers we need into builtin ones (statically linked, no dlopen). Possible solutions: 7.6: Turn xio driver "pipe" into a builtin driver 7.7: Stop turning xio drivers into builtin drivers, now that we dynamically link with the Globus libraries Ignore this problem and drop support for GRAM4

title: Ticket #2398: Setting hold=true when spooling a job's files causes it to fail
description: If you put 'hold=true' in your submit file and then submit your job with the -spool or -remote option to condor_submit, the schedd doesn't modify the file paths in the job ad to point at the spool directory. The schedd will then be unable to run the job. The schedd looks at the HoldReasonCode of a newly-submitted job to determine whether to expect spooling of the job's files. It's expecting the value to be CONDOR_HOLD_CODE_SpoolingInput. But when 'hold=true' appears in the submit file, condor_submit sets HoldReasonCode to CONDOR_HOLD_CODE_SubmittedOnHold. The subsequent spooling of files releases the job, negating the effect of the hold attribute.

title: Ticket #2377: support pilot job management
description: On July 29, Miron, Igor, Brian, Jaime, and I (Dan) met to begin coming up with a plan for first-class support for "resource provisioning." Concretely, what this means is managing generic pilot jobs in a distributed computing environment such as OSG. Milestones: [DONE] 2011-08-19, Dan - create a first draft of the plan, based on what was discussed Objectives Design a resource provisioning service to be deployed at grid sites. Existing job management services, such as the OSG CE, have been used for resource provisioning through the use of pilot jobs. This approach works but requires that the demand for resources be expressed indirectly by instantiating individual pilot jobs rather than by an explicit statement of what is desired. Therefore ... The service should provide an interface for clients to request the provisioning of resources. An example of a "provisioned resource" is a pilot job running on a batch slot possessing a specified minimal amount of RAM and disk. Other types of provisioned resources may also be considered. If the pilot job terminates or the resource it was using becomes unavailable, it is the responsibility of the service, not the client, to attempt reprovisioning the resource, as long as the request remains in force. (For convenience, it may be appropriate to have a special type of request where the termination of the pilot job automatically reduces the size of the request and is therefore not restarted. However, this would be an added feature, not the mainstay of what we mean by resource provisioning.) Arbitrary types of pilots should be supported (i.e. an executable supplied by the client). The translation of pilot requests to jobs should be configurable by the site. For example, the site admin might want to use specific queues for some types of jobs, without exposing this detail to outside users. The service should support multiple VOs. Clients should be able to reliably remove their previously submitted requests. Clients should be able to conveniently modify their previously submitted requests. For example, the number of desired resources of a specific type may increase or decrease over time. Requests for resources should have a renewable lease. If the lease is not renewed, the request is removed and resources are freed. Clients should be able to monitor the status of requests. For example, the number of current and recently allocated resources could be queried. Clients should be able to access relevant error logs for ease of debugging. Question: do we require that the service support multi-instance requests, or is this not a core principle? e.g. Should the service be required to support requests for N>1 pilots, or is it acceptable for an implementation to only support requests for N=1. implementation A - glideinWMS The glideinWMS could be extended to meet the design goals. The framework already provides a protocol for making requests, but the requests are not for generic pilots of type X. The factory component could be implemented using something very close to the existing glideinWMS factory. It would run at the target site and would submit pilots into the batch system, either directly or via a schedd that forwards jobs to the local batch system via the blahp. The broker component would be another instance of the glideinWMS factory, but instead of submitting pilot jobs, it would send aggregate requests to the pilot factories at the sites. The existing protocol for sending requests from the frontend to the factory could be used, but it would need to be extended to support arbitrary types of pilots. Retrieval of pilot failure diagnostics would need to be implemented. This is already on the wish-list for glideinWMS as it exists today. implementation B - Condor This is an exercise to think about Condor components (existing or missing) that could be used to implement the design goals. We considered implementing the factory as a schedd plus additional appendages that implement the factory logic. The broker could communicate with the schedd using the Condor-C protocol. B.1 scheduler universe factory Pilot jobs could exist in the schedd queue with the expression OnExitRemove=False, so they keep running until removed. These jobs are forwarded to the local site batch system via the blahp. The broker could manipulate these pilot jobs directly, but that violates one of our design goals of having the broker only deal in aggregate requests. Alternatively, the broker could submit scheduler universe jobs that translate aggregate requests into operations on individual pilots. There are two models for how this could work: the scheduler universe tasks submitted by the broker could be crondor tasks that periodically evaluate state and perform actions; the broker can modify the request by updating attributes of the crondor job's ad or by removing/replacing the job. This way of doing things sounds similar to Derek's Campus Grid Factory, as pointed out in Brian's comment below. the scheduler universe tasks are long-running jobs that have their own internal event loop. For example, an early-stage prototype that modified dagman to keep N jobs running could be adapted to this role. One problem with implementing pilots as jobs that automatically resubmit themselves with OnExitRemote=False is how to collect failure diagnostics for run attempts that fail. One solution would be to have failed glideins go on hold until their logs are harvested. Another solution would be to make Condor support logging to files with names that change with each run attempt (e.g. support $$([RunCount]) in the stderr/stdout names). B.2 JobRouter factory This idea is based on Brian's patch, which is attached to this ticket. The JobRouter could be modified to do 1-to-N transformations instead of 1-to-1 job transformations. This allows it to become a pilot factory. The source job would serve as a pilot request. The destination jobs would be the pilots. Attributes of the source job specify the desired number of pilots to instantiate. The routing table (i.e. the transformation description) would be designed to do whatever is necessary to make the jobs run on the local site (e.g. use the blahp or Condor-C or Globus). Aggregate stats about the pilots could be fed back into attributes of the pilot request ad, which could be conveniently queried by the broker. We would need to work out how error diagnostics could be fed back to the broker.
remarks: 2011-Aug-11 18:35:27 by bbockelm: At first blush, implementation (B) looks a lot like Derek's Campus Grid Factory (CGF). (Of course, a lot of this is theme and variation) CGF is a crondor job that runs at the remote site. It inserts some offline ads - one per defined pilot type - into the collector. The remote negotiator matches against the offline ad and notifies the collector. If the CGF sees a recently matched ad, it will submit a job. If we wanted to extend it to this use case, we would need to Instead of looking to see if the slots have been negotiated with and submitting a few jobs at a time, we would want the broker to be able to request N running and M idle. Concretely, VO A could write a ClassAd for a job, push it to the collector, and then update it as its requested job load changes. Note that this changes semantics of what is kept in the offline ad: job descriptions instead of machine descriptions. Need to think through the consequences of that. Note we've got a push-based system, and a mechanism to auto-expire requests. Do we want push or poll? Think deeper about security. We don't necessarily need to associate a proxy with a pilot, but we need to make sure that users can't change each other's requests. I.e., VO B can't change the number of requests in the VO A, or mess with its startup script. It seems like the extension could be done with small changes to the collector and keep the existing authorization scheme. Truthfully, the factory is very simple in this case. If it could be DC-based, could we do something clever with condor_fetchlog to deliver logs back to the broker upon request? How does this differentiate from using the gWMS factory at each site? Authorization is done entirely within Condor. No proxies are required for the whole scheme, but it is completely compatible with the OSG security infrastructure. All the non-Condor pieces are run and managed by Condor. The non-Condor parts are simple enough that it's plausible to replace with a Condor daemon; this way, we would tap into the existing ecosystem (auth, log fetching, configuration, etc). Other than that, its very, very similar. Existing CGF uses gWMS libraries. Stray, unrelated thought that might be off-the-wall: Consider submitting to a Condor site. When you submit a gWMS pilot to Condor, you start a condor_starter within a condor_starter. Even in the case of PanDA, you submit a starter-like-executable inside a starter. What if the startd launched the custom starter from the pilot system? attachments: multicast_router.patch 29962 bytes added by bbockelm on 2011-Aug-12 03:27:58 UTC. What about something along the lines of the attached patch? Currently, the jobrouter knows how to do arbitrary translation of jobs, but does a one-to-one translation between source and destination. With this patch, given a specific ClassAd, will do a one-to-many translation. Internally, I introduce a new class (PilotJob) that can hold one or more RoutedJobs. In the event loop, the PilotJob creates RoutedJobs until it has hit the target number running or the target of queued jobs. NOTE/CAVEAT: this compiles, but doesn't likely work (it represents a plausible idea). I have not put in any mechanisms for failure recovery if the job router is killed. I also have not put in any counter to track how many RoutedJobs the PilotJob creates. Finally, I have not considered the impact of the RoutedJobs updating the source job directly; likely we want something different if it's a pilot. The jobrouter can handle proxies; I haven't thought it through, but I don't see any reason why this scheme wouldn't be able to do the same. This would use the existing callout mechanism to do arbitrary transformations of jobs. So, if you would submit a GT2 on Condor-C job to an enabled schedd, the site admin could change the job router's transform to match the site setup (i.e., vanilla -> pbs/blahp). This is really the minimal amount of work I can think of to implement the project. Thoughts? PilotProvisioningDesignDoc.docx 133889 bytes added by danb on 2011-Aug-12 18:15:36 UTC. title: Ticket #6764: TCP_FORWARDING_HOST vs PRIVATE_NETWORK_*
description: The following five-line configuration does not result in an advertised private network (name or interface/address): USE_SHARED_PORT = FALSE # This line may be superfluous / redundant NETWORK_INTERFACE = $(IP_ADDRESS) PRIVATE_NETWORK_NAME = tannenba PRIVATE_NETWORK_INTERFACE = $(IP_ADDRESS) TCP_FORWARDING_HOST = 1.2.3.4 It appears that DaemonCore::InfoCommandSinfulStringMyself() has a bug where TCP_FORWARDING_HOST changes the public IP of the sinful /after/ the determination of whether to advertise the private network attributes (we don't if the public and private sinfuls aren't different). This problem doesn't happen when USE_SHARED_PORT is TRUE (the default), which probably means that the above test is probably broken.
remarks: 2018-Sep-14 18:37:58 by tlmiller: After further investigation, this may have been a testing problem. We deliberately don't set TCP_FORWARDING_HOST in the .address files, because those are intended only for local communication. So, using the test configuration: $ condor_status -master -af MyAddress <1.2.3.4:32845?PrivAddr=%3c69.130.241.97:32845%3e&PrivNet=tannenba&addrs=1.2.3.4-32845&noUDP> $ cat ../install/local/log/.master_address <69.130.241.97:32845?addrs=69.130.241.97-32845> $CondorVersion: 8.7.10 Sep 14 2018 BuildID: UW_development PRE-RELEASE-UWCS $ $CondorPlatform: X86_64-Debian_7 $ You see that without shared port, the address file uses the specified NETWORK_INTERFACE. The address file does not include the private network name, which make no sense for local communication, but the actual advertised Sinful does. (Arguably, you could have a private network address that you'd rather use for local communication, but since we don't support that, using the specified NETWORK_INTERFACE is the most likely to result in locally-routed packets, since the kernel must know about that interface for anything else to work.) With shared port: $ condor_status -master -af MyAddress <1.2.3.4:40095?PrivAddr=%3c69.130.241.97:40095%3fsock%3d29510_4c4b%3e&PrivNet=tannenba&addrs=1.2.3.4-40095&noUDP&sock=29510_4c4b> $ cat ../install/local/log/.master_address <1.2.3.4:40095?PrivAddr=%3c69.130.241.97:40095%3fsock%3d29510_4c4b%3e&PrivNet=tannenba&addrs=1.2.3.4-40095&noUDP&sock=29510_4c4b> $CondorVersion: 8.7.10 Sep 14 2018 BuildID: UW_development PRE-RELEASE-UWCS $ $CondorPlatform: X86_64-Debian_7 $ You can see that the address file uses the same address as the advertised address, because it's using (must use) the shared port's address. Arguably, the on-disk shared port ad should include what would otherwise be in its .address file, but that's not what we do for whatever reason. 2018-Sep-17 13:34:42 by tlmiller: Resolving since we can't reproduce. Best guess is that ToddT forgot to restart the shared port daemon after making the changes.

title: Ticket #4923: Cannot restart the collector on Windows, or shutdown takes a long time
description: On Windows, the master is unable to restart the collector (or any daemon using a well-known port). Upon attempting to restart the collector, the MasterLog would contain errors like the following: 03/04/15 14:00:45 Collector port not defined, will use default: 9618 03/04/15 14:00:45 Sock::bind failed: WSAError = 10048 03/04/15 14:00:45 Failed to listen(9618) on TCP/IPv4 command socket. Does this computer have IPv4 support? 03/04/15 14:00:45 Warning: Failed to create IPv4 command socket. 03/04/15 14:00:45 ERROR: Create_Process failed trying to start C:\condor\bin\condor_collector.exe The problem is the master is unable to restart the collector because port 9618 is already in use because when the master started the collector the first time, DaemonCore::Create_Process() posted a listen on 9618 and marked that listen socket as inheritable. It then starts a condor_procd if one is not already running (as of #2911). The result is the condor_procd inherited the 9618 listen socket, and thus that socket will stay in use until the procd is killed. Besides failing to restart the collector, this bug also manifested itself when sometimes doing a net stop condor or "condor_master -master" on Windows would take a really long time. The reason was the master is waiting for all other daemons to exit, but if the collector shuts down first, other daemons may have to timeout waiting for the condor_procd to respond to collector commands sent to 9618. By fixing this bug, these timeouts will no longer occur, since now as soon as the collector shuts down clients will receive a connection refused error immediately.
remarks: 2015-Apr-06 15:30:47 by johnkn: CODE_REVIEW: change looks good.

Before this change, for instance, the condor_master could not restart the collector because the listen socket on port 9618 was in use by the procd! (By Todd Tannenbaum )

title: Ticket #4889: WriteUserLog has poor user id hygiene
description: Some constructors for WriteUserLog accept a username argument, which is used to call init_user_ids(). This call is immediately preceded by a call to uninit_user_ids(). uninit_user_ids() isn't called anywhere else in WriteUserLog. Thus, after a WriteUserLog object is deleted, the user uid is still set in the Condor privilege handling code. The next time the daemon wants to act as a different user, the call to init_user_ids() will result in this daemon log message: warning: setting UserUid to 11021, was 6004 previously We see this error a lot in the schedd's log when it spawns a scheduler universe job or needs to access a job's files. If the WriteUserLog calls init_user_ids(), then it should call uninit_user_ids() when it is deleted.
