title: Ticket #4535: Reject DAGs that try to write to read-only file systems
description: On Tue, 12 Aug 2014, Tom Downes wrote: I'm receptive to the idea that you can only do so much to stop stupid but... I have 2 users who were running DAGs that were attempting to write to a read-only filesystem. I think these DAGs are bonked for their own special-snowflake reasons and it so happens that when they were first submitted long ago it was a rw filesystem. It got filled up along the way, brought down the cluster and I decided to make it read-only; these users did not change their jobs accordingly. But, at some point, these DAGs probably started up OK and successfully submitted jobs. After upgrading to 8.2.2 today and rebooting to get a kernel patch installed, I found that after restarting the schedd, these condor_dagmans would get stuck in idle and condor_q was unresponsive to the point where I had to turn the tool multiplier up to 100 and run, e.g.. condor_rm -constraint 'JobUniverse == 7' user It did not go unnoticed that these tools now allow translate a username argument into the appropriate constraint, thanks. strace -p pid_of_schedd showed a lot of hits involving the read-only filesystem and an error like -1 O_RDONLY (my strace output is lost to sands of time). It moved on from each error quickly but would move right on to another instance of the error (in one case a user had ~15 DAGs all making the same mistake). So, it would be nice if condor_schedd could detect this problem and reject a DAG. I'm not sure if it was a DAG job trying to write to the filesystem or the condor_dagman itself but the fact that the JobUniverse=7 jobs were idling suggests it was the condor_dagman. Okay, I'll make a gittrac ticket for this. We'll have to do some thinking about how things should work, and where the detection should happen. For example, if the problem is that the workflow log is on a read-only filesystem, DAGMan itself could detect that before submitting any jobs. If the dagman.out file is on a read-only filesystem, I think that would have to get detected in daemoncore. Kent
remarks: 2015-Sep-22 11:51:34 by tpdownes: In-person discussion Kent+Tom. We both think it's worthwhile to pursue ability of DAGMan to test writability of nodes.log file prior to submitting jobs because DAGMan simply won't know jobs are completing unless this file exists. Targeting 8.5 series so prioritize at 3.
creator: wenger

title: Ticket #5324: HTCondor Annexes
description: We should create a tool to help users create and manage HTCondor "annexes" in the cloud. Initially, we will target EC2, using CloudFormation and AutoScaling Groups, as described by the attached document (see the link at the bottom of this ticket). See https://cdcvs.fnal.gov/redmine/projects/glideinwms/wiki/GlideinwmsCondorAnnex for a friendly user's report about the prototype. See https://docs.google.com/document/d/1vvt9BJsbPuPA4cJznQ41VkfTBZ28R2C8_U4JRj6RtQ0 for our response. Ticket #5787 is part of this development effort, and is intended to simplify the construction of AMIs that can participate in a Spot Fleet -based annex, which is our current goal. We've demonstrated good behaviour with 'one-shot' Spot Fleets, in terms of finding a bulk-request mechanism that doesn't interfere with our or our user's ability to terminate instances (permanently), and with ticket #5787, also demonstrated a method for customizing annex instances which avoids the use of the user data -- preserving it for our users. We intend to maintain the size of Spot Fleet -based annex with the daemon we'd want to have monitoring it anyway, and ticket #5816 tracks progress in that direction. (Not report 86.) title: Ticket #7319: Provide docker images for building HTCondor from source
description: Compiling HTCondor from source, especially doing so with all the functionality of the HTCondor RPMs/DEBs at htcondor.org, requires a huge pile of dependencies. Kerberos, Globus, CREAM, Sphinx, Boost, the list goes on and on. We want to provide, in the HTCondor git repo, Dockerfiles to produce to create images on supported platforms containing all the dependencies needed to build from source all the HTCondor packages, tarballs, and documentation as released on htcondor.org. The official HTCondor area on Docker Hub will host the images (for both dev and stable branches), and Docker Hub will be configured to automatically rebuild the images whenever updated in the HTCondor git repo.
remarks: 2019-Oct-11 12:29:46 by karpel: I set up build rules for the CentOS7 image on the repo htcondor/build-centos7: (git branch/tag) -> (docker tag) master branch -> latest stable tag -> stable latest tag -> dev VX_Y_Z tag -> VX_Y_Z As far as I know there's no way to test whether any of these but the master branch one actually work. Will need to check in with this after our next release to see if the rules fired as expected. 2019-Oct-11 13:14:01 by karpel: I think that we should COPY . home/build/CONDOR_SRC (or whatever), so that when you pull the image you get the source for the version its tagged for. If you do a bind mount because you want to work with your local copy it will silently hide the source in the image, so I don't think there's much user impact beyond having to download the repo as part of the image. Thoughts? 2019-Oct-12 21:21:32 by karpel: I made a branch 7319-jtk-revisions, with the following commits (so far): The first just runs yum clean all inside each RUN (running it outside will actually increase the image size, not decrease it). This is basically a bugfix. The second is more drastic; it copies the source tree into the image. This means that the image build needs to be done from the repository root, like docker build -f build/docker/centos7/Dockerfile . For faster image builds, this second commit also adds a .dockerignore at the repository root which excludes everything in .gitignore, as well as a few other directories that shouldn't be needed inside the image. Unfortunately, the build context is still a few hundred MB. It would be around 100 MB if we didn't include the .git directory (without it, you couldn't easily checkout a different version of the repo from inside the image). If we want to keep that commit, it implies that even if you're planning to bind mount a local source tree into the container, you should pull the closest version of the image from Docker Hub and use that, rather than building the image locally (because every time you build locally, you'll have to re-send the build context even if the entire image build is cached, and that can take a long time). Or, at the least, you should build the image once in the morning and re-use it all day. This is possibly a little kooky. I think the main question is: is this container self-contained (har har), or do you always have to bind mount local source/do a clone inside the container? 2019-Oct-14 10:24:12 by karpel: After consulting with GregT, I went ahead and pushed these commits to master. 2019-Oct-30 18:34:40 by karpel: After discussion with ToddT, have reversed course: we're no longer going to bundle the source tree into the image. It's only a git clone/checkout away, and we think people should be bind-mounting source into the container anyway. 2019-Oct-31 11:23:59 by tannenba: ^^^ Actually, I said we should not include the src in the container, but the container on startup should look at a well-known mount point (e.g. /condor_src ) and if the src is not there it should automatically fetch the source (of a specified tag) from github. I do not think the source should have been removed until the functionality to fetch the source has been added. I want people to be able to build HTCondor with one docker command line... 2019-Oct-31 11:25:51 by karpel: Mmm, yes, should have referenced my notes when writing the comment :) My mistake on pulling the source too soon - I can change it back if you'd like. title: Ticket #3966: No definition of local universe in condor_submit manpage
description: The condor_submit documentation mentions but does not define local universe. Here is the 8.1.1 text for "universe" in the condor_submit manpage today: Specifies which HTCondor Universe to use when running this job. The HTCondor Universe specifies an HTCondor execution environment. The standard Universe tells HTCondor that this job has been re-linked via condor_compile with the HTCondor libraries and therefore supports checkpointing and remote system calls. The vanilla Universe is the default (except where the configuration variable DEFAULT_UNIVERSE defines it otherwise), and is an execution environment for jobs which have not been linked with the HTCondor libraries. Note: Use the vanilla Universe to submit shell scripts to HTCondor. The scheduler is for a job that should act as a metascheduler. The grid universe forwards the job to an external job management system. Further specification of the grid universe is done with the grid_resource command. The java universe is for programs written to the Java Virtual Machine. The vm universe facilitates the execution of a virtual machine.

title: Ticket #3435: negotiator-side resource consumption with consumption policies
description: I've put together a draft implementation of two interlocking new capabilities: configurable resource consumption policies (for what we currently call p-slots) enhancement to the negotiator to allow multiple jobs to match against a single p-slot during a negotiation cycle The draft currently lives on this topic branch on my github fork: https://github.com/erikerlandson/htcondor/tree/V7_9-prototype-negside-pslot-splits I wrote up a discussion and demonstration of the proposed features here: http://erikerlandson.github.com/blog/2012/12/03/a-demonstration-of-negotiator-side-resource-consumption/ Motivation Some advantages of negotiator-side consumption: each match only charged for cost of resources consumed - cleaner relationship between quotas, share, slot weights and match costs (e.g. solves #3013) resources consumed where there is direct access to the centralized accounting logic for concurrency limits and accounting groups resource constraint checking is just another kind of match requirement not restricted to exact requirements match, as with scheduler-side multiple claiming Configurable resource consumption policies: consumption logic lives on resource ad: consistent and accessible everywhere, e.g. on both negotiator and startd Generalizes MODIFY_REQUEST_EXPR_* static slots become just a particular kind of consumption policy (you get everything, regardless of what you ask for) Requirements resource consumption in matchmaking: Support ability to match multiple jobs against a single resource ad (p-slot) Resource limits must be respected Use consumption policy that resides on resource ads, in a manner consistent with startd and any other contexts Support extensible resources match costing policy must sanely extend current slot weight logic Properly respect all other current constraints and logic (quotas, submitter shares, concurrency limits, requirements expressions, preemption policies, etc) consumption policies: Support a configurable consumption policy for each resource (p-slot) ad. Consumption policy should be respected consistently in every context where it is relevant. Currently, this includes the startd claiming logic and negotiator matchmaking. "Legacy" slots without a configured consumption policy should be supported in backward compatible "mixed-pool" fashion Proposal Consumption policies Each resource Xxx has a corresponding attribute on a resource ad called ConsumptionXxx ConsumptionXxx has a classad expression that is evaluated to obtain the amount of that resource a job/match will consume. The scope 'target.' refers to a job ad Example: ConsumptionMemory = quantize(target.RequestMemory, {128}) To be considered for consumption policy logic, an ad must have one of these attributes for every resource, including extensible resources. configuration of consumption policies is now exposed to config file params (see below), with defaults consumption policy logic is abstracted so it can be shared between startd, negotiator, etc determine if a resource ad supports consumption policy evaluate Consumption* to obtain resources actually subtract resources from slot ad .../condor_utils/consumption_policy.{h,cpp} When (all) present, Consumption* expressions are used to determine the resources used while claiming a slot, instead of Requested* or _condor_Requested* _condor_RequestedXxx still allowed to override value of RequestedXxx when evaluating ConsumptionXxx MODIFY_REQUEST_EXPR_* are still applied to RequestedXxx prior to above Configuration of consumption policies CONSUMPTION_<asset> (applies to any slot in startd) e.g. CONSUMPTION_CPUS = quantize(target.RequestCpus, {1}) defaults: CONSUMPTION_CPUS = quantize(target.RequestCpus, {1}) CONSUMPTION_MEMORY = quantize(target.RequestMemory, {128}) CONSUMPTION_DISK = quantize(target.RequestDisk, {1024}) extensibles: CONSUMPTION_XXX = ifthenelse(target.RequestXxx ? undefined, 0, target.RequestXxx) SLOT_TYPE_<N>_CONSUMPTION_<asset> e.g. SLOT_TYPE_2_CONSUMPTION_MEMORY = Memory Configuration of slot weight expressions SLOT_WEIGHT = <expr> e.g. SLOT_WEIGHT = Cpus default is 'SLOT_WEIGHT = Cpus', as usual SLOT_TYPE_<n>_SLOT_WEIGHT = <expr> e.g. SLOT_TYPE_2_SLOT_WEIGHT = floor(Memory / 25) Example of consumption policy configurations: https://gist.github.com/erikerlandson/4731965 negotiator-side resource consumption To support negotiator-side claiming logic, p-slots now generalized to hold multiple claim ids each match removes one id from the set during a cycle. a legacy slot is detected and induces a set of size 1. number of supported claims configurable per slot type, currently defaults to number of cpus The code for computing asset consumption values, and deducting those assets from an ad, is factored and reused between startd and negotiator .../condor_utils/consumption_policy.{h,cpp} slot weight is generalized slightly to become 'match cost' (or alternatively 'claim cost') match cost is SlotWeight for legacy slots for resources supporting consumption policy, match cost is computed as W(S) - W(S'), where W(S) is SlotWeight evaluated on resource ad prior to deducting the resources consumed by a job ad, and W(S') is SlotWeight evaluated after the deduction. insufficient resources to satisfy a job's consumption is a new match requirement consumption policy is now addressed as another facet of match constraint checking in matchmakingAlgorithm() Testing Testing needs to cover the following categories of behavior: respect for configured consumption policies validate resources deducted from parent resources (p-slots) granularity of resources allocated to claims (d-slots) any default policies, if we go that way negotiator side resource consumption achieving multiple matches per resource during a negotiator cycle correctness of resource management resource limits as a matching constraint compatability with legacy/mixed-pool resources static slots legacy p-slots Effort implementation implementation is largely done, the main exceptions being migration of negotiator resource constraints to matchmakingAlgorithm() (2 days) default values for policies (1 day) testing initial testing will be by hand (5 days) hand testing needs to be codified into regression testing environment (5 days) doc (3 days) review/feedback (all stages) (5 days?)

A way to solve that unit analysis problem is to define slot weights so that slot weights represent units of 'jobs able to be run against slot': http://erikerlandson.github.io/blog/2012/11/15/rethinking-the-semantics-of-group-quotas-and-slot-weights-claim-capacity-model/ So, this ticket "solves" the problem by enabling a consumption policy to be matched up with a slot weight in such a way as to make weights equal jobs, which makes it possible to ensure that surplus sharing logic plays properly with slot weights. Really, this is just a generalization of the logic that was already present for counting Cpus: int count_effective_slots(ClassAdListDoesNotDeleteAds& startdAds, ExprTree* constraint) 2013-Apr-11 19:20:54 by eje: I had a request to verify that consumption policies can operate when schedd-side "leftover" slot splitting is also enabled. My initial test was to create a consumption policy that granted the entire slot. My original theory was that the schedd could split that, however I had forgotten that I designed consumption policies to operate consistently across the negotiator and startd. So the initial negotiator match obtains its claim, that represents all the resource assets. The schedd has no problem attempting to further allocate leftovers, however there are no leftovers, as the first job acquires them all with its claim. The first test did demonstrate that nothing pathological happens. It just means that the negotiator will tend to acquire the matches/claim first, and the schedd will generally have nothing further to do in that case. However, I did do a further test where I declared two startds. Each startd has a p-slot, but only one has a consumption policy, and the other operates in traditional mode. This test demonstrates that the system can operate in "mixed pool" mode, where some startds advertise traditional slots, and others can advertise slots with consumption policies, and the system correctly handles both. the configuration was: # spoof some cores NUM_CPUS = 5 STARTD.ST1.STARTD_LOG = $(LOG)/Startd_1_Log STARTD.ST1.STARTD_NAME = st1 STARTD.ST1.ADDRESS_FILE = $(LOG)/.startd_1_address STARTD_ST1_ARGS = -f -local-name ST1 STARTD_ST1 = $(STARTD) STARTD.ST2.STARTD_LOG = $(LOG)/Startd_2_Log STARTD.ST2.STARTD_NAME = st2 STARTD.ST2.ADDRESS_FILE = $(LOG)/.startd_2_address STARTD_ST2_ARGS = -f -local-name ST2 STARTD_ST2 = $(STARTD) USE_PROCD = FALSE DAEMON_LIST = MASTER, COLLECTOR, NEGOTIATOR, SCHEDD, STARTD_ST1, STARTD_ST2 # configure an aggregate resource (p-slot) to consume SLOT_TYPE_1 = 100% SLOT_TYPE_1_PARTITIONABLE = True # declare multiple claims for negotiator to use # may also use global: NUM_CLAIMS SLOT_TYPE_1_NUM_CLAIMS = 20 NUM_SLOTS_TYPE_1 = 1 # turn on schedd-side claim splitting to test with a consumption policy CLAIM_PARTITIONABLE_LEFTOVERS = True # turn this off to demonstrate that consumption policy will handle this kind of logic MUST_MODIFY_REQUEST_EXPRS = False # configure a consumption policy. This policy is modeled on # current 'modify-request-exprs' defaults: # "my" is resource ad, "target" is job ad # startd-wide consumption policy config # defaults for cpus/memory/disk consumption STARTD.ST2.CONSUMPTION_POLICY = True # a consumption policy where match consumes whole slot each time STARTD.ST2.CONSUMPTION_CPUS = 2 STARTD.ST2.CONSUMPTION_MEMORY = 32 STARTD.ST2.CONSUMPTION_DISK = 128 # keep slot weights enabled for match costing NEGOTIATOR_USE_SLOT_WEIGHTS = True # weight used to derive match cost: W(before-consumption) - W(after-consumption) SlotWeight = Cpus # for simplicity, turn off preemption, caching, worklife CLAIM_WORKLIFE=0 MAXJOBRETIREMENTTIME = 3600 PREEMPT = False RANK = 0 PREEMPTION_REQUIREMENTS = False NEGOTIATOR_CONSIDER_PREEMPTION = False NEGOTIATOR_MATCHLIST_CACHING = False # verbose logging ALL_DEBUG = D_FULLDEBUG NEGOTIATOR_INTERVAL = 300 SCHEDD_INTERVAL = 15 spin up the pool, and verify that there are two p-slots: $ condor_status Name OpSys Arch State Activity LoadAv Mem ActvtyTime slot1@st1@localhos LINUX X86_64 Unclaimed Idle 0.500 1897 0+00:00:04 slot1@st2@localhos LINUX X86_64 Unclaimed Idle 0.460 1897 0+00:00:04 Total Owner Claimed Unclaimed Matched Preempting Backfill X86_64/LINUX 2 0 0 2 0 0 0 Total 2 0 0 2 0 0 0 Now submit 10 jobs: universe = vanilla cmd = /bin/sleep args = 300 should_transfer_files = if_needed when_to_transfer_output = on_exit queue 10 You should see three match-events in the negotiator: $ grep Matched NegotiatorLog 04/11/13 16:57:36 Matched 1.0 none.user0000@localdomain <10.0.1.3:52463> preempting none <10.0.1.3:50396> slot1@st1@localhost 04/11/13 16:57:36 Matched 1.1 none.user0000@localdomain <10.0.1.3:52463> preempting none <10.0.1.3:54095> slot1@st2@localhost 04/11/13 16:57:36 Matched 1.2 none.user0000@localdomain <10.0.1.3:52463> preempting none <10.0.1.3:54095> slot1@st2@localhost Notice that only one match can occur against the "traditional" p-slot slot1@st1@localhost, but two matches are allowed against slot1@st2@localhost, since its consumption policy consumes 2 cpus per match and it has 5 cpus. title: Ticket #3823: Use stale info in passwd_cache for a short period
description: When an entry in the passwd_cache becomes stale, the next query about that user account results in consulting the OS, in case the information has changed. If the OS call fails, then the passwd_cache also returns failure. We have seen a server at CERN where for a minute every day, queries to the OS about user accounts return "no such account", due we believe to maintenance on the local ldap server. If a Condor daemon looked up any user account during this time and the passwd_cache entry was stale, the daemon got a failure. This could lead to a job failing to run or the daemon exiting. When a call to the OS about a user account fails and we have stale information in the passwd_cache, we could use that stale information for a short period of time. That would make Condor more resilient to short-lived ldap server failures.

title: Ticket #7163: Schedd doesn't write core files after clone()
description: After any use of clone() in DaemonCore::Create_Process(), daemons will not write a core file on a crash. As the only current user of clone(), the schedd is the only affected daemon. Glibc caches the pid and tid values for each thread in a process in an attempt to reduce calls it has to make to getpid() and gettid(). When clone() is called with the CLONE_VM flag, glibc sets these cached values to -1. They are never reset to the actual values. In DaemonCore's signal handler for SIGSEGV and friends, it calls raise() to re-raise a caught signal. The raise() call uses the cached pid and tid values to call the tgkill() syscall. This will fail with an EINVAL. DaemonCore's signal handler then fails back on _exit(4) to terminate the process. Glibc's clearing of the cached pid and tid values will have consequences for a number of thread-related operations. So far, I haven't found a way to maintain or restore the proper cached values via any public interface. Linus's opinion on glibc caching these values is entertaining: https://yarchive.net/comp/linux/getpid_caching.html To fix this, I plan to call kill() instead of raise() in DaemonCore's signal handler. The use of clone() will likely cause other bugs if/when we employ actual threads in the schedd.
remarks: 2019-Aug-07 13:08:54 by gthain: CODE REVIEW Looks good.

This is due to cached values for the current pid and tid in glibc being invalidated. To work around this, we call kill() instead. (By Jaime Frey )

title: Ticket #4466: Starter Suggestions
description: Our MATLAB bin directory is mounted on the exec nodes as a read-only filesystem. When a MATLAB job dumps core, the condor_starter tries to rename the /cluster/MATLAB/R2008b/bin/core file to core.1234567.0 - the associated cluster/process ID - under the UID of the job owner. I assume it's looking in the bin directory because that's where the executable or the working directory is set. However, the core file would never be created since that directory is read-only, and so the rename() attempt wasn't necessary in the first place. Also, I have adjusted my core pattern so that core dumps are centrally stored and managed, so there wouldn't have been a file simply named "core" even if the directory were writable, and some sites here prevent creation of core dumps entirely by setting a zero size limit in /etc/security/limits.d. I've tweaked my audit rules to filter these events, but you may wish to have the starter do a stat() and/or a permissions check before it assumes the uid of the job submitter and tries to rename a file which may or may not exist.

title: Ticket #3209: Add support for spot instances to EC2 GAHP
description: Tony Tiradani writes: > I have recently received requests from both CMS and HCC to provide EC2 > Spot Instance support in glideinWMS since spot instances are > significantly cheaper than ordinary instances. In order to do this, we > need Condor to support EC2 Spot Instances. > Could we have the following API calls added to the support list? > These calls are required to get spot instance to work: > RequestSpotInstances > CancelSpotInstanceRequests > DescribeSpotInstanceRequests > This one would be a second order request. I envision using it to provide > matching capabilities per availability zone. > DescribeSpotPriceHistory
remarks: 2012-Aug-24 16:25:18 by tstclair: Really...? wow, you would want DMTCP or something to ensure job recovery. 2012-Aug-24 16:29:09 by tlmiller: I've added the following commands to the EC2 GAHP: EC2_VM_START_SPOT EC2_VM_STATUS_SPOT EC2_VM_STOP_SPOT EC2_VM_STATUS_ALL_SPOT all equivalent to the commands without the _SPOT suffix, and corresponding to the RequestSpotInstances, DescribeSpotInstanceRequests, CancelSpotInstanceRequests API commands, respectively. (EC2_VM_STATUS_ALL_SPOT issues an unfiltered DescribeSpotInstanceRequests command.) After discussion with Jaime, I've decided to extend to EC2Job class's state machine with five new states: GM_START_SPOT, GM_SPOT_SUBMITTED, GM_PROBE_SPOT, GM_CANCEL_SPOT, and GM_CHECK_FOR_SPOT (used during recovery). To summarize, we're going to change the rest of the state machine as little as possible, and instead jump into a subgraph that deals with spot instances. We can do this by forbidding persistent spot requests and spot requests which can spawn more than one instance; if requested by our users, we can emulate/implement those features in Condor proper. (Effectively, once we've cancelled the spot request and removed its information (and added the instance ID), the job is a normal instance job, and can be treated as such.) 2012-Aug-24 16:30:48 by jfrey: Or calibrate your spot instance price so that average instance lifetime is longer than a job's lifetime. We'll let them worry about figuring that out. 2012-Aug-24 16:32:03 by tstclair: We should have some type of clause to say use at your own peril. 2012-Sep-28 11:55:09 by tlmiller: In branch 'V7_9-spot_instances-branch'. 2012-Sep-28 11:56:25 by tlmiller: Jaime, please review; I'll start working on the tests. Thanks. 2012-Nov-07 14:12:02 by tlmiller: Merged to master. Still to do: Finish handling the StateReasonCode (extensive comments in code). Add regression test(s). 2012-Nov-08 13:49:14 by tlmiller: Took care of the state reason code. Remaining: Regression tests. Documentation. 2012-Nov-14 13:48:37 by jfrey: CODE REVIEW General note: try to match the tab/space style of surrounding code. In GM_PROBE_JOB, EC2Job::errorString shouldn't have newlines. In GM_CLEAR_REQUEST, you should be setting ATTR_EC2_SPOT_REQUEST_ID to Undefined. You need to do this before the check for dirty attributes and in such a way that subsequent calls into doEvaluateState() don't re-dirty the attribute. One way to do this is to check whether m_spot_request_id is empty. If it isn't, set to the empty string and set the attribute to Undefined in the job ad. In GM_SPOT_CANCEL, when you clear m_spot_request_id, you could also set ATTR_EC2_SPOT_REQUEST_ID to Undefined in the job ad and call requestScheddUpdate(this, false). That would avoid an unnecessary EC2 command on any subsequent failure recovery. In GM_SPOT_START, you switch to GM_SPOT_CANCEL if the job is held or removed. Nothing will happen in GM_SPOT_CANCEL, as we don't have a spot instance request id. Also, if we have an ec2_spot_start command in progress, we have to wait for the result before leaving this state. Otherwise, we can leak a spot instance request. In GM_SPOT_QUERY, the comments say that ec2_spot_status() should return 0 or 1 spot instance request, and in the case of 1, it'll be the one we're interested in. The code handles getting multiple requests, but assumes our request is one of them. The code could be improved to handle receiving results that don't include our own request. In GM_SPOT_QUERY, you switch to GM_DONE_SAVE if the spot instance request's status isn't "active" or "open". Shouldn't it be putting the job on hold, and possibly canceling the request first? 2012-Nov-15 09:59:18 by tlmiller: DOCUMENTATION The sooner the better, but these changes require documentation. In particular: condor_submit has gained the 'ec2_spot_price' submit file attribute The EC2 section in the grid manual needs to talk about spot instances, how Condor handles them (lifecycle and other concerns from the design doc), and how they can be requested. The attributes EC2SpotPrice, EC2SpotRequestID, and EC2StatusReasonCode need to be added to, and explained in, the job ad documentation. 2012-Nov-15 10:00:15 by tlmiller: REGRESSION TESTING ... 2012-Nov-19 11:21:17 by tlmiller: CODE REVIEW Complete and changes pushed.

title: Ticket #6908: Migrate the manual to Read the Docs
description: The current HTCondor manual is built on ancient technology, is difficult to update, even more difficult to build, and looks awful. We want to move the manual into a modern framework, namely Sphinx, and host it on Read the Docs. The first part of this project called "Read the Docs" (and the goal of this ticket) is to do a full migration of current manual into reStructuredText format, get it hosted on Read the Docs, and integrate it into our release workflow. The vast majority of this work can be automated with scripts, but some manual tidy up will be required to make the new pages look right. This does not however solve the problem that our manual is bloated, badly organized, poorly written and not user-friendly. A later project called "Fix the Docs" will deal with these (far more complicated) problems in a separate ticket.

title: Ticket #5332: Address doc confusion for DAGMan maxjobs and maxidle
description: There is conflicting information for DAGMan maxjobs and maxidle on the DAGMan and condor_submit_dag pages of the manual. For example, maxidle is sometimes defined as counting jobs in terms of DAG nodes and sometimes relative to job processes (not clusters, which would be closer to DAG nodes in definition). Additionally, there is no formal association of DAGMAN_MAX_JOBS_IDLE with "maxidle", and therefore no definition for it. It's only provided as an example for the CONFIG feature. In CHTC, we've had MANY users struggle with the differences, specifics, similarities, etc., which has led to submit server performance issues when too many jobs are in the queue. I can only imagine (and htcondor-users threads show) that many outside of CHTC struggle as well.

title: Ticket #5762: Collector asserts if NO_DNS = True when updating developers collector
description: If config knob NO_DNS = True, the condor_collector process will exit with an error several times per hour, asserting when sending an update to the developer collector with the following error message in the CollectorLog : ERROR "Unknown protocol (1) in Sock::bind(); aborting." at line 741 in file /home/tannenba/condor/CONDOR_SRC/src/condor_io/sock.cpp The patch fixes the underlying problem, which is a failure to check for errors when converting a no-dns hostname to an ip sockaddr. title: Ticket #5298: File transfer timestamps broken
description: In Condor 7.7, we added information in the job ad about file transfer times (#2783). This includes the attribute JobCurrentStartTransferOutputDate, which records the timestamp when output transfer began. In 7.9, improvements to file transfer management broken this attribute (#3333), so that it no longer appears in the job ad. The problem is that the FileTransfer object records the start and end times of transfers in the Upload() and Download() methods. When a transfer is done in non-blocking mode, this happens in the child process, and the times are not sent back to the parent process.

title: Ticket #714: Idle system checking is broken on Vista and higher
description: Condor uses the function GetLastInputInfo on Windows to check if the system is idle. However, due to a change in how services run on Windows, this function no longer has access to the current running context and will not see any user input. This was also noticed by the Marquette people and they are using the same function. The only way to work around this that I have found is to start up a separate process under the current running user's context and have it check for any input using GetLastInputInfo and report back to the parent the values. Currently waiting for access to MSDN to doublecheck if this is the only option and whether this will cause problems in the future.
remarks:
2009-Sep-04 10:57:50 by burnett: Yeah, this is the new Windows world order, services have their own window station that is separate from the interactive user's station. I suspect we will see the same type of problem with the mouse idle code. Maybe try something like the code bellow. It assumes you have a great deal of privileges (which you will in Condor), and prints the the idle time for each. It uses WTSEnumerateSessions() which "retrieves a list of sessions on a specified terminal server," so that we can check all sessions, even the interactive one. We use this because Vista simply uses the Terminal Services framework to provide support for multiple logins and privilege separation between the interactive desktop and the services' "desktop". void printSessionIdleTimes() { DWORD count = 0, idle = 0; HANDLE token = INVALID_HANDLE_VALUE, session_token = INVALID_HANDLE_VALUE; WTS_SESSION_INFO *session_info = NULL; __try{ if(!WTSEnumerateSessions(WTS_CURRENT_SERVER_HANDLE, 0, 1, &session_info, &count)){ cout << "WTSEnumerateSessions failed!
"; __leave; } for(DWORD i = 0; i < count; ++i){ if(WTSActive == session_info[i].State){ if(!WTSQueryUserToken(session_info[i].SessionId, &token)){ cout << "WTSQueryUserToken failed!
"; __leave; } if(!DuplicateToken(token, SecurityImpersonation, &session_token)){ cout << "DuplicateToken failed!
"; __leave; } if(!ImpersonateLoggedOnUser(session_token)){ cout << "ImpersonateLoggedOnUser failed!
"; __leave; } LASTINPUTINFO input_info; GetLastInputInfo(&input_info); idle = GetTickCount() - input_info.dwTime; RevertToSelf(); cout << "Idle time: " << idle << "
"; } } } __finally { RevertToSelf(); if(INVALID_HANDLE_VALUE != session_token){ CloseHandle(session_token); } if(INVALID_HANDLE_VALUE != token){ CloseHandle(token); } WTSFreeMemory(session_info); } } 2009-Sep-04 11:02:12 by burnett: Also, when you say you need access to the MSDN, do you mean the disks, newsgroups, documentation, ..., magazines? I'm not quite sure from our statement; let me know what you need and I'll do my best to point you in the right direction. 2009-Sep-04 11:07:47 by ziliang: Access to the newsgroups. 2009-Sep-11 09:47:15 by david.herzfeld: I don't believe the proposed solution will work since the !ImpersonateLoggedOnUser() function does not allow the application to run in the session of the impersonated user (rather, it merely impersonates the "security context" of the requested user). Therefore, getLastInputInfo() will still return the information for session 0 (the service session) rather than for the session of the logged on user. Also, as I understand it, impersonating a logged on user is rather expensive - especially if you need to perform this impersonation for each logged on user at regular intervals. I think a better solution might be to register for changes (logon, etc) with Terminal Services via !WTSRegisterSesssionNotification(). Once a logon occurs, duplicate the user token (duplicateTokenEx()) and use CreateProcessWithToken() to start a new executable in the desired session. This executable would then have to communicate back to the Windows service - probably via a named pipe - at regular intervals. Care would need to be taken to ensure that the named pipe maintained adequate security between session 0 and session 1-n. Much of this could be accomplished with modification of the code that burnett proposed. 2009-Oct-01 14:08:16 by ziliang: After investigating having the master monitoring and starting up keyboard daemons on demand, it turns out that if the timing is just right, a user could log out, effectively killing the daemon, and log back in, before the master is aware of the log out, so the next time the master checks to see if there are any new logins it will not know that the logged on user had just logged in again. So I'm going with modifying the installer to dump the daemon into the startup Registry. 2009-Oct-02 12:27:01 by david.herzfeld: I will attach the Marquette implementation of the service that I referenced above. Note: there is a fair amount of code specific to POVB, which can be ignored. Also, the code is written in VB.NET, but it should be trivial to convert it to C++/C#, etc. The main points about the implementation: When the service starts, it enumerates all of the active sessions. For each active session it finds, it duplicates the user token, and starts a daemon process in the user's session. Every time Windows notes a session change (Logon/Logoff/Fast User Switch/System Lock, etc) the OnSessionChange subroutine in the service is called. This checks to see if the event was a new logon, in which case it performs the same process as in (1) with the new session. Idle information is sent back to the service from every daemon via a Named Pipe every 5 seconds. Results from all sessions are saved by the service and the lowest value is taken to be the "system idle time." For every daemon that the service starts, it notes the PID. When the service stops, all of these daemon processes are killed (although, some may no longer be around due to a log off). It would be possible (and perhaps convenient) to change the security context of the running daemon processes, which would prevent users from killing them except in the case of a logout. This service should work in the case that you described above (fast user logon/logoff -> as the service is event driven not polling) as well as user switching (as opposed to logoff/logon), multiple sessions, remote desktop connections, etc. I have performed very preliminary testing on the application on Windows 7 (x86_64) and Windows Vista (x86/x86_64) although it "should" work on all Windows versions 2000 - 7. Feel free to disregard if you feel a different direction is more appropriate. David 2009-Oct-02 12:32:20 by david.herzfeld: Sorry, can't attach the file as it is over the 300KB limit. I would be happy to email it to you. 2009-Oct-02 20:56:57 by ziliang: From a practical perspective, what is the advantage of having Condor/whatever monitor user logins and inject applications into the user session instead of having the application be set to automatically start up on user login? I ask mainly because doing the monitoring does require a bit more invasive of a change to Condor, so I'd be reluctant to make it unless we gain something from it. 2009-Oct-04 10:30:10 by david.herzfeld: A number of points come to mind - but as I am rather unfamiliar with the logon scripts you mentioned, it is hard to offer anything concert. However, perhaps you can answer a concern that I have regarding the logon script usage: can you confirm that the addition of a logon script to a system attached to a domain (eg, actively controlled by a domain controller) will run your script for domain users without some GPO? 2009-Oct-04 10:35:30 by ziliang: It's not a login script, it's a registry key that you can add things to to tell Windows to start that application at user login. http://social.msdn.microsoft.com/Forums/en/winformssetup/thread/7d728ee5-6bb8-409c-9f13-35b4c05bdd6d The registry key itself is HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE/Software/Microsoft/Windows/CurrentVersion/Run and I presume it's what keeps getting changed whenever an application like Adobe Reader tries to start up with the user login. 2009-Oct-04 10:50:09 by ziliang: That said, I do not know exactly how this will come into play with an active directory domain without actual testing. I don't think it will since this is in the local machine hive and not user, but depending on how draconian the group policy is set up, there may be a conflict. 2009-Oct-04 16:00:55 by david.herzfeld: You may also want to look into the effect of some virus software on registry key. This location seems to be a fairly prevalent place for worms and trojans to attack. It is possible that some pretty standard virus software would remove your Condor key. 2009-Oct-16 13:56:48 by zmiller: this has been committed to the V7_4_0-branch and merged appropriately. i'm resolving this ticket. 2010-Aug-23 14:34:59 by ziliang: That commit about reenabling kbdd registry was by me. title: Ticket #4489: Collector runs very slowly on 3.14 Linux kernels
description: In the collector, in order to improve performance, we try to increase the size of the per-socket TCP send and receive buffers, with the setsockopt system call. However, there's no guarantee that the OS will honor a request of any given size, so what condor does on startup is to progressively request an ever increasing buffer size, starting at 1024 bytes (!), going up to the desired value of 500k. Every time the code tries to set the buffer, we check what it was set to. HTCondor stops trying to increase the size when either we hit the required size, or the system isn't increasing the buffer size since the last request. Apparently, on the 3.14 kernel, the kernel doesn't support setting the send buffer less than about 4k bytes, so our initial two attempts to set it to 1k and 2k both result in setting it to 4k. Condor notices that the size isn't going up, and stops trying, even though the actual size is bigger than the requested size. Oddly, we follow the same algorithm for the receive buffer, but there's no kernel surprises there. SO, the collector ends up with a TCP send buffer smaller than the usual cedar packet size, which causes the collector to run in lock-step with its clients, and then things get very slow indeed.
remarks: 2014-Aug-06 16:32:36 by tannenba: CODE REVIEW Before the patch, set_os_buffers(X) would set the size of UDP/TCP buffers to the greater of either a) the parameter given (X), or b) to the largest value allowed by the OS. The patch got rid of clause (b). This is a problem because set_os_buffers() is used not only by TCP, but also by UDP to set the incoming collector UDP buffers very large (attempts to go with 10MB by default). Patch [40769] effectively gets rid of the large collector UDP incoming buffer by default on many platforms, so I reverted it. Instead, I made a patch that keeps the original ramp-up behavior of set_os_buffers(), but a) fixes the specific problem described above on the 3.14 kernels, and b) ramps up 4k at a time instead of just 1k at a time. title: Ticket #6660: condor_submit should exit early if executable script has CRLF EOLs
description: This is an issue that has surfaced several times in the CHTC - A user edits their (bash) shell script on a windows machine, saves it with DOS/Windows line endings, and copies the script back to the submit machine. The job is submitted, and on the execute node, the executable script fails to execute because technically the CR in the CRLF line ending is interpreted as part of the script name, as if the script intended to use /bin/bash<CR> as an interpreter. The error usually looks something like: 012 (110929593.000.000) 04/21 02:50:35 Job was held. Error from slot1_2@e347.chtc.wisc.edu: Failed to execute '/var/lib/condor/execute/slot1/dir_26337/condor_exec.exe': (errno=2: 'Nosuch file or directory') Code 6 Subcode 2 Which (1) is not especially helpful/obvious to the user in determining the problem (the line endings in the script) and (2) does not even appear to the user until the job lands on an execute node and fails there. Instead, we can do a simple check at submit time (there are other such checks there already) to fail right away with a useful error message. We can #ifdef this check to apply only to non-windows platforms, just in case #! interpreter scripts are somehow being used in windows also.

Note that it has to be applied slightly different in master, due to some restructuring in submit.cpp on master: https://github.com/edquist/htcondor/commit/fed07158f1b54c59b1d664e821f8dd3ff8d60173 on V8_6: https://github.com/edquist/htcondor/commit/7d4d4670476fa4c5963331dfd65a4ff4b312b565 I can make a merge commit off of master that includes both, if that's helpful. 2018-May-07 16:21:53 by edquist: I've added [54879] with the change on branch master-gt6660_crlf_submit_check-branch against master, as the change is a bit different between 8.6 and master. If it's a hassle to include both, maybe just get it into master. TJ, TimT, what do you guys think? 2018-May-09 10:14:23 by edquist: Feedback from TJ in person yesterday was: use the safe_fopen* wrappers instead of fopen directly remove the #if !defined(WIN32) conditional, as a windows submit host could still submit onto a linux exec node either make this check a warning instead of an error, or else make an option to allow crlf #! scripts (in case someone is running a #! python script on windows) I've pushed [54891] and [54892] to master-gt6660_crlf_submit_check-branch to address these. For TJ's last item, I made a -allow-crlf-script option, and left the default to error out and mention the option. (Having an error by default seems more useful, since with a warning the jobs will still end up in the queue, and you either have to kill them or wait for them to fail on the exec nodes.) I've tested a build with these changes and everything works as expected.

title: Ticket #893: Require GRIDFTP_URL_BASE for CREAM jobs
description: For the current CREAM support in Condor-G, we ask the CREAM server to perform the file staging via gridftp. The CREAM API doesn't provide a way to specify what DN to expect for gridftp transfers, so the client machine must have a gridftp server with a host certificate. This means Condor-G's trick of starting a gridftp server with the user's credential won't work, and GRIDFTP_URL_BASE must be set. The gridmanager should check whether GRIDFTP_URL_BASE is set and put CREAM jobs on hold if it isn't.

Ticket #3931: Asynchronous Stageout for dynamic slots
description: This approach has been abandoned. See #4291 for latest Full details available in Design Doc There's a relatively straightforward way to do asynchronous stageout -- allow the dynamic slot starter release the CPU resources it currently holds back to its parent slot. The partitionable slot gets a new CPU resource and can be rematched. There are two circuit breakers relevant here: There should be a way to limit the number of simultaneous asynchronous stageouts; I suggest having a config knob which defaults to the number of CPUs in the parent partitionable slot. This would currently cause a lot of shadow churn - the dynamic slot will no longer match the next job, meaning the schedd has to go back to the negotiator to reuse the resource. Hence, the starter shouldn't try async stageout until the stageout has lasted at least X seconds. Another config knob; default is 60. This could go away once the shadows only match against the p-slot; we don't need to wait for this, however. Hence - the starter could request to give up its resources but the startd could deny the request. For the implementation, we already have a command socket between starter and startd - we can use this for the communication. We would also need to switch stageout to non-blocking in the starter; not so bad, as allJobsDone is already non-blocking (from the job exit hook implementation).

title: Ticket #939: Issue single status command for all cream jobs
description: The cream api allows the client to query the status of all jobs. Condor should take advantage of this, rather than querying each job separately, as it currently does. In a recent test run of 2000 jobs, the cream status command was executed 14284 times in 33 minutes. Equivalent code for this already exists for several other job types in the gridmanager. For Condor-C jobs, condorresource.cpp's CondorResource::DoScheddPoll implements this on a timer setup in the constructor. Nordugrid jobs use nordugridresource.cpp's NordugridResource::DoJobStatus, again, set up in a timer in the constructor. Can we factor out a shared implementation? virtual bool BaseResource::WantBulkStatusTimer() { return false; } virtual int BaseResource::BulkPobeInterval() { EXCEPT("Invalid call to BaseResource::BulkPobeInterval); } virtual const char * BaseResource::ResourceName() { EXCEPT("Invalid call to BaseResource::ResourceName); } BaseResource::BaseResource { ... m_bulkPollTid = daemonCore->Register_Timer( 0, (TimerHandlercpp)&BaseResource::DoBulkStatus, "BaseResource::DoBulkStatus", (Service*)this ); m_bulkStatusActive = false; ... } int BaseResource::DoBulkStatus() if ( ( registeredJobs.IsEmpty() || resourceDown ) && m_bulkStatusActive == false ) { // No jobs or we can't talk to the schedd, so no point // in polling daemonCore->Reset_Timer( scheddPollTid, BulkPobeInterval() ); return 0; } // TODO: Nordugrid jobs use a dedicated m_statusGahp? if ( gahp->isStarted() == false ) { if ( gahp->Startup() == false ) { // Failed to start the gahp server. Don't do anything // about it. The job objects will also fail on this call // and should go on hold as a result. daemonCore->Reset_Timer( m_bulkPollTid, BulkPobeInterval() ); return 0; } } daemonCore->Reset_Timer( m_bulkPollTid, TIMER_NEVER ); if(m_scheddStatusActive == false) { dprintf(D_FULLDEBUG, "Starting bulk job poll of %s\n", ResourceName()); int r = StartBulkPoll(); return r; } else { int r = FinishBulkPoll(); if(r == TRUE) { dprintf(D_FULLDEBUG, "Finished bulk job poll of %s\n", ResourceName()); } daemonCore->Reset_Timer( m_bulkPollTid, BulkPobeInterval() ); return r; } }
remarks: 2009-Nov-25 11:22:16 by adesmet: Done. 100 jobs, each running 10 minutes, took 105 calls to CREAM_JOB_STATUS, down from 401. 1000 jobs, each running for 10 minutes made 1,130 calls, down from a predicted 3,000-4,000. Longer running jobs will have larger payoffs. In general, given N jobs running M minutes, the old system would generate about N*M/5 calls, the new one will generate about N+M/5.

title: Ticket #2336: SCHEDD_ASSUME_NEGOTIATOR_GONE description out of date
description: 7.6 manual says - SCHEDD_ASSUME_NEGOTIATOR_GONE This macro determines the period, in seconds, that the condor_schedd will wait for the condor_negotiator to initiate a negotiation cycle before the schedd will simply try to claim any local condor_startd. This allows for a machine that is acting as both a submit and execute node to run jobs locally if it cannot communicate with the central manager. The default value, if not specified, is 4 x $(NEGOTIATOR_INTERVAL). If $(NEGOTIATOR_INTERVAL) is not defined, then SCHEDD_ASSUME_NEGOTIATOR_GONE will default to 1200 (20 minutes). The code says - // Check when we last had a negotiation cycle; if recent, return. int negotiator_interval = param_integer("NEGOTIATOR_INTERVAL",60); int claimlocal_interval = param_integer("SCHEDD_ASSUME_NEGOTIATOR_GONE", negotiator_interval * 20); //, // default (20 min usually) //10 * 60, // minimum = 10 minutes //120 * 60); // maximum = 120 minutes The manual can be more accurate by saying the macro defaults to 20*NEGOTIATOR_INTERVAL, not 4*NEGOTIATOR_INTERVAL. Gotcha, the NEGOTIATOR_INTERVAL may not be defined to the same value for both the Schedd and Negotiator.
remarks: 2011-Jul-28 13:52:55 by matt: Note: For 7.6, the default is 20 * NEGOTIATOR_INTERVAL. For 7.7.1+, the default is simply 20 minutes (20 * 60 seconds), see [22626].

title: Ticket #5559: Limit the update rate for absent submitters
description: In order to reduce the rate of updates to the collector, submitter ads for users that have no jobs in the queue should not update as often as the ads for active users. The update currently happens in the schedd's count_jobs function. The fix will be to keep track of the last time and update was sent, and whether that update was for an absent submitter (i.e a user with no jobs in the queue). Updates will be skipped when at least one update has been sent for the absent user, and the last update was more recently than the ABSENT_SUBMITTER_UPDATE_RATE, which defaults to 5*60 sec. It should be noted that prior to this change, it appears that the code would send absent submitters TWICE each time any subnmitters were updated.

title: Ticket #2766: Warn of restart-only config changes on reconfig
description: Condor daemons should be aware of configuration settings where changes are ignored on a reconfig. If one of those settings changes, the daemon should note it and emit a warning that the change is being ignored to the log. The daemon should always compare against the value seen at start up. That way if a confused admin runs condor_reconfig repeatedly, the warning will keep popping up. Proposed message: 09/26/11 13:56:19 Warning: Ignoring change of NUM_SLOTS from "2" to "4". You will need to restart this daemon for the change to take effect. This came up in the LIGO discussion of #876; they suggested it would be helpful to be warned if a setting it being ignored on reconfig.

title: Ticket #4348: CONDOR_IDS should be ignored if not running as root
description: When running with root priv, CONDOR_IDS tells condor what UID/GID to use during normal operation. However, if you start condor without root, it should really have no effect. For the most part, that's true, but a call to get_real_condor_uid() returns the value from CONDOR_IDS even though this can never be the case, as a non-root install can't switch to said UID. This can lead to problems operating on jobs because OwnerCheck will fail, and the resulting message is entirely non-obvious. There's no good reason that I can think of to look at CONDOR_IDS in a non-root install, and as such I propose to modify the code so it is ignore in such a scenario.
creator: zmiller

title: Ticket #256: Track file sizes in checkpoints
description: This is part of the large patch set contributed by Dan Forrest. This patch includes information about the sizes of a stduniv application's files in the file table in its checkpoint. This avoided a problem that Dan often tripped over where an application would: run for a while produce a periodic checkoint run for while longer adding more data to its files get evicted without producing a checkpoint restore from the periodic checkpoint At this point, the data that was added after the periodic checkpoint was taken but before it was evicted is still in the files, and if the application appends to a file that data will remain there (and likely end up being duplicated). Tracking the file size in the file table allows files to be truncated to the size stored in the checkpoint when an application is resumed. Chunks from the annotated diff of Dan's changes (which Todd has) that are associated with this ticket are labeled with a (8).

title: Ticket #1633: Change OpSys from WINNT51, WINNT61, etc to simply WINNT
description: For Windows computers, Condor includes the version number in the OpSys. So Windows 7 is WINNT61, Vista is WINNT60, Server 2008 might be WINNT60 or WINNT61, XP might be WINNT51 or WINNT52. This is surprising, since it means that if I submit a job on a Vista box, by default I'll end up with OpSys == "WINNT60" my Requirements expression and my job won't run on a Windows 7 box, despite the fact that my job will almost certainly run fine on Windows 7. Crafting a Requirements expression that says, "Anything Windows NT based is okay" is a nuisance, requiring one to fiddle around with substr() or regular expressions. This is also different from our other major platform, Linux, which always advertises an OpSys of LINUX, without regard to the version. If anything, different distributions of Linux are less compatible than Windows, and we don't distinguish them. For users who care, the version information is available already; machine classads contain things like: WindowsMajorVersion = 5 WindowsMinorVersion = 1 WindowsBuildNumber = 2600 WindowsServicePackMajorVersion = 3 WindowsServicePackMinorVersion = 0 Proposed: Remove the version number from the OpSys. So simply advertise WINNT. To consider: this is an opportunity to tweak the name. "NT" is a dead name, it's all just Windows now. Might might consider options like WINDOWS, MSWINDOWS, or MSWIN. Compatibility This is likely backwards incompatible change. Old jobs and old submit files will do the wrong thing. We'll need to call this out for people who are upgrading. What can we do to minimize the pain? new jobs, old startds New jobs will be looking for WINNT, but old startds will only offer WINNT61, WINNT51, or similar. Possible fixes: Do nothing. Announce it widely. Either upgrade your startds or craft custom Requirements. new jobs should require any WINNT we know about: (OpSys == "WINNT" || OpSys == "WINNT51" || OpSys == "WINNT52" || OpSys == "WINNT60" || OpSys == "WINNT61"). On the down side, this is messy. Instead of using WINNT or WINDOWS, declare all versions of Windows to be WINNT51 (or whatever the most widely deployed version is). This breaks some old startds, but might minimize compatibility problems. old jobs, new startds Old jobs will require WINNT51, WINNT61, or whatever, but a new startd will advertise WINNT (or WINDOWS, or whatever) and so the jobs won't match. Possible fixes: Do nothing. Announce it widely. Update your jobs with condor_qedit or update the submit files before reusing. Detect old Requirements expressions or dependent expressions and rewrite them. Leave OpSys as it is and add a OpSysNew (or some better name). New jobs will use OpSysNew (and perhaps also OpSys as a fallback). Declare OpSys to be WINNT51 forever and ever. While misleading, it's backward compatible with many old jobs.

remarks: 2014-Sep-22 12:05:29 by wenger: We currently have a FindNodeByName() method in the Dag class; I guess we could also add a FindNodeByRegex() method. My thought is that, to avoid a lot of inefficiency, the only time we'd call FindNodeByRegex() is during parsing, if we called FindNodeByName() and didn't find anything. If we just call FindNodeByRegex() all the time I think that will slow down the parsing a lot. One thing to think about -- how this interacts with the VARS code for #1780. 2014-Sep-22 12:13:09 by wenger: We clearly want to do this for VARS if we do it, even though that's not included in the original title. Maybe clean up the VARS implementation first... 2016-Jun-06 11:01:26 by wenger: If we do this, I think we need to disallow characters like *, etc., in node names. The reason is that, for performance, we don't want to do a regex lookup every time we process a command -- that will get super-slow for really big DAGs. What I think we should do is look up the specified name in the node name hash table, and, only if that fails, run a regex against the node names. I guess another option would be to look for special regex characters in the node name in VARS commands, etc., and if we find them, run the regex lookup. Either way, though, we probably want to prohibit special regex chars in node names.

title: Ticket #6549: ProvisionedGPUs wrong
description: The symptom is that the user log's usage report claims that a set of jobs had more simultaneously-provisioned GPUs than actually existed. When the startd accepts a schedd's claim to a partitionable slot, that schedd does a bad job of converting the match ad it got from the negotiator into the slot ad for the dynamic slot on which the startd will actually run the job. (The startd should just tell the schedd what the deal is, but that's GregT's problem.) In particular, and aside from assuming that Request{Cpu,Memory,Disk} = Provisioned*, the schedd does not deal with custom machine resources at all. As a result, the job running in the first dynamic slot (even when it's reused) will always have Provisioned* = Total* for each custom machine resource. The second dynamic slot will have Provisioned* = Total* - <AssignedToFirstJob*>, and so forth. The simplest work-around is to have the starter report the correct values from the copy of the slot ad it gets from the startd.

title: Ticket #4827: Option to treat absent ads like offline ads
description: Currently, the tools in HTCondor to wake up hibernating machines when there are jobs that can run on them only work with offline ads. A machine ad becomes an offline ad if HTCondor initiates the hibernation of the machine. If something else hibernates the machine, then the ad doesn't become an offline ad. It can become an absent ad, but those can't be used to wake up the machine. It would nice to allow condor_rooster to wake up machines that were hibernated by someone other than HTCondor. There are a couple ways we could do this. First, we could have the negotiator and condor_rooster treat absent ads like offline ads. Second, we could have an option to have the collector convert absent ads to offline ads.
creator: jfrey

title: Ticket #7708: procd inefficiencies on macOS
description: Taking a snapshot of all processes in procapi is highly inefficient on macOS. ProcAPI::buildPidList() calls sysctl() to retrieve information about all processes on the system. It extracts the pids and discards the rest. Then, in ProcAPI::getProcInfoRaw(), sysctl() is called to get the same information about each process individually. We can avoid these per-process calls to sysctl(), which would can greatly reduce the time to take a snapshot. The inefficient snapshot code is having a major impact on batlab machines. On the macOS 10.15 machines, it's common for test suite jobs to get bogged down with 450 procds monitoring 3000 processes. Each procd snapshot is taking up to 10 minutes. A ps auwx command also takes about 3 minutes. With no active procds, a ps auwx takes less than a third of a second. Eliminating the per-process sysctl() calls would reduce the time to take a snapshot by 80%. Doing so for all of the procds in a test suite run could result in even greater performance.

title: Ticket #1832: Interaction of STARTD_JOB_EXPRS and STARTD_ATTRS is undocumented
description: If an attribute appears in both STARTD_JOB_EXPRS and STARTD_ATTRS, at the moment STARTD_JOB_EXPRS, so the job's ClassAd value stomps the configuration file's value. If the job's ClassAd lacks the attribute, the matching entry from the machine ClassAd is deleted. This behavior surprised at least one user (condor-admin 21457). We should document this. Options I see: Declare it undefined behavior and discourage it. Document it in the documentation for both STARTD_JOB_EXPRS and STARTD_ATTRS. Putting an attribute in both STARTD_JOB_EXPRS and STARTD_ATTRS seems pretty suspicious. Declare it illegal, changing the code to report warnings or errors if it happens. Declare it legal and document it in the documentation for both STARTD_JOB_EXPRS and STARTD_ATTRS.

title: Ticket #1131: mixing authenticated and unauthenticated users problematic
description: There are two issues with policies that deal with a mix of authenticated and unauthenticated users: Currently, if security negotiation determines that authentication will happen, then failure to authenticate causes rejection of the connection, even if neither side required authentication. The use of the ANONYMOUS authentication method can mostly overcome this problem, but the current implementation of this method is not safe to use (i.e. it is less safe than not authenticating). Unauthenticated users are not mapped to a name, so the only way to refer to them in the allow/deny list is with a *, which also matches all authenticated users. Cases where these issues have caused problems: It is not possible to have a policy that allows both unauthenticated administrative access from the central manager and authenticated administrative access from the local host. Authentication methods such as FS which are not mutual result in the server remaining unauthenticated from the client's point of view. This has resulted in the inability to use ALLOW/DENY_CLIENT to achieve a desired policy, because there is no way to refer explicitly to the unauthenticated servers vs. servers that were authenticated. Finally, it is simply confusing and unexpected that a policy that says authentication is optional will reject connections that fail to authenticate. Zach and I (Dan) talked about possible solutions. The one we think is worth pursuing is this: if authentication was not required by both parties, then allow connections to proceed even if authentication fails. assign a name to all unauthenticated connections. Currently we are thinking it will be unauthenticated@unmmappeduser. This includes assigning a name to the unauthenticated side of an asymmetric authentication method such as FS. commands that require authentication (such as submitting a job) should automatically disallow the unauthenticated user, or for that matter, all unmapped users. This addresses an unintended "feature" in the current implementation where authenticated users who were not mapped can submit jobs as gsi@unmappeduser or ssl@unmappeduser or whatever. The special unmappeduser domain would be rejected in all cases where the requirement of authentication is currently hard-coded.
remarks: 2010-Jan-22 11:08:33 by danb: I personally find "unmappeduser" ugly and would prefer to replace it with "anonymous". 2010-Jan-26 12:55:10 by danb: I have attached a patch that implements unauthenticated@unmappeduser plus the other changes outlined in this ticket. I would like to get it reviewed and I would like to finalize the name of the unauthenticated user before committing. 2010-Mar-30 13:49:58 by danb: Zach and I talked. We agreed that "unmappeduser" should be changed to "unmapped". So unauthenticated people will appear as "unauthenticated@unmapped". Someone authenticated via GSI but not found in the map file will appear as "gsi@unmapped".

title: Ticket #3419: condor_submit won't expand macros directly inserted into job classad

This works for "normal" submit file entries, but not for things directly inserted into the job's classad using +Name=blah. For example, given a submit file of: universe=vanilla requirements=false executable=/bin/date arguments=foo=$(foo) qux=$(qux) foo=foo +qux="qux" queue Actual output: sh-4.1$ condor_submit submit Submitting job(s). 1 job(s) submitted to cluster 45. sh-4.1$ condor_q -format '%s\n' Args 45 foo=foo qux= Expected output: sh-4.1$ condor_submit submit Submitting job(s). 1 job(s) submitted to cluster 45. sh-4.1$ condor_q -format '%s\n' Args 45 foo=foo qux=qux This was an actual nuisance, as I was setting a variable used by the machine's requirements, and that I had done so I wanted to pass to the arguments. I wanted to say something like: arguments=--log-level=D_FULLDEBUG --identity=$(TrustedUser) +TrustedUser="username" queue +TrustedUser="someoneelse" queue +TrustedUser="bob" queue but had to say: arguments=--log-level=D_FULLDEBUG --identity=username +TrustedUser="username" queue arguments=--log-level=D_FULLDEBUG --identity=someoneelse +TrustedUser="someoneelse" queue arguments=--log-level=D_FULLDEBUG --identity=bob +TrustedUser="bob" queue This is more verbose and more prone to mistakes. Tangentially related: Ticket #2091: Condor_submit should warn or fail if undefined macro used. If that was implemented, as least you'd be warned that it hadn't worked, instead of silently being an empty string.

title: Ticket #2208: Don't crash GDB in daemon core
description: For the most part, GDB crashes in daemon core when condor forks. This is due to the fact that it uses libthread_db to get internal state information from libpthread. We use clone() without asking the kernel to set up new thread level storage (TLS). Having the parent's TLS, but being in a different TGID, causes a corruption in gdb's state. This corruption appears to happen when gdb is notified of the exec invocation. I propose to ask the kernel to create new TLS for the child, use the parent's TLS for any non-locking call (when traced, the parent holds an internal pthreads lock; calls in the child where glibc internally tries to grab the same lock such as seteuid end badly), and return to the child's TLS for the exec. Patch forthcoming.
remarks: 2011-Jun-02 17:32:50 by bbockelm: Additional narrative: I think Condor is the only batch system "lucky" enough to be able to crash GDB during normal running. Basically, the use of clone() and pthreads is causing this; gdb uses a library, libthread_db, that talks to libpthreads, to support threaded debugging. This allows pthreads to trigger breakpoints in the debugger whenever significant events occur in the lifetime of a process. When we call clone(), we copy the parent's thread local storage which includes pthread's thread state information but the PID changes (making the information invalid). When GDB gets the signal when exec is called, it will retrieve the thread state information, but find it is invalid and assert (boom!). The naive solution is have the kernel create a default, empty TLS. Unfortunately, this causes various glibc functions to SIGSEGV, such as malloc (I believe because glibc started using pthread information and isn't prepared for it to disappear; malloc uses TLS for lock-free allocations, for example). In the child, we can restore the parent's TLS for everything but the exec call (which is when GDB asserts), but a few glibc calls will try to hold the TLS's mutex (seteuid is one used by condor). When in tracing mode, the parent also holds said lock and, as we use CLONE_VFORK, the parent doesn't release the mutex until after the child exits... causing a deadlock. The attached patch carefully weaves a combination of using the child and parent's TLS when in the child in order to avoid pthreads deadlocks, GDB asserts, and glibc segfaults. It's tricky.
attachments: condor_gdb_noworries.patch 2332 bytes added by bbockelm on 2011-Jun-02 22:17:50 UTC.

title: Ticket #5037: Restructure Callbacks and event handling
description: Event Handling It has long been true that any event which did not have a call back would cause a failure. There was no method to preset events as expected and ok. So now there is a call to allow events and another one to clear them. Condor::SetAllowedEvents("RegisterEvictedWithoutCheckpoint,RegisterSubmit,RegisterExecute,RegisterAbort"); This makes the events legal and bypassed until removed with ClearAllowedEvents. When an event happens a routine called CheckAllowed looks to see if the event is registered and if so no failure is declared. More on this in the Call back changes. Call Back Changes It used to be that we reset the test module on every call to RunTest RunTestDag and SimpleJob::RunCheck. Set events and callbacks now only clear from an explicite call to Condor::EventReset. Ending the test will remove the impact on any event or callback. This persistenceof the new allowed events and callbacks is a very substantial change. Since so much is done the SimpleJob:RunCheck including multiple uses per test, The module had to have memory of set callbacks so that a second call to RunCheck would know this. The routine which lears events remembered in SimpleJob.pm is SimpleJob::CallbackReset. You may reset any callback by passing a new handler. Runcheck at the beginning will over ride saved handlers if a new one is passed in. The RegisteredTimed callback had conflicting usage from tests and from SimpleJob::RunCheck. The Condor.pm module now wathches the use of this timer and unless it is reset by a test which already has the timer. NOTE the timer is a callback and as such make sure you remove it at the right time or it might fire after you had moved on. SimpleJob::Runcheck will now get it's own timer Daemon log searching tools in Check::CondorLog.pm needs their own timer too or we will loose callbacks.

title: Ticket #2658: privsep + gid tracking + fork does not work
description: The implementation of privsep gid tracking is broken when USE_CLONE_TO_CREATE_PROCESSES is not true in the starter. This problem is especially relevant in 7.6.4, because [27874] forces use of fork() instead of clone() in all but the schedd. The problem is that in the child branch of clone/fork, the tracking gid is recorded in a data structure belonging to the parent process. The parent then sends this gid over a pipe to the privsep switchboard. When using clone(), this happens to work, because the child and parent share the same memory. When using fork(), the parent's variable holding the tracking gid remains uninitialized, so it writes a garbage value to the switchboard. Depending on shared memory between the parent and child is not a good design. We suspect that this was not done intentionally.
remarks: 2011-Nov-23 13:45:44 by danb: The user-visible symptom of this problem is that jobs fail to start. They appear as running briefly and then return to the idle state. The starter log contains the following error message: privsep_get_switchboard_response: error received: error switching to uid 201, tracking gid 11060: code -13 the tracking group was not safe Another type of problem that is possible is that a valid gid happens to appear in the garbage value. Then the job will be started with a different tracking gid than the one expected by the procd. In this case, I believe everything would appear to work, but it might be possible for some job processes to not be properly tracked/killed. 2011-Nov-23 15:54:36 by tannenba: CODE REVIEW Patch looks good (+10 points for using full_read()!), however, in the current patch the code EXCEPTS if it fails to read the tracking gid from the pipe if the tracking gid was expected. I think instead of EXCEPTing, Create_Process should fail the same way as if we read an errno (e.g. do a waitpid() to prevent a zombie, return failure). Also, a comment that currently only the starter expects a tracking gid at this point in the code would be helpful. Also in v7.7.x we should ideally do something in the event of an uninitialized tracking gid (e.g. tracking gid of zero). However, in v7.6.x (stable), the complications of dealing w/ a tracking gid of zero is likely not worth the risk... a tracking gid of zero should almost assuredly end up with the switchboard not accepting it.

title: Ticket #5467: Prevent bad privilege state change sequences
description: Certain sequences of privilege state change calls can result in the process being in an incorrect privilege state. If the user uid/gid is reinitialized when already in user priv-state, then supplemental groups are lost. If a daemon tries to switch to user priv-state before initializing which account to use, then the process ends up in root priv-state. We attempted to prevent these situations in 8.4 (#4522), but reverted the change when it broke otherwise-working production installations. We plan to retry in 8.5 and fix the resulting failures. We will make the following changes: set_user_ids() and init_user_ids() will return failure if the process is in PRIV_USER or PRIV_USER_FINAL state and the requested id is different. Otherwise, supplement groups will be lost. Switching to PRIV_USER or PRIV_USER_FINAL will cause an EXCEPT() if the user id hasn't been set. We EXCEPT() because the privilege-switching functions can't return an error to the caller.

title: Ticket #692: local universe job with unwritable job log leaks spool directory
description: If a local universe job is submitted, but cannot write to its job log, when it tries and fails to run it will leak a subdirectory at $SPOOL/local_univ_execute/dir_$PID . Worse, the schedd complains: Local starter pid 30992 for job 3.0 exited with status 1 ERROR: Local Starter exited with unknown value 1! and immediately re-runs the job. The problem loops, eventually consuming all 32000ish possible subdirectories. No further local universe jobs can run; all will fail trying to create the subdirectory. Condor will never clean up these directories. This process also leaks disposable run accounts created on Windows. If the computer also run the startd, the next time the startd starts up, the run accounts will be deleted (possibly while still in use by the local universe!). Otherwise the run accounts are never deleted. Problem 1: In this case the job should be put on hold, not left in idle. Cause: The schedd.cpp Scheduler::jobExitCode isn't prepared to handle "1" as a failure from the starter, and just tosses the job back into idle. Fix: In schedd.cpp Scheduler::jobExitCode's default case, if(exit_code==1 && IsLocalUniverse(srec)), then put the job on hold. Problems: The HoldReason is non-specific and less helpful. Jobs may be put on hold not because the job has a problem, but because the condor_starter has an unrelated problem . Better Fix: Have the starter send a message with the problem to the schedd so that the job can be put on hold with a useful reason. I haven't yet dug into what would be involved. Problem 1a: The fix for problem 1 leaves the job with an unhelpful hold reason. Fix: TODO Look to how jobs get put on hold when the starter explodes for the same reason on a vanilla job. Problem 2: Leaked directory. (This user also had a pretty aggressive PeriodicRelease, so fixing problem 1 isn't enough.) Cause: starter normally cleans up after itself, but terminated abnormally. When running under a startd, the startd has a copy of the cleanup code and will manage it. As duplicates, they may drift apart. Fix: Having moved CStarter::removeTempExecuteDir's implementation into a shared location, have cleanup_execute_dir call it instead of reimplementing it. Problem 4: The schedd doesn't clean up leaked local universe execute directories on startup. The startd does. Fix: Move cleanup_execute_dirs out of the startd and into a shared location (probably condor_c++_util again). Call cleanup_execute_dirs in schedd.cpp:7568 Scheduler::initLocalStarterDir. Current plan plan: Investigate and propose fix plan only. Identify other possible problems, leaks, etc stemming from same core problem (starter self manages, but may EXCEPT or otherwise exit uncleanly) As part of plan: schedd should probably clean up on unexpected starter exit, schedd should probably clean up rogue (all?) on startup. Email fix plan to Miron, Todd, Alain. Alternate Fix As an alternate solution, we could run/contact a startd and run the starters under the startd. This may necessitate running shadows as well. The pieces may already be in place. A schedd can contact and use a local startd without needing a negotiation cycle. A startd can dynamically repartition itself into "more" slots. Advantages: Existing, known good, startd cleanup code works. Some existing redunant policy evaluation duplicated between the schedd (for local universe) and the startd can potentially be eliminated, simplifying code. More work will be moved out of the schedd into the startd/shadows, increasing parallelism and reducing load on the typically loaded schedd. Disadvantages: More processes with attendant FD, memory, and processor consumption. Increased configuration complexity. If we reuse the existing startd, do we need to craft a policy to handle a mix of vanilla and local jobs? Do we run two, in which case we need multiple sets of configuration? This may create the public impression that Condor is always heavyweight, and not appropriate for the sorts of jobs that the local universe exists for.
