title: Ticket #368: Add functionality to the GC code to optionally use a tool to hibernate
description: It has been suggested that it would be nice to be able to give Condor hints with regards to how to "hibernate" a machine. We've discovered, with some user feedback, that it can be difficult, if not impossible, to always automatically determine which "hibernation" states a particular machine can enter; further, it is also difficult to determine the tools to use in order to enter the desired "hibernation" state. As such, it seems reasonable that an administrator could explicitly specify which "hibernation" states are supported as well as the tools required to enter these states. For instance, an administrator could approximate S5 support with shutdown. Edit: This will be used a general framework for all hibernation capabilities in Condor. The code from the startd will be ripped out and embedded into the condor_power tool. The startd will then only be in charge of evaluating the HIBERNATE expression and passing the result to the defined hibernate command. In the general case, the command will be a script that uses condor_power to affect the state of a given machine. If the tool is exercised on the startd, the machine will likely enter hibernation; conversely, if the tool is invoked on the negotiator, it will likely wake the machine in question.

title: Ticket #2988: add an input file cache
description: Igor discussed caching of transferred input files with Todd and Miron, because UCSDGrid users frequently have short jobs with large input sandboxes that contain files shared by many jobs. There was concern about how to guarantee that the file in the cache is the same as the file the next job is requesting. Igor says it would be useful to support caching without solving the general case. We should limit ourselves to only the use case where the user tells us he is not going to change a file between jobs, and the (absolute path) file name is enough to guarantee uniqueness. Of course, this requires the user to opt in (possibly on a job-by-job basis), since we cannot assume all users are able or willing to guarantee this. But that would solve a large fraction of use cases and definitely Igor's current problem. The files in the cache would not be directly accessible to the user job; they would be owned by the condor user. Only the copy of the file would be available to the job. This way we do not need to worry about the user corrupting the cached file (intentionally or by mistake).

title: Ticket #2822: Improve cleanup of chroot execute dirs
description: Right now, the chroot implementation has a few drawbacks: It creates $CHROOT/var/lib/condor/execute with too-restrictive permissions if it doesn't already exist. It implements the parsing of the NAMED_CHROOT param twice via the miracle of copy/paste It bind-mounts /var/lib/condor/execute -> $CHROOT/var/lib/condor/execute. If we would instead bind-mount /var/lib/condor/execute/dir_12345 -> $CHROOT/var/lib/condor/execute/dir_12345, the running jobs wouldn't be able to scribble in each other's sandbox, even if they are running as the same unix user. This is an important isolation/security protection! If (3) is implemented, we would need to cleanup the various dir_12345 directories in the starter and startd. All simple things to fix; patch incoming.

title: Ticket #3730: document the specification of a trusted CA for EC2
description: From ToddM, who received the request from Fermi. When you specify a service with a https://, x509://, or euca3s:// URL, HTCondor validates that service's certificate, checking that a trusted certificate authority (CA) signed it. Commercial EC2 service providers generally use certificates signed by widely-recognized CAs; these will usually work without any additional configuration. For other providers, you may need to specify which CAs you trust. For these providers, you may see errors like the following in the EC2 GAHP log: 06/13/13 15:16:16 curl_easy_perform() failed (60): 'Peer certificate cannot be authenticated with given CA certificates'. You specify which CAs you trust by including their certificates in a group of trusted CAs: either an on-disk directory or a single file, either of which may contain multiple certificates. Unfortunately, which way will varies from system to system, depending on its SSL implementation. (HTCondor uses libcurl; see http://curl.haxx.se/libcurl/c/curl_easy_setopt.html#CURLOPTCAINFO and http://curl.haxx.se/libcurl/c/curl_easy_setopt.html#CURLOPTCAPATH for details.) Some versions of HTCondor (those with the standard univese enabled) ship with their own libcurl, which will be linked against OpenSSL. The behavior when specifying both is undefined, although the EC2 GAHP allows it. The EC2 GAHP will set the CA file to whichever variable it finds first, checking in the following order: (1) The environment variable X509_CERT_FILE (set when the HTCondor master starts up) (2) The HTCondor configuration variable SOAP_SSL_CA_FILE The EC2 GAHP supplies no default value if it doesn't find one. The EC2 GAHP will set the CA directory to whichever variable it finds first, checking in the following order: (1) The HTCondor configuration variable GSI_DAEMON_TRUSTED_CA_DIR (2) The environment variable X509_CERT_DIR (set when the HTCondor master starts up) (3) The HTCondor configuration variables SOAP_SSL_CA_DIR The EC2 GAHP supplies no default value if it doesn't find one. The descriptions of SOAP_SSL_CA_DIR, SOAP_SSL_CA_FILE, and GSI_DAEMON_TRUSTED_CA_DIR should probably mention that the EC2 GAHP may also use them.

title: Ticket #7289: Implement secure S3 transfers using pre-signed URLs
description: Downloading from a secure S3 bucket normally means dealing with a tuple of security tokens (two if permanent, three if temporary). Rather than deal with distributing and managing those tokens, Brian Bockelman suggests that we instead transform 's3://' URLs into pre-signed 'https://' URLs in the shadow before we send the list during file-transfer. Doing so for uploads would require an additional round-trip, but keeping the tokens on the submit machine seems like a big win for security. The function generate_presigned_url() will be implemented in libcondorutils, and based off of the EC2 GAHP's createV4Signature(). While the S3 and EC2 signing protocols are almost identical, the bigger difference deals with moving all of the signature metadata out of the HTTP headers and into the query parameters. For this reason, generate_presigned_url() will share subroutines (which will be moved into libcondorutils) with createV4Signature(), the two functions will not call the same implementation with different flags. The shadow will recognize three types of s3:// URLs. # This form is distinguished by having no '.' before the slash. s3://<bucket>/<key> # We check for this pattern so we can automatically extract the region, since AWS cares about it. s3://<bucket>.s3-<region>.amazonaws.com/<key> # All other S3 URLs, presumed to be for Ceph or Minio. s3://<host>/<key> If the user needs to specify a region, they will be able to do so in the submit file. This region applies to all 's3://' URLs that don't specify a region. Likewise, the same key pair is used for all files, both downloaded and uploaded. (It wouldn't be hard to allow the user to specify a key pair for each direction. Specifying a key pair per file would be hard.) The shadow will silently rewrite 's3://' URLs for download. For upload, the starter issues a new command to the shadow, asking it to translate a list of URLs; the starter sends the list because support for output file globs means that shadow doesn't actually know them all.

title: Ticket #6924: Python Bindings: cluster handle objects
description: Right now, the Python bindings API is mostly built from the point of view of a pool admin: when you want to submit, query, act, or edit, you go to the Schedd. This makes perfect sense for admins because they don't own any particular cluster of jobs, and they are aware of the topology of the pool. However, users don't typically care about the Schedd. They care about submitting a cluster of jobs and then monitoring its progress, possibly editing its attributes or querying it. The first half of this was made much easier by the introduction of the Submit object in the bindings. This ticket addresses the second half (query, act, edit) by having a rich Cluster object. This object knows which Schedd its jobs live on and implements query, act (and possibly specialized hold, release, etc.), and edit methods that automatically target only the clusterid the jobs belong to. Depending on exactly how much (if any) of the existing API we want to break, there may be a variety of ways to get a Cluster: 1. The existing Submit.queue and Submit.queue_with_itemdata methods could return Cluster. This can be done without breaking queue_with_itemdata by pulling the SubmitResult methods up into the Cluster as well, but it would break users of queue. 2. Introduce a new Submit.submit method which has the semantics of queue_with_itemdata, but returns a Cluster. 3. Ask a Schedd for a handle to a cluster: Schedd.handle(clusterid). 4. Construct it directly: Cluster(clusterid, schedd). (All names up for debate...) All of this will be implemented via pure-Python wrappers over the existing C++ bindings code. One change may be necessary in the underlying bindings: it would be useful for a Transaction to store and expose which Schedd it was created from. This could maybe be implemented in the Python wrapper as well, although it would probably be less stable.

title: Ticket #2064: Allow Condor to keep the file descriptor open between writing logs
description: On Windows when opening files it is possible to deny write access to them. Many applications do this when reading a file, including Explorer when it is copying files between locations. This will result in Condor failing when it tries to write its logs out. The proposed solution is to provide a flag that will keep the file open on Windows, if and only if file locking is not also enabled. As the shadow is the only daemon that needs file locking and its failure does not bring down all of Condor, the other daemons should not be affected by this. The current plan is to only offer this on Windows due to a global FD limit on Linux. The current default is also to turn this off until more testing is done.

Seems like if and only if D_FDS is specified, the logging code would need to open a separate file to identify the (highest) active fd number. Seems like you need to close the file at rotation time, so is the original problem really solved, or is the window of vulnerability just made smaller? What do we do (and what can we do) if someone opens the daemon log file right between when we close the file and then attempt to rotate it? While the immediate problem is Windows specific, it might be nice if the functionality of keeping the fd open worked on both Unix and Windows. By default, perhaps we could keep all daemon logs open on Windows, and on Unix we keep all daemon logs open EXCEPT for the shadow and dagman which should still open/close at each entry (since we don't want to exhaust system or uid wide fd limits on unix). IF locking on the daemon log is specified (no longer the default anywhere, incl the shadow), I assume we still open/close the log as we always did? 2011-Apr-21 08:39:41 by tstclair: For the 7.7 series why don't we just look into a pluggable non-blocking logging daemon.... Seriously...? You could still preserve the base case, but redirect calls if plugin override exists. I have example code for this which is on my public directory @ UW. 2011-May-02 15:28:56 by bbockelm: Two thoughts: I think the community would prefer a pluggable logging daemon. The condor logging systems has great things about it, but the lack of choice is frustrating. The maximum number of file descriptors on the servers I can find are dynamically adjusted based upon the amount of RAM on the machine (maybe it's a RHEL5 thing? I can't find this documented online anywhere). It's not possible for me to exhaust the FDs this way: the virtual memory system would go first. Mileage may vary on other distros; something worth investigating. [bbockelm@red ~]$ cat /proc/sys/fs/file-max 1600885 2011-May-02 15:42:53 by ziliang: So to address the issues so far. Todd: 1. D_FDS is handled by opening the NULL file to get the FD count. 2. On Windows, the window of vulnerability still exists, in a much smaller form, during log rotation. So - I think that, if a decision is made, it shouldn't be made based upon the global FD limit. Brian 2011-May-02 19:37:51 by ziliang: Right now the functionality has been added to Linux. After a brief discussion with TJ, the answer, at least initially, is none. About attribute naming: a monitor may watch more than resource, e.g., GPU[Core]s and GPU memory. The metrics configuration defines a metric type for each named resource: SUM:GPUs, PEAK:GPUsMemory. The monitor writes attributes named Uptime<Resource>Seconds or Uptime<Resource>PeakUsage, respectively; this could change in the future, but makes the current implementation easier (because the aggregation functions don't have to change the name of the attribute). The startd generates the job-specific <Resource>Usage automatically. For SUM metrics, this is the change in cumulative Uptime<Resource>Seconds divided by the job duration; for PEAK metrics, this just the Uptime<Resource>PeakUsage (during/as of the end of the job). The startd does not presently but should also generate the Recent<Resource>[Seconds|PeakUsage] and Recent<Resource>Usage automatically. Of these names, <Resource>Usage corresponds to the job ads' MemoryUsage and DiskUsage (both of which are PEAK metrics); the corresponding CPUsUsage is not reported in the user log (and therefore, the job ad); this should be corrected (we have the necessary data and even publish most of it). The machine ad currently has LoadAvg and its cousins; we should add RecentCPUsUsage for consistency. This got me worried about more-subtle problems that might be hiding in the 5/6 to 7/6 range of allowed values, so I took a closer look to see if we could just allow 5/6, 6/6, and 7/6.* The answer is no, because the startd presently computes usage as of when it writes the update ad (based on the total usage computed from the previous sample), which means we're occasionally too high because we're not dividing by the full length of the job. The obvious solution is for the startd to compute the usage as of the last sample time, which is more accurate anyway, especially since -- as noted above -- we're not waiting around for the last sample interval anyway. title: Ticket #6359: dprintf inside _set_priv during clone cause problems
description: It turns out that the parameter "dologging" is not a true/false boolean. (This is the 999 case for dologging) The fix is to only dprintf if "dologging" is not zero and also not 999.

title: Ticket #4734: Improve debugging tools for JobRouter
description: Note: a (very) preliminary version of the condor_job_router_info tool was secretly added to 8.2.4. as ticket #4569. This ticket is for the devel series where we address the limitations and non-maintainable code issues of the preliminary version. We've received strong feedback from OSG site admins that the job router is quite difficult to debug. We'd like to see some client tools to help analyze setups. Suggestions we've received: Have a tool which can print all the routes (with or without defaults) and warn about any syntax errors (people often forget line continuations). Have a tool which can print all jobs matching the umbrella requirements and, for each job, print the route names which match. Given a single job and a route name, determine whether the job passes the umbrella requirements, passes the route requirements, and print the changes the router would make. To help motivate why we ask for these tools, See Bob Ball's notes from deploying the HTCondor-CE: �https://www.aglt2.org/wiki/bin/view/AGLT2/CondorCE Not all bullet-points result in bugs or work item - it should give an flavor of what a knowledgable sysadmin finds confusing. issues brought up on review of #4569 by Alan De Smet Things to change: Implementation of the class Scheduler is duplicated in job_router_tool.cpp and schedd_main.cpp, and they are slightly different. This will likely surprise anyone updating the code in the future. There is non-obvious behavior hiding in there. The code should be unified. Perhaps an additional constructor argument triggering different behavior (if a ClassAdCollection * is passed in, don't new up a m_consumer and m_mirror, instead store the pointer and return it from GetClassAds.) The tool version of Scheduler::GetClassAds only returning something for m_id==0 is magical. Perhaps instead call some sort of Scheduler::SetClassAds to set the pointer on the first instance instead of relying on the m_id being 0. It looks like JobRouter::set_schedds leaks whatever Schedulers were present before. I think the old ones should be stop()ed and deleted. It also seems like a landmine for an external party to hand in newly allocated memory for JobRouter to manage. Perhaps just pass in the two param names and let JobRouter handle instantiation. Or maybe have a second JobRouter::JobRouter that takes the param names to use. Scheduler::id() is unused; strike. In job_router_tool's main, if read_classad_file fails, should probably exit after the message. By continuing it seems likely that the message will be overlooked and the user will get unexpected behavior. job_router_tool's main, checking !job_files.isEmpty() before iterating over it seems unnecessary. Shouldn't it merrily iterate 0 times? class CondorQClassAdFileParseHelper is duplicated 3 times with minor variations: src/condor_q.V6/queue.cpp,src/condor_utils/compat_classad.cpp, src/condor_job_router/job_router_tool.cpp. (It's called CondorClassAdFileParseHelper in compat_classad.cpp) They should be unified as much as possible. (Perhaps adding sub-classes to handle any necessary differences?) The same goes for the function read_classad_file() duplicated in src/condor_q.V6/queue.cpp and src/condor_job_router/job_router_tool.cpp. class JobLogMirror in job_router_tool.cpp appears to be unused. Strike. Other things to consider: JobRouter::dump_routes: Consider using the iterator interface (m_routes->begin()/end()) as more robust, just in case someone later adds an inner loop over the routes. JobRouter::dump_routes: Consider looking up Universe string when writing TargetUniverse. JobRouter::dump_routes: Why is CurrentRoutedJobs not reported? JobRouter::~JobRouter: Do we want to stop() the scheduler objects if m_operate_as_tool? What does Scheduler::stop do? job_router_tool.cpp my_exit: Seems unnecessary to flush stdout/err. Do we have systems where stdout/err don't get auto-flushed on exit? job_router_tool.cpp usage: Seems silly to rely on tabstops; why not space indent? job_router_tool.cpp: Why replace the default dprintf behavior? Why discard early dprintf messages (dprintf_set_output_intercept)? Future work: Expunge the disabled part of #if 1 in Scheduler.h Should Scheduler::~Scheduler call m_mirror->stop() and eliminate Scheduler::stop to reduce possibilities of mis-use. submit_job.cpp and job_router_tool.cpp duplicate a bunch of functions: claim_job, yield_job, submit_job, push_dirty_attributes, push_classad_diff, finalize_job, remove_job, Write*EventToUserLog, Initialize*Event, and EmailTerminate Event. The job_route_tool.cpp are simple stubs. Perhaps this would be more cleanly expressed by moving the functions into a pure virtual class, then letting the two files implement overrides. It would be more verbose, but would make the intent more obvious and provide more specific error messages if a function was added to one but not the other. JobRouterHookMgr's implementation is duplicated between JobRouterHookMgr and job_router_tool.cpp. job_router_tool.cpp's version is basically all stubs. Perhaps move the interface and any shared functionality into a parent class, give each case it's own child class, then either pass in the specific child class into JobRouter::init, or have an option to JobRouter::init that selects which one to new into existance.

title: Ticket #5826: Improve documentation of concurrent job limits
description: From htcondor-support #8571: I was thinking it would be a good idea to add some verbiage to the manual in the section on concurrency limits about the SubmitterUserResourcesInUse ClassAd, and how it can be used to limit the number of concurrent jobs through the requirements expression without having to implement a configuration change on the system: requirements = (isUndefined(SubmitterUserResourcesInUse) || SubmitterUserResourcesInUse <= 100) ... or whatever the correct incantation is. Presently, this ClassAd is only mentioned in the "Priorities in Negotiation and Preemption" section of the manual, and so most "howto" guides you find online don't mention this as a way to enforce concurrency limits.
remarks: 2016-Aug-04 14:02:57 by wenger: Hmm -- I've been playing around with this to understand things, and I'm not sure it works the way it should... If my requirements expression is this: requirements = (isUndefined(SubmitterUserResourcesInUse) || SubmitterUserResourcesInUse <= 0) only one job runs at a time, as you'd expect. But if the requirements expression is this: requirements = (isUndefined(SubmitterUserResourcesInUse) || SubmitterUserResourcesInUse <= 1) as many jobs run as I have slots available. I'm trying to figure out whether there's something I'm missing... 2016-Aug-04 14:39:39 by tannenba: It basically works, but only if you disable matchlist caching by adding to the condor_config in your central manager # Disable Matchlist caching (defaults to True) NEGOTIATOR_MATCHLIST_CACHING = False Note disabling this cache can result in substantially increasing the time it takes to do a negotiation cycle. In pools with just a few hundred slots it probably doesn't make much difference. But in pools with many thousands of slots, it explode the negotiation time by an order of magnitude. I'm not sure we should be recommending this technique to people without a big warning about the impact to scalability... 2016-Aug-04 14:48:10 by wenger: Okay, good to know that -- I'll put some kind of warning in the docs.

title: Ticket #5125: Python bindings for the negotiation protocol
description: Currently, the negotiation protocol is tied to the condor_negotiator implementation. There's no way to perform large-scale experimentation with how condor does matchmaking. I'd like to expose the basic pieces of the negotiation protocol to the python bindings so alternate matchmaking approaches (parallel matchmaking, iterative matchmaking for new glideins) can be explored. I think the API should look along these lines: claims = htcondor.Collector().getClaims() # TODO schedd = htcondor.Schedd() with schedd.negotiate("bbockelm@unl.edu") as session: for request in session: candidate = myGreatMatchmaker(request, claims) if candidate: session.sendClaim(claim) The above would be a very silly negotiator indeed - but the basic building blocks would be there. As the aim is to allow experimentation, API coverage is purposely light: no support for consumption policies, no support for p-slot claiming, etc.
remarks: 2015-Jun-30 12:05:34 by bbockelm: First version of the API is posted. Here's the world's least-useful negotiator implementation using the API: import htcondor coll = htcondor.Collector() private_ads = coll.query(htcondor.AdTypes.StartdPrivate) startd_ads = coll.query(htcondor.AdTypes.Startd) claim_ads = [] for ad in startd_ads: if "Name" not in ad: continue found_private = False for pvt_ad in private_ads: if pvt_ad.get('Name') == ad['Name']: found_private = True ad['ClaimId'] = pvt_ad['Capability'] claim_ads.append(ad) with htcondor.Schedd().negotiate("bbockelm@unl.edu") as session: found_claim = False for resource_request in session: for claim_ad in claim_ads: if resource_request.symmetricMatch(claim_ad): print "Sending claim for", claim_ad["Name"] session.sendClaim(claim_ads[0]) found_claim = True break if found_claim: break Nevertheless, it's sufficient for chucking matches at a schedd.

title: Ticket #7118: condor-annex-ec2 startup script needs better throttles
description: The University of Manchester, via AWS, is reporting that they not infrequently don't see all of the instances which start as a result of their Spot Fleet request join the pool. The error they sent along was An error occurred (RequestLimitExceeded) when calling the DescribeInstances operation (reached max retries: 4): Request limit exceeded. title: Ticket #5430: deadlock on windows when daemon talks to itself via shared port
description: When a daemon (say the collector) tries to send a TCP message to itself via shared port, it will deadlock on Windows because the outgoing message holds the big fat mutext, but the socket handoff (via pipe from shared port) cannot complete until the big fat mutex is released. This happens routinely when the collector sends updates to COLLECTOR_HOST because it is usually a member (or the only entry!) in that list. The fix for this should be 3 fold. Since this communication will fail anyway, and lockup the shared port daemon in the process, the shared port daemon should just fail the connection attempt early instead. The code in the collector to remove itself from the collector list before sending updates should be fixed - clearly it is not working on windows (or anywhere?). The shared port on windows code should be modified so hand the socket off from the helper thread to the main thread without needing to take the big fat mutex.
derived_tickets: #5431 shared port should fail when source and destination are the same #5432 collector doesn't always remove itself from collector list #5433 shared port on windows should hand sockets off without taking bigmutex
creator: johnkn

title: Ticket #446: collector is freezing up after a forked child exits
description: Soon after merging in the thread code (#17), some regression tests would occasionally fail. DanB reported the following via email: Looking in all of the other failed test logs from last night, I see the same pattern. The collector is freezing up after a forked child exits and the collector has not yet processed the SIGCHLD. Here's one: 04/30 02:15:48 (fd:6) (pid:15426) ForkWork: Child 15426 done, status 0 04/30 02:15:48 (fd:5) (pid:15294) Entering thread safe start [select] in selector.cpp:311 unknown() And another: 04/30 09:00:36 (fd:6) (pid:22825) ForkWork: Child 22825 done, status 0 04/30 09:00:36 (fd:5) (pid:22806) Entering thread safe stop [select] in selector.cpp:317 unknown() 04/30 09:00:36 (fd:5) (pid:22806) Leaving thread safe stop [select] in selector.cpp:317 unknown()
remarks: 2009-Apr-30 18:29:00 by tannenba: Looks like the problem is with the mutex in dprintf, which was added to make dprintf() thread safe to aid in thread-related debugging. The issue is in dprintf, we grab the mutex before blocking signals that could generate dprintfs (like SIGCHLD). So if the SIGCHLD signal is delivered in the small window between grabbing the mutex and blocking dprintf-generating signals, we deadlock. Will commit simple patch to master branch to grab mutex after signals are blocked, and of course release the mutex before signals are released.

title: Ticket #2176: Hierarchical Groups can cause starvation
description: Hierarchical groups can cause starvation. Consider this configuration as an example: GROUP_NAMES = \ foo, \ cms, \ cms.prod, \ cms.other, \ GROUP_QUOTA_foo = 200 GROUP_QUOTA_DYNAMIC_cms = 1 GROUP_QUOTA_cms.prod = 200 GROUP_QUOTA_DYNAMIC_cms.other = 1 GROUP_ACCEPT_SURPLUS = True Ok, consider the case of a cluster with 300 slots, no jobs from "foo", 300 cms.prod jobs, and 300 cms.other jobs. How many job slots should each group get? I would claim the desired distribution of jobs is 200 for cms.prod and 100 for cms.other. Unfortunately, the algorithm as implemented will give 300 slots to cms.prod and 0 to cms.other. This is because we first calculate the number of job slots, then allocate the surplus. First, the allocation: 300 slots in the cluster. At the top level, 200 go to foo leaving 100 slots for dynamic quotas, all going to cms. Because cms only has 100 slots, cms.prod's allocation gets trimmed to 100 slots and cms.other receives a quota of 0. Then, the allocation of surplus: There's no foo jobs, so 200 surplus slots go to cms (for a total of 300 slots). In Matchmaker::hgq_allocate_surplus, surplus is allocated to groups with >0 quotas, then groups with =0 quotas. cms.prod (quota is 100) is allocated all 300 slots, as it has sufficient demand and there are 300 slots to hand out. cms.other gets 0 slots as there is nothing left. I don't have a solution - but I think the implementation is not what is desired.
remarks: 2011-May-19 15:04:19 by eje: Declaring static quotas larger than the quota available to the parent (which is what tkt #2176 configuration does, as you correctly describe) is somewhat of a no-no, although it will do its best by rescaling (with a warning). Part of the issue is that quotas are by necessity assigned prior to the redistribution of surplus. The logic of mixed static and dynamic quotas requires that static quotas are serviced first, which is why you ended up with zero quota left for group cms.other. Quota surplus is then shared in proportion to quota for nonzero quotas (with any remaining given to zero quotas equally). Therefore cms.prod, with nonzero quota, gets all the surplus, and so cms.other gets none. Given the dynamic nature of slot availability on a condor pool, I tend to recommend that static quotas are not used at all, unless there are compelling reasons to use them. When they are used, they should ideally be declared small enough that a dip in reporting slots does not cause a static quota to become larger than the quota available to its parent. 2011-Dec-22 16:56:22 by eje: Will #2678 and #2679 resolve this in a satisfactory way?

title: Ticket #7724: condor_config_val should be able to validate the configuration
description: condor_config_val and condor_reconfig should be enhanced so that they can validate all of the configuration variables as well as verifying that the config files will all load and parse. Motivation When an admin changes the config files, and then runs condor_reconfig, there is a possibility that the daemon being reconfiged will abort because the new configuration is invalid. If the config files themselves do not parse, then condor_reconfig will detect this and it report the error with filename and line number, and the reconfig command will never be sent. But then the problem is the contents of configuration variable, condor_config_val will not see the error. The most common reason for this is that some configuration variables can be classad expressions, and if the expression does not parse, this is only detected at the time the daemon tries to fetch the configuration variable. In some cases, the daemon will then abort. It would be useful if there was a way to validate that all of the keys in the configuration files that have classad expressions have valid classad expressions. In order to do this, it must be known which of the keys are expected to parse as classad expressions. Since nearly all keys are listed in the param table and the param table has information about what type of data the key should hold, we can use this information to figure out which keys to check for validity. Since we have never tried to use the param table in this way before, it is likely that some of the information there is incomplete or inaccurate, so it will have to be verified and brought up to date. It may also be necessary to enhance the type information there. Configuration keys that are based on a pattern rather than having a fixed name do not currently live in the param table, so we will have to come up with a scheme for adding these key patterns. (This would be useful for other reasons) Once the param table has the necessary information. It would be a simple matter to have condor_config_val and condor_reconfig check the validity of all keys in the config. Tasks Write code to walk the configuration and parse as classad expression all keys that are known to be expressions. Hook that code up to condor_config_val -validate, and condor_reconfig Enhance the param table to indicate which keys are or may be expressions Enhance the param table so that we can express key patterns for keys that do not have fixed names such as SUBMIT_REQUIREMENT_<TAG>
creator: johnkn

title: Ticket #5719: Negotiator writes duplicate data to AccountantnewLog, slows negotiatio
description: LIGO reports that their negotiator runs so slowly at Caltech that it the negotiator ad ages out of the collector unless the Accountantnew.log file is put in /dev/shm. Also, they have a large number (> 2k) of accounting groups. Inspection shows the following problems: For users or groups with no current or recent historical usage, and whose HTCondor priority has aged out to the minimum value (0.5), we first calculate a new value < 0.5, write it to the accountant log, then check to see if it is below the threshold, cap it up to the threshold, and write the new value out. The result of this is that every negotiation cycle, we write two entries to the log file for every idle group or user when we should be writing none. Also, at the end of every negotiation cycle, we write out all the accounting info for every group and user, even when it doesn't change. As a result, we tend to rotate (compress) the Accountantnew.log file on every cycle, which defeats the purpose of storing it in a transaction log format. note that the MAX_ACCOUNTANT_DATABASE_SIZE knob doesn't quite do what you'd expect -- it sets the maximum size of the file until it is hit the first time. After compression, the accountant sets it to 2x the compressed size. So, for this ticket, we will only write to the accountant's transaction log when values actually change, instead of unconditionally.

title: Ticket #6565: Remove duplicate strlen calls in cedar
description: In the depths of cedar, there are three interfaces which put a string on the wire. One takes a const char , one a std::string, and the third a MyString. The non-char versions simply pull the char * out of the object, and call the char * version. The first thing the char * version does is call strlen, and pass the results to a function which takes that as an argument. As strings have the length, we should skip the middleman and the extra strlen call.

title: Ticket #2875: Jobs with new style arguments don't show args in condor_q
description: If a job is using new style arguments, then the arguments won't appear under "CMD" in the output of condor_q. % cat submit-1 executable=/bin/echo universe=vanilla hold=true arguments=arguments bare 1 2 3 queue % condor_submit submit-1 Submitting job(s). 1 job(s) submitted to cluster 58. % cat submit-2 executable=/bin/echo universe=vanilla hold=true arguments="arguments quoted 1 2 3" queue % condor_submit submit-2 Submitting job(s). 1 job(s) submitted to cluster 59. % condor_q -- Submitter: puffin.cs.wisc.edu : <128.105.185.14:36212> : puffin.cs.wisc.edu ID OWNER SUBMITTED RUN_TIME ST PRI SIZE CMD 58.0 adesmet 3/8 17:29 0+00:00:00 H 0 97.7 echo arguments bar 59.0 adesmet 3/8 17:29 0+00:00:00 H 0 97.7 echo 2 jobs; 0 idle, 0 running, 2 held In the above, it is expected that the "CMD" entry for both jobs would be identical. The code that collects the information is in /src/condor_utils/condor_arglist.cpp in ArgList::GetArgsStringForDisplay. That code's attempt to look up ATTR_JOB_ATTRIBUTE2 appears to always fail. Hypothesis: the ClassAd projection code that only sends requested attributes doesn't realize that ATTR_JOB_ATTRIBUTE2 is needed in addition to ATTR_JOB_ATTRIBUTE1. Possible fixes: Ensure that whenever ATTR_JOB_ATTRIBUTE1 is included in a projection, automatically include ATTR_JOB_ATTRIBUTE2. A bit special case. You could do this on the schedd's side (very magical and non-obvious) or on the condor_q side. Change condor_submit. to ensure that ATTR_JOB_ATTRIBUTE2 ("Arguments") is always present. See #2876: Ensure Arguments is always in job ad, even if old Args is being used

title: Ticket #4108: document how all the different logs work
description: Our variety of logs can be confusing. Write a new section within the Administrator's manual chapter to categorize and identify how the various logging methods work.
remarks: 2014-Nov-25 15:59:44 by smoler: job event log - a chronological listing of events for a single job. Created because the submit description file has log = <file name>. The events are documented in section 2.6.7. daemon (or subsystem) logs - each daemon records events as it executes file name of each log is inconsistent; when not explicit in param_info.in, set by configuration variable <SUBSYS>_LOG. Many of the daemon logs use a camel case for the daemon name, which is concatenated with Log. size/rotation/locking are specified by a variety of configuration variables events have a time stamp; contains detail of start up for a daemon, statistics (when enabled) job queue log - a transaction log that is the schedd's database of all current jobs in the queue default file is $(SPOOL)/job_queue.log event numbering in src/condor_utils/ClassAdLogEntry.h At intervals set by QUEUE_CLEAN_INTERVAL, condor_schedd goes thru the job_queue.log file and "truncate all transactions" to clean the file. Default is once per day. Thus, there is no maximum size for this file, so it needs to be in a partition with plenty of space. If SCHEDD_BACKUP_SPOOL is True, make a backup copy of the job queue on schedd start up. Default is False. MAX_JOB_QUEUE_LOG_ROTATIONS is maximum number of history files that are saved before deleting the one with the oldest timestamp. event log - logs all job events for all jobs and all users file name is set by configuration variable EVENT_LOG size/rotation? accountant log - a transaction log that is the negotiator's database of all accounting information, which are priorities written by negotiator ?? file name is not configurable? $(SPOOL)/Accountantnew.log users are represented in the DB by username@uid_domain MAX_ACCOUNTANT_DATABASE_SIZE sets max size in bytes of the file before it is "cleaned" or "compacted," rewriting the file in a more compact form. admins interact with the DB by using condor_userprio schedd audit log - optional log to record user-initiated events that modify the job queue file name is set by configuration variable SCHEDD_AUDIT_LOG size/rotation set by MAX_SCHEDD_AUDIT_LOG and MAX_NUM_SCHEDD_AUDIT_LOG events are timestamped and the message identifies what changed for which job. Should be for any _rm _hold _release _submit command. value of NEGOTIATOR_MATCH_LOG - a second log from the negotiator, written only with items that have DEBUG level D_MATCH file name is set with configuration variable NEGOTIATOR_MATCH_LOG, and the default value is $(LOG)/MatchLog size/rotation? history log - optional log for info about all jobs that have completed defaults to $(SPOOL)/history written by schedd size/rotation set by ENABLE_HISTORY_ROTATION, MAX_HISTORY_LOG, MAX_HISTORY_ROTATIONS admins can view historical info with condor_history For DAGMan, there are more logs: the default node log -- used to enforce the dependencies of the DAG default file name is set by configuration variable DAGMAN_DEFAULT_NODE_LOG size/rotation? one per DAG submission; each SUBDAG has its own log dagman.out file - like a daemon log (for dprintfs) file name is ?? size/rotation? one per DAG submission; each SUBDAG has its own log jobstate.log file - ?? (for Pegasus) file name is ?? size/rotation? one per DAG submission; each SUBDAG has its own log node status file - not really log, as it forms a snapshot of the current status of a DAG file name is ?? one per DAG submission

description: HTCondor GSI (and SSL?) authentication should honor the Subject Alternative Names in x509 certificates. See ticket #6127 for details. title: Ticket #2930: Allow "weak" parent/child relationships
description: Brooklin says that a user would like to have the option of specifying "weak" parent/child relationships in a DAG -- in other words, not all of a job's parents have to finish before it runs. It seems like the simplest possibility would be to specify that a job runs when a certain percentage of its parent jobs have completed, but we may want other options besides that. (We need to think about both the user's perspective and the implementation perspective.) Also, we need to think about what happens to "unneeded" parent jobs -- do they get removed? We'll really have to be careful when implementing this -- I think there are a lot of ways that the internal logic of DAGMan could get goofed up. We need to make sure that recovery mode and rescue DAGs work correctly with this feature.
remarks: 2012-Apr-20 14:45:54 by wenger: Miron just mentioned that he is concerned with this introducing a statistical bias into people's results, if jobs don't finish because of some characteristic of the job itself, as opposed to landing on a bad machine or something (e.g., are all of your outliers the ones that take a long time to finish, and therefore if you exclude them you are really biasing your results). 2012-May-15 20:59:04 by nwp: Perhaps DAGman would be better implemented as a "schedd on the side", that is, a schedd with some additional capability to control job submission---a la the dependency graph of DAGman. e.g,. users could then query the "schedd on the side" for job status. Also implement a (classad) library so that users can write their own policies, like "start jobs in cluster B after 80% of jobs in cluster A have completed" or "Do not submit any jobs if more than 50 jobs are idle (or such)" 2012-Jun-18 12:55:53 by nwp: If I remember Brooklin's original email correctly, this would be better implemented as a master-worker program, rather than DAGman. 2015-Oct-29 14:05:44 by wenger: I think another option for this is something like, "the child is submitted after the parent has been successfully submitted" or "the child is submitted after the parent has submitted and started running". title: Ticket #3622: RFE: condor co-scheduling with openstack
description: So an idea I've had running around my head, now that brianb has exposed the .py bindings, was: "What if we were to overload a Openstack nova-scheduler driver to use condor as a co-scheduler to "share" a cluster and play nicely together." Openstack is written in python and is very extensible, at almost every layer one can override and configure their own optimized widget. One such place, is the nova-scheduler.driver, which basically chooses the resource where openstack can schedule it's job. title: Ticket #6420: Python submit object does not behave the same as condor_submit
description: The Python binding object htcondor.Submit() is supposed to allow users to use the familiar submit-file keywords to submit jobs. Unfortunately, submitting the same job with condor_submit results in a different job classad than submitting via the Python the htcondor.Submit() object. Primary reason appears that the python Submit.queue() always does the most backward compatible thing, while condor_submit command-line tool checks the version of the schedd you are trying to submit to and will use the most up-to-date features that the schedd will support. This impacts file transfer, as well as the way the job’s environment is specified, and possibly a few other things. First reported by Xin Wang in this htcondor-users thread. Here is code that demonstrates the problem by submitting the same job via Python and via condor_submit, and then comparing the respective job classads that end up in the schedd: #!/usr/bin/env python import os import htcondor # # Create a submit object with a simple job # sub = htcondor.Submit() sub['universe'] = 'vanilla' sub['environment'] = '"PYTHONHOME=/my/path/to/anaconda3"' sub['executable'] = '/usr/bin/python' sub['arguments'] = '/my/path/to/scripts/myrun.py' sub['log'] = '/tmp/job.log' sub['output'] = '/tmp/test.log' sub['error'] = '/tmp/test.err' sub['should_transfer_files'] = 'YES' sub['hold'] = 'true' # # Use HTCondor python bindings to submit the job, and # save this job id in jobId1 # schedd = htcondor.Schedd() with schedd.transaction() as txn: jobId1 = sub.queue(txn) # # Now convert the job described in the submit object into a # string containing name=value pairs, and use this string as stdin # to condor_submit. Save this job id in jobId2 # job = "" for x in sub.items(): job += x[0] + " = " + x[1] + "\n" job += "queue \n" jobId2=os.popen("echo '" + job + "' | condor_submit -terse - | awk '{print $1}'" ).read().rstrip() # # Finally compare the two jobs. Hopefully they are the same. # os.system("condor_q -l " + str(jobId1) + " " + jobId2 + " | sort | uniq -u") The only job attributes that should be different between the two jobs should ClusterId and GlobalJobId, but unfortunately that is not the case. Behold when testing on HTCondor v8.6.6: [tannenba@localhost test]$ ./pytestrun.py ClusterId = 34 ClusterId = 35 CumulativeRemoteSysCpu = 0.0 CumulativeRemoteUserCpu = 0.0 EnvDelim = ";" Environment = "PYTHONHOME=/my/path/to/anaconda3" Env = "PYTHONHOME=/my/path/to/anaconda3" Err = "_condor_stderr" Err = "/tmp/test.err" GlobalJobId = "localhost#34.0#1506453150" GlobalJobId = "localhost#35.0#1506453150" Out = "_condor_stdout" Out = "/tmp/test.log" TransferOutputRemaps = "_condor_stdout=/tmp/test.log;_condor_stderr=/tmp/test.err"

title: Ticket #7231: Add dataflow jobs to HTCondor
description: LIGO would like an optional "dataflow" mode, wherein jobs whose declared output files all exist and whose mtimes are all later than the declared input files mtimes would be skipped. This allows a quick re-run of large workflows.
remarks: 2019-Oct-14 17:20:02 by coatsworth: I've completed a code prototype for this dataflow mode that seems to work well. ToddT asked me to put together a design document, although it's straightforward and simple enough that I'm just going to explain it here in the ticket. We can implement this dataflow mode almost entirely in the condor_shadow, after the condor_schedd has claimed a resource. Before the shadow activates the claim (and hence invokes the condor_starter) it checks if the declared output files are newer than the claimed input files. It does this by sending the job ad to a static function in the FileTransfer object called AreOutputFileNewerThanInputFiles() (this needs a better name). If the output files are newer, the shadow_v61_main.cpp::startShadow() function sets a few attributes in the job ad to indicated the job completed successfully, then invokes the BaseShadow::shutDown() method. This skips the process execution and drops us off at the point where the shadow is about to exit. We ensure that both "Job submitted" and "Job terminated" events show up in the log so that DAGMan can process these jobs correctly. The prototype I've put together seems to work just fine, so unless anybody has objections to this approach I'll start working on production code shortly. 2019-Dec-03 10:07:33 by pfc: As soon as this is released, the ball is in LIGO's court to test it.

title: Ticket #6973: Improve minicondor configuration / better secure-by-default
description: This ticket is (for now) a TO-DO for a design document. Once the TOKEN (multiple pool password) authentication method is ready for prime-time, a number of interesting possibilities for improving the default configuration become available. The primary concern with the current FS-only / localhost-only configuration is that there's a lot of configuration to change to allow other machines to join the pool, and that the simplest of the historically-available protocols has been pool password, which precluded flocking; it also had a very flat trust model. The TOKEN protocol has neither of those problems, so we should consider switching the minicondor configuration to use it. To this end, it may be worthwhile to extend TOKEN so that if a (master) password file is specified, but does not exist, HTCondor will create it and fill it in with a sufficiency random bits. This would eliminate some coding in the packaging materials. This is not a complete answer, because user authentication would require the administrator to create tokens, or HTCondor to allow FS (only for user authentication); the latter may be acceptable if we assume that there will not, initially, be any remote submission. We should consider a Puppet-like 'promiscuous mode' for initial key distribution, or something very much like it; we may decide that we actually trust administrators of more than one machine to have a mechanism for key distribution (if nothing else, scp). Since our administrators may not be their networks' administrator, we would at least want to offer some simple way of restricting which machines get keys. We should also consider a simple TUI and/or a Python API (the former perhaps implemented on the latter); the latter may allow us to simplify the construction of annexes (if not of glide-ins). We will also need to consider the ALLOW lists for the minicondor; we have an opportunity to establish convention and/or best practice, and we should take advantage of that. For instance, we may want to suppose the existence of a master key used only to sign tokens for (local) startds, or (another?) one only for users who are authorized to submit jobs. (Is it possible and do we want to identify users, and/or configure Condor, in such a way that the submit node's FS-authenticated identity (after mapping?) is the same as the token-based identity (after mapping?)? That seems like it would have substantial simplicity benefits. This may change the default identity issued by condor_token_create and/or condor_token_fetch.)

title: Ticket #2199: Inconsistent job status for gt2 jobs between condor-g and ce
description: UCSD is reporting that jobs marked running in their Condor-G queue were in fact idle at several CEs using Condor. The problem appears to be caused by the jobs becoming held on the CE. GRAM ignores hold events when determining a job's state. GRAM also makes no attempt to release or remove held jobs, so absent admin-set system periodic expressions, held jobs will remain held forever, with their status reported as running (or possibly idle) to the client. More details here: http://crt.cs.wisc.edu/SelfService/Display.html?id=9237

The GRAM perl code needs to be overhauled to look at what event appears last in the Condor user log. 2015-Feb-11 20:29:21 by bbockelm: UCSD has since switched to HTCondor-CE; abandoning this for now.

title: Ticket #7661: condor_procd spontaneous EXCEPTs which causes a condor_startd EXCEPT
description: The condor_procd erroneously claims that the master has exited and EXCEPTs. Then, the condor_startd asks the newly started condor_procd about a process family that it has been tracking and EXCEPTs when it cannot update usage data. In all of the cases examined to date, the procd believes most or all of the pids that it's tracking have exited, including the condor_master. Death of the master (which started it) causes the procd to exit. in the case of e2015 on 05/28/20, the procd thought the startd and starters had exited but not the master. So the procd remained running, and stopped tracking the process families that the startd and starters had asked it to track. This still caused grief for those daemons. When the procd exits, the master restarts it. All of the daemons notice, kindly wait a second, and reconnect to the new procd process. But they are wholly unprepared for the consequences. All of their requests relating to previously-registered process families fail, because the new procd doesn't know about the registrations. Chaos ensues. Each daemon can't even kill its children, because that's generally done via a kill_family request to the procd. A first look through the procapi snapshot code and the procd logs suggests that when the procd reads /proc to get the set of current pids on the system, it's getting few or no results. OOM Events After a restart of the procd, each starter running a vanilla job says it got an OOM event, logging one of the following: Job was held due to OOM event: Job has gone over memory limit of 4096 megabytes. Peak usage: 32626 megabytes. Spurious OOM event, usage is 0, slot size is 4096 megabytes, ignoring OOM (read 8 bytes) In all cases examined so far, the reported job memory usage is either very small or approximately 32GB (exact values vary). /var/log/messages doesn't show any OOM events.

title: Ticket #5133: accounting groups clarification/example
description: when the +AccountingGroup attribute was first defined for use in submit files it was not used to describe an accounting group in modern terms at all. Instead it was use to define what would be more reasonably be called a user alias. So lets say that I run a submit a job like this: Universe=Vanilla Executable=sleep Arguments=600 condor_userprio will show Effective Priority Res Total Usage Time Since User Name Priority Factor In Use (wghted-hrs) Last Usage ------------------------------- ------------ --------- ------ ------------ ---------- johnkn@machine 500.00 1000.00 0 421.03 1+21:53 and the relevant attributes of condor_userprio -long are AccountingGroup26 = "<none>" Name26 = "johnkn@machine" IsAccountingGroup26 = false Since my username is johnkn. But if I run this job, I'm telling the account to treat "Science" as my NAME for accounting purposes Universe=Vanilla Executable=sleep Arguments=600 +AccountingGroup="Science" And so condor_userprio shows this. Effective Priority Res Total Usage Time Since User Name Priority Factor In Use (wghted-hrs) Last Usage ------------------------------- ------------ --------- ------ ------------ ---------- Science@machine 500.00 1000.00 0 421.03 1+21:53 and the relevant attributes of condor_userprio -long are AccountingGroup17 = "<none>" Name17 = "Science@machine" IsAccountingGroup17 = false Thus the use of +AccountingGroup="Science" is NOT setting a group in the sense that the group accounting uses the term So far this agrees with the above sentence. But for a short period of time HTCondor would treat a . in the AccountingGroup attribute as triggering new behavior. so +AccountingGroup="Science.johnkn" would give be treated as a group specification rather than a user alias. title: Ticket #1520: paths specified in transfer_output_files have undefined meaning
description: When something other than a basename is specified in the transfer output file list, the meaning of this is not well defined. We propose that a path in the transfer output file list should indicate the path from which the output file on the execute machine should be read. Relative paths are relative to the job's scratch directory on the execute machine. The path to which the output file is written on the submit machine is defined by the output file remaps. If no remap is specified, the basename is used. There are two known problems with paths in the output file list: For spooled jobs, the output file list is rewritten by the schedd in the reaper of the input file spooler. It takes the basename of each item in the list and prepends the path to the spool directory. When we try to stage out from the execute machine, we then try to read the output files from these paths into the spool directory, which is just wrong. If we do not mess with the paths in the output file list, stage-out from the execute node works, but then stage-out from the spool (e.g. using condor_transfer_data) fails, because the files in the spool are stored as the basename of the original path, but we are still trying to read from the original path. When condor_submit checks accessibility of output files, it assumes that the path that will be written to is identical to the path in the transfer output files list, rather than applying remaps or taking its basename.

title: Ticket #4688: Fine-grained match auth
description: Scenario: CMS would like users to be able to run their own startds in our global pool. These startds are completely controlled by the user - START expressions, etc. - and authenticate using the user's identity. By default, we do not trust the user's identity to do anything but run their own jobs; how do we enforce this policy? As extra credit - but not necessary for first implementation - the job should be able to specify a list of "trusted users". That way, ToddT can say he trusts the startds launched by BrianB. Thoughts on this scenario: We can't rely on START or Requirements expressions to enforce this policy because we can't trust the contents. We can utilize START / Requirements to optimize the matchmaking, just not as the authorization mechanism. We can trust the AuthenticatedIdentity attribute in the collector, as the collector inserts this (not the startd). We don't want to re-authenticate / re-authorize the startd when the shadow first claims it. We can't afford the authentication costs. Proposed implementation: Add an option for the schedd: SEC_ALLOW_MATCH_PASSWORD = user1@domain1, user2@domain2, ... This is a comma-separated list of identities of startds who are allowed to use match auth (the startd's identity is taken from the AuthenticatedIdentity value in the startd's ad - this means the schedd trusts the collector to do all the work). If unset, any startd is allowed to use match auth with this schedd. Otherwise, match auth is ONLY allowed for users on this list. There's a special token, self, which allows match auth to be used if the startd's identity matches the job's User attribute. Would be nice: It would be nice if the user could also specify an TrustedStartds attribute that can extend the SEC_ALLOW_MATCH_PASSWORD. However, one complication is shadow recycling - we'd have to be OK with the possibility of job A from ToddT trusting BrianB's startd, then having job B from ToddT use the same startd regardless of whether or not it trusted BrianB. How CMS would use this: CMS places a wrapper around the pilot startup script in CVMFS such that anyone with a X509 proxy can launch a "personal pilot". This pilot would launch with the user's proxy and use a START expression to only accept their own jobs. CMS sets up a dedicated child collector for personal pilots. This child collector authenticates startds against the CERN Argus service (same thing we use for schedds). Child collector feeds into the global pool. We set SEC_ALLOW_MATCH_PASSWORD = condor@cms, SELF on all our schedds. Users would submit their tasks to the central CRAB3 service and then be able to launch as many pilots as they wish on whatever resources they can find.
remarks: 2015-Jan-08 10:36:31 by bbockelm: Alright, some updates on the implementation - I ended up using the SecMan logic, so MATCH_AUTH is now just a new authorization level in the security table. There's still a self token that allows jobs to run on startds owned by the job owner. Turns out the match logic is duplicated in the shadow and the schedd. I refactored this centrally as much as possible into src/condor_utils/match_auth_verify.{h,cpp}. To test, I added the following lines to my security configuration: ALLOW_MATCH_AUTH = condor@hcc-briantest.unl.edu ALLOW_ADVERTISE_STARTD = $(ALLOW_DAEMON), bbockelm@hcc-briantest.unl.edu STARTD.SEC_CLIENT_AUTHENTICATION_METHODS = GSI SCHEDD_DEBUG=D_FULLDEBUG, D_SECURITY SHADOW_DEBUG=D_FULLDEBUG, D_SECURITY I setup GSI auth so the host cert mapped to bbockelm@hcc-briantest.unl.edu. Overall, this made the startd to authenticate as my user: $ condor_status -l | grep Auth AuthenticatedIdentity = "bbockelm@hcc-briantest.unl.edu" Then, I turned on D_SECURITY and looked at the security sessions to make sure {execute-side,submit-side}@matchsession only shows up when self is in ALLOW_MATCH_AUTH. 2015-Feb-17 16:30:03 by jfrey: Would this set of config parameters be sufficient: APPEND_REQUIMRENTS = AuthenticatedIdentity =?= Undefined || \ AuthenticatedIdentity == "condor@cms" || \ AuthenticatedIdentity == User || \ member( AuthenticatedIdentity, TrustedStartds ) TrustedStartds = { } SUBMIT_EXPRS = TrustedStartds Like your plan, the AuthenticatedIdentity attribute set by the collector is the root of trust. But here, jobs state which startds they trust, with the default being the Global CMS identity and the job owner. Additional trusted identities can be named in the submit file. The AuthenticatedIdentity=?=Undefined clause is needed for when the startd checks the requirements at job start time. This should be safe, as AuthenticatedIdentity is set by the collector. This requires no code changes in HTCondor. 2015-Feb-18 16:23:02 by jfrey: Addendum to my proposal based on today's phone call: SUBMIT_REQUIREMENTS can be used to ensure that submitters are picking up the appended requirements that restrict which startds the job trusts. Hobble-in startds should include in their START expression the set of job owners they trust.

title: Ticket #450: deadlock errors in quill
description: If quill tries to init the job queue while dbmsd is calling quill_reindextables() or (possibly) quill_purgehistory(), there is a deadlock. Postgres was detecting the deadlock and aborting one of the transactions, but this was causing the job_quill_basic test to fail. Similar errors may exist with other types of updates done by quill. It may be the case that all such errors are recoverable, so the main problem is just when they cause real performance problems or cause the nightly test to fail. I have observed this problem after switching quill over to using buffered i/o when reading job_queue.log. Apparently this changed the timing of some things so that quill's initial update to the db happened at the same time as dbmsd's initial call to the mentioned PL/SQL functions. The two platforms where I observed the problem were ppc64_sles9 and ps3_ydl_5.0. Why only these platforms had problems is likely just a matter of how fast certain operations happened to run on these systems during the test.
remarks: The deadlock problem has been addressed for the specific case that was affecting the job_quill_basic test. I have therefore reapplied the patch to switch quill over to buffered i/o when reading the job queue.

Postgres was detecting the deadlock and aborting one of the transactions, but this was causing the job_quill_basic [...] (By Dan Bradley )

title: Ticket #4237: DaemonCommandProtocol isblocking
description: In DaemonCommandProtocol::ReadCommand, we have: // read in the command from the sock with a timeout value of just 1 second, // since we know there is already some data waiting for us. m_sock->timeout(1); m_result = m_sock->code(m_req); While the comment is technically correct (there is indeed data), the original author forgot that Sock::code reads from the socket until an EOM is sent. For some RPCs, this may be a significant amount of data; in some cases (the CMS glideinWMS pools), even a small amount of data may cause us to hit the timeout. If the timeout is hit, the socket gets closed, causing a significant amount of network churn (assuming updates are sent via TCP). In #4139, as a part of the non-blocking collector work, I posted a branch that includes a non-blocking read command for CEDAR. With that, correctly handling this case is relatively straightforward.
remarks: 2014-Mar-13 11:23:29 by tannenba: Hi Brian, do we have any data on how often this occurs in CMS/glidein? Are we talking a few times per minute, per hour, per day? 2014-Mar-13 12:15:53 by bbockelm: Hi, I count 200k instances of disconnects in the last 2-ish days (logs rollover on size, not time, so it's just an estimate). Brian 2014-Mar-16 22:26:24 by bbockelm: Pushed as branch V8_1-gt4237. Todd, can you please review? 2014-Mar-26 14:56:12 by bbockelm: Here's an example message from the collector: 03/25/14 17:30:10 condor_read(): timeout reading 4075 bytes from <194.67.74.194:43539>. 03/25/14 17:30:10 Buf::read(): condor_read() failed 03/25/14 17:30:10 IO: Packet read failed: read -1 of 4075 03/25/14 17:30:10 DaemonCore: Can't receive command request from 194.67.74.194 (perhaps a timeout?) 2014-Mar-26 17:22:10 by tannenba: Hi Brian, Little concerned after looking over [39640]. This commit implies that condor_read() returns 0 when a read would block (makes sense), but several other places in the code from other commits still assume that condor_read will return -3 when it blocks (which it looks like it never does). What was your thinking moving forward? A few places where callsites to condor_read() are now expecting a different interface than is implemented: C:\home\tannenba\condor\CONDOR_SRC\src\condor_io>grep "\-3" *.cpp . buffers.cpp: if (nr < 0 && (!non_blocking || nr != -3)) { buffers.cpp: if (!non_blocking || nr != -3) { condor_rw.cpp: * Returns < 0 on failure. -1 = general error, -2 = peer closed socket, -3 = read would block. reli_sock.cpp: if ( retval == -3 ) { // -3 means that the read would have blocked; 0 bytes were read reli_sock.cpp: if (p_sock->is_non_blocking() && (tmp_len == -3 || tmp_len >= 0)) { 2014-Mar-29 17:14:03 by tannenba: Latest round of changes looks good, thanks! Cherry-picked into V8_1_5-branch. 2014-Apr-01 08:34:34 by bbockelm: To record some knowledge on the ticket that we discussed already on the phone: This improvement, while important, isn't as earth-shattering as it might first appear. This will make sure the first CEDAR is completely buffered before progressing. However, in most cases, the first CEDAR message is the security handshake. This means that the first message of the security handshake may be non-blocking but the payload could still block. If the command socket is reused, there is no handshake and there is no blocking for the payload after this patch is applied. The two currently-existing places in the code where command sockets are reused are for shadow->schedd communication and for daemon->collector updates over DC. Testing has confirmed that these are now appropriately non-blocking. ToddT is planning a follow-up ticket to provide a "peek" functionality for CEDAR to allow us to make the payloads non-blocking.

title: Ticket #2249: back to back condor_hold + release can cause job removal
description: Steps to repro: get a series of long running sleep jobs to execute: once your schedd is sufficiently busy run 2 times in a row"_condor_q && condor_hold -a && sleep 1 && condor_release -a && condor_q_" watch your queue decrease in size.
remarks:
2011-Jun-16 15:27:34 by tstclair: when looking through the Log you will notice a lot of Job #.-1: not runnable ^^ then they are removed from the queue 2011-Jun-16 15:55:37 by jfrey: I just reproduced with 30 running jobs. Only one of them left the queue during the second hold/release cycle. I see a lot of 'Job 253.-1: not runnable' in the schedd log, so I'm not convinced that's directly related to the problem. Also, the details look different than #1900. That is, the shadow isn't setting JobStatus to 6 (TRANSFERRING_OUTPUT) in the schedd just before exiting. 2011-Jun-16 16:46:17 by tstclair: In tracing it looks to be a race condition on shutdown, because it appears that the shadows are cleaning up after the status has changed from the 2nd modification. Maybe there needs to be some additional logic here. case JOB_KILLED: // If the job isn't being HELD, we'll remove it if ( q_status != HELD ) { set_job_status( job_id.cluster, job_id.proc, REMOVED ); } break; 2011-Jun-17 09:28:35 by matt: I'm able to reproduce by removing the "sleep 1" and running >30 jobs. Only the running jobs appear to be removed, which supports with Tim's theory. This bug is possible from the beginning of time itself. A pain to track down due to numerous code reformattings. commit e36960755e96ac142669df746b95ed43a7111668 Author: wright <wright> Date: Thu Mar 15 21:48:08 2001 +0000 Fixed bug for condor_hold on NT (and any using of the new shadow). If the job we put on hold was running, we used to remove it from the queue. Now, in child_exit(), we check the status of the job in the queue, and if it's HELD, we don't change the job status when the shadow exits w/ JOB_KILLED, JOB_COREDUMPED, etc. This insures that check_zombie() won't remove the job from the queue. commit 209f5873b9c08fe2d7ef7d837ff0f20b985deba9 Author: adiel <adiel> Date: Thu Feb 19 21:40:45 1998 +0000 Jobs that are killed/coredumped are set to status REMOVED instead of COMPLETED Before this the race would have show up as COMPLETED jobs, oops. 2011-Jun-17 10:06:22 by tstclair: So making a simple switch to: case JOB_KILLED: // If the job isn't being HELD, we'll remove it if ( q_status != HELD && q_status != IDLE ) { set_job_status( job_id.cluster, job_id.proc, REMOVED ); } break; fixes this particular issue, but I wonder if it handles all. So the question would be: Is there ever a case where the shadow exits 102, +JOB is marked as idle, and the job should be removed? title: Ticket #903: Remove authorization levels from SETTABLE_ATTRS
description: SETTABLE_ATTRS is an overly flexible set of parameters. It can work with any authorization level, e.g SETTABLE_ATTRS_OWNER checks for OWNER authorization while SETTABLE_ATTRS_CONFIG checks for CONFIG authorization. This flexibility allows for SETTABLE_ATTRS_OWNER=A,B,C and SETTABLE_ATTRS_CONFIG=X,Y,Z to be configured at the same time. However, what's the practical utility of being able to do this. I propose a simplification, updating and making the configuration more clear. The _<Authorization Level> should be removed and all SETTABLE_ATTRS should always require the CONFIG level. An added pain is confusing log messages from configurations such as: ALLOW_OWNER = * SETTABLE_ATTRS_OWNER = A ALLOW_ADMINISTRATOR = * SETTABLE_ATTRS_ADMINISTRATOR = B ALLOW_WRITE = * SETTABLE_ATTRS_WRITE = C $ condor_config_val -neg -rset D=1 Attempt to set configuration "D=1" on negotiator robin.local <127.0.0.1:37239> failed. title: Ticket #3321: make KVM checkpointing user experience like universe=standard
description: The goal is that all a user has to do to switch from standard universe to vanilla+KVM checkpointing is change "universe=standard" to "universe=vanilla; enable_checkpoints = true". This should probably decompose into a number of other tickets, including: implement periodic checkpoints for vanilla+KVM checkpointing allow KVM checkpoints to be stored/retrieved to/from checkpoint server etc. Random things to keep in mind before this hits production: If Condor will write KVM checkpoints to disk and then copy them to the checkpoint server (rather than stream them like it does for standard universe), then with local checkpoint servers on each execute node, the max_vacate_time needs to be at least as long as it takes to write all of RAM (plus some virtual memory for good measure) to disk twice.
remarks: 2013-Jul-09 22:45:07 by bbockelm: Is there any compression for DMTCP checkpoints? In CMS, using crtools, we found that our checkpoints compress by about a factor-5. It'd seem something like Google Snappy would help out here in terms of saving disk activity. FWIW - you write out to disk twice in the worst case, but not the average case. Page cache will probably save you (writes to disk only occur if a certain threshold percentage of RAM is dirty).

title: Ticket #6123: add collector stats to show query and fork time
description: In order to scale the collector even further, we need to know where it is spending its time during queries, how much time we spend forking, and how much time we spend handling an existing query inline because we ran out of fork workers. We will do this by adding 6 new Miron probes, and 2 additional new attributes: HandleQuery Miron probe for time spent handling query commands where Fork was not attempted. HandleLocate Miron probe for time spent handling locate query commands where Fork was not attempted. HandleQueryForked Miron probe for time spent forking to handle query commands HandleLocateForked Miron probe for time spent forking to handle locate query commands HandleQueryMissedFork Miron probe for time spent handling queries the the main Collector because we could not fork HandleLocateMissedFork Miron probe for time spent handling locate queries in the main Collector because we could not fork PeakForkWorkers The largest number of active fork workers in the lifetime of the collector CurrentForkWorkers The number of active fork workers.

title: Ticket #329: Condor-C over-reports RemoteWallClockTime
description: I noticed that when Condor-C jobs finish, on the submit side, the RemoteWallClockTime stored in the job ClassAd is about double what it should be.
remarks: 2015-Apr-16 11:18:12 by jfrey: This is because the CondorJob object in the gridmanager propagates the RemoteWallClockTime value from the remote job ad into the local job ad in the schedd. Then, when the job completes, BaseJob::UpdateRuntimeStats() adds its own calculation of how long the job's been running (calculated from ShadowBday in the local ad). We should use BaseJob::calcRuntimeStats to eliminate this double-counting of runtime.

title: Ticket #779: CMake and Directory restructuring Port
description: The following bug is used for tracking updates and changes made for CMake port, and directory restructuring. For more details see: BuildModernization Goals and Objectives The goal of updating the condor build mechanism is far more reaching then using the latest wiz-bang tool to build code, and is meant to address the following issues: Build consistency across platforms (Including Windows): Currently Imake does a good job for build consistency across *nix variants, however there is an entirely different set of mechanics for dealing with builds on Windows, which few people really understand. To make matters a bit more confusing, is that the mechanism by which we build & test on Windows is quite non-standard which presents an issue as condor becomes a more open source project. This plurality causes several issues in maintaining two desperate build files, with completely different mechanisms. It would be in the best interests for the group in the long run to employ a single build mechanism which has support on all condor platforms. Support for unit testing within the build: For the purposes of testing it is advantageous to have a build tool which supports running automated unit tests as part of a "unit" build, with a minimal amount of external overhead. Packaging: Many build systems provide automated packaging for it's native environment. This can be highly useful as it eliminates and automates custom build steps and scripts and makes it easier to maintain. Having this requirement can reduce the overhead on condor developers and allow them to focus on bug fixes and new features. It also allows flight worthy to get out of the packaging business and simplifies the consumption for downstream folks. Milestones [Completed] Stage 1: Feasibility 9/25/09 Estimated: ~1 Month - likely less Time Elapsed: ~1.2 Months X - Setup existing environment build and analyze. X - Create full configuration (auhtmlonf-cmake) X - Build for linux and Windows X - Simplify build files (done through cmake macros and updated file extensions .unix .linux .window) X - Develop plan for dealing with externals - Currently the plan is to stage uw-externals prior to building and update include and link paths to this loc by default. (everything is external) - This greatly simplifies the build process and cleans up the questions of who does "what" "when" X - Build all code with c++ compiler cleanup non-ansi C-code X - Analyze packaging options CPack will likely meet our needs and eliminate separate steps X - Eliminate unnecessary linkage where possible. tools <tbd>... daemons procd ... libs ccb cedar classad_analysis classad.old daemon_client daemon_core privsep procapi sysapi tt utils tests <tbd> include <previous condor_include> scripts <tbd> examples <tbd> <release_dir> ... Analysis: I was surprised at the levels of "over complexity" within the builds and code dependencies. So in my work going forwards, my primary goal is to simplify. I believe that a cleaner structure would help for future open source progress. IMHO it should easy for a developer / researcher to obtain the source, build, and install a package. Also the directory structure should be easily to follow and navigate. [In Progress as of 11/14/09] Stage 2: Evaluation, Adoption, & Continuation Estimated: ~1 - ? Months Time Elapsed: 2 Months (Near completion) X - Cleanup and cruft and provide tracking branch for UW. (origin/CMAKE) X - Setup an wiki page ticket X - Have an evaluation with RedHat folks X - Cleanup windows build, build against the latest sdk. X - Full Parallel Build including externals [Windows] - Setup Initial Packaging [In Progress] - Have an eval with UW Folks [Next Week? 1/25/10] - add checks for perl, awk, and flex (right now I believe it is assumed) Stage 3: Full Parallel Build, Test, and Packaging (Last Month) - Establish NMI auto-builds - Verify all tests build and pass on all platforms (including windows) - Establish packaging using CPack for all platforms - Setup Unit Testing w/CTest
