title: Ticket #7732: Metrics to measure avoidance of repeated drains.
description: Added the following attribute to the machine ad to implement the corresponding metrics: LastDrainStopTime, which records when the last (unix epoch) time when draining stopped (was cancelled), as distinct from the last time draining completed. Added the following attributes to the defrag daemon's ad: RecentDrainsList, which is a list of ClassAds describing the 10 most-recent drain commands sent by the defrag daemon; and when -- the Unix epoch time the command was issued, who -- the name of the slot being drained, and what -- one of "graceful", "quick", or "fast". RecentCancelsList, which is a list of ClassAds describing the 10 most-recent drains cancel commands sent by the defrag daemon. when -- the Unix epoch time the command was issue, who -- the name of the slot whose drain is being cancelled. Added the recent_counter_timer stats "Drain" to the machine ad, resulting in the usual set of attributes, list below. RecentResMgrDrain RecentResMgrDrainRuntime ResMgrDrain ResMgrDrainRuntime These attributes may be read from a startd in the usual ways, including condor_status -l -statistics ALL:2 -direct <slot-name> original ticket body Context: the CHTC uses the default DEFRAG_RANK, which is -ExpectedMachineGracefulDrainingBadput. If a machine has no jobs, and doesn't get any (because it's been dedicated to a user who's idle right now), it will repeatedly sort to the top of the DEFRAG_RANK. It would not normally be drained more than once, but the CHTC has DEFGRAG_WHOLE_MACHINE_EXPR constructed in such a way that this machine is never considered "whole." Before we can talk about solving the problem, we need to define (and implement as necessary) some metrics so we can know what success means. We came up three simple metrics during our discussion: (a) Add an explicit attribute in the machine ad for when a startd most recently finished draining. (We have EnteredCurrentState, but that's super-obscure.) To match EnteredCurrentState, this should include cancellations. (b) Add an attribute to the machine ad, perhaps using the "stats" implementation, for number of "recent" drains. (c) The defrag daemon should record and advertise the last ?? draining commands it issued, specifically when and to whom. Recording draining metrics in both the defrag daemon and the startd allow us to account for manually-issued drain commands. We don't know right now if the difference between a daemon- and admin- issued drain will be important, so don't distinguish in (a) for now. It would be nice to know, to see if we're draining efficiently, if the job(s) which ran on the just-drained machines would not have run without the draining. This seems like a rather complicated (and configuration-specific) question to answer directly in one of the daemons, so think about what would be required and how to gather it.

We can have LastDrainStopTime report when the drain actually stopped (possibly even preserving it against the drain being cancelled), if we feel that would be more useful. 2020-Jul-22 16:01:19 by tlmiller: I'm making RecentDrainsList and RecentCancelsList reverse-chronological, so that the most recent drain or cancel is always index 0. 2020-Jul-24 15:45:28 by tlmiller: ResMgrDrain ResMgrDrainRuntime RecentResMgrDrain RecentResMgrDrainRuntime 2020-Jul-24 15:49:27 by tlmiller: The ResgMgrDrain* attributes are part of the usual statistics package; I don't know if that's desirable or not. 2020-Oct-19 16:18:11 by tannenba: Design Review Attribute names seem fine, but would be helpful if the ticket description was updated to reflect what actually got implemented. title: Ticket #6820: Improve Python bindings' JobEvent interface
description: After more consultation, we've determined that the JobEvent API would be better (and more Pythonic) if the event-specific data were not represented as JobEvent object attributes, but by making JobEvent objects more dict()-like. Specifically: Add the __getitem__ function, remove the __getattr_ function, and implement cluster, proc, and timestamp. Add __contains__(), keys(), values(), items(), and get(). Add __iter__(), iterkeys(), itervalues(), and iteritems(). Add __len__() and has_key(). Since JobEvent=s are immutable, do NOT implement =clear(), setdefault(), update(), pop(), popitem(), __missing__(), __setitem()__, or __delitem__(). Don't bother implementing __reverse__(), either. Don't bother implementing copy(), either; it's a pain due to C++ pointer management in the underlying object, and seems like there's no reason to want an immutable object anyway. Leave Python 3 issues for another ticket. (It may not be so bad; since a JobEvent is immutable, we don't need to worry about the 'live update' aspect of things, but can get away with just changing the mapping of keys(), values(), and items() to Py_{IterKeys,IterItems,IterValues}()

To avoid having to support the attribute API for 8.8, let's try to get rid of it before the 8.8.0 code-freeze. To avoid losing access to event-specific data, add the __getitem__ function. To avoid losing access to non-event-specific data, make type, cluster, proc, and timestamp normal attributes. We would like to implement the rest of the dictionary interface as time permits, but a keys() method would address a specific probem; see #6814. title: Ticket #2160: Avoid having to truncate node job user log files
description: Right now DAGMan truncates a node job log file to zero length the first time it "sees" it in a run. (This is done because we haven't implemented a way for DAGMan to filter out events in a log file that don't belong to the current run.) Anyhow, it would be really nice if we could avoid this truncation, for several reasons: * Avoid erasing history that might be useful. * Avoid having log file "collisions" be a fatal error. To do this we'd have to add some extra info to the log file events so that any DAGMan instance could identify the events that belong to it. One idea is to add the DAGMan's condor ID, and maybe the schedd name. (One issue with this is that we'd have to do some special work to make recovery mode work correctly if the recovering DAGMan had a different condor ID than the original one.)

title: Ticket #7677: Detect Singularity failure to launch container vs job failure
description: As part of our effort to improve HTCondor's Singularity support so that it can manage container launches instead of glideinWms, we want HTCondor to distinguish between failure of a job running under Singularity vs a failure of Singularity to start a container. As a reference, consider this glideinWMS code - looks like their approach is to have the container drop a success-of-launch file before running the job, and if Singularity exits with a failure it will look if this file exists or not. Upon detection of a Singularity failure, we want the ability to prevent future Singularity jobs from running (at least for a time, to prevent black holes). glideinWMS simply sleeps for 20 mintes... perhaps a first-class HTCondor mechanism can do better. We should have the same unified approach for Docker, Java, and VM universe.... in other words, how we handle failure of a runtime environment should be consistent from the point of view of the user / admin (not necessarily saying the code/implementation has to be unified, but that would be nice).

title: Ticket #6436: Version information asymmetric.
description: In some cases -- perhaps only when a daemon is born with a security session? -- the server (parent) will know the client's (child's) version, but the client (child) will know nothing about the server's (parent's) version -- get_peer_version() will return NULL. This can easily cause severe protocol problems. In particular, CommitTransaction() in 8.3.4 gained the ability to send back a ClassAd on failure; we have since used this ability to add submit requirement reasons (and most recently, warnings). If the client doesn't know the server's version number, the client assumes the server does NOT send such a classad and will fail if it does. This problem was easy to miss previously because this would only happen in the case where there had been some other problem, so it probably just looked like part of that problem (and would go away when that problem was fixed). This did not cause the whole test suite to fail because the shadow doesn't care about successfully updating the schedd until the final update, which must succeed. Since the protocol error happens /after/ the transaction committed, the job ad the shadow checks after being restarted is correct and the shadow exits with a happy job-complete exit code. Other clients, like the gridmanager, are more sensitive to failure.
remarks: 2017-Oct-31 11:40:46 by jfrey: This imbalance can occur due to how the peer versions for the socket are set when resuming a cached security session. The client gets the server's version from the session, if it's there. The client always sends its version to the server as part of starting a new command. The server uses that as the client's version for the socket. Since there's no reply from the server to the client on a session resumption, there's no opportunity for the server to send it's version back to the client. For a negotiated security session, this works ok. RemoteVersion is set in the session policy info on both sides, and it should match the version of the actual peer process. But things can go wrong for a non-negotiated security session (e.g. parent/child, match password). RemoteVersion would need to be explicitly set when calling CreateNonNegotiatedSecuritySession(), and we don't do that (sometimes because we don't know that information). If the session info doesn't include RemoteVersion on either side, then when using the session for a new command, the client doesn't know the server's version, but the server does know the client's version (because the client always sends it). 2017-Oct-31 11:54:00 by jfrey: If we want to maintain peer version symmetry, here's a proposed fix: When using a cached session, either the client doesn't send RemoteVersion to the server, or the server ignores RemoteVersion for setting the socket's peer version, relying on only the cached session info. For the parent/child non-negotiated session, explicitly set RemoteVersion to the parent's version in the session info. Adding version info to other non-negotiated sessions will be tricky, and is beyond the scope of this ticket. 2017-Dec-20 11:33:01 by jfrey: This ticket has no user-visible changes, so no version history. 2017-Dec-20 12:00:33 by zmiller: CODE REVIEW: Also, I did discuss these changes with Jaime long ago, so I sign off on them.

The client's sock object won't have peer [...] (By Jaime Frey ) 2017-Nov-02 10:52 Check-in [52904]: Insert peer version info for parent/child session. #6436 We can assume that a parent and child daemon are the same version, so explicitly set that in the their non-negotiated security session. title: Ticket #6318: Update HTCondor-managed AFS creds when new jobs are submitted or run
description: All of this is assuming you are using the SEC_CREDENTIAL_DIRECTORY, SEC_CREDENTIAL_PRODUCER, CREDMON, etc. to manage creds (krb5 tickets, AFS tokens, whatever) for jobs. Currently, when a job is submitted it sends a "cred" which is opaque to HTCondor to the credd before actually submitting the job. If the credd already has a cred for that user stored in the SEC_CREDENTIAL_DIRECTORY, it simply discards the new cred rather than update them. Instead we should update them every X minutes. We shouldn't update them every time, as then the CREDMON will likely make a fresh call to the KDC and the KDC could become overwhelmed. Likewise, on the execute side, if a job from a user is about to run, and a cred for that user already exists, we currently don't bother updating it. Again, if the existing credential is more than X minutes old, we should update it.
remarks: 2017-Jun-28 17:48:19 by zmiller: I'm proposing to add a configuration variable called SEC_CREDENTIAL_REFRESH_INTERVAL. If it the value is negative, HTCondor will never update the credential if it already exists. (Current behavior, and will remain the default) If the value is zero, HTCondor will always update the credential. Any positive integer then is the number of seconds in which we say the credential is "fresh enough" and doesn't need to be updated. So for one hour you would say: SEC_CREDENTIAL_REFRESH_INTERVAL = 3600 Any comments on the name or behavior?
check_ins: 2017-Jul-07 11:05 Check-in [51834]: Add a knob, SEC_CREDENTIAL_REFRESH_INTERVAL, that controls if and when we update credentials in the SEC_CREDENTIAL_DIRECTORY. #6318 (By zmiller )

title: Ticket #542: job_core_basic_par fails randomly

When the test fails, some resources are still in STARTUP when the master node exits. It is not clear to me why this test is only failing on the master branch. The earliest cases of this failure that I see are from 5/19. I will go ahead and check in a fix for the above race condition in the stable series to be code reviewed by Greg.

Example: 12/21 12:16:54 ********** STARTER starting up *********** 12/21 12:16:54 ** $CondorVersion: 7.4.4 Oct 13 2010 BuildID: 279383 $ 12/21 12:16:54 ** $CondorPlatform: X86_64-LINUX_RHEL5 $ 12/21 12:16:54 ****************************************** 12/21 12:16:54 Submitting machine is "REDACTED HOST NAME" 12/21 12:16:54 EventHandler { 12/21 12:16:54 func =3D 0x4fcd4a 12/21 12:16:54 mask =3D SIGALRM SIGHUP SIGINT SIGUSR1 SIGUSR2 SIGCHLD SIGTSTP 12/21 12:16:54 } 12/21 12:16:54 Done setting resource limits 12/21 12:16:54 *FSM* Transitioning to state "GET_PROC" 12/21 12:16:54 *FSM* Executing state func "get_proc()" [ ] 12/21 12:16:54 Entering get_proc() 12/21 12:16:54 Entering get_job_info() 12/21 12:21:54 condor_read(): timeout reading 5 bytes from <REDACTED IP ADDRESS>. 12/21 12:21:54 IO: Failed to read packet header Stack dump for process 13598 at timestamp 1292962914 (13 frames) condor_starter(dprintf_dump_stack+0xb7)[0x4f8348] condor_starter[0x4f85b6] /lib64/libpthread.so.0[0x3b2c40eb10] /lib64/libc.so.6(gsignal+0x35)[0x3b2b830265] /lib64/libc.so.6(abort+0x110)[0x3b2b831d10] /lib64/libc.so.6(__assert_fail+0xf6)[0x3b2b8296e6] condor_starter(REMOTE_CONDOR_startup_info_request+0x1a1)[0x4f132f] condor_starter(_Z12get_job_infov+0x52)[0x4c296a] condor_starter(_Z8get_procv+0x21)[0x4c2a87] condor_starter(_ZN12StateMachine7executeEv+0x20e)[0x4fd056] condor_starter(main+0x157)[0x4c3923] /lib64/libc.so.6(__libc_start_main+0xf4)[0x3b2b81d994] condor_starter(__gxx_personality_v0+0x3e1)[0x4c2149] 12/21 12:21:54 ERROR "Can't find transition out of state "GET_PROC" for event "CHILD_EXIT"" at line 326 in file state_machine_driver.cpp This is not particularly helpful and suggests something scary is happening. Connections timing out are not particularly rare problems. We should eliminate the noise. The key bit there is "timeout reading 5 bytes." (Why would this happen? If it's a previously checkpointed job using a checkpoint server, but the checkpoint server cannot be accessed, the standard universe shadow will keep trying to contact the checkpoint server with exponential backoff for about an hour, leaving the poor starter hanging. Those interested and with access can see condor-admin 21467 to see the real world example that the above is based on.)

title: Ticket #5534: No IPv6 interfaces detected on Windows.
description: HTCondor's interface detection code uses SIO_GET_INTERFACE_LIST on an AF_INET socket, and doesn't return an IPv6 addresses. The Windows documentation (https://msdn.microsoft.com/en-us/library/windows/desktop/ms741621%28v=vs.85%29.aspx) states that won't work with anything other than IPPROTO_IP. Quick Googling reveals that other people have tried and failed to get IPv6 addresses with this interface. The SIO_ADDRESS_LIST_QUERY ioctl can return IPv6 addresses, but it's not clear if it will return both IPv4 and IPv6 addresses at the same time. Googling reveals that GetAdaptersAddresses() may be the function we want to call.

title: Ticket #7159: Allow users to utilize the token request workflow
description: The token request workflow currently requires ADMINISTRATOR access to utilize. This was done purposely in 8.9.3 to avoid too many changes at once. However, this limitation was a bit artificial - in 8.9.4, we can relax it slightly. Instead of requiring ADMINISTRATOR authorization for all requests, additionally allow users to list/approve tokens for their own identity. That is, if there is a request for the bbockelm identity, then either an administrator or user bbockelm should be allowed to approve the request. Users can already generate their own tokens from a login session (so this isn't allowing new privileges) - but allowing them to additionally utilize the token request workflow reduces the likelihood the user copy/pastes their tokens into random places.

title: Ticket #5164: Bulk submits for condor_dagman
description: When fully loaded, we're seeing pretty huge penalties for our dagman-based workflows versus our non-dagman workflows. Looking at a strace of the schedd, I think one big contribution is the fact dagman submits a cluster-at-a-time while all our other submission methods do bulk submits (multiple procs; 10-100). Our schedds see about 10 condor_submit processes in parallel at any given time and 200-300 condor_dagman processes. We are bottlenecked on accept() new sockets, giving further credence to the idea that a bulk condor_submit would be helpful. Since we want to convert condor_submit into a library anyway for the 8.5 series, I wonder if we could change condor_submit / condor_dagman to do something along the line of: condor_submit file1 file2 file3 where each fileX is a separate submit file and creates a separate cluster.
remarks: 2015-Jul-28 14:33:14 by bbockelm: Unassigning from myself as this is a huge piece of work - just wanted to record the need and use this as a conversation starter. 2015-Jul-29 10:59:16 by wenger: From the DAGMan point of view, there are several complications with this: Often various nodes that are submitted in the same cycle don't have the same set of condor_submit arguments (e.g., VARS, parent node names, etc.). DAGMan currently parses the output of condor_submit, so we'd have to make sure the multi-submit condor_submit produced output containing all of the information DAGMan needs, and DAGMan would have to be changed to parse that output. 2015-Jul-29 11:05:00 by bbockelm: Another possible approach would be to pre-create a schedd socket and let condor_submit inherit that. That way, each condor_submit is completely independent (and unchanged) but the security session and socket are reused. The schedd would see the benefit of bulk submits, but the client side would look "mostly" the same. 2015-Aug-09 11:31:16 by bbockelm: A third, even simpler idea (but with less impact) is to automatically disable the reschedule for condor_submit and perform a condor_reschedule at the end of the cycle when there was at least one successful submit.

title: Ticket #5471: HTCondor View: fix delta
description: The "delta" step is just broken. It starts at index 1 instead of 0, ensuring that the second data value (index 1) is always returned instead of the delta to index 0. Strictly a bug. Proposal: Just fix it. The test requires the new value to be strictly larger than the previous one; otherwise undefined is returned. This is hidden by our automatically converting undefined to 0, but is still buggy. I strongly argue this is a bug. Proposal: Just fix it. 0 is fine. Finally, not strictly a bug, but surprising: if the new number is smaller, the result is undefined. For reasons I don't understand, we get the new number, not undefined/0. Proposal: we really want 3 functions.: delta - Strict delta, may be negative deltainc - delta, but increasing only. If it ever goes backward, return the new value. Useful for things that (theoretically) are monotonically increasing, but may reset. deltadec - deltainc, but decreasing only and converted to an absolute value (that is, make it positive). Useful for hypothetical monotonically decreasing values.

title: Ticket #4260: condor_submit segfaults
description: CMS would like to start testing the 8.1.x series, but cannot because condor_submit segfaults. Valgrind reveals: ==21912== Invalid read of size 8 ==21912== at 0x4D82B78: find_macro_item(char const*, macro_set&) (in /data/srv/glidecondor/lib/libcondor_utils_8_1_4.so) ==21912== by 0x4D82C0F: lookup_macro_exact(char const*, macro_set&, int) (in /data/srv/glidecondor/lib/libcondor_utils_8_1_4.so) ==21912== by 0x4D82CCA: lookup_macro(char const*, char const*, macro_set&, int) (in /data/srv/glidecondor/lib/libcondor_utils_8_1_4.so) ==21912== by 0x4D82F3B: expand_macro (in /data/srv/glidecondor/lib/libcondor_utils_8_1_4.so) ==21912== by 0x411315: SetArguments() (in /data/srv/glidecondor/bin/condor_submit) ==21912== by 0x41EF7E: queue(int) (in /data/srv/glidecondor/bin/condor_submit) ==21912== by 0x420ED2: read_condor_file(_IO_FILE*) (in /data/srv/glidecondor/bin/condor_submit) ==21912== by 0x4215F9: main (in /data/srv/glidecondor/bin/condor_submit) ==21912== Address 0x732d8d0 is 0 bytes after a block of size 512 alloc'd ==21912== at 0x4A07152: operator new[](unsigned long) (vg_replace_malloc.c:363) ==21912== by 0x4D83F6E: insert (in /data/srv/glidecondor/lib/libcondor_utils_8_1_4.so) ==21912== by 0x40D730: set_condor_param(char const*, char const*) (in /data/srv/glidecondor/bin/condor_submit) ==21912== by 0x41F579: queue(int) (in /data/srv/glidecondor/bin/condor_submit) ==21912== by 0x420ED2: read_condor_file(_IO_FILE*) (in /data/srv/glidecondor/bin/condor_submit) ==21912== by 0x4215F9: main (in /data/srv/glidecondor/bin/condor_submit) It appears when the macro table is re-allocated, we don't update the current allocation size. Thus, if we ever go over the default table size, We reallocate the whole table each time we insert something. We segfault if we insert more than twice the number of elements the table is initialized with (or more than 32 items if there is no default size). So, the segfault can possibly trigger if there's ever more than 32 lines in a submit file. This makes sense above because each macro item is 16 bytes and the default size is 32, explaining the 512-byte allocation. As a meta-grumpy-comment: there's nothing here that can't be done with std::vector and std::algorithm's sort and binary_search. Using the standard tools instead of rolling our own would have prevented this.
remarks: bug is fixed, version history needed.

title: Ticket #5922: Improve linux distro detection
description: The cmake build code detects the linux distro by looking at /etc/redhat-release (if it exists) and /etc/issue. title: Ticket #4630: Updates to partitionable slot documentation
description: In /doc/admin-man/multi-core.tex around line 665 it says: "To enable dynamic provisioning, define a slot type with machine resources." It is not necessary to assign it any resources; if you don't you'll get the "normal" definition (ie. "mem=auto, cpu=auto, swap=auto, disk=auto"). What is necessarily is to allocate at least one slot of that type using NUM_SLOTS_TYPE_<N>. The bare minimum to set up partionable slots is: NUM_SLOTS=1 NUM_SLOTS_TYPE_1=1 SLOT_TYPE_1_PARTITIONABLE=TRUE This creates a single partitionable slot that has all of the resources of the machine.

title: Ticket #5308: Docker Universe should allow admin to specify volume mounts
description: Docker containers provide, by default, complete file system isolation -- jobs running in containers see only the files in the filesytem image they booted from, and processes on the host machine outside of the container can't see any files within the container. While is is good for isolation, it is problematic for sharing datasets prestaged on a host, or accessing remote filesystems, which the container may not have credentials to mount. Docker containers can optionally share a directory with the host filesystem via a "volume mount". This is a Linux bind-mount that makes a directory tree on the host visible, readable and writeable by the processes running in the container. Today, Docker Universe always bind-mounts the condor scratch directory into the container. Several users have expressed a desire to have directories other than the scratch directory volume mounted into the docker universe container. One use case is a large dataset prestaged on the host, too big to put into an image. Another use case is access to a network file system that is mounted on the host, because admins are unwilling or unable to grant access to that filesystem to an arbitrary container. Although the requirement to use a volume-mounted filesystem is really an aspect of the job, we'd like to make it easy for administrators to say "always volume mount these directories for any docker universe job that lands on this machine". At the same time, we'd like to provide advanced users the ability to say "this machine can volume mount any of these directories, but will only mount those the user requests". Because these requests will be first class job attributes, the machine will also be able to say "Even though I have volume A, I won't allow user u to access it". We assume there will be a small, fixed number of these. The first set of configuration knobs will be on the startd side. The first will list names of filesystems available to mount: DOCKER_VOLUMES = NAME1, NAME2 Each Volume will then need a path DOCKER_VOLUME_DIR_NAME1 = /path/to/name1:/optional/mount_point DOCKER_VOLUME_DIR_NAME2 = /path/to/name2:/optional/mount_point If the colon and following optional mount point is ommitted, condor treats the entry as if the optional mount point is the same path as the source path. The admin can then tell the start which volumes to always mount: DOCKER_MOUNT_VOLUMES = NAME1 this will cause the condor_start to add the command line parameter --volume /path/to/name1:/optional/mount_point to the docker run command. The above will be the first milestone. Then, we will add to the submit file the ability for the job to request additional volume mounts: docker_volume_mount = name1:/override_default_mount_point, name2 Where the optiona /override_default_mount_point tells condor to mount this volume in a non-default directory in the container. For this to work, the startd will advertise each of its available docker volume mounts as separate entities HasDockerVolumeName1 = true HasDockerVolumeName2 = true and the job's requirements will be modified by condor_submit to require these: Requirements = ... && HasDockerVolumeName1 When the job lands on the machine, the starter will double check the volume mounts, and mount the correct volumes at runtime.

title: Ticket #5758: Docker volume mounts should be an expression
description: Docker volume mounts should be an expression, not a fixed list. The expression should be evaluated within the context of the machine and job ad. Use case: We have local users who need a particular NFS server volume mounted for their jobs, but we don't want to expose this for grid-based jobs that may be running on the same cluster.

That matches what I'd expect HTCondor to do. 2016-Aug-03 07:51:03 by gthain: We talked a lot about naming. _EXPRS often means insert this expression into the ad, like SUBMIT_EXPRS. We though about _REQUIREMENTS, but rejected it for various reasons 2016-Aug-03 14:05:34 by bbockelm: Indeed, that's what EXPRS means. However, for _EXPR: DEFRAG_WHOLE_MACHINE_EXPR STARTD_AD_REEVAL_EXPR The following additionally use the value of the evaluated expression: TRANSFER_QUEUE_USER_EXPR MODIFY_REQUEST_EXPR_* GRIDMANAGER_SELECTION_EXPR However, _IF is not used anywhere.

title: Ticket #7765: Remove C bindings for internal APIs
description: A lot of our functions have C linkage and some of our header files hide C++ symbols when included in C source files. This is due to our lineage of C source code, the last of which disappeared with the standard universe. Most of this is now clutter that can be removed. But we need to be careful to leave in C-linkage that's visible to external code (unless we want to discourage external usage).

title: Ticket #6524: startd may delete a starter object before the starter is reaped.
description: While working on #6500, I discovered a race condition in the STARTD whereby a claim object can be deleted before the condor_starter corresponding to the Starter c++ object that it tracks has been reaped. When this happens, the STARTD never attempts to delete the job sandbox, and also does not add the sandbox to the deletion retry list. (because Starter::exited is never called, and that is where that code lives) The STARTD should be changed so that the instance of the Starter class is not deleted until the condor_starter has been reaped. This will involve making the Starter object not owned by the Claim object, but instead have independent lifetime, with the pid of the condor_starter being used to lookup the Starter object when it is needed. (note that in the current code, there is no need for Starter objects to exist beyond the scope of a single function if there is no condor_starter pid to associate them with) As a part of this fix, the s_starter member of the Claim class will be removed, as well as the c_claim back pointer in the Starter class. Mostly these pointers will just become function arguments, but in a few cases they will be looked up using the condor_starter pid as the key. Because the fix for this race condition requires quite a lot of code refactoring, we will not be making the fix in stable.

We saw this same problem of ignoring SIGINT independently from a different Condor user. If you send me e-mail ( gene@ccs.neu.edu ), we can exchange further information. Here are the things that we know so far: 1. The "unrelated bug" in DMTCP-1.2.4 has now been fixed in DMTCP-1.2.5 (latest Debian package). 2. The issue of ignoring SIGINT turns out to be unrelated to DMTCP. When this bug is present, all Condor jobs will ignore SIGINT. (Could you verify that this is also the case at your site?) 3. To see if the bug is present, it's enough to do something like: cat /proc/`pgrep condor_master`/status | grep SigIgn where `pgrep condor_master` is the pid of condor_master on the machine that starts Condor. If the bug is present, you will see something like: SigIgn: 0000000000001002 The 2 in that bitmastk expands into 0010 in binary. The 1 bit (second from the right) says that signal 2 (SIGINT) is being ignored. You will see this for all condor_* processes -- not just condor_master. 4. We're still trying to track down what configuration of Condor or Debian could cause this behavior. We're seeing this on Debian squeeze (2.6.32-5-amd64 kernel) with Condor 2.8.1. title: Ticket #2971: Add limits to stdout/stderr
description: CMS has a use case where we have servers acting as schedulers submitting jobs on behalf of users. These servers can be quite busy, and it would be useful to be able to limit the size of the stdout/stderr coming back from the job. We don't want to limit DiskUsage for the job itself, since the actual output files get staged elsewhere, but it is possible for CMS users to accidentally generate multi-GB stdout and stderr. Additionally, if we do hit a size limit, I think we'd like to tail rather than truncate, since that's marginally more likely to have useful information in it.

title: Ticket #6031: Improve RANK documentation
description: On 11/30/2016 2:00 PM, Aaron Moate wrote: > Below is HTCondor manual section 3.5.1.4 regarding RANK > expressions. I believe RANK only effects jobs that are > already running in comparison to jobs that are being > considered for matches (as opposed to two jobs that are > not yet running and being considered for matches)? > And that if preemption is disabled then RANK is meaningless? > If this is so, I would suggest making section 3.5.1.4 > more clear. Reading it gives me the impression that > RANK will effect matchmaking while the slot is idle > (which it may? This has always confused me). > > -Moate Hi Moate, Your belief is correct; startd RANK only effects jobs that are already running. People on htcondor-users often have the same confusion; in fact, I answered a question about this very topic just a few days ago --- see the below email thread. You do subscribe to htcondor-users, right? ;-) Kent, below may have text you can lift for improving the documentation in the section Moate referenced. regards, Todd -------- Forwarded Message -------- Subject: Re: Jobs taking a long time to match Date: Tue, 22 Nov 2016 13:28:38 -0600 From: Todd Tannenbaum <tannenba@cs.wisc.edu> To: Szabolcs Horvátth <szabolcs.horvatth@gmail.com>, htcondor-users@cs.wisc.edu On 11/22/2016 1:00 PM, Szabolcs Horvátth wrote: > Hi, > > I'm trying to find the reason why some of our condor jobs can take a > really long time to get matched. The situation is the following: > > - There are submitted jobs that have high machine rank so they are > supposed to start as soon as slots are available. > - There are available slots that match the job requirements, condor_q > analyze confirms that, but other users' lower ranked jobs get matched to > these slots. Setting the startd rank (i.e. RANK = .... in condor_config) does not control how fast slots get matched, nor does it prevent lower ranked jobs from getting matched to those slots. What startd rank DOES do is tells the startd "if possible, preempt and replace the currently running job with a higher ranked idle job". Essentially, it is a way for the machine to rank how much it likes the job it is currently matched with, and tells the condor_negotiator to keep looking for a match it likes better than its current one. So if a machine has an unclaimed slot, it will first be offered to the highest priority user (regardless of startd RANK). Once the slot is claimed by the highest priority user with a job that matches the slot, startd RANK kicks in and the condor_negotiator will continue to look to see if there are jobs from a different user that RANK higher - if so, the job from the highest priority user will be preempted and replaced with the job that ranks higher. Note that startd RANK always implies preemption- if you don't want job to be preempted, startd rank does not help you. If you want to control who gets "first shot" at a slot, you would normally adjust user priorities (aka condor_userprio -setfactor user@domain 1) or group quotas. If you want to increase the frequency at which matchmaking occurs (it only happens every NEGOTIATOR_INTERVAL seconds, or when someone run condor_submit, condor_reschedule), decrease NEGOTIATOR_INTERVAL. Hope the above helps, Todd
remarks: 2016-Dec-01 09:17:52 by wenger: ... except that the default NEGOTIATOR_PRE_JOB_RANK includes My.Rank, which according to the manual, refers to the machine rank, not the job rank. (The manual appears to say that the sort goes in the following order: NEGOTIATOR_PRE_JOB_RANK job's rank NEGOTIATOR_POST_JOB_RANK PREEMPTION_RANK where the job's rank is a hard-coded sort key and can't be ignored. This I'm less sure about.) - ToddM

title: Ticket #2455: CREAM leases set in the past
description: Rod Walker reports instances where the gridmanager calculates a job lease for CREAM jobs that's in the past. The CREAM server rejects this lease expiration time and job submissions fail. Milestones Diagnose when this behavior occurs
remarks: 2011-Oct-24 13:55:41 by jfrey: We need more information to debug this further. I've been unable to reproduce this problem and it hasn't reoccurred on Rod Walker's machines. I'm deferring this ticket until we have more information. 2011-Dec-01 15:30:01 by jfrey: I now understand why this bug occurs. When a lease update attempt fails, the gridmanager sets LastJobLeaseRenewalFailed=True in the job ad. On subsequent update attempts, the expiration time from the first failed attempted is used until there's a successful update, even if that expiration time elapses. When a lease is shared across multiple jobs, this poisons all of the jobs, as the earliest expiration time is used. The lease management code in the gridmanager needs to be overhauled. As a short-term fix, we can ignore LastJobLeaseRenewalFailed and always base the new lease expiration time on the current time. 2011-Dec-05 14:00:38 by jfrey: I've pushed a patch to V7_6-branch and posted a pre-release binary for Rod Walker, Xin Zhao and Igor Sfiligoi to try: ftp://ftp.cs.wisc.edu/condor/temporary/forrod/2011-12-01/condor_gridmanager 2012-Jan-06 14:32:40 by jfrey: Rod Walker reports that lease problems have not reoccurred since installing the patched binary.

title: Ticket #6046: Fix build on Mac OS 10.12 Sierra
description: Apple continues to discourage use of the OpenSSL libraries it provides. Starting with Xcode for macOS 10.12, the libraries are no longer in the default search path. Although the libraries are present in /usr/lib, the compiler doesn't look there when linking. Instead, it looks in /Applications/Xcode.app/Contents/Developer/Platforms/MacOSX.platform/Developer/SDKs/MacOSX.sdk/usr/lib. The compiler does this by using the -syslibroot option when calling ld. Adding -L/usr/lib to the compile line doesn't help. But making symlinks to the libraries in a different location and using -L with that directory does work. CMake's find_library() gives us the full path to the OpenSSL libraries under /usr/lib. So our problem comes from externals that link to the libraries using -lssl -lcrypto.

title: Ticket #1279: New jobmanager version command crashes gt2 gahp
description: Gram client library function globus_gram_client_get_jobmanager_version() returns a hashtable of information about a remote gram jobmanager. The validity of the hashtable argument when an error is returned is not well-defined. For some errors, it is defined and must be freed by the client. For other errors, it's undefined and must be ignored by the client. The gt2 gahp server assumes it's always defined and attempts to access it, frequently resulting in a seg-fault. When an older gram jobmanager returns an error that it doesn't understand the version command, the gram client library returns gram error 91 and a valid, though sparse, hashtable. When a jobmanager closes the connection without sending a reply, the client library returns gram error 10 and an undefined hashtable reference. Due to another bug (#1280), the latter case is most common. The gram client documentation says that the hashtable reference is always undefined when an error is returned, but ignoring the hashtable in the error 91 case results in a memory leak. A viable workaround appears to be possible. Set the hashtable reference to NULL before the call to globus_gram_client_get_jobmanager_version(). If it's still NULL after the call, then leave it alone. Otherwise, it's a valid hashtable that can be consulted and must be freed. This ambiguity in the gram client interface has been reported to Globus: http://jira.globus.org/browse/GRAM-142

title: Ticket #4581: Local hostname and IP address unrelated
description: In init_local_hostname() in ipv6_hostname.cpp, the hostname and IP address selected to identify the local machine have no explicit relationship to each other. On a machine with multiple network interfaces, we can end up using the hostname of one interface and the IP address of another interface. In addition, setting NETWORK_INTERFACE only affects the IP address we use and setting NETWORK_HOSTNAME only affects the hostname we use. In init_local_hostname(), it appears on casual inspection that we'll set the IP address based on the hostname, when we examine the records returned by ipv6_getaddrinfo(). But the IP address is always initialized earlier in the function, because we always have a value for NETWORK_INTERFACE (with '*' as a default). We should do a better job of having the hostname and IP address we use correspond to the same network interface.

title: Ticket #6416: condor_config_val -expand has unexpected new behavior
description: In versions of HTCondor prior to 8.7.2 condor_config_val -expand foo behaved the same as condor_config_val foo. title: Ticket #3301: Improve gridmanager reaction to gahp failing to start
description: Whenever a GAHP server exits unexpectedly, the gridmanager exits as well. This makes recovery in the gridmanager easier and works well enough if a GAHP failure is a rare event. With BOSCO, we start GAHPs on remote machines over SSH. Now, GAHP failures can be very common, caused by things such as network failure, remote machine failure, invalid ssh credentials, and incorrect platform for the remote binaries. The gridmanager's suicide reaction can now be overkill. An easy improvement is to have the gridmanager not suicide if the GAHP fails to start up properly. Instead, the gridmanager can put the affected jobs on hold with a meaningful hold reason.

title: Ticket #2843: Have Starter set MemoryUsage into the job ad
description: The STARTER needs to set or update the MemoryUsed attribute in the job ad, and the value needs to be reported into the user log so that users can learn what their actual memory requirements are. The value set into MemoryUsed should be configurable on the execute node, on the theory that different operating systems may have a different 'best measure' of memory used. The current plan is to use ResidentSetSize on Linux and Windows. Note that the ResidentSetSize attribute has been defined as the sum of the MAX working set values for the process tree, not the current values. This will tend to overstate memory used, but not quite so much as ImageSize does. In order for users to learn what to set for request_memory in their submit file, we should report the value changes for MemoryUsed into the user log just as we report changes in ImageSize. These extra values will be added to the end of the existing updated ImageSize event (so it is fully backwards compatible).

title: Ticket #6553: GPUsUsage accounts for multiple GPU devices improperly.
description: This was easy to test with partitionable slots, and is broken.
remarks: 2018-Feb-02 16:10:28 by tlmiller: There were a number of problems. The first problem was that we were copying the StartOfJob* attributes on every Aggregate() call, which meant that the second GPU's StartOfJob* attributes were over-writing the first's... which would still be wrong, because we need to aggregate StartOfJob* across all devices in the slot ad. In fact, because slot ads are recomputed every time, we need to store device-specific StartOfJob* attributes in the device-specific ad and aggregate them every time in the Aggregate() ad. We also needed to move the ResetStartOfJob code so that it would only trigger when a new sample came in. 2018-Feb-02 16:11:50 by tlmiller: No need to add documentation for a bug fix to an unreleased branch.

title: Ticket #6800: Fix job priority sorting to have a well-defined ordering of jobs
description: When the schedd sorts a user's jobs based on their priority, it actually uses an 8-part sort key of the these job attributes (strongest is first): PreJobPrio1 (higher is better) PreJobPrio2 (higher is better) JobPrio (higher is better) PostJobPrio1 (higher is better) PostJobPrio2 (higher is better) QDate (lower is better) ClusterId (lower is better) ProcId (lower is better) The Pre and Post attributes are undefined by default. When comparing two jobs, if a given Pre or Post attribute is undefined in either job ad, then they are considered equal and the next part of the sort key is examined. This can result in sets of jobs where there's no clear ordering. Consider the following set of jobs: Job ID PreJobPrio1 JobPrio 12.0 2 1 13.0 Undefined 2 14.0 1 3 Job 12.0 sorts before 14.0 (both have PreJobPrio1 and 12.0's value is larger). Job 13.0 sorts both before 12.0 and after 14.0 (13.0 doesn't have PreJobPrio1 defined, so JobPrio is used for the sort comparison). There's no clear ordering. The sorting algorithm should be changed so that an undefined attribute is treated as the value 0.
remarks: CODE_REVIEW: change looks good. as a side note, we should probably drop one of the PreJob prios and one of the PostJob prios. this is insanely overdesigned....
check_ins: 2018-Oct-17 15:05 Check-in [55581]: Docs for bug fix in sorting jobs in priority order. #6800 (By Jaime Frey ) 2018-Oct-17 10:27 Check-in [55578]: Fix job priority sorting to have a well-defined ordering of jobs #6800 If the (Pre|Post)JobPrio(1|2) attributes are undefined in a job ad, use the value 0 for sorting purposes. The old behavior of skipping these sort keys if undefined in either ad lead to cases where there was no correct sort order. [...] (By Jaime Frey )

title: Ticket #7342: Add interactive (console) mode to classad_eval
description: For more serious debugging of ClassAd expressions, it might be nice to have an interactive / console mode for classad_eval, probably entered if you specify nothing on the command line. (Or explicitly; it may be useful to pre-populate the ad with the -file option, for instance. Maybe go interactive whenever there are no expressions are on the command-line?) The idea of course, is that you type an expression and the evaluated form is spit back out. It's unclear if the ad should always be printed, be printed only when changing it, or only when explicitly requested. It seems obvious that full GNU readline(-ish) command-line editing (and history?) should be supported; otherwise, it'll be easier to use the command-line editing supported by your shell in many cases.

title: Ticket #3478: shared_port on dynamic port fails after restart
description: If shared_port is using a dynamic port, and the master is using shared port, then if shared_port dies, all subsequent attempts to restart it on a different port fail, because the newly started shared_port tries to send a keepalive to the master by connecting to the address of the old shared port.
remarks: 2013-Feb-04 16:23:00 by danb: The submitted patch allows shared_port to restart and communicate with the master. There will still be transient communication problems until the address of the old instance of shared_port works its way out of the system. Daemons periodically refresh their address to incorporate changes to the shared_port address, which may include dynamic info such as CCB stuff. Expect up to 10 minutes of chaos. Bottom line: it is still best not to use a dynamic shared port. An additional improvement could be made. The master could remember the dynamic port that was chosen for shared_port (or any other daemon, for that matter), and it could attempt to reuse this port in subsequent restarts. That is orthogonal to this patch, which is still needed in the worst case. 2013-May-21 16:29:49 by tannenba: CODE REVIEW Patch looks good, thanks.

title: Ticket #5955: Improve custom GCE attributes to merge with those set by Condor
description: In our initial support for custom GCE attributes in the submit file (gce_json_file, #5893), the GAHP pastes the text of the custom attributes into its JSON instance description without examination. Thus, the custom attributes can't override or modify ones set by the GAHP. Overriding these attributes is useful and required in many cases. The disk and network configurations are prime examples. The GAHP needs to do a better job of merging the custom attributes into its instance description. An easy first step is to allow the custom attributes to override those written by the GAHP. Thus, if both set the networkInterfaces attribute, the value from the custom attributes wins.

title: Ticket #3182: Getting loadavg does not work on non-English versions of Windows
description: The PDH library we use for getting CPU usage takes locale specific names for performance counters. Since we hardcode the name we use, this means on non-English versions of Windows, the API fails to find the requested counters. Guilty code is in condor_sysapi/load_avg.cpp at around line 323 in the sample_load function. Specifically, the PdhAddCounter function wants the localized counter name. Vista offers an "alternative" function called PdhAddEnglishCounter, which unfortunately we cannot use since we still support XP. The alternative is to follow the suggestions here: http://support.microsoft.com/kb/287159 to acquire the localized name by searching for it using the counter index. The counter we are using is a system counter so I do not believe it is ever liable to change, so we could hardcode that. A third alternative would be to avoid using the pdh helper functions.
remarks: 2012-Aug-07 15:16:29 by johnkn: I propose that we dynalink to the Vista/Win7 function and use it if it is available, otherwise fall back to the current code. That gives us non-english support on Vista and Win7, but not on XP, which would be acceptable to most of our users. -tj

title: Ticket #3028: Condor-C will create non-executable executable in the spool directory
description: When Condor-C submits a job to a remote schedd, if the source executable is not marked as executable, the job will not be marked as executable in the remote spool. The spool directory looks something like this: -bash-3.2$ ll /var/lib/condor-ce/spool/1626/0/cluster1626.proc0.subproc0/test.sh -rw-r--r-- 1 condor condor 46 Jun 2 15:28 /var/lib/condor-ce/spool/1626/0/cluster1626.proc0.subproc0/test.sh This can cause strange job failures on the remote side. In the case of the Condor-CE submitting to PBS, PBS will not do anything and report exit code 0 - no out or err though. When Condor-C is doing the transfer, it should automatically at the executable bits to the appropriate file.

title: Ticket #4217: GT2 GAHP fails badly when it runs out of file descriptors
description: Brian Bockelman and Bockjoo Kim report numerous failures of Condor-G GRAM jobs in GlideinWMS due to the gahp server running out of file descriptors. The errors can occur in many different places in the gahp server (can't open file for transfer, can't accept connection, can't open CA file for authentication). In many cases, no useful error message is propagated anywhere. Eventually, the gahp crashes, taking down the gridmanager and its other gahps with it. This causes a lot of extra recovery work and possibly more failures. Keeping GRIDMANAGER_MAX_PENDING_REQUESTS small can help prevent running out of FDs, but many FDs are used to handle incoming connections to the gahp (for file transfer and job status notifications), which the gridmanager and gahp don't have direct control over. An email from Brian describing the problem: It appears that the gahp_server processes on gfactory-1 has a limit of 1024 open file handles. This is causing various random errors to happen on gahp_servers which are servicing many jobs (in particular, UFL and Purdue, although there are others). When running out of FDs (or almost run out), it appears that the gahp_server has relatively unpredictable behavior. For example, it can sometimes accept a new connections (for example, from globus-url-copy), but not open the file to write the output. This results in a HTTP 400 error, which you are seeing (but the error is not logged anywhere). Another way this manifests is being unable to open the CA cert in /etc/grid-security, causing what appears to be "network issues" when communicating with the remote CE. The appropriate error messages do not appear to be logged. Watching a few, it does not appear to be a leaked FD; rather, it seems the pending queries eventually are returned. It's possible the factory's setting of 500 pending queries per gahp does not help here. Eventually, the gahp_server segfaults and dies (segfaults appear to be happening at least once a minute) -- but causes various issues until then. It's difficult to see exactly what's happening because the logs rotate once every 5 minutes or so. The gahp server dying causes the grid_manager to EXCEPT, causing all other gahp servers serviced by that grid_manager to get nuked -- meaning that other sites are going to have GT5 stdout/err issues if one does. So, recommendations for the factory: 1) Decrease the number of pending queries from the grid manager and set the status query limit rate for the gahp servers. 2) Increase the maximum file descriptors per gahp server. 3) Keep logs for more than a few minutes. 4) Keep core files and report them to the HTCondor team. There are some obvious improvements for the HTCondor team too (log failures, take appropriate action when FDs run low in the gahp_server); I've CC'd them. It's quite possible (but not guaranteed) that all the stdout/err issues - and many of the status issues - are caused by this.
remarks: 2014-Feb-18 21:09:52 by bbockelm: Random Thoughts: Does GT5 have job status notifications? I thought condor-g polls (or, at least, that's the impression I got from strace). If this is true, we have a mechanism to throttle. my_ez.cpp limits the number of accepted connections to 20. After that, connections are backlogged because accept() isn't called. This has always bugged me because we basically have no clue how many stageouts are being silently failed. It would be much better to connect, then immediately deny, attempts over the limit (and log appropriately). The limit probably ought to be configurable too. If open() fails for writing or reading in my_ez, it's not logged. Knowing that we were looking for an EMFILE would have saved considerable time. The GAHP needs a logging mechanism to provide feedback to the GridManager. I suspect that Globus has a very nice error message when CA certs fail to open that is getting swallowed. File descriptors increase slowly - we could periodically record this and tell the grid manager to back off. Even giving a "fake result" back to the grid manager may be helpful. We probably need to make the FD limit configurable throughout the grid_manager / gahp stack. As a correction, in the case of the factory, it was an unrelated gahp (cream_gahp) which was pulling down the grid_manager. Didn't exactly do wonders for GT5 (uploads of file transfers from the CE failed while things were down). 2014-Feb-19 10:59:57 by jfrey: Random Responses: GT5 has job notifications from the jobmanager to the client, which is why they don't feel the need to have a bulk query option. There's no way for the client to tell if it has missed a notification, so Condor-G does polling of all of the individual jobs as a backup. title: Ticket #889: Split up the WriteUserLog class
description: Synopsis Currently, the WriteUserLog class has several issues: There's a lot of duplicate logic to accommodate the addition of the event log For the schedd, which likely has a lot of WriteUserLog objects, there are man open file handles to the event log file. This intertwining of these functions has increased the complexity of the code, making it increasingly more difficult to maintain. Fixes To fix this, I propose: Split up WriteUserLog into a base class, and two thin derived classes WriteUserLogBase would be the class with logic shared between the "normal" user log and event log WriteUserLog would be very small, containing only logic specific to the user log. Included in this would be a static pointer to a singleton WriteEventLog object WriteEventLog would contain all of the event log specific logic' As noted above, there would be only a single instance of this object, with pointers to it shared by all of the WriteUserLog objects The pointer to the WriteEventLog singleton would be available to the application through a static accessor method in the WriteUserLog class The schedd would thus be able to directly interact with the WriteEventLog object In particular, it would disable reconfigure events from being propagated through the WriteUserLog objects to the WriteEventLog object, and would instead directly reconfigure the WriteEventLog object.

title: Ticket #2639: # in ALLOW_READ list spams nameserver
description: A user had something like the following in their configuration file: ALLOW_READ = foo.example.com, bar.example.com #, qux.example.com (You can see the exact configuration in condor-admin 22800 ) This assumes that foo, bar, and qux are actual hostnames. This wouldn't have been too bad, but the user reports: "condor suddenly polls our nameservers for a host named "#" at a rather high rate (roughly 1000 requests per minute)." It is highly likely that other invalid hostnames, possibly all non-resolving hostnames, will cause the effect. Under no circumstances should we be spamming a nameserver repeated for a non-resolving address. title: Ticket #923: Better handling of released gt2 jobs with no job-manager
description: When a gt2 gram job with the GridJobId attribute set is released, the gridmanager attempts to determine whether there's a job-manager running on the remote machine for that job by issuing a callback register command to the URL in the gram job contact string. If the result is gram error 79 (GLOBUS_GRAM_PROTOCOL_ERROR_CONTACTING_JOB_MANAGER), the gridmanager assumes there is no job-manager for the job and starts monitoring the job normally. If the result is gram error 7 (AUTHORIZATION), 10 (PROTOCOL_FAILED), or 156 (JOB_CONTACT_NOT_FOUND), the gridmanager thinks something has gone wrong and tries restarting a job-manager for the job. Error 10 is particularly annoying as the gridmanager first tries to send a stop command to the potentially running job-manager. If that also fails, the job ends up on hold. I believe error 10 is a common result when another service (speaking a different protocol) is using the port that the gridmanager is trying to contact. Errors 7, 10, and 156 will occur frequently when a relatively small port range restriction (a couple hundred ports or less) is in place on the CE. When trying to contact a potentially running job-manager for a job that's just been released, all of these errors should be treated the same: assume there's no job-manager running for this job and resume normal monitoring (what's currently done for error 79).

description: I'm looking at the event writing code because of some weird problems Bill ran into (events getting overwritten). title: Ticket #5810: After shared_port restart, master should send update w/o addresses.
description: Currently, immediately after the master restarts the shared port daemon, it will send an update ad (indicating that the shared port daemon is down). That update ad -- because the shared port daemon is down and the way the fix to the rewrite code works -- will contain an old* and not-rewritten address. Instead, it should contain no addressing information at all, as it would if a condor_reconfig were issued while it was waiting for the shared port daemon's address file. This more accurately and consistently reflect the actual situation. * : Old is probably OK -- the shared port daemon's port will generally be fixed except in personal condors -- but not-rewritten could be bad (since address rewriting is necessary for backwards compatibility).

Ticket #1500: Shadow exception when shadow is recyled for use with another job
description: Seen in 7.5.3 but may exist in other versions. The shadow blows up if it is recycled for use with another job. This happens because of the way the user token on Windows is handled (i.e. it's NULL 'd out of existance before switching back to "root"). I've only seen this happen in the shadow for this reason, but it concevably it would happen any time the user is re-initialized the way it is done in the user log code: first it calls uninit_user_ids() followed imediatly by init_user_ids(). Ultimatly what happens is that some piece of code calls set_priv() to switch to the user, when the user's token is NULL. In the case of our shadow exception this happens in dprintf() (which is called by inside init_user_ids()) after it has done the actualy printing thing, and is reverting the the previous priv level.
remarks: 2010-Jul-12 20:03:15 by matt: Ben, do you have a test procedure that demonstrates the issue? Bonus points if it runs in the test suite. Dan, will you code review? 2010-Jul-12 21:38:59 by burnett: It can be reproduced with the printname example that is shipped with the Windows distribution. All I did was add +ShadowWaitForDebug=true and queue 20 so that I could track down the source of the error. As far as I can tell it only will happened on a shadow recycle right now, so unless the shadow looks for another job, things will go on working fine. So it shows up rather erratically if you don't use a debugger on it. For instance, I used the same printname with just queue 20 I only saw the exceptions start after the first 10 jobs had been run. 2010-Oct-08 11:34:24 by tannenba: It may be that in order to reproduce this bug, you need dprintf set at a high-enough level. The issue is the shadow blows up inside dprintf when priv stating, so if your dprintf level is not verbose enough, you may not step on the landmine. title: Ticket #1384: reduce round-trips between schedd and shadows
description: There are numerous interactions between the shadow and the schedd that involve the shadow sending something over a TCP socket and waiting for the schedd to send back a response and then the schedd waiting for the shadow to send the next request. I found that by removing the round-trip in SetAttribute(), the sustained throughput in jobs/s that the schedd could achieve increased by about 30% (from 169 jobs/s to 217 jobs/s). This is nearly as much improvement as I observed when completely disabling job queue updates in the shadow, so, although a few more round-trips could likely be removed, it appears that SetAttribute() was the main culprit. Both of these observations were made with the job queue log on /dev/shm. With the job queue log on a local disk, I only see about a 15% improvement in throughput, and things are almost entirely limited by fsync.
remarks: 2010-Apr-30 09:51:02 by tstclair: We see little/no performance benefit on this one. Do you have more details on your submission and server side config? Our baseline tests are following: 20k sleep 60 jobs. 3072 slots on 6 16-core machines each running 32 startd's SHADOW_WORKLIFE=CLAIM_WORKLIFE=7200 in order to elim negotiation blibs and see raw schedd perf. logs are on an ssd drive. 2010-Apr-30 10:27:33 by danb: With 3072 slots and 60s jobs, I don't think you are pushing the schedd hard enough to see the benefit from this patch. 3072 jobs/60s = 51.2 jobs/s I am testing with 20k 0-second sleep jobs on 400 slots. Although the jobs are 0-second sleep jobs, it seems to often take a second for the starter to complete the task. I haven't investigated why. With no user log and with spool in /dev/shm, stack sampling of the schedd showed that it was spending a sizable fraction of its time (approx 1/3) waiting for the shadow to respond in the qmgmt command handler. After removing the round-trips in SetAttribute, it spends much less time waiting on the shadow, and I see about a 30% increase in throughput. At the rate my jobs are running, I find that with more than 400 slots, my schedd can't keep up with all the shadows and I get increased failures. This decreases throughput somewhat. I haven't investigated this aspect in much detail. My config: MAX_JOBS_RUNNING = 400 MAX_ACCEPTS_PER_CYCLE = 0 SHADOW_WORKLIFE = -1 SPOOL = /dev/shm/spool SHADOW_LOCK = My submit file: executable = /bin/sleep arguments = 0 notification = never should_transfer_files = yes when_to_transfer_output = on_exit transfer_executable = false queue 20000 2010-Apr-30 10:35:52 by tstclair: ack, we will give this a whirl b4 & after.

title: Ticket #7600: Implement resource provisioning in condor
description: We want to implement resource provisioning into the HTCondor system. Specifically, we want to introduce a special kind of job, a "provisioner job", whose purpose is to acquire compute resources on remote clusters (ie. Amazon EC2, Argonne Cooley). The main use case is for users to put a provisioner node in their DAGMan workflows, such that other nodes in the DAG execute on the allocated resources. This is a master ticket for this work, which loosely includes the following tasks: Define a special type of provisioner job which the condor_schedd recognizes as different from regular jobs. If a provisioner job fails, the condor_schedd always wants to recover it so we don't leave expensive compute resources running indefinitely. Implement a provisioner node in condor_dagman. Create an Amazon EC2 provisioner script which uses the condor_annex to allocate EC2 compute resources. Child tickets: #5622 adds a basic, minimal provisioner node into condor_dagman. It's mostly just plumbing at this point, still lots of DAGMan work to be done in future tickets. #7333 implements an Amazon EC2 provisioner based on the condor_annex. This is the executable that actually requests and later terminates the compute resources.
remarks: 2020-Dec-04 12:36:28 by coatsworth: Miron's thinking has evolved on this topic. Resource provisioning was initially envisioned as a first-class citizen in DAGMan; more recently, Miron is thinking about provisioning happening in a regular node as part of a DAGMan workflow. This work is currently being continued in https://opensciencegrid.atlassian.net/browse/HTCONDOR-95, in which a Slurm provisioner is built into a regular DAGMan workflow. If we ever decide to revisit implementing a first-class DAGMan provisioner, I'll add links to it here as well as the above Jira ticket. For now, I'm closing this ticket.

title: Ticket #7315: Additional S3 improvements
description: After talking to a few folks around CHTC - and demoing what we have done for S3 integration, a number of solid ideas for future improvements have come about. I'll write them into this ticket - but once we are ready to work on these, they really ought to be separate tickets. "Process each object in a bucket" - that is, have a straightforward mechanism to generate a job per object in a given S3 bucket. "Transfer in all files to a S3 bucket" - Lauren mentioned some user fan-out / fan-in DAGs may result in 100 output files from the "fan out" step all needing to be downloaded by a single "fan-in" job. As it is today, users would need to list out 100 S3 URLs to accomplish this. "Check credentials early" - try issuing a HEAD against a presigned URL to verify the credentials are valid prior to submitting jobs to the queue. "Check space early" - As a part of (3), record the resulting file size and ensure request_disk is sufficiently large to transfer the input sandbox. "Allow default key files" - add a config knob for each key file. (Feel free to add other user-facing ideas...)
creator: bbockelm

title: Ticket #4169: Speed up schedd restart time by eliminating uneeded fsyncs
description: CMS AnaOps reported to htcondor-support: Dear HTCondor team. I just restarted the schedd on a node that was handling 7k running jobs. At start time, the schedd wasted ~3mins printing out the remaining job lease times! The CPU usage during that time was in the ~2% range. That's a lot of wasted time! I expect a non-negligible fraction of the job leases expired due to this :( Is the schedd at least doing anything useful in that time, or is it really just waiting on log file being written to disk? Upon investigation, the problem was not so much the printing of remaining lease times into the SchedLog, but that the schedd does one fsync during recovery for every job that was running at the time of the crash in order to reconcile committed run times. The proposed patch will fsync just once after correcting committed run times for all jobs (instead of an fsync per job), and move the dprintf mentioned from D_ALWAYS to D_FULLDEBUG.

title: Ticket #1691: Gridmanager should use DelegatedProxyExpiration for cream jobs
description: The gridmanager uses job attribute DelegatedProxyExpiration to avoid refreshing proxies to all gram2 jobs on restart. Without this attribute, on restart, the gridmanager doesn't know when the previously-delegated proxy will expire. Refreshing proxies for all jobs is an expensive operation to be avoided if possible. With Cream, there's only one proxy delegated for many jobs, so refreshing it is inexpensive for the gridmanager. But it's very expensive on the Cream side when it has to push the proxy out to hundreds or thousands of jobs. Thus, the gridmanager should use the DelegatedProxyExpiration attribute for Cream jobs to avoid unnecessary proxy refreshes on a restart.

title: Ticket #974: NMI Glue is a Pit of Despair
description: While testing my glue changes for #715, I've run into an ever deepening pool of suck. The high level view of it is that apparently, years ago when the glue (specifically nmi_tools/ and nmi_glue/) was written, an assumption was made that there would be only a single authoritative source for this glue, for all branches, and that it would live at the end of the trunk. Our nightly builds assume it, the workspace build assumes it, even building a certain tag or branch assumes it. Due to the happy coincidence that our glue scripts, and how they interact with our sources and tests, are identical across all of our branches at this time, our builds and tests work on a day to day basis. This assumption has made it nearly impossible for one to test any changes in a branch to the glue without propagating it all the way to the master and thereby contaminating the nightly builds and whatnot with untested code. After moderate inspection of condor_nmi_submit, how our nightlies work, and so forth, I've come to the conclusion that there were initial design problems which were never solved, punted on, and are now causing the pain. Some design problems are: All of our branches have nmi_glue and nmi_tools, yet only the origin/master instance is actually used during BUILD and TEST runs. This is especially apparent in the nightlies, no matter which tag you are building. The existence of those directories in each branch produced an implication that glue scripts are local to a branch and will only affect the building of that branch. From a developer point of view, the glue associated with the branch *should be* the glue used to make and test that branch. Fixed. See #1195 In workspace builds, it is somewhat unclear to me which glue actually gets used. It appears to me that the glue used in the BUILD stage is the one from the workspace, but the glue used in the TEST stage is the one from origin/master. From a developer's point of view, both instances of the glue should be from the workspace itself. One cannot correctly test glue changes without contaminating all builds and tests for all branches including nightlies. In the nightlies, condor_nmi_submit is responsible for finding the nightly tags file and submitting the builds and tests. Since we don't have a condor_nmi_submit, we get one from origin/master and call that one. This means we use origin/master's glue for all branches built. From a developer's point of view, the nightly.pl script should parse the tags, checkout the correct version of nmi_tools and nmi_glue, and then invoke that with the right branch tags so the build and tests gets the right glue. Fixed. See #1195 / #1397. Even though there is one branch for the glue, the submit_info file is actually checked out from the individual branches in question in the nightlies and read by the condor_nmi_submit. This is crazy, as it means the format and meaning of that file must be identical across all branches because it is only read by one version of the glue! Made obselete by #1195 / #1397. The SubmitInfo.pm file now matches the condor_nmi_submit that uses it. While doing work for #366, I came across another problem. I was adding new targets to condor_tests/Imakefile and found that the NMI glue builds the tests in the test suite in a radically different manner than how a developer does it. Basically, the test glue builds a few named targets, then each test actually needing to be run is build independently. Since some of those tests rely on a new dependency which has to exist in the toplevel condor_tests/ directory, I'd have to add a new make invocation in the glue to ensure it exists. Make can't do it itself, because there are completely separate Makefiles in condor_tests/ condor_tests/gcc condor_tests/g77 condor_tests/gpp condor_tests/f90 that don't really know about each other. I found that changing the glue in a certain manner, suppose altering the syntax or presence of the submit_info file, causes the new glue to be unable to build previous incarnation or tags of Condor which predate the glue change. This is due to the head of the master trying to find what it think to be the correct files or state in older tags or branches. Basically, the NMI Glue not only expects to see an identical version of itself across all branches, but also across all time on those branches. The nightly.pl script, which fires off the nightly builds is only valid at origin/master. Worse than that, the nightly.pl script updates itself as it is running from cron, meaning if you make a change to it, the nightlies on the day you made the change won't see it, but the next nightlies will, unless you manually update the copy in ~cndrauto/condor on nmi-s006. See #1195 / #1397 for now it works sanely.

title: Ticket #6787: Default value for DEFAULT_JOB_MAX_RETRIES too high
description: I believe that the default value of 10 for DEFAULT_JOB_MAX_RETRIES is too high. Obviously you may disagree and you should feel free to mark this ticket resolved. The case I'm worried about is that a user intentionally or via cut-and-paste sets success_exit_code in his/her submit command. Doesn't matter the value, just that it is explicitly set, rather than defaulting to 0. The user may be doing this in order to define the condition for job failure and get a consequent notification. Regardless of the notifications settings, such a job will be retried 10 times with the "out of the box" configuration. This is almost certainly wasted cycles. "Fool me once" and all that. If the user does want a notification, this is almost certainly not the behavior they desire because notifications (appear to be) are generated when the job exits the queue. In this instance, the user won't get a notification until the job has failed 10+1=11 times. A default value of 0 or 1 seems more appropriate.

title: Ticket #427: Make proxy refresh handling consistent in the gridmanager
description: The gridmanager's handling of forwarding renewed proxies is very inconsistent across the different grid-types. The handling should be made more consistent. The different behaviors are outlined here: In gt2, the proxy is immediately forwarded to a running jobmanager, but a stopped jobmanager will be restarted only if the old proxy has less than 6 hours of life left. In gt4, the renewed proxy is forwarded if the old proxy has less than 11 hours of life left, and failed attempts are retried at most every 5 minutes. In cream, the renewed proxy is forwarded immediately, and failed attempts are retried at most every 5 minutes. In condor, the renewed proxy is forwarded immediately, and the interval between failed attempts is controlled by GRIDMANAGER_PROXY_REFRESH_INTERVAL. In lsf/pbs, the renewed proxy is forwarded immediately and there's no control of retries on failure. In nordugrid, there is no forwarding of renewed proxies. Some difference in behavior may be appropriate between systems where forwarding is done per job (gt2, condor, pbs/lsf) vs per site (gt4, cream). In the latter case, more aggressive forwarding is acceptable.

title: Ticket #1107: Change Dynamic Slot names to slotX_Y from slotX.Y
description: See, https://bugzilla.redhat.com/show_bug.cgi?id=483666 Basically, a dynamic slot's Name is "slotX.Y@Machine". This is displayed by condor_status and can be used in constraints. When using STARTD_SLOT_ATTRS, other slots on a Startd get attributes of the form slotX.Y_Attr. This is a problem because attribute names should not include a period (.), and expressions referencing slotX.Y_Attr -> ERROR. It is possible to replace the . with a _ before sharing Attr, but that will create a special case and users will need to know the displayed name of the slot is not the same as the name used in policy. To fix this problem and avoid special casing, a dynamic slot's name should use a _ instead of the .. It does not appear possible to quote slotX.Y_Attr in policy expressions, as new classad grammar suggests.
