title: Ticket #4446: Secure sandboxing for glideins
description: (This ticket is more of an open brainstorm) HTCondor has made great strides in the last few years in terms of process isolation (cgroups, namespaces) by taking advantage of new kernel features. Unfortunately, almost all of this progress is useless for users of glideins as they typically run as unprivileged users and all the new kernel techniques require some sort of privilege. Because there's no built-in way to do process isolation, CMS has turned to glexec - this is quite the can of worms! A few ideas: The introduction of user namespaces in the kernel allows most of our process isolation techniques. Unfortunately, this isn't available in RHEL7.0 (although I found a random blog post from a RedHat employee saying there's interest in adding it during the RHEL7.x series. This would be set in condor_master and no changes to the startd would be required. Unfortunately, even the latest Fedora doesn't have this enabled so I don't really have a good development platform. Bah. Use a combination of a ptrace jail and seccomp filter. Modern ptrace ain't your father's ptrace. seccomp mode 2 allows us to filter out the syscalls. We can suppress the payload's ability to call ptrace or send signals and ENOSYS syscalls we don't recognize. Safe syscalls can be passed through to the kernel. PTRACE_O_TRACESECCOMP allows us to pop syscalls that we can't examine from the BPF. This allows us to examine things like which file is being opened by the syscall. We wouldn't need to emulate the syscalls like parrot - just check the arguments and filter them out as necessary. This would allow us to filter filesystem operations. Because we can whitelist the syscalls we want to examine with ptrace, we won't suffer the ptrace overhead for things like futex / clock_gettime. PTRACE_O_EXITKILL prevents the traced processes from escaping in case the sandbox screws up. See http://pdos.csail.mit.edu/~taesoo/pubs/2013/mbox/mbox.pdf for a clever example of how to mitigate TOCTTOU attacks. Signals, filesystem operations, ptrace. What else would we need to look at?

title: Ticket #671: RFE: reverse direction of alive messages, go with startd->schedd
description: By default the Schedd sends ALIVE messages to all Startds executing jobs. For a long time now Condor has had the, undocumented, ability to reverse these ALIVES. The mechanism for sending the ALIVEs is also overly complex, see #32. Condor should change the direction to Startd->Schedd by default. This change should accompany simplification for the ALIVE process and MUST include good documentation so existing administrators with strong firewall policies know how to upgrade their systems. A benefit of the direction reversal is to offload work from the Schedd.
remarks: 2009-Aug-17 10:02:04 by tannenba: I have some additional wisdom about this issue in the associated RUST ticket. 2009-Aug-17 12:25:53 by matt: By having the Schedd send ALIVEs, it has the ability to renew all leases before gracefully shutting down. While this isn't done right now, doing so would help limit the number of leases that expire on jobs while the Schedd is gone. 2010-Aug-16 16:43:56 by jfrey: Pushed changes to master for 7.5.4. In 7.5.4 and beyond, the default is for the startd to send keep-alives to the schedd. If a daemon detects that it's talking to a pre-7.5.4 peer, it will revert to the old default of the schedd sending the keep-alives.

title: Ticket #4016: Knob to control scratch-directory default permissions
description: Between versions 7.8 and 8.0 the default permissions of the starter-created job scratch directory in a regular (non-privsep) setup changed from 0777 & ~umask to 0700 & ~umask. Some jobs PHENIX cluster relied on there permissions being at least group-readable. The analysis-train software runs as a special user who invokes a custom setuid program to copy-as-user to NFS. This was done to allow quotas to be respected during the stage-out of each user's data (anatrain runs jobs on behalf of a user). The program checks the destination, becomes the user, then begins the copy -- which failed when they could no longer read the file because of the directory permissions. This is easily fixed by the job chown'ing its own scratch dir, however it would be nice to be able to configure this as an admin. This small fix adds a new knob to do just that. The fix doesn't take into account privsep, which creates directories with fixed permissions based on if glexec is in use. See Design Document (text version available here).

title: Ticket #4915: Collector reuses invalid socket for forwarding
description: OSG is observing issues with our central collector. The HTCondor-CE instance use the CONDOR_VIEW_HOST configuration variable to forward schedd ads from the site collector to a central collector at GOC. We've observed many HTCondor-CE instances disappear from the collector after the biweekly maintenance, only to come back after a "condor_reconfig" is done at the site. CMS has seen something similar when a top-level collector dies; since this (thankfully) doesn't happen often, we don't have a good way to reproduce. We've been working under the assumption that this is tied in to issues with invalid security sessions. However, OSG just got the server-logs and I no longer think this is security-related. Here's the server logs at D_FULLDEBUG,D_NETWORK: 02/26/15 12:39:29 ACCEPT bound to <129.79.53.205:9619?alias=collector1.opensciencegrid.org%2cvip-collector.grid.iu.edu> fd=13 peer=<129.93.239.132:41134> 02/26/15 12:39:29 condor_read(fd=13 <129.93.239.132:41134>,,size=4,timeout=1,flags=2,non_blocking=0) 02/26/15 12:39:29 condor_read(fd=13 <129.93.239.132:41134>,,size=5,timeout=0,flags=0,non_blocking=1) 02/26/15 12:39:29 condor_read(fd=13 <129.93.239.132:41134>,,size=481,timeout=0,flags=0,non_blocking=1) 02/26/15 12:39:29 Stream::get(int) incorrect pad received: ffffffd1 Here's the sendto() statement from strace: sendto(4, "\1\0\0\1\341\321@\312\375l\253\211\30\1c\354\351\257R\16V\0\0\0\0\0\0\352j\0\0\0\0\0\0\0\20Command = 1\0SessionDuration = \"86400\"\0AuthMethods = \"FS,GSI\"\0Authentication = \"OPTIONAL\"\0Enact = \"NO\"\0Subsystem = \"COLLECTOR\"\0ServerCommandSock = \"<129.93.239.132:9619?noUDP&sock=collector>\"\0ParentUniqueID = \"red-gw1:1561060:1423603964\"\0Integrity = \"OPTIONAL\"\0RemoteVersion = \"$CondorVersion: 8.3.2 Dec 29 2014 $\"\0NewSession = \"YES\"\0CryptoMethods = \"3DES,BLOWFISH\"\0OutgoingNegotiation = \"PREFERRED\"\0Encryption = \"OPTIONAL\"\0SessionLease = 3600\0ServerPid = 1561113\0\0\0", 502, 0, NULL, 0) = 502 In particular, look at the header: \1\0\0\1\341\321@\312\375l\253\211\30 Bytes 5-13 are supposed to be a command int, properly padded; it looks like garbage (FWIW, the command int should be "\0\0\0\0\0\0\352j" instead). Ah-ha! Poking around in the collector code, we create a list of DaemonClient objects and ReliSocks during the config process. In CollectorDaemon::send_classad_to_sock, we have the following code: if (!view_sock->is_connected()) { // We must have gotten disconnected. (Or this is the 1st time.) .... if (view_sock_timeslice.isTimeToRun()) { ... view_coll->connectSock(view_sock,20); Looking in the ReliSock code, it doesn't seem that we flush message buffers on state transitions. I think we are seeing leftover gunk in the buffers from the previous disconnect. I see two approaches: We delete-and-recreate the ReliSock object. We fix ReliSock to not have crap in its buffers. (1) is an easy fix. (2) is probably more appropriate, as I have no clue where else we might reuse ReliSock objects for multiple connections!
remarks: 2015-Feb-27 16:35:53 by jfrey: If integrity checking is enabled, then bytes 5-20 are the checksum, and the command int is after that. And the expected command int is there after 16 bytes of checksum. This isn't corruption. 2015-Feb-27 16:38:35 by jfrey: However, we did find a problem with buffers not being fully cleared on a close and reconnect when non-blocking mode is used for writing. ReliSock::SndMsg::m_out_buf needs to be deleted and set to NULL in ReliSock::init(). But the more we think about this, the more we're being convinced that a ReliSock or SafeSock should not be reused after it's closed. 2015-Feb-27 17:03:17 by jfrey: It appears that when the ReliSock is closed and reopened, the state for whether to do integrity checks isn't cleared. So in the new connection, the client starts out doing checksums when the server isn't expecting it (since they've yet to establish a security session). And CCB reuses closed ReliSocks, so we can't just ban that code path. 2015-Mar-16 15:44:08 by tannenba: Condierations while creating a patch for this ticket: I didn't want to just change how the collector uses relisock, since there is at least one other place in HTCondor where a relisock is closed and then subsequently reused (ccb client). I didn't want to simply obliterate all state when a relisock is closed, because some of the state (like bytes send/received) still makes sense to query after a close(), and some places in the code assume this. Ideally I wanted a patch that fixed as much of the underlying cedar problems as I felt safe to do in a stable series. So after much back and forth, I decided to tackle this problem by fixing just the specific problems in CEDAR with reuse of a relisock that were causing observable problems: the fact that buffers and security state lingered on after a close(). So the patches do not clear out the entire minefield, but it did clear out some mines from known code paths. Someday we should make close() private to just cedar destructors and ccb, and make the Sock copy constructor private as well (currently the copy ctor is being used by daemoncore Create_Thread). Assigning this ticket over to Jaime for a code review. I tested this patch by recreating the problem described above by starting a view collector on port 9666, and then starting up a personal condor on the same machine using the following config: NETWORK_INTERFACE = 127.0.0.1 CONDOR_HOST = 127.0.0.1 DAEMON_LIST = MASTER,COLLECTOR,NEGOTIATOR,SCHEDD,STARTD UPDATE_INTERVAL = 2 SEC_DEFAULT_INTEGRITY = REQUIRED CONDOR_VIEW_HOST = 127.0.0.1:9666 COLLECTOR.UPDATE_COLLECTOR_WITH_TCP = True Before the patch, restarting the view collector resulted in the view collector failing to receive any further updates until a condor_reconfig of the personal condor. After the patch, behavior worked as expected: a restart of the view collector caused it to send an out-of-band session invalidate to the collector at port 9618, after which updates were received. 2015-Mar-16 15:48:41 by jfrey: Code Review These changes look good.

title: Ticket #3100: New ClassAd::Insert() doesn't handle attribute names properly
description: The new ClassAd method Insert(std::string&) doesn't handle attribute names properly. It takes a single string which should consist of an attribute name, a '=', and an expression. First, it assumes the only whitespace around the attribute name is a possible single space between the name and the '='. Second, it doesn't handle quoted attribute names at all. Quoted attribute names can contain a '=', fouling the method's search for the '=' that separates name and value. And quote attribute names need to be unquoted before being passed to Insert(const std::string& attrName, ClassAd *& expr, bool cache).

title: Ticket #6302: file transfer of directories windows to linux directory delimiter bug
description: From htcondor-users: I am currently running into an issue trying to transfer output from a Windows (2012R2) Exec back to a Linux (SLES11SP3) schedd. The job creates a directory named results in the condor execute directory and writes output there. Then based on the submit file Condor tries to copy the results directory back to the schedd. However it looks like it gets confused about the file name and ends up creating a file called results\output.h5 on the schedd instead of putting output.h5 into the results directory. The full description on htcondor-users is available here. This appears to be a case of HTCondor not properly understanding the directory delimiter (backwards vs forwards slash) when transferring the contents of directories, and requires a code patch to fix. In the meantime, there is a work-around available to the end user by leveraging transfer_output_remaps in the job submit file. For instance, to workaround the problem described above the user could put transfer_output_remaps = "results\\output.h5=results/output.h5" in their submit file.

title: Ticket #7840: Make DEACTIVATE_CLAIM command more robust to failure
description: When the shadow decides to abort a job execution (e.g. because the job is removed), it sends a DEACTIVATE_CLAIM command (or a DEACTIVATE_CLAIM_FORCIBLY command) to the startd. To maintain backwards compatibility with pre-7.0.5 startds, the shadow doesn't expect a response to its request. Recently in the BaTLab, we've seen cases where the startd doesn't receive a DEACTIVATE_CLAIM connection request from the shared port daemon before the shared port daemon and the shadow time out. With an existing security session, the shadow assumes the command has been delivered when it was not. The shadow then waits forever for the starter t exit, which will not happen before the job exits. We should change the shadow to require a response from the startd. If there is no response, the shadow should make a new DEACTIVATE_CLAIM request.

title: Ticket #7513: Customized job classads appended to Requirements depending on name
description: With 8.9.5 and using the python bindings, customized classads that start with the word 'Request' and evaluate to numbers are automatically added to the Requirements expression, expecting to find a counterpart in the machine classads. This does not happen with e.g.: 8.8.1 or 8.9.2 for example. E.g.: RequestJobNumber will expect to find 'JobNumber' in the machine classads and (TARGET.JobNumber >= RequestJobNumber) will be automatically added to the job Requirements, preventing the job from matching if JobNumber is not present in the machine classads. Expected behavior: +RequestJobNumber should be added to the job classads, but not expect anything on the machine classads side. How to reproduce: # Results with condor 8.9.5 $ condor_version $CondorVersion: 8.9.5 Dec 30 2019 BuildID: 493601 PackageID: 8.9.5-1 $ $CondorPlatform: x86_64_RedHat7 $ $ cat submit.py import classad import htcondor schedd = htcondor.Schedd() sub = htcondor.Submit(""" universe = vanilla executable = test.sh arguments = 3 Output = out.$(Cluster)-$(Process) Log = log.$(Cluster) """) sub['My.JobName'] = classad.quote("jobtest1") sub['My.AnotherJobNumber'] = '4' sub['My.RequestJobNumber'] = '4' with schedd.transaction() as txn: submitRes = sub.queue(txn) print("ClusterId: {}".format(submitRes)) $ python submit.py ClusterId: 2654 $ condor_q 2654 -l | grep Requirements Requirements = (TARGET.Arch == "X86_64") && (TARGET.OpSys == "LINUX") && (TARGET.Disk >= RequestDisk) && (TARGET.Memory >= RequestMemory) && (TARGET.JobNumber >= RequestJobNumber) && ((TARGET.FileSystemDomain == MY.FileSystemDomain) || (TARGET.HasFileTransfer)) ## Results with 8.8.1 $ condor_version $CondorVersion: 8.8.1 Feb 18 2019 BuildID: 461773 PackageID: 8.8.1-1 $ $CondorPlatform: x86_64_RedHat7 $ $ cat submit.py import classad import htcondor schedd = htcondor.Schedd() sub = htcondor.Submit(""" universe = vanilla executable = test.sh arguments = 3 Output = out.$(Cluster)-$(Process) Log = log.$(Cluster) """) sub['My.JobName'] = classad.quote("jobtest1") sub['My.AnotherJobNumber'] = '4' sub['My.RequestJobNumber'] = '4' with schedd.transaction() as txn: submitRes = sub.queue(txn) print("ClusterId: {}".format(submitRes)) $ python submit.py ClusterId: 774 $ condor_q 774 -l | grep Requirements Requirements = (TARGET.Arch == "X86_64") && (TARGET.OpSys == "LINUX") && (TARGET.Disk >= RequestDisk) && (TARGET.Memory >= RequestMemory) && ((TARGET.FileSystemDomain == MY.FileSystemDomain) || (TARGET.HasFileTransfer))

E.g.: Requirements = (((REQUIRED_OS =?= "any") || (GLIDEIN_REQUIRED_OS =?= "any") || stringListMember(GLIDEIN_REQUIRED_OS,REQUIRED_OS)) && (AuthenticatedIdentity =!= "volunteer-node@cern.ch")) && (TARGET.Arch == "X86_64") && (TARGET.OpSys == "LINUX") && (TARGET.Disk >= RequestDisk) && (TARGET.Memory >= RequestMemory) && (TARGET.Cpus >= RequestCpus) && (TARGET.Disk_RAW >= RequestDisk_RAW) && (TARGET.ResizedCpus >= RequestResizedCpus) && (TARGET.HasFileTransfer) 2020-Mar-02 09:12:08 by khurtado: Okay, the bug in my comment (when schedd round attributes for Disk and Memory are enabled) only happens with: Schedd: HTCondor 8.9.2+ Python bindings: HTCondor 8.8.3 It does not happen if I use python bindings 8.9.2+. title: Ticket #5484: Allow longer leases?
description: It should be possible to implement longer leases, given the ability of the current lease function to reset the alarm. Basically, set an expiration date in the stack [parameters] and check that, with the lease function adding a new heartbeat when the alarm goes off as appropriate.
creator: tlmiller

title: Ticket #2341: Copying a classad in schedd should collapse chained ads
description: We have had multiple instances of the schedd crashing because "deep" copies of job classads from the job queue do not collapse in attributes from chained classads (aka cluster ads). We should always collapse chained ads into a copy of a job ad (aka in the copy ctor and assignment operator). In other words, make a deep copy of a classad instead of doing a deep copy of most things and a shallow copy of the chained ad. Hopefully this will prevent bugs like #2294 from being introduced in the future.
remarks: This may have originated as the indirect result of a LIGO ticket (#2294), but it's not something LIGO is asking for, so I'm removing us as the customer group.
creator: tannenba

remarks: 2019-Aug-07 11:43:16 by jfrey: The core of this bug is a race between DaemonCore::Driver() and SharedEndPoint::PipeListenerThread() operating on the DaemonCore variables async_pipe and async_pipe_signal. PipeListenerThread() calls DaemonCore::Register_PumpWork_TS() and none of the functions in this call stack grab a lock for operating on these variables. Certain interleavings of the of the instructions in the two threads can result in async_pipe_signal set to true and the async_pipe connection empty. This condition is never cleared. The main fix is to unconditionally set async_pipe_signal to false in DaemonCore::Driver() on windows (this is already the behavior on unix). This clears the bad state if the daemon gets into it. We also add usage of InterlockedExchange() when modifying async_pipe_signal reduce risks from cache incoherency. All other changes in this ticket are error detection and reporting. 2019-Aug-07 11:43:32 by jfrey: Code Review This code looks good.

title: Ticket #1994: transfer queue needs better support for dealing with job suspension
description: The file transfer queue on submit.chtc.wisc.edu has been observed in several instances to become backlogged for hours without making much progress. At least one cause of this problem is suspension of jobs that are transferring input files. This happens in CHTC to whole-machine jobs that are suspended while waiting for jobs on all other slots to finish. I don't know if suspension always causes file transfer to be suspended, but in CHTC, that is what I observe. Here is output from ps --forest that shows the condor_starter child process in a suspended state: USER PID %CPU %MEM VSZ RSS TTY STAT START TIME COMMAND condor 30284 0.0 0.0 27120 3384 ? Ss 12:59 0:00 \_ condor_starter -f -a slot10 submit.chtc.wisc.edu condor 30286 0.0 0.0 26988 1604 ? T 12:59 0:00 \_ condor_starter -f -a slot10 submit.chtc.wisc.edu The workaround is to disable queueing of stage-ins: MAX_CONCURRENT_UPLOADS = 0 As an aside, I also note that the starter appears to stop sending ALIVEs to the startd when in this state. In the StartLog I observe the following after the job (file transfer) has been suspended for an hour: 03/23/11 13:59:13 ERROR: Child pid 30284 appears hung! Killing it hard. When this happens, the file transfer is aborted, and the count of active transfers is decremented as it should be. However, the likely result is that a new whole-machine job will soon come along and plug things up again. (But at least it must enter at the end of the queue, so deadlock is avoided.)
remarks: 2011-Mar-23 14:35:00 by tannenba: Strange. So when the startd decides to suspend, it should daemon core signal the starter to suspend the job, but that should not suspend the starter itself. So i do not know why the starter would fail to send daemoncore keepalives. Also, not certain why the starter child process is being suspended .... is something going on due to privsep and/or procd involvement? 2011-Mar-23 15:45:08 by danb: I also see that the file transfer communication timeout is rather large, which may explain why the shadow doesn't give up sooner: STARTER_UPLOAD_TIMEOUT = 3600 With a shorter timeout, the problem of the file transfer queue getting plugged up by suspended transfers may be less of a problem. 2011-Mar-25 17:02:48 by danb: The suspension of the starter's file-transfer sub-process is being done explicitly in the file-transfer object: int FileTransfer::Suspend() { int result = TRUE; // return TRUE if there currently is no thread if (ActiveTransferTid != -1 ) { ASSERT( daemonCore ); result = daemonCore->Suspend_Thread(ActiveTransferTid); } return result; } And in the starter: // If we have a file transfer object, we want to tell it to // suspend any work it might be doing... if( filetrans ) { filetrans->Suspend(); } 2011-Mar-25 22:11:23 by danb: I have committed a patch that improves the reporting of transfer queue state, which should at least make this problem easier to manage in the future. The state of the queue is logged periodically and is published in the schedd ad. Transfers that exceed the maximum age limit are reported via the log and email to the administrator. What remains to be done: decide whether it is desired that file transfer is suspended when the slot is suspended. if so, then is it good enough to rely on the read/write timeouts to avoid hanging for too long? The default read/write timeout is 5 minutes. In CHTC we had jacked this up to 1 hour to workaround problems with parallel universe. also, can the default of 2 hours for MAX_TRANSFER_QUEUE_AGE be improved? Should this mechanism take per-job information into account? 2011-Oct-24 17:02:20 by danb: We now understand why the starter stops sending heartbeats to the startd. The starter hangs when doing a syscall to the shadow, which is stuck doing file transfer, because the starter's file transfer child process is suspended. The shadow does file transfer in its main process because parallel universe breaks if a sub-process is used. (The file transfer object only supports having one sub-process at a time.) 2011-Oct-24 17:10:05 by danb: In a conversation with Todd and Greg, we came up with the following short-term plan for improving things: add a configurable knob that controls whether the starter suspends file transfer or not. Longer-term we would like to be able to set this policy from the startd's SUSPEND/CONTINUE expressions. This means that somehow the file transfer status needs to be made visible. 2011-Nov-03 10:33:59 by danb: Our belief that a shorter STARTER_UPLOAD_TIMEOUT could help avoid transfers plugging up the queue while the transfer is suspended for a long time turned out to be false hope. As the name implies, STARTER_UPLOAD_TIMEOUT only applies to the starter's side of the connection. There is no timeout on the shadow's side. In fact, I now see that we explicitly avoid having a timeout on the shadow side for the very reason we are now wishing we had one. Here's the code in FileTransfer::HandleCommands() that is responsible: // turn off timeouts on sockets, since our peer could get suspended // (like in the case of the starter sending files back to the shadow) sock->timeout(0);

title: Ticket #7456: Fix fine-grained token auth with ALLOW and alternate permissions
description: In 8.9.3 (ticket #7006), we allowed daemon core to implicitly give the ALLOW authorization to fine-grained tokens, even if it's not listed in the token's scopes (the idea being that ALLOW is always allowed). However, it appears this broke in the handling of alternate permission levels in #7225; if ALLOW only shows up in the alternate permission, then daemon_command.cpp requires it to show up in the token. Marking this as a regression in 8.9.4.
remarks: 2019-Dec-31 08:34:07 by bbockelm: It appears there's a similar issue with Sock::isAuthorizationInBoundingSet; however, it's not possible to trigger any bug in that method. We should still fix the issue as it might bite someone in the future. 2020-Jan-15 14:42:22 by tlmiller: Code Review This looks good to me, but I don't know enough about the alternate permissions table to say if it makes sense. Holding off on the merge for now. 2020-Feb-01 14:48:27 by bbockelm: Coming back to this - did you have any particular question on the alternate perms table? Basically, if there are more than one permission levels the command is registered with, we need to use a specific permission level to build the security policy. So, suppose we have something that is accessible via DAEMON and WRITE - which security policy do we use? Instead of trying to do a merge of two policies, one permission level becomes the "primary" (and that security policy is used) and the other(s) becomes the "alternate(s)". So, let's say you have a command (such as requesting tokens) that you want to enable for EVERYONE but want to use a specific security policy (such as DAEMON); for example, you may want the ALLOW authorizations but distrust the CLAIMTOBE that the admin set for ALLOW and instead use the authentication methods for DAEMON. In such a case, you set the primary auth to DAEMON and alternate to ALLOW. That gets to this bug -- all TOKENs are assumed to have the ALLOW authorization. We currently only check if the primary auth'z is set to ALLOW; if the alternates are set to allow, they are ignored. The change in this branch tracks to see if any of the alternate permissions are ALLOW and, if so, accepts the TOKEN. 2020-Feb-03 15:10:05 by tlmiller: So the previous HTCondor solution to wanting multiple authorization levels -- for instance, with the queue management commands -- was to "upgrade" the security of the connection once the appropriate level was determined. That approach won't work with single-authorization-level TOKENs because daemon core will reject them at the lower authorization level. (For instance, an ADVERTISE_SCHEDD token doesn't -- and we don't want it to -- include a WRITE authorization. Without it, daemon core will reject the WRITE-level connection before the command handler is called and can do the "upgrade".) Instead of carrying around an otherwise-unnecessary authorization and requiring the client know to use it for certain commands, we instead updated daemon core to check the "alternate" table for the ALLOW/DENY lists of other authorization levels. This check ignores the other authorization levels' methods (preventing privilege escalation). 2020-Apr-10 07:46:37 by tim: Bulk change of target version from v080906 to v080907 using ticket-target-mover.

title: Ticket #7006: Add support for a token request workflow
description: Whenever we (such as the schedd) can't authenticate with a remote host, but accept tokens, we should have the option to request a token be created for us. This would allow for various token bootstrapping workflows. See https://docs.google.com/document/d/1pxgbs35CiKe_ymGlu4nWDtfH8oKmg-FCAHPS-EA4c2o/edit for a full description.
remarks: 2019-May-08 15:08:58 by tlmiller: Some notes on the design doc, for the record: The attack listed under "denial-of-service" is actually, as noted in the text, more like a brute-force attack. Mitigated by [56651], it seems like it would be wiser -- as hinted at by [56656] -- to at least require the token reply to go to the original token requester's IP. (My initial thought for better-yet was to leave the connection open until the request was approved, but that may be its own DoS attack, and might not actually be any safer if the connection isn't using SSL.) The design doc does not explicitly mention the client ID, which is a second ID used for the request that (if SSL is used) is never shared in the clear. Since the user never ever sees the client ID, we can make it as long and random as we desire, which significantly improves the security of this protocol. (Unless the attack can read the memory of the client process, in which case we're boned anyway.) The protocol as-drawn is deceptive, since it doesn't indicate polling on part of the client between step 4 and 7, which is key to understanding the potential attack models. Other notes: Step 1 in the "implementation" section is ticket #6981. 2019-May-09 15:02:34 by tlmiller: From (implicit -- the variable was not named) commentary in the code, the client ID is intended to be a "human-friendly ID that will help the request approver to identify the request." It is, however, checked during the polling phase to make sure it matches the request ID. We might be better off, instead of an arbitrary client-supplied string, to return a client ID with the request ID (see above). As regards the example client ID (the hostname), it seems like it would be better to have that generated by trusted code (the server), so it can be relied upon (at least as far as your network properly disallows spoofing) for decisions. 2019-May-10 13:38:25 by tlmiller: code review notes Sorted by not ordered by commit ID. title: Ticket #2204: Declare test a failure if "non-printable" characters found in log.
description: There is already logic in the test suite to declare a test failed if "ERROR" appears in the logs. There should be similar logic to declare a test failed if any "non-printable" characters appear in the logs. Such characters almost universally indicate corruption of some sort and thus a bug. Proposed definition of "non-printable": c<8 || c> 127

title: Ticket #1078: Be able to have NOOP jobs in a DAG that are not actually submitted
description: (See condor-gnats 951.) LIGO wants DAGMan to avoid actually submitting NOOP jobs. Pete and I have discussed this, and we'd like to designate jobs as NOOP jobs at the DAG level (as opposed to looking for noop_job in the submit file (or maybe in addition to that?). We haven't figured out the syntax yet, but the idea is that you'd mark a job in the DAG as a noop job, and it wouldn't really get submitted. We could probably implement this by just writing an appropriate submitted and terminated event pair to the right log file, instead of calling condor_submit. If we do this, the existing DAGMan log reading code should correctly mark the node job as done. (PRE and POST scripts, if they exist, would get run as normal.) Once this is implemented, it should allow us to have a nightly test of a truly large DAG (with all noop jobs).
remarks: 2009-Dec-22 15:45:35 by wenger: Ah, I just realized something about this: when we write the "fake" submit and terminated events, we have to have a Condor ID that's not going to conflict with other jobs in the DAG. I wonder if negative values for the cluster ID will work? At any rate, we should have a function that does the fake submit and keeps track of the fake cluster IDs. 2009-Dec-22 16:06:09 by wenger: Oh, yeah -- we have to worry about initialdir in the submit file, too... 2010-Jan-15 13:44:26 by wenger: Pete just suggested using 0 for the cluster ID of the noop jobs, rather than the DAGMan's cluter ID. I think that's a good idea. 2010-Jan-29 09:38:48 by wenger: The code for this is actually committed now, and the test passed last night. I'm leaving the ticket open for now, though, because the documentation isn't finished yet. 2010-Feb-05 19:16:48 by wenger: Just finished documenting this, so I'm going to resolve the ticket.

title: Ticket #3045: Badly-formed XML causes problems in new ClassAd XML parser
description: Some varieties of invalid XML classad documents will send classad::ClassAdXMLParser into an infinite loop. One example is when content data is found outside of an attribute element, like so: <c>ad</c> There may be other instances where an infinite loop can result. Some varieties of invalid XML classad documents will cause classad::ClassAdXMLParser to leak memory. It returns immediately when it encounters the invalid input without deleting the ClassAd it's constructed so far. Invalid input can also result in the parser returning a partially-constructed ClassAd without indicating there was an error or trying to read to the end of the enclosing classad element.

title: Ticket #6617: JobCurrentStartTransferOutputDate incorrect in job ad
description: The attribute JobCurrentStartTransferOutputDate in the job ad is the time at which transfer of the output sandbox started (represented as seconds since the unix epoch). When the FileTransfer object's timings were enhanced to sub-second resolution, this value was no longer a timestamp for most users (linux, possibly windows). The new timing values used a clock that's valid for computing elapsed time within a process but not for generating a timestamp.

title: Ticket #3415: Cream grid jobs fail when no input or output files to transfer
description: When a Cream grid job has no input files or no output files to be transferred, the gridmanager passes invalid URLs of NULL to the nordugrid_gahp for file transfer. The gahp responds with an error message of "Transfer failed: globus_ftp_client: an invalid value for url was used". The job ends up on hold with this as the hold reason. The trouble is that the CreamJob always instantiates a TransferRequest for staging, regardless of whether there are any files to stage. But TransferRequest doesn't expect to be invoked with an empty list of transfers.

title: Ticket #1306: Stop/Start daemons on a master reconfig
description: There is currently no way to have the master start/stop daemons w/o completely restarting the master. This can cause a bit system impact if you are trying to add an additional schedd, or other such daemon, to improve scalability. It would be nice if a reconfig sent to the master would start/stop daemons if DAEMON_LIST has changed.

title: Ticket #333: Condor_submit fails on filesystem with 64-bit timestamps
description:
An OSG user installed a Compute Element that uses Condor to manage fork jobs. Unfortunately, he was unable to submit jobs from any NFS directory, because condor_submit failed. There is no easy workaround, because Globus uses a user's home directory, and these are on NFS. The error that is reported looks like this: % condor_submit submit Submitting job(s) ERROR: No such directory: /home/VCELL/aroy ===== Problem 1 (The easy problem) ===== That error message is totally wrong. The directory exists, but Condor thinks it is inaccessible. This is a low severity, low priority thing, but it should be fixed to report a more accurate message. ===== Problem 2 (The hard problem) ===== The error occurs in condor_submit.v6/submit.C in ComputeRootDir(). The code looks like this: if( access(rootdir, F_OK|X_OK) < 0 ) { fprintf( stderr, "
ERROR: No such directory: %s
", rootdir ); DoCleanup(0,0,NULL); exit( 1 ); The access() function call is actually access_euid(), which is our implementation of access() in condor_util_lib. The call fails here: if ((F_OK == 0) || (mode & F_OK)) { if (stat(path, &buf) < 0) { if( ! errno ) { /* evil! stat() failed but there's no errno! */ dprintf( D_ALWAYS, "WARNING: stat() failed, but " "errno is still 0! Beware of misleading " "error messages
" ); } return -1; } already_stated = 1; } stat() fails and provides an errno of 75 (Value too large for defined data type). This isn't specific to Condor: I wrote a simple program that just calls stat(), and it gets the same error. It only gets this error on NFS, and not for local disks. I figured that this was a problem with the filesystem, so I passed it back to the user. Fix your filesystem! I cried. Unfortunately, they passed the buck back to me. Here is their response: > Ah, but this makes perfect sense... There is no "problem" with the > shared file system... > > The reason for failing with EOVERFLOW error (errno 75 - Value too > large...) is 64bit file support of the shared filesystem. Alain, if you > compile your program with large file support it will not fail: > > [moraru@vdgateway Wed Mar 18 19:01:01 /tmp/stat2] $ gcc > -D_FILE_OFFSET_BITS=64 -o stat stat.c > [moraru@vdgateway Wed Mar 18 19:02:13 /tmp/stat2] $ ./stat /home/VCELL/ > name = /home/VCELL/ > rc = 0 > errno = 0 > > OK - so now you may ask: why did it fail before, even though it didn't > actually encounter any file > 2GB? > > The reason is that our shared file system not only supports large files > using 64 bits, but also supports 64bit timestamps... This is required > for proper synching with NTFS file systems (that always use 64bit > timestamps). See below a comparison between the timestamps on the > shared filesystem and the plain vanilla local Linux filesystem: > > [moraru@vdgateway Wed Mar 18 19:02:21 /tmp/stat2] $ stat /tmp > File: `/tmp' > Size: 4096 Blocks: 16 IO Block: 4096 directory > Device: fd00h/64768d Inode: 491521 Links: 14 > Access: (1777/drwxrwxrwt) Uid: ( 0/ root) Gid: ( 0/ root) > Access: 2009-03-18 18:50:41.000000000 -0400 > Modify: 2009-03-18 19:02:13.000000000 -0400 > Change: 2009-03-18 19:02:13.000000000 -0400 > [moraru@vdgateway Wed Mar 18 19:02:41 /tmp/stat2] $ stat /home/VCELL/ > File: `/home/VCELL/' > Size: 1134 Blocks: 34 IO Block: 4096 directory > Device: 1eh/30d Inode: 4329963743 Links: 45 > Access: (0755/drwxr-xr-x) Uid: ( 0/ root) Gid: (10000/Domain > Users) > Access: 2009-03-18 13:26:34.914135705 -0400 > Modify: 2009-03-18 13:26:34.914135705 -0400 > Change: 2009-03-18 13:26:34.914135705 -0400 > > So, basically a stat() call to **any** path on the shared filesystem > will **always** return 64bit timestamps (atime, ctime, mtime) and > generate EOVERFLOW errors if #define _FILE_OFFSET_BITS=64 was not used. Indeed, I rebuilt my simple stat() program with -D_FILE_OFFSET_BITS=64, and it worked. So the claim is that Condor is in the wrong here. Frankly, I find it weird that every program that runs on their filesystem may need to be recompiled. But what can I do? I talked to Nick about this, and he thinks that if access_euid() used his stat wrapper class, the problem might go away. I don't know if that's the correct solution or not. (Should we have built with this flag?) Also, this problem might be all over Condor: if we fix this call site, will there be others that exhibit the same problem? I don't know. I'll try to keep access to this site. If I can, I'll be happy to work with someone to test potential bug fixes by deploying a personal (non-root) Condor and running tests. Thanks, -alain, on behalf of an OSG site.

title: Ticket #1756: Be able to dynamically add nodes to a running DAG
description: This was requested by the Pegasus folks (and I think other people have wanted it in the past). I think the main thing we'd have to define is the interface for doing this. One thing that was suggested recently is that we have places in the DAG where DAGMan reads a designated "DAG addition" file and incorporates it into the current DAG. That should be fairly simple to implement, I think.
remarks: 2010-Nov-04 10:27:38 by wenger: We need to define exactly how this would work. I'm not sure whether we'd be better off having an entirely new keyword like "INSERT DAG" or whether this should be a special case of "JOB". Internally in the code it probably needs to be a Job object (or maybe a subclass of Job), but instead of actually submitting a job we'd parse the given DAG file. For example: INSERT DAG foo_sub.dag 2011-Apr-12 12:28:53 by wenger: Maybe also allow the "insert" DAG files to declare an existing node to be a NOOP (re yim with Matt F). 2014-May-08 10:43:45 by wenger: I talked with Karan about this at HTCondor Week. For a first cut, at least, they'd be happy with just specifying a "node" in the DAG that would parse a specified "snippet" DAG file and incorporate it into the existing DAG (not as a splice, just directly). I don't think that should be too hard to do -- basically we can just call the existing parse code on the snippet. Some things to watch out for: We'll have to check for a bunch of illegal actions, like adding a parent to a node that's already run. I have to think about how to make this work for rescue DAGs and recovery mode. We'll have to figure out exactly what actions should be illegal -- obviously, adding a parent to an already-run node must be illegal. But I suspect there are other things that could cause problems. At any rate, I need to write up a detailed design for this. 2016-Apr-12 10:37:15 by wenger: Hmm -- something else to think about is handling syntax errors in the dynamic parts. I guess the question is whether a syntax error should be immediately fatal, or whether it should be treated like a node failure. Also, we need to make sure that this works with rescue DAGs and recovery mode... 2016-Apr-12 10:41:53 by wenger: We also need to think about how to handle this internally. I guess there should be a Job object to represent the dynamic parts, since it will have to have parents and children, at least potentially. But either we could subclass Job or have a special flag that says, when you get to this job, don't submit something, parse the specified file. 2016-Apr-12 11:31:18 by wenger: Here's a link to the relevant Pegasus document: https://docs.google.com/document/d/11bqnjiQEsIO8nShkeqBTrpmTqi02okm2tBc7c3cUftM/edit 2016-Apr-12 12:08:39 by wenger: My initial thought is that the syntax could be something like this: DYNAMIC INCLUDE NodeX my_include.dag or JOB INCLUDE NodeX my_include.dag (although the second option would cause problems if anyone already has nodes named "include"). I guess, though, that a way to do this without syntax changes would be to simply make splices parsed dynamically, but I don't think that would be any easier to implement, and I like the increased flexibility of not forcing the dynamic nodes to be a splice (if we implement dynamic include, the include DAG file could just have "bare" nodes). The really tricky thing, though, is that Pegasus wants to use this to do looping. My initial thought on this is that you'd do something like this: DYNAMIC INCLUDE NodeX ... SCRIPT PRE NodeX ... PRE_SKIP NodeX ... RETRY NodeX ... However, looking at the Pegasus document, it looks like they are thinking more in terms of recursion than actual looping. In other words, something like this: == top.dag: DYNAMIC INCLUDE It0 it0.dag SCRIPT PRE It0 ... == it0.dag: JOB calculate ... DYNAMIC INCLUDE It1 it1.dag SCRIPT PRE It1 PARENT calculate CHILD It1 ... I think the "recursion" would actually be easier to deal with from the DAGMan point of view than retries on the dynamic includes. The problem I see with allowing retries on dynamic includes is the interaction with rescue DAGs -- if the same dynamic include file gets overwritten, when you start up the rescue DAG, you'll have lost the nodes for all but the last iteration of the loop. If we use recursion, each "iteration" has its own include DAG, so then we should be okay. Assuming we go with "dynamic include" instead of "dynamic splice", I see possibly implementing this in three phases: Dynamic includes work with "bare" nodes. Dynamic includes work with splices. Dynamic includes work with loops (optional). Anyhow, we clearly need a design document for this, and I need to think more about whether the "recursion" option will actually work with rescue DAGs. 2016-Apr-12 12:20:36 by wenger: Hmm -- something else I just thought of: if we go with "dynamic include" instead of "dynamic splice", what happens if the included DAG file has nodes that have no parents? How will that interact with rescue DAGs? Maybe the way to go is just to make all splices dynamically-parsed, and be able to have PRE and POST scripts on them. (Hmm -- now that I think about it, it would be fairly easy to have PRE scripts on either dynamic includes/dynamic splices, but having POST scripts would be much harder unless we implement socket nodes (gittrac #3587). I haven't really looked at how much work adding the socket nodes is, although we might not absolutely need POST scripts to do what Pegasus wants.) 2016-Apr-12 12:43:14 by wenger: Hmm -- now I'm wondering whether the way to do this is to add socket nodes and make the splices dynamically parsed all at once. I'm thinking that, when we parse the splice command in the top-level DAG, we'd create the parent and child socket nodes, with a parent-child relationship between them. That would give us a place to "attach" PRE and POST scripts, and parent/child relationships to the parents and children of the splice. The parent socket node could then do the parsing of the splice DAG when we get to that point in the DAG -- when we parse the splice DAG, we'd create the proper parent/child relationships between the "internal" splice nodes and the socket nodes. 2016-Apr-26 11:30:16 by wenger: As per phone conference with Karan today -- I need to create a design document for this from the DAGMan point of view, with some examples of what would and would not be allowed. 2016-Apr-28 13:13:40 by wenger: Hmm -- need to think about how this would work (if at all) with the new splice connect feature (also see #3587: Add "socket" nodes for splices). Maybe we wouldn't allow connected splices to be dynamically parsed? 2016-Apr-28 14:54:51 by wenger: Just had a discussion about this with Miron. A few points from this discussion: Add socket nodes first, without dynamic capability (see #3587). Splices should not be dynamic by default -- we should have some new keyword for dynamic splices. The first version, at least, of dynamic splices will not support pin connections. Note: my thought is that maybe we could have a keyword like SPLICE_DYNAMIC or something, but the exact keyword isn't critical.

title: Ticket #3291: Enable syslog output for dprintf
description: It's been a long-standing request to have improved support for improving the integration between Condor and syslog. Based on the new refactoring of dprintf code, it's possible to have multiple output targets - an opportunity for adding a syslog output. In fact, the implementation is fairly trivial and this is implemented in https://github.com/bbockelm/condor.git, branch dprintf_syslog. When the word "SYSLOG" is the target (for example: SCHEDD_LOG = SYSLOG), syslog integration is enabled. Any output which would have been printed by condor logging is sent to syslog level INFO and facility DAEMON. Control of the output contents is handled by the "typical" condor methods. However, I have no Windows box available to me - can you test it? Brian 2012-Nov-12 16:34:20 by johnkn: Todd has some concerns about the consequences of turning on syslog output. title: Ticket #4554: Exceeds MAX_JOBS_RUNNING
description: batches of jobs go past the limit and the excess are then removed. Removal of extra jobs not based on last started first out. killing seems random. set MAX_JOBS_RUNNING at 8 write a submit file which submits 12 jobs against 12 slots. submit and look at user and starter and schedd logs etc.
remarks: 2014-Sep-05 15:50:10 by bt: This seems to be a regression from 8.0.7 2014-Oct-01 16:11:09 by jfrey: This was introduced with the new send-multiple-matches feature of the negotiator (#3585), introduced in 8.1.1. The schedd sees 12 identical jobs, so it sends the negotiator one job ad (one auto cluster) and asks for 12 matches. As each match arrives, the schedd checks whether the next job in the auto cluster can run on it. This includes a check of MAX_JOBS_RUNNING (counting the matches it has been receiving). For the first 8 matches, everything's fine. For the final 4 matches, the check fails. So the schedd falls back to seeing if any job in the queue can run on the match, without a check of MAX_JOBS_RUNNING. The jobs checked include the unmatched jobs it just decided can't run. The schedd then proceeds to claim the startd and start a shadow. Later, the schedd rechecks the entire job queue and notices that there are too many shadows running, and picks 4 random ones to kill. In particular, ScheddNegotiate::nextJob() includes a check of MAX_JOBS_RUNNING (via scheduler_skipJob()) and skips jobs in the auto cluster if it fails. If it runs out of jobs, it sets the id of the next job to -1.-1. The old code that negotiates one job at a time checks for this value and says it has no more jobs to be matched. In the new code, it can keep receiving matches after nextJob() runs out of jobs and starts using id -1.-1. It will call scheduler_handleMatch() with this job id and the additional matches. scheduler_handleMatch() doesn't properly detect that no jobs can be started with the match (it could be dealing with a grid universe job, which doesn't have this limit). It then calls FindRunnableJob() and doesn't do an additional check. 2015-Jan-30 10:29:03 by jfrey: This problem has gone away with the newer negotiation protocol introduced by #4460 for 8.3.0. 2015-Apr-07 14:06:33 by tannenba: CODE REVIEW Patch looks good, thanks.

title: Ticket #7728: Make BaTLab docs build more stable
description: I accidentally broke the BaTLab docs builds for a few hours last week because I added a new extension in docs/conf.py. This broke the build because we do a stripped-down Sphinx run that only builds the man pages, and therefore doesn't need any extra extensions. The problem is that this is driven by a patch file that needed to be updated when I changed the extensions list. This was annoying, and was doubly-annoying because it wasn't obvious that it would be happen. I propose a fix: since the extensions Sphinx configuration attribute is just a list built up at runtime, we should set an environment variable during the BaTLab docs build that explicitly switches it to the more constrained list. title: Ticket #6990: Introduce "secure" random numbers
description: While tinkering with a separate branch, I had the need to create a random request ID that is difficult for an attacker to guess. Looking at the HTCondor random number generator (e.g., get_random_int inside src/condor_utils/get_random_num.cpp), we currently use lrand48. This is a fine generator for doing things like generating random sleep intervals as it has a known distribution across its range. However, lrand48 is not a cryptographically secure RNG: that is, from a small sequence of output values, it's possible to reverse-engineer the state of the generator -- and hence possible to guess the next values in the sequence. So, for example, it should not be used to generate credentials, shared secrets, etc: if an attacker can get HTCondor to generate a sufficient number of secrets, they can guess the next secret sent to a user. I propose we separate out the two use cases: rename the existing get_random_int to get_random_int_insecure and introduce a get_random_int_prng that is appropriate for credential or secrets generation.

title: Ticket #7378: condor_update_machine_add doesn't seem to take -name argument
description: The man page of condor_update_machine_ad indicates it should be able to take a -name argument: Name condor_update_machine_ad update a machine ClassAd Synopsis condor_update_machine_ad [ -help | -version ] condor_update_machine_ad [ -pool centralmanagerhostname[:portnumber] ] [ -name startdname ] path/to/update-ad Description condor_update_machine_ad modifies the specified condor_startd daemon's machine ClassAd. The ClassAd in the file given by path/to/update-ad represents the changed attributes. The changes persists until the condor_startd restarts. If no file is specified on the command line, condor_update_machine_ad reads the update ClassAd from stdin . Contents of the file or stdin must contain a complete ClassAd. This will cause OfflineUniverses , VMOfflineTime , and VMOfflineReason to change. title: Ticket #4942: Improve RANK preeemption for partitionable slots
description: We want to make several improvements to the code for preempting partitionable/dynamic slots (#3667, #4580). Here are the things that have been done in Condor 8.3.6: Negotiator will not directly preempt individual dslots if ALLOW_PSLOT_PREEMPTION is true. For pslot preemption, the negotiator will ignore dslots that have retirement time remaining or are in preempting state. Fixed bug that selected the claim ids of the wrong dslots when preempting a pslot. When a preempting pslot claim is requested, the startd immediately returns resources of the preempted dslots to the pslot, then creates a new dslot with the requested resources. Design doc is on google drive. The following is future work after 8.3.6: Negotiator should not do pslot preemption calculations if NEGOTIATOR_CONSIDER_PREEMPTION is false. When consumption policies are enabled, don't consider dslots for multiple preemptions. Negotiator should sort eligible pslots that require preemption by applying rank expressions to all dynamic slots to be preempting and using minimum value. Allow NEGOTIATOR_CONSIDER_EARLY_PREEMPTION to be an expression applied per slot ad. Startd should wait for preempted dynamic slots to return resources to partitionable slot before creating dynamic slot for preempting claim. This would allow preemption of dslots that have retirement time remaining, like is possible with static slots. Startd should verify that preempting claim is eligible to preempt existing claims. Startd should update preemption stats properly.

title: Ticket #4041: RFE: Provide additional statistics and counters in negotiator
description: From downstream RFE: Provide Rejection counts broken down by the unique values you'd expect to see in LastRejMatchReason when looking at a job classad - e.g. "no match found", "concurrency limit reached", "group quota exceeded", etc. This will help resolve utilization problems. We can't just count these messages as we encounter them since we now stop negotiation in some cases to avoid seeing the messages. But, I think this can be gleaned from using autocluster size, number of submitters. ... I think the stats could either be tracked in the accountant log on a per user/group basis or attached to the submitter ads. The idea being that one could query things like users or #users hitting "no match found" and submitters not negotiating because of concurrency limits. Also from downstream (copied from #4042) (from downstream rfe) Provide a timing stats that correspond to various stages within Phase 4. This is to help resolve utilization/performance problems. ... Ideally what I'm trying to get in a Phase4Duration breakdown are answers to questions like: What percentage time is being spent in the negotiator vs. in communication with the schedd's? If the negotiator is spending all it's Phase4 time not communicating, there's likely a code problem. How much time am I spending in each schedd? Is there a particular schedd that I'm spending all of my time in? Was I experiencing communication problems with that schedd in addition to spending lots of time with it, and how much wait time was introduced due to communications recovery? How much time is being lost to rejections vs. valid matches? Today we just get 1 number, total time spent.
remarks: 2013-Nov-05 15:11:29 by tannenba: Agree that having more useful statistics in the negotiator would be good. Next stop is a specific design document that spells out the statistics to add and the motivation/reason/usage scenario for the stat (e.g. why the majority of admins would want to see it), and for each statistic identifying name, which stat class will be used, default reporting level. We have failed in the past because we have added a huge pile of raw statistics into the code without thinking about if/who/when the statistics would ever be used. Most have not. I do not want to make the same mistake again; I would rather see a design that identifies a very small set of useful statistics than a design that adds in a dozen (or dozens) of "might be useful sometimes to someone" statistics. 2013-Nov-21 18:37:44 by eje: Design doc: https://docs.google.com/document/d/1kRmlQHiO-Ow90xHW0PJkJLWdGPUx4vNHS6DxEKEUWZ8 2014-Jan-28 15:43:36 by gthain: This design looks good. description: Memory Tracking Test job_memory_tracking We want to ensure reported memory after a job completes is the high water mark for resident memory used and that we have consistency in the image size reported to the user log and that we have the same values in the machine and job ads. title: Ticket #4411: condor_advertise -multi should block until the collector has added all
description: condor_advertise -multi can send multiple ads to the collector in a relatively short amount of time, but those ads will actually be processed by the collector one at a time while doing other work in between each ad. So on a busy collector this can take a long time for the ads to show up. We have seen 291 ads take more than 10 minutes to be read by the collector out of the message stream. It would be better feedback to the user if condor_advertise could be told to wait until the collector had read the ads before returning. Because the behavior of not waiting is long-standing. We will make this an opt-in behavior via a new command line argument -wait. -wait will imply -tcp since that is required to make this feature work without changing the collector.
creator: johnkn

title: Ticket #626: Improve interaction between VM and host startds
description: The parameters VMP_VM_LIST and VMP_HOST_MACHINE allow a startd in a VM to interact with a startd running on the host OS. The current code assumes the two startds are vying for the same cpu(s). Thus, it tries to ensure that only one of the two startds can run a job at a given time. The VM startd periodically polls the host startd. If the host startd is not in Unclaimed or Owner state, the VM startd sets its START expression to False. If the host startd is in Unclaimed or Owner state, the VM startd using the normal START expression and the host startd sets its START expression to False. Once a VM startd decides it can match jobs, the host startd will leave START = False until the VM start exits. All of this behavior is hard-coded. There are situations where the admin may want jobs running on both the host and VM startds, particularly on multi-core machines. The only-one-startd-can-run-jobs behavior should be removed from the startd, replaced with a more flexible policy system.
creator: jfrey

title: Ticket #1613: [RFE] New ClassAd function - unparse()
description: The ClassAd language contains two types that are intimately related: strings and expressions. The language also contains tools to dissect and manipulate strings. It does not contain tools to manipulate expressions. Proposed is the first tool for expression manipulation: quote(). Unlike string(), which evaluates the expression before converting it to a string, quote() directly converts the expression into a string. The string tools become available, and the existence of eval() becomes even more interesting. One concrete use case for quote() is parsing Requirements expressions. For example, detecting if DiskUsage is referenced within job ads: condor_q -constraint 'regexp(".*DiskUsage.*", quote(Requirements))'
remarks:
2010-Sep-30 06:16:24 by matt: http://www.cs.wisc.edu/condor/classad/refman/node4.html#SECTION00043900000000000000 string(any x) returns string. If x is a String, the result is x. Otherwise, the result is the canonical unparsing of x (see Section 3.3.3). http://www.cs.wisc.edu/condor/classad/refman/node3.html#sec:unparsing The canonical unparsing of an expression is completely parenthesized and has no comments and no whitespace outside of string literals or attribute names. For example, the strings ``-x + 3 * (y + 1)'' and ``((-x)+(3*(y+1)))'' both parse to the same internal form. The second string is the canonical unparsing. 2010-Sep-30 06:18:37 by matt: $ ./condor_status -format "%s
" 'string(-x + 3 * (y + 1))' $ ./condor_status -format "%s
" 'string(-10 + 3 * (100 + 1))' 293 $ ident ./condor_status ./condor_status: $CondorVersion: 7.5.5 Sep 29 2010 PRE-RELEASE-UWCS $ $CondorPlatform: X86_64-LINUX_F13 $ $CondorVersion: %d.%d.%d %s %d %d $ 2010-Sep-30 10:17:09 by danb: Hmm. I haven't thought about it deeply, but the spec for string() seems quite unexpected to me. I would expect string() to coerce its evaluated argument to a string, just like int() coerces its evaluated argument to an integer. I think we need two separate functions: one for coercing and one for unparsing. I'd recommend calling the unparser unparse() rather than quote(). Note that the spec for string() doesn't quite match what you are hoping for. "The canonical unparsing of an attribute name is simply the name itself." It seems that you were hoping for the attribute name to be expanded. Perhaps we need both "deep" and "shallow" variants of the unparser. 2010-Sep-30 11:11:53 by jfrey: I suspect the spec assumes when an expression is a valid function argument, it's evaluated before use. The definition of 'const' arguments to functions probably needs refinement as well, but that's for another ticket. I could see several behaviors desired for this quote()/unparse() function with regard to expanding attribute references: No expansion. This could be useful if you want the unparsed expression in canonical form as a string. Single expansion. If the expression consists of a single attribute reference (including scoping), expand that reference to its value, if possible, before unparsing. title: Ticket #7544: Document minimum GPU job duration to ensure recorded usage
description: If I recall correctly, HTCondor requires a full sampling interval before recording any usage. That sampling interval is computed for each GPU (being a third of the max sampling duration?) at run-time, but last time I looked was in practice one of two values which I don't presently recall.
remarks: 2020-Mar-11 16:18:34 by tlmiller: The documented minimum duration for a sample is 1/6 of a second. At run-time, condor_gpu_utilization finds the GPU device with the smallest maximum sample count and divide that count by six; this give us the largest number of seconds we can wait between samples. It then divides this count by three and samples at that interval. However, it buffers the results and reports them at intervals not smaller than ten seconds each (but only immediately after a sample), so the delay between samples may be as large as 10 plus the sample interval. (Two reference points: both a TITAN RTX and a Tesla V100 have max sample counts of 100. We therefore sample every (100/6)/3 =~ 5.6 seconds.) The other piece of the puzzle is that condor_gpu_utilization reports on a regular interval from when the startd started up, not from the beginning of any of the jobs. The startd, therefore, receives a GPU utilization update roughly every 11 seconds in our example. (The first sample is obtained after ~5.6 seconds, and the second at ~11.2 seconds, which is longer than 10 and triggers a report.) To make sure we're reporting only the current job's utilization, the startd only counts full intervals. Thus, if condor_gpu_utilization reports on GPU utilization at 21:00:00, a job which starts at 21:00:01 will not record any GPU usage until (just after) 21:00:22. There's additional complications regarding watching gpu utilization for jobs or slots based on how often the job and machine ads in the schedd and collector are actually updated, but the problem was with regard to short GPU jobs exiting without recording any activity. If those jobs lasted for more than 23 seconds, however, that may indicate a problem in how we're reporting final GPU usage. 2020-Mar-17 10:23:36 by tlmiller: (This ticket may be about the "RIFT" tool?) 2020-May-12 10:44:53 by pfc: James will check with Richard (yes this is RIFT). 2020-Jun-09 10:31:57 by pfc: Deferring until we can reconstruct the ultimate user-facing (or admin-facing) accounting problem (0 usage reported where we expect >0?) that produced this bug report.

title: Ticket #2746: Remote, no-DAGMan POST scripts (and maybe PRE)
description: In the CHTC, we're frequently running jobs under DAGMan for a single purpose: to use a POST script to verify job success, and on failure RETRY the job. This adds a lot of complexity to the process, making it harder to teach users, harder to debug, chews up scheduler universe slots, and is a general nuisance. Instead of DAGMan and RETRY, you can use an on_exit_remove expression to gain much the same effect. Unfortunately, on_exit_remove is limited to information in the job's classad. Some programs (Matlab programs are a common culprit) will return 0 on success or failure, so the exit code isn't useful. Thus, we use DAGMan to run a POST script that validates the output. You could get the same effect by wrapping your executable in a script that runs your read executable then does the check. However, this adds the various problems in writing a wrapper. In particular, we're sharing one exit status for two executables. If "1" is returned, did it come from your executable, or from the script? Either one probably indicates a problem, but it's harder to track down the source. Also, you co-mingle your output and error streams. If you're hoping that the stdout from your program will be clean, your wrapper script can't print any debug messages there. I'm tired of using DAGMan to handle retries and detecting if jobs failed. I'm tired of wrappers complicating interpreting the output of a job. I think Condor can do better. Relatedly, one might want to run a script on the remote end to validate the machine before starting your real work. Might also be useful for downloading input files from unusual locations on a machine where you can't install file transfer hooks. Also, a remote post script would be a good opportunity to compress files, delete unneeded temporary files, or handle result upload to an unusual place. Proposed: Individual jobs gain the concept of a PRE and POST program. In a submit file, it might look like this: pre_executable = validate_machine pre_arguments = 1024MB input.txt pre_output = pre-output.txt pre_error = pre-error.txt executable = my_job arguments = --obscure-argument=1 52 input.txt --output=output.txt output = main-output.txt error = main-error.txt post_executable = validate_output post_arguments = output.txt post_output = post-output.txt post_error = post-error.txt universe = vanilla transfer_input_files = input.txt log = log.txt queue When a job starts up, if there is a pre_executable, it will be run. If it returns non-zero, then ExitBySignal, ExitCode, and ExitSignal are set appropriately as though pre_executable was the executable. PreExitBySignal, PreExitCode, and PreExitSignal are set to match. The job then stops, matching the behavior of a failed PRE script in DAGMan. If the pre_executable returns 0, then PreExitBySignal=FALSE and PreExitCode=0. If there is no pre_executable, or it returned 0, then run the actual executable. When it exits, ExitBySignal, ExitCode, and ExitSignal are set as normal. MainExitBySignal, MainExitCode, and MainExitSignal are set to match. Finally, the post_executable, is assigned, is run. When it exits, ExitBySignal, ExitCode, and ExitSignal are set as normal. This intentionally overwrites the output of the executable. PostExitBySignal, PostExitCode, and PostExitSignal are set to match. The final values of ExitBySignal, ExitCode, and ExitSignal are what is written into the job log, and thus what a tool like DAGMan will use to decide if the job succeeded or failed. at_exit_remote and other policies can make decisions based on the result of any of the pre, main, or post executables. Simpler policies can simply test all of them by looking at the ExitBySignal, ExitCode, and ExitSignal results. The flow of exit codes roughly matches that of DAGMan are the moment: if the PRE fails, nothing else runs. Is a POST runs, its result decides if the job succeeded or failed. As yet unconsidered: We should pass the exit code from the main executable into the post_executable. DAGMan uses a special $RETURN in the arguments to the POST script; we could do something similar, but probably a different pattern since $RETURN will match attributes in the job ad.

title: Ticket #4738: [EC2] Investigate EC2 GAHP memory usage
description: The EC2 GAHP, even with an upgraded version of libcurl (one that doesn't leak memory) uses a lot of RAM (up to 1.2GB in Fermi's use case). This doesn't seem, on the face of it, wholly reasonable; it doesn't (seem to) have much state to retain. (Peak memory usage, I expect, would occur if each worker thread got its result from curl back almost simultaneously, and all results were large; but that still seems like it shouldn't be more than a few megabytes, at most.) During the course of proving that the leak was in libcurl, I looked at a ~475MB EC GAHP. The /proc/maps file showed huge chunks of memory (5x60MB) allocated to/by the process but unreadable by it (marked private but without the readable, writable, or executable bit set). Identifying these may be a good place to start.
creator: tlmiller

title: Ticket #3507: Handle OpenStack's stopped state.
description: HTCondor, when managing an instance on an OpenStack resource, will report that instance as running even after it has shut itself down. title: Ticket #4368: Checksum always fails on non-blocking read for ReliSock
description: The non-blocking read code recently added in ReliSock introduces a bug in checksum checking. In ReliSock::RcvMsg::rcv_packet(), when a partial CEDAR packet is read, the checksum in the header (if there is one) isn't saved. Thus, when the rest of the packet is read in a later call, uninitialized data from the stack is used as the checksum that the packet's contents are checked against, which will always fail.
attachments: rcv_packet.patch 1880 bytes added by jfrey on 2014-May-19 16:22:03 UTC. Patch to preserve CEDAR packet checksum across multiple reads of the packet.

title: Ticket #1490: condor_hold + condor_rm of DAG goofs things up
description: If a DAG is held, and then removed without being released, none of the normal "condor_rm of DAG" cleanup takes place. I think fixing this would take changes to the schedd, because it would have to do something special in terms of releasing the DAGMan job before removing it...
remarks: 2010-Jul-07 16:33:49 by matt: Stopping submission of jobs while letting existing jobs complete is a useful feature - one you can implement by holding a dag. 2010-Jul-07 16:37:08 by wenger: Yes, condor_hold as it now exists is useful. But if the user does condor_hold and then condor_rm without a condor_release in between, the DAG job gets taken out of the queue, but the node jobs continue running, which is probably not the behavior we want. 2010-Jul-07 16:39:17 by matt: I don't disagree, but it would be sad if the solution was to make dagman rm its children on a hold. 2010-Jul-07 16:45:06 by wenger: Ah, no, my idea is not that the behavior on condor_hold would change; it's something like when the schedd sees the condor_rm, if the job is on hold and it's a DAGMan, the schedd does a condor_release before the condor_rm. (Or something like that -- it actually would be better if we didn't do a normal condor_release to DAGMan, because that will send it into recovery mode -- maybe we can have some special mode where DAGMan just removes its child jobs before exiting.) I don't know enough about the schedd to know exactly what the best way is to do this, but I agree that condor_hold on the DAGMan should leave the node jobs alone, as it does now. 2011-Jan-15 15:19:50 by wenger: I'm doing some tests on this, and one other issue is that if we remove a DAG that's on hold we leave the lock file hanging around -- I'm not sure whether we want to do that or not... 2011-Jan-20 15:03:39 by wenger: Pete and I just met and came up with a more general way of dealing with this: we'd have a bunch of "job state transition actions" (e.g., auto_action_remove, auto_action_hold, auto_action_checkpoint, etc.). Probably initially we'd just implement auto_action_remove to deal with LIGO's DAG issue. This would be an expression in a job's submit file that would act on other jobs when the first job is removed. The one for DAGMan would be something like this: auto_action_remove = target.DAGManJobId == my.ClusterId eventually this could be extended to something like: auto_action_remove = if (expression) job_hold(constraint) so that removing one job could do something to other jobs besides removing them. title: Ticket #4692: URL transfer plugin and should_transfer_files broken if input URL only
description: If should_transfer_files is not set in the submit file, and transfer_input_files contains URLs, they are not transferred, which is highly unintuitive. Also, when should_transfer_files = if_needed, URLs again need special treatment since they have nothing to do with whether or not the file system domain matches between submit and execute. Full report from Brian Candler on condor-users: (1) Running a personal condor (8.0.7), given the following submit file (foo.sub) with the input from a URL: universe = vanilla executable = /bin/sh arguments = "'-c' 'cat condor_submit.html'" transfer_executable = no transfer_input_files = http://research.cs.wisc.edu/htcondor/manual/current/condor_submit.html output = foo.out error = foo.err queue I find that the file is not transferred at all. foo.err says: cat: condor_submit.html: No such file or directory The documentation says: "For vanilla and vm universe jobs only, a file may be specified by giving a URL, instead of a file name. The implementation for URL transfers requires both configuration and available plug-in." but these are indeed present (/etc/condor/condor_config has FILETRANSFER_PLUGINS which includes /usr/lib/condor/libexec/curl_plugin) WORKAROUND: I was able to make it work by setting "should_transfer_files = yes". However, is this right? Surely a URL should always be fetched, regardless of whether or not you are in the same filesystem domain, since URLs don't appear in the filesystem anyway? (2) Given a unimplemented URL scheme (like "https"), I found a difference between my test personal condor node and my production condor node. The former would leave the job idle because of a classAd matching condition which was never true: 1 ( TARGET.HasFileTransfer && stringListMember("https",HasFileTransferPluginMethods) ) but the latter puts the job into a "held" (H) state, saying Hold reason: Error from slot1@dar2.example.net: STARTER at 192.168.6.42 failed to receive file /var/lib/condor/execute/dir_24716/xxxx.xxxx: FILETRANSFER:1:FILETRANSFER: plugin for type https not found! (Aside: if a plugin for https is not present, wouldn't it be better to abort the job rather than put it into a 'held' state indefinitely, as this isn't a condition which is likely to fix itself?) Anyway, I managed to drill down to find the difference, and it turns out to be different behaviour depending on whether you set should_transfer_files = if_needed or should_transfer_files = yes I cannot find this behaviour documented anywhere. Looking at http://research.cs.wisc.edu/htcondor/manual/current/2_5Submitting_Job.html#SECTION00354000000000000000 it says the default value is "should_transfer_files = if_needed" and this will enable the file transfer mechanism if the machines are in different filesystem domains. This implies to me that if the machines are in different filesystem domains this should behave the same as "should_transfer_files = yes", but actually the generated requirements expressions are different in these two cases. You can reproduce it with the following test case: ---- bar.sub ---- universe = vanilla executable = /bin/sh arguments = "-c true" transfer_executable = no transfer_input_files = https://example.net/ should_transfer_files = if_needed #should_transfer_files = yes error = bar.err requirements = ( TARGET.Machine == "nonexistent" ) queue Submit with "condor_submit bar.sub" then use "condor_q -analyze <pid>" [Results with should_transfer_files = if_needed] The Requirements expression for your job is: ( ( TARGET.Machine == "nonexistent" ) ) && ( TARGET.Arch == "X86_64" ) && ( TARGET.OpSys == "LINUX" ) && ( TARGET.Disk >= RequestDisk ) && ( TARGET.Memory >= RequestMemory ) && ( ( TARGET.HasFileTransfer ) || ( TARGET.FileSystemDomain == MY.FileSystemDomain ) ) [Results with should_transfer_files = yes] The Requirements expression for your job is: ( ( TARGET.Machine == "nonexistent" ) ) && ( TARGET.Arch == "X86_64" ) && ( TARGET.OpSys == "LINUX" ) && ( TARGET.Disk >= RequestDisk ) && ( TARGET.Memory >= RequestMemory ) && ( TARGET.HasFileTransfer && stringListMember("https",HasFileTransferPluginMethods) ) This to me also seems like a bug, as I was expecting should_transfer_files = (yes|if_needed) to behave the same when the nodes are in different filesystem domains. But if it's not, I think it should be documented accordingly. To me the correct behaviour would be something like this: if any input or output file is a URL, then add stringListMember("<scheme>",HasFileTransferPluginMethods) to the requirements if should_transfer_files = yes, then add ( TARGET.HasFileTransfer ) if should_transfer_files = if_needed, then add ( ( TARGET.HasFileTransfer ) || ( TARGET.FileSystemDomain == MY.FileSystemDomain ) )

title: Ticket #6640: Jobs dont start on windows if INTERACTIVE login is disabled
description: USGS was having a problem where jobs could be submitted, but would always fail to transfer input because the shadow was unable to impersonate the user. There was a valid user/password in the CREDD store (i.e. set by condor_store_cred), but it could not be used because their LDAP server had a group policy that disabled INTERACTIVE logon, only allowing NETWORK logon. The difference between NETWORK login and INTERACTIVE, is that INTERACTIVE tells Windows to cache the login info, so that a user can subsequently login to their machine even if the LDAP server cannot be conctacted at the next logon attempt. NETWORK login will always query the LDAP server. Thus HTCondor should not care which type of logon is used, and indeed, condor_store cred will first use NETWORK and then INTERACTIVE when it tries to validate a credential. But the SCHEDD, SHADOW, and STARTER will only use INTERACTIVE login. This should be changed so that the SCHEDD first tries INTERACTIVE, and if that fails with the correct error code, it should then try NETWORK logon. Also so that system administrators can avoid this inefficiency or force a certain type of logon (BATCH mode is also a type), a new knob should be added to choose which logon type the schedd,shadow and starter will use. If this knob is set to AUTO (the default) then it will try INTERACTIVE and then NETWORK. The new knob is windows specific, it will be called WINDOWS_LOGON32_TYPE and allowed values will be (not case sensitive): AUTO - try INTERACTIVE, if that fails with ERROR_LOGON_TYPE_NOT_GRANTED then try NETWORK. This is the default INTERACTIVE - always use LOGON32_LOGON_INTERACTIVE NETWORK - always use LOGON32_LOGON_NETWORK BATCH - always use LOGON32_LOGON_BATCH Any unrecognised value will be treated as AUTO.
