title: Ticket #7051: GSI authentication protocol bug
description: We've diagnosed a long-standing bug in the GSI authentication protocol. Condor's CEDAR layer had a workaround dating back 17 years, but it causes problems in some cases (#7024). On certain authentication failures, the client doesn't send data expected by the server. For most use cases (non-Condor), the client will then close the connection. But Condor CEDAR may want to try other authentication methods on the same connection. In this case, the GSI bug leaves the two sides out of sync. Since this bug only occurs on some types of GSI authentication failures, it's difficult for CEDAR to compensate for the possible out-of-sync problems. The problem is in gss_init_sec_context() in libglobus_gssapi_gsi. If globus_i_gsi_gss_handshake() returns failure, then globus_i_gsi_gss_get_token() is called to extract any reply for the server (stored in output_token), and then the code jumps to the error_exit label. There, gss_delete_sec_context() is called, which discards the previous reply for the server and makes its own call to globus_i_gsi_gss_get_token(). This second call indicates no additional data to send (again in output_token). The fix is to not pass output_token to gss_delete_sec_context() if it already contains data.

title: Ticket #5703: An /etc/condor/groups file?
description: I proposed, for condor_annex, that the annex daemon map from authenticated Condor user to EC2 credentials. After some additional thought, this seemed like too limited a mechanism, for the following to reasons: A glideInWMS user (or other factory) may be making EC2 requests on behalf of many users. Any individual user may well have more than one set of credentials (will certainly have at least one set per service, in the glorious future where condor_annex & co support services other than AWS). The obvious solution was to permit the user to specify which credential(s) to use. The obvious way to do that, since we don't want to be in the business of transferring credentials around, is to allow the user to specify credentials by (partial?) path name on the annexd's machine. This has some obvious security implications, so it seems wise to require a whitelist, and make the user-to-credentials map one-to-many. If no credential is specified, the first one is used. So I asked Zach about the security implications of this (sounds generally OK), but he also pointed out that users could also share credentials in this manner, and as such the credential names were like group names, which is a problem we've been wanting to solve for our users for years. So the proposal is as follows: an /etc/groups -like file for mapping authenticated Condor users to groups, and another file (or set of files, e.g., /etc/condor/groups.d) with group-specific ClassAds. Certain attributes would have specific meaning to HTCondor -- like "allowed_ec2_credentials" and "default_accounting_group" -- but others would be arbitrary and available for use by the admin (as a subclassad?) in SUBMIT_REQUIREMENTS (and/or SUBMIT_TRANSFORMATIONS, or whatever we end up calling it). I further propose a special attribute that would be a list of attributes from the group ad for the schedd to insert in the job ad at submit time, after the user's group has been validated.
remarks: 2016-Jun-03 15:26:52 by tlmiller: ToddT points out that this entire proposal could be subsumed into the rewrite-on-submit code, as long as we make that available outside of the schedd and add a few things to handle the special case of validating group membership (that is, if Zach is in both the Physics and CS groups, he should be able to submit jobs with either Physics or CS, but not with any other group; attempts to do so should fail. That could done with a function which returns the special mapping-rejected group, and having SUBMIT_REQUIREMENTS reject that job by default). Tickets #4804 and #5613 are about submit-time job (ClassAd) rewriting.

title: Ticket #775: Optimize daemon-core timer code for gridmanager usage
description: Stress-testing of the gridmanager with 10,000s of jobs has revealed that daemon-core's timer code doesn't handle 10,000s of timers that get reset frequently very well. It's unclear yet whether we need to redesign the timer code's data structures to better handle the gridmanager's use-case. But I have identified some simple changes that should provide significant improvements. Some of these save time, others save space. These are all changes to the TimerManager class. Change Timer::timeslice to a pointer and remove Timer::has_timeslice. If Timer::timeslice is NULL, then there isn't a Timeslice for that timer. Also fix up calls that take a Timeslice to pass by reference rather than by value. Maintain a tail pointer in TimerManager. If a timer's 'when' member is TIMER_NEVER, just throw the timer on the end of the list. Remove Timer::is_cpp and just test if Event[cpp] and Release[cpp] are NULL. TimerManager::ResetTimer() ends up traversing the list three times, once in ResetTimer(), once in CancelTimer(), and once in NewTimer(). At least one of these can be eliminated. In many places, a timer that's rescheduled is destructed and its components passed to NewTimer() for recreation. Should break insertion out into a separate, private method and hand it filled out Timer structs.

title: Ticket #3287: Invalid submissions to EC2 can't be removed.
description: If you submit an invalid EC2 job -- for instance, one with a bogus AMI ID -- the RunInstances command will fail and the job will go on hold (with a useful error message -- I know, I'm doing it wrong). However, condor_rm'ing the held job will cause the gridmanager to go into recovery mode and wrongly call RunInstances again. (This isn't as insane as it sounds -- because of the idempotent ClientToken, Amazon will ensure that we only start the one instance.) Of course, doing so puts the job back on hold. The grid manager needs to check before entering recovery if the job is held, and if so, ignore it. If the job is in the removed state, it needs to make sure it's finished cleaning up after it; this may require additional machinery. (We can't just call RunInstances to convert the ClientToken into an instance ID because we don't want to start an instance if we haven't already.) Discovered by Anthony Tiradani.
remarks: 2012-Oct-23 16:05:22 by tstclair: Version needed here, because I fixed a very similar issue to this months ago. 2012-Oct-23 17:14:00 by tlmiller: I don't know how far back the problem goes (which is why I left the corresponding field blank), but it looks like (based on code inspection) that it exists in the present master branch. It certainly exists (I have experimentally verified it) on my branch for the spot request implementation, which isn't all that old. I took a quick look back to July and didn't see anything in the git logs from you that looked likely. Could you send me (the hash of) your fix? Thanks. 2012-Nov-29 15:02:42 by tlmiller: In fact, anything that causes the call to ec2_vm_start() to fail will cause the job to become held, rather than removed (particularly including authentication failures). 2012-Dec-17 18:54:06 by tlmiller: We could correct this problem by either not putting the job on hold when the call to RunInstances() fails, or by not making the call to RunInstances() at all. The former requires a great deal of knowledge, which may change from service to service, about the failure modes of RunInstances(), because we must put the job on hold unless we're certain that the error could not result in a running instance whose ID we do not know. The latter seems simpler: during recovery, if we have a client token but an instance ID, and we're removing the job, go to a special state where we check to see if any instance has that client token. If it does, we go back GM_START_VM (as if we hadn't checked if we removing the job at all); if it does not, we go to GM_DELETE (since we know we have nothing to cancel, we should just get rid of the job). This, however, leaves jobs with AuthFailures (see #2274) unable to be removed from the queue, because the call to DescribeInstances() in the new state above (GM_SEEK_INSTANCE_ID) will fail. Shoul the GM_SEEK_INSTANCE_ID delete the job instead of putting it on hold for AuthFailures? Maybe if-and-only-if the job's hold reason (hopefully uncleared by being removed) is also an AuthFailure? 2012-Dec-18 11:41:30 by tlmiller: Changed 'broken version' to 7.9.2, presuming 7.8.2 to be a typo. title: Ticket #4542: Maintain [Last]EvictReason in job ad.
description: We should use the job ad to tell the user why the job was evicted. For instance, a common reason in the VM universe would be because of a failure to launch. Other common reasons might include the job being preempted, the machine failing, or the running past its allotted time. We currently record many of these reasons in the user log, but doing so in the job ad has two benefits: it makes it easier to run without the log; and it if we choose the attributes carefully, should permit better policy-making. The latter suggests we should follow the HoldReason[[Sub]Code] pattern.
creator: tlmiller

title: Ticket #6085: Missed shadow updates causes a death spiral
description: We have a Schedd that is killing of shadows at a rate of about 1-5Hz; seems mostly due to missing keepalives. Randomly killing shadows results in a lot of chaos through the system (including the issue fixed in 8.4.11 about disconnecting glexec-based jobs) that could otherwise be avoided by processing the keepalive. I have verified this is simply a too-busy schedd: no obvious blocking is going on, the UDP buffer (from /proc/net/udp) is indeed at the limit of 128KB. Can we better detect UDP drops or standing buffers? Can we record killed shadow processes as a metric? Could we switch to using a unix socket as the command socket? The unix socket would report failures to enqueue data back to the client. It seems that one keepalive is processed per duty cycle, despite the fact the keepalive is "light" to process and expensive when missed. Todd suggested it would be plausible to process multiple of these in a cycle. In the end, we had to just crank up SHADOW_NOT_RESPONDING_TIMEOUT to a value where the update rate is below what the schedd can handle.

title: Ticket #1605: support host certificate DNS name validation
description: The GSI and SSL authentication methods do not currently do any check that the hostname in the server's certificate matches the DNS name of the server. This makes it awkward to use Condor-C as a replacement for GRAM. Proposal Add knobs to enable/disable hostname checks in the client-side of GSI and SSL authentication methods: GSI_SKIP_HOST_CHECK SSL_SKIP_HOST_CHECK These settings are analogous to the existing SOAP_SSL_SKIP_HOST_CHECK used by the amazon gahp. The default for the above knobs is false, do not skip host checking. When the global toggle is false (do not skip host checking), exceptions may be made: GSI_SKIP_HOST_CHECK_CERT_REGEX SSL_SKIP_HOST_CHECK_CERT_REGEX Any DNs matching the above regular expressions are not required to pass the DNS check. For backward compatibility, any DNs listed in GSI_DAEMON_NAME are also not required to pass the DNS check. At some point, we may also want to apply DNS checks on the server side to clients doing DAEMON-level commands. I am proposing that we ignore this for now and just focus on the client side, since that is all that is relevant to Condor-C. Alternative Proposal After discussion with Igor, we agreed that the above proposal is good for many cases, but it would be nice to additionally provide some features that would allow something similar to be achieved via the map file. The idea is to have a list of flags that specify what pieces of information are desired for mapping. For example, there could be a flag that extracts the authenticated host name. Let's call it AUTHENTICATED_HOST. This could trigger a DNS check if one hasn't happened already. If the check fails, then the mapping entry requesting AUTHENTICATED_HOST is skipped. If the check succeeds, then the authenticated host name will be matched against the corresponding matching field in the map file. Example: GSI AUTHENTICATED_HOST ".*" gsiserver If you want to look at the DN and the host name, you would specify both: GSI AUTHENTICATED_HOST,DN ".*" "/DC=org/DC=doegrids/OU=Services/CN=.*" \1@cs.wisc.edu More generically, GSI FLAG1,FLAG2,FLAG3,... "REGEX1" "REGEX2" "REGEX3" ... NAME Ideally, it should be possible to refer to extracted bits of previous REGEXes in ones that follow it. For example, REGEX2 might want to say that the authenticated host name matched in REGEX1 should appear in the DN. Ideas for flags that we could support, IP, AUTHENTICATED_HOST, DN, VOMS stuff, condor authorization level. I haven't thought about exactly how the regexp substitution references would work across the multiple regexes, but presumably we can just index across them. There is ambiguity in what we should yield for the authenticated host name. It could be the name we get when we do a reverse lookup of the IP address of our peer, or it could be the name in our peer's certificate. The two are not necessarily identical even when gsi_compare_names() is successful. I'm not sure if there is an advantage of one over the other. I'd be tempted to use the name from the certificate. Implementation Notes Some code to perform the hostname check already exists in Condor_Auth_SSL::post_connection_check(). It is commented out and so likely needs some work. For GSI, we can just change the "GSI-NO-TARGET" argument to globus_gss_assist_init_sec_context() in order to enable hostname checking. However, that doesn't allow us to make exceptions. Instead, we can use gss_compare_names() to do the check as a separate step.

title: Ticket #3638: Unified HTCondor Source RPM
description: HTCondor comes packaged in RPM form by at least three significant communities: UW, OSG, and Fedora. Each one has its own version of the RPM, built & packaged differently and including different features. This ticket represents the project to create a unified RPM that incorporates the features provided by each of these RPM versions, and (more importantly) required by each of the major communities consuming them. remarks: 2013-May-20 16:44:22 by edquist: The following can be turned into a design doc, but this is the current list of features we hope to include in the unified RPM, and the implementation plan. Working list of condor rpm features: follow fedora rpm guidelines provide a source rpm (currently UW's does not) have correct / consistent locations for everything (libs, config files) conditional support for various features standard universe UW-style vs PROPER-style build parallel universe well defined subpackage relationships procd in particular shouldn't pull in all of condor separate out standard universe if possible reconcile config file differences (condor_config, sysconfig, init.d) handle upgrades reasonably when to do condor_off -fast vs -graceful, etc provide a proper place for customizations to init script that won't get blown away on upgrades Note that we do not plan to support relocatability in the RPM. Technical TODO / game plan: start with OSG condor.spec add in any missing features from Fedora's spec add conditional support to do a UW style build (instead of PROPER) UW style build will initially include standard universe, but see if it's possible to build standard universe each way (UW/PROPER) see if standard universe can reasonably be made into a subpackage fix dependencies so that procd doesn't pull in all of condor automate parallel universe configuration, if enabled automate cgroups configuration, if enabled investigate any differences in locations of installed files between uw/osg/fedora versions (eg, condor_config.local), find out which ones are likely to cause trouble if they change same with content of config files between uw/osg/fedora; see if there is any trouble reconciling them implement Steve Timm's suggestions for fixing / improving the init.d script behavior look into different upgrade scenarios, when it makes sense to end services immediately vs when to wait for jobs to finish, etc. try to find a way to have it do the right thing either way 2013-May-30 09:18:28 by cat: I would like to see the design document, as started in the first remark, on a separate, standalone wiki page linked from here. The document will evolve over time, and I do not want to try to reconstruct its current state from a series of comments here. Plus, the design document needs to be viewable and clear to external folks as well.

title: Ticket #7381: condor should tell users what output files were NOT transferred back
description: Design document. If manifest or manifest_dir is set in the submit file, write a file containing the names of the files and directories of the top level of the sandbox immediately after file transfer in, and a different file for the same immediately after file transfer out. These files will be manifest_dir, if it is specified, or in <cluster>_<proc>_manifest if not. Transfer this directory, if created, automatically. original description #usability One of the most common user errors when constructing new jobs and workflows with Condor file transfer is an output file not existing. Often this is because the output wasn't named what the user expected. Another common user error when constructing new jobs and workflows is a job failing with no indication of why in stderr, and no way to see what unanticipated output files, core files, etc. may have been written on the execute node and not sent back. One of the most common wrapper scripts Condor forces users who use Condor file xfer to write, in order to debug jobs, is one that runs "ls -l" before and after a job. All of this could be helped if Condor simply told the user what files were there. I'm agnostic as to how/where Condor communicates this info, but please let's not force everyone to do it themselves, when Condor is perfectly positioned to do it for them.

title: Ticket #2479: startd SUSPEND trumps user continue, and user suspend trumps startd CO
description: So this may be a bit different then what we had discussed and after some thought the following seems to make the most sense. STARTD SUSPEND trumps user continue user suspend trumps STARTD CONTINUE Please post comments below.
remarks: 2011-Sep-20 13:00:43 by matt: +1 You don't want the Startd policy CONTINUE trumping the user desire to suspend their job. The user is making a move in a direction to limit resource use on the machine represented by the Startd, instead of trying to use more resources. A middle ground may be to mark the job in such a way that the Startd CONTINUE policy can conditionally follow the user's desire. However, this may be complex as following the user's desire should be the default behavior. 2011-Sep-23 09:59:16 by tstclair: For the sake of brevity (not opening another ticket) I've also updated the logic to ensure it will try to reconnect when in the SUSPENDED state. How many places is the Resource::eval_continue expression called and do all of them expect this type of behavior? If I recall, when a job is moving from the claimed/suspended state to the vacating/killing state, the job is first continued in order to send it the killsig (which you can specify in the submit file) so the job can checkpoint or clean up or whatever. title: Ticket #2183: fetch-work changes advertised ClaimId
description: The following situation has been observed in the startd log: 05/16 06:52:55 State change: Finished fetching work successfully 05/16 06:52:55 slot4: Changing state: Unclaimed -> Claimed 05/16 06:52:55 slot4: Warning: starting ClaimLease timer before lease duration set. 05/16 06:52:55 slot4: Got universe "VANILLA" (5) from request classad 05/16 06:52:55 slot4: Changing activity: Idle -> Busy ... 05/16 06:53:04 Received UDP command 440 (MATCH_INFO) from <10.9.2.120:39783>, access level NEGOTIATOR 05/16 06:53:04 Calling HandleReq <command_match_info> (0) 05/16 06:53:04 Error: can't find resource with ClaimId (<10.9.2.120:55421>#1305060839#656#...) So first a fetch-work job started on slot4 and then shortly after that, a match to this slot was rejected because it presented the wrong ClaimId. I have not dug into the code, but I suspect that this happened because fetch-work caused the slot's ClaimId to be changed, thus creating a race condition between fetch-work and the negotiation cycle. This problem was particularly bad because of #2170.

Possibly preemption policy should be taken into account in these situations. 2012-Feb-10 14:43:26 by pfc: Todd claims that this is only an issue when fetch-work jobs run for less than ~1 minute before exiting. If that's true, then this is a lower-priority issue (but still an issue). If that's not true, then this is important.

title: Ticket #5996: SCHEDD_USE_SLOT_WEIGHT causes infinite loop if RequestCpus is expr
description: If SCHEDD_USE_SLOT_WEIGHT is true, the schedd fakes up a STARTD ad with Cpus = RequestCpus Disk = RequestDisk Memory = RequestMemory And then uses it to evaluate job wieght of the job. This works when the job has constant values for RequestCpus, RequestDisk and RequestMemory. But when one or more of these are expressions referring to the STARTD ad, evaluation of the slot weight of the job turns into infinite recursion. (actually the classad evaluator aborts when it gets to a depth of 1000) The fix for this must be to have the SCHEDD's slot weight expression be expressed directly in terms of job attributes (and getting rid of the faked-up STARTD ad). This will require having a new knob for the SCHEDD's slot weight expression - SCHEDD_SLOT_WEIGHT. The fix should include a dprintf message when the SCHEDD_SLOT_WEIGHT expression has a Cpus, Memory, or Disk attribute reference.
remarks: 2016-Nov-08 12:02:32 by tannenba: I am not enthralled with the proposed fix above, which requires the poor admin to deal with yet another arcane and hard-to-understand knob else risk the schedd flying off into neverland? Not good. I have no problem with adding a knob SCHEDD_SLOT_WEIGHT and having the schedd use that if it is defined instead of using SLOT_WEIGHT assuming we do not require it to be defined. But I think we can do better in the default case of SCHEDD_SLOT_WEIGHT is not defined, SLOT_WEIGHT is defined (to the default value of Cpus), and SCHEDD_USE_SLOT_WEIGHT is True (which is the default). I.e., I think we can make the startd ad that is faked up by the schedd smarter/more resilient to avoiding the recursion problem. 2016-Nov-08 14:19:59 by johnkn: Jaime and I discussed ways to make the fake ad smarter - its not possible. We could try and re-write the SLOT_WEIGHT expression so that it refers to job attributes instead, but that's risky. And in any case, whenever the job uses an expression for RequestCpus, etc the schedd calculation of slot weight will be bogus. The real solution is to get rid of the need for the schedd to make a reasonable guess of slot weight. 2016-Nov-09 14:06:01 by johnkn: [49559] is the initial commit, which add SCHEDD_SLOT_WEIGHT [49567] ads code to use SLOT_WEIGHT when SCHEDD_SLOT_WEIGHT is not defined 2016-Nov-28 17:03:30 by gthain: CODE REVIEW Code is good, but would like to fix this in the negotiator so that we don't need to guess the slot weight of unmatched, idle jobs.

title: Ticket #1486: Condor account are not granted correct privileges on local machines
description: The problem may be due to Condor or the slot users not having sufficient privileges to allow Condor to login the condor slot accounts as an interactive users (thus the error ERROR_LOGON_TYPE_NOT_GRANTED). To enable access we need to grant the Condor accounts the SE_INTERACTIVE_LOGON_NAME (i.e. "SeInteractiveLogonRight") privilege. This should fix the problem. So of the point in here may help: http://support.microsoft.com/kb/257346 I believe this problem cropped up when we first moved away from using batch login account, in favour of interactive ones. We did this for several reasons, but primarily it was because the batch login accounts three major limitations: batch users had trouble running certain types of applications that were becoming popular at the time, also because newer versions of Windows did not allow batch users to run batch files (via the cmd.exe tool), and finally, because batch accounts were found not to work when using Samba as a Primary Domain Controller. Batch accounts were initially used because it was thought they would allow Condor to process a login faster. It was found, however, that in practice the latency incurred from using interactive accounts was far outweigh by its benefits. The only reason I could think of that Condor should optionally be using batch accounts, is when it is running a (very) large number of short lived jobs. Even then, the overhead of spawning a starter process will dwarf the login time an interactive login would invite.
remarks: 2010-Jul-12 21:54:19 by burnett: I don't really know what the correct priority for this should be, but it is a huge pain for people with stricter network policies that limit the privileges of regular users (which we restrict our accounts to be).

title: Ticket #2245: INSANE showing up in NegotiatorLog
description: When MatchList caching is enabled in the negotiator (which is the default), the negotiator scans through all the startd ads to find the machine ad (called bestSoFar) that is the highest ranked match to a particular job. During this same scan, it puts all the machine ads that match the job into a list (the MatchList), and sorts the list based on the ranking criteria. It then pops the top entry off the MatchList (called bestCached) and compares it to the machine ad it found during the scan. If these do not match, then a scary entry appears in the NegotiatorLog: INSANE: bestCached != bestSoFar It then returns bestSoFar. The end result is not only a scary message in the log, but also whenever this happens the negotiator ends up matching the same slot twice in the same pie spin! The reason this is all happening is because the sort is qsort(), which is not a stable sort - i.e. if you give qsort an already sorted list, entries with the same weight may be swapped. The patch below gets rid of the unnecessary comparison, and also always returns the top entry from the MatchList to the schedd if MatchList caching is enabled. This fixes both the INSANE warning in the log and also the bug of giving out the same match twice.
remarks: 2013-Aug-06 08:42:03 by johnkn: CODE REVIEW: Code looks good. Although if bestSoFar is always pulled from the match list, it's time to remove the redundant sorting code at lines 4171 to 4218. 2013-Aug-06 12:00:52 by tannenba: Thanks for review, but disagree w/ above re time to remove redundant sort code... it is still needed for the case when matchlist caching is disabled in the config file. We could get rid of the code if we knew nobody used the knob to disable matchlist caching, but iirc folks do use that knob in certain situations (condor-g matchmaking where matches get reused perhaps? don't recall off the top of my head).

title: Ticket #5979: Full disk + shared port = broken ssh-to-job
description: Based on an incident today, it appears that having a full disk while running shared port breaks ssh-to-job, because the starter(?) needs to create a new listen socket for the remote client, which means that the shared port daemon's address needs to be known. On matlab-build-1, we look this up out of /var/lock/condor/SharedPortAd, which is not the "usual" address file. That file was of length 0 at the time I observed it with the full disk. This is probably because this file is updated regularly with certain metrics, and the update process probably truncates the file, either before writing or after writing but without checking to see if the write was for the full length of the buffer. (On a full disk, a write of 0, etc...) This behaviour is bad if we really care about the metrics; if we don't, we should store them in a file whose absence doesn't cause things to break.

We need to think carefully about what failure in that case would really mean (do we currently arrange for the shared port daemon to reconfig first, so nobody else has to change their address twice if that's going to happen?).

title: Ticket #1193: Better handling of full checkpoint server
description: Currently checkpoints are removed from the checkpoint server if the job completes or 60 days (configurable) pass without updates. In a disk full situation new checkpoints are just dropped. We can do better. Proposal: give checkpoints short leases, may 14 days by default. A schedd will ping the checkpoint server every lease/10 days, updating the lease. When the lease expires, the checkpoint is not necessarily removed. A checkpoint is removed after 60 days of inactivity (still configurable), or if the lease is expired and disk space available is "low" (% used for checkpoints versus configurable size limit, or perhaps if disk as a whole is over 90% full).

The linux queue works well, but in the windows queue, jobs fail to execute at the startd: =============================================================== 06/18 22:22:08 Starting a VANILLA universe job with ID: 37.0 06/18 22:22:09 Tracking process family by login "condor-reuse-slot1" 06/18 22:22:09 IWD: C:\Progra~1\Condor\execute\dir_428 06/18 22:22:09 Output file: C:\Progra~1\Condor\execute\dir_428\_condor_stdout 06/18 22:22:10 Error file: C:\Progra~1\Condor\execute\dir_428\_condor_stderr 06/18 22:22:10 Renice expr "10" evaluated to 10 06/18 22:22:10 About to exec C:\Progra~1\Condor\execute\dir_428\condor_exec.gass_cache/local/md5/32/4a5afa0e96a19fa2244e8dd70116ce/md5/f4/91c2ba79ec192a3e127340f8999f71/data 06/18 22:22:10 GetExecutableAndArgumentsByExtention: failed to find extension *.gass_cache/local/md5/32/4a5afa0e96a19fa2244e8dd70116ce/md5/f4/91c2ba79ec192a3e127340f8999f71/data in the registry (last-error = 2). 06/18 22:22:10 Create_Process(): Failed to find an executable for extension *.gass_cache/local/md5/32/4a5afa0e96a19fa2244e8dd70116ce/md5/f4/91c2ba79ec192a3e127340f8999f71/data 06/18 22:22:10 ERROR: C:\Progra~1\Condor\execute\dir_428\condor_exec.gass_cache\local\md5\32\4a5afa0e96a19fa2244e8dd70116ce\md5\f4\91c2ba79ec192a3e127340f8999f71\data.exe is not a valid Windows executable 06/18 22:22:10 ERROR "Create_Process(C:\Progra~1\Condor\execute\dir_428\condor_exec.gass_cache/local/md5/32/4a5afa0e96a19fa2244e8dd70116ce/md5/f4/91c2ba79ec192a3e127340f8999f71/data,, ...) failed: " at line 530 in file ..\src\condor_starter.V6.1\os_proc.cpp 06/18 22:22:10 ShutdownFast all jobs. =============================================================== The gass_cache part should not be there.. if I understand correctly, condor-g uses gass internally to transfer files to the gt5 resource, but once they are there and a condor_submit is generated, condor's own file transfer mechanism kicks in and the startd should never see the cache url? title: Ticket #2992: Have Condor manage OOM
description: When a job runs inside a cgroup, it basically has its own personal virtual memory subsystem. Part of this includes its own OOM-killer. As a part of cgroups, we can actually have the OOM-killer for inside the container be subservient to the procd. I propose two changes: If using the memory controller, the procd should manage the OOM-killer for the job. In the event the kernel detects the OOM-killer needs to run, the procd should hard kill the entire job. title: Ticket #722: Remove Insert() and Append() variants in our List class
description: Our List class has two variants for its Insert() and Append() methods. One takes a pointer to the item to be added and the other takes a reference. The reference variant just takes the address of the item and calls the pointer variant. The code comments say that the reference variant is useful for adding items on the stack or in global data space. Since the List always stores a pointer to the item, adding stack variables is dangerous, as the List then can't leave the local scope. I've found a couple places in the code that use the reference variant and assume the items are copied, rather than a pointer taken. One function inserts a local variable and returns the List to the caller. Another inserts the same variable multiple times, assigning different values in between calls. The reference variants of these two methods are only used in four source files. To avoid misuse, we should remove them and convert the few callsites to the pointer variant. We should also fix the existing faulty code.
remarks: Committed changes for 7.4.0.

title: Ticket #7339: It should be simpler to test ClassAd(s and) expressions
description: Mat and I both griped about the clumsiness of using condor_status to test/demonstrate ClassAds and expressions while we were reviewing #7206, and Mat observed that it should be a very short Python script to implement a tool with a much simpler interface. classad_eval <ad> <expr>[ <expr>]+ or classad_eval <ad> <expr>[ <expr>]+ We've decided on classad_eval rather than condor_eval -- even though the tool will evaluate using HTCondor ClassAd semantics -- because classad_eval is less obscure/confusing to the people who don't know the difference, and the people who do won't care. We want classad_eval packaged as a command-line tool, but in the Python bindings. At least initially, it doesn't have to much behave like a "normal" HTCondor command-line tool, particularly in terms of error-handling.
remarks: 2019-Oct-24 14:13:30 by tlmiller: Thinking about it a little, I think we can do the following without much more code, and it would make certain expression testing easier: classad_eval <expr> Where having exactly one argument implies that no ad is necessary to evaluate expr. 2019-Oct-24 14:23:30 by matyas: Not a big fan of changing the meaning of the first parameter based on whether the second parameter is present (aside: Unix cal(1) has a place of honor on my hate list for that exact reason). How about classad_eval <expr> [<expr>...] classad_eval -a <inline ad> <expr> [<expr>...] classad_eval -f <ad from file> <expr> [<expr>...] 2019-Oct-24 15:58:57 by tlmiller: After discussion, see child tickets. 2019-Oct-25 08:28:24 by karpel: Could we use entry_points instead of scripts for packaging? It makes it much easier to test and makes editable installs work. See https://python-packaging.readthedocs.io/en/latest/command-line-scripts.html 2019-Oct-25 10:50:04 by tlmiller: "Editable installs"? But yes, we can do that. 2019-Oct-25 10:52:22 by karpel: pip install -e <path/to/pkg/dir> symlinks local package source into your Python package directory instead of copying it, so you can pretend like it's installed without having to re-install it every time you make changes (for dev purposes only, really). 2019-Oct-25 18:44:13 by tlmiller: [58275] implements simplify(), but the lifetime of ExprTree 's return from simplify() is probably tied to the lifetime of the scope argument. I find this moderately absurd even in C++; it's probably flat-out wrong in Python. If a scope argument is not supplied, and the ExprTree has a parent scope, the lifetime of the return is probably the same as the lifetime of the original ExprTree -- which is the lifetime of the parent scope. This is also a model which I imagine will cause infinite confusion. Finally, if the scope argument is not supplied, the lifetime of the return really should be the natural lifetime of the Python object in question. It may even be more problematic that the answer varies than that it isn't always the natural lifetime of the Python object. We will have to have to have words with BrianB. 2019-Oct-29 14:58:47 by tlmiller: We need to document: the new tool that Python's ExprTree.eval() no longer accepts raw dictionaries (wrap them in classad.ClassAd() first) the existence of simplify(), and if we do, that attempts to use a temporary ClassAd, or the resulting ExprTree past the lifetime of the non-temporary context argument, is a terrrible, terrible plan. 2019-Oct-31 12:32:40 by tlmiller: Also, we need to make sure the new tool: is packaged in the tarballs is packaged by RPM and Deb is packaged by anaconda/pip ... and that it ends up in a sane place, and runnable, in all three cases. 2019-Oct-31 16:35:02 by tlmiller: Documentation is done. 2019-Nov-12 11:22:25 by tlmiller: We discussed the packaging problems at Flightworthy; HTCondor will now just require the Python bindings, and we'll "just" install this script into the usual binary directory, not using setup.py at all. (We'll thus have to duplicate or leverage its shebang-line rewriting powers until we can actually drop Python 2 support.) 2019-Dec-20 10:59:44 by tlmiller: For the 8.9.5 release, we'll just package classad_eval like we do condor_top (in the python bindings RPM/deb, but not in the PyPI/pip/conda package(s)), and not make the Python bindings a hard dependency.

title: Ticket #5304: Need more permissions for match password auth
description: For SEC_ENABLE_MATCH_PASSWORD_AUTHENTICATION to work, authorization entries must be made for the match principals, submit-side@matchsession and execute-side@matchsession. Currently, some of these entries are made automatically when the feature is enabled, but others need to be explicitly added in the configuration files. Now that we have SEC_ENABLE_MATCH_PASSWORD_AUTHENTICATION enabled by default, we should have all of the authorization entries added automatically. The following authorization entries currently need to be done explicitly in the configuration files: schedd: CLIENT shadow: CLIENT startd: CLIENT and DAEMON starter: CLIENT and DAEMON The CLIENT entries do not need to be made if ALLOW_CLIENT isn't set in the configuration files (because the default is to allow all). Most of the new automatic entries will not be limited by IP address (i.e. the entries will act like submit-side@matchsession/*). We don't believe this adds any security problems, and it's necessary for the startd, which has no way to know what schedds may want to claim it.

title: Ticket #7786: Add tool to shut down + resume condor_dagman and provisioner jobs
description: We want tools that will allow us to shut down and then later resume provisioner jobs (as per #7600), as well as condor_dagman jobs. This is different from removing a condor job using condor_rm. Removing a job implies that the job is finished. However when we shut down a job, we assume that we'll want to resume that job at a later point, picking up from the state where it left off. We'll need to make new tools for this feature, presumably called condor_shutdown and condor_resume. This work is described in detail in a design document: https://docs.google.com/document/d/1O1dcSDclEp_gN5IkHza4TKtkjT5nJCjYveD1IA-hnfs/edit#

title: Ticket #1652: Schedd controls who sends alives
description: STARTD_SENDS_ALIVES is an error-prone knob, especially when flocking. If the submit and execute machines don't have it set the same, then you can end up in a situation where neither daemon is sending keep-alives, and all jobs die an early death. There should be one place where the decision of who sends the keep-alives for a given claim is made. The schedd makes the most sense. At the start of the claim, the schedd should inform the startd who is responsible for sending keep-alives. The default should be for the startd to send them. And both daemons should be backwards-compatible with older versions.

description: Note: this is a nonpublic, never released branch. It will eventually be merged into master once problems like this are sorted out. ./tmp exists when job_ckpt_io-async_std tries to run. This is a fatal error. See http://nmi-s006.cs.wisc.edu/rundir/m/2011/03/m_nmi-s006.cs.wisc.edu_1299801231_31219/userdir/nmi:x86_rhas_3/job_ckpt_io-async_std-1.out for an example. ./tmp is a directory, and when the tests finish, it is and contains the following: drwxr-xr-x 4 4096 Mar 11 03:30 tmp drwxr-xr-x 3 4096 Mar 11 05:06 tmp/condorLocks drwxr-xr-x 3 4096 Mar 11 04:35 tmp/condorLocks/34 drwxr-xr-x 2 4096 Mar 11 04:01 tmp/condorLocks/34/38 -rw-r--r-- 1 0 Mar 11 04:01 tmp/condorLocks/34/38/451316.lockc drwxr-xr-x 2 4096 Mar 11 01:18 tmp/full_dir The contents suggest two people using ./tmp: condorLocks: File locking. The file locking code uses this directory under tmp_dir_path() if it can't find LOCAL_DISK_LOCKDIR (/src/condor_utils/file_lock.cpp 679 FileLock::GetTempPath). tmp_dir_path will try in order, param("TMP_DIR"), param("TEMP_DIR"), and then /tmp. (/src/condor_utils/directory_util.cpp 30 tmp_dir_path). I think ./TestingPersonalCondor/condor_config(.local) is being used, and that sets TMP_DIR=$(LOG)/tmp. LOG is $(LOCAL_DIR/log). LOCAL_DIR is the full path to ./TestingPersonalCondor/local, as expected. And sure enough, ./TestingPersonalCondor/local/log/tmp exists and contains condorLocks and general evidence of the locking system being used. So, who is getting the wrong idea to use ./? tmp/condorLocks could be created by an earlier test, in which case we don't know which configuration is in use. So far, no luck correlating timestamps on the files with matching start times and durations in the NMI reports; the timestamps don't agree with each other at all. Guilty party is almost certainly job_dagman*.run. The various condor_dagmans started by those tests somehow decide that CWD(?) is the appropriate place for log files. full_dir: /src/condor_unit_tests/OTEST_StatInfo.cpp and /src/condor_unit_tests/OTEST_Directory.cpp will create a directory by this name. title: Ticket #5168: Increase rate of schedd job completion
description: We have some schedds where the average job finish rate is greater than the duty cycle rate. This results in an accumulation of jobs in 'C' state - more than 100k in one case. As there are lots of unnecessary ads in the queue, queue scanning and hash table operations take longer - resulting in a longer duty cycle and more jobs in queue. We should expose a knob to manage the number of completions done per duty cycle
remarks: 2015-Jul-28 08:02:55 by bbockelm: Just to follow up - This has been a complete lifesaver within CMS. We found that our schedds could sustain a higher rate of "real job completion" (i.e., shadow finished the job) than they could sustain removing the proc from the queue. We observed multiple cases over the past two weeks that were only solvable by this patch (or by having an operator log in and setting MAX_JOBS_RUNNING=0 and waiting until the issue has resolved). On nodes with the patch applied, this issue has not returned. I see no reason why someone would want to tune this knob; hence, I am not creating a param table entry. Jaime, can you review? Brian 2015-Jul-28 09:30:02 by jfrey: Code Review I'm hesitant to increase the default count-per-interval setting of job_is_finished_queue to 8 without additional changes. Several jobs that have spool directories with a large number of files could block the schedd for a prolonged period. I'd like to see the addition of a time-based limit or make spool directory cleanup less of a synchronous operation. 2015-Jul-28 14:03:08 by bbockelm: What about just waiting to merge until after #5152? 2015-Jul-28 16:08:28 by jfrey: That depends on how #5152 is implemented. If the schedd doesn't block waiting for the spool directory removal to finish, then sure.

Ticket #5538: Bad accounting group names can kill negotiator
description: If an accounting group name contains a space, the negotiator will write bad entries to the accountant log, which it cannot read back on restart. This will kill matchmaking until the accountant log file is manually corrected. The negotiator uses the account group name as part of a ClassAd log key, but keys cannot contain spaces, as space delimits the fields of a ClassAd log entry. The negotiator needs to validate accounting group names and reject those that have invalid characters (which may extend beyond space). Condor_submit and condor_schedd should probably do the same. At a lower level, the ClassAd log should validate its keys, and refuse to write entries that it can't read back.

title: Ticket #3815: Projection introduced in #3366 breaks concurrency limits
description: The resource ad projection introduced on #3366 does not include the ConcurrrencyLimits attribute, which is required to recompute concurrency limit counts at the beginning of each negotiation cycle. The effect is that concurrency limits used in previous cycles are not counted, and so concurrency limits won't be respected across multiple cycles.
remarks: 2013-Jul-26 11:13:31 by eje: TEST/REPRO A good way to exercise the behavior across multiple cycles is to set up a p-slot with (say) 4 cpus, and configure a concurrency limit of 3. It's crucial to set "NEGOTIATOR_CONSIDER_PREEMPTION = False" for repro. title: Ticket #1828: schedd does not fork if condor_q authenticates
description: When condor_q authenticates, the schedd never forks when processing the query, no matter what the setting of SCHEDD_QUERY_WORKERS. This is because the client does not call InitializeReadOnlyConnection(). This affects glideinWMS, because the frontend requires integrity (and therefore authentication) when running condor_q. I am fixing this in the 7.5 branch, because in 7.5 we have a separate CEDAR command for read-only connections, so there is no need to rely on an additional message from the client to indicate that the connection is read-only. This means that the fix will work for 7.5.5 schedds talking to condor_q from 7.5.0 and beyond.
remarks: 2010-Dec-30 09:38:38 by danb: It turns out that forking on all QMGMT_READ_CMDs doesn't work. The problem is that clients older than 7.5.0 always send QMGMT_READ_CMD, even when they are intending to do write operations. Also, even newer versions of condor_qedit were using QMGMT_READ_CMD (fixed for 7.5.5). So instead of fixing things in the schedd, I am fixing things on the client side. As of 7.5.5, qmgmt cleints that want a read-only session will always call InitializeReadOnlyConnection(), regardless of whether they are using an authenticated security session or not.

title: Ticket #7856: Proxy refresh for Condor-C jobs ignores lifetime job attribute
description: When delegating a GSI proxy, the lifetime of the delegated proxy is controlled by config param DELEGATE_JOB_GSI_CREDENTIALS_LIFETIME and job attribute DelegateJobGSICredentialsLifetime. When a refresh proxy is forwarded for a Condor-C job (grid universe, type condor), the job attribute is ignored when doing the delegation in the c-gahp, but is consulted when the gridmanager calculates the lifetime of the delegated proxy. This can result in the gridmanager thinking the delegated proxy has a longer lifetime that it actually does. This will delay when a proxy with a shortened lifetime needs to be refreshed, potentially until after the existing proxy expires. CERN encountered this with some of their ATLAS jobs. The proxies have 4-day lifetimes and are refreshed once a day. Config parameter DELEGATE_JOB_GSI_CREDENTIALS_LIFETIME is set to the default of 24 hours. DelegateJobGSICredentialsLifetime is set to 0 in the job ads, indicating that the delegated proxies should have the full lifetime of the source proxy. The jobs are submitted with the full multi-day lifetime for the proxy. After the first refresh, the delegated proxy has a 24-hour lifetime, but the gridmanager thinks it has the full multi-day lifetime. Thus, the delegated proxy expires around the time the gridmanager will refresh it (when the source proxy is refreshed). To make matters worse, the destination schedd has a SYSTEM_PERIODIC_HOLD expression that triggers if the proxy expires.

title: Ticket #4283: Improve synchronization of the job log.
description: For updates, there's no reason to use fsync (which sync's data and metadata) on the job_queue.log; only fdatasync (which only sync's data) is really needed. The metadata probably only needs to be synchronized on rotation... ...speaking of which, our current code for job_queue.log rotation is not safe. We use rename() to rotate the file; there's no guarantee which copy of the data is in which file after a crash. description: I just ran into a case working with BMRB where jobs were failing because of a problem on an OSG execute machine, and retries weren't doing any good because jobs kept landing on the same machine. It would be really nice to just have a flag in DAGMan to say "force retries to land on a different execute machine than the job failed on". title: Ticket #5884: Prefer depth-first matching of pslots in negotiator
description: When the negotiator matches a job to a pslot, by default, it hands out the whole pslot to the schedd, which the schedd can us to match further jobs. Although, the negotiator will charge the user for the whole weight of the pslot, and stop handing out pslots when the submitterLimit is hit, this assumes that all jobs match all slots. If this isn't the case, and jobs are selective, it is possible that the negotiator will hand out too many pslots, and cause unneeded fragmentation of the pslots. CMS is seeing pslot fragmentation, so we will add a knob that will assume that if one job in an autocluster matches part of a pslot, the negotiator will ignore as many subsequent jobs in that autocluster which should fit it that pslot. This knob is called NEGOTIATOR_DEPTH_FIRST.

title: Ticket #6251: condor_history occasionally shows RemoteHost and other attributes
description: Lukas reported on the htcondor-users email list that condor_history occasionally shows the RemoteHost classad attribute for terminated jobs. This is a minor bug, which can occur if a job happens to complete while the schedd is in the process of a graceful shutdown. The issue is job attributes like RemoteHost are normally removed whenever the shadow associated with the job exits. However, these attributes must be preserved to enable a new shadow to reconnect to the job in the event the schedd is restarted. Thus in the situation where the shadow exits because the schedd is shutting down, the schedd always preserves these attributes --- even if the job is in a terminal state! This ticket will submit a patch so the schedd will not bother to preserve these reconnect attributes in the event that the job is in a terminal state (Completed or Removed).

title: Ticket #5187: Improved concurrency interfaces for python bindings
description: A common use case for the python bindings are the equivalent of "condor_q -g ..." -- finding all the jobs in a pool matching a constraint. This is typically implemented as: all_ads = [] for ad in collector.query(htcondor.AdTypes.Schedd, schedd_const): schedd = htcondor.Schedd(ad) all_ads += schedd.xquery(jobs_const) This is inherently serial, however - even though the returned iterator is non-blocking. I'd like to introduce a gather function: queries = [htcondor.Schedd(ad).xquery(jobs_const) for ad in collector.query(htcondor.AdTypes.Schedd, schedd_const)] all_ads = [] for query in htcondor.gather(queries): all_ads += query.nextAdsNonBlocking() gather will keep track of the given iterator objects and return any that has events ready to read. If all iterators are complete, then throws a StopIteration exception. QueryIterator.nextAdsNonBlocking() will return all the currently available ads. Returns an empty list if no ads are available. Returns an empty list if the query has completed. QueryIterator.next() will be extended to optionally not block. Still throws StopIteration if the query has completed. QueryIterator.tag() will return the query's tag. Schedd.query will get a new keyword argument, tag. When set, it'll set the created =QueryIterator='s tag. If not set, the =QueryIterator='s tag will be set to the schedd's name. The tag allows us to identify queries: queries = [htcondor.Schedd(ad).xquery(jobs_const) for ad in collector.query(htcondor.AdTypes.Schedd, schedd_const)] ads_per_schedd = {} for query in htcondor.gather(queries): schedd = query.tag() if schedd not in ads_per_schedd: ads_per_schedd[schedd] = [] ads_per_schedd[query.tag()] += query.nextAdsNonBlocking() Hmm - that's a bit more complex than I had hoped. Suggestions?
remarks: 2015-Aug-01 12:51:19 by bbockelm: Here is the serial test script used: $ cat test_query_old.py #!/usr/bin/python import time import htcondor coll = htcondor.Collector("vocms099.cern.ch") job_counts = {} print "Querying collector for schedds" start = time.time() coll_query = coll.query(htcondor.AdTypes.Schedd) end = time.time() for schedd_ad in coll_query: schedd_obj = htcondor.Schedd(schedd_ad) if True or not schedd_ad['Name'].startswith('crab'): print "Starting query to", schedd_ad['Name'] # job_counts[schedd_ad['Name']] = len(list(schedd_obj.xquery(opts=htcondor.QueryOpts.AutoCluster))) job_counts[schedd_ad['Name']] = len(list(schedd_obj.xquery())) end2= time.time() print "Found %d schedds to query." % len(job_counts) print job_counts print "Collector query time: %.2f" % (end-start) print "Schedd query time: %.2f" % (end2-end) print "Total time: %.2f" % (end2-start) And concurrent version: $ cat test_query_poll.py #!/usr/bin/python import time import htcondor coll = htcondor.Collector("vocms099.cern.ch") queries = [] start = time.time() print "Querying collector for schedds" coll_query = coll.query(htcondor.AdTypes.Schedd) end = time.time() for schedd_ad in coll_query: schedd_obj = htcondor.Schedd(schedd_ad) if True or not schedd_ad['Name'].startswith('crab'): print "Starting query to", schedd_ad['Name'] # queries.append(schedd_obj.xquery(opts=htcondor.QueryOpts.AutoCluster)) queries.append(schedd_obj.xquery()) end2= time.time() print "Found %d schedds to query." % len(queries) job_counts = {} for query in htcondor.poll(queries): schedd_name = query.tag() job_counts.setdefault(schedd_name, 0) count = len(query.nextAdsNonBlocking()) job_counts[schedd_name] += count print "Got %d results from %s." % (count, schedd_name) print job_counts end3 = time.time() print "Collector query time: %.2f" % (end-start) print "Schedd query startup time: %.2f" % (end2-end) print "Schedd query finish time: %.2f" % (end3-end) print "Total time: %.2f" % (end3-start) Note that they are somewhat the equivalent of "condor_q -g -l". I ran both scripts on the CMS global pool on a relatively sleepy Saturday (68k jobs total). Doing things serially: Collector query time: 4.63 Schedd query time: 239.67 Total time: 244.31 versus concurrently: Collector query time: 4.67 Schedd query startup time: 9.40 Schedd query finish time: 71.15 Total time: 75.82 So, about a 3x speedup. Note the CPU usage from the latter: real 1m15.952s user 0m59.239s sys 0m2.827s Basically, the larger the pool, the closer we get to being CPU-bound (as we do so much network IO concurrently). The CMS global pool has 38 schedds at the time of writing. Now, an important lesson here comes by switching from job queries to autocluster queries (uncomment appropriate lines above). First, serial: Collector query time: 4.61 Schedd query time: 22.83 Total time: 27.43 Then, concurrent: Collector query time: 4.75 Schedd query startup time: 7.41 Schedd query finish time: 7.93 Total time: 12.67 real 0m12.745s user 0m0.607s sys 0m0.068s This is a 6x speedup! So, while going parallel is indeed worthwhile, there are bigger savings in utilizing auto-clusters instead of jobs (keep in mind that not all queries can do this - but I suspect many can!). Note also, when querying auto-clusters, the penalty for opening connections and security sessions to schedds increases significantly. At some point, we may want to do a follow-up ticket to make this phase non-blocking. However, this would first require making the client-side of the authentication stack non-blocking.

title: Ticket #958: Prioritizing GAHP commands
description: The gridmanager restricts the number of concurrent commands it will issue to a GAHP server, with a default of 50. Additional commands are queued up and issued on first come, first served basis. This can cause a time-sensitive command to be stuck behind a long string of less-important commands. For example, a command to renew the leases of all submitted jobs may have to wait behind 5000 submit commands for new jobs. In a recent test run of cream jobs, 1500 jobs were submitted simultaneously. The submission process consists of a REGISTER, then a START command. The REGISTER command for all 1500 jobs were executed (50 at a time) before the START command for any could execute. The specific case of a deluge of job submissions used to be mitigated by the parameter GRIDMANAGER_MAX_PENDING_SUBMITS_PER_RESOURCE. But that parameter has been removed, and the sudden removal of a large number of jobs can create a similar delay in the execution of commands that may be more time-sensitive. We need a way to prevent a large number of job submits or removals from delaying other GAHP commands. One possibility is to indicate certain commands as high or low priority. This could be done in the gridmanager or the gahp. If done in the gahp, then the throttle on concurrent gahp commands would need to be widened or removed. That would require all gahps to do their own throttling of concurrent command execution, which some already do.

title: Ticket #2513: NETWORK_INTERFACE does not work as expected
description: As of 7.7.0, the following configuration does not cause the daemons to bind only to 127.0.0.1: BIND_ALL_INTERFACES = FALSE NETWORK_INTERFACE = 127.0.0.1 It does not even cause the daemon to advertise 127.0.0.1 as its public address. I have verified that in 7.6.2, the above configuration does have the expected effect. Here's what appears to be causing this problem: Checkin [22136] attempted to fix problems in the new 7.7.0 IPv6 init_local_hostname(). However, this code caches the result of my_sin_addr(), among other things. The problem with caching the result is that if my_sin_addr() is called before the configuration has been fully initialized, NETWORK_INTERFACE is not taken into account. init_local_hostname() is called early during configuration in order to fill in config macros such as HOSTNAME. From then on, the cached value is used, so NETWORK_INTERFACE is effectively ignored. Note that all cached values in my_hostname.cpp are cleared and re-initialized by the config system after the configuration has been loaded. Something similar needs to be done for the new IPv6 code, or it just needs to avoid caching.

title: Ticket #7341: Make multi-attributes easier to classad_eval
description: If users could be able to specify ClassAd attributes one at a time on the classad_eval command-line, that would be much easier than dealing with quoting newlines. Example: classad_eval -insert 'x = y' 'y = "7"' 'z = "foo"' -eval y z 7 "foo" We could support -insert and -eval as mode-modifying flags (so that you could insert/eval/insert/eval if you wanted to), but Mat thinks that it'll be simpler and less confusing just to have people run classad_eval twice. We'll probably have to test that with actual users. It's unclear what the semantics should be if we allow -insert or -eval to be optional. (On the other hand, given that the name of the command is 'eval', maybe nouns for the options is better: -ad and -expr?) For instance, a lone -eval should mean that anything before it is an insert, but instead of -none, it would be nice just to say that if neither -insert nor -eval appear, all positional arguments are evaluated rather than inserted. TJ maintains that if we restrict ourselves to HTCondor ClassAds, it will be easy to distinguish attributes from expressions; if that is so, I agree that we should make both flags optional and just do the right thing.

title: Ticket #2840: glexec causes jobs to 'exit' without running
description: When condor is configured to use glexec, we have observed a situation where the job appears to exit with status 1, even though the job in fact was never started. The stderr of the job contains the following message: fdpass_recv error on new_sock_fd This was observed at DESY with Condor 7.6.4. Here is the story: Condor starts condor_glexec_run with only one open file descriptor: fd 0, which is a socket for communication with the starter. condor_glexec_run calls glexec to run condor_glexec_job_wrapper. By the time condor_glexec_job_wrapper is run, file descriptors 1 and 3 but not 2 are also open. They point to some socket (not sure where that came from). condor_glexec_job_wrapper does not behave correctly if file descriptor 1 and/or 2 are not open. The fact that 2 is not open therefore triggers the bug. The bug was introduced in [11658] (7.2). Prior to 7.6.2 (#1642), the effect of this bug in condor_glexec_job_wrapper was different. It could have caused failure to detect exec() failure when starting the job. Starting in 7.6.2, the effect of the bug is worse: it causes condor_glexec_job_wrapper to fail to start the job and for Condor to think that the job did start. In 7.7, this bug does not get triggered, because Condor opens a pipe for stdout/stderr from glexec (#2259) and hence is not dependent on how glexec behaves when stdout/stderr are not open when it is called. At DESY, glite-GLEXEC_wn/node-version contains the version string 3.2.6-3, which I believe means glexec is version 0.8.1-1.
remarks: 2012-Feb-22 17:18:40 by danb: The following shell script can be used to mimic the way condor calls glexec. #!/bin/sh exec 3>&1 1>&- 2>&- /opt/glite/sbin/glexec /bin/sh -c '/usr/sbin/lsof -p $$ 1>&3' At DESY, this shows the problematic 'hole' in the open file descriptors: bash 12522 cmsplt012 0u CHR 136,0 2 /dev/pts/0 bash 12522 cmsplt012 1u unix 0xffff810424a14f00 60858654 socket bash 12522 cmsplt012 3u CHR 136,0 2 /dev/pts/0 bash 12522 cmsplt012 4u unix 0xffff810424a14f00 60858654 socket bash 12522 cmsplt012 5r REG 8,3 646 590363 /opt/glite/etc/lcmaps/lcmaps-glexec.db The lcmaps-related file that is open makes me wonder if this problem has something to do with the lcmaps configuration. When I run this test at T2_US_Wisconsin, I get the following (no holes) bash 16878 osg_cmsuser01 0u CHR 136,0 2 /dev/pts/0 bash 16878 osg_cmsuser01 1r CHR 1,3 2215 /dev/null bash 16878 osg_cmsuser01 2r CHR 1,3 2215 /dev/null bash 16878 osg_cmsuser01 3u CHR 136,0 2 /dev/pts/0 The Wisconsin glexec is from rpm glexec-0.8.10-8.osg. 2012-Feb-23 17:17:33 by tannenba: CODE REVIEW Wow, what a find, nice detective work. Patch looks good. Just need a quick version history blurb, so moving ticket to doc pending state. 2012-Feb-28 11:45:33 by danb: It turns out that DESY had glexec configured in log-only mode. This means glexec was not setuid-root. Linux forces opening of /dev/null for the stdio descriptors for setuid-root programs running as non-root. This explains why we do not normally see this problem: it only affect log-only mode. Though Condor no longer cares, Mischa has now fixed gLExec 0.9.3 to open /dev/null for missing stdio descriptors, even when running in log-only mode.

title: Ticket #4097: On Windows files are not always truncated when they should be
description: If a user submits a job like executable = foo output = foo.out queue and runs it, and then after it completes runs it a second time, one would expect HTCondor to erase (truncate) the results from the first run of foo.out before writing out the results from the second run. Unfortunately on Windows this is currently not happening, and the user may be left with a mish-mash of the two runs in foo.out. The problem is in our safe_open utility library, the flag O_TRUNC is removed from the open() system call and ftruncate() is called afterwards. But the ftruncate() call is in a block of code that's only compiled on unix. Thus, on Windows, safe_open effectively ignores O_TRUNC and thus the opened file is never truncated. The functions where this occurs are safe_open_no_create() and safe_open_no_create_follow(), though many other calls in the safe_open API end up calling these functions.

title: Ticket #6045: The Startd should put docker "universe" offline if Docker hangs
description: In CHTC we are seeing cases where a Docker job is causing the Docker daemon to stop responding. When this happens, all subsequent docker jobs will fail on this machine, making the machine a black hole for Docker jobs. To Fix this: The DockerAPI should be enhanced so that it will time out all communication with the Docker daemon. When the Startd is unable to communicate with the Docker daemon, it should put the docker "universe" offline using the same mechanism we added for VM universe.
remarks: 2016-Dec-08 14:08:45 by johnkn: Since the DockerAPI currently uses my_popen for most communication with the Docker daemon, we will need to add the capability to do reads from the resulting pipe with a timeout. More particularly, since we only really care about whether or not the my_popen process FINISHES within a certain amount of time, a new class will be created on top of my_popen that will run a program and capture its output into a memory buffer with a timeout on the entire operation.

title: Ticket #6415: schedd should have a way to blacklist a site of execute nodes
description: CMS global pool operators want the ability to blacklist a site from accepting new jobs on a schedd basis. LIGO would also like set a per-schedd limit on the number of running jobs per user. We think we can do both with one new schedd expression. We plan to implement this via a constraint config knob in the schedd, which must evaluate to true for a job to activate on a slot. The idea here is that, like the current START_LOCAL_UNIVERSE and START_SCHEDULER_UNIVERSE config knobs, that control when jobs of these universe types are allowed to start - there should also be a START_VANILLA_UNIVERSE knob that controls whether the schedd is willing to start a job for other universes (the name is tentative, this would apply to all jobs that need a condor_shadow process - not just vanilla jobs). This check would happen when a new match arrives from the negotiator, and also when the schedd is about to re-use a claim. The START_VANILLA_UNIVERSE expression would be evaluated in the context of the slot ad, the job ad, and a new "owner" ad that contains username and number of jobs that the current user has running, idle & held. Attribute references will be required to be scoped, but to make this clearer, the scopes will be JOB, SLOT, and OWNER. (i.e. not MY and TARGET). For instance. The schedd could ban a site using the expression: START_VANILLA_UNIVERSE = SLOT.Site =!= "badsite" or it could ban a site only for a certain user with the expression: START_VANILLA_UNIVERSE = IfThenElse(OWNER.Name =?= "bob", SLOT.Site =!= "badsite", true) The flexibility of this mechanism means it could also be used to stop or limit new job starts for a user or for jobs of a certain type. For instance, you could refuse to start new jobs for a user that has a lot of jobs on hold with this expression: START_VANILLA_UNIVERSE = OWNER.JobsHeld < 10 The OWNER ad will have counts of jobs in the queue, Idle, running and held jobs that are kept up-to-date in order to facilitate this use case. To prevent this new expression from becoming a large drain on CPU time in the Schedd, it will analyze the expression and optimize certain use cases - For instance. When a new match arrives, the expression will first be analyzed without any JOB ad, and if it evaluates to true or false rather than undefined, it will not be evaluated again while the schedd looks for idle jobs in the queue that match the resource. A further optimization will be made where the schedd reduces the expression to a sub-expression that refers to the SLOT ad and sends that sub-expression to the negotiator as part of the resource request ad. The negotiator would then be able to skip sending matches to the schedd that the schedd would never activate. While reducing the expression for the negotiator, the schedd will notice if the expression would resolve to true or false without referring to any SLOT attribute. If that is the case, then the schedd will leave the resource request unmodified (if true), or skip negotiating for the job entirely (if false). For example if START_VANILLA_UNIVERSE = IfThenElse(OWNER.Name=?="bob", SLOT.Site=!="badsite", true) && OWNER.JobsHeld < 10 and bob has jobs with Requirements = OpSys=="LINUX" When negotiator asks for resource requests from bob, If bob has less than 10 jobs on hold, the schedd will send a resource request with Requirements = OpSys=="LINUX" && IfThenElse(true, TARGET.Site=!="badsite", true) . If bob has more than 10 jobs on hold, then the schedd will tell the negotiator that it doesn't want any resources for bob. One caveat here is that the negotiator doesn't know anything about job Owners, it thinks in terms of submitters, and there can be a many to many relationship between owners and submitters - so it is not possible to reliably communicate constraints that refer to OWNER attributes to the negotiator that will prevent the negotiator from repeatedly trying to negotiate for bob. What we can do is short circuit the negotiation process so that the negotiator will not actually make matches for a bob's jobs when they will never be activated.
remarks: 2017-Sep-26 12:28:19 by johnkn: When the START_VANILLA_UNIVERSE expression refers to a JOB attribute. that attribute will have to be added to the set of significant attributes. If this is not done, then there will be jobs that share an autocluster id, but have different results from evaluating the START_VANILLA_UNIVERSE. This will either result in not getting matches for jobs that could run, or for getting matches that cannot be used. 2017-Oct-26 16:54:09 by johnkn: We are not enthusiastic about the name START_VANILLA_UNIVERSE for this knob, and will defer documenting it until we have come up with a better name, or have decided to go with the current name.

title: Ticket #3617: Gathering pid list on mac os x and bsd can cause crashes
description: On Mac OS X and BSD, the procapi code uses sysctl() to get a list of all processes on the system. In ProcAPI::buildPidList(), it calls sysctl() with a NULL pointer to determine how much space is required to hold the information, allocates a buffer of that size, then calls sysctl() again with that buffer. If either call fails, buildPidList() returns failure and leaves the ProcAPI::pidList linked list containing one entry with uninitialized data. The callers ignore the return value and always assume pidList contains all pids on the system. Depending on the uninitialized contents of pidList, this can cause ProcAPI to crash or to think only one random pid is left on the system. This can cause the behavior seen in #2537 and #3549. The first call to sysctl() returns a size that's a little larger than required, to account for new processes showing up between calls. But if enough new processes are born in that short time, the buffer may be too small when sysctl() is called the second time. If this happens, it will return ENOMEM and a new buffer size estimate. By making the following changes, we can make this code more robust and easier to debug on failure: On ENOMEM failures, retry sysctl() several times, increasing the buffer size appropriately If sysctl() still fails after retries, log the error When buildPidList() returns failure, always leave pidList as an empty list. Callers to buildPidList() should be prepared for it to fail, either checking the return value or otherwise reacting appropriately to an empty pidList.

title: Ticket #5393: HTCondor View: Filter on timestamps relative to "now"
description: You can currently filter based on dates and perhaps timestamps, but it would be a fixed date/timestamp. What we generally want are time relative to "now." So a display of the last day's worth of data would be "filter=timestamp>=now-24 hours" or somesuch. We could do the filter when we build the graph. On the up side, it would allow some meaningful zooming out. On the down side, it could potentially double the amount of data being considered; early filters are faster. title: Ticket #4701: The obvious way to configure a personal condor is broken.
description: The configuration use role : personal use security : host_based seems like an obvious way to get a personal condor, but doesn't actually create a working pool, because: use role : personal sets CONDOR_HOST to 127.0.0.1 use security : host_based sets ALLOW_NEGOTIATOR to $(CONDOR_HOST) Based on NETWORK_INTERFACE (default *) and BIND_ALL_INTERFACES (default TRUE), the collector drops an address file containing the host's public IPv4 address. The negotiator reads that address file and contacts the collector accordingly. The host's public IPv4 is NOT in ALLOW_NEGOTIATOR. We don't want to turn off BIND_ALL_INTERFACES, because we think it's a good idea to allow users to expand a personal condor into a pool by only changing the ALLOW_* lines. I think setting NETWORK_INTERFACE to 127.0.0.1 would prevent address rewriting, so querying the original collector would return useless addresses for the original daemons. The proper solutions is probably something along the lines of: have 'use role : personal' set some variables (LOCAL_ADMINISTRATOR, LOCAL_NEGOTIATOR?) and have 'use role : host_based' add append them unconditionally to the corresponding ALLOW entries (including SCHEDD_NEGOTIATOR). Empty entries at the end of the list are harmless, so this should just work (regardless of the ordering of the two use commands).

title: Ticket #5813: shared_port daemon should be careful about FD use

(It may have to be two FDs per MAX_ACCEPT, because the shared port daemon both accept()s a connection and almost immediately opens the corresponding domain socket (or whatever) to shove that FD down.) title: Ticket #1153: per-test-run subdir / allow repeated runs of batch_test.pl
description: Even if you're luck and "./batch_test.pl -b -c" runs without errors, "./batch_test.pl -b -c && ./batch_test.pl -b -c" is pretty much guaranteed to have errors. Many of the tests pollute the condor_tests directory, and some require no pollution to be present. As a workaround you can run "x_makeclean.pl" which is also available as "make resubmit", but that's fundamentally a relatively fragile workaround. Tests should always run in an isolated subdirectory that they're free to pollute to their hearts content. This will: Make finding relevant output files easier. Allow someone to see multiple runs output Make cleaning up a run easier (rm -rf runs/therun) If directories nested at least one deep, you can clean up all runs easily (rm -rf runs) Tests won't risk stomping on each other; you'll be able to run the tests in a loop. Some tests write files in the condor_tests that other tests need, so transitioning will be slow. We'll probably want to make a whitelist of older tests that are allowed to pollute until we can fix them.

title: Ticket #7592: Add an include dir feature to condor mapfiles
description: For HTCondor-CE, we'd like the ability to add lines to our condor_mapfiles to include directories containing additional mapfiles. If the original DAG was submitted with 7.9 or 8.0.0, DAGMan would have used the "single log file" feature initially; but on restart (because of the missing version in the .condor.sub file) the new instance of DAGMan falls back to the old "individual submit file" behavior. 2013-Sep-03 16:31:27 by wenger: As per today's LIGO phone conference, the plan is as follows: I produce an 8.0.3-pre release DAGMan that doesn't do the "fall back to individual log files" check. title: Ticket #3928: Improve readability of ClassAd reals in Condor
description: In 8.1.1, we made Condor print floating-point values in ClassAds the same way they're printed in native new ClassAd syntax, using printf format string %1.15E (#3363). This preserves the full precision of doubles when unparsed into text representations. But this format is much harder for humans to read. A compromise is to use format %.16G. It keeps the same precision, while using scientific notation only for especially large or small values. This representation is only used if old ClassAd syntax is requested in ClassAdUnParser. Native new ClassAd syntax will still use %1.15E, as described in the specification.

title: Ticket #1915: schedd EXCEPTs on shutdown due to bad reference count
description: The following error happens when the schedd is shut down: 02/14/11 15:55:32 (pid:20530) ERROR "Assertion ERROR on (m_ref_count == 0)" at line 98 in file /scratch/danb/CONDOR_SRC/src/condor_utils/classy_counted_ptr.h This is happening in DaemonCore::Cancel_And_Close_All_Sockets(). The problem is that one of the sockets that is closed has a non-zero reference count, because the asynchronous negotiation code increments the reference count before registering the socket. Currently, Cancel_And_Close_All_Sockets() does not call the socket callback, so any code that is waiting to receive a callback will never happen. There are two possible solutions: Get rid of DaemonCore::Cancel_And_Close_All_Sockets(). Fix DaemonCore::Cancel_And_Close_All_Sockets() to call socket handlers after closing the sockets. This gives the handler a chance to clean up. Doing the second option correctly would require some care. For example, the socket handler might try to register more sockets or delete the socket we are currently dealing with. We would probably need to prevent more sockets from being registered. Since no daemon but the schedd calls this function, I am going to just go with the first option: get rid of the function. The only purpose it is serving is to clean things up to make memory leak detection easier. If we decide we need that, we can try to implement this function the right way, and use it uniformly in all condor daemons, rather than just in the schedd.

title: Ticket #920: Startd crash can leak VMs
description: When the Startd starts it removes everything under the EXECUTE directory, but first checks for .recover files. The .recover file contains the job ad of the running job. If the job was a VM job, the startd will invoke the condor_vm-gahp in "KillMode". KillMode eventually invokes VirshType::killVMFast to terminate the VMs. However, on 26 Aug 09 (155e821), the killVMFast function was commented out. The result being the Startd's attempt is effectively ignored. The end result is libvirt VMs are left running after a startd restart after a crash.
remarks: 2009-Nov-09 10:26:27 by jfrey: Some related tickets: #514 Original ticket detailing leaking of VMs on startd crash #688 Change of VM GAHP to link against libvirt
attachments: startd_crash_vm_cleanup.patch 6001 bytes added by rrati on 2009-Nov-09 16:16:42 UTC. This patch moves the VM shutdown functionality out of killVM and back into killVMFast.
