title: Ticket #4890: Mistakes and confusion around documentation of CPU core detection
description: The documentation surrounding CPU core detection and counting seems to be a mess, and should be fixed asap. Below I cut-n-pasted the relevant knob notes as they currently stand in the manual. I think the blurb for $(DETECTED_CORES) is the only one that looks fine :). With DETECTED_CPUS, I think the documentation says the exact opposite of the truth! The rest are confusing and/or use inconsistent language (mixing the idea of number of CPUs vs the number of CPU cores, interchanging terminology like 'hyper-threaded cores' vs 'virtual CPUs' vs 'hyperthread CPUs' vs 'hyper-threaded processors' vs 'CPUs/cores'). For NUM_CPUS, it says it is "disabled by default", and then goes on to give a default value. The documentation on DetectedCpus attribute in the machine ad is also meaningless - is it equal to $(DETECTED_CORES), or $(DETECTED_CPUS), or something else? I have no idea. Current wording of Manual Entries we should improve - $(DETECTED_CORES) The number of detected CPU cores. This includes hyper-threaded cores, if there are any. $(DETECTED_PHYSICAL_CPUS) The integer number of physical (non hyper-threaded) CPUs. $(DETECTED_CPUS) The integer number of physical (non hyper-threaded) CPUs, as given by $(DETECTED_PHYSICAL_CPUS), when COUNT_HYPERTHREAD_CPUS is True. The integer number of hyper-threaded CPUs, as given by $(DETECTED_CORES), when COUNT_HYPERTHREAD_CPUS is False. COUNT_HYPERTHREAD_CPUS This macro controls how HTCondor sees hyper-threaded processors. When set to True (the default), it includes virtual CPUs in the default value of NUM_CPUS. On dedicated cluster nodes, counting virtual CPUs can sometimes improve total throughput at the expense of individual job speed. However, counting them on desktop workstations can interfere with interactive job performance. NUM_CPUS An integer value, which can be used to lie to the condor_startd daemon about how many CPUs a machine has. When set, it overrides the value determined with HTCondor's automatic computation of the number of CPUs in the machine. Lying in this way can allow multiple HTCondor jobs to run on a single-CPU machine, by having that machine treated like a multi-core machine with multiple CPUs, which could have different HTCondor jobs running on each one. Or, a multi-core machine may advertise more slots than it has CPUs. However, lying in this manner will hurt the performance of the jobs, since now multiple jobs will run on the same CPU, and the jobs will compete with each other. The option is only meant for people who specifically want this behavior and know what they are doing. It is disabled by default. The default value is set by $(DETECTED_CPUS). Startd Ad attribiute DetectedCpus: The number of detected machine CPUs/cores.

title: Ticket #5852: Eliminate need to set <SUBSYS>_ARGS.
description: We shouldn't have to pass anything on the command-line of a "cloned" daemon (e.g., a second negotiator), because we don't have to for the original; making this true should make adding a cloned daemon much easier. This may entail adding <DAEMON_NAME>.PORT and <DAEMON_NAME>.SOCKET_NAME to the things DaemonCore and/or the master pay attention to, among other things. To the extent that DaemonCore will pay attention to <DAEMON_NAME>.<parameter>, it's potentially exceedingly confusing if the master does not, as the master will claim one thing about the networking it prepared for the daemon, and which the daemon inherits; and the daemon itself will believe something else (and/or make it come true). On the other hand, one could also argue that <DAEMON_NAME>_PORT (or <DAEMON_NAME>_<paramter-read-by-the-master> is both more in-line with the existing names and makes more sense, because telling the master to do should be a configuration parameter for the master, not some random DAEMON_NAME.

title: Ticket #3085: Add (certain) invalidated ads to absent list.
description: The BaTLab uses absent ads to maintain a persistent idea of what platforms "should" be in the pool, assuming that we intend all "clean" shut-downs to happen. However, it has become obvious that is is not the case; the startd is simply "too good" at getting its invalidation messages to the collector before it goes away, even if we'd prefer it didn't. This breaks absent ads because the ads immediately leave the collector upon invalidation; they don't get a chance to time-out and "go absent" that way. To correct that: > However, I like your idea for a knob in the collector that would > cause to ignore invalidation requests (for ads that meet the > ABSENT_REQUIREMENTS), or maybe just immediately force the invalidated ad > into the absent list. Our pool doesn't change all that fast, so manually > correcting the absent list won't be too much of a pain -- until we get > our run-as-root service working, at which point we'll need a way to > handle it automagically, since those machines will be rather transient. > Perhaps the knob could be INVALIDATION_REQUIREMENTS? That is, only ads > which match that expression could be invalidated, and all others would > go absent instead. This would allow the BaTLab to keep track of which machines "should" be in the pool for automation purposes -- most noticeably, whitelisting platforms for job submission -- automatically.
remarks: 2012-Jul-03 13:58:56 by tlmiller: Implemented as described. However, the collector plugin API doesn't presently permit a plugin to decline (or force the collector to decline) to invalidate an ad. This may require further consultation with ToddT. Why does the collector have hard-coded calls to the offline plugin? Can the calls to the plugins be safely moved to before the call to process_invalidation() in CollectorDaemon::receive_invalidation()? How much of the code after that call needs to be called even if a plugin declines to invalidate? 2012-Jul-03 16:18:41 by tlmiller: Instead of answering either of those questions, we had to look at the question of how many ads a single call to the plugin could invalidate. The answer is: the collector passes the plugin the same /query/ ad that it uses to determine which ads to remove. The key is that, by definition (construction?), any query for which a hashkey can be constructed refers to only one ad; every other query must be handled by an O(n) scan of the table. The collector handles the latter case (directly above the call to the plugin). The plugin (presently) does not; instead, it ignores queries without hashkeys. This also applies to update(), although it may semantically invalid to update multiple ads simultaneously. The expire() function can return false (unlike invalidate() and update()) because the collector is handing it a specific ad (not query) from out of the table to examine. 2012-Sep-28 14:19:32 by tlmiller: Design: right now, absent ads are all "unexcused absences" -- the startd vanished without excusing itself. It would suffice to add "excused absences" to the absent list: as an option in the collector, force all invalidated ads to become absent. Additional elaboration could include recording the excuse status in the ad, and adding -excused and -unexecused flags to condor_status. This may be faster to get committed because it doesn't change the plugin API. 2013-Mar-01 16:16:44 by tlmiller: After further investigation and consultation with GregT and ToddT, the plan is as follows: (1) Turn the IGNORE_INVALIDATE knob, see if allowing invalidated ads to expire instead (eventually) generates the list that we (the BaTLab) are looking for. (2) If so, add an EXPIRE_INVALIDATED_ADS knob which, instead of deleting invalid ads, sets them to expire immediately. This code may be substantially similar to the HOUSEKEEPING_ON_INVALIDATE code. (It will need to set the LastHeardFrom attribute to something other than 0 (1?), because the collector engine treats those ads as invalidated, and doesn't call the offline code's expire() function for them.) Work for another ticket: (3) Have the EXPIRE_INVALIDATED_ADS code add an attribute (AbsentReason?) to the ad saying that the ad was invalidated. This will help users write their ABSENT_REQUIREMENTS expressions when we implement 'condor_off -reason' or similar. (4) Likewise, the expire() function should set the AbsentReason (?) to 'expired' if there isn't one already. 2013-Mar-08 10:53:22 by tlmiller: (1) Turning the IGNORE_INVALIDATE knob causes condor_off'd startds to become absent, as desired. (kill -9'd startds become absent as well.) 2013-Mar-08 15:47:17 by tlmiller: The attached patch implements the EXPIRE_INVALIDATED_ADS knob. However, since it's composed mostly of cargo-cult programming, I'd like it reviewed before committing, instead of after. :) In particular, CollectorEngine::expire() is a mix of CollectorEngine::remove() and code from cleanHashTable(). 2013-Apr-09 16:52:38 by gthain: CODE REVIEW Looks good to me -- a few comments would be handy here. I had to look up that offline_plugin::expire returning "true" meant 'keep the ad'.

title: Ticket #127: condor.boot.generic init script will kill wrong condor_master
description: /src/condor_examples/condor.boot.generic will kill (with QUIT) the wrong condor_master. This script just uses ps|grep to find any process with "condor_master" in its name (or anywhere else in the ps output) and kill -QUIT's the lot of them. If there are more than one copy of Condor running, this will kill all of them. So, for example, if a user is running a personal Condor, and the admin runs "condor stop" in preparation for an change, the user's personal Condor also goes away. VDT users are actually hitting this case. An admin will "/etc/init.d/condor stop" while working on the "main" Condor install, and in the process kill off unrelated Condor installs installed by the VDT. /src/condor_examples/condor.init doesn't have this problem, and generally works better. Unfortunately it relies on Linux LSBisms (and perhaps Red-Hatisms). Possible improvements: Option 1: Warn users that condor.boot.generic is dangerous. Simple, but users will likely ignore it, install it as is, and get surprises if a second Condor instance even ends up on the machine. Option 2: Drop condor.boot.generic. If condor.init doesn't work for you, you have to work it out for yourself. Depending on how portable condor.init proves to be, this may be Good Enough. Option 3: Make condor.boot.generic safer. Possibly port condor.init to be more portable (will simply inlining the "functions" file be good enough?) Possibly set CONDOR_CONFIG (default to empty) and use condor_off -master? (While imperfect, since Condor may not have shut down by the time the script exists, the current condor.boot.generic suffers from this same bug. There is a risk is that ALLOW_ADMINISTRATOR won't allow localhost's root to issue this command, and so it will be silently ignored. condor.boot.generic's current implementation can't be ignored by the security layer.) No matter what we do, we'll have users using the old scripts, so it may be worth publicizing that better options are available. The release notes are an obvious location. VDT ticket 4328 tracks this from the VDT's point of view. To do This is a todo list for condor.boot.2.generic (attached) If stop() times out, it might try harsher (kill -KILL) measures. More fully comply with LSB comment guidelines If we can find the LSB /lib/lsb/init-functions we should use their functions. spec If we can find Red Hat's /etc/init.d/functions, we should use their functions (preferring the LSB ones if both are present) Review chkconfig defaults start() should wait "a bit" to confirm that `condor_pid` returns a PID. If more than "a bit" passes without it, report failure. status() should report more cases: pid file exists, but pid is gone. Known to not work on: Mac OS X: Condor apparently fails to drop a PID file? May be failing to start? HPUX: not investigated. When the test is committed, add a new ticket to factor out the log watching code into a proper Perl class and add it to be shared testing library for general use.

title: Ticket #1112: Fix mixed use of TARGET scope in expressions
description: We need to use the target attribute scope correctly for the switch to new ClassAds. All attributes in an expression that refer to the target ad need to have a 'target.' prefix. Currently, many don't. We will need to change expressions that Condor creates to use proper scoping. Condor daemons will need to correct expressions received from other (older) daemons and users to enforce proper scoping. Milestones Change behavior of EvalBool() Improve methods to add/remove target scoping in attribute references Enforce proper scoping in query constraints in the collector and its clients Enforce proper scoping in job constraints in the schedd and its clients Details In old ClassAds, attribute references in expressions with no scope (i.e. no 'target.' in front) are looked up in both the local scope and the target scope. In new ClassAds, they are only looked up in the local scope. If you want to refer to an attribute in the target scope, you must put 'Target.' in front. Due to old ClassAds' looser scoping rules, many expressions have attribute references to the target ad that don't have a 'target.' prefix. These won't work as-is with new ClassAds. Any expressions that Condor itself writes can be corrected to use target correctly. But expressions that come from a user or an older version of Condor need to be accepted as well. For these expressions arriving from the outside, we need functions that will correct them, adding or removing target scopes where appropriate. Some of this already exists, but we need more. EvalBool() The stand-alone EvalBool() function is odd, as it evaluates an expression in the context of a target scope, but no local scope. In most places where it's used, the opposite appears to be expected (local scope provided, but no target scope) and the expressions never have attributes with a target scope. It could be simplified to have no target scope, with an interim check that strips target scopes in the places where they do occur.

title: Ticket #5151: Exceptions are not recorded after hung shadow processes are killed
description: If the schedd kills a shadow because it was hung, you see the following error messages: 07/15/15 15:12:22 (pid:1363748) Shadow pid 1890816 successfully killed because it was hung. 07/15/15 15:12:22 (pid:1363748) Shadow pid 1890816 died with signal 4 (Illegal instruction) After this, the job stays in 'R' (I haven't figured out how long though). No shadow is restarted - I suppose the lease eventually times out? According to the code, the intent is to record a shadow exception and have the job exit. However, here's the relevant code: if ( daemonCore->Was_Not_Responding(pid) ) { <snip/> dprintf( D_ALWAYS, "%s pid %d successfully killed because it was hung.\n", name, pid ); status = JOB_EXCEPTION; } <snip/> if ( WIFEXITED(status) ) { <snip/> For POSIX, WIFEXITED looks at the upper 8 bits. Hence, WIFEXITED returns false and HTCondor interprets this a signal. jobExitCode is not invoked and the job stays running. I think we want to set: status = JOB_EXCEPTION << 8; This causes the job to exit and a shadow exception recorded. Further, I don't understand the intent of the WIFSIGNALED branch of the conditional. It seems to not update the job state. Don't have the time to poke at it right now. (I noticed this when a CMS schedd reported 7k jobs running but only 1k shadows. According to git blame, this bug was introduced by tannenba in 1999.)
remarks: 2015-Jul-15 14:42:00 by jfrey: I agree with the proposed change, but I can't replicate the behavior reported. If the schedd isn't in the middle of a shutdown, then the shadow exiting via a signal should result in the job going to idle status. When I tried replicating this situation by sending a SIGKILL to the shadow, the schedd marked the job idle and attempted to reuse the claim to start a new job. That failed because the slot was still Claimed/Busy, so the schedd killed the claim. 2015-Jul-16 22:22:13 by bbockelm: I think you're right about jobs going back to running. Even after we disabled timeouts for shadows, we still see massive issues with the wrong number of running jobs. I think #5158 is to blame.

title: Ticket #7479: MAX_PROCD_LOG does not honor units suffix
description: the MAX_PROC_LOG config knob ignores a units suffix (such as Mb) which can lead to the effective size of the ProcdLog being quite small. This in turn can lead to the procd rotating it's log on every message. The problem here is that the procd actually gets its log filename and size from command line arguments, and the code that is constructing those arguments is doing the param() calls, but not interpreting the results correctly. There should also be a hard-coded floor in the procd so that very small values for the log file size should be rounded up to something more reasonable, maybe 64K?

title: Ticket #7880: condor_chirp on windows aborts in c-rutime after successful command
description: G-Research reports that when they upgraded to 8.8.9, condor_chirp on Windows began to exit with status -1073740791 which is STATUS_STACK_BUFFER_OVERRUN, even when the command was successful. In attempting to reproduce the problem, I discovered that condor_chirp 8.8.7, 8.8.9 and 8.9.9 would all exit with an error status (but a different one) in the c-runtime process teardown code while trying to close open files. This does not seem to be because anything in condor_chirp changes, but rather because Microsoft changed the c-runtime to automatically call _fcloseall() after main exits. condor_chirp has always done something that is technically illegal - it calls fdopen twice against the same fd. This results in an error when the second FILE* is closed because the first one closed the underlying file. On Linux error is quitely ignored, and on Windows it was as well for many years, but a recenty it began to cause an abort instead. We believe that a recent update of Windows is what changed. If we fix the underlying bug - the incorrect re-use of an fd, the abort no longer happens.

title: Ticket #6792: Allow modification of CEDAR timeouts in python bindings
description: ATLAS is using the python bindings to query their schedds. These queries occasionally time out, likely due to heavy load on the schedd. They would like a way to increase the timeout for these query operations from within the python bindings. Currently, the best way to modify the timeouts is to set TIMEOUT_MULTIPLIER in the config file.
remarks: 2018-Oct-17 13:46:48 by jfrey: The timeouts can be lengthened from within python by setting TIMEOUT_MULTIPLIER via the environment. This code snippet will double all of the network timeouts in subsequent Condor calls: os.environ["_condor_TIMEOUT_MULTIPLIER"] = 2 htcondor.reload_config()
creator: jfrey

title: Ticket #6546: Investigate custom machine resource monitor behavior in edge cases
description: We need to find out what happens to custom machine resource monitors (specifically, the contents of the startd's extra ads) when HTCondor is reconfigured. We should document the behavior as soon as possible; we can decide later what to do if the behavior is undesirable. We also need to verify that a continuous cron job which crashes and restarts is not handled differently than a periodic cron job (that is, its "extra" ads are maintained). We also need to test that usage reporting functions properly when claims are reused. We may also or alternatively need to test that starting a job on a slot with large Uptime* value(s) works properly.
creator: tlmiller

title: Ticket #2856: add pow function to ClassAds
description: ClassAds needs to have a pow function so that we can use it in an expression when defining the 'cost' of carving off more than 1 cpu from a partitionable slot. At some point in the near future we will also want to be able to quantize request_memory etc before we use the value to carve off a dynamic slot.
remarks: 2012-Mar-07 10:59:30 by jfrey: My comments on the code: pow(): Why add 0.5 to the result in the integer case before casting? In the integer case, you cast one int argument to double, but not the other. We have unintuitive behavior where pow(2, 3) returns an integer, but pow("2", "3") returns a real. Probably not worth worrying about. We try to catch division by zero and make the result Error. For pow(), we're not catching results that are infinity or NaN. Should we? quantize(): I think it's ok to return Error if elements in the list can't be converted to reals. Inconsistency: quantize(0.5,1) evaluates to a real, but quantize(0.5,{1}) evaluates to an integer.
derived_tickets: #3967 ClassAd quantize() can fail when in a cached expression

title: Ticket #5690: systemd socket activation causes host-based security grief
description: When HTCondor is "using passed TCP socket from systemd," and CONDOR_HOST is set to $(FULL_HOSTNAME), then 'use security : host_based' will cause condor_reconfig (and condor_off, etc) to fail, saying something like ERROR SECMAN:2010:Received "DENIED" from server for user unauthenticated@unmapped using no authentication method, which may imply host-based security. Our address was '::1', and server's address was '::1'. Check your ALLOW settings and IP protocols. This error message is expected, in one sense, because $(FULL_HOSTNAME) almost never resolves to the IPv6 loopback address; and unexpected the other sense, because why is the client connecting from that address to that address. I speculate that this has to do with some combination of only getting a single socket from systemd -- on a mixed-mode system HTCondor would normally have one for each protocol version -- and systemd binding the same socket simultaneously to IPv6 and IPv4 (probably all interfaces as well). This may cause weird code problems, although I haven't investigated. (Having one socket is generally OK, but potentially unexpected in mixed mode; having a socket which doesn't have a well-defined protocol may be a little upsetting; and I'm not sure how we'd handle accept()ing on the same socket and getting different protocol sockets back, which is how I expect this randomness (is supposed to) works.) Additionally, there may be a serious meta-problem where the socket (and listening address(es) handed to us from systemd is (and is/are) completely independent of HTCondor's configuration. For instance, it's possible to configure HTCondor to listen to one address and systemd to another. I assume things would break horribly, but I'm not sure of precisely how. It seems reasonable to at least investigate how hard it would be to determine what address(es) and protocol(s) our shared port socket is actually listening to and compare that to its configured/expected value(s). It seems like this should be investigated, even if we decide to solve the problem with an alternate approach (e.g., a magic 'self' identifier or config variable and/or cleverness dealing advertising for local vs remote clients*, versus advertising a GUID so the client can make that decision). * : If the AddressV2 stuff were available, we could just advertise the loopback addresses as a private network. We'd need to name the private network with some globally-unique identifier; it could be a GUID or maybe the global address of the daemon in question (if available). IIRC, our preference sorting checks for private networks first already; we may need additional tweaking to prefer this type of private network.
creator: tlmiller

title: Ticket #6815: Pslot preemption with non-fungible custom resources crashes the startd
description: Pslot preemption doesn't work with non-fungible custom resources. That is, custom resources that have distinct identities, like GPUs. This is because the startd assigns the resources to a new dslot before the preempted slots are completely deallocated, and you can't share between two jobs. But the negotiator will happily make a pslot preemption match in this situation, and the startd will EXCEPT() at claim time. The negotiator and startd should be patched to refuse pslot preemption involving non-fungible custom resources.
remarks: 2018-Nov-05 15:41:06 by jfrey: You can use PREEMPTION _REQUIREMENTS to prevent the negotiator from making matches that will crash the startd. For example, you can do the following for GPUs: PREEMPTION_REQUIREMENTS = RequestGPUs =?= Undefined || GPUs =?= Undefined

title: Ticket #2440: HGQ improperly handling partitionable slots
description: The HGQ quota assignment does not properly account for partitionable slots with multiple cpus. When accept-surplus is disabled, it will result in slot starvation, as the quota will count a partitionable slot once instead of how many cpus it has available. From Jon Thomas: GROUP_NAMES = a, b GROUP_QUOTA_DYNAMIC_a = 0.5 GROUP_QUOTA_DYNAMIC_b = 0.5 Simple case: NUM_CPUS = 4 SLOT_TYPE_1 = cpus=2 SLOT_TYPE_1_PARTITIONABLE = TRUE NUM_SLOTS_TYPE_1 = 2 Submit jobs to a. Users in will not use more than one slot. Seems to hit in other configs too: NUM_CPUS = 20 SLOT_TYPE_1 = cpus=2 SLOT_TYPE_1_PARTITIONABLE = TRUE NUM_SLOTS_TYPE_1 = 10 Will only use 9 slots NUM_CPUS = 20 SLOT_TYPE_1 = cpus=4 SLOT_TYPE_1_PARTITIONABLE = TRUE NUM_SLOTS_TYPE_1 = 5 Will only use 4 slots.
remarks: 2011-Sep-03 13:44:34 by eje: repro/test: Using the following configuration, with both regular and partitionable slots: NEGOTIATOR_DEBUG = D_FULLDEBUG SCHEDD_INTERVAL = 15 NEGOTIATOR_USE_SLOT_WEIGHTS = FALSE GROUP_QUOTA_MAX_ALLOCATION_ROUNDS = 1 GROUP_NAMES = a, b GROUP_QUOTA_DYNAMIC_a = 0.5 GROUP_QUOTA_DYNAMIC_b = 0.5 GROUP_ACCEPT_SURPLUS = FALSE NUM_CPUS = 22 SLOT_TYPE_1 = cpus=4 SLOT_TYPE_1_PARTITIONABLE = TRUE NUM_SLOTS_TYPE_1 = 5 SLOT_TYPE_2 = cpus=1 SLOT_TYPE_2_PARTITIONABLE = FALSE NUM_SLOTS_TYPE_2 = 2 The unused slot profile should look like this: $ svhist Machine _SlotType_ State Activity Cpus 5 rorschach.localdomain | P | Unclaimed | Idle | 4 2 rorschach.localdomain | X | Unclaimed | Idle | 1 7 total submit 12 jobs to group "a". The group should be allowed to run 11 jobs: universe = vanilla cmd = /bin/sleep args = 1800 should_transfer_files = if_needed when_to_transfer_output = on_exit +AccountingGroup="a.user" queue 12 Submit the above jsub file, and let several negotiator cycles pass. Before fix: the slots provided by partitionable slots are not properly accounted for, and slots are starved. "a" is only allowed to run 6 jobs, instead of its quota of 11: $ qvhist AccountingGroup JobStatus 6 a.user | 1 6 a.user | 2 12 total After the fix, group "a" quota is filled, and 11 jobs are allowed to run: $ qvhist AccountingGroup JobStatus 1 a.user | 1 11 a.user | 2 12 total Here is an additional test variation for the fixed version that exercises the code path for GROUP_DYNAMIC_MACH_CONSTRAINT / NEGOTIATOR_SLOT_POOLSIZE_CONSTRAINT This configuration adds 42 slots, which will be ignored by the HGQ algorithms and by the job submission: NEGOTIATOR_DEBUG = D_FULLDEBUG SCHEDD_INTERVAL = 15 NEGOTIATOR_USE_SLOT_WEIGHTS = FALSE GROUP_QUOTA_MAX_ALLOCATION_ROUNDS = 1 GROUP_NAMES = a, b GROUP_QUOTA_DYNAMIC_a = 0.5 GROUP_QUOTA_DYNAMIC_b = 0.5 GROUP_ACCEPT_SURPLUS = FALSE NUM_CPUS = 22+42 SLOT_TYPE_1 = cpus=4 SLOT_TYPE_1_PARTITIONABLE = TRUE NUM_SLOTS_TYPE_1 = 5 SLOT_TYPE_2 = cpus=1 SLOT_TYPE_2_PARTITIONABLE = FALSE NUM_SLOTS_TYPE_2 = 2 # I intend this slot's quota to be ignored by # GROUP_DYNAMIC_MACH_CONSTRAINT / NEGOTIATOR_SLOT_POOLSIZE_CONSTRAINT SLOT_TYPE_3 = cpus=42 SLOT_TYPE_3_PARTITIONABLE = TRUE NUM_SLOTS_TYPE_3 = 1 # ignore slots of type 3 for quota counting GROUP_DYNAMIC_MACH_CONSTRAINT = (Cpus < 42) This version of the job also ignores the 42-cpu slot, so it does not get partitioned: universe = vanilla cmd = /bin/sleep args = 1800 should_transfer_files = if_needed when_to_transfer_output = on_exit requirements = (Cpus < 42) +AccountingGroup="a.user" queue 12 Because the 42-cpu slot is ignored both by the HGQ algorithms and the job, we should see that group "a" is still allowed to run 11 jobs, as before: $ condor_submit t.jsub Submitting job(s)............ 12 job(s) submitted to cluster 1. $ qvhist AccountingGroup JobStatus 1 a.user | 1 11 a.user | 2 12 total 2011-Sep-23 17:38:26 by danb: Code review: This patch conflicts quite a bit with a patch TJ recently committed on the master branch: #2277. You might have beaten him to the punch if I hadn't taken so long to review. Sorry! The basic idea looks okay to me, though one wonders if it would be better to just simplify the negotiator by always using slot weights. --Dan 2011-Sep-23 18:10:04 by eje: For this particular situation, I don't think slot weights would work quite the right way, since in the case of partitionable slots you want a job to be able to peel off a single slot, and not worry about paying for a weight tagged to # of cpus. I think we want partitionable slots to be "weighted" on the resource side (summing up available resources for allocation) but not on the consumption side (paying for weight when negotiating). (I expected this might be a race condition with #2277, regardless)
attachments: gt2440-part-slot-usage.patch 5098 bytes added by eje on 2011-Sep-03 15:55:55 UTC. Patch to allow HGQ quota assignment to correctly account for the effective number of slots provided by partitionable slots. This patch is against V7_6-branch, will probably require manual merge against master.

title: Ticket #6403: Rehaul of the openmpiscript and related scripts
description: A number of issues have been brought up with using the openmpiscript to run Open MPI jobs in the parallel universe: 1. Environment variables are not passed to the user's executable. When condor_ssh connects to a slot's sshd and sets up the worker process to run the executable, few-to-no environment variables are passed. This can be a problem for, e.g., OpenMP-OpenMPI hybrid jobs that need OMP_NUM_THREADS defined. We should probably pass as many vars as possible? 2. The number of CPUs is not included in the contact file. mpirun and/or the user's executable could make use of that information. 3. Using the proc number may not be the best way of distinguishing condor slot ids to "trick" mpirun in to sending a unique SSH command to every slot. 4. There may be better ways of finding open ports for the SSHDs to run on.
remarks: 2017-Oct-05 15:16:52 by jpatton: [52496] and [52497] address (1) and (2) above directly, and (4) indirectly. 1. The big change in this version of openmpiscript is the use of two new helper scripts, get_orted_cmd.sh and orted_launcher.sh, to remove the need of using ssh and sshds to set up the execute nodes. The former script gets the orted command that would normally be sent via ssh to the execute node and chirps it the spool directory. The latter script fetches the command from spool and runs it directly under the starter rather than under a sshd. Thus the environment is preserved for the user's executable. 2. request_cpus is now handled in the hostfile where appropriate (i.e. when not using OpenMP to do threading). If the use of OpenMP is desired, there's a boolean option in openmpiscript. Also, options are set to no longer allow Open MPI to bind to cores; no binding is permitted (so long as the relevant MCA variable is not changed in the script). This does mean a small performance reduction in the best case (no accidental oversubscription of the first n cores) but prevents huge performance problems in the worse case (oversubscription...). 4. No longer need ports to run sshd. Ports are still needed for communication between the orted processes. As for (3), by prevent binding to cpu cores, I believe the user's problem that brought (3) to light is solved. We still use "fake" hostnames based on the node id number, but the correct number of slots are accounted for now in the hostfile.

title: Ticket #4594: Fix time-slicing for ClassAd iterator
description: We took a shortcut in the ClassAd iterator implementation when it comes to time slicing. The query protocol returns to DC whenever there is blocking on the network socket when writing out a matching ad. However, if we are iterating through the ClassAd log and there are no matching ads, we periodically need to return to DC to prevent the query from significantly blocking the schedd. To "periodically" return, we simply return once every 1000 non-matching ads. This isn't a great metric - could be quite disjoint from actual wall clock time. In the example of a very busy schedd with a million jobs, this means we would return to DC (and hence wait to get rescheduled) 1000 times We should switch to actually timing things - spending a fixed amount of time in rejecting ads.

title: Ticket #1846: FileTransfer::CommitFiles is not fault tolerant
description: If there is a crash or filesystem error in the middle of FileTransfer::CommitFiles(), the job's spool can get into an inconsistent state that is not detected by Condor on restart. If it is a job that uses the spool as a checkpoint, the job could rerun with some files as they were prior to the failed commit and some as they were in the failed commit. This commit happens in a tight loop, uninterrupted by communication or copying of data, so the window of vulnerability is small. In #1844 I had to make some changes to CommitFiles() to support replacement of non-empty directories within the sandbox. In order to do this, a third directory (swap) was introduced where files/directories to be replaced are moved. This "swap" directory could be used to implement rollback in case of an aborted commit. Some additional bookkeeping would be needed to clean up new files added during the failed commit.
remarks: 2011-Jan-10 12:25:28 by danb: Wait, I was wrong! When CommitFiles() is interrupted, the operation is completed on the next run attempt before uploading files to the starter. Condor is perfect.

title: Ticket #7091: Shadow EXCEPTs too readily
description: The shadow calls EXCEPT() or ASSERT() in a lot of common error conditions that aren't programmer errors and frequently are not fatal. When ABORT_ON_EXCEPTION is set to True, this can lead to a lot of unnecessary core files. The shadow should be made more resilient to common failures. When such failures are non-recoverable, the shadow should have a less drastic way to notify the schedd. Here are some failures we've observed recently in CHTC: Starter failed to contact the transfer queue manager (i.e. schedd). Starter began output transfer while input transfer was active (main cause fixed in #6728) RPC connection closed when sending a reply. Starter timed out because shadow was blocked connecting to schedd.

title: Ticket #2293: param system can't specify default-over-null
description: Some param settings must be non-null; if they are null then the code simply uses the default. It is not possible to represent this clearly at the moment and it leads to default values being in the code multiple times, creating a possibility for drift. For example, this is a summary of actual code. It has been abridged. /src/condor_utils/param_info.in [PRIORITY_HALFLIFE] default=86400 Accountant::Initialize in /src/condor_negotiator.V6/Accountant.cpp HalfLifePeriod=86400; tmp = param("PRIORITY_HALFLIFE"); if(tmp) { HalfLifePeriod=(float)atof(tmp); free(tmp); } Note that 86400 appears twice and must stay in sync to behave correctly in all cases. If you omit the logic in Accountant.cpp, if the user puts PRIORITY_HALFLIFE= in their configuration file, the PRIORITY_HALFLIFE ends up going un-set. This is a reasonably common situation, and the param system should be improved to better handle it. Proposed: Add default_overrides_null=true as a valid setting in param_info.in. If present and true, and if the parameter is set to empty in the configuration file, the default value is returned. (Having an empty default and default_overrides_null=true is nonsensical and should probably be a compile error.)

title: Ticket #6680: late materialization itemdata should be spooled
description: When submitting late materialization jobs, itemdata from the QUEUE statement should be sent to the schedd and stored in the SPOOL directory beside the spooled submit digest. a new RPC will be added to the SCHEDD qmgr. SendMaterializeData which will accept a cluster id and a stream of lines of data. The RPC can only be called during submission (after NewCluster is called) and the cluster id must be the one returned by NewCluster The schedd will write the stream of materialize data into a file at $(SPOOL)/$(Cluster)%10000/condor_submit.$(Cluster).items It will also store the materialization data into a pending job factory in anticipation of getting a SendJobFactory RPC and then a cluster ad. This RPC will then return the full path name to the spooled itemdata so that the client can include that filename in the submit digest that it sends using a subsequent SentJobFactory RPC The spooled materialize data file will be used when the Schedd is restarted. In order to future-proof the file format, and to support submit from python bindings. The materialization itemdata will support using the 0x1F character as a field separator as an optional alternate to the current space and/or comma field separator used by the current submit file parser. When the queue statement indicates that there are multiple fields, the itemdata splitter will check for the 0x1F chararacter, and if it finds one, then it will split only on the 0x1F character. If not, then it will split on space and/or comma as it does now. It is recommended (but not required) that clients using the SendMaterializationData RPC use 0x1f as the field separator.

title: Ticket #1903: Temporarily larger JobLeaseDuration
description: JobLeaseDuration defaults to 20 minutes, which is a reasonable default for brief, unexpected outages. But it's not long enough for a longer outage, especially a planned one. "We're doing a major rewiring, and the network will be down for the day," or "We're doing a major hardware upgrade on the submit machine" type outages. A administrator could benefit from the ability to say, "Temporarily extend all JobLeaseDurations to X hours from now." At now + X, the old JobLeaseDurations reassert themselves. Notably, running jobs would also need to respect the updated duration, something not currently done, (see ticket #1904). Strawman proposal: add JobLeaseNoEarlierThan, which is a timestamp (set to now +X). In the various locations where either side is considering the JobLeaseDuration, if the current time < JobLeaseNoEarlierThan, then the lease is considered still valid Another strawman proposal: JobLeaseIsValid, which defaults to: JobLeaseIsValid = ((LastJobLeaseRenewal + JobLeaseDuration) > CurrentTime) || JobLeaseNoEarlierThan > CurrentTime JobLeaseNoEarlierThan = 0 On the up side this is more flexible and potentially allows very clever policies ("The lease is 20 minutes, except it's 60 minutes between midnight and 1 AM when nightly maintenance takes place.") On the down side, it becomes very possible to write a policy so that the schedd and startd will come up with different answers, potentially leaving a job "running" when the startd drops it, or having a job return to idle while the startd is still running it (violating the "once at a time" promise). Credit to psilord for mentioned that it should be an expression.
creator: adesmet

title: Ticket #3894: condor_config_val -dump should work remotely
description: Add to daemon core the ability to query the names of all configuration knobs, and add to condor_config_val the ability to use that to provide the functionality of condor_config_val -<daemon> [-dump|-verbose] where <daemon> is master, startd, etc. Current daemons already support the DC_CONFIG_VAL function, but only condor_who uses it - condor_config_val does not. This gives us the oppotunity to extend the behavior of DC_CONFIG_VAL so support more complex queries by using characters not allowed in param names. And to return more than a single string result back. The DC_CONFIG_VAL command will be extended to look for ? in the first character position of the input argument. If it exists, what follows will be a command rather than a parameter name. Initially, the supported commands will be ?names[:<regex>] - return all of the param names. Optionally return all of the names that match the given regex. Additionally, the normal DC_CONFIG_VAL query, which passes a single param name, will now return multiple strings in the following order. HTCondor daemons prior to 8.1.2 will return only the first line, so clients of the DC_CONFIG_VAL command must be prepared to deal with getting back either 1 string or an arbitrary number of strings - future versions of daemon core may return more additional strings after <default-value> <expanded-value> <name> = <raw-value> (like the line would appear in the config file) <source>[, line <lineno>] <default-value> where <source> can be a filename, or <Detected>, <Default>, <Environment>, <Over>, or <Internal>. condor_config_val will be enhanced to make use of the expanded return values of DC_CONFIG_VAL and of the new ?names query to add support for -dump and and -verbose modes for remote queries.

title: Ticket #2786: Race condition in parallel universe can cause job to hang unstarted
description: When the dedicated scheduler spawns a parallel job, it has a set of matches it wants to give the shadow. After the shadow starts, it makes a daemon core call to the schedd, running a DC command to get the matches. If, for some reason, one of the planned claims is released after the schedd makes it's decision and before the shadow asks for the claim, the shadow will block forever, as it will get a subset of the number of claims, and it will wait, trying to get the last ones.

title: Ticket #7584: libcondor_utils has RPATH set instead of RUNPATH
description: Some cmake changes made for 8.9.5 ([58207], no associated ticket) accidentally changed the libcondor_utils shared library to have RPATH set instead of RUNPATH. This changes the search path for libraries that are dlopen()d by libcondor_utils. The search path for libraries at process start time is determined by the executable, which still has RUNPATH. Commit [58207] attempted to set linker flag --enable-new-dtags (which sets RUNPATH instead of RPATH) globally, but it only does it for executables, and not for shared libraries. It should set CMAKE_SHARED_LINKER_FLAGS in addition to CMAKE_EXE_LINKER_FLAGS. The old code set the linker flag via target_link_libraries() for libclassad as well as most executables. This method adds the given flags to the link line of the target and all of its dependencies. Thus, libcondor_utils picked it up because it depends on libclassad. This caused a problem for some CMS submit machines, where LD_LIBRARY_PATH is used to point to an alternate version of the OpenSSL libraries from cvmfs for their condor_dagman processes. At startup time, condor_submit (run by dagman) loads libcrypto from cvmfs (LD_LIBRARY_PATH overrides condor_submit's RUNPATH). Later, when it needs to read a GSI proxy, it dlopen()s libssl from /lib64 (using libcondor_util's RPATH, which precedes LD_LIBRARY_PATH). The two libraries are from slightly different versions and the dlopen() fails. This causes condor_submit to fail, as it can't interpret the proxy file.
remarks: 2020-Apr-07 21:33:18 by jfrey: The change from RUNPATH to RPATH also affects the python bindings libraries. Any dlopen() calls they do will be similarly affected.

title: Ticket #7793: Group mapping in the negotiator
description: When flocking into a pool, the accounting group configuration of the schedd may not line up with the accounting group setup at the remote pool. This is because the schedd's group configurations are in the local pools "namespace" whereas the flocked-to pool has a distinct namespace. We should provide the ability for the flocked-to negotatior to "map" from the incoming namespace to the local one (the ACCOUNTING_DOMAIN). The ACCOUNTING_DOMAIN, defaulting to UID_DOMAIN, peels off another bit of the functionality of UID_DOMAIN - leaving the latter more focused on OS-level identities (especially after the rework of the User/Owner attributes). I propose using the mapfile mechanism to provide a group prefix for the remote schedd. That is, suppose the submitter has the accounting principle of bbockelm@example.com flocking to the pool chtc.wisc.edu. Then, if you have a group mapfile with the following entry: * example.com remote_group The submitter will then be mapped to remote_group.bbockelm@chtc.wisc.edu by the remote pool's negotiator. title: Ticket #6881: User Job Log Improvements
description: part (a): reduce clutter / length by removing the useless image size update events. (Continue to send and receive them, just don't write them to the log.) part (b): replace "your job's usage looks sane after start-up" functionality with a starter-side event that dumps the *Usage values from the job ad after five minutes (or maybe the second update from the starter). part (c): keep #6854, but consider eliding whichever transfer event's timing is redundant (with job start and with job end, presumambly).
remarks: 2019-Jan-27 18:23:30 by tlmiller: Based on Friday's team meeting, it sounds like there's some interest in making the user job log more useful; people seemed to like the idea of the file transfer events. People seemed broadly in favor of removing the image size updates themselves, but weren't sure about the proposed replacement, or what to do about the secondary "liveness" function of the image size updates. Regarding the more philosophical questions, I guess the distinguishing feature of the user job log is that can and does provide more information about the history of a job than its ad does. Certain questions about the current state of the job may be better answered by improving condor_q, but some current-state information may be useful to provide in the log for provide debugging context (under the assumption that nobody looks at the log unless something has gone wrong). There is or was a secondary function regarding a non-polling alternative for job status updates, but I think that's been entirely superceded by the DAGMan event log. 2019-Jan-27 18:33:06 by tlmiller: As ToddT observed, it may no longer be necessary for the log to be a formal log any longer. For example, using zero- or space- filled fields in a periodic (notice of liveness -style) event would reserve space for us to update the event (atomically, or at least in a single write) when the new event comes in, rather than clutter the log with new events. Certain diagnostic or historic data could also be stored directly by the shadow in a directly usable format (e.g., storing *Usage attributes over time in an RRD). 2019-Jan-27 21:03:48 by karpel: Two thoughts: HTMap is using the event log as a non-polling job status tracker (and also one that doesn't depend on being able to talk to the daemons), but could presumably be switched to use DAGMan and its event log internally. On image size events: perhaps a reasonable criteria would be to only write them to the event log if they're larger than the previously-largest image size event recorded? This is the information many people (and admins) actually care about. (That information is also in terminated events, but if I remember correctly there's some problem with being able to pull it out of them programatically.) 2019-Jan-29 14:01:22 by tlmiller: ToddT also asked why or if the user event log still needed to be a formal log; one idea that sparked in my mind was the possibility of writing a bunch of extra zeros or spaces in the usage/image size event and then just updating the information in-place. That could be bad if it included the event time-stamp; maybe it makes more sense to add another event-internal field that's the last-update time-stamp. (You could also only update the event if it's the last one in the log, but that won't have the desired effect in multi-job logs. I guess each writer could only update an event if there had been no intervening event?) 2020-Apr-10 07:46:13 by tim: Bulk change of target version from v080906 to v080907 using ticket-target-mover.

title: Ticket #5254: bad permissions on config files cause master to kill itself on reconfi
description: If /etc/condor/config.d contains a configuration file that is not readable by the condor user, then the master starts up normally, but a reconfig will cause it to exit without a log message or killing its daemons. Looks like the master is acting as root when it reads the config files on initial startup, but is acting as the condor user when doing a reconfig. This inconsistency can keep admins from discovering the error in their config files in the first place. The master prints the error message to stderr instead of logging it, and exits without shutting down any of its children. These should probably both be fixed. The logging is most important to me, though I think that from an admin's point of view, the ideal behavior is that if a reconfig fails due to broken files (or any other reason), that Condor should keep running with the old config. I have no idea how feasible that is with the Condor codebase.

title: Ticket #7269: support an explicit list of checkpoint files
description: Duncan M wrote: As I see it, an ideal outcome would be something like this: should_transfer_files = YES when_to_transfer_files = ON_SUCCESS transfer_input_files = infile1.txt, infile2.txt transfer_output_files = outfile1.txt, outfile2.txt checkpoint_files = checkpoint.dat (plus the current +SuccessCheckpointExitCode etc options to perform self-checkpointing) Here checkpoint.dat is sent between the sandbox/spool as needed to follow the job around if it gets evicted (IF IT EXISTS - if it doesn't exist when the job gets evicted, that should not present an error, maybe a warning would be good, for debugging). Note that if I (the user) want to have the checkpoint as part of the output files I can (and should) specify it in transfer_output_files (as now). Also, it would be great to have condor keep track of those elements of transfer_output_files that happen to exist when a job is evicted, and have those transferred to/from spool so that they exist in the sandbox of the restarted job. This means that if a job creates a file, then gets evicted and restarted in a new sandbox, the file is moved into that new sandbox so that it doesn't have to be regenerated again (which in general it wouldn't if the job restarts from a checkpoint) and transfer_output_files is complete when the job finally exits (successfully).
remarks: 2019-Sep-18 13:51:02 by pfc: This is related to #7270. 2019-Sep-18 15:28:09 by tlmiller: So to summarize: If checkpoint_files is specified, it's a list of optional (not existing is not an error) files to transfer whenever we do any file transfer other than the 'final' transfer. This does not interact in any way with when_to_transfer_output = ON_SUCCESS, which governs the behavior of only the 'final' file transfer. This use of 'final' hopefully coincides with the existing flag in the file transfer object, but for this specification means "when the job exited of its own accord and that exit did not indicate a successful checkpoint". HTCondor should always act as if checkpoint_files included $(transfer_output_files). 2019-Sep-25 14:40:04 by pfc: Bumping to priority 2 since Josh Willis informed me that this is effectively blocking lalinference from using Condor file i/o. 2020-Apr-10 07:46:37 by tim: Bulk change of target version from v080906 to v080907 using ticket-target-mover.

title: Ticket #4916: Implement "submit many" interface in python bindings
description: The "submit" interface for the python bindings is not entirely equivalent to condor_submit. It only allows you to set one classad per cluster (note the transaction interface does allow you to at least submit multiple clusters in a single connection). This is the equivalent of only allowing one "queue N" statement in the submit file. We should provide an interface that is equivalent to having an arbitrary number of "queue N" statements in the python bindings. I'm thinking: int submitMany(ClassAd cluster_ad, list proc_ads, bool spool, list ad_results) - ClassAd cluster_ad: The base ad for the entire cluster. All jobs inherit from this base ad. - param proc_ads: A list of 2-tuples. The tuples have the format (proc_ad, count). This will result in "count" jobs being submitted, inheriting from the proc_ad and cluster_ad. - param spool: Boolean specifying whether the jobs will be spooled. - param ad_results: A list object; the resulting job ads will be appended to this list. - return value: The cluster ID.

title: Ticket #3380: Foolproof mechanism for JobRouter routes
description: Right now, the HTCondor-CE job routes are defined in the configuration file using a simple, declarative language. This allows us to evaluate, set, and delete attributes from the source ad when creating the destination ad. There are a few problems: Some things are impossible to do in this framework. For example, OSG puts all its environment variables in an external file; this file is read by Globus and the proper variables are inserted into the ClassAd. It's not possible to do this in a JobRoute - you can't do IO or loops with classads. Hence, we need to make the job router hooks plausible for a normal sysadmin to use. There is no mechanism to test or validate job routes. Everyone, including me, who has worked with HTCondor-CE has lost a few hours of time due to a misplaced ";" or using "#" as a comment character in the new-classad. Job hooks exist for the transform, but it's nearly impossible to write them well. Most admins will be tempted to write a shell script. ClassAd parsing rules are pretty complex, especially when it comes to quoting. I suspect writing a compliant classad parser is well outside a normal admin's skillset. To fix this, I propose two improvements: Building a python wrapper library for libclassad. This will allow admins to safely parse and manipulate ClassAds in a job hook. Build a job route tester and validator. It should, given the on-disk configuration Validate the job routes can be parsed Given a job classad, show which routes would match. Does not need to analyze why routes do not match; we don't need a "condor_router_q -analyze" at this point. Given a job classad and a router, print the resulting classad.

title: Ticket #1217: race condition in MAX_JOBS_RUNNING accounting
description: On the CMS CE at Fermilab, it was observed that the schedd kept saying that it was preempting jobs due to a change in MAX_JOBS_RUNNING, even though this configuration variable was only ever increased, never decreased. Below is a typical sequence of events in the logs (grepping for MAX_JOBS_RUNNING and matched). 02/15 13:02:36 Reached MAX_JOBS_RUNNING: no more can run, 8 jobs matched, 10 jobs idle 02/15 13:02:36 Out of servers - 8 jobs matched, 10 jobs idle, 0 jobs rejected 02/15 13:02:37 Reached MAX_JOBS_RUNNING: no more can run, 8 jobs matched, 443 jobs idle 02/15 13:02:37 Out of servers - 8 jobs matched, 383 jobs idle, 0 jobs rejected 02/15 13:02:42 Reached MAX_JOBS_RUNNING: no more can run, 8 jobs matched, 59 jobs idle 02/15 13:02:42 Out of servers - 8 jobs matched, 41 jobs idle, 0 jobs rejected 02/15 13:02:44 Preempting 1 jobs due to MAX_JOBS_RUNNING change 02/15 13:02:50 Preempting 2 jobs due to MAX_JOBS_RUNNING change I believe the problem is that we do not count matches that are in limbo (waiting for the startd to respond) when computing how much of MAX_JOBS_RUNNING is used up: // figure out the number of active shadows. we do this by // adding the number of existing shadows + the number of shadows // queued up to run in the future. CurNumActiveShadows = numShadows + RunnableJobQueue.Length(); The longer matches stay in limbo, the more likely this race condition is to strike. This can be a very long time if the startd does not quickly preempt its existing job (e.g. if MaxJobRetirementTime is being used or if the KILL expression allows jobs to take a long time to do a graceful shutdown). If this theory is correct, then this appears to be a very old bug. The code fragment above dates back to 2002 if not earlier. There are two ways to fix this problem: Add num_pending_startd_contacts and startdContactQueue.Length() to CurNumActiveShadows. Get rid of CurNumActiveShadows and use matches->getNumElements() instead. I prefer the second option, because it is more direct. This same technique should be used in the preemption code so that the two are in sync. (Currently, the preemption code uses a slightly different formula and is not always consistent with the formula used during negotiation.) This method would prevent us from falling into the same race condition on the other end if we ever add the ability to hold onto an idle match for a short time after a job finishes (no shadow, no job in the runnable queue, but we probably shouldn't try to get more resources when the sum of busy and idle matches that we already have adds up to MAX_JOB_RUNNING). It should be noted that the second option would change the behavior of MAX_JOBS_RUNNING to only apply to jobs with matches. Currently, it also applies to local and scheduler jobs. Therefore, in the stable series, it seems that we should go with the first option. In the developer series, stronger medicine should be considered. See #642 for other ideas.

title: Ticket #4015: Bad work fetch jobs leave slot in Claimed/Idle state
description: If the starter fails to start a work fetch job and exits, the slot remains in Claimed/Idle state. It should return to Unclaimed/Idle. One easy way to trigger this condition is to have an invalid executable. This happens with both static and partitionable slots.
remarks: 2013-Oct-31 14:21:30 by jfrey: It turns out after a work fetch job completes or fails to start, the slot remains in Claimed/Idle until the next UPDATE_INTERVAL, when the startd runs the fetch hook again to see if there's another job. If there isn't, the slot returns to Unclaimed. If the starter fails to start the job, the Job Exit hook is still called, but there are no exit status or runtime attributes. The startd could be made to run the Fetch Work hook immediately after the starter exits. But that could create a rapid black hole for misconfigured work fetch jobs.

title: Ticket #4500: Condor-C should distinguish auth failure from dead machine
description: Currently, the C-GAHP doesn't make any distinction between different failures in connecting to the remote schedd. Thus, the gridmanager marks the remote machine as being down on any failure. If the failure is due to authentication or authorization, it should instead put the job on hold with an appropriate error message. When the C-GAHP calls ConnectQ(), it should provide a CondorError object, and examine that object if ConnectQ() returns failure. If the CondorError object indicates a security problem, the C-GAHP should indicate that in the message returned to the gridmanager, which can then put the job on hold.

title: Ticket #4150: Failure to transfer files larger than 4GB on 32bit platforms, Windows
description: On 32bit platforms and ALL Windows platforms (since we always use a 32bit compiler on Windows to build), the shadow would stop the file transfer prematurely at the point when there was less than a multiple of 4 GB remaining to transfer on a file larger than 4 GB. I was able to reproduce an incident report on htcondor-users on Windows. The issue was a coding bug involving the overflow of a 32bit integer. Here is the offending line: nrd = ::read(fd, buf, (size_t)(bytes_to_send-total) < sizeof(buf) ? bytes_to_send-total : sizeof(buf)); Note: type size_t is a 32bit integer on 32bit platforms, and "bytes_to_send" and "total" (total bytes already sent) are 64bit integers. The third parameter to read() is the number of bytes to read. Essentially this line just reads X bytes from the file, where X is either the size of the buffer or the number of bytes left to read in the file, whichever is smaller. The above code meant to cast the result of the conditional expression to a size_t, but instead due to order of operator precedence, it is just casting the subtraction sub-expression. This can result in an overflow, resulting in the code passing 0 as the number of bytes to read, resulting in read() returning zero, which is interpreted as end-of-file and thus the transfer stops. Inserting a couple ()'s fixes the problem. Here is the fixed line: nrd = ::read(fd, buf, (size_t)((bytes_to_send-total) < sizeof(buf) ? bytes_to_send-total : sizeof(buf)));

title: Ticket #3695: Accounting Group with accept_surplus = false can go above quota
description: We are able to reproducibly configure HTCondor accounting groups to go above their configured quota. The description at a high level: We have two child groups, and want to limit the sum of their allocation to a fixed value, but are willing to let the usage for the individual groups float from zero to the sum. To implement this, we set accept_surplus = true for the children, and false for their parent, and assign a fixed quota to the parent. If there is infinite demand for one child group and zero for the other in the first negotiation cycle, the first group will correctly be assigned the sum. However, if demand then springs up in the next cycle for the other child group, the system, ignorant of usage, assigns the full static quota (with no surplus) to the group with no usage, and the sum allocated to the two groups exceeds the parent's quota. To reproduce NUM_CPUS = 100 MEMORY = 8192 GROUP_NAMES = group_atlas_analysis, group_atlas_analysis.long, group_atlas_analysis.short GROUP_QUOTA_group_atlas_analysis = 80 GROUP_QUOTA_group_atlas_analysis.short = 40 GROUP_QUOTA_group_atlas_analysis.long = 40 GROUP_ACCEPT_SURPLUS_group_atlas_analysis = false GROUP_ACCEPT_SURPLUS_group_atlas_analysis = false GROUP_ACCEPT_SURPLUS_group_atlas_analysis.long = true GROUP_ACCEPT_SURPLUS_group_atlas_analysis.short = true GROUP_AUTOREGROUP = false GROUP_ACCEPT_SURPLUS = false NEGOTIATOR_ALLOW_QUOTA_OVERSUBSCRIPTION = false # long.submit universe = vanilla executable = /bin/sleep arguments = 3600 output = o error = e notification = never log = log +AccountingGroup = "group_atlas_analysis.long.longUser" queue 100 # short.submit $ cat short.submi3 universe = vanilla executable = /bin/sleep arguments = 3600 output = o error = e notification = never log = log #copy_to_spool = true +AccountingGroup = "group_atlas_analysis.short.shortUser" queue 100 $ condor_submit long.submit Submitting job(s).................................................................................................... 100 job(s) submitted to cluster 436. # note that after submitting 100 jobs in the first group, 80 are running, as expected, # using the quota of 40 for the group, and borrowing the surplus 40 from the other group. # But, capped at the 80 of my parent group. $ condor_userprio Last Priority Update: 6/11 11:05 Group Config Use Effective Priority Res Total User Name Quota Surplus Priority Factor In Use --------------------------------------- --------- ------- ------------ --------- ------ ------------ group_atlas_analysis.short 40.00 ByQuota 1.00 0 shortUser@chevre.cs.wisc.edu 3.77 1.00 0 group_atlas_analysis.long 40.00 ByQuota 1.00 80 longUser@chevre.cs.wisc.edu 5.68 1.00 80 $ condor_submit short.submit Submitting job(s).................................................................................................... 100 job(s) submitted to cluster 437. # However, here, although my parent group has a quota of 80, and accept_surplus is false for the parent, the sum of the two children is above the quota. $ condor_userprio Last Priority Update: 6/11 11:08 Group Config Use Effective Priority Res Total User Name Quota Surplus Priority Factor In Use --------------------------------------- --------- ------- ------------ --------- ------ ------------ group_atlas_analysis.short 40.00 ByQuota 1.00 20 shortUser@chevre.cs.wisc.edu 3.76 1.00 20 group_atlas_analysis.long 40.00 ByQuota 1.00 80 longUser@chevre.cs.wisc.edu 5.76 1.00 80
remarks: 2013-Jun-17 15:47:26 by eje: From email discussion, for posterity: OK, I see what's happening. The surplus logic is working properly -- that is, no surplus is awarded to anybody on the 2nd cycle. Here's the state of play coming into the 2nd cycle: 06/12/13 10:54:53 group quotas: group= <none> cquota= 0 static= 0 accept= 1 quota= 20 req= 0 usage= 0 06/12/13 10:54:53 group quotas: group= group_atlas_analysis cquota= 80 static= 1 accept= 0 quota= 0 req= 0 usage= 0 06/12/13 10:54:53 group quotas: group= group_atlas_analysis.long cquota= 40 static= 1 accept= 1 quota= 40 req= 180 usage= 80 06/12/13 10:54:53 group quotas: group= group_atlas_analysis.short cquota= 40 static= 1 accept= 1 quota= 40 req= 100 usage= 0 "group_atlas_analysis.long" is using the 80 it was given from last round, since at that point it was able to accept the surplus from "group_atlas_analysis.short". Note, now both ".long" and ".short" are requesting more than their quota. So, here we can see that the outcome was that both ".long" and ".short" were allocated up to their quota of 40: ("allocated= 40"). Note, this logic is not designed to penalize any group if it currently has more than its quota. 06/12/13 10:54:53 group quotas: group= <none> quota= 20 requested= 0 allocated= 0 unallocated= 0 06/12/13 10:54:53 group quotas: group= group_atlas_analysis quota= 0 requested= 0 allocated= 0 unallocated= 0 06/12/13 10:54:53 group quotas: group= group_atlas_analysis.long quota= 40 requested= 180 allocated= 40 unallocated= 140 06/12/13 10:54:53 group quotas: group= group_atlas_analysis.short quota= 40 requested= 100 allocated= 40 unallocated= 60 Also note: ".long" does not negotiate this round, because it does skip negotiation for groups whose current usage is >= their allocation: 06/12/13 10:54:55 Group group_atlas_analysis.long - sortkey= 2 06/12/13 10:54:55 Group group_atlas_analysis.long - skipping, at or over quota (usage=80) Now, the pertinent bit: ".short" was allocated its quota of 40. There are 20 unused slots laying around, and so it negotiates and manages to get those 20. If there had been other groups contending, recall that this is currently dealt with by the group-negotiation sorting order, which defaults to a starvation metric, so the most-starved groups always get first shot at negotiation. In this case, that was only ".short" > Once this specific fire is put out, seems like we really need a list of > common HGQ usage scenarios, and for each scenario a configuration > example and a regression test.... So, I think this all touches on the semantics of (a) what factors "should" be taken into account during resource allocations, and (b) what does it mean to be a child group. I recall Steve Timm once said that his intuition about group hierarchy was that if a parent group's quota was "Q", then it "should" mean that child groups are constrained to never use more than Q groups, total. That is not the currently implemented semantic. Implementing such a semantic would require a new kind of logic, where a group's current usage is also checked against rolled-up totals for its parents, on up to root, prior to being allowed to negotiate for a next resource. 2013-Jun-18 11:07:26 by jrt: This is a regression. The children groups should not go outside of the parent's quota. Not sure where it was introduced, however condor-7.8.8-0.4.1.el6.x86_64 (which does have some additional patches in it) does not show the issue, but 7.9.1 does. Also, with 7.9.1 dynamic quotas seem to work as designed with the parent bounding the children. So this seems to be specific to handling of static quotas. 2013-Jun-18 11:12:46 by gthain: Note there's a race condition here -- if demand for both groups exist at one negotiation cycle, the parent's quota is honored. If the new demand shows up in the second, then the quota is exceeded. 2013-Jun-18 12:43:47 by jrt: 7.8.8 and 7.9.1 still test good as in my previous comment even separating submission across different cycles. 2013-Jun-21 18:07:25 by eje: REVIEW of patches: I think Jon's patch does the right thing in terms of examining "allocated" values in a way that is compatible with both static and dynamic quotas (our customers will want this to work with dynamic quotas). Greg's patch examines parents up the stack, which I think is the right thing for cases where a group's immediate parent doesn't have surplus disabled, but some other ancestor does. Recomputing the usages each round seems good, although with large hierarchies it might have a measurable cost. 2013-Jun-22 14:52:43 by eje: Another question about proposed semantics: both patches seem to only enforce a maximum for groups where accept-surplus is disabled. One possible interpretation is that all groups enforce maximums, and if a group happens to accept surplus, then that surplus correspondingly increases the maximum. In the code, this would actually be simpler. It would amount to removing the check for accept_surplus in the logic. 2013-Jun-24 09:40:30 by gthain: s/enabled/disabled/ in the previous remark? 2013-Jun-24 14:25:39 by jrt: The other way to do it is integrate it in the fairshare routines so there is no low level accept_surplus check in negotiationTime. NegotiationTime remains unchanged and sum of allocated values for children never exceeds parent quota - subtree usage. Any unused slots are handled out in RR fashion, so each starved group gets a shot at some of the remaining. Both patches simply limit. Conceivably, the first group could get the bulk of slots, a second group a limited number, and a third group none. This would be a more complicated patch and I think would probably require at least one additional recursive tree walk, maybe two. For Greg's patch, I think calculate_subtree_usage can be eliminated and instead get usage in fairshare as I did in the patch I attached. Also, it looks like the check for static_quota should be removed because it does repro with dynamic quotas too. 2013-Jun-24 16:07:53 by eje: to elaborate on my comment above, suppose you have: # hierarchy four deep GROUP_NAMES = a, a.b, a.b.c, a.b.c.d # only "a.b" has surplus disabled GROUP_ACCEPT_SURPLUS = true GROUP_ACCEPT_SURPLUS_a.b = false In the current patch, the child(ren) of "a.b.c" would not be restricted to "a.b.c"'s quota, because it has surplus enabled. However, whether or not surplus is enabled can be thought of as orthogonal to whether parent groups limit the sum of child (subtree) quotas. Put another way, the config var NEGOTIATOR_STRICT_ENFORCE_QUOTA could apply to all parent groups, not just ones with surplus disabled. With this semantic, "a.b.c.d" would be limited by its quota, but also "a.b.c", "a.b" and "a" -- the quotas of all parent groups would have to be respected. Tangentially, maybe something like NEGOTIATOR_ENFORCE_PARENT_QUOTAS as an alternative to NEGOTIATOR_STRICT_ENFORCE_QUOTA.

title: Ticket #2987: Hard links in sandbox cause privsep to fail, and job goes on hold
description: When the execute node is running in privsep mode, the privsep switchboard attempts to chown the sandbox back to the condor user after the job exits. When chowning files, the privsep code attempts to detect attempts to chown hard-links outside the sandbox by only chowning files with the correct source (i.e. "from") uid. However, if the job has hardlinked two filenames together in the sandbox, the privsep switchboard will only correctly chown the first one. When it stats the second one, it will see that it has already been chown'd, and thus is owned by the target uid. In this case, it exits with an error, and the job goes on hold. It should be safe to detect that the target file is already owned by the target uid, and skip this chown.

title: Ticket #7286: the condor_config_val -write:upgrade option needs a better name
description: The best way get a quick look at the configuration of a machine is condor_config_val -write:upgrade. This operation shows ONLY the knobs that differ from the defaults (it also has some special code to recognize old defaults) it was intended as a way to make an 'effective config' after an upgrade - i.e. to delete knobs that have the same value as the new default. But in practice it's also a very good way to get an overview of the configuration of a machine you are not familiar with. In this role, the option really needs a better name - and also it should probably print a few additional bits of information, such as the condor_version. The new option will be called condor_config_val -summary And it will behave like condor_config_val -write:upgrade - . Writing the effective config to stdout and prefixing it with the condor_version of condor_config_val. In support of this, we will also add the option condor_config_val -root-config <file> which will specify that the root config file should be <file>, rather than looking in the usual places for the root config.

Ticket #6244: Build python bindings for MacOSX
description: Tony Tiradani would really like to use the python bindings in the MacOSX tarball. Python Versions Our cmake scripts currently require that the versions of the python library and interpreter match exactly. Otherwise, we disable the python bindings when building. On our MacOSX build machines, the versions that come with the OS are slightly different (2.7.6 library and 2.7.10 interpreter). If we don't set PythonInterp_FIND_VERSION_EXACT in cmake, then the PythonInterp module will accept an older library and newer interpreter (as long they're still the same major version). We should allow this looser matching of versions. Our build machines also have an older version of python under /usr/local/bin, which comes earlier in the PATH. We're planning to remove that copy, so that /usr/bin/python is used. Plugins The build fails on the python collector plugin, because CollectorPlugin::CollectorPlugin and CollectorPlugin::~CollectorPlugin can't be resolved at link time. These class methods are defined in CollectorPluginManager.cpp, which ends up in a library named libcollectorlib.a. This library isn't distributed, and is only used to link the condor_collector executable. One solution is to move the definitions of these methods into the class declaration in CollectorPlugin.h. The same may need to be done for other plugin types. Library Paths In MacOSX, shared libraries contain the path where they can be found at runtime. This can be an absolute path or a path relative to the executable loading the library. This can be set at link time with the -install_name flag. When an executable or shared library is linked, the install_names of the shared libraries it depends on are saved in the new executable/library. These values are used at runtime to find the libraries. Additional search locations for libraries can be provided at runtime via the DYLD_LIBRARY_PATH environment variable. A library's install_name and the install_names of dependent libraries can be queried with otool -L. These values can be modified in existing executables and libraries with install_name_tool. When building HTCondor executables and libraries, we include cmake rules to rewrite the dependent library install_names to be relative paths appropriate for the file layout in the tarball. In the NMI build scripts, we set DYLD_LIBRARY_PATH so that we can run the executables, including unit tests, without having to assemble everything with make install first. This setup breaks with the python unit tests. The python interpreter in /usr/bin is covered by SIP, which protects OS programs from potential malicious abuse. This includes removing DYLD_LIBRARY_PATH from the environment. Thus, the python bindings can't find their libraries. Running a shell script that runs a binary in the build tree would similarly fail (unless the script itself set DYLD_LIBRARY_PATH). The best fix for this (for both NMI and interactive builds) is to change how we set library install_names. For executables and libraries residing in the build tree, the library install_names should be the full paths to the library files. During the install step, the executable and library files in release_dir should be rewritten so that the library install_names have the appropriate relative paths.

title: Ticket #4783: Add stats for job reconnects after schedd restart
description: We'd like to have statistics on how the schedd recovers from a restart, specifically how many jobs it's able to reconnect with. The following schedd statistics will be added: JobsRestartReconnectsFailed (job count) JobsRestartReconnectsLeaseExpired (job count) JobsRestartReconnectsSucceeded (job count) JobsRestartReconnectsAttempting (job count) JobsRestartReconnectsInterrupted (job count) JobsRestartReconnectsBadput (accumulated time) At startup, the schedd initializes JobsRestartReconnectsAttempting to the number of shadows it will start in reconnect mode, initializes JobsRestartReconnectsLeaseExpired to the number of jobs it won't create reconnect shadows for because the job lease has already expired, initializes JobsRestartReconnectsBadput to the current run time of jobs counted in JobsRestartReconnectsLeaseExpired, and initializes the other stats to zero. The shadow_rec struct has a new bool member named reconnect_succeeded, which is initialized to false. If the shadow is born with the -reconnect argument and exits because it cannot reconnect to the job (either because the lease expired or the startd/starter refused it), it should use the new exit code JOB_RECONNECT_FAILED instead of JOB_SHOULD_REQUEUE. Note that if the shadow successfully reconnects and then subsequently fails to reconnect if disconnected in the future, it should still exit with JOB_SHOULD_REQUEUE. When a shadow exits with the new shadow exit code JOB_RECONNECT_FAILED, the schedd decrements JobsRestartReconnectsAttempting, increments JobsRestartReconnectsFailed, and increases JobsRestartReconnectsBadput by the current run time of the job. For all other purposes, JOB_RECONNECT_FAILED should be treated like JOB_SHOULD_REQUEUE. When a shadow updates the job attribute NumJobReconnects (and increases the value), if the shadow_rec has is_reconnect==true and reconnect_succeeded==false, the schedd decrements JobsRestartReconnectsAttempting and increments JobsRestartReconnectsSucceeded and sets reconnect_succeeded=true.
