title: Ticket #3046: create a condor_who tool.
description: add condor_who as a new tool for use by glide-in hosts to find out what users and jobs are making use of the local machine. It is intended to run on an execute node and provide information on jobs running on that node. Ideally, condor_who would be able to return useful output even when the node that it is querying is running an earlier version of Condor. To facilitate this, the initial version of condor_who should be developed without any changes to code outside of the tool itself. It should be able to gather useful information from address files in the LOG directory and by scraping the log files themselves. It should also be able to directly interrogate STARTDs to get information from the Machine Ad, and then merge that with information from system calls and log files to produce a picture of running jobs. The output might look something like this OWNER SUBMIT-HOST SLOT PID RUNTIME MEMORY COMMAND johnkn submit1.chtc.wisc.edu 1 2345 2:00:00 20 Mb sleep 30 condor_who needs to know the command port of each STARTD or STARTER that it wants to talk to, in order to make this tool useful to administrators in glide-in scenarios, condor_who will accept a variety of command line arguments that tell it were to look for STARTD/STARTER addresses. -pid <pid> find the condor daemon that owns this PID -addr <addr:port> use the given addr:port to talk to the STARTD or STARTER -logdir <dir> look in address files in the given directory to find STARTD or STARTER Idea: In order for -pid option to be possible without a great deal of disk scanning, daemon core will be modified so that when an ephemeral port is used for the command port, the value of the port will be passed on the command line as an argument intended to be used by viewers of ps. --ephemeral_port=NNN Idea: If condor_who is running as root, it can correlate the output of lsof and ps to locate condor daemons and their listen ports, then query for machine and job ads. In phase 2, the MASTER, STARTD and STARTER can be ehanced to have new query commands for condor_who to use. The MASTER should be enhanced to return a list of daemons that is managing and which ones are currently running. For glide-ins It should also return an indication of who created the master, we can possible use DC_CONFIG_VAL for this. The STARTD and/or STARTER should be enhanced to provide more information about running jobs. In particular they should provide information from the ProcD about the job�s process family tree and resource usage.

title: Ticket #4629: Drmaa library breaks when SCHEDD_HOST is used
description: The HTCondor DRMAA library uses the hostname of the local machine in the job ids that it returns to the user. When these job ids are used subsequently, the library uses the hostname with the -name parameter of the HTCondor command line tools. The -name parameter is not used with condor_submit. For most configurations of HTCondor, this will work fine, as the local schedd's name is the machine's hostname. But if SCHEDD_HOST is set, then jobs will be submitted to the schedd named by SCHEDD_HOST, but condor_q and friends will attempt to talk to a different, possibly non-existent, schedd.

title: Ticket #6614: STARTD_RECOMPUTE_DISK_FREE ignored during dslot creation
description: the knob STARTD_RECOMPUTE_DISK_FREE is ignored during dslot creation, but honored during later updates. This has the effect of creating the dslot using a percentage that is derived from the pslot's c_total_disk (which hasn't updated since the startd started) and applied to the current disk free space at the time dslot is created. This can result in under-provisioning of the dslot DISK attribute, which then causes the job not to match. Todd Tannenbaum also pointed out that we should make sure that the initial value of Disk in the pslot should be set only after the startd has done its initial cleanup of the execute directory.

title: Ticket #5468: Have only one timestamp in the ULogEvent class
description: Right now we have two different timestamps in the ULogEvent class: time_t eventclock; struct tm eventTime; The really scary thing is that when a ULogEvent object is created by reading an event from a log, these two don't agree -- the eventTime is set according to the time in the log, but the eventclock is just the time at which the ULogEvent object was constructed(!). I can fix the immediate problem by also setting eventclock when we read an event; but I think we should only have one of these in the actual class, to avoid confusion and future problems like the current one.
remarks: fix for #6936 resolves this issue. it removes the eventTime field and makes the eventClock field the only timestamp in the event object.

title: Ticket #7005: Allow multiple jobs to share a GPU
description: We would like to be able to have multiple jobs sharing a GPU. This works today in a sort of hacky way, but there are issues. The total number of jobs that can share a GPU is set by configuration, but you would do this by post-processing the output of condor_gpu_discovery, or skipping the discovery step which is a bit ugly. There is no accounting of the GPU memory, and no way for a job to claim whole GPU, if the Startd is configured to allow say 2 jobs per GPU. Future versions of the CUDA runtime will require that processes that share a job all be owned by a single user, but there is no way to enforce this at present. Currently you can configure a GPU to be sharable between two jobs merely by declaring that there are 2 instance of the GPU with that name. For instance, this configuration configuration fragment MACHINE_RESOURCE_GPUs = CUDA0, CUDA1, CUDA0, CUDA1 ENVIRONMENT_FOR_AssignedGPUs = CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES ENVIRONMENT_VALUE_FOR_UnAssignedGPUs = 10000 Will result in the STARTD being willing to create up to 4 slots each of which has one of 2 GPUs assigned. Using the above configuration means that you don't get the extra attributes you get by using of using condor_gpu_discovery -extra. If you want to use condor_gpu_discovery, then you would need to wrap that program in a script that rewrites the DetectedGPUs attribute to duplicate all of the devices listed there. We could add an argument to condor_gpu_discovery telling it to over-report the GPUs it finds, to simplify the above configuration. But since the above configuration is a bit of hack, it seems like a bad idea to further entrench it. What we really need is a way to deal with the fact that not all GPUs are the same, and that they contain fungible resources like memory and cores within themselves. There needs to be a way to request only part of a GPU, and to have a specific GPU assigned to a slot, but only part of its internal resource set assigned to that slot. One way to do this would be to marry a collection of sub-resources to a single GPU resource. We might be able to get away with adding a constraint along with the request for a GPU, something like this.. submit fragment request_gpus = 1 request_gpus_constraint = ResourceAttr("Name") == "Tesla" && ResouceAttr("AvailableMemory") > 1000 The details of this syntax and it's capabilities would need to be worked out, it is unlikely that the exact syntax above would serve the purpose, but I hope that it gets the idea across. Or perhaps all we need to do is support requesting only a fraction of a GPU. like this submit fragment request_gpus = 0.5 If there is only one pool of GPU memory (i.e. multiple GPUs share a pool of GPU memory because they are on the same physical card), then we can probably just switch from allocting GPUs to allocating GPU memory. For instance this configuration: configuration fragment # at least one instance of CUDA0 per CPU (or less to allow a maximum of N simultaneous users) MACHINE_RESOURCE_GPUs = CUDA0 CUDA0 CUDA0 CUDA0 ENVIRONMENT_FOR_AssignedGPUs = CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES ENVIRONMENT_VALUE_FOR_UnAssignedGPUs = 10000 MACHINE_RESOURCE_GPUMemory = 4000 and this submit submit fragment request_gpus = 1 request_gpumemory = 1000 would be sufficient to allow up to 4 jobs to share a GPU, with each being allocated 1000 of the memory. A job could claim the whole GPU merely by having submit fragment request_gpumemory = TARGET.GPUMemory If it were not for the fact that the CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES environment variable needs to be set, there would be no need have the job request a GPU at all, the request for gpumemory would be sufficient.

title: Ticket #3800: Notice system shutdown and react appropriately.
description: In the context of an HTCondor startd running in a spot instance on Amazon, we have a (relatively) limited amount of time to shut down when outbid. Although proper configuration of the system shutdown scripts can extend this time to 120 seconds, we should start simple, and just make sure that the startd invalidates its ad as quickly as possible after we notice that the machine is shutting down. This is part of a larger effort to sort startd shut-down activities by priority, to that we make the best use of the time we have before the system shuts down. We could potentially detect shutdowns by polling /sbin/runlevel (or doing whatever it does) from the master. However, without configuring the system to stall during shutdown, this will have to be a relatively high-frequency poll (on the order of once a second). It's probably better just to check the runlevel once, when shutting down, and react appropriately. (This check may be performed in the initscript, as well.) It may be possible for the master to delay shutdown for some time by declining to die (catch SIGTERM); however, the system will probably SIGKILL the master 5 seconds after SIGTERMing it (if the HTCondor initscript does not). It may be possible to delay system shutdown in the initscript; I don't know if those usually have time-outs. (If they do, the highest-level script can be modified to block instead, which is what was done to empirically demonstrate the two-minute grace period.) It would also be nifty for the startd to invalidate its active claims on the way out the door.
remarks: 2014-Feb-18 15:07:45 by bbockelm: It'd be extremely useful if the startd could invalidate claims on its way out. I don't know about EC2, but "service condor restart" results in an unusable personal condor instance for about 20 minutes until reconnect timeouts pass.
creator: tlmiller

title: Ticket #2712: RFE: new dprintf() format-modifying flag to output flag info
description: A new format-modifying flag that instructs dprintf() to include the 'regular' flags (D_FULLDEBUG, D_MATCH, etc) as part of log output for grepping would be helpful for selecting subsets of log output using 'grep' or other tools. So, a new format flag to go with D_PID, D_FDS and friends: D_FLAGS. If D_FLAGS was set, then a line of log output might look like: 12/13/11 10:01:19 D_FULLDEBUG|D_ALWAYS Phase 1: Obtaining ads from collector ... One use case is suggested in #2711, for selecting parsable log output lines from the log stream using grep.

title: Ticket #2342: negotiator updates user priorities with one transaction per user
description: The CMS glidein pool negotiator is effectively broken because it takes so long to update user priorities in each negotiation cycle: 08/01/11 10:10:27 Phase 2: Performing accounting ... 08/01/11 10:48:08 Phase 3: Sorting submitter ads by priority ... The problem is that each user is updated in its own transaction and there are over 4k user records. Igor requested that we fix this in the stable series, if possible. The problem is so easy and safe to fix that I think we should do it in 7.6.3.
remarks: 2011-Aug-16 16:41:04 by danb: We found that there is an additional fsync-related performance problem, this time in Accountant::CheckMatches(). This took over an hour in a case where a large number of machines transitioned from claimed to unclaimed. I assert that AddMatch() and RemoveMatch() should commit "nondurable" transactions, meaning no fsync. This would solve the problem in CheckMatches() and it would also avoid any similar problem during matchmaking when large numbers of new matches are created. In the current model, the match records do not need to be durable, because in the event of a negotiator crash, any discrepancies between the match records and the advertised state of the startds will be corrected in CheckMatches() itself. I propose making this change for 7.6.3.

title: Ticket #6301: Add knob to prevent startd from recomputing free disk space periodical
description: The startd periodically computes the amount of free disk space. However, this is a problem for partitionable slots -- this represents the amount of free disk space, minus any reserved for dynamic slots. However, we don't keep track of how much space is reserved for all the dynamic slots. Moreover, the amount of disk space used on the execute partition could be used by the dynamic slot, or could be used external to condor. This causes all kinds of problems. To fix this, let's add a knob that assumes that the execute disk directory is on a partition that only has condor job on it. STARTD_RECOMPUTE_DISK_FREE, default to true, which is the existing behaviour.

title: Ticket #625: Rework how startd handles VM resources
description: The startd handles system resources for VM universe jobs like a poor man's dynamic slot partitioning. All slots advertise the total number of cpus and memory left for use by VM jobs on the machine. When a VM job is matched and starts executing, the cpu and memory totals advertised by all slots are decremented. The VM cpus and memory can be over-provisioned in a given negotiation cycle, as all slots advertise the total amounts available. This VM universe-specific behavior is confusing to users and unnecessary. The same effects can be obtained using slot-specific requirements and dynamic slot partitioning. The VM-specific cpu and memory totals should be eliminated and the standard per-slot allocations used. Each slot ad currently contains a list of all IPs and MACs for running VMs. Each slot should contain just the IP and MAC for the VM running on that slot.

title: Ticket #2196: Run same classad daemon hook (hawkeye/cron) once per slot
description: A user might want to run a classad daemon hook once per slot on a multi-slot startd. At the moment this requires copying the hook configuration repeatedly, once per slot. This is a nuisance, creates a possibility of the various copies accidentally diverging. For example, a user might be using classad daemon hooks to advertise the presence of GPUs. Each slot should only advertise a single single GPU, so slot 1 advertises GPU ID # 0, slot 2 GPU ID # 1 and so on. You can do this today (see HowToManageGpus), but it could be better. Proposal: Add "STARTD_CRON_<HOOK NAME>_SLOTS_INDIVIDUALLY" to the configuration. Boolean, defaults FALSE. If TRUE, the hook will be executed once for each slot available (or once for each slot named in "STARTD_CRON_<HOOK NAME>_SLOTS" if present). Each slot will advertise the output only for the instantiation associated with it. Of course, the hook will need to know which slot it is reporting for. Since hooks are highly Condor specific anyway, put the slot number in an environment variable named "SLOT_ID". Before This only works for machines with up to 4 GPUs. For machines with more, just keep copying, pasting, and editing. Be sure to not make any mistakes! STARTD_CRON_JOBLIST = $(STARTD_CRON_JOBLIST) GPUINFO1 STARTD_CRON_GPUINFO1_MODE = OneShot STARTD_CRON_GPUINFO1_RECONFIG_RERUN = FALSE STARTD_CRON_GPUINFO1_PREFIX = GPU_ STARTD_CRON_GPUINFO1_EXECUTABLE = $(MODULES)/get-gpu-info STARTD_CRON_GPUINFO1_ENV = SLOT_ID=0 STARTD_CRON_GPUINFO1_SLOTS = 1 STARTD_CRON_JOBLIST = $(STARTD_CRON_JOBLIST) GPUINFO2 STARTD_CRON_GPUINFO2_MODE = OneShot STARTD_CRON_GPUINFO2_RECONFIG_RERUN = FALSE STARTD_CRON_GPUINFO2_PREFIX = GPU_ STARTD_CRON_GPUINFO2_EXECUTABLE = $(MODULES)/get-gpu-info STARTD_CRON_GPUINFO2_ENV = SLOT_ID=1 STARTD_CRON_GPUINFO2_SLOTS = 2 STARTD_CRON_JOBLIST = $(STARTD_CRON_JOBLIST) GPUINFO3 STARTD_CRON_GPUINFO3_MODE = OneShot STARTD_CRON_GPUINFO3_RECONFIG_RERUN = FALSE STARTD_CRON_GPUINFO3_PREFIX = GPU_ STARTD_CRON_GPUINFO3_EXECUTABLE = $(MODULES)/get-gpu-info STARTD_CRON_GPUINFO3_ENV = SLOT_ID=2 STARTD_CRON_GPUINFO3_SLOTS = 3 STARTD_CRON_JOBLIST = $(STARTD_CRON_JOBLIST) GPUINFO4 STARTD_CRON_GPUINFO4_MODE = OneShot STARTD_CRON_GPUINFO4_RECONFIG_RERUN = FALSE STARTD_CRON_GPUINFO4_PREFIX = GPU_ STARTD_CRON_GPUINFO4_EXECUTABLE = $(MODULES)/get-gpu-info STARTD_CRON_GPUINFO4_ENV = SLOT_ID=3 STARTD_CRON_GPUINFO4_SLOTS = 4 After STARTD_CRON_JOBLIST = $(STARTD_CRON_JOBLIST) GPUINFO STARTD_CRON_GPUINFO_MODE = OneShot STARTD_CRON_GPUINFO_RECONFIG_RERUN = FALSE STARTD_CRON_GPUINFO_PREFIX = GPU_ STARTD_CRON_GPUINFO_EXECUTABLE = $(MODULES)/get-gpu-info STARTD_CRON_GPUINFO_SLOTS_INDIVIDUALLY = TRUE

title: Ticket #4941: Preserve time zone info in python bindings
description: ClassAd absTime() values include a time zone offset. Python datetime values can include timezone information. When converting between the two types, we should preserve the time zone information.
remarks: 2015-Mar-17 13:45:14 by jfrey: I've attached a patch that handles the time zone information in the Python->ClassAd value conversion. To do the same for ClassAd->Python conversions, we need to define a subclass of datetime.tzinfo that encapsulates the time zone offset. I don't know how to do that from within the C++ bindings. 2015-Mar-17 14:03:39 by jfrey: The Python module pytz provides subclasses of tzinfo for every hour offset from GMT. But that doesn't help if the offset isn't an even number of hours. Also, can we assume that pytz is available everywhere? The following Python code would do the trick, but can we define and then use a chunk of Python code from within the bindings library? class FixedOffset(tzinfo): """Fixed offset in minutes east from UTC.""" def __init__(self, offset, name): self.__offset = timedelta(minutes = offset) self.__name = name def utcoffset(self, dt): return self.__offset def tzname(self, dt): return self.__name def dst(self, dt): return timedelta(0) Or can we define and wrap a C++ class that implements all of the methods of tzinfo without being derived from it? 2015-Mar-17 14:24:20 by jfrey: The dateutil module includes the tzoffset class, which implements a fixed offset timezone with a granularity of seconds. Can we assume that will be available everywhere? 2015-Mar-17 14:34:06 by jfrey: It appears dateutil is not part of the base install for Red Hat 5, but is available.

title: Ticket #5716: if NEG_CONSIDER_PREEMPTION=false, ignore exhausted partitionable slot
description: CMS runs a very large pool with NEGOTIATOR_CONSIDER_PREEMPTION=false, and an increasing percentage of partitionable slots. In the steady-state cause, most of the partitionable slots will have exhausted their resources -- out of CPUs, Memory, or other attributes; having given them out to their child dynamic slots. These partitionable slots won't ever match anything, in the same way that Claimed slots can't match anything. However, unlike Claimed slots, the NEGOTIATOR_CONSIDER_PREEMPTION code doesn't remove them from future matching consideration. In the case with a full pool in steady state, the majority of Unclaimed slots might be these exhausted partitionable slots. We should add code to trim out these slots, to improve negotiator performance. We could test the impact of this by adding a (Cpus > 0) clause to NEGOTIATOR_SLOT_CONSTRAINT.

title: Ticket #4804: Managed condor_submit transforms
description: NOTE: This ticket abandoned as we ultimately implemented the functionality in #5885 instead We live with two kinds of wrappers in our lives: condor_submit wrappers: The sysadmin wants to set some sort of non-trivial transformation for the user's job (i.e. setting accounting_group to something that can't be done with SUBMIT_ATTRS). Executable wrapper: Think dmtcp_shim or parrot_run; these are put in front of the executable; typically, arguments are added, new environment variables are inserted, and additional files are transferred. These are ugly, but a common pattern. We should provide a built-in mechanism for transforms. We are considering two possibilities: one based upon the job router functionality, and a second that would introduce some simple schedd knobs. Option 1 - JobRouter based solution It turns out, HTCondor already has a transform mechanism for job ClassAds - job routes! I propose we use job routes (as currently configured -- although I want to make it less miserable to add new routes separately); the user can add a list of these to their submit files to apply the route to their job. For example: features = route1, route2, route3 where routeX is the name of the route. These are applied in order. Further: If the route's requirements expression evalautes to error, then the condor_submit fails. If the route requirement evaluates to false, then the route is not applied and the next one is considered. If the route requirement evaluates to true, the route is applied. The idea is that something like: features = DMTCP would do all the client transforms to submit the job with the dmtcp_shim. A configuration variable, DEFAULT_FEATURES, would specify the features to apply to all jobs by default. This would give sysadmins a mechanism for setting things like accounting_group. [Per usual, this only applies to condor_submit-based jobs; support for other clients. JobRouter or python bindings would have to come later.] Option 2 - Simple Schedd Knob solution The thinking here is we would have some simple schedd config knobs to handle common transformation situations, like "insert this attribute into every incoming ad". ON_SUBMIT_SET_XXX = ON_SUBMIT_SET_EVAL_XXX = ON_SUBMIT_SET_DEFAULT_XXX = ON_SUBMIT_SET_EVAL_DEFAULT_XXX = ON_SUBMIT_NOTREADY_STATE =
remarks: 2015-Feb-25 16:02:27 by bbockelm: We found another use case for this: The intensity frontier would like to prioritize resource provisioning. They have three classes of resources: Owned CPUs at FNAL Owned CPUs at select collaboration universities. The rest of OSG For FNAL CPUs, they'd like to provision glideins instantly; for university CPUs, they want to provision after the job has been in queue for 2 hours; for the rest of OSG, 4 hours. However, in order to implement this scheduling or provisioning policy, we need to take queue date into account; this currently has a second-level granularity and will basically break auto-clustering. Hence, we would like to be able to implement a submit feature which quantizes the QDate with an eval_set and copies it into a separate attribute. Hence, all jobs submitted during the same hour will possibly be in the same auto-cluster. We would not like to use attribute rounding for this feature as we don't want to change the QDate itself; it's used in too many places in HTCondor. 2015-Mar-04 16:06:39 by bbockelm: Another use case: CMS has group information in an external service (could be a flat file, could be a web service call). We would like to use this group information for provisioning and matchmaking information. Concretely, we want to be able to use the fact that user bbockelm is in group nebraska and send pilots to site Nebraska which will run only jobs in this group (assuming site Nebraska is interested in prioritizing this group). We could put a list of all users in the group in the glidein's start expression: START = $(START) && ((Owner=?="bbockelm") || (Owner=?= "joe") || ...) However, this would get tedious at a site like FNAL which may have >1,000 users in a given group. Instead, we would like the group information calculated at submit time; suppose we put this in an job attribute called GroupName. Then, the start expression would be: START = $(START) && (GroupName =?= "nebraska") This is scalable from the matchmaking and administrative POV. 2015-Apr-08 15:28:53 by bbockelm: Discussion from today's OSG/HTCondor call: This gets assigned to Jaime, but he's got a handful of other items in the priority queue. This needs to be moved from submit utilities into the schedd. Transform logic probably needs to be extracted from JobRouter and made stand-alone. 2016-Apr-13 13:58:51 by tpdownes: This is very similar to LIGO request #5613. I don't see LIGO presently having a large need for users to specify the transformation. I agree with the conclusion that integrating the logic into the scheedd makes more sense than adding extra "distance" between a .sub file and its corresponding ClassAd. I'd really like to see this make it in for 8.6 at least at the fairly simple level described in #5613. I am happy to do LIGO's transformation logic entirely in the Python bindings.

updates later but this appears to be a problem with condor registering itself as a OOM manager for jobs managed under the condor cgroup while memory.use_hierarchy is enabled. This restriction is lifted in kernels 3.16 and later. http://lkml.iu.edu/hypermail/linux/kernel/1404.2/00715.html http://kernelnewbies.org/Linux_3.16 Initial testing with a 3.16 backports kernel suggests the problem is resolved. Tom 2015-Nov-24 15:46:35 by tpdownes: The line that prints the error about subscribing should probably be changed to D_ALWAYS 2015-Nov-24 20:23:25 by tpdownes: These are the 2 issues. HTCondor fails to register itself as the OOM killer for HTCondor jobs when memory.use_hierarchy is enabled. The memory hierarchy is integral to putting a firm cap on RAM usage by all Condor jobs and reserving space for the OS and Condor itself. But I believe Condor still attempts to act the OOM killer and gets in the way of kernel OOM killer on rare occasions (the crash that forms the basis for the ticket) This failure is not properly logged (D_FULLDEBUG rather than D_ALWAYS) They are resolved by upgrading to a 3.16+ kernel as noted in previous remakers. Nevertheless, Condor needs to gracefully handle a failure to register itself as the OOM killer. 2016-Apr-27 14:08:19 by gthain: As per our phone call today, we're going to close this ticket, as LIGO hasn't seen this since a kernel upgrade.

title: Ticket #6090: mutability of StringList breaks history_helper, probably other things
description: LIGO reports crashes in condor_history_helper. Among other problems, this program crashes in the static object destructor for StringList. This is because the next method has been marked const, with the underlying List<char> it uses as mutable. StringList::next is certainly not conceptually const. Compiler optimization of const StringLists are free to elide repeated calls to next, which cause problems with duplicate frees.

title: Ticket #3292: condor_master crashes after reconfig with controller changes
description: When changing a daemon's configuration from non-controller to controller and issuing a reconfig, the daemons are started correctly. However, when reversing the process (going from controller to non-controller) setup the master crashes. This can be reproduced by setting: MAX_HAD_LOG=640000 MASTER_NEGOTIATOR_CONTROLLER=HAD HAD_LIST=$(IP_ADDRESS):$(HAD_PORT) DAEMON_LIST = MASTER HAD NEGOTIATOR STATE_FILE=$(SPOOL)/Accountantnew.log HAD_CONNECTION_TIMEOUT=2 HAD_PORT=51450 HAD_LOG=$(LOG)/HADLog HAD_ARGS=-p $(HAD_PORT) Start condor. Now edit the config by removing HAD from D_L: DAEMON_LIST = MASTER NEGOTIATOR Then issue a condor_reconfig.
remarks: 2012-Oct-25 17:52:16 by johnkn: Bulk change of target version from v070806 to v070807 using ./ticket-target-mover. 2012-Oct-29 14:25:51 by jfrey: CODE REVIEW The HA code in the master is completely unprepared for changes in what daemons are under HAD control after startup. This patch doesn't fix things completely. I'm not sure how much of an improvement it is, but it's no worse than before, with the exception of a controllee being added to a controller's list multiple times (mentioned below). It appears a daemon with a controller gets added to the controler's controllee list on every reconfig. There's no check on whether the daemon is already in the list, so it will be added multiple times. Once the list fills, RegisterControllee() will start to fail. The one place you call your new DeregisterDaemon() method is unnecessary. We know from the preceeding call that the daemon isn't in Daemons::daemon_ptr. To minimize lookups, I'd expect DeregisterDaemon() to either delete the daemon* that's being unregistered or return the pointer to the caller to handle cleanup. There's no code to remove a daemon from the controler's controllee list. If a controller and controllee are both removed from the list, I believe the object for the controllee is now leaked. 2012-Oct-30 16:01:56 by rrati: Code Review Updates: Daemons will now deregister from their controllers on a reconfig It's not possible for a controllee to register multiple times with a controller Removed DeregisterDaemon, it wasn't needed anymore I don't believe there is a memory leak in the case where the controller and controllee are both removed. There are 2 cases to this: The controllee is running. When they are both removed in this case, StopDaemon is called in main_config:956 because the daemon is no longer in DAEMON_LIST. StopDaemon will see the daemon running and mark it as ok to exit and be cleaned up. When the daemon exits, the DefaultReaper or AllReaper will delete the daemon. The controllee is not running. In this case, the StopDaemon is called like in case 1, but the daemon is seen as not running and is removed from the running daemon list (and deregistered from the controller) and deleted. 2012-Nov-07 13:50:48 by jfrey: Code Review In daemon::DeregisterControllee(), the compacting of the controllees list doesn't work properly if there's more than one controllee after the removed one in the list. It also doesn't work properly if there's a duplicate entry in the controllees list, though hopefully that wouldn't happen. In daemon::DeregisterControllee(), why use strncmp() instead of strcmp()? You'll get false matches if one controllee's name matches the start of another controllee's name. 2012-Nov-08 14:03:27 by jfrey: Code Review Scratch the comment about problems in daemon::DeregisterControllee() when there are multiple entries after the controllee being removed. I was misreading the code. 2012-Nov-28 14:55:57 by smoler: Minimum documentation of a version history item in the 7.8.7 manual is needed for this bug fix.

title: Ticket #4557: HTCondor-C should gracefully handle authentication issues
description: When a HTCondor-C submitter receives an authentication denied, the GAHP does not translate this appropriately to the gridmanager. We expect the job should go on hold with an appropriate message (similar to GRAM). Instead, the user gets a "Globus resource down"-style message and the job stays idle.
remarks: 2014-Oct-09 14:40:32 by jfrey: Detecting and handling authentication failures is easy to do. The CEDAR network layer can return an error string describing the methods attempted and why they failed. The same is not true for authorization failures. If the daemon doesn't like the authenticated user id, it just closes the connection. No explanation is given to the client. The daemon could have crashed or had some other internal error as far as the client can tell. title: Ticket #760: Gridmanager bottlenecks affecting BNL stress testing
description: The BNL ATLAS group has been conducting Condor-G stress tests with 10,000's of jobs submitted to one Condor-G machine at BNL destined for to 1-4 CEs at UW-Madison. This testing has turned up several scaling problems in the gridmanager daemon. This ticket summarizes the main problems. Sub-tickets will detail individual changes. #769 Jobs objects waiting for job ad changes to be pushed to schedd can wait extra long due to unrelated changes to job ad. #771 Job state evaluation sometimes called unnecessarily when job ad changes are pushed to the schedd. #772 A refreshed proxy file causes all related jobs to have their state evaluation called, often unnecessarily. #773 Check for GRID_MONITOR_NO_STATUS_TIMEOUT highly inefficient. #775 Simple optimizations to daemon-core timer code for 10,000s of timers that get reset frequently. The main problems stem from the gridmanager's extensive use of daemon-core timers as a form of callback. Each Job object has a timer registered for its state evaluation function. When other parts of the code detect events that may be of interest to a job, they reset the job's state evaluation timer to fire immediately. Most of the time, the job's timer is set to TIMER_NEVER (i.e. don't fire), although sometimes it's set to go off in the near future (to do a periodic probe of the remote job's status, for instance). Daemon-core keeps its timers in a linked list sorted by when they will fire next. This doesn't scale well when there are 10,000s of timers that get reset frequently. It's particularly bad when an event occurs that is of potential interest to all jobs, like a proxy file being refreshed. We have observed the gridmanager take 8 minutes to reset timers for 65,000 jobs to fire immediately. Floods of timer resets like this present an additional problem of delaying other events in the gridmanager. When 65,000 timers are reset to fire immediately, previously-registered timers that will fire in 2 seconds can be delayed by 10s of minutes. Examples of delayed timers we saw in our testing: Child Alive commands delayed more than 40 minutes, causing the schedd to kill the gridmanager, believing it to the hung. Gahp RESULTS commands that should occur every minute occurring every 20 minutes. Updates to the schedd that are scheduled for 5 seconds into the future delayed 15-20 minutes. When a schedd update or gahp command completes, a job waiting for that event doesn't have its state evaluation called for 20-30 minutes. Many times when a job's timer is reset to 0, its state evaluation function doesn't need to be called immediately, preceding events like Child Alives or schedd updates. Rather, the state evaluation needs to be called in the near future. We need a way to handle calling of jobs' state evaluation that is efficient and won't cause prolonged delays for other tasks in the gridmanager. We could add low-priority timers to daemon-core. This would minimize the changes required in the gridmanager. Or we could use a modified SelfDrainingQueue for job state evaluations. This would require potentially extensive changes in the gridmanager. There are a couple changes we can make short of re-architecting how the gridmanager uses timers. First, there are a couple places where a large number of job timers are reset unnecessarily. These are when a proxy is refreshed (insert ticket number) and when a grid monitor report arrives (insert ticket number). Also, there are a couple minor changes that can be made to daemon-core's timer code to optimize the gridmanager's use of it (insert ticket number).
remarks: 2009-Oct-10 10:04:47 by jfrey: After implementing the changes in #769, #771, #772, #773, and #775, the gridmanager can easily manage 35,000 jobs going to a single CE.

title: Ticket #2250: Feature Request: Fast start for DAGMan jobs.
description: Metronome uses DAGMan to watch each run's monitor. The monitor creates the run ID in the database. For ease of use, nmi_submit normally waits for the monitor to generate the run ID, and then prints it for the user. Most of that waiting time is not, however, for the monitor itself, but for DAGMan, primarily to ensure a unique process ID. I would like to shorten this wait. My initial thought was to "attach" DAGMan to a Condor job I've already submitted. This turns out not to work as easily as Kent suspected. One possibility would be some way to extract the condor_submit command-line(s) DAGMan would use to submit the jobs once it was ready. Then the user (Metronome, who knows that the jobs haven't been run yet, since it just created the .sub files) could submit them and run DAGMan in recovery mode. Another option would be to do the above, but internally to DAGMan -- that is, have some command-line option (--fast-start?) that would submit jobs before or while it was waiting for its unique process ID. Obviously, this carries the risk that two DAGMans will conflict, but perhaps in the fast-start case that would be OK, or DAGMan could check for the lockfile early and refuse to proceed if exists, regardless of its contents (or lack thereof, because it would touch it before it had its process ID in this mode).

title: Ticket #1885: optimize fetching of ads by negotiator from collector
description: Every negotiation cycle, the negotiator fetches all ads from the collector. For very large pools, this can take considerable time and chew up a lot of memory. Ads of any type other than startd, schedd, and submitter are fetched but not used for any purpose by the negotiator. When the negotiator is not considering preemption, the claimed ads are thrown away after getting the total count. The total count is used in the resource allocation algorithm. If there were a more efficient way for the negotiator to count the ads without actually fetching them, this process could be much more efficient.
remarks: 2011-Jan-28 16:53:14 by matt: One idea that has been discussed previously is turning the Negotiator into a Collector, make it a sink like a view collector. Check with eje for exact numbers, but the query phase during negotiation is very much non-trivial overhead. 2011-Jan-28 17:01:05 by matt: Or better yet, ask your own Negotiator - A quiet negotiator - $ condor_status -neg -l | grep Phase LastNegotiationCyclePhase1Duration0 = 0 LastNegotiationCyclePhase2Duration0 = 0 LastNegotiationCyclePhase3Duration0 = 0 LastNegotiationCyclePhase4Duration0 = 0 2012-Dec-10 10:01:19 by danb: Since the negotiator spends a lot of time in the matchmaking code and is thus not very responsive to network activity, I'd be worried about lots of ads getting dropped if it were trying to keep up with updates from a large pool. Anybody have evidence that this is not a problem? 2012-Dec-10 10:32:09 by sfiligoi: Making the Negotiator a Collector would not really save you much; all ClassAds are updated (on average) every 5 minutes. In my experience, one does not re-negotiator much more often than once every 5 mins, so the Negotiator would still process (close to) ALL the ads... And gathering the data would of course be worse; instead of a orderly query, it would have to process the updates in a highly chaotic bursts. 2012-Dec-10 14:18:59 by matt: @danb The negotiator is already partially async during the negotiation cycle. A direct melding of collector engine + negotiator would not work because the matchmaking code currently assumes an immutable set of machine ads. The melding would need to replicate that feature of the machine set, which can be achieved with parallel sets. Outside a cycle there is one set, setA, at the start of a cycle a second set, setB, is created and async populated as updates arrive, matchmaking can operate on setA, at the end of the cycle setB can be merged into setA. This is an operable step toward an even more async negotiator. Or a negotiator that maintains ads in a form already prepared for matchmaking, e.g. filtered, sorted and sig attr calculated. I am not aware of evidence that consuming updates is an expensive operation on the collector engine. Additionally, invalidating ads has an constant time implementation. Anecdotally observing "Query info" data, I postulate that the bulk of the collector engine's work is spent servicing queries and encoding classads. With Tim's ClassAd optimizations, that cost should be reduced. @sfiligoi Negotiation in most of our environments is a near continuous process, with only a 20 lag between cycles to let Match information to propagate. The cost of query + process dominates the cycle. Once a pool is at high utilization the negotiator only sees a small % of resources as available, with spikes associated with claim worklife expiration. However, each cycle the negotiator must gather and process the entire pools worth of machine ads. 2012-Dec-10 14:58:26 by danb: Presumably the two sets of machine ads that you propose would share memory with copy-on-write semantics. Perhaps the recent classad expression caching work would be enough? Without some sort of copy-on-write, I fear the memory allocation overhead could make things worse. If the negotiation cycle is quite long compared to the machine ad update interval, the classad sink overhead in the negotiator could be higher when directly receiving updates than the bulk query case. If it is acceptable to increase the update interval, then this effect could be controlled somewhat. However, state changes can trigger a new update at any time. If the negotiation cycle is short compared to the average update interval, the bulk query could be optimized to take advantage of that: "send me all ads that have been updated since time T". Since the negotiator probably doesn't care about a lot of the attributes in the ads, perhaps the forwarding mechanism would benefit from the same sort of attribute white-list as the query mechanism. 2012-Dec-11 14:46:57 by matt: @danb - Re CoW: Not having CoW would be no worse than what currently exists, which is Collector serializing entire contents of memory to the wire followed by the Negotiator deserializing the wire into memory. This commonly happens on a single machine. Re update rate: Yes, the real update rate (periodic plus edge triggered) will dictate the elbow in the performance curve. Re MODIFIED-SINCE queries: That sounds like a reasonable step, which keeps the collecting role in the Collector and allows for merging in the Negotiator. For long delays between cycles, it will tend to a full dump. A high real update rate will accelerate the tendency. I posit the delays are decreasing rather than increasing, both wrt claim eviction and MTTS for new jobs. Re query projection: The Negotiator does not know upfront what attributes are present in job Requirements & Rank and may miss w/ a projection. 2012-Dec-11 14:53:04 by sfiligoi: Re query projection: There are some use cases where the attributes used for the requirements are uniform in a Condor pool... e.g. the glidein pools CMS is using. So we should put in place autoclustering of machine ads, similarly to what is done in the schedd. Not sure where this should be done; maybe the Negotiator could just incrementally learn (with occasional re-query on wrong assumption). The other option, of course, is for the admin to tell the Negotiator to only look at the ones that are expected. Could be a short term solution, like it was for the schedd clustering. 2012-Dec-12 11:53:25 by danb: Regarding projection: the collector already expands the projection to include all dependencies. So if the negotiator asks for requirements and rank, it will also get all attributes referenced by those expressions. This sounds like a non-trivial amount of work per ad, but it's probably still a big win for over sending full ads to the negotiator.

title: Ticket #7402: Python bindings install doesn't see changes to CMAKE_INSTALL_PREFIX
description: The cmake code that installs the python bindings invokes setuptools by wrapping and running a command like: python setup.py install --root=${CMAKE_INSTALL_PREFIX} --install-lib=${C_PYTHONARCHLIB} --install-scripts=${C_BIN}. This command string is parsed and coded into the resulting Makefile when cmake is run. This means that changes to any of the cmake variables (e.g. ${CMAKE_INSTALL_PREFIX}) after running cmake are not seen by setup.py. Instead, we should "install" the scaffolding that setuptools generates to a well-known location at build time and then use cmake's normal install behavior to copy the scaffolding at install time, since the normal install behavior can understand changes to cmake variables.

title: Ticket #3011: large accountant logs cause very long negotiator reconfigs
description: There is a scaling problem with large accountant logs that can be seen when using reconfigs and also on startup. A 25MB log can require a 60 sec reconfig. This causes problems when trying to keep negotiation cycles short and the period between cycles stable. I've tracked this down to n^2 in Accountant::Initialize. The accountant reads the accountant log into a table. Accountant::Initialize runs through this table looking at all the CustomerRecords and creates a user list. Then it iterates through the user list and for each user calls Accountant::ReportState. Accountant::ReportState iterates through the table looking at every ResourceRecord to match the user.
remarks: 2012-Aug-21 13:32:47 by eje: REPRO: No special configuration is required except to enable D_ACCOUNTANT: NEGOTIATOR_DEBUG = D_FULLDEBUG | D_ACCOUNTANT The important thing is to generate a large accountant ClassAd log table, which can be done by starting up a pool, and using condor_setprio to generate entries in the accountant table: $ condor_master # create 5000 user entries in the accountant: $ time for j in {0..5000}; do condor_userprio -setprio user"$j"@localdomain 1.0; done > /dev/null real 7m18.727s user 1m20.221s sys 0m49.676s Next, stop the negotiator, then begin listening on the NegotiatorLog: $ condor_off -neg $ tail -f NegotiatorLog | grep -e 'Sanity check' -e 'NEGOTIATOR_POST_JOB_RANK' In another terminal, now re-start the negotiator using "condor_on -neg". Verify that sanity checking happens, and that it takes some measurable time (in my case, it was about 15 seconds, with 5000 user entries): $ tail -f NegotiatorLog | grep -e 'Sanity check' -e 'NEGOTIATOR_POST_JOB_RANK' 08/21/12 11:21:07 Sanity check on number of resources per user 08/21/12 11:21:22 NEGOTIATOR_POST_JOB_RANK = 0 Next, in the other terminal, invoke "condor_reconfig -neg" to reconfigure the negotiator. Back on the log output, verify that the sanity check happens again - this sanity check is redundant, since the negotiator has already started and checked its entries: 08/21/12 11:21:33 Sanity check on number of resources per user 08/21/12 11:21:47 NEGOTIATOR_POST_JOB_RANK = 0 2012-Aug-21 13:46:37 by eje: TEST: to test the fix, use the same procedure as the REPRO above. However, there should now be two differences. After invoking "condor_on -neg", the initial sanity check should be faster. In my case, I measured about 5 seconds instead of the original 15 seconds: $ tail -f NegotiatorLog | grep -e 'Sanity check' -e 'NEGOTIATOR_POST_JOB_RANK' 08/21/12 11:43:03 Sanity check on number of resources per user 08/21/12 11:43:08 NEGOTIATOR_POST_JOB_RANK = 0 After invoking "condor_reconfig -neg" to reconfigure, there should be no sanity check from the reconfiguration: 08/21/12 11:43:18 NEGOTIATOR_POST_JOB_RANK = 0 2012-Oct-22 14:59:14 by zmiller: Bulk change of target version from v070901 to v070902 using ./ticket-target-mover.

title: Ticket #6213: User tracing plugins for HTCondor-CE
description: OSG has been working to replace glexec (which provides both traceability and isolation); the first - and most difficult - part of this was to add singularity for isolation. However, FNAL has asked us to all improve on the traceability capabilities. Currently, glexec leaves a message (critically, containing a user's name) in syslog each time a user invokes the program. They want an alternate mechanism to provide information about what users have been running locally. Since glideinWMS currently sends the startd ad to the HTCondor-CE, the agreement is that if the condor_collector running on the CE records the username of the payload user, then we will meet the traceability requirements. To do this, we propose implementing a new condor_collector plugin. Unfortunately, it appears the collector plugin infrastructure is unusable: It appears that the linking of the condor_collector binary hides necessary symbols for any plugin to function. Unusable ABI design: There's no C++ ABI guarantee across HTCondor versions nor any versioning mechanism in place. Unusable API design: There's no API versioning mechanism nor are the necessary headers shipped. HTCondor-CE is currently python/shell/config files only and we'd like to keep it that way. Hence, the new plugin will be a python-based plugin. A new knob, COLLECTOR_PLUGIN_PYTHON_MODULES will provide a comma-separated list if python module names (not filenames!). If specified and the module is loadable, there will be three functions invoked: update(command: str, ad: ClassAd): Invoked each time a new ClassAd is received by the collector. command is the string version of the collector command and ad is the provided ad. invalidate(command: str, ad: ClassAd): Analogous to update, but invoked whenever a daemon explicitly invalidates its ad. shutdown: Invoked when the collector is being shutdown. As a result, a python module that implements FNAL's requirements might look like the following: import htcondor def update(command, ad): if command != "UPDATE_STARTD_AD": return if ad.get('State') == 'Unclaimed': return info = {} keys = ['RemoteOwner', 'GlobalJobID', 'State', 'Name', 'ClientMachine', 'x509UserProxyVOName', 'ProjectName', 'x509userproxysubject', 'x509UserProxyFQAN', 'x509UserProxyEmail', 'Group', ] for key in keys: if key in ad: info[key] = ad[key] htcondor.log(htcondor.LogLevel.Audit, "Startd user trace: %s" % info) The corresponding configuration addition might be: COLLECTOR.PLUGINS=/some/path/to/libcollector_python_plugin.so COLLECTOR_PLUGIN_PYTHON_MODULES=audit_payloads COLLECTOR_AUDIT_LOG = $(LOG)/AuditPayloadLog COLLECTOR_DEBUG = D_AUDIT, $(COLLECTOR_DEBUG) MAX_COLLECTOR_AUDIT_LOG = 1d MAX_NUM_COLLECTOR_AUDIT_LOG = 90

title: Ticket #7814: Fix test_custom_machine_resources.py
description: This Ornithological test is currently disabled; fix it and enable it. This test not pass consistently in the BaTLab, maybe "because job ads don't get update synchronously".
remarks: 2020-Sep-08 10:59:57 by karpel: The part of this test that fails is test_reported_usage_in_job_ads_makes_sense. This is the most intricate part of the test: it tries to verify that the reported usage number is actually reasonable given the resource increments we set up in the configuration. All of the other parts of the test pass, and cover the "user-facing" part of the CMR API. The failing part is much harder than it sounds, because there are a lot of things that can go slightly weird when calculating usage that end up showing up in the final number reported to the user. The main problems have to do with rounding the period between monitor triggers and how many triggers occur while the job is running (i.e., how many increments occur while the job is running). The test attempts to account for all of these effects deterministically and decide whether the usage number is reasonable. The test is occasionally failing because it looks we haven't accounted for all possible effects: the reported number is never actually "unreasonable", it just doesn't match one of the finite possibilities we have accounted for. The reported number seems to always be within the bounds set by the smallest and largest of the finite possibilities we generate. Ultimately, this part of the test is trying to capture some of the gooey internals of the CMR code. I think it is debatable whether we should even test it to this level of specificity (though it was a fun exercise), since it is certainly implementation-dependent. Given that, what should we test here? I think we want some kind of test that checks that the usage is within reasonable bounds given the setup. 2020-Sep-09 09:41:12 by tlmiller: I would rather only test for the specific values that we know are actually being reported by the monitor(s); the Perl test's approach was the smallest set of specific values that could be right. Since I don't trust coincidences, I'd like to understand why we're seeing the values we are, rather than just hope for the best. 2020-Sep-09 09:45:15 by karpel: Just remember what "because job ads don't get update synchronously" was about... Occasionally, the test fails because the AssignedXXX attribute is missing from job ads in the query. That is, the job would run, but the job ad wouldn't be updated with CMR information. That error was fairly ephemeral, presumably only occurring under high load (I only ever saw it in the batlab). If it crops up again, the jobs may need to run for longer to allow time for updates to propagate through the system.

title: Ticket #6706: cmd_drain_scavenging intermittent failures
description: Initial analysis indicates that that cmd_drain_scavenging is failing intermittently on Windows because we send WM_CLOSE when we would send SIGTERM on Linux, and perl doesn't (and can't?) convert that to SIGTERM internally, meaning that the job actually exits when requested, and HTCondor never transitions to preempting/killing, which is something the test is checking for. TJ can provide a (tiny) 'sleepw.exe' binary that is a sleep command with a window, and have it ignore WM_CLOSE messages. This should enable us to actually test MAX_VACATE_TIME after draining on Windows, but may require nontrivial rewrites of the test, whose perl script sleeps but can be interrupted via a file.

title: Ticket #6356: Consolidate + deploy code for cached HTTP public file transfers
description: We previously made progress towards adding an HTTP-based mechanism for transferring public input files (#3818, #4900). However this code is now several years old and was never deployed. In order to do HTTP file transfers, we'll need an active web server. The existing code provides a basic HTTP handler via the shared port daemon; however for now we won't use this, and instead we'll assume a standalone web server. We want to consolidate these changes into our 8.7.x codebase and deploy them: Develop a new branch which merges these changes into the modern master branch Make any updates/changes so it builds and works correctly Test in our batlab environment and fix accordingly Use #ifdef statements to isolate the code that implements this functionality in order to enable it to be conditionally compiled via cmake Use different #ifdef statements to isolate sections we don't want to use right away (ie. shared port HTTP handler) Update the hashing function to generate hash links based on both file name AND last modified time Verify that all the knobs are well-named Add functionality into condor_preen to remove stale webroot links Shadow should make sure execute node supports input remaps before sending it mapped URLs Shadow should use root privileges to store the hash links, so web_root_dir doesn't need to be 777 Merge back into master
remarks: 2017-Aug-02 14:23:36 by tannenba: For item # 5 above, I do not want the code "we don't want to use right away" merged back into the master branch at all, even it is if #ifdef-ed, until you (Mark) can explain to me specifically what these code pieces are intended to do and how it was implemented. The code pieces we don't want now can continue to live on Carl's branch. Thanks. 2017-Aug-03 13:58:00 by coatsworth: Updated. I'll deal with the shared port stuff in a different ticket then. Also included a line item to update the hashing function like we discussed. 2017-Aug-03 16:40:34 by coatsworth: One thing I'm finding confusing with Carl's code: whenever the public file transfers are misconfigured (ie. wrong web server address, webroot not defined, etc.) it silently falls back to a CEDAR transfer. This doesn't seem like desirable behavior to me. A user could easily make a configuration error, then send massive amounts of data over CEDAR without ever realizing it. A couple different options here: 1) Preserve the existing behavior but add error messages to the logs. 2) In the event of a configuration error, hold the job. Same behavior as when there are problems with transfer_input_files. Force the user to fix the problem before moving on. Any thoughts, other ideas? 2017-Aug-03 18:55:34 by zmiller: Let's be clear about the distinction between "users" and "HTCondor sysadmin". It's the sysadmin that does the configuration. It's the user that specifies the submit file. So putting the job on hold due to the sysadmin's error may not be helpful since the user can't do anything about it (other than complain to their sysadmin). Really, they just want the job to run and probably don't care too much how the file gets there, which is why Carl decided to just falling back to transferring it via CEDAR. That said, this failure shouldn't happen silently. I'd suggest we log something via dprintf(D_ALWAYS, "ERROR: ...") but still let the job run, or in a more extreme version we EXCEPT() so that we get the sysadmin's attention right away. The incentive for users to use the "public_input_files" feature is just that they get to run their jobs more quickly in theory. But I'm sure they'd rather have them run slowly than not at all, and it's the sysadmin who should be concerned about good utilization of the network and caches. My $0.02. 2017-Aug-11 10:36:22 by tannenba: Re item 10 above that says "Shadow should use root privileges to store the hash links, so web_root_dir doesn't need to be 777" Why root? Isn't root a really big hammer for this? Also, if your web_root_dir is on a shared file system like NFS (which is likely to be pretty common if folks want to run their web server on a different machine from their schedd), root squash will make writing the links as root a really bad choice. Isn't condor privileges good enough? Or maybe even better, allow a config knob to specify the user to use when writing to web_root_dir ? (and maybe 'condor' could server as a reasonable default here) 2017-Aug-14 11:25:41 by zmiller: Responding to Todd regarding item 10. Sorry for the confusion here. In the original version of the code, the links were written as the user running the job. This meant that the directory used for web_root_dir had to be chmod 777 (or 1777 perhaps). I did not want to make a world-writable directory necessary for this feature to work which is why I raised this issue initially. My idea was to have HTCondor use root to create the link and then change the ownership to the user, so that the directory could be locked down to something chmod 755. This is the exact same approach we take for creating spool and execute directories for a user, where the "execute" dir itself is owned by "condor" but each subdir/sandbox is owned by the user. That doesn't seem like an outrageously "big hammer", it follows our existing model, and it helps make it trivially obvious to the admin which users are using public_input_files since the symlinks would have their ownership. As Todd mentioned, that does run into potential trouble with NFS and root_squash, though. In general, that seems like an odd configuration since you wouldn't be able to (usefully) link to local files on the submit machine if the httpd server is running on a different machine. It would only work if you linked to files that were also already in NFS and probably already available via NFS on the execute machine, since that IMHO is the most common reason to have NFS or other shared filesystems deployed. If these public input files are in NFS, the shadow needs to read the entirety of each file over the network just to calculate the hash, then the web server needs to read the entire thing from the NFS server, and then send it yet again over the network to the execute machine. Doesn't seem terribly efficient, especially given that the ostensible goal of this work is to reduce the amount of times we transfer files to ease the load on the network. The design doc doesn't specify allowing a third-party (separate host using shared filesystem) web server explicitly, and definitely seems to make the assumption that the web server is running on the same host as the schedd/shadow (with references to linking to local files, having the shadow potentially be the server, navigating shared port, etc.). Despite all those caveats, supporting that "split server" mode is not difficult to add to the design. In that case, the web_root_dir can, as Todd suggested, simply be owned by "condor" (or some other configurable user, perhaps "httpd") and the links inside web_root_dir can be created as the same user. All the files pointed to are already required (and checked) to be world-readable anyways. So let's create a new knob, "HTTP_PUBLIC_FILES_USER", which defaults to the user that is running condor. Typically this is "condor" but if the admin has changed this using CONDOR_IDS then we should honor that piece of configuration. To that end, I propose that the value of this knob can either be set to: a raw username, like "httpd" or "nobody", or I guess a raw UID, like 1377. The token "<condor>" (case insensitive) which means the same user as the condor daemons run as. The token "<user>" (also case insensitive) which means the user who submitted the job. The default could then be "<condor>"... (or "<user>"?) Any problems with that? It allows as much flexibility as I think anyone would ever need for both regular and NFS deployments. 2017-Aug-14 14:18:38 by zmiller: If we decide to go with my proposal, I now have code to do exactly that. 2017-Aug-15 13:53:07 by zmiller: I just went ahead and committed my code yesterday to fix issue 10 as described in my previous comment. 2017-Oct-17 12:24:32 by coatsworth: Hi all, this work is implemented and documented, so I'm going to mark this as resolved. There is some follow up work that needs to be done (hard link security, possible integration with shared port daemon) which we'll address in new tickets.

title: Ticket #1169: Add a lease to cached security sessions
description: The Problem Cached security sessions currently have an age limit, which defaults to 1 day for daemons and 60s for command-line tools. Daemons that sometimes don't live for very long, such as the shadow or glidein daemons may therefore result in a lot of unnecessary security sessions bloating the cache. A misconfigured command-line tool could also cause severe bloating of the cache. Proposed Solution To address this, we would like to add a session lease which defaults to 1 hour, but which is configurable and negotiated between client and server. Leases are automatically extended whenever sessions are used. Sessions which are not used for the lease time will be removed from the cache. This allows for more aggressive garbage collection of daemon sessions without incurring greater authentication overhead in typical cases. All daemons which communicate on a regular basis do so with a default frequency higher than once per hour. Those that communicate less frequently than once per hour are unlikely to suffer much from reauthenticating at this low frequency. The session lease time will be controlled by SEC_<auth-level>_SESSION_LEASE, which defaults to 1h in all cases. We don't think users will need to adjust this in most cases. The shorter of the server's and client's values will be used. Sessions with older versions that do not support session leases will be given an infinite lease time. The server will add a small grace period (20s by default) before expiring a session due to its lease running out. This is the same as the server's existing treatment of expiration due to the session duration running out. Error Handling There is no in-line ACK from the server to the client when a session is requested, so we will have the client blindly renew its lease whenever it tries to use a session. If the server does not successfully receive the request, there is therefore a possibility of the server's cached session expiring before the client's. The error handling in this case is identical to the case where the server is restarted and therefore has lost all prior cached sessions: the server responds out-of-band to inform the client that the session is invalid. This may result in failure of the operation that the client was attempting when using the invalid security session.

title: Ticket #2745: Better handling of output files that have unreadable permissions
description: If Condor encounters a file whose permissions block reading while transfering output back to the submit point, the job will be put on hold. The normal error message is: 012 (034.000.000) 01/04 12:25:51 Job was held. Error from dot.cs.wisc.edu: STARTER at 128.105.165.118 failed to send file(s) to <128.105.185.14:59241>: error reading from /scratch/condor/execute/dir_20718/eraseme.badpermfile: (errno 13) Permission denied; SHADOW failed to receive file(s) from <128.105.165.118:40408> Code 13 Subcode 13 although if you have privlege seperation on, the error message is: 012 (68230.000.000) 01/04 11:26:46 Job was held. Error from slot4@e019.chtc.wisc.edu: error changing sandbox ownership to condor Code 31 Subcode 0 Transfer unreadable files: If the problem is just permissions, Condor is perfectly able to chmod() them to readability, then transfer them. This will eliminate a cause of problems for users and potential wasted work. Unify behavior: The behavior when privlege seperation is on should be identical to the behavior when it is off. The privlege seperation error at the moment is less useful. Restore unreadability: Optionally, when the files are copied to the submit machine, restore the exact permissions the file used to have. This ensures that the output files are as similar as possible to those on the execute node. It also will clue the user in that their job is setting suspicious permissions. Why might it bad to retrieve a file marked as unreadable? What problems might we create. Brainstorming: Perhaps the user doesn't want the file to be retrieved. If so, this is clumsy solution, and ineffective at the moment as the job fails and is held. The correct solution is unlinking the file. What is the file is export controlled and needs to never be retrieved? Are there good reasons to mark is as unreadable temporarily to block it's retrieval? Seems like a poor solution. How might an attacker take advantage of this? I can't imagine any circumstances in which an attacker might insert an unreadable file that he couldn't just insert a readable file to the same result.
remarks: 2012-May-16 16:33:31 by adesmet: An additional thought: this can bite jobs doing self-checkpointing. The implicit promise is that when a self-checkpointing job (when_to_transfer_output=on_exit_or_evict) restarts after being evicted, the files in the current working directory should be identical to the what was there when the job was evicted. If you had an unreadable file when you were evicted, that unreadable file should be there when you restart. Admittedly, a valid use of this is unlikely, but I find it entirely plausible that a job might erroneously create unreadable files and instead of fixing the cause might just fix the permissions when needed.

title: Ticket #7382: Don't copy strings from classad cache on gcc's with small string opt
description: The classad caching code today assumes that std:string is implemented as a copy-on-write shared string, except on Windows. However, starting with gcc version 5, all std:strings are implemented as the so-called "small string optimization", or SSO, where they are never shared or C-O-W. Today, the classad cache code assumes that WIN32 compilers are all SSO, and everything else is COW. We'll fix this to define COW string for gcc < 5, and SSO for everything else.

title: Ticket #5645: Schedd EXCEPTs on job proxy update
description: In 8.5.0, we made the permissions on jobs' directories under spool more restrictive by default (#4896). This broke the code in the schedd that accepts an updated proxy from a client. If the job's spool directory is chown'd between condor and the job owner (no longer done by default), the schedd needs to know which priv state to be in to write the proxy file. It does this by stat'ing the proxy file and looking at the ownership. With the restricted directory permissions, this will fail if the stat is done as the wrong user. The schedd doesn't notice the failure and EXCEPTs when it tries to use an uninitialized uid. To fix, the schedd can stat the job's spool directory instead of the proxy file. Both should have the same ownership, and we know at this point in the code that the proxy file is in the spool directory.

title: Ticket #6593: On dslot claim reuse, schedd checks resources of pslot
description: When the schedd searches for a job to run on an idle dynamic slot, it compares the job's resource request to the available resources of the partitionable slot that the dynamic slot was created from. This can result in the schedd attempting to run a job that's too big for the dynamic slot. When the shadow attempts to activate the claim, the startd rejects it, and the schedd then relinquishes the claim. This happens because the schedd optimizes the slot ad's Requirements expression when the ad arrives in the schedd (in AddMrec()). This does constant propagation and expression inlining for attribute references internal to the slot ad. This includes the checks of whether the job fits in the slot in the WithinResourceLimits attribute. Later, when the schedd is about to contact the startd to request a claim, it modifies the partitionable slot ad to look like the dynamic slot ad that the startd will create for the claim. It overwrites the Cpus, Memory, and Disk attributes to match the amounts requested by the job it intends to run on that slot. But it doesn't update the copies of those attribute values that were propagated into the optimized Requirements expression. Thus, when the schedd looks for the next job to run on that slot, it will use an inaccurate Requirements expression that will match jobs that it shouldn't. A simple fix for this bug is to redo the Requirements optimization after the partitionable slot ad is modified to look like a dynamic slot ad.

title: Ticket #3284: Change default MODIFY_REQUEST_EXPR_REQUESTMEMORY
description: At least at our CMS T2, the default MODIFY_REQUEST_EXPR_REQUESTMEMORY does more harm than good. Right now, it is something like: quantize(RequestMemory, TotalCpus / TotalMemory / 4). This basically rounds-up to the nearest 25% of the per-slot memory. Two issues with this: If the memory request is slightly more than the per-slot memory, this can cause significant loss. Example: Suppose there are 32 slots and 2000 MB RAM per slot. If each job asks for 2001 MB, then the request is rounded to 2500 MB. So, a maximum of 25 jobs can be run - idling 7 cores instead of 1 core. If there are many node types, then this is causing quite a bit of fragmentation of match lists. If you quantize based on the RequestMemory, you cause fragmentation of the auto-clusters. A priori, I don't really see any advantage based on using the per-slot memory size. I propose we have a limit on the absolute amount of per-slot memory loss. Let's change the default to: quantize(RequestMemory, 100)

title: Ticket #4541: ordering of configuration files not well documented
description: Which configuration files are local, and which are global? What is the exact order of evaluation? How is this different on Windows from Linux? Many of these details are documented, but some of the information is buried in the installation section, and other parts are in section 3.3 (Configuration). Details are to be placed and revised as this ticket's content, and after that, all the info will get into the manual, in a single location. Ordering is important. The last time a variable's value is set wins, where there are multiple locations/files that set a particular variable. The various kinds of files or environment variables that might specify configuration have an ordered evaluation. In order: a single configuration file; we tend to call this the global configuration file other configuration file(s), referenced and parsed due to specification within the global configuration file; we tend to call these local configuration files, and there may be more than one environment variables So, if variable FOO is set in both the global configuration and in a local configuration file, the value that sets FOO is the local configuration file one, as it is evaluated later than the global configuration one. For Linux, we search for a single global configuration file, starting at the top of the following list. We use the first one that exists, and then remaining possible file locations from this list become irrelevant. File specified in the CONDOR_CONFIG environment variable $(HOME)/.condor/condor_config (Ticket #3158 for version 8.3.1: this file is removed from this list of possibilities for the global configuration file. It becomes an automatically checked location for use as a local configuration file.) /etc/condor/condor_config /usr/local/etc/condor_config ~condor/condor_config For Windows, the location of the global configuration file is determined by the contents of the environment variable CONDOR_CONFIG. If this environment variable is not defined, then the location is the registry value of HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE/Software/Condor/CONDOR_CONFIG. The global configuration file may contain a specification of one or more local configuration files. Since the last definition of a variable sets the value, we must fully specify the ordering of parsing these local configuration files. In order: The value of LOCAL_CONFIG_DIR lists one or more directories which contain configuration files. The list is parsed from left to right. The leftmost (first) in the list is parsed first. Within each directory, a lexicographical ordering by file name determines the ordering of file consideration. The value of LOCAL_CONFIG_FILE lists one or more configuration files. These files are considered in left to right within the list. If one of these steps changes the value (RHS) of LOCAL_CONFIG_DIR, then LOCAL_CONFIG_DIR is processed for a second time, using the changed list of directories. An unrelated detail to get correct in updated documentation: If the value of LOCAL_CONFIG_FILE ends in the pipe character (|), then the variable's value cannot be as defined (a list of files). It must instead be the command to execute.

title: Ticket #1743: condor_ssh_to_job is harmful during stage-in

Once the file transfer finishes, the starter's attempt to do the final update goes ahead, but then the starter hits an exception: 10/29/10 15:33:33 ERROR "FileTransfer::UpLoadFiles called during active transfer! Furthermore, when using privsep, the sshd_setup script fails when file transfer is happening, because the sandbox is owned by condor rather than the user. 10/28/10 17:56:51 START_SSHD failed: condor_ssh_to_job_sshd_setup failed: Failed to create /var/lib/condor/execute/slot5/dir_29041/.condor_ssh_to_job_1 How To Fix It seems best to have the starter reject ssh attempts during file transfer. It may also be a good idea to reject ssh attempts until the job has started, since the starter may get confused if sshd is ever the first and only task that it is managing. Either way, we should understand why the starter gets confused and also fix that, because it seems like the logic must be buggy.

title: Ticket #326: sh-like control of stdout/err for jobs
description: (This is based on a discussion between adesmet, gthain, and psilord.) Condor's handling of stdout and stderr is pretty primative. You either capture it or now. If you capture it, it must be to a unique file. If both stdout and stderr go to the same file, the result is undefined (but you'll probably lose data). If multiple jobs write to the same stdout or stderr, you'll probably lose data. /bin/sh supports a rich set of options, and it would be nice to offer this level of option to Condor users. Key features: Redirect stdout and stderr into a single file, interleaved as the lines were emitted. This would be similar to "cmd 2>&1 > outfile" in sh. This is handy for, say, compiler output. (Because of buffering you can't guarantee that the lines interleave correctly, but the niave implementation will likely be Good Enough; after all, it works for /bin/sh.) Append to stdout and stderr, instead of truncating and writing. This is potentially useful for 1. programs doing their own checkpointing, and 2. lots of jobs that you want to merge the output on. Possible syntax: Ad hoc: append_stdout = true append_stderr = true stdout = output.txt stderr = output.txt sh-like io = 2>&1 >> output.txt
remarks: 2009-Mar-16 14:29:11 by gthain: Another syntax might be perl-like: output = ">>append_to_me" error = ">&1" 2009-Apr-08 15:27:29 by tlmiller: This problem becomes possible to solve with post-processing if #370 is implemented, although doing it "natively" would be nicer to the user. As an extension of this idea, for the parallel universe, if would be cute to allow streaming output from one job to be streaming input to another. I'm not sure, however, to what extent Condor really wants to support pipelining without intermediate files as a computational model. (In addition to the latency advantages of concurrency, you also wouldn't have buffer or track potentially large intermediate files. If you explicitly support pipelining as a computation model, what you probably want to do is let Condor co- or not co- schedule pipelined computations as the matchmaker sees fit. This would require some special support from Condor, even if the interface ended up in DAGMan, with explicit data dependencies, rather than ordering dependencies.) 2010-Oct-20 15:59:08 by jfrey: Bulk change of target version from v070504 to v070505 using ./ticket-target-mover. 2011-Jan-27 14:21:33 by danb: Bulk change of target version from v070505 to v070506 using ./ticket-target-mover. 2011-Feb-01 14:49:30 by tannenba: Bulk change of target version from v070506 to NULL using ./ticket-target-mover.

title: Ticket #7697: SHARED_PORT_PORT is never honored
description: When the master chooses the port to assign to the shared_port daemon, if the master is not starting a collector, it will ignore SHARED_PORT_PORT and instead attempt to use the same port as the pool's collector. This is clearly wrong in the case where of a node that is not running a collector (i.e. a submit node, or execute node), but the local machine is using shared port. The user who ran into this problem wanted to start a Schedd and use shared port and specify a specific port for shared port because he was running in a container under k8s. It turns out this configuration never works - SHARED_PORT_PORT is always ignored. The reason is that the master first scans the COLLECTOR_LIST looking to see if there is a local collector with a port assignment. If this list is not empty, then there is a bug in the use of same_host() that results in the master thinking it has found a matching collector. It then uses the port from that entry, and that entry does not have an explicit port, it uses the default port. Only when the COLLECTOR_LIST is empty, does the master param for SHARED_PORT_PORT or COLLECTOR_PORT to get the port number. The code in the master should be changed so that if it is not starting a local primary collector (i.e. the daemon list has COLLECTOR), it will never look at COLLECTOR_LIST to determine the port. This is the immediate bug. In a separate ticket, we will fix the bug where same_host() is being used incorrectly. workaround If the COLLECTOR_LIST is empty, or the first entry in the list uses the desired port, then the master will assign that port to the shared-port daemon. This has the undesirable property of having the master try and send it's ad to at non-existent collector, but since COLLECTOR_LIST can be a list, it can be configured to also send it's ad to the real collector config fragment # The first entry in the list is what defines the local shared port port MASTER.COLLECTOR_LIST = $(IP_ADDRESS):$(SHARED_PORT_PORT) $(COLLECTOR_HOST) # If the collector list is empty, the master will use SHARED_PORT_PORT MASTER.COLLECTOR_LIST =
