title: Ticket #6655: Spooling empty input sandbox fails
description: When spooling the input sandbox to the schedd, if there are no files to send, then the transfer fails. % cat noxfer.desc executable=/bin/bash transfer_executable=false arguments=--version queue % condor_submit -spool noxfer.desc Submitting job(s). 1 job(s) submitted to cluster 310. DCSchedd::spoolJobFiles:7002:File transfer failed for target job 310.0: SUBMIT at 128.105.121.64 failed to send file(s) to <128.105.121.64:12345> ERROR: Failed to spool job files. % This was first first reported on condor-users; see the post for details. The problem is in FileTransfer::DoDownload(). It switches to user priv just before receiving the first file from the client. If there are no files, then the priv change doesn't occur. At the end of the transfer, it always writes a commit file. But if no files were transferred, then it's in the wrong priv state. This only affects daemons running as root. The priv state change should be hoisted above the per-file for loop. This bug was introduced by #5226 in HTCondor 8.5.0, which changed the ownership of the job spool directory at file transfer time.
remarks: 2018-May-02 16:25:57 by coatsworth: CODE REVIEW This is a fairly simple fix, and DoDownload makes extensive use of return_and_resetpriv() so I'm not worried about leaking privileges. All looks good. Only minor detail would be an updated comment, so that people know why you put the code block where you did, and they don't move it around later.

title: Ticket #4392: CREAM external built incorrectly
description: When I upgraded the CREAM external to version 1.14.0, I made a couple errors that caused communication with the CREAM server to fail. First, I dropped a patch to glite-lbjp-common-gss where it passes an invalid buffer length to gss_import_cred(). The patch is still required for the new version of glite-lbjp-common-gss. Second, I needed to switch from gcc to g++ to build glite-lbjp-common-gsoap-plugin. This was due to the newer version of gsoap. The same header file (stdsoap2.h) is used for both C and C++. When the header file is used in a C++ compilation, the struct soap it defines gains a constructor and a virtual destructor. This means the layout of the struct soap is different between C and C++. Since glite-ce-cream-client-api-c is C++ code that uses stdsoap2.h, glite-lbjp-common-gsoap-plugin must also be compiled as C++ and we need to link against the C++ gsoap library. While making and testing these fixes, I also reorganized the CREAM externals so that each one installs into its own installation directory, rather than all of them installing in the glite-ce-cream-client-api-c installation directory.

title: Ticket #7414: Use callbacks to implement curl_plugin timeout
description: In #7316 we addressed a performance bug in the curl_plugin by adding a version check for the libcurl library. A better way to work around this bug (for all versions of libcurl) would be to use callbacks to abort a transfer if it's taking too long. I don't know exactly what the implementation looks like right now, so I'll do some homework and will update this ticket with details shortly.
remarks: 2020-Jan-02 17:35:22 by coatsworth: Hi Brian, I've written some code that users SIGALRM and callbacks to track progress of a file transfer. The good news is that it's straightforward and easy to identify when a transfer is not making progress. The bad news is that it's difficult to actually abort the transfer, put an error message in the output and then exit the process with a non-zero code. I've looked around online for other approaches. The best suggestion I've been is to use the libcurl CURLOPT_PROGRESSFUNCTION callback, which is called at regular time intervals (whether or not progress is actually being made) with information about current progress. We can implement our timeout logic in the callback function, and if the transfer isn't moving forward, just return a non-zero code and libcurl will abort the transfer. There's more information here: https://curl.haxx.se/libcurl/c/CURLOPT_PROGRESSFUNCTION.html Let me know if you think this makes sense, or you have other ideas. 2020-Apr-10 07:46:37 by tim: Bulk change of target version from v080906 to v080907 using ticket-target-mover.

title: Ticket #2616: Create a command-line tool to communicate with DAGMan
description: Right now the user can basically communicate with a running DAGMan only via the condor_rm and condor_hold commands, and we (Pete and I) think that this is too coarse-grained. (A couple of examples -- on condor_rm, should a final node be run or not, and should a rescue DAG be created, or should things just be killed off as quickly as possible; and, on a condor_hold, should the DAGMan job actually be killed, or should it be told to just stop submitting node jobs.) There are plenty of other possibilities, too, such as querying the state of the DAG. We're thinking that this should be a new command-line tool, like condor_dag_tool or something. Since DAGMan is daemoncore, it has a command socket; it could put the address for that into its classad, and then the DAG tool could get the address from the schedd, and talk to DAGMan directly after that.
remarks: 2011-Nov-07 16:45:23 by wenger: This tool should also be able to change configuration settings for DAGMan (e.g., maxjobs). It might also eventually become a way of dynamically changing the actual DAG, although we also had other proposals for how to deal with that. 2011-Nov-07 19:37:39 by nwp: #2438 is duplicate of this ticket. I will delete that and point to this. 2012-Apr-06 10:52:46 by pfc: Just to import another use-case from #2663, which was closed as a dup with this ticket, this tool should replace/support controlling the <dagname>.halt files to gracefully halt a running DAG. 2012-May-02 15:01:14 by nwp: This is something I would like to do for 7.9. Instead of deriving from #2213, I will repoint to #2810 2014-Aug-11 13:23:59 by wenger: What are some things such a tool should be able to do?: Halt/un-halt DAG. Add nodes. "Manually" re-try specified nodes. Possibly various flavors of removing the DAG (such as having DAGMan stay in the queue until all child jobs have exited the queue). Maybe change node priorities on the fly. Peacefully pause the DAG (see #3756). Dump a rescue DAG but continue to run. Get and report stats on the state of the DAG. Probably a bunch of other things... (I wonder if this would be something that it would make sense for Zach to work on, because he knows daemoncore better than I do.) 2014-Aug-11 13:25:05 by wenger: What should such a tool be named? condor_dag_cmd? 2014-Aug-11 15:10:35 by wenger: More stuff for this tool to do: Change DAGMan settings, such as maxjobs, maxidle, DAGMAN_USER_LOG_SCAN_INTERVAL, DAGMAN_MAX_SUBMITS_PER_INTERVAL, etc. 2014-Aug-11 15:14:26 by wenger: The command-line format maybe could be something like this: condor_dag_cmd [-name scheddname] <cluster id> <command> <command> ... Maybe have the option to specify -addr <a.b.c.d:port> instead of "[-name scheddname] <cluster id>" to be able to bypass the schedd. 2014-Aug-12 09:27:01 by wenger: There are a number of tickets that could benefit from this functionality: #2831: Be able to "manually" retry nodes during a DAG run #3756: provide command to peacefully pause a DAG #1756: Be able to dynamically add nodes to a running DAG #1311: Be able to configure DAGMan's actions when condor_rm'ed #4356: Have some way to do a reconfig on a running DAGMan 2015-Jun-04 12:47:45 by wenger: Hmm -- I just thought of a simpler way to do this that would be easier and quicker to implement: each time through the submission loop, DAGMan looks for a specific file (foo.dag.cmd or something), and, if the file exists, DAGMan executes whatever commands are in the file, and then removes the file. One other thing I was thinking about is this: if we allow commands (whether via the file or other means) that do things like adding nodes, we need to have some way of recording them for rescue and recovery modes -- otherwise, the new nodes won't get created in those modes. One possibility I thought of is this: we create a rescue DAG file when DAGMan first starts up, and we record the "dynamic" commands in that file as we go. Then, if we finish successfully, we remove the rescue DAG file. I think that might work for both rescue and recovery modes, although I need to do a little more thinking to make sure that it would work for recovery mode. Also note that we might not need to record all commands -- for example, if a command is to do a reconfig, any changes to the config file(s) would take effect automatically in recovery or rescue mode anyhow. 2016-Oct-30 18:25:07 by wenger: Okay, probably the most obvious use for this would be changing parameters like maxjobs on the fly...

title: Ticket #7044: param calls in submit_utils should happen only when used by tools
description: There are several places in submit_utils where param() is called. We must NOT invoke param() when materializing jobs in the Schedd, the value of param() from the tool must be used instead. For the most part we will fix this by refactoring submit_utils to use the param() only when building the cluster ad (which always happens on the tool side and never in the Schedd), or we will capture the value of the param() and stuff it into the submit digest - like we currently do with the current working directory. A similar correctness issue is that there are many places in submit_utils where a default action is taken when the submit file has no keyword. The is the correct behavior when processing a submit file, but NOT the correct behavior when processing a submit digest (which may have been pruned back to the essential statements). When materializing in the presence of a clusterAd, the values of the clusterAd should always be used when a submit keyword is unspecified.

title: Ticket #1201: DAEMONLIST=VIEW_SERVER without a CONDOR_VIEW_HOST segfaults master
description: If VIEW_SERVER is in the DAEMON_LIST (and points to the same binary as COLLECTOR), but CONDOR_VIEW_HOST is not set, the condor_master will try to dereference a null pointer and falls over dead. Two layers could have caught and handled the error: StringList::initializeFromString (string_list.cpp:66) doesn't notice it was passed in NULL. It should instead notice the NULL pointer, then either EXCEPT or behave as though an empty string ("") was passed in. EXCEPTing may help catch bugs in callers layers who are being sloppy and handing around bad data. Treating it as an empty string almost certainly yields the desired behavior. Daemon::getCmInfo (daemon.cpp:1330) didn't notice that getCmHostFromConfig returned NULL. If that happens, it should silently return false; the layer one up will notice and will fall back to using COLLECTOR_HOST.

title: Ticket #4453: Improve scalability of CCB
description: There are three somewhat-wacky things we do in the CCB that could be improved: CCB has a timer which, when fires, calls select() individually on every socket for every target. 10,000 targets connected? That's 10,000 invocations of select(). DanB left a message saying that, because CCB has so many targets registered, we keep things out of DC. Instead, we can register a single epoll FD with DC and add all the targets to the epoll watch for an O(1) operation. CCB blocks on reading off the initial CEDAR message. This is similar to what we've hit before - if we change readReady for ReliSocks to reflect whether there is a CEDAR message to read instead of bytes on the sock, then we should only invoke the registered callback when a complete message has arrived. This should greatly decrease the chance we block on the network in the CCB. When we read from a socket, we typically call select() with one file descriptor in order to have the desired timeout behavior. The runtime of select is a function of the largest passed file descriptor number. If we switch to poll for this situation (relatively unobtrusive change), the runtime is O(1). Branch posted: https://github.com/bbockelm/htcondor/tree/ccb_epoll

I don't like defining dummy poll macros and structs in the Selector header file. I'd prefer that to be confined to selector.cpp and not affect other source files that include selector.h. * I don't like the trickery of the epoll fd masquerading as a pipe to daemon-core. But I also don't want to add an array for yet another type of handler in daemon-core just for this one use. * This is in the existing code, but I hate that for the object named BlockingModeGuard, a value of true means non-blocking. title: Ticket #1651: Have master daemon create security sessions for its child daemons
description: Communication between Condor daemons over TCP must be done over an authenticated security session. This results in a potential deadlock situation on Windows due to its increased reliance on network communication for emulating signals. This can occur when the child daemon attempts to communicate with the parent by establishing a session when the parent also initiates an authentication attempt with the child. This effectively kills scalability on Windows. A way to avoid this is to have the parent daemon create a security session and pass it off to the child so that the parent can communicate with the child without having to set up a session from scratch. Components Have Create_Process create a security session whenever it is starting a daemon. Currently the method for detecting this is determining if want_command_port is true, as so far every daemon seems to require one and there does not appear to be a case where a non-daemon program will ask for it. Embed the session information into the environment variable. We will need to create a second, private environment variable as D_DAEMONCORE debug level will print out the ENV_INHERIT variable contents and this would be a potential security hole. We will also have to disable this functionality entirely on Solaris as apparently environments are not private to processes on that OS. Reconstruct the security session on the child side and punch a hole in IpVerify so that the child will accept commands through it. Future Work See if there's an alternative method for Solaris support that doesn't require major modifications. Also confirm if the issue with environment variables still holds true in newer versions. Allow the child to use the session to send messages to the parent. Currently only the parent can use the session. This will require a bit of thought with respect to making sure the child only tries to use the session if it knows it is communicating with its parent. The PID for the parent seems to be also passed through the environment variable, which offers a possible way to check. Branch name: V7_5-parent-child-session

For now, we are only implementing a security session for use by the parent process when sending signals to the child. Use of the session for other purposes should be straightforward, but we'd like to get this step done first. 2010-Sep-24 12:53:40 by danb: Z, here are some comments from my review of the code: It's cumbersome to have #ifdef Solaris sprinkled everywhere that this code lands. When coming across this, one wonders, "what does this have to do with Solaris?" And the answer is nowhere to be found. I would recommend including most of this code on all platforms, even in the Solaris case (e.g. still have a session_id in PidEntry). The only place where you need to be platform-dependent is when you decide whether to create a session id or not. Please put a comment there explaining why Solaris is a special case. It is not clear in the code why creation of a security session is conditional on want_command_port. Please add a comment explaining that this is how we know whether the child is DaemonCore. In daemon-core, session_key is leaked in a couple spots where you 'goto wrapup' without freeing it. Also, session_id is leaked if anything prevents us from sticking it into the PidInfo object (numerous possible error cases). It often is best to immediately copy char pointers into a std::string and then free them immediately, rather than having to deal with all the different paths for exiting from a function. The following line should not be conditional on want_command_port or Solaris. It should be conditional on whether privateinheritbuf is empty or not. job_environ.SetEnv( EnvGetName( ENV_PRIVATE ), privateinheritbuf.Value() ); When creating the security session in the parent, do not specify CONDOR_PARENT_FQU. We aren't currently using the session to connect from the child to the parent, but if we did, we would not want the child to be authenticated as condor@parent. For now, create CONDOR_CHILD_FQU=condor@child and use that. The following log line needs to be improved. It sounds like you are removing a session key from the session cache, which is the opposite of what you are doing. dprintf(D_DAEMONCORE, "Removing session key.\n"); I just looked at the implementation of PunchHole(). I was surprised to find that the following does not quite work. PunchHole() expects "fqu/ip". So giving it "fqu" means incoming requests will never match this rule. id.sprintf("%s", CONDOR_PARENT_FQU); ipv->PunchHole(DAEMON, id); So we have to decide what to do. We could punch holes for all IP addresses on the machine. I am worried that this will be more complicated and fragile (e.g. if network interfaces change dynamically). Therefore, I think we need to add support in PunchHole() for matching just the fqu, from any IP. That will also fix a similar problem with PunchHole() in the starter's implementation of ssh_to_job. Let's not make that fix in this patch. I'll make it separately. 2010-Oct-05 17:16:50 by danb: Z, your latest patch looks good. If it were me, I would merge with the --squash option and put one short description of the patch, rather than pulling in lots of little pieces that are not logically independent. 2010-Oct-06 14:36:42 by ziliang: The same assumption is being made in the code that read in the public environment variable. title: Ticket #7785: Failure to spawn local universe job crashes the schedd
description: LIGO and others report that the schedd is asserting when running many local universe jobs. For some reason, the schedd is unable to register a local universe job with the procd, with the procd complaining that this pid already exists. I haven't been able to reproduce that problem, but when that happens, the schedd marks the local universe job as idle and tries again. However, at that point, the srec for the failed local universe job hasn't been completely removed from the schedd's tables, and when the schedd goes to start the now-idle local universe job a second time, it finds the srec in the table of srec's by job id, and asserts. We'll fix this immediate problem, and keep an eye on the procd problem.

description: Grid universe jobs submitted via SOAP that make use of the spool directory fail when attempting to write to the spool directory. This usually results in jobs becoming held. title: Ticket #2092: Negotiator miscounts resources it hands out
description: In each pie spin in Phase 4.x, we keep a running total of the number of resources used by the schedd's which were active in that pie spin. This number is cumulative across all pie spins. This doesn't make any sense to me. If you have schedd's that hit their submitter limit, they are added to scheddUsed. Hence, in the second spin, their usage is double-counted. I see this in our 7.5.6 negotiator; in phase 4.1, the group usage is counted as 563 (correct), but there are no matches. In 4.2, it counts 1100 resources used by the group (incorrect), and hence has stuff like this: 04/26/11 09:29:05 maxAllowed = -366.000000 groupQuota = 734.000000 groupusage = 1100.000000 In addition to counting groupusage correctly, we can probably halt the spin if maxAllowed is currently negative. This is seriously affecting our ability to use 7.5.6 at our CMS T2.

title: Ticket #3379: Race condition in file stageout
description: If we have a remote job with grid universe, there is a race condition in retrieving the sandbox. I believe this is because the gridmanager or schedd marks the job as complete prior to doing the chown of the spool. If the remote user attempts to read out from the spool during that time, it may get a permission denied. This is a HTCondor-CE job: another possibility is the issue is in the sandbox management of the JobRouter. I'll attach the "condor_transfer_data" session at D_FULLDEBUG|D_SECURITY. I can reliably reproduce this by using "condor_submit -remote" to the HTCondor-CE, query for job completion every second, and call condor_transfer_data immediately after the job hits state 4.
remarks: 2013-Jan-14 14:33:51 by jfrey: The gridmanager sets the job's status to COMPLETED when the job is done and all output has been retrieved. The gridmanager then cleans up any job-related state on the remote server, and then calls DestroyProc(). The DestroyProc() triggers the chowning of the sandbox (it would also remove the job from the queue if LeaveJobInQueue wasn't True). Here are a few possible solutions: Check for CompletionDate in the job ad. This is set when DestroyProc() is called. Still leaves a (much smaller) race condition, as sandbox chowning can be delayed. Allow gridmanager to trigger sandbox chowning when setting JobStatus to COMPLETED. Still leaves a (much smaller) race condition, as sandbox chowning can be delayed. Allow schedd to transfer output before sandbox is chowned. 2014-Nov-17 15:40:47 by blin: #4719 was marked as a duplicate of this ticket 2014-Dec-10 11:00:04 by tlmiller: Code Review Looks good; approved. (Review note: since we can't know when the schedd will get around to actually chown()ing the directory, we have no choice but to poll for it; but it the schedd has already chown()ed the directory by the time we notice the state change, we won't poll twice.)
attachments: condor_transfer_data_race 21478 bytes added by bbockelm on 2012-Dec-13 23:22:04 UTC. condor_transfer_data output at high level of debug. NOTICE the misleading error message - complains about a failure to auth using FS. It tried FS, failed, then succeeded with GSI; likely there's an error stack that someone failed to clear.

title: Ticket #371: Timezone handling in new ClassAd functions inconsistent
description: In new ClassAds have a basic datatype call AbsTime, which represents a timestamp including a timezone offset. There are several ClassAd functions that split an AbsTime into its component parts (year, month, day, hours, etc). The splitTime() function returns a ClassAd with each component stored in a separate attribute. formatTime() is a printf-like function that returns a string containing the time in whatever format is given. A set of functions called getYear(), getMonth(), getHours(), etc. return the appropriate component of the given AbsTime. When splitTime() and formatTime() split up an AbsTime into its components, they do so in the timezone given in the AbsTime, which may be different than the local timezone. getYear() and friends split up the given AbsTime() according to the local timezone. In the following classad snippet, a and b will evaluate to different values if the local timezone isn't UTC: t = AbsTime("2009-4-8T12:00:00z") a = splitTime(t).hours b = getHours(t) This inconsistency is likely to be confusing to users. We should make all of these functions consistent.
creator: jfrey

title: Ticket #7013: Make the main branch of HTCondor FIPS compliant
description: Update HTCondor so it is FIPS-compliant without needing to do a special custom build. New Plan Switching to AESGCM will remove the need for MD5 integrity checks on network traffic. Using SHA256 for checksums in HAD will be another step towards getting us into FIPS compliance (for now). This ticket is essentially dead, but if you want to follow the removal of MD5 and related commits, see JIRA ticket <HTCONDOR-XYZ>. Old Plan There are some major milestones: Create diagram showing types of TCP traffic, how it is packetized, where the checksums and headers are, etc. Analyze and create Milestones for non-negotiated sessions Allow negotiation for Integrity methods (currently only encryption methods are negotiatied) Add SHA(X) as a new Integrity method Change UDP to not use MD5 (or perhaps any crypto) when talking to local processes. Change UDP to throw a big noticable error if trying to use MD5 for non-local traffic. Make MD5 libraries explicitly dlopened() so as not to trigger the FIPS bailout code when no MD5 is actually used. After some period of MD5 and SHA coexisting for a long-enough time, we can eliminate MD5 completely in a future release. Header Formats and Notes The basic structure of the TCP header is: ReliSock (CEDAR TCP) Header if Integrity is enabled: Byte Offset Size (in bytes) Descrip 0 1 1 if last packet in msg, else 0 1 4 Length of packet as integer (network order) 5 16, or 32 if FIPS Message Digest <data> ReliSock (CEDAR TCP) Header if Integrity is NOT enabled: Byte Offset Size (in bytes) Descrip 0 1 1 if last packet in msg, else 0 1 4 Length of packet as integer (network order) <data> Questions and Notes What is the higher-level protocol for establishing a key and enabling Integrity on a brand-new connection with a new session? Header size is 5 bytes initially. (flag for last packet, size of packet) "Security Negotiation" is done in the clear using classads. (One round trip) Authentication is performed (X round trips) and key is exchanged. Send/receive buffers are now empty. If requested, INTEGRITY is now enabled for sender and receiver. Header size is now 21 bytes (or 37 in FIPS) (additional 16 or 32 bytes for checksum) What is the higher-level protocol for establishing a key and enabling Integrity on resuming a session? Header size is 5 bytes initially. "Security Resume" is done in the clear using classads and includes the session ID. (receive only, no response) EOM is called after sending/receiving message in the clear. (i.e. the resume message is one packet by itself) Send/receive buffers are now empty. If requested, INTEGRITY is now enabled for sender and receiver, using the key from the session we looked up. Header size is now 21 bytes (or 37 in FIPS) (additional 16 or 32 bytes for checksum) Are checksums computed over the entire packet or only the bytes for which an MD was enabled when doing a put()? The MD is computed over the whole packet. Calling init_MD in the middle of a message is not supported and will in fact return failure to avoid any accidental use outside of this mode. How do we know if Integrity is enabled (i.e. whether there is a checksum in the header) ? Whether or not Integrity is enabled is state within the socket object. It is enabled when establishing or resuming a session (see 1 and 2 above) and from there on out we know how to interpret additional incoming packets. If Integrity is enabled, how do we know how big it is or what method was used? Currently there is no state saying "what type" of Integrity check we are using, and therefore if there are different header sizes or interpretations. This is state we will need to add to the socket object that can be reference inside the message object when interpreting headers. How is put_bytes_nobuffer() handled? All buffers are flushed before sending bytes_nobuffer. If integrity is enabled those packets will have checksums in the headers. The data is then encrypted (if enabled), but no checksum is computed. The packets are then pushed out using condor_write() which does no explicit packetizing and does not compute any checksums or integrity checks. How are non-negotiated sessions handled? What methods do they use? Can those be disabled by admin if needed? In Progress...

title: Ticket #2641: DiskUsage and request_disk relationship backward
description: misc/jobad.tex %%% ClassAd attribute: DiskUsage \index{ClassAd job attribute!DiskUsage} \index{DiskUsage!job ClassAd attribute} \item[\AdAttr{DiskUsage}:] Amount of disk space (Kbytes) in the Condor execute directory on the execute machine that this job has used. The initial estimate may be specified in the job submit file using the \SubmitCmd{request\_disk} command. If not initialized by the job's request, \SubmitCmd{vm} universe jobs will default to an initial value of the disk image size. If not initialized by the job's request, non-\SubmitCmd{vm} universe jobs will default to an initial value of the sum of the job's executable and all input files. DiskUsage doesn't care at all about request_disk. You can only set it with +DiskUsage, as in: # This example is 1 megabyte +DiskUsage = 1024 man-pages/submitcmds.tex %%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%% %% request_disk %%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%% \index{submit commands!request\_disk} \item[request\_disk = $<$quantity$>$] For pools that enable dynamic \Condor{startd} provisioning (see section~\ref{sec:SMP-dynamicprovisioning}), the amount of disk space in Kbytes requested for this job, setting an initial value for the job ClassAd attribute \Attr{DiskUsage}. If not specified, the initial amount requested under dynamic \Condor{startd} provisioning will depend on the job universe. For \SubmitCmd{vm} universe jobs, it will be the size of the disk image. For other universes, it will be the sum of sizes of the job's executable and all input files. Seems to suggest that request_disk will set DiskUsage. This is backward. If request_disk is not specified, it is set to DiskUsage. Not the value of DiskUsage, it is set to the expression DiskUsage. (It's identical to "+RequestDisk=DiskUsage" in a submit file.) The details on how that size is calculated is correct for DiskUsage, but only indirectly here. misc/jobad.tex %%% ClassAd attribute: RequestMemory \index{ClassAd job attribute!RequestMemory} \index{RequestMemory!job ClassAd attribute} \item[\AdAttr{RequestMemory}:] The amount of memory space in Mbytes requested for this job; results in setting an initial value for the job ClassAd attribute \Attr{ImageSize}. Utilized when dynamic \Condor{startd} provisioning is enabled. RequestMemory has no impact on ImageSize. However, if RequestMemory is not set by the user, it will be set to this expression: RequestMemory = ceiling(ifThenElse(JobVMMemory =!= UNDEFINED, JobVMMemory, ImageSize/1024.0)) man-pages/submitcmds.tex %% request_memory %%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%% \index{submit commands!request\_memory} \item[request\_memory = $<$quantity$>$] For pools that enable dynamic \Condor{startd} provisioning (see section~\ref{sec:SMP-dynamicprovisioning}), the amount of memory space in Mbytes requested for this job, setting an initial value for the job ClassAd attribute \Attr{ImageSize}. If not specified, the initial amount requested under dynamic \Condor{startd} provisioning will depend on the job universe. For \SubmitCmd{vm} universe jobs that do not specify the request with \SubmitCmd{vm\_memory}, it will be 0. For other universes, it will be the size of the job's executable. Seems to suggest that request_memory will set ImageSize. If request_memory is not specified, it is set to "ceiling(ifThenElse(JobVMMemory ! UNDEFINED, JobVMMemory, ImageSize/1024.0))". The details on how that size is calculated is correct for ImageSize, but only indirectly here.

title: Ticket #5184: CLASSAD_USER_PYTHON_MODULES crashes for UW builds
description: For UW builds, the following segfaults starting in 8.3.5: _condor_CLASSAD_USER_PYTHON_MODULES=foo /usr/bin/condor_q After some detective work, it is due to the how libstdc++ implements std::string. There's a special static symbol, empty_rep_storage, which represents the empty string (the most common libstdc++'s implement string as copy-on-write). When a string destructor is called, there is special logic - if (this == &empty_rep_storage), then the underlying storage is not destroyed. In the above segfault of condor_q, the setting of CLASSAD_USER_PYTHON_MODULES causes a dlopen of libclassad_python_user.so with RTLD_DEEPBIND. Objects in that library initialized to the empty string utilize empty_rep_storage from libstdc++. Outside that library, empty_rep_storage is provided from the data segment of the executable itself. Hence, the conditional (this == &empty_rep_storage) is false and the code calls free() on a statically-allocated array outside the heap (segfaulting the program). Because we have two memory addresses for empty_rep_storage, we have violated C++'s One Definition Rule. It's an obscure issue - to trigger it, we needed to have empty_rep_storage in the binary, in libstdc++, and a library dynamically-loaded with RTLD_DEEPBIND. We can't remove empty_rep_storage from libstdc++; RTLD_DEEPBIND is needed due to #4998. It turns out that empty_rep_storage is not in the binary for PROPER builds, however. This is because PROPER builds use '-fPIC', which is required for "code that is suitable for dynamic linking" - our use case! If we are going to keep the CLASSAD_USER_LIBS mechanism (and hence CLASSAD_USER_PYTHON_MODULES), we'll have to add -fPIC to the UW build.

title: Ticket #7443: privately mount /dev/shm for vanilla universe jobs
description: CHTC single-node openmpi jobs are failing because they write files to /dev/shm, and mmap them. If more than one job of this type lands on the same machine, they can collide with each other and cause problems. Also, if the job is rm'd, the files are left behind in /dev/shm and aren't cleaned up. This ticket will add support for privately mounting /dev/shm for each job. This will give each job its own view to /dev/shm, and automatically clean it up no matter how the job exits. Just in case users want a shared /dev/shm, the knob MOUNT_PRIVATE_DEV_SHM can be set to false to disable this. Defaults to true.

title: Ticket #6252: TIMER_NEVER broken on 32-bit systems
description: Passing TIMER_NEVER as a period is supposed to result in a timer that fires once and only once, but is not automatically destroyed later (because you know you'll need it again, just not when). condor_timer_manager.h defines TIMER_NEVER as const unsigned TIMER_NEVER = 0xffffffff; On systems where 'unsigned' is a 32-bit value, that results in all the code in timer_manager.cpp that adds Timer.period to Timer.when overflowing. (Timer.when is a time_t, which is a 32-bit signed word on 32-bit systems). Since this causes the timer to sort to the front of the timer list ('when' became a second smaller), it immediately gets called again; this causes an infinite loop. The user-visible effect is, for instance, that condor_annex hangs.

A better patch would check for overflows everywhere, but this one seems to work. 2017-May-09 17:15:17 by tannenba: CODE REVIEW Perhaps the attached patch is not comprehensive, but it is surgical, fixes the immediate problem, and should not regress anything. Please commit to v8_6-branch, thanks! 2017-May-14 15:42:30 by tlmiller: Since we don't currently build condor_annex on any of the 32-bit platforms we release, and condor_annex was the only externally-visible problem we (or as far as we know, anyone else) had noticed, I'm thinking this doesn't need a version history item.

title: Ticket #6747: output and error files cannot be absolute paths on Windows
description: The filename remapping code treats \ as an escape character in order to support = or ; in a filename. We should fix this by having the remapping code only strip \ when followed by = or ;.

title: Ticket #4280: Slot config needs new features to support async stageout
description: New capabilities are needed in the STARTD configuration to support transfer slots for asynchronous configuration small resource usage, especially < 1 CPU designating which transfer slot belongs to which normal (execute) slot option to have transfer slots not advertised to the collector ability to configure START, PREEMPT and other expressions separately for each slot type. We will achieve this with new configuration option for SLOT_TYPE_<n>, and several new knobs with a SLOT_TYPE_<n> prefix. SLOT_TYPE_<n> = minimal triggers new behavior in the resource allocator. Assignment of fractional CPU will be allowed, and fractional CPU values will not be accounted for in the determination of whether there are enough CPUs for the requested slots. minimal can be used the same way that auto is, either as the only slot definition, or as just one of a set of resource options for SLOT_TYPE_<n>. For instance the amount of disk & memory may be explicitly specified while the minimal keyword is used to permit fractional CPU assignment. SLOT_TYPE_2 = minimal, memory=100 disk=auto SLOT_TYPE_<n>_PAIRED_WITH = SLOT_TYPE_<x> causes each slot of type <n> to be assigned a pair slot of type <x> when the slot is created. This relationship is advertised in all of the slots, type <n> and type <x> in the attribute SlotPairName SLOT_TYPE_<n>_VISIBLE = false tells the STARTD to not advertise slots of type <n> to the Collector. These slots will still be returned to a condor_status -direct query. SLOT_TYPE_<n>_NAME_PREFIX = xfer will create slots of type <n> will names that begin with "xfer" instead of the default of "slot". This feature is nice to have but not strictly necessary. It may be removed if it turns out that there are parts of HTCondor that depend on the prefix being "slot". SLOT_TYPE_<n>_<knob> = <expr> where <knob> is one of the config knobs that control slot matchmaking behavior: START, SUSPEND, CONTINUE, PREEMPT, KILL, WANT_SUSPEND, WANT_VACATE, RANK WANT_HOLD, WANT_HOLD_REASON, WANT_HOLD_SUBCODE, CLAIM_WORKLIFE, MaxJobRetirementTime, MachineMaxVacateTime, PERIODIC_CHECKPOINT, SUSPEND_VANILLA, CONTINUE_VANILLA, PREEMPT_VANILLA, KILL_VANILLA, WANT_SUSPEND_VANILLA, WANT_VACATE_VANILLA, START_BACKFILL, EVICT_BACKFILL, ATTR_FETCH_WORK_DELAY, SLOT_WEIGHT, SlotWeight, IsOwner, CpuBusy It is expected that these new features will be used to create transfer slots using a configuration similar to the following. NUM_SLOTS_TYPE_1 = $(NUM_CPUS) NUM_SLOTS_TYPE_2 = $(NUM_SLOTS_TYPE_1) SLOT_TYPE_2_PAIRED_WITH = SLOT_TYPE_1 SLOT_TYPE_2_VISIBLE = false SLOT_TYPE_2_NAME_PREFIX = xfer SLOT_TYPE_2_START = undefined SLOT_TYPE_2 = minimal, memory=100 disk=auto Here is a file to use with condor_status -print-format to see slot pairs # condor_status query for slot pairs, use with condor_status -direct to see hidden pairs. SELECT Machine WIDTH AUTO splitslotname(Name)[0] AS SlotName WIDTH -8 IfThenElse(SlotPairName isnt undefined,splitslotname(SlotPairName)[0],"-") AS Paired Strcat(Arch,"_",IfThenElse(OpSys=="WINDOWS",OpSysShortName,OpSysAndVer)) AS Platform Cpus AS Cpus PRINTF "%.3f" # IfThenElse(GPUs isnt undefined,GPUs,0) AS GPUs PRINTF "%4d" Memory WIDTH 6 Disk WIDTH 8 EnteredCurrentActivity AS " StatusTime" PRINTAS ACTIVITY_TIME NOPREFIX Strcat(State,"/",Activity) AS Status WIDTH -14 TRUNCATE ifthenelse(JobId isnt undefined, JobId, "") AS JobID

title: Ticket #1578: Removing jobs via SOAP interface does not set terminal status on job
description: The history file contains jobs with their JobStatus set to non-terminal values if you use the SOAP interface to remove a job the status of the job in the history file remains as it was when the job was removed. It's not set to C or X, which is what happens if you remove a job condor_rm. Example: >condor_history 48.10 ID OWNER SUBMITTED RUN_TIME ST COMPLETED CMD 48.10 Administrator 8/12 22:44 0+00:00:00 I ??? \\htpc\nas\jobs And for a held job: >condor_q 48.16 -- Submitter: winxpcm : <192.168.0.173:4501> : winxpcm ID OWNER SUBMITTED RUN_TIME ST PRI SIZE CMD 48.16 Administrator 8/12 22:44 0+00:00:00 H 0 0.0 run.bat -- sanity check to make sure there's nothing about job in the history file -- >condor_q 48.16 -- Submitter: winxpcm : <192.168.0.173:4501> : winxpcm ID OWNER SUBMITTED RUN_TIME ST PRI SIZE CMD -- job was removed via the SOAP interface -- >condor_history 48.16 ID OWNER SUBMITTED RUN_TIME ST COMPLETED CMD 48.16 Administrator 8/12 22:44 0+00:00:00 ??? \\htpc\nas\jobs Technically all jobs in the history file should be jobs that are in terminal states. Easy to reproduce: put jobs in queue, issue SOAP calls to remove them when they are in states other than queued. Only tested, reproduced on WinXP so far. Looks like the SOAP remove is just missing: jobStatus = REMOVED; jobAd->Assign(ATTR_JOB_STATUS, jobStatus); Before AppendHistory() is called. I'm attaching a history file that shows jobs in states not terminal in it.

title: Ticket #3115: Slow Condor tests when hostname != FQDN.
description: This stems from a problem where tests on exec-13 would run slowly enough to cause time-out failures. This problem started on the same day as the upgrade from RH 6.2 to 6.3, but may have been only tangentially related. One symptom (or perhaps cause) of the slow tests was the personal condor reporting slots as slot1@exec-13, not slot1@exec-13.batlab.org, as the main/C1 Condor -- the one reporting the BaTLab collector -- was doing. We were unable to isolate the problem, but examining the 32-bit version of the same platform revealed that its /etc/sysconfig/network file was setting the hostname to the FQDN. Making this change and rebooting exec-13 corrected the symptom; TJ will know shortly if it corrected the slowness as well.

title: Ticket #5491: Negotiator should advertise accounting ads to collector
description: The negotiator internally keeps information about each submitter in the accountant. This is information that condor_userprio and condor_q -analyze query. Information about each submitter includes their effective priority, priority factor, current usage, etc. This information really belongs in the collector, where it can be forwarded to the gangliad for monitoring, and more efficiently queried, instead of querying the frequently busy (and single threaded) collector. To keep the memory used by the collector bounded, we will not forward information about every submitter ever seen (which the accountant stores), but only for active submitters.

title: Ticket #3816: Have example use cases
description: Note: I'm not sure whether this is something that should be in the Wiki or the actual HTCondor manual. Anyhow, this comes out of a discussion from a meeting today with Miron and people from BMRB (this is a request from Miron). Miron wants to add a bunch of uses case examples that we can point people at. These would have details of how people got their particular application running on HTCondor. An example might be, "I have a bunch of analysis jobs that each take 48 hours to run, and I want to run 1000 of them". So details would be stuff like, "how did they actually get their jobs to run on HTCondor at all"; "how did the break the 48 hour chunks up into smaller pieces"; "how big were the input and output files, and how did they deal with them"; "how did the fit the whole thing into some kind of DAG", 'here's a problem to watch out for", etc., etc. The goal would be to eventually have a number of these, each representing a fairly common case, that we could point a new HTCondor user to and say, "Okay, here's an example of how someone did something similar to your use case." I think Miron sees these being developed by talking to actual HTCondor users and finding out what they had to do to get their stuff to run.

title: Ticket #3861: automatically detect NVIDIA/CUDA GPU resources
description: This can be an inventory discovery script as outlined in #2905 or another mechanism, but the goal is to avoid the need for Condor administrators to manually configure NVIDIA GPU resources and CUDA environment variables. This will make life easier for administrators -- but equally importantly, it will establish a consistent naming scheme for users to address these resources. (E.g., right now on the LDG, every site has its own bespoke GPU naming and environmental conventions users have to sort out.) [Note: #3862 is an equivalent ticket for Intel MIC resources.]

title: Ticket #32: Replace MAX_CLAIM_ ALIVES_MISSED with DEFAULT_CLAIM_ LEASE_DURATION
description: (Replaces Drupal 1648 (backup) 1648 (public)) MAX_CLAIM_ALIVES_MISSED is almost never used in Condor. When it is, it’s behavior is surprising. Claim leases on startds default to job_lease_duration/JobLeaseDuration (from the job). job_lease_duration defaults to 20 minutes. If and only if job_lease_duration is missing is MAX_CLAIM_ALIVES_MISSED used. (A user can use job_lease_duration=0 to get this behavior.) In that case, the claim lease duration is MAX_CLAIM_ALIVES_MISSED*current_alive_interval_on_schedd. The current alive interval on the schedd changes! It starts at ALIVE_INTERVAL, but if the current value is ever larger than the job_lease_duration/3 of a starting job, it is permanently lowered (until the schedd restarts). So, MAX_CLAIM_ALIVES_MISSED is a multiplier based on a number that is actually under the control of user job submissions! So this knob will almost never be used, and when it is used it’s hard to guess exactly what it means. Documenting it is clearly is difficult because so many parts are involved. Proposed change: remove MAX_CLAIM_ALIVES_MISSED. When the schedd send the current alive interval, the startd should ignore it. Replace the c_lease_duration calculations in condor_startd.V6/claim.C where multiplies max_claim_alives_missed against the new_alive/c_aliveint with a simple PARAM for DEFAULT_CLAIM_LEASE_DURATION. Now the documentation is straightforward: the claim lease is the job_lease_duration; if not present DEFAULT_CLAIM_LEASE_DURATION is used.

title: Ticket #2323: Clear nmi externals cache daily
description: On several occasions, code changes related to the externals that broke the build went unnoticed for a week or more due to caching of the externals on the nmi machines. In order to reduce the chance of this happening, we want to clear the externals cache on nmi machines once a day. Rebuilding the externals once a day shouldn't be a significant increase in usage of the machines.

title: Ticket #7121: Reduce DAGMan memory footprint by deduping strings in nodes
description: Each node defined in DAGMan contains several strings, such as the path to submit file, a working directory path, a set of VARS values. These strings often contain the same value(s) in each node. If the DAG contains tens of thousands of nodes, this duplication of the same string over and over consume a significant RAM. This ticket will simply deduplicate the submit-file and current-directory strings contained in DAG nodes by using the /src/condor_utils/stringSpace.h class. Relatedly, a child ticket also will modernize the stringSpace utility class, and yet another child ticket will dedup VARS.

Ticket #6360: per-thread keyring sessions not supported in pre 3.0.0 kernel
description: If we are using clone() to spawn shadows, kernel versions before 3.0.0 do not support creating a new session within the clone. If we detect this configuration, we should EXCEPT right away. The sysadmin can set USE_CLONE_TO_CREATE_PROCESSES = false to workaround the issue. Although that does impact performance on heavily-loaded schedds, the alternative is not being able to spawn shadows at all. The proposed patch will not allow HTCondor to start if we detect an invalid combination of kernel version, USE_KEYRING_SESSIONS, and USE_CLONE_TO_CREATE_PROCESSES. All in all, it seems like setting USE_KEYRING_SESSIONS=True on anything older than a v3.x Linux Kernel (i.e. anything older than RHEL7) is just a bad idea for several reasons, including both this ticket and the fact that creating a new session on RHEL6 is several orders of slower than on RHEL7 (on RHEL6 creating a new session takes ~7.5ms!).

title: Ticket #3498: Use relative timestamps for condor_status
description: condor_status is echoing "Communications Error" when the client's absolute (epoch) timestamp is beyond a one minute difference from the time on the collector. A discussion I had with TJ Knoeller yielded that the timestamp should be relative to the beginning of the conversation instead of based on the time of the client machine. This issue causes much confusion for users running condor_status from the command line, since "Communications Error" doesn't indicate the nature of the problem. The CollectorLog on the collector side shows the "Received an expired query" line as follows: 02/18/13 14:19:08 Received TCP command 5 (QUERY_STARTD_ADS) from unauthenticated@unmapped <128.104.101.139:59040>, access level READ 02/18/13 14:19:08 Calling HandleReq <receive_query_cedar> (0) for command 5 (QUERY_STARTD_ADS) from unauthenticated@unmapped <128.104.101.139:59040> 02/18/13 14:19:08 Got QUERY_STARTD_ADS 02/18/13 14:19:08 Received an expired query (old by 22s), ignoring 02/18/13 14:19:08 Return from HandleReq <receive_query_cedar> (handler: 0.000s, sec: 0.005s, payload: 0.000s) 02/18/13 14:19:08 Return from Handler <DaemonCommandProtocol::WaitForSocketData> 0.0051s

title: Ticket #3532: Anonymously report software metrics
description: (This is from Karan Vahi at ISI.) As part of the SI2 proposal, one of the requirements imposed on us by NSF is to track usage of the software. For Pegasus 4.2, we implemented reporting of anonymous metrics to a server at ISI in the planner. An overview of that is covered here http://pegasus.isi.edu/wms/docs/latest/funding_citing_usage.php#usage_statistics However, to close the loop we need to have metrics reporting in Condor DAGMan also. Ewa and Miron talked about it last week. He mentioned that it might be possible to implement this in DAGMan . By default in the planner we have metrics reporting turned on. However, for DAGMan it was felt that it should be enabled initially only for Pegasus workflows. That should be possible for us to do , when we launch dagman for Pegasus workflows. The configuration is controlled by an environment variable that is set in the environment. We could use that or pass a specific command line option to dagman. We have covered some metrics that will be useful for DAGMan to report. https://confluence.pegasus.isi.edu/display/pegasus/DAGMan+Metrics+Reporting

title: Ticket #6730: DAGMan should coordinate with parent JobPrio
description: There is almost no coordination between an active DAGMan instance and the scheduler universe job running it. The only time these ever talk to each other is when running the condor_submit_dag command, with the -Priority flag. For example, condor_submit_dag -Priority 500 file.dag sets an internal DAGMan member variable such that all jobs under file.dag will get submitted with JobPrio = 500. It does not, however, set the JobPrio of the scheduler universe job itself. Moreover, if we ever run condor_prio on the scheduler universe job running DAGMan, the change in priority does not trickle down into the nodes/jobs running under the DAG. We want to make the following changes: When calling condor_submit_dag -Priority N file.dag, we want to submit the scheduler universe job with priority = N When calling condor_prio or condor_qedit on the scheduler universe job, we want to communicate that change to DAGMan, and update all unsubmitted jobs with the difference in priority. The schedd should write events to the user log to communicate the change. To fully enable this functionality we need to do some additional work in the schedd to submit scheduler universe jobs in order of JobPrio. This is covered in #6703. A design document is available here: https://docs.google.com/document/d/1m6RG2Up2IqCT4Y2fKQYGD0KoPFSWqgIFgghi4WVouPE

title: Ticket #4218: Merge gridmanager's queries of job ads from schedd
description: The gridmanager makes two different queries of job ads to the schedd. One is for new jobs the gridmanager should be managing. The other is looking for jobs managed by the gridmanager whose status has changed to Held, Removed, or Completed (and the gridmanager needs to react to that change). The second query is done on every connection to the schedd. The first is done on startup and whenever the schedd sends an ADD_JOBS or REMOVE_JOBS signal to the gridmanager. These two queries could be combined, so that the schedd only has to iterate once over the job queue.

title: Ticket #3477: Keypairs of EC2 jobs may not be cleaned up.
description: It is permissible for an EC2 job to go on hold without deleting its keypair. (The keypair may belong to the user; or the user may wish to use the keypair; or the keypair should be left active to avoid invalidating a spot request.) When such a job enters recovery, we correctly avoid recreating the keypair. However, we do not set the flag which marks the keypair as created; so when the job eventually leaves the queue, we don't clean the keypair up. It is presently problematic to determine from the job ad if we created the keypair. This fix will have three parts: (1) Prevent the user from specifying both a keypair name and a filename for saving the created keypair. Since this options are mutually exclusive, this won't cause any problems. (2) Now that we know both keypair name and filename can be set only when we created a keypair, use that information to determine when to remove a keypair from the cloud. (3) If and only if the job we see in GM_DELETE is exiting the queue (for good), delete the on-disk copy of the keypair. This allows the user to (potentially) access the instance started by the held job.
remarks: 2013-Feb-20 16:07:19 by jfrey: Code Review I think the keypair cleanup code in GM_DELETE is too aggressive. When is it OK to destroy a keypair on the EC2 server without interfering with instances that want to use that keypair? It's entirely possible for a job to end up in GM_DELETE state after the instance has been requested but before the server has started it, and for the job to be healthly and recoverable and will be seen by the gridmanager in the near future. 2013-Feb-21 15:13:05 by tlmiller: After discussion with Jaime, the code will be amended to be much less aggressive: only remove keypairs from the server under the same conditions as from disk. Discussion, however, revealed the problem discussed in the child ticket (#3508).

title: Ticket #1919: support streaming output in condor_q to reduce memory usage
description: condor_q reads all ads into memory before generating any output. This is intended to prevent the schedd from getting blocked by condor_q being blocked on output. However, this also means that very large queues require a lot of memory for condor_q, even if all it is doing is dumping the ads to a file. If memory runs low and swapping results, then the schedd can get blocked anyway. We ran into this problem on glow.cs.wisc.edu. condor_q is periodically run to monitor demand. The code that measures demand carefully avoids ever needing to have all of the jobs in memory, but it relies on condor_q to fetch the ads and dump them in a file, so any schedd with a large job queue can cause trouble. Proposed Solution Add -stream-results option to condor_q. This will cause it to generate output as each ad is fetched.

title: Ticket #2266: Condor should optionally enforce rlimits on RAM, file size
description: Condor should optionally set various rlimits on jobs to provide a weak limitation on misbehavior. Possibilities: Set to Memory*1024*1024. This won't stop a multi-process job from using more memory than advertised, but it does provide a bit of limiting behavior. All of these may be limited to 2GB on 32-bit machines! RLIMIT_AS - virtual memory (address space) RLIMIT_DATA - data segment (probably redundant given RLIMIT_AS) RLIMIT_RSS - resident set size (probably redundant given RLIMIT_AS. Also ignored on modern Linux) RLIMIT_STACK - stack size (probably redundant given RLIMIT_AS. Probably silly) Set to Disk*1024 RLIMIT_FSIZE - Maximum size of a single file. title: Ticket #1299: scheduler jobs can start during schedd shutdown
description: When in shutdown mode, the schedd still calls StartLocalJobs() in the poorly named schedd houskeeping function scheduler::timeout(). This allows scheduler universe jobs to start up, which can lead to a cycle of killing and restarting scheduler jobs until the graceful shutdown time finally expires. Local universe jobs get queued to start but the runnable job queue is not processed while in shutdown mode, so they don't actually run. To reproduce, submit 20 scheduler universe jobs that sleep for an hour. Set SCHEDD_INTERVAL=5. Run condor_off -schedd. Rather than exiting within ~20 seconds, the schedd keeps killing and restarting the scheduler jobs until the graceful shutdown time expires.

title: Ticket #1763: disk usage not correctly monitored in privsep mode
description: If a job creates a directory that is not accessible to the condor user, then disk usage is not correctly monitored in privsep (or glexec) mode. The following type of error appears in the starter logs: 11/04 13:51:57 (pid:31610) Can't open directory "/scratch/condor/var/lib/condor/execute/dir_17225/glide_c17435/execute/dir_31610/cms_XEaGVGH32545" as PRIV_CONDOR, errno: 13 (Permission denied) The error could be avoided by monitoring disk usage by launching a separate process that runs under the same account as the job. However, it is unfortunate that in this case the job could mess with the monitoring process. To avoid that, one would need to run the monitoring process with real user id root and effective user id of the job. I'm not aware of any existing feature of glexec that would support this. Note that this problem can also happen in the non-privsep case if the job creates a directory that the job user itself does not have permission to access and condor is not running as root (or the filesystem does root squashing). Solving that would require changing permissions on the directory, which is not ideal.

title: Ticket #1333: GSI cert settings ignore config settings from environment
description: Setting _CONDOR_GSI_DAEMON_TRUSTED_CA_DIR and/or _CONDOR_GSI_DAEMON_DIRECTORY in the environment does not override configuration file settings for condor tools such as condor_status or condor_q. This is caused by the placement of the call to condor_auth_config() before the loading of configuration settings from the environment. Furthermore, setting X509_CERT_DIR has no effect on condor tools, contrary to the manual. This change appears to be a side-effect of the addition of ALLOW/DENY_CLIENT in 7.1.0. We needed tools to look for the map file in the same default location as daemons do, and we accidentally also made tools share code with the daemon for finding the trusted CA directory. We could revert to the old behavior in which tools rely on X509_CERT_DIR to find their trusted certificates. However, it is tempting instead to continue having tools and daemons share the same configuration. If we decide to do that, then the following things need to be fixed: configuration settings need to be settable from the environment, as normal [DONE in 7.4.3] GSI_DAEMON_DIRECTORY and GSI_DAEMON_TRUSTED_CA_DIR both have 'DAEMON' in their name, which makes them unsuitable for being the settings that apply to both daemons and tools. Perhaps we could just remove 'DAEMON' from the name. The old settings could be preserved for backward compatibility. the manual needs to be updated

title: Ticket #6049: Race condition at job exit causes errors in StarterLog
description: When a job exits normally, the starter first transfers the output sandbox back to the shadow (if needed), then sends a remote system call to the shadow to inform it the job is done and the exit code. The starter then waits for the startd to kill it. The shadow deactivates the claim on the startd, and either exits, or virtually exits, and grabs another job from the schedd. In either case, it closes the syscall socket. When the startd gets the deactivate claim message from the shadow, it kills the starter. However, the starter also tries to detect a disconnected shadow or broken network by listening on the syscall socket and putting it into daemon core's select loop. If it goes hot, we assume the socket is closed, and go into disconnected mode. The race condition is if the shadow exits (and closes the syscall socket) before the starter is killed, the starter will log a confusing warning, go into disconnected mode, before getting killed. To fix this, we will unregister the syscall socket from select before we send the final exit rsc to the shadow.

title: Ticket #1108: Improving the locking situation of the logging systems
description: The different logging systems have different file locking strategies for log file access and rotation. Some of them cause problems in shared file systems (such as NFS). The goal is to design the new unified logging system in a way, such that locking does not constitute a point of failure anymore. A quick overview of the current locking strategies: History files : - write : No actual locking. Solely a reference counter assures that all started write processes will also be finished before closing. - AppendHistory(ClassAd *) // condor_c++_util/classadHistory.cpp -> OpenHistoryFile() // -- " -- -> safe_open_wrapper (if not open yet) + refCount increase -> fwrite -> RelinquishHistoryFile() : decrease of refCount after successfully finished write process - CloseHistoryFile() : makes sure that refCount is 0 - rotation : File is simply renamed. This assures that the file is closed at the time (therefore the last write process was finished; otherwise it wouldn't be closed, according to the close-file semantics) - int rotate_file(const char *old_filename, const char *new_filename) ( condor_util_lib/rotate_file.c ) dprintf : - write : mutex/critical section for every write process; seems to have a queue for waiting messages - rotation : rename of the old file; creation of a new one Event-/User-Logs : - write : Event file is opened with either locking en- or disabled. If enabled, a lock file is created that indicates that the file is accessed. If disabled, a fake lock will be created to simplify API usage; no effect on read/write access. ( condor_c++_util/write_user_log.cpp ) - WriteUserLog::openFile( const char *file, bool log_as_user, bool use_lock, bool append, FileLockBase *&lock, FILE *&fp ) -> uses condor_includes/file_lock.h API for creating a lock file and managing thereof - Write processes in WriteUserLog class obtain a WRITE_LOCK prior to writing to the file. - rotation : separate lock file (same API) as for "write". The lock file is already created in the Configure() process and cannot be turned off (makes sense). An actual lock status is obtained during the write process before rotation takes place (the actual rotation function does not deal with locking) and released after. BENCHMARKS average dprintf call with locking (personal Condor): 0.03 ms Event logs (average) including write process (personal Condor) : 0.13 ms (max values around 1 ms) API suggestions Essentially two options: either stick to integrated logging functions of one logging class or let a separate logging daemon handle all logging-related things. (1) Logging daemon: - Pro: Locking question becomes obsolete, because only one process will ever access file - Con: Daemon independence is not guaranteed; what happens if logging daemon is down? Assumption: something like syslog will manage the logging itself; therefore it is possible to forward log messages to another host Logd(); Init(Type, Level, Location = NULL) // whereas location could also be another host; NULL default means local // Level is the max level that will be written (according to D_ALWAYS, D_FULLDEBUG, ... ) // Type: Which process requests logging (History, Daemon dprintf (Schedd, Shadow,...), EventLog...) int Write(Type, Level, Msg) // write message Read(...) // Read function .. will be more complex. TODO: Which args would be necessary? Close(Type) // Finishing log process Open questions: How to track number of log entries that will be discarded by deleting old log files in order to not exceed disk space? How to prevent daemons from waiting for logd to come up or to stop working or to just discard log messages in case logd is failing? (2) Integrated logging functions: Problem: Locking needs to be taken care of -> how to avoid a) deadlocks, b) incompatibilities of different file systems/ interactions of different OS
remarks: 2010-Jan-20 09:50:57 by tstclair: It is highly unlikely for a logging daemon such as syslog to go down, as most if not all systems heavily rely on it. I believe there is recovery built in, but it should be verified independently. 2010-Oct-20 16:03:30 by jfrey: Bulk change of target version from v070504 to v070505 using ./ticket-target-mover. 2011-Jan-27 14:46:04 by danb: Bulk change of target version from v070505 to v070506 using ./ticket-target-mover. 2011-Feb-01 14:49:30 by tannenba: Bulk change of target version from v070506 to NULL using ./ticket-target-mover. 2011-Aug-16 14:47:55 by cweiss: Even though this is probably a never-ending story, I'll go ahead and close this ticket. If more work in this area is going to be done, this ticket can be a reference.

title: Ticket #3135: Specify dependencies in the schedd
description: We would like the schedd to support simple job dependency workflows.
remarks: 2012-Sep-27 15:01:27 by wenger: My first question with this is, "What is the use case?". The main case where I can see that this would really provide an advantage over what we already have is when a user submits a job, and then later wants to submit another job that depends on the first one. I've had users request something similar to this -- basically, "Can I make a DAG where the first job is already running?" I'm kind of skeptical whether this would allow us to simplify the DAGMan implementation -- all of the existing dependency code would have to be there in case jobs have scripts, retries, etc., but then we'd have some extra code that would take advantage of the schedd dependencies. Also, if DAGMan did the "submit everything and exit" mode of operation, you'd lose the capability to delete an entire workflow by condor_rm'ing the DAGMan job. And I don't think it would work for nested DAGs, either. So if DAGMan did have this capability, we'd have to have a flag to disable it. Another thing to think about is error handling -- a big part of the DAGMan code is for dealing with errors, so if we're going to implement this I think we should get a pretty good handle on the error conditions we'd have to deal with. For example, what if a job specifies a parent ID that doesn't exist? What if a job is submitted with dependencies but then manually released? I guess one possibility is that we'd implement this functionality, but not necessarily have DAGMan take advantage of it. My thought at this point, though, is that I'd like some more specifics about what we think we'll gain from doing is, and also at least an idea of how elaborate the error handling will have to get. 2012-Oct-20 05:26:43 by matt: Four use cases where this request appears - First, desire for full materialization of a DAG within the Schedd. The benefit here is all jobs in a workflow are readily available within the queue for inspection. All jobs can be managed and monitored with standard tools without having an extra step of processing the dag file to figure out what is yet to come. For instance, how close is a dag to completion using standard tools? Second, DAG editing, with full materialization of a dag within the schedd, the dependency relationships can be modified. Right now that modification requires stopping dagman, changing the dag, restarting dagman. Third, team collaboration, when one user has a workflow that needs to depend on another user's workflow, or a specific step in another user's workflow. Fourth, scheduler migration, simply users who are used to this functionality within other schedulers and do not want to move to dagman when moving to condor. 2012-Oct-20 05:56:28 by matt: First blush comments on design - Avoid using the HOLD state. Using hold will introduce noise into a state the provides valuable signal about jobs that cannot run, often because of errors, and require manual intervention. Instead, add a new policy that defines if a job is runnable. The job would remain Idle, but not be considered for execution until the policy expression evaluated to true. Note: this functionality could eventually be used for cron jobs as well. Another reason not to piggyback on Hold and PERIODIC_RELEASE is the rate at which PERIODIC_RELEASE is evaluated. Job runnability wrt dependencies should be edge triggered, i.e. when dependencies completes a job should immediately be runnable. The process of updating child jobs can also reevaluate their runnability without having to process the entire potential PERIODIC_RELEASE set, which is everything based on how periodic policies are implemented. Consider what will happen if a big dag user, O(10K+) nodes, tries to use this functionality instead of DAGMan. For instance, ChildJobs w/ O(1000) entries. If you don't want people to replace DAGMan with this functionality, provide information/guidance what a workflow looks like that should use DAGMan instead, e.g. if you want pre/post, if you have more than 100 children per node, etc. For users, jobs ids are only ClusterId.ProcId. Technically there's a third component that DAGMan can see, but it does not have to be exposed to users. It will also be .0 in all cases. A simplification would be to have ParentJob_110_0_JobStatus instead of Exit* attributes, but I can see how Exit* may be easier to manage (attr mirroring happens less frequently) and provide more information. Some conditions to consider: parent not in queue when child submitted (error or assume completed?), parent removed from queue without running (remove child? hold child as never runnable, an error?), dependency modification (multiple qedits) won't be atomic, dependency modifications on a running job (add parent when child is starting) condor_q -analyze will need to learn about jobs dependencies. Teaching it about a runnable policy will be cleaner than teasing the information out of Hold. 2012-Oct-22 13:15:11 by tstclair: I think you could be opening pandoras box. Why not just use JobPrio, because you still can't get cross schedd deps without a massive snafu, and JobPrio should ensure "relative" ordering within a single schedd. 2012-Dec-11 16:38:39 by johnkn: Bulk change of target version from v070902 to v070903 using ./ticket-target-mover.

title: Ticket #7526: Shadow wrongly does not recogize or log JOB_NOT_STARTED.
description: In BaseShadow::logEvictEvent(), we check for JOB_CKPTED, JOB_NOT_CKPTED, and JOB_KILLED; if the evict reason isn't one of those, we don't log it, claiming the reason is unknown. This log message -- and absence of a log entry -- can regularly occur if the schedd starts a job's shadow before the previous occupant of that slot has finished evicting, because the eviction reason in that case is JOB_NOT_STARTED. Until we rearchitect the startd, this race condition is unavoidable; but since we explicitly check for it, we probably should print a scary message to the log and not tell the user what happened.

title: Ticket #7033: Job lease not updated in shadow
description: A code change in 8.7.4 accidentally removed the shadow's updating of the timestamp on when it last heard from the starter. Thus, when a disconnect happens, the shadow acts as if it last heard from the starter when the job began execution.
remarks: 2019-May-15 11:23:00 by jfrey: This bug does not affect reconnecting after a restart of the schedd. This is because the schedd updates LastJobLeaseRenewal for all running jobs periodically (every 5 minutes). The bug only affects a shadow that experiences a closing of its network connection to the starter. 2019-May-15 14:11:49 by jfrey: The whole job lease machinery of the schedd and shadow should be revisited. Both the schedd and the shadow are updating LastJobLeaseRenewal. Since the shadow's updates are delayed, the value in the job ad can jump backwards to any earlier time. Also, the schedd sets this attribute to the current time for every single running job. This is basically an "I was alive at time X" marker. It should be able to store this timestamp once persistently. This also applies to the WallClockCheckpoint attribute. We should consider removing all of the machinery for supporting the older job lease protocols, like the schedd sending alive messages and the startd sending alive messages while the starter is alive. 2019-May-15 15:49:51 by jfrey: Another update: This bug will affect reconnecting after a schedd restart, but only for some of the shadows. When the shadow wants to set LastJobLeaseRenewal to the current time because it heard from the starter, it instead re-sets the existing value (from an unuqdated last_job_lease_renewal variable). ClassAds marks the attribute as dirty, even though the value is unchanged. On the next periodic push of changed attributes to the schedd (every 15 minutes by default), the old value for LastJobLeaseRenewal is included. If this periodic push occurs between the schedd's last update of LastJobLeaseRenewal and its restart, then the job will be affected by this bug. 2019-May-15 16:00:13 by gthain: CODE REVIEW All is good.

[root@ip-172-31-1-111 config.d]# condor_config_val -v CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES VALUE Not defined: CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES # at: /etc/condor/config.d/01gpus.config, line 3 # raw: CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES = $ENV(CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES:) VALUE = "defined" # at: /etc/condor/config.d/01gpus.config, line 5 # raw: VALUE = "defined" [root@ip-172-31-1-111 config.d]# CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=foo condor_config_val -v CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES VALUE CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES = foo # at: /etc/condor/config.d/01gpus.config, line 3 # raw: CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES = $ENV(CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES:) VALUE = "defined" # at: /etc/condor/config.d/01gpus.config, line 5 # raw: VALUE = "defined" We'd like to understand this behaviour. It appears to be checking if CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES is in the hashtable, not if it's empty. TJ suspects there's a whitespace trimming issue. empty as a conditional that either (a) is what we expect defined = to be or (b) like =defined, but succeeds on whitespace-only variables. environment as a conditional that combines the call to $ENV() -- with the unexpectedly required trailing colon -- with the defined / empty conditional. Changing $ENV() to not return UNDEFINED (but rather the empty string), or adding another expansion that behaves that way. something else I don't recall right ATM.

title: Ticket #6788: Add process family security session
description: There should be a pre-made security session shared between all daemons in a process tree (e.g. amongst a master and all of its descendants). It would work like the existing session between parent and child daemons, but apply to all daemons in the same family. A daemon whose real uid is different its parent's would not inherit this family session. When a daemon attempts to connect to another daemon, it first checks whether it has a security session specific to that peer. If it does, then it uses that session, as it does today. Otherwise, it would attempt to use the family security session if both are using the same shared port daemon or, if shared port is disabled, if both are on the same machine. If the family session is rejected, the daemon would fall back to negotiating a new security session. This would simplify making Condor secure out of the box. No security settings would needed to be set for a single-node Condor setup to be secure, without interfering with admins configuring the security settings themselves.

title: Ticket #6272: condor_q reports wrong totals for materialized jobs
description: Wrong totals are visible only when CONDOR_Q_SHOW_OLD_SUMMARY is false, which is not the default in 8.7.1. Thus, this is (mostly) a bug that was invisible to users before. But when CONDOR_Q_SHOW_OLD_SUMMARY is false, and a late-materialize job is submitted, the total for idle jobs will not show any of the materialized idle jobs, and when those jobs go to the running state, the count of idle jobs will be decremented. This results in a low, or even negative count of idle jobs.
remarks: 2017-May-19 13:30:56 by johnkn: While chasing this bug. I realized that CommitTransaction in qmgmt.cpp will start a new transaction for jobs that have just been submitted in the hold-for-job-spooling state. This nested transaction breaks the transaction triggers callback mechanism which is used to track jobs changing state and to update per-job-state counters. The particular work done by this nested transaction doesn't change the job state, but this is still a potential problem for future transaction trigger'd callbacks, so work done in the nested transaction will instead by moved into the same function that currently does job transforms and submit requirements. This will cause the changes to happen before the current transaction is committed. Only creation of the job spool directory will happen (as it does now) after the transaction is committed.

title: Ticket #6858: Pass credentials through to the file transfer plugin
description: After much discussion at the SciTokens retreat, we came up with the following scheme for specifying a particular HTTPS file transfer should be done with a given credential: Each credential foo is contained in a file in $_CONDOR_CREDS/foo.use. If a user wants to specify the HTTPS transfer https://download.com/bar needs the foo credential, then they specify the URL foo+https://download.com/bar. The schedd and starter do matching of the file transfer plugins based on everything right of the +. That is, it forces foo+https:// URLs to match with a plugin advertising https support. The corresponding HTTPS plugin is responsible for locating and using the correct credentials in the $_CONDOR_CREDS directory. We work with the facilitators to determine whether users would prefer to write transfer_input_files = foo+https://download.com/bar or have a simpler alias of foo_input_files = https://download.com/bar ,. If necessary, the latter would be transformed into the former by the submit library.

title: Ticket #4865: cream_gahp fails at startup due to native package Globus
description: In the cream_gahp, Globus uses lt_dlopen() to load a thread library. lt_dlopen() ignores the executable's RPATH, so it won't find the copy of the library that we include in UW builds of HTCondor. In #4440, we attempted to solve this problem by using dlopen() to load the library at the top of main(). lt_dlopen() would then use the already-loaded copy of the library. It turns out this only works if lt_dlopen() can't find the library in all of the places where it looks. If it finds a copy of the library under /usr/lib, it will load that copy of the library, in addition to the copy loaded by dlopen(). In the UW native packages for HTCondor, the RPATH is set to prefer libraries in /usr/lib/condor over any in /usr/lib. If Globus libraries are installed in /usr/lib, then the cream_gahp ends up using Globus libraries in /usr/lib/condor plus the Globus thread library in /usr/lib. The Globus libraries from EPEL appear to be incompatible with those we distribute with HTCondor. With Globus libraries from EPEL and the UW RPM of Condor 8.3.2 installed, the cream_gahp fails on startup with this error: dlsym: /usr/lib64/libglobus_thread_pthread.so: undefined symbol: globus_extension_module We can fix this by modifying the RPATH in our native linux packages to explicitly list /usr/lib before /usr/lib/condor. Then, the cream_gahp and other HTCondor binaries will use Globus libraries in /usr/lib if they are present. The tarball release already works this way.
