title: Ticket #5777: Procapi flooding Mac OS system log due to SIP
description: We have a report from htcondor-users that the condor_procd on Mac OS X El Capitan swamps the system log with errors about denying attempted operations. We believe this is due to procapi calling task_for_pid() on every process in the system to get memory and cpu usage. This call is not allowed for processes protected by SIP (System Integrity Protection). The user also reports reboots and process freezes that may be related. HTCondor can be more intelligent about this. It doesn't need to collect cpu/memory usage on processes that it doesn't manage. If we can identify processes protected by SIP and avoid calling task_for_pid() on them, I believe that would fix this problem.
remarks: 2016-Jul-07 15:12:07 by jfrey: This was reported by kkauder@gmail.com on June 23, 2016. The email subject line was 'El Capitan and Sandbox'. Post a followup on htcondor-users when we have a fix ready. 2016-Jul-15 11:29:37 by jfrey: This is a bit more complicated than I thought. All executables in /bin and /usr/bin are protected by SIP, thus all instances of them are protected, no matter what user they're running as. So a user job started by HTCondor that's a shell script can't be queried. 2016-Jul-22 16:26:22 by jfrey: The function proc_pid_rusage() does what we need. It allows you to query user and system cpu time and memory usage for a given process, including those protected by SIP. But it was added in Mac OS X 10.9. So we'll need to drop support for older versions or do a fallback. 2016-Sep-28 13:53:00 by tim: CODE REVIEW: I approve this change. (I had one question as to how the units were determined. Jaime did it empirically (by measurement)).

title: Ticket #1364: job queue hooks
description: Igor wants to try using Condor-C as an alternative to Globus for glidein submission. The sites need to be able to modify jobs as they are submitted. Currently, this sort of thing is done in the globus jobmanager (condor.pm). For example, OSG environment variables are inserted and the VO of the user may be looked up and inserted into the ad. The proposal is to add job queue hooks to the schedd. At the very least, a job submission hook would be needed. However, Igor proposes going a step further and having a hook that is called on every event that is logged to the user log. One way of doing things would be to make the guarantees for calling of the hooks the same as for logging of events to the user log. So if a particular event is "at least once" then the hook would also be "at least once", and if the event is best effort then the hook would also be best effort. For "at least once" we should be able to wrap together the logging of the event and the calling of the hook into a single logical transaction so that no additional syncs to the job queue are required. If there is just a single hook that is called an all types of user log events, for efficiency, we might want to provide a way to whitelist/blacklist which events result in a call to the hook. The writing of the submit event is currently being moved from condor_submit to the schedd. This is convenient for our purposes here, because we would not want hooks to be called from the user tool. They should only be called from the schedd and shadows. Question: are there places where we would want a job queue hook but where no user log event happens? Question: if the hooks are used to force the value of some job attributes, what should be done about condor_qedit? One idea would be to have a configurable whitelist/blacklist of attributes that condor_qedit can/cannot touch.
remarks: 2010-Apr-18 12:57:25 by gthain: The performance implications of running a script on every log update would require a bit of analysis. Is it possible to implement the kind of job modifications he needs in a more declarative manner? e.g. we've talked about having an XSLT like thing for classads. Perhaps the schedd could be modified to allow this kind of modification to all incoming condor-c jobs? 2010-Oct-01 11:39:05 by bbockelm: Can I bump this ticket? This is relevant to the sort of things we want to do at HCC also. We are very interested in investigating replacing our Globus-based gatekeepers with a Condor-based one where plausible. 2011-Mar-21 14:42:13 by bbockelm: Hi, After a discussion with danb, I think there's (almost) a way to implement this today: the job_router. Using SUBMIT_EXPRS and APPEND_REQUIREMENTS (assuming we move them to the condor_schedd), have all submitted jobs automatically "blacklisted" so they cannot match. Inserting an attribute or two would be very "cheap". See #1989 Use condor_job_router to perform the site contextualization / job transformation. Maybe you just want to add the OSG environment variables to the job. Maybe you want to do something drastic like move them into PBS. Because the transformation is done by a separate daemon, it is naturally rate-limiting and doesn't block the schedd. This is doable in 7.5.6. Prevent the user from coming back and doing a condor_qedit and overriding your settings. I think it's somewhat questionable this item is compatible with the "Condor philosophy" though. Brian 2015-Aug-01 20:43:54 by bbockelm: Marking as abandoned. OSG eventually went the jobrouter-based route with the HTCondor-CE. For arbitrary submit transforms, the current approach is #4804 (which doesn't involve arbitrary scripts...).

title: Ticket #701: condor_submit_dag -r documentation
description: The documentation for the "-r" option for condor_submit_dag is misleading. The following should be a correct complete replacement.: -r schedd_name Submit DAGMan to a remote schedd. The \Condor{dagman} job will not run on the local \Condor{schedd}, but on the specified schedd. This is implemented using the "-remote" option to \Condor{submit}. Note that this option does not currently specify input files for DAGMan or individual nodes to be taken along! It is assumed that any necessary files will be present on the remote computer, possibly via a shared file system between the local computer and the remote computer. It is also necessary that the user has appropriate permissions to submit a job to the remote schedd; the permissions are the same as those required to use \Condor{submit}'s -remote option. If you want other options, including transfer of other input files, consider using the -no\_submit option, modifying the resulting submit file for your needs, then using \Condor{submit} on that.

title: Ticket #1671: Detecting clock skew
description: A customer has been having problems with clock skew between his machines, especially virtual machines where that can be a problem. Condor would seem to be a in a good position to detect serious clock skew and potentially alert administrators to the problem. This might not be built into Condor, but might take the form of an external tool, perhaps doing something as simple as: condor_status -master -constraint '((MyCurrentTime-LastHeardFrom) > 60) || ((MyCurrentTime-LastHeardFrom) < -60)' Some initial investigation: The most promising existing ClassAd entries are MyCurrentTime and LastHeardFrom. MyCurrentTime is automatically added to ClassAds on their way to the collector in DaemonCore::publish (/src/condor_daemon_core.V6/daemon_core.cpp). LastHeardFrom is automatically added by the collector in CollectorEngine::updateClassAd (/src/condor_collector.V6/collector_engine.cpp). Both values are based on time(), which should be relative to the epoch in UTC. Quick testing confirms this. As such, MyCurrentTime and LastHeardFrom are appropriate as it. How will the user discover the problem? The above condor_status report run via crondor and sending email? Should the collector itself detect the situation and complain? We have developed systems in the past for monitoring ClassAds in the collector; is one appropriate here? This requires further consideration.
remarks: 2010-Sep-22 16:42:13 by adesmet: My personal opinion is that 1 is too prone to confusing administrators and third party tools, and 3 is too clever for negligible payoff. 2 seems like the best balance of benefits. 2010-Sep-22 22:50:19 by matt: time(2) should be independent of timezone 2012-Feb-01 11:32:20 by tannenba: This blog post is perhaps of interest to anyone looking at this ticket.

title: Ticket #5632: Managing per-thread security configs in python
description: CMS and ATLAS have a multi-threaded program where, in each thread, we may want to establish a remote security session with a unique credential. CMS is interested in having multiple GSI credentials in use, one per user, to submit to a variety of schedds. ATLAS is interested in having multiple pool passwords for querying different remote pools. I propose a python context manager that will set a thread-local variable specifying the current python thread's security configuration. Then, in the existing mutex for entering/exiting condor library code, we'll set/restore the config. This way, HTCondor doesn't have to understand the thread-local -- only the python binding code does. CMS will need a small tweak in the security code -- they need multiple security sessions cached per schedd (one for each CMS user). Hence, we'll need a new global in the security manager code specifying a tag. If the tag is present, we'll prepend it to the hash for security session lookup. In terms of interfaces, here's what I was thinking: with htcondor.SecMan().context() as ctx: ctx.setTag('bbockelm') ctx.setPoolPassword('foo') ctx.setGSICredential('/path/to/bar') # ... do something that needs a security session ... For any HTCondor calls inside the indented block, the ctx variable overrides the security session. Other threads are unaffected, as well as code outside the block. This work lives on the V8_5-gt5632 branch.

title: Ticket #7530: Fix negotiator diagnostic in "condor_q -analyze"
description: Starting in #3585, schedds provide resource request lists (RRL) to the negotiator -- not jobs. When a job associated with an RRL is rejected by the negotiator, the schedd makes a note of this in the job's ClassAd. condor_q -better-analyze understands this attribute and will inform the user whether or not the job has been considered by the negotiator. title: Ticket #73: Use Daemon() constructor that takes a ClassAd*, not a char*
description: The Daemon object (condor_daemon_client/daemon.*) has two constructors for initial creation. One takes a ClassAd* for the daemon to contact, the other takes a char * that is the "name". The ClassAd version has lots of smarts built it: it recognizes that a daemon may have multiple addresses (because of GCB) and can intelligently pick between them. The char* version is dumb and just connects up to the hostname/port or sinful string given. Right now this means that the GCB PRIVATE_NETWORK_NAME optimization doesn't work on these connections. It also means that future smarts (say, better handling of multi-homed machines) won't work either. So... Whenever feasible, we should use the Daemon(ClassAd*,...) constructor, not the Daemon(...,char*,...) constructor.

title: Ticket #7160: condor_history should optimize the search for a single job by id
description: condor_history can take a very long time because when operating from a constraint, it must search the entire history file looking for matches. This is made worse by the fact that parsing classad is very slow, so much so that grep of the same file is at least an order of magnitude faster than running condor_history. We could optimize the search for a single job in the history file in two ways. parse only the banner between classads and only parse the full ad when the banner matches the query. stop at the first match when the query is for a single job by id. This optimization is complicated by the fact that condor_history is always operating using a constraint expression, this is especially true for remote history. But we could analyze the constraint expression, detect when it is of the form ClusterId == <number> && ProcId == <number> and then optimize the case when the constraint expression is equivalent to this. and convert this into a search for a single job by id. We could also optimize the case when expression refers only to ClusterId ProcId and Owner, as this information is in the banner between job classads.

title: Ticket #6321: condor_annex status
description: Miron feels that condor_annex status is less confusing than condor_status -annex, so we should certainly implement the former and possibly remove the latter. We've also agreed that the unit of interest in annexes is the instance, so the default format should report on that basis. So far, so easy a pass-through (just add -annex -compact, or -const ... -compact, since condor_status just ANDs together multiple -const flags). However, the current condor_annex -status also reports on instances in the annex but not in the pool; this is valuable and should not be lost. So we have to decide how to include this information in the output.
remarks: 2017-Jun-27 16:42:50 by tlmiller: The first implementation should probably just invoke condor_status and pass the appropriate arguments through (including most of condor_annex 's). The missing instances summary should probably be printed at the bottom, so we'd have to fork() rather than exec(). Once condor_status was done, condor_annex would contact EC2 to get the full list of annex instances, and then (have to) contact the collector a second time to get the list of instances in the pool to find the difference (since it couldn't depend on the output format). One way to avoid making the second collector query would be to enforce the condor_status output format, so that condor_annex could parse it (before printing it out). This would require people who want better formatting control to use condor_status for that and then call condor_annex for the missing instances summary; even an option to suppress the per-instance data would be still result in two queries being made, so this is distinctly suboptimal. Discussion with TJ revealed four other options: Call condor_status and get a fixed format output on standard error, but the usual output on standard out; condor_annex could then parse the standard error, instead. The fixed format could be a compile-time constant, or supplied on the command line (before the other options); in either case, once set, those options would have to be immutable by further command-line options. Probably not useful for anyone else. As above, except that the fixed format is printed on standard out, separated from the usual output with a well-known (or given) separator. This would probably be a little easier to program in condor_annex, but not any more useful. Pass the data from EC2 about an annex's instances to condor_status via stdin and use a custom summary/footer format function (the ability to specify such does not presently exist) to read from it, compute the difference, and print the summary. Extremely specific to condor_annex, except, potentially, the part about specifying custom footers. Extend condor_status with a 'merge' mode: accept ads on standard in, and from the query, and a join condition. Print three differently-formatted outputs: those ads which were in both the "left" and "right" sets of ads; those ads only from standard in, and those ads only from the query. (Be sure to allow for the null format, which prints nothing.) This would be of general interest and use. condor_annex would synthesize ads for instances it found and feed them to condor_status 's standard in, specifying the join condition as the AnnexName attribute. 2017-Jun-28 14:16:01 by tlmiller: A use case for point 4: A user reported (to GregT and/or TJ) that some accounting ads were missing from the list in the collector. These ads, were, however, available directly from the negotiator, so something like $ condor_user_prio -negotiator | condor_status -any -const 'MyType == "Accounting"' -merge:left-only would have been handy to have (where the default join condition would have to be on the Name attribute). 2017-Jul-03 14:49:57 by tlmiller: Since 'condor_annex status' should report on instances that aren't currently in the pool, we need some way to identify those instances. That is, #6313's third point is actually relevant. While I'm OK with telling the user not to use an annex name as a client token prefix (that is, ignoring the possibility of mistaken identity when dealing with a name annex), I'm less happy about pulling in any instance (or spot fleet request) which matches the pattern <name>_<guid>, since it seems a pretty obvious one to use. Luckily, all instances can be tagged (max of 50 tags), and since AWS reserves the 'aws:' key prefix for itself, it makes sense to say that our users shouldn't tag things with 'htcondor:AnnexName', and use that, instead. Unluckily, while we can tag at creation time for on-demand instances, we can't yet do so via a spot fleet request. title: Ticket #3573: Execute directories left behind when privsep is in use
description: I have tracked this down and I am writing down what I learned: What we knew going in: execute directories were being left behind for some strange reason. Looking at the StarterLog, it looks like the execute directories correspond to jobs that were hard-killed (kill -9) (or maybe the power went out) -- there is no statement corresponding to the end of a job in the StarterLog. What I found out: first off, the code was doing the wrong thing. Here is a line from /etc/condor/privsep_config: valid-dirs = /var/lib/condor/execute/slot1 The code was doing a simple string comparison against this and "//var/lib/condor/execute/slot1", so the two slashes at the beginning were screwing up the comparison. Second problem, after I fixed the above: privsep was still barfing. It barfed because of the following: $ ls -ld /var/lib/condor drwxr-xr-x 4 condor condor 4096 Apr 12 00:15 /var/lib/condor Note that the owner of the directory is condor, but user condor is not in the trusted-uids list in /etc/condor/privsep_config! (The execute directories are under /var/lib/condor/execute on this machine.) Indeed the configuration is valid-caller-uids = condor valid-caller-gids = condor : 1100-1199 valid-target-uids = nobody : boinc : ghostusr : slot1 : slot2 : slot3 : slot4 : slot5 : slot6 : slot7 : slot8 : slot9 : slot10 : slot11 : slot12 : slot13 : slot14 : slot15 : slot16 : slot17 : slot18 : slot19 : slot20 : slot21 : slot22 : slot23 : slot24 : slot25 valid-target-gids = boinc : nobody: ghostusr : slot1 : slot2 : slot3 : slot4 : slot5 : slot6 : slot7 : slot8 : slot9 : slot10 : slot11 : slot12 : slot13 : slot14 : slot15 : slot16 : slot17 : slot18 : slot19 : slot20 : slot21 : slot22 : slot23 : slot24 : slot25 : 1100-1199 So I ran # chown root.root /var/lib/condor # chown root.root /var/lib/condor/execute Then I restarted the startd, and it cleaned up the execute directories. Possible solutions/workarounds: condor should be in the valid-target-* lists, or the execute directories should be owned by nobody or root.
remarks: 2013-Apr-12 09:40:17 by nwp: Pushed onto V7_9-gittrac_3573-branch, which is based off of V7_9_5-branch. Would like to get this reviewed and merged, to be released with htcondor version 7.9.5 if possible. 2013-Apr-12 09:41:19 by zmiller: the directory may end up owned by condor if for whatever reason the starter is killed while the sandbox is being staged in. the reason for this is that in PrivSep mode, the transfers are done as the condor user and then the sandbox is chowned to the real user. hence, if it gets interrupted there, the directory will still be owned by condor. i do not see any problem in adding condor to the target user list. the switchboard can only be called by the condor user. the condor user should be able to act on behalf of the condor user without any security implications. 2013-Apr-12 10:00:15 by nwp: It looks like we don't have a default privsep config in the git tree. title: Ticket #4259: examine ".throttle.io_service_bytes" instead of ".io_service_bytes"
description: I'd like to verify this a bit more, but my understanding of the blkio controller semantics is that "blkio.io_service_bytes" counts a subset of "blkio.throttle.io_service_bytes", which suggests it would be better to examine the "throttle" version. https://www.kernel.org/doc/Documentation/cgroups/blkio-controller.txt - blkio.throttle.io_service_bytes - Number of bytes transferred to/from the disk by the group. These are further divided by the type of operation - read or write, sync or async. First two fields specify the major and minor number of the device, third field specifies the operation type and the fourth field specifies the number of bytes. These numbers should roughly be same as blkio.io_service_bytes as updated by CFQ. The difference between two is that blkio.io_service_bytes will not be updated if CFQ is not operating on request queue.
remarks: 2014-Mar-14 14:37:39 by eje: I got some additional confirmation of this: <eje> ... then anything counted by blkio.io_service_bytes is also counted by the "throttle" version ? <vgoyal> yes <vgoyal> first IO passes through throttling layer and is counted <vgoyal> then it passes through CFQ and is counted again <vgoyal> so same IO shows up both in blkio.io_service_bytes as well as blkio.throttle.io_service_bytes I'm pretty sure I've caught this happening. "blkio.io_service_bytes" unpopulated and non-zero measurements in "blkio.throttle.io_service_bytes" 2014-May-21 14:21:00 by tannenba: This appears to be a bug fix to the cgroup code that went in back in 7.7 or so. If so, why is it not marked as a defect ticket and merged into v8.0? (instead was marked as enhance and put in v8.1) Also would be nice if the ticket description described the symptom of the bug, i.e. "When using cgroups, the BlockReadKbytes attribute in the job classad will be incorrect by....". For that matter, would be nice if the ticket was titled "Fix incorrect block read/write values in job classad" instead of title being an implementation detail. This is all assuming I understand what is going on here, I am not super familiar with this part of the code... Thanks.

title: Ticket #3066: create a tool to tell condor that the machine is going to sleep
description: Some pool administrators have a situation where condor is a guest on a set of machines that may be put to sleep for some reason. They need a way to ask condor to put the machine into the sleeping state in the central mananger even though condor_rooster isn't being used to put the machines to sleep. This request came from Stephen McGough at Newcastle U. He writes: We have a Windows based cluster where we have a pre-existing (to Condor) mechanism to allow computers to go to sleep when idle for longer than a set amount of time. Given that we couldn't persuade the powers that be to use the Condor mechanism to sleep computers we opted to write a small piece of code which posts a replacement class-ad to the collector (using condor_advertise) with an offline status for the box. This is obviously fragile as if Condor itself posts a new class-ad before the box enters the sleep state then the status is lost. Also if anything changes in Condor about how a resource works then our code will be broken. It would therefore be ideal if we could have a condor_sleep (or something similar) command which will set up an offline status for the resource.
creator: johnkn

title: Ticket #7475: Add a Getting Started section to the manual
description: Our manual lacks simple, clear instructions for how to get started with HTCondor. There are several different angles to consider: installing Condor, submitting your first job, setting up a basic Condor pool, possibly some basic management. The most immediate need (and reason for this ticket) is a simple guide for setting up + administering a HTCondor pool. This will be focused towards smaller university campuses who are setting up new clusters and need basic, clear instructions. We want to provide a short, concise recipe that doesn't get bogged down by all the different options and flavors available. Next, we'll add the existing Quick Start Guide (https://research.cs.wisc.edu/htcondor/manual/quickstart.html) directly into the manual. We also eventually want an "Easy Install" page, describing how to set up a personal Condor with as few steps as possible. We already have a webpage with some basic install information (https://research.cs.wisc.edu/htcondor/instructions/) but even this gets too bogged down with options and details. This should be one page maximum. Once we have enough content ready, we'll publish this all under a new top-level section called Getting Started.

We can reduce the number of steps and complexity. For instance, the first steps of installing from the repository requires wget to be installed (it is not installed in the Centos 7 basic image btw), leaves garbage files behind, requires answering questions. Why not instead just two commands: $ sudo yum-config-manager --add-repo https://research.cs.wisc.edu/htcondor/yum/repo.d/htcondor-stable-rhel7.repo $ sudo yum install -y condor Note the easy install above is dependent on the one-line change to our RPM repos specified in #7710. Next, I think the suggested contents for security file config.d/50-security suffers from the following problems: unnecessary reverse DNS requirements no encryption, meaning private claim id information is being passed over the network in the clear host-based authorization for administrator commands (like condor_userprio) contains lines that are not needed like SEC_PASSWORD_FILE, which is already defined upon installation of the RPM is not completely cut-n-paste and yet it seems like it could be; for instance, references "condor-cm.mydomain.com".... could we replace this with $(CONDOR_HOST), since earlier in the instructions we tell people to define that? no comments in this config file... not a single one... I suggest instead something like: config.d/50-security # Require authentication, encryption, integrity use SECURITY: Strong # Set things up so authentication must happen via the local filesystem # or a pool password. The local file system will be used to authenticate # users submitting, removing, or editing jobs; this means we assume users will # be logged into submit nodes. HTCondor daemons themselves will only trust # other daemons with the same pool password, a secret contained in file on each # node that requires root access to read. It seems like a problem that is specific to my testbed, but if we are going to mention it then I don't think disabling ipv6 is the best approach. Any thoughts or suggestions? 2020-Jul-27 12:23:15 by karpel: Just gave this a read since it was linked on a Nikhef email. Thoughts: I'd really like to see some more "conversational" text in this guide, describing what's going on instead of just puking out things to copy-paste. title: Ticket #1958: -schedd-{daemon-ad,address}-file options to condor_submit_dag
description: Arguments -schedd-daemon-ad-file and -schedd-address-file were added to condor_submit_dag. They take full paths to a file dropped by the condor_schedd. Either SCHEDD_DAEMON_AD_FILE or SCHEDD_ADDRESS_FILE from config, which default to $(SPOOL)/.schedd_classad and $(SPOOL)/.schedd_address respectively. title: Ticket #2677: condor_softkill doesn't work reliably on Windows 7
description: condor_softkill fails to enumerate desktops when run non-interatively on Windows 7 (and probabably Vista as well). The softkill log shows entering enum_winsta_proc, winsta_name = msswindowstation OpenDesktop error: 2 This indicates that the "mswindowstation" does not have a desktop called "default". Thus condor_softkill fails to find a window associated with the given pid and thus never tries to send a WM_CLOSE. No other window stations show up in the enumeration (not even WinSta0 which is known to exist). On windows XP, the log contains entering enum_winsta_proc, winsta_name = WinSta0 OpenWindowStation error: 5 entering enum_winsta_proc, winsta_name = Service-0x0-3e7$ OpenWindowStation error: 5 entering enum_winsta_proc, winsta_name = Service-0x0-3e4$ OpenWindowStation error: 5 entering enum_winsta_proc, winsta_name = Service-0x0-3e5$ OpenWindowStation error: 5 entering enum_winsta_proc, winsta_name = SAWinSta OpenWindowStation error: 5 entering enum_winsta_proc, winsta_name = Service-0x0-39442180$ entering enum_winsta_proc, winsta_name = Service-0x0-3ab729de$ entering enum_winsta_proc, winsta_name = Service-0x0-3f9ccea7$ entering enum_winsta_proc, winsta_name = Service-0x0-41a60219$ entering enum_winsta_proc, winsta_name = Service-0x0-43973610$ entering enum_winsta_proc, winsta_name = Service-0x0-45b7e4c4$ entering enum_winsta_proc, winsta_name = Service-0x0-48ffeb71$ entering enum_winsta_proc, winsta_name = Service-0x0-4b303c9a$ entering enum_winsta_proc, winsta_name = Service-0x0-4cc682fc$ entering enum_winsta_proc, winsta_name = Service-0x0-4fb2968b$ entering enum_winsta_proc, winsta_name = Service-0x0-6d022906$ entering enum_winsta_proc, winsta_name = Service-0x0-83367cfe$ entering enum_winsta_proc, winsta_name = Service-0x1-5c993e20$ entering enum_winsta_proc, winsta_name = Service-0x1-68ad4cd2$ entering enum_winsta_proc, winsta_name = Service-0x1-6f835ca4$ entering enum_winsta_proc, winsta_name = Service-0x1-73874238$ posting WM_CLOSE to window 0x16D012E owned by thread of pid 1344 executable for process is perl.exe It seems likely that the more locked-down security model of Vista/Win7 had made the strategy of enumerating all window stations/desktops to find the window associated with a PID is no longer viable. Since we KNOW what window station we created the process with in the first place, we should probably use that information. At the very least we should start by checking the current desktop for rather than enumerating all desktops.

title: Ticket #7025: Python bindings: Submit.__delitem__ causes SIGSEGV kill
description: This Python script: # crash.py import htcondor s = htcondor.Submit({'foo': 'bar'}) del s['foo'] will cause an error like “python crash.py” terminated by signal SIGSEGV (Address boundary error) TJ believes the problem is that Submit.__delitem__ tries to insert a null pointer which ends up being dereferenced elsewhere. title: Ticket #717: CGAHP protocol updates
description: http://www.cs.wisc.edu/condor/gahp/cgahp_protocol.txt claims: At startup, allowable commands are limited to the following: COMMANDS INITIALIZE_FROM_FILE INITIALIZE_FROM_MYPROXY QUIT VERSION Once a successful INITIALIZE_* command is completed, any other command may be issued. If any command outside of the above list is issued before a successful INITIALIZE_* command, the Result Line should consist of : E <CRLF> This is wrong. The CGAHP doesn't need to be INITILIZEd to accept other commands. The gridmanger relies on this. The actual behavior should be identified and the documentation updated.

title: Ticket #4170: missing job ClassAd attributes in the manual
description: A user noticed that there were some job attributes not documented in the manual: DiskProvisioned CpusProvisioned MemoryProvisioned <name>Provisioned These pair up with the job attributes Request<name>. They don’t appear in the job ClassAd on the schedd, only in the job ClassAd that’s written in the job’s execute directory while the job is running. They indicate how much of each machine resource has been allocated to the job. For statically partitioned slots, they will match the amount of resource given to the slot when the startd started. For partitionable slots, they will be based on the job’s Request<name> attributes, but may be larger to make the partitioned slot more likely to be reusable for additional jobs. In all cases, they should be equal to or greater than the job’s Request<name> attributes.

title: Ticket #4465: Improve DAEMON_SOCKET_DIR
description: I sat down to merge #3813 and was surprised to see BOOM - tests fail across the board. It turns out that the default value of DAEMON_SOCKET_DIR is $(LOCK)/daemon_sock; unfortunately, $(LOCK) is sometimes a deeply nested directory and DAEMON_SOCKET_DIR results in being more than 100 characters long. In turn, the name of shared port sockets is more than 108 characters, which is the limit for Unix sockets, resulting in the master excepting. So, unfortunately, we must handle this situation better before USE_SHARED_PORT can be set by default. We expect this would be a common situation for glideins - I suspect this will render CMS unable to use shared port on the execute side for now. Bummer. I propose the following solution: On Unix platforms, default DAEMON_SOCKET_DIR to "auto"; this results in the current default of $(LOCK)/daemon_sock or have mkstemp create a directory of the form /tmp/condor_daemon_sock_XXXXX. The value of DAEMON_SOCKET_DIR is encoded in the environment of any daemon core process when launched via Create_Process. This causes an entire process tree to agree on the value in the case where it is randomly generated. *: The master is responsible for cleaning this directory on graceful exit. On Linux, we use abstract Unix domain sockets of the form condor_daemon_sock_XXXXX/$ID. Thus, the sockets will get automatically cleaned when the process exits; DAEMON_SOCKET_DIR effectively does not exist on the filesystem.
remarks: 2014-Jul-17 12:36:26 by tannenba: I would love to use abstract domain sockets... do they exist on MacOS as well, or only Linux? Also, do we know if the limit on the path name size exists primarily just on linux and other platforms like macos have more reasonable size limits? If there is no such silly path name size limit on MacOS, perhaps we can just use abstract domain socks on Linux and keep everything else the same on macos and friends. 2014-Jul-17 13:56:18 by bbockelm: Abstract domain sockets are, unfortunately, Linux-only. They do seem to work perfectly for what we need, however. The limit on the path name seems to be uniform across the Unix platforms; when I ran the default shared port branch through the unit tests, they all blew up. Batlab tests look good so far (still in progress) with this branch. I'll try to merge it into V8_3-gt3813 and see how much that helps. There may still be some testing framework changes we need to do for that branch (not certain). 2014-Jul-17 21:11:17 by bbockelm: Ok, this passed all the batlab tests and I can confirm #3813 now passes on most platforms when merged with this branch (some Windows issues remain...). Todd, can you do a review before I commit? 2014-Jul-17 21:27:48 by bbockelm: Igor pointed out the DAEMON_SOCKET_DIR documentation gives an example of where condor_ssh_to_job needs access to DAEMON_SOCKET_DIR (when the execute node is behind the CCB and the condor_ssh_to_job is run on a node where shared port is used). Since abstract sockets have no filesystem permissions, I considered the location of the "directory" for a HTCondor instance to be a secret. Now, we could allow it to divulge the secret if configured to do so -- or, alternately, open a FD on behalf of the client and use file descriptor passing techniques to give an endpoint to the client without letting it know where it came from. Thoughts? 2014-Jul-23 08:03:38 by bbockelm: Reviewed this with Jaime on the phone. After a bit more tuning in batlab, I merged this in last night. 2014-Jul-25 10:49:47 by jfrey: I'm starting a review of the actual code now, and this ticket can't be resolved yet. So far, I've found that the code in DaemonCore::Create_Process() to handle CONDOR_PRIVATE_SHARED_PORT_COOKIE is dead code. It's wrapped in linux-only and windows-only ifdef's. And the code won't compile if it isn't dead. 2014-Jul-25 15:48:02 by jfrey: Code Review * Code in DaemonCore::Create_Process() is wrapped in nested linux-only and win32-only ifdefs, so it's never compiled. On linux, there's no 'newnev' object, so the code won't compile anyway. As it is, the CONDOR_PRIVATE_SHARED_PORT_COOKIE environment variable will be inherited by all child processes where we don't explicitly scrub the whole environment, including user jobs. * In DaemonCore::Create_Process(), when we don't want the child process to receive the CONDOR_PRIVATE_SHARED_PORT_COOKIE value, we should remove the variable from the environment, not set it to "unavailable". This would require adding a remove method to the Env class. * In SharedPortClient::PassSocket(), change pipe_name to a std::string and eliminate tmp_name. * In SharedPortState::HandleUnbound(), is a stringstream and extra copying better than using formatstr_cat()? This also makes the construction of the socket name different than in SharedPortEndpoint, which uses formatstr(). * In SharedPortState::HandleUnbound(), if there is no primary socket name (because there's no CONDOR_PRIVATE_SHARED_PORT_COOKIE set) and the alternate socket name is too long, then the helpful error message about the name being too long isn't printed. It will instead attempt and fail to connect to a bogus primary socket name. * I'd prefer a more descriptive name than USE_ABSTRACT, like USE_ABSTRACT_DOMAIN_SOCKET. * In SharedPortEndpoint::RealInitializeDaemonSocketDir(), the string pointed at by keybuf is leaked. * In SharedPortEndpoint, you use a socket name of "collector" to see if the full socket pathname will be too long. You should use a longer test name. Right now, our pool has a daemon with a shared port sock named "15337_9022_90". * In SharedPortEndpoint, I think we should also do the length check when DAEMON_SOCKET_DIR is set to something other than "auto", and refuse to use any DAEMON_SOCKET_DIR path that's too long. 2014-Jul-29 11:35:45 by bbockelm: Hi Jaime, I think I took care of all the issues in the latest commit. title: Ticket #6458: DEFAULT_MASTER_SHUTDOWN_SCRIPT ignored on Windows
description: When running on Windows as a service, the condor_master ignores the shutdown script, this includes the DEFAULT_MASTER_SHUTDOWN_SCRIPT knob, as well as the MASTER_SHUTDOWN_xxx configuration variables and associated condor_set_shutdown command. When not running as a service, the condor_master does attempt to run the shutdown script, but it just hangs, most likely because execl() in the Windows C-runtime can only be used by programs that don't use most of the other c-runtime calls - this is documented behavior. The fix is to have the master do an explicit CreateProcess call and then just exit rather than try and use execl(), and the code to do this needs to be in the exit path for running as a service as well as the normal exit path.

title: Ticket #4035: precomputing surplus does not work with HGQ and slot weights
description: The current negotiator logic where quota surplus is computed prior to actual negotiation prevents certain categories of use cases for group quotas and slot weights. Example: <tannenba> Imagine a parent group P (quota 100, no surplus), and child groups A (quota 50 w/ surplus) and B (quota 50 w/ surplus). Group A has 100 jobs submitted, group B has 5. <tannenba> Negotiation starts. <tannenba> Negotiator starts negotiating with group A, cuz it is furthest from its quota. <tannenba> it compues for group A a scheduler limit of 95, which is the sum of 50 (its quota) plus 45 (its surplus). <tannenba> so its starts negotiating w/ group A with a scheduler limit of 95. <tannenba> turns out that all of group A's jobs request 25 cores each. <tannenba> if slotweight=CPU, the negotiator will stop after it matches 3 jobs from group A, since the slot weight for each job is 25. <tannenba> and 3 jobs * 25 slot weight < 95 <tannenba> lets also assume that all the jobs from group B are 25 cores, to make things simple <tannenba> What SHOULD have happened is group A should have 2 jobs, and group B should have 2 jobs. But what WILL happen (i think) is group A will get 3 jobs, and group B will only be left running 1 job. <tannenba> Because of how HGQ computes surplus, the policy is off by 25% <tannenba> again, this problem does not happen unless you have surplus enabled (but without enabling surplus, you don't have hierarchical groups). Ideally, jobs could match and have their usages updated by whatever slot weight the match cost. If a particular submitter runs out of jobs that can match, slot quotas can be re-computed without that submitter, and with remaining resources, and negotiation can proceed. That form of 'surplus' inherently takes into account what matches are costing, as they happen. This would make quota allocations work analogously to how submitter shares are recomputed now. A side effect of this would be that GROUP_QUOTA_ROUND_ROBIN_RATE and GROUP_QUOTA_MAX_ALLOCATION_ROUNDS (and associated loops) would become irrelevant.
remarks: 2018-Feb-09 10:51:42 by tannenba: Abandoning this ticket.... HTCondor has been modified so that if slot weights only references attributes Cpus and Memory, then it will work with HGQ surplus...

title: Ticket #5809: peaceful shutdown command not behaving as messages indicate
description: There is no evidence that this command actually sends any messages to the startd despite what it prints out. I've tried variations on this command including the FQDN and slot1@FQDN. root@condorcm:~# condor_off -peaceful execute1034 Sent "Set-Peaceful-Shutdown" command to startd execute1034.nemo.phys.uwm.edu Can't find address for schedd execute1034.nemo.phys.uwm.edu Can't find address for execute1034.nemo.phys.uwm.edu So I RTFM'd and see that you recommend including -startd in the argument list. I tried that. It outwardly looks better root@condorcm:~# condor_off -peaceful -startd execute1034.nemo.phys.uwm.edu Sent "Set-Peaceful-Shutdown" command to startd execute1034.nemo.phys.uwm.edu Sent "Kill-Daemon-Peacefully" command to master execute1034.nemo.phys.uwm.edu And the jobs go into the retiring state, which seems reasonable enough. But the StartLog actually prints that it's doing a graceful shutdown. 07/27/16 10:27:34 Got SIGTERM. Performing graceful shutdown. 07/27/16 10:27:34 shutdown graceful So I think the right command is doing the right thing but logging inaccurately. I think a command that should be right-enough is print half the right-message but doing nothing.
remarks: 2016-Jul-27 11:24:37 by wenger: Hmm -- seems like there are several problems here: Without -startd, the right thing is not even happening. The message is confusing/incorrect. (BTW, condor_off -help says that -startd, etc., are deprecated. So apparently, "-daemon startd" is preferred.)
creator: tpdownes

title: Ticket #6726: Make interactive submission more first-class
description: For a variety of reasons, some forward-thinking, the user experience for interactive jobs needs improvement: 1) Submit files from interactive jobs should be able to be submitted for non-interactive batch jobs, without modification. Currently, the "executable" line is ignored and an error given if it's included in a submit file submitted with "condor_submit -i". Improvement: HTCondor should accept jobs submitted this way, and transfer the executable (as for a non-interactive job), but not run the executable. Could: give the user a warning statement that the executable will be transferred, but not executed 2) A better, less error-looking message should be given to the user if the job environment is not ready. Roughly monthly CHTC RCFs encounter a user who thinks they've done something wrong. E.g: --- The last error occurs sometimes when I submit a job. My request is rejected but I am still assigned to some cluster. Following is an error message: [szhao64@submit-3 ~]$ condor_submit -i debug.sub Submitting job(s). 1 job(s) submitted to cluster 121316375. Waiting for job to start... slot1_12@e185.chtc.wisc.edu: Rejecting request, because the job execution environment is not yet ready. Welcome to slot1_12@e185.chtc.wisc.edu! Can you help me fix these problems? Do I need to add some options in the command line? --- Improvement: make the "Rejecting request..." message more informative and less scary. Maybe something like "Preparing job environment." 3) Interactive jobs in the queue are hard to identify and decode. Currently, interactive jobs (a) list "sleep" as the executable in the condor_q output, and (b) may go on hold and stay on hold if the interactive job overuses resources (or other hold reason). There should be a more informative error message in these cases and the job should probably be removed from the queue rather than going on hold. Improvement: (1) replace "sleep" with "(interactive job)" in the condor_q output (2) remove interactive jobs from the queue if held, and perhaps give hold reason as an error message when the SSH is terminated.

title: Ticket #3524: GT5 does not return job's exit code.
description: [This ticket for work being done on behalf of Eric Heien.] Metronome (and DAGMan) really need to know the exit code of the GT5 job in order to have proper reporting and semantics. For instance, the platform_post step isn't run if the platform_job (the GT5 job) fails. According to Jaime, this is simply unimplemented (as opposed to broken). Metronome can fake this in a DAGMan postcript (probably); this will probably be even more troublesome for other users.
creator: tlmiller

title: Ticket #1519: spooled input files getting uploaded twice
description: In condor's file transfer mechanism, the shadow transmits some spooled input files twice to the execute side. This happened if the file was listed in the transfer_input_files list as a simple basename (no directory part). The origin of this problem is probably earlier than 7.0.0. I have not done a thorough investigation of the history.

title: Ticket #6376: Dedicated Scheduler not releasing claims in some cases
description: If the dedicated scheduler claims a startd, but the job is removed before it is started, the claim is never released, even after UNUSED_CLAIM_TIMEOUT seconds.
remarks: 2017-Sep-07 14:56:31 by jpatton: CODE REVIEW Looks good. Some additional context (please correct if wrong): Prior to fix, after a condor_rm of a PU job, resources could still end up claimed (and "scheduled") by the DS if multiple negotiation cycles happened during the scheduling. This fix removes the protection of such resources in such state.

title: Ticket #486: [RFE] Vacate and Hold command
description: We needed a feature where we could suspend a running VM without loosing the snapshot files. For this we needed to vacate the job (vm universe) and then hold it instead of re-starting it somewhere else. We achieved it by setting Job Requirements to FALSE before vacating the job. Is any one aware of any problems with this approach? Vacate will transfer the modified files to the spool directory, while hold will not. That's why we went for this approach. Commands used are: condor_qedit <jobid> Requirements FALSE condor_vacate_job <jobid> Thanks, Sateesh

title: Ticket #7137: Improve token request auto-approval UX
description: #7080 hasn't (as of this writing) implemented two features. We may decide not to implement them, but if we do, we should record why in this ticket. Use PRIVATE_NETWORK_NAME to determine a default netmask for the auto-approval tool's CLI. We were really thinking that we had a netblock or mask in the configuration already; PRIVATE_NETWORK_INTERFACE optionally has a wildcard (e.g., 129.168.*) which could be converted, but if it's not required, let's not bother.) The CLI should confirm that the auto-approval rule it's going to install is the one the user wanted. This should include converting the lifetime value in seconds to fractional hours before installing the rule, as well as printing the netblock out in both styles. Instead of trying to guess a good time-out for historical auto-approval, the CLI should list all of the requests from that time period (just like the list tokens command) and say "to approve all these requests, run the following command." It should also mention, if there are any requests older than that, how to get a list of them (e..g, condor_list_tokens <num... num>). The "rule text" included with each auto-approval log message looks brief enough that only printing it for the first auto-approval by each rule is probably worse than repeating it.

title: Ticket #2335: long addresses overflow user log event buffers
description: SubmitEvent contains a static buffer of size 128 to hold the address of the schedd. No bounds checking is done when writing into this buffer. Since the schedd address may contain information such as the private network name, shared port id, and CCB information, it is possible for the address to exceed the buffer size. The result is a crash of the schedd whenever a job is submitted with a user log. This problem was observed on the new morgridge submit node, which uses tcp forwarding, shared port, and private network address and name, which resulted in an address string longer than 128 characters. Similar problems exist in the following events: ExecuteEvent, NodeExecuteEvent. These bugs likely go back long before 7.6.0. I haven't bothered to trace them back to find out.
remarks: 2011-Aug-02 18:40:41 by cweiss: All in all I think the patch looks reasonable. It looks actually significantly better than before. A couple of remarks: 1) Why don't we just initialize executeHost , remoteName , and submitHost with "" in the constructors? That would save the checks later on (in the average case where the values will be actually set, this would lead to an additional delete[], that's true). I could go either way with that, just want to throw it in. 2) We should strip obtained values by default where fscanf has been replaced (re: LogNotes). Otherwise I could imagine we may run into more DAGman-related issues down the road. If we don't already have a strip function lying around, one could be added and used. 2011-Aug-05 11:50:36 by danb: Cathrin, Thanks for the review. I agree that initializing to "" would have simplified things slightly. I'll likely leave things as they are, because I've heavily tested it as is and would rather not touch it any more unless I have to ;-) Regarding your second concern, there was only one instance of the fprintf("...%s\n") usage. It is fixed. So I think we are safe.

title: Ticket #2270: spinning pie algorithm + preemption = unfair allocation
description: Here is a simple scenario in which the spinning pie algorithm does not converge to the expected fair share allocation. In fact, it is wildly off. 1000 slots and 2 submitters: A & B At time T1, A & B are running 501 and 499 jobs respectively and have steady-state priorities of the same (i.e. roughly equal shares of the pool but not exactly equal). At time T2, the 1000 running jobs are still running and the priorities of the users have diverged sufficiently so that B could preempt A if B had any idle jobs. User B submits 1000 more jobs. Condor has free reign to preempt in order to reallocate resources to the fair share levels as quickly as possible (PREEMPTION_REQUIREMENTS = True). What happens in the next negotiation cycle? B preempts all of A's jobs and claims all 1000 slots. This is not what I would expect! This happens because in the first spin of the pie, A gets dropped from future consideration, because A has no more jobs that match. Then in the second spin of the pie, B is alone and gets a computed "fair share" of 100%. It seems that the intent of the spinning pie is to avoid portions of the pie going uneaten when some submitters have big enough appetites to keep eating. However, as it iterates, it doesn't appear to correctly take into account portions of the pie that have already been dished out fairly. I believe we have obscured this problem in the past by using PREEMPTION_REQUIREMENTS expressions that only allow preemption when the user priorities are sufficiently different that we are not surprised to see big shifts in resource allocation. But this does not really solve the quirkiness of the allocation. The current matchmaking algorithm also does not handle immediate resource allocation when a user with a worse priority currently has fewer than his fair share of resources claimed (e.g. user A in the negotiation cycle after the one described above where A loses everything). We only allow preemption when the preempting user has better priority than the existing user, irrespective of whether the preempting user deserves more machines based on fair share considerations. This is the case even if PREEMPTION_REQUIREMENTS is true. We rely on the longer-term effect of user-priority decay to eventually promote the unfairly treated user to a position that allows preemption.
remarks: 2012-Dec-07 10:52:44 by danb: Another quirk relating to resource allocation and preemption: while in preempting state, the resources are counted towards the total usage by the preempted user and not at all towards the total use of the preempting user. Therefore, if preemption lasts for longer than a matchmaking cycle, the preempting user may be given a bigger chunk of the pool than desired. In the extreme case, this can lead to an oscillation in which the entire pool flops back and forth from one user to the other, rather than converging on the fair share ratio. This effect also applies to the Claimed/Retiring state. Since this state can last for considerable time, the problem can be quite noticeable. 2013-Mar-28 17:16:00 by johnkn: Bulk change of target version from v070808 to v070809 using ./ticket-target-mover.

title: Ticket #7588: cross-slot posting of p-slot Child attrs needs work to be reliable
description: CHTC was attempting to use a bologna-backfill style configuration to allow GPUs to be assigned to both a primary p-slot and a set of backfill static slots, with the backfill slots getting out of the way when the p-slot was using the GPUs. This did not work because the configuration to do this requires that the static backfill slots be able to see the assigned gpus of the d-slots. This can be configured by config fragment STARTD_PARTITIONABLE_SLOT_ATTRS = AssignedGPUs STARTD_SLOT_ATTRS = Cpus Memory ChildAssignedGPUs This should result in the following attributes being advertised in all slots which allows them to be used in the backfill slot START and PREEMPT expressions slot attributes slot1_ChildAssignedGPUs = {<list of GPU devices in use by d-slots>} slot1_Memory = <unused p-slot memory> slot1_Cpus = <unused p-slot gpus> This problem is that the order of operations inside the startd makes the value of slot1_ChildAssignedGPUs very likely to be out of sync with the actual value. When a d-slot is destroyed, it tends to be wrong for quite a long time. Even worse, in the general case, where STARTD_CRON or custom expressions are in use, and also cross-slot posted, the slot<x>_* values can end up being out of sync all or most of the time, and the behavior is not even stable, since the evaluation order of slots within the Startd changes over time (the state of the slot affects the order) The solution to this is many fold. Surgery on the Startd to make the evaluation/update order stable and ordered to support the most common case, which is to always to Child* rollup before SLOT_ATTRS. Introduce a new cross-slot reference mechanism that is not (as) dependent on update order and is more point-to point than broadcast. This will take the form of a custom classad function specific to the Startd. Expressions in STARTD_ATTRS can use this function config fragment STARTD_ATTRS = PslotGpusInUse PslotGpusInUse = SlotEval("slot1",join(",", ChildAssignedGpus)) SLOT_TYPE_2_START = !StringListIMember(AssignedGpus, PslotGpusInUse) The SlotEval classad function will exist only in the Startd, when it is evaluated, the result of the expression will be the same in all slots, it will only reference attributes in the named slot. (slot1 in this case). Possible future work to change the Startd so that all slot ads are built before any cross-slot posting is done. This is quite a large change to the way the startd operates, but may desirable for other reasons as well. more on SlotEval When an expression containing SlotEval is sent anywhere outside the Startd, it will be replaced with the current evaluated value as part of the process of unparsing the ad to put it on the wire (or write it to a file, etc). So the negotiator will see this slot ad fragment ChildAssignedGpus = {"CUDA0", "CUDA1"} PslotGpusInUse = "CUDA0, CUDA1" SlotEval is a direct cross-slot lookup at evaluation time, so it is immune the relative order in which STARTD_SLOT_ATTRS and STARTD_PARTITIONABLE_SLOT_ATTRS are processed. It also does not result in a large number of undesireable attrributes being cross posted to all slots. Contrast this with each slot slot getting 40 attributes from one STARTD_SLOT_ATTRS value when there are 40 slots on the machine. config fragment # this results in slot1_Foo through slotN_Foo in all slots STARTD_SLOT_ATTRS = Foo # this results in slot1_Foo (and ONLY that) in all slots and all slots get the same result from evaluating Foo STARTD_ATTRS = slot1_Foo slot1_Foo = SlotEval("slot1",<epression>)

title: Ticket #890: gahp writing lots of data to stderr can wedge gridmanager
description: The gridmanager and gahp_server can get into a deadlock. If the gahp writes a lot of data to stderr (more than will fit in the pipe buffer) at the same time that the gridmanager writes a new request to the gahp's stdin, the gahp will block trying to write to stderr while the gridmanager busy-loops trying to read from the gahp's stdout. With the number of gahps around with third-party software that could be writing to stderr, making the gahp not block writing to stderr seems impractical. The best solution is to make the gridmanager read from the gahp's stderr in addition to the gahp's stdout (both non-blocking). Better yet (though more work) would be to have the gridmanager talk to the gahp completely non-blocking, returning to daemon-core if reads/writes to the gahp's stdin/out would block. #648 is related.
remarks: 2010-Jun-17 11:14:51 by jfrey: Pushed a commit to master for 7.5.4 that fixes most of the problem. Now, whenever the gridmanager reads a gahp's stdout, it also reads it's stderr. There's still a potential deadlock between the gridmanager writing to the gahp's stdin and the gahp writing to its stderr. That should be harder to trigger, because it requires the data being written to both pipes to be larger than the pipe buffer. 2010-Oct-20 15:59:08 by jfrey: Bulk change of target version from v070504 to v070505 using ./ticket-target-mover. 2011-Jan-27 14:46:04 by danb: Bulk change of target version from v070505 to v070506 using ./ticket-target-mover. 2011-Feb-01 14:49:30 by tannenba: Bulk change of target version from v070506 to NULL using ./ticket-target-mover.

title: Ticket #2620: crondor job misfired due to daylight saving change
description: We run a daily crondor job at 00:15am to report usage of GLOW. On 2011-11-06, the day time changed back to normal time from daylight savings time, the crondor job ran twice in one day: once at 00:15am and once at 23:15pm. It behaved as though the extra hour was not taken into account when computing the next time to run on 2011-11-06. After the extra run on 2011-11-06, the crondor job ran as normal at 00:15am the next day, 2011-11-07. The above problem happened to a crondor job on glow.cs.wisc.edu. Strangely, this same problem did not affect an identically configured crondor job on cm.chtc.wisc.edu. The condor version is close but not identical between these machines, but I don't know if that is the cause of the different behavior. glow.cs.wisc.edu: $CondorVersion: 7.7.2 Aug 23 2011 BuildID: 363342 PRE-RELEASE-UWCS $ $CondorPlatform: x86_64_rhas_3 $ cm.chtc.wisc.edu: $CondorVersion: 7.7.2 Sep 27 2011 BuildID: 372978 PRE-RELEASE-UWCS $ $CondorPlatform: x86_64_rhas_3 $ The cron-related attributes in the jobs are: CronMinute = "15" CronHour = "0"

The man-page for mktime() in linux says that if tm_isdst is set to -1, it will figure out what daylight savings time setting is applicable for the specified time. Why aren't we using that? 2011-Nov-08 11:26:08 by danb: I think the reason cm.chtc.wisc.edu was not affected is that there was a reconfig at 21:05pm on 2011-11-06. A reconfig causes recalculation of cron schedules. Since this reconfig happened after the daylight savings shift, it used the correct value for tm_isdst. title: Ticket #193: Allow startd to grow and shrink slots on demand
description: As part of multicore support, we need to add and shrink slots from the startd on demand. Questions: Should this be persistant? On a lease? We need to support drainage. As the slots aren't uniform on many startds, do we need to turn off specific slots? And what does that mean?
remarks: 2009-Feb-20 10:46:03 by gthain: The current plan is to leverage work for pool upgrades. Fundamentally, we aren't going to change any given startd, rather, we will launch a new startd, potentially with a different configuration, which will run alongside the old one, until the old one drains out. This allows us to effectively change anything about the startd, including number of slots and policies. When the process is startd, the old startd essentially goes into graceful shutdown mode, and can't come out. The name of the old startd is changed to something like old-name. The master forks a new startd, which polls the old startd for the job status. There is a mapping of old slots to new that describes which running old slots block new slots, not necessarily one-to-one. Thus, if we switch from an 8-way machine to a 1 way machine, all 8 old slots block the one new slot.

title: Ticket #6663: condor_vacate_job -fast leaves starters stuck in Preempting/Vacating
description: condor_vacate_job -fast leaves the corresponding starters stuck in 'Preempting/Vacating'. condor_vacate_job issues an ACT_ON_JOBS command to the schedd. The schedd (correctly) sends a SIGQUIT to the shadow. Daemon core catches the signal and calls main_shutdown_fast(), which calls Shadow->shutDown( JOB_NOT_CKPTED ), which calls evictJob( JOB_NOT_CKPTED ), which calls cleanUp( jobWantsGracefulRemoval() ) and then DC_Exit() without re-entering the event loop. The starter tries to tell the shadow that it, as instructed by cleanUp(), evicted the job. It can't (the shadow has already exited), causing it ignore the startd's subsequent SIGTERM, as it's waiting for its job lease to expire. jobWantsGracefulRemoval() returns true by default (and unless it's otherwise configured or the job specifically says not to). So one problem is that the shadow doesn't hang around for the starter. It seems like the shadow should either always wait for the starter to call it back or that the starter to stop calling it; the former is much easier. (When the schedd really is trying to shut down quickly, e.g. for an upgrade, and it wants to preserve jobs, it just SIGKILLs the starters.) The other problem is that the shadow asks the starter to shut down gracefully when it itself is shutting down quickly. I was worried that correcting this would be a semantic change, but the condor_vacate_job man page says that -fast means a hard kill: "If the -fast option is used, the job(s) will be immediately killed, meaning that standard universe jobs will not be allowed to checkpoint, and the job will have to revert to the last checkpoint or start over from the beginning." So the fix ought to be to (a) wait for the starter to finish shutting down and (b) tell it to shut down the correct way (fast), which has the nice effect of making the wait for (a) shorter.

It may suffice to set a timer which knows about recycling vs. calling DC_Exit(); it may be that terminateJob(), despite calling cleanUp(), will never actually ask the startd/starter to do anything because it should only be called when the starter has already sent us the job_exit RPC (and exited), and we also therefore have nothing to wait for. 2018-May-02 10:59:44 by tlmiller: So holdJobAndExit() actually really does need to exit immediately to function properly. title: Ticket #2159: Various daemons are bypassing dprintf for access to the log file
description: Dagman and the amazon/ec2 gahp are directly manipulating the FILE pointer for the log file, bypassing dprintf. With the change that allows daemons to keep their log files open instead of opening and closing on every write, there does not exist a singular FILE pointer. There is instead an array, due to the fact that dprintf needs to support the ability to route its output to multiple files. As such, dagman and gahp both need a solution to achieve whatever it is they needed direct access to the FILE pointer for in the first case.
remarks: 2011-May-18 10:48:26 by ziliang: condor_amazon and EC2 gahp implementation of redirecting output had a broken design. They attempted to change the file pointer out from under dprintf, except dprintf would go and reopen the file every time regardless, so it would overwrite the file pointer the gahp tried to sneak in. The gahp also tried to default output to stderr, which was already happening in dprintf itself if it did not find a file to output to. I can conceivably think of a way to do this correctly, but will refrain from implementing it until such time as someone actually wants it, since passing a log file to the gahp never worked in the first place. 2011-Jun-01 11:39:34 by jfrey: I believe the situation in the amazon_gahp and ec2_gahp resulted from a half-successful attempt to remove all dependencies on Condor libraries. Calls to param() are done in the gridmanager passed to the gahps via the environment or command line. But dprintf() is still used to write to a log file. As long as they are using dprintf(), I see no reason from them not to consult the config file for the value of AMAZON_GAHP_LOG to determine which, if any, log file to write to. Since the subsystem is set to 'amazon_gahp' already, I don't think any special calls are required.

title: Ticket #4127: Disconnection during job cleanup can crash shadow
description: If the shadow becomes disconnected from the starter during job cleanup, it can crash as it starts running another job. I haven't traced the exact course of events, but this is an outline of what I'm seeing: Transfer of output files completes shadow becomes disconnected job termination code executes shadow is recycled for a new job shadow crashes At the point of the crash, daemonCore is attempting to call a timer named "RemoteResource::attemptReconnect()". The destination of the call is bogus and the process segfaults. It appears that the shadow is in the process of cleaning up the terminated job when the disconnect happens. A timer is registered to attempt a reconnect. Before the timer can fire, the job termination code path completes and the shadow is recycled, including deleting the RemoteResource object. The destructor for RemoteResource does not cancel the timer. Then the reconnect timer fires, invoking a method on a RemoteResource object whose memory has been reused. The destructor for RemoteResource should cancel the reconnect timer (the identifier is stored in data member next_reconnect_tid).
remarks: 2013-Dec-18 10:59:25 by jfrey: BaseShadow::m_cleanup_retry_tid is another timer that should be canceled when the object is destroyed. 2014-Jan-24 16:23:50 by tlmiller: CODE REVIEW Looks good. Checked for other TIDs missing deregistration, didn't see any. (Resolving, since it looks like the docs are done.)

title: Ticket #1260: Privsep should look for permission and uid errors at condor startup.
description: When using privsep there are a number of items that can be validated at startup or reconfig time. This leads to a machine looking like condor is running happily until a job schedules. It would be better to fail earlier so that a problem can be identified. This is what a user probably expects. For example, if SLOT12_EXECUTE is /home/slot5/execute, but /home/slot5/execute is not in valid-dirs in the privsep config, we know there will be an error at job run time. Condor should error out at this point and show that there is a configuration error. What happens, however, is that we don't get an error until a job runs. And condor will happily continue to match jobs and then reject them at run time.

title: Ticket #605: Claim activation failure due to shadow/startd communication issue
description: NOTE: Details, logs, and Todd's initial response in the associated RUST email. $CondorVersion: 7.0.5 Sep 20 2008 BuildID: 105846 $ $CondorPlatform: INTEL-WINNT50 $ The problem is that on many jobs (definitely over half if not almost all) the startd and the shadow fail to connect properly resulting in the job being evicted and the shadow exiting with status 108. You can see the behavior in the attached SchedLog, ShadowLog, and StartdLog files. You can see the scheduler start up the shadow for that job and match it to a slot2 on the execute node. And you can see the shadow and startd talking. But it appears that there is a communication issue - possibly security related - that causes the shadow to think it hasn't heard from the startd and to then evict the job.

title: Ticket #5673: After a failed GSI authentication, FS doesn't work.
description: There is a race condition in the non-blocking handshake code such that if a method that uses non-blocking reads (currently GSI, FS) fails, the next method in the list will also fail. The reason is that we do not properly reset the do_authenticate flag on a continuance of authentication that results in failure and then moves to the next method. As such, the server decides not to authenticate while the client does do the authentication, and the resulting out-of-syncness causes badness, typically in form of both sides reading at the same time. The server then times out after 20 seconds and declares failure.

title: Ticket #5223: Better error message when job is shell script without #! header
description: If you submit a shell script as your job, but it lacks the #! line specifying the interpreter, HTCondor will put your job on hold with a message like: Error from slot8@potatoes.example.com: Failed to execute '/path/to/test/exe': (errno=8: 'Exec format error') That's the error from exec, and while accurate, isn't helpful. Especially since the user can probably run /path/to/test/exe and have it run as their shell covers for them. We should provide a more helpful message: Possibilities: Add "If your job is a shell script, ensure the correct interpreter is specified on the #! line of your program." As above, but try to be clever and sniff that it's not a binary. Perhaps first 1kB is ASCII or valid UTF-8?

title: Ticket #7459: Rootly docker universe jobs need /tmp mounted 01777
description: When HTCondor is built to allow docker universe jobs to run as root, it bind mounts /tmp into the scratch directory, just as usual. However, this directory it created 0755, owned by the non-root user the job would have run as. This isn't a problem for jobs that stay as root, but if they su to a non-root user, then they can't write to tmp. Note that we can't make the bind-mounted /tmp 01777 for non-docker jobs, as that would allow random people to write into our /tmp, which is the problem that bind mounted is intended to fix. So, we'll make /tmp 01777 for all docker jobs.

title: Ticket #5872: Unneccessary EXCEPT()ion in starter.
description: The following EXCEPT()ion occurs in FileTransfer::abortActiveTransfer(). title: Ticket #4760: Ignore additional files in config directory
description: The current default list of files to ignore in the configuration directory is insufficient. At a minimum, cfengine backup files should be added to the list. From Tom Downes on the HTCondor-LIGO mailing list: I'd like you to consider changes to how you manage the /etc/condor/config.d directory. I suggest that you either explicitly exclude some common extensions that are produced as backups (.*~$ .*\.cfsaved$ .*\.dpkg-dist \*.rpmsave etc) or only poll for files with an explicit extension (like /etc/ld.so.conf.d). Reasoning: cfengine produces cfsaved backup files all over the place unless you ask it not to. Because these backups occur lexically after their intended replacement, they overwrite the values that you were actually trying to change! I have managed to find LOCAL_CONFIG_DIR_EXCLUDE_REGEXP and I think you should just expand it to include more default values. ^((\..*)|(.*~)|(#.*)|(.*\.rpmsave)|(.*\.rpmnew)|(.*\.dpkg-dist)|(.*cfsaved))$ I'm not sure the interior parens are necessary if this is an extended regular expression... but maybe you need them because of the parentheses everywhere rule in condor configurations.

The only concern was the dpkg-old file (which are equivalent to the rpmsave files). However, a problem would only occur if we screwed up the packaging in a major way or some other package would be providing HTCondor configuration files. In the end, it made more sense to exclude backup files from RPMs and debs in the same way as from editors and cfengine.

title: Ticket #557: Unexpected copy_to_spool setting
description: It is observed that copy_to_spool set in the .sub file to false ends up being true in the actual job ad. See rust ticket for details.
remarks: 2009-Jul-07 16:27:43 by mccardel: Here's an explanation why this is happening. In the submit file, everything is a command unless it has a + in front of it. When something has a + in front of it, it becomes an attribute, and it is inserted into the classad. A command is simply something that tells condor_submit what to do and may also insert attributes into the job ad based upon the command's action and feature it controls. An attribute (made with the + sign) has no effect on what condor_submit does. As an example, let's say there was a (non-existent) command called ProduceFreeEnergy which interacts with the (non-existent) condor_energy_module. If in your submit file you had: ... ProduceFreeEnergy = TRUE ... then this would tell condor_submit to have the condor_energy_module start creating some nice free energy. This would not show up in the classad though. But if you had: ... +ProduceFreeEnergy = TRUE ... then "ProduceFreeEnergy = TRUE" would show up in the classad, but condor_energy_module wouldn't start producing free energy. Now lets say you wanted to produce free energy AND have the classad report this. You would need the following in your submit file: ... +ProduceFreeEnergy = TRUE ProduceFreeEnergy = TRUE ... The first line would add that to the classad, the second line would actually start making free energy. Now in the RUST ticket, the following was said to be in the condor_config file: WantRemoteIO = False WantBadgers = True Notification = Error JOB_LEASE_DURATION = 3600 copy_to_spool = True SUBMIT_EXPRS = WantRemoteIO, Notification, WantBadgers, JOB_LEASE_DURATION, copy_to_spool So it would appear that they are setting copy_to_spool to a default value of true. However, this isn't what's happening. SUBMIT_EXPRS adds attributes to the classad. Putting "copy_to_spool" in SUBMIT_EXPRS is semantically equivalent to putting "+copy_to_spool = TRUE" into the submit file. So what this means is that all classads created will have attributes called "copy_to_spool" with the value TRUE. This does NOT insert the command "copy_to_spool = TRUE" into the submit file, which is what the submitter intended to do. Now in the submit file, the person who submitted the RUST ticket said that they had the following line: copy_to_spool = false So this is what was happening: the condor_config file inserts an attribute called "copy_to_spool" with the value "TRUE" into the classad that condor_submit is creating based on the submit file. But condor_submit reads the "copy_to_spool = false" line, and then doesn't copy the executable to the spool. However, when the submitter types in `condor_q -l XXXXX`, "copy_to_spool = TRUE" is printed out, since that is what is in the classad. The solution to this is the following: Take "copy_to_spool = TRUE" out of the condor_config file. In the submit file, have copy_to_spool be either TRUE or FALSE. Also in the submit file, have the same exact line as above, but with a + in front of it. Example: ... copy_to_spool = TRUE +copy_to_spool = TRUE ... This will both tell condor_submit to copy to spool, and also add an attribute into the classad that tells whether copy_to_spool is true or false. This will allow the user to type in `condor_q -l XXXXX` and see whether copy_to_spool was true or false for XXXXX. 2009-Jul-09 10:26:43 by smoler: The manual's definition of the configuration variable SUBMIT_EXPRS has been modified to more clearly state that it cannot be used to cause an action on behalf of a submitted job (like trying to insert a submit description file command forgotten in the file). 2009-Aug-28 13:36:43 by psilord: New comments added to rust ticket, should we act on it?

title: Ticket #1562: startd slotad policy evaluation is out of synch with reality
description: When the startd starts up and has some hawkeye scripts, the hawkeye attributes show up in the collector's view of the slotad in the first published ad to the collector, but NOT in the emitted slotad in the StartLog when using D_MACHINE. So, the job matches the slot from the negotiator's point of view the startd rejects it if the job's requirements use any attributes from the hawkeye scripts since the policy matcher uses the slotad which D_MACHINE prints out. After UPDATE_INTERVAL amount of time passes and a new ad is sent to the collector, the internal ad is reconciled and now contains the attributes. This is insidious, because both the collector AND condor_status -direct -startd both return the merged ad--which is not the ad used when matching against the job! There is obviously multiple copies or views of the ad and there hsould only be one. In DanB's words, "How could the collector have a more correct view of the slotad than the startd itself?" Due to this sync'ing problem of reality and the collector vs internal policy slotad description, one could construct a scenario where a job will NEVER match to a slotad if it depends upon hawkeye attributes which are updated faster than the slotad is published. Synchrony will never be achieved and the job will match from the negotiator's point of view, but always be rejected directly by the startd. This also may explain certain scenarios where even with a Start = True job policy, a job will be refused to run for UPDATE_INTERVAL seconds because the State of the internal machine ad used by the policy matcher is "Matched".

title: Ticket #107: PrivSep: Switchboard's mkdir operation doesn't clean up when it fails
description: The PrivSwp Switchboard has a "mkdir" operation that allows Condor to create job sandbox directories in the EXECUTE directory (which is modifiable only by root in PrivSep mode). Creation of a directory occurs in two steps. Create the directory as root. Use chown() to give the directory the correct ownership. If a problem occurs and the operation fails, it can leave behind the root-owned directory created in step 1. As part of looking at this issue I'd like to reconsider whether root-ownership of the EXECUTE directory is strictly needed. If not, we could do away with the Switchboard mkdir operation altogether.
