title: Ticket #2420: preen finds stale ickpt files in spool directory --- why?
description: Igor asks why preen found stale ickpt files in the spool directory: The condor_preen process has found the following stale condor files on <glidein-1>: /opt/glidecondor/condor_local/schedd_glideins3/spool/3474/cluster233474.ickpt.subproc0 - Removed /opt/glidecondor/condor_local/schedd_glideins3/spool/3861/cluster233861.ickpt.subproc0 - Removed /opt/glidecondor/condor_local/schedd_glideins3/spool/3760/cluster233760.ickpt.subproc0 - Removed /opt/glidecondor/condor_local/schedd_glideins3/spool <many more cases like the above --- 121 in total> One thing that I find quite disturbing is the logic in condor_preen for deciding if a spooled file is still associated with a job that is in the queue. It queries the schedd to see if the job still exists. It does not distinguish between failure of the query and non-existence of the job! The connection to the schedd is created with no timeout on the client side, but other things could go wrong: schedd times out, schedd dies in the middle of the query, network interruption. Unfortunately for this theory, I see no evidence in the ScheddLog that any query errors happened when preen was running. I also confirmed that the cluster ids mentioned in the preen message do not appear in the job queue or in the history, which goes back two days. Therefore, I think these deletions by condor_preen were legitimate garbage files. The question then is why these files got left behind. I don't yet have an explanation for that.
remarks: 2011-Sep-01 16:49:51 by danb: Another incident of this problem happened. This time, I noticed that the job was removed forcibly: LastHoldReason = "Globus error 131: the user proxy expired (job is still running)" HoldReason = "Globus error 121: the job state file doesn't exist" RemoveReason = "via condor_rm -forcex (by user gfactory)" I experimented in 7.7.2 with submitting both vanilla and gt2 jobs and getting them into a state where they were removed (status appears as X). When in this state, preen still correctly sees that the file should not be removed. Then when I remove the job with condor_rm -forcex, the file is correctly removed. So I failed to reproduce the problem. 2012-Oct-31 15:46:00 by jfrey: Igor found the source of this problem. When copy_to_spool is set to True or the job is standard universe, condor_submit spools the executable to the schedd as part of the queue-management transaction, before setting any of the job's attributes. If the transaction is aborted, the job is never submitted but the file isn't cleaned up by the schedd. In Igor's case, the submission was aborted because the job's proxy was expired. 2012-Nov-02 16:47:46 by jfrey: A possible solution is to call ClusterCleanup(), or some subset of it, in the schedd for each uncommitted cluster when aborting a transaction.
creator: danb

title: Ticket #6930: Support Windows AMIs in condor_annex
description: Presently, condor_annex does not (readily) allow for Windows AMIs: there are a few things that any instance started by an annex must do in order to join the annex, and we don't supply any means for Windows instances to do those things. We are investigating what it would take to change that. As a first step, it will dramatically simplify implementation to convert the Linux initscript back to a script called at config time by HTCondor. This approach was abandoned previously because the config time script ran once and only once, and really needs to be run once per boot (if for no other reason that the IP address of the instance changing). It was equally unattractive to run the script once per config parse and have it manage the cache by itself. The first step is therefore TJ's ticket, [number-to-follow], in which the master (and only the master) purges the config cache when the master starts up (but not when it restarts). Since we don't expect the master to restart often, this should approximate once-per-boot closely enough to work well. The second step is to rewrite the initscript to work on Windows. The immediate task is to determine what APIs AWS makes available on Windows; this will allow TJ to decide how to proceed with the rewrite. We may have to additionally alter the condor_annex tool to produce .zip files for Windows AMIs (or universally, and edit the initscript to handle them).

We'll talk more later.

title: Ticket #7622: Difficult to run personal condor under Kubernetes
description: HTCondor, in various places, checks that the owner of a job does not have user or group id (uid or gid) 0 (i.e., is not root). When it notices this it generally rejects any attempt to do work on their behalf (submit jobs, write event logs, etc.). Kubernetes, since v1.14 (June 2019), has the feature gate RunAsGroup default to true. When this feature gate is false, Kubernetes always runs pods with the gid set to whatever is in the image metadata. With the feature gate set to true, Kubernetes runs pods with the gid set in the pod security context (https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/configure-pod-container/security-context/#set-the-security-context-for-a-pod). If no gid is set in the pod security context, Kuberentes runs the container as gid 0. There does not appear to be a way to recover the pre-1.14 behavior to run as the gid in the image metadata if the feature gate RunAsGroup is enabled. We initially noticed this issue in the HTMap tutorials on mybinder.org, which hosts Jupyter Notebooks inside Kubernetes pods. The effect of the above is that, inside the pod, id showed jovyan@jupyter-binder-2dexamples-2djupyter-2dstacks-2dshd85tff:~$ id uid=1000(jovyan) gid=0(root) groups=0(root),100(users) ... and since the personal condor we use to back the examples is started in the entrypoint (and therefore by the user), the personal condor had the same uid and gid. It therefore rejected attempts to submit jobs (because of the gid). It also seemed to get very confused about whether it was a rootly condor or not, because it had some privileges by virtue of being gid 0. I haven't tried it, but I believe this can be replicated by simply starting our HTC notebook image locally with docker run --user 1000:0. As a hotfix for the HTC notebooks I did https://github.com/htcondor/htc-notebook/pull/7/commits/012e190d1636eb30936495428bd971bc7e371084#diff-4095c27189dcd85cefd5ff73ea166601R29 , which runs the master under sg in the entrypoint script. This solves the immediate issue of using the HTC notebooks under Kubernetes v1.14 or greater with default settings, but doesn't help anyone else trying to build their own images to run under Kubernetes. ZKM suggested that we could /MAYBE/ use the config knob CONDOR_IDS as a workaround for this problem, if that code is implemented properly. I haven't experimented with that. In the HTC notebooks in particular, the expected uid and gid are available as environment variables. ZKM also suggests that a possible general solution is to add a flag that forces condor to drop privileges regardless of whether it actually has them. Related issue on the BinderHub issue tracker: https://github.com/jupyterhub/binderhub/issues/1088

title: Ticket #6199: Harmonize periodic job policy evaluation parameters
description: The config parameters that control how often the job policy expressions are evaluated are a confusing mess. The documented default for PERIODIC_EXPR_INTERVAL is 60 seconds, but the parameter defaults table has a default value of 300. But everywhere that we query the value, we pass in an explicit default value of 60 (except the gridmanager, which uses 300). The param table wins over the call sites, so functional default is 300 everywhere. The parameters MAX_PERIODIC_EXPR_INTERVAL and PERIODIC_EXPR_TIMESLICE aren't in the defaults table. The schedd and job router supply the documented defaults when querying them. The gridmanager, shadow, and starter ignore these parameters, as they don't use a Timeslice to limit the aggregate evaluation time. We should make the following changes: Change the param defaults table entry for PERIODIC_EXPR_INTERVAL to say 60 Add param defaults table entries for MAX_PERIODIC_EXPR_INTERVAL and PERIODIC_EXPR_TIMESLICE with the documented values Change the gridmanager to use a Timeslice for job policy evaluation with a default PERIODIC_EXPR_INTERVAL of 60

title: Ticket #393: Allow use of "DAG templates"
description: Miron wants some kind of capability to use a "DAG template" for cases where we have to do many similar workflows with slightly different data. The template files would have a bunch of $(xyz) variables in them, which would then be substituted when creating the "real" DAG. So the user would be able to do sort of a 'foreach ...' where for each value you create and run a DAG. It's not clear whether this capability should be part of condor_dagman or condor_submit_dag themselves, or part of some external tool (maybe SOAR). title: Ticket #6463: Change IS_OWNER default to False
description: The current default value for IS_OWNER (START =?= False) has repeatedly bitten people with surprising and bad behavior. We should change the default to False, and require people to opt-in to the current behavior. The following START expression attempts to limit matches to a certain class of jobs. But it results in the machine staying in Owner state forever: START = TARGET.Matlab =?= True The following START expression will crash the startd with an infinite recursion in state changes between Owner and Unclaimed: START = State != "Unclaimed" || time() - EnteredCurrentState > 300 The Owner state (and IS_OWNER) is an artifact of Condor's cycle-scavenging roots. Most of our users today run Condor on dedicated resources and don't need the Owner state. By changing the default value of IS_OWNER to False, we avoid the issues above for these users with no detriment. Users working in a cycle-scavenging mode can opt into the old behavior. We should restore the old setting in the Desktop POLICY.

title: Ticket #4848: Address rewriting only considers first command socket
description: (Split off from #4833.) If shared_port, IPv6, and IPv4 is enabled, address rewriting does not work. The address rewriting code seems to have a somewhat-fatal flaw: instead of comparing the ad's address against all command sockets, it only compares the address against the first command socket. So, if the initial command socket is IPv4, an IPv4 address may get bumped to IPv6; an IPv6 address will not get rewritten to IPv4. This results in IPv4 connections getting told the IPv6 address; hilarity ensues. The issue comes up is because we determine the command socket from the shared_port_ad; if the shared port advertises the IPv4 socket (the default!) but the ad in the collector is the IPv6 address (true if the IPv6 address is first in the DNS for the collector). This affects the collector ad (assuming issue 1 is fixed). I fix this by tracking all command socket sinful strings and try address rewriting for each.
remarks: 2015-Jan-16 11:21 by tlmiller: I'm certain I tested this. I may have missed something, but I'm sure I tested it -- so I'd like to know what, precisely, is broken. The address rewriting code should never see an IP address other than the first command socket's -- we (should) never insert anything else. I don't necessarily object to checking all of sinfuls, just to be safe, but I think something else is going on. Have you verified that the on-disk shared port ad contains an IPv6 address? The shared port daemon uses the initial command socket (as we would expect) to populate the ad, and address rewriting only occurs when sending ClassAds over the wire. (And only when the address in question is the address of the sender, because we don't otherwise know what to substitute.) More generally, yes, even an IPv4-only client is going to see IPv6 addresses in the collector. There's nothing we can do about that; we plan to avoid the problem with matchmaking, in the future. 2015-Jan-17 07:48:35 by bbockelm: Yes, when you tested it, this worked correctly. However, when we fixed #4830, the daemons started connecting to the collector using IPv6 (as designed) - including the collector itself! This means the collector ad contained the collector's IPv6 address - no longer IPv4. When subsequently serving the collector ad - which contains the IPv6 address, but the initial command socket is IPv4 - address rewriting breaks. 2015-May-27 14:44:26 by tlmiller: I believe this was deliberately left undocumented.

title: Ticket #6875: Explicit token management protocol between starter and shadow
description: Based on a suggestion from tlmiller in #6859 (I suspect others have discussed the same thing, but I didn't see a ticket): While the file transfer protocol is asynchronous -- a single ACK is only sent by the starter after the whole transfer is done -- we would like for the shadow to better manage the transfer queue slots without having to guess about which stage of the transfer the starter is in. For 8.9.0, the shadow guesses that the starter is done with the queue slot after it has sent the last transfer and before it receives the ACK (under the theory that this is when the multifile transfers occur). For 8.9.1, we should do better. I propose we: 1. Partition the file transfers into URLs and non-URLs, and lexigraphically sort the URLs. 2. Introduce a new SYN integer in the protocol that allows the shadow to indicate an ACK is requested. 3. When the SYN is received by the starter, it responds with the transfer status ACK. 4. Once the transfer ACK is received by the shadow, it does transfer token management - releases the token for now. The intent is that multiple partitions or synchronizations may happen in the future. For example, we can have one partition for each protocol we use for transfers -- or, for special ones such as HTTP/HTTPS, one partition per origin server. The first step seems to be appropriate sorting and synchronization, however.
creator: bbockelm

title: Ticket #7767: condor_shadow activate/deactivates claim with wrong privilege
description: PR#124 Report from OSG is that, if all the schedd has token (say, in /etc/condor/tokens.d/) and the CCB is necessary to talk to the starter, then the condor_shadow will invoke the activateClaim RPC with PRIV_USER. Unfortunately, since the token is owned by PRIV_CONDOR, doing a RPC which involves going to the CCB results in a permission denied. title: Ticket #2565: WANT_HOLD doesn't put jobs on hold
description: The following configuration in 7.7.1 and 7.7.2 results in the job being evicted and returning to the idle state, rather than going on hold: PREEMPT = True WANT_HOLD = True However, WANT_HOLD succeeds if the hold subcode is set to something non-zero: WANT_HOLD_SUBCODE = 1 The problem was introduced in #2329. If I revert 3de9e262 and 2e4eddc4, the problem goes away. The strange dependence on hold subcode comes from this code in UniShadow::holdJob(): // exit immediately if the remote side is failing out or has already exited. if ( hold_reason_subcode != 0 || ( iPrevExitReason != JOB_SHOULD_HOLD && iPrevExitReason != -1 )) { // don't wait for final update b/c there isn't one. DC_Exit( JOB_SHOULD_HOLD ); } I think this code is using hold_reason_subcode to determine whether this is a remote hold event or periodic_hold. This is not the right way to differentiate. In fact, hold_reason_subcode may be non-zero for periodic_hold if the user sets periodic_hold_subcode, so this test can be wrong in both cases.

title: Ticket #4632: Documentation for SIZE field of condor_q is misleading
description: The manual entry for condor_q: SIZE - The value of job ClassAd attribute MemoryUsage (in Mbytes), when the attribute is defined, and ImageSize (in Kbytes), otherwise. This is confusing, incomplete, and (I think) inaccurate as evidenced by user confusion in ticket 38026 to CHTC-requests. The documentation above implies that SIZE could be in Mbytes or Kbytes, when in fact I think it is always in Mbytes. It also never gives the "big picture", but instead just gives the gritty-low-level info. Suggest it say instead something like: SIZE - The peak amount of memory in megabytes consumed by the job; note this value is only refreshed periodically. The actual value reported is taken from the job ClassAd attribute MemoryUsage if this attribute is defined, and from job attribute ImageSize otherwise. TJ, please confirm what I am saying above is true, and if so, please correct the manual in the V8_2-branch (and merge forward). Also take a look at ticket 38026 in CHTC-requests and see if you think there is an additional problem beyond just misleading documentation.

title: Ticket #5920: Blocking log event reads with Python bindings can return prematurely
description: Blocking reads of log events (i.e. read an event with no specified timeout) are broken with the Python bindings, using either the LogReader or EventIterator classes. For example, with EventIterator.poll, when given a positive timeout argument it seems to work fine. But if timeout is the default value of -1, it returns within a second with no event: The following code will demonstrate the bug: x = htcondor.read_events(open('EventLog')) for _ in x: pass # fire through all events so nothing's left x.poll(4000) # blocks for 4 seconds as expected x.poll() # should block indefinitely but returns after a second In addition, sub-second LogReader blocking polling on platforms without inotify (mac, windows) is also broken for no good reason.

title: Ticket #1430: SUBMIT_EXPRS docs vs code disagree on overrides
description:
The documention for SUBMIT_EXPRS claims: Note that adding an attribute to a job's ClassAd will not function as a method for specifying default values of submit description file commands forgotten in a job's submit description file. The command in the submit description file results in actions by condor_submit, while the use of SUBMIT_EXPRS adds a job ClassAd attribute at a later point in time. The implication is that job ClassAd attributes added with SUBMIT_EXPRS are apply after the submit file is processes, and thus overrides them. This doesn't match what the code actually does. The code actually behaves as a default. Using ImageSize as an example, I can specify the image_size in the submit file as expected: % /bin/echo -e "executable=/bin/true
image_size=12345
queue
" | condor_submit -verbose -dump /dev/null | grep ^ImageSize ImageSize = 12345 I can specify ImageSize in the configuration file as expected: % /bin/echo -e "executable=/bin/true
queue
" | env _CONDOR_ImageSize=4242 _CONDOR_SUBMIT_EXPRS=ImageSize condor_submit -verbose -dump /dev/null | grep ^ImageSize ImageSize = 4242 But if I specify both, I would expect the configuration file (4242) to win, but in practice the submit file (12345) does: % /bin/echo -e "executable=/bin/true
image_size=12345
queue
" | env _CONDOR_ImageSize=4242 _CONDOR_SUBMIT_EXPRS=ImageSize condor_submit -verbose -dump /dev/null | grep ^ImageSize ImageSize = 12345 This seems to function as a default just fine, disagreeing with the claims of the manual. First: figure out which is correct, the code or the manual. Second: Fix the code or the manual to conform with the other. Third: If the code is correct, resolve #404 as SUBMIT_EXPRS solves the problem. Open a new ticket: "Feature request: allow config file to always override submit file."

title: Ticket #956: We should have a backtrace log
description: We should have a subsystem dependent log file devoted strictly to backtraces. The dprintf system could keep a cyclic buffer of N lines in the current debugging modes so that when the back trace happens, those N lines plus the backtrace get emitted to the file with demarcation lines around it. Then one can simply look at the backtraces as they happen with a little bit of context without having to dig around in much faster rotating logs. This is a regular log file and would rotate normally. The purpose of this would be catching bad, but not fatal, semantic misunderstandings in our code base. Examples follow: calling scheduler_timeout() inside of itself produces a backtrace, but we don't EXCEPT

title: Ticket #1963: Failure to write a UserLog event is not fatal
description: With the v7.5.6 release candidate, on CHTC we have observed jobs running to completion and leaving the queue, and yet both the global and job event logs only have a running event - no execute or terminate event. One big problem is the shadow does nothing beyond a dprintf when writing a user log event fails. For example, when writing the job terminate event log fails, the shadow just does a dprintf and then merrily tells the schedd everything was fine, and the schedd then removes the job from the queue.
remarks: 2011-Mar-11 17:48:23 by tannenba: Commit [21031] was code reviewed by gthain - pushed into v7.5.6-branch. We will be installing a shadow with these changes onto submit.chtc.wisc.edu to see if we can catch the problem in the act. 2011-Mar-14 11:59:20 by tannenba: After running the v7.5.6 prelease 2.5 days with the additional userlock log messages, we caught it in the act. Interesting shadow log snippet attached to this ticket. What we see is Shadow's attempting to grab the lock on the global event log, and chronically failing to do so for a period of a few seconds apparently because the underlying call to fcntl() is failing. When the underlying fcntl fails, apparently we ultimately fail to log the event anywhere. Our handling of fcntl failures is apparently not very robust. Note this brief period of locking failures did not happen while the global event log was being rotated, so the rotation code is in the clear for the moment. This may not be a regression. The lock failures appeared to happen grabbing the lock on the global event log (lots of shadows all locking the same file), and happened when there was a flood of events to log (many job evictions happened at the same time for some reason). The global event log has only been enabled on CHTC since end of Dec. 2011-Apr-06 08:45:03 by tannenba: GregT, please code review [21277] and [21278] 2011-Apr-06 14:09:23 by cweiss: A comment concerning changes in file_lock.unix.cpp: For the non-blocking case we loop w/o an additional break condition in case of ​EINTR. I know that this has been that way since the dawn of time and unlikely to end up in an infinite loop, but I think I'd feel more comfortable if this loop also had a deterministic upper bound , maybe also num_retries < _lock_file_num_retries ?

title: Ticket #813: Remove MASTER_NEW_BINARY_DELAY param
description: http://www.cs.wisc.edu/condor/manual/v7.3/3_3Configuration.html#17412 MASTER_NEW_BINARY_DELAY Once the condor_master has discovered a new binary, this macro controls how long it waits before attempting to execute the new binary. This delay exists because the condor_master might notice a new binary while it is in the process of being copied, in which case trying to execute it yields unpredictable results. The entry is defined in seconds and defaults to 120 (2 minutes). It sounds like this param was introduced to avoid a race condition. Copying binaries onto a system was taking longer than it took the condor_master to restart the binary. This param just gives the copy a 2 minute window to finish - surely that's all that'll ever be needed. It seems this is a hack-workaround. A fix would be for the master to record some stat info for each binary and only restart when the info stabilizes. A TOCTOU still exists there of course, but a user doesn't have to remember about the delay. Why care? I've run into situations where the delay is rather unexpected and causes user confusion - especially while restarting an entire pool. It's also yet another behavior people need to remember to understand how Condor will behave - Condor's cognitive footprint.

title: Ticket #4777: ClassAd references don't handle nested ads properly
description: When calculating the internal references of a ClassAd expression, attribute references that delve into a nested ad aren't handled properly. Often, the attribute name in the nested ad is listed as if it were in the main ad. The problems are mainly with GetInternalReferences(), but some of changes will also affect GetExternalReferences(). This ensures the two remain complementary. GetInternalReferences() and GetExternalReferences() create an EvalState with rootAd set to the immediate parent scope of the ExprTree being evaluated. This suggests that references that go into any outer parent scopes should be considered external. We should change the lookup and evaluation code to treat EvalState::rootAd as the root of the tree, even if that ad has a non-NULL parentScope. It will be difficult to support the full-names option of GetInternalReferences() in all cases, particularly when you have references inside nested ads. I propose we eliminate the full-names option and always use short names, and the short names are attributes of the ClassAd that GetInternalReferences() was invoked on. For the attribute reference My.UidDomain (assuming UidDomain is in the ad), both My and UidDomain would be included in the internal references. The compat layer can filter out My.

Now, only B is returned. 2015-Jan-27 16:22:10 by jfrey: The effect of this bug on users is minimal and hard to characterize. No version history.

title: Ticket #7858: Global Job Priority breaks flocking
description: Fermi reported some schedds doing little or no flocking to one of their pools. Investigation shows that the main pool (the CMS global pool) has global job priorities enabled (USE_GLOBAL_JOB_PRIOS=True). This causes the schedd to see multiple negotiation sessions during a negotiator cycle, each for a small range of job priority values. At the end of each session, the schedd recomputes the flocking level. If no jobs were rejected, then the schedd thinks all jobs for the submitter have a match and lowers the flocking level to that of the pool just negotiated with. This is very similar to #7549 (Negotiator prefetch breaks flocking). The negotiator config parameter NEGOTIATOR_JOB_CONSTRAINT can also cause this problem.

title: Ticket #6434: event log reader should tolerate well formed events it does not know
description: The event log reader library currently aborts if it sees an event ID that it doesn't know. This makes it dangerous to add new event types because older readers might see them and then abort. Since the first part of is well defined, and the termination marker is also well defined, it is possible for the event log reader to skip past them and even to read and re-write them as long as we are not trying to convert from XML logs to non-XML logs and visa versa. The proposed fix is to define a FutureEvent, which will be instantiated whenever the event log reader reads an event with an event ID that is not in it's list of known IDs. This event will capture the event id, the remainder of the event line (after the timestamp) in a field called 'head' and all of the lines before the ... terminator in a field called 'payload'. This event will be able to write the event back out from these fields, but the primary use is to be able to skip over them when scanning for fields that the read does recognise, such as the submit event and remove event.

title: Ticket #5648: too much time recomputing autoclusters
description: Some SCHEDD's at the Brookhaven site are spending many MINUTES (sometimes almost an hour) rebuilding the PrioRec array. More detailed profiling seems to indicate that the time is being spent in the code that removes jobid's from one autocluster -> jobidset because the code is doing a brute force scan through all of the autoclusters to find the correct one to remove the job from. This can apparently take up to 15 seconds per-job when the number of autoclusters is quite large. This is unacceptably slow. Fortunately, the index into the autocluster->jobidset map is known just one layer up in the call tree, so this removal can be hugely improved, and even if the old clusterid is NOT known or is wrong, the jobidset will still be garbage collected correctly by the mark/sweep code.

title: Ticket #2532: Finishing a unit test you're not in should be an error
description: If there is a bug in the testing code, and one of the PASS, FAIL, or ABORT macros is called, but we're not currently in a test, the unit test binary will merrily mark it up as a pass/fail/abort and continue on. This will lead to a summary claiming that more tests finished that started. The batch test wrapper (lib_unit_tests.run) will correctly treat this as an error. Tracking down the rogue code is a pain in the butt. Having run into exactly this situation, I propose: Implement #2531, so we know which file contains the unexpected PASS/FAIL/ABORT Modify class Emitter to add "bool in_test" Modify Emitter::Emitter to initialize in_test = false Modify Emitter::emit_test: if(in_test == true) { freak out } in_test = true; Modify Emitter::emit_result_success, Emitter::emit_result_failure, and Emitter::emit_result_abort if(in_test == false) { freak out, reporting the file and line number } in_test = false;

title: Ticket #7730: blahp temporary directories include hash character
description: To prevent cross-talk between multiple jobs with the same initialdir, the blahp makes a temporary subdirectory for each job, in which the job is run. After the job exits, output files are moved to the initialdir and the temporary directory is removed. To avoid leaking the temporary directory on failure, the gridmanager picks the name of the directory and ensures it's removed after the blahp reports the job is done. To guarantee each job's temporary directory name is unique, the gridmanager uses the GlobalJobId job attribute as part of the value. GlobalJobId values include the # character. We have a report on htcondor-users that the # character in a directory name is causing problems for software at one site. We should fix the gridmanager so that the directory name it gives to the blahp does not include the # character. Additionally, we should consider changing the blahp to allow disabling the creation of a temporary subdirectory. In a CE configuration, each job has its own initial dir, so the subdirectory is unnecessary. As a workaround, the user or admin can put Remote_JobDirectory=Undefined in the job ad. This prevents the gridmanager from dictating the name of the temporary directory to the blahp, which falls back to picking a random name that doesn't contain any problematic characters.
remarks: 2020-Jul-09 11:05:41 by jfrey: The '@' character can also appear in GlobalJobId and should probably be sanitized. 2020-Jul-16 09:18:25 by jfrey: I don't plan to include a backwards-compatibility check with this fix. As a result, for jobs in the queue when Condor is upgraded, the gridmanager won't use the current filename when cleaning up a leaked blahp temporary directory. I'm not concerned about this for two reasons. First, the cleanup in the gridmanager is a backstop for the blahp, which does the removal except in infrequent failure cases. Second, in an HTCondor-CE or BOSCO setup, a leaked directory won't be transferred to the submitter and will be cleaned up with its parent directory when the job is ready to leave the queue. 2020-Jul-28 10:38:12 by johnkn: CODE_REVIEW looks good.

title: Ticket #2162: Condor-C and file transfer plugins
description: I'm using Condor-C with file transfer plugins. I'd like the file transfer plugin to be executed on the worker node. However, it does not seem this is possible. If you give the following input file: +remote_TransferInput = "srm://srm.unl.edu:8443/srm/v2/server?SFN=/mnt/hadoop/dropfiles/condorc-test-hda.raw" it gets transformed into TransferInput = "srm://srm.unl.edu:8443/srm/v2/server?SFN=/mnt/hadoop/dropfiles/condorc-test-hda.raw" on the remote schedd. Then, Condor-C will spool to the remote schedd. The spool process will transform the TransferInput to: SUBMIT_TransferInput = "srm://srm.unl.edu:8443/srm/v2/server?SFN=/mnt/hadoop/dropfiles/condorc-test-hda.raw" TransferInput = "condorc-test-hda.raw" Hence, the file transfer plugin gets called on the remote schedd (a blocking operation, stopping the machinery of the schedd) and the file is transferred from remote schedd to remote worker node using condor file transfer. My preferred way of fixing this is to have any URL get ignored when spooling and passed to the worker node.
remarks: 2011-May-16 21:34:07 by bbockelm: Actually, this affects more than Condor-C: the same thing happens on condor_submit with spooling. Try the below submit file with "condor_submit -spool"; the URL plugin gets invoked by the schedd for the srm:// file and the other file is spooled, then the schedd does condor file transfer of both files to the worker node. I'm pretty sure this is not the intended behavior, especially as it defeats one of the purposes of the URL plugins (scalability) if everything goes through the schedd. universe = vanilla executable = test.sh output = test_local.out error = test_local.err log = test_local.log ShouldTransferFiles = YES WhenToTransferOutput = ON_EXIT transfer_input_files = condor-7.5.4-1.rhel5.x86_64.rpm, srm://srm.unl.edu:8443/srm/v2/server?SFN=/mnt/hadoop/dropfiles/condorc-test-hda.raw queue 1 2011-May-18 16:09:59 by psilord: Ok, I reviewed the patch and it looks good. I've committed it into V7_6_1-branch, merged to V7_6-branch, and merged to master.

title: Ticket #7360: macro default does not allow - character and workaround is broken
description: Michael Pelletier reports: "The following leaves the trailing ")" at the end of the BASENAME macro's output when expanding." IMAGE_FILE = $(IMAGE_FILE:/user/1127883/DOCKER/singularity/c5-tf-container.simg) IMAGE_BASE = $BASENAME(IMAGE_FILE) MY.ImageBasename = "$(IMAGE_BASE)" hold = true executable = /bin/sleep arguments = $(IMAGE_BASE) queue :!condor_q 29243 -af args ImageBasename c5-tf-container.simg) c5-tf-container.simg)
remarks: 2020-Mar-09 16:12:08 by johnkn: The problem here is that IMAGE_FILE is not self-substituting in the first line so it's value ends up being $(IMAGE_FILE:/user/1127883/DOCKER/singularity/c5-tf-container.simg) which looks to the $BASENAME function like file with a URL prefix of $(IMAGE_FILE: and a file extension of .simg) It turns out the actual problem here is the use of - in the filename. This is not a legal character to follow the : in the $(name:default) pattern, the use of - causes the parser to skip over the entire $() expansion thinking that it is not actually a $() expansion. There is an intended work-around DEF_IMAGE=/user/1127883/DOCKER/singularity/c5-tf-container.simg IMAGE_FILE=$(IMAGE_FILE:$(DEF_IMAGE)) But there is a bug that prevents that from working. For now, your workaround should be if !defined IMAGE_FILE IMAGE_FILE = /user/1127883/DOCKER/singularity/c5-tf-container.simg endif 2020-Apr-10 07:42:27 by tim: Bulk change of target version from v080808 to v080809 using ticket-target-mover. 2020-May-06 12:17:52 by tim: CODE REVIEW: Looks good.

title: Ticket #3323: getProcInfoRaw performs useless retries
description: Current code has the number of attempts to find the pid in /proc hard coded at 5. That's 5 passes per pid. Logs are showing as much as 68010 failed tries in 12 minutes. Looking at the logs further, I find that the scenario is that either there is 5 failed attempts per pid or success on the first try. Multiple attempts aren't required. The issue with multiple attempts is that the Master is spending upwards of 30s processing these while also failing to process Childalives.
remarks: 2013-Jan-22 10:54:51 by johnkn: Bulk change of target version from v070903 to v070904 using ./ticket-target-mover. 2013-Mar-05 10:58:27 by johnkn: Bulk change of target version from v070904 to v070905 using ./ticket-target-mover. 2013-Apr-22 11:10:10 by johnkn: Bulk change of target version from v070905 to v070906 using ./ticket-target-mover. 2013-Aug-23 19:05:55 by eje: TESTING config requires disabling procd: USE_PROCD = False MASTER_DEBUG = D_FULLDEBUG D_PROCFAMILY # new option to reduce failed attempts to get proc info PROC_INFO_NUM_ATTEMPTS = 1 To repro failed attempts at get-proc-info, spin up a pool, and run a few jobs. Watch MasterLog: $ tail -f MasterLog | grep 'does not exist' Now shoot the job processes in the head. It may be most effective to do this a few times repeatedly. $ pkill -9 condor_starter $ pkill -9 condor_shadow Eventually you should see master fail to find some of these processes. The original behavior is that it will try each pid 5 times: $ tail -f MasterLog | grep 'does not exist' 08/23/13 16:40:52 ProcAPI::getProcInfo() pid 15867 does not exist. 08/23/13 16:40:52 ProcAPI::getProcInfo() pid 15867 does not exist. 08/23/13 16:40:52 ProcAPI::getProcInfo() pid 15867 does not exist. 08/23/13 16:40:52 ProcAPI::getProcInfo() pid 15867 does not exist. 08/23/13 16:40:52 ProcAPI::getProcInfo() pid 15867 does not exist. 08/23/13 16:40:52 ProcAPI::getProcInfo() pid 15868 does not exist. 08/23/13 16:40:52 ProcAPI::getProcInfo() pid 15868 does not exist. 08/23/13 16:40:52 ProcAPI::getProcInfo() pid 15868 does not exist. 08/23/13 16:40:52 ProcAPI::getProcInfo() pid 15868 does not exist. 08/23/13 16:40:52 ProcAPI::getProcInfo() pid 15868 does not exist. With the new code update, you can set 'PROC_INFO_NUM_ATTEMPTS = 1', and it will only attempt each pid once: $ tail -f MasterLog | grep 'does not exist' 08/23/13 16:46:27 ProcAPI::getProcInfo() pid 27424 does not exist. 08/23/13 16:46:27 ProcAPI::getProcInfo() pid 27425 does not exist. 08/23/13 16:46:27 ProcAPI::getProcInfo() pid 27426 does not exist. 08/23/13 16:46:27 ProcAPI::getProcInfo() pid 27427 does not exist. 2013-Aug-23 19:06:52 by eje: topic branch: V8_1-gt3323-get-proc-info-optimize 2013-Sep-13 10:52:08 by johnkn: CODE_REVIEW: this patch is rejected. The problem is not the number of retries, the problem is that there are some failure conditions that should be treated as a reason to break out of the retry loop because there is no reason to expect to get a different answer on retry. Instead of adding a configuration knob for retry count, the PROCAPI_NOPID & PROCAPI_PERM errors should just unconditionally break out of the loop. 2013-Sep-13 11:23:55 by jrt: I don't disagree, but I don't know the history of the code. Evidently the original author thought there would be a different answer on a retry. Hence a knob that preserves old behavior vs. a change that has no way to revert. 2013-Sep-13 12:37:41 by johnkn: If you feel that there should be a knob to disable bailing out of the loop on NOPID and NOACCESS conditions, then I won't object to that. But I don't believe that the knob is necessary. Review the commit history of this code to see why the author though the loop was necessary. I'm convinced that the retries are sometimes necessary. 2013-Sep-13 13:02:21 by eje: If there are return codes that are guaranteed unrecoverable, then a hard breakout on those seems like a good strategy. The original motivation for the ticket was that multiple retries were causing condor_master performance problems. With that in mind, a return-independent throttle on retries seems like the only way to guarantee that repeated failures can't swamp condor_master. 2013-Sep-26 17:20:56 by eje: The code history for ProcAPI::getProcInfoRaw() indicates that the read of the /proc/* files themselves is unreliable: // read the entry a certain number of times since it appears that linux // often simply does something stupid while reading. I found no indication whether or not /proc/* read failures were fixed at a later date. The source of failure is independent of any particular return code, so retaining the iteration on failure is still prudent. 2013-Oct-11 16:51:53 by tannenba: The retries in procapi are mainly there for dealing with failing to read consistent info out of the /proc/pid file (it is not 'snapshot' safe). We have no reason to think that we need to retry if we fail to open the pid file due to ENOENT or EPERM. Thus after discussion with eje and others, decided to not add yet another knob but instead fix the root of the issue: do not do the retries in the event of ENOENT or EPERM (as suggested in the code review). All the reported problems were related to ENOENT, so we should be good. p.s. not sure this warrants a version history item, as it isn't really user visible... resolving.

title: Ticket #3773: Put path to bin, sbin, libexec, and CONDOR_CONFIG in job's environment
description: When starting a job, we should put the paths to HTCondor's bin, sbin, and libexec directories into the job's environment, perhaps as _HTCONDOR_BIN, _HTCONDOR_SBIN, and _HTCONDOR_LIBEXEC. These paths would just be to the patching BIN, SBIN, and LIBEXEC paths in the configuration file. We should also ensure the CONDOR_CONFIG is set as it was set when HTCondor was startedd. Rationale: There are good reasons for a job to want to use various HTCondor programs. condor_chirp is the obvious one; it exists for the specific purpose of being called by jobs. (See #3753 for an example.) A job might also be doing clever things like running on a remote machine and wanting to submit a new job, perhaps a whole DAG. But it's HTCondor doesn't make this easy. The tools are not in the PATH, nor is CONDOR_CONFIG set if it's required. A job needs to experimentally search for the correct configuration, or pools need to be specially configured to make this practical. If we advertise the paths to the directories and set CONDOR_CONFIG for the job, running other HTCondor programs because much easier. Worth considering: a fair number of users are running HTCondor under HTCondor. (Glide-ins. The BaTLab for our own tests). Depending on which things we're setting, it's possible we might confuse a nested HTCondor.

title: Ticket #3289: Grid manager prematurely destroys keypairs.
description: The GM_DELETE state in ec2job.cpp attempts to destroy the keypair created earlier in the job's lifecycle. This state unconditionally follows GM_HOLD, which is entered when, for instance, a network burp prevents GM_PROBE_JOB from discovering the state of a (previously noted to be) running instance. It may be OK to destroy the keypair -- if doing so doesn't destroy the instance's copy of the key, because if the job isn't still running by the time we get back to it, we can just make another one for resubmission -- but we shouldn't delete the user's copy of the private key until we know that the instance is gone, because otherwise they can't log in to it. While we could destroy the keypair in GM_SAVE_INSTANCE_ID -- under the condition above, since the instance has started running and has its own undeletable copy of the public key -- it won't hurt anything to leave the keypair active longer, until, say, GM_DELETE. Checking in GM_DELETE to see if the job is REMOVED or COMPLETED should suffice to only delete the user's key until we know the instance is terminated. (If we have a problem terminating the instance when the user removes the job, we'll go into HOLD instead.) This is probably the smallest code change that will resolve the problem. We also need to make sure that we handle recovering a job whose instance has a destroyed keypair.

title: Ticket #3909: Make UPDATE_JOBAD handling more efficient in the schedd
description: When a user runs condor_qedit to modify job ads, there are several cases where the schedd will repeatedly try to send useless UPDATE_JOBAD signals. When multiple attributes are modified in the same job ad, whether in one or multiple condor_qedit commands, the UPDATE_JOBAD signal is sent multiple times. When attributes in multiple jobs managed by the same gridmanager are modified, the gridmanager is signaled multiple times. The schedd will repeatedly try and fail to send UPDATE_JOBAD signals for local and standard universe jobs, even though the local starter and standard shadow don't support them. When resending an UPDATE_JOBAD signal, the schedd doesn't recognize when the job no longer has a shadow or gridmanager managing it, and will keep trying to send the signal periodically.

title: Ticket #7419: Cleanup crufty man page creation in CMake
description: When working on some man pages for #7361, I noticed that our man page creation is filled with Rube Goldberg-esque gadgetry for what appears to be a fairly simple process. Things I noticed: Manpages only build in-source, which would break Todd's Docker images that suggest to mount the source code directory read-only. If the in-source outputs are present, then re-running CMake will disable the creation of the manpages. So, if you ever switch branches - or otherwise touch CMakeLists.txt, you must "rm -rf" all the manpage build products. There is a comment from 2009 saying that this crazy setup is for an "old version of NMI". Hopefully the need is passed! CMake actually only gets as far as invoking a Makefile; the latter simply runs a single command The CMake custom_command does not provide the right dependencies, meaning the docs are re-generated on every build -- even if no source files have changed. I suspect a lot of this is coming from the old manual build -- which was far more complex. For 8.9, it appears far simpler to invoke sphinx-build directly and with the appropriate command line arguments to place the build products in the build directory. Here's some documentation I found to help this along: https://eb2.co/blog/2012/03/sphinx-and-cmake-beautiful-documentation-for-c---projects/

title: Ticket #452: remote job in grid universe can be killed even after lease renewed
description: In Condor-C, the gridmanager on the submit side will renew the job lease attributes in the job ClassAd on the remote schedd. However, if the remote job is already running, the remote side schedd will have spawned a shadow. This shadow has a cached copy of the job classad upon which it evaluates job policy expressions, such as the expression that says the job should be killed when the lease expires. The problem is the submit side gridmanager updates the copy of the remote job ad in the schedd, but the job can still be killed because the remote side shadow never sees the update. This problem is blocking the BatLab's ETICs deployment. Note we have observed this problem w/ Condor-C, but the same trouble may very well exist for Condor-G due to caching of the job ad by the gridmanager. In addition, the job router caches the job ad... maybe another problem area. Two solutions are proposed, an immediate short term work-around for BatLab, and the real fix. Short Term. Detailed in #453. Real Fix. The schedd should signal the shadow (and/or gridmanager and/or jobmanager) when the shadow should refresh its copy of the job ad from the schedd. The schedd would send this signal whenever a job ad is changed by a tool other than the shadow itself. This distinction could be made because the schedd has a public port (used by tools like condor_q) and a private port used for shadow/gridmanager connections. Changes to the ad initiated by the private port should be ignored.

title: Ticket #4720: Files fail to spool using python bindings to an 8.0.x host
description: Symptoms of the Error Using the condor_ce_trace tool against an 8.0.x host, an error occurs when trying to spool files: RuntimeError: DCSchedd::spoolJobFiles:7002:File transfer failed for target job 790.0: Failed to receive GoAhead message from 128.230.171.6. condor_ce_trace uses the python bindings to submit to the remote schedd. Using `condor_submit -spool` and `condor_transfer_data` appears to work ok. Cause of the Error For file transfer commands, if the DCSchedd object doesn't know the version of the schedd, it assumes it's the same version as itself. Thus, it assumes the schedd supports the disk-load-based throttling protocol change introduced in HTCondor 8.1.0. The python bindings construct a DCSchedd object by providing it with only the sinful string of the schedd. Thus, the DCSchedd object doesn't know what version the schedd is. Reproducing the Error Grab htcondor-ce-client from the 'osg' repo to get the condor_ce_trace tool and run: condor_ce_trace --debug its-condor-ce.syr.edu Alternatively, use condor_submit using the schedd's sinful string: condor_submit -spool -address <sinful string> Proposed Solution The security negotiation that occurs at the start of most CEDAR commands (and forced for these file transfer commands) includes an exchange of the versions of the peers. The DCSchedd object could extract the version information from the CEDAR layer when it's not already known.

title: Ticket #1522: support directories in the input/output file transfer lists
description: It would be useful to support transfer of directories. For example, it may sometimes be convenient to describe workflows using directories as containers for input/ouput so that the specifics of the files produced and consumed by a given run of the application don't have to affect the workflow description. In some cases, handling directories would also simplify or eliminate the need for job wrapper scripts that untar inputs and tar up outputs. I propose supporting the following: A directory in the file transfer list is copied, along with all of its contents. The directory is named on the remote side in the same way that files are treated: i.e. if a path to the directory is specified, only its basename is created on the remote side, unless a name remap specifies otherwise. Analogous to rsync syntax, if a directory name in the file transfer list is followed by a slash, this has special meaning. It means that the contents of the directory should be copied but not the directory itself. Symlinks to files should be followed when opening files for transfer, because that is the existing behavior. Symlinks to directories are forbidden until we have time to implement support for them. When we do implement it, internal symlinks should be recreated as relative symlinks on the remote side (i.e. we don't follow internal symlinks). External symlinks should be followed and we must detect circularity and treat it as an error. When output is auto-selected (i.e. by looking for new files in the output sandbox), we keep the existing behavior of ignoring subdirectories. If the user wants output from subdirectories, then explicit output selection should be used.

What remains to do should be proposed in separate tickets: support directories in other grid universes, and support symlinks to directories. 2010-Sep-16 14:56:13 by danb: Jaime found a bug with this feature. condor_submit no longer complains if the stdout/stderr point to directories.

title: Ticket #4370: Memory leak when reusing cached collector connection
description: Whenever a cached connection to the collector is reused to send a new command, if the collector can't read the full CEDAR message immediately, it leaks a DaemonCommandProtocol object. This appears to have resulted in a large amount of leaked memory in GlideinWMS's collectors when they upgraded to HTCondor 8.1.5. When a daemon needs to handle a new incoming command on a socket, it creates a DaemonCommandProtocol object. This object handles security negotiation, determining which command is being requested, and calling the appropriate callback for that command. It can do a lot of the requisite network I/O non-blocking, allowing the main event loop to run when it needs to wait for data. It does this by registering the socket with DaemonCore, requesting to be called back when there's data available for reading. This is a problem when a new command arrives on a socket that the collector has cached from a previous command. The socket is already registered in DaemonCore as a command socket and the same socket can't be registered for two different callbacks. Before HTCondor 8.1.5, the new registration would fail and the collector would close the connection. With the new non-blocking code added in 8.1.5, DaemonCommandProtocol avoids re-registering the socket if it's already registered. That leaves the original registration in place, the DaemonCommandProtocol object's callback is never called, and the object hangs around forever. To fix this, DaemonCommandProtocol needs to replace the existing socket registration with its new registration, then restore the old one when its callback is invoked.

title: Ticket #5561: [EC2 GAHP] Retry on AWS' RequestLimitExceeded
description: John Hover writes: > Last Friday we attempted a very large scale AWS test, using 3 submit hosts, > all three Amazon regions, and many instance types. Each submit host was > configured the same, and submitted to all three regions/endpoints. > > Everything went OK until hitting the ~5000 machine level, at which point, > over a couple hours, each submit host began seeing AWS RequestLimitExceeded > messages. Getting that error sent the VM job into HELD state. We should instead respond to RequestLimitExceeded by retrying the limit-exceeding request after a(n exponential) back-off (based on the number of RequestLimitExceeded errors received since the last success or failure). Milestones Milestone 1 - Respond to RateLimitExceeded messages Planned completion date: 2016-03-28 For this milestone, we plan to complete implementation of responding to an Amazon RateLimitExceeded error via an exponential back-off algorithm recommended by Amazon engineers. More specifically, the EC2 GAHP will now examine each Amazon result code for the RateLimitExceeded error. If the GAHP finds it, it will wait until the exponential back-off period has expired before re-sending the failed request and sending any subsequent requests. If that back-off period would result in waiting long enough for the signature on the RPC we need to retry to expire (~5 minutes), the GAHP will fail the request immediately. We will add a configurable throttle to limit the rate at which the GAHP will send requests to the EC2 server. Milestone 2 - Reduce number of requests sent to Amazon Planned completion date: 2016-03-28 We plan to significantly reduce the number of job-specific requests made by HTCondor to Amazon. This should reduce the frequency with which we encounter the RateLimitExceeded error. Currently each EC2 job submitted to HTCondor results in four requests made to Amazon: submit spot instance request cancel spot instance request tag instance remove instance upon a condor_rm We believe we can reduce this to just one request. Item 2 can be eliminated by making the spot request a "fire-once" request upon submission. Item 3 can be eliminated by not requesting a tag in the job submit file (currently Johns does not typically use the tags). Item 4 can be eliminated by having the glidein jobs themselves shutdown the instance when the startd has not had any claimed slots for more than X minutes, instead of relying on the factory to perform a condor_rm of the EC2 job. To facilitate this, we will produce an HTCondor config recipe for John to use. At completion of Milestone 1 and 2, we will ask John Hover to test incremental release for regressions by using his small EC2 pool in its quiescent low-cost state (40-50 instances). Milestone 3 - Complete extensive synthetic testing Planned completion date: 2016-04-04 We will use extensive synthetic testing to develop confidence that the binaries produced upon completion of Milestone 1 and 2 will function as expected both during "normal" operation and in rarer cases. The approach will be for the HTCondor code to pretend to receive a RateLimitExceeded error at specific corner cases and/or according to a defined random distribution. Any problems we discover will be fixed and a new pre-release sent to John Hover to help verify continued forward progress. Our goal at the completion of this milestone is to allow John Hover to be able to perform the first functional full-scale (10k instances) tests as early in the first week of April, and have reasonable confidence in success since we understand performing a full-scale test has a non-negligible monetary cost. Milestone 4 - Addition of metrics Planned completion date: 2016-04-13 HTCondor will report, via the grid manager resource ads which are sent to the condor_collector, statistics about i) how many requests were sent, ii) how many received RequestLimitExceeded errors, and iii) how many times the GAHP returned failure for a request because the signature expired. In addition, the EC2 job classad will include an attribute LastRemoteStatusUpdate which will contain the time HTCondor last heard from Amazon about the state of this job; this will allow the user to discern if the information in the job classad is stale (perhaps due to exponential back-off). Milestone 5 - Prioritize commands sent to Amazon Planned completion date: 2016-04-18 When the grid manager has multiple commands to issue to the GAHP, it will issue them in priority order: status commands highest and commands to generate more work lowest. Design Document Work on a design doc is in progress. A draft is available at the following address: https://docs.google.com/document/d/1g9F5Vx1YSDfC-ieBeGUxTSZ-sBKDI4IL7nWSzo-8K_I

title: Ticket #7399: condor_wait without inotify (lustre)
description: A user has a set-up where their users submit jobs from hosts with no running HTCondor daemons. To find out when their DAGs completed, these users were running condor_wait on a DAGMan log file on a (Lustre) shared file system. This worked for them using HTCondor 8.4.12, but broken when upgraded to HTCondor 8.8.5, because the Linux ports assume that if the kernel supports inotify, it's available for all log files, but Lustre does not currently support inotify. In an attempt to see if we could get a quick fix, we tried building the condor agent with a modified version of file_modified_trigger that did not use inotify (simply changed the ifdef to use the polling-based fallback). We re-deployed this newly built version to schedds and remote hosts, but this version also seemed to have issues - the dagman could no longer write to its log file if a condor_wait was being called (possibly locking?). I was able get it working if I pushed the standard 8.8.5 release to schedd hosts, and my modified version to a remote host; but we probably don't want to live in this modified build forever (in fact, we've just rolled back these remote hosts to using 8.4.12). > To make sure I understand: condor_wait built without inotify > prevents a DAGMan built without inotify from writing to its log (while the > condor_wait is running), but a DAGMan with inotify can write to its log > (while the same condor_wait is running)? That's correct - it seems the fallback for not using inotify may do some sort of locking. > Actually, I guess it might be even faster to check -- if the > schedd is running 8.8.x, what happens if condor_wait is from 8.4.x? This is actually what we're doing right now, and it seems to work fine. So it sounds like there's two problems: 8.8.5 does not fall back to the polling implementation if inotify is unavailable for a specific file. (This needs to be a run-time, not a compile-time decision.) The 8.8.5 polling implementation is broken (or used incorrectly by the new log-reading code?) -- the reader blocks the writer. We also need to verify that the inotify-based and polling-based implementations properly interoperate (as both reader/writer and writer/reader), because some set-ups, like sshfs, permit/require both.

title: Ticket #6971: Add timeouts to curl plugin
description: While debugging some squid issues with Moate, we realized that the curl_plugin basically has no timeouts. Basically, a particular CHTC-run squid had an issue where the server would allow clients to establish a TCP connection - but then one of the three worker processes would instantly lose track of the request. That means a request could be made from the curl_plugin but no response would be sent - ever! There are two timeouts we should be setting: Connection timeout: amount of time we're willing to wait for a TCP connection to be established. Useful when a firewall is silently dropping packets. Note this isn't the case described above. Minimum speed timeout: useful to ensure the transfer is making forward progress. (There is also an overall request timeout - but if the response size can vary from 1KB to 1GB, it's not clear what the value should be!) The speed timeout has two settings: sampling interval and the minimum average speed. If the average transfer speed falls below the minimum over the course of a sample interval, then the transfer is killed. For example, if the minimum average speed is set to 1KB/s and the sampling interval is set to 10 seconds, curl will kill the transfer if it does not receive at least 10KB over the course of 10 seconds. There is an infinite amount of tuning that can be done to pick out the values for the minimum speed timeout. I propose we don't spend too much time here and set something very minimal, like 1KB/s and 30 seconds. It would solve the problem at hand (zero bytes are sent out over the course of hours) but not the case where the file transfer is so slow to be unusable. Given that any default is likely wrong, we should additionally allow the user to override the values via an undocumented ClassAd setting. This would allow us to tune at CHTC without iterating over multiple versions of the code. If we decide this could be safely set by any user, we can document it. When the timeout occurs, we should consider it a transient error (as it was in this case -- squid was actually only a blackhole for approximately 1/3 of the transfers).

We should explicitly call this somewhere else, probably in InitializeCurl() or even the main() function. Lines 718 and 727: use safe_fopen_wrapper() instead of fopen(). The ParseAds() function makes me queasy for a bunch of reasons: No comments and confusing logic flow. Why do you bail out of the function if ad is unset but not if ad2 is unset? Why are you dynamically allocating the classad::ClassAd objects? This seems prone to leaks and doesn't offer any obvious advantages. Similarly, shouldn't job_ad and machine_ad just be non-pointer std::string objects? ad and ad2 should have more descriptive variable names. file_transfer.cpp Line 4816: This dprintf statement should happen inside each of the preceding if-statements (where we know the strings are non-empty), not outside. Line 4923: same as above file_transfer.h Why does setRuntimeAds() have const std::string & input parameters, instead of just basic std::string objects?

title: Ticket #6072: condor_status fails inside Docker container
description: When running a personal HTCondor inside a Docker container using default networking, the following fails: condor_status -schedd `hostname` It appears this is because get_daemon_name fails to behave reasonably for hosts without a FQDN. Docker sets the hostname to a randomly generated string, such as eb4f00c8f1ca. Docker correctly sets up forward and reverse host<->IP resolution using /etc/hosts. However, both hostname and hostname -f (which returns the FQDN) returns eb4f00c8f1ca. Unfortunately, get_fqdn_from_hostname considers any FQDN without a period (. character) invalid and returns the empty string. Then, get_daemon_name will happily return the empty string to the caller. Finally, condor_status errors out when the daemon name to query is the empty string. I believe get_daemon_name or get_fqdn_from_hostname should be updated to simply pass through hostnames where there is no registered DNS name. I only see two uses of get_fqdn_from_hostname in the code base, meaning it might not be so bad to change semantics. The other user is build_valid_daemon_name (which has some really unfortunate semantics - allocates memory via new[], meaning it must be disposed of via delete[]. title: Ticket #2898: mktime() is dominating compute cycles when used in non-DST timezone
description: While profiling the collector, I noticed that mktime was using an amazing 60% of the collector's cycles. It appears to happen due to CondorVersionInfo invoking mktime with tm_isdst = 1, which causes mktime to mysteriously burn a gigantic amount of time when invoked in a timezone not observing DST (e.g. Arizona, where I happen to live): For more info, see: http://erikerlandson.github.com/blog/2012/03/19/interaction-between-mktime-and-tm-isdst-a-compute-cycle-landmine/ When I was profiling, the collector, I set up a pool with 50 slots, and ran 200 jobs with 100 submitters, and also set up a "condor_status -any" every few seconds, to simulate a pool with a busy collector.

title: Ticket #1758: Aggregate submit file access checks
description: After submitting its jobs, condor_submit sends requests to the schedd to check whether it can access the jobs' files. Submit uses a new connection for each file check. Thus, if you submit more than 15,000 jobs, each with stdout and stderr, you burn through all of the ephemeral ports on the machine. For the next 30 seconds or so, they are in TIME_WAIT state. We've seen problems with the gridmanager being unable to connect to the schedd or any remote machines due to a lack of ports. The ATTEMPT_ACCESS command should be replaced with a more efficient version that takes a list of files to check in one command.

description: We need to be able to submit a standalone checkpoint image as a standard universe job. The only thing preventing this from working is the chdir() call that happens when restarting. Years ago Pete implemented a -_condor_relocatable argument that, if defined, would skip the chdir(), but it never made it into a release (only because we dropped the ball). It's now becoming very important again, as it would allow us to take advantage of a huge (3k-10k core) opportunistic Condor pool on campus. If for some reason this isn't trivial (i.e., it's more complicated than adding an "if arg_condor_relocatable == False" before the chdir) then it can be bumped to a Priority 2 -- but if it's not a complicated fix it's a very high priority for us. Usage: [general-opts] are -global Query all Schedulers in this pool -submitter <submitter> Get queue of specific submitter -name <name> Name of Scheduler -pool <host> Use host as the central manager to query -jobads <file> Read queue from a file of job ClassAds -userlog <file> Read queue from a user log file -constraint <expr> Add constraint on job ClassAds [restriction-list] each restriction may be one of <cluster> Get information about specific cluster <cluster>.<proc> Get information about specific job <owner> Information about jobs owned by <owner> [output-opts] are -cputime Display CPU_TIME instead of RUN_TIME -currentrun Display times only for current run -debug Display debugging info to console -dag Sort DAG jobs under their DAGMan -expert Display shorter error messages -globus Get information about jobs of type globus -goodput Display job goodput statistics -help [Universe|State] Display this screen, JobUniverses, JobStates -hold Get information about jobs on hold -io Show information regarding I/O -run Get information about running jobs -stream-results Produce output as jobs are fetched -version Print the Condor Version and exit -wide Widescreen output -autoformat[:V,ntlh] <attr> [attr2 [attr3 ...]] Print attr(s) with automatic formatting -format <fmt> <attr> Print attribute attr using format fmt -long Display entire ClassAds -xml Display entire ClassAds, but in XML -attributes X,Y,... Attributes to show in -xml and -long [analyze-opts] are -analyze[:<qual>] Perform matchmaking analysis on jobs -better-analyze[:<qual>] Perform more detailed match analysis <qual> is a comma separated list of one or more of priority Consider user priority during analysis summary Show a one-line summary for each job or machine reverse Analyze machines rather than jobs -machine <name> Machine name or slot name for analysis -mconstraint <expr> Machine constraint for analysis -slotads <file> Read Machine ClassAds for analysis from <file> <file> can be the output of condor_status -long -userprios <file> Read user priorities for analysis from <file> <file> can be the output of condor_userprio -l -nouserprios Don't consider user priority during analysis -reverse Analyze Machine requirements against jobs -verbose Show progress and machine names in results What's new from 7.8 series: -jobads, -userlog, <qual> on -analyze and -better-analyze, -machine, -mconstraint, -slotads, -userprios, -nouserprios, -reverse, -verbose, -autoformat -jobads <file> reads job classads from a file rather than from the schedd. this file can be the output of condor_q -long. -userlog <file> - reads job classads from a user/job log rather than the schedd. only a few fields of the job ad can be read from the userlog, but this is sufficient to determine the job status, and avoids loading the schedd when polling to see if the job has started or completed. -machine <slot_or_machine_name> - analyze only this slot or machine, rather than the whole pool. use only one of -machine or -mconstraint. -mconstraint <expr> - analyze only slots that match this expression, rather than the whole pool. may also be specified as -slotconstraint. use only one of either -machine or -mconstraint. -slotads <file> - read slot/machine ads from a file rather than the collector. this file can be the output of condor_status -long. -userprios <file> - read user priorities from a file rather than from the negotiator. this file can be the output of condor_userprio -long. this option forces the priority qualifier for -analyze and -better. -nouserprios - analyze without considering user priority, this is now the default unless -userprios <file> is specified or the priority qualifier is passed to -analyze or -better. -reverse - another way to specify reverse analyze, see -analyze:reverse. -verbose - include additional information about the progress of analyze and the names of machines that matched or did not match. not all machine names are output, the limit is about 1k. -analyze and -better-analyze now have optional qualifiers, one or more qualifiers may be specified, comma or : separated, without spaces. Like this -analyze:summary,reverse. qualifiers may be abbreviated sum, rev & pri. priority - consider user priority when doing analysis. this will fetch priorities from the negotiator unless -userprios <file> is also specified. Fetching user priorities from the negotiator may take a few minutes - it may wait until the negotiation cycle has ended. reverse - analyze slot (machine) Requirements and START expression against jobs. (default is job Requirements against machines). summary - print one line per job (or machine if used with reverse). title: Ticket #1308: Do-it-yourself meta-scheduler toolkit
description: DAGMan is a great metascheduler, but its quite clear in its goal. If you need to do metascheduling based on disk space management or you need cyclic workflows, DAGMan becomes a poor match. We can keep extending DAGMan, but these tasks seem out of scope. It would be nice to provide a simple toolkit that makes writing DAGMan-like systems easier. I'm envisioning a sort of message pump API. Something like void initial_jobs(CondorMetaScheduler & m) { m.submit_job(step_1); } void job_done(CondorMetaScheduler & m, unsigned int cluster, unsigned int process, int result) { if(result == 0 && job_is_step_1(cluster)) { m.submit_job(step_2); } } int main() { CondorMetaScheduler m; m.job_done_callback(job_done); m.initialize(initial_jobs); // If all you need is the simple pump, you can just call "m.pump()", but // the expanded form is shown for completeness. // "done" is defined as "No jobs in queue, no misc work to do" while( ! m.done()) { m.process(); } } It might also be implemented by inheriting from CondorMetaScheduler and overriding the default no-op implementations of CondorMetaScheduler::job_done or similar. class MyScheduler : public CondorMetaScheduler { public: virtual void initialize() { submit_job(step_1); /* Provided by CondorMetaScheduler */ } virtual void job_done(unsigned int cluster, unsigned int process, int result) { if(result == 0 && job_is_step_1(cluster)) { submit_job(step_2); /* Provided by CondorMetaScheduler */ } } }; int main() { MyScheduler m; // Automatically calls m.initialize() while( ! m.done()) { m.process(); } } No matter the API, it would include functionality to: Automatically watch log files Submit jobs Call back as jobs exit the queue Attach simple data to a job that I can query (so I can, say, flag a job with a useful human friendly name, or a CATEGORY ala DAGMan.) Ideally this shouldn't be implemented alongside DAGMan. Instead, the core logic of DAGMan would become this toolkit, and DAGMan would be implemented in terms of it. That would ensure that the toolkit receives real testing. Use case This is based on a real world system I worked on: There are 500 disconnected backup tasks to do. Each task consists of: tar (create a tar file), scp (copy it to the archive server), rm (delete the local copy), wait 4 hours (yes, really), validate (ensure the archive server copied it to tape) We faced several limits: Don't run more than 2 tar commands simultaneously to avoid choking the system in I/O. Don't run more than 2 scp commands simultaneously; that's plenty to saturate the bandwidth. It at all possibly run a tar and an scp simutaneously; we're pressed for time and need to keep the entire pipeline full. Between the tar and rm steps, we're using up local disk. We have enough local disk to have anywhere from 1 to 5 tar files on disk simultaneously. We can predict how big a given tar file will be in advance, but completely filling the disk is not an option. There are further challenges: The archive service sometimes is down, sometimes for days. We'll need to retry the scp and validate steps; if the error is unable to connect, we should retry on a slow basis (say, every 5 minutes?) for days. If the error is something else, we should probably retry a few times quickly, then give up. If any step fails, and retries don't help, we want to retry the entire chain, going all the way back to tar. Once a filename is claimed on the archive server, it is claimed forever. It is an error to try and rewrite it. As a result if the scp fails, we might need to rewrite the names of the tar files. For example, "-attempt-01.tar" becomes "-attempt-02.tar". If validate fails, when we retry the entire chain we need to signal that tar and later steps need to rewrite the names. All of this is relatively straightforward, but proved extremely complex to implement using just DAGMan and Condor. The implementation in production has a number of crude limitations. I seriously considered writing a new metascheduler from scratch, but the overhead of worrying about following user logs, checking the output from condor_submit, and the like seemed infeasible given the very short deadline. With a library like I describe above, I believe writing a new metascheduler would have been faster to create and better fitted to the problem than the Frankenstein creation I stitched together.

title: Ticket #7726: Add int-to-string map of JobStatus attribute to Python bindings
description: Seriously, this is absurd. Let's just do this. I propose a new rule for the bindings: API changes should be reviewed, since changing them is such a pain. I propose a new rule for the bindings: API changes should have a justification, particularly discussing alternatives, extensions, and why the change is the smallest useful one. I actually don't have much of a justification, other than to say that an enumeration is clearly the correct thing to do for an enumerated set of values. This change does not provid an implementation of __str__, so str(JobStatus(1)) will be "JobStatus.IDLE", not "IDLE". I feel like we should be able to change this later; should we explicitly reserve that right in that documentation? (JobStatus(1).name is already "IDLE".) This change does not provide a look-up table or function. It's arguably a smaller change to provide such a table or function, but an enum seems like a natural approach that lends itself to use elsewhere.
remarks: 2020-Jul-06 16:58:25 by karpel: A quick-and-dirty pure-Python solution: import enum class JobStatus(enum.IntEnum): IDLE = 1 ... print(JobStatus.IDLE) print(repr(JobStatus.IDLE)) print(JobStatus(1)) print(JobStatus.IDLE.name) # the string "IDLE" print(JobStatus.IDLE.value) # the integer 1 # JobStatus.IDLE # <JobStatus.IDLE: 1> # JobStatus.IDLE # IDLE # 1 2020-Jul-14 13:21:06 by karpel: Code Review Given that I suggested the implementation, I am fine with it :) re: implementing __str__, I think we can skip it. We can point to the Python enum docs and say "it behaves like that; do whatever you want". From one perspective, the job status really is 1; we just happen to give it the name (see what I did there?) IDLE. This API reflects that. re: lookup table, the enum is actually its own lookup table in both directions! (Though I neglected to mention the other direction in my initial comment...) import enum class JobStatus(enum.IntEnum): IDLE = 1 ... assert JobStatus(1) is JobStatus["IDLE"] I think the more interesting question is: do we think we'll ever want to return one of these from a C++ method? If so, I think this definition (unfortunately) needs to live inside the C++ layer.

title: Ticket #6834: FindRunnableJob() causes aggressive rebuilding of PrioRec array
description: FindRunnableJob() will rebuild the PrioRec array if it's marked as dirty. When iterating over the PrioRec array, it will mark the array as dirty if it sees a job in the array that's already been matched to a resource. This will force a rebuild of the PrioRec array the next time FindRunnableJob() is called. If there are frequent calls to FindRunnableJob() in a short period of time, many of those calls will see the job returned in the previous call as already matched and mark the array as dirty, forcing a rebuild in the next call. The rebuilds in this case are meant for efficiency, not correctness. But they end up rebuilding the entire array to remove one entry. A couple changes can reduce this unnecessary work: FindRunnableJob() shouldn't trigger a rebuild of the PrioRec array every time it sees non-runnable jobs in the array. It could either not trigger a rebuild at all or there could be a rate limit on rebuilds for efficiency. When building the PrioRec array, skip jobs that are Idle but are in a match record.
