title: Ticket #1959: Implement per-job PID namespaces.
description: Since Linux kernel 2.6.24, it is possible to create PID namespaces. This makes a process believe it is PID 1, while processes in the global namespace see the "normal" PIDS for the process and its descendants. Reference: http://lwn.net/Articles/259217/ If a Condor job is launched with its own namespace, we'd have the following advantages: Cleanup: when "PID 1" dies, the kernel kills the rest of the processes in the namespace. Separation: two jobs running under the same Unix user account cannot see each other. In order to implement this, one also has to implement a separate mount namespace for the job as you must remount /proc for "ps" to work as expected. That leads to the tantalizing possibility of having a per-job /tmp and /var/tmp; I'll address this in a later ticket. Here's what the job runtime environment will look like: [bbockelm@rcf-bockelman condor]$ condor_run ps faux USER PID %CPU %MEM VSZ RSS TTY STAT START TIME COMMAND bbockelm 1 0.0 0.0 106200 1132 ? SN 14:15 0:00 /bin/bash /home/bbockelm/projects/condor/.condor_run.17238 bbockelm 2 0.0 0.0 108052 1000 ? RN 14:15 0:00 ps faux Patch to come.
remarks: 2011-Mar-28 12:23:12 by tannenba: 2011-Mar-28 12:19:35 by tannenba: Initial Feedback First off, thanks for the interesting work and the patch! Thoughts below. Should the code to create a new pid namespace be implemented in daemon core, or should it be a standalone command-line tool? Since it would need to run as root, options are this tool could be setuid or invoked as a hook via Condor or via the switchboard. If the pid namespace creation stays in daemon core, we need at least a road map plan for how this functionality would work with priv sep enabled. As written, the patch uses pthread conditionals to synchronize between the parent and child processes for procd registration. This is not desired, nor required. One way to eliminate both the pthread calls (nothing but the CondorThreads class should call pthreads directly) and the need for this synchronization is to always have the child process register with the procd as before, and have the parent pass the global pid to the child via the already in-place pipe. Another idea would be for the parent to always register w/ the procd, and to have the child block pending a message on the pipe from the parent telling the child a successful procd registration has occurred. The former may be preferred due to less code churn. In either event, the same codepath to register w/ the procd should be used regardless of if a new pid namespace is being created or not. Functionality to remap /tmp and friends should be a different patch/ticket. Though not ideal, it is ok to rebase the patch off of this one if it makes it easier, but it needs to be a seperate commit that could be merged/revoked independently w/ a separate discussion thread (ticket). 2011-Mar-28 13:07:54 by bbockelm: Hi Todd, 3, 4 are no problem. I think the main part to discuss is 1 and 2. One aspect of privsep I don't understand is the propagation of error messages. If the switchboard is successfully invoked, but exec fails, how does this error message propagate back? Since CLONE_NEWPID can definitely fail on an otherwise-functional system, I would prefer proper error propagation. Brian 2011-Mar-30 08:43:17 by bbockelm: Hi, I did some more research into implementing this with privsep. There appears to be no way to have a process "switch PID namespace". It can only be done when clone() is called. Unfortunately, the only thread in a process that will perform exec (regardless of the thread that calls exec) is the thread group leader, preventing us from playing games with CLONE_THREAD. Hence, any use of PID namespaces requires a parent and child process. For non-privsep this is OK: the parent is the starter, the child is the job. To implement this in privsep, we would need to have an additional process in the tree: starter -> shim -> job. We would need to make the shim correctly reap the job, have the same lifetime of the job, and have the same exit code as the job. In other words, we'd have a non-trivial, long-lasting process with elevated privileges (and change the running semantics on sysadmins! Right now, PID namespaces is rather invisible to admins, although it does change semantics for users): quite a project to do and security audit. Another, more-plausible, approach would be to have the shim short-lived and reparent back to the starter (CLONE_PARENT). This would require the switchboard to synchronize with the starter and inform it of the child's final PID. In general, I think the switchboard ought to do this sort of synchronization with the starter in order to gracefully communicate other exec failures. However, if the infrastructure isn't already there to synchronize via pipe ... I would personally call it out of scope for this ticket. Thoughts? I'll add ZKM to the ticket to see what he thinks. Brian 2011-May-02 18:26:50 by bbockelm: Hi Todd, all, Can I bump this ticket? Been about a month ready for another review, I think. Brian 2011-Nov-29 14:21:06 by eje: One open issue is generalizing current checks for "small pid" relating to preventing security holes, so they don't trigger when pid namespaces are in effect. Places I identified: ./src/condor_procd/procd_main.cpp:247: if (root_pid == 1) { ./src/condor_procd/procd_main.cpp:340: if (own_pi->ppid == 1) { ./src/condor_utils/killfamily.cpp:234: if ( (*old_pids)[i].ppid == 1 || (*old_pids)[i].pid == 0 ) { ./src/condor_daemon_core.V6/daemon_core.cpp:5716: if ( signed_pid > -10 && signed_pid < 3 ) { Pete Keller suggested abstracting these checks into a function, like "bool is_safe_pid(int pid)", which allows small pids when it knows pid namespaces are being used, but otherwise does not for legacy behavior. 2012-Apr-05 11:42:49 by adesmet: Possibly related: #2558. clone() was causing grief for the startd, so it was disabled for all daemons except the schedd. 2012-Jul-25 15:56:08 by tstclair: Patch doesn't apply cleanly and wasn't targeted to release. 2012-Oct-22 14:58:32 by zmiller: Bulk change of target version from v070901 to v070902 using ./ticket-target-mover. 2012-Dec-11 16:37:58 by johnkn: Bulk change of target version from v070902 to v070903 using ./ticket-target-mover. 2013-Jan-10 11:55:33 by gthain: A key requirement here is that many OSG site do not run with slot users, and all users from any given site are mapped to the same OS user. title: Ticket #7024: GSI authentication failure can lead to skipping other auth methods
description: During CEDAR authentication, if the GSI authentication functions return failure, the client sends an integer value of 0 to the server before negotiating the next method to try. The server isn't expecting this, and interprets it as the client's mask of additional authentication methods. The value 0 means no other methods to try, so authentication fails and the connection is aborted. The client code that sends the unexpected 0 includes the following comment: // Following four lines of code is added to temporarily // resolve a bug (I belive so) in Globus's GSI code. // basically, if client calls init_sec_context with // mutual authentication and it returns with a mismatched // target principal, init_sec_context will return without // sending the server any token. The sever, therefore, // hangs on waiting for the token (or until the timeout // occurs). This code will force the server to break out // the loop. My reading of the GSI code shows that globus_gss_assist_init_sec_context() can return failure before any network activity if the target_str is set to a string other than GSI-NO-TARGET. But we never use a value other than GSI-NO-TARGET, so that shouldn't be a concern for us. After a successful SSL handshake, the client sends a "0" or "D" character to indicate whether it wants to do a proxy delegation. Sending of this character may be skipped if gss_init_sec_context() 's checks of the server's credential fail. These include an unexpected subject name (not an issue for us) and an unexpected limited proxy (also not an issue for us). This will leave the server waiting for data. I assume the client's expected reaction is to close the connection, but we don't do that. I need to check the code some more to see if any of the failure conditions can arise with how we invoke these calls.
remarks: 2019-May-02 09:46:26 by jfrey: It appears that all of the situations where the client doesn't send data that the server is expecting occur when the caller in the client provides an expected subject name for the server. We never do that, so I believe we can just remove the kludge at the CEDAR level. 2019-May-02 14:36:03 by zmiller: CODE REVIEW: Jaime and I discussed this and these changes look good! 2019-May-13 21:05:19 by jfrey: After removing the CEDAR-level kludge, I quickly encountered a situation where it's required. When the client doesn't like the server's credentials, it aborts the SSL handshake before sending its own credentials. The SSL code on the client generates a final packet of data to send to the server, but the error handling code in gss_init_sec_context() accidentally drops it. In the failure case initially observed in this ticket, it appears the server didn't like the client's credentials and aborted the handshake at a later point in the protocol (after both sides sent their credentials). In that situation, the client wasn't expected to send any additional data. In all observed situations (client abort, server abort, and success), the final packet of data exchanged is small (10-40 bytes). I will restore the CEDAR-level workaround, but trigger it only in the case where the last data exchange was a large packet (greater than 100 bytes) received by the client. 2019-May-20 11:57:19 by zmiller: CODE REVIEW: Looks good. Docs in... resolving! 2019-Jul-25 11:22:33 by jfrey: We've submitted a patch for the underlying GSI bug to the gridcf/gct repository (#7051).

title: Ticket #6859: End-game for introducing the multifile_curl_plugin
description: There are currently two libcurl-based file transfer plugins - the curl_plugin (used in production but doesn't support the new multifile protocol) and the multifile_curl_plugin (not used in production, but also a cleanup and supporting the multifile protocol). This is an awkward setup: developers have to put code into both (duplicate work as there is no common code base), or decide whether they want to put it into the new plugin (and not have code used) or the old plugin (and know it's a waste of time going forward). I propose we use the new 8.9.x series as an excuse to switchover to the new plugin. That is: We immediately claim the curl_plugin is in bugfix-only mode: all new development and features go into the multifile_curl_plugin variant. 8.9.0 we distribute both and enable multifile support by default. To support developer testing, the multifile_curl_plugin claims to provide support for dav:// and davs:// URLs. The curl_plugin is still the primary plugin for HTTP/HTTPS. Once 8.9.0 is deployed to CHTC, all testing is based on the multifile_curl_plugin. In 8.9.1, we distribute both codebases but the multifile_curl_plugin is renamed to curl_plugin and the curl_plugin is named legacy_curl_plugin. In 8.9.2, only the multifile_curl_plugin (now called simply curl_plugin) is distributed and we delete the code for legacy_curl_plugin. At any point, if testing goes poorly or other unexpected issues come up, we stop and re-evaluate the next steps.
remarks: 2019-Jan-16 10:14:50 by coatsworth: This is ambitious but I can get behind it :) TJ has identified some flaws with the multifile_curl_plugin that are important and need to be fixed before we turn it on by default. I'm pretty tied up with HTTP scale-out in the short term so not sure if I can do any work on this in time for 8.9.1, but agree we should push forward sooner rather than later. 2019-Jan-17 12:02:56 by tannenba: When the multifile plugin is enabled, I am not a fan of the current behavior where the starter lies to the shadow about URL transfers being immediately completed (when in fact the starter shuffles that transfer to anther list to transfer after everything is pulled from the shadow). I would like the shadow to know how long it took to transfer each file, or at least how long it needed to stay connected to each origin. I haven't yet had time to think about if we should make these changes before enabling multifile by default or if this change is something we can introduce in a backwards-compatible way later in the v8.9 series. Both sides of the file transfer object know the version of their peer, so maybe not a big concern, but I wanted to note it here. 2019-Jan-17 14:31:50 by bbockelm: The branch attached to the ticket implements the pieces necessary for the 8.9.0 proposal. HOWEVER, note that the multifile protocol is not implemented / used for file upload. That implies a more significant amount of work besides "just debugging" scheduled prior to 8.9.1. 2019-Jan-17 16:23:43 by coatsworth: CODE REVIEW In multifile_curl_plugin.cpp, you've set "SupportedMethods = \"http,https,ftp,file,dav,davs\". We only want this plugin to support dav and davs for now. Otherwise it could override the curl_plugin and become the default plugin for all http transfers. In param_info, need to add $(LIBEXEC)/multifile_curl_plugin to the FILETRANSFER_PLUGINS knob default. Otherwise I think everything looks good. 2019-Jan-17 21:08:18 by bbockelm: Forgot to mention - tested this by transferring the same large file twice, once with http and once with dav. Confirmed that the file transfer statistics recorded in the schedd log show that a transfer queue slot is held for the http transfer but not for the dav transfer. 2019-Jan-18 13:20:42 by tlmiller: I concur with ToddT's concern about the starter lying to the shadow, primarily because that will make the implementation of file transfer events way more complicated. 2019-Jan-18 14:41:08 by bbockelm: @tlmiller, @tannenba, I am not a fan of the current behavior where the starter lies to the shadow about URL transfers being immediately completed (when in fact the starter shuffles that transfer to anther list to transfer after everything is pulled from the shadow). I would like the shadow to know how long it took to transfer each file, or at least how long it needed to stay connected to each origin. The starter does not lie to the shadow as this is an asynchronous protocol. As far as I can tell, there is no ACK per transfer. The schedd shoves as many URL-based file transfers requests as will fit into the TCP socket's kernel buffers (a thousand?). At some undefined point later after the shadow requests a file transfer, if a transfer fails, there will be an asynchronous message that the schedd receives. 2019-Jan-18 16:11:17 by tlmiller: And yet, the shadow knows when the starter succeeds. That may just be implicit, when the forked child that is the file-transfer object exits, but it implies that the right thing to do is add a mechanism so the starter can either explicitly return the transfer token (probably the right thing, since we'll want to have multiple transfer tokens in the near future) or explicitly signal success. 2019-Jan-19 08:38:25 by bbockelm: tlmiller - Right, completely agreed. Definitely no time for it this weekend, but I wrote up a ticket as a reminder: #6875. 2019-Jan-19 18:30:08 by tlmiller: Thanks. I like the look of the new ticket. 2019-Apr-08 14:53:39 by coatsworth: CODE REVIEW Everything here looks good. This isn't much by way of code changes here. These updates mostly just focus on turning on the new multifile curl plugin by default. Brian did make some significant code changes to the new plugin in #6885 which I'll review separately.

title: Ticket #4167: VM universe assumption shared filesystems breaks compressed FT plugin
description: If you submit a VM universe job which mentions base.img in the vm_disk parameter, and you don't specify base.img in transfer_input_files, condor_submit adds a requirement that the submit and execute nodes share a filesystem. I think that's more of a heroic assumption than a user-friendly feature, but at least the solution is clear: mention your input disks in transfer_input_files. However, this breaks down when your URLs don't include (after the last slash, apparently) the filename in question, e.g.: transfer_input_files = httpz://host.tld/base.img.gz This has cause TimC grief in CHTC. Brainstorming: Require a convention-maintaining remap syntax for file-transfer plugins (if the URL doesn't match the convention). Pros: only the new compression plugin requires changes. If generally implemented (e.g., transfer_input_remaps), could be useful. Con: Rather verbose (especially if it becomes as common as I'd expect). If generally implemented, could be super-confusing, because some plugins would do their own remaps and others wouldn't. A specific solution may look like: transfer_input_files = httpz://host.tld/base.img.gz?basename=./base.img Another option might be something like: transferred_input_files = base.img transfer_input_files = ftp://host.tld/vm-image-generator?param=$(PROC) but this is also clumsy. Decline to assume a shared filesystem in VM universe. Pro: Neatly solves this problem. Cons: May mean missing out on opportunities to help our users notice problems with their jobs. May require add assume_shared_filesystem or similar (so that users could request the old behavior). Not backwards-compatible. Add a flag (assume_shared_filesystem) and require users using the compress plugin (or others, in the future) unless it's set to false. Pros: backwards-compabitible, concise. Cons: Annoying and non-obvious.
remarks: 2014-Jan-21 14:37:09 by tlmiller: JaimeF will be adding some documentation here (and hopefully in the manual) about what the VM universe currently does, with respect to file transfer, with the vm_disk filenames. 2014-Jan-21 14:39:44 by tlmiller: You can work around part of this assumption by adding a null (tautological?) requirement that mentions FileSystemDomain, but the VM universe job will then fail looking for the disk image that's not mentioned in transfer_input_files in a directory based on the submit node. 2014-Jan-21 15:03:02 by tlmiller: TimC has a reasonable suggestion: (4) Everybody except the starter (and/or VM GAHP) ignore the contents of the vm_disk filename field (the exceptions may need to know to convert relative paths to absolute paths by prepending the location of the (execute-side) sandbox for libvirt API reasons). Pros: Simple, easy to explain, flexible. (Works for a pre-staged or shared-FS base image with a delta disk.) Cons: Makes it impossible for HTCondor to try and warn the user about a missing file. 2014-Feb-25 16:44:59 by tlmiller: Complication: doing anything other than a flag in the submit file will break old submit files which assume a shared filesystem. The following is a quick hack that seems to address the problem, albeit in a user-hostile way. diff --git a/src/condor_submit.V6/submit.cpp b/src/condor_submit.V6/submit.cpp index a144a28..36601e1 100644 --- a/src/condor_submit.V6/submit.cpp +++ b/src/condor_submit.V6/submit.cpp @@ -7980,6 +7980,13 @@ bool make_vm_file_path(const char *filename, MyString& fi } } + // File-transfer plugins can confuse us, so if the user says to, + // trust them and don't require a shared FS -- or change the filename. + char * vm_disk_trusted = condor_param( "vm_disk_trusted" ); + if( isTrue( vm_disk_trusted ) ) { + return true; + } + // This file will not be transferred // filename should have absolute path fixedname = full_path(fixedname.Value()); 2014-Feb-26 14:07:52 by tlmiller: So if we're OK with breaking submit files with relative paths on a shared file system (e.g., submitting from the base image's directory), the good news -- as TimC points out -- is that the fix for users with broken jobs is relatively simple - just list the files in question in transfer_input_files. This may make HTCondor look a little stupider, but it's for a good cause. :) (Also, TimC thinks a flag that changes the behavior of vm_disk would be less confusing than having another very similar attribute that behaves differently.) 2014-May-15 17:10:53 by tlmiller: Patch applied in V8_1-trustVMDisk-branch (in git repo for safekeeping). 2016-Apr-25 16:10:50 by jfrey: For 8.5.5, no new attributes. Just have condor_submit stop rewriting vm_disk, xen_kernel, and xen_initrd. Also, condor_submit no longer makes any assumptions about the need for a shared filesystem based on whether files are mentioned in transfer_input_files. Filenames in these attributes need to be valid on the execute machine: either absolute paths, or paths relative to the execute directory. 2016-Apr-28 13:54:13 by cat: Jaime, I do not understand your recent comment. In the case where transfer_input_files mentions a compressed filename ending in, say, .tgz but the actual sandbox filename does not include that suffix (after decompression), will things work now? 2016-Apr-29 09:48:41 by jfrey: Yes, the scenario you describe will work now. Condor no longer examines the filenames in the vm_disk, xen_kernel, and xen_initrd submit attributes before it's time to launch the vm. At that time, the filenames need to point to valid files on the execute machine. How those files come to be there is up to the user (pre-staged, transferred normally, transferred compressed and extracted via a plugin, etc). There's no longer any comparison with filenames in transfer_input_files or rewriting of file paths.

title: Ticket #1735: AccountGroup can't be set by SUBMIT_EXPRS
description: When using accounting groups, the typical form is something like this in the submit file: +AccountGroup="group_staff.adesmet" Both halves are necessary for proper prioritization. A given submit machine might be exclusively used by a single group. The admin might want to automatically add the correct group, reducing mistakes. The admin might try something like this in his configuration: AccountingGroup = strcat("group_staff.", Owner) SUBMIT_EXPRS = $(SUBMIT_EXPRS) AccountingGroup This doesn't work, as AccountingGroup is only ever read with AttrList::LookupString, not AttrList::EvalString. Proposed: an administrator should be able to automatically add a suitable AccountingGroup to jobs using SUBMIT_EXPRS. Option 1: EvalString Change all uses of LookupString on ATTR_ACCOUNTING_GROUP to EvalString. Pros: Leverages existing Condor functionality. Potentially allows further clever tricks with other functions an attributes. Cons: The policy to set is non-obvious. The AccountingGroup might change when re-evaluated; will that cause problems? (Already a potential problem thanks to condor_qedit, but with an expression it might change while the negotiator is considering it.) Option 2: Break user off of AccountingGroup If the AccountingGroup lacks a specific user (say AccountingGroup="group_condor.") assume the Owner of the job. Pros: Simple to use, both for job submitters and admins. Cons: May require changing a bunch of code; ATTR_ACCOUNTING_GROUP is looked up about 13 times in our code base. They would presumably need to be replaced with a unified "GetAccountingGroupFromClassAd" Option 3: Break AccountingGroup into two fields Instead of AccontingGroup containing the user and the group, have it only contain the group and add AccountingGroupUser to hold the user name. eje has an extended proposal that includes this at https://lists.cs.wisc.edu/archive/condor-devel/2012-January/msg00017.shtml

title: Ticket #3708: Do upgrade test before new stable series
description: I think that maybe we should do an upgrade test from the previous stable series before the first release of any new stable series. (This issue arose because of the problem with upgrading from 7.8 to 8.0.0 with running DAGs that has bitten LIGO.) I guess we should probably have realized that the DAG upgrade would be a problem, but in general I think we need a more systematic way of finding out this kind of thing before our users do... Anyhow, I'm saying that maybe doing such a test should be part of the standard procedure before any new stable series (along with running on the pool for 3 weeks, etc.).

title: Ticket #4537: Incorrect default for GANGLIAD_METRICS_CONFIG_DIR in RPMs
description: In the RPM, GANGLIAD_METRICS_CONFIG_DIR defaults to $(RELEASE_DIR)/etc/condor/ganglia.d. This resolves to /usr/etc/condor/ganglia.d, which isn't shipped by the RPM (and causes condor_gangliad to EXCEPT). We probably want /etc/condor/ganglia.d. Better yet - we should have all the defaults in /usr/share/condor/ganglia.d and just allow sysadmins to override things in /etc/condor/ganglia.d. That way, there is always a clean upgrade path when we add/remove default metrics. Looking at the code, I think this would work with minimal code changes: GANGLIAD_METRICS_CONFIG_DIR=/usr/share/condor/ganglia.d,/etc/condor/ganglia.d We do a similar trick with the HTCondor-CE to keep sysadmins honest when overriding defaults.
creator: bbockelm

title: Ticket #4022: Use pre-built libraries for Windows builds
description: On Windows, there is very little reason to want or need to build third party libraries from source by default. It is considerably more convenient to just build once or use supplied prebuilt binaries of third party libraries. Doing so will not only decrease the build times for Windows, but also remove one of the biggest impediments to creating a native 64bit version of HTCondor, namely the need to rig the building of externals through some haphazard CMake macro magic. This would also be a good opportunity to actually update some of the externals we use considering how old some of them are.

description: In #5064, the original branch parsed X509 attributes from delegated proxy files or the GSI connection. Later commits had the condor_schedd parse x509userproxy on schedd side. That code doesn't work: Schedd doesn't switch to user priv to parse the file. This means the proxy is parsed schedd-side only if the proxy is world-readable or owned by condor. If a condor_qedit changes the proxy file to an invalid / unparsable file, the prior x509 attributes are overwritten. Marking as fairly high priority because all condor submits now are missing x509 attributes.
remarks: 2016-Apr-18 13:04:52 by zmiller: Will fix the first issue right away. As a possible workaround you can use an older version of condor_submit. The second issue is how it was designed to work. The attributes should reflect what is contained in the current proxy. 2016-Apr-18 13:12:14 by bbockelm: In that case, we should seriously consider rejecting qedit's that point to an invalid proxy. Put another way - we did this so we could have some level of "trust" in these attributes to make reasonable decisions (i.e., put it in queue A instead of queue B). The trust is established by the fact the user could prove he has a certain identity (can provide a proxy, authenticate a connection). That goes away if a user can arbitrarily clear out the related attributes. 2016-Apr-18 13:18:24 by zmiller: Right. If the user clears out their proxy, they have lost the ability to prove those things about themselves, and so clearing them from the job attributes reflects that reality. Is there a situation where a user somehow has MORE access to things by not proving who they are? That seems odd. That said, I can get on board with rejecting updates to x509userproxy when the proxy is not valid. Do you want them also not to be able to clear the value? 2016-Apr-22 16:26:59 by zmiller: NOTE: Ticket #5064 was reopened and the work plan for fixing this is in the remarks of that ticket. 2016-Oct-19 10:27:05 by jfrey: I believe the latest work on ticket #5064 resolves the issues with this ticket. Assuming no one objects, I plan to resolve this ticket. 2016-Nov-21 14:00:10 by zmiller: No one objected, resolving.

title: Ticket #1559: QUILL -> add on, and no longer distro'd
description: In FW 8/3/10 the ok has been given to move QUILL to add-on's and remove from mainline distribution. It is debatable if we should remove the code entirely from the tools condor_q, etc.
remarks: 2010-Aug-04 09:21:07 by matt: The decision was to remove the code from q and history producing a quill_q and quill_history. 2010-Aug-12 14:48:28 by epaulson: A quill_q and quill_history is about the worst possible way to make things better. 90% of the code in a quill_q or quill_history will be identical and any bug fixes or feature enhancements would have to be done twice. It basically ensures that quill will quickly become broken and useless. A far better way is to rip all of the quill code out of condor_q and condor_history, and instead fix the biggest mistake we made in quill -> quill++: restore the ability of the quilld to speak the schedd protocol. What you really want is an unmodified condor_q being able to talk to a schedd or a quill daemon and not care what it is. In the schedd ad, you take all of the quill crap out, and just advertise something like MX records - "if you want to do read-only queries, here is who you talk to". This has the happy bonus of isolating condor_q/history from having to have any knowledge of the schema or RDBMS involved, and isolates what needs to link with the Postgres libraries (and Oracle/MySQL/MSSQL/etc libraries) to just the quill daemon. It also means you can better control access to your RDBMS instead of having your firewall wide-open, and we can add caching of materialized classads or aggregate stats without having to pound the database. The downside is now you're stuck with Condor concurrency, ie the quilld is still single-threaded, so if you have a ton of clients querying the quilld it may be slower than talking straight to the database. However, from a software maintenance standpoint, it's probably worth it, and it's certainly better than a quill_q 2010-Oct-20 16:03:30 by jfrey: Bulk change of target version from v070504 to v070505 using ./ticket-target-mover. 2010-Dec-07 14:54:09 by tstclair: modifications have been made to master to remove, but there is still a non-trival amount of work needed in order to complete. namely tool cleaning. 2011-Jan-27 14:46:04 by danb: Bulk change of target version from v070505 to v070506 using ./ticket-target-mover. 2011-Feb-01 16:19:13 by tannenba: Bulk change of target version from v070506 to NULL using ./ticket-target-mover.

title: Ticket #7177: Should transfer finished events have success/failure information?
description: The transfer-finished events in the job log don't specify if the transfer completed successfully, but in at least one case (see below), appear even if the transfer failed. I previously argued that transfer-finished events should appear even -- or perhaps especially -- for failed transfers; it's information that could be very useful, but we don't people (or programs) to have to infer it, for the same reason(s) that explicit transfer events are useful at all. The obvious follow-up argument is that determining success or failure should also not require looking at other events. I will have to investigate to see if the specific failure case that we know appears in the log is unique or not; there may be a counter-argument that we should instead make transfer-finished-and-failed events uniformly not appear in the log, and make the presence of an event signal success. The obvious counter-argument may be identical in the case. ;)
remarks: 2019-Jul-31 16:05:45 by karpel: The philosophical issue seems to be whether you should be able to determine a job's state uniquely from the last event you read, or whether you need to reconstruct its entire history to determine the current state. (1) Normal termination (return value 0) Usr 0 00:00:00, Sys 0 00:00:00 - Run Remote Usage Usr 0 00:00:00, Sys 0 00:00:00 - Run Local Usage Usr 0 00:00:00, Sys 0 00:00:00 - Total Remote Usage Usr 0 00:00:00, Sys 0 00:00:00 - Total Local Usage 10730 - Run Bytes Sent By Job 10737418240 - Run Bytes Received By Job 10730 - Total Bytes Sent By Job 10737418240 - Total Bytes Received By Job Partitionable Resources : Usage Request Allocated Cpus : 0 1 1 Disk (KB) : 10485797 11534336 11702622 Ioheavy : 0 Memory (MB) : 1 50 50 ... There are gaps after the "finished transferring output files" events where you would expect the next event to be a "terminate" according some imagined state transition diagram that doesn't actually exist, but it will in fact be a "reconnect". title: Ticket #7527: MemoryUsage in Docker Universe does not show maximum observed
description: The MemoryUsage attribute in the job classAd for Docker Universe jobs can be incorrect. Specifically, it represents the immediate memory usage, and not the maximum memory used. The result it can end up being set to zero in the job event log and in the history file if HTCondor polls Docker for memory usage after the job completes and the container is shutting down or output files are being transferred. There are two problems here: The condor_starter does not poll the Docker daemon for memory usage often enough, meaning it could "miss" observing the job's maximum. The polling interval should be controlled by the config knob POLLING_INTERVAL (which defaults to 5 seconds), but instead the polling interval was hard-coded to 20 seconds. Neither the condor_starter nor the condor_shadow actually calculates the maximum of the observed memory values. (sigh) This patch changes the starter to actually honor the polling interval for Docker Universe jobs, and also take the maximum of the observed values. Note we attempted to fix the problem of not storing the maximum observed value months ago in the shadow via #7049, but that patch failed to do the job because of conflicts with commit [54199] in #6549 which ended up incorrectly rewriting the value for MemoryUsage. The patch in [54199] needs to be revised, but that is another ticket. In the meantime, this ticket makes a simpler patch to the shadow which will take the maximum memory value for Docker universe jobs as well (so that the max is taken even if the starter has not been updated yet).

title: Ticket #2725: ResidentSetSize appears to get reset when job is put on hold
description: It appears ResidentSetSize is reset to zero when a job is put on hold. Locally, we have a SYSTEM_PERIODIC_HOLD expression based on RSS - anything hitting 1.6GB is put on hold. Here's the memory-related classad attributes for a job in the schedd after it has been put on hold: ProportionalSetSizeKb = 1750000 ProportionalSetSizeKb_RAW = 1626303 ImageSize = 2000000 ImageSize_RAW = 1838488 ResidentSetSize = 0 Notice the values of PSS and VSIZE from the last run have been preserved, while RSS is reset to 0. I also note that _RAW for ResidentSetSize is missing. This is from Condor from trunk; I do not know when this behavior started.
remarks: 2011-Dec-22 09:14:00 by bbockelm: The attached patch causes RSS to work in a manner similar to PSS. However, it's not obvious why the patch works (the "correct" PSS behavior is likely some unintended side-effect of rounding). Discussing this with danb, there likely should be a MaxResidentSetSize and MaxProportionalSetSizeKb; this would record the largest available value, not the most recent. There are some small race conditions here - what if RSS/PSS is measured as the job is shutting down? 2011-Dec-23 11:02:57 by danb: In my tests, rounding ResidentSetSize does not reliably prevent this attribute from getting reset to 0. I can't come up with any theory that would explain why it should. The reason RSS is getting reset to 0 is that in the starter's final update, it computes a total of 0 RSS for the job. The reason PSS is not reset to 0 is an artifact of the way PSS is handled. Instead of getting 0 for the total PSS, the starter gets the result "no PSS available", so it doesn't send an update to PSS in the final update. I discussed with Todd and he agrees that we should change the definition of ResidentSetSize and ProportionalSetSizeKb to be maximums, like ImageSize. This seems more useful for batch jobs. If instantaneous values are ever desired, new attributes could be added to provide those.

title: Ticket #2230: negotiating groups with no submitters
description: Artifact of #2054 and #2194 when using round robin that leads to entering negotiateWithGroup with no submitters attached to the group. 06/07/11 21:20:38 Group <removed> - BEGIN NEGOTIATION 06/07/11 21:20:38 Phase 3: Sorting submitter ads by priority ... 06/07/11 21:20:38 Phase 4.1: Negotiating with schedds ... 06/07/11 21:20:38 numSlots = 365 06/07/11 21:20:38 slotWeightTotal = 365.000000 06/07/11 21:20:38 pieLeft = 0.000 06/07/11 21:20:38 NormalFactor = 0.000000 06/07/11 21:20:38 MaxPrioValue = 0.000000 06/07/11 21:20:38 NumSubmitterAds = 0 06/07/11 21:20:38 resources used by are 0.000000 06/07/11 21:20:38 resources used scheddused 0.000000 groupUsed 0.000000 06/07/11 21:20:38 negotiateWithGroup resources used scheddAds length 0
remarks: 2011-Jun-15 17:52:55 by eje: Note -- I don't think this is related to #2054 (which does not remove submitters, only halts negotiation). It appears to happen due to an interaction of (1) the fix for #2194, (2) round-robin, and (3) update latency for submitter ads on the collector (another argument for grabbing submitters directly from schedds). For simplicity, assume a single group "a" and a single submitter "a.u1", and RR rate = 1. The repro scenario is: "a.u1" has >= 2 jobs that are running. Then, all its jobs complete: the accountant gets updated, but the collector does not. It enters negotiation. The negotiator grabs (running+idle) from the collector, sees this value is > 0 (in fact, >=2), so it allocates some quota for "a". But the usage comes from accountant, which is zero (why? because its values are more current than the collector!), so it concludes it needs to negotiate. It then goes into 1st RR iteration, but discovers "a.u1" has no idle jobs, so it removes "a.u1". This leaves group "a" with no submitters, but now it's got more RR iterations. And on all subsequent RR iterations, it's entering negotiateWithGroup with zero submitters for "a". 2011-Jun-15 18:06:07 by eje: Test/Repro: Using configuration: CLAIM_WORKLIFE = 0 NEGOTIATOR_CONSIDER_PREEMPTION = FALSE NEGOTIATOR_DEBUG = D_FULLDEBUG NEGOTIATOR_INTERVAL = 30 SCHEDD_INTERVAL = 15 NUM_CPUS = 10 GROUP_NAMES = a, b GROUP_QUOTA_a = 5 GROUP_QUOTA_b = 5 GROUP_QUOTA_ROUND_ROBIN_RATE = 1 Spool up the test pool, and then follow along on negotiator log: $ tail -f NegotiatorLog | grep -e 'RR iter' -e 'skipping, no sub' -e 'Filtering.*no idle jobs' Submit this job: universe = vanilla cmd = /bin/sleep args = 20 should_transfer_files = if_needed when_to_transfer_output = on_exit +AccountingGroup="a.u1" queue 2 After the fix, you should first see it go through 2 RR iterations. Then, after the job completes, you see "a.u1" removed on first RR iteration, followed by it skipping the subsequent iteration. Note, it may occasionally get correct up-to-date values from the collector, in which case the fix will not execute, so if you do not see the behavior after job completes, try again. [root@rorschach log]$ tail -f NegotiatorLog | grep -e 'RR iter' -e 'skipping, no sub' -e 'Filtering.*no idle jobs' # First negotiation (two RR iterations) 06/15/11 15:24:58 group quotas: entering RR iteration n= 1 06/15/11 15:24:59 group quotas: entering RR iteration n= 2 # ... # After job completes, you see this: 06/15/11 15:25:29 group quotas: entering RR iteration n= 1 06/15/11 15:25:29 Filtering submitter a.u1@localdomain with no idle jobs 06/15/11 15:25:29 group quotas: entering RR iteration n= 2 06/15/11 15:25:29 Group a - skipping, no submitters (usage=0) Before the fix, you should see two RR iterations on job completion (no skipping message) (unless the collector got lucky and had up-to-date values)

title: Ticket #7462: Different token types should be distinguished in the cred dir
description: NOTE: Documentation work to be done in ticket #7646 Currently, $(SEC_CREDENTIAL_DIRECTORY)/<username> could contain many different types of tokens, and we rely on the user and/or admin to know enough about the token storage configuration to avoid naming conflicts. I propose that we should distinguish the type of tokens by creating subdirectories either under $(SEC_CREDENTIAL_DIRECTORY) or <username>, e.g.: /var/lib/condor/credentials/jpatton/oauth/box.top /var/lib/condor/credentials/jpatton/oauth/box.use /var/lib/condor/credentials/jpatton/kerberos/krb5.cc /var/lib/condor/credentials/jpatton/s3/chtc.access /var/lib/condor/credentials/jpatton/s3/chtc.secret Perhaps for getting multiple credmons to work nicely together, the distinguishing subdirectories should be up a level, with logs and such placed there instead of at the root of $(SEC_CREDENTIAL_DIRECTORY): /var/lib/condor/credentials/oauth/jpatton/box.top /var/lib/condor/credentials/oauth/jpatton/box.use /var/lib/condor/credentials/kerberos/jpatton/krb5.cc /var/lib/condor/credentials/s3/jpatton/chtc.access /var/lib/condor/credentials/s3/jpatton/chtc.secret However, this means naming conflicts could still show up in the execute sandbox unless some care is taken by the starter to reorganize the sandbox's cred dir. replace SEC_CREDENTIAL_DIRECTORY with multiple knobs We will solve this problem, by switching the code to have more than one credential directory knob, there will be a separate knob for each credential directory namespace: password, krb, and oauth. passwords will be stored in SEC_CREDENTIAL_DIRECTORY. The *nix builds do not normally store passwords other than the pool password, but this may change in the future. In any case the plumbing for this has always been in the code. Kerberos credentials will be stored SEC_CREDENTIAL_DIRECTORY_KRB. It may be reasonable to default this to $(SEC_CREDENTIAL_DIRECTORY)/krb OAuth tokens will be stored in SEC_CREDENTIAL_DIRECTORY_OAUTH. It may be reasonable to default this to $(SEC_CREDENTIAL_DIRECTORY)/oauth Enable multiple instances of credmon In the current code, the admin must add the credmon to the daemon list, we will need to have multiple instances of the credmon, so we will need to extend this mechanism to allow for multiple instances of the credmon, each managing a different credential directory. This will be handled by adding a daemon to the DAEMON_LIST for each credmon. Schedd must block for multiple CREDMON_COMPLETE files Since we may have multiple instances of the credmon, we will need multiple CREDMON_COMPLETE files. We will extending the existing pattern for this, such that each credmon directory will have it's own CREDMON_COMPLETE FILE. If SEC_CREDENTIAL_DIRECTORY_KRB is configured, then the schedd will wait for a CREDMON_COMPLETE file to appear in this directory before it begins running jobs. optional If SEC_CREDENTIAL_DIRECTORY_OAUTH is configured, then the schedd will wait for a CREDMON_COMPLETE file to appear in this directory before it begins running jobs. THE Master will delete these files as part of it's startup processing. configuring possible config fragment DAEMON_LIST = $(DAEMON_LIST) CREDMON_KRB CREDMON_OAUTH CREDMON_KRB = $(LIBEXEC)/credmon_krb SEC_CREDENTIAL_DIRECTORY_KRB = $(SEC_CREDENTIAL_DIRECTORY)/krb # The knob above will cause the Schedd to wait for $(SEC_CREDENTIAL_DIRECTORY_KRB)/CREDMON_COMPLETE CREDMON_OAUTH = $(LIBEXEC)/credmon_oauth SEC_CREDENTIAL_DIRECTORY_OAUTH = $(SEC_CREDENTIAL_DIRECTORY)/oauth # The knob above will cause the Schedd to wait for $(SEC_CREDENTIAL_DIRECTORY_OAUTH)/CREDMON_COMPLETE

title: Ticket #3071: Does condor_power work?
description: Does condor_power ever work? I'm dubious. The key code is in /src/condor_utils/udp_waker.cpp . The rough flow: UdpWakeOnLanWaker::UdpWakeOnLanWaker (ClassAd *ad ) (line 71) Gets a classad. It hands the add to a Daemon object just so it can call Daemon::addr(). The returned address appears to be the local machine's address. The code claims to "retrieve the IP from the ad," but there isn't any reason that the ad would contain the target machine's IP address. The local machine's address is put into m_public_ip. For example, m_public_ip=1.2.3.4, where 1.2.3.4 is the machine I'm running condor_power on. UdpWakeOnLanWaker::initializeBroadcastAddress () line 283 initializes m_broadcast. Assuming a subnet was not passed in on the command line, or that the submit passed in was "255.255.255.255", m_broadcast.sin_addr.s_addr will be initialized to 0xffffffff. This is as expected. line 313 inverts m_broadcast.sin_addr.s_addr. It's not clear why it's doing this. m_broadcast.sin_addr.s_addr is now 0x00000000 line 317 ors broadcast.sin_addr.s_addr against the address found in m_public_ip. (0x01020304 | 0x00000000) -> 0x01020304 That decidedly seems wrong UdpWakeOnLanWaker::doWake () (line 467) usess m_broadcast as the destination for sendto(). So we're sending a UDP packet to 0x01020304, which is 1.2.3.4, which is the local machine, not the target machine. condor_rooster calls "condor_power -d -i", where -i means "pass a ClassAd in on stdin." I need to check this code path; it's possible it works. I think it probably sends a UDP packet directly to the off machine, which might actually work. The behavior remains weird. To do: Figure out what the hell this code is doing. A simple local broadcast should be as a simple sending to 255.255.255.255, and that code isn't doing it. It might be trying to do a subnet directed broadcast, but I don't think it's doing that either, at least not correctly. Fix -m. Presumably it should do a local broadcast. Tim St. Clair is confident that it used to work. Check if -m -s works. What's it supposed to? Probably subnet directed broadcasts. Fix if broken. Investigate -i. Why does it work? Does it fail in some cases? In particular, is it using local broadcast or subnet directed broadcast, and should we bother supporting the other if it only doesone?

title: Ticket #6789: Use instance role credentials when available for EC2
description: Problem Statement Users running HTCondor in an AWS instance, even if the instance('s role) has the privilege to start new instances, must still copy-and-paste their credentials into the instance. We regard this as a UX bug. Goals A user who starts an instance (with a sufficiently-privileged IAM role) should be able to successfully run condor_annex in that instance without additional configuration. Overview Amazon runs a (mostly?) private webserver for each instance called the metadata server. This server provides a JSON file at a particular URL that contains the temporary credentials (and their expiration date). The AWS infrastructure regularly renews these credentials; the documentation recommends checking for new credentials once an hour, or at least fifteen minutes before the specified expiration date. These credentials, unlike the permanent credentials we've been using until now, come in three parts; all three parts are necessary to use them. Specifications For the specific use-case of condor_annex, we won't concern ourselves with credential caching or renewal; the GAHP will simply obtain the necessary tokens from the meta-data server when it needs them. We also declare it to be acceptable to have to 'sudo' when using condor_annex, in case the machine has been configured (as annex nodes are by default) to limit access to the metadata server to root processes. The GAHP will know to obtain the necessary tokens from the metadata server if given a specific "magic" value for access or secret key files, or perhaps if those values are empty, instead. The condor_annex tool will use this mode either because of a command-line flag or if the appropriate config knobs are not set. Future Considerations For longer-duration and/or larger-scale uses, like with the grid manager, we'll need to worry about caching and renewal. One possibility is to manage that process in the grid manager, and teach the GAHP to get the three tokens from files. To avoid rewriting all of the call sites, we could add a GAHP command which associated key filename pairs with the filename of the third token. (We could also simply use conventions about the naming, but that would prclude the user from naming these files as they see fit.) This would also allow the user to supply only temporary credential; more research is required to determine how to renew those.

title: Ticket #4560: Unable to release held OpenStack (any non-idempotent EC2 service) jobs
description: We compensate for EC2 services which don't support idempotent submits by using SSH keypair IDs. Naturally, if a user specifies a keypair ID, we put the job on hold when we discover that the service the specified doesn't support idempotent submits. However, when we put a job on hold, we don't clear the SSH keypair ID in the job ad, and so if the grid manager has to restart to handle releasing the job (as it might if it's the only EC2 job in the queue, for instance), it puts the job on hold for the same reason, not recognizing that it created the SSH keypair in the first place. We have two fixes to make, then: first, if we should never put the job in a state where the above hold would trigger. In practice, this means removing the SSH keypair ID from the job ad (and synchronizing with the schedd) after removing the SSH keypair ID from the service. (To be more conservative, if the user supplied the SSH keypair ID, we could never unset any of the remote job ID, client token, and SSH keypair ID without unsetting all of them.) The second is to check in the hold if we created the keypair in the first place. Unfortunately, we can't presently do so if we created the keypair only because we needed it for idempotence (that is, the user did not supply a keypair file name). More thought is required.
creator: tlmiller

title: Ticket #1762: Core limits not set correctly for DAG node jobs
description: Todd M ran into this problem, and I've done a bit of investigating -- it seems like DAG node jobs end up with a core size limit of 0, unless CREATE_CORE_FILES is true for the schedd. It seems like something in daemoncore sets the soft limit to 0 inside the DAGMan process.
remarks: 2010-Nov-08 21:04:48 by wenger: I've done some investigating, and what's going on is this: In check_core_files() in daemon_core_main.cpp, RLIMIT_CORE gets set to zero if the param CREATE_CORE_FILES is false. The manual says that CREATE_CORE_FILES defaults to undefined, but it actually seems to default to false. So by the time the DAGMan process is going to run condor_submit for a node job, its own soft core limit has been set to zero unless CREATE_CORE_FILES is true. Condor_submit then inherits the core limit from DAGMan, and sets CoreSize accordingly. So the summary is that CREATE_CORE_FILES, which is supposed to apply to the Condor daemons, ends up also applying to any DAG node jobs. 2010-Dec-03 16:54:45 by wenger: This got fixed (and documented) a few weeks ago, but for some reason I forgot to resolve the ticket, so I'll do that now...

title: Ticket #5371: schedd crashes during fast shutdown intermittently
description: During a fast shutdown, the schedd will crash if there are running forkwork'ed children, perhaps from a condor_q in flight. The stack trace looks like this: Stack dump for process 63178 at timestamp 1446687642 (17 frames) /slots/07/dir_14290/userdir/condor/lib/libcondor_utils_8_5_2.so(dprintf_dump_stack+0x12d)[0x2ba86881eaad] /slots/07/dir_14290/userdir/condor/lib/libcondor_utils_8_5_2.so(+0x15af92)[0x2ba868831f92] /lib64/libpthread.so.0[0x33fb20f790] /slots/07/dir_14290/userdir/condor/lib/libcondor_utils_8_5_2.so(_ZN10DaemonCore11Send_SignalE18classy_counted_ptrI11DCSignalMsgEb+0x57)[0x2ba868970517] /slots/07/dir_14290/userdir/condor/lib/libcondor_utils_8_5_2.so(_ZN10DaemonCore11Send_SignalEii+0x76)[0x2ba868971416] /slots/07/dir_14290/userdir/condor/lib/libcondor_utils_8_5_2.so(_ZN8ForkWork7KillAllEb+0x88)[0x2ba8688c46d8] /slots/07/dir_14290/userdir/condor/lib/libcondor_utils_8_5_2.so(_ZN8ForkWork9DeleteAllEv+0x15)[0x2ba8688c4735] /slots/07/dir_14290/userdir/condor/lib/libcondor_utils_8_5_2.so(_ZN8ForkWorkD1Ev+0x1b)[0x2ba8688c4a4b] /lib64/libc.so.6(exit+0xe2)[0x33faa35b22] /slots/07/dir_14290/userdir/condor/lib/libcondor_utils_8_5_2.so(__wrap_exit+0x73)[0x2ba86896a4f3] /slots/07/dir_14290/userdir/condor/lib/libcondor_utils_8_5_2.so(_Z7DC_ExitiPKc+0x219)[0x2ba868959a59] condor_schedd[0x449680] /slots/07/dir_14290/userdir/condor/lib/libcondor_utils_8_5_2.so(_Z17handle_dc_sigquitP7Servicei+0x31)[0x2ba8689557a1] /slots/07/dir_14290/userdir/condor/lib/libcondor_utils_8_5_2.so(_ZN10DaemonCore6DriverEv+0x946)[0x2ba868978576] /slots/07/dir_14290/userdir/condor/lib/libcondor_utils_8_5_2.so(_Z7dc_mainiPPc+0x1799)[0x2ba868958d89] /lib64/libc.so.6(__libc_start_main+0xfd)[0x33faa1ed5d] condor_schedd[0x4213a9] The problem is that the ForkWork object is a global in qmgmt, and the destructor is called by the system after exit is called. However, when the ForkWork destructor is called, the DaemonCore singleton instance is guaranteed to already be deleted (we do it explicitly, before calling exit). The ForkWork destructor kills any running child proceses via DaemonCore::Send_Signal, but the daemonCore instance has already been deleted and set to null, so we crash. Note this isn't a problem for a graceful shutdown of the schedd, for there we explicitly tell ForkWork to kill all the children before calling DC_Exit for this very reason. For 8.4, I'll just duplicate this code in the graceful shutdown code, but we should probably move ForkWork into DaemonCore for 8.5, as it depends on Dc.

title: Ticket #4833: IPv6 bugfixes for 8.3.2
description: Very very sorry to keep on finding bugs in IPv6; I really hope this is the last one! If shared_port, IPv6, and IPv4 are enabled, then the collector does not listen on IPv6 UDP 9618. Moved to Ticket #4847: Collector doesn't listen on UDP 9618 with shared_port, IPv6, and IPv4 This is because DaemonCore::InitCommandSockets assumes that TCP and UDP sockets are on the same port. In the case of the collector using shared port, the collector listens on UDP port 9618 and the shared_port listens on TCP 9618 - breaking the code's assumption. If shared_port, IPv6, and IPv4 is enabled, address rewriting does not work. Moved to Ticket #4848: Address rewriting only considers first command socket The address rewriting code seems to have a somewhat-fatal flaw: instead of comparing the ad's address against all command sockets, it only compares the address against the first command socket. So, if the initial command socket is IPv4, an IPv4 address may get bumped to IPv6; an IPv6 address will not get rewritten to IPv4. This results in IPv4 connections getting told the IPv6 address; hilarity ensues. The issue comes up is because we determine the command socket from the shared_port_ad; if the shared port advertises the IPv4 socket (the default!) but the ad in the collector is the IPv6 address (true if the IPv6 address is first in the DNS for the collector). This affects the collector ad (assuming issue 1 is fixed). I fix this by tracking all command socket sinful strings and try address rewriting for each. (It's not really a bug, but an issue when using dual-stack for the HTCondor-CE - so important for the OSG.) In the case where all daemons are on a single node, we can perform address rewriting for all ads leaving the collector. Moved to Ticket #4849: Rewrite all ads leaving collector on single-node pool We should loosen the IP address rewriting rules to only match the IP, not the whole sinful. Less aggressive, but would still fix the HTCondor-CE case is only rewriting ads when the sinful strings match or the same shared_port server is used. The issue fixed in #4830 hid the issues above. However, since 8.3.2 does not support shared_port and dual stack anyway, this ticket can be considered internal.
remarks: 1. As far as I can tell, it's a bug that the collector is trying to bind to a UDP port when shared port is enabled at all. The port should never be used. (Who would the collector ever tell about it? I guess maybe a collector tree, but it seems like this shouldn't generally be happening.) That being said, I think you've misidentified the code's assumption. The target ports can only differ from the requested ports if the requested ports were dynamically assigned. If they are, then we assume that InitCommandSocket() (singular) will do what it's supposed to and fail if it can't bind both the TCP and the UDP port. In point of actual fact, I don't think it does -- neither TJ nor I could find where, if InitCommandSocket() were given fixed port numbers, it actually binds the TCP port. Our best guess as to why it actually works right now is that the master uses a different method when it creates sockets for people to inherit, and nobody ever actually asks for an extra command socket on a specified port. This would tend to imply the master isn't doing the right thing here, but I need to investigate further. 2. I'm certain I tested this. I may have missed something, but I'm sure I tested it -- so I'd like to know what, precisely, is broken. The address rewriting code should never see an IP address other than the first command socket's -- we (should) never insert anything else. I don't necessarily object to checking all of sinfuls, just to be safe, but I think something else is going on. Have you verified that the on-disk shared port ad contains an IPv6 address? The shared port daemon uses the initial command socket (as we would expect) to populate the ad, and address rewriting only occurs when sending ClassAds over the wire. (And only when the address in question is the address of the sender, because we don't otherwise know what to substitute.) More generally, yes, even an IPv4-only client is going to see IPv6 addresses in the collector. There's nothing we can do about that; we plan to avoid the problem with matchmaking, in the future. 3. I don't recall it at the moment -- more later, possibly, or maybe on Tuesday when Alan gets back -- but there's a really good reason we can't rewrite based only on IP address; it may not apply in this special case. I guess we could offer a knob to force the collector to rewrite other people's ads? 2015-Jan-17 07:48:35 by bbockelm: Hi Todd, Thanks for the review. A few responses. When the collector and shared_port are enabled (and if COLLECTOR_USES_SHARED_PORT is left to the default of true), then the shared_port will listen on TCP 9618 (forwarding non-shared-port requests to the collector). Then, the collector will bind to UDP 9618 and a dynamic TCP port (this is because the remote daemons will still try to update via UDP). Hence, for the case where the collector host is using shared port, port=-1 and udp_port=9618. However, the code targetTCPPort = targetUDPPort = rs->get_port(); make an invalid assumption that port = udp_port. This causes the collector to break when shared_port is enabled in master. Yes, when you tested it, this worked correctly. However, when we fixed #4830, the daemons started connecting to the collector using IPv6 (as designed) - including the collector itself! This means the collector ad contained the collector's IPv6 address - no longer IPv4. When subsequently serving the collector ad - which contains the IPv6 address, but the initial command socket is IPv4 - address rewriting breaks. Yeah, I went back and forth whether to rewrite based on (IP address) or (IP address+port+using shared_port). I picked the less conservative choice in the commit; however, rewriting only sinfuls on the same shared port server would be fine with me and fix this use case. 2015-Jan-23 14:39:49 by adesmet: Broken into three tickets: #4847: Collector doesn't listen on UDP 9618 with shared_port, IPv6, and IPv4 #4848: Address rewriting only considers first command socket #4849: Rewrite all ads leaving collector on single-node pool This ticket is now obsolete.

title: Ticket #5664: Review usage of getHostFromAddr().
description: [See #5659 for the genesis of this ticket.] I'm concerned about not using the Sinful class to do the parsing in getHostFromAddr(); we've already got at least one Sinful format (v1) that it won't handle correctly, and we may make it (or a further revision) the default at some point. We should also take a look at who calls getHostFromAddr(); callers who know they're looking at Sinful strings should just use the Sinful object, instead. This may simplify things. (The Sinful object may also have "hostname:port" parsing in it for backwards compatibility...) If we do need getHostFromAddr(), it should probably use the Sinful object. We should also worry about why the callers are obtaining the host name (or IP address -- in the Sinful parlance, the primary address), since we can no longer assume, with shared port and CCB, that those are unique identifiers.

title: Ticket #1277: Use SIG_TERM on windows instead of WM_CLOSE
description: Condor uses WM_CLOSE on windows to signal processes to shut down, but this causes complexity in daemoncore and non-daemoncore daemons developed by 3rd parties that want to be used in a cross platform context. Windows does support a few signals, one of which is a SIG_TERM, and using a SIG_TERM instead of WM_CLOSE eases the cross-platform support burden. In addition, master reports that it is attempting to send a signal 15 (SIG_TERM) to the process even though it is actually sending a WM_CLOSE on windows.
remarks: 2010-Mar-16 23:24:34 by tannenba: Condor sends a WM_CLOSE message to an app to tell it to gracefully go away, analogous to sending a SIGTERM on Unix. A WM_CLOSE message was selected as the mechanism to tell a job to nicely go away since that is what Windows does when you close a window by pressing the "x" in the upper right corner (thus a well-understood and common execution path for practically every program ever written for Windows), it can be easily caught by either a windows console app or a windows gui (message-pump) app, the default action if not explicitly caught by the app is to terminate, and it isn't particular to any language-specific runtime support library. What do you mean windows supports "SIG_KILL" ? Specifically, what Win32 system call are you talking about? Or did you mean that daemonCore on Windows support SIGKILL? If that is what you mean, note a daemonCore sigkill on windows just sends a WM_CLOSE message, waits a small amount of time, then follows up with a hard-kill. 2010-Mar-18 12:59:38 by pmackinn: I think Rob would like to set an asynch signal handler in his Python daemon that would be portable between POSIX and Win32 platforms. However, there really is no kill(pid,signum) for Windows CRT thus making signal-based IPC on Windows impossible. Happy to be corrected on this. You can raise(signum) a signal but that is internal to that process. Ctrl-C is mapped by the Windows CRT to SIGINT and thus can be captured, but that is still a console event that has to be generated. 2010-Mar-18 14:37:25 by tannenba: Agree w/ ^^^... Using WM_CLOSE on Win32 for all the reasons mentioned in the remarks above was the best we could come up with. Lord knows I share frustrations w/ Rob, but not certain what, if anything, we could do to improve upon the situation... Should this ticket be marked as abandoned? 2010-Mar-18 14:43:25 by rrati: Windows supports about 5 signals, one of which is SIGTERM. I discovered that SIGTERM wasn't being sent because of a python program I wrote and wanted managed by master, but that isn't the only place this could come up. What I'm suggesting is use SIGTERM instead of WM_CLOSE for daemoncore and non-daemoncore processes. From my understanding, WM_CLOSE is equivalent to SIGTERM, and since windows supports SIGTERM why add the additional complexity of deciding which platform condor is one to send a SIGTERM vs. WM_CLOSE. I'm suggesting send SIGTERM on all platforms that support it (which should be just about all of them). Is there something a WM_CLOSE can achieve on windows that a SIGTERM can not? 2010-Mar-18 15:21:14 by tstclair: My bad, my previous example will just kill the process.. from some other win-goop I believe you will need to attach both processes to a console in order to send the signals, then you can write to the console (CTRL+C, CTRL+BREAK), and that write will be interpreted by the "signal handler" on the other side.. 2010-Mar-18 15:50:07 by tstclair: http://msdn.microsoft.com/en-us/library/ms682541(VS.85).aspx && http://msdn.microsoft.com/en-us/library/ms683155(VS.85).aspx 2010-Mar-18 19:44:06 by tannenba: @ Rob, you say "Windows supports SIGTERM". Please be specific... what Win32 system call you are talking about? Some method that only exists in the C runtime support library is not acceptable (e.g. signal()) as millions of programs on Windows are not linked w/ the C runtime support libs (think anything written in Visual Basic, or even apps written using a C compiler other than Microsofts). Likewise, some mechanism that relies on the existence of a console window is not acceptable (e.g. GenerateConsoleCtrlEvent()) as attaching both processes to a console is not feasible unless we want to say Condor can only run console applications. @ Tim, what previous example? @ everyone - I sympathize with Rob, but unfortunately asynch signals do not exist on Win32 like they do on Unix. Repeating the requirements that are met by the current way of doing things from my first remark on this ticket: a well-understood and commonly tested execution path for practically every program ever written for Windows it can be easily caught by either a windows console app or a windows gui (message-pump) app the default action if not explicitly caught by the app is to terminate it isn't particular to any language-specific runtime support library Any replacement mechanism would need to meet the above requirements. I'd be happily surprised if such a mechanisms exists. But I doubt it does. :(. Thus I again move to abandon this ticket... 2010-Mar-18 19:49:32 by matt: Possibly moot, but we could distinguish between signals the master will send to a daemon it is managing and the signal condor will send to an executable run under the starter. 2010-Mar-18 20:28:17 by tannenba: Not sure how distinguishing between apps under the master -vs- apps under the starter would help in this particular instance ... but thinking along the same lines, maybe distinguish between console and gui apps for how Condor asks apps to go away ? Not certain that making this distinction is worth it, however... catching a WM_CLOSE in a console apps seems about the same level of difficulty as catching any other console event like ctrl-c or ctrl-break. Rob, I am not a python guy, but doesn't calling win32api.setConsoleCtrlHandler() to catch a CTRL_CLOSE_EVENT work for you? 2010-Mar-19 09:15:36 by tstclair: Say for the sake of argument, I wanted to hook up a perl or god forbid a prolog daemon, that means I would have to bind in Win32 deps to intercept the WM_CLOSE to clean up nicely? I find that to be a little onerous... Daemon core directly binds these deps, maybe an alternative compromise would be a C-Style binding DLL/.so which would allow you to jig in a condor-esk-DAEMON without eating 3rd-party (or plat) deps for whatever lang you are working on. This would give any would-be daemons a contract so everyone can play nicely. This would not be a near term solution but it would solve a annoying dependency issue if one wants to make a platX daemon which is not in C/C++... 2010-Mar-19 09:24:40 by rrati: Again, this ticket was sparked by a python issue but the problem is far from python specific. The master daemon can control any program written in any language, which means the daemons could be written in languages common on multiple platform, be it compiled or interpreted. My intention with this ticket was to find a better means to be kind to non-daemoncore cross-platform programs, and hopefully that solution would simplify daemoncore processes as well. It sounds like signals on windows are a joke, which is hardly surprising.

title: Ticket #6048: Have separate Dag objects for splices?
description: Thinking about the option of having separate Dag objects for splices, instead of "lifting" the splice nodes into the parent Dag object. This would make a whole lot of other things way simpler to implement: PRE/POST scripts on splices. Per-splice throttling (#5653). Retries on splices. DIR on splices (#4824). Lazy creation of splice DAG files. Also see #2980: RFC: Unify SPLICE and SUBDAG EXTERNAL in DAGman. The biggest problem I see with this is how it would work with splice connections. (In a way, now, I'm kind of unhappy with the splice connection feature, because it really breaks the correspondence between sub-DAGs and splices.) Maybe we could have cross-Dag-object dependencies? I'm not sure how hard that would be. Anyhow, one way that we could avoid that problem is by making a new "sub-DAG internal" feature, that would be like splices (no extra DAGMan instance) other than that it wouldn't allow splice connections. The main problem I see with that is that we'd then have three sets of code to maintain, whereas now we only have two. Maybe we could initially implement a separate sub-DAG internal feature, and then eventually merge it with splices? Maybe we want a separate sub-DAG internal feature anyhow, though, because splice connections really conceptually complicate some of the other things we want to do with splices. For example, if you have PRE and POST scripts on a splice that has splice connections, when should they get run? I guess a lot of this depends on how far we want to go with making splices and sub-DAGs work alike -- if we just want to add PRE and POST scripts to splices, it would be way easier, I think, to just add socket nodes. But if we really want to do retries on splices, per-splice throttling, etc., it probably makes more sense to convert to separate Dag objects. Unfortunately, we kind of need to decide that up front, because if we implement socket nodes, and then later go to separate Dag objects, the socket node work will be pretty much wasted...
remarks: 2017-May-16 13:29:24 by wenger: Another advantage of this I just thought of: it would probably make it easier to be able to have individual configuration for a splice (e.g., different MAXIDLE settings for splices within the DAG).

title: Ticket #3860: PRIVATE_NETWORK_INTERFACE ignored by stduniv starter
description: This prevents dual-homed submit machines that need to talk to both private-network clusters and public-network clients from working correctly. (Details in the linked rust-admin ticket.) There is a hacky workaround (also outlined in the RUST ticket) for our current, very specific use-case but I'm not convinced it's going to work for all the cases we will need to support soon, so I think this either needs to be addressed in the old starter before v8.2, we need a better hack, or else DMTCP needs to save the day (#3321). Since we have a workaround at the moment I'm leaving this as a priority==4 ticket, but it will become priority==2 if/when the current hack doesn't work any more.
remarks: 2013-Aug-20 15:11:04 by wenger: Fixed RUST ticket number... 2013-Aug-20 15:43:31 by pfc: Background from the ticket: We need to configure a schedd on a dual-homed machine such that it can manage standard-universe jobs running on a private network, and yet respond to queries over the public network. Our desired configuration is as follows: spice001: Private Network Cluster Node eth0 10.20.3.1 NETWORK_INTERFACE=eth0 PRIVATE_NETWORK_INTERFACE=eth0 PRIVATE_NETWORK_NAME=sugar sugar-dev2: Dual-Homed Submit Machine eth0 10.20.5.33 eth1 128.230.146.15 NETWORK_INTERFACE=eth1 PRIVATE_NETWORK_INTERFACE=eth0 PRIVATE_NETWORK_NAME=sugar its-condor-submit: External Querier eth0: 128.230.171.183 NETWORK_INTERFACE=eth0 With this configuration, the external querier (its-condor-submit) can successfully query the schedd (sugar-dev2) via "condor_q -name", however standard-universe jobs submitted from the schedd (sugar-dev2) fail to successfully run on our cluster nodes (e.g, spice001) because the stduniv starter doesn't observe PRIVATE_NETWORK_INTERFACE and tries to contact sugar-dev2 over its NETWORK_INTERFACE, which isn't valid. The only configuration which allows stduniv jobs submitted from sugar-dev2 to successfully run on spice001 is where sugar-dev2's NETWORK_INTERFACE is eth0 (the private network) -- which prevents its-condor-submit from being able to contact it. However, after thinking this through, and much destructive experimentation (oh, the users I've hosed tonight), I discovered an ungodly hack that allows this to work. Instead of this desired configuration on our dual-homed schedds, which doesn't work: NETWORK_INTERFACE = 128.230.146.15 PRIVATE_NETWORK_INTERFACE = 10.20.5.33 PRIVATE_NETWORK_NAME = sugar …we can use this bizarro-configuration, which does work: NETWORK_INTERFACE = 10.20.5.33 PRIVATE_NETWORK_INTERFACE = 128.230.146.15 PRIVATE_NETWORK_NAME = public Caveat: this work ONLY if the external public network clients which wish to query our schedd set their PRIVATE_NETWORK_NAME=public, like so: % _CONDOR_PRIVATE_NETWORK_NAME=public condor_q -pool condor.phy.syr.edu -name sugar-dev3.phy.syr.edu The reason this works is that a matching PRIVATE_NETWORK_NAME tells the external public network clients to route over the public IP, while the private-network NETWORK_INTERFACE allows the brain-dead standard-universe starter to do the right thing and try to contact the schedd over the private network. NOTE: This also ONLY works if our dual-homed central manager is changed to have "NETWORK_INTERFACE = *". For reasons I don't understand, if the central manager has the same bizarro configuration as the schedds, no one can talk to it. Why? 2013-Sep-03 15:22:38 by tlmiller: If by "central manager" you meant "collector", remember that HTCondor must use the resolved DNS name or IP literal from the configuration file to contact the collector -- the private network information isn't available. If you meant the negotiator, I don't know, but I'd check BIND_ALL_INTERFACES.

title: Ticket #2322: Improve bad hostname handling in the gridmanager
description: The gridmanager needs to handle bad hostnames better. If a user mistypes the hostname in the GridResource attribute, the gridmanager will usually mark the resource as down and wait (potentially forever) for it to become reachable (which it never will). The gridmanager could do some basic sanity checks on the hostname and put the job on hold an informative message if the name doesn't resolve. A common variant of this problem is a gram jobmanager that returns a non-fully qualified hostname in its contact URL. Currently, the gridmanager will repeatedly try and fail to contact the jobmanager, attempting to restart the jobmanager in between tries. As above, the gridmanager should try resolve the hostname and put the job on hold if that fails.

title: Ticket #3476: CCB reconnect can fail due to race conditition
description: The following race condition causes CCB reconnection to fail, making the daemon unreachable via CCB until it is restarted. Reverse connection is requested. Expecting callback when non-blocking connect to target daemon finishes ... The connection to the CCB server fails. Reconnection is scheduled. Waiting for timer callback ... Callback for 2. CCB reconnect is initiated. Expecting callback when non-blocking connect to CCB server finishes ... Callback for 1. Reverse connect to target daemon has finished (or failed). Incorrectly, attempt to send report to CCB server on socket that is not yet connected. This fails and triggers a second reconnect attempt without correctly cleaning up the in-progress reconnect attempt. An invalid state is entered. The daemon waits forever for the reconnect callback to 3, but the operation has been canceled, and no callback will ever happen. The minimum time between 2 and 3 is one minute, and 4 must come after 3 but before the callback to 3 for the race to cause incorrect behavior. This makes the race fairly unlikely. However, in the cases we have observed, the network problem that causes 2 also delays 4, creating the conditions for the problem to strike.

description: Original idea from gthain. New configuration setting: SUBMIT_REQUIREMENTS. When a job is submitted, this expression is evaluated in the context of the job's ClassAd. If FALSE, the job is rejected. Example use cases: # Jobs must explicitly set (Can't test =!=UNDEFINED since # ImageSize defaults to executable's size SUBMIT_REQUIREMENTS = ImageSize > 1000 #Forbid scheduler universe jobs SUBMIT_REQUIREMENTS = JobUniverse != 7 # Require an AccountingGroup SUBMIT_REQUIREMENTS = AccountingGroup =!= UNDEFINED Possible extension: allow a list of tests so we can give more useful rejection messages: SUBMIT_REQUIREMENT_LIST=SUBMIT_REQUIREMENT_SCHEDULER_UNIVERSE_FORBIDDEN,SUBMIT_REQUIREMENTS_IMAGESIZE_MUST_BE_SET SUBMIT_REQUIREMENTS_IMAGESIZE_MUST_BE_SET_SCHEDULER_UNIVERSE_FORBIDDEN = ImageSize > 1000 SUBMIT_REQUIREMENTS_SCHEDULER_UNIVERSE_FORBIDDEN = JobUniverse != 7 then when a submit fails: % condor_submit myjob Submitting job(s).
