ERROR: Submit requirement SCHEDULER_UNIVERSE_FORBIDDEN not met. 2015-Jan-08 21:44:11 by bbockelm: Hi, The auto-generated message is better than none - but significantly worse than what we would do locally with "SUBMIT_REQUIREMENTS_REASON" that was there before. I really would not want to expose the auto-generated ones to users. Could you put it back? Other than that, the other refactors look fine. Brian 2015-Jan-09 14:39:23 by tlmiller: I'm not sure what you don't like about the auto-generated ones; as long as the administrator chooses reasonable names for the requirements, they seem useful. I strongly oppose the previous solution; writing nested conditionals to determine which clause failed and then returning the corresponding string is error-prone and mostly useless. Instead, I'd rather implement SUBMIT_REQUIREMENT_<NAME>_REASON, which would be a string to return instead of (or in addition to?) the default string. If you can come up with a good example, I'd be OK making it a ClassAd expression which evaluates to a string, although I might prefer SUBMIT_REQUIREMENT_<NAME>_REASON_EXPR for that. 2015-Jan-09 14:40:51 by tlmiller: Retroactive design doc draft -- https://docs.google.com/a/wisc.edu/document/d/1HywDThmWKoJVWIPOrgN58oaiiR0myYl8NPLaafIJ4Lk 2015-Jan-12 14:43:59 by tlmiller: Implement SUBMIT_REQUIREMENT_<NAME>_REASON as an expression, figuring people wouldn't mind adding quotes if they just wanted to use constant strings. 2015-Jan-12 15:04:57 by tlmiller: (Documentation draft/notes -- Admin Manual) Submit Requirements You may wish to restrict which jobs may enter the queue of a particular scheduler. For instance, you may not wish to clog up your queue with jobs you know will never be able to run (for instance, standard universe jobs in a queue with restricted networking). Or you may require that all jobs in the queue request a minimum amount of memory. To do so, set the configuration knob SUBMIT_REQUIREMENT_NAMES. This comma- or space- separated list tells HTCondor the names of your submit requirements; pick something descriptive, since the name is a major component of the default error message if a user attempts to submit a job which fail to meet the requirements. For our example: SUBMIT_REQUIREMENT_NAMES = NotStandardUniverse, MinimalRequestMemory The names in this list must be valid configuration knob names. HTCondor sets each named requirement by looking up the configuration knob SUBMIT_REQUIREMENT_<NAME>. Each knob must contain a valid ClassAd expression that evaluates to a bool (or something convertible thereto). For our example: SUBMIT_REQUIREMENT_NotStandardUniverse = JobUniverse != 1 SUBMIT_REQUIREMENT_MinimimalRequestMemory = RequestMemory > 512 Note that JobUniverse and RequestMemory are both job ad attributes. Each submit requirement is evaluated (in the listed order) in the context of the the schedd ad (in the MY namespace) and the job ad (the TARGET namespace); attributes not found in the job ad will be look up in the schedd ad, as usual. The first requirement that fails terminates evaluation and is the only reason reported. You may also set a rejection reason for each requirement: SUBMIT_REQUIREMENT_NotStandardUniverse_REASON = "This schedd does not accept standard universe jobs; try again elsewhere." SUBMIT_REQUIREMENT_MinimimalRequestMemory_REASON = strcat( "The job only requested ", RequestMemory, " megabytes. If that's really how much memory your job needs, contact me at ..." ) A rejection reason has the same name as the corresponding requirement, except with _REASON appended, and must be a ClassAd expression which evaluates to a string. Thus, in our first example, we had to put double quotes around the whole explanation. In the second example, we construct a string using ClassAd's string manipulation funcations. If you submit multiple jobs per cluster, please note that while we evaluate the submit requirements against individual jobs, any individual job failing the submit requirements will cause the entire submit to fail; the other jobs in the cluster will not enter the queue. 2015-Jan-12 15:09:21 by tlmiller: Brian also suggested, as long as we're changing the protocol, that we should return a ClassAd instead of a bare string, for future-proofing. This is probably a good idea. 2015-Feb-12 14:22:04 by tlmiller: Design doc updated; hopefully it became clearer. 2015-Feb-18 14:37:54 by tlmiller: ToddT reviewed the design and found it generally acceptable. His concerns will be addressed in a child ticket.

title: Ticket #7442: Get cgroup memory usage from memory.usage_in_bytes, not rss fields
description: Today, when cgroups are enabled, the memory usage by a job come from summing the total_rss, total_mapped_file, and total_swap fields of the memory cgroup. However, this is not the total amount of physical memory used. There are several other sources of memory, like kernel data structure, caches, etc. In addition to under-reporting memory, the memory limit that we currently report is less than the limit used to kill processes that have reached their provisioned limit. This causes all kinds of surprises with users, and difficulty with condor, which ignores the OOM killer, if it thinks the job is under the allocation. Therefore, we will switch the memory reporting to the field memory.usage_in_bytes, which is the total physical memory used by processes in the cgroup, and the limit against which the OOM is checked.

title: Ticket #6603: HTCondor can't run jobs when HTCondor is started in a docker container
description: If condor is started inside a docker container, the default settings give it uid 0, but many of the rootly capabilities are removed. In particular, the cgroups are mounted read-only, so no new cgroups can be created. As condor 8.6 now uses cgroups if they are visible, this creates problem. Users can work around this by starting the docker container with the --privilege flag today. This ticket will change the starter to check not just that the starter has root, but also the appropriate capability to create new cgroups.

title: Ticket #4281: Change default settings so that jobs are not preempted by default
description: One of the most common questions for new HTCondor admins is how to turn off job preemption. This ticket proposes to change the default out-of-the-box configuration for HTCondor so that jobs are not preempted by default, and thus enabling job preemption as before is opt-in.
remarks: 2014-Mar-27 15:32:48 by tannenba: NOTE: This code must undergo a code review before v8.1.6 2014-May-22 14:48:17 by tannenba: CODE REVIEW Looking over this patch, it looks like it essentially comments out and/or removes a bunch of settings from the condor_config file and places the below defaults into the param table: PREEMPTION_REQUIREMENTS = False START = True PREEMPTION_RANK = NEGOTIATOR_PRE_JOB_RANK = RemoteOwner=?=UNDEFINED NEGOTIATOR_POST_JOB_RANK = (RemoteOwner=?=UNDEFINED) * (ifthenElse(isUndefined(KFlops),1000,Kflops) - \ SlotID - 1.0e10*(Offline=?=True)) WANT_SUSPEND=FALSE WANT_VACATE=FALSE SUSPEND=FALSE CONTINUE=TRUE PREEMPT=FALSE KILL=FALSE PERIODIC_CHECKPOINT = ((time()-LastPeriodicCheckpoint)/60.0)> \ (180.0+$RANDOM_INTEGER(-30,30,1)) CLAIM_WORKLIFE = 3600 Looking this over, I think we can do better before v8.2.0. Some items noticed: CLAIM_WORKLIFE of an hour seems a bit long esp with preemption disabled by default; seems like 20 minutes seems better in absence of preemption. Wouldn't it be better to disable preemption via MaxJobRetirementTime instead of changing PREEMPTION_REQUIREMENTS ? This way, the no preemption policy is honored even in the face of draining, for instance. Also it would be easier for an admin to re-enable preemption by simply adjusting the MaxJobRetirementTime to whatever they want instead of messing around with a potentially complicated expression. condor_config.annotated should be released, i.e. the CMakefile should be modified to copy it into the release examples directory. Right now it looks like the only place condor_config.annotated can be found is in the source code. should metaknob policy always_run be enabled by default, just like the host security metaknob is? BTW, if this metaknob, MaxJobRetirementTime is 0 - what does that mean? should preemption_rank go by inverse wall clock time by default? the "uwcs" preemption_requirements expression looks to be broken. guessing it evaluates to undefined most of the time due to bug #4369 we should have negotiator_pre_job_rank do some local best fit with respect to cpu and memory. Going to resolve this ticket and open a new ticket for v8.2.0 to address the above items.

title: Ticket #1579: Fix collector query expressions
description: Query ads are sent to the collector to query for and invalidate groups of ads. They include a requirements expression that filters the desired ads. The collector does a one-way match between the query ad and the candidate ads. Clients use expressions with a mixture of TARGET-scoped and unscoped attribute references. These will cause problems when we start using new ClassAd's strict scoping rules. The new standard will be that the requirements expression of query ads should not have any TARGET scoping. The expression will be evaluated directly in the context of each candidate ad. Here are some reasons why: No current expression references attributes in the query ad Most current expressions have no TARGET-scoping Some expressions come from the user and won't have TARGET-scoping

title: Ticket #3544: no AVX machine attribute causing stduniv job resumes to fail
description: Vladimir Dergachev writes: I think I figured out why some of my jobs are getting killed with signal 4 - illegal instruction. During program startup libc automatically determines CPU capabilities and if the job was started on a newer CPU (say with AVX) it will use AVX variant of math functions such sin, etc. However, if the job is checkpointed and then restarted on an older node it runs into a problem as the CPU is no longer capable to execute these instructions. So it seems that condor needs to know which nodes are newer and that a checkpoint made on AVX node cannot be restored to an SSE only node. Stuart asks: What is the current best way to handle this problem of checkpoint images getting started on non-compatible CPU's? Ideally, Condor would take care of this automatically by registering what type of CPU is needed when a checkpoint image is taken, and then using that information when match making to restart a job.
remarks: 2013-Mar-18 14:18:36 by gthain: Just to be complete, this is on RHEL6? 2013-Mar-18 14:26:15 by pfc: SL6 to be precise, but yes. 2013-Mar-18 15:15:33 by bbockelm: Be careful what you wish for here - AVX is one of many subtle differences you can run into between CPU instruction sets. CMS has found that AMD and Intel love to leapfrog each other on slightly different, incompatible processor-specific instructions. It'd be a bummer to have to tie things to a specific CPU model, but OTOH, the list of CPU flags is long: [bbockelm@brian-test condor]$ cat /proc/cpuinfo | grep flags | tail -n 1 flags : fpu tsc msr pae cx8 apic cmov pat clflush mmx fxsr sse sse2 ss syscall nx lm constant_tsc pni vmx ssse3 cx16 sse4_1 sse4_2 popcnt lahf_lm Not all are going to be relevant to all executables either. CMS has been looking at newer features in GCC 4.8 which allow us to make a single binary optimized for multiple CPU architectures. Unfortunately, I think GCC 4.8's approach may not work transparently with stduni. Brian 2013-Mar-19 10:11:55 by tlmiller: Since AVX is the only instruction-set difference currently causing us grief, the consensus seems to be that adding it to the standard universe platform string is the right approach. 2013-Mar-19 12:15:39 by bbockelm: Hi Todd, Other common things that will likely cause issues: sse3, sse4_2, aes, fma4. avx2 processors are around the corner, but I don't have access to any right now. I would really strongly advise against doing a one-off knowing there are already several further issues down the road. I'd hate to have this become like OpSys in that it needs several redesigns to make it useful. Brian 2013-Mar-19 13:32:22 by tlmiller: After discussion with GregT, I'd like to take a step back and figure out why this isn't happening in our pool -- it may just be good luck -- and then reproduce it locally. I'm loathe to partition people's pools any more than we have to: if glibc is only using AVX, then I'd prefer (even if we add the rest of the cpu flags infrastructure) to include only AVX in the checkpoint string. Maybe this could be made configurable, and default to whatever the craziness inflicted on us by glibc is? 2013-Mar-19 13:33:50 by pfc: Once again, I'd love a general, all-singing, all-dancing abstractastic solution that handles all cases, but if that's not on the table in the short-term it would be great to solve the actual problem in front of us. The OpSys point is well-taken but one important difference is that OpSys is user-visible so users have to know to change their submit files whenever it changes, whereas this is "under the hood" and can be fixed now for this one case and still improved later for the general case without users having to adjust. 2013-Mar-19 13:35:34 by pfc: Punting to the user / adding a knob / making this configurable would be a fine solution for us, if you'd prefer not to affect anyone else. 2013-Mar-19 13:37:50 by tlmiller: How long is the "short term" for you? 2013-Mar-19 16:27:22 by bbockelm: What about advertising this with something like STARTD_CRON for now? 2013-Mar-22 10:18:46 by tlmiller: What do people think about making CheckpointPlatform something that can be configured by the administrator? Then they can partition (or not) their pool depending on their particular needs (including AVX), and HTCondor doesn't have to try to make one decision to fit every situation. 2013-Mar-22 11:50:55 by pfc: LIGO would be very happy with that solution. 2013-Mar-28 10:18:20 by tlmiller: I have a build which I think will do the above. It's provisionally in 7.9.6; I need to do some more research to determine if this is really the right fix (since we don't understand why we haven't seen this problem locally). I'd like you to test it and see how it works for you; which platform(s) do you need binaries for? 2013-Mar-28 10:45:38 by pfc: For now, just RHEL6 x86_64 since that's what CIT runs. 2013-Mar-29 09:56:02 by tlmiller: Link sent, will be tested. Still need to reproduce the problem here. 2013-Apr-10 14:20:06 by tlmiller: Found a user who /did/ get hit by this problem and swiped their binary. Can now reproduce (even in the debugger!). Confirmed that the problem is that glibc caches __cpu_features and calls optimized routines as indicated; in this particular case, HTCondor code was calling strcmp() (in order to deal with the file table). 2013-Apr-10 16:27:47 by tlmiller: Our heavy-hearted decision, made with tears in our eyes, is that we have to partition the pool, and add the bits that glibc cares about to the standard universe platform string. Based on code inspection, those bits appear to be SSSE 3, SSE 4.1, and SSE 4.2; although the glibc code uses two other bits, having them set wrong will only incur a performance penalty. ("Prefers SSE for memory operations" and "Fast REP string". The latter instruction prefix exists on all x86 processors, but are only faster than the alternative on some; SSE has existed since the Pentium III, so I don't think we need to worry about detecting it.) I've confirmed that (shockingly) the Linux kernel and glibc agree about which bits mean what, so we can simply grovel in /proc/cpuinfo and add which of those flags are present to the checkpoint platform string. 2013-Apr-11 14:21:35 by tlmiller: DESIGN PARAGRAPHS PROBLEM A series of optimized functions in glibc are causing the standard universe grief: by detecting, at the time of the first call to these functions, if the processor supports particular instruction set extensions (SSE2, SSSE3, SSE4.1, SSE4.2), glibc can improve its performance. Naturally, the detection is cached, so if we restart a checkpointed job on a machine without those extensions, the process will execute an illegal instruction the next time it calls these functions. SOLUTIONS One option for a solution is to hack glibc never to use these optimized functions. This has the advantage of keeping the pool unfragmented, but has two major disadvantages: it removes what glibc thinks is a worthwhile speedup, but more importantly, requires us to maintain another patch for glibc. We would rather, in fact, be removing patches, rather than adding them. Because this decision is made by glibc at runtime, we also can't solve this problem with matchmaking -- before start-up, the job could run on any machine. Luckily, we already have a mechanism in place to handle this problem: the checkpoint platform (string). By extending the platform string to include the bits that glibc cares about, we can partition the pool but also make sure that jobs don't crash after they migrate. IMPLEMENTATION The sysapi already grovels /proc/cpuinfo, so we'll start there. (This makes sense: as far as we know, nobody else uses glibc.) We'll do two things with the attributes glibc cares about: advertise them, and add them to the checkpoint platform string. By advertising them as individual attributes, we make it easier for admins to add new ones as or should they become necessary, and improve the ability of condor_q to analyze them usefully. (We could just forward the 'flags' field into the job ad, substituting commas for spaces, in order to use the ClassAd match-out-of-the-list function; but that would be harder to analyze. It would also either include a lot of useless information or be harder to extend, when something new shows up.) It will also standardize the representation of these attributes, which will help pools interoperate. Likewise, we'll leave the existing patch in place, so that the checkpoint platform string can be updated by administrators as necessary. (That is, before we the developers hear about the problem.) 2013-May-20 16:38:46 by adesmet: Code Review Code passes as is. strongly recommended The idiom "Check for ATTR_CHECKPOINT_PLATFORM, fall back to sysapi_ckptpltfrm" [35281] repeats several times . May be overlooked if someone adds another call to sysapi_ckptpltfrm later. Proposed change: create get_ckptpltfrm with encompasses the "try param, then sysapi_ckptpltfm" and use that instead. Ensure that sysapi_ckptpltfrm is commented to warn that get_ckptpltfm is probably what you want. low importance /src/condor_sysapi/processor_flags.cpp sysapi_processor_flags_raw Hard coded buffer of 1024. The comment ("see ncpus.cpp") is silly; just copy that comment over. Or better: don't make it a hard coded buffer. If this ever fails, it will fail cryptically as flags are silently lost. Perhaps time to write a small "safe_fgets" that returns a newly malloced string (with a warning that the user needs to free it) and solve the problem once and for all? low importance /src/condor_sysapi/processor_flags.cpp sysapi_processor_flags_raw Any possibility that we'll have different flags on different processors? Seems unlikely, but I can envision a future where hyperthreaded core advertise different features. Probably not worth trying to fix, but for bonus points: detect if the flags vary across cores and complain to the log. low importance /src/condor_sysapi/processor_flags.cpp sysapi_processor_flags_raw For paranoia in case the /proc/cpuinfo format changes, assert that colon[1] == ' '? Handing back to tlmiller 2013-May-21 14:22:40 by tlmiller: In the course of investigating item 1, I discovered that CHECKPOINT_PLATFORM already existed as configuration file attribute to be used for setting the machine ad attribute CheckpointPlatform, and confirmed that it worked. I'll be removing that portion of this patch and updating the docs.

title: Ticket #5490: add a -batch-name argument to condor_submit and condor_submit_dag
description: The new condor_q can summarize a batch of jobs by grouping them by "batch name" where batch name is either the dag id, cluster id or a common command string. But it would be even more useful if users could set the batch name explicitly as an argument to condor_submit and condor_submit_dag or as a statement in the submit file or .dag file. The command line option is more useful because it is more likely that submit and .dag files are re-used across batches of jobs than that they are recreated each time a new batch is desired. a new argument -batch-name <name> should be added to both condor_submit and condor_submit_dag. title: This attachment is private.
Ticket #2705: condor_schedd misreports submitter ads for running jobs on restart
description: Description of problem: So a relatively subtle fairshare issue has been affecting us due to our schedd stability issues lately. This is what I believe to be going on: * Jobs for a particular AccountingGroup are running in a condor_schedd. * The submitter add for the jobs reports running & idle jobs with Name equal to the AccountingGroup, and there's another submitter ad with the Name equal the User attribute of the jobs but 0 for running/idle/held. * The schedd dies and is restarted * The running jobs are reported in a submitter ad with Name equal to User, not Name equal to AccountingGroup. The submitter ad with Name equal to AccountingGroup shows idle jobs but 0 running jobs. * During the negotiation cycle the negotiator sees 0 running jobs for the group and allocates slots for additional jobs. When it connects to the schedd it sees a larger number of jobs running than shares were initialized for, decided the group has received enough allocation, and doesn't dispatch any more jobs to it. A "trapped" AccountingGroup can often receive no other jobs until existing running jobs finish. The misreporting submitter ad is a fairly severe bug due to the fairshare miscaluation and how new job dispatching is blocked until job completion. Can you kindly repro this and look at providing us a patch?
remarks: Root cause is that the schedd does not properly restore accounting group info on restart. REPRO/TEST: Using the following config: NEGOTIATOR_DEBUG = D_FULLDEBUG NEGOTIATOR_USE_SLOT_WEIGHTS = FALSE NEGOTIATOR_INTERVAL = 30 SCHEDD_INTERVAL = 15 CLAIM_WORKLIFE = 0 NUM_CPUS = 10 # turn off round robin and multiple allocation rounds HFS_ROUND_ROBIN_RATE = 100000000 HFS_MAX_ALLOCATION_ROUNDS = 1 GROUP_NAMES = a, b GROUP_QUOTA_a = 5 GROUP_QUOTA_b = 5 GROUP_ACCEPT_SURPLUS = FALSE GROUP_AUTOREGROUP = FALSE Submit the following job (you may wish to replace 'eje' with your username) universe = vanilla cmd = /bin/sleep args = 6000 should_transfer_files = if_needed when_to_transfer_output = on_exit +AccountingGroup="a.eje" queue 5 After the jobs negotiate, you should see submitter 'a.eje' with 5 jobs running: $ condor_status -submitter Name Machine Running IdleJobs HeldJobs a.eje@localdomain localhost. 5 0 0 RunningJobs IdleJobs HeldJobs a.eje@localdomain 5 0 0 Total 5 0 0 Now restart the schedd: $ condor_restart -schedd Before the fix: After schedd restarts, you will see that the jobs have been improperly re-constituted with submitter 'eje' instead of 'a.eje': $ condor_status -submitter Name Machine Running IdleJobs HeldJobs a.eje@localdomain localhost. 0 0 0 eje@localdomain localhost. 5 0 0 RunningJobs IdleJobs HeldJobs a.eje@localdomain 0 0 0 eje@localdomain 5 0 0 Total 5 0 0 After the fix: if you repeat the repro steps above, you should see that after the schedd is restarted, the jobs are correctly reconstituted with 'a.eje' for the submitter name: $ condor_status -submitter Name Machine Running IdleJobs HeldJobs a.eje@localdomain localhost. 5 0 0 RunningJobs IdleJobs HeldJobs a.eje@localdomain 5 0 0 Total 5 0 0

title: Ticket #1650: Submitting multiple VMWare jobs with single submit doesn't work
description: Trying to submit multiple VMWare vm universe jobs with a single submit file doesn't work when the vmware_dir attribute isn't used. Condor_submit gives this error: ERROR: no vmx file for vmware can be found. The problem is that the VMware code in condor_submit adds vm-related files to TransferInput in the job ad, then searches the list of files in TransferInput to find .vmx and .vmdk files. This is done as a part of #1351, which allows VMware files to be given in vmware_dir or transfer_input_files in the submit file. However, condor_submit's code to collect job attributes with identical values in the cluster ad causes the ads of jobs after the first in a cluster to be mostly empty. So for the second and subsequent jobs in the cluster, the job ad in condor_submit doesn't have a TransferInput attribute, so the VMware-related code complains that there is no .vmx file. The proposed fix is to improve how condor_submit decides which attributes go into the cluster vs the proc ad. Before, InsertJobExpr() kept a hash table of attribute name/value pairs that went into the cluster ad. For subsequent jobs in the cluster, it would return immediately if the name/value pair was in the hash table. Thus, the job ad would only taken values that differed from the cluster ad. Now, a copy of the cluster ad is saved in memory. InsertJobExpr() always inserts values into the job ad. Then, when SaveClassAd() sends the ad to the schedd, it compares each name/value against the cluster ad and skips those that match.

Is this intentional? 2011-Jan-05 11:04:39 by jfrey: Custom attributes don't always go into the proc ad, although maybe they should. If you set one for the first job in the cluster, it ends up in the cluster ad. But I just noticed that if you set a custom attribute for the first job in the cluster, you can't unset it using the '-' notation for any subsequent jobs in the cluster.

title: Ticket #6195: Job Router crash on error reading job_queue.log
description: The Job Router can crash when it has trouble reading the schedd's job_queue.log file. This is due to fclose() being called twice on the same FILE struct. Reported by CERN. The ClassAdLogReader object shares one FILE struct between two ClassAdLogParser objects. One parser checks whether the job log has grown or rotated, and the other reads the log events for processing. On certain errors reading the file, both parser objects will close the FILE struct. I propose to modify ClassAdLogParser such that if it is given a FILE struct (instead of calling fopen() itself), it will not call fclose() on it. That will remove this double-close situation. I will make some further changes to reduce the chance for leaking open files when the caller isn't careful about calling closeFile() when necessary.

title: Ticket #5613: how best to transform job classad prior to submission
description: NOTE: This ticket abandoned as we ultimately implemented the functionality in #5885 instead It was communicated to LIGO users before O1 that they needed to add "accounting_group" and "accounting_group_user" values to their submit files to track the consumption of individual users and of search groups. Unfortunately this decision binds you to use the group scheduling system of Condor, something that no LIGO site ultimately chose to do. LIGO users were quite good about adding the right lines to their submit files. These are also easy knobs to turn in Pegasus. So rather than tell them to stop, I wrote a wrapper that transforms: accounting_group = ligo.bla.bla.bla to +LigoSearchTag = ligo.bla.bla.bla in the submit file before submission by using the "-dump" argument to submit and normal shell scripting tools. There are also some rules concerning the values which were being enforced by a Python helper which I have successfully re-implemented using CLASSAD_USER_PYTHON_MODULES and SUBMIT_REQUIREMENT_NAMES. I would like to see the transformation replaced with something that doesn't require replacing condor_submit in the user's PATH. Something like SUBMIT_REQUIREMENT_NAMES would be nice, e.g.: I'd really like to see this look more like SUBMIT_REQUIREMENTs. This is described in greater detail in the ticket. For example, CLASSAD_USER_PYTHON_MODULES = ligojob SUBMIT_TRANSFORM_NAMES = LIGOJOB SUBMIT_TRANSFORM_LIGOJOB = ligoxform(Target.ClassAd) The last line is not intended to be literal but to evoke the idea. In the meantime, my wrapper solution is below. condor_submit wrapper #!/bin/bash CONDOR_SUBMIT_BINARY=/usr/bin/condor_submit CONDOR_SUBMIT_XFORM=/home/tpdownes/wrapper-testing/test.py if [ $# -eq 0 ]; then ${CONDOR_SUBMIT_BINARY} -dump - - | ${CONDOR_SUBMIT_XFORM} else ${CONDOR_SUBMIT_BINARY} -dump - "$@" | ${CONDOR_SUBMIT_XFORM} fi exit 0 condor_submit transformation #!/usr/bin/python import htcondor import classad import sys adString = sys.stdin.read() ad = classad.parseOne(adString) ad['LigoSearchTag'] = ad['AcctGroup'] ad['LigoSearchUser'] = ad['AcctGroupUser'] del ad['AcctGroup'] del ad['AcctGroupUser'] htcondor.Schedd().submit(ad)

title: Ticket #5243: Avoid DAGMan restarts on dprintf failure, etc.
description: We ran into this problem on CHTC: What was the problem you ask? User "smallegan" had three dagman jobs that were starting, exiting, and being restarted over a million times because the user filled up his disk quota at 12:30pm. DAGMan could not write to its logs and so it immediately exited (with exitcode 44, which is what all HTCondor daemons do when they cannot write to their logs), at which point the schedd immediately restarted it as fast as it could. I put user "smallegan"'s jobs on hold and the duty cycle immediately dropped and all was happy again. Just discussed this with ToddT -- he suggests that DAGMan should be removed from the queue on exit with anything other than SIGTERM, SIGKILL, or SIGQUIT. My initial thought is that that's probably fine, but I want to investigate a bit before saying yes for sure. (Part of the idea is that we don't just want to say, "DAGMan should be removed from the queue if it exits with exit code 44, because there might be similar issues in the future that would not cause that specific exit code.)

I set OnExitRemove to true, but condor_dagman still stays in the queue after being condor_held... 2015-Aug-28 14:56:35 by wenger: Created V8_5-gittrac_5243-branch for this. 2015-Aug-28 15:38:39 by wenger: Okay, I've committed a fix on the branch that removes DAGMan from the queue on an exit code of 44. That will fix the immediate problem with re-starts on dprintf failures, and I'm 99% certain that it doesn't break anything. My thought is that if we want something out in the next few days we should go with this, and then revisit a more comprehensive fix when we have a little more time to think about it.

title: Ticket #6896: Disable DAGMan graph metrics reporting by default
description: There's a bug in the DAGMan code that provides graph metrics for completed DAGs. For certain graph structures, the algorithms to calculate height and width can send the code into a (very CPU heavy) infinite loop. Instead of debugging the core problem, which could take a long time, I'm simply adding a knob to disable this code by default. title: Ticket #7784: condor_qedit should not adversly affect condor_schedd operations
description: In stable versions 8.8.9 and earlier, as well as development version 8.9.8 and earlier, there were some issues with the condor_schedd validating the input provided by condor_qedit. Deleting Attributes There are certain attributes that the SchedD will not let you modify, such as Owner. However, the same checks were not applied when deleting attributes, which can leave jobs in a state that they are not runnable. Possibly, if the administrator has configured submit attributes, job transforms, and set PROTECTED_ATTRIBUTES, the user would be able to remove an attribute that should be protected which could influence policy used in matchmaking. Special Attributes Certain internal attributes in the SchedD should not be editable by users, but the SchedD was not correctly enforcing this. While there are no known security issues with this, the user can disrupt the SchedD by modifying the state such that the next time the SchecD attempts to start up, it cannot. It is suggested that you upgrade to the latest stable or development release. However, if you cannot, there is a workaround for this issue which is to set: SECURE_JOB_ATTRS=NextClusterNum, NextJobSetNum
creator: tim

title: Ticket #2569: Submit event not written for spooled jobs when running as root
description: When a job is submitted with a user log and spooled input files to a schedd running as root, the schedd fails to write the submit event to the user log (in the spool directory). The schedd writes to the user log as the job owner. When it writes the submit event, the spool directory (if there is one) is owned by condor, so the write fails. We can either chown the spool directory just before writing the submit event (at transaction commit time), or write the submit event as condor if the user log is in the spool directory. This wasn't detected in previous changes in how the submit event is logged because testing was done with personal Condors (i.e. non-root).
remarks: 2011-Oct-21 14:44:07 by jfrey: I've attached a patch for this bug. If the schedd fails to open the user log as the user and the log is in the job's spool directory, the schedd will then try to open the log as user condor. 2011-Oct-21 16:17:22 by zmiller: PATCH REVIEWED, LOOKS GOOD
attachments: log_as_condor.patch 1050 bytes added by jfrey on 2011-Oct-21 19:43:05 UTC. Allow user logs in the spool directory to be written to as user Condor.

title: Ticket #6879: condor_ssh_to_job doesn't work from 8.8.0 schedd to 8.9.0 startd
description: As part of the SciTokens work, we replaced the base64 encoding/decoding routines from ones that came from openssl to homebrew implementations. The OpenSSL base64 encoder always inserts a newline after every 76 bytes of output. Our homebrew one does not. The OpenSSL base64 decoder can't handle lines longer than 76 bytes, but our homebrew one can. So, for 8.9.0, I've changed our encoder to append a newline every 76 bytes. In general, seems like this line wrapping should work at a higher level, but this fix allows ssh_to_job to work for now. Also, we should fix the base64 encoder/decoder interfaces -- one takes an unsigned char as input, the other a signed char. One returns the output, the other sets it as an output parameter. One takes an input length and a char *, the other just a char *, and assumes it is null terminated.

Isn't that the bug? 2019-Feb-06 11:17:44 by tim: Restored old base64 encoding. We are back to two implementation. This was never released. No docs.

title: Ticket #6480: FileLock functions isLocked() isUnlocked() don't call fcntl() to check
description: On Linux, Instantiating a FileLock object and then calling isLocked() or isUnlocked() doesn't actually make any calls to fcntl(). It just returns the value of a member variable. That member variable m_state is initialized to the UNLOCK state and only updated if we call obtain(). This means that if another process has already obtained a lock, and we instantiate a FileLock and call isUnlocked() the answer will always be true. Unless I'm misunderstanding the intended use of these functions, it seems like if they don't actually call fnctl() to check the lock status that this couldn't possible come up with the correct answer. Am I missing something? As is, it seems like the function should be named pleaseDontTellMeIfSomeoneElseDidButDidIPersonallyLockThisFileIForgot()
remarks: 2017-Nov-09 14:19:34 by tannenba: Yes, the isLocked/isUnlocked methods do exactly as you describe - they just tell the caller the current state of the object. It would be nice if a comment told folks this in the header file, but changing these methods to do fcntl() to test things is not a good idea imho. First of all, you'd be changing the semantics of a public method which is currently in use elsewhere, which could have large consequences. Secondly, implementing the semantic of "tell me if any process has this file locked" by polling is nonsensical imho. Process i/o happens asynchronously. If "isUnlocked()" returns True, you cannot act on that information, because by the time the function returns another process may have locked the file. The only way to truly determine the state of a lock on a file is to try and actually obtain and hold the lock. (and even that can be messed up iirc, due to incompatibilities between fcntl, flock, lockf, etc) Thus these helper methods simply return the state of the object. I am going to mark this ticket as abandoned. 2017-Nov-09 19:38:24 by zmiller: I'm re-opening this ticket. As you said: It would be nice if a comment told folks this in the header file, I agree that would be nice. I have other reservations beyond that, however, so until we chat and resolve this, I'd like to keep it open.

title: Ticket #1345: Clearly document cross-platform portability
description: I was recently contacted by a user who wanted binaries for RHEL4 and didn't see them on the web site. They didn't realize that the RHEL3 binaries work fine on RHEL4. We hide that information in several different non-obvious places, all of which are slightly out of date and disagree with each other. http://condor-wiki.cs.wisc.edu/index.cgi/wiki?p=PortsTable http://www.cs.wisc.edu/condor/porting/port_table.html http://www.cs.wisc.edu/condor/manual/v7.4/1_5Availability.html#948 This is a mess. We should have canonical information in one place, not three. We might automatically copy that information elsewhere, but updating that information should be done in one place, not three. The download page (that is, the page which lets the user select binaries for download, e.g. this one) should include this information. Ideally it should be copied from the canonical location directly into the table, adding additional rows that point to the same binaries elsewhere in the table. If the user selects the same binary several times, the download page should note the platforms the user selected so he knows why, say, 3 platforms turned into 2 downloads. If that proves too complex, at least have a prominent link at the top, "My platform isn't list" or similar, with a link to the canonical table.

title: Ticket #3682: Reintroduce SSH keypair -style two-phase commit for OpenStack
description: Although it doesn't complain when you supply a client token, OpenStack doesn't support the idempotent RunInstances(). We must therefore reintroduce the SSH keypair ID -style of two-phase commit. Because we can't really tell if we're contacting a (broken version of) OpenStack, we must have the user tell us. (A job attribute might be appropriate, given that the logic changes will fall mostly in the grid manager, but since we already use 'euca3' as a "protocol", it may be less ugly to add 'openstack' as a protocol as well.) This also implies using something like GM_SEEK_INSTANCE_ID (or, rather, its batched-request replacement) during recovery, since we need to make sure we only call RunInstances() once per job.

title: Ticket #1191: Windows job_queue.log rotation not atomic
description:
A user noticed his windows schedd daemons (Condor 7.2.4) were emitting this error: 1/27 12:50:15 (pid:2528) ERROR "JOB QUEUE DAMAGED; header ad NEXT_CLUSTER_NUM invalid" at line 893 in file ..\src\condor_schedd.V6\qmgmt.cpp His environment is XP SP3 and Server 2003 SP2 and he does a patching scenario where his machines will come up, apply a patch, then reboot, 5-10 times, and the machine being up 20 seconds to 5 minutes each time before stabilizing. He's been doing thid for a long time, and his Condor 6.8.8custom version hadn't shown the problem, but his 7.2.4 version did. Upon inspection of the job_queue.log, it was found corrupted. Most notably, there was an instance of NextClusterNum being 1, when it should have ~700. Guessing that file rotation might be an issue, I tracked down the portion of the code which deals with it. here it is on the head of the V7_2-branch: /* HEAD of V7_2-branch */ int rotate_file(const char *old_filename, const char *new_filename) { #if defined(WIN32) /* We must use MoveFileEx on NT because rename can not overwrite an existing file. */ if (MoveFileEx(old_filename, new_filename, MOVEFILE_REPLACE_EXISTING) == 0) { DWORD err = GetLastError(); dprintf(D_ALWAYS, "MoveFileEx(%s,%s) failed with error %d
", old_filename, new_filename, err); return -1; } #else if (rename(old_filename, new_filename) < 0) { dprintf(D_ALWAYS, "rename(%s, %s) failed with errno %d
", old_filename, new_filename, errno); return -1; } #endif return 0; } Notably, here is the same piece of code at the head of the V7_4-branch: int rotate_file(const char *old_filename, const char *new_filename) { #if defined(WIN32) /* We must use MoveFileEx on NT because rename can not overwrite an existing file. */ if (MoveFileEx(old_filename, new_filename, MOVEFILE_COPY_ALLOWED | MOVEFILE_REPLACE_EXISTING | MOVEFILE_WRITE_THROUGH) == 0) { DWORD err = GetLastError(); dprintf(D_ALWAYS, "MoveFileEx(%s,%s) failed with error %d
", old_filename, new_filename, err); return -1; } #else if (rename(old_filename, new_filename) < 0) { dprintf(D_ALWAYS, "rename(%s, %s) failed with errno %d
", old_filename, new_filename, errno); return -1; } #endif return 0; } Notice the difference? Those flags showed up in this checkin: commit a4fad2c73e9076e3a26bc5c6e392844de9cc1b98 Author: Ben Burnett <burnett@cs.wisc.edu> Date: Thu Dec 11 19:08:24 2008 -0600 A first attempt at eliminating the access denied error we are seeing in some of the tests when rotate_file() is called. My hypothesis was verified when he found this in the logs: 1/15 18:42:46 (pid:480) Cleaning job queue... 1/15 18:42:46 (pid:480) About to rotate ClassAd log D:\Condor/spool/job_queue.log 1/15 18:42:47 (pid:480) MoveFileEx(D:\Condor/spool/job_queue.log.tmp, D:\Condor/spool/job_queue.log) failed with error 5 1/15 18:42:47 (pid:480) failed to rotate job queue log! It needs to be verified that the new flags in V7_4-branch either fix, or don't fix, this problem. If it is still a problem, then a lock file should be used to perform the rotation. You create the lock file, rotate the log, delete the lockfile, then delete the old job queue log. If the schedd wakes up (say from reboot) and sees that the lock file is still there, then it needs to start over the rotation procedure.
remarks: 2010-Jun-03 10:55:16 by cweiss: Attached commit (as described in ticket #1215) prevents corruption of the job_queue.log in case rotation fails. We still can run into trouble if a file descriptor is open on either file (with different error codes), e.g. caused by a virus scanner currently scanning. Therefore, I will still leave this ticket open to be addressed at some point. 2011-Aug-16 14:44:59 by cweiss: As I am cleaning up tickets, I am going to close this one, because there is not much we can do at this time if virus scanners et al have a handle on log files (except for waiting and retrying).

title: Ticket #4393: Make listen() backlog configurable
description: When calling listen() for a daemon's command socket, we currently use a backlog of 500. We should make this configurable, as heavy users may want a larger value. We'll have a new config param named SOCKET_LISTEN_BACKLOG, whose value will default to 500. There are two locations where we want to do this. The first is in ReliSock::listen(). The second is for SharedPortEndpoint::CreateListener(), where a daemon creates a unix domain socket for being given connections from the shared port daemon. Currently, if listen() fails, we retry several times with smaller backlog values. On all of our current platforms, if the given backlog is too large for the OS's liking, it just caps the value and listen() still succeeds.
remarks: 2014-Jun-02 16:15:29 by tannenba: CODE REVIEW Looks good, please push w/ a version history entry. Little worried about calling param() from inside relisock as relisock is used in the syscall library, but I think we are likely ok in this instance. 2014-Jun-05 16:09:13 by bbockelm: For historical record - One case where one might increase the backlog is very busy schedd (many thousands of running jobs) using shared port. The shared port will use the backlog as of 8.1.5; prior versions would fork child shared_port instances and use those as a queue. So, effectively, from 8.1.4 to 8.1.5, the default queue size went from 1000 to 128 (Linux default max backlog) and the max configurable went from basically unlimited to 500. So, this will allow large installs to restore the prior behavior. The investigation for this bug uncovered many places where shared_port is used unnecessarily by the shadow and startd; these will be fixed in 8.2.x and 8.3.x, respectively.

title: Ticket #2617: Document USE_VISIBLE_DESKTOP for win7 etc.
description: re: condor_users Part of the new Vista/Win7 security features is the prohibit services from sharing a desktop with users. It is no longer possible on Vista/Win7 to see the job's window on the same desktop as programs that were started interactively. Services now have their own desktop. So to see the window from the Condor job, you have to configure Vista/Win7 to detect interactive services, and then it will give you a way to switch desktops. The instructions on how to enable interactive services are here http://ben.versionzero.org/wiki/Condor_Enable_Visible_Desktop_on_Vista Once you have done that, when a Condor job starts, Windows will pop up a message box asking if you want to switch to the services desktop, where the Condor job's window is.

title: Ticket #1938: Run blahp over ssh on remote pbs/lsf machine
description: Currently, for Condor to submit jobs to a PBS or LSF cluster, a schedd must be running on the frontend node of the cluster. We would like to remove that requirement and allow job submission to a PBS/LSF cluster with no prior software installation on the frontend node and only SSH access. Ideally, a user's local schedd would be able to submit jobs to multiple remote clusters via SSH. As a first step, we will demonstrate the ability to submit jobs when the blahp is preinstalled on the frontend node and all job files remain on the frontend node. The gridmanager will start and communicate with the blahp remotely via ssh. Summary We have been working on a job universe type in Condor-G that allows a user to submit a job destined to run on a remote PBS or LSF cluster in which the head node of the remote cluster does not have any grid gateway software installed (such as Condor-C, Globus, Cream, etc). Instead, all that is required is for the user to have ssh access into the head node. On the Condor-G submit side, the user needs to enumerate all the cluster front ends in which he/she has ssh access, where the blahp is installed on each, and an ssh key file and passphrase to authenticate with each. On each cluster frontend, the blahp must be installed. At this point, we don't do any file transfer, so all job executables and data files must be installed on each cluster frontend as well. Job output files will be left on the cluster frontend. The user can then submit their jobs to Condor-G as a standard LSF/PBS grid universe job. New parameters in the submit file specify which cluster frontend to use and where the job's files are located on the remote machine. Aside from file transfer, all Condor-G functionality should work as normal. We plan to add file tranasfer in the future if demand warrants. Milestones Setup a local PBS cluster for testing. [DONE] Submit a job by running the blahp remotely via ssh with no file transfer and hacky handling of ssh credentials. [DONE] Allow disabling of all file existence and permission checks in condor_submit. Determine best handling of ssh credentials. [DONE] Test submitting many jobs. [DONE] Test failure recovery. [DONE] Setup test installation useable by Josh. [DONE] Plan how to handle file transfers. (#2386) Figure out how to determine whether jobs are progressing through batch queue (Marco) Ideas for future work

title: Ticket #3905: stduniv jobs with want_remote_io=false still do remote i/o sometimes
description: Short story: even if WantRemoteIO=false, Condor falls back to remote i/o when a local-to-the-job file operation fails, instead of propagating the failure. Long story: We have condor configured correctly to inhibit remote i/o for standard-universe jobs (including matching UID_DOMAIN and FILESYSTEM_DOMAIN on the submit and execute side, USE_NFS=true, want_remote_io=false in the submit file, etc.). The precipitating external-to-Condor problem was that on a large subset of our pool a certain NFS server was denying mount permission to a directory needed by the jobs. So on most of our nodes, the jobs successfully opened the files it needed locally. However, on the bad subset of nodes, the open()s failed -- and apparently in that case, Condor helpfully (?) tries remote i/o as a fallback instead of failing. At least in our case, this was unexpected and undesired given our want_remote_io=false directive, and led to thousands of jobs /appearing/ to run, but indefinitely consuming zero CPU while simultaneously blocked on i/o through the submit machine. I suspect this will understandably get chalked up as "won't fix because DMTCP is coming to save the day", but I'm becoming more and more worried that the DMTCP hero has not yet arrived...

title: Ticket #2247: procd dies after hardkilling starter
description: I suspect that when the startd tells the procd to hard-kill the starter, there is a chance that the procd will hit an exception caused by a broken connection attempt from the starter. This then causes both the procd and then the startd to exit, which means all running jobs are stopped. This may explain some of the cases of "ProcD has failed" errors which have been reported by various sites for quite some time. I observed this error in CHTC with a pre-release of 7.7.0. I suspect the problem dates back much earlier than 7.7.0, so I am setting the broken version to be 7.6.0 in order to suggest fixing this in the stable series. StartLog: 06/16/11 10:31:13 slot4: starter (pid 22119) is not responding to the request to hardkill its job. The startd will now directly hard kill the starter and all i ts decendents. 06/16/11 10:31:13 slot4: In Starter::kill_kids() with pid 22119, sig 9 (SIGKILL) 06/16/11 10:31:13 slot4: In Starter::kill_kids() with pid 22119, sig 9 (SIGKILL) 06/16/11 10:31:14 error reading from named pipe: watchdog pipe has closed 06/16/11 10:31:14 ProcFamilyClient: failed to read response from ProcD 06/16/11 10:31:14 kill_family: ProcD communication error 06/16/11 10:31:14 ERROR "ProcD has failed" at line 587 in file /home/condor/exec ute/dir_31058/userdir/src/condor_utils/proc_family_proxy.cpp ProcLog: 06/16/11 10:31:14 : sending signal 9 to family with root 22161 06/16/11 10:31:14 : error opening /var/lock/condor/procd_pipe.STARTD.22119.0: No such device or address (6) 06/16/11 10:31:14 : ERROR: ProcFamilyServer: failed trying to accept client
remarks: 2011-Jun-16 12:46:07 by tstclair: I've actually been tracing this exact issue, b/c of signal escalation issues. 2011-Jun-16 14:05:42 by danb: I confirmed the suspected sequence of events that leads to this problem. I attached to the procd and set a breakpoint on the line where the server opens the pipe for writing to the client. (I had to patch the procd to not die when gdb attaches, because the procd did not like having select() get interrupted.) Here is the line in LocalServer::accept_connection() where I set the breakpoint: if (!m_writer->initialize(client_addr)) { When it got there, I then hard-killed the client (which was the starter). The procd then failed to open the pipe and died. The solution is to make the server resilient to communication errors that could be caused by a client that is interrupted. 2011-Jun-16 14:38:18 by tstclair: It also appears that the startd is following non-happy path to killing the starter. When searching through the procd it looked like it had it's own killing path. Is there any reason to choose one method over the other? Why does the startd fire indiscriminately without any notification to the procd? 2011-Jun-16 15:00:25 by danb: The problem of the procd dying due to a dead client has been fixed, so I am closing this ticket. I'll leave the cleanup of the startd killing logic for another ticket. (I agree that it is suspiciously confusing.)

title: Ticket #848: Merge execute directory cleanup code
description: The code to clean up an execute directories is duplicated between condor_starter.V6.1/baseStarter.cpp:2665 CStarter::removeTempExecuteDir and condor_startd.V6/util.cpp:284 cleanup_execute_dir. This is due to pre-existing entries in the session cache, based on the following log: 07/13/11 14:32:40 (pid:19461) SECMAN: failed to create session <10.1.3.72:58072>#1310575699#5. 07/13/11 14:32:40 (pid:19461) SEC_ENABLE_MATCH_PASSWORD_AUTHENTICATION: failed to create security session for <10.1.3.72:58072>#1310575699#5# ..., so will try to obtain a new security session Why would the session already exist in the cache? Hash key collision? Reuse of the same claim id? (When a match is deleted the old session is kept around for 10 minutes, so there is a 10 minute window in which reuse of the same claim id would collide.) More information needs to be added to the log when a collision occurs in order to diagnose the problem. It may be a good idea to have a mode in which the match password session is not optional. This would prevent the fallback to potentially performance-killing authentication protocols. In the mean time, I have recommended a much smaller timeout during authentication with a setting such as this: SEC_CLIENT_AUTHENTICATION_TIMEOUT = 5

title: Ticket #7100: Per-submitter Flocking
description: It currently is quite complex for a user to "bring their own resources" to an existing HTCondor setup. It requires careful coordination with the schedd's sysadmin and a very deep level of trust: the sysadmin basically must trust that user with any job (from any user) within the schedd. We should allow the user to control which collectors they would like their jobs to flock to; in the case where the collector is not on the list of admin-approved flocks, the user should have to maintain their own authentication mechanism (only starting with TOKENS is acceptable). This way, Anyone With A Credit Card can launch some startds and a collector on Amazon, setup TOKEN auth, and condor_qedit existing jobs to be able to flock to their new condor-in-the-cloud. title: Ticket #4686: DAGMan node status file incorrect on remove
description: Our users are complaining that they kill DAG tasks but then the jobs show up as running or idle in the monitoring. Poking around, it seems to be because the node status file isn't updated when the DAG is killed. For example, see this task: http://submit-5.t2.ucsd.edu/CSstoragePath/22/cmsprod/141027_165621_crab3test-1:sciaba_HC_96_T2_UK_London_IC_20141027173502/node_state.txt From this, we see: [ Type = "DagStatus"; DagFiles = { "/home/glidecondor/condor_local/spool/8496/0/cluster3468496.proc0.subproc0/RunJobs.dag" }; Timestamp = 1414430189; /* "Mon Oct 27 10:16:29 2014" */ DagStatus = 6; /* "STATUS_ERROR (removed)" */ NodesTotal = 31; NodesDone = 0; NodesPre = 0; NodesQueued = 31; NodesPost = 0; NodesReady = 0; NodesUnready = 0; NodesFailed = 0; JobProcsHeld = 0; JobProcsIdle = 31; ] So, the DAG was successfully killed. However, [ Type = "NodeStatus"; Node = "Job1"; NodeStatus = 3; /* "STATUS_SUBMITTED" */ StatusDetails = "idle"; RetryCount = 0; JobProcsQueued = 1; JobProcsHeld = 0; ] For this particular task, I copied the dagman output into the file RunJobs.dag.dagman.out into the same web directory. remarks: 2014-Oct-30 09:57:22 by wenger: What's causing this is that, when you condor_rm DAGMan, DAGMan doesn't wait around for all of the node jobs to exit before it exits itself. (And I can't remember without looking at the code whether the schedd condor_rm's all of the node jobs right away, or waits for the DAGMan job to go away first.) (Hmm -- the schedd should probably wait for DAGMan to go away, to make sure that there isn't a race condition where DAGMan could submit a new node job after the node jobs are condor_rm'ed.) I can see at least a couple of ways to fix this: When DAGMan gets condor_rm'ed, just internally mark all queued nodes as removed, and update the status file accordingly, even though the node jobs haven't actually been removed yet. Actually wait for the node jobs to go away, and don't exit until we've seen all of the terminated/aborted events (see #3995). I'm not thrilled with either of these, but at least for a short-term fix I'd go with number 1. Number 2 has a lot of complications -- how do we modify the schedd to remove the jobs before DAGMan goes away, but still avoid the race condition mentioned above? Do we need a timeout on how long we wait for jobs to exit the queue? What if you want to immediately remove DAGMan?, etc. 2014-Oct-30 10:09:39 by bbockelm: Hi Kent, For the urgent part of this issue, I'm fine with solution (1). For the long-term, I like (2) better and will follow up in #3995. If we take the first approach, we need to do a bunch of tweaking for final nodes. If we take the second approach, things may get goofed up by seeing aborted events for the nodes we've already marked as removed. 2014-Oct-30 12:05:29 by wenger: My initial idea was that if you condor_rm a DAG with a final node, the status file would be "correct" (show non-final nodes as removed) while waiting for the final node to run. title: Ticket #1484: Lock file deletion foils locking of daemon logs
description: The config parameter <subsys>_LOCK can be used to cause the daemons to use a lock file to ensure exclusive access to the daemon log. It's more commonly used with the shadow and gridmanager, which can have many daemons writting to the same daemon logfile. The daemons keep the lock file open constantly, locking and unlocking it as required. If the lock file doesn't exist when the daemon starts up, it creates the file. This causes problems if the lock file is deleted. Older daemons continue to use the unlinked lock file, while any new daemons will use a newly-created lock file. This can lead to concurrent writes which can be interleaved. Also, when a daemon rotates the file, it can EXCEPT if other daemons continue to write to the log mid-rotation. In particular, the rotating daemon checks whether the old filename still exists after a rename() and blows up if it does. The BNL ATLAS group is seeing this happen on their Condor-G systems. A possible solution is for the daemons to close and reopen the lock file each time it's used, or at least stat the filename and ensure the inode hasn't changed.
remarks: 2010-Jul-02 14:31:54 by jfrey: Good way to mostly reproduce: start a vanilla job running, then delete the ShadowLock file, then submit another vanilla job. When the second job starts running, look at the files both shadows have open (lsof -p or ls /proc/<pid>/fd). Both will have the ShadowLock file open, but for the older shadow, it will show the file as '(deleted)'. This won't reproduce the daemon EXCEPTing, but will demonstrate the underlying problem. Once we have a fix, it'll be easy to test on BNL's systems. They have multiple gridmanager daemons that are constantly writing to the daemon log. 2010-Jul-08 10:35:08 by jfrey: I've found another cause for a daemon dying during log rotation (due to the old file still existing after a rename). When the logging code is initialized (in dprintf_config()), the log file is opened and immediately closed. If the log file doesn't exist, it's created. This is done without regard to the lock file. This can be fixed by having dprintf_config() initialize the lock filename, then call the debug_lock() instead of directly opening the log file. 2010-Jul-08 15:39:33 by jfrey: Pushed patch dprintfFileLock2.patch to V7_4-branch for 7.4.4.

title: Ticket #7229: Collector under shared port can forward ads to itself
description: When the collector is sitting behind a shared port server and CONDOR_VIEW_HOST is set to refer to itself, the collector can fail to notice the self-reference and end up forwarding ads to itself. This can easily happen when using an array of child collectors that do authentication with daemons in the pool and forward ads to one parent collector (a collector tree), like CMS does. CONDOR_VIEW_HOST is set for all daemons, but the parent collector is supposed to refuse to forward ads to itself. The problem occurs when the parent collector is using the shared port service and CONDOR_VIEW_HOST is set to a simple hostname or IP address and optional port. The collector uses Sinful::addressPointsToMe() to detect if the CONDOR_VIEW_HOST value refers to itself. In this case, the collector's internal sinful address includes a shared port id of collector, while the sinful address constructed from the CONDOR_VIEW_HOST setting has no shared port id. In this case, Sinful::addressPointsToMe() returns false, indicating the address refer to different daemons. But the shared port daemon will forward connection requests lacking a shared port id to the collector.
remarks: 2019-Oct-15 14:29:25 by tlmiller: Code Review The patch is well-formed, but I'm not sure it's a good idea. There's a lengthy comment at line 1817 of condor_collector.V6/collector.cpp about the exact same problem, except for the COLLECTOR_HOST list, the gist of which is that context matters: when the collector asks, while trying to contact another collector, if the sinful it's about to contact is itself, we can be sure that in either sinful, the intended target is a collector. The same is not true for all all other daemons. While I can't think of a case that would arise naturally where this would misidentify a daemon, it doesn't seem impossible. My preferred solution would thus be to turn the special-case code that follows the comment into a function and call it from both places (line 1817 and 1897) that need the fix. On the other hand, I could be talked out of this, and we won't get a chance to test any changes I make in production. Given that this hasn't caused any problems in testing so far, I will therefore mark this ticket as resolved, and open another one which tells Jaime and I to discuss this patch when he gets back.

title: Ticket #2928: Hide jobs in X within job lease duration from condor_q
description: Jobs may linger in X (Removed) for a while. So long as the job lease hasn't expired, this is probably fine, it most likely indicates some sort of communication problem between the shadow and the starter. Eventually either communications will be restored or the lease will expire, the shadow will be killed, and the job in X will politely move into the history. However, users see jobs in X and worry. They asked the job to go away, and it just won't go away! So they are prone to resorting to -forcex. This is not a good idea. A forcex'd job may unnecessarily continue running. We may lose information about real problems. This is particularly a problem on systems where the execute "machines" are virtual machines that are frequently killed with little notice, and so see jobs in X with some frequency, and thus become habitual uses of -forcex. Proposed: condor_q should, by default, hide jobs where (unverified!) (JobStatus==3)&&(CurrentTime < (LastJobLeaseRenewal+JobLeaseDuration)) Now for properly functioning jobs a user will never see a job in X. After the job lease passes, if a job is still in X Something Has Gone Wrong, and we want it visible. Hopefully these will be far less common and users will be prone to asking their administrator or us for help. For administrators there would be a "-all" or "-showx" to include the excluded jobs.

title: Ticket #3285: Add new tool for cluster summaries
description: I've found condor_status less useful over time (as our cluster grows and when we switched to p-slots) - I think we're at a point where a new tool would be beneficial. When I use "condor_status", I use it as a mechanism to get an overview of my pool. I often have the following questions about the basic dimensions of the poool: How large is my pool? How full is my pool? How busy is the pool? (I.e., if a slot is claimed, is it also fully utilized by the job?) And questions about nodes in abnormal state: Are there idle nodes (in the face of large queues)? Are there poorly utilized nodes? I claim that for a 100-node cluster using p-slots, condor_status does not provide meaningful answers for any of the above questions. Here are some deficiencies I've noted: Entirely too verbose for large pools. Our site is 3k cores and growing. No human can get process that many lines of output. Does not take into account the significant differences between p-slots and "traditional" slots. State, LoadAv, Mem, and Activity time have different meanings for p-slots. Does not advertise number of cores in the output. Uses outdated terminology - "Machines" in the summary means "Slots". Slots don't have a significant meaning when the slots are transient. The "Name" column is truncated for every node I own. I have a 300-character wide terminal, yet the Name is limited to about 30 characters! The Arch and OS column is the same for every node I own; quite the waste of space. I can't easily determine if the occupancy rate is reasonable for the current load. A 50% occupied pool is "no problem" if there are no jobs in queue. There might be a big problem if there are 10k jobs in queue. 1 No units on memory numbers! I propose we do not touch condor_status - changing output has too high a chance of breaking user scripts. Instead, I propose we have a new tool - "condor_pool_summary" - which addresses the needs of sysadmins (condor_status is plenty powerful for machine-readable needs). No XML format, no stable output guarantees, maybe limited query semantics, not entirely grep-friendly. I'd start with Matt's work here: http://spinningmatt.wordpress.com/2012/10/01/partitionable-slot-utilization/ and extend it in light of the comments above. title: Ticket #1742: Create a sandbox manager to decouple transfers from job completion
description: Currently, after a job completes the file transfer back to the submit node is still considered part of the job itself. This means that a slot remains blocked although it is not actually running anything computationally expensive anymore. A joint effort with Parag Mhashilkar from Fermi will introduce a sandbox manager to decouple the file transfer from the actual job execution: Once the job completes, it will change into a different state (as already introduced by Jaime in ticket #1641). After that the sandbox can be requested right away from the startd (invoking the sandbox manager) or at a later point in time. In the meantime, a new job can take over the slot and be run. Timeline: Milestone 1 Startd maintains the slot manager Old Condor behavior with new implementation, changes are not user-visible: After job execution, execution Starter terminates and transfer Starter starts up to transfer data back (same starter invoked w/ command line argument to skip job execution and go straight to transfer) terminology: data slot holds state for creation time, expiration time, physical location, sandbox id schedd creates slot id (random-generated 64 byte string) created by schedd. Startd could potentially create the id as well, but would require two-phase commit protocol. Additionally if the schedd creates it, the ids could be tied to a workflow). Also, data slots need to maintain state about themselves: stagein, bound to cpu slot , stageout, expired, unused, (no disk space) Milestone 2 Advertise if a CPU slot is bound to a data slot, require binding in start expression. Advertisement should be minimal for now ('is data slot available?). Milestone 3: schedd should mark claim as deactivated when job assoc w/ that claim goes into job transfer state. Milestone 4: restart semantics : lease renewal, schedd re-attach to stards, startd crash Milestone 5: advertise in classads (of startd? Seperate?) data slot info Milestone 6: data slot partitioning and characteristics. Future work seperate capability string and claiming protocol for data slot. Right now it is piggy backed on cpu slot capability - this is ok until you want to claim a data slot w/o a cpu slot for data stage in. data ads seperate from startd ads, gang matching lite

title: Ticket #7696: GPU discovery should report stable GPU ids
description: We have discovered that when a GPU goes bad on a machine with multiple GPUs, Docker will refuse to use any of the GPUs until that GPU is taken offline (via nvidia-smi drain). Once a GPU is taken offline, however, it disappears from GPU enumeration, and the GPUs after it move down 1 index. Since GPU ids are currently GPU indices, this essentially shuffles the GPUs behind the Startd's back causing who knows what problems. We need to change condor_gpu_discovery so that it reports stable identifiers for the GPUs. This can be done by using the GPU uuid instead of the GPU index. Also NVIDIA allows the uuid prefix to be used, so long as it is not ambiguous. So we will use either the first 8 characters of the uuid, or the whole uuid. DetectedGPUs then becomes DetectedGPUs="GPU-5498e439, GPU-bc8c14c7, GPU-112d9b26, GPU-d298c6e0" instead of DetectedGPUs="CUDA0, CUDA1, CUDA2, CUDA3" And GPU specific attributes become GPU_5498e439DevicePciBusId="0000:3E:00.0" GPU_5498e439DeviceUuid="5498e439-bec3-fa72-ed65-a45d5f53e1b5" GPU_bc8c14c7DevicePciBusId="0000:60:00.0" GPU_bc8c14c7DeviceUuid="bc8c14c7-ad51-371f-de8e-36ae559b39ed" instead of CUDA0DevicePciBusId="0000:3E:00.0" CUDA0DeviceUuid="5498e439-bec3-fa72-ed65-a45d5f53e1b5" CUDA1DevicePciBusId="0000:60:00.0" CUDA1DeviceUuid="bc8c14c7-ad51-371f-de8e-36ae559b39ed"

title: Ticket #4813: Infinite recursion with ClassAd eval() function
description: In the ClassAd library, it's possible to set up an infinite recursion during evaluation when using the eval() function in an expression. With the following ClassAd, evaluating attribute A or B2 will overflow the stack. [ A = eval("A"); B = "eval(B)"; B2 = eval(B); ] The EvalState object prevents infinite recursion when there's a loop in attribute references, by halting the evaluation when it has gone more than 1000 levels deep. We should do the same for eval() calls.

title: Ticket #1884: support changing ownership of claims in the schedd
description: Miron wants the schedd to reallocate claims between users. Initially, the following features are desired: when a job finishes, support reassignment of the claim to a different user. Initially, do this by consulting a static configuration that specifies the desired share for each user. Give the claim to the user who has the greatest deficit. Keep track of current usage, but do not save to disk (yet). (Should accounting groups be supported here? Not for the first version.) status of this: patch is attached to this ticket but not included in a released version add usage records for the users of the schedd. Does it make sense to synchronize these records with the pool accountant? If there are multiple pools, that does not seem easy to do. add support for preemptive reassignment of a claim to a different user. How will we know when preemption should be used? Perhaps use a policy expression similar to PREEMPTION_REQUIREMENTS. (Should we support preemption of jobs belonging to the same user?) All of the steps after the first one are somewhat speculative still. Focus on just getting the first step done.
remarks: 2011-Jan-28 18:25:40 by bbockelm: I don't follow the logic here - to me, a claim is a contract/lease between a user and a resource, not between the scheduler and a resource. What's the usage case here? 2011-Jan-28 19:34:10 by matt: From an accounting perspective it certainly is. Every negotiation cycle that the Schedd holds onto a claim is a little longer that the claim's owner (user) is charged for the resource. Would the claim be scoped within accounting groups, or the ability to re-claim a resource for accounting purposes be added? 2011-Jan-31 10:07:01 by danb: As I understand it, the goal is to keep the negotiator relatively simple and to start making more scheduling decisions in the schedd, which has access to the full job queue. There was no discussion of restricting the change of claim ownership to members of the same accounting group, but that is an interesting idea. The new user should be charged for using the claim, not the original user. One can imagine scenarios in which the allocation policy of the schedd and the policy of the negotiator tend to want to reverse each other's decisions. This may not be desirable. Understanding the net effect of combined schedd and negotiator allocation policies could be complicated and confusing to users. 2011-Mar-24 14:57:36 by danb: One use-case for this feature is a schedd that lies to the matchmaker about the identity of its users. For example, the schedd might tell the matchmaker that all jobs belong to GroupPhysics when they actually belong to PhysicistA, PhysicistB, and so on. Alternatively, the matchmaker might ignore the schedd's user identities and substitute something else, such as a group name assigned by the matchmaker administrator for all jobs coming from that schedd (e.g. GLOW_VO). The main benefit of this is that the administrator of the schedd could control individual user priorities without administrative access to the matchmaker. This would be advantageous in situations where the schedd and matchmaker are administered separately, such as when a schedd flocks from one campus or department to another. The ability to substitute different identities for matchmaking purposes is not implemented or even proposed thus far. This is just something I can imagine that could make use of the schedd doing resource allocation.
attachments: 0001-Allow-schedd-to-change-ownership-of-claims.-1884.patch 18392 bytes added by danb on 2011-Mar-24 19:26:30 UTC. This patch implements changing ownership of claims on job boundaries when recycling claims within the schedd. The decision of who should get the claim is made by consulting a configurable list of user shares. The user using the least fraction of their share relative to the other listed users is given first priority. If that user does not have a suitable job, the schedd continues down the ordered list of most deserving users until it finds one. Claims belonging to users who are not listed in SCHEDD_USER_SHARES are not eligible for change of ownership.

title: Ticket #7403: Knob DAGMan illegal character checking
description: In #5966 we prohibited the use of certain characters ('.', '+') in DAGMan node names because they created problems with the parser in splices. As it turned out, many people were using these characters in their workflows and this changed caused a lot of headache. Let's knob this behavior so that people can use illegal characters when they want, but prohibit them when necessary.
remarks: 2019-Dec-04 13:15:25 by coatsworth: All done. The new knob is called DAGMAN_ALLOW_ANY_NODE_NAME_CHARACTERS and is set to false by default. Additionally we removed the period character (.) from the list of illegal characters. 2019-Dec-04 14:51:06 by coatsworth: Also, I've figured out why we decided to disallow periods in the first place. It has to do with submitting multiple dags at once and mungeing node names. If we were to submit multiple dags as follows: condor_submit_dag mydag1.dag mydag2.dag Then the parser prepends the dag number before the node names. So in mydag1.dag, a job called FirstJob gets munged to 0.FirstJob, SecondJob gets munged to 0.SecondJob. In mydag2.dag, FirstJob gets munged to 1.FirstJob and SecondJob gets munged to 1.SecondJob. This is described in more detail at https://htcondor.readthedocs.io/en/latest/users-manual/dagman-applications.html#single-submission-of-multiple-independent-dags. So re-allowing the period opens up the possibility of name collisions. I think this is still safe. Not only are collisions very rare, but there are multiple workarounds: 1) don't submit multiple DAGs at once, 2) set the DAGMAN_MUNGE_NODE_NAMES macro to False, 3) if you must submit multiple DAGs at once, make sure they have unique node names. 2019-Dec-13 14:14:29 by johnkn: CODE_REVIEW change looks ok. although a param_call is kind of expensive to be doing for each node name check.

title: Ticket #6212: Milestone 1 for schedd late materialization
description: Milestone 1 of schedd late materialization will have opt-in via condor_submit -factory, and set max_materialize=<n> in your submit file. master off switch in the schedd SCHEDD_ALLOW_LATE_MATERIALIZE condor_submit -factory will create a digest of your submit file into a file in the current working directory. The file will be called condor_submit.$(cluster).digest. It will then make a cluster ad and transmit it to the schedd. then send the schedd the filename of the digest using a new RPC. if there is foreach data that is not already a file, it will also make a file called condor_submit.$(cluster).items out of the foreach item data. On commit of the submit transaction. The schedd will make an instance of submit_utils and attach it to the cluster ad, and initialize it from the submit digest by reading the given file. It will then add the cluster to a list of clusters needing attention and start a 0 tick timer if one is not already queued. It will then return success or failure to the condor_submit. When the timer fires, it will examine each cluster needing attention and materialize proc ads as needed. Each proc ad will be in its own transaction. When DestroyProc decrements the proc count for a cluster, it will check to see if the cluster has a job factory, and if it does, it will put the cluster into a list of clusters needing attention - and it will NOT remove the cluster even if the current proc count is 0. It will then start a 0 tick timer just like submit does. actOnJobs in the schedd will look at cluster ads as well as job ads and will handle RM, HOLD and RELEASE on the cluster ad that match the constraint expression. RM will pause the job factory in a permanent way. HOLD will pause the job factory, and RELEASE will resume a paused job factory. a RELEASE will also put the cluster into the list of clusters needing attention and start the timer. When the clusters needing attention timer fires, it will materialize new jobs for clusters that have less than the max_materialize limit, and remove clusters that have 0 procs and will never materialize any new jobs - either because they have been permanenently paused, or because all of the jobs have already been materialized.
