title: Ticket #5828: Initial Singularity support
description: CMS / OSG / WLCG is starting to look seriously at singularity (http://singularity.lbl.gov). It is indeed Yet Another Approach to containers, but has several features that make it heavily oriented toward batch systems. Instead of a separate daemon, it is a single setuid executable. Its images (can be a raw disk image or loopback device) are meant to be read-only with a few scratch directories. The focus is on providing alternate OS environments for batch system users - hence there's no treatment / isolation of networking and does not try to own the cgroups for the job. It is also not quite as heavy hammer as glexec - for example, if you use singularity to contain a payload job, you do not need to change UIDs. This resolves an immense number of problems that we see in glexec from surprising batch systems with processes inside a job that are not the same UID as the job itself. Here is a summary of the changes: condor_startd detects the presence of singularity and tests to see if it is functional, then the machine ad advertises HasSingularity=True if it is found, along with version info. (just like Docker, Java, etc) Setting SINGULARITY_JOB = true forces the job to be run inside singularity. Evaluated in the context of the job (TARGET) and machine (MY) ad. SINGULARITY_IMAGE_EXPR specifies the image. Evaluated in the context of the job (TARGET) and machine (MY) ad. SINGULARITY overrides the default path to the singularity binary. MOUNT_UNDER_SCRATCH is respected. Currently, specifying both USE_PID_NAMESPACES=True and SINGULARITY_JOB evaluating to True is not supported and will result in failure to start jobs. Need some improvement here? HTCondor automatically bind mounts the $_CONDOR_SCRATCH_DIR and IWD. (additionally, singularity options can be set in /etc/singularity/singularity.conf). On modern platforms (Ubuntu and Fedoras - almost anything past RHEL7), Singularity can run without the setuid bit. As part of the support detection, we ought to automatically switch to the non-setuid version if we detect it is working. In such a future, if HTCondor had reasonably good singularity support, we can start to discuss dropping the glexec code.

Updated some notes above. 2016-Nov-10 09:53:55 by wenger: Brian, could you attach an example config and submit file to this ticket? That would help a lot in writing the documentation. 2016-Nov-10 10:16:46 by tim: I think that this work is preliminary. Here are the plans from Brian Bockelman's email on October 29th: - Merge the existing branch into 8.5.8. Document just the raw variables. - hence, the "raw" integration is available in 8.6.0. - this allows integrators and glideinWMS to add support in 2017 instead of 2018. - Add first class condor_submit support in the 8.7.x series. - Expect that users really start to pick this up in 8.8.x. 2016-Nov-11 15:20:02 by bbockelm: Here's an example config file: # Only set if Singularity is not in $PATH. #SINGULARITY = /opt/singularity/bin/singularity # Forces _all_ jobs to run inside singularity. SINGULARITY_JOB = true # Forces all jobs to use the CernVM-based image. SINGULARITY_IMAGE_EXPR = "/cvmfs/cernvm-prod.cern.ch/cvm3" # Maps $_CONDOR_SCRATCH_DIR on the host to /srv inside the image. SINGULARITY_TARGET_DIR = /srv # Writable scratch directories inside the image. Auto-deleted after the job exits. MOUNT_UNDER_SCRATCH = /tmp, /var/tmp This provides the user with no opportunity to select a specific image. Here's an example configuration file to allow the user to specify an image path: SINGULARITY_JOB = !isUndefined(TARGET.SingularityImage) SINGULARITY_IMAGE_EXPR = TARGET.SingularityImage Then, users could add the following to their submit file: +SingularityImage = "/cvmfs/cernvm-prod.cern.ch/cvm3" (note the quoting) Finally, let's pick an image based on the OS - not the filename: SINGULARITY_JOB = (TARGET.DESIRED_OS isnt MY.OpSysAndVer) && ((TARGET.DESIRED_OS is "CentOS6") || (TARGET.DESIRED_OS is "CentOS7")) SINGULARITY_IMAGE_EXPR = (TARGET.DESIRED_OS is "CentOS6") ? title: Ticket #6707: Fix handling of missing local config files
description: When initializing Condor's config system, the caller can pass a flag that suppresses calls to exit() on errors. When this flag (CONFIG_OPT_NO_EXIT) is used, the initialization call returns false instead of calling exit(). This flag is doesn't affect the case where a required local config file is missing or unreadable. These errors do result in a call to exit() (except when using config_host() with a non-NULL host argument). This flag also doesn't affect parse errors, like a missing '=', which always cause an exit(). The use of CONFIG_OPT_NO_EXIT is dubious. If config_ex() returns false, then much of the initialization of the config system hasn't been done. The caller should abort or try to fix the problem and call config_ex() again. All current callers proceed as if config_ex() was successful.
creator: jfrey

title: Ticket #3505: Leaking mount points, on filesystems originally mounted w/shared prop.
description: In an effort to explore how we handle cleaning up mount points, I've stumbled upon an issue that exists as a result of mounting the root filesystem with shared propagation which is now done by default in F18 &> (yay systemd). Thus, when using knobs such as MOUNT_UNDER_SCRATCH, condor will leak mount points to the system namespace to the point there it can no longer mount, or run jobs. In reading through the docs LWN Article 1 and LWN Article 2 It appears what we are looking for is: Under "Use cases" 4.B) B) A process wants its mounts invisible to any other process, but still be able to see the other system mounts. Solution: To begin with, the administrator can mark the entire mount tree as shareable. ## TSTCLAIR: Already done now in F18 && > mount --make-rshared / A new process can clone off a new namespace. And mark some part of its namespace as slave mount --make-rslave /myprivatetree Hence forth any mounts within the /myprivatetree done by the process will not show up in any other namespace. However mounts done in the parent namespace under /myprivatetree still shows up in the process's namespace.

title: Ticket #1538: exponential backoff with job rescheduling
description: I have a context where I'd like X number of jobs submitted into a pool and they should only leave the queue with a certain exit code. No problem. However, something external to the jobs is adjusting something the jobs require to exit with an exit code of 0. In the current incarnation of Condor, the schedd will try and reschedule all the jobs as fast as it can. What I want is a means by which I can implement an exponential backoff concerning a particular job to when it'll be scheduled next to stop the pressure in the pool to schedule jobs which might not be schedulable. This is similar to deferring the job to run at a particular time, but I don't even want the job to be considered to scheduling until a particular amount of time in the future. I just want it to be ignored.

title: Ticket #6357: Transmit submit digest to schedd as text to be spooled
description: As part of late materialization milestone 2 - we should transmit the submit digest to the schedd as a text blob and have the schedd write it into the spool directory. This will save the schedd the work of reading it from disk on submit, and also reduce the likelihood of user error causing factories to fail to load on restart. We will follow the same pattern that the schedd uses for spooled executables for spooling the submit digest. The file will be named $(SPOOL)/$INT(ClusterId%10000)/condor_submit.$(ClusterId).digest This change also opens up the possibility that the schedd will write the digest into the job queue log rather than writing it to a separate file, but for this milestone, a file will be used.

title: Ticket #1168: RFE: /proc/<pid>/io data available to job ad policy and archive
description: Condor currently reports CPU usage information in Job ads during execution. The linux kernel provides other information, such as io statistics for processes. It would be useful to report the io statistics in the Job ad as well. http://www.kernel.org/doc/Documentation/filesystems/proc.txt 3.3 /proc/<pid>/io - Display the IO accounting fields ------------------------------------------------------- This file contains IO statistics for each running process Example ------- test:/tmp # dd if=/dev/zero of=/tmp/test.dat & [1] 3828 test:/tmp # cat /proc/3828/io rchar: 323934931 wchar: 323929600 syscr: 632687 syscw: 632675 read_bytes: 0 write_bytes: 323932160 cancelled_write_bytes: 0 Description ----------- rchar ----- I/O counter: chars read The number of bytes which this task has caused to be read from storage. This is simply the sum of bytes which this process passed to read() and pread(). It includes things like tty IO and it is unaffected by whether or not actual physical disk IO was required (the read might have been satisfied from pagecache) wchar ----- I/O counter: chars written The number of bytes which this task has caused, or shall cause to be written to disk. Similar caveats apply here as with rchar. syscr ----- I/O counter: read syscalls Attempt to count the number of read I/O operations, i.e. syscalls like read() and pread(). syscw ----- I/O counter: write syscalls Attempt to count the number of write I/O operations, i.e. syscalls like write() and pwrite(). read_bytes ---------- I/O counter: bytes read Attempt to count the number of bytes which this process really did cause to be fetched from the storage layer. Done at the submit_bio() level, so it is accurate for block-backed filesystems. <please add status regarding NFS and CIFS at a later time> write_bytes ----------- I/O counter: bytes written Attempt to count the number of bytes which this process caused to be sent to the storage layer. This is done at page-dirtying time. cancelled_write_bytes --------------------- The big inaccuracy here is truncate. If a process writes 1MB to a file and then deletes the file, it will in fact perform no writeout. But it will have been accounted as having caused 1MB of write. In other words: The number of bytes which this process caused to not happen, by truncating pagecache. A task can cause "negative" IO too. If this task truncates some dirty pagecache, some IO which another task has been accounted for (in it's write_bytes) will not be happening. We _could_ just subtract that from the truncating task's write_bytes, but there is information loss in doing that. Note ---- At its current implementation state, this is a bit racy on 32-bit machines: if process A reads process B's /proc/pid/io while process B is updating one of those 64-bit counters, process A could see an intermediate result. More information about this can be found within the taskstats documentation in Documentation/accounting.

title: Ticket #2894: Condor writes logfiles as root user
description: It appears that the logrotation code and/or the stack-trace dumping code do not play well together. About once-or-twice a week, when a daemon dies, it will cause the log file - or the rotated log file - to be owned by root instead of Condor. When this happens, condor_master will continuously try to restart the daemon, which then fails immediately. I suspect there's some badness in the stack-trace code. Anyhow, this has taken down our T2's schedd twice in two weeks: I'd be really interested in having an expert take a crack at it. This last time this happened had an interesting twist - SchedLog.old and job_queue.log both got owned by root.
remarks: 2012-Aug-29 19:42:54 by bbockelm: I think this was caused by #183 and commit c8265d1b33ca9059fe94a087f10b08447df56538, by danb. If the daemon wants to do a stack dump and is not PRIV_CONDOR, it will switch to the real UID (root, in most cases), and open the logfile with O_CREAT. I propose one of two things: In this case, drop the O_CREAT flag. We lose the stack trace. Tough cookies. The first time we compute the Condor UID, cache it in a global. If this is set, use it. If this is not set, go to case 1. Reassigning to Dan.

title: Ticket #6584: Glide-ins misreport GPU device names
description: CUDA devices have indexes, not names. If CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES is set in the startd's environment, condor_gpu_discovery will (not wrongly) report that it found devices named with the first k indices, rather than with the indices given in CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES. We worked around this problem in condor_gpu_discovery by unsetting CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES (and GPU_DEVICE_ORDINAL) before calling doing GPU detection. This gives us the correct device indices. We then filter out all the devices not listed in the original CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES (or GPU_DEVICE_ORDINAL). In condor_gpu_utilization, we just unset CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES, and report using the correct indices; the startd already matches devices to slots, so nothing else is necessary.
remarks: original description: CUDA devices have indexes, not names. If CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES is set in the startd's environment, condor_gpu_discovery will (not wrongly) report that it found devices named with the first k indices, rather than with the indices given in CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES. This causes grief for glide-in pools, because (for example) every GPU on a machine providing one-GPU slots will be reported as using the "CUDA0" device. David Schultz has provided a "proof a concept" patch to condor_gpu_discovery so that it will report that it found the CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES. Investigation will be required to extend this patch to OpenCL (does OpenCL have the concept of visible devices?), as well as to condor_gpu_utilization. This patch is a quick work-around; it's not clear what will happen in the upcoming CUDA versions that support multiple processes for each GPU. We also think that filtering/aliasing should be an explicit option, in both configuration and on the tools' command lines; this should be easy to arrange with if $(ENV(..)) in the metaknob. It will additionally probably work better for future CUDA versions and/or for OpenCL if the detection code unsets the appropriate environment variables, gets all the data, and then only outputs what's listed in the explicit filter request. A longer-term option would be a startd config knob to skip custom machine resource detection entirely and instead report everything based on polling the parent HTCondor's .update.ad. 2018-Mar-22 15:41:56 by tlmiller: Found a decided infelicity in the config system that I've discussed with TJ. I validated (using a hack-around) the approach on a multi-GPU system for detection purposes, but since I'll need to test the non-hack-around code (and as a metaknob) with 8.7 anyway, I haven't tested our approach to the utilization code yet. (Also still need to verify that the doc update builds!) 2018-Mar-22 16:10:45 by tlmiller: Actually, we could proceed by adding another metaknob, use policy : preserve_cude_device_names, which would append '-filter -device-list $ENV(CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES)' to GPU_DISCOVERY_EXTRA and '-filter' to the new GPU_MONITOR_EXTRA variable (which use feature : GPUsMonitor would updated to include). Actually, we might be better off appending '-filter -device-list $(CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES)' and requiring the glidein to pull CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES from the environment if they so desire, rather than risk the weirdness that comes with the config potentially being different depending on who's asking. 2018-Mar-26 11:44:15 by tlmiller: So ToddT reminded me that we have to make sure that CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES is set properly for (each of) the slots, so there's no reason we'd ever want to have the detection or utilization binaries report the nonglobal device indices. Following that, the detection code should record CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES and then unset it, do its normal detection work, and then filter out everything not in CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES (including for the total device count). The utilization code needs only unset CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES because of the slot-matching code in the startd. All of the above also applies to GPU_DEVICE_ORDINAL, as well. 2018-Mar-28 14:44:58 by tlmiller: ... and that should take care of it.

title: Ticket #2197: General statistics architecture for Condor
description: We would like to be able to gather statistics for the purpose of improving the Condor software and providing guidance to users. The data is to give us insight in to what the daemon is doing, and in particular intended to help us determine the reasons for badput. General Guidelines: We will do the bare minimum of processing of data. The onus of processing will be on the user. Thus the data we collect will observe the following constraints. Instantaneous values or totals from the time the daemon was started will be published. Statistical data is not persistent and will be lost when the daemon process exits. The set of statistical values is defined at compile time, based on actual user requests or plausable use cases. Dynamic or user-defined statistics are not envisaged. Calls to increment and update raw statistical values will need to be added in various places in the code that we are trying to measure, but an effort should be made to minimize the amount of code needed outside of the statistics module. It will be straightforward to change or add new statistical values, and to change which ClassAds statistics are published into. Implementation: A module will be created to aid in the storage, updating and publishing of statistics. Storage of temporary values and much of the code for windowing and calculating statistical data will be collected into a class or set of classes. The class will have a simple interface for callers to increment various counters, and to publish the collected values. There will be three main types of statistical values Simple values or time durations that will increase throughout the lifetime of the daemon Windowed values for the most recent RecentStatWindowTime seconds Histograms returned as a list of values In most cases statistical values will be available as both Simple values and Recent window values. The statistics will be collected internally in the daemons, and published in the daemons' ClassAds. The collection will occur in a statically allocated table, with the exception of the binning for the lists (e.g., in JobLifetimes). The binning is envisaged to be a config knob. The initial implementation will define what statistics exist and where they will be published at compile time. But it is expected that we may want to make changes at run-time in the future, so care will be taken to not preclude that. Because the changes #2006 have already been shipped by Red Hat, we will make it easy to publish some of the values under the names indicated in #2006 as well as under the names given above. This behavior will be controlled by a new param called PUBLISH_STATISTICS_USING_OLD_NAMES_ALSO. Proposed values: ## Schedd Ad statistics. StatLifetime RelTime total the schedd has been collecting statistics. (schedd lifetime) JobsStatLastUpdateTime AbsTime corresponding to the most recent update of the Schedd Ad statistics. JobsSubmitted int number of jobs submitted over lifetime of schedd JobsStarted int number of jobs started over schedd lifetime JobsCompleted int number of jobs successfully completed over schedd lifetime JobsExited int number of jobs exited (successful or otherwise) over schedd lifetime JobShadowExceptions int number of shadow exceptions over schedd lifetime # these supercede (2006 ExitCodeXXX) and JobsExitedWithCodeXXX above # JobsExitedNormally int number of jobs that exited with JOB_EXITED or JOB_EXITED_AND_CLAIM_CLOSING JobsCheckpointed int number of jobs that exited with JOB_CKPTED JobsKilled int number of jobs that exited with JOB_KILLED (or JOB_NO_CKPT_FILE?) JobsCoredumped int number of jobs that exited with JOB_COREDUMPED JobsExitException int number of jobs that exited with JOB_EXCEPTION, DPRINTF_ERROR, or any unknown code JobsShadowNoMemory int number of jobs that exited with JOB_NO_MEM JobsExecFailed int number of jobs that exited with JOB_EXEC_FAILED (or JOB_NO_MEM?) JobsShouldRequeue int number of jobs that exited with JOB_SHOULD_REQUEUE JobsNotStarted int number of jobs that exited with JOB_NOT_STARTED JobsShouldHold int number of jobs that exited with JOB_SHOULD_HOLD JobsShouldRemove int number of jobs that exited with JOB_SHOULD_REMOVE JobsMissedDeferralTime int number of jobs that exited with JOB_MISSED_DEFERRAL_TIME JobsExitedAndClaimClosing int number of jobs that exited with JOB_EXITED_AND_CLAIM_CLOSING ShadowsRunning int current number of running shadows ShadowsRunningPeak int largest number of simultaneously running shadows ShadowsStarted int total number of shadow processes that have been started over daemon lifetime ShadowsRecycled int number of times shadows have been recycled over daemon lifetime ShadowExceptions int number of shadow exceptions during StatLifetime (2006 ShadowExceptionsCum) JobsAccumTimeToStart RelTime sum of job wait times to first start, over schedd lifetime JobsAccumRunningTime RelTime sum of job running times for goodput over schedd lifetime JobsAccumBadputTime RelTime sum of job running times for badput over schedd lifetime ## Schedd Ad window'ed statistics RecentStatWindowTime RelTime size of the time window for 'Recent' stats. grows until it reaches WINDOWED_STAT_WIDTH and then holds there. RecentJobsSubmitted int number of jobs submitted over most recent sampling window RecentJobsStarted int Number of jobs started in stat window WINDOWED_STAT_WIDTH RecentJobsCompleted int number of jobs completed (successfully) over sampling window RecentJobsExited int number of jobs that exited (successful or otherwise) over window RecentJobsExitedWithCodeXXX int number of jobs exited with code XXX (100, 115, etc) over window RecentJobShadowExceptions int number of shadow exceptions over window RecentJobRunningTime int running (wall-clock) time of jobs in schedd, over stat window # these are currently in the code but aren't needed, can be calculated from the above. # RecentJobStartedPerSec int rate (jobs/sec) of jobs starting in stat window RecentJobsSubmittedPerSec int rate of job submission (jobs/sec) over sampling window RecentJobsCompletedPerSec int rate of successful job completions over window ## ## Histograms of job runtimes and sizes for goodput and badput ## JobsRunningSizes list counts of jobs for each of <job_size_set> for actively running jobs JobsCompletedSizes list counts of jobs for each of <job_size_set> for jobs that succeeded JobsBadputSizes list counts of jobs for each of <job_size_set> for jobs that failed in some way. ## <job_set_set> is ( < 64k < 256k < 1Mb < 4Mb < 16Mb < 64Mb < 256Mb < 1Gb < 4Gb < 16Gb < 64Gb < 256Gb ...) ## This is possibly a user configurable set. JobsRunningRuntimes list runtimes of jobs for each of <job_runtime_set> for actively running jobs JobsCompletedRuntimes list runtimes of jobs for each of <job_runtime_set> for jobs that succeeded JobsBadputRuntimes list runtimes of jobs for each of <job_runtime_set> for jobs that ran and failed in some way. ## <job_runtime_set> is ( < 30 sec < 1 min < 10 min < 30 min < 1 hour < 3 hours < 6 hours < 24 hours < 2 days < 7 days < 30 days > 30 days) ## possibly user configurable set? ## for each daemon ## DCStatLifetime RelTime total time the daemon has been collecting statistics. (uptime) DCStatLastUpdateTime AbsTime time of last update of DCxxxx statistics values DCSelectWaittime RelTime total time spent waiting in select DCSignalRuntime RelTime total time spent handling signals DCSocketRuntime RelTime total time spent handling socket messages DCPipeRuntime RelTime total time spent handling pipe messages DCSignals int number of signals handlers called DCSockMessages int number of socket handlers called DCPipeMessages int number of pipe handlers called DCSockBytes int number of bytes passed though the socket (can we do this?) DCPipeBytes int number of bytes passed though the socket DCDebugOuts int number of dprintf calls that were written to output. Milestones 20110909 Implement the generic plumbing, and simple and windowed stats for the schedd. 20110817 #2354 Statistics in DaemonCore 20110819 #2353 Statistics histogram 20110915 #2355 Unit tests for Ring buffer implementation 20110915 #2356 Condor tests for statistics implementation 20110830 #2429 create AddingStatisticsValues page to document how to use the classes in generic_stats.h
remarks: 2011-May-31 14:30:44 by eje: Performance stats are fairly daemon-specific in my experience. What is the expected payoff for a generic cross-daemon 'stats collecting' object and/or service? As part of #2006 I implemented a template widget called timed_queue<> which can be limited by either a time-window or a particular size (or both) -- it provides ring-buffer functionality. It also demonstrates some basic accumulation methods: .../src/condor_utils/timed_queue.h 2011-May-31 14:54:48 by nwp: Payoff from having cross-daemon object/service is that it is something that the schedd does not have to do; It seems that the schedd is getting overloaded, and not adding more to it seems like a good idea. As it is, the timed_queue has got two objections that I have heard here around UW: first, it is not a priori bounded in memory usage; second, there is an objection to deriving from std::deque, because condor is not set up now to handle C++ exceptions very well. 2011-May-31 17:31:32 by eje: Regarding timed_queue<> questions: 1) It's memory can be bounded in a well defined way using the max_len() method, if desired. 2) Regarding exceptions, the STL data structures that are used in the condor code already include string, vector<> and map<>. Adding deque<> to that list doesn't introduce a qualitative change. 2011-May-31 17:39:31 by eje: Regarding schedd computational load, it doesn't feel obvious to me that updating a given statistic is more compute-expensive than executing the machinery of sending data to a third party so the third party can maintain it. 2011-Jun-01 12:04:26 by nwp: Yes, STL has snuck into Condor, for better or worse. Hopefully, the upside is better than the downside. I do not know that the statistics daemon is a good idea; I am just throwing it out there. I could see some lunatic asking for statistics 30 times/sec and then it would probably make sense to offload it from the schedd. 2011-Jun-01 12:18:21 by tstclair: I think we need to create some clear objectives & requirements, based on use cases, similar to some of the other tickets. It might become more obvious what the best path will be then. As it stands, this is pretty nebulous, and prone to conjecture atm. It might be worth a mtg with some folks to gather/define requirements. 2011-Jun-01 12:19:06 by nwp: Amen 2011-Jun-03 10:20:39 by bcotton: From our Research Services group, who do the statistical finagling: There are three distinct types of things that we cannot (to our knowledge) get from Condor right now that would be very helpful: 1. Full job run attempt history. Right now, all that is logged in the history log is the last, second-to-last, and some info about the first run attempted. A lot of the discussion and proposal seems to be centered around the notion of reporting statistics on a job. We don't want or need Condor to do statistics--we have real statistics packages for that. What we would like is for Condor to log the raw data those need about every attempted run. 2. Information on jobs in progress or in queue. Right now, history only logs anything about a job after it completes. This is very problematic. It would be much more useful to get information about jobs before they complete, as things happen. This really is a fundamental shift in thinking about logging, from a job-based log to an event-based log. Even if something wholly different from the current history log, a real event-based log would be far more useful. Many jobs will stay in progress for days or even weeks, and not being able to report on them until they finish makes truly accurate reporting on the current state of the system simply impossible. 3. Centralized logging. Being reliant on access to logs from the schedd hosts is a really big problem. It means that we cannot get accurate information on what our pool resources are doing if any of them allow jobs from hosts outside of our control, either directly or through flocking. This creates a huge disincentive for anyone to allow any jobs from outside of their own organization, because they have no way of tracking what work or even how much work they are supporting by those outside schedds. Note, this doesn't have to be a fancy DB-based custom system. Simply having event-based remote syslog support would solve all of (1), (2), and (3) above. 2011-Jun-03 10:36:52 by tstclair: bcotton - love the comments! and there may be 2-3 side-tickets just from that! But I'm not sure it relates 100% to the root of this specific ticket. For example, most of the stats we are looking to obtain, or already exist, are internal performance measurements of the code itself. The question(s) we've been trying to figure out are: What the possible use cases? What's the scope we want to attack here? 2011-Jun-03 11:06:06 by eje: bcotton, fyi - I think some of what you want will be available via new schedd stats in 7.7 (#2006) 2011-Jun-04 12:16:44 by eje: see also: #2211 (collector stat rfe) 2011-Jun-06 13:35:56 by gthain: Note that I'm not worried about using deque, but deriving from std::deque is a bit hinky, as the stl containers aren't really designed for this. 2011-Jun-06 16:04:43 by johnkn: I propose that the sort of statistics that are relevant to this ticket are. Instantaneous values or totals from the time the daemon was started. Not persistent - statistical data is lost when the daemon process exits. Designed to give us insight in to what the daemon is doing, and in particular intended to help us determine the reasons for badput. title: Ticket #7395: Escape newline in file transfer hold messages
description: If the file transfer object includes a hold message with a newline character (not impossible, considering part of the hold message can come from a file transfer plugin -- which outputs in new ClassAd format), then the hold message is completely ignored by the schedd as newlines are invalid characters. title: Ticket #5717: Handle multiple negotiators in a single pool
description: The global CMS pool has three negotiators, each matching a third of the machines in their pool. Most of HTCondor is built on the assumption that a pool has only one negotiator active at any time. Thus, the CMS configuration presents problems that we'd like to fix. Config knob NEGOTIATOR_NAME to set Name attribute of negotiator ad. Otherwise, negotiator ads overwrite each other in the collector. NEGOTIATOR_NAME should also show up in an attribute in the accounting ads, and be part of the hash key. Add options to condor_userprio to specify which negotiator to query. If specific negotiator not selected, and multiple negotiator ads returned by collector, contact all negotiators. [WONT CHANGE] If specific negotiator not selected when querying accounting ads from the collector, show all accounting ads.
remarks: 2017-May-09 12:50:51 by jfrey: One annoyance with the new default negotiator name is that Condor assumes daemon names are fully-qualified hostnames if they don't have an '@' character. Thus, this doesn't work: condor_status -negotiator NEGOTIATOR And adding a -name option to condor_userprio would have similar problems: condor_userprio -name NEGOTIATOR The names for CMS's alternate negotiators (NEGOTIATORT1 and NEGOTIATORUS) are similarly affected. 2017-May-11 13:53:30 by jfrey: We are changing the negotiator naming behavior to match that of master and schedd daemons. The default name is provided by default_daemon_name(). If an alternate name is configured, it's passed through build_valid_daemon_name(). The upshot is that the default negotiator name is the hostname, and an alternate name that doesn't have an '@' will have the hostname appended with an '@'. 2017-May-15 16:16:08 by jfrey: Status Update Everything in this ticket has been implemented, except for querying of multiple negotiators. condor_userprio looks up one negotiator ad for locate. If there are multiple negotiator ads are present and the new -name option isn't used, then condor_userprio will receive one ad. Which ad it receives is undefined. When condor_userprio talks to the negotiator and -name isn't used, it's similarly undefined which negotiator it will talk to.

title: Ticket #4805: putClassAd non-blocking mode doesn't work
description: The refactor of putClassAd in #4448 contains a small bug which breaks the non-blocking mode. BlockingModeGuard is used as following: BlockingModeGuard(rsock, true); However, this causes the object to be destroyed immediately. We really want this to stay in scope until the end of the code block. For that: BlockingModeGuard guard(rsock, true); In particular, this prevents the V3 query protocol to actually be non-blocking (probably not a big deal in 8.3.2, as the query protocol forks a child in most cases).

title: Ticket #6838: Improve JobEvent (Python) API - Python 3 idioms
description: Ticket #6814 added Python 2.7 container-type methods to JobEvent. These methods work in Python 3, but the idiomatic interface is different. Primarily, Python 3.7 removes the iter*() methods but changes keys(), values(), and items() to return 'view objects'. While leaving the iter*() methods in should be harmless, we should see if it's possible to implement 'view objects' in such a way that they're also compatible with the return type in the Python 2.7 API.
creator: tlmiller

title: Ticket #2178: Condor-C GAHP Worker Thread using the wrong credentials
description: I found the following error message in the CondorC GAHP Worker Thread: 05/20/11 08:42:03 [30007] ChildAliveMsg: failed to send DC_CHILDALIVE to parent daemon at <129.93.239.174:32804> (try 1 of 3): CEDAR:6002:failed to send EOM|GSI:5004:Failed to gss_assist_gridmap /DC=org/DC=doegrids/OU=People/CN=Brian Bockelman 504307 to a local user. Check the grid-mapfile. It is using the credential of the user to talk to the parent daemon and failing because, on purpose, random users don't have DAEMON-level authorization on the submit node. The parent should have created an authz session for the worker thread, right? Not sure when this broke.
remarks: 2011-May-23 10:03:52 by danb: I think there are two issues here: DC_CHILDALIVE requires DAEMON level access, which is more broad than one would like---especially when the child process is running as some user other than condor. Do we really want the condor-c-gahp to be able to send arbitrary DC signals to other Condor daemons? That is one thing that DAEMON level access allows. DC_CHILDALIVE must create a security session to the parent. In the 7.5 series, children are born with a security session for the parent to signal the child. The same thing should be done (but has not been) for the child to send DC_CHILDALIVE to the parent. If parents always use a specific security session for signalling children, and children always use a specific security session for sending heartbeats to the parent, perhaps we can stop allowing DAEMON-level access to these commands and restrict them to these specific security sessions. The one thing I'm not sure about is whether there are any cases where DC signals are sent from processes that are not direct parents, or whether we would want to keep this option open. 2011-May-23 17:43:16 by bbockelm: Ouch - so, in order for Condor-C to work, anyone must be able to signal a Condor process? FWIW, I can temporarily give this permission only to the C_GAHP, an unsatisfactory but functioning workaround: C_GAHP.ALLOW_DAEMON = $(ALLOW_DAEMON) bbockelm@unl.edu 2011-May-24 08:18:05 by tannenba: I am 99% certain signals are only passed from parents to direct/immediate children, and vice-versa, so binding to a specific security session is an idea. As I don't like the idea of a process running as the user having permission to send signals to the gridmanager any more than Brian, here is another idea: don't have the C-Gahp even attempt to send alives to its parent. The gridmanager has other means of knowing if the gahp is non-responsive. Maybe the below attached patch? 2011-May-24 09:58:58 by danb: Todd, The patch looks safe to me. There is no need to make a special case for dagman, because dagman does not inherit DaemonCore info from its parent. 2011-May-24 13:17:38 by tannenba: Patch pushed to v7.6.1, resolving.

title: Ticket #7680: condor_q -name useless for some hosts
description: Mat reports: Got an issue: I've got a minicondor in a Docker container. The container's hostname -f is "c0a0000e013f". It's in the host file so ping resolves but when I try to do condor_q -name `hostname -f` , I get Error: unknown host c0a0000e013f After some analysis, it seems like the problem is that get_daemon_name() barfs when given a hostname that doesn't have a corresponding FQDN. Supposedly get_daemon_name() is only called by client code prior to doing a collector query, so that's the wrong behavior; clearly, the daemons do something something else. (Changing get_fqdn_from_hostname() seems likely to cause a lot of subtle issues, so let's avoid that.) It's not clear what other side effects, if any, of this change would be, but Jaime points out that the following is absurd, and would be fixed by this change also: [jfrey@submit-1 ~]$ condor_status badname condor_status: unknown host badname [jfrey@submit-1 ~]$ condor_status badname.nogood [jfrey@submit-1 ~]$

title: Ticket #5347: Initialize OpenSSL threading in python bindings
description: CERN noticed that if python bindings are used in a multithreaded python process and the native python HTTPS is invoked while a HTCondor GSI auth is ongoing, OpenSSL fails. We suspect this is due to the fact that the GIL is released by the condor python bindings yet OpenSSL is not thread-safe by default. We should implement the pithy callback functions to make sure OpenSSL is thread safe. See: https://www.openssl.org/docs/manmaster/crypto/threads.html
creator: bbockelm

Ticket #3339: manual description of parallel universe needs improvement
description: From Sam F, the start of suggestions for improved prose: \subsection*{Parallel Universe: Clusters, Processes, and Subprocesses} When a user submits a job to HTCondor with \verb=condor_submit=, HTCondor in Parallel Universe processes the submit file and assumes that all jobs submitted in this file are part of a parallel (e.g.~MPI) job. HTCondor processes the job and creates a new cluster with a new clusterID for the job. The user though can specify different requirements for different parts of the job and queue each part separately with each part being part of the same cluster but receiving a different ProcID (process ID). Within each processes, the user (by using partitionable slots) can also request more than one CPU (\verb+num_cpus = 2+). Each request for a slot is known as a subprocess; each subprocess has the same cluster ID and proc ID as the over-arching process but has its own unique subprocID (or whatever the actual name is). The way to create multiple processes is to place a number after the \verb=queue= command, such as \verb=queue 8= to create eight different processes with the same cluster. After a particular \verb=queue= command, the user can also change parameters previously specified in the submit file or add parameters not previously specified. For example, suppose that the head node of a parallel job needs additional RAM compared to the rest of the nodes. The user can write request_memory = 5G queue request_meory = 1G queue 31 If a user wishes to submit multiple independent Parallel Universe jobs, the user cannot simply append a number to the \verb=queue= command. HTCondor will assume that each job is not independent -- as by definition, a parallel job is a job is at least setup to handle multiple (sub)processes.

title: Ticket #331: Code review patch from Cycle Computing for resource weights.
description: See more details here: 1699 (backup) 1699 (public) (http://nmi.cs.wisc.edu/node/1699) This is a patch that was contributed for 7.1 in October 2008. Our customers are actively interested in this functionality. This patch adds support for having different slots "cost" different amounts against the group quota (right now every slot costs 1). In the config file for a startd, ResourceWeight is a ClassAd expression which evaluates to the weight or cost of the resource. For example: ResourceWeight = ifthenelse(SlotID == 1, $(Slot1ResourceWeight), $(OtherSlotResourceWeight)) Slot1ResourceWeight = 10.0 OtherSlotResourceWeight = 1.2 GROUP_NAMES = group_a GROUP_QUOTA_group_a = 15
remarks: # 1 Submitted by danb on Tue, 2008-10-28 17:41. Nice, Ian! Without running your code, I can't tell if the following dprintf provides enough context or not: + if(candidate->EvalFloat(ResourceWeightAttr.Value(), NULL, + ResourceWeight) == 0) { + dprintf(D_FULLDEBUG, "Can't get ResourceWeight; using 1.0\n";); Is the negotiator log just going to have this message show up out of the blue, or will it be obvious which machine ad is responsible? Also, is "ResourceWeight" a better name than "SlotWeight"? -Dan # 2 Submitted by Ian on Tue, 2008-10-28 23:35. Dan, I'm reworking this patch after discussing some issues with Todd, to make sure that we're fair within groups. I'll take a look at the context of this message - in the tests I've performed I have D_ACCOUNTING on. It's a good idea to identify the candidate explicitly. Todd suggested ResourceWeight but he might like SlotWeight. Thanks for the suggestions. -Ian # 3 Submitted by Todd Tannenbaum on Wed, 2008-10-29 10:55. SlotWeight is fine imho if folks like it better than ResourceWeight, I have no strong feelings. The patch as it currently exists (attachment resource_weight.diff) cannot go into the code because it looks like it breaks fair-share amongst users within a specific group. This functionality is required and cannot be removed. But once we get this aspect cleaned up, it looks very nice. At first blush it seems fair-share within a group can be restored (or at least as fair as spinning-pie allows) by totaling the ResourceWeight of all candidate startds, and then multiplying this sum by the priority ratio instead of just using the number of startds. Course if ResourceWeight is not defined, it should default to be 1.0, and so the summation of ResourceWeights should equal # of startds and all is like it was before. Another less attractive (but maybe safer) option if folks see a problem with the above idea is a knob that tells Condor to either honor fair-share within a group, or honor ResourceWeights. Any other comments / thoughts? Thanks for the patch Ian!!!!! # 4 Submitted by Ian on Thu, 2008-10-30 14:23. I've reworked the patch to add two things: adding computation of total resource weight as Todd suggests, and a knob NEGOTIATOR_USE_RESOURCE_WEIGHTS that if set to false (the default) will do things exactly as they are done now (resource weights have no effect, almost exactly the same code path is followed). The way this works is by having a separate accounting system. The existing system is unaltered; the new system works alongside it. The limitation of this work right now is that the priority system still uses the old integer weights to calculate usage and priority; so a user using one slot with ResourceWeight = 2 will have the same priority as a user using a slot with ResourceWeight = 0.5. In other words, NEGOTIATOR_USE_RESOURCE_WEIGHTS only affects group quotas, not priorities. I think this is useful as is, and I'll work on extending this feature to priorities as well as time permits (and again, using a parallel implementation). 2009-Apr-08 13:38:13 by tannenba: Note - this patch also adds a matchmaker diagnostic 'rejected for group quota'. Nice. :) 2009-Apr-08 15:21:12 by matt: Quick thoughts... Can the ResourceWeight reference attributes from a potential or current job? A slot may have some amount of memory, but a job may know it'll only ever use half. The job may just happen to not be using all the memory (might be possible already with STARTD_JOB_EXPRS). The node and system policy may have exceptions for certain Owners. Is there a reason this can't just be on all the time (avoid YAK, yet another knob)? There is already a default for ResourceWeight of 1, should probably be Cpus, which will allow for removal of code in the accountant that checks Cpus to do a primitive form of this feature. It could avoid multiple tests for NEGOTIATOR_USE_RESOURCE_WEIGHTS and duplicate code blocks (see "if(useResourceWeights)"). 2009-Apr-08 15:25:57 by tannenba: If resource weights are not being used, aka NEGOTIATOR_USE_RESOURCE_WEIGHTS is set to false, the patch should be more careful to not introduce significant additional CPU demand into the negotiation cycle. For instance, looks like the v2 patch below always calls sumResourceWeights() even if resource weights are not desired. And this is a very CPU-demanding function (evaluation on every machine ad). Also, re the lets try to not introduce more knobs rule, couldn't the NEGOTIATOR_USE_RESOURCE_WEIGHTS knob be set automatically and thus not have to be a knob at all? Maybe a simple algorithm of if no machine ads contains a resource weight attribute then in the code useResourceWeights=false else true. 2009-Apr-08 15:59:27 by matt: Assuming sumResourceWeights() is conditional... Is sumResourceWeights() even necessary? It ads an extra iteration over all the ads and doubles the number of times EvalFloat(ResourceWeight...) is done. Re: Auto Knob - Sounds cool as long as it does not require another iteration over the ads. 2009-Apr-13 11:49:12 by alderman: See the above copied comments (#3) for why the sumResourceWeights function is necessary; it's to ensure fair share within groups. In terms of turning this feature on automatically or all the time, I'd think it's an OK direction to go in but maybe it would be worthwhile to get a better sense of the performance impact w.r.t. summing the weights, etc. by having it be a knob for now. It seems to me that it would be better to have a knob until we can show that there's no performance penalty to 1) sumResourceWeights or 2) look through all machine ads for a ResourceWeight attribute. 2009-Apr-17 11:10:57 by matt: Re comment 3: The goal was to provide fair-share amongst users within a group. That could be achieved using an upfront sum, but doing so introduces another iteration over the startd ads making it less likely to be on by default, results in evaluation of the ResourceWeights attributes multiple times, and doesn't allow for the possibility of referencing job attributes within the ResourceWeight. Rephrased: Is it necessary to sum weights upfront? Re the knob: The more I think about it the more an auto-knob is scary, especially if this feature is slow. Assuming it is slow and can't be on by default - debugging why negotiation gets slow as a side-effect of a machine specifying a ResourceWeight, ouch. 2009-Apr-17 11:25:24 by alderman: Agreed about the knob. Todd points out that fair-share within a group is essential. In order to divide up the pie fairly, we need to know the size of the pie. Right? Do you see a way to retain fair share that but not sum the weights? 2009-Apr-17 11:46:50 by matt: If you don't have any ideas on how it could be worked around let me know and I'll think about it too. If you think it's a necessity that cannot be worked around maybe we shouldn't bother. 2009-Apr-17 12:06:51 by alderman: I think we need to do some performance testing to determine whether there's a problem at all before we try to find a work-around. 2009-Apr-17 12:12:09 by matt: By all means, but there is still the functionality component. I don't think you can sum the weights upfront and let them reference job ads. Is that functionality just not possible? 2009-Apr-17 12:23:54 by alderman: That's an interesting question. The problem is that, if the resources cost differing amounts for different members of the group, the size of the per group pie will vary. So, we might be able to make the weights per group but not per user? 2009-Apr-17 12:52:15 by matt: Off the top of my head, summing for groups is the same as summing for jobs. You may not know the exact size of the pie upfront. Though with groups you'd have a smaller set of possible pie sizes. So, you can think of doing something more probabilistic as you go along to estimate the pie size and existing slices. However, maybe you don't even need fair-share across weights and just across # of slots is enough. What's the goal of this feature - what do you expect it to give you overall, what's a concrete use? Maybe fair-share across # of slots is enough, but the charge back will be different across slots, which will effect shares in the future. 2009-Apr-20 11:41:20 by tannenba: I think the earlier we get this code into the developer series the earlier we will know the answers to some of the above performance issues (or non-issues?). Merged and pushed resource_weight_v4.diff attachment below into the master branch as commit [14512]. Will resolve this ticket, can create child defect tickets if required if problems are encountered. Thanks for the patch, Ian.

title: Ticket #6091: DAGMan cannot submit jobs with AFS / Kerberos support enabled
description: With HTCondor configured to use the AFS / Kerberos support added in v8.5 for CERN: when DAGMan invokes condor_submit to submit jobs in a workflow, it invokes SEC_CREDENTIAL_PRODUCER, which then fails do to lack of tickets. The root of the problem is the condor_starter sets up the environment correctly with KRB5CCNAME and friends, but with scheduler universe there is no starter, and thus the SEC_CREDENTIAL_PRODUCER callout fails. The patch presented in this ticket avoids the problem by simply telling any condor_submits that occur as part of a scheduler universe job to not run the SEC_CREDENTIAL_PRODUCER in the first place if the scheduler universe job classad has attribute SendCredential equal to True. The thinking here is if SendCredential is True in the scheduler universe job classad, then a credential for that user was already stored on submit machine when the scheduler universe job was submitted (i.e. when the user ran condor_submit_dag), and thus having DAGMan attempt to produce a store a credential at every condor_submit is an unnecessary waste of time/resources. The implementation has such scheduler universe jobs run with an environment variable setting SEC_CREDENTIAL_PRODUCER to "CREDENTIAL_ALREADY_STORED", which tells the condor_submit to NOT invoke the credential producer but to act as if it did (i.e. still set SendCredential to True in the job).
remarks: 2017-Jan-18 11:39:39 by zmiller: CODE REVIEW: Looks good.

title: Ticket #761: matchmaker diagnostics not visible to JobRouter or Quill
description:
In the schedd, LastRejMatchTime, LastRejMatchReason and a few similar things are inserted into the job ClassAd in memory only. This means these attributes are not persistent and they are not visible to JobRouter and Quill. There is no comment in the code excusing this way of doing things, so I am planning to make it update the ad the normal way, which logs to job_queue.log. I think I would make this a "non-durable" transaction, so we would not fsync after updating these attributes. I would like to do this as a bug fix for 7.4.0, because the documented use-case for JobRouter depends on these attributes. Todd suggested getting some rough performance numbers for the different methods of updating ClassAds in the schedd. Here's what I got: Time in seconds to perform 10,000 SetAttributeInt operations, to memory only, NONDURABLE (no fsync), and DURABLE (fsync). NO-DISK NONDURABLE DURABLE SYSTEM 0.04 0.2 4 My MacBook 0.04 0.2 50 My MacBook with busy disk 0.03 0.3 300 tonic 0.03 0.3 500 tonic with busy disk I think the NONDURABLE option demonstrates reasonable performance for something called as frequently as the matchmaker diagnostic updates in the negotiation handler. It's 8-10 times slower than a pure memory update, but it can handle over 10,000 updates per second on the systems I tested. Fortunately, we don't need a DURABLE update, because the performance of that looks a bit more iffy. I made the disk busy by doing cp -r of CONDOR_SRC. I confirmed by reading the code that the NONDURABLE option skips both the fsync and the fflush. The patch I used to test is pasted below. diff --git a/src/condor_schedd.V6/schedd.cpp b/src/condor_schedd.V6/schedd.cpp index e8f5afa..56cf7d9 100644 --- a/src/condor_schedd.V6/schedd.cpp +++ b/src/condor_schedd.V6/schedd.cpp @@ -5069,6 +5069,29 @@ Scheduler::negotiate(int command, Stream* s) host_cnt = max_hosts + 1; JobsRejected++; cad->Assign(ATTR_LAST_REJ_MATCH_TIME,(int)time(0)); + { + time_t tt = time(0); + UtcTime start1(true); + for(int cc=0;cc<10000;cc++) { + cad->Assign(ATTR_LAST_REJ_MATCH_TIME,(int)tt); + } + UtcTime stop1(true); + dprintf(D_ALWAYS,"DAN TESTING: time to update in memory 10000 times: %f
",stop1.difference(start1)); + + UtcTime start2(true); + for(int cc=0;cc<10000;cc++) { + SetAttributeInt(id.cluster,id.proc,ATTR_LAST_REJ_MATCH_TIME,(int)tt,NONDURABLE); + } + UtcTime stop2(true); + dprintf(D_ALWAYS,"DAN TESTING: time to update non-durable 10000 times: %f
",stop2.difference(start2)); + + UtcTime start3(true); + for(int cc=0;cc<10000;cc++) { + SetAttributeInt(id.cluster,id.proc,ATTR_LAST_REJ_MATCH_TIME,(int)tt); + } + UtcTime stop3(true); + dprintf(D_ALWAYS,"DAN TESTING: time to update durable 10000 times: %f
",stop3.difference(start3)); + } break; case SEND_JOB_INFO: { // The Negotiator wants us to send it a job.
remarks: I made a patch for 7.4 that changes the in-memory updates to mathcmaking diagnostics into NONDURABLE (to disk with no fsync) updates.

title: Ticket #4556: UDP invalidations can be sent to hosts without a UDP command socket
description: Currently, if SEC_INVALIDATE_SESSIONS_VIA_TCP is set to false (default is true), then UDP-based invalidations will always be sent - even if the daemon's sinful string indicates no UDP command port is available. This could be fixed with the patch below: --- a/src/condor_daemon_core.V6/daemon_core.cpp +++ b/src/condor_daemon_core.V6/daemon_core.cpp @@ -10660,7 +10660,7 @@ void DaemonCore::send_invalidate_session ( const char* sinful, const char* sessi msg->setSuccessDebugLevel(D_SECURITY); msg->setRawProtocol(true); - if( m_invalidate_sessions_via_tcp ) { + if( !daemon->hasUDPCommandPort() || m_invalidate_sessions_via_tcp ) { msg->setStreamType(Stream::reli_sock); } else { This logic goes against the sysadmin's wishes - but should be OK because these are non-blocking and the logic is consistent with how the schedd sends vacate messages to the startd. We have not observed this to be a problem "in the wild" so a fix only on master would be fine.

title: Ticket #3293: Tunnel Bosco file transfers over ssh
description: In Bosco, the connections made from the ft-gahp to the gridmanager for file transfer should be tunneled over the ssh connection. That eliminates the need to have network connectivity from the cluster front-end node back to the submit machine. When starting the ft-gahp, we can use the -R option to tell ssh to create a port on the remote machine and forward connections from there to the gridmanager's command port. This code almost certainly doesn't work with IPV6.

title: Ticket #4782: Recognize My in native ClassAds
description: In the ClassAds compatibility class, we add and remove a My attribute every time we do an evaluation or reference tracking. The native ClassAds library already has a special self attribute that refers to the current ad (which we use to implement My). If we had the library recognize My the same as self, then we eliminate lots of temporary modifications of the ad in the compatibility class and callers could use the native ClassAd evaluation methods. We could make the recognition of My contingent on _useOldClassAdSemantics being set to true, so users of ClassAds other than HTCondor wouldn't see it.

title: Ticket #4628: Should condor_rm'ed DAGMan wait for nodes to exit before FINAL runs?
description: In the course of working on #4618, it occurred to me that maybe DAGMan should wait for removed node jobs to exit the queue before submitting a FINAL node. (This is in the case that the DAGMan job itself is condor_rm'ed or an ABORT-DAG-On fires.) Right now DAGMan condor_rm's any queued node jobs before submitting the FINAL node, but doesn't wait for them to exit from the queue. I think this probably makes sense -- if, for example, the FINAL node is supposed to do some kind of cleanup, we should run it after any other nodes have generated whatever output they're going to create. Maybe there should be an option for waiting or not waiting before submitting the FINAL node? (Also see #3995.)
creator: wenger

title: Ticket #5469: Job Router handling of job policy exprs needs work
description: When the Job Router claims a job to route, it evaluates the periodic job policy expressions of the source job. It also forwards those expressions into the destination job, where the schedd (or one of its delegates) will evaluate those same expressions. In many situations, the periodic remove expression will evaluate to True in both ads at about the same time, and there is a race as to which one will occur first. If it fires first in the source job, then the Job Router will remove the destination job and then let the source job leave the queue. If it fires first in the destination job, then the Job Router will return the source job to schedd control and try rerouting it later. Returning the job to the schedd may alter the ad such that the periodic remove will no longer fire. This can result in a loop of a source job being routed and aborted multiple times. If the source job has the TimerRemove attribute (set by Condor-C when a job lease is used), then the initial lease time is forwarded to the destination job, but none of the lease renewals are forwarded. Thus, the TimerRemove will not fire in the source job, but will fire in the destination job after the initial lease expires. If the destination job cannot complete before the lease expiration that was set when that job was submitted expires, the job ends up in the loop described above. The problem with TimerRemove can be easily solved by having the Job Router always remove this attribute from the destination job ad. It's unclear to me whether we can do the same for the other policy expressions, as they may be sensitive to the differences between the source and destination job ads.

title: Ticket #1979: Installer throws a warning if the firewall service is deactivated.
description: The Windows firewall service can be turned off and any attempt by installers to punch holes in it will result in a warning message box popping up. This is only a problem if the service itself is turned off explicitly. Turning off the firewall through the control panel does not turn off the service. This could potentially be a problem during unattended installs and is also likely to confuse end users. Ignoring the error will allow the installation to complete successfully but the best solution is to find a way to conditionalize the firewall hole punching. Determine if there is a way to detect what services are running on a system. See if the firewall exception schema can be conditionalized. Depending on results of previous two efforts, determine best course of action for dealing with unattended installs.

title: Ticket #7004: Add Docker for Windows support
description: Now that Windows supports Docker, we should add support for Docker to our Windows Starter. This ticket will be the parent ticket for that work. The main issues that we need to resolve are Detect whether Docker for Windows is configured to support Linux or Windows containers (done) and decide how we are going to handle/report that. investigation needed Figure out how to automatically configure Docker on Windows to work with HTCondor. This may involve stuffing username/password into the Docker configuration so that it will use an account created by HTCondor for that purpose. We may also need to change the ACL's on the HTCondor execute directory to make this work, possibly other things we haven't thought of yet. investigation needed. Determine if we can start a docker container from a Starter running on the Services desktop. Is it necessary that Docker Desktop be running for this to work? Is it necessary for a user to be logged in? Investigation shows that at present is is necessary for docker desktop to be running, and that a user be logged in (this is what starts docker desktop). It has been suggested that the HTCondor startd try starting up docker desktop. This seems iffy because docker desktop is designed to hook into the taskbar, and the services desktop doesn't have a taskbar, but it's worth trying (on a throw-away windows installation, in case we damage the docker setup in a way that can't be fixed) investigation needed Figure out what UID to use when running Docker jobs, or decide that using the default UID of 0 is OK here. at present docker for windows does not accept the -user option, so we have no way to do this. Figure out how to transfer files into and out of the container in a way that is consistent with the current HTCondor file transfer mechanism. Three alternative mechanisms are being considered here. Use the experimental LCOW mode to run Linux images on a docker configured to default to Windows containers, then bind mounting of a Windows directory into the docker job works. This allows us to use the current HTCondor file transfer mechanism, but work is needed so that the Starter understands that the path that job sees to the transferred files isn't the path that the Starter sees. Work has begun to make a version of the Starter that can handle this. see https://blog.docker.com/2018/02/docker-for-windows-18-02-with-windows-10-fall-creators-update/ Use the SMB share mechanism that Docker supports to have the sandbox actually shared between the Windows host OS and the Docker container. This option will likely have the best performance, but is more uncertain - We don't currently know how to get this working for HTCondor running as a service. This isn't needed if we use the experimental LCOW mode for docker. Use a Docker Volume to stage files into and out of the Hyper-V VM using a Docker image that we control and/or Docker cp to do the actual file transfer. This will mean that files will be transferred first to the Windows file system. Then copied from there into the Docker volume and only then can we start the job. Experiments prove that this can work for input files, but it's a slower and more expensive solution than the experimental LCOW mode for docker, and it's a hard to use this for output files because it's hard to transfer only changed files. Use a Docker image containing a HTCondor Starter to do file transfer directly into and out of a Docker Volume. This will result in a very different code flow than our usual, but should give us performance as good as using the SMB share without needing the SMB share. This option is probably the most work. Enhance the Startd/Starter to understand that the path to the sandbox from that the job sees may not be the same as the path the Startd/Starter sees. Improving this will have the side benefit of allowing us to use a standard path like /home/condor/sandbox for all jobs inside the docker container, which in turn make it a bit simpler to build docker images. work has begun on this.
creator: johnkn

title: Ticket #2206: CondorThreads should hand around "arg" as objects, not void *
description: CondorThreads pass around a void* ("arg") to pass to the actual worker code. It's a void* since different code might want different things. The down side is that we can't validate that the arg is valid in any way. Proposed: Create class CondorThreadArg; it has no methods Change CondorThreads::pool_add to take a CondorThreadArg* instead of a void*. (And thus in the back-end store and pass around CondorThreadArgs) Change the prototype for the callback function to take CondorThreadArg* instead of void* Change all users to wrap their data in a class derived from CondorThreadArg. Benefits: Instead of unsafe casts to and from void*, we can use a safe(r) dynamic_cast. If the dynamic_cast returns NULL, we know that we were passed invalid data and can EXCEPT with a helpful error. Further thoughts: should we go whole hog and instead of passing around a function pointer and a argument, instead pass in an object with a "RunThreadTask()" function?

title: Ticket #2713: RFE: extend dprintf flag parameter to 64-bit integer
description: To support any additional dprintf() flags, for example #2712, it looks like we need to increase the width of the flag bit parameter. Simply extending to 64-bit integer would be one straighforward option.
remarks: 2011-Dec-14 14:52:33 by johnkn: I have no real objection to this, but I noticed that more than half of the debug 'flags' are mutually exclusive, and if we switched them from from individual bits to an enum, we could get even MORE headroom without going to 64 bits. Redefine the debug 'level' as a set of mutually exclusive flags (D_PID, etc) OR'd with one category value from the set of categories. This would also give us room for a few bits of 'verbosity'. something like this #define D_CATEGORY_MASK (0xFF<<16) #define D_NO_CATEGORY (0<<16) #define D_CONFIG (1<<16) #define D_PROTOCOL (2<<16) #define D_PRIV (3<<16) #define D_SECURITY (4<<16) #define D_DAEMONCORE (5<<16) #define D_COMMAND (6<<16) #define D_MATCH (7<<16) #define D_NETWORK (8<<16) #define D_KEYBOARD (9<<16) #define D_PROCFAMILY (10<<16) #define D_IDLE (11<<16) #define D_THREADS (12<<16) #define D_ACCOUNTANT (13<<16) #define D_VERBOSITY_MASK = (3<<14) #define D_LACONIC = (0<<14) #define D_CHATTY = (1<<14) #define D_VERBOSE = (2<<14) #define D_DIAGNOSTIC = (3<<14) so a dprintf call might be dprintf(D_SECURITY, "message that everyone who sets D_SECURITY should see"); dprintf(D_SECURITY | D_VERBOSE, "message for those who set D_SECURITY_VERBOSE") This leaves us with room for 50 more categories, and it frees up a bunch of bits to use as new flags. 2011-Dec-14 15:45:52 by eje: I see that there are two "unused" in flags, and another in format-flags: #define D_UNUSED2 (1<<13) #define D_UNUSED3 (1<<14) //... #define D_UNUSED4 (1<<30) So arguably I could service #2711 and #2712 with those. 2012-Jun-25 14:51:23 by eje: TJ's refactor of dprintf on #2933 makes this RFE moot, I'm abandoning

title: Ticket #52: Condor Connection Broker (CCB)
description: This ticket will hold information about CCB, the Condor Connection Broker. The sinful string for a daemon now includes all contact information. This includes public address, private network info, and CCB info. We plan on CCB essentially replacing GCB at some point in the v7.3.x development series.
remarks: 2009-Jan-21 15:21:48 by tannenba: Some wisdom (snagged from a message from Dan to Igor on 1/21/09): I have not yet had time to optimize the security session in the connection to the collector. So if a daemon is advertising itself to the same collector as is acting as its CCB server, there will currently be two authentication's per daemon. (Because the first one is DAEMON level and the second one is ADVERTISE_STARTD or ADVERTISE_MASTER, which implies DAEMON, but is not implied by DAEMON.) Client's wishing to request a connection from a daemon do so at READ authorization level when they talk to the CCB server. I don't recall whether that requires authentication in your setup or not. I found that there were a number of places where having the CCB info in a separate attribute was problematic, because Condor passes around address strings rather than full daemon classads in some cases. Therefore, the CCB info is always packed into the address string. As things stand, that means daemons with CCB turned on are incompatible with other condor components from before 7.3.0. Same goes for daemons with a private network name defined, because I had to pack that into the address as well. Even in the GCB case, that helps, because of all the places where the extra contact information was slipping through the cracks. 2009-Mar-10 17:55:02 by danb: Unfortunately, I just discovered that CCB doesn't work at all with standard universe. Why? Because the sockets that the shadow opens to communicate with the starter are created by connecting to the startd. It doesn't connect to the startd's command port (or all would be well). Instead, the startd creates two new listen ports and the shadow connects to those. One solution would be to have the shadow create the connections by connecting (in advance of ACTIVATE_CLAIM) to the startd command port with some kind of command that indicates to the startd that it should just hold on to those connections until ACTIVATE_CLAIM happens. There are other possible solutions, but I think this one would be the simplest. If that problem were solved, it would be possible to run standard universe jobs on a private execute node from a public submit node. It would still not be possible to run on a public execute node from a private submit node (or with a private checkpoint server). The reason is that the checkpoint is sent to the shadow (or checkpoint server) by creating a new connection, but the shadow and checkpoint server are not daemonCore, so this connection cannot be reversed via CCB.

title: Ticket #7141: Replace Python bindings tutorials in docs with rendered notebooks
description: The best and most recent version of our Python bindings tutorials are at https://github.com/htcondor/htcondor-python-bindings-tutorials. The versions in the manual have not tracked recent changes in that repository. In fact, doing so would be difficult because the tutorials in the manual are plain RST files, while the ones in that repo are Jupyter notebooks. This ticket removes those RST files and replaces them with pre-run Jupyter notebook files, rendered via https://nbsphinx.readthedocs.io/en/0.4.2/ Making this change does not remove the maintenance burden: whenever a change is made to the tutorial repo notebooks, that notebook should be executed and the resulting .ipynb file copied into the /docs in the main HTCondor repo. The files in the HTCondor repo should be considered read-only. This is a pain, but at least it will keep the content in sync without needing to interpolate between RST and notebooks. The above maintenance procedure will be described in plain-text files in both repositories.

title: Ticket #4297: Prototype vanilla universe self-checkpointing support.
description: (Also see #4968, this ticket's new parent.) I have code that will eat your babies. It will also periodically send a vanilla-universe job its "soft kill" signal (defaults to SIGTERM, can be adjusted via the submit-file attribute kill_sig), at intervals defined by the PERIODIC_CHECKPOINT (as respected by the standard and VM universes). It does so if and only if the job ad has WantCheckpoint and UserLevelCheckpoint set. Immediately after sending the signal, it performs intermediate file transfer. Under the above two conditions, this will result in periodic application-level checkpointing, with the caveat that the checkpoint stored by the shadow will always be one checkpoint interval old. If you would like this code to eat your babies, let me know for which platform and I'll send you the binaries. I would like to see if this approach can be made to work for people in practice before trying to clean it up. Obvious extensions include: some way of telling when the application is done checkpointing (watch a signal file?), which could be tricky, but would weaken condition (b), above; adding another job attribute to specify the checkpoint signal distinct from the kill signal, which should be simple but may be useless; and making the intermediate files go some place more useful than the shadow, which will probably be a pain. This is not any other ticket. (;)) In particular, it does not address the general use of third-party checkpointing. It does not address the use of standard universe binaries in stand-alone mode. It does not do fast evict/restarts. It is my understanding that this specific and narrowly-defined use case meets an existing user need, and if that is so, we'll get it for basically free in the process of doing vm-assisted checkpointing.
remarks: 2014-May-15 16:38:41 by tlmiller: Use V8_1-gittrac_4297-branch for follow-ups until V8_1-vc-branch is close to production. 2014-May-19 16:51:28 by tlmiller: Tannenbaum points out that requirement (b) is tough if the application stores state on-disk during normal operation, because the on-disk state will diverge from the stored state of the checkpoint. The application must either recover from this problem on resume, or ensure that the on-disk state visible to HTCondor only changes atomically. (For instance, if you specify the checkpoint file as 'checkpoint.tar.gz', a wrapper script could catch the signal and direct the application to take a checkpoint and pause (or exit). It could then tar up the whole of the required disk-state in a temporary file, (atomically) rename it to 'checkpoint.tar.gz, and then continue (or restart) the application.) This punts a lot of complexity to the user, which is not The HTCondor Way. However, if this will work for LIGO, it may be worth offering at least temporarily. A number of more-general solutions are outlined in #3138; the "intelligent starter" sounds like the least intrusive. Other tickets of interest may include: #1000, which could replaced by providing a wrapper script for stand-alone checkpointing (probably -- see #2007) #317, made obsolete by the above if nobody wants remote I/O (confirmed by HTCondor Week 2014 attendees) #1956, also made obsolete by the above #1323, assumed in this ticket #2007, which may be overkill for self-checkpointing #3771, which may have relevant bugs 2014-May-19 17:30:27 by tlmiller: Thoughts on the "intelligent starter" design: In VanillaProc::Ckpt(), send soft_kill_sig and set the isCheckpointing flag. Because we don't want to transfer files right away, return false. In the reaper, check isCheckpointing. If we are, and the process exited normally (with return code 0), do intermediate file transfer and then restart the job. Unset isCheckpointing. Do not send the "final job update". If we are but the process did not exit normally, assume it was our fault and exit appropriately. If told to vacate while checkpointing, set the vacate timer. (Verify that we don't (normally) do file transfer when hard-killing.) When the vacate timer fires, unset isCheckpointing and proceed as normal. 2014-May-19 17:39:55 by tlmiller: Thoughts on #2007: If we're assuming user-level self-checkpointing (even if that's standard universe stand-alone checkpointing), we can ignore the requirements for identifying the required checkpointing infrastructure. We could use chirp in the wrapper script to edit the Requirements expression to require the checkpoint platform, if it were available to the user. This may require some hacking (since condor_ckpt_probe doesn't report the whole checkpoint platform string). This would avoid privileging any given checkpointer in the vanilla universe without having to define the whole infrastructure in #2007. By adopting the convention that a cleanly exited return-code 0 job means a successful checkpoint, we can avoid both the problem of determining when the checkpoint is done and the need to specify the checkpoint assets. (Ignoring superfluous files is an orthogonal issue about dealing with intermediate files.) 2014-Sep-17 16:30:07 by tlmiller: We discussed this proposal with Peter Couvares on 2014-09-17, and he pointed that the exit code from a successful checkpoint must be a user-specified "special" one, to avoid a race condition where the job finishes between when HTCondor sends the periodic checkpoint signal and when the job finishing triggers the job reaper. 2014-Nov-05 12:45:18 by tlmiller: Tom Downes did some testing of the proof-of-concept. He noticed two issues. First, the standard out (and presumably, error) files we return to the user only include output (or error) since the most recent checkpoint (restart). This is at best disconcerting, and certainly counter to expectations; and it should be a relatively simple fix. Second, after a condor_vacate_job, we report an explicitly application-level checkpointing job as "not checkpointed", regardless of the actually success or failure of the checkpoint. This was at least in part to avoid accidentally triggering any standard universe -specific code, but it's deceptive and should be fixed (at a lower priority than the first, because it could get complicated). 2015-Mar-11 17:47:30 by tlmiller: Consider, even if this feature goes in as experimental, modifying condor_submit to know about WantCheckpointSignal. 2015-Mar-13 10:09:36 by tlmiller: Marked as experimental until we're sure we want people to be trying to use it without support for any kind of checkpoint server at all. 2015-Mar-13 10:14:21 by tlmiller: Added concatenation of output and error streams across runs. Doesn't work with streaming I/O yet. 2015-Mar-16 10:51:43 by tlmiller: ... and now it does. 2015-Mar-18 14:05:13 by tlmiller: Retro design doc: https://docs.google.com/a/wisc.edu/document/d/1leCtRalvU8YOEiNfwBD0j46pQv3yH4f3YrKgXDT_e4I/ 2015-May-20 16:24:57 by tlmiller: Example submit file... universe = vanilla executable = self-checkpointing transfer_executable = true should_transfer_files = true when_to_transfer_output = ON_EXIT_OR_EVICT +WantCheckpointSignal = true +CheckpointSig = "SIGUSR1" stream_output = true stream_error = true Note that the periodicity of the signal is defined by the startd, not the job; see the standard universe documentation for details. 2019-Sep-18 14:35:58 by tlmiller: I don't know why this was marked defer, but after four years, I'm certain it's no longer relevant.

title: Ticket #6750: A single cpu job may never match a pslot
description: The negotiator calculates how much slot-weight each submitter should get. However, we ignore the fact that when we give out a matching p-slot, we charge the whole amount of the pslot. This is particularly noticeable when Group Quotas are enabled, although the problem can happen even without group quotas. So, for example, in a newly-booted pool of 40 core machines, each with 40-core pslots, any group with a quota of < 40 will never match any machines. This ticket will patch the code so that one submitter per negotiation cycle is allowed to go over the limit.
