title: Ticket #6880: Python bindings don't build with python 3
description: The Boost 1.66 python bindings don't build with the python 3.7 that's commonly available on linux distros. This can be fixed with some small patches to Boost. There are two problems here, which both must be addressed. First, the signature of _PyUnicode_AsString() changed in python 3.7, and a use in Boost needs to add a cast. This is a back-port of a fix in later versions of Boost. Second, the python 3 include directory in rhel and fedora includes an 'm' suffix (i.e. /usr/include/python-3.7m). This indicates that python was built with the pymalloc custom allocator. The Boost python module thinks the directory doesn't have an 'm', and fails to build. This is a long-standing bug that others have hacked around by telling boost where the directory is. Multiple issue tickets about python include directory name bug in boost: https://svn.boost.org/trac10/ticket/6826 https://svn.boost.org/trac10/ticket/11120 https://github.com/boostorg/build/pull/250 https://github.com/boostorg/python/issues/187

Initial tests with installing the wheel package in my and karpel's Python 3.7 environments look good as well.

title: Ticket #5255: startd history should log if badput was due to policy or user
description: When a job is evicted, it can be because the user requested it, via condor_rm/condor_hold, or because the system evicted it due to policy (startd RANK, user prio preemption, draining). Otherwise, any preempted job will be from user action.

title: Ticket #1646: create StdUnivSock
description: Currently, standard universe uses ReliSock plus a number of things ReliSock depends on. Standard universe doesn't actually depend on a lot of the functionality of ReliSock. As a result, we end up including stuff in the syscall library that we don't really need (such as openssl). This also makes it difficult for us to maintain both standard universe and the rest of Condor, because we have to be careful about introducing new dependencies that break standard universe. Some things are stubbed out when linking with standard universe in order to avoid adding dependencies. Some object files are compiled twice with different precompiler flags. In general, this all makes it difficult to understand and maintain the code. Without investing much effort, we can derive a new socket class StdUnivSock that just includes the functionality that standard universe needs. I have found that it does not take much effort to refactor Stream so that we can reuse that code as the base class. More refactoring could lead to more code sharing (e.g. would be nice to get rid of std_univ_buffers.cpp), but we all agreed that sharing Stream was good enough.

title: Ticket #2969: The Directory object can't handle long paths on Windows
description: The condor directory object uses the Ansi entry points for the Windows API's. These entry points can't deal with paths > 260 characters. title: Ticket #4014: Starter selection for work fetch is error prone
description: When the startd wants to start a job, it calls StarterMgr::findStarter() to find the appropriate starter to use. If the job comes from a shadow, the startd already knows which starter it wants to use (indicated by the starter_num argument). In that case, findStarter() ignores the other starter types. For work fetch, startd passes -1 for starter_num, indicating it doesn't know which type of starter should be used. In this case, findStarter() will try all starters and use the first one for which the job's requirements are met. If the job's requirements don't mention any starter ability attributes, then it will match the first starter in the list. Fortunately, the daemon-core starter is first, which is what we want for anything other than standard universe. But if the order changes or someone wants to run a standard universe work fetch job (is the latter possible without a shadow?), then we'll get unexpected results. Whatever the startd does to determine which starter it wants before calling StarterMgr::findStarter(), that should be done for work fetch jobs.
remarks: 2013-Oct-28 14:50:34 by jfrey: When a job comes from a shadow, the shadow says which type of starter should be used. Maybe the best we can do for work fetch is to ensure that the new starter is always first in the list.

title: Ticket #1703: allow different semantics for multi-job clusters
description: (This was requested by Igor.) Currently, the semantics of multiple-job DAG nodes are that, if any job in the cluster fails, all remaining jobs are removed, and the node is considered failed. Igor wants to have an option to have different semantics: if any job succeeds, the node succeeds. We are proposing several changes to implement this: 1) There would be a new keyword NVARS, which would be similar to VARS, except that it would apply to the DAG semantics of a node, as opposed to getting passed to condor_submit. So we'd have something like: NVARS A permissive_cluster="true" We are also proposing new macros RETURN_LIST and RETURN_LIST_LEN that could be passed to a POST script. RETURN_LIST would be the exit codes for all jobs in the cluster, in procid order. RETURN_LIST_LEN would be the number of values in RETURN_LIST. This would enable users to implement more complex semantics if the needed to. RETURN_LIST and RETURN_LIST_LEN should be defined even if the old node semantics are used.
remarks: 2011-Mar-31 15:30:25 by wenger: Also see gittrac #349.

title: Ticket #366: Allow our ckpt tests to run against DMTCP
description: I really, really, really want to see if DMTCP checkpointing can pass our ckpt tests in our test suite. Ideally I'd like to know how well it does by/before 4/20/09. The work on this ticket is being performed on the V7_5-dmtcp_tests-branch. Milestones 12/06/09 - Checkin tarball of DMTCP and have test suite build it properly. [DONE] Figure out how the stduniv tests are currently built. [DONE] Make test suite build DMTCP tarball for the right machines with right flags. [DONE] Write a small source to link in libdmtcpaware.a and a helper object file which implements our checkpoint API. [DONE] Write new Imake.rules functions to build DMTCP-ified test programs. [DONE] Write the new link rules for all of our test programs. [DONE] 01/11/2010 - Run DMTCP test programs outside of Condor. Implement test harness in CondorDMTCP.pm to set up, run, and manage a DMTCP program. This is hard, and not yet done. Probably 2 weeks left or so. Write an example .run file for job_ckpt_combo-sanity_std. Found problems with DMTCP, this ticket is on hold at this stage. Future - Write all .run files for DMTCP tests outside of Condor Future - Run DMTCP test programs inside of Condor. Figure out how to utilize and check in my shim script and associated goo. Write a single test and see if it works. Write the rest of the tests. ... Plan Building DMTCP into our test suite For the initial plan, we have to determine exactly what DMTCP is in relation to the test suite, is it an external? A Prereq? Or what? Due to certain constraints: DMTCP will have many bugs fixed or features added incrementally. DMTCP exists in the layer between Condor and the User Job and so isn't really an external. Turnaround time for NMI reinstalling a new prereq or reconfiguring the compilation flags of DMTCP is high. I've decided that I'm going to check in a tarball of DMTCP into condor_tests and have the test suite build it for me. This allows the fastest development scenario for me because it prevents be blocking on NMI to update a prereq. Since DMTCP isn't used by the Condor source code itself, making it an external seems wrong--in addition the sync time between the afs directory and the externals web server slowing me down. After getting the test suite to build it, I will add in new Imake.rules functions similar to CLINK() which will link together the test executable with the dmtcp libraries and the condor-specific checkpointing API library. These rules should be called DBUILD(), DBUILD_DEP(), and DLINK() and be aware of if HAVE_DMTCP_ABILITY is defined along with IS_CLIPPED. Running DMTCP tests in the test suite For this aspect, I'm initially going to have a .run file which just runs and checkpoints/restarts the DMTCP executable outside of Condor all together. This is easier for me to implement as a first pass, and checkpointing inside of Condor or outside of Condor are functionally identical from the point of view of DMTCP. Each .run file will start a unique coordinator for the purposes of the test under consideration. This models what would happen inside of Condor and I don't have to worry about checkpoint requests stomping on other simultaneously running DMTCP test jobs. (In the DMTCP world view, there is one coordinator for many processes, related or not. In Condor's world view, there is a unique DMTCP coordinator per slot alive only when the job is running). Later, I'll check in the shim_script and have the checkpoints done inside of Condor itself. This will test the movement of the files and checkpoints back and for from the spool. It seems to me that the .run logic for running DMTCP tests inside of Condor is sufficiently different that it warrants a different .run file from that of running the DMTCP test program outside of Condor. Having different ones for running inside of Condor is a feature since it allows us to alter how we integrate DMTCP with Condor without compromising the bare testing of DMTCP with our stduniv programs.

title: Ticket #3694: short hostname no longer usable in condor_status
description: condor_status now requires use of FQHN. [jrthomas@small BUILD]$ condor_status small [jrthomas@small BUILD]$ condor_status small.mydom.com Name OpSys Arch State Activity LoadAv Mem ActvtyTime slot1@small.mydom. LINUX X86_64 Unclaimed Idle 0.000 3828 0+02:44:44 Machines Owner Claimed Unclaimed Matched Preempting X86_64/LINUX 1 0 0 1 0 0 Total 1 0 0 1 0 0
remarks: 2013-Jun-12 07:50:53 by jrt: Earliest version I see this in is 7.8.6, but I also see it in 7.9.1. The change in behavior came out of the switch to ipv6 code. 2013-Jun-27 12:31:24 by tannenba: Doing condor_status chevre results in the following query going to the collector (note the blank Name and Machine constraints): Projection = "Name Machine Opsys Arch State Activity LoadAvg Memory ActvtyTime MyCurrentTime EnteredCurrentActivity" MyType = "Query" TargetType = "Machine" CurrentTime = time() Requirements = ( ( ( Name == "" ) || ( Machine == "" ) ) ) But try it with condor_status chevre.foo.edu, that is the name is fully-qualified (i.e. it has a period character in it), then a proper query is sent: Projection = "Name Machine Opsys Arch State Activity LoadAvg Memory ActvtyTime MyCurrentTime EnteredCurrentActivity" MyType = "Query" TargetType = "Machine" CurrentTime = time() Requirements = ( ( ( Name == "chevre.foo.edu" ) || ( Machine == "chevre.foo.edu" ) ) To make an active connection, the only directory service consulted should be the collector. Kinda looks like the daemon locate method is using DNS to try and convert a short name into a fully-qualified name before sending a query to the collector - I would love to see this crazy behavior from the dawn of Condor go away. The behavior in HTCondor of the daemon locate method making any calls at all into DNS is, imo, broken design. Instead of leaning on DNS to go from short to fqhn (full qualified host name), why not just send a query to the collector that is appropriate if given a short name? I.e. a query that uses regular expressions to strip out the short name from Name and Machine if the locate method is only given a short name. I realize the above may be more appropriate for the dev series, and we still need something in the stable series... but I would hate to see DNS used even in v8.0.x.... Thoughts? 2013-Aug-01 08:07:27 by jrt: We also saw the same behavior with condor_config_val. Further investigation and the original problem is looking like a bug in glibc in RHEL6 using AF_INET. $python >>> from socket import * >>> getaddrinfo("small", "80", AF_INET, 0, 0, AI_CANONNAME) >>> getaddrinfo("small", "80", AF_UNSPEC, 0, 0, AI_CANONNAME) both of the above should return the FQDN. 2013-Aug-09 18:58:43 by eje: Regarding Todd's comments above, I'm personally agnostic about whether expansion is best driven by DNS or from a collector query. Regarding timing, now our stable series is 8.0 -- It would serve my purposes best to get this in as-is for 8.0 series, however it seems reasonable to spawn a ticket for 8.1 for migrating to a collector-based name resolution if there is sufficient interest. 2013-Aug-12 14:58:42 by eje: topic branch for review: V8_0-gt3694-short-hostnames TEST: Spin up a pool. execute condor_status to check behavior: # short hostname $ _CONDOR_TOOL_DEBUG=D_HOSTNAME condor_status -debug localhost 2>&1 | grep -e 'Requirements =' -e 'Returning daemon name' 08/12/13 12:57:09 Returning daemon name: "localhost.localdomain" Requirements = ( ( ( Name == "localhost.localdomain" ) || ( Machine == "localhost.localdomain" ) ) ) # long hostname $ _CONDOR_TOOL_DEBUG=D_HOSTNAME condor_status -debug localhost.localdomain 2>&1 | grep -e 'Requirements =' -e 'Returning daemon name' 08/12/13 12:57:24 Returning daemon name: "localhost.localdomain" Requirements = ( ( ( Name == "localhost.localdomain" ) || ( Machine == "localhost.localdomain" ) ) ) # no hostname $ _CONDOR_TOOL_DEBUG=D_HOSTNAME condor_status -debug 2>&1 | grep -e 'Requirements =' -e 'Returning daemon name' Requirements = true 2013-Aug-12 16:25:51 by johnkn: I'm not really qualified to review this patch. It appears to me to have the potential for for LOTS of side effects, and I'm quite certain it won't solve the problem for our RUST user. I'd like to see it actually work over some period of time in the developer series before we inflict it on stable. In any case, Alan De Smet needs to be one to review it. 2013-Aug-12 17:24:02 by adesmet: Changing the query to eliminate DNS is the "right" answer. However, that may constitute new behavior and thus be better suited for 8.1. If we don't want the "right" answer in 8.0, this approach seems broadly reasonable... but, it may not fix the case TJ mentions (that will require a proper code review). And it needs a review. I can review, but it's not happening until the week of the 19th at the earliest, and it may be later as I have a backlog of priority interrupts. 2013-Aug-22 16:02:39 by jfrey: This patch restores the functionality of the old get_full_hostname() and get_full_hostname_from_hostent() (before Min's ipv6 code went in). We should be checking h_name before h_aliases in the hostent struct. get_fqdn_and_ip_from_hostname() and get_hostname_with_alias() are similarly broken. 2013-Aug-22 16:22:59 by jfrey: On closer inspection, it appears get_hostname_with_alias() is ok as-is. The list it builds should already contain the canonical hostname, obtained from get_hostname(). 2013-Sep-12 15:46:47 by adesmet: CODE REVIEW: Approved hostnamev4.patch is approved with no changes.
attachments: hostnamev3.patch 617 bytes added by jrt on 2013-Jun-12 12:48:27 UTC. In some cases, getaddrinfo doesn't get the FQDN in the result addrinfo. Calling it with a short hostname can in some cases return only the short hostname. In these cases, it appears that gethostbyname and subsequent alias check will fail too because there is no FQDN alias. So, get_fqdn_from_hostname will fail on a known hostname. However, it appears that in these cases, the hostent from the gethostbyname call will have the FQDN in it's h_name. Unsure of exact case where this happens. I see it with dnsmasq as dns server. hostnamev4.patch 956 bytes added by jfrey on 2013-Aug-22 22:09:12 UTC. Updated patch for hostname resolution.

title: Ticket #1353: New DaemonCore::Register_Timer: take param name for repeat rate
description: When you DaemonCore::Register_Timer a timer, you can set a one-off time, or a repeating timer. Repeating timers have a fixed repeat interval. Many timers are set based on param_integer("SOME_NAME", default_val). You could pass this value into Register_Timer as the repeat rate, but then you'd need to pay attention to reconfig requests and DaemonCore::Reset_Timer it. This can be a nuisance if your code isn't already fretting about the reconfig request. As a result, there is a lot of code that sets one-off timers and upon firing immediately re-adds itself. For example, dc_touch_log_file in /src/condor_daemon_core.V6/daemon_core_main.cpp : int dc_touch_log_file( Service* ) { dprintf_touch_log(); daemonCore->Register_Timer( param_integer( "TOUCH_LOG_INTERVAL", 60 ), (TimerHandler)dc_touch_log_file, "dc_touch_log_file" ); return TRUE; } This is redundant. Instead we should offer a Register_Timer that takes a param name and default and automatically does this for us. The interface might look something like: // Param name default val if no param daemonCore->Register_Timer_param( "TOUCH_LOG_INTERVAL", 60 (TimerHandler)dc_touch_log_file, "dc_touch_log_file" ); This would eliminate some redundancy. It can also eliminate complexity where code watches for the reconfig and Reset_Timers itself. Reduced complexity will hopefully lead to fewer bugs, especially when people are working on related tasks (see #1337 for an example of how a minor mistake in the timer system can trash the entire entire system)

title: Ticket #5310: Subsystem-specific config params sometimes ignored
description: If a configuration parameter is set to something other than the default, and then the default value is set for a specific subsystem, the subsystem-specific setting is ignored. If the subsystem-specific value is different than the default, then it is treated as expected. For example, take a config file that contains the following: # The default in the param table is False USE_SHARED_PORT = True SCHEDD.USE_SHARED_PORT = False STARTD.USE_SHARED_PORT = 0 The value of USE_SHARED_PORT will be True everywhere, including in the schedd. % condor_config_val USE_SHARED_PORT True % condor_config_val -subsystem schedd USE_SHARED_PORT True % condor_config_val -subsystem startd USE_SHARED_PORT 0 %

title: Ticket #2085: Write shim script for blahp-over-ssh
description: For blahp-over-ssh, we need a simple script that the gridmanager will invoke as a gahp server. The script needs to ssh to the appropriate remote system, dealing with authentication in the process, invoke the blahp on the remote side, and forward all data on stdio between the gridmanager and blahp. Ssh will handle the forwarding of stdio for us. The script needs to invoke it in the correct way. We can't assume ssh-agent is already running to allow password-less login. We'll need to store the passphrase protecting the ssh credentials in a safe manner and provide it to ssh on demand. Here is a list of required features: Select one of multiple servers, as indicated by the gridmanager. The gridmanager will pass the name of the desired server as the first command-line argument. Read the passphrase to decrypt the ssh credentials from a file and supply it to ssh when required. Store the passphrase to decrypt the ssh credentials in an encrypted form. Forward all stdin, stdout, and stderr between gridmanager and blahp. Extra text written by ssh to stdout should not be forwarded to the gridmanager. These are optional features we may want to add at a later date: Allow blahp path and ssh credentials to be different for different remote servers. Allow name from gridmanager to be a label, with script translating to real hostname.
remarks: 2011-Apr-27 13:43:19 by jfrey: We have a test system setup on tonic and glow-c004. I have a Condor installation built from V7_7-blahp_over_ssh-branch on tonic under /scratch.1/jfrey/condor-blahp_over_ssh. Included are a bare-bones ssh shim script and sample submit file. Josh can copy this installation, modify the shim script, and submit test jobs. glow-c004 is our one-machine pbs cluster. On it, I have a Condor installation, including the blahp, under /home/jfrey/condor-7.7.0. I also have a wrapper script for invoking the blahp remotely under /home/jfrey/remote-test/batch_gahp.wrapper. The wrapper is necessary because the blahp requires an environment variable to be set telling it where to find the rest of its files. 2011-May-05 12:13:02 by jfrey: The shim script looks good. Here are a couple changes I'd like to see: The scripts needs to be able to connect to one of several remote systems. The first command-line argument to the script should name the system to use. You can ignore the rest of the command line arguments. Ideally, the script would have a switch statement that can set the variables differently for different servers. The passphrase for the ssh key file should be read from a file, not stored directly in the script. The passphrase shouldn't be passed as a command-line argument to the expect script. title: Ticket #2768: Monitor startd swapping rates
description: We have several handles on the node swap rate (either for the whole node, or per-job). We should report these statistics, both in the startd ad and the job ads. It's likely the swap rate is a more interesting number than the absolute amount of swap used, as high swap usage but very low swap rate affects the resource utilization differently from low swap usage but high swap rate. Note - the per-job swap rate is based on the availability of this information in the memory cgroup. While this is available on RHEL6 by default, Fedora 16 has turned it off by default (it's now an optional boot parameter), complaining about the overhead of instrumenting swap. We should try to understand the direction the community is going on this topic.

title: Ticket #6681: bake-in relevant functions of singularity wrappers to Condor
description: From a few sources, I've heard that the OSG uses a job wrapper to handle a lot of the corner cases of Singularity jobs. Finally saw it today and I'm told this one is in use at Madison. I think Singularity (2.5.1) might be doing this now, because running singularity shell gives me a prompt with the name of the target in it rather than the link. Hard-coded binding a few mountpoints in (e.g. /hadoop). This can be realized with SINGULARITY_BIND_EXPR. Bring in some extra bind points based on Job ClassAd (e.g. GPU, CVMFS). Are these generic enough to bake in? Set --contain (if not GPU jobs) and --ipc and --pid. It looks to me like Condor now uses -C (which is equivalent) by default but do not know if that is uniformly used for all jobs. Fix working directory in OSG-appropriate manner. I have filed #6676 to discuss precisely this point. Although the ticket has "shared filesystems" in its name, I believe the issue to be more generic. Fix X509 environment variables. This may have been resolved by #6625 and the recent release? So, for starters, this probably isn't a full enumeration of the functionality. But, since it's in use at Madison, there must be a reason for it and some local expertise with it. In the grand spirit of HTCondor, there should be a knob / standard-ish job transform snippets for the bits that are generic. I'm particularly concerned about #6676 and IWD handling. I'm pushing Singularity very hard with some interested users and I'll admit to some frustration that a lot of effort must of gone into this wrapper but not so much into helping the HTCondor team identify the problems it's solving. To give an example, I believe the X509 problem was resolved in a week or two in response to a report by Matthias Schnepf from Germany. When... quite literally you have someone fixing it in a job wrapper down the hall from you. Can we view this as a starting point for understanding where Singularity support stands and what might be snuck in before 8.8?

title: Ticket #171: Be able to save output of PRE and POST scripts.
description: Currently, stdout and stderr of PRE and POST scripts in DAGMan is lost -- it would be nice to be able to save it somewhere.
remarks: 2013-Dec-13 10:04:29 by wenger: I was just thinking about this (after TimC asked about it yesterday), and one question is where the output should go. In general, the submit file for the job doesn't have to be defined before the PRE script runs, so we can't really do something based on, say, the output value in the submit file. (And, of course, the user doesn't have to define output.) Right now I can see two ways to do it: Add some new keywords to the DAG to specify where the output should go. Cons up some kind of default, like foo.dag.nodeX.pre.out. title: Ticket #3529: Multiple file transfer worker threads can crash daemon
description: The FileTransfer object keeps a hash table to track child processes created to perform transfers. A pointer to the hash table is a static member of FileTransfer. An entry is inserted when a child process is created and removed when a child process is reaped. Whenever a FileTransfer object is created, the hash table allocated if it isn't already. When a FileTransfer object is destroyed, the hash table is also destroyed (and the pointer set to NULL) if it doesn't have any entries. If a daemon creates two FileTransfer objects, deletes one, then creates a child process to perform a transfer for the other object, the process crashes due to a NULL pointer deference. We should leave the hash table in place once it's created, never deleting it. The amount of memory used by an empty table is tiny. This problem was first observed in the condor_gridmanager and condor_ft-gahp with Bosco. Everywhere else in HTCondor, no more than one FileTransfer object is in existence at a time. (Well, also the transfer daemon, but that's not used.)

title: Ticket #3196: SPOOL is wrong with multiple schedds
description: John Wiegand at Fermi noticed a bug in Condor when multiple schedds are defined. See the initial message, reply, and simple demonstration of the bug.
remarks: 2012-Aug-21 22:40:22 by nwp: The easy solution is to eliminate the default value of JOB_QUEUE_LOG in the param table (that is, revert 395c915). Or, is it envisioned that something like the following is supposed to work? SCHEDD.xxyyz.SPOOL=/foo SCHEDD.yywwt.SPOOL=/foo2 JOB_QUEUE_LOG=$(SPOOL)/bar Then JOB_QUEUE_LOG evaluates to /foo/bar for schedd xxyyz and to /foo2/bar for schedd yywwt. What is the downside of a simple revert? 2012-Aug-22 08:37:11 by tstclair: From what I recollect about the param system, the above is not possible in some cases. Thus the only solution that is valid is removal from the param table. 2012-Aug-22 09:38:52 by nwp: I am setting this to review for Greg T, since Greg put this in the param table in the first place. 2012-Sep-12 13:42:06 by nwp: Let's get some wisdom written down on this topic. For concreteness, lets consider an example from a configuration file. LOCAL_DIR= /scratch/nwp/personal-condor SPOOL= $(LOCAL_DIR)/spool SCHEDD.SCHEDDJOBS2.SCHEDD_NAME = schedd_jobs2 SCHEDD.SCHEDDJOBS2.SCHEDD_LOG = $(LOG)/SchedLog.$(SCHEDD.SCHEDDJOBS2.SCHEDD_NAME) SCHEDD.SCHEDDJOBS2.LOCAL_DIR = $(LOCAL_DIR)/$(SCHEDD.SCHEDDJOBS2.SCHEDD_NAME) SCHEDD.SCHEDDJOBS2.SPOOL = $(SCHEDD.SCHEDDJOBS2.LOCAL_DIR)/spool I think this configuration is enough to show what is involved. At this point in the code, there are two ways to look up a configuration/param macro. The code either calls param and associated param_*; functions, or it can call lookup_macro. Now, with the configuration above, what happens? Let's assume we are in the schedd, with a local-name set to SCHEDDJOBS2. When the code calls param("LOCAL_DIR"), param first tries to lookup "SCHEDD.SCHEDDJOBS2.LOCAL_DIR", then "SCHEDD.LOCAL_DIR", then "LOCAL_DIR". Of course the first lookup succeeds (and the other two are not looked up), and param will find "$(LOCAL_DIR)/$(SCHEDD.SCHEDDJOBS2.SCHEDD_NAME)". Then param calls lookup_macro. The lookup_macro code does not try to scope the LOCAL_DIR on the right-hand side, so it returns "/scratch/nwp/personal-condor", and it looks up "SCHEDD.SCHEDDJOBS2.SCHEDDNAME", to get "schedd_jobs2". So param("LOCAL_DIR") returns "/scratch/nwp/personal-condor/schedd_jobs2" and lookup_macro("LOCAL_DIR") returns "/scratch/nwp/personal-condor". I tried to simply add the param scoping behavior into lookup_macro, but I just got into an infinite loop, since the code kept expanding SCHEDD.SCHEDDJOBS2.LOCAL_DIR over and over; essentially, the code was trying to figure out what SCHEDD.SCHEDDJOBS2.LOCAL_DIR = $(SCHEDD.SCHEDDJOBS2.LOCAL_DIR)/$(SCHEDD.SCHEDDJOBS2.SCHEDD_NAME) means; on its face, it is not clear what is the meaning; so I stopped working on it.

title: Ticket #937: outgoing security session caching is broken with CCB
description: Outgoing security sessions are being cached by IP:port of the peer, but in the case of a CCB connection, the port is an ephemeral port, which is likely to be different each time we connect to the same daemon. This typically results in renegotiation security in situations where we could have used a cached session. It could also result in an inappropriate security session being used if two different daemons on the same IP use the same ephemeral port in different instances. We did not notice this problem before, because SEC_ENABLE_MATCH_PASSWORD_AUTHENTICATION sidesteps the problem by forcing the use of a pre-created security session.
remarks: 2009-Nov-12 15:32:47 by danb: This problem is fixed for 7.4.1. 2009-Nov-12 15:41:32 by danb: I should also note a related problem addressed by the same patch: when the connection is closed in response to DC_AUTHENTICATE, secman tries to send a raw command int (no security negotiation). It does this by closing the socket and reconnecting. The address it was using to reconnect to was the peer's connected address, which in the case of a reversed CCB connection contains an ephemeral port, not appropriate for reconnecting to.

title: Ticket #5412: HTCondor View: rolling file name format
description: Requirements The HTCondor View client needs to be able to identify which files available on the HTCondor View server it must load to display a given date range's worth of data. The client should do so without asking the server for dynamic information. We cannot assume that the server will provide any sort of automatic, parseble directory listing. The files will be in multiple sampling resolutions, which more dense sampling kept in files covering smaller intervals. The number of old files will vary based on the interval. Server Specifications Summary End up with a bunch of files like: machine.oldest.json machine.monthly.2015-11.json machine.monthly.2015-10.json machine.monthly.2015-09.json machine.weekly.2015-W48.json machine.weekly.2015-W47.json machine.daily.2015-11-23.json machine.daily.2015-11-22.json submitter.oldest.json submitter.monthly.2015-11.json submitter.monthly.2015-10.json submitter.monthly.2015-09.json submitter.weekly.2015-W48.json submitter.weekly.2015-W47.json submitter.daily.2015-11-23.json submitter.daily.2015-11-22.json * .daily. *, * .weekly. *, and * .monthly. * are JSON files with data covering the specified period. * .oldest are JSON files identifying the oldest data available for each type of data. For example: { "monthly": "2015-09", "weekly": "2015-W47", "daily": "2015-11-22" } All dates and times are in UTC. Details The data files are JSONish, notably missing the framing "[]" that an array would normally require and allowing an extra "," after the last entry. The "[]" and "," are allowed, although if the framing "[]" is present, the extraneous "," after the last record is not. Otherwise data is in any format Afterquery understands. A set of files will be kept for each TYPE of data. Types might include "submitters" and "machines." For each TYPE, there will be files for several intervals: daily, weekly, and monthly. For each TYPE and interval there will be a file for each period. Intervals will start at midnight. Weekly intervals start on Monday (matching ISO 8601). Monthly intervals start on the first of the month. File may be missing because the server was down for that period, or no records have yet been written to the current period. All dates and times are in UTC. For weekly files, the year rolls over on the Monday of the first week to include a Thursday in the new year. (Or put another way: the week that includes January 4th.) This means the "year" can be ahead or behind the year as generally understood. For example Sunday, January 3rd, 2016 is 2015-W53 while Monday, January 4th, 2016 is 2016-W01. Monday, December 31st, 2018 is 2019-W01. If you're using strftime %G may get you the year you want. The file name will consist of the TYPE (eg "submitters"), the period description ("monthly"), and the shortest ISO 8601 data that will uniquely identify the start of the period. Unneeded fields in the data can be dropped. Monthly: TYPE.monthly.2015-11.json - strftime("%Y-%m") Weekly: TYPE.weekly.2015-W48.json - strftime("%G-W%V") Daily: TYPE.daily.2015-11-23.json - strftime("%Y-%m-%d") Hourly: TYPE.hourly.2015-11-23T15.json (This is an example. Hourly logs are not currently planned.) Old files will be deleted on a regular basis. While likely user configurable in the future, as a starting point: Daily: Keep 2 files, sample every 5 minutes Weekly: Keep 2 files, sample every hour Monthly: Keep 12 files, sample every 2 hours The server will also maintain an additional file with the TYPE and ".oldest." It contains information on the oldest data available for each interval for that type. It is a JSON list of Objects. Each object has an "interval" (eg "monthly") and "oldest" (eg "2014-12") When the server starts up, it will fill in this file if it's missing. When the server deletes old data, it will replace this file with updated information. It is acceptable to set an oldest date that does not yet exist; it is likely on initial server startup. Example TYPE.oldest.json file: { "monthly": "2015-09", "weekly": "2015-W47", "daily": "2015-11-22", "hourly": "2015-11-22T15" } File Data The dated JSON files contain data in any form that Afterquery can parse. However, every record must have a "Date" field which contains a UTC time and date stamp in a form Afterquery can parse. (Non-UTC times are acceptable so long as they contain time zone information in a way that Afterquery can correctly interpret.) Client Notes The most common use case is "for a given interval, give me the two most recent files". We need two because the most recent file will only contain up to a given interval's worth of data. Two files ensure we receive at least an interval's worth of data. This is being treated as a special case of the more general case. The more general case is "Get me data between these two timestamps. All data must use the same interval. If possible no more than two files will be loaded. Given those constraints, select the highest resolution possible." The client will use the In both cases the client is almost guaranteed to end up with more data than requested. The client will filter it out. The client will not just display all of the data; doing so would leave to automatically-updating graphs slowly expanding the period covered, then suddenly snapping back to the minimum. Strictly limiting the range will provide smooth animations. Rationale The files could have ended with ".0" ".1" and so on, and be rotated. Files with time/date stamps in the name were chose so that: Easy for the client to calculate which files it should read. A server which is down for an entire period doesn't need to stub in an empty rollover file to ensure the client's calculations match. Eliminates race conditions when the client is requesting files while the server is rolling them over. I considered one .oldest file per TYPE and interval ("TYPE.monthly.oldest" "TYPE.weekly.oldest"). Rejected as requiring additional unnecessary file writes and HTTP requests. In particular, the client will often need to check multiple oldest entries to decide which files to load. The file is small enough that that overhead will drown out the tiny file savings. Dates are all in UTC because the client has no idea what time zone the server is in. It's more straightforward for everyone to work in UTC than for the server to publish time zone information and the client to convert into it (with bonus points for dealing with daylight savings).

title: Ticket #4829: ENABLE_IPV6 only works in top-level condor_config
description: GSI auth fails unless ENABLE_IPV6 is set in the global condor_config. This is because GSI auth relies on verification of forward-resolution; forward resolution relies on ipv6_getaddrinfo, which calls get_default_hint(). get_default_hint invokes _condor_is_ipv6_mode; this function caches the param value on the first call (which is invoked after the global condor_config but before the rest of configuration has been done). So, unless ENABLE_IPV6 is set globally, get_default_hint forces the use of IPv4 addresses in ipv6_getaddrinfo. Accordingly, GSI clients will reject GSI servers. There are probably other users of forward resolution that are expecting it to work. I see no reason to cache the value of the param_boolean call; if the lookup was done from the config system each time, this would work.

I'm not sure what the caching was intended to accomplish. 2015-Jan-14 12:53:50 by bbockelm: I think, as part of the work for 8.3.2, the dependency on the cached value was reduced to only get_default_hint() for getaddrinfo(). title: Ticket #6814: Improve JobEventLog (python) API
description: Josh has found a number of infelicities while working with the JobEventLog in a non-testing capacity. The JobEventLog doesn't close its FDs until it's been garbage-collected. This causes problems on Windows, where the open FDs prevent directory removal. Proposed solution: add a close() method which closes any open FDs and prevents the JobEventLog iterator from returning any events. The JobEventLog should also be an iterable context manager. (Implement __enter__ (sets timeout to 0) and __exit__ (calls close). The JobEvent doesn't provide access to its underlying ClassAd. The goal here is to make attributes discoverable, so maybe the right thing to do is to add the various dictionary methods (maybe not including writes); see how to emulate container types for Python 2.7 and Python 3.7. The advantage of doing this over just exposing the ClassAd would be (a) no copies or no worries about exposing a mutable internal data structure and (b) the job event "ClassAds" really are dictionaries -- they should never contain an ExprTree. See #6820 for the Python 2.7 implementation. Python 3.7 drops the iter*() methods, but changes keys(), values(), and items() to return 'view objects'. Not sure what the idiomatic solution here is. We should implement __str__ and __repr__.
remarks: 2018-Nov-01 14:21:44 by tlmiller: I think this list is up-to-date. Let me know, or if I've misrepresented something. 2018-Nov-01 14:32:56 by karpel: Looks right to me. A rationale for exposing the entire classad (maybe through a .classad() method?) is that it could help a lot when developing. You grab the classad and can then print it out to look at all the attributes. When you know what you want, you go back to . syntax to extract them efficiently. A significant part of my frustration with figuring out how to use the events is figuring out which names have what information behind them. 2018-Nov-01 15:23:23 by tlmiller: Thanks. Body text updated. 2018-Nov-02 14:27:54 by karpel: TJ asked me to give some thoughts on possible __str__ and __repr__ methods. __str__ should probably return the message that shows up in the actual event log on disk. If not, there should probably be a event_msg() method that does do that. This would make it easy to use the bindings to stream the event log as-written to somewhere else (stdout is obvious, but maybe over a network to somewhere else). __repr__ is murkier, but a somewhat-common convention is to return something that looks sort of like a constructor call with keyword arguments. So maybe it would look something like <SubmitEvent(cluster=1, proc=2, timestamp=1234)> Different event types could then include different parameters. Alternatively, all events could just look like <JobEvent(type=Submit, cluster=1, proc=2, timestamp=1234)> The main purpose of the __repr__ is for programmers to look at, so I don't think there needs to be a lot of information there - just a little more than the default, which is to show the memory location :) 2018-Nov-07 11:06:52 by tlmiller: We should also think about dictionary- vs attribute- based accessors. Arguably, the properties we guarantee should be attributes and the ones we don't in the dictionary (and maybe decline to do anything in __setAttr__() for the constants?). 2018-Nov-07 13:13:00 by karpel: That divide between attributes and other items makes sense to me. This: >>> x = (0, 1, 2) >>> x[0] = 5 Traceback (most recent call last): File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module> TypeError: 'tuple' object does not support item assignment indicates that the correct thing to do for __setattr__ and __setitem__ is to raise a TypeError, which seems like an odd choice to me, but I guess it's what's done... I don't see any reason to have any mutable attributes or items visible from Python. People can build a mutable object of their own by getting data from the event if they want, but the event itself should always represent exactly what came out of the log. 2018-Nov-08 14:45:46 by tlmiller: After talking with TJ and Mat, our plan is to basically deprecate / actually remove the __getattr__ method, make type, cluster, and proc immutable attributes, and implement __getkey__ but not __setkey__, where __getkey__ will throw if asked for a key that doesn't exit, rather than return None. The TypeError thing seems a little weird to me, but I'll investigate that a little further; I expect that if we just don't define __setkey__, the right thing(s) will happen. 2018-Dec-11 14:18:22 by tlmiller: At this point (with everything else implemented), I'd like to make Python 3 container type stuff a different ticket. title: Ticket #2011: Investigate Condor / GPU integration for LIGO
description: DONE.... Contact Carsten DONE.... Review Carsten's RFC on condor-users DONE.... Give feedback on immediate possible improvements DONE.... Update this ticket with info. DONE.... (Long deadline due to other deadlines pressing and Condor Week) - Have another chat with Carsten, update this ticket with info. ???????? Ongoing discussion; some basic experimentation with CUDA/OpenCL to try and answer a few technical questions. ???????? Identify functionality that we can provide immediately. ???????? Identify places where Condor is can't provide that functionality. Random notes General implementation ideas Manage GPUs as part of the resources partionable with dynamic slots Current "one dynamic slot per machine per negotiation cycle" limit applies, but we may be working on that separately. Suffers slot fragmentation problems. Manage GPUs similar to existing concurrency limits (typically used for software licenses). "I have 4 GPUs available. Oh, someone just claimed one, now I have 3." Simpler model, with attendant loss of nuance. Notably messy if a machine has mixed GPUs. Current concurrency limits are global; this would need to be per machine. Usage open questions Do users want/need coallocation? "I need 3 GPUs and 2 CPUs"? Carsten reports that developers are currently interested 1 GPU and N CPUs, but expected interest in M GPUs and N CPUs eventually, especially if the functionality is available. What information should Condor automatically detect and advertise? Probably start with Carsten's configuration. Some benchmarks? Is there anything good? Make it easy to add more benchmarks with Condor cron support! Do a minimal smoke test? (Specifically mentioned by Carsten, but probably not important.) Are pools likely to have mixes of GPUs? Is a given machine likely to have different GPUs? (Say, replacement of failed parts when the original is no longer available.) Can Condor help make GPU programs more portable or easier to start up by providing a "GPU" universe (or more likely feature) akin to the "Java" universe"? We might recompile GPU programs (although isn't this usually done at run time via the normal API), or provide paths to local libraries/binaries. Technical open questions Is is possible to hard limit a job to a particular GPU, to prevent misuse of GPUs as a result of malice or error? Slot user accounts and permissions on Linux? Carsten expressed interest in this. Can we make it easier for a job to use the correct GPU? Currently limited to passing in the GPU identifier (0-n) on the command line or in the environment. Do we need to do any cleanup of a GPU job to ensure that old GPU programs aren't left running and old data isn't left on the card? Who handles the cleanup? If it's a library, we probably need to clean up to recover abnormal terminations. If it's the OS, we can probably trust it. Hybrid CPU/GPU devices (AMD's Fusion, surely others) need consideration. AMD and nVidia's implementations may not co-exist. Is it enough to have suitable library on disk and (maybe) set LD_LIBRARY_PATH for the job? Might we need to relink the job with the suitable library? Random notes ziliang has previously worked with CUDA/nVidia and OpenCL/AMD (and possibly OpenCL/nVidia?) and has offered advice and assistance. Carsten Aulbert Carsten's configuration runs a program that emits a section of condor_config file that advertises GPU information. It is run on machine boot, so it should be up-to-date assuming no one invents hot-swappable GPUs on us. The relevant information is: Attribute/Setting Example Meaning SLOT1_GPU_CUDA_DRV =3.20 Driver version (Requires CUDA runtime 2020 or later) SLOT1_GPU_CUDA_RUN =3.20 Runtime version (Requires CUDA runtime 2020 or later) SLOT1_GPU_DEV =0 Device number, unique per GPU, as known to the CUDA API SLOT1_GPU_NAME ="Tesla C2050" Device name SLOT1_GPU_CAPABILITY= 2.0 Device's compute capability major.minor SLOT1_GPU_GLOBALMEM_MB =2687 Device memory in MB (CUDA API provides in bytes, this is X/(1024*1024)) SLOT1_GPU_MULTIPROC =14 Number of multiprocessors (Requires CUDA runtime 2000 or later) SLOT1_GPU_NUMCORES =32 Number of cores per multiprocessor (Requires CUDA runtime 2000 or later) Is directly based on GPU_CAPABILITY. A given GPU_CAPABILITY has a given number of cores per multiprocessor. SLOT1_GPU_CLOCK_GHZ =1.15 Clock in GHz (CUDA API provides kHz, this is X*1e-6f) Carsten is interested in using dynamic slots with GPUs. They are planning on moving the machines in question to dynamic slots anyway, and it would be nice if GPUs were part of the partitionable resources.

title: Ticket #6951: Allows schedd to mistrust certain startds
description: Currently in HTCondor, the startd is a highly-trusted daemon, even if the startd advertised itself to the pool with the identity of a minimally-trusted user. If that user misconfigured their startds, that could have serious negative effects on other users' jobs. CHTC minimizes this problem for annex users by only allowing the annex startds to report to a different collector; a user must therefore opt in to danger by requesting flocking. This is hardly ideal. Although this could be a problem with GSI, in practice, everyone goes through glideInWMS, which correctly configures its startds. Multiple pool passwords (#6947) are in part designed to make this situation more common, by making it easier to establish potentially lower-trust relationships. However, with multiple pool passwords, we could establish a connection between the identity used by a startd to join the pool and which jobs the schedd is willing to start running there. The collector already records the authenticated identity with which the startd advertised itself; if we don't already, we should be simple to add this to the match ad. At this point, the initial proposal is for the schedd, when looking for a job to run on a claim whose authenticated identity is not trusted, to restrict its search to those jobs whose owner matches the authenticated identity of the startd. The schedd could reduce pointless matches by including this constraint in its resource request(s) for that user. It would seem fair to also teach the accountant not to count resources contributed by the user against their priority in the rest of the pool. Follow-up work could include more sophisticated constraints, or a way for users to opt-in to using another user's startds (if allowed).
remarks: 2019-Mar-10 23:24:09 by bbockelm: One use case this wouldn't cover is a "PI who purchases a HTCondor annex for his group"; this would only allow a PI to consume hosts from a HTCondor annex which she bought for herself. It wouldn't allow her to "gift" CPU time to her grad students. Another confounding factor to consider is the child collector: forwarding from child to parent would cause the authenticated identity to change from the startd identity to the child identity. (Not saying that these exceptions negate the approach, just they are something to think about!) 2019-Mar-11 11:19:55 by tlmiller: > One use case this wouldn't cover is a "PI who purchases a HTCondor annex for > his group"; this would only allow a PI to consume hosts from a HTCondor annex > which she bought for herself. It wouldn't allow her to "gift" CPU time to her > grad students. This exact scenario was the motivation behind "more sophisticated constraints" in the follow-up work. A simpler option, for pools with schedd-enforced accounting groups, would be to allow the schedd to match the accounting group against the ID instead. This would mean the admin would have to be involved, but that may be no bad thing when talking about groups. > Another confounding factor to consider is the child collector: forwarding from > child to parent would cause the authenticated identity to change from the > startd identity to the child identity. I hadn't thought about that. That sounds buggy to me, but maybe we'll have to add an OriginalAuthenticatedIdentity instead.

title: Ticket #3250: Create script to preserve DAGs across 7.8.5 upgrade at LIGO
description: When LIGO upgrades to 7.8.5 their running DAGs will hit the problem noted in #3207. (Subsequent upgrades will be okay.) We want to create a script to automate the re-starting of DAGs in recovery mode after the upgrade.
remarks: 2012-Oct-03 14:35:58 by wenger: My first thought on this is that they'll have to run a script before the upgrade to gather information on all of the running DAGs, and that script will create another script that they'll have to run after the upgrade to re-start things. A few issues I've thought of: What if a DAG finishes between the running of the first script and the Condor upgrade? I guess the post-upgrade script could look for the lock files and not re-start a DAG if it doesn't find one. Will each user who has DAGs run the script themselves, or do we have to set things up to just have the script run by one user? In the latter case, it would have to be run as root so it can su to the right user to re-submit the DAGs. Do the LIGO people use command-line flags like -usedagdir on the condor_submit_dag command line? That might make things trickier. Are all of their DAGs submitted on one machine, or do they submit from a bunch of machines? The latter would obviously add complication... 2012-Oct-03 14:41:29 by nwp: Here is the plan according to Stuart. Date: Wed, 26 Sep 2012 17:38:42 -0700 From: Stuart Anderson To: Nathan Panike Nathan, When Condor 7.8.5 is released and we upgrade the LIGO Condor pools we will give our users the option of running condor_rm on any running DAGMan jobs prior to the upgrade (and submitting the rescue dag after the upgrade) versus running condor_submit <DAGFile>.condor.sub after the upgrade and potentially needing to do the manual cleanup as described by Duncan. Thanks. 2012-Oct-03 16:16:41 by wenger: Hmm -- the restart script should probably also make sure that the relevant job (the DAGMan job) is no longer actually in the queue before clearing out the lock file and re-submitting... 2012-Oct-03 16:18:54 by nwp: The whole point is that it is known not to be in the queue. 2012-Oct-03 16:26:38 by wenger: Well, I guess I'm thinking about a scenario like the user accidentally running the re-start script before the Condor upgrade actually happens, or something like that... But it should be easy to add a check to make sure that's not the case. 2012-Oct-04 09:26:43 by nwp: Indeed, here is a script that checks the history before resubmitting the DAG: cat<<PRINT_FUNC condor_history -const 'JobStatus=?=4 && ExitStatus=?=0 && isUndefined(ExitCode)' -format '%d.' ClusterId -format '%d\n' ProcId > suspicious-jobs resubmit_dag () { if grep -q \$1 suspicious-jobs; then \ su - \$5 -c "echo -n > \$4; cd \$2 && condor_submit \$3" else echo echo "**************************************************" echo "DID NOT FIND JOBID \$1 IN CONDOR HISTORY" echo "**************************************************" echo fi } PRINT_FUNC condor_q -const 'regexp("condor_dagman",Cmd,"i")' | \ sed -n '/^\s*[0-9]\+\./p' | \ awk '{print $1}' | \ while read jobid; do dir=$(condor_q $jobid -f '%s' Iwd) dag=$(condor_q $jobid -f '%s' UserLog | \ sed 's/\.dagman\.log$//').condor.sub lock=$(echo $dag | sed 's/\.condor\.sub/\.lock/') username=$(condor_q $jobid -f '%s' Owner) echo "resubmit_dag $jobid $dir $dag $lock $username"; done 2012-Oct-04 13:02:00 by wenger: This looks good except that the resubmit_dag script needs to clear out the lock file. (That's the best thing to do, as opposed to trying to stick some different PID into it -- if you just truncate the lock file to zero size, the new DAGMan will definitely continue, as opposed to possibly deciding that the old DAGMan still exists.) I was able to duplicate the problem by running a 7.8.4 personal Condor and doing a condor_restart -- I think that's very close to the upgrade scenario. Nathan -- I'm going to assign this ticket back to you, since it looks like you're close to having something working. 2012-Oct-04 13:18:37 by nwp: The script above clears out the lock file now. 2012-Oct-04 15:22:13 by wenger: Another issue I just thought of -- what if some node jobs are scheduler universe? (Although when I test by doing a condor_restart a scheduler universe node job stays in the queue, even though DAGMan is removed -- I'm not sure what's going on with that.) 2012-Oct-04 15:53:00 by nwp: Per the discussion on CondorLIGO, the script will now use su to invoke condor_submit as the user. Also, fix it so that we do not run condor_history for every job. Complain loudly if we do not find the job in the history, and do not restart the job in that case. Also we ran across a case that when only a few jobs have run, the sed script does not print out any job lines; this is fixed. 2012-Oct-04 15:55:18 by nwp: If the scheduler job stays in the queue, DAGMan should be fine, right? The log file will say it is running and that will be correct. If the scheduler job exits with nonzero status, DAGMan should keep going until it cannot make any forward progress, then dump a rescue dag and exit: the user will resubmit the rescue dag. 2012-Oct-18 16:20:40 by wenger: Did some more testing on this, here's a modified script that looks for the lock files rather than the ExitCode to decide whether a DAG should be restarted. To use this script, do the following: Put the code into a file, say fixit.sh. Run this command: "bash fixit.sh > restart.sh" Do the Condor upgrade Run this command: "bash restart.sh" cat<<PRINT_FUNC condor_history -const 'JobStatus=?=4' -format '%d.' ClusterId -format '%d\n' ProcId > suspicious-jobs resubmit_dag () { if grep -q \$1 suspicious-jobs; then if [ -e \$4 ] then echo "Restarting DAGMan job \$1" su - \$5 -c "echo -n > \$4; cd \$2 && condor_submit \$3" else echo echo "**************************************************" echo "Lock file \$4 not found" echo "DAGMan job \$1 apparently finished normally -- not restarting" echo "**************************************************" echo fi else echo echo "**************************************************" echo "DID NOT FIND JOBID \$1 IN CONDOR HISTORY -- not restarting" echo "**************************************************" echo fi } PRINT_FUNC condor_q -const 'regexp("condor_dagman",Cmd,"i")' | \ sed -n '/^\s*[0-9]/p' | \ awk '{print $1}' | \ while read jobid; do dir=$(condor_q $jobid -f '%s' Iwd) dag=$(condor_q $jobid -f '%s' UserLog | \ sed 's/\.dagman\.log$//').condor.sub lock=$(echo $dag | sed 's/\.condor\.sub/\.lock/') username=$(condor_q $jobid -f '%s' Owner) echo "resubmit_dag $jobid $dir $dag $lock $username"; done 2012-Oct-18 16:24:21 by wenger: There are at least a couple of things to watch out for with this: Once you've re-submitted DAGs this way, doing a condor_rm of the DAGMan job won't remove the node jobs (see #3278). You need to make sure that su'ing to a given use correctly sets up everything for that user to run Condor (e.g., they don't have to do any manual fixing up of their path or anything like that). If someone wants to run this as a normal user instead of root, it will all work just by changing 'su - \$5' to 'bash' in the script. 2012-Oct-18 16:28:25 by wenger: Oh, yes -- as a further clarification, this script is designed to be run as root, one time on each machine that any running DAGs have been submitted from. It should take care of DAGs started by any users on the machine on which it is run. 2012-Oct-18 17:18:23 by wenger: Another thing to watch out for: Make sure you don't run the restart.sh script more than once -- if you do that, you'll end up with multiple instances of DAGMan running the same DAG, and you'll have problems. 2012-Nov-13 14:08:28 by nwp: We confirmed in the LIGO conference call on 13 November 2012 that this can be resolved.

title: Ticket #3084: Negotiator will repeatedly wait for wedged schedd; slows negotiation
description: (Based on a report by roy. See "Thoughts on bad negotiation cycles" to condor-team, June 22, 2012.) If the negotiator times out talking to a schedd, it will go to the next submittor and try to connect, even if that submittor is on the same schedd. If you have a bunch of submittors on a non-responsive schedd, this might mean a multi-minute wait. Alain Roy has seen the negotiator waste 5.5 minutes out of every negotiation cycle trying to connect to the same unresponsive schedd for multiple submittors. This dragged the cycle from about 5 minutes out to 10 minutes. Proposed: If a schedd times out, drop all submittors from that schedd from the list to be processed, at least until the next negotiation cycle. Representative NegotiatorLog, anonymized. 06/22/12 01:56:56 Socket to user1@node.example.com (<XXX.XXX.XXX.45:56330>) not in cache, creating one 06/22/12 01:57:26 condor_read(): timeout reading 5 bytes from schedd user1@node.example.com. 06/22/12 01:57:26 IO: Failed to read packet header 06/22/12 01:57:26 Error: Ignoring submitter for this cycle ... 06/22/12 01:57:26 Socket to user2@node.example.com (<XXX.XXX.XXX.45:56330>) not in cache, creating one 06/22/12 01:57:56 condor_read(): timeout reading 5 bytes from schedd user2@node.example.com. 06/22/12 01:57:56 IO: Failed to read packet header 06/22/12 01:57:56 Error: Ignoring submitter for this cycle

title: Ticket #1543: Startd handles statfs overflow poorly
description: The condor startd, via sysapi, calls statfs to get the free disk space. statfs measures free disk space in an unsigned long number of blocks. If the number of free blocks is more than an unsigned long, statfs returns -1 and sets errno to EOVERFLOW. This is happening for igor when running on lustre-mounted huge distributed filesystem. The Disk startd attribute then doesn't get set and no jobs match. This patch checks for EOVERFLOW, and sets the free space to INT_MAX number of k.
remarks: 2010-Jul-28 16:47:49 by matt: Todo or Defect? 2010-Jul-28 16:49:17 by matt: Setting INT_MAX is a rather ugly hack. If a 64 bit compiled Condor has a problem that should just be logged and fixed. The user should run 64 bit versions of Condor to avoid statfs overflowing. 2010-Jul-28 17:08:57 by gthain: The ultimate problem is that this info is recorded and forwarded as a classad integral value, and classad integers are always 32 bits.

title: Ticket #5150: Tools should apply reasonable projection for daemon location
description: When querying the collector for daemon location, tools such as 'condor_q' get the kitchen sink - no projection is applied. CMS has very large schedd ads (~100KB) because of the monitoring we have enabled. I've noticed that, on high-latency and/or low-bandwidth links, this transfer back to the client can contribute significant portion of the overall query time. We should apply a projection on MyAddress.
remarks: 2015-Jul-17 11:07:27 by jfrey: There will need to be a few more attributes in the projection, like CondorVersion. 2015-Jul-28 14:21:20 by jfrey: The following attributes are consulted in the Daemon object. They would have to be part of the projection. <subsys>IpAddr Name MyAddress CondorVersion CondorPlatform Machine AddressV1 and AddressV2 (for IPv6) Additionally, the daemon's ad can be retrieved via a public method. In several places, callers query additional attributes, requiring potentially the full daemon ad. This could be handled by having an option to fetch the full ad. Here are the current places where more of the daemon ad is required: condor_pigeon: a fragile attempt to lookup an attribute whose name ends with "PORT" from a pigeon ad. condor_q: SwapSpaceExhausted, MaxJobsRunning, TotalRunningJobs, StartSchedulerUniverse, StartLocalUniverse condor_config_val: -evaluate takes a config parameter's value and evaluates it in the context of the daemon ad condor_history, condor_load_history: JobQueueBirthdate python bindings: the daemon ad appears to be visible to python callers 2015-Aug-06 17:26:00 by tannenba: I would like daemon location queries sent to the collector to be tagged specifically as "location lookups", not just as generic queries with a small projections. Ie the query ad to the collector should state that this is an address lookup. One reason for this is instead of just shortening the projection, I'd like these lookups to always use an index on the collector. 2015-Aug-09 05:37:37 by bbockelm: The solution I ended up with was to differentiate between "LOCATE_FAST" and "LOCATE_FULL" in the Daemon::locate method (defaulting to LOCATE_FULL). When LOCATE_FAST is used, CondorQuery indicates to the collector that this is a "location query" (in addition to providing a reasonable projection). I went through and tagged as many tools as I had time to test (and, crucially, the negotiator lookup for the schedd's RESCHEDULE -- CMS has previously noted that this is an expensive lookup as it is done for every condor_submit; there's a ticket somewhere...). If we go further down this road, we could consider flipping the default to LOCATE_FAST and marking just the tools Jaime noted which pull out the daemonAd. ( NOTE: we essentially did this in #6223 for v8.7.2 ) Finally, I changed the default for locate in the python tools to LOCATE_FAST. This was always the intent behind exposing a different "locate" versus "query" in the first place. We'll just note to users that they will need to switch to 'query' if they want the full ad. 2015-Aug-10 10:51:34 by tannenba: Thanks Brian.... I'd be happy to code review when the time comes if nobody else does so... 2015-Aug-10 10:57:11 by tannenba: Brian re your comment above about the expensive collector lookup that the schedd does upon a reschedule.... Hopefully that has been significantly improved after #4821 got pushed into v8.3.3. 2015-Aug-10 11:19:34 by bbockelm: Yup - that should make a good improvement. However, there's still RTT between California and CERN to deal with - still seems silly to do it multiple times a second if every 'condor_submit' invokes a reschedule. Anyhow, there ss a separate ticket for this: #4274 2015-Oct-21 10:55:22 by tannenba: ToddM must sign off on this from an IPv6 perspective. Greg will consult with ToddM on some details here. 2015-Nov-06 11:06:19 by tlmiller: This doesn't look like it will cause any problems for the IPv6 / multi-address work in the short-to-medium term. In the long term, we may introduce yet another address attribute, but this can be readily extended to cover that.

title: Ticket #5500: linux kernel tuning script should set dirty_bytes for cgroups
description: When Linux kernels of a rhel6 vintage are running starters configured to use cgroups to limit memory usage, and the cgroup memory policy is set to hard, the kernel will incorrectly OOM kill the cgroup when the cgroup has hit the memory limit, including the memory used by the kernel to buffer file system writes. Usually, the kernel will simply flush this memory, but under some conditions, it doesn't, and OOM kills the cgroup. To work around this problem, condor should limit the amount of memory used by the kernel for file system caching. By default, it is 40 percent of all physical memory, which is way too much, especially on large-memory systems. HTCondor's linux_kernel_tuning script will set /proc/sys/vm/dirty_bytes to 100Mb if cgroups is enabled.

title: Ticket #3968: Nested ads not detected properly by ClassAd caching code
description: In the ClassAd caching code, a nested ad cannot be cached and shared across multiple enclosing ads. This is because the nested ad contains a pointer to the enclosing ad for its parent scope. This pointer needs to be set properly for attribute references to resolve properly during expression evaluation. CachedExprEnvelope::cache() checks whether the value of an attribute is a ClassAd and doesn't cache it. But if the value contains a nested ad, it does cache it. For example, this attribute/value pair will be cached: A=[Z=User].Z This should evaluate to the value of the User attribute in the enclosing ad, if it's defined. If caching is enabled, it always evaluates to Undefined. The caching code needs to examine the entire expression tree to look for any occurrences of a nested ad and not cache if one is found.
creator: jfrey

title: Ticket #960: add heartbeat to CCB listener connection
description: Craig at Marquette observes problems where CCB listener connections are disconnected by the NAT and the daemon doesn't notice until over a day later. We have seen similar behavior for one of the CHTC users. Condor is fairly resilient in the face of network disconnects, but since it can take so long for the listener to notice the problem, this can lead to very inefficient operation. Like all CEDAR connections, the CCB listener connection should already be using TCP KEEPALIVE, so I don't understand how it can take so long to notice the disconnect. But even if TCP KEEPALIVE could address the problem, the default interval is not aggressive enough and it is not convenient to configure since it is a system-wide setting. Therefore, CCB should do application-level heartbeats to detect disconnects earlier and possibly to keep the connection alive by generating a guaranteed minimum rate of activity that is easily configured.

title: Ticket #5445: Add support for workflow log to be on SSD
description: I had suggested a while ago that we put workflow logs for CHTC on SSDs for performance improvement. Just doing that wouldn't require any DAGMan changes, but we're thinking that, when the workflow finishes, DAGMan should move the log off of the SSD (e.g., to the directory where the DAG file lives). This would require some support in DAGMan. Also, we'd have to decide what to do if the file moved failed (e.g., if there's not enough disk space in the directory we're moving to). My first thought is to put the DAGMan job on hold, with an appropriate hold reason. Then the user could clear out disk space and release the job, and it should re-try moving the log file.

description: This came up during a previous LIGO call -- they wanted to be able to have the PRE and POST scripts run on the same machine as the job, and it was suggested that a way to do this was by actually running them as starter Pre and Post scripts. It was then suggested that it would be good if there was some way to get DAGMan itself to automatically translate a DAG PRE/POST script to a starter PRE/POST script. (I don't know if the way to do this would be to have some global setting that would run all of the scripts in the starter, or maybe a different keyword for scripts that should be run by the starter.) Hmm -- something I just thought about -- this obviously won't work for scheduler-universe node jobs. If you try to do this for a scheduler-universe node job, DAGMan should issue an error if Condor itself doesn't.
remarks: 2012-Apr-20 14:29:42 by wenger: Starter scripts are now documented in 7.7.6 (see #2379). I can't really link to the docs yet, because 7.7.6 isn't released yet... 2013-Jan-25 12:23:42 by wenger: I was thinking about how to specify in the DAG file that you want to run your scripts as starter scripts, and I was thinking something like this: SCRIPT [STARTER] PRE JobName ExecutableName [arguments] SCRIPT [STARTER] POST JobName ExecutableName [arguments] or else maybe: STARTER_SCRIPT PRE JobName ExecutableName [arguments] STARTER_SCRIPT POST JobName ExecutableName [arguments] Anyone have a strong preference for one way or the other? 2013-Jan-25 12:36:14 by wenger: Just created V7_9-gittrac_2380-branch for this... 2013-Jan-25 13:16:50 by tannenba: Kent, you should write a design document for what you are thinking before writing a lot of code.... thanks. 2013-Jan-25 13:23:27 by wenger: Yes, I need to do some testing to fully understand how the starter scripts work before I come up with a design... 2013-Feb-22 16:21:12 by wenger: Note: the starter pre and post scripts are documented on the condor_submit man page. 2013-Feb-25 15:22:03 by wenger: DAGMan should be able to specify starter pre and post scripts using the PreCmd, PostCmd, and Pre/PostArgs and/or Pre/PostArguments classad attributes. Without some changes to condor_submit, though, I don't think there's any way for DAGMan to add the pre or post script to the input file list for file transfer -- I need to do a little more checking on that. If I'm right, though, we'll have to make some changes to condor_submit to implement this. 2013-Feb-25 15:51:57 by wenger: Hmm -- another issue is that the semantics of starter post scripts are different than that of DAGMan POST scripts, in that the starter post scripts are not run if the job is evicted -- we need to think about how to deal with that. Hmm -- here's another issue -- getting back the exit code of the starter post script! We really need to do that -- I'll have to look at the code, I guess, and see whether that gets saved anywhere... 2013-Mar-05 10:26:59 by wenger: Hmm -- something else I just thought of (assuming we don't have a shared filesystem): if a PRE or POST script uses an input file that's not specified as an input file in the submit file, we'd have to add that to the list of files that gets transferred. It may be tricky to figure this out -- we can't really know if an argument to one of the scripts is a file name or not. We can obviously figure out that we need to add the scripts themselves, but input files are much trickier. 2013-Mar-05 15:03:29 by wenger: Just to clarify what I was referring to in the previous remark: Say we have an input file in1 that the PRE script transforms to in2, which is then the input to the actual executable of the job. Then, if we run the PRE script in the "normal" way, the file we have to transfer is in2. But if we run the PRE script as a starter script, we have to transfer in1. (My goal is to be able to have everything work in the same way whichever way you're running the scripts, but I think that may not be possible in all cases.) 2013-May-03 13:58:56 by wenger: I just talked with Carsten about this at HTCondor week and clarified their use case, which is as follows: They have jobs for which data has to be copied onto the execute machine, and copied back after the job runs. (They are doing this copying outside of HTCondor's file transfer mechanism.) The big thing is that they need to throttle the "input copying" separately from the compute jobs (and maybe throttle the "output copying" too (although that's not as much of a problem because the compute jobs don't all finish at once)). So running the PRE and POST scripts as starter scripts is not really what they need, because if they do that DAGMan can't throttle the scripts separately from the actual jobs. I can think of a couple of ways to address this, maybe there are others: Make the copying tasks actual HTCondor jobs, with a capability to make a given input, compute, and output job all land on the same machine. Then you could do the throttling with DAGMan node categories. Have the PRE and POST script know what machine the job will run/ran on. I'm wondering if we could do something like this: submit the job in a special state where it gets matched with a machine but not actually run; then DAGMan runs the PRE script, and when that finishes does something to allow the job to continue. Once the job finishes, it goes into a special state that doesn't do stuff like transferring files back; in the mean time DAGMan runs the POST script, and when it's finished tells the job to do the normal HTCondor post-job stuff. (We'd have to add some special PRE and POST script arguments to tell the scripts the machine that the job landed on, and probably its directory.) Then you could do the throttling with maxpre/maxpost. 2014-May-20 11:40:46 by wenger: I'm going to reduce the priority of this one because we don't need it as much if we implement the more flexible retry feature (#1309). 2015-Dec-09 13:21:38 by wenger: Resurrecting this ticket as per discussion on today's LIGO call. 2015-Dec-16 11:11:11 by wenger: ToddT thinks we should do this -- probably combined with checksumming all file transfers by default. 2019-Apr-10 15:03:46 by pfc: I'm assuming solely based on the age of this ticket that it's safe to demote to priority 5 and defer. If I'm wrong, please speak up.

title: Ticket #91: PrivSep: Create_Process errors do not result in job being held
description: In the Starter, we respond to certain failure conditions by placing the job on hold. Examples include the executable not being found or not having execute permission (i.e. ENOENT or EACCES from exec()). When PrivSep is enabled on the execute-machine, some of these types of failures do not have this effect.

title: Ticket #1406: Processor Affinity setting doesn't work with privset
description: Processor Affinity setting is done in DaemonCore::Create_Process, which privsep doesn't use. So, if you have privsep on, processor affinity doesn't work.
remarks: Fixed in 7.4.3. Note that glexec doesn't support processor affinity, so it doesn't work it that world, only with the condor switchboard.

title: Ticket #5916: Warn when we encounter only invalid VOMS ACs
description: When an invalid VOMS AC is encountered, it is silently ignored by the VOMS library. This will occur either because it actually is invalid - or VOMS has not been configured correctly on this host), it is silently ignored. While maliciously faked VOMS ACs are rare, this can be triggered by a common misconfiguration and cause HTCondor to behave in unexpected ways (i.e., mappings that are based on VOMS information will no longer match). I propose that, whenever VOMS verification is enabled, we call VOMS_Retrieve twice: once with verification enabled and once without. If we get zero attributes the first time and nonzero attributes the second time, we print out a loud warning message about failed verification. If there are actually zero attributes at all (plain-old grid proxy), then we pay a minimal overhead: basically, the VOMS library will iterate through the list of attributes, see the lack of VOMS information, and return. While this approach isn't perfect (it doesn't handle the cases where there are N attributes and only N-1 are invalid), it's probably going to catch almost all the errors - while minimizing the impact on valid proxies.

title: Ticket #2103: Control GSI_AUTHZ_CONF environment variable via condor configuration
description: Condor should set the environment variable GSI_AUTHZ_CONF in an analogous way to how it sets GRIDMAP. Currently, it does nothing to manage this environment variable. As of 7.5.6 (#1834), this environment variable controls where the globus mapping library looks for the mapping callout configuration. Until Condor provides control over this setting, admins will need to be careful to set this environment variable if desired before launching condor. This may be particularly important for glideins. title: Ticket #1685: no documentation of specification of expression for -constraint option
description: On 8-11-2010, a condor-users post expresses frustration in generating a correct expression for use with condor_status -constraint. There are many references in the manual to condor_status, and a few to the section on ClassAds, but none explains the usage of single quote vs. double quote, and when backslashes might be appropriate as escape characters. More explanation and more examples within the condor_status manual page will help.
remarks: 2010-Sep-30 10:15:32 by smoler: From Greg T: For most (all?) Unix shells, the single quote mark (') is a way to cause the command-line interpretation to not expand anything within single quote marks. Therefore, it becomes the right way to delimit a single expression that has white space characters which would otherwise cause the expression to be broken into multiple command-line arguments. From TJ: Not so on Windows machines (old, normal command shell). A single quote mark would be passed through for the Condor tool to deal with. So, double quote marks are the right way on Windows to delimit a single expression with white space characters. Further gotcha is that an embedded (and needed) double quote mark must be escaped on Windows by using 2 consecutive double quote marks (""), whereas a Unix escape would be a backslash followed by a double quote mark (\"). Conclusion: virtually all our examples with the manual are Unix-specific.

title: Ticket #3207: Jobs in scheduler universe ignore OnExitRemove
description: Jobs in scheduler universe ignore OnExitRemove, and go directly to "Completed" state, disregarding policy expressions. A job running under scheduler universe would improperly be marked as "Completed", instead of using the OnExitRemove attribute to decide if it should leave the queue. The message below is a symptom of this bug. To be explicit, the OnExitRemove expression for condor_dagman reads on_exit_remove = ( ExitSignal =?= 11 || (ExitCode =!= UNDEFINED && ExitCode >=0 && ExitCode <= 2)) Thus, when condor_dagman exits with status 3, the schedd should move it to "Idle" state and restart it. But this was not happening because the schedd was moving it to "Completed" state, rather than "Idle". All scheduler jobs that exited would be marked as "Completed" state, regardless of the OnExitRemove expression.
