Ticket #4192: Allow "manual" node retries within a DAG
description: This is for the case where a node fails, but then the user fixes something in the submit file that will cause the node to succeed if it's re-tried. This is what Brian had to say: Yes - to be clear, I don't want to edit the nodes of a DAG - but change the status of a node. Here's what I would want: 1) For node N, kill any existing job and/or script. Do not retry this node or make forward progress.. 2) For node N, clear any error state and change the number of retries to R. Allow it to be scheduled for forward progress. We can already do # 1. For # 2, the re-submission of the job has to happen within DAGMan. Internally I think it should be pretty simple -- we just need to reset the node's status from failed to ready, and reset a few things like the retry count. The question is how the user communicates to DAGMan that a node should be "manually" re-tried.
remarks: 2014-Feb-04 11:27:46 by bbockelm: Shoot, I must have missed it - how to do #1 today? 2014-Feb-04 11:55:55 by wenger: Well, it depends on the exact behaviour you want: If you just condor_rm the node job, any children of that job will not be run, but other "paths" in the DAG will continue. If you halt the DAG with a halt file, and then condor_rm the node job, other already-submitted node jobs will continue, but no new node jobs will be submitted, and when the submitted jobs finish DAGMan will create a rescue DAG and exit (unless you unhold it first). If you condor_rm the entire DAGMan, all progress will obviously stop and a rescue DAG will get created. 2014-Feb-04 12:02:37 by bbockelm: Ah - so, that wouldn't work because: The node may be in the post-script (and stuck). The node may have additional retries left. I want to kill it and prevent any future retries. However, it gets us pretty close - most of the time, the use case is "job X should run for 4 hours and it's been running for 24 hours. Kill and resubmit it because something must have gone wrong." The submit case is usually "site X broke this morning and killed 100 of 10,000 jobs. The sysadmin emailed me to say it is fixed and to retry things this afternoon." 2014-Feb-04 12:07:17 by wenger: Ah, okay, so we need something like "manually fail a node", too. (In other words, condor_rm the job, or kill the PRE or POST script, and immediately put the node into failed state, bypassing any remaining retries.) Again, internally I don't think that should be so hard. What we need to do is define a mechanism for communicating this to DAGMan. 2014-Feb-04 12:20:22 by bbockelm: My initial thoughts - Allow scheduler universe jobs to notify the schedd they will be listening onto a given domain socket. Schedd will have a new command called "INTERACT_WITH_JOB". If the remote side authenticates as the same user as the running job or as a super-user, invoke the shared port code to pass the ReliSock to dagman. At this point, DAGMan has a DC command socket authenticated by the schedd. The client can perform additional commands against the DAGMan process. (Why so complicated? CMS doesn't have filesystem access to the schedd node...)

title: Ticket #2945: standard universe breaks glob() on SL6
description: A 7-year-old standard universe glob() bug is back on SL6. It is insidious, as we can only reproduce it in the LIGO inspiral code, and not yet in a simple test program. The same LIGO inspiral code condor_compile'd on Centos 5 (or non-condor_compile'd on SL6) works fine. The problem is likely related to the fact that the libc glob() code on SL6 internally calls newfstatat() which is failing, even though the files exist: newfstatat(5, "L-L1_LDAS_C02_L2-953081600-128.gwf", 0x7fff8096ad20, 0) = -1 EBADF (Bad file descriptor) ...whereas the libc glob() on CentOS 5 calls stat(), which is working: stat("/home/dbrown/projects/cbc/dax/ihope-4.1/953078343-953114343/full_data/./L-L1_LDAS_C02_L2-953102336-128.gwf", {st_mode=S_IFREG|0644, st_size=16122709, ...}) = 0 Pete may have somehow special-cased stat() to deal with this (maybe to avoid remote io?), but the same may need to be done for newfstatat(). This is pretty urgent, since it means we can't compile a working LIGO inspiral workflow on SL6 -- we can only do so on Centos 5, which LIGO no longer supports. This may be difficult to reproduce at UWCS given the complex software environment, but we can give an account to Todd or Alan or anyone else who needs one to reproduce this at Syracuse.
remarks: 2012-Apr-20 13:23:34 by tannenba: Best guess here is the table that virtualizes file descriptors is getting out of whack because the new stat syscall is not being trapped. Pfc will try enhancing the toy test program... 2012-Apr-20 17:01:01 by tlmiller: It may be worth trying to run your toy program with the -_condor_aggravate_bugs flag. This flag, by avoiding using FDs 3 to 31, should help "to uncover bugs due to untrapped system calls." 2012-Apr-23 11:20:42 by tlmiller: The test program from the referenced condor-admin ticket fails when run with -_condor_aggravate_bugs on SL6.x. (Oddly enough, under Condor 7.7.5, it reports error: bad file descriptor; under 7.7.6, it reports error: success.) Investigating... 2012-Apr-24 13:40:24 by pfc: Re: the differing errno, I believe it's is not being set by glob() itself, but rather is inherited from the last stat() call that glob() made. So depending on how glob() is failing within the standard universe, the errno may not always be relevant or useful... 2012-Apr-25 15:03:48 by tlmiller: Patched in 7.8, but only for stand-alone checkpointing. (GregT reviewed.) 2012-Apr-25 15:18:18 by pfc: Any chance we could get a pre-release RPM for SL6? We're desperate to kill the Centos 5 machine that we're keeping around just to run these jobs... thanks! 2012-Apr-25 15:29:22 by tlmiller: cough s/for stand-alone checkpointing/without remote system calls/. Sorry about that. 2012-May-08 16:26:43 by pfc: Thanks for the quick turnaround on this, guys. We really appreciate it, since it was blocking an urgent project.

title: Ticket #5279: lib_job_router_local on Windows broken with shared port active
description: The lib_job_router_local test currently turns shared port off for the job router on Windows. It's unclear why this is necessary -- the resulting hang has been inexplicable. According to the logs, the job router simply stops doing anything after it updates its ad with the collector the first time. The last line in the log is consistently 09/24/15 16:35:23 DaemonCore Timeout() Complete, returning 5, which should be followed by no more than five seconds later by the timer firing again. In a normal run, a few seconds later, the job router accepts what is probably a connection from a condor_who invoked by the test harness; and shortly afterwards, the other timers fire again, the job router finds a job, and the test (eventually) passes. This may be entirely a coincidence, or it could be that accept()ing that connection kicks daemon core out of a bad state. It is suspicious because shared port, of course, changes how that connection works. The shared port daemon logs that it has written a number of bytes to the named pipe, but there's no corresponding record in the job router. Since it's unlikely that the timer code is just flat-out broken on Windows (then nothing would work) I wonder if we're somehow wedging in the daemon core event loop.

title: Ticket #999: Document IwdFlushNFSCache Job Ad attribute
description: A Job Ad attribute introduced in 7.4.0, IwdFlushNFSCache is an expression defaulting to TRUE. It controls the Condor feature of attempting to flush a submit node's NFS cache to refresh a job's IWD. The feature is currently implemented by the condor_schedd, but could be implemented by the condor_shadow in the future. The goal of the feature it to allow files written by the job into an NFS mounted IWD to be immediately visible on the submit node. For instance, if a process is managing the job's presence in the Schedd, such as a meta-scheduler, needs access to the job's output written to the job's IWD and does not perform NFS cache flushing itself (why it doesn't is unknown), then Condor can perform the cache flushing on behalf of the process. This flushing operation can be expensive, requiring multiple round trips with the NFS server. In 7.4.0, the only way to disable the flushing if a job's IWD is on NFS and the provided semantics are not required is to +IwdFlushNFSCache=FALSE.

title: Ticket #7481: condor_off -startd -peaceful continues to run new jobs
description: condor_off -startd -peaceful continues to run new jobs, and a subsequent -graceful is ignored. My expectation is that "condor_off -startd -peaceful" should prevent any new jobs from starting and request running jobs to checkpoint, but not kill any that ignored that request. And that a subsequent "condor_off -startd -graceful" would re-request checkpoints but then after some minutes kill jobs that ignored that request. Note, I forgot about -force-graceful, which did set a timer and forcefully kill jobs. However, please remind me why that option is needed? title: Ticket #5146: MAX_ACCEPTS_PER_CYCLE not respected by shared port endpoint
description: We are seeing severe priority inversion on some CMS schedds under load. It's taking ~45 seconds for condor_submit to get to the schedd, despite the fact that there's a DC cycle every 200ms or so. Looking into the issue, it appears to be because MAX_ACCEPTS_PER_CYCLE is not respected when shared_port is in use. This is priority inversion because new sockets (condor_submit) are at a pretty significant disadvantage compared to others. I'd like all clients to be considered equally (here, I mean 'one callback processed per duty cycle on ready sockets').
remarks: 2015-Jul-14 15:26:16 by tannenba: To achieve what you want, could you just set MAX_ACCEPTS_PER_CYCLE=1 ? ;-) But I agree the shared_port_endpoint should honor MAX_ACCEPTS_PER_CYCLE, thanks for the patch! Re the patch, looks like the loop logic needs a quick change to honor the knob semantics - documentation that says if MAX_ACCEPTS_PER_CYCLE has value of zero or less, it means no limit. Please post the results of your before/after observations and tests as remarks to this ticket. Ie with the same workload, schedd was taking ~45 seconds per submit, after change ~X seconds. Assuming the testing and before/after observations look good, please merge for inclusion into v8.3.8. Final comment - as these are all developer tuning knobs, it may be interesting for our own benchmarking/experimentation purposes to have a SHARED_ENDPOINT_MAX_ACCEPTS_PER_CYCLE knob that, if defined, overrides MAX_ACCEPTS_PER_CYCLE in the shared_port endpoint code. 2015-Jul-15 10:16:40 by bbockelm: I did some performance tests last night. At the worst, the schedd took 8 minutes to respond to condor_q -const false; the negotiator timed out waiting on response for every negotiation cycle (negotiation timeout is set to 10). The average was somewhere in the 30s range. After the change, the average query time when using condor_shared_port was <5 seconds (identical performance to using the TCP port opened for the shadows).

title: Ticket #3138: Periodic evicts/fast restart in vanilla universe (checkpoints)
description: Overview Periodically evict a job, sending its sandbox home, then immediately restart it in the same claim. This is part of work to do checkpointing in the vanilla universe (see parent #2007 "Can stduniv run as a vanilla job with standalone checkpointing?" and grandparent #1956 "Move stduniv to new starter/shadow"). By itself, this will massively simplify doing periodic checkpoints in the vanilla universe. This will solve problems LIGO has today, primarily because the standard shadow/starter combination lack modern niceties, including CCB. (This may be useful for DMTCP or KVM. I'm just mentioning them so this will show up in searches.) Architecture: "Clueless Starter" The startd will decide when a periodic checkpoint is desired, using existing functionality with some tweaks. Upon deciding, the startd will signal the starter that it is time to exit while internally noting this special case. The signal will note "this is a periodic checkpoint". The starter will signal the shadow that this is a periodic checkpoint. When the starter exits, the startd will note that it is prepared to accept the old claim again. It will not clean up the execute directory as it normally would. When the shadow finishes talking with the starter, the shadow enters a "try to claim" mode, nothing that it's a reclaim. When the shadow reclaims and starts talking to the new starter, it avoids re-sending any files. Everything presumable restarts and all is well. Specific steps are described in the development plan below. Development Plan This only happens if a vanilla universe job specifically requests periodic checkpoints with "+WantCheckpoint=TRUE". If Universe==$(vanilla) && WantCheckpoint && PERIODIC_CHECKPOINT, then it's time to do a checkpoint. 03 days - Change startd: startd tells starter to shut down for periodic checkpoint. startd enters a new state "shutting down, but not really." Probably involves changing /src/condor_startd.V6/Resource.cpp Resource::periodic_checkpoint around line 352 to know about this case (and not to do so for the VM universe, which has its own rules!) and instead kill off the starter. 02 days - Change starter: On periodic checkpoint shutdown, shutdown 03 days - Change starter and shadow: On periodic checkpoint shutdown, signal to the shadow that this is a periodic checkpoint shutdown. 03 days - Change startd: when starter exits, transition to "being re-claimed" maintaining the old claim information. Ensure we don't clean up the working directory! Work probably needs to be done in Starter::exited (/src/condor_Startd.V6/Starter.cpp around line 670) 03 days - Change shadow: When files sent back, transition to "(re)claiming slot mode". It should have the old machine ad with the claim information, so it should be able to reconnect. 03 days - Change startd: if we're in "being re-claimed" and someone shows up with the correct claim ID, reuse the existing execute directory. Maybe change starter: when starting the starter be sure to pass in "assume file transfer is done". (May not be necessary) 04 days - Change shadow and/or starter to be able to be skip file transfer. Might it be enough to have the shadow simply not bother? 02 days - Change condor_vacate and condor_vacate_job: Add --and-restart which will initiate a periodic checkpoint shutdown? Useful for testing, as well as forcing a checkpoint now without (kinda) interrupting the job. 02 days - change condor_startd to respect --and-restart flag from condor_vacate/condor_vacate_job Open issues What if a competing claim shows up while waiting for a reclaim? title: Ticket #1555: make condor_q jobid efficient
description: condor_q <jobid> results in a linear search in the schedd. Instead, the schedd should do an efficient hash table lookup. This is a possible STUDENTTASK. proposal There are two possible solutions: Make the tool provide more hints to the schedd. Make the schedd do a query optimization pass. It could be really stupid and just look for a query that matches a specific template. If it is easy to insert the hint in a backward compatible way, 1 is probably better than a stupid optimizer that matches to a template. Explicit interfaces are better than implicit ones that can silently break. However, since 2 would be so easy to implement, we should keep it in mind in case 1 turns out to be difficult. If we are worried about silent breakage, we should add a test that asserts expected behavior in the schedd.

title: Ticket #4757: Let user know when scheduler or local universe job limits are hit
description: BMRB just ran into an issue where scheduler universe jobs weren't starting because StartSchedulerUniverse = TotalSchedulerJobsRunning < 200 and TotalSchedulerJobsRunning = 200 The problem is, it is really hard for the user to figure this out. The jobs just stay idle; there's nothing in the job user log or even the SchedLog that indicates that you hit this limit, and, of course, you can't use condor_q -analyze to figure out what's going on. I can see a number of possible things to do (kind of in order of increasing work): Print something in the SchedLog when jobs don't start because of this limit. Put this information in some event in the job's user log, if it has one. Print this information when you do condor_q -analyze on a scheduler or local universe job. Print a warning when you submit a scheduler or local universe job, and the schedd has hit (or is close to) one of these limits. One other bizarre symptom: this apparently causes newly-submitted scheduler universe jobs, at least, to not appear at all in the SchedLog.

That way, things like SCRIPT commands would have something to attach their script to even before the splices are "lifted". I think the thing to do would be to have the socket nodes have special names, like <splice_name>_socketpre and <splice_name>_socketpost. Then, the Dag::FindNodeByName() method would need an extra argument that would specify one of three choices: Never give me a socket node Give me the socket pre node if a node with the specified name doesn't exist Give me the socket post node if a node with the specified name doesn't exist 2016-Apr-27 11:04:02 by wenger: Hmm -- now I'm thinking that we'd be better off having the PRE socket node just have the splice name, and then have the POST socket node have some special name; the PRE socket node would also have to have a flag that it's a PRE socket node. Then, if you have a command like: SCRIPT PRE <splice> ... the code could just search for the node with the appropriate name, and add the PRE script to it. For SCRIPT POST <splice> ... the code would find the PRE node, but because we're adding a POST script, we'd know that we have to add it to the POST node. Similarly, for PARENT/CHILD relationships, PARENT could only get added to a POST node, and CHILD could only get added to a PRE node (except when we're "lifting" the actual splice nodes -- obviously some nodes in the splice would be children of the PRE node, and some would be parents of the POST node. 2016-Apr-28 13:12:51 by wenger: Hmm -- need to think about how this would work (if at all) with the new splice connect feature. title: Ticket #6785: Starter should assume shadow on same machine has trustable UID_DOMAIN
description: On a machine that doesn't have working DNS or is configured to be a personal Condor (using interface 127.0.0.1), it's easy for UID_DOMAIN (default $(FULL_HOSTNAME)) to not match the hostname associated with the network interface used between the starter and shadow. This causes the starter to run the job as user nobody. If file transfer isn't enabled, this is likely to fail, as nobody won't have permission to access the job's files. If the starter and shadow are on the same machine, it's reasonable to assume they share the same UID namespace. Add a new knob, TRUST_LOCAL_UID_DOMAIN. If it's true (the default) and the shadow's end of the TCP connection is on a local network interface, then the starter doesn't do the matching test between UID_DOMAIN and the hostname of that interface. This is the same as TRUST_UID_DOMAIN, but only for shadows on the same machine. We should still do the matching of UID_DOMAIN values between starter and shadow, as that makes testing easier.

title: Ticket #425: OS specific fork() detection
description: Condor's process tracking code (these days, the procd) jumps through a lot of hoops to make sure that child processes don't slip away. It polls repeatedly. It uses magical environment variables. In some cases it uses dedicated accounts. Despite all of this, it's possible for a malicious or extremely odd user job to escape Condor's detection and escape management. This is bad. As best we know, there is no portable way to track all of your child processes and their processes. We should consider using OS-specific hooks to accomplish the task. Here is a place to collect possibilities: Linux: System Tap, specifically process.create. The argument new_pid and the function ppid() should provide everything we need with essentially perfect reliability. Down side: Requires: root, gcc, kernel-dev packages, System Tap, none of which we're guaranteed access to. Solaris: DTrace

title: Ticket #5453: HTCondor View: constant date_end-date_start but changing graph range
description: If date_start/date_end are specified, we limit the data to that graph, then graph it. However, unless we happen to have data right at those ends, the actual graph will expand to show the actual range of data. This is surprising: it doesn't seem like it's showing what you asked for. Also, if you are refreshing the graph regularly, it means that the exact duration shown will not quite be constant. Worst case, if you have a gap, it will suddenly jump! The ideal solution is to capture one more set of samples on either side of the requested range, then limit the graph to the exact range. The extra samples ensures we have data running all the way up to the end of the range. This is a Very Hard problem, it's hard to even specify. Samples may not be arriving simultaneously; identifying all of the samples you need to ensure all lines continue may be very tricky. There is certainly no way to specify this now. As a possibility, we could just set the graph to the exact range. However, this almost guarantees that there will be gaps on either side, which looks like missing data (which is sort of is). I don't have any good answers here. Perhaps we just live with the graph not quite matching expectations.
creator: adesmet

title: Ticket #6506: NETWORK_INTERFACE=127.0.0.1 on Windows causes collector to crash ...?
description: ToddT reports that setting NETWORK_INTERFACE to 127.0.0.1 on his personal condor on Windows is causing his collector to crash when it sends an update the world collector. It blows an assert in condor_sockaddr::from_ip_str(), called from ConvertDefaultIpToSocketIp() (the address-rewriting code) with the return of s.my_ip_str(). s is UDP, which is the default for updating the world collector, and s._who is the IPv4 address of the world collector. However, s.my_ip_str() returns NULL and leaves a message in the log claiming that this is because it the address was unreachable (10051). (1) ToddT will avoid the assert by checking to see if s.my_ip_str() returns NULL and bailing before calling condor_sockaddr::from_ip_str() if so. (2) (design) We should reconsider the wisdom of the assertion in question: should we instead check if all callers check the return value, and if they do, return false if the parameter is NULL instead of blowing an assert? (3) (optimization) ConvertDefaultIpToSocketIp() only does anything aside from write log messages if the undocumented knob SHARED_PORT_ADDRESS_REWRITING is set. We should find out if that can be removed (see tickets #4848 and #4849). Otherwise, we can certainly optimize the function by checking for it first, and for the various debug flags if we decide to keep caring about them. (4) (bug) ConvertDefaultIpToSocketIp() should have been bailing out because network_interface_to_ip() should be setting enable_convert_default_IP_to_socket_IP to false if the NETWORK_INTERFACE only matches one interface, and no machine should have interfaces with the same address. (5) (we were confused) Why does connect() think the address is unreachable? We looked (briefly) and didn't find where we bound UDP (or TCP) sockets to the NETWORK_INTERFACE when binding w/o an address or on a connect.
remarks: 2017-Dec-12 18:29 by tlmiller: (4) Oh, hey, look at that. If condor_sockaddr::from_ip_string() works on NETWORK_INTERFACE, we don't unset enable_convert_default_IP_to_socket_IP. We should maybe fix that. 2017-Dec-12 18:39:24 by tlmiller: (5) In Sock::bindWithin(), if bind_all isn't set, then we call get_local_ipaddr(proto), which will return the NETWORK_INTERFACE if it's of the right protocol, that is, 127.0.0.1; this is the address we later pass to condor_bind(). Either Sock::bindWithin() is called from Sock::bind() or Sock::bind() calls if the port is dynamic, which it was in the debugger, and we're not binding to all interfaces, which we weren't. 2017-Dec-13 12:49:31 by tlmiller: (1) #6507 (2) #6510 (3) #6509 (4) #6508 2017-Dec-13 12:50:49 by tlmiller: Resolving on the basis that all of the incident's components have their own tickets now, of which we only really care about one.

Imagine running a tool like ssh_to_job or condor_fetchlog that needs to contact an execute machine behind a firewall via CCB; in this case, the reversed CCB connection may need to arrive via shared_port and the tool will need to know this. 2017-Feb-20 16:23:55 by tannenba: Random thought -- does DAGMan need a command port at all on LINUX platforms? Of course, on Windows, I think a command port is required since that is how DAGMan receives signals from the schedd.... 2017-Feb-20 16:47:43 by tlmiller: DAGMan is started with -p 0, which the code says and Jaime empirically confirmed prevents the creation of a command socket. However -- presumably to enable shared pot with CCB -- daemon core unconditionally initializes shared port in reconfig(), which is typically called during start-up. Our brief testing and looking at the error message make us wonder if there's (also) a problem with DAGMan changing the LOG directory or something (why is the shared port endpoint looking in '.' for the shared_port_ad?), but it's probably the case -- we'd have to check the initializer code -- that just turning off shared port for dagman would work fine. We should ask Kent if we want to continue/finish our investigation. 2017-Feb-21 15:01:19 by jfrey: If you pass -port 0 on the command line, DaemonCore doesn't create a TCP/UDP command port. But it does try to create a shared port command port. This is a bug. For DAGMan, the attempt to create a shared port command port is messed up by the "-l ." command line argument, which overrides the value of the LOG parameter. Thus, it can't find the shared_port_ad file and creates a daemon_sock directory under its current working directory. If I create symlinks for shared_port_ad and daemon_sock in the current working directory to point to the real locations, then I can send commands to DAGMan by using an appropriate sinful string. We can set DAGMAN_USE_SHARED_PORT=False in the param table to avoid these problems. title: Ticket #3354: condor_root_switchboard performance problem with large fdset size
description: Burt reports performance problems because of condor_root_switchboard closing all the FDs up to getrlimit(rlimit_NOFILE). On the glidein factory, it is common to have ulimit -n around 50k. I'm not aware of a better solution than to use an OS-specific technique such as iterating through /proc/pid/fds to avoid iterating through all 50k FDs, most of which are not open. Since reducing the limit does not force higher-numbered fds to be closed, one may need to be careful if there is a concern about leaving some FDs open.

title: Ticket #1369: New ClassAd function: switch
description: Lets say you're writing a report similar to the default condor_q report, but with tweaks for your own needs. condor_q's -format option can get you there, but sometimes the expressions you end up writing are a mess. For example, to generate the "ST" (Job Status) field, you use something like this: -format '%-2s ' 'ifThenElse(JobStatus==0,"U",ifThenElse(JobStatus==1,"I",ifThenElse(JobStatus==2,"R",ifThenElse(JobStatus==3,"X",ifThenElse(JobStatus==4,"C",ifThenElse(JobStatus==5,"H",ifThenElse(JobStatus==6,"E",string(JobStatus))))))))' That's a pain in the ass to write or read. Essentially I'm doing a lookup, or something similar to a switch statement, and a briefer form would be nice. For example, it might look like this: -format '%-2s ' 'switch(JobStatus,string(JobStatus),0,"U",1,"I",2,"R",3,"X",4,"C",5,"H",6,"E")' The arguments above would be: switch( value to switch on, default, value 1, result 1, value 2, result 2, ...) Or perhaps something more verbose, but also more flexible: -format '%-2s ' 'switch(string(JobStatus),JobStatus==0,"U", JobStatus==1,"I", JobStatus==2,"R", JobStatus==3,"X", JobStatus==4,"C", JobStatus==5,"H", JobStatus==6,"E")' With the tests evaluated in order, the first one to return true being the answer. If none are true, the first argument is returned at the default. This more verbose form allows simple testing of ranges or regular expressions.

Ticket #6855: transfer file transfer plugin along with the job
description: It should be possible to transfer a file transfer plugin along with a job. This would allow file transfer plugins to be managed on the submit node, or event to be created by advanced users. It would also allow for a much faster development cycle for transfer plugins. The proposed solution is to add an attribute to the job that specifies the name of the plugin, and the URL tags that that plugin supports. Something like this transfer_plugins = ZKM=/path/to/zkm_plug.exe; HTTP,HTTPS=my_http_plugin.exe This would add the following to the job. TransferPlugins = "ZKM=/path/to/zkm_plug.exe; HTTP,HTTPS=my_http_plugin.exe" Then when the job has transfer_input_files = ZKM://myfile, HTTP://stuff, HTTPS://morestuff Condor submit would NOT add the ZKM and HTTP file transfer plugin tags to the job's requirements expression, but would instead it would add TARGET.HasJobTransferPlugins to the job's requirements expression. Starters that support file transfer plugins supplied by the job will advertise this attribute. If there are plugin prefixes in the list of files to be transferred that are not included in the TransferPlugins list, then those plugins would still be added to the job's requirements expression. so transfer_plugins = ZKM=/path/to/zkm_plug.exe; HTTP,HTTPS=my_http_plugin.exe transfer_input_files = ZKM://myfile, HTTP://stuff, HTTPS://morestuff, FTP://file Would result in a requirements expression that had Requirements = .. && (TARGET.HasJobTransferPlugins && stringListIMember("FTP",TARGET.HasFileTransferPluginMethods)) When the file transfer class is initialized, it will be passed the job ad, so after it loads the transfer plugins from configuration, it will then parse the job's TransferPlugins attribute and add the plugins it finds there to the list of available plugins. Thus plugins transferred by the job will be preferred to plugins available on the execute node. Because there is no way to indicate whether a plugin is single or multi-file, multi-file will be assumed for plugins transferred with the job. Plugins transferred with the job will never be run as root.
remarks: 2019-Jan-30 12:30:21 by johnkn: See the patch file for an implementation. The patch works with the following submit file. The "transfer plugin" in this case is myplug.cmd, which I have verified gets transferred to the execute sandbox and then invoked as a multi-file plugin. plug.sub executable=simple.bat transfer_executable=true transfer_input_files=payload\, simple.in, JMK://foo Transfer_plugins=JMK:myplug.cmd arguments = 2 log=plug.log output=plug.out error=plug.err should_transfer_files=yes when_to_transfer_output=ON_EXIT queue I think the patch works when the plugin has an absolute path, but I have not tested that. Also, I know that the file transfer class is used for spooling input files, but I have not tested that case either. I should have noted in the patch comment, it is for master branch. SHA 3dfdb5dd80988e49ba20feca1a3368fa97dd7e74 2019-Jan-31 08:48:04 by bbockelm: Code comments are here: https://github.com/htcondor/htcondor/pull/29 The bigger question is about the format of the map itself in the submit language. It's unlike how we do transfer_output_remaps; I'd like to see some consistency between the two. 2019-Jan-31 08:48:46 by bbockelm: Oh - the other question I had was more general: is there case sensitivity in matching the protocols? Does the HTTP plugin work with a http:// URL? 2019-Jan-31 08:55:40 by johnkn: URL tags are case-insensitive by definition, although the current file transfer code does this wrong, and treats them as case-sensitive. The matchmaking expression that condor_submit emits in the current code correctly does case-insensitive matchmaking, so we will match an HTTP://file to a STARTD that reports "http" support, which will then fail (sigh). We should fix that, but my patch does not since that would be a much more extensive change. 2019-Jan-31 09:09:52 by johnkn: I see no value in making it consistent with transfer_output_rempaps, these are entirely different things. On the other hand, swapping the URL tag and the filename and switching from : to = as the separator doesn't really matter either way. 2019-Jan-31 09:53:27 by bbockelm: Right - I'm not saying that transfer_output_remaps is related, but it's syntactically a list of key-value pairs, just like transfer_plugins is here. We should use the same separators unless there's a strong reason not to. Can you open a separate ticket for case sensitivity of the protocol schema? 2019-Jan-31 11:54:58 by johnkn: we should avoid confusing this with transfer_output_remaps unless there is a strong reason treat them as similar.

title: Ticket #5280: Need to set cgroup hard memory limit for memsw limit to work
description: If an admin has set a soft memory limit for a cgroup-enabled slot, then setting the memory + swap limit often fails. This is because the kernel prohibits setting memory + swap lower than the hard limit, and if we haven't set the hard limit, the default is often infinite. So, when setting the memory + swap limit, if condor only has a soft limit, we will also set the hard limit to be memory + swap minus one page.

title: Ticket #4184: [Miron] Determine if|how KVM can checkpoint & continue
description: What can KVM do, especially via libvirt, to implement a periodic checkpoint? Does it have built-in support for checkpoint-and-continue, or would we need to checkpoint and restart? What restrictions, if any, must or should we place on the VM? Is it necessary, for instance, to use qcow2 disk images?
remarks: 2014-Feb-03 13:54:04 by tlmiller: As of the RHEL7 beta, the libvirt (virsh) / KVM / QEMU troika can not save the state of the VM while it is running. (They claim this capability will be arriving shortly; I don't know if that means in time for RHEL 7 or Fedora 20 or what.) We must therefore pause the VM in order to checkpoint. The troika does support a method of operation in which they pause and resume the VM around a checkpoint automatically. However, this method of operation does not result in anything useful, because the checkpoint is taken "internally", which means as part of the existing disk image(s). Since we can't copy those while the emulator is running, this ability is mostly useless. (We'd have to pause the VM again, as well as make sure that the hypervisor flushed its buffers, or, possibly, had the proper caching mode set on all of the VM's disks.) However, we can bypass both of these problems by using the 'virsh save' command, which writes the memory (and other volatile) state of the VM to disk in a file specified by the user. This process terminates the VM, but the save/restore cycle for my test VM was only 2.5 seconds. (I wouldn't be surprised if this number increased by an order of magnitude for more RAM-intensive VMS.) However, because save and restore are distinct commands, we have as long we need to copy the memory image (and the disk image(s), known to be in a consistent state) wherever we like. Once the "live checkpoint" functionality is available, we'll be able to do pretty much the same thing without interrupting the VM. (There's already functionality for merging the external checkpoint disk back to the base image once you're done backing it up.) In the interim, we could try to be clever with setting up delta disks, which should allow us to ship back just the changes from the base image; but there may be (bad) performance implications. The methodology suggested above also has the nice consequence that we remain indifferent to the format of the disk image(s).
creator: tlmiller

title: Ticket #649: new param() system should have patterns
description: Currently, the param default table specification file does not have the ability to specify patterns for when Condor code does param("%_LOG") and such things. I have a test piece of definition in which the actual layout of the patterns are defined. The important thing to remember is that there are two classes of variables, patterned ones, and non-patterned ones. When param() does its deal, it should look into the hash of non-patterned entries first, then failing to find one, linearly search the pattern entries until a match is found. When a match is found, then specific string is associated to the pattern entry via memoization table. This will make the initial search linear, but later search use hash table complexity. This is an optimization, to be sure, but most likely a needed one immediately.
creator: psilord

title: Ticket #6443: Allow custom names to refer to the two ads in a MatchClassAd
description: When matching two ads with a MatchClassAd, expressions can reference attributes in their own ad using a MY or SELF scope prefix and attributes in the other ad using a TARGET or OTHER scope prefix. In some situations in Condor, we want to evaluate an expression in the context of both ads, and neither ad is the natural home for the expression. So we pick one ad as the local context of the expression. Users have to remember this arbitrary choice to use the correct attribute scope names, and can easily get it wrong. One example of this is the negotiator's preemption expressions. It would be very useful if descriptive names were available to refer to the two ads in a MatchClassAd. In the negotiator, these could be Job and Slot. Then, the expression writer doesn't have to worry about which ad the expression is evaluated in. They can just prefix all of the attribute names with correct descriptive ad name. Note: We can't use Machine as the ad name for the machine ad, as the ad contains an attribute called Machine.
remarks: This is a purely internal change. No version history required.

title: Ticket #6013: Collect JVM statistics for Java Universe jobs
description: From Michael Pelletier: We ran into a situation here where jobs were choking out because their heap space was too small, which was driving their garbage collectors to extremes, and it occurred to me that it would be handy if the Java universe used "jstat" or something like that to collect useful statistics about the operation of the JVM during the run. I'm not familiar enough with Java to know everything that might be useful, but at least in this case knowing things like the number of GC events and GC time would have been helpful. In addition, the min, max, and current heap sizes could be placed in immutable job attributes. This would increase the usefulness of the Java universe, I suspect.

title: Ticket #4700: Document how to restart DAGMan in recovery mode
description: We don't really document how to re-start DAGMan in recovery mode. A situation where you might need to do this is as follows: the filesystem that your dagman.out file is on fills up while DAGMan is running, causing dprintf to fail, which makes DAGMan exit. In this case, I believe that DAGMan will exit the queue, and we don't document how the user should re-submit it without re-running the jobs that already succeeded. If the user just does "condor_submit_dag <dag_file>" I think it will complain about the .condor.sub file, etc., already existing. So they may end up doing condor_submit_dag -f, which will re-run all jobs. They can do the right thing by doing "condor_submit <dag_file>.condor_sub", but I can't remember whether "condor_submit_dag -recovery <dag_file>" will work. (I think you can kind of simulate this by removing a DAG that's already on hold.)

title: Ticket #167: GitTrac: Diff fails for new files
description:
See [13632], observe that the HTML is busted. Problem: /setup_diff claims: "If you leave the above entry blank, the following command is used: GIT_DIR='%RP' git-diff --full-index -t -p -r '%V1' '%V2' -- '%F' 2>/dev/null" Lies. If the file is new (or probably deleted), it merrily passes an empty string as V1 (or probably V1 on deletion). This causes git-diff anguish and it complains, "fatal: bad revision ''" and trashes the HTML as a side effect. So in reality, for new (and probably deleted) files, GitTrac doesn't do anything at all. But, if you set the entry, it always calls it. Fix: Instead of calling GIT_DIR='%RP' git diff --full-index -t -p -r '%V1' '%V2' -- '%F' | /scratch.2/gittrac/bin/diff2html.py 2>/dev/null we should call a wrapper script that detects an empty V1 or V2 and instead just spits back something more useful. Perhaps a simple

%F was added

or

%F was deleted

Of course, if V1 and V2 are both present, call the above command as usual.
creator: adesmet

title: Ticket #6697: coordinated retirement while draining breaks HOLD_IF_MEMORY_EXCEEDED
description: The HOLD_IF_MEMORY_EXCEEDED policy doesn't immediately put jobs which exceed their requested memory on hold, as intended, because the 'immediately' part is implemented as a modification to MAXJOBRETIREMENTTIME. While draining (with backfill), a job which exceeds its memory will have /its/ MJRT become 0, but that's ignored in favor of coordinating retirement times. The latter has always seemed a questionable thing to do while allowing backfill, but now it breaks things. Leaving as an incident report until we decide what to do. Moate reports being somewhat concerned about jobs on a draining machine having their maximum lifetimes extended. This happens for the same reason: a job is evicted for running too long, but eviction obeys MJRT, and the MJRT is not zero because it's been computed as the largest MJRT for any slot. The relevant policy expressions follow. PREEMPT = (JobUniverse != 13 && MemoryUsage =!= UNDEFINED && MemoryUsage > Memory) || TotalJobRunTime > ( 72 * 3600 ) MAXJOBRETIREMENTTIME = ifthenelse((JobUniverse != 13 && MemoryUsage =!= UNDEFINED && MemoryUsage > Memory),0,MAX_PREEMPT) MAX_PREEMPT = (3600 * (72 - 68 * (WantGlidein =?= true)))

title: Ticket #7593: Lots of FDs cause my_popenv_impl() grief
description: It can take several (approximately four) seconds to close a million FDs. This causes a long cumulative delay in starting up the startd, which makes a few calls to my_popenv, and blocks waiting for the starter (running -classad), which makes quite a few of its own calls to that function. (It's not clear right now it DaemonCore::Create_Process() has the same problem or not.) We noticed this because the default ulimit -f is ~1 million in a Docker container we were testing; we should check if that's normal (inherited from the Docker daemon?). We should commit a quick improvement almost immediately, where we move the call to getdtablesize() out of the loop (cutting the syscall count in half). See https://gitlab.freedesktop.org/libbsd/libbsd/blob/master/src/closefrom.c for ideas on a better approach.

title: Ticket #5054: file transfer appears to not always encrypt files when requested
description: Using the default security settings, it appears that HTCondor will transfer files unencrypted on the wire even if the submit file explicitly requests an encrypted transfer. To reproduce the problem the same way I did, set STARTER_DEBUG = D_SECURITY D_FULLDEBUG and then submit a test job that transfer a couple of input directory (that are populated with some files), and request that all job input files are encrypted on the wire. My test.sub submit file: executable = c:\utils\sleep.exe arguments = 10 encrypt_input_files = * transfer_input_files = c:\temp\swamp_configs, c:\temp\patch should_transfer_files = YES when_to_transfer_output = ON_EXIT log = test.log universe = vanilla queue After the job ran, I observed the following in the StarterLog on the execute machine: 05/13/15 14:46:03 FILETRANSFER: incoming file_command is 2 05/13/15 14:46:03 NOT enabling crypto - there was no key exchanged. I did the same test on both Linux and Windows using v8.3.5 pre-release, and got the same results. I did not change any SEC_* settings in my condor_config file(s).
remarks: 2015-May-13 16:27:03 by tannenba: On a related note: I boldly assert that if HTCondor is told to encrypt a file transfer and it cannot comply, the file transfer should fail - it should not fall back in transferring the file in the clear. Looking at the source code in /src/condor_utils/file_transfer.cpp, we see the following lines: dprintf( D_SECURITY, "FILETRANSFER: incoming file_command is %i\n", reply); if( !reply ) { break; } if (reply == 2) { s->set_crypto_mode(true); } else if (reply == 3) { s->set_crypto_mode(false); } else { s->set_crypto_mode(socket_default_crypto); } Seems to me that this code should check the return values from method set_crypto_mode(), and if this method fails, the file transfer should fail (ideally propagating a reason to the user log). 2015-May-27 15:16:37 by zmiller: I looked into this in depth. There is no crypto key to use if authentication between the shadow and starter does not occur. This is currently the default in both the CHTC pool and HTCondor version 8.3.5. I propose the following changes: Change the CHTC to use a special kind of authentication called "match password". I have emailed our sysadmin to request this change and will let you know when it is in place. This causes crypto keys to be exchanged and per-file encryption is then possible. Change the default in HTCondor 8.3.6 to have "match password" enabled by default. This obviates the need for item 1 above, but item 1 does no harm and this item is a good change to make for ALL pools, not just CHTC. When doing file transfer, put the job on hold if encryption for a file was requested but unable to happen due to lack of encryption keys. I have already completed this code, am testing it, and will check it in for 8.3.6. This way you can be assured your job will never run and files will never be transferred if encryption was unavailable for any reason. Due to other various hold-ups, we will not have release candidate binaries for 8.3.6 until Monday (slipped from Thursday this week). I suggest we all check in then. 2015-May-28 08:54:21 by bbockelm: Match auth should only really be used if the channel from negotiator->schedd is secure. Should we also change defaults so that is true also? I'm somewhat uncomfortable making a significant security default change as a side-impact of a different ticket. 2015-May-28 10:09:53 by zmiller: Brian: I disagree. Are you saying that using match password is somehow worse than no auth at all? It only uses information that was already being sent. Let's talk later today if you have a chance. title: Ticket #3929: Log rotation broken when MAX_NUM_SUBSYS_LOG > 1 w/o date rotation
description: when MAX_NUM_<SUBSYS>_LOG is set to 2 or more, the log rotation code generates a log file with the extension 1969* and never actually rotates beyond it. It appears that there is some crosstalk between time based rotation and size based rotation. Also, on Windows. if there is a log file with an extension that sorts after .old. cleanupOldLogFiles will go into an infinite loop. Note this bug does not occur if one is using date-based rotation instead of size-based rotation.
remarks: 2013-Oct-02 17:50:23 by tannenba: CODE REVIEW Ticket shows no evidence of how the patch was tested. While the problems with rotation when MAX_NUM_SUBSYS_LOG > 1 appear resolved, unfortunately cleanUpOldLogFiles() still goes into an infinite loop. The infinite loop problem seems related to this code: // catch the exception that the file name pattern is disturbed by external influence if (strcmp(oldFile, empty) == 0) break; The break statement never happens, because in my test case empty is c:\condor/log/NegotiatorLog, and oldFile is NegotiatorLog.20131002T173421. The problem is one path is fully qualified, and the other is not, thus the break will never happen. Even if both paths were fully qualified, another issue is the directory delimiters are not canonicalized before the pathnames are compared. Please modify patch and include in the ticket screen output of it failing to work before your fix and working correctly after your fix. 2013-Oct-15 13:50:23 by johnkn: Further analysis of the code shows that the above is indeed a problem, but that the code is even more broken than previously believed. Fixing the above mentioned problem actually makes things worse because findOldest on Windows always returns the .old file if one exists, but that test causes us to never delete that file. On *nix, findOldest actually returns the youngest file with a file extension, so it's broken in a different way. The fix for these bugs requires more changes than can be safely made before 8.0.4 is released - I'm retargeting for 8.0.5 2013-Nov-07 15:35:46 by bt: We now have some tools which test the logging code. A test exercises those tools and can be run by hand in a preconfigured condor to test. The test is called "job_test_logrotation.run" and it uses a custom tool condor_testwritelog. When called with any args, it does not start any person condors but does change config settings between tests. Status as of 11/8/13.

title: Ticket #7439: Remote query to a schedd with a localname reads wrong history file
description: If a secondary schedd is given a localname, and then that localname is used to configure a different history file config fragment SCHEDD_TWO = $(SCHEDD) DAEMON_LIST = $(DAEMON_LIST) SCHEDD_TWO HISTORY = /opt/condor/history/history SCHEDD_TWO.HISTORY = /opt/condor/history/two.history When a remote history query is sent to schedd two, it will start a local instance of condor_history, passing on the query socket and query args, but NOT passing on the localname, so the local condor_history will use the HISTORY knob and read from the wrong history file. We should fix this by adding a -localname argument to condor_history and having the schedd pass it's localname argument down to it.

We have a test low-latency dag that was running at CIT in /home/gstlalcbctest/observing/1/trigs_ts The dag was restarted ar 11/11/15 06:27:29 and one of the jobs that we are trying to understand was submitted and began to be executed 11/11/15 06:32:38 Event: ULOG_SUBMIT for Condor Node gstlal_inspiral_0002 (27941471.0.0) 11/11/15 06:32:54 Event: ULOG_EXECUTE for Condor Node gstlal_inspiral_0002 (27941471.0.0) 11/11/15 06:42:54 Node gstlal_inspiral_0002, Condor ID 27941471, status STATUS_SUBMITTED but then later 11/12/15 21:23:00 Node gstlal_inspiral_0002, Condor ID 27941471, status STATUS_SUBMITTED 11/12/15 21:48:52 Event: ULOG_EXECUTE for Condor Node gstlal_inspiral_0002 (27941471.0.0) 11/12/15 22:11:14 Node gstlal_inspiral_0002, Condor ID 27941471, status STATUS_SUBMITTED So the job stopped executing for some reason and was restarted. We tracked down that the job was originally running on node628 and restarted on a new node around 21:48. Unfortunately, I don't know which node it was restarted on because I forgot to take a note of that before the dag was stopped. I did log into node628 and there is an indication of a vacate request going to that node on 11/12/15 around 21:46, but we're not 100% sure what that was or where it came from. Is there an easy way to understand? More than one jobs was affected by this. We don't have the details, but it could be extracted from the dagman.out file if needed. Thanks for your help, P #### REPLY #### Patrick, It looks like this is due to the following kernel bug that was introduced in the kernel we are currently running but has been fixed upstream, http://oss.sgi.com/archives/xfs/2015-09/msg00263.html I need to look a bit further but I suspect we will schedule a kernel patch/reboot on the cluster next Tuesday that will hopefully clean this up (along with another annoying warning we have been seeing for a while). title: Ticket #921: Expose Schedd's NFS cache flushing feature as controllable by job ad
description: The Schedd has a feature to mkstemp&unlink a file in a completing job's Iwd, if that Iwd is in NFS. This clears the NFS cache to assist programs on the submit node that read the job's Iwd after it completes. Original Issue: programs reading the Iwd on the submit machine could read cached data and not the job's actual output. In 7.4.0, this cache flushing happens for any job with an Iwd in NFS. if ( job_ad->LookupString( ATTR_OWNER, owner ) && job_ad->LookupString( ATTR_JOB_IWD, iwd ) && fs_detect_nfs( iwd.Value(), &is_nfs ) == 0 && is_nfs ) { FLUSH_CACHE (using condor_mkstemp and unlink) } It is assumed that the mkstemp and unlink is expensive. The FLUSH_CACHE should be a feature exposed to jobs. This would mean other processes could also implement it, i.e. the shadow. I'm going to introduce job attribute IwdFlushNFSCache, an expression, that will guard the fs_detect_nfs() check. The benefit here is to avoid the FLUSH_CACHE and avoid the fs_detect_nfs(). For 7.4, this attribute, undocumented, will default to TRUE, but should be considered for documentation and a default of FALSE for 7.5. Additionally, the FLUSH_CACHE may be better implemented as closedir(opendir(Iwd)), to be lighter weight.

description: Handling several repositories for Condor is a pain. When possible, we want to reduce the number of repositories we have to manage. Three of our current five repos (CONDOR_EXT, CONDOR_TST_CNFDTL and CONDOR_TST_LRG) hold large tarballs that don't change and which we don't want to pollute the CONDOR_SRC repo. title: Ticket #1447: dedicated scheduler doesn't check concurrency limits for claim reuse
description:
When the dedicated scheduler considers an unexpired claim for re-use, it does not check that concurrency limits also match between job ad and the claimed resource. The repro below assumes a two-slot dedicated scheduler configuration, with: TEST_LIMIT = 4 In the following repro example, the second job should not be able to re-use the claim from the first job, however it does: % echo -e 'universe=parallel
cmd=/bin/sleep
args=20s

' | condor_submit % echo -e 'universe=parallel

title: Ticket #6382: Python bindings parse old ClassAds with new ClassAds escaping rules
description: The python bindings understand both old and new ClassAds syntax. But when parsing old ClassAds format, they use the string escaping rules from new ClassAds. This causes string literals that contain a backslash to be parsed wrong, and some valid string values to result in a parse error. In the python bindings, the OldClassAdIterator class passes each name=value string to classad::ClassAd::Insert(const std::string&), which doesn't know about old ClassAd escaping rules. This can be fixed fairly easily in 8.7 by using ClassAdParser set to old ClassAd mode. In 8.6, we'll need something equivalent to ConvertEscapingOldToNew() from the Condor util lib. This was first reported at https://ticket.opensciencegrid.org/34573

title: Ticket #4645: Stats publication should be configurable using a whitelist
description: Currently, the publication of statistics is controlled by configuring a verbosity level for the publication of each set of statistics. The stats themselves have a verbosity level set by the programmer, the user can choose what verbosity level to publish by setting the STATISTICS_TO_PUBLISH configuration variable. If verbosity 2 is chosen for SCHEDD stats, then all stats of verbosity 2 or lower will be published. This is a huge amount and will flood the collector, so in practice only verbosity 0 or 1 is useful. But some of the stats that we wish to track are set at verbosity 2. So a way is needed to specify a list of stats that should always be published, regardless of the current publication verbosity. A new configuration variable STATISTICS_TO_PUBLISH_LIST will contain a comma or space separated list of classad attributes, each statistic that matches at least one entry in that list will be have it's verbosity set to the current STATISTICS_TO_PUBLISH verbosity level. Thus these will always publish. Because some stats are published in sets (i.e. a count,total,min,max,avg & std). Enabling one member of the set will enable all of them.

title: Ticket #2142: KILLING_TIMEOUT overrides KILL policy
description: I'm wondering if the change in behavior of preemption in 7.5 was really intended to be as broad as it is. Due to #1198, the KILL expression is useless by default, because when a job is preempted, it is hard-killed as soon as KILLING_TIMEOUT expires. The default KILLING_TIMEOUT is just 30s. We've received complaints in CHTC from users who have self-checkpointing jobs that cannot save state in this amount of time. The desired policy was configured via the KILL expression, which gave jobs 10 minutes to vacate, but this is being trumped by the new behavior of KILLING_TIMEOUT.
remarks: 2011-May-09 13:32:27 by danb: I reproduced this problem using the following configuration, which is supposed to hard-kill the job after it has been running for 120 seconds, but which instead hard-kills it when KILLING_TIMEOUT expires, 60s after the job started. PREEMPT = (time() - JobStart) > 30 WANT_VACATE = true KILL = (time() - JobStart) > 120 I then submitted a job: executable = my_preempt notification = never log = ulog output = mydir/stdout error = mydir/stderr should_transfer_files = yes when_to_transfer_output = on_exit queue The script my_preempt is as follows: #!/bin/sh Killed() { echo Received SIGTERM } trap Killed SIGTERM sleep 3600 2011-May-10 10:17:35 by rrati: The issue was that in the ShutdownGraceful case the starter was setting the escalation timer, when when it expires would hard kill the job. This shouldn't happen in the graceful shutdown case. The starter should send the signal to the job and wait for outside influence to escalate to a Fast case if needed (rm, policy, etc). 2011-May-10 10:34:57 by tannenba: fwiw, I did a quick code review of the 3 line change, looks good :)
check_ins: 2011-May-10 10:05 Check-in [21808]: Signal escalation should only occur in the ShutdownFast case, but the ShutdownGraceful case was starting the escalation timer. This caused a conflict with the KILL policy expression. Removed setting the escalation timer during ShutdownGraceful. (#2142) (By Robert Rati )

Ticket #6414: cgroup limits not getting set on some OSes due to signed'ness of memsw
description: The starter reuses its cgroup from one invocation to the next. When setting the memsw limit, it must always be higher than the memory limit. This is hard to ensure, given that a 2nd run of the starter doesn't know what the previous settings of memsw and mem were. To fix this, the starter first sets memsw to a very high value, then sets memory to the correct value, then lowers memsw to the correct value. We were setting memsw to a high value by setting it to ULONG_MAX, the max unsigned value. However, some kernels (RHEL6, but not the Fedora 25 kernel) threw an error with ULONG_MAX, and then refused to set any other cgroup memory or cpu limits thereafter. Changing the "high value" setting to LONG_MAX seems to fix the problem on all platforms.

title: Ticket #3616: schedd fails to restart after writing unparseable values into log
description: The classad log code can write unparseable values into the log file (e.g. job_queue.log), and as a result of #3069 it could EXCEPT on restart when it replays the log and hits the invalid line. The most common way to trigger this landmine is perform a condor_qedit using a illegal classad value such as $$$ (no quotation marks), or even spaces. If you then try to restart the schedd before the schedd rotates the log (which is currently only every 24 hours by default), the schedd will EXCEPT on restart. The fix should not be at the level of the schedd, but at the level of the classad log code -- note that this is where the bug resides, and that the classad log code is used by more than just the schedd (e.g. it is also used by the accountant inside the negotiator, by the collector for offline and absent ads, ...). Before writing an attribute value to the log (aka job_queue.log), make certain the value can be parsed. Because parsing is relatively expensive, this should be done efficiently by parsing only once when the log event is created. The resulting parse tree could then be stored in ram and reused when the log is played. If the value fails to parse, the value will be changed to UNDEFINED. As an aside, it would be nice if "condor_qedit" validated the attribute value and gave an immediate error back to the user.

title: Ticket #6947: Extend PASSWORD auth to support multiple and derived secrets
description: We would like the pool password mechanism to be extended such that the admin (or daemons) with access to the master password can create derived passwords with limited trust and that there can be multiple master passwords per pool. Each pool should have a self-identified key domain which indicates to clients which set of derived passwords should be used. See design doc (https://docs.google.com/document/d/10uSYp6sePbHPFzKmkTMAwr1uKzuSxebr_Om89IUgyUs/edit) for more details.

This token will later become the JWT used by the user. 2019-Mar-08 11:36:46 by tlmiller: I'll review the design doc (shouldn't be any major issues -- I think we agreed on all the major points of the plan in my office on Thursday) and then the existing code (per your request). 2019-Mar-08 13:38:37 by bbockelm: Thanks! I assume they don't fall back to PASSWORDv1, but that when a daemon is acting as a client and has a master key, but it not otherwise configured, it will use some standard fixed identity (from which, of course, it can readily generate the derived keys when that becomes necessary). I think the document should be explicit that "associate it with additional metadata" specifically includes simply passing an authenticated identity into HTCondor's existing authorization mechanisms, and that this will probably be the default. (When the document says "the set of authorizations" later on, it makes this work sound very ambitious, inasmuch as HTCondor does not presently have a capabilities model.) It might be helpful to mention the default settings and expected scenarios as they relate to the initial set-up of a secure pool, flocking (to and from another pool), connecting an annex, and Condor-C. This would include ideas like using the first entry in the collector list as the default key domain, and -- since PASSWORDv2 should just disable itself without a password file -- a default configuration where all the admin has to do to turn on PASSWORDv2 is drop the client's keyblob in the conventional place on disk. 2019-Mar-08 19:32:51 by bbockelm: > How two processes which both have access to the same master key communicate Actually, if the token is an empty string, the PASSWORD2 protocol is equivalent to the PASSWORD1 wire protocol. title: Ticket #5668: Don't cache classad attributes that are pre-parsed
description: When inserting attributes into a classad, the code can either take an unparsed string as input, or a pre-parsed ExprTree. Today, if we get an ExprTree, we first unparse it back to a string, in order to see if we have a cached value for that string. This is rather expensive, and unlikely to be a cache hit. Instead, we will only cache inserts where we already have the string value to parse in hand.

title: Ticket #7655: Python bindings transaction behavior is confusing and undocumented
description: (I've labelled this for 8.9.8 because I think we need to decide what to do about it before doing anything, and we should decide soon, because we need to think about whether to break compatibility for 9.x) The current behavior of the Transaction object in the bindings is very confusing because it tries to serve several distinct roles. TJ, please correct me if any of this is wrong... You must acquire a transaction before submitting jobs using a Submit object. You must explicitly pass the transaction to the queue method. You may acquire a transaction object before Schedd.edit. If you do, the edits will all be part of the same transaction, even though you don't have to pass the transaction to the edit method. The edits implicitly use the transaction through global state in the bindings. You must not Schedd.act inside a transaction with anything else in it, because the actual schedd doesn't support acting and editing/submitting in the same transaction. It's unclear to me whether you can edit and submit in the same transaction; based on my understanding the answer is no. As I recall, we've also had problems with submitting twice in the same transaction. Perhaps TJ can clarify? Even worse, making a transaction object immediately acquires the write lock in the schedd for the entire duration of the transaction context in Python. This is not documented anywhere and has obvious implications for how users should write code in transaction contexts (get in and out as quickly as possible). The easiest and most immediate approach is to actually document all of these quirks in the manual (basically, stick the above text in the manual). In the long-term, I think we should consider completely scrapping the current transaction model in Python and coming up with one that reflects the transaction model in the schedd (which we could also improve) more accurately and clearly. The new model should also defer actually acquiring the underlying write lock until the "transaction" context ends in Python (in particular, in the __exit__ method of the context manager, so that the user doesn't get to run code as easily during the real transaction).
