title: Ticket #2007: Can stduniv run as a vanilla job with standalone checkpointing?
description: Motivation The users of Condor's stduniv constitute a small userbase. Of that small user base, an even smaller group relies in remote I/O. The larger group specifically turns it off. There are multiple user space third party checkpointers, such as DMTCP, cryopid, etc., and several application specific checkpointers, like Gromacs, that people would like to use with Condor. Problem Statement What services would Condor have to provide to make it easy for third party checkpointing systems (with DMTCP as the motivating example) to use the vanilla universe to maximize goodput and correctness of execution restart? If we thought of Condor's standard universe as a third party system (without remote I/O) and used it in the vanilla universe, what, if anything, would have to change about the stduniv? Goal These goals presume the assumption of no remote I/O capability by any of the "third party" checkpointers, including our own stduniv library when used in this context. Identify what special features about the stduniv we need to propogate to the vanilla universe. Identify what functionality we need from third party checkpointers to allow their integration into Condor's vanilla universe. Identify how Condor Users and Administrators will interact with the new feature. State of the Art The Standard Universe This describes the current high-level behavior of the Standard Universe. Each resource slot in the pool computes (via internal code and a binary tool we ship called condor_ckpt_probe) a "checkpoint signature" of the machine and stores it into the slot ad. This is stored in the CheckpointPlatform classad attribute. The value represents an opaque token. The START expression of each slot has in it a reference to the expression IsValidCheckpointPlatform. This expression is false if the job is a standard universe job whose defined LastCheckpointPlatform value does not match the slot's CheckpointPlatform attribute. It is true in all other cases. When a job initially starts, it must start on a machine that matches the arch/opsys of the submitting machine. Upon successful checkpoint or vacation, the CheckpointPlatform value from the slot ad is stored into the LastCheckpointPlatform in the job ad. When a job restarts, not only must the arch and opsys match from the submit machine, but it must also match the jobad's LastCheckpointPlatform in the slot ad's CheckpointPlatform attribute. This ensures that the checkpoint is compatible with the restarting kernel, memory layout, etc. When a job doing remote i/o checkpoints, there is a logical checkpoint of the jobs' files in that they stay unmolested on the submit machine. In the case of a job where remote i/o has been turned off, the files are in a shared location and implicitly preserved when the job moves from one machine to another. Periodically, the startd tells the starter to send a periodic checkpoint signal to the job which tells it it should emit a checkpoint and keep going. There is a difference between a periodic checkpoint and a checkpoint when the job is vacating. The former is SIGTSTP, which means to checkpoint and keep going, and the latter is SIGUSR2, which means to checkpoint and exit. At vacate time, a checkpoint signal is sent to the job to tell it to checkpoint and then exit. Using the tool condor_checkpoint_job, a user on the submit machine can tell a single job to checkpoint, no matter where it may be runnning. Using the tool condor_checkpoint, a user (with the right permissions) can tell a host to checkpoint all stduniv jobs running on that machine no matter who owns them. The storage and retrieval location of the job's checkpoint image is determined by the shadow and told to the job just before it reads or writes it. The job will read/write the checkpoint image from a socket which is either connected to the shadow (and it gets/puts the file from the submit machine) or a checkpoint server, where it will contact it on a specified port and get/put the file. The standard universe job may only be one process throughout the life of the job. This means only a single checkpoint image. The Vanilla Universe This describes the state of the art in how a user today uses the vanilla universe for checkpointing with a third party (or application level) checkpointer. In both of these cases, checkpoint files are treated as intermediary files which are moved back and forth along with the job's files. They are kept in the spool directory and are basically files to which the user has no access. Even though file transfer plugins exist, I don't know of any third party checkpointer using it. Using a Wrapper Script A generally hand-written wrapper script is submitted as the vanilla job. The actual job executable(s) is often stored as a tarball or something else that the script unpackages, prepares, and executes. The wrapper script may start other services needed by the third party checkpointer. The wrapper script can be active after forking the application in the background, but the wrapper script must exit with a return code of the application when appropriate. Using the submit file command KillSig, the submittor of the job sets it to a signal that the wrapper script expects. When the job is being vacated, the wrapper script receives this signal and enacts a checkpoint. The wrapper has KILL expression amount of time to finish the checkpoint. While the wrapper script can initiate periodic checkpoints, the checkpoint images, which may be a collection of files and/or directories, are not moved out of/into the sandbox except at vacate and job start boundaries. Checkpoint files without the data files near to the time of checkpoint are basically useless. A significant problem faced by a user of a third party checkpointer is the lack of signature matching between the machine upon which the checkpoint was originally take and a resuming machine. This will often cause hard to find and frustrating failures. Application Level Using the submit file's KillSig signal, an application can write out one or more checkpoint files at vacate time. The KillSig is only sent at vacate time. It is up to the application to decipher its own checkpoint files and ensure that they start properly on the resumption machine. New Design Checkpointer Identification Checkpointing system need to identify themselves in name, version, and an opque token which represents a computed checkpoint signature of a machine. Checkpointer Identification, Startd Side The vanilla universe must provide a means for a checkpointer to record a checkpoint signature and restart on a machine with the same checkpoint signature. Each checkpointer must provide a tool which emits a classad that describes the third party checkpointer. The tool must accept the "--classad" option on the command line. The ad it will emit must have this form: # XXX is an arbitray length AlphaNumeric name of the checkpointer # with NO underscores AAA is a zero padded major number BBB is a zero padded minor number CCC is a zero padded patch number # And the classad itself HasCheckpointer_XXX_AAABBBCCC = TRUE CheckpointerSignature_XXX_AAABBBCCC = "opaque string" The startd will look into a directory defined by the CKPT_SIGNATURE_PROBES_BIN_DIRECTORY config file parameter where the Condor Administrator has placed the checkpoint signature identifcation tools for each third party checkpointer and execute each program upon startup/reconfig. Each returned classad is merged into the slot ads for the resource. Checkpointer Identification, Submit Side The user will place: # A comma delimited list of checkpointers the user is willing to use. UseCheckpointer = XXX_AAABBBCCC in their submit file. This informs the Condor system that this job cares about what machine with which it will be matched and to keep track of the signature of that checkpointer/version in the job ad. A new signal definition attribute called ckpt_sig will be defined in the submit file. It will denote a signal number that will be sent to the vanilla job under certain conditions. A new attribute called PeriodicCkptInterval will be defined in the submit file which tells the Condor system to send the ckpt_sig to the job every N seconds. The shadow tells this information to the starter and may override it. Use of the Checkpoint Signature Identification The START expression of the slot will have IsValidCheckpointPlatform removed. It will be the onus of the job ad's Requirements Expression to know about the LastCheckpointSignature_XXX_AAABBBCCC stored in the job ad and that it should match with the slot ad. When condor_submit sees the UseCheckpointer attribute in the submit file, it will modify the Requirements Expression to be a conjunction of HasCheckpointer_XXX_AAABBBCCC =?= TRUE} expressions, one for each specified checkpointer. This forces jobs onto slots that have the checkpointer available. Condor_submit will also inspect the name of each checkpointer and revision and then add additional disjoined expressions which will be true if LastCheckpointSignature_XXX_AAABBBCCC (one for each) is not present in the job ad or if it is present and matches the slot ad's appropriate CheckpointerSignature_XXX_AAABBBCCC signature related to the name/version of the desired checkpointer. This forces jobs which previously checkpointed back onto machines with the same signature. Checkpointer Identification, Starter Side & Shadow Behavior When a checkpointable vanilla universe job has run (and possibly checkpointed) the first time on a machine, the Starter sends back the LastCheckpointerSignature_XXX_AAABBBCCC attribute (knowing which one to pick by analysis of the job ad) filled in with the correct opaque value so that the shadow places it into the committed job ad. The StarterKnows to do this because LastCheckpointerSignature_XXX_AAABBBCCC won't be in the job ad on the first run. Limitation: It might be too difficult to know that a checkpoint was taken succesfully, so assume it had and set the attribute anyway. Checkpoint Asset Management Checkpoint files (or sets of checkpoint images) are meaningless without the rest of the application's files at the time of (or just after) the checkpoint. Here we describe the concept of a "Checkpoint Asset", which is a collection of everything an application needs to resume its computation at a later time. When a checkpoint is taken, and known to be completed, the entire sandbox must be moved off of the machine to another storage location. However, certain subsets of those files have different properties as other subsets of the files. The submit file must expressly identify, via regexs, files or directories which will comprise temporary and storage subsets of checkpoint assets. These assets shall be identified in the submit file by: CheckpointVolatileAssets = <regex>, <regex>, ... CheckpointVolatileAssets are be explcitly managed and only needed during the time that the process isn't actually running. For example, after a job resumes, the volatile checkpoint image could be deleted. This makes the CheckpointVolatileAssets different from the set of application files. These files are usually the checkpoint images themselves. CheckpointStorageAssets = <regex>, <regex>, ... CheckpointStorageAssets are explicitly managed files which are preserved with a checkpoint, but cannot be deleted. They are treated like intermediate files and this attribute trumps the calculation of immediate files. If this attribute is left unspecified it is exactly the set of files which are all files minus the CheckpointVolatileAssets. The term CheckpointAssets refers to a union of the CheckpointVolatileAssets and CheckpointStorageAssets subsets. We could utilize the (not merged yet) dataflow code to identify checkpoint assets that are not being written any longer. In the initial implementation, only the most recent checkpoint assets for a job will be stored. We will use File Transfer Plugins to get/put checkpoint information from/to distributed storage or some other kind of storage. XXX Ideas that do not have a place in the design document yet: Who allocates of storage for Checkpoint Assets. Do we keep a sequence of Checkpoint Assets for a job? Who cleans up the Checkpoint Assets? Who manages the Checkpoint Assets sequencing (LRU eviction, etc). Where do the CheckpointAssets go? How is this determined? Checkpoint Initiation Events Third party checkpointers may perform their own periodic checkpoints. When the schedd receives a condor_checkpoint_job request for a vanilla universe job, it will inform the shadow for the job to send a message to the starter to send the ckpt_sig to the job. If ckpt_sig is not defined, it is a NOP. An alternative implementation is that the schedd tells the startd which tells the starter to do it. It has not been thought out which is the better option other than that it is likely less resource consumption for a schedd to contact a daemon on the localhost for a short message than on a machine far away. Assumptions There will be no remote I/O by the Condor standalone checkpointer. A portion of the integration of a third party checkpointer will be done by administrators and a portion by the submittors. This specifically means that when supporting a new third party checkpointer, the Condor administrator must perform work to allow it to be used. The application undergoing checkpointing will not perform read AND write operations on the same logical file. Performing read/write operations on the same logical file during checkpointing will produce inconsistent or undefined results. Requirements for Third Party Checkpointers The writing of the checkpoint assets must be atomic. Behavior in Failure Scenarios TBD Limitations There appears to be no perfect way to know if a checkpoint is happening or has successfully occured. TBD Known Customer Requirements LIGO On the CheckpointPlatform signature: Currently we have two pools here in Hannover, the regular one yields: 6654 CheckpointPlatform = "LINUX X86_64 2.6.x normal 0x2aaaaaac7000" the test pool with GPUs and a few newer nodes yield: 256 CheckpointPlatform = "LINUX X86_64 2.6.x normal 0x2aaaaaac7000" 17 CheckpointPlatform = "LINUX X86_64 2.6.x normal 0x2aaaaaac9000" So, this means that they could get away without having the checkpoint signature codes working. Instead they could hand specify an attribute that their jobs must match against. However, they need a tool which will calculate the above value so they can see when it changes. However, if they phase change the pools and a new signature shows up, they have to deal with it by hand! On preemption or periodic style checkpointing: They absolutely require preemption style checkpointing for a significant majority of their stduniv usage. They have one user, though, who has been running a 68+ day job and relies on periodic checkpoints. On choice of where to write the checkpoints: They currently run a checkpoint server on each compute node. When asked the question if they would want their checkpoint images written to the shared partition that all their machines use, they said they fear 4000 or 8000 jobs under a single user suddenly bursting their checkpoints to the shared file system. They are tempted by the siren call of ease of use, but fear the consequences. On versioned checkpoints: They never had a need for it and wonder about expiration dates for older checkpoints. They didn't mention it, but forking the checkpoint lineage has to be thought about too. This isn't important to them. On checkpoint/restart policy (and the fact we don't let you specify it): It has bitten them a few times, usually with the schedd blocking on a "broken" checkpoint server which isn't responding. They can easily fix for the few times it happens. They don't consider this an issue. On condor_ssh_to_job and CCB: They require this behavior. On other topics (what else do you need in this feature?): As quoted from Casten: "Not to my knowledge, but (our) users are very creative, thus together with dynamic slots expect users to start looking heavily into multi-core programming and/or using "CPU-external" processing. For example, one of the largest stduniv pipelines we currently have is being reworked to use gstreamer(?) as a way to move data hence and forth between different tasks (could be threads - possibly p-threads, processes, processes with GPU parts). If we needed more on that, we would need to talk to the designer/programmers from that project. Currently, they are aiming for generic vanilla jobs AFAIK." Milestones Fix condor_ckpt_probe to accept the "--classad" option and emit the proper classad to use Condor's standalone checkpointer as the first third party checkpointing system. Fix condor_startd to understand CKPT_SIGNATURE_PROBES_BIN_DIRECTORY, find and run all programs contained therein, deal with the usual erroneous situations, and ensure the attributes show up in the slot ad. Give a good default for this knob. XXX Maybe that config knob should just list full paths to executables vis $(SBIN) or something instead. Mostly because the permission the code runs under needs to be non-priviledged and if an attacker succeeded placing a new binary there, could get Condor to run it as some other user, which is bad. Ensure our build system and RPMS place the condor_ckpt_probe executable in the right place if needed. Fix condor_submit to accept: UseCheckpointer = XXX_AAABBBCCC CheckpointVolatileAssets = <list of regexes> CheckpointStorageAssets = <list of regexes> ckpt_sig = <integer> and to adjust the requirements expression properly. When the starter runs the job, have it notice if it is a checkpointable job and have it insert the appropriate LastCheckpointerSignature_XXX_AAABBBCCC attribute into the jobad regardless if the job actually completes or not. Implement the behavior condor_checkpoint_job into the schedd such that ultimately the user job gets the checkpoint signal. TBD The simpler version For a very first pass, just to implement what ligo needs, we'll do this: Goals We will initially suppose LIGO's needs. LIGO only desires condor_ssh_to_job, ccb, and the richer job policy mechanisms of vanilla universe. Assumptions Homogeneous pool wrt CheckpointPlatform. It'll only work with Condor's Checkpointer. The Plan We write a tool to act as a client to a Condor checkpoint server. This tool will move checkpoints to and from the checkpointer server and has the ability to rename them and delete them as well. We will implement this tool with the current client libaries that already embody this functionality. We will write a wrapper script which will start the user job ala the dmtcp_shim script. This will look into the jobad, find out if it had previously checkpointed, and if so, retrienve the checkpoint image and restart the job. The pool admin should specify in the machine ad the location on the local machine in which user checkpoints may be written. This must be writable by the uid of the job. The wrapper script will pick this location out of the .machine_ad file and start the user job with it. When it comes time to checkpoint at vacate time, the wrapper script will transfer the checkpoint as a temporary file to the checkpoint server, rename it as the correct checkpoint file, then using chirp, update the job ad with the correct LastCkptServer information. [There may be races here, but just look to see how we do it in stduniv and copy that algorithm.] The user job must specify +WantIOProxy = TRUE in their submit file in order to be able to use chirp.

title: Ticket #6366: corrupt job_queue.log entries
description: In the process of tracking down another bug, the schedd on submit-4 repeated crashed with an invalid job_queue.log. The entries in question: 103 4416990.0 LastRejMatchTime 1501776513 16654.0 LastRejMatchTime 1501776512 103 4416686.0 LastRejMatchReason "no match found " 103 4416686.0 LastRejMatchTime 1501776512 103 4416724.0 LastRejMatchReason "no match found " 103 4416724.0 LastRejMatchTime 1501776513 103 4416769.0 LastRejMatchReason "no match found " 103 4416769.0 LastRejMatchTime 1501776513 103 4416928.0 LastRejMatchReason "no match found " 103 4416928.0 LastRejMatchTime 1501776513 103 4416929.0 LastRejMatchReason "no match found " 103 4416929.0 LastRejMatchTime 1501776513 103 4416948.0 LastRejMatchReason "no match found " 103 4416948.0 LastRejMatchTime 1501776513 16654.0 LastRejMatchTime 1501776512 103 4416686.0 LastRejMatchReason "no match found " 103 4416686.0 LastRejMatchTime 1501776512
remarks: 2017-Aug-08 11:47:15 by jfrey: The job_queue.log contained 16 invalid lines, written over the course of 12 minutes. All of the lines appear to be incomplete entries that are missing a variable number of their initial characters. 2017-Aug-08 11:55:32 by jfrey: When the schedd first opens the job_queue.log file (LoadClassAdLog()), it does not use O_APPEND. When the schedd opens a new file for truncation (TruncateClassAdLog()), it does use O_APPEND. If the file is "clean" when initially read in (i.e. no transactions and no incomplete entries), the schedd will use the non-append file descriptor for further writes. If the file isn't "clean", then it immediately does a truncation (resulting in a file descriptor in append mode). The corruption we're seeing could be explained by a forked child process writing to the log file in non-append mode. Always opening the file in append mode would help prevent this, but we should also understand how the extra writes are happening. 2017-Aug-10 12:55:08 by jfrey: The log corruption appears to be caused by valgrind. I wrote a simple program that called fopen(), fprintf(), and _exit(). When I run it normally, the file is empty. When I run it under valgrind, the file contains the text from my fprintf(). The corruption always occurs around updates of LastRejMatchTime and LastRejMatchReason, which are done non-durable, which means they aren't fflush()d. The corrupted job_queue.log was generated while the schedd was run under valgrind (while Greg investigated a crash). Throughout the file, groups of updates to LastRejMatchTime and LastRejMatchReason are duplicated, sometimes jumping backward in time (duplicating entries from a second ago). I believe whenever the schedd forked a child helper process when ad updates were buffered by stdio, valgrind caused those updates to be flushed when the child process exited.

title: Ticket #5819: htcondor sets the watchdog timer for systemd too low
description: In the condor.service file, we set various parameters for systemd: RestartSec=5 WatchdogSec=5 TimeoutStopSec=5 5 seconds is too short. If the master blocks for (Time/2) systemd will kill it. So, for example, if a single DNS query were to take 3 seconds, the master might be killed (depending on the timing).

title: Ticket #7824: Further Python binding exceptions improvement
description: The following are unaddressed issues from JoshK's review: There are a few places that something like THROW_EX(ClassAdEvaluationError, "Unable to evaluate expression"); happens; it would be nice if we could get a more detailed error message in. I would maybe call HTCondorEnumError something like HTCondorInvalidEnumMember to make it more specific. In general, exception don't need to be *Error... though I don't think there are really better names for most of these. One could argue between HTCondorLocateError and e.g. FailedToLocateDaemon; I don't think it matters much. Other ideas: Add one or more THROW_EX() variants (possibly exception-specific) to make it easier to create exceptions with more data members (e.g., errno). This of course implies adding data members to the exceptions. THROW_EX_FORMAT() THROW_EX_WITH_ERRNO()?

title: Ticket #3867: condor_ssh_to_job / condor_submit -i and held jobs
description: If you run condor_submit -i and the resulting job goes on hold, condor_submit will not notify you; it instead assumes that the hold is a transient condition, and the command hangs. (It may, in fact, just be very patient.) Likewise, condor_ssh_to_job -auto-retry appears to hang when you specify a job that's on hold. Since this will only be useful is in the case that you have a periodic release expression defined (which I understand to be relatively uncommon), it would seem that we could do better. For condor_ssh_to_job -auto-retry, we should report to the user (on each retry?) that the job is on hold, why (the hold reason), and that you will probably need to manually intervene. For condor_submit -i, we should report the job going on hold to the user, as above, but because we know the job was submitted for the sole purpose of interactive access, also ask the user if they'd like to release the job (perhaps reminding them that interrupting the console will remove it). If condor_submit -i (as I would expect) just calls condor_ssh_to_job, this could be trickier to arrange. Implementing the first suggestion for EC2 jobs should be simple (condor_ssh_to_job already has the EC2 job's status attribute), but implementation for other jobs would probably best done in the schedd (getJobConnectInfo()), by altering the 'retry_sensible' output parameter, but this may have other implications. Perhaps the second suggestion could just implement as an undocumented flag to condor_ssh_to_job?

title: Ticket #34: bad error message: gethostbyname(SOME.MACHINE.NAME) failed, errno = 25
description: (This replaces 1557 (backup) 1557 (public).) If your DNS or /etc/hosts is "bad" (for various definitions of "bad"), Condor will fail with errors that look something like: "gethostbyname(SOME.MACHINE.NAME) failed, errno = 25" (from my_hostname.C, line 187ish). This is a deeply unhelpful error that provides absolutely no clue about what is wrong or how to fix it. There are reports on Condor users that some modern Linux distributions default to creating a wonky /etc/hosts file, which makes this error all the more common. This is a multi-part problem: The EXCEPT message reports the errno, which is 25 (ioctl failure) and completely useless. Given that the function that failed is Condor code, is errno ever likely to be valid? The code called (get_full_hostname) should either try to always set errno, my_hostname should not print the errno. The code that is actually failing is get_full_hostname (get_full_hostname.C). It only logs at D_HOSTNAME. Should it debug at D_ALWAYS for error cases, possibly helping debugging? There are reports that some distributions are doing surprising things in their /etc/hosts files by default. We should figure out what they're doing and either give useful error messages, some details in the manual, or ideally just go to war with the /etc/hosts we have. User discussions about the problem: https://www-auth.cs.wisc.edu/lists/condor-users/2008-May/msg00174.shtml https://lists.cs.wisc.edu/archive/condor-users/2007-May/msg00008.shtml We see regular rust about this. It frequently doesn't get resolved. admin: 12587, 14025, 15179, 15498, 18092
remarks: 2010-Jun-30 15:23:27 by psilord: gethostbyname() actually set h_errno, not errno. The man page explains it and what to do about it in more detail. 2010-Oct-20 15:59:08 by jfrey: Bulk change of target version from v070504 to v070505 using ./ticket-target-mover. 2011-Jan-27 14:21:33 by danb: Bulk change of target version from v070505 to v070506 using ./ticket-target-mover. 2011-Feb-01 14:49:30 by tannenba: Bulk change of target version from v070506 to NULL using ./ticket-target-mover.

title: Ticket #3922: Stderr from job hooks run by starter should end up in log files
description: If a job hook run by the startd (eg *_HOOK_FETCH_WORK) outputs to stderr, the message will be put in the START_LOG (see /src/condor_startd.V6 in FetchClient::hookExited; look for "Warning, hook"). If a job hook run by the starter (eg *_HOOK_PREPARE_JOB) outputs to stderr, the message is discarded. (see /src/condor_starter.V6.1/StarterHookMgr.cpp, look for HookPrepareJobClient::hookExited and HookPrepareJobClient::hookExited). This makes debugging a hook harder; a hook writer must manage their own log file of some sort. This should be changed to behave like the startd case: copy the hook's stderr into STARTER_LOG.
creator: adesmet

title: Ticket #7432: Job router should use a list of job transforms for the route
description: The JobRouter should use the same configuration model and syntax for routes that the schedd does for JOB_TRANSFORMs This is a follow-on to work to apply the routes in the order in which they are declared. There will be new knobs JOB_ROUTER_PRE_ROUTE_TRANSFORM_NAMES a list of transforms that will be applied in order when an incoming job matches a route but before the routing transform is applied. JOB_ROUTER_POST_ROUTE_TRANSFORM_NAMES a list of transforms that will be applied in order after a route transform is applied Names in these two knobs will refer to pre-and post route transforms defined by JOB_ROUTER_TRANSFORM_<name> knobs. These knobs will allow, but not require REQUIREMENTS statements, so that not all pre/post route transforms need be applied to all jobs that are routed. There will be a new knob JOB_ROUTER_USE_DEPRECATED_ROUTER_ENTRIES that will default to true for now, but will be set to false some time in the future. When this knob is false, the JobRouter will longer parse the 3 JOB_ROUTER_ENTRIES* knobs and the JOB_ROUTER_DEFAULTS knob, and will generate a warning if any of these are configured. Google doc for job router config redesign: https://docs.google.com/document/d/1IkEV907Jsc2Wu6HIhhrH9QdFTiGkFzuUn5CTVPRZzNs/edit?usp=sharing

title: Ticket #880: Condor issues in ETICS production pool
description: ETICS is running a Condor 6.9.5 prerelease on their pool, because as of last year it was the newest set of binaries we could provide to them that did not have a critical component broken. The SL5 machines don't appear to work well with the RHEL 3 binaries running on them. Jobs are not completing and are getting stuck in the middle of their build processes. This is in the ETICS production pool and is affecting production users. There is no indication of error caused by Metronome in the Metronome logfiles. An example of a recent problem from the StarterLog.vm1 on a SL5 platform: 10/8 23:34:46 Process exited, pid=3808, signal=9 10/8 23:34:46 condor_write(): Socket closed when trying to write 305 bytes to <128.142.142.97:23356>, fd is 5 10/8 23:34:46 Buf::write(): condor_write() failed 10/8 23:34:46 Failed to send job exit status to shadow 10/8 23:34:46 JobExit() failed, waiting for job lease to expire or for a reconnect attempt 10/8 23:35:07 Got SIGTERM. Performing graceful shutdown. 10/8 23:35:07 ShutdownGraceful all jobs. 10/8 23:35:07 Result of "get_usage" operation from ProcD: ERROR: No family with the given PID is registered 10/8 23:35:07 error getting family usage in VanillaProc::PublishUpdateAd() 10/8 23:35:07 condor_write(): Socket closed when trying to write 67 bytes to <128.142.142.97:23356>, fd is 5 10/8 23:35:07 Buf::write(): condor_write() failed 10/8 23:35:07 Failed to send job exit status to shadow 10/8 23:35:07 JobExit() failed, waiting for job lease to expire or for a reconnect attempt 10/8 23:35:12 **** condor_starter (condor_STARTER) EXITING WITH STATUS 0 RHEL5 builds were available for Condor 6.9.5, though it would take a bit of digging/work to resubmit the prerelease build and obtain binaries that may end up working on that platform. This does not seem like the best solution, as it requires a lot of time and effort spent on older binaries and may not resolve the problem. I have experimented with several newer versions of Condor in the ETICS test pool for the job migration work, which is when I uncovered the 7.1 <-> 7.2 incompatibility problem. The BatLab pool is stuck running Condor 7.1.4. In order to maintain versions at ETICS and UoW that are compatible for job migration work, I recommend we upgrade both pools to the same version of Condor. ETICS prefers the stable series for their production pool. Which version to choose? 7.4.0 pros: - new, latest, best release, will work with 7.4.0 built for old platforms, pool is happy, etc. cons: -not out yet 7.3.2 pros: - stable series cons: - Do we know of the 7.4.0 binaries Nick built for our older platforms will work with a 7.3.2 submitter? - Any Condor upgrade for ETICS will require Condor config file changes and some of my time for assistance. They are still using vms instead of slots, for example. - If any bugs found after 7.3.2 affect us or ETICS, namely any of the 7.4.0 blockers, we'll have to perform a second upgrade to 7.4.0 at UoW and ETICS when it's released.

title: Ticket #2260: Optional compression during file transfer
description: Sometimes a user has some large input or output files that are easily compressed. Plain text is common. Compressing them over the wire would speed up transfers and reduce bandwidth usage; good for everyone. The cost in process time is minimal if zlib is set to use the lowest compression level (1 AKA Z_BEST_SPEED). The current workaround is to compress the files manually, then teach your program to uncompress them or add a wrapper script to do the uncompression. Either option adds unnecessary complexity. Proposal 1: Always enable compression during file transfer. If investigation shows that the CPU overhead is trivial, this will help users with compressible data at negligible cost to everyone else. Proposal 2: if the CPU cost isn't negligible, allow users to toggle the option on a per job or perhaps per file basis.
creator: adesmet

title: Ticket #7598: condor_drain -off
description: The defrag daemon was causing Stuart grief by cancelling drains (after they were complete) that Stuart had ordered. We should implement condor_drain -off, which turns off a startd when draining completes (and maybe the complementary condor_off -drain). We should also have the startd set an attribute in each draining slot which notes if the drain came from the condor_drain command-line tool or from the daemon. Since we'll probably need to extend the protocol to handle the first point, we may as well put the plumbing in for the second point at the same time. We can decide if the defrag daemon should ignore machines with the latter's attribute set by default later. The -off flag must fail if issues to a startd which doesn't support it.

Ticket #6223: Use a location lookup collector query by default
description: In #5150, the HTCondor Daemon::locate() method was enhanced so the caller could specify LOCATE_FOR_LOOKUP (with a small projection), or LOCATE_FULL (send back the full classad). The default locate() method was set to LOCATE_FULL, and just a few surgical locations were specified as LOCATE_FOR_LOOKUP. Most of the call sites do not specify which type of lookup to perform, and thus resulted in receiving the full classad with no projection. In this ticket, we flip the default for locate() to be LOCATE_FOR_LOOKUP. To locate call sites that needed changing and to prevent future land-mines, we remove the public method Daemon::daemonAd() which is used to retrieve the full classad after LOCATE_FULL. Call sites that want to invoke the daemonAd() method must now instantiate a child class DaemonAllowLocateFull instead of using class Daemon. DaemonAllowLocateFull operates just like Daemon, except it includes a daemonAd() method and the locate() method must be specified. This way, the code is future-proofed in that if someone edits the code to invoke method daemonAd() on a Daemon object, they will end up with a compile-time error.
remarks: 2017-Apr-12 12:51:18 by tannenba: Looks like there are about 82 places in the code where we call Daemon::locate() without specifying what type of lookup to perform. Behold: C:\home\tannenba\CONDOR_SRC\src>git grep "locate(" | grep -v tests | grep -v "daemon.h" | grep -v "daemon.cpp" | grep -v "daemon.t.cpp" | grep -v LOCATE_ | wc -l 82 As for the places that are left which actually need a full lookup, see remark 2 by Jaime in #5150. description: Running the debian 4.0 binaries on debian 5.0 have shown a really good bug: Imagine this cycle, repeating for tens of thousands of stack frames until you run out of stack to allocate: #14 0x083c5a51 in kill () #15 0x083c587e in raise () #16 0x083c5cfb in abort () #17 0x083c1156 in __assert_fail () #18 0x084088da in __nscd_getgrouplist () #19 0x083f876f in internal_getgrouplist () #20 0x083f8878 in initgroups () #21 0x0811206e in passwd_cache::cache_groups (this=0x9e86b48, user=0x9ebe0e0 "sl2-user") at passwd_cache.C:109 #22 0x08112474 in passwd_cache::num_groups (this=0x9e86b48, user=0x9ebe0e0 "sl2-user") at passwd_cache.C:236 #23 0x081124d2 in passwd_cache::init_groups (this=0x9e86b48, user=0x9ebe0e0 "sl2-user", additional_gid=0) at passwd_cache.C:386 #24 0x0811078a in set_user_egid () at uids.C:1364 #25 0x0811164f in _set_priv (s=PRIV_USER, file=0x843e0cc "dprintf.c", line=1187, dologging=0) at uids.C:1148 #26 0x080ab569 in dprintf_dump_stack () at dprintf.c:1187 #27 0x0809ceaa in linux_sig_coredump (signum=6) at daemon_core_main.C:631 #28 <signal handler called> Cool eh? Apparently, while trying to printf the stack trace, we fault again and go right back into the loop. Funny thing is, glibc is calling abort() since initgroups() is a call into glibc. The fix appears to be to set the default signal handler in linux_sig_coredump() before calling a lot of code which could result in another signal, instead of after.

"); /* raise(SIGABRT);*/ abort(); return 0; } The solution is to add this block of code to the top of the handler: static int foo = 0; if (foo) { return; } foo = 1; This prevents the secondary abort() from reentering the handler. title: Ticket #479: Accept --double-dash form for long arguments
description: --double-dash appears to be the dominant form for long arguments, but Condor users -single-dash. The error message isn't terribly helpful: mustardseed(condor) condor_q --global Error: unrecognized argument --global Usage: condor_q [options] where [options] are -global Get global queue -submitter <submitter> Get queue of specific submitter Option 1: Better error message. Detect the case and offer the obvious correction. mustardseed(condor) condor_q --global Error: unrecognized argument --global. Perhaps you meant -global? Option 2: Silently parse it as a single dash. For example, if the argument matches the pattern ^--[A-Za-z], just remove the first dash before trying to parse. This Just Works. It also provides a long term path to making the --double-dash form the recommended default in the future.

title: Ticket #5376: Allow involuntary Spot terminations without shrinking ASG.
description: Investigate what happens in our current set-up if the Spot instance is involuntarily terminated. We do not want the size of the ASG to change if we're not shutting down for lack of work. An involuntary termination should trigger the initscript first; whichever HTCondor shutdown mode the init script uses, the daemon shutdown config knob should use the other, and may need to configure a very short retirement time to make the one behave like the other.
remarks: An involuntary termination should trigger the initscript first; whichever HTCondor shutdown mode the init script uses, the daemon shutdown config knob should use the other, and may need to configure a very short retirement time to make the one behave like the other.We shouldn't have to set a very short retirement time if we're only shutting down voluntarily because of a lack of work. (We may have to give up on a master-triggered lease to allow updating.) More importantly, MASTER_SHUTDOWN triggers on all shutdowns (that is, including fast ones). We need some way to determine from the shutdown script which type of shutdown we're doing, or some other way to determine if we should shrink the ASG. (We should always change the termination type, and should arguably do that on start-up. It would be nice to be able to do that in the template....) 2015-Nov-11 14:36:27 by tlmiller: I'm checking to see if the 'spot/termination-time' metadata is available after the power off occurs, since that's the actual condition we care about. 2015-Nov-17 11:14:18 by tlmiller: It didn't seem to behave reliably, although testing -- especially for Spot -- is hard. Instead, since what we want to do is distinguish between just HTCondor shutting down and the whole system shutting down, just check -- before we call shutdown ourselves -- to see what the system's runlevel is. This seems reliable with externally-terminate dedicated instances; tests for Spot proceeding. 2015-Dec-10 16:06:22 by tlmiller: This seems to be working pretty well.

title: Ticket #5726: Fix HAD/REPLICATION problems with shared port.
description: See #5301 for the previous work-arounds. It appears that the HAD and REPLICATION daemons expect to be born with an active command socket, so it shouldn't be too hard to make them accept shared port connections. The problem comes with the HAD_LIST and REPLICATION_LIST configuration knobs, which expect to be [hostname|IPv4 literal]:protNo. The least-incorrect solution is probably to have the HAD and REPLICATION daemons rendezvous in the collector(s); then we don't have to worry about configuration at all. Arguably, the next-best solution would be to accept full Sinfuls, but that has some serious usability drawbacks (since full Sinfuls are tricky to generate except by running the daemon in question, and even then don't compensate for DNS drift the way hostnames do). The next possibility is to implement the list as full Sinfuls, but carefully craft the documentation so that only something like <1.2.3.4:5?sock_id=had> is necessary. However, it occurred to me, in the spirit of user-friendliness, rather than make the user specify a shared port ID in the config file, we should supply a default identifier. Then it occurred to me that there's really no reason to run more than one HAD and/or more than REPLICATION daemon behind the same shared port daemon -- that is, if we just had the master (if using shared port) set those two daemon's sock ids to their subsys names, we'd avoid the issue of the user having to specify the shared port ID entirely: the existing [HAD|REPLICATION]_LIST entries carry enough information to connect to the shared port daemon. On the other hand, they don't say if that daemon is using shared port. ToddT then suggested that we could just assume that they were -- try using shared port and see if it works; if it doesn't, try again without it. Since daemons just ignore unregistered commands, this should be safe. (The shared port daemon will forward unknown commands to the collector, but the collector will then ignore the HAD or REPLICATION daemon command sent to it. This is a little unfortunate, because it clutters up the wrong log, but since shared port will be on by default in 8.6, it still makes sense to try shared port first.) This then raises the question about why we don't name all (except the shadow and starter) shared port daemon sockets after the subsys name, but that's another issue for another time.
remarks: 2016-Jun-14 15:19:46 by tlmiller: Jaime points out the CMS is currently using three negotiators, so we can't assume that each shared port daemon has one HAD and one REPLICATION daemon. However, the master does understand and respect the -sock option in each daemon's ARGS, so if we tell people to use that, we could then have the HAD or REPLICATION daemon use its own shared port ID to append to the _LIST elements. The question then becomes if we try both shared port and non-shared port when we do. Although it seems fair to assume/require that an explicitly-set port or shared-port name flag is indicative of intention for other daemons in the group, this may run into problems setting defaults. ToddT and I decided that I'd implement the retry if it didn't take too long to do so (the default, using shared port, we try first, so that the creepy unknown-command messages would more likely show up in the HAD or REPLICATION logs than the collector). Current configuration is highly manual (no defaults at all?), so at least for the first pass, we don't have to do anything clever.

title: Ticket #750: DeferralTime jobs should only list as "R"unning when actually running
description: (Based on a report by Scot Kronenfeld for the VDT.) If I have a job with deferred execution time, it always shows up as running, even when it's in between runs. For example, I run the following script with these attributes in the submission file: DeferralPrepTime = 180 DeferralTime = (CurrentTime + 300 + random(30)) DeferralWindow = 99999999 Notification = never OnExitRemove = false PeriodicRelease = (HoldReasonCode =!= 1) && ((CurrentTime - EnteredCurrentStatus) > 60) Universe = local When I run condor_q, I see that it is in the 'R" state. But I can check my process table and see that it is not currently executing. It never leaves the 'R' state that I've seen. -- Submitter: vdt-rhas4-ia32.cs.wisc.edu : <192.168.0.204:32999> : vdt-rhas4-ia32.cs.wisc.edu ID OWNER SUBMITTED RUN_TIME ST PRI SIZE CMD 13.0 vdttest 9/15 14:44 0+00:00:11 R 0 0.0 gratia-script-cons We shouldn't force people to look at the process table to tell if a job is currently running. Note: When I run a job with the cron* attributes instead of the deferral* attributes, jobs do get listed as idle when they are not running. Proposed behavior, by Alan De Smet: Good: If the job is actually running, list it as Running. If no resources (that is, a starter) are allocated, list the job as Idle. If the starter is running in the DeferralPrepTime but waiting for the exact DeferralTime, the job can be listed as Idle or Running. (If you list it as Idle a user might not realize that he is using a startd slot. If you list it as running, the user might wonder why it isn't actually doing anything.) Better: As above, but during the DeferralPrepTime window put the job into some other state, probably a new one. Perhaps "P"reparing?

title: Ticket #4137: Non-blocking authentication
description: Authentication has always been a sore spot for blocking. We do the first few round-trips in a non-blocking manner - but as soon as we hand off to the ReliSock to do the "real work", everything blocks. It's straightforward work to give the same treatment to the remaining condor_io layers involved in authentication. Branch posted here: https://github.com/bbockelm/htcondor/tree/non_blocking_auth Includes a non-blocking version of FS and GSI auth.
remarks: 2013-Dec-29 08:39:02 by bbockelm: After a few bugfixes, this branch passes NMI tests. 2014-Jan-02 10:56:12 by tannenba: Here is the significant wisdom here (ideally to be part of the design doc): Previously, HTCondor interfaced with GSI using using globus_gss_assist_init_sec_context() and globus_gss_assist_accept_sec_context(). This is problematic because these APIs block the caller while performing multiple synchronous network round-trips. However, the GSS API does have have non-blocking native interface; the "assist" part of "globus_gss_assist_init_sec_context" is a wrapper library around the GSS API which provides a blocking API. This work will change HTCondor to use the non-blocking interface, allowing a return to the main event loop handler between GSI network round trips. Hooray!!!! :) :) :) 2014-Aug-07 16:20:33 by jfrey: Code Review In DaemonCommandProtocol, remove the call to CommandNumToTableIndex() in Authenticate(), PostAuthenticate() and ExecCommand(). m_cmd_index should already have the correct value, set in ReadCommand(). In DaemonCommandProtocol, does the CondorErr m_errstack need to persist between calls? Otherwise, why make it a class member? In DaemonCommandProtocol::Authenticate(), you always call ReliSock::authenticate() in non-blocking mode. Shouldn't you consult m_nonblocking to decide if you want to be blocking or nonblocking? In DaemonCommandProtocol::AuthenticateContinue(), you always call ReliSock::authenticate_continue() in blocking mode. Shouldn't you call it in non-blocking mode? In SecManStartCommand::authenticate_inner(), ReliSock::authenticate() is always called in non-blocking mode. Should this be based on SecManStartCommand::m_nonblocking? Should Authentication::authenticate_finish() be protected or private? No one outside of the class should be calling it, correct? In Authentication, these new data members aren't initialized in the constructor: m_auth, m_continue_handshake, m_continue_auth. The destructor should delete m_auth, and m_auth should be set to NULL when the pointer is moved to authenticator_. In Condor_Auth_FS, in the FS_REMOTE code, you dprintf() an empty m_new_dir instead of the template path. In Condor_Auth_FS, for both the local and remote cases, the code around condor_mkstemp is overly convoluted. Why not leave new_dir as a char* that's strdup()'d and then free()'d after use? When condor_mkstemp() fails, it's clearer if you set m_new_dir to "". In Condor_Auth_X509, authenticate_server_gss_complete() could be folded into authenticate_server_gss(). That may allow you to turn m_client_name into a local variable. In Condor_Auth_X509, I don't see why m_input_token and m_input_token_desc need to be class members. They're only used in authenticate_server_gss() and they're always freed before the function returns. It appears that m_input_chan_bindings and m_mech_type are unnecessary as well. You could just use GSS_C_NO_CHANNEL_BINDINGS and GSS_C_NO_OID when calling gss_accept_sec_context(). 2014-Aug-07 20:28:17 by bbockelm: I believe I took care of everything except m_errstack; I'm not convinced that a badly written authentication object won't stash and use it between calls. Ran the code through batlab and tests looked good. Per our phone, merging this - any further fixes can go straight to master. 2014-Sep-10 13:43:31 by jfrey: You didn't address the concern about SecManStartCommand::authenticate_inner() also calling ReliSock::authenticate() in non-blocking mode.

title: Ticket #4588: Export a log reader API from the python bindings
description: The ClassAd log is an important concept - especially for the schedd - which we should expose through the python bindings (currently, it's only exposed through libcondorapi). This would allow easier development of appropriately-privileged external daemons to tail the activity of the schedd and synchronize out to external systems. Why use this versus ... Global user log? The log reader API provides details at the level of the individual attributes. The Global user log only includes state transitions. Schedd plug-ins? Plug-ins run in-process (potentially causing security issues, memory leaks, or crashes) and wouldn't provide an easier development path - C++ plugin versus python code. As seen in recent issues with classad loadable plugins, the HTCondor plugin infrastructure provides no versioning help -- there's no way to know if you are loading an incompatible plugin and about to cause the schedd to crash. The API design would expose a new class with the following methods: constructor: given a filename, returns a new instance. Unfortunately, this must be based on filename (as opposed to an open file pointer) due to the Next (and __iter__): Returns the next event in the log. Appropriate for for-loops. A slight twist, Poll, will be provided that is appropriate for while-loops. Wait: Block until a new event is available. setBlocking: Determine whether or not "next" should block when there are no events available. Watch: Return a file descriptor which will be marked as "ready for read" in a select() call when there are new events available. Meant to be used for event-loop-based programs. Basically, the object is meant to behave as a pythonic iterator (i.e., appropriate for for-loops). The various iterators should return a dictionary which is a rough equivalent of the existing ClassAdLogEntry. Note this inverts the control flow from the existing ClassAdLogReader (which is callback-based) to allow better interaction with event loops.
remarks: 2015-Feb-19 12:26:05 by smoler: There is no documentation yet for this new class. This ticket is to remain open until the documentation is complete. 2015-Feb-21 11:37:52 by bbockelm: Hi Karen, Sorry for the belated documentation. Here's a few explanations: LogReader The LogReader provides a parser for reading and tailing ClassAd transaction logs; the best example of a ClassAd transaction log is the one kept by the schedd in job_queue.log. This is meant to allow a python program to mirror the contents of a schedd's log. The LogReader is iterable, meaning it can be used in loop constructs, such as: for event in LogReader("/var/lib/condor/spool/job_queue.log"): print event The events produced by the iterator are python dictionaries describing the next event in the log file. LogReader methods Constructor: Takes in the name of a file to parse. next(): Returns a python dictionary containing the next event in the log file. If blocking mode is enabled, this blocks indefinitely until a new event is available. If blocking mode is disabled, this raises a StopIteration exception when no new event is available. poll(timeout): Returns a python dictionary containing the next event in the log file. This will block until a new event is available or a timeout is hit. The timeout parameter is specified in milliseconds; set 0 to return immediately or -1 to block indefinitely. Returns None on timeout. setBlocking(blocking): Set whether or not the next() function should block when no event is available. Returns the previous value of the object's blocking state. wait(): Wait until a new event is available; no value is returned. watch(): Returns a file descriptor. When select() indicates there is data available on this descriptor, a new event may be available. If -1 is returned, the API is not available on the current platform.

title: Ticket #1270: UDP message not properly closed in DaemonCore::HandleReq()
description: When encountering some types of errors in DaemonCore::HandleReq(), the incoming UDP message was not properly closed, resulting in an error message that looks like this: ERROR: receiving new UDP message but found a long message still waiting to be closed (consumed=0). Closing it now. One type of error in HandleReq() that could cause this is failure to set up the message digest object, which results in this message: DC_AUTHENTICATE: unable to turn on message authenticator, failing. Ultimately, the problem was that HandleReq() was setting the socket into encode mode before doing the final end_of_message() to close the UDP message. The problem of the unclosed UDP message did not actually cause any further errors, as far as I know--just annoying log messages. I did not try to see when exactly this error was introduced--probably much earlier than the version 7.4 that I listed in the ticket header.

title: Ticket #5663: Log TCP statistics for file transfers
description: HTCondor is now transfers petabytes of files in the OSG over many WANs. However, we have no visibility into the performance of these transfers. There is a socket option on Linux, TCP_INFO, which returns many low-level statistics about the performance of a single network socket. In this ticket, we will extract these statistics on a per-file-sandbox transfer, and log them to a distinct file for later processing. We will add a new dprintf category, D_STATS, and allow the starter and shadow (via the FileTransfer class), to log these statistics to this category. By default, both the starter and shadow will log to a file name XferStatsLog, one line per transfer. This line will contain human readable statistics the the job id, number of bytes up/dowloaded, the peer IP address of the connection, and the low-level TCP statistics.
remarks: 2016-Jun-14 15:11:28 by gthain: With this ticket, by default we create a new HTCondor log file, in the usual $(LOG) directory, called XferStatsLog. This file is rotated every time it reaches a configurable size limit, by default 10Mb. This file contains lines like the following (wrapped in this ticket for readability, but presented in one line in the log file for parseability. 6/09/16 14:53:10 File Transfer Download: JobId: 626.19 files: 7 \\ bytes: 391021382 seconds: 1.0 dest: 128.105.14.141 rto: 203000 ato: 40000 snd_mss: 33408 \\ rcv_mss: 65468 unacked: 1 sacked: 0 lost: 0 retrans: 0 fackets: 0 pmtu: 65520 \\ rcv_ssthresh: 1964430 rtt: 3000 snd_ssthresh: 2147483647 snd_cwnd: 10 \\ advmss: 65483 reordering: 3 rcv_rtt: 1000 rcv_space: 4451824 total_retrans: 0 This line starts with a timestamp the transfer successfully finished, the direction of the transfer with respect to this machine (Download or Upload), and the condor job id. Any further job attributes can be extracted from the condor_history command on the schedd's history file, or the startd's startd_history file on the execute side. This is then followed by the number of files transferred, the total size of the files, and the IP address of the peer, either IPv4 or IPv6. After these items, the contents of the Linux TCP_INFO getsockopt call are returned. These are only fully documented in the Linux kernel source, but many would have meaning to a network engineer. Probably the most important counters here are "lost", the number of packets lost, and "retrans", the number of re-transmitted packets, though the computed path mtu (pmtu) may also be interesting. We would expect remote transfers to have roughly the same performance and statistics per site that we transfer to, it is up to a higher level tool to extract these data, and present them in a more user friendly format. In vanilla universe, this file is written by the starter on the execute side, and by the shadow on the submit side. The default file name is set by the STARTER_STATS_LOG and SHADOW_STATS_LOG config knobs, respectively, and the maximum size before rotation is set by MAX_STARTER_STATS_LOG and MAX_SHADOW_STATS_LOG. Alternatively, and admin could add D_STATS to the SHADOW_DEBUG or STARTER_DEBUG and have these lines interweaved into the usual log files. When the file transfer is initiated from a user-owned process, like the c-gahp or condor_submit -remote, who don't have permissions to write to a condor-owned log file, these lines will be written to their usual debug files. title: Ticket #3563: Schedd commands to audit
description: We want the audit log for HTCondor-CE to include entries for all commands to the schedd coming from users. For all of these commands, we will record basic security information (source IP address, authenticated identity, HTCondor identity, command name). This information will be written by DaemonCore before the command callout to the schedd code. For most commands, we will record additional information specific to that command. For example, the ids of any submitted jobs. This information will be written from the relevant schedd functions. This ticket will track what commands should be logged at all and what command-specific information should be included. Some commands are received from both users and trusted daemons. When these commands are received from a trusted daemon, then no logging is required. You can write to the audit log by calling audit_log(). It works like dprintf(), but the first argument is a ReliSock* instead of a debug category. The Commands Here are all of the READ, WRITE and DAEMON level commands registered by the schedd, ignoring commands registered in DaemonCore for all daemons. These are the commands we may want to log. When we say that the expected client is the "job owner", this could be a user running a command-line tool, the condor_c-gahp, or the Job Router. In any of these cases, the client will authenticate as the job owner, not as a Condor daemon. DAEMON Level Commands DAEMON and WRITE levels are mostly synonymous. Many configurations may allow users to issue DAEMON level commands GIVE_MATCHES Expected clients: shadow Don't log WRITE Level Commands WRITE level commands are the ones we're most interested in, as they modify state. TRANSFER_QUEUE_REQUEST Expected clients: shadow Don't log RESCHEDULE Expected clients: job owner, site admin Don't log ACT_ON_JOBS Expected clients: job owner, site admin Log Extra information: command (rm, rm -rf, hold, release, vacate, vacate fast, suspend, continue), job id list or constraint SPOOL_JOB_FILES Expected clients: job owner Log Extra information: job ids, job proxy info (if transferred) SPOOL_JOB_FILES_WITH_PERMS Expected clients: job owner Log Extra information: job ids, job proxy info (if transferred) TRANSFER_DATA Expected clients: job owner Log Extra information: job ids TRANSFER_DATA_WITH_PERMS Expected clients: job owner Log Extra information: job ids UPDATE_GSI_CRED Expected clients: job owner Log Extra information: job id, job proxy info DELEGATE_GSI_CRED_SCHEDD Expected clients: job owner Log Extra information: job id, job proxy info REQUEST_SANDBOX_LOCATION Expected clients: job owner Don't log Extra information: job id RECYCLE_SHADOW Expected clients: shadow Don't log ATTEMPT_ACCESS Expected clients: job owner Don't log Extra information: read/write, file path STORE_CRED Expected clients: job owner Windows only Don't log QMGMT_WRITE_CMD Expected clients: job owner, shadow, gridmanager, site admin Log Extra information: CONDOR_NewCluster: Clusterids of submitted jobs CONDOR_SetAttribute*: job id, attribute name, and attribute value for changes to existing jobs GET_MYPROXY_PASSWORD Expected clients: gridmanager Don't log GET_JOB_CONNECT_INFO Expected clients: job owner Log Extra information: job id CLEAR_DIRTY_JOB_ATTRS Expected clients: shadow, gridmanager Don't log READ Level Commands For the most part, READ level commands are not interesting, but some may be of concern. RELEASE_CLAIM Expected clients: startd Valid claimid must be presented Don't log ALIVE Expected clients: startd Valid claimid must be presented Don't log QUERY_SCHEDD_ADS Expected clients: job owner, site admin Don't log QUERY_SUBMITTOR_ADS Expected clients: job owner, site admin Don't log QMGMT_READ_CMD Expected clients: job owner, site admin Don't log DUMP_STATE Expected clients: site admin Tool condor_squawk only on Windows Don't log

title: Ticket #4619: Shadow error causes job to be un-removed
description: If a running job is removed, and then shadow exits with JOB_SHOULD_HOLD, the schedd puts the job in the HELD status without setting JobStatusOnRelease. Then, if the job is released, it goes to IDLE status instead of back to REMOVED. SetAttribute() already has a check for JobStatus, to save the previous value as LastJobStatus. We can expand that code to ensure that JobStatusOnRelease is set appropriately when the status changed away from REMOVED, and that once the status has been REMOVED, it can only switch between HELD and REMOVED. In Scheduler::jobExitCode(), if the shadow's exit status is JOB_SHOULD_HOLD and the job's current status is REMOVED, then the schedd should leave JobStatus as REMOVED and let the the job leave the queue. The same goes for DedicatedScheduler::reaper().

title: Ticket #6274: DAGMan doesn't work right with late materialization
description: DAGMan currently doesn't work right if one of its node jobs uses late materialization. title: Ticket #4249: condor_q extremely large memory usage
description: Currently, dprintf buffers all statements until 'dprintf_config' is called. For a tool (condor_q), this never happens so the buffer grows indefinitely. When using "-userlog" mode, there's 2 log lines per event (one for locking and one for unlocking). In my testing, this caused >100MB of RAM to be used by a condor_q invocation. For now, the workaround is to add the "-debug" flag and pipe stderr to /dev/null. This causes dprintf_config and prevents the buffering.
creator: bbockelm

title: Ticket #3076: Startd slot stuck in Preempting/Vacating
description: Observed in the CHTC pool running 7.7.6: slots are sometimes hanging around in Preempting/Vacating indefinitely. At the moment 150 slots out of about 2,000 are in Preempting/Vacating, and have been for at least 2 days, and in some cases as long as 45 days. In all cases examined, the associated starter exited as expected, many, many days ago. There don't appear to be any leak processes; we're using slot users so they're easy to detect. Unfortunately our startd logs were too small, 50 MB with D_FULLDEBUG so about 12 hours, so we don't know if the startd even detected the starter exiting. Ken increased the logs to 240 MB, but the problem hasn't happened since we started digging more deeply. As a side effect, jobs are trying to match to preempting slots, only to be rejected. The appearance to the user is that there jobs take a long time to match, when in fact they're matching but are immediately rejected. Observed on a Windows XP machines in new batlab (exec-102) running 7.8.0. Both slots were stuck. This time the StartLog was spammed with entries in this form: "06/21/12 16:08:01 DaemonCore: async_pipe is signalled, but async_pipe_signal is false." The warning may be unrelated, #3079 was created to track is separately if necessary.
remarks: 2012-Jun-27 15:53:10 by adesmet: Immediate cause isolated to /src/condor_startd.V6/startd_main.cpp around line 752 in the function reaper: int reaper(Service *, int pid, int status) { /* [snip */ foo = resmgr->getClaimByPid(pid); if( foo ) { foo->starterExited(status); } return TRUE; } resmgr->getClaimByPid(pid) is returning NULL, so we silently skip over foo->starterExited(status). This appears to only happen with fetchwork jobs (but it may be that something about fetchwork jobs, or how we have CHTC configured makes fetchwork more likely to tickle the bug. In particular, fetchwork jobs can be interrupted at any point while we don't normally interrupt other jobs until 24 hours has passed. Also, fetchwork jobs can start very quickly, while other jobs have more overhead. A representative StartLog is: 06/27/12 15:44:42 Starter pid 9991 exited with status 0 06/27/12 15:44:42 Starter pid 9995 exited with status 0 06/27/12 15:44:42 Starter pid 9998 exited with status 0 06/27/12 15:44:42 slot7: State change: starter exited 06/27/12 15:44:42 slot7: State change: No preempting claim, returning to owner 06/27/12 15:44:42 slot7: Changing state and activity: Preempting/Vacating -> Owner/Idle 06/27/12 15:44:42 slot7: State change: IS_OWNER is false 06/27/12 15:44:42 slot7: Changing state: Owner -> Unclaimed 06/27/12 15:44:42 Starter pid 9999 exited with status 0 06/27/12 15:44:42 Starter pid 10001 exited with status 0 06/27/12 15:44:42 slot2: State change: starter exited 06/27/12 15:44:42 slot2: State change: No preempting claim, returning to owner 06/27/12 15:44:42 slot2: Changing state and activity: Preempting/Vacating -> Owner/Idle 06/27/12 15:44:42 slot2: State change: IS_OWNER is false 06/27/12 15:44:42 slot2: Changing state: Owner -> Unclaimed The jobs in slots 2 and 7 exited preempting successfully. Slots 1, 6, and 8 (associated with PIDs 9991, 9995, and 9999, but in an unknown association) do not. Current technique to reproduce in a few minutes: Set up condor; ./condor_configure --make-personal-condor Add to your configuration: STARTD_JOB_HOOK_KEYWORD = ALAN ALAN_HOOK_FETCH_WORK=/scratch/adesmet/V7_8-branch/release_dir/hooks/fetch-work-infinite FetchWorkDelay=1 NUM_CPUS=8 # FetchWorkDelay means the log will be full of garbage, make it big MAX_START_LOG=100000000 Create fetch-work-infinite #! /usr/bin/perl -w use strict; my $exe = '/bin/sleep'; my $args = 3600; my $owner = 'adesmet'; print <<END; Cmd="$exe" Args="$args" Owner="$owner" JobUniverse=5 Requirements=TRUE RequestCpus=1 RequestMemory=8 RequestDisk=1024 END exit 0; Start up condor Run spam-vacate, a Perl tool that follows: #! /usr/bin/perl my $MAX = 90; while(1) { my $val = rand($MAX); print "Sleeping for $val\n"; sleep($val); system('condor_vacate'); my(@wedged) = `condor_status -const 'State=="Preempting" && ( CurrentTime-EnteredCurrentActivity ) > 20' -format '%d\n' CurrentTime-EnteredCurrentActivity`; if(@wedged) { die "Wedged something, huzzah!" } } New question: Why isn't resmgr->getClaimByPid(pid) finding the claim? Presumably there is a window when the PID exists, but the claim isn't registered. 2012-Jun-27 16:09:05 by adesmet: Testing to see if I can reproduce with vanilla jobs. Guessing no, but just in case. 2012-Jun-28 18:03:51 by adesmet: Cannot reproduce with vanilla jobs. Healthy code path: Starter::kill (sometimes called twice?!) reaper notices condor_starter exited Claim::resetClaim deletes the Starter Unhealthy code path Starter::kill (sometimes called twice?!) Claim::~Claim deletes the Starter associated Starter is deleted reaper notices condor_starter exited It's not yet clear why the Starter is being deleted. 2012-Jun-29 13:49:13 by adesmet: Stack during an unhealthy ("early") call to Claim::~Claim which destroys the associated Starter object. Claim::~Claim() Resource::createFetchClaim(compat_classad::ClassAd*, float) Resource::createOrUpdateFetchClaim(compat_classad::ClassAd*, float) StartdHookMgr::handleHookFetchWork(FetchClient*) FetchClient::hookExited(int) HookClientMgr::reaperOutput(int, int) DaemonCore::CallReaper(int, char const*, int, int) DaemonCore::HandleProcessExit(int, int) DaemonCore::HandleDC_SERVICEWAITPIDS(int) DaemonCore::Driver() dc_main(int, char**) main __libc_start_main CronJob::Reaper(int, int) 2012-Jun-29 14:41:55 by adesmet: Current hypothesis: Current job (probably fetchwork but not necessarily) is preempting. Startd is waiting for the starter to exit Fetchwork hook for the slot returns, Startd decides to hand the slot over to the new fetch job; why not, it's already preempting. Fetchwork hook deletes the old Claim (/src/condor_startd.V6/Resource.cpp line 2476 inside Resource::createFetchClaim). As a side effect, the Starter object is destroyed, along with any connection of the PID to this slot. The starter exits (ot at least the startd notices that the starter exited). It ignores this, since it no longer know which slot its connected to. As such, the code path that codes Preempting to Unclaimed never fires. Open questions Can this happen to a non-fetchwork job? I suspect yes. Can this happen when the new job is a non-fetchwork job. Not sure. What's the right behavior? When the new fetchwork job decides to stomp on the old claim, should it force the slot into Idle? Seems dangerous in general to stomp on an unresolved job. Refuse new fetchwork (any work?) until we're out of preempting? 2012-Jun-29 17:02:19 by adesmet: Why complicate things? Just do what happens if the fetchwork job arrives and the machine is claimed: mark it as the next/preempting claim (r_pre) and carry on. "startd exiting because of fatal exception."? Oh, alright then. 2012-Jul-03 15:23:44 by adesmet: Went with the straightforward option: if a fetchwork job shows up and we're preempting, just refuse it. Also, log if we see unexpected processes exit; don't just silently ignore them. Work is on V7_8-preempting-fix-branch pending review and eventual merge to V7_8-branch. 2012-Jul-10 16:04:57 by adesmet: Bounced by johnkn, who correctly points out that in this case we won't invoke the reply fetch hook, a violation of the API. Fixing. 2012-Jul-12 11:10:05 by adesmet: Better solution checked in to V7_8-preempting-fix-branch. Handing back to TJ for re-review. 2012-Jul-18 11:08:49 by johnkn: Better fix looks good to me.

title: Ticket #5008: ssh_to_job should not run a login shell by default
description: The intent is for the environment of ssh_to_job to be the same as the batch job. But looking at the code, it appears that the below environment variables are likely to be missing/different between a vanilla batch job and an ssh_to_job session. Ticket #4943 fixed part of the problem. But in addition to the issues addressed in #4943, ssh_to_job tends to have many more environment variables set than a batch job does because ssh_to_job initiates a login shell, and thus it picks up environment variables from the system's .profile and/or .bashrc. We should have ssh_to_job just set the terminal related environment variables by default instead of initiating a login shell by default, and perhaps provide an command-line option to request a login shell.
creator: tannenba

title: Ticket #7465: Container jobs don't respect pre- and post- script exit codes
description: The SWAMP would like Docker and Singulariy jobs to respect their pre- and post- script exit codes in the same way that VM jobs do. After speaking with Tom Bricker on 2020-02-28, the problem (at least as he remembers it) was that the SWAMP had been using a hack to make it possible for their VM universe pre-script to prevent the job from running, that is, deleting the image. The fix we added for them shortly later has always applied to all pre- and post- scripts, where you can specify Success[Pre|Post]ExitCode, and the job goes on hold if the pre- or post- script's exit code doesn't match. Tom needed the job to be removed in those cases, but that was a simple extension of their existing periodic_remove expression.

title: Ticket #8: Add "use warnings" and "use strict" to test scripts
description: Our regression tests (src/condor_tests) are built primarily on Perl. Ideally all of our Perl scripts would "use strict" and "use warnings". The combination catches a lot of bugs, both serious and minor. For example, I discovered a script that printed a variable that could not possibly be assigned. This meant the resulting message was a bit nonsensical, since part of the output was missing. Either "use strict" or "use warnings" would catch the bug quickly (complaining that the variable wasn't defined, or that undef was being printed, respectively). So: Add "use strict" and "use warnings" whenever possible in our test scripts. Attached is a script that will scan a directory and report perl scripts that need attention.

title: Ticket #1948: StarterLog should indicate user changes more clearly
description: The StarterLog is confusing and it leads it difficulty in debugging problems. It would not be hard to make it less confusing. From RUST #21737, here is an extract from the StarterLog which almost helps the user: 03/01 10:52:23 Submitting machine is "mansun" 03/01 10:52:23 setting the orig job name in starter 03/01 10:52:23 setting the orig job iwd in starter 03/01 10:52:23 ERROR: the submitting host claims to be in our UidDomain (wrc.xerox.com), yet its hostname (mansun) does not match. If the above hostname is actually an IP address, Condor could not perform a reverse DNS lookup to convert the IP back into a name. To solve this problem, you can either correctly configure DNS to allow the reverse lookup, or you can enable TRUST_UID_DOMAIN in your condor configuration. 03/01 10:52:23 Job 12.4 set to execute immediately I think the StarterLog should add messages about attempting to change the user. It could look something like this when successful: 03/01 10:52:23 Submitting machine is "mansun" 03/01 10:52:23 setting the orig job name in starter 03/01 10:52:23 setting the orig job iwd in starter 03/01 10:52:23 Attempting to change from user "root" to user "roy" 03/01 10:52:23 Now running as user "roy" 03/01 10:52:23 Job 12.4 set to execute immediately And it could like this when it failed: 03/01 10:52:23 Submitting machine is "mansun" 03/01 10:52:23 setting the orig job name in starter 03/01 10:52:23 setting the orig job iwd in starter 03/01 10:52:23 Attempting to change from user "root" to user "roy" 03/01 10:52:23 ERROR: Failed to change from user "root" to user "roy" because the submitting host claims to be in our UidDomain (wrc.xerox.com), yet its hostname (mansun) does not match. If the above hostname is actually an IP address, Condor could not perform a reverse DNS lookup to convert the IP back into a name. To solve this problem, you can either correctly configure DNS to allow the reverse lookup, or you can enable TRUST_UID_DOMAIN in your condor configuration. 03/01 10:52:23 Now running as user "nobody" 03/01 10:52:23 Job 12.4 set to execute immediately Note that in both cases, the new user is indicated, and in the failure case, the explanation for the failure mentions that the attempt to change users failed. Of course, since you understand what is happening better, you might have an even better suggestion of how to change the message. I hope that this change can go into Condor soon. It might be too late for 7.6.0, but I think it's a good change to consider for 7.6.1 because it will help us debug problems more quickly and solve RUST tickets more quickly. Thanks!

title: Ticket #357: WS-GRAM and RFT on different machines for GT4 grid jobs
description: In the gt4 grid-type, a WS-GRAM service can be configured to use an RFT service in a different container. As a delegated credential can only be accessed from within the same container, this setup requires the client to delegate the credential to two different Delegation services, one in GRAM's container and one in RFT's container. The client can query the WS GRAM service for the RFT service it uses. globusrun-ws handles this split case, while Condor-G does not. The Condor-G job will fail due to RFT being unable to retrieve the credential. This setup (GRAM and RFT in different containers) appears to be rarely used in the wild.

title: Ticket #7609: Submit.queue_with_itemdata() segfaults if iterator raises an exception
description: Paul Skopnik reports on HTCondor-users: The Submit.queue_with_itemdata method causes a segmentation fault when the iterator passed raises an exception during next(it). Submit.queue_with_itemdata() should check whether an exception occurred during next(it) and pass on this exception to its Python caller. Minimal reproducible example: import htcondor def my_it(): raise Exception() yield {} sub = htcondor.Submit() schedd = htcondor.Schedd() with schedd.transaction() as txn: result = sub.queue_with_itemdata(txn, itemdata=my_it()) I'd love if we could re-raise the exception that is raised inside the iterator instead of our generic RuntimeError. Further update from Paul: I discovered further details about the bug while attempting a workaround. I believe there are two separate but related issues. ## No 1: Segfault during queue_with_itemdata The segmentation fault is caused not by the exception inside next(it) but by the Iterator yielding no elements ("length" of 0). This code causes a segfault: import htcondor sub = htcondor.Submit() schedd = htcondor.Schedd() with schedd.transaction() as txn: result = sub.queue_with_itemdata(txn, itemdata=iter([])) ## No 2: Late checking for exception This is not a bug from a user perspective, but might be a programming issue. The reason for the segfault in my original example is, that there is no immediate check whether an exception occurred during iteration. Hence, PyIter_Next returning NULL is interpreted as the iterator being exhausted. The exception is then detected and raised to the caller later on. This can be seen in this code which sort of works as expected: import htcondor def my_it(): yield {'executable': '/bin/ls'} raise Exception() sub = htcondor.Submit() schedd = htcondor.Schedd() with schedd.transaction() as txn: result = sub.queue_with_itemdata(txn, itemdata=my_it())
