title: Ticket #1289: Custom Signals can be defined for vanilla universe jobs
description: It is now possible to define a custom kill signal to be used when a vanilla universe job is killed instead of always hard killing the job. If 'kill_sig' is defined in the job description file, then the specified signal will be sent to the job in the case the job is to be killed (like condor_rm). By default, the starter will wait 'killing_timeout-1' seconds before sending the job a kill signal to forcibly kill the job. If the job description file contains 'kill_sig_timeout', then the starter will wait the shorter of killing_timeout-1 and kill_sig_timeout before sending the job the kill signal. The signal definition/escalation described above is not available on windows. Change sourced from GT#1198
remarks: kill_sig_timeout is a new submit description file command. It is associated with the job ClassAd attribute KillSigTimeout These submit commands and associated attributes apply to all universes other than the standard universe, so this ticket (and derived from #1198) are incorrect.

title: Ticket #1773: condor_q is significantly slower due to new classads
description: When running condor_q against a queue of 100k jobs, I found that 7.5 after the introduction of new classads takes 4 times as long to complete as before new classads. The main reasons for the slowdown that I have found are: linear searches in ClassAdList creating an intermediate copy of the classad in compat_classad::ClassAd::initFromStream expensive ClassAd instantiation due to initialization of expr and name iterators that may not even be used on the schedd side, putOldClassAd() is slow because iterating through a hash_map appears to be fairly expensive on the schedd side, when applying a projection of which attributes to send, it constructs a temporary ad; deletion of this ad is fairly expensive, again due to iteration through the hash_map The patches that I have committed to address the above problems make condor_q on 100k jobs perform at the same speed as the same test in 7.4.

title: Ticket #5730: Make node job ClassAd visible to DAGMan POST script
description: Miron today expressed a desire to have a node job's ClassAd visible to its POST script. (I didn't think of this during our discussion, but the POST script can access the ClassAd via condor_history. I'm not sure if that would satisfy what Miron wants or not.) I'd have to think about what a good way would be to do this -- the first thing that comes to mind is that we could have a $(CLASSAD_FILE) argument to the post script, and DAGMan would write a file with the relevant ClassAd, and fill in the file name as the argument. (One issue with that is garbage-collecting the ClassAd files.) (One problem with using condor_history is that it may not work real well for node jobs with multiple procs. If we did the file method, I guess the file could contain the ClassAds for all of the procs, so that might work a little better.)

title: Ticket #7648: Job submission without Unix account on schedd
description: I'm looking at supporting a use case where we are providing Jupyter notebooks to anyone within CMS (using their CERN account via OIDC). We are generating an IDTOKEN on the fly for the container to allow them to submit Dask workers to a local schedd. We do not want to create a Unix user in our LDAP for everyone using the JupyterHub, however. Just as when a job from a different UID domain gets mapped to Unix user 'nobody' when running on a starter, I would like to explore the idea of a user from a different UID domain getting their Owner attribute mapped to Unix user 'nobody' when submitting to a schedd. What does this imply? User becomes an immutable attribute that reflects the authenticated identity at job submit time. This is likely worth doing regardless!! SetAttribute code for generating the Owner attribute should set the owner to nobody if the user is from a different domain. QMGMT owner checks become "user" checks. Authenticated users from a different UID domain should not be able to change each other's jobs. No longer "fix" the user attribute if the Owner is set to nobody. Ban jobs from user nobody as that's now a reserved attribute. For backward compatibility reasons, perhaps we can rename the string nobody for people submitting under that name. Review tools that currently query on Owner to see if they should instead query on User (and then silently truncate the results if the UID_DOMAIN matches the one on the authenticated socket)
remarks: 2020-Jun-10 12:33:56 by bbockelm: The first draft of this work is here: https://github.com/htcondor/htcondor/pull/120 While it currently contains some code relevant to the proposed feature, the more important aspect is it refactors the meaning of User and Owner as proposed (will also attach the longer document written with Miron & Todd). It has some minimal testing (personal condor functions) but not a full test run. Modulo bugs (which I'm sure exist), it should have the same observable behavior as current HTCondor installs. Ticket #6059: Count prefetch time as part of schedd interaction
description: Right now, prefetching is "free" communication: time spent in the prefetch loop doesn't count against a schedd's time. I think this is wrong: in CMS, we've observed a "bad schedd" timing out every one of several prefetch loops. We shouldn't give the unresponsive schedd a free pass just because prefetching is enabled. We should add time spent prefetching (from when the first prefetch request is sent until the last request finishes, regardless of how many schedds we are processing in parallel) to the time spent negotiating with the schedd.

title: Ticket #1636: Report operating system, distribution, and version in world ads
description: Problem: We have no idea what our users are actually running Condor on. Condor may report "x86 RHEL3", but that's not terribly helpful since the RHEL3 binaries run on a wide variety of actual distributions. This makes it hard to determine which old platforms can be dropped, and which new platforms we should consider native ports for. Proposal: Add new logic to the condor_master to detect the operating system, distribution (if Linux), version of distribution, and architecture. This information should be added to the master ad. It might be something like "ActualPlatform=Linux,Red Hat,5,x86" Add new logic to the condor_collector to collect this information up and add it to the world ad or world email. Something like "ActualPlatforms="20,Linux,Red Hat,5,x86;7,Windows,Windows,6.1,x86" for 20 RHEL5 boxes and 7 Windows Server 2008 boxes. In addition to giving us a better sense of what our users are actually running for porting, it gives users an incentive to report world ads. The CONDOR_DEVELOPERS and CONDOR_DEVELOPERS_COLLECTOR documenation can have added to it, "The Condor team uses this information to decide which platforms to support. If you disable this, the Condor team will not know what platforms you are using and will be unable to take it into consideration." The task of doing OS/distribution/version detection is ticket #653; until that is at least partially done, we can't start this. Once #653 is implemented, we'll have a choice: does the master link in the detection code, or do we keep it in a separate binary that the master calls into. A separate binary may help keep the master small, and provides a handy tool for user support ("Please run condor_detect_os and tell me what it returns"). (#653 originally encompassed the above as well as development of the detection library. I'm breaking into smaller, more focused tickets.)

title: Ticket #2919: Parallelize classad matchmaking
description: As part of my ME964 project, I am working to find points where ClassAd work can be done in a parallel fashion. The first step is seeing if matching of classads can be parallelized. Currently matching is done using the IsAMatch function inside compat_classad_util. This operation can be parallelized by passing in the classad we want a match for and a list of candidates and, perhaps using openmp, by using a parallel for loop to create MatchClassAd instances for each potential pair. Because the original classads are modified during the matching operation, we would need to make copies of the target classad, as depending on the classad we are matching against, the change is different. The original candidate classads can be modified themselves. One possible performance enhancement is to create a pool of MatchClassAd instances that the parallel matching algorithm can use instead of constantly creating and destroying MatchClassAd instances, assuming this is ever a problem.
remarks: 2012-Apr-06 20:58:10 by ziliang: Some preliminary numbers where I am trying to find a match for a job from amongst 1136 machines. Note that each pair of numbers is using a different job ad but the same set of machines. Also note that I am not stopping the search the moment I find a match, this is a straight up comparison to see how much time it would take to run a comparison against all the machines. Job 1: OpenMP: 1404 Sequential: 1435 Job 2: OpenMP: 1404 Sequential: 2636 Job 3: OpenMP: 2418 Sequential: 4399 Job 4: OpenMP: 1653 Sequential: 5226 Comments: This is running with 4 threads for each comparison, since that's how many cores I have on my workstation. My implementation sets that the amount of threads equal to the number of cores. The first job also had to initialize the memory pool used to hold the MatchAd classes and the copies of the target ad. We need a better way to clean those up. This speedup for the others is also, unfortunately, not linear. That may have something to do with the synchronization that happens to add matching ads to the shared vector. Am open to suggestions of how to make that more efficient. Another possibility is the cost of the copying operation I have to do for the target ad, which is not done in the sequential matching. 2012-May-15 15:38:16 by ziliang: We'll need to declare openmp as a dependency in the packaging glue if we roll this out. 2016-Sep-27 10:40:06 by gthain: Let's leave this one undocumented until it has some more mileage under its belt.

title: Ticket #5931: Inefficient JobRouter updates
description: Updates are pushed from the job router to HTCondor-CE schedd in the following manner: for each job: connect to schedd set effective owner setattribute (with ACK) disconnect This results in a huge number of connects / disconnects. title: Ticket #4623: TotalSlots is not documented
description: In GlideinWMS to verify if partitionable slots are used we are using in the startd daemon shutdown expression: ((PartitionableSlot =!= True) || (TotalSlots =?=1)) This expression seems to work but TotalSlots is not documented (at least not in the index). remarks: 2014-Nov-19 15:49:38 by smoler: Revised documentation task is to update and add documentation for all aspects of machine ClassAd attributes Disk, TotalDisk, and TotalSlotDisk, where each is given in KiB Cpus, TotalCpus, and TotalSlotCpus Memory, TotalMemory, and TotalSlotMemory, where each is given in MiB Total<Resource> is the amount per machine (not per slot). For static slots, <Resource> and TotalSlot<Resource> will be the same value For partitionable slots, TotalSlot<Resource> is the total amount assigned to the partionable slot. <Resource> is the quantity remaining in the partitionable slot, given that dynamic slots may have been carved off this partitionable slot. Total<Resource> and TotalSlot<Resource> are going to be the same value if there is 1 slot per machine. This is the ordinary case for partitionable slots, where we have 1 partitionable slot per machine. 2014-Nov-19 16:25:57 by smoler: TotalSlots is the number of total slots on the machine right now. This will be sum of the number of static slots, the number of partitionable slots, and the number of dynamic slots. Quick example: if there are 2 partitionable slots configured for this machine, and 3 jobs have each carved off 1 dynamic slot (1 slot per 1 job), then TotalSlots is 5. 2 partitionable slots + 3 dynamic slots = 5.

title: Ticket #947: Remove NEGOTIATOR_SIMPLE_MATCHING
description: Setting config param NEGOTIATOR_SIMPLE_MATCHING to True causes machine ads to be referenced after deletion in the negotiator. It also causes some machine ad munging related to WantAdRevaluate and NegotiatorRequirements to be skipped. This parameter was added specifically for Micron 5 years ago, whose negotiator was being slowed down too much by the negotiator grabbing all ads from the collector, rather than just startd and submitter ads. Back then, the collector was changed to pull all ads in order to support gangmatching-lite. Gangmatching-lite is no longer in the code-base and the extra ads are now ignored. NEGOTIATOR_SIMPLE_MATCHING has never been documented. If we assume Micron has a modern machine for their central manager, we can remove the NEGOTIATOR_SIMPLE_MATCHING code. At some point, we may want to reconsider whether the negotiator should be grabbing all ads from the collector.

title: Ticket #1972: execution_history - startd/er equivalent to the job history
description: Answer questions about goodput/badput across a pool is hard. Indeed, lots of information about what happens on execute machines is hard to collect. jmeehean ran into this exact problem trying to ask the seemingly simple question, "How much badput does CHTC have?" The information is scattered about. The local history can't help you because it doesn't know about jobs that were suspended and it doesn't know about work fetch. The daemons that actually know what is running, for how long, and the like are the startd and starter. They could keep a log of classads of jobs they've run (similar to the history the schedd keeps). For each job, it would track: Source schedd, fetch work script, etc username cmd arguments Time/Date the job was accepted to Cumulative time spent running Cumulative time spent suspended Cumulative time spent in input file transfer before the jobs starts Cumulative time spent in output file transfer after the jobs finishes Size of the sandbox after transfer in, and before transfer out. Cumulative time spent in overhead (from the time the startd forgets about the job - the time the startd accepted the job, minus all of the above cumulative entries) Reason the job stopped running (exited, exited with signal, preempted, removed) Exit code (if appropriate) exit signal (if appropriate) Slot number Machine name (useful if aggregating multiple logs) Like the job history it needs options, probably defaulting to on, to roll this log over. This isn't everything, it ignores complexities like aggregating results across machines. However, the information to be able to answer a question like, "What percentage of our work time is badput?"
creator: adesmet

title: Ticket #802: VM configuration status changes have delayed visibility
description: Description of problem: The new VM_RECHECK_INTERVAL parameter force condor to check again VM configuration status after the specified amount of time. If VM support was disabled (xend/libvirtd not running) but it is enabled again after the interval is elapsed, the new status is not sent to the Collector. Steps to Reproduce: 1. Configure condor enabling VM support, disable xend/libvirtd and start condor. 2. Re-enable xend/libvirtd, wait for VM_RECHECK_INTERVAL seconds and check again condor_status -long. Actual results: Most of the time condor_status -long contains HasVM = FALSE, even if condor_status -long -direct <vmnode> reports HasVM = TRUE. The status is updated after a while. Expected results: condor_status -long should report the new status, i.e. an update should be triggered on a state change for HasVM.
remarks: 2009-Oct-01 07:58:56 by tstclair: Initial Investigation: -------- Begin Manual Excerpt (Note the bold) VM_RECHECK_INTERVAL An integer number of seconds that defaults to 600 (ten minutes), representing the amount of time the condor_startd waits after a virtual machine error as reported by the condor_starter, and before checking a final time on the status of the virtual machine. If the check fails, Condor disables starting any new vm universe jobs by removing the VM_Type attribute from the machine ClassAd. -------- End Manual Excerpt When I looked into the code and re-read the statement it is rather literal, it only adjusts the VM_Type attribute. It appears to me that HasVM will be updated the next time the classAd is "published", which it appears can happen for several reasons. Desired functionality is to publish the data on the event. Patch will be forthcoming. 2009-Oct-02 17:03:35 by danb: Tim, Looks good to me! My only minor nitpick is a case of whitespace being messed with in a completely unrelated function.

title: Ticket #7849: AES non-negotiated session backwards compatibility
description: This work was moved to https://opensciencegrid.atlassian.net/browse/HTCONDOR-233 Previous ticket content below break I'm adding some content here to capture a Zoom meeting between Zach, ToddT, and BrianB on Nov 12, 2020. On the call, we were discussing that there may not be a need for (all) the below mechanism(s) to implement backwards compatibility when using AES in non-negotiated sessions. However, see in the discussion, I believe parts of the solution in this ticket are still necessary. In versions of condor 8.9.10 and earlier: When a startd creates it's private ad that it sends to the collector, it is including the list of supported crypto methods. It creates a non-negotiated session using the private capability as the session key and with the method that is listed first in the list of SEC_*_CRYPTO_METHODS. The Schedd also looks at just THE FIRST CHARACTER of this list, and creates an out-going non-negotiated session using the capability and crypto method associated with that character, either 'B'lowfish or '3'des. In versions of condor 8.9.11 and later: The startd will append "B," to the list of methods that it includes in its ad sent to the collector The schedd will take the first entry in the list that is a VALID name of a method. "BLOWFISH" and "AESGCM" are the valid names. "B" is not. An old schedd will see "B,AESGCM" and will select BLOWFISH due to the first letter being 'B'. A new schedd will see the "B" method, disregard the invalid name, and then select "AESGCM'. Discussion I believe this on its own is not suffecient. The startd still needs to know which method the client is using when it is "resuming" the non-negotiated session. So, as proposed below, new SchedDs should add an attribute in the resume classad that indicates what method they are trying to use. In that case, the startd still needs to either: 1) Create a session of both Blowfish and AES, so it is ready when a resume command comes in for either, or 2) Delay binding of the crypto type to the session until the command comes in. I think I'm still in favor of the startd creating multiple sessions, one for each type of allowable crypto type. To distinguish between which Either there should be an additional attribute in the resume classad, or new schedds could attach "-AES" to the session name, or something similar. Older Content For non-negotiated sessions, how can we start using AES but maintain backwards compatibility? In this ticket we'll brainstorm approaches with pros/cons. Here's one rough crazy idea: The startd creates two non-negotiated sessions to receive claims. One uses 3DES and the private claim ID as the key. The other uses AES. Maybe they have different names. The startd would have a knob to only use AES. (Avoiding an old TLS-style exploit involving forced selection of an older protocol). The negotiator could put something in the match that it gives to the schedd depending on whether the match is given to a new or old schedd and whether its an old startd since it knowns the versions of both. New schedds would then resume the AES session when talking to new startds, and everything else would use the 3DES one. This requires the CM to be running an AES-supported negotiator. Or, maybe better, the startd adds a special new attribute to its ad that new schedds then notice, and new schedds then do something in the resume session classad to indicate that they are resuming an AES session instead of a 3des one. Old schedds would ignore the new startd attribute and resume the session without the special attribute. New schedds can look at the version of the StartD they are claiming and not use it on old startds. Something like that. Other ideas?
remarks: 2020-Sep-09 22:55:55 by jfrey: Here's a variation on your initial ideas: The startd puts a new attribute in the security policy ad of the claim id indicating it supports AES in addition to the stated crypto method for the session (3DES or BLOWFISH). A new schedd will recognize this attribute and put a new attribute in the resume session ad that indicates it wants to use AES. Old schedds would ignore the new attribute in the claim id and resume the session without the use-AES attribute. The negotiator doesn't need to do anything. And this can be used for any non-negotiated session, like the ones the schedd can now send to the negotiator and collector. If the startd only wants to support AES, then it just gives AES as the crypto method in the claim id. 2020-Sep-10 09:07:08 by zmiller: Yeah, perfect. That's kind of what I was thinking with my last paragraph but didn't quite have it spelled out. I think that will work! 2020-Sep-10 09:07:55 by zmiller: The question now is: how do we future-proof this mechanism for when we add <ZKM65536> encryption down the road? Perhaps the startd advertises all of the methods it supports, the schedd can pick any one it likes and send that in the "session resume" and the startd does some kind of "late binding session creation" or "late crypto method instantiation" where it can resume a session that is known and pre-registered but with different crypto methods (as long as they are supported by the startd... i.e. the schedd can't pick one the startd has purposely disabled). 2020-Sep-10 09:18:17 by jfrey: The new attribute in the claimid session info could be a list of all additional crypto methods the startd is willing to use. If the schedd wants to use a method other than the primary one in CryptoMethods, it can say which one in the resume session ad. This same idea could be applied to introducing new integrity algorithms. 2020-Sep-10 09:20:27 by zmiller: Slightly off-topic: I think we could also use this trick to eliminate a round trip in normal (negotiated) session negotiation. Likely an optimization for 9.1.X and it doesn't have as much gain now that the session resume is non-blocking, and more and more things are using pre-existing non-negotiated sessions, but here it is anyway: If the client has the ad of the daemon it wants to connect to (e.g. because it got it from the collector, as most things do) then it could already know the list of methods that daemon supports. It picks anything that it knows the server supports and in the initial resume message it just informs the server which methods they will be using and it immediately goes to authenticate. This eliminates the [client->server: here are my methods ; server->client: okay, here's what we'll do] round trip. The server of course still needs to enforce that whatever the client requests is allowable. But otherwise I think this will work. 2020-Sep-10 09:31:07 by jfrey: I like the security negotiation optimization idea. We'd have to add the security policy stuff to the daemon ads and include the new attribute(s) in the locate projection. If the server doesn't like what the client says, it'd have to slam the door and send an out-of-band message, like with a rejected session resumption. 2020-Jan-11 11:47:35 by zmiller: Due date pushed back because of dependency on #6226.

title: Ticket #4336: Make dict-like objects in Python bindings even more dict-like
description: the htcondor.param module in HTCondor's Python bindings is "dictionary-like." They should be even more dictionary-like, and in a perfect world would implement the complete dict interface. Specifically requested are: keys, vals, items, __len__, __iter__, __contains__.
remarks: 2014-May-07 07:47:07 by bbockelm: I just pushed this in checkin [40075] but forgot to reference the ticket from the commit. I implemented everything requested except values(); this did not seem to have a reasonable use case. If you really want it, you can now convert the htcondor.param object to a dict. This forced some minor cleanup work [40072] in the config system. In particular, I consolidated the boolean arguments to config_ex into the flags argument. I also caught a few cases where calling config() can cause exit() being called despite CONFIG_OPT_NO_EXIT being given. This means the python bindings will no longer exit the interpreter when the module is loaded. Now, config() will just return false (note - I don't currently do much with this fact from within the python bindings). The param object now returns the correct types; for example, htcondor.param[UPDATE_INTERVAL'] returns the integer 300 instead of '300'. This forced some cleanups ([40073] [40074]) where the default values were not valid values for the given type. For example, HAVE_EXT_KRB5 defaulted to the string "HAVE_EXT_KRB5" due to a problem in the code generator instead of "1". 2014-May-07 13:52:54 by johnkn: CODE REVIEW: review for parameter changes, not necessarily bindings The parameter changes look good. I particularly like the flags cleanup for config_ex(). I'm a little worried about treating the param table as a python dictionary though. The values stored in the dictionary will have to be the 'cooked' values, which are valid only until the next call that changes the param table. Also, there are several Boolean parameters that are type 'string' because the value is actually an expression that must be evaluated. In the c++ code, this evaluation happens each time param_boolean is called, but it appears to me that with the dictionary, this evaluation will happen only for parameters that are type bool and only at the time the dictionary is created.

title: Ticket #2061: Fetch work hooks not implemented for standard universe jobs
description: Part of the message from condor-users, Joan J. Piles on April 13: We have a hook that must be called for each job running in our cluster, an instance of xxxxx_HOOK_JOB_EXIT. In the Vanilla universe (the one most of our jobs use), there is no problem, and it works almost as expected (I say almost because the exit reason is shown as "evict" even when "condor_rm" is used, but that's not an important problem for us). We have recently found that this hook is completely ignored for Standard universe jobs. According to the documentation it should work, and it is condor_starter's job to run the hooks. However, there seem to be two condor_starter executables, one for most jobs, and another one (condor_starter.std) for Standard universe jobs. Furthermore, in the sourece code there are two completely different implementations, and the Standard universe one seems to have no hook capability at all, so I don't know if this is a bug or a feature ;-) What are our options for implementing hooks for Standard Universe jobs? Is this being worked upon (in development versions), or we should find a workaround? We already tried ditching condor_starter.std, but the default condor_starter doesn't seem to be able to start Standard Universe jobs. Thanks in advance, Joan And here is part of Todd T's response: You are correct, standard universe has its own shadow/starter pair that does not support a bunch of mechanisms found in the newer shadow/starter pair that supports other universes like Vanilla, Java, etc. Besides hooks, other features like ssh_to_job and CCB do not work in standard universe for this reason. So, we should clearly document this limitation in the hook documentation.

title: Ticket #7799: Remove intentional delays in daemon startup
description: Several of the daemons have intentional delays of a second or longer at startup. These are unnecessary and can be removed. When the master starts the shared port and collector daemons, it delays starting other daemons until these ones create their address files. It polls the status of the files at 1-second intervals, but the files are typically present after less than a tenth of a second. We can't schedule daemoncore timers a sub-second resolution, but the handler can sleep for 100 milliseconds when the file isn't present yet. This should be ok, as the master isn't doing anything else in these cases. When the schedd starts up, it creates a Timeslice object to handle calling of the Scheduler::timeout() daemoncore timer. It sets a minimum interval (default 5 seconds) but not an initial interval. Thus, the first call to timeout() does't happen for 5 seconds. This delays count_jobs(), which sends ads to the collector, among other things. When the startd starts up, it creates all of its Resource objects and their associated machine ads. It then delays 3 seconds before sending ads to the collector "to allow the startd's state to quiesce". This principally means ensuring attributes that are advertised cross-slot are accurate. After recent changes by TJ, this should not be necessary. The delay can be reduced to 0 seconds (though still in a separate daemoncore timer).
remarks: 2020-Sep-01 14:42:36 by jfrey: Improving the master's startup time tickles a bug related to one observed in #7502. When the shared port daemon sends its first child-alive message to the master, the master sees no data on the passed socket. When the shared port daemon forwards a connection for the collector's child-alive, the master reads the data from the passed socket just fine. The failure to read data for the shared port's child-alive appears to be tied to the master sleeping and not immediately responding to the connection from the shared port daemon. Reverting the master's behavior on macOS mostly fixes the problem, but the underlying cause should still be investigated.

title: Ticket #7263: Build RTD with most mature Python bindings available for version
description: Per site policy, any wheel that is uploaded to PyPI must have a unique version string compared to any prior uploaded wheels. That includes wheels that have been deleted. So if we somehow flub a release to PyPI, the only way to correct this is by uploading a post-release version. (For PyPI, this is signified by adding ".postN" to the version string.) This creates a problem when building documentation for Read The Docs, as our configuration for our documentation build is coded to pip install htcondor==${VERSION_STRING}, which will not grab a post-release version (e.g. ${VERSION_STRING}.post1). We can do better by taking advantage of =pip='s ability to do logic with version strings. It's valid, for example, to do this: pip install htcondor>=8.9.3,<8.9.4 This will grab the latest version of the python bindings labeled as part of the 8.9.3 release, even if that includes a post release. I will change our doc build config file to use this logic (>=${CURRENT_VERSION},<${CURRENT_VERSION_MINOR+1}) instead of being coded to look for ${CURRENT_VERSION} and only ${CURRENT_VERSION}.

title: Ticket #3220: Allow different submit limits for grid resources
description: Many groups would like to be able to set different job submission limits (i.e. GRIDMANAGER_MAX_SUBMITTED_JOBS_PER_RESOURCE) for different remote servers. There is code in the gridmanager to allow this, but it's been broken for a long time. We could get it working pretty easily. The revived old syntax works like this: GRIDMANAGER_MAX_SUBMITTED_JOBS_PER_RESOURCE=5,foo.edu,10,bar.org,15 It's a comma-separated list. The first entry is the default limit. title: Ticket #228: glibc opens nscd socket and defers checkpointing until exit()
description: I need a program written that will be tested on RHEL 5 x86, x86_64, and Debian 5.0 x86, x86_64. The machines chosen must have the nscd daemon running and the glibc actively using it to resolve questions like getpwnam(), among other things. You can tell if a machine is configured correctly by seeing of nscd is running with ps -aux, and using this command (adjust to your shell): Linux nmi-0199 > strace whoami |& grep nscd connect(3, {sa_family=AF_FILE, path="/var/run/nscd/socket"...}, 110) = 0 If you notice, a connect is made to the specific socket which represents the connection to the nscd daemon. It is this successful socket connection that I am interested in. The question I specifically want this ticket and the program associated with it to answer is: under what conditions is this socket closed? The reason why it is important to me is because check pointing of a stduniv program is deferred while sockets are open and I have a belief that once glibc connects to that socket it caches it and never closes it until the application is exiting. Currently, we disable the nscd feature in the glibc we compile and distribute with Condor and it is one of the reasons why we have to do this in the first place. So, the program you will write will have a few stages: Stage 0 Call sync() three times. Call getpwnam() on yourself, this should cause a connect to happen. Stage 1 Call sync() once Print out "BEGIN Stage 1" Write a select time loop which waits on the stdout fd, but times out after .5 seconds, if the socket comes back ready, print a period, if it times out, print an X. In both cases, resume the loop. The entire loop should execute for 2 hours (use gettimeofday() to compute how long the loop has been running) Print out "END Stage 1" Stage 2 Call sync() once Print out "BEGIN Stage 2" Write a tight loop which, using gettimeofday() to limit it to 2 hours, that simply adds some numbers together and doesn't print anything out. Print out "END Stage 2" Now, at this point, the two stages called back into glibc via gettimeofday() and technically gives glibc an opportunity to close the socket since we are not using the nscd service during the two previous stages. Whether or not it does is the open question. The next does not provide an opportunity to go back into glibc. Stage 3 Call sync() once Print out "BEGIN Stage 3" Write a tight nested for loop to waste time, hand tweak it until it runs for two hours on your machine. A hint on how to do this is write a different small program to count how long it takes to count to UINT_MAX/2 and then to UINT_MAX and linearly interpolate that to how long you'd have to count to get to two hours. Print out "END Stage 3" Stage 4 Call sync() three times. Call exit(EXIT_SUCCESS) Analysis Once you get this program written and it works like how you expect, this is what you do. Run (adjusting for your shell) strace -ttt -e trace=open,connect,close,sync,exit_group your_prog >& output which will save a long inorder sequence of open,connect,close,sync calls that your program is doing. Once the program finishes, this is the final output which needs to be analyzed for when the socket in question gets closed. Ensure that the connect to /var/run/nscd/socket returns 0, which means your program is actively using the nscd daemon. Perform the analysis by telling me when the /var/run/nscd/socket fd is opened and when it is closed with respect to the stages. You can use the sync() barrier calls to determine what stage you are in.

title: Ticket #1358: Make operations on invalid timers an EXCEPTion
description: TimerManager currently allows attempts to CancelTimer or RemoveTimer an invalid timer id. It will complain "Timer %d not found" to the log, but who really notices. (See /src/condor_daemon_core.V6/timer_manager.cpp ) Generally speaking, attempting to manipulate an invalid timer is a symptom of a more serious bug. It's possible we take advantage of the ability to modify no-longer valid timers, but usually it's suspicious. That it's just a minor warning makes it easier for bugs to hide. #1337 is a serious bug in the kbdd that was hidden for several months, from 7.4.0 through 7.4.2 by this. Proposed: Modify CancelTimer or RemoveTimer to EXCEPT on an invalid timer. This would have caught #1337 almost immediately. This will likely find other bugs that need to be fixed and it might find some places where we rely on this sketchy behavior, which will need to be changed.

title: Ticket #3735: chirp wire protocol incompatible between 7.8.x and 8.0.x
description: Too aggressive removal of unneeded code in the shadow and starter (#3390) resulted in a change to the wire protocol for chirp between 7.9.4 and 7.9.5. This wasn't noticed until we tried to run a mixed 8.0.0 and 7.9.4 pool in the batlab. Because 7.8.x uses the same protocol as 7.9.4, and 8.0.0 uses the same protocol as 7.9.5, this represents an incompatibility between successive stable versions. Because this protocol change shipped in 8.0.0, it is now necessary to fix the problem by detecting the version of the other side of the chirp conversation and either using the old or new protocol based on that information. The command that was actually failing in the batlab was condor_chirp put -mode wac - $file it was failing because the chirp open() call was failing in the starter because it was not expecting a filename prefixed with "remote:" (new protocol) but the shadow was sending the file with that prefix (old protocol). Testing reveals that when the Shadow is 8.0 and the Starter is 7.8, we see the bug. But when the Shadow is 7.8 and the Starter is 8.0 we don't see it. This is because the 8.0 starter calls REMOTE_CONDOR_get_file_info_new to translate a pathname, and gets back "remote:original_path", then it ignores the translated path and uses the original path instead. Because the 8.0 Starter is immune to all changes in the translation algorithm, the bug can be fixed by merely reinstating the code in the Shadow that adds the url prefixes "remote:". This will work for 7.8 starter because it expects the "remote:" prefix, and for the 8.0 starter because it ignores the translation entirely.

I believe that Sinful::addressPointsToMe() is the best place for this code for the following reasons: Anyone adding new calls to Sinful::addressPointsToMe() in the collector may forget to call a special collector-specific function. It is possible to configure share port to default forward to a different daemon. (Others can argue whether this would ever be a good idea.) 2019-Dec-12 14:41:28 by tlmiller: My argument was addressPointsToMe() can't know which daemon is asking if a sinful string without a shared port ID points to itself, but the new version doesn't actually check that -- it checks to see if the default shared port ID is the same as the only shared port ID in the pair of sinfuls we're comparing. I can't conceive of a reason why a daemon would get its own shared port ID wrong, so this should actually just work in all cases. It won't work if the daemon fails to determine its own shared port ID and is passing a sinful without a shared port ID to addressPointsToMe(), but that's true for the existing code. Code Review Change looks good. 2019-Dec-12 14:44:32 by tlmiller: I don't think this needs a release note. title: Ticket #5065: Provide support for immutable job attributes (esp. x509 ones)
description: SUBMIT_REQUIREMENTS provides a powerful tool for sysadmins - jobs must pass a given expression in order to be accepted in the queue. This is great for making sure jobs enter the queue in a certain state - but because of condor_qedit, there's no guarantee they stay in that state. We propose adding a new configuration knobs: IMMUTABLE_JOB_ATTRS a list of attributes provided by the admin that, once they have committed values, cannot be changed. SYSTEM_IMMUTABLE_JOB_ATTRS same as above, but would be hard-coded in the param table by the developers to contain items like ClusterId, ProcId, MyType, etc. PROTECTED_JOB_ATTRS a list of attributes provided by the admin that, once they have committed values, can only be altered by the queue super-user. SYSTEM_PROTECTED_JOB_ATTRS same as above, but would be hard-coded in the param table by the developers. Example use cases: Accounting groups: If SUBMIT_REQUIREMENTS checks the validity of an accounting group (for example, by validating that a given user is indeed a member of a certain unix group), then we shouldn't allow users to change it post-submit. X509 attributes: If we implement #5064, we would automatically set X509/VOMS attributes from cryptographically secure sources (connected socket, delegated proxy). We shouldn't allow these to be changed later.

title: Ticket #4224: DAGMan retry count counter-intuitive
description: The DAGMan retry counter is counter-intuitive (at least to us). It counts the number of times the node is run to "normal completion". That is, the number of times the post script (if present) exits normally (zero or non-zero). Our users have been complaining that if they kill the DAG and resubmit (which sends SIGUSR1 to the DAG), the retry counter is not incremented the next time the job is submitted. This is especially irritating because we create a copy of the stdout per DAGMan retry; since the retry counter is not incremented before the job is submitted, we overwrite the stdout of the previous job run. In other words, the job is run multiple times per retry. I propose we introduce a DAGMan "start count". That is, the number of times the pre-script has been started. So, we will have an ordering of (node start count) <= (job run count) <= (node retry count) Is this behavior a bug or intended?
remarks: 2014-Feb-22 17:43:05 by bbockelm: Shoot, thinking more - we really want to know how many jobs have been submitted, not how many times the pre script has been run. We don't care how many pre-scripts are run ... no logs from those we want to preserve. That might be easier to implement anyway.

title: Ticket #4674: Allow sub-collector queries
description: When working with a collector tree (esp. in the glideinWMS case), we often don't forward Master classads from parent to child due to the lack of memory. If you want to "condor_off" a glidein, you have to write a for-loop to iterate across all the child collectors, find the master ad, and then issue the condor_off. I propose we extend the CollectorList class to first query the pool collector for known child collectors, then issue the query to each returned child collector (in order). The child collectors selected will be controlled by COLLECTOR_QUERY_EXPR; if set to false (default), the parent collector is queried directly. If, for example, this is set to "true", all child collectors and the parent are queried; the parent is queried because it advertises itself. Similarly to how "condor_q -g" works, I propose the following error semantics: if there's at least one child collector that returns successfully, the whole operation is marked as a success. Otherwise, the operation fails.

title: Ticket #1499: increase throughput during upgrade
description: Currently, an upgrade of condor requires either draining or killing all jobs running on a machine. On a multi-slot machine, either choice results in reduced throughput. It would be nice if the old version of condor could drain while the new version of condor takes over running jobs on slots which have finished draining. One potential problem with this idea is what to do about slots with policies that interact with each other. For example, there might be a whole-machine slot that, when busy, disables the other slots. If the whole-machine slot is busy in the old condor, one would not want the new condor to start running jobs. Some possible approaches: Have the new condor use the draining slot ClassAds verbatim from the old condor. Have the new condor read state from the old Condor (e.g. job ClassAds) and go through all the motions of running the jobs. It might launch a dummy starter process or it might stop short of that.

title: Ticket #5570: Add PreCmdEnvironment and PostCmdEnvironment support
description: From the rust ticket: It would be nice to set additional or replacement environment variables for the PreCmd and PostCmd. MATLAB uses a wrapper shell script to set up the correct LD_LIBRARY_PATH for tools compiled with "mcc," and thus using compiled MATLAB as a PreCmd or PostCmd requires transferring both the wrapper and the binary and then executing the wrapper. This environment may not be suitable for the job itself, however, so setting these elements in the submit description's environment is not the best approach. In some cases I've had to work around, the MATLAB environment for very old releases actually prevented HTCondor commands from running due to antiquated MATLAB-supplied libraries. If we had a (Pre|Post)CmdEnvironment attribute, it could set environment variables specific to the PreCmd and PostCmd, such as the required MATLAB Compiler Runtime variables, eliminating the need for the wrapper script while avoiding interference with the job's environment. Default behavior would continue as currently exists, with the job's environment being applied to the PreCmd and PostCmd, but if the Pre or PostCmdEnvironment is defined, it would set the variables specified and override matching variables in the job environment, then return to the original environment when the command is finished.
remarks: When I went to go implement this, it turned out that it already existed in the code. As such, I just updated the manual and am resolving the ticket. Docs will appear in the 8.4.6 and 8.5.4 manual. For reference, just put this this in the submit file: +PreEnv = "one=1;two=2" +PostEnv = "three=3"

title: Ticket #5120: Change outcome of transfer_output_files failure
description: Currently, if user specifies "transfer_output_files" and such files do not exist when the job completes (success or failure) the job goes on hold, without any return value reported in the user log, and without stderr or stdout, which leads to the following: User can't troubleshoot job Users have to release said jobs, or often remove them and resubmit (two steps) if they don't know about "release" options. Users aware of "release" options often resort to a PeriodicRelease, which, if the jobs fail immediately, results in jobs "thrashing" between held > idle > running > held > (so on). We've seen this render the schedd unresponsive in many cases. Instead, can a change be made to: Let jobs fail if the files in "transfer_output_files" did not exist, reporting the return value in the user log (which might still be "0"). Transfer back, anyway, the stderr and stdout, for troubleshooting purposes. Add information in the user log or elsewhere that tells the user the contents of the sandbox when the job exited, but only including the top level - not recursive.) Perhaps add submit file "knobs" to specify which option (current 'hold' method, or remove job from queue and transfer what "can" be transferred, but with an indication of transfer issue in the user log.) Though the jobs will fail instead of going on hold: It is unlikely that the user can "fix" the job while it's in the queue by using condor_qedit, anyway. There are options to retry failed jobs, both with submit file specifications AND with DAGMan features, which would be the better way to handle cases where some jobs fail to produce the desired output (and where a retry might actually result in job success.) Thank you, Lauren (CHTC)
remarks: 2015-Jun-24 14:49:22 by tannenba: A few comments on the above.... Things are not quite as bad as Lauren writes above (unless functionality has regressed). Specifically if a file listed in transfer_output_files does not exist, HTCondor is still supposed to transfer back all the files that do exist (including stderr, stdout, etc) - see #487. set all job classad exit attributes like ExitStatus, ExitSignal, etc, as well as set hold reason codes, allowing policy expressions using on_exit_remove and periodic_release to take the exit status of the job into consideration. See #1587. Also note that many of the items requested in this ticket are a duplicate of items requested in #1587. Since Zach code reviewed and resolved both #1587 and #487, he now gets to deal with this ticket as well :). Perhaps a simple immediate workaround for the "send these files back if they exist, but it isn't a big deal if they dont" behavior is to have zero-length files of the same name in the input file set. That way those files will always exist :). Seems like what we really need is a new event log event, or add more information to an existing file transfer completed log event. Also, the file transfer code should distinguish between 1) "failed to transfer back output file" and 2) "output file did not exist upon job exiting", provide a first-class switch for saying if the job should go on hold for reason 2 (false by default?), and use different hold reason subcodes for these two failures.

title: Ticket #6425: Windows limited to 80% of open socket limit for no good reason.
description: The maximum number of open sockets in any HTCondor daemon is limited to FD_SET_SIZE, which is 1024 on Windows and (effectively) the size of the fd table on Linux. On Linux, daemon_core limits the socket count to 80% of the size of fd table because the table is also use for open files. On Windows, the socket table and the file handle table are separate, so it makes no sense to use only 80% as the socket limit.

title: Ticket #2935: Teach Condor to run as a BOINC-like backfill system
description: A potential UW campus user is interested in using Condor as a BOINC-like system. Perhaps Condor should have better built in support. Such a system should Be robust in the face of firewalls and NATs. CCB can help, but tunneling over HTTP(S) would be even better. We'd need to assume outbound only connections. Internet access may be spotty, so we'll want to download a lot of work when we do connect. We'll need to be able to run for long periods with no connection to the internet. However, we don't want to wait until all of the work is done before sending results, and as some smaller tasks finish we want to top-off our queue of work while we have an internet connection. Work fetch can do this today, but requires writing custom hooks and generally adding complexity. Should be very cautious to stop using CPU and minimize RAM usage very quickly when a user tries using the machine. Doable today with suitable policy. Should detect, as much as possible, situations in which it shouldn't run: low battery and no wall power, overheating. Can do this today, but we'd need to add a bunch of currently non-existent startd cron programs. Highly customizable so a power user can tune the sorts of jobs they accept. Doable today with suitable policy. However, users might want to configure that policy from a centralized web site, which complicates the matchmaking system. Needs to be highly portable, at least across Windows computers. Done. Needs to be extremely simple to set up for common configurations; run a single program and you're done. Doable, just a matter of packaging.

title: Ticket #3277: ENABLE_IPV6 must be set in the main config file
description: Observed behavior: ENABLE_IPV6=TRUE is ignored if placed into a local configuration file. It only works in the global configuration file. Expected behavior: ENABLE_IPV6=TRUE should work if placed into any configuration file, be it the global one, or a local one specified by LOCAL_CONFIG_FILE or LOCAL_CONFIG_DIR. Workaround:: Put ENABLE_IPV6=TRUE in your global configuration file. Why: As the configuration system is bootstrapping it needs to identify the machine's hostname so that LOCAL_CONFIG_FILE=condor_config.$(HOSTNAME) works. This chases into the ipv6_getaddrinfo() (/src/condor_utils/ipv6_addrinfo.cpp ), using a default argument of get_default_hint() (/src/condor_utils/ipv6_addrinfo.cpp ) to identify which family (IPv4/6) to ask for. That calls into _condor_is_ipv6_mode() (/src/condor_utils/condor_ipv6.cpp ) to determine the family. But we haven't yet loaded any local configuration files, just the main one. ENABLE_IPV6 isn't set, it defaults to false, and away we go in IPv4 mode. Future calls into _condor_is_ipv6_mode() use a cached result, so the real value is never noticed. Why did it ever work? Because the caching code in _condor_is_ipv6_mode() was buggy. Commit a5801a023f8390a40536b256af22a724b80a7d45 [33275] fixed the caching. Why not just remove the caching? I'm not confident that it's a deep fix. That Condor briefly spends some time thinking its IPv4, then suddenly IPv6 seems dangerous. For example, if you don't have IPv4 at all, attempts to figure out HOSTNAME may fail. It would become subject to being changed by condor_reconfig. The IPv6 is not currently prepared to change mode mid-run; the behavior would be undefined. Initial thoughts on fixing: calls to ipv6_getaddrinfo can specify the addrinfo hints instead of relying on get_default_hint(). With a suitable addrinfo, you can request both IPv4 and IPv6 addresses (should just be a matter of setting addrinfo::ai_family to 0). The bootstrapping code should do so. If it only needs an IP address briefly, to figure out the HOSTNAME, either one should work. If it actually cares, it may need to deal with the possibility of getting one of each and using both for a while until the configuration system has settled down.

title: Ticket #5209: cannot shutdown condor_shared_port on Windows
description: condor_master is unable to shut condor_shared_port down cleanly. Instead it will wait 10 minutes before killing it. This is generally undesirable and means many tests fail. condor_shared_port's ideal behavior is that a process connects to it, provides a shared port ID ("sock"), and then condor_shared_port hands the file descriptor off to the correct daemon. On Linux the file descriptor is handed through a named pipe. If no shared port ID is provided, the connection is handed off to the condor_collector. This allows a process to find the collector without knowing the shared port ID in advance; it can then learn full Sinful addresses, including the shared port ID, from the collector. On shutdown condor_master sends SIGTERM to the child processes, including condor_shared_port. This works fine on Linux. But on Windows sending a signal is implemented by sending a DaemonCore command. The condor_master sends that command without a shared port ID because condor_shared_port has no ID. condor_shared_port proceeds to send the command to the condor_collector. If the collector is already gone (and it likely is), condor_shared_port eventually times out, the command undelivered. Relatedly, it appears that (based on behavior) that condor_shared_port proxies data to the collector when no shared port ID is present on Windows. We haven't looked into exactly which cases this behavior happens in (does it on Linux? Always on Windows?). (After quick investigation, I can't find logic that would do proxying. But condor_shared_port was definitely logging complaints when a condor_config_val -dump to the collector was interrupted. Something about the pipe being used to hand the information over?) At some point we should overhaul the "signal" delivery system on Windows, but that is a much bigger task. Possible solutions: condor_shared_port already processes at least one command (SHARED_PORT_CONNECT) to take a shared port ID and hand the FD off. Perhaps it should process a few administrative commands directly, maybe just DC_RAISESIGNAL. So long as anyone sending administrative commands intended for the collector has the full Sinful, they'll work find since they have a shared port ID. condor_master almost certainly does. (Question, why doesn't condor_shared_port already handle DC_RAISESIGNAL? Is it avoiding InitDCCommandSocket? Come to think of it, why is DC_RAISESIGNAL set in InitDCCommandSocket and not in dc_main (/src/condor_daemon_core.V6/daemon_core_main.cpp ) like the rest?) condor_shared_port should have a special shared port ID that means "myself" which it should ensure the condor_master has to use.

Possible solutions: condor_shared_port accepts the authentication, and if the following command should go to the collector, re-authenticates to the collector, then hands off the command. Seems likely to be complex. Establish a trusted connection between the master and shared_port daemons. Can we re-use the channel used for child "I'm still Alive" messages? Either implement a one off "treat this as SIGTERM", or allow sending of arbitrary "signals". Add a new command DC_SHUTDOWN_WITH_COOKIE, which is sent without authentication. It has no authentication, but ignores any commands without a correct cookie attached. The cookie was created by the master and passed to the shared_port daemon on startup using some secure channel (we have one, right?). Support WM_CLOSE. TJ's vision for better signal handling. description: When getHostFromAddr() is given a sinful string with an IPv6 address in the supplemental data (stuff after the '?'), it returns the wrong result. For example, for the sinful string <128.142.201.170:51450?addrs=128.142.201.170-51450+[--1]-51450> , it returns 128.142.201.170:51450?addrs=128.142.201.170-51450+[--1 . title: Ticket #6833: Stale autocluster data
description: The autocluster data structures in the schedd often contain stale data. While some of this data is updated frequently on a busy schedd, some of it is never updated. Most of this staleness is harmless to the schedd's proper operation, but it makes the autocluster query results given to clients confusing and much less useful. Some small changes in the schedd could greatly reduce the staleness with minimal performance effects. When one of a job's significant attributes changes, the AutoClusterId attribute is deleted from the job ad, but the job isn't removed from the membership list in the object of that autocluster. When the job is assigned to a new autocluster on a rebuild, its membership in the old autocluster still isn't cleared. Thus, a job can appear to be in multiple autoclusters at the same time. This will persist until the old autocluster has no more jobs and is deleted. Autocluster membership isn't updated when a job leaves the queue, either. When one of a job's significant attributes changes, the PrioRec array isn't marked as dirty. Thus, it will be treated as being in the old autocluster until the PrioRec array is marked as dirty by another trigger and then rebuilt. This includes for matchmaking with the negotiator. Autoclusters are updated (including deletion) when the PrioRec array is marked as dirty (usually by a job entering IDLE status or FindRunnableJob() seeing a non-runnable job in the array) and then rebuilt (when a negotiation session begins or FindRunnableJob() is called). When the schedd has no new jobs entering the queue, this won't happen. A quiet schedd can have autoclusters that persist forever that have no jobs in them. Here are changes that would greatly reduce this stale data: When a job's AutoClusterId attribute is cleared (due to a significant attribute being modified) or a job is removed from the queue, do the following: Remove the job from the autocluster object's membership list. Mark the PrioRec array as dirty. Force a rebuild of the PrioRec array periodically. (this was done for #6834)
remarks: CODE_REVIEW : changes look good. we should keep an eye on whether these changes increase the frequency at which the prio-rec array is rebuilt. There's too many moving parts to know just from looking at the code if this will happen.

title: Ticket #6130: speed up reading a Classad from a socket
description: We can dramatically speed up reading a classad from a socket by removing copies from the parsing code paths, and by pre-parsing literal values and inserting them into the ad without ever invoking the classad parser. A bit more savings can be had by parsing the expressions lazily. A new function, getClassAdEx will be added to classad_oldnew.cpp (where the code to read a classad from a socket currently lives) that can take an argument to enable these speedups, and the code in the collector that handles updates will be changed to use these speedups. With this change, the unparsed values that we put into the classad cache will always be wire form, making it possible to unparse directly from the cache when we want to put a classad on the wire.

title: Ticket #4398: STARTD_CRON should have a way to set slot specific values
description: In configuration files, one can use the configuration STARTD_ATTRS = FOO SLOT1_FOO = 1 SLOT2_FOO = 2 to publish FOO in slot1 & slot2 will a different value in each slot, so the above configuration will result in the following STARD slot ads containing: slot1 = [ FOO = 1 ] slot2 = [ FOO = 2 ] This is complicated by the fact that one can also use the configuration STARTD_SLOT_ATTRS = FOO To request that the value of for each slot be published in each slot, so if you had 2 slots as indicated above. This additional configuration would result in STARTD slot ads containing: slot1 = [ FOO = 1 slot1_FOO = 1 slot2_FOO = 2 ] slot2 = [ FOO = 2 slot1_FOO = 1 slot2_FOO = 2 ] Note that FOO = 1, in slot1 and FOO = 2 in slot2. A hawkeye script can return slot1_FOO = 1 and slot2_FOO = 2 and this will result in both of these attributes in both of the slots. But there is no way for hawkeye (STARTD_CRON) scripts to set different values of FOO in each of the slot. One possible solution would be for the output of hawkeye scripts to be parsed so that an attribute slot1_FOO would be treated as setting FOO only in slot1 rather than in all slots. This could be combined with STARTD_SLOT_ATTRS = FOO to achieve the same output as can be achieved by config statements. Another possible solution would be to extend the hawkeye script to accept multiple ads as return and either use classad nesting syntax or parse the SlotId or SlotName attributes of the returned ads to determine what slots to publish them into.
remarks: 2014-Jun-11 10:01:46 by johnkn: From investigation the current behavior of STARTD_CRON is: attributes are read from stdout one at a time, and accumulated into a temporary classad until the script exits or until it writes a line beginning with '-'. scripts of type WaitForExit can run forever, but they must write line starting with a '-' periodically or they have no effect on the startd ad(s). STARD_CRON can be combined with STARTD_SLOT_ATTRS but there appears to be a delay of one update cycle or so before the STARTD_SLOT_ATTRS propagates slot attrs to other slots. STARTD_CRON_*_SLOTS can be used to set the output slots for a script, so (at least on a machine with only static slots) advertising different values to different slots can be achieved with the current code. Advertising different values to different dynamic slots is impossible to do because currently all dynamic slots share a slot id. 2014-Jun-16 11:06:00 by johnkn: It now seems clear to me that part of the solution to writing different values to different slots should be permitting the STARTD_CRON scripts write multiple ads. This would allow for the possibility of having different merge rules for the different ads. There would then need to be way to designate which ads are merged into which slots. My thought was to look in the STARTD_CRON ad(s) for a SlotId or SlotTypeId or SlotName attribute and use that to direct the merge. Since we don't want to allow a STARTD_CRON script to change these attributes of the slot, there is no ambiguity with using them (if they exist) to control the merge. Todd suggested that we might also look for a new attribute containing a boolean expression that would control which slots the ad merged into. This seems powerful, but I'm inclined to begin by looking for SlotId, SlotTypeId and SlotName since we want to prevent these from merging anyway. 2014-Jun-16 17:17:32 by johnkn: patch [40449] makes it possible to set different values into different slots, but in a different way than originally proposed. Its comprised of two basic changes. a line starting with '-' can now be followed by arguments. the '-' line has always indicated end-of-classad. It can now be followed by a uniqness tag to indicate the 'name' of the ad that should be replaced by the new ad. This name is joined to the name of the STARTD_CRON job to produced a full name for the ad. This allows a single STARTD_CRON script to return multiple ads - by giving each a unique name. And to replace multiple ads - by using the same unique name as a previous invocation. The optional uniqness tag can be followed by an optional keyword update:<bool>, which can be used to override the STARTD_CRON configuration and suppress or force immediate updates. Each ad can return one of 4 possible attributes to control what slots the ad is merged into when the STARTD sends updates to the collector. These attributes are, in order of priority. SlotMergeConstraint Expression The current ad is merged into all slot ads for which this expression is true. The expression is evaluated with the slot ad as the TARGET ad. SlotName String The current ad is merged into all slots whose Name attributes match the value of SlotName up to the length of SlotName Name String - Alternative to SlotName SlotTypeId Integer The current ad is merged into all ads that have the same value for their SlotTypeId attribute. SlotId Integer The current ad is merged into all ads that have the same value for their SlotId attribute. Attributes are checked in the above order. If the attribute exists, the it controls the merge, otherwise the next higher priority attribute is checked. If STARTD_CRON_<tag>_SLOTS configuration is set, then the actual slots published to will be the intersection of configuration and script output. For example - if the STARTD_CRON job returns: Value=1 SlotId=1 -s1 Value=2 SlotId=2 -s2 Value=10 - update:true This script will set Value=10 into all slots except slot1 & slot2. On those slots it will set Value=1 and Value=2 respectively. It will also send updates to the collector immediately 2015-Nov-16 16:12:35 by tannenba: This ticket should never have been resolved, the documentation is useless. I opened a new child ticket (#5403) to deal with the Manual. 2016-Aug-24 11:30:39 by wenger: TJ says there are now meta-knobs for this.

title: Ticket #1933: Free'ing of objects from globus_utils.cpp
description: Hi, I noticed the doc string of x509_proxy_subject_name says the following: /* Return the subject name of a given proxy cert. On error, return NULL. On success, return a pointer to a null-terminated string. IT IS THE CALLER'S RESPONSBILITY TO DE-ALLOCATE THE STIRNG WITH free(). */ However, in the implementation of *get_subject_name from Globus, their docstring says: * @param subject_name * The subject name as an X509_NAME object. This should be freed * using X509_NAME_free when the user is finished with it So, the Condor docstring appears incorrect. It's possible we're also free'ing the resulting subject_name incorrectly. Brian

This should be freed * using free() when the user is finished with it The body of the Globus function also has this: /* ToDo: This logic needs fixing. The subject_name is passed up and is freed by the caller - but it must be freed with OPENSSL_free(), not free() and the caller cant be expected to know that */ So it's a problem in the Globus code. If we're worried about it, I suppose we could have Condor make a copy of the string and use OPENSSL_free() on the one returned by Globus.

title: Ticket #5136: Starter can wait forever when connection to shadow closes
description: With the new job lease keep alive protocol introduced in 8.3.2, the starter needs to start a timer when its connection to the shadow goes away. If the job lease time elapses with a reconnection, then the starter exits in a way that notifies the startd that the lease has expired. Currently, if the connection closes after the job as exited, the starter doesn't start the timer, and so will wait forever for a reconnect attempt. If the shadow/schedd sends a DEACTIVATE_CLAIM or RELEASE_CLAIM to the startd, this isn't a problem. But if they don't, then the startd/starter will wait around forever. This can happen very easily if the startd is using CCB and the CCB server goes down.
remarks: 2015-Jul-07 11:39:36 by bbockelm: One approach I'd like to see is to have the condor_starter send a heartbeat to the startd each time the lease is renewed with the shadow. Having the startd delegate all responsibility to the starter (by simply looking at the starter's exit code) is insufficient. This would help prevent future bugs along these lines. In this case, if the condor_startd knew that the lease updates were not going out, it could have contacted the schedd about the claim and found out that it was no longer valid. 2015-Jul-07 15:08:33 by jfrey: We can consider that for a future release. I think it's too big a change for 8.3.7.

title: Ticket #843: New test: detect excessive CPU usage
description: New test: Is condor excessively using the CPU? This would detect bugs like the one fixed in [16011]. As a first pass, it be easiest to detect if CPU usage as a whole is excessively high, but ideally we would limit it to the set of Condor daemons we spawned. Test 1: Start up the deamons, and give them "a bit" to settle in. Check CPU utilization: it should be negligable. Test 2: Start up a very lightweight run; perhaps a handful of vanilla jobs that just run /bin/sleep. Check CPU utilization: it should be very low. Defining "too much" CPU utilization is an area for consideration. 1-minute load average is probably a good start; an idle Condor pool should generate negligible load. Actual CPU utilization may also be useful; I'm not sure how to measure it, but both Windows and Gnome are happy to offer me a number, so it's measurable.

title: Ticket #3148: Condor checkpointing should setarch automatically
description: Wishlist item for existing standard universe support: Because of address randomization and other changes to Linux, Condor's checkpointing support requires that the executable be run in backward compatibility mode. On the command line this is done like so, replacing x86_64 with i386 for 32-bit systems, and possibly not setting -B (thus allowing > 32 bit addresses) in some undefined circumstances. Presumably when run under Condor, something similar happens. setarch x86_64 -L -B -R ./my-condor-compiled-executable That you need to do this is non-obvious, and the failure is cryptic; the binary will crash when checkpointing without any clue that setarch could fix the problem. For the sake of ease of use, I propose that the condor syscall library should detect if the appropriate backward compatibility options are set. If they are not, it should set them itself, then exec itself. (You need to exec, because the options only take effect at exec time. By the time you're in user code, it's too last.) This will simplify things for users using Condor's checkpointing support outside of Condor, as well as for developers testing.
creator: adesmet

title: Ticket #1175: Good error messages for invalid configuration settings
description: When faced with an invalid configuration setting, Condor usually blunders along with some sort of guess. Exactly how it blunders along varies from setting to setting. This can surprise users. For example condor-admin 20228 discovered that "vm_networking=nat" is silently identical to "vm_networking=false". They spent some time diagnosing the problem. Better behavior would be to either emit a warning to the log, possibly followed by EXCEPTing. EXCEPTing increases the chances that the administrator will notice and fix the bad setting, but if we can't detect the problem until runtime, I expect users will be angry if a daemon runs for several days before needing to consider a setting, then trips over the landmine. A solution might be related to the grand unified param() system (#123, #988). Perhaps, at least for some settings, it could know the range of allowed values. "vm_networking is boolean", "num_cpus is a positive, non-zero integer", etc.

title: Ticket #4377: DNS query while holding event log lock is bad
description: When writing the job execute event to the job event logs, we call gethostbyaddr() to convert the IP address of the executing machine into a hostname. This can be a blocking network operation that can take many seconds to complete. We do this while holding the lock on the event log file. This is a bad combination. On a LIGO submit machine, we've observed gethostbyaddr() take 5 seconds to complete. With hundreds of shadows attempting to write to the same user job log, we saw shadows taking multiple hours to acquire the lock on the file before writing their events. In the meantime, their starters timed out while waiting for responses to their RPCs and aborted job execution. The call to gethostbyaddr() occurs in ExecuteEvent::writeEvent(). Originally, this call was used to report the execute hostname in the Quill log of events. Later, the Quill code was changed so that the upper layer provided the name to record via the ExecuteEvent::setRemoteName() method. But the gethostbyaddr() was kept for a dprintf(). The dprintf() should use the name given in setRemoteName() and the gethostbyaddr() call should be removed.

title: Ticket #6960: shared port on Windows can make damons slow to notice signals
description: When shared port is enabled on Windows, daemons can be slow to notice "signals" that are sent using the DC_RAISESIGNAL command. The problem is that after the command handler for HandleSigCommand updates the daemon core signal table. the daemon core pump goes back into select, and only notices the pending signal in the table after select wakes again - usually after a timeout. For example StartLog fragment 03/19/19 14:39:31.372 (D_ALWAYS) PERF: leaving select 03/19/19 14:39:31.372 (D_ALWAYS) State = TIMED_OUT 03/19/19 14:39:31.372 (D_ALWAYS) max_fd = 756 03/19/19 14:39:31.372 (D_ALWAYS) Selection FD's 03/19/19 14:39:31.372 (D_ALWAYS) Read {756 } = 1 03/19/19 14:39:31.372 (D_ALWAYS) Write {} = 0 03/19/19 14:39:31.372 (D_ALWAYS) Except {} = 0 03/19/19 14:39:31.372 (D_ALWAYS) Timeout = 1.000000 seconds 03/19/19 14:39:31.372 (D_ALWAYS) PERF: entering select. timeout=59 03/19/19 14:39:58.129 (D_ALWAYS) PERF: leaving select 03/19/19 14:39:58.129 (D_ALWAYS) State = FDS_READY 03/19/19 14:39:58.129 (D_ALWAYS) max_fd = 756 03/19/19 14:39:58.129 (D_ALWAYS) Selection FD's 03/19/19 14:39:58.129 (D_ALWAYS) Read {756 } = 1 03/19/19 14:39:58.129 (D_ALWAYS) Write {} = 0 03/19/19 14:39:58.129 (D_ALWAYS) Except {} = 0 03/19/19 14:39:58.129 (D_ALWAYS) Ready FD's 03/19/19 14:39:58.129 (D_ALWAYS) Read {756 } = 1 03/19/19 14:39:58.129 (D_ALWAYS) Write {} = 0 03/19/19 14:39:58.129 (D_ALWAYS) Except {} = 0 03/19/19 14:39:58.129 (D_ALWAYS) Timeout = 59.000000 seconds 03/19/19 14:39:58.129 (D_COMMAND) Calling HandleReq <HandleSigCommand()> (0) for command 60000 (DC_RAISESIGNAL) from ... 03/19/19 14:39:58.129 (D_COMMAND) Return from HandleReq <HandleSigCommand()> ... 03/19/19 14:39:58.129 (D_ALWAYS) PERF: entering select. timeout=32 03/19/19 14:40:30.129 (D_ALWAYS) PERF: leaving select 03/19/19 14:40:30.129 (D_ALWAYS) State = TIMED_OUT 03/19/19 14:40:30.129 (D_ALWAYS) max_fd = 756 03/19/19 14:40:30.129 (D_ALWAYS) Selection FD's 03/19/19 14:40:30.129 (D_ALWAYS) Read {756 } = 1 03/19/19 14:40:30.129 (D_ALWAYS) Write {} = 0 03/19/19 14:40:30.129 (D_ALWAYS) Except {} = 0 03/19/19 14:40:30.129 (D_ALWAYS) Timeout = 32.000000 seconds 03/19/19 14:40:30.130 (D_ALWAYS) Calling Handler <handle_dc_sighup()> for Signal 1 <SIGHUP> 03/19/19 14:40:30.130 (D_ALWAYS) Got SIGHUP. Re-reading config files. 03/19/19 14:40:30.248 (D_ALWAYS) History file rotation is enabled. 03/19/19 14:40:30.248 (D_ALWAYS) Maximum history file size is: 20971520 bytes 03/19/19 14:40:30.248 (D_ALWAYS) Number of rotated history files is: 2 03/19/19 14:40:31.097 (D_ALWAYS) PERF: entering select. timeout=3 Notice that HandleSigCommand is processed at 14:39:58.129, then select is entered and returns ~30 sec later at 14:40:30.129 having timed out. Only then does the pump notice the SIGHUP and does the reconfig. Analysis The problem is that when shared port is enabled, the DC_RAISESIGNAL command might be handled in SharedPortEndpoint::DoListenerAccept which is processed by DoPumpWork on Windows because the socket actually arrives via named pipe on a different thread. DoPumpWork is processed with the timers, after the signal handlers and before select. If DoPumpWork were before the signal handlers, then there would not be this delay. Alternatively, if we forced the select timer to be 0 when the signal table is set, this would also avoid the delay.
remarks: 2019-Mar-20 12:15:44 by tlmiller: Code Review This looks good. There should be no further implications of moving the (Windows-specific) work pump in front of the signal handling, because Windows doesn't actually have signals. (It may be possible for the DC_RAISESIGNAL to be handled during normal socket-handling, depending on the security settings, if the work pump handles security but the command packet is delayed, but that's fine: select() will exit when the command packet arrives and the signal will be handled after pumping work on the next go-around.) 2019-Mar-20 12:16:52 by tlmiller: This might be worth mentioning in the version history (and maybe to fill out a release announcement).

title: Ticket #7672: schedd should not block when asking negotiator to reschedule
description: GregT and ToddT found the following evidence of the schedd blocking: 06/02/20 09:40:52 (pid:2188) (D_ALWAYS) Can't find address for negotiator cm0.cs.wisc.edu 06/02/20 09:40:52 (pid:2188) (D_ALWAYS|D_FAILURE) Failed to send RESCHEDULE to negotiator cm0.cs.wisc.edu: 06/02/20 09:41:52 (pid:2188) (D_ALWAYS) attempt to connect to <128.104.109.26:9618> failed: timed out after 60 seconds. Note that 128.104.109.26 is vultur.ssec.wisc.edu, not cm0.cs.wisc.edu. (description updated to match commentary) Turning the debugging all the way up, this is happening as a result of a blocking lookup of the negotiator in question in its collector. Details of the code are below, but it looks like all collector queries are blocking. The assumption that collector queries are blocking is baked pretty deep into the daemon client (among, presumably, others), and it seems like it would be quite difficult to correct the problem generally (because of language limitations). Instead, it might be easier to avoid the problem and implement a non-blocking variant of Daemon::locate(); it would have to accept a callback. GregT wisely observes that we could minimize the need for these collector queries by caching the results.
