Many years back when I did more profiling this would bubble up into the top uses of the schedd's time. 2020-Jun-03 14:01:45 by tlmiller: Yeah, I just figured that out. :( I'll confirm by twisting the QUERY_TIMEOUT knob, but I'm pretty sure this is the low debug level being deceptive, and the blocking is actually happening in the collector query. 2020-Jun-03 14:07:46 by tlmiller: OK, twisting the knob didn't change the timeout messages to the number I set the knob too, but they did shrink considerably from the 60 second default for QUERY_TIMEOUT, so I'm calling that confirmation. 2020-Jun-03 14:59:26 by tlmiller: // condor_daemon_client/daemon.cpp:1350; _pool is the entry in FLOCK_COLLECTOR_HOSTS // which corresponds to the flocked negotiator we're asking to reschedule. CollectorList * collectors = CollectorList::create(_pool); if (collectors->query (query, ads) != Q_OK) { // This goes to condor_daemon_client/daemon_list.cpp:352 -- result = cQuery.processAds (callback, pv, daemon->addr(), errstack); // which calls condor_utils/condor_query.cpp:248 -- int mytimeout = param_integer ("QUERY_TIMEOUT",60); if (!(sock = my_collector.startCommand(command, Stream::reli_sock, mytimeout, errstack)) || !putClassAd (sock, queryAd) || !sock->end_of_message()) { So I'm guessing it's probably least disruptive to make a nonblocking variant of Daemon::locate() available (one that takes a callback, I guess, to invoke when the locate succeeds, fails, or times out); that seems like the least-painful way to proceed. 2020-Jun-03 15:13:22 by tlmiller: I should explicitly state: as far as I can tell from reviewing the log with higher debug levels set, the reschedule itself is correctly sent non-blocking. 2020-Jun-17 11:56:24 by tlmiller: Miron wants a document with: what blocking calls to a collector does the schedd make? which of those calls are done to a collector to which the schedd is flocking?

title: Ticket #793: Grand unified param() system uses too much RAM
description: The grand unified param() system uses too much RAM, apparently because it strdups items into the heap for reasons that should be investigated. The original idea was the grand unified param code would put the param table in shared static data via the perl script that would generate static code. We need to avoid using heap space because (1) on principle: the table is all just static initialized data and (2) to be practical: if it is implemented as static code, memory usage will be shared across all shadow processes. For 7.4.0, we should simple make the function(s) generated the perl script a no-op since we aren't using it anyway [15724]. For 7.5.x, we should get rid of the (most likely) unneeded heap allocations in the generated code.

title: Ticket #6599: remove the need for most wrapper scripts
description: It is our belief in most cases, the use of job wrapper scripts by users or administrators is an indication that HTCondor is lacking in necessary features. This ticket is an examination of some specific wrapper scripts in use with the 8.6 stable release with analysis of what features should be added to make these scripts unnecessary Wrappers come in 2 forms Administrator defined wrappers (aka USER_JOB_WRAPPER) User defined wrappers - a submit file where the executable is a script that wraps the real job. Administrator defined wrappers On the STARTD, the USER_JOB_WRAPPER configuration knob can be set to provide a wrapper script for all jobs that run on that node. These are undesirable because they don't compose - only one wrapper is allowed for all jobs, so it must handle all forms of wrapping. In this category we have two examples singularity-job-wrapper.sh - a wrapper for singularity jobs used by OSG condor-docker - a wrapper for docker jobs used by Fermi singularity-job-wrapper In pseudo-code this wrapper does the following: if the job has a SingularityImage attribute AND the STARTD supports singularity add "-bind /cvmfs" to singularity args if the slot has GPUs add "-bind <nvidia drivers/libs>" to singularity args set home and pwd for singularity job to /srv exec singularity using SingularityImage and input args else exec the job There is also code to modify environment variables and paths in the arguments [[anonymous: to adjust for the existence of the wrapper script itself?]] recommendation None - this wrapper script does not appear to do anything we cannot do with HTCondor's native Singularity support, but it does enable the use of Singularity jobs on versions of HTCondor that have no native Singularity support. docker-wrapper in pseudo-code the docker wrapper does add arg to set the hostname of the container to a well known, unique value add args to disable swapping add environment variables from FERMIHTC_DOCKER_ENV config variable if the docker job is using a trusted docker image enable --cap--add items from FERMIHTC_DOCKER_CAPABILITIES config variable If pull configured pull the docker image run the docker job with modifed args recommendation add support for --cap-add for trusted docker images add support for STARTD_JOB_TRANSFORMS in order to customize the environment. User defined wrappers We consider the user to have written a wrapper script when the executable statement in the submit file is a script but what the user thinks of as their job is a different executable or script. For instance, most R jobs in CHTC are an R script, with a bash script wrapper. In this sort of job, the wrapper script is really a setup script, preparing the environment for the job itself. We have many examples, but they all boil down to one or more of these basic operations download an executable or runtime unpack a tarball or zip file from file transfer or from step 1 adjust the environment to be correct relative to the current working directory validate the results and report a job failure if validation fails delete extraneous files after the job runs and before output transfer tar/zip the results recommendation add tar/zip packing and unpacking to file transfer add file transfer blacklist make sandbox directory path available to $$() expansion OR add a mechanism to modify the final environment in the starter before launching the job.

title: Ticket #6063: Improve handling of job workflows with different memory requirements.
description: Over the next year, CMS will have an increasingly diverse set of memory requests due to two factors: Increasing use of multicore. Typically, memory usage in a multicore job is M*(#cores) + B. For some workflows, M=200; for others, M=500. Once we set (# cores) = 8, then we have a "swing" of 2.4GB even if B is similar for both workflows. Concurrently running upgrade workflows (for future detector designs) that require significantly more memory than workflows that process the existing detector. For many years, we've been able to assume 2GB RAM / core; in 2017, we'll have workflows ranging from .6GB to 4GB / core. Currently, we try to submit workflows with identical memory requests regardless of the actual workflow's need. As an example, I attach a PNG that is a histogram of actual memory usage for jobs who request 5.9GB. I'd like to get to the point where we could, in a scalable manner, actually set the the workflow's needed memory without doing 2GB of quantization. Why? Say we have: One 8-core p-slot with 17GB RAM. Assume all jobs are in the same schedd. All jobs are from the same submitter but at different priorities. An infinite number of "backfill" jobs that require 600MB RAM; 8 are currently running on our p-slot. An infinite number of "medium prio" jobs that require 2GB RAM. One "high prio" job that requires 3GB RAM. Goal: Run the 'high prio' job as soon as possible. Currently, in order to avoid creating work for the negotiator, we set the claim worklife to be relatively long (24hrs?). To avoid massive priority inversion, we round up the RequestMemory of the backfill jobs to 2GB; that way, the schedd will at least switch to the medium prio job after a backfill job finishes. We do not round everything to 3GB because then we would not utilize the available cores. However, this means each d-slot is too small for the high prio job. One possible mechanism to help the backfill job run is p-slot claiming (willing to consider other mechanisms in this ticket). Then, it would be safe to submit the backfill jobs with RequestMemory=600 because they won't starve medium prio jobs. Further, the schedd has sufficient resources claimed to start the high prio job once a backfill job finishes.
attachments: CMS-Memory-Histogram.png 15998 bytes added by bbockelm on 2016-Dec-20 17:43:37 UTC. Histogram of used memory for all jobs submitted with RequestMemory=5900. You can clearly see peaks around 2GB and 3GB, but almost no usage around the requested 5.9GB. CMS-Memory-2300-Histogram.png 23805 bytes added by bbockelm on 2016-Dec-20 17:53:16 UTC. Histogram of actual memory usage from jobs with RequestMemory=2300 run in the last 30 days. Not the peak is around 600MB; as current quantization rounds this to 2500MB, that means we are over-requesting by about 4x.

Ticket #6433: Condor jobs stuck with spurious OOM
description: The thread beginning here (list membership/auth req'd): http://lists.aei.mpg.de/cgi-bin/mailman/private/condorligo/2017-September/005011.html outlines cgroups issues that Carsten has had since upgrading from 8.6.3 to 8.6.5. He cannot entirely rule out that the upgrade is unrelated but this change was introduced in 8.6.4: https://htcondor-wiki.cs.wisc.edu/index.cgi/tktview?tn=6294 There appear to be 2 issues: Jobs can get stuck in D state when swapaccount is enabled in the kernel and swap is disabled. (this is an oversimplification of the thread, please read it) Take a system configured with... 64403MB of RAM and 19530MB of swap (using powers of 2, some RAM lost to BIOS) swapaccount=1 enabled in the kernel Condor configured for soft limits and not to book-keep for swap BASE_CGROUP = htcondor CGROUP_MEMORY_LIMIT_POLICY = soft slot_type_1 = swap=0 slot_type_1_partitionable = True num_slots_type_1 = 1 Outside of condor I set the parent cgroup limits # enable RAM limit based upon ratio of 2000MB per core CONDOR_MEMORY_LIMIT_RAM=$((`nproc`*2000)) CONDOR_MEMORY_LIMIT_SWAP=0 CONDOR_MEMORY_LIMIT_SWAP_RAM=$((CONDOR_MEMORY_LIMIT_RAM+CONDOR_MEMORY_LIMIT_SWAP)) # create htcondor cgroup and ensure that subgroups inherit memory limits /usr/bin/cgcreate -g blkio,cpu,cpuacct,freezer,memory:htcondor -a root:root -t root:root /usr/bin/cgset -r cpu.shares=1000 htcondor /usr/bin/cgset -r memory.use_hierarchy=1 htcondor /usr/bin/cgset -r memory.limit_in_bytes=${CONDOR_MEMORY_LIMIT_RAM}M htcondor /usr/bin/cgset -r memory.memsw.limit_in_bytes=${CONDOR_MEMORY_LIMIT_SWAP_RAM}M htcondor /usr/bin/cgset -r memory.swappiness=1 htcondor ... we see these cgroups values for a slot for a job that requested 2GB of memory: ==> memory.limit_in_bytes <== ## this is the cgroups hard limit on RAM (unset because I use soft limits) 87391088640 ==> memory.memsw.limit_in_bytes <== ## this is the cgroups hard limit on combined RAM and swap (no corresponding soft limit) 87391092736 ==> memory.soft_limit_in_bytes <== ## this is the cgroups soft limit on RAM 2147483648 The problem here is that memory.memsw.limit_in_bytes has been set to a value that is either exactly or very nearly all of RAM and swap on the system. And, of course, there has been no hard limit placed either (except via the parent cgroup). The upshot is that on a system with no other jobs this job would be allowed to consume all of RAM and swap. My outside-of-Condor magic prevents it from consuming combined RAM+SWAP than there is RAM, but it doesn't prevent swapping. I read what Carsten is saying to mean that memory.memsw.limit_in_bytes is being set to this (very large) value even when he has hard limits configured. This is definitely not right. I would further argue that the hard limits you've set include swap when I've assigned none to the slot. So you're not really doing the right thing for soft limits either. For soft limits, I think you'd be better off (for every job) setting memory.limit_in_bytes=MEMORY and memory.memsw.limit_in_bytes=MEMORY+SWAP_FOR_SLOT. Or, instead of MEMORY, something like N*RequestMemory.

title: Ticket #6576: Remove code that adds/removes TARGET. scoping in ClassAd expressions
description: This code was added in the initial transition from old to new ClassAds. At the time, during match evaluation, references to attributes in the peer ad had to have a TARGET scope prefix in new ClassAds (but didn't in old ClassAds). This code was an attempt to hide this change in evaluation semantics from users. It was prone to a lot of problems, so we ultimately added a hack in the new ClassAds library to allow the evaluation semantics of old ClassAds. We haven't tried to make users change their expressions to follow the new ClassAds semantics, so this code is just dead weight. In the one place where this code is in actual use (the EvalBool() that takes an unparsed expression string), none of the callers need the removal of TARGET scope prefixes.

title: Ticket #2866: Named instance settings are not overriding global settings
description: I've run in to a weird situation running multiple schedds on one machine using the more modern named daemon configuration syntax. The following settings are defined by their default values: SPOOL = $(LOCAL_DIR)/spool SCHEDD_ADDRESS_FILE = $(SPOOL)/.schedd_address SCHEDD_DAEMON_AD_FILE = $(SPOOL)/.schedd_classad I started out with the following definition for a named schedd instance: SCHEDD1 = $(SCHEDD) SCHEDD1_ARGS = -f -local-name Q1 SCHEDD1_LOG = $(LOG)/ScheddLog.1 SCHEDD1_SPOOL = $(SPOOL)/1 SCHEDD.Q1.SCHEDD_NAME = Q1@$(HOSTNAME) SCHEDD.Q1.SPOOL = $(SCHEDD1_SPOOL) SCHEDD.Q1.SCHEDD_LOG = $(SCHEDD1_LOG) This kind of worked. The spool directory for the instance was created and the scheduler was using it as expected. But the .schedd_address and .schedd_classad file for the scheduler were showing up in the spool/ directory instead of the spool/1 directory where they were expected. This was causing errors in the log file on shut down when the schedds on the machine were >1 because of collisions and races to delete these files from the multiple schedulers. I had to override SCHEDD_ADDRESS_FILE and SCHEDD_DAEMON_AD_FILE explicitly for each named scheduler on the machine to get things to work: SCHEDD.Q1.SCHEDD_ADDRESS_FILE = $(SCHEDD1_SPOOL)/.schedd_address SCHEDD.Q1.SCHEDD_DAEMON_AD_FILE = $(SCHEDD1_SPOOL)/.schedd_classad I was fairly certain this wasn't required in previous versions of Condor though I'd have to go back to make sure now. Should the SCHEDD.<name>.SPOOL setting not have overridden the global value for each of the named instances here? It seems to be an error that the global SPOOL value was used for these settings and not the per-named-instance values.

title: Ticket #6825: Enable condor_ssh_to_job into a singularity container
description: When a job is running inside singularity, condor_ssh_to_job works, but leaves the user's shell outside the container, which is less than optimal. We can put the shell inside the container in the same way we do for docker universe -- by having the sshd outside the container, as we do for vanilla universe, and implementing a special command to enter the container. Unfortunately, singularity doesn't have the equivalent of docker exec. We can simulate this, though with a combination of nsenter and chroot. This requires root, so when singularity is enabled, and the starter has root, we'll drop a unix domain socket in the sandbox dir. When a connection is made to this sock, the client will pass stdin, stdout and stderr to the starter, which well then fork and exec nsenter, passing chroot as the command to nsenter. This allows the resulting shell under the chroot to run inside the singularity container.

title: Ticket #7367: Jobs not getting OOM killed when out of memory
description: When cgroups are enabled in the vanilla universe, the starter subscribed to per-cgroup OOM killer notification. When the OOM killer fires, it can be because 1 of 2 reasons: 1) Processes in this cgroup are using more memory than their limit. 2) Processes in this cgroup are below their memory limit, but processes outside cgroup limits (usually everything on the system that isn't a condor job. A while back, we decided to not kill a job in case #2, and continue running, to allow the system to choose something else to kill. To make this decision, we compare the amount of memory used by the processes in the cgroup vs the limit. However, there's a bug in our implementation. Our code to measure the amount of memory used simply totals rss + total_mapped_file. The OOM limit is based on all used pages, including various kernel structures. When we first implemented this, we hacked around this by coding a 10% buffer. This buffer was removed in ticket #6925. Since this commit, CHTC gets jobs stuck, repeatedly hitting the OOM killer, but not putting them on hold. In the short term, I'm going to restore the 10% buffer, and in the long term, give condor the ability to read the total amount of memory a cgroup is using, as viewed by the OOM limit.

title: Ticket #2165: Rescue DAGs should not be a complete DAG file?
description: In today's discussion with the botany people, one of the things we talked about is why they don't use rescue DAGs more. It turns out that at least one reason is that when they fix things up after a failure, they often want to make slight changes to the DAG file itself (renaming the DAG file of a subdag external, for example). But you can't really do this in a clean way, because if you edit the original DAG file, the change won't take effect when the rescue DAG is run; and, of course, if you edit the rescue DAG, you lose the change if the original DAG is re-run from scratch. So I think the solution to this is that the rescue DAG file should no longer be an actual DAG file; rather, it should just be a list of which nodes are marked as done. So then, when you run a rescue DAG, the original DAG file would be parsed, and then the appropriate (latest) rescue DAG file would be read, and the nodes would be marked as done appropriately. Note that if we do this, it would probably mean eliminating the -oldrescue option that we currently support.

title: Ticket #3959: Implement Pegasus/DAGMan/Condor integration testing
description: This is just kind of a reminder that we should deal with this issue -- there are lots of things to resolve before we can actually do it. One big issue, clearly, is whether the testing should happen at the Pegasus end or the Condor end. I think the Pegasus end is more logical, but it sounds like that's not likely to happen. Another thing is, we need to do a bunch of cross-version testing; for example, we should test the latest released Pegasus with the tip of the development and stable branches, to make sure we don't make changes that will end up breaking Pegasus. Probably we should also test the tip of Pegasus development against some version of Condor. Right now we don't have any testing like this, so if we introduce some incompatibility, we usually find out about it from our users...

However, I have one job which has been evicted twice so far and each time the data did not get transferred back to spool. I am currently trying to catch this behavior live in order to collect some log information. Maybe more information on this matter: I see ShadowLog output such as 03/12/11 15:09:12 (2429403.0) (1894): Failed to remove /var/condor/spool/9403/0/ cluster2429403.proc0.subproc0.swap: Permission denied (errno 13) ... 03/12/11 15:09:17 (2408019.0) (20653): Directory::setOwnerPriv() -- failed to fi nd owner of /var/condor/spool/8019/0/cluster2408019.proc0.subproc0 03/12/11 15:09:17 (2408019.0) (20653): Directory::Rewind(): failed to find owner of "/var/condor/spool/8019/0/cluster2408019.proc0.subproc0" Looking into recent code changes (warning squashing, etc) I see various initializations with priv_state saved_priv=PRIV_UNKNOWN; However, the only code path that ever leads to "failed to find owner" is Directory::getIds() returning false. title: Ticket #951: DaemonCore signal handlers should return void not int
description: DaemonCore's Signal code makes callbacks into function pointers or member function pointers. These functions return int. However, the Signal code doesn't care and ignores the return value. See /src/condor_daemon_core.V6/daemon_core.cpp roughly line 2940 in DaemonCore::Driver(). This is confusing, as a developer might think the return value has some significance. Fix: the typedefs SignalHandler and SignalHandlercpp (condor_daemon_core.h) should return void, not int. functions passed into DaemonCore::Register_Signal should return void, not int. function pointers passed into DaemonCore::Register_Signal should not be cast; either they match and are correct, or don't match. This change should not be user visible in any way, and thus does not need a version history entry.

title: Ticket #7449: Improve token revocation/blacklisting capabilities
description: There are two mechanisms currently for removing authorization from tokens: you can remove the signing key (which invalidates all tokens signed with that key) or set DENY_* to remove authorization from the mapped identity. Neither are particularly great. For example, suppose I issue a token for all users at my site in order to enable remote submission. What should I do if a user contacts me saying they lost their token? If all user tokens were signed with the same password, I can remove that password and disable all remote submits to my site. I can permanently disable access to HTCondor for that user by adjusting the configuration. Given each token looks a bit like a ClassAd - and we have a rich expression language for matching ClassAds, I propose: Allow the admin to set an configuration parameter, TOKEN_BLACKLIST. Once authenticated, the token is converted to a ClassAd. The TOKEN_BLACKLIST is converted to a ClassAd expression and evaluated in the context of the "token ad". Any token matching this blacklist will be rejected.

title: Ticket #4265: CKPT_SERVER_HOST=127.0.0.1 doesn't work
description: Greg asked if there was a ticket for this and there wasn't, so here it is. Background: in order to take advantage of a fast distributed filesystem (Lustre) on Stampede which promises ~100GB/s aggregate performance, we want to run a checkpoint server on every compute node, all of which write checkpoints "locally" to a common directory on Lustre. Since individual compute nodes may come and go from our Condor pool, we cannot use the LAN IP address of the compute node because any given IP may be gone when we need to restore. However, localhost will always work. We know the many-ckpt-servers-writing-to-the-same-directory part of this works (we've tested it), but the if we set CKPT_SERVER_HOST=127.0.0.1, Condor fails to store or restore checkpoints. Any non-loopback IP address works, leading us to believe that there is some kind of inappropriate special-case in the code for localhost. This is urgent as we are unable to scale individual checkpoint servers to support more than ~30 simultaneous checkpoints[*], and would like to support many 100's or 1000's. [*] The math: ~3GB ckpt per job + ~150MB/s local disk throughput on the checkpoint server + 10min timeout == >30 simultaneous checkpointers causes all checkpointers to timeout before completion. With Luste we should be able to support >10k simultaneous checkpointers.

title: Ticket #1437: Make submit file option for equivalent of -disable
description: condor_submit has an option called -disable, which disables checks for files. There is is an equivalent option in the configuration file called SUBMIT_SKIP_FILECHECKS. I think that the submit file should have an option for this. That is, you should be able to put something like: skip_filechecks = True in the submit file. There are two reasons for this: 1) When you need a DAG where some jobs need to disable file checks, there is no easy way to pass "-disable" via condor_submit_dag or the DAG description file. 2) The configuration option SUBMIT_SKIP_FILECHECKS applies to all jobs. If you argue that it can be set in the environment per-job, I would argue that's both ugly, and it's hard to make it apply to some jobs in a DAG but not others. There is someone at Argonne's APS that wants this feature (Claude Saunders), so there is a real customer. For the moment he can use workarounds, but they're much uglier. Thanks!

title: Ticket #4635: The CMS IPv6 Requirements and Problems
description: Todd Miller and Alan De Smet discussed CERN's coming IPv4 purge. CMS/CERN limitations CMS will run a single glide-in pool including external worker nodes and CMS's own internal worker nodes. All execute nodes will be glided-in; no nodes will report directly. CMS will run two collector machines at CERN in a HAD configuration. Each collector machine hosts a collector tree for scaling reasons. The collector machines will have globally routable IPv4 and IPv6 addresses. CERN's firewall will allow both inbound and outbound connections to port 9618 for the collector machines. These nodes will use shared_port. CMS's schedds at CERN will have globally routable IPv4 and IPv6 addresses. CERN's firewall will allow both inbound and outbound connections to port 9618 for the collector machines. These nodes will use shared_port. CERN's internal worker nodes will have a CERN-routable IPv4 address with no external connectivity, and a public, globally-routable IPv6 address. The firewall will allow outbound connections for the startds. Inbound connections will be blocked; CCB can be used to traverse this firewall. There may be schedd nodes external to CERN. They must be dual-protocol with globally routable IPv4 and IPv6 addresses. A single protocol schedd is not welcome. There may be glided-in startds external to CERN. They may have an IPv4 address, an IPv6 address, or both. GlideinWMS does not have the ability to detect IP (v4 or v6) addresses and change the configuration file accordingly. Hence, we need the same config to work for the whole site - worker nodes may have: Local IPv6, global IPv4 Global IPv6, local IPv4 No IPv6, global IPv4 We believe that, in all cases, the worker nodes will have an IPv4 address. It just might not be globally routable. Goals All schedds (CERN internal and external) should be able to run jobs on all startds (CERN internal and external). We're relying on schedds all being dual-protocol, and thus able to connect to a single-protocol startd. CERN internal schedd to CERN internal startd: Should Just Work, using globally routeable IPv6 addresses at all steps. CERN internal schedd to external startd: Should Just Work, using globally routeable IPv4 or IPv6 addresses at all steps, whichever protocol the startd supports. CERN external schedd to internal startd: Works with CCB, using globally routeable IPv6 addresses at all steps. CCB will allow the schedd to make connections to the firewalled startd. CERN external schedd to external startd: Should Just Work, using globally routeable IPv4 or IPv6 addresses at all steps, whichever protocol the startd supports. Potential problems / Work to be done An external submit node with a globally-routable IPv6 address would run jobs on a CERN worker node in the following manner. This is the most complicated connection, as it requires CCB. Sub-bullets indicate potential problems. The worker node registers at its CCB using IPv6. We propose that the worker node chooses to use IPv6 because it knows that its only globally-routable address is IPv6. (More generally, the worker node sorts its addresses and uses the protocol of the one we rank most highly.) How to identify the most highly ranked address? We already try to figure out a best option that we store in local_ipaddr in ipv6_hostname.cpp; that may work. Currently no function directly exposes it. On the down side, the ultimate goal is to eliminate it. Does CCB do IPv6 at all? If the CCB is specified as a hostname, we need to deal with wacky DNS issues. Current code may not be able to code with multiple addresses being returned, may not be able to ever return an IPv6 address, and certainly won't be able to cope with only getting IPv4 addresses when an IPv6 address was desired. The broker (CCB) returns its existing IPv6 port and address. The worker node includes that in its own Sinful string that is advertised. (Proposal: the broker (CCB) returns the socket with same protocol as the request.) No, really, the broker... quit laughing! The submit node contacts the broker on IPv6. We don't need to worry about DNS resolution or choosing a protocol, because we only have the one. If the schedd is forwarding its own address, make sure it either chooses a protocol-appropriate one or that its choice is rewritten by the existing ConvertDefaultIPToSocketIP function. The broker directs the worker node over their existing IPv6 connection to make an outbound IPv6 connection to the external submit node. This really should already work. The submit node sends the worker node three(?) address/port pairs: one for file transfer, one for chirp, and one for the shadow? All need to be IPv6. Proposal: more address rewriting. The existing connection is going to be IPv6. This should already work once we've gotten mixed-mode flocking working. The collector contains a mixture of IPv4 and IPv6 ads. Because all schedds are dual-protocol, it's okay. No intelligent matchmaking based on protocol is necessary. #4494: IPv6: mixed-mode submit node (schedd/shadow) #4715 Security #4714 CCB #4712 Shared port

title: Ticket #1122: Add methods for adding TARGET scope in expressions based on ad type
description: The existing methods to add TARGET scoping to expressions in the new ClassAd compatibility layer are aggressive, adding a 'Target.' scope for any attribute reference that doesn't appear in a provided list. This list is usually all attributes currently in the expression's ad. There are places where this won't work very well, because the ad can change after we modify the expression, or the full ad isn't available when we modify the expression. We can define a new, less-aggressive set of methods that only modify attribute references that appear in a given list. We can then define lists of attributes known to occur in job and machine ads. Anytime a daemon or tool receives an expression from an external source (either a user or a potentially older Condor binary), it can call one of these methods to modify the expression as appropriate. The lists of job and machine attributes can be built from the following: Attributes known to be added to these ads by Condor SUBMIT_EXPRS for job attributes STARTD_ATTRS for machine attributes STARTD_JOB_EXPRS for machine attributes STARTD_SLOT_ATTRS for machine attributes NEGOTIATOR_MATCH_EXPRS for job attributes A pair of new config params to allow admins to add additional attributes We will need some form of pattern matching for some of the attribute entries (e.g. slot attrs). StringList's wildcard matching should be sufficient. Milestones Define function signatures [DONE] Write expression modification code [DONE] Write code to create lists of job and machine attributes

title: Ticket #1088: NeverCreateJobSandbox is wonky in Condor-C
description: NeverCreateJobSandbox introduces a subtle Condor-C issue. Basically, the NeverCreateJobSandbox attribute gets set at submit time and then Condor-C copies this attribute into the remote job ad. The value of NeverCreateJobSandbox may be inconsistent with the value of remote_ShouldTransferFiles used in the Condor-C submission. This is not a terrible bug, because I don't think it hits in the normal Condor-C usage case where the original job and the remote job both use file transfer. (But sorry I didn't think of this when we discussed this method of doing things, Will!) How to reproduce: universe = grid grid_resource = condor FULL_HOSTNAME COLLECTOR_HOST executable = /bin/date output = simple.out error = simple.err log = simple.log remote_universe = vanilla +remote_requirements = True +remote_requirements = True +remote_ShouldTransferFiles = "YES" +remote_WhenToTransferOutput = "ON_EXIT" queue The starter fails with the following message: FileTransfer: DownloadFiles called on server side This illustrates two problems: The starter and the shadow do not use the same logic to determine whether file transfer should happen. (Seems like this should be shared code in a static method of the file transfer object.) Specifically, JICShadow::initFileTransfer does not pay attention to NeverCreateJobSandbox. Either or both of the following should be done: A) the starter should use the same logic as the shadow to decide whether to do file transfer B) the shadow should set ShouldTransferFiles="NO" if it is not consistent with NeverCreateJobSandbox. Condor-C should be smart about NeverCreateJobSandbox when submitting the remote job (same logic as condor_submit). Or this logic should be moved into the schedd.
remarks: 2010-Nov-23 11:25:29 by bbockelm: Ouch - just got hit by this one. I would note that the "how to reproduce" is basically the same job as the example in the manual. If this can't be fixed quickly, can we change the manual so the example is functional? 2010-Nov-24 17:59:14 by danb: The solution I am trying is to get rid of NeverCreateJobSandbox. In the file transfer object, rather than always creating the spool directory, it will only created when it is needed. The schedd still creates/chowns the sandbox for spooled jobs and for jobs that specify JobRequiresSandbox. For backward compatibility, it also does this for all parallel universe jobs.

title: Ticket #5531: Unifiy submit files for docker and vanilla universe
description: Currently, the semantics of the job executable for docker and vanilla universe are a bit different. In vanilla universe, if the executable is transferred to the scratch directory we notice that, and prepend the scratch directory to the basename of the command. In docker universe, we just try to run the command verbatim. This makes it difficult to switch between docker and vanilla universe by just changing the condor universe.

title: Ticket #1821: Add support for EC2 REST interface to grid universe
description: Condor speaks the EC2 SOAP interface under the grid universe type 'amazon'. A lot of cloud services speak the EC2 REST interface, but not the SOAP interface. Thus, Condor cannot submit jobs to them. Adding EC2 REST support to Condor should be pretty simple, reusing the SOAP-based code where-ever possible. Much of the existing amazon_gahp should be reusable. We would rip out the gsoap layer and replace it with something that talks simple HTTP. That could be gsoap's http layer or libcurl or something else, as deemed appropriate. If we want to replace the SOAP support for REST support, no other parts of Condor would have to change. If we want to continue handling SOAP requests, some changes would be required in condor_submit and condor_gridmanager. References http://docs.amazonwebservices.com/AWSEC2/latest/APIReference/ Describes all the commands and their attributes, with examples. http://docs.amazonwebservices.com/AWSEC2/latest/DeveloperGuide/ Section Making API Request > Making Query Requests describes how to speak the REST interface.

We could use the same attribute names but tell users to use the other credentials. That can be confusing, though. I'm really tempted to introduce a new grid-type of 'ec2' and deprecate 'amazon'. 2011-Jan-11 14:35:09 by tlmiller: Current status: All AMAZON_VM_* GAHP commands (START, STOP, STATUS, STATUS_ALL, RUNNING_KEYPAIR, CREATE_KEYPAIR, DESTROY_KEYPAIR, and KEYPAIR_NAMES) have been implemented using the Query API. These commands have been tested against Amazon's EC2, at the level of the GAHP's stdio interface. Build changes: I added one library (cURL) to those required (although I haven't removed the now-superflous gSOAP or Kerberos). I used PCRE (which could be coded around), expat, and OpenSSL, but these did not require new linking. I made additional use of standard Condor libraries/functions (condor_base64.h and Regex.h). I have not eliminated gsoap_commands.cpp, although it's unused by the Query API. (Trying to avoid mucking about too much with cmake.) Code changes: I eliminated the contents of gsoap_commands.cpp, since I wouldn't be using it, and didn't want to keep updating it to match the amazonCommands.h header, to which I made moderate changes. The layout is broadly similar, although I implement the core of the Query API functionality in AmazonRequest::SendRequest(), as opposed to handing the job off to another source file. The key implication here is that I used a common std::map< std::string, std::string > in AmazonRequest instead of explicit variables in the subclasses for the different parameters. While this is obviously less efficient (although the Query API does require that parameters be sorted by name), it allows AmazonRequest::SendRequest() to be completely generic in a natural and simple way. I made a small tweak to the class heirarchy, as well (AmazonVMStatus now inherits from AmazonVMStatusAll). I replaced the StringList in AmazonStatusResult with a std::vector< std::string > > because StringList had some problem with its assignment function. amazonCommands.cpp has been (almost; I haven't purged the #include list) totally replaced by the Query API implementation. I erred on the side of simplicity in the implementation; it undoubtedly makes too many copies of various bits and pieces. However, I'm reasonably confident that it doesn't leak memory. title: Ticket #5161: Serialize concurrent collector updates
description: When a "condor_reconfig -schedd" is done, current security sessions are flushed from the schedd and count_jobs is invoked. It appears this is a poor combination. If I'm reading our pstack correctly, this fires off a bunch of non-blocking updates to the collector. Since there's no established session, many of these will start a new security handshake before the first one creates a new session. This has turned out badly for CMS as our largest schedds have 400 submitters and we maintain two HA collectors (so, ~800 updates). The resulting effect is our schedds block for a few minutes (all the callbacks appear to fire at once), especially as the client-side of GSI auth is blocking.
remarks: 2015-Jul-20 21:49:50 by bbockelm: Assigning to Jaime for review. Note the change in behavior for UDP updates (one per DC cycle instead of all in the same DC cycle). Since we are changing the default updates to TCP, I'm not sure if we care deeply here. I think it's possible to get the prior behavior if desired. 2015-Jul-27 13:51:47 by jfrey: Code Review As noted in the code, if there's a cached TCP socket, then it is used to send all pending updates, including ones that request UDP. Assuming that and the other behavior changes described in the ticket are acceptable, the patch looks good to me. 2015-Jul-28 14:28:34 by bbockelm: Per discussion with Jaime, assigning to another set of eyes to think about potential pitfalls of this approach. 2015-Aug-06 16:55:38 by tannenba: Code Review Looks good, thanks for the patch!!!! The shortcomings mentioned above do not concern me, and the benefits are great. Would like a few more comments in the code, I suppose I could add those. title: Ticket #6464: Reduce frequency of DAGMan updates to the schedd
description: DAGMan currently updates the schedd every time its internal metrics change (number of jobs, number of submits, number of jobs completed, etc.) In a rapidly evolving DAG, this means an update will happen every submit cycle (5 seconds). title: Ticket #2974: Support Eucalyptus 3.x in EC2 GAHP
description: Eucalyptus 3.x does not recognize the InstanceInitiatedShutdownBehavior parameter in RunInstances, and refuses to start the instance. This parameter is required by EBS-backed instances to conform to Condor's semantics (until the Grid universe gains a stopped/suspended state), but does not apply to S3-backed instances. After discussion with Jaime, the plan is to add a parameter to EC2_VM_START that determines whether or not the IISB parameter is sent. The grid manager can determine this from ATTR_EC2_EBS_VOLUMES in the job ad, which it already stores in each EC2Job as m_ebs_volumes; the changed call should occur at ec2job.cpp, line 529.
remarks: 2012-May-25 11:07:00 by tstclair: The logic does not seem correct, the lack of ebs_vol's causes InstanceInitiatedShutdownBehavior to not be set. This will break ec2. Use case of breakage, and ebs backed image starts up with no ebs volume attached. Shutdown will cause a "stop" not terminate which the customer will be billed for. 2012-Jun-08 16:42:32 by tlmiller: That is, a given AMI is backed by EBS or not: it isn't up to the client to decide, so we can't tell based on anything in the job whether or not a given instance (image) is. We can either require a specific per-job attribute -- for backwards-compability, flagging when /not/ to set IISB -- which is ugly; we can add another URL type (https, x509, eucalyptus), which is also ugly; or we could ask (via DescribeImages), if the AMI in question uses EBS, which would be cleaner, but adds another round-trip. 2012-Jun-14 18:16:53 by tlmiller: Decided to go with ugly option number 2, because it's a very small change. 2012-Jul-02 13:08:57 by tstclair: option 2 looks ok

description: For full details see: https://bugzilla.redhat.com/show_bug.cgi?id=1000106
remarks: 2013-Oct-25 15:44:52 by gthain: Note that a trunk build seems to work fine on f19, as does the rhel6 tarball, all running as root and with USE_CLONE_TO_CREATE_PROCESSES=true 2013-Oct-25 15:54:52 by tannenba: Given Greg's remark above, sounds like the problem is specific (somehow) to how the Fedora 19 build or packaging takes place.... 2013-Nov-18 15:47:41 by johnkn: when the ProcFamilyClient attempts to contact the PROCD. the UNIX NamedPipeReader code allocates a fd_set on the stack, but the SCHEDD can have more fd's than the standard allocation. if the named pipe fd used to communicate with the procd is > sizeof(fd_set), then NamedPipeReader::read_data will trash the stack and the caller will very likely fault on return. We saw EPB getting set to either 0, or a value with only 1 bit set. This will cause either a NULL deref, or in rare cases a SIGBUS. When the ProcFamily code is called from within clone, it's possibly to trash the clone stack so hard the the main SCHEDD thread's stack is also overwritten with 0's. We have seen the IP of the main schedd thread set to 0, which can will cause the SCHEDD to hang rather than exit. The clone thread will only call the ProcFamily code in the SCHEDD when starting a local universe job. 2013-Nov-20 11:43:05 by tim: This will be fixed under #4088 2013-Nov-26 11:12:43 by gthain: #4008 doesn't solve this problem. I can reproduce this now on my F19 laptop, but only when building with -O2. 2013-Dec-04 17:19:35 by gthain: The problem is that we we call clone(2), we need to pass a stack for the clone'd thread to use. clone requires that we pass a pointer either to the lowest address of this stack or the highest, depending on whether the architecture we are running on has the stack growing up or down. To determine this, there's the static function in daemon_core.cpp: static int stack_direction(volatile int *ptr=NULL) { volatile int location; if(!ptr) return stack_direction(&location); if (ptr < &location) { return STACK_GROWS_UP; } return STACK_GROWS_DOWN; } With the gcc 4.8 compiler series, which is the default on Fedora 19, this code return STACK_GROWS_UP if compiled with -O2, which is the default in nmi. Interestingly, it returns the correct STACK_GROWS_DOWN when compiled with either -O0 or -O3. Given that the linux clone(2) man page says that the only Linux architecture where the STACK GROWS UP is HP-PA, I'm just going to hardcode STACK_GROWS_DOWN. I'm curious if this is true for our CMS friends currently experimenting with ARM? 2013-Dec-04 17:45:26 by eje: There might be a way to improve the detection by making it less vulnerable to optimization, e.g. https://bugs.r-project.org/bugzilla3/show_bug.cgi?id=15011 "To get reliable results, you need to compare the address of a variable local to Rf_initialize_R with the address of a variable local to a function called from Rf_initialize_R, that is defined in another source file (to stop the compiler from inlining it)." or: http://www.devx.com/tips/Tip/37412 2013-Dec-05 09:17:47 by gthain: As this impacts none of our released platforms, I'm not putting a version history note in the file. 2013-Dec-05 10:09:40 by jfrey: Code Review The change to ​stack_direction() looks good. 2014-Jan-21 10:48:59 by tim: This problem is not specific to Fedora. It also happened with Debian testing. They are both using a newer version of gcc. So, this is compiler dependent. Not OS dependent.

title: Ticket #6034: Work around my_popenv error sensitivity.
description: When condor_submit_dag calls condor_submit, it logs the error stream. One of users noticed a new warning in this log, which came from the following new line in the new default base Condor config: include ifexist command into $(LOCAL_CONFIG_DIR)/49ec2-instance.config : \ /etc/condor/config.d/49ec2-instance.sh The include-command syntax invokes my_popenv(), which will print the warning; the ifexist does not suppress warning messages (as you might expect). Although we suspect checking for existing won't have any false negatives (that a command which doesn't exist can still be executed), rather than worry about that and redo the my_popenv() plumbing, we decided it would better if we could move this line out of the base condor config and into a config file supplied by the EC2 package. The reason for not doing that in the first place was that 49ec2-instance.config may download new configuration files, which would be ignored if they appear after processing of the config directory began. TJ pointed out an escape hatch: the config directories, plural, are processed one at a time, so that a script run from, say, /etc/condor/config.d/49ec2-instance.config could populate /etc/condor/config.d/dynamic and the config system would pay attention. However, we can't change the config directories list from a config directory file. Therefore, the plan is to remove the problematic line from the default base config file, but change the default config directories to include config.d/dynamic (the config directories aren't searched recursively). To avoid warnings, we'll also alter the packages (or condor_install, for the tarballs) to ensure that directory exists at install time. Finally, the EC2 RPM (no deb yet, IIRC) will be adjusted to include the problematic line in config.d/49ec2-instance.config. See #5787.
remarks: 2016-Dec-01 14:37:14 by tlmiller: TJ points out that the hard-coded path to the script in the problematic config line should /also/ be $(LOCAL_CONFIG_DIR). However, since that will be a list in this solution, some additional cleverness may be required. 2016-Dec-01 14:38:52 by tlmiller: The first thing that comes to mind is to add a new variable in the root config when we add the dynamic directory to LOCAL_CONFIG_DIR, say, DYNAMIC_CONFIG_DIR, which we know will be singular. 2016-Dec-01 16:26:24 by tlmiller: New plan, after discussion: Immediately -- for 8.5.8 -- remove the line in question from the default root config and stop distributing the EC2 RPM. Later -- consider rewriting the EC2 RPM as something which installs an extra initscript (which configures HTCondor with the instance-specific data (unconditionally/ignoring cache) and (re-; see previous parenthetical remark) downloads the new configuration. 2016-Dec-02 14:15:12 by tlmiller: Reverting the previous two commit seemed safer than partial removal, and reversions don't require code review. 2016-Dec-02 14:17:48 by tlmiller: We also don't appear to have documented the EC2 package anywhere yet, so I guess this doesn't need documentation changes.

Ticket #2077: Remove circular dependencies from condor_utils
description: There are a few circular dependencies between condor_utils/qmgmt and condor_utils/stdu starter. There is also a global symbol, SigNames, which is defined twice in condor_utils. Both issues are currently handled because we statically link condor_utils, and the static linker is able to ignore missing symbols. This is a bit of a ticking-time-bomb: if Condor ever decides to provide a shared lib, then there might be a huge mess of circular deps to untangle. Better start now rather than later. To see the exact symbols that need to be untangled, set BUILD_SHARED_LIBS true in the cmake macros and remove "STATIC" from add_library in the definition for condor_static_library
remarks: 2011-Apr-21 08:33:33 by tstclair: I treaded down this road during the cmake transformation. The idea to turning the the lib+header dependencies into a DAG, but it was quite the nightmare when teasing out the header inclusion issues. I agree it should be done, but IMHO this is quite a thorny, and folks should plan on this being a non-trivial amount of work. Also I would revise this to saying: "remove circular dependencies..." because there are many not just in condor_utils.

title: Ticket #6937: Successful Application-Level Checkpointing Misidentified as Failure
description: Duncan Brown reports: I've encountered the following error: 6070226.0 dbrown 2/27 17:41 Error from slot1@CRUSH-SUGWG-OSG-10-5-228-85: Job did not exit as promised when sent its checkpoint signal. Promised exit was with exit code 255, actual exit status was with exit code 255. More information: I did straces which suggests that condor_pid_ns_init and condor_exec.exe are both exiting with status 255, as they are supposed to. The problem also happens when I try and use a signal for checkpointing, rather than an exit code: +CheckpointExitBySignal = True +CheckpointExitSignal = 10 6070287.0 dbrown 2/28 10:42 Error from slot1@CRUSH-SUGWG-OSG-10-5-228-85: Job did not exit as promised when sent its checkpoint signal. Promised exit was on signal 10, actual exit status was on signal 10. It's a bug in the starter. The code to figure out what a successful checkpoint is... inconsistent with the docs on the wiki page and the code ... that generates the error. The former wants +SuccessCheckpointExitBySignal = True +SuccessCheckpointExitSignal = 10 to see if the checkpoint was successful and the latter looks for +CheckpointExitBySignal = True +CheckpointExitSignal = 10 (as per the docs on the wiki) to construct the hold error message. Adding both sets of class ads to the submit file works around the problem.

title: Ticket #5618: Bad behavior with CCB+SP and failures during claiming
description: During the recent 100,000-slot scale test, before we turned on the claiming throttle (MAX_PENDING_STARTD_CONTACTS), the reverse connections from the startds initiated when the schedd connected to the startd in order to claim it, would frequently get dropped on the floor by the schedd's shared port daemon (because the schedd's domain socket's listen queue was full). This meant that the schedd would (effectively) never retry claiming that slot. (This may be because the default time-out for failing to claim is calibrated assuming that the failure to hear back from the startd was because the startd was preempting (retiring?).) However, the schedd would also refuse new attempts to claim the slot (during the negotiation cycle) because the pending claim was still in its table. Furthermore, it appears that the failure of the reverse connection didn't prompt a retry from the startd. (This may be on purpose; the contact_er_ is supposed to do the retries, not the contact_ee_.) Perhaps if the startd is using CCB (and the schedd is using shared port), the schedd should put claim attempts waiting the startd's reverse connection in a different state (in the pending-connection table) with a shorter time-out. Once the startd connects -- even if it has nothing to say because it's preempting/retiring or whatever -- the state could move to the current intermediate state, with the longer timeout.

remarks: 2011-Oct-19 14:51:10 by eje: If this idea is implemented, it will be important to consider what to do if somebody tries this: NEGOTIATOR_ROOT_ACCOUNTING_GROUP_NAME = root GROUP_QUOTA_root = 1 The above "GROUP_QUOTA_root = 1" would be ignored by the current code, and it would need to be forbidden, or ignored with a warning. Generally, which acct grp attributes have well-defined semantics for "root" (<none>) and which don't would need to be documented and/or addressed in some way.

title: Ticket #6872: Remove dependency on capability library for running in a containter
description: The HTCondor starter checks to see if it is root (technically can_switch_ids) before it tries to contain a job with cgroups or issue a MOUNT_UNDER_SCRATCH. WHen running in a docker or singularity container, HTCondor has uid root, but the linux capabilities to do these operations have been removed. So, the starter now checks not just that it is root, but that it has cap_sys_admin. Unfortunately, the library we use to wrap the system call to get the capability is not installed by default with the kernel headers, so we can't use it. The code today, if it couldn't find the capability-checking library, assumed that the system didn't support capabilities, and thus fell back to the "if I have uid 0, I can do anything", and thus a condor built this way started inside a container would fail to run jobs. To fix this, we will not use the capability library, but check the capabilites directly with a system call.

title: Ticket #7760: Python ClassAds do not define equality operator
description: Python ClassAds do not define equality, so we get results like this: >>> c = {"foo": "bar"} >>> d = {"foo": "bar"} >>> c = classad.ClassAd(c) >>> d = classad.ClassAd(d) >>> c == d False >>> print(c) [ foo = "bar" ] >>> print(d) [ foo = "bar" ] or >>> import classad >>> x = classad.ClassAd() >>> y = classad.ClassAd() >>> x == y False ... which is why I've been converting classads to dicts before comparing them for a while, thinking that we just didn't have sensible comparison operators for them, when it turns out we don't have them at all. We should defer to the C++ ClassAd equality operator here.

title: Ticket #2831: Be able to "manually" retry nodes during a DAG run
description: Earlier this week Bill ran into a problem where a node failed during a large DAG (but other paths in the DAG still continued to run). He was able to fix the problem that caused the node to fail, but there's no way to get DAGMan to retry the node at that point without condor_rm'ing the DAG and resubmitting it (which he didn't want to do because that would have caused a lot of badput). So it would be nice to be able to tell DAGMan during a run, "go back and retry a certain node" or "retry all failed nodes" or something like that. If we build the command-line tool (see #2616) it seems like this would be a good function for it to implement. It's also possible that we could implement it in a different way.
remarks: 2013-Mar-05 10:09:57 by pfc: FWIW, this would be useful for LIGO as well. Our users are constantly resubmitting DAGs to rerun jobs that failed due to external factors (e.g., NFS server issues), but it would save them time if they could do it for individual jobs while the initial DAG is still running. 2013-Nov-06 16:18:51 by wenger: Brian Bockelman would like this, as well. 2014-Aug-11 10:29:42 by wenger: A few things to think about with this: How does the user communicate which node(s) they want to retry? How do we handle errors (e.g., the user attempts to retry a node that doesn't exist or has succeeded)? If a node has retries already, and they're all used up, does a "manual" retry just give us one more retry, or does it essentially reset the retry count to zero? What if we have a node with retries, and the user specifies a "manual" retry on that node before all of the specified retries are used up? How would this get implemented? My initial thought on how the user would specify this is that they could create a file called something like foo.dag.retry, which would contain lines specifying the node names to retry. DAGMan would read this file and then delete it or rename it after reading it, so that it wouldn't get into a cycle of retrying the nodes multiple times, unless the user specifies multiple manual retries. 2014-Aug-11 10:41:06 by wenger: Hmm -- something else to think about is this: how will this work with recovery mode? If a node fails, you do a manual retry, the node runs, and then you go into recovery mode, I'll bet DAGMan will be unhappy... Do we need to put something into the workflow log about the manual retry? Hmm -- have to think about this. (If we do need to put something into the workflow log, we'd have to require DAGMan to use the workflow log -- I can't remember whether we already do that or not. Also, if we go that route, I think the "real" code should just write the event, and then the actual retry should happen as a result of DAGMan reading and processing the event.) 2014-Aug-11 10:51:48 by bbockelm: Hi Kent, Sorry - we can only use it if it is remotely queryable; no filesystem operations. As part of the "shared port default" work, I think we'll end up having a client class that would allow authenticated clients to get a command socket from the schedd. Would that work here? Brian 2014-Aug-11 11:05:18 by wenger: Hmm -- a socket to the schedd would only do you any good if the schedd then communicated to DAGMan. We've talked for quite a while about having a command-line tool to communicate with DAGMan -- maybe this is the time for that? 2014-Aug-11 11:15:36 by wenger: Note: See #2616 for notes about the command-line tool.

title: Ticket #3723: Frequent shadow crashes on CMS machine at CERN
description: Igor Sfiligoi reports that he's seeing frequent shadow crashes (about 12 a day) on machine vocms83.cern.ch. Examination of the logs and core files indicates the crashes are due to the passwd_cache class being called recursively inside of _set_priv() due to a getpwnam() call failing. passwd_cache isn't designed to be called this way, and is probably corrupting memory as a result. The getpwnam() failures claim that the user doesn't exist, though we know the user existed when the job was submitted and when the shadow was born. Almost all of the failures occur at 17:44 local time each day. This suggests that there is a regular, short-lived outage of the ldap service each day. Here is the sequence of events shown by the stack trace quoted below: Shadow wants to write a job usage update log event Log event code calls _set_priv() to switch effective uid/gid to the job user _set_priv() calls into passwd_cache to lookup and set supplemental groups for the user passwd_cache decides cached information about the user and their groups is stale, starts updating cache entry with new information passwd_cache calls getpwnam(), which returns failure passwd_cache calls dprintf() to log failure dprintf() calls _set_priv() to switch effective uid/gid to condor dprintf() writes failure to log dprintf() calls _set_priv() to restore previous effecive uid/gid, which is the user _set_priv() calls into passwd_cache to lookup and set supplemental groups for the user passwd_cache starts to update cache with new information about user and supplemental groups BOOM! _set_priv() takes an argument indicating when it shouldn't call dprintf(), used when dprintf() calls _set_priv(). This avoids a crash-inducing recursion. The passwd_cache object doesn't have a similar flag, so when _set_priv() calls into passwd_cache, it has no way to tell passwd_cache not to call dprintf(). There's a similar problem when _set_priv() is called during process creation on unix, between the fork()/clone() and exec() in the child process. _set_priv() has to be careful about any modifications to memory. passwd_cache won't respect that restriction. In this Condor installation, the Condor user is "_condor", rather than the usual "condor". There is no "condor" user on the system. The CONDOR_IDS variable is set to indicate the "_condor" user. [DONE] In passwd_cache, when a cache entry is stale, if getpwnam() or friends fail, keep and use the old cache entry for a limited period of time. When CONDOR_IDS is set, don't try to lookup the "condor" user in passwd_cache at daemon startup. [DONE] Lengthen the default passwd_cache entry lifetime from 5 minutes to 20 hours. This is config param PASSWD_CACHE_REFRESH. [DONE]

title: Ticket #6521: Optimal preen connections to schedd
description: In #6490 we fixed a defect in how preen cleans up the spool directory. Previously, preen established a blocking connection to the schedd for the entire time it spent cleaning the spool directory -- whether it was needed or not. We changed this to only connect to the schedd when needed, then to disconnect after a certain time interval expired. However this was only a stopgap measure, not an optimal solution. We want to implement a better approach into preen, as follows: 1. When scanning through the spool directory, do not initially establish a connection to the schedd. Keep a list of any files we need more information about. 2. After finishing the scan, now connect to the schedd (if needed) and request information about the files. Do not delete files at this point, which could incur expensive disk accesses. Just keep track of which files are stale and need to get deleted. 3. Disconnect from the schedd. Now delete the files indicated as stale. It's worth noting there is a possible race condition between steps 2 and 3; the schedd might indicate a file is stale, but then delete it before preen gets a chance. This is correct behavior, we just need to be prepared to handle it.

title: Ticket #3689: Remove hard-coded policies on how schedd can reuse claims
description: Currently, the Claim that is given out by the Negotiator to the Schedd is very open ended. As long as it matches the Startd requirements, the only additional restrictions on the Claim are hard-coded : it cannot be used for a different user, and it must be used for a job with the same set of concurrency limits. This situation has shown to be a problem when implementing the “Global Priority” feature. While the Negotiator will pick the globally higher priority job for a user, all bets are off once that job finishes, since the Schedd will pick the next job using local criteria. Other policies based on the global state of the system would equally be impossible to implement. The proposal is thus to remove the hard-coded claim reuse logic and for the negotiator to explicitly embed the restrictions on jobs that can reuse the claim in the requirements that are sent back to the Schedd.

title: Ticket #6805: Fix cleanup after failed azure instance creation
description: If the AZURE_VM_CREATE command fails, it can leave behind some resource related to the instance in the Azure service. For example, we could have a resource group with network, public IP address, and disk resources, but no compute resource. This partial set of resources doesn't show up in AZURE_VM_LIST. Currently, the gridmanager won't attempt cleanup if AZURE_VM_LIST doesn't show anything. The resources can be cleaned up with AZURE_VM_DELETE, but that command will fail if there's no resource group at all. A failure would cause the gridmanager to put the job on hold. To ensure proper cleanup, we need to do one of the following: Have AZURE_VM_LIST include partial resource sets with an indication that they are in a failed state. Have AZURE_VM_DELETE return success if there's no resource group for the given name. Have the gridmanager recognize a "no such group" error from AZURE_VM_DELETE and treat it as a success.
creator: jfrey

title: Ticket #4838: HTCondor 8.3.3 excepts on start-up on SL 6.3
description: Turned out the problem was that if asked to resolve a host with one AAAA DNS and one A DNS record, the version of getaddrinfo() on SL 6.3 would return a two-element list, where the first element was the correct IPv4 record and the second element was completely bogus. This tripped an except in the condor_sockaddr code, which checks to make sure that the address family of the socket is something we can work with. Enabling IPv6 works around this problem. Worked around by never asking getaddrinfo() to filter by address family. Instead, filter them out in our address info iterator class.
remarks: 2015-Jan-29 10:43:13 by tlmiller: Confirmed as a bug in 8.3.3 and fixed before release; no version history necessary. 2015-Feb-02 14:03:48 by tlmiller: Coverity discovered a problem with this fix, which the patch in the check-in below remedies); this will not need documentation if merged to 8.3.3 (see above). Please code review. (The flag could be a global, but then we'd have to be sure to reset it on every reconfig; I don't think we maintain an address iterator across reconfigs, but changing one in mid-iteration seems like a good way to break things. And this is a way smaller change.)

title: Ticket #7347: Discuss ClassAd memory management
description: We should talk when Jaime gets back. I've hated the way we do memory management in ClassAds for quite some time, but I'm increasingly convinced by recent experiences, particularly in writing the classad_eval tool using the Python bindings, that the way ClassAds manage memory (in particular, ownership) is fundamentally incompatible with the way Python does. This may not be 100% true; it may just be that we need to be really careful and explicit about generating new Python objects, managing their reference counts, and handing ownership over to them. In addition to being hard, I think we'd need to add a bunch of things to the ClassAd library in order to be able to make deep copies and/or reassign ownership. On the other hand, I think it would benefit us, moving forward, to have a predictable and consistent memory model for ClassAds. (For instance, some types of Values are actually references.) It may make sense to leave the existing API alone, because of the large body of code that's been tweaked to work well with it, and create another one -- initially used by the Python bindings -- that might be less efficient, but is easier to code against.

title: Ticket #2450: schedd fails to parse its transaction log
description: A schedd in the glidein factory at UCSD failed to restart after a power outage. It failed with the following exception: ERROR "Error: bad record with op=103 in corrupt logfile" at line 1060 in file /home/condor/execute/dir_22626/userdir/src/condor_utils/classad_log.cpp Note the complete lack of helpful information about where in the transaction log this error was encountered. It turned out that there were numerous entries in the transaction log of the following form, where XXXX is replaced by random garbage characters: 103 541891.0 HoldReason "CREAM error: CREAM_Job_Register Error: XXXXodName=[jobRegister] ErrorCode=[0] Description=[The CREAM service cannot accept jobs at the moment] FaultCause=[Submissions are disabled!] Timestamp=[Wed 07 Sep 2011 17:54:52]" Removing the garbage characters made the schedd happy.
remarks: 2011-Sep-12 13:37:10 by danb: The problem is caused by ascii 0xFF characters. These are treated as an error by the log reading code in LogRecord::readline(), because they happen to match the value of (char)EOF: buf[i] = fgetc( fp ); if( buf[i] == EOF && !feof( fp ) ) { free( buf ); return( -1 ); } But these characters are not forbidden by the log writing code, so it is possible to write a record that is not accepted on read-back. This code that treats EOF as an error dates back to at least 6.4.0 if not earlier. This failure to distinguish between (char)0xFF and EOF is a bug. I therefore propose fixing the log reader rather than forbidding the writing of 0xFF characters. It is a shame that the quill log reader is implemented completely separately, duplicating much code. It happens that while fixing a different sort of problem, that code was fixed to distinguish between (char)0xFF and EOF in [17674]. 2011-Sep-12 20:56:21 by danb: Note: some of the commits associated with this ticket are for 7.7.2. The commits that went into 7.6.4 are [27176] and [27182].

description: Milestones [? days] Milestone 1 [gthain] EMBED: Status Table of Derived Tickets TN: Developer # Status Type Pri Created Changed Target Due Date Days left Title No records match the report criteria History Work to support Paritionable slots in Condor is an ongoing effort. Current support for partitionable slots in Condor: A startd can be configured to support zero or more paritionable slots, in addition to the traditional static slots. Static and partitionable slots can be mixed, and we do see demand from user for having machines running with both static and partitionable slots. This can be to have a static slot for administrative purposes, or to support specific kinds of resources like GPUs. Partitionable slots can be given fixed or remaining amounts of disk, cpu and memory resources. Today, the negotiatior knows nothing special about partitionable slots -- they are advertised to the collector, matched in the negotiator, just like a static slot, and assigned to a schedd. Only when the claim is in the schedd does their partitionable nature become noticed. When the schedd claims a partitionable slot, the startd splits the claim into the requested amount (perhaps rounded by itself), creating a new claim we call the dynamic slot, and decrements the existing partitionable slot, so that it represents the remaining claim. The schedd can then repeatedly try to claim the partitionable leftovers until they are exhausted. However, the partitionable slot never itself goes into the claimed state, it stays unclaimed for the whole life cycle. Defragmentation is handled by a defragmentation daemon, which periodically sends draining requests to selected startds, in order to drain the whole machine. Problems with current support for partitionable slots There are several operational problems with the current partitionable slot implementation. These stem from a few root causes. The first root cause is that the negotiator doesn't know about partitioning, and hands out the whole resource, or tries to, to the schedd. This means that in cases where there are many resources per machine, and each submitter, for whatever reason, is only allowed to currently use less than a whole machine's worth of resources, the negotiator will fail to match the resource to the job, because it can only allocate the full slot to the submitter. A related problem is that it is impossible to specify a policy where the admin can "fill up" one machine with jobs before moving on to the next machine. Again, this is because the negotiator believes it is matching one job to a resource which eventually may split into multiples. Because the negotiator implements concurrency limits, these don't work correctly in the paritionable slot case either. Another result of this is that startd rank doesn't work correctly -- the rank and the match only apply to the partitionable slot, not to the dynamic slot which is created by the start at claim time. A minor consequence is that the partitionable slot stays unclaimed, which is confusing in condor_status output. Another root cause of several problems is that there is no naming or identification of partitionable slots. While static slots aren't explicitly named, many sites use the slotd as a de-facto name. For example, one static slot might be special in some way, and be bound to jobs that need licenses or whole machine slots, or GPUs or other specialness. Because the slot id of dynamic slots is dynamic, there is no fixed binding even of the slot id to a name, and thus there is no way to consistently identify dynamnic or partitionable slots. A related problem is that the CPU affinity knobs are bound to slot ids, which don't really exist as one might expect in the partitionable slot world, so there is no way to express the common idiom of "use Linux CPU affinity to give each slot one core". Yet another problem related to this is custom slot attributes. With static slots, there is the ability to set SLOTxx_SomeConfigKnob, to just change the config knob for that slot. This is not possible in the partitionable slot world. Perhaps the most common example of this is the Start expression itself -- this is global per startd, instead of per slot, or per slot type. Proposed fixes To improve upon this situation, in this work we will make the partitionable slots named and claimable. Each partitionable slot will have it's own id, and it will be possible to assign configuration values and classad attributes to the partitionable slot, which are copied into that slot's dynamic slot at claim time. Specifically, it should be possible for each slot type to have it's own START expression, independent of the other slot types. The workflow will also be changed to that the negotiator and schedd will collaborate to claim the partitionable slot, and only perform fast leftover claimed from the claimed partitionable slot. This will show up in the condor_status output, so that the partitionable slot will, less confusingly, end up in the Claimed/busy state. There will then be a tree of partitionable slots, with each partitionable slot having one dynamic slot associated with it, and a child partitionable slot, which can be itself claimed and partitioned. Any of these partitionable slots in the tree can be preempted by the usual RANK conditions, which results in a preemption of all the dynamic slots recursively under that partitionable slot.

title: Ticket #1786: review treatment of undefined policy settings in startd
description: Miron suggested that we review the treatment of undefined policy expressions, starting with the startd. I have summarized below the current treatment as of 7.5.4. Meaning of the columns in the following table: Unconfigured treatment when not specified in configuration Undefined treatment when expression evaluates to undefined Error treatment when expression evaluates to error Meaning of the values in the following table: (S) silent treatment; no log message Ignore use more generic policy variable in place of this one Error shut down the startd and log the reason why Variable Unconfigured Undefined Error START Error False (S) False (S) PREEMPT Error Error Error SUSPEND Error Error Error CONTINUE Error Error Error WANT_HOLD False (S) False Error WANT_SUSPEND Error False (S) False (S) WANT_VACATE Error Error Error KILL Error Error Error PERIODIC_CHECKPOINT False (S) False (S) False (S) PREEMPT_VANILLA Ignore (S) Ignore (S) Ignore (S) SUSPEND_VANILLA Ignore (S) Ignore (S) Ignore (S) CONTINUE_VANILLA Ignore (S) Ignore (S) Ignore (S) WANT_SUSPEND_VANILLA Ignore (S) Ignore (S) Ignore (S) WANT_VACATE_VANILLA Ignore (S) Ignore (S) Ignore (S) KILL_VANILLA Ignore (S) Ignore (S) Ignore (S) Prior to 7.4.2, if WANT_SUSPEND evaluated to undefined, this was treated as an error. This was changed to be treated as false because numerous instances occurred in which admins were surprised to have their startd exit when a job showed up lacking some attribute the WANT_SUSPEND expression referenced. In discussion, it was concluded that in every known case of this problem, the desired behavior was for WANT_SUSPEND to be treated as false, so a change was made to the code to implement this behavior (#1001). Proposal Treat 'unconfigured' and 'undefined' and 'error' as semantically equivalent. For all the cases mentioned in the table above where 'undefined' leads to an error, it should instead be equivalent to 'false'. We should, however, provide useful diagnostics. For example, it should not log that SUSPEND is false when it is actually 'undefined' or 'error'.

title: Ticket #6043: Fix pslot preemption for parallel universe jobs
description: The dedicated scheduler doesn't know how to request a claim that involves pslot preemption. It ignores the claims for the dslots, and can't claim the pslot because it has insufficient resources.
remarks: 2016-Dec-06 14:08:35 by jfrey: This fix is more involved then I initially thought. The dedicated scheduler pulls machine ads from the collector and does its own matchmaking before talking to the negotiator. If it doesn't see machine ads that satisfy the requirements of its jobs, it doesn't send those jobs to the negotiator. So it needs code equivalent to the pslot preemption code in the negotiator.
creator: jfrey

title: Ticket #6413: Make HAD replication work with shared port and IPv6
description: In HAD, replication of the accounting data is done by one side binding and listening on a new, dynamic IPv4 port, and the other side connecting to it. This breaks with IPv6 and when shared port is needed to navigate through a fire wall. The code should be updated to work in these situations. When HAD wants to replicate data, the transfer is initiated by the receiving replication daemon. It spawns a transferer process in download mode and gives it the sinful string of the remote replication daemon. The transferer binds and listens on a dynamic IPv4 port, initiates a REPLICATION_TRANSFER_FILE command with the remote (sending) replication daemon, and sends the address of the newly-bound socket as a sinful string. The sending replication daemon spawns its own transferer process in upload mode and gives it the sinful string it just received. The upload transferer connects to the given address and sends the data. I propose we change this setup to work like claim activation when starting a vanilla job. When the download transferer connects to the sending replication daemon, the replication daemon would hand the connection to the upload transferer that it spwans. The two transferers would then talk to each other as before. For backwards compatibility, we would introduce a new command for the new communication pattern. If the replication daemon detects that its peer is too old (or doesn't know its peer's version), it would use the old command.
