title: Ticket #38: Unhelpful hold reason when periodic expression is UNDEFINED
description: (Copied from Drupal 1364 (backup) 1364 (public).) If a job has a periodic expression, but it evaluates to UNDEFINED, the resulting job is put on hold. The hold reason is not helpful. The hold reason is HoldReason = "The UNKNOWN (never set) PeriodicRemove expression '' evaluated to UNDEFINED" This is particularly confusing, since it suggests that the PeriodicRemove expression was never set, when indeed it was. It also has a blank where it looks like the expression should be placed. The expected output might look something like: HoldReason = "The PeriodicRemove expression 'DoesNotExist > 0' evaluated to UNDEFINED" To reproduce, try this submit file on a reasonably supported Linux: universe=vanilla executable=/bin/date log=eraseme.log periodic_remove = DoesNotExist > 0 queue Wait a few moments and the job should go on hold. The hold reason will be visible via `condor_q -format '%s\n' HoldReason` or in the eraseme.log userlog.
remarks: Put this into the master. 2010-Jul-16 17:04:36 by mccardel: The problem was that the function AnalyzeSinglePeriodicPolicy in condor_c++_util/user_job_policy.cpp couldn't tell the difference between when an attribute was undefined and when something inside the expression was undefined. This function was called from AnalyzePolicy() in the same file, which in turn was called from PeriodicExprEval() in condor_schedd.v6/schedd.cpp. The call to ASPP would generate a return value of UNDEFINED_EVAL, and this would propagate up to PeriodicExprEval(). Following this, the UserPolicy is checked again; this time to see what the firing reason was. Originally, FiringReason() would see that the variable m_firing_source hadn't been set yet, and would set part of the error string to be "UNKNOWN (never set)", because the type of thing that tripped the firing code was never set. It should've been set in ASPP, but that quit before it could set the firing source. However, the code in ASPP now differentiates between when an attribute is undefined and when its expression is undefined. This was done by adding an if-block that looked up the attrname in the classad, and made sure it wasn't null. If it isn't null, then we know that we can set m_firing_source to be a job attribute and that the expression is undefined. Thus, the error message is now the following: The job attribute PeriodicRemove expression 'DoesNotExist > 0' evaluated to UNDEFINED

title: Ticket #2779: allow checkpoint before startd auto-restarts due to an updated binary
description: We would like to revisit the question of live upgrading of Condor. In particular, the sequence of events that occur when the condor daemons auto-detect a new binaries on disk and auto-retart. Here is a typical sequence of events: 01/18/12 19:23:34 /usr/sbin/condor_master was modified, restarting /usr/sbin/condor_master. 01/18/12 19:23:34 Sent SIGTERM to CKPT_SERVER (pid 8168) 01/18/12 19:23:34 Sent SIGTERM to STARTD (pid 5234) 01/18/12 19:23:34 DaemonCore: pid 8168 exited with status 0, invoking reaper 1 <Daemons::AllReaper()> 01/18/12 19:23:34 The CKPT_SERVER (pid 8168) exited with status 0 01/18/12 19:23:34 DaemonCore: return from reaper for pid 8168 01/18/12 19:23:34 DaemonCore: pid 5234 exited with status 0, invoking reaper 1 <Daemons::AllReaper()> 01/18/12 19:23:34 The STARTD (pid 5234) exited with status 0 01/18/12 19:23:34 All daemons are gone. Restarting. What would it take to add some dependencies in the shutdown process so that in the typical LIGO case the CKPT_SERVER is given time to checkpoint jobs from the STARTD on the same server?
remarks: 2012-Jan-24 17:23:07 by bbockelm: Oh! Maybe I can hijack this ticket for something our admins complain bitterly about. I should be able to configure the condor startd to "peacefully restart" when it auto-restarts. That is, it should either vacate or drain the running jobs (pros and cons to each approach), then restart. I.e., something analogous to the difference between a "fast shutdown" versus a "peaceful shutdown". Our site admins have indicated that a reason they don't update Condor more frequently is because of the lack of a "peaceful restart" for upgrades. This ticket references checkpointing explicitly, but I think a solution may be able to cover both use cases. 2012-Feb-10 14:46:08 by pfc: Updated priority to match Todd's new scheme (1=fire, 2=soon, 3=time permitting, 4=not yet prioritized, 5=wishlist/ideas). 2012-Feb-13 11:37:57 by johnkn: I propose to solve this by stopping the STARTD first on peaceful stop, then stopping the rest of the daemons. This should allow job to checkpoint, which solves the specific problem. I also propose to add a config knob to allow setting the restart mode when new-binaries are detected so that restarting peacefully would be an option. -tj 2012-Feb-17 11:05:58 by johnkn: The patch https://condor-wiki.cs.wisc.edu/index.cgi/chngview?cn=30633 changes the master so that it restarts in either GRACEFUL or PEACEFUL mode, it will shut down the STARTDs and wait for them to exit before it shuts down any other daemon. This should give the jobs a chance to checkpoint before any local checkpoint servers are shut down. In order to fix a race condition with this change, it was necessary to change the master to that it looks only with the timestamp of the condor_master binary. Otherwise daemons would shut down in the order that the master noticed the timestamps on their binaries change. This patch also introduces a new config param MASTER_NEW_BINARY_RESTART which can have the value GRACEFUL, PEACEFUL or NEVER (with NONE or NO being accepted as synonyms for NEVER). This patch also fixes as stumble upon bug where condor_off -master -peaceful would tell the master to shutdown peacefully, but the master would not tell it's children to shut down peacefully. It is worth nothing that I noticed another design flaw in the way peaceful shutdown is implemented. Once a daemon as been told to shut down peacefully, it can no longer be shut down gracefully. (it can still be shutdown fast). 2012-Feb-22 16:23:10 by jfrey: Here are my comments on [30633]: Now, master never restarts a daemon when that daemon's binary changes. It only does so if the master's own binary changes. If that's the desired behavior, we need to clearly document this loss of functionality. Daemons::CheckForNewExecutable() shouldn't call CancelNewExecTimer(). That timer should be canceled or not started in Daemons::StartTimers() and/or Daemons::StartNewExecTimer(). Unfortunately, getting it right is a bit of a mess with where these methods are called. As it is, you can't change MASTER_NEW_BINARY_RESTART from NONE to PEACEFUL/GRACEFUL and have the master start checking again on a reconfig without also changing MASTER_CHECK_NEW_EXEC_INTERVAL. Daemons::SetAllReaper() parameter fStartdsFirst is always false. Remove the parameter and setting of stop_other_daemons_when_startds_gone. There is a DC_OFF_PEACEFUL command that the master can send to children instead of DC_SET_PEACEFUL_SHUTDOWN followed by SIGTERM. But the daemon class seems to only want to use real unix signals, and not CEDAR signals. This isn't a request to change the code, just an observation. 2012-May-02 14:30:41 by tstclair: Now, master never restarts a daemon when that daemon's binary changes. It only does so if the master's own binary changes. If that's the desired behavior, we need to clearly document this loss of functionality. Why is this delta a requirement given the ticket (startd constraint). 2012-May-07 14:16:38 by tstclair: It should be noted that the work-around is to send the -peaceful to the daemon that a user wishes to restart.

title: Ticket #530: RFE: long submission sessions with condor_submit
description: condor_submit can read job descriptions from standard input. It's the default if you don't provide a submit file. This is quite nice for scripting condor_submit. However, there's a catch. After the first queue command is sent the clock is ticking. When the queue command is received condor_submit makes a connection to the condor_schedd. If queue commands aren't sent fast enough after that the connection will be silently broken - an error is raised on the queue following the disconnection. A second problem is that the condor_schedd is blocked during this time. It won't handle other connections, e.g. condor_q or other condor_submits. Seems this could be mitigated in two ways: 1) (Todd's initial thought) allow the Schedd to have multiple CEDAR transactions open at once; 2) (Matt's initial thought) have condor_submit make a new connection to the Schedd for each queue command and don't keep the connection open for long between them. (1) is probably the ideal, and may even eliminate other contention issues such as concurrent submissions. It'd probably be a few solid weeks of Todd's time to get right. (2) has an obvious downside of probably causing each queue to create a new cluster, though that's maybe not a big deal. It'd probably take anyone 3 days to get done by only touching condor_submit, and probably touch condor_schedd and double the time to handle any downsides. An alternative is to use something like the SOAP interface to condor_schedd, which already supports multiple concurrent transactions.

description: From Florian Weimer - Scheduler::abort_job() in src/condor_schedd.V6/schedd.cpp does not require authentication beyond the WRITE level and does not check if the job owner matches the user making the request. As a result, local users can abort any idle job, bypassing the restriction enforced by condor_rm. From Matt - KILL_FRGN_JOB was introduced in, commit 6ad56fef0a28d1399c63dffce20411aeb47614ef Author: sashwin <sashwin> Date: Sat Apr 12 22:30:36 1997 +0000 Added a function to abort a job [abort_job_myself()] and made abort_jo() call it. The new function is also called by qmgmt.C functions which were updated earlier to automatically abort a job when it was deleted from the Q. KILL_FRGN_JOB was renamed to DEACTIVATE_CLAIM_FORCIBLY in, commit 9423470db636f8e90133e3a12ed9ce955ae655e1 Author: wright <wright> Date: Thu Oct 30 21:21:07 1997 +0000 Added more startd commands At its introduction it was used by condor_rm to remove jobs. Sometime ~6.3 (2002, closest ref is d1486a76) condor_rm changed to use ACT_ON_JOBS, but KILL_FRGN_JOB was still exposed from the condor_schedd. There are currently (~2c386c41) no uses of the condor_schedd's KILL_FRGN_JOB or DEACTIVATE_CLAIM_FORCIBLY.

title: Ticket #6690: Ensure that Docker jobs run on condor_annex default AMI
description: We realized during HTCondor Week that we need to make sure that condor_annex produces Docker-ready instances by default.
remarks: 2019-Jul-20 18:58:13 by tlmiller: This idea hit a snag during testing: Docker jobs can't run if the execute directory is encrypted. GregT indicates that the problem isn't readily resolvable -- the container is in a different process tree than the starter -- but if we just disable encryption for Docker jobs, I think that would violate the principle of least astonishment for many people. If we make a code change, handling this problem in matchmaking might be a better one, but that doesn't answer the question about that to do w.r.t. the default annex AMIs. Maybe we could argue that if a job doesn't explicitly ask for encryption, it's OK to run it unencrypted, even if that's a little surprising from the machine point of view? It's wildly unclear how many people are worried enough about their data to encrypt the execute directory on the cloud but not worried enough about it to avoid using the cloud at all. 2019-Aug-02 17:10:43 by tlmiller: We'll just not encrypt the default Annex AMI for now.

Ticket #3492: EC2 GAHP doesn't like the new Eucalyptus XML
description: Eucalyptus now returns (or can return) a different style of (valid) XML, in which all the tags are explicitly in the 'euca' namespace. The parsers in the EC2 GAHP presently search for tag only in the default namespace. Unfortunately, Expat (our XML parser) doesn't appear to have an option to recognize and discard namespaces, so this fix will require a lot of little code changes.
remarks: 2013-Feb-13 18:47:52 by tlmiller: I had a clever idea that made this quick to work around. Testing this work-around revealed an incompatibility in the XML that I also worked around. However, that incompatibility also had a simple work-around. Testing this revealed a serious bug in the response-parsing code. Although we usually just ended up ignoring the spurious empty status report thereby created, sometimes the bug would eat important information about an instance and cause it go on hold, claiming that the cloud service had purged its records. With this fix, all three of the EC2 implementations I could test (the Nimbus server is down at the moment) now seem to work. I need to do some further investigation to see what this might mean for 7.8.x. 2013-Feb-18 13:27:11 by tlmiller: Since 7.8.x doesn't support the euca3 'protocol', that part of this fix is irrelevant. Its response-parsing code also appear to be adequate, although I don't know if this is a result of asking for statuses one at a time, or that it uses a different version of the REST API. 2013-Feb-20 16:12:34 by jfrey: Code Review This code looks good. 2013-Feb-21 13:14:31 by tlmiller: Documentation in commit.

title: Ticket #475: Option to run w/ one gridmanager per remote site.
description: Currently, the schedd will start a new gridmanager instance per UID of the submitter. We think it would be advantageous to provide greater isolation based upon remote site destination, so if Condor-G is submitting to a slow site over a slow WAN for example, it would minimize impact upon job throughput to fast/nearby sites. In theory it should not matter since the GRAM interface in Globus is supposedly non-blocking, but in practice we'd sleep better at night. ;-) Thus, we'd like an option for the schedd to start a new gridmanager instance based upon a tuple of both submitter UID and remote destination.

title: Ticket #4642: Avoid condor_history DoS attacks on schedd
description: Peter Couvares reports that they've essenitally suffered denial of service attacks because of part of the OSG infrastructure running so many condor_history commands, thereby goofing up the schedd. We're not sure what the best way is to ameliorate the problem. Some ideas: Fork off a separate process to service condor_history commands (but there might still be problems with disk bandwidth). Throttle the condor_history processing somehow -- possibly limit the number of condor_history commands that will be serviced within a certain time window, or limit the number of concurrent condor_history commands (if the command keeps an open connection to the schedd).
remarks: 2014-Oct-09 16:02:57 by tannenba: The schedd already does fork off a separate process to service condor_history commands. Also, remote condor_history queries can already be throttled. But I am not surprised you were not aware of this, because somehow these knobs did not get documented! I added ticket #4643 to address this. Assuming the information in #4643 is sufficient for Peter's needs, I am abandoning this ticket. Peter, feel free to reopen and/or remark why the existing throttling mechanism is not sufficient, or if you feel the defaults are stupid... thanks.

title: Ticket #6385: Always try to send alive messages to systemd on linux
description: Someone on htcondor-users reports that their master daemon dies every 20 minutes on their ubuntu 14 machine. It turns out that systemd is killing the master because it's not reporting that it's alive. Ubuntu 14 doesn't use systemd as its init system by default, but can be configured to do so. Our code to send alive messages to systemd is only enabled if the related header and library files are present at compile time, which they aren't by default on ubuntu 14. The code should be changed so that the daemon always tries to interact with systemd (if the requisite environment variables are set). The values we need at compile time (SD_LISTEN_FDS_START and LIBSYSTEMD_DAEMON_SO) are the same across all distros, so we can set defaults if the header and library files aren't present.

title: Ticket #1440: ClassAd interval() function doesn't work as advertised
description: The ClassAd function interval() is used to take a number of seconds (as an integer) and returns a string representing the corresponding interval of time expressed in days, hours, minutes, and seconds, like so: days+hours:minutes:seconds. Any leading values of 0 are dropped, along with their punctuation. So interval(67) should evaluate to "1:07". The descriptions of this function in old and new ClassAds agree on this. However, the function never drops leading 0s and the days field is padded out to a minimum of 3 characters with leading spaces. So interval(67) actually evaluates to "<space><space>0+00:01:07". The code should probably be changed to match the documentation.

title: Ticket #7594: Efficiently close FDs after fork
description: See parent ticket for details. Splitting this ticket across a code freeze.
remarks: 2020-Apr-10 15:27:21 by tlmiller: Implementing a libbsd-style fix make be too radical for the stable series. 2020-Apr-14 13:09:14 by tlmiller: The V8_9-gt7594-branch appears to work. Asking for a review both for code quality (we really don't want to screw this up) and to determine if the change is safe for the stable series (probably not). 2020-Apr-14 13:44:32 by jfrey: Code Review This code will attempt to close the FD associated with the DIR object. It happens after closedir(), so is harmless. I don't think a change is needed. Otherwise, this looks good. As mentioned already, not recommended for the stable series. 2020-Apr-14 13:55:14 by bbockelm: Thoughts: Factor this out into a library call. We're going to want it later for Create_Process. This might fail if /proc isn't mounted inside a container or if HTCondor is already at its ulimit for fds. Needs a fallback. I'm a bit nervous to buffer a vector of all fds. What about having it break every 1K close() invocations and reopen the directory? As long as we are making forward progress... 2020-Apr-14 14:16:43 by tlmiller: Jaime: We could call dirfd() to avoid close()ing that FD redundantly, but I'm not sure which way is faster. 1. Agreed, but it seemed a good idea to get it reviewed first. 2. I feel like not mounting /proc should break all sorts of things, but fair enough, if the rest of HTCondor works without it, we should have a fallback. 3. I guess if we avoided closing the dir FD, that would work, and I guess a fixed-size buffer would be faster anyway. Thanks for the feedback, both of you. 2020-Apr-15 08:22:09 by bbockelm: Revisions look much better. I also noticed we don't have much sanity checking for the strtol call; it might be worthwhile to check errno and that the value is positive (perhaps switching to std::stol while we're at it).k Again, mostly paranoia -- but sometimes paranoia is OK too. 2020-Apr-15 11:33:18 by tlmiller: I think that the endptr check handles the only case we care about - did we convert the whole filename into an int or not, and even that's being really paranoid. If the kernel suddenly spazzes out and drops non-numeric names or negative numbers in /proc/self/fds, I think we have other problems. I suppose somebody could have not mounted /proc and filled self/fds with garbage? Do we care about that case? I'd rather not use std::stol() and have to deal with exceptions. 2020-Apr-15 11:34:06 by tlmiller: I have a patch to close only 1024 FDs at a time, but I don't like it (it involves cleverness to detect when we're done). How strongly do we feel about that? 2020-Apr-20 15:28:35 by bbockelm: Heh: exceptions, that's the reason why I prefer the std version of the function :) I'll let you be the judge on whether buffering the file descriptors is worthwhile. If it's too much complexity, I agree it can be skipped. 2020-Apr-20 15:37:32 by tlmiller: According to BrianB, for clone(), we can't call opendir() or readdir() before the exec, or allocate memory, so we'll have to have a version where the list of FDs is populated in the parent and passed into the child. (Which renders an attempt to only close() 1024 at a time meaningless.)

title: Ticket #1913: negotiator does not publish updated address
description: Changes to the negotiator's address are not published to the collector until the negotiator is reconfigured or restarted. This problem was observed when using shared_port. The negotiator started up at a time when the shared port ad file did not contain a valid address for some (unknown) reason. The negotiator detected the problem and kept retrying until it successfully read the shared port address, but the negotiator continued to publish an incomplete address until it was restarted. If the shared_port address were to change, a similar problem would happen. The negotiator would detect the new address but would continue to advertise the original address.

title: Ticket #7740: Port BLAHP to gcc 10
description: So, my little fedora box got a new version of gcc, and now the BLAHP fails to compile, or link really: gcc -g -O0 -o BLClient BLClient.o blah_utils.o BLfunctions.o -ldl -lpthread /usr/bin/ld: BLfunctions.o:/home/gthain/condor/b/externals/bundles/blahp/1.16.5.1/blahp-prefix/src/blahp/src/BLfunctions.h:73: multiple definition of `argv0'; BLClient.o:/home/gthain/condor/b/externals/bundles/blahp/1.16.5.1/blahp-prefix/src/blahp/src/./BLfunctions.h:73: first defined here Hmm. gthain@gthain src]$ nm BLClient.o | grep argv0 0000000000000000 B argv0 [gthain@gthain src]$ nm BLfunctions.o | grep argv0 0000000000000000 B argv0 Well, the linker seems to have a point here -- linking together two .o's, each with a global data variable with the same name (argv0). And why did the compiler do that? both BLClient.c and BLfunctions.c include BLfunctions.h, and in this header file, we see on line 73: char *argv0; no extern, no static, just a definition. And there's a bunch of other variables like this causing multiply-defined symbols, but let's ignore that for now. So, how did this ever work, I ask myself? Compiling this on older versions of gcc shows that older versions of gcc put these symbols in the "C"ommon block. Turns out, there's a gcc command line option, -fcommon that controls whether global variables with "tentative definitions" are put into the Common block (-fcommon) or put into the BSS (-fno-common). And, the default from time immemorial was -fcommon, but gcc 10 changed this to -fno-common, without much fanfare. Note this is one of these oddball corners where C is different than C++: the c++ language definition says these can't go in the common block, and must create multiply defined symbols, and the blahp is written in C, not C++. So, the immediate fix is to add -fcommon to the command line, but in the long term we should extern these in the header file and define them in a c file.

title: Ticket #4496: Predictable hostname detection
description: We need to document the current hostname detection algorithm and improve it. CURRENT deficiencies: condor_gethostname (the default UTS hostname detection) doesn't appear to work with IPv6 if NO_DNS is enabled Hostname is a function of the configuration file (depending on ENABLE_IPV6 or ENABLE_IPV4). However, the configuration is a function of the hostname. Hence, it's quite possible to have a non-convergent configuration. We show no preference for the local hostname - instead taking the last hostname from the highest desirability. There's no way to override the hostname. Summary of proposal: Default the "local hostname" to the value of environment variable CONDOR_HOSTNAME; if this is not present, use the UTS hostname through gethostname. If NETWORK_INTERFACE is set in the config file as non-default, issue a warning. Allow it to be set as the CONDOR_NETWORK_IP environment variable instead. (Upgrade the network_interface_to_ip function to work with IPv6 addresses.) Do a reverse lookup for all IP addresses, v4 and v6. Use the existing desirability rankings algorithm for iterating through addresses; introduce a level "4" for IP addresses which match the local hostname. The first IP address with highest desirability is used as the default IPv4/6 address. As suggested in #4461, track the default IPv4 and IPv6 addresses separately. The default IP address (if v4 or v6 is not specified) will be determined by the IP address above with the highest desirability.
remarks: 2014-Jul-29 15:35:07 by bbockelm: The biggest outcome of the proposed algorithm is that the hostname and IP address detection becomes independent of the configuration file - meaning we don't have to worry about non-convergent configurations! I think it's OK to take the key configuration variables from the environment because, currently, NETWORK_INTERFACES and ENABLE_IPV6 only function if present on the global config file. Accordingly, the only way to change these are to go against best practices for managing configuration files. Another change to note is we could utilize a hostname derived from an IPv6 interface even if ENABLE_IPV6=false. This would be the wrong hostname if the IPv6 hostname is different from the IPv4 hostname and the default hostname is the IPv6 one). I'd argue this is a sufficiently rare setup (and really, quite a bad idea!) that we can instruct affected users to override using the CONDOR_HOSTNAME environment variable. With the patches in #4461 and the changes set above, the correct local IPv4 address would still be used even in this case.

title: Ticket #3353: custom attributes published by user code in job
description: Note - beyond the below, see the design doc at http://goo.gl/rVnIFq Use Case Stefano Belforte who is co-coordinating the CMS Physics Support project within CMS Computing has requested the ability to have the job publish custom attributes in the job ad at job completion. Specifically, he needs to be able to publish an application-specific error code that is not expressible in the job exit status published by condor. Having this information in the job ad will make it possible to write better job policy expressions (e.g. automatic retry for specific types of failures). It will also make it easier for users to query the status of their completed jobs using condor_history --- obviating the need to dig through output files to gain access to this information. Weakness of Current Solutions Currently, the user code in the job can publish custom attributes by using condor_chirp's set_job_attr command. There are two reasons why this is not a good solution for CMS: To enable chirp, one must submit the job with WantIOProxy=True. This tells the shadow to allow all chirp commands. This gives the job a great deal of power. It can read and write any file on the submit machine that the user has permission to access. It can also change any attribute in the job that the user has permission to change. The user's submit environment is therefore quite vulnerable in the event of a security compromise of any execute machine. The chirp set_job_attr command generates a durable transaction in the schedd job queue log each time it is called. Any extra transactions are undesired, because they can severely impact performance of the schedd. Proposed Solution We propose that the job write attributes into a file, and on exit of the job, these attributes get published into the job ad in the same transaction as other attributes that are updated in the final job update (exit status, memory usage, etc.). If this file exists while the job is running, it will also be used to update attributes in the periodic update of the job ad. The submit side will control which custom attributes are allowed to be set using a white-list that is the union of a schedd-wide configuration and a job-specific setting. For flexibility, the white-list should support wildcards. If the job attempts to set an attribute that does not match the white-list, the shadow will log a complaint but will proceed without error. Failure to open, read, and parse the attribute file for any reason other than that the file does not exist will cause the job to go on hold with a descriptive error message if the error happens after the job has exited. If the error happens while the job is still running, the starter will log an error message but will otherwise ignore the failure. Failure to update the job ad during the final update will be handled as it is today: if all retry attempts fail, the job stays in the queue and may be restarted at a later time. Failure to update the job ad during a periodic update will also be handled as it is today: the periodic update is not critical and is handled in a non-durable transaction (no sync to disk). If the same attribute is set multiple times, the last setting takes effect. Details The file written by the job to publish custom attributes will be named .job.report.attrs. The full path to it (including its name) will be in the environment variable $_CONDOR_JOB_REPORT_ATTRS_FILE. It will be located in $_CONDOR_SCRATCH_DIR. The white-list will be configured with JOB_REPORT_ATTRS. The per-job white-list will be set in the submit file with the command job_report_attrs, which will create a job attribute named JobReportAttrs. Alternate Solutions A new chirp command could be added set_job_report_attr to add an attribute to the list of attributes to be bundled into the periodic and final updates. This list should be maintained by the starter so that shadow restarts do not lose the information. Additional controls could be added on the submit side to limit the chirp operations that are allowed. For example, if the submit side is configured with a white-list of job report attributes, but WantIOProxy is false, chirp could be enabled only for set_job_report_attr and not for other operations. The chirp mechanism has the advantage of allowing independent processes within the job to publish attributes without coordinating with each other. If the job is composed of different software packages, glexec pluggins, wrappers, etc. that were written by different authors, this could be important. The file-based mechanism, on the other hand, would require the different processes to avoid clobbering each other's updates to the file. The latter could be achieved, for example, if the file is only ever appended to, never truncated or replaced.
remarks: 2013-May-13 08:35:58 by bbockelm: Hi, I have a tree for the alternate solution posted here: https://github.com/bbockelm/htcondor/tree/V7_9-remoteupdates-branch I added: Split authorization between remote I/O and remote updates. You can now choose to enable one but not the other. New chirp command, "set_job_attr_volatile". This causes updates to travel via the existing periodic update mechanism used for resource updates. The update is sent to the schedd via a non-durable transaction (no job log fsync) in the same classad as the other updates (no extra DC operations). This makes chirp-based updates essentially zero-cost in terms of resources, but possibly lossy and delayed by a few minutes. This makes the mechanism appropriate for large-scale monitoring. Allowed condor_chirp to locate the chirp.config file (renamed to .chirp.config to match .machine.ad and .job.ad) via environment variable. Previously, you had to send the update from the job $IWD - possibly hard to maintain in a glidein environment. The environment variable is (I think) a more flexible mechanism. title: Ticket #6151: Make documented flag names human-readable.
description: In particular, 'odi' and 'sfr' are odious. Flags that are specific to AWS should probably begin -aws (we can add a general version of the flag later, if it turns out be generalizable). We probably have better things to do than to think about this too hard, but I'm proposing the following based on our discussions. Some of the option names get rather long, but if we're worried about them not working for Azure, we don't have a lot of choice (but see below for an idea about that). This help assumes GT# 6113 in the 'user data' section. -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- usage: condor_annex -annex-name <annex-name> -count|-slots <number> For on-demand instances: [-aws-on-demand] -count <integer number of instances> For spot fleet instances: [-aws-spot-fleet] -slots <integer number of weighted capacity units> To set the lease or idle durations: [-duration <lease duration in decimal hours>] [-idle <idle duration in decimal hours>] To customize the annex's HTCondor configuration: [-config-dir </full/path/to/config.d>] To set an instance's user data: [-aws-[default-]user-data[-file] <data|file> ] To customize an AWS on-demand annex: [-aws-on-demand-instance-type <instance-type>] [-aws-on-demand-ami-id <AMI-ID> [-aws-on-demand-security-group-ids <group-ID[,groupID]*> [-aws-on-demand-key-name <key-name>] To use a customize an AWS Spot Fleet annex, specify a JSON config file: [-spot-fleet-config-file <path/to/config.json>] To reprint this help: [-help] Expert mode (specify account and region): [-aws-access-key-file <path/to/access-key-file>] [-aws-secret-key-file <path/to/secret-key-file>] [-aws-ec2-url https://ec2.<region>.amazonaws.com] [-aws-events-url https://events.<region>.amazonaws.com] [-aws-lambda-url https://lambda.<region>.amazonaws.com] [-aws-s3-url https://s3.<region>.amazonaws.com] Expert mode (specify implementation details): [-aws-spot-fleet-lease-function-arn <sfr-lease-function-arn>] [-aws-on-demand-lease-function-arn <odi-lease-function-arn>] [-aws-on-demand-instance-profile-arn <instance-profile-arn>] -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- I discussed this briefly with TJ, and it seems like some of the option names are getting rather long. My proposal to address this, which we agreed seemed both reasonable and implementable, had two parts: (1) Break the -aws off the front of the options and make it its own flag, which is set by default. That way you only have to type it (or -azure, if and when that happens) once. (2) Break the -on-demand off the new front of the options and make it its own flag, which is set by default. That way you only have to type it (or -spot-fleet) once. This has the nice implementation side-effect of allowing the AWS-, on-demand-, and spot- specific parsing/setup to happen in different functions. To further encourage parsimony, we thought it would make sense for the -on-demand and -spot-fleet flags to become options whose argument specifies the size of the annex. We could keep -count as a general flag of you don't specify an annex type; TJ and like the idea, however, of having a general flag for the count as well, because having a single positional argument sometimes looks real funny.

title: Ticket #1381: PCRE compilation issues in "proper" mode
description: Brian Bockelman submitted the following to condor-admin: I noticed that there appears to be no way to compile 7.5.1 in "proper" mode. This is apparently because the new ClassAd library depends on PCRE, and "-lpcre" is not added to the linking set if proper mode is set (or --without-externals is thrown). The patch below fixes the autoconf file to do two things: If externals are on, but no external for PCRE is set, it will try to take it from the build environment. If externals are off, take PCRE from the build environment. Using the patch below, I can compile even on the latest Fedora with this command ./configure --disable-gcc-version-check --disable-glibc-version-check --disable-static --without-externals (Some hand-hacking remains to get vm-gahp to not be enabled in proper mode; --without-libvirt is apparently not strong enough, and the version of libvirt in the latest Fedora does not appear to be compatible with vm-gahp. I'm sure someone else will tackle this.) Brian diff --git a/src/configure.ac b/src/configure.ac index d52eac0..5c1b558 100644 --- a/src/configure.ac +++ b/src/configure.ac @@ -3075,11 +3075,16 @@ fi CHECK_EXTERNAL([pcre], [7.6], [hard], [use PCRE (provides regular expression support)], MF_LIB_CHECK([pcre], [[pcre pcre_compile]], [PCRE])) + AS_IF([test "x$cv_ext_pcre" = xyes], [CPPFLAGS_save="$CPPFLAGS" CPPFLAGS="$CPPFLAGS $PCRE_CFLAGS" AC_CHECK_HEADERS([pcre.h pcre/pcre.h]) - CPPFLAGS="$CPPFLAGS_save"]) + CPPFLAGS="$CPPFLAGS_save"] + [AC_CHECK_HEADERS([pcre.h], [], [AC_MSG_ERROR([PCRE headers not found or incompatible])]) + AC_CHECK_LIB([pcre], [pcre_study], [HAVE_PCRE="yes"; PCRE_LDFLAGS="$PCRE_LDFLAGS -lpcre"], [AC_MSG_ERROR([PCRE library not found or incompatible ])]) + ] +) AC_SUBST(PCRE_LDFLAGS, $PCRE_LDFLAGS) AC_SUBST(PCRE_CFLAGS, $PCRE_CFLAGS) @@ -3333,6 +3338,11 @@ else AC_SUBST(want_ext_glibc,NO) AC_SUBST(ext_glibc_version,UNUSED) +# We still need PCRE, even if we're not using externals, due to ClassAd library + AC_CHECK_HEADERS([pcre.h], [], [AC_MSG_ERROR([PCRE headers not found or incompatible])]) + AC_CHECK_LIB([pcre], [pcre_study], [HAVE_PCRE="yes"; PCRE_LDFLAGS="$PCRE_LDFLAGS -lpcre"], [AC_MSG_ERROR([PCRE library not found or incompatible ])]) + AC_SUBST(PCRE_LDFLAGS, $PCRE_LDFLAGS) + fi # END of if $ac_cv_has_externals = "YES" or $enable_proper = yes

title: Ticket #4479: Invalid security sessions re-used repeatedly.
description: If a client (a Condor-C GAHP) contacts a server (a remote schedd) with an invalid session (as it would after the schedd crashes and restarts), and the network does not permit a reverse connection (to the client's UDP command port?), the client will never realize its connections are being dropped because of an invalid session. The lease added in #1169 is ineffective because the lease is renewed on each attempt to use it, rather than each success. This prevents Condor-C from working after a schedd restart. The recommended course of action is to shoot our protocol into the sun. Failing that, we could move session lease renewal to after a successful security negotiation (handshake?).
remarks: 2014-Jul-22 15:02:57 by bbockelm: Currently, when an invalid security session is used, IIRC, we immediately close the socket. Don't suppose it's possible to send back an error message? For the python bindings, we basically have to fork a subprocess any time we want to do an authenticated session in order to avoid this issue. 2014-Jul-22 15:44:37 by tlmiller: > Currently, when an invalid security session is used, IIRC, we immediately > close the socket. That's why it's so hard for the client to know that the problem is an invalid security session. > Don't suppose it's possible to send back an error message? We do, but not on the connection before we close it -- we open a wholly new reverse connection which doesn't succeed (because of the firewall, I assume). Unless you mean "is it possible to change the protocol to send back an error message on the same connection", to which the answer is "probably, but I'd have to ask Zach." I assume the reason we used an out-of-band message in the first place is because it was less painful than changing the protocol. > For the python bindings, we basically have to fork a subprocess any time we > want to do an authenticated session in order to avoid this issue. We should be able to do better, especially since we _already_ forked a sub process (the CGAHP worker thread). 2014-Jul-22 16:15:58 by tlmiller: An important note: this can only happen because the schedd is reacquiring the same port number. This is happening because the firewall only has one port open, but because we don't need to talk to anything other than the schedd (and to minimize other configuration changes in the SWAMP), I didn't use the shared port daemon. The shared port daemon would rebind to the same port, but the second instance of the schedd would get a different shared port ID, so the old session couldn't be used again. (This will stop helping if we change the shared port daemon to reuse IDs for restarted daemons, as we've been thinking about.) In normal situations, the only HTCondor daemon that would rebind to the same port on restart would be the collector. It's possible that we don't see this problem with the collector because collectors can usually reach their startds via UDP. title: Ticket #4183: Preemption due to stale public ads
description: There's currently a race condition in the negotiator. It queries for the startd public ads and, in a separate query, queries for private ads. It's possible for the startd to update the ads between the two queries - resulting in the negotiator having a copy of the old public ad and new private ad. Because the old public ad may indicate the slot is unclaimed, it will match jobs to the slot - and the jobs will successfully preempt using the preemption claim from the new private ad. Two fixes are proposed: (Stable and dev series) Query for private ads first, then public ads. The race condition is that the negotiator may try to preempt based on a new public ad but the preemption will fail due to a stale private ad. A bit of waste is an improvement over improper preemption! this is #4185 (Dev series only) Have the startd advertise the public claim ID and use this as a foreign key to join with the private ad. The two should always match if the ads were updated at the same time. Any slots that would have triggered the race condition will fail to negotiate this round (but work in the next). While a more thorough solution than above, it also requires the startds to be updated (so we must do this along with the prior suggestion). We want to avoid any fixes that assume the results returned are an atomic snapshot of the collector database (this is true now, but we may want to change this in order to avoid having to fork child collector processes). This is why we do not query the private ads and public ads at once.

title: Ticket #4029: condor_sos - a tool for the admin to manage a swamped daemon
description: Imagine a HTCondor daemon like the condor_schedd under such extreme load that client commands like condor_q timeout. To fix the problem, the administrator would like to inspect what is going on, run a few condor_q commands to see what is happening, maybe run some condor_hold or condor_rm commands, etc. But unfortunately, the administrator cannot get in a word edgewise to the swamped daemon, and therefore cannot really do anything intelligent to fix/diagnose the problem! Proposed enhancement is for daemons to have an unadvertised "super" command port for use by the administrator; incoming commands to this port are serviced ahead of all other incoming commands. This way the administrator has a reasonable chance of not having their commands time out, even if the daemon is extremely busy. For now, this super command port will not be advertised in any classads. To create a super command port, place <SUBSYSTEM>_SUPER_ADDRESS_FILE in the config file to specify where to write a file with the super command port (just like the regular ADDRESS_FILE). Administrators will then be able to use the condor_sos command line tool to access this special port, for instance "condor_sos condor_q" or "condor_sos condor_hold abusiveUser". In addition, if the user running a client tool to talk to a local daemon happens to be root, then the super command port will also be used. In other words, if root runs "condor_q" it is equivalent to running "condor_sos condor_q".

title: Ticket #5268: Fix manual page for condor_transfer_data
description: Per htcondor-staff email with Todd Miller, and acknowledgement by Todd Tannenbaum
remarks: 2015-Sep-23 15:16:05 by tlmiller: I came across the section of the manual for "condor_transfer_data", and believe it could use a bit of clarification, as I found myself very (SUPER) confused. See: http://research.cs.wisc.edu/htcondor/manual/current/condor_transfer_data.html Some example text, below, and my confusion: *"condor_transfer_data* causes HTCondor to transfer spooled data. It is meant to be used in conjunction with the *-spool* option of *condor_submit*, as in condor_submit -spool mysubmitfile Submission of a job with the *-spool* option causes HTCondor to spool all input files, the job event log, and any proxy across a connection to the machine where the *condor_schedd* daemon is running. After spooling these files, the machine from which the job is submitted may disconnect from the network or modify its local copies of the spooled files." For "causes HTCondor to transfer spooled data": In which direction, from what machine to what machine, and under what other conditions, is data transferred? What is the order of events? Is this at the end of the job or when data is first transferred to the sandbox on the execute node? What does it mean to "spool" all input files. What happens to them and where do they go if "spooled"? Should this section point to a better explanation of "spool"? Why or in what instances would I want this? In which cases (desired or undesired) would the submission machine disconnect from the network or modify its local copies of the spooled files? What's different if "-spool" isn't used? I think the use of "may" with "or" also adds ambiguity here. Is a disconnection something that is more prone to happen (not of the user's desire) if spool is used or is it a disconnection easier to recover from when using spool? How do I know if/when/why the machine would disconnect -OR- modify it's local copies of the spooled files? "When the job finishes, the job has JobStatus = 4, meaning that the job has completed. The output of the job is spooled, and *condor_transfer_data* retrieves the output of the completed job." So condor_transfer_data retrieves the data from the spool and then copies it to the submission directory? If not to the submission directory, then to where? 2015-Sep-23 15:17:00 by tlmiller: I agree. The man page could be a lot better -- I think it was trying to compactly explain the intended usage scenario, but ended up being less helpful than a simple link to a longer introduction. > For "causes HTCondor to transfer spooled data": In which direction, from > what machine to what machine, and under what other conditions, is data > transferred? The first sentence should probably read something like "condor_transfer_data transfers a spooled job's output to the current directory." Hopefully that makes it clear that the transfer happens immediately (when you call condor_transfer_data). > What is the order of events? Is this at the end of the job or when data is > first transferred to the sandbox on the execute node? Likewise, I hope this question is answered by the reformulation above. > What does it mean to "spool" all input files. What happens to them and > where do they go if "spooled"? Should this section point to a better > explanation of "spool"? Why or in what instances would I want this? I agree that the man page should point to a longer introduction, and tend to think that we should just omit the smaller inline explanation. My longer attempt to actually answer your questions follows. (It may save you some time to note here that the '-remote' option to condor_submit is equivalent to '-spool -name'.) Suppose that you're working on your laptop. You've made some clever change to your Matlab code, or maybe just come some interesting data from some instrument you attached to the laptop. Either way, uploading files to the submit node is a pain (whether it's using scp or if you don't have access to gluster from your laptop or whatever); or maybe you're just not sure which files you changed, and don't want to spend the time to transfer all of them. Instead of transferring files and then submitting a job, you can use 'condor_submit -spool -name submit-3.chtc.wisc.edu ...' (or wherever) and Condor will transfer the job's input files from your laptop to the submit node for you. Rather than picking some random part of your home directory to store your job's files, Condor (the schedd) takes responsibility for managing them and stores them its 'spool' directory. Once condor_submit has finished transferring the job's input files, the job proceeds as normal with its directory in spool effectively being its submission directory. At this point, the job is entirely independent of your laptop -- whether you disconnect it from the network (because you went home, because it's low on battery), change the files that were part of the job, or whatever. At some point, you learn that the job has finished. (Condor can send you mail. ;)) When you do, you can run condor_transfer_data to get the output sandbox. (Since the job's spool directory is its submission directory, the output goes there.) In older version of Condor, running condor_transfer_data before the job finished may not have worked, depending on file permissions. You can also use -spool without -name, in case all you want the ability to continue to change your files while the job is in queue, but I think we generally don't like it when people do that (it uses a lot of disk space and can be abused in the presence of quotas). 2015-Sep-23 15:17:40 by tlmiller: Lauren also mentioned a mail from ToddT that she found considerably more illuminating than the manual, and much shorter than my own. :) 2015-Sep-23 16:30:08 by tlmiller: Proposal, pending a better example to crib from. \Description Use \Condor{transfer\_data} to fetch a job's output after submitting it with the \Opt{-spool} or \Opt{-remote} options. You may call \Condor{transfer\_data} at any time, but if you call it before the job attribute \Attr{JobStatus} equals 4 (completed), you may not get the all of the job's output. Data transfer begins immediately and will be complete when \Condor{transfer\_data} returns (unless an error occurs). After transfer, the location(s) of output on disk will be the same as if the job had not been submitted with the \Opt{-spool} or \Opt{-remote} options. For more details on HTCondor file transfer, please consult [FIXME]. For more information about why you might choose to use the \Opt{-spool} or \Opt{-remote} options, please consult [FIXME].

title: Ticket #5792: Problem with default JOB_DEFAULT_REQUESTMEMORY
description: Reported by Stuart via Tom to Condor ticket system. The default setting of JOB_DEFAULT_REQUESTMEMORY, ifThenElse(MemoryUsage ! UNDEFINED,MemoryUsage,(ImageSize+1023)/1024) appears to be problematic for jobs submitted without RequestMemory under HTCondor 8.4.7 and Partitionable slots if they are preempted and need to match/run again. In particular, I noticed that a number of jobs in the LIGO CIT SL7.2 pool that where relying on this default where being rejected by partitionable slot STARTD’s with, 07/09/16 15:07:44 slot1_3: New machine resource of type -1 allocated 07/09/16 15:07:44 Setting up slot pairings 07/09/16 15:07:44 slot1_3: Slot requirements not satisfied. 07/09/16 15:07:44 slot1_3: Job ad was ============================ However, if I condor_qedit RequestMemory to be quantize(ImageSize/1024,1) then jobs are not rejected and start in a dynamic slot. I believe there are a few problems: 0) Sec 3.5.1.19 states a different default default value, http://research.cs.wisc.edu/htcondor/manual/v8.4/3_5Policy_Configuration.html#37135 JOB_DEFAULT_REQUESTMEMORY = ifThenElse(MemoryUsage =!= UNDEFINED, MemoryUsage, 1) then what I observe and what is stated in Sec 3.3.13, http://research.cs.wisc.edu/htcondor/manual/v8.4/3_3Configuration.html#25623 ifThenElse(MemoryUsage =!= UNDEFINED,MemoryUsage,(ImageSize+1023)/1024) 1) It looks like RequestMemory must be an integer to be effective. I first tried manually calculating a reasonable RequestMemory value for a test job and entered that via condor_qedit as a real number. However, even when I seriously inflated the value STARTD for the partitionable slot would still reject the job until I rounded that to an integer. 2) Even with STARTD_DEBUG = D_ALL I was unable to find a mention in StartLog of what “Slot requirements” where not satisfied. I think it would be very helpful to log this and make it easy to access, e.g., from a submit machine I would love to see “condor_q -better-analyze JobId” report details on the last failed attempt to start a job (if there was a match that was rejected). 3) Attempting to use the ResidentSetSize directly (or via MemoryUsage) in RequestMemory did not work (even after rounding to an integer). I did not investigate this very much, but I believe startd is not happy if RequestMemory is less than ImageSize. At any rate, the following was successful in getting a number of otherwise idle jobs running, A) Make a list of idle jobs requesting less memory than ImageSize before and after running qedit, condor_q -constraint "(jobstatus == 1) && (RequestMemory < ImageSize/1024)" -af globaljobid RequestMemory ImageSize/1024 B) Set all of those jobs to track their ImageSize, condor_qedit -constraint "(jobstatus == 1) && (RequestMemory < ImageSize/1024)" RequestMemory "quantize(ImageSize/1024,1)" C) Change the default setting for new user jobs being submitted, [root@ldas-pcdev2 ~]# cat /etc/condor/config.d/memory JOB_DEFAULT_REQUESTMEMORY = quantize(ImageSize/1024,1)

title: Ticket #137: Improve documentation for testing system
description: The current testing system (in /src/condor_tests ) is documented, but it's erratic, incomplete, complex, and in some cases out of date. Documentation is scattered between several files. They have a recommended reading order. The reader is encouraged to ignore the WISDOM* files. These should be unified. (The files in question are: /src/condor_tests/README /src/condor_tests/README.filenames /src/condor_tests/README.imake /src/condor_tests/README.running /src/condor_tests/README.testclass /src/condor_tests/WISDOM.C-tests /src/condor_tests/WISDOM.Fortran ) The documentation needs to be reviewed to ensure that it is up to date. src/condor_tests/README.filenames suggests that output goes into the condor_tests directory, but new practices are to give each test its own subdirectory. The documentation needs to be complete. For example, /src/condor_tests/README.testclass documents 4 different test classes, but the code currently contains about 15 (btdebug condorc core dagman env filexfer framework full lib local long performance quick quicknolink simple) CondorTest.pm needs better, and more complete documentation. Every function a test might use should be documented. The file as a whole needs some general guidelines on a big picture usage, perhaps with a simple test case. The documentation should probably be valid POD, so that someone can generate a nice document if they want. We might want to move sort or all of the documentation into the the wiki. Advantages to keeping it in the code: it's Right There; and it's visible to external collaborators until the wiki is public. Advantages to the wiki: Details about the test are usually cross-version, so we don't need to maintain and merge forks of the documentation; the wiki becomes increasingly The Place for developer documentation; and pretty formatting.
remarks: The Readme files are as they originally were and are still accurate. There have been a few instances of new tests going in separate directories but the mass of 1000s of files has been this way since derek set it up. I'd love to not find things by using ls and sub patterns. Its just another case of priorities... :-(
creator: adesmet

title: Ticket #4300: Job left queue after failed file transfer w/ MAX_TRANSFER_QUEUE_AGE
description: Customer reports the following problem: I had a file transfer failure (download) due to the transfer exceeding the MAX_TRANSFER_QUEUE_AGE. That is not the problem. I like that feature. The problem is that condor treated the job like it had succeeded. This was particularly problematic because the job was part of a much larger DAG job. Dagman assumed the job completed successfully and submitted all of its children. The children in turn failed because they depend on the output file of the parent job as an input file. I can see how someone might want it both ways (fail or not based on a failed file transfer). Would it be possible to add a flag to the submit file stating that if the file transfer fails the job should be treated as incomplete and run again?

title: Ticket #4750: Excessive port usage when using shared port and CCB (HIGHPORT/LOWPORT)
description: This problem probably affects version earlier than 8.2.2, but that's the earliest version I've confirmed. In the following scenario, the shared port daemon will rapidly become unable to forward/complete (CCB) connections. I'm not sure what those connections do, but the visible symptom is slots falling out of the claimed status for no discernible reason. condor_shared_port will fail to forward/complete connections because it can't bind a port when it calls connect_socketpair(), which it does under certain circumstances. The following log snippet demonstrates the problem: 12/03/14 11:40:58 CCBListener: received request to connect to STARTER <128.104.103.7:9787?CCBID=128.104.100.22:9764%3fnoUDP%26sock%3dcollector#3& sock=24920_24ee_651> on <128.104.103.7:34013> with reverse connect address <128.104.103.7:9787?CCBID=128.104.100.22:9764%3fnoUDP%26sock%3dcollector#3& sock=28485_025f_3>, request id 6536. 12/03/14 11:40:58 Bypassing connection to shared port server <128.104.103.7:9787?CCBID=128.104.100.22:9764%3fnoUDP%26sock%3dcollector#3>, because that is me. 12/03/14 11:40:58 get_port_range - (LOWPORT,HIGHPORT) is (9700,9800). 12/03/14 11:40:58 Sock::bindWithin - failed to bind to port 9739: Address already in use ... 12/03/14 11:40:58 Sock::bindWithin - failed to bind any port within (9700 ~ 9800) 12/03/14 11:40:58 connect_socketpair: failed in tmp_srv.bind() 12/03/14 11:40:58 CLOSE <128.104.103.7:0> fd=14 12/03/14 11:40:58 Failed to connect to loopback socket, so failing to connect via local shared port access to daemon at <128.104.103.7:9787>. 12/03/14 11:40:58 CLOSE <128.104.103.7:9730> fd=13 12/03/14 11:40:58 CCBListener: failed to create reversed connection for request id 6536 to <128.104.103.7:9787?CCBID=128.104.100.22:9764%3fnoUDP%26sock%3dcollector#3 &sock=28485_025f_3>: failed to initiate connection where "because that is me" appears to mean that the reverse address ("call me back at this number") includes the same shared port daemon as is currently doing the CCB reversal. Do not depend on this analysis. GregT suggests the problem is that connect_socketpair() is creating a socket either without SO_LINGER set to false (which I'm not sure is possible in our codebase), or perhaps SO_REUSEADDR (which is normally only set for command ports). There may (also?) be another problem where we don't close sockets properly as part of our normal operation -- as far as I can tell, things are working as expected before this problem occurs. The scenario is as follows: I have a central manager with a schedd and an execute node. The execute node is configured to use CCB and shared port, and has HIGHPORT and LOWPORT set to a range of 100 ports. (This generally seems to be sufficient for normal operation in the BaTLab.) This configuration is useful for testing, but it also currently our only way of specifying a range of ports for the shared port daemon to choose from, which is useful for glide-ins. I submit 300 10-second sleep jobs; the execute node has 24 slots. After about 100 jobs, this problem appears, and 'netstat' is full of sockets in TIME_WAIT. title: Ticket #7193: Schedd blocked for 5 minutes on ssh_to_job
description: Today, I encountered a situation where the schedd on submit-1.chtc.wisc.edu was blocked for 5 minutes. The cause was a deadlock triggered by ssh-to-job, which I don't believe has been reported before. Here are the legs of the deadlock: In response to a GET_JOB_CONNECT_INFO request, the schedd is making a blocking connection to the starter to do a CREATE_JOB_OWNER_SEC_SESSION command. The CEDAR timeout is 300 seconds. The starter is about to start the job and is making a begin_execution RPC to the shadow. Having just finished input file transfer, the shadow is attempting to connect to the schedd to push job ad changes related to the transfer. The CEDAR timeout is 300 seconds. As a short term fix, the schedd's timeout for CREATE_JOB_OWNER_SEC_SESSION could be shortened (years of careful research would suggest 20 seconds). In the long term, making one of the connection attempts non-blocking would be better.
remarks: 2019-Aug-08 15:34:27 by jfrey: The timeout for schedd connecting to the startd and starter was originally 20 seconds. It was increased to 300 seconds in #5070. 2019-Aug-20 13:56:46 by jfrey: Restoring the old timeout value of 20 seconds for now.

title: Ticket #422: Fetch hook broken on Windows.
description: From: https://bugzilla.redhat.com/show_bug.cgi?id=497895 Description of problem: A simple fetch hook that does "exit 0" on Windows will run a number of times and then block the startd. The result is the startd is killed and restarted by the master, which starts the cycle again. While hung the startd does not advertise itself and is not responsive to condor_status -direct. Version-Release number of selected component (if applicable): 7.2.2 How reproducible: 100% Additional info: It is presume that this is related to pipe closing code, and potentially fast pid re-use on Windows. It may also be a timing problem, wherein the hook exists, closes its fds before the call to DaemonCore::PidEntry::pipeFullWrite(), with then fails. Looks like Ian Chesal and friends on condor-users have gathered up additional information on this problem (or a very closely related one).
remarks: 2009-May-14 12:28:36 by burnett: Problem break down: Fetch Work code creates a HookClient object with pipes to capture input, output, etc. if requested. The fact that it creates a pipe to capture stdin is most important to us. The registration of the stdin pipe calls PipeEnd::set_registered() and PipeEnd::set_watched(); which is to say, the pid watching code in daemonCore will monitor the pipe's state. The pipe watching code, now in control, first calls ReadPipeEnd::pre_wait() to "simulate the semantics of select" by starting asynchronous reading on the pipe (returning an event hadle that can be monitored for a signal--used in place of a process or thread handle by the pid watcher). This is quickly followed by a call to ReadPipeEnd::post_wait() which finishes any outstanding i/o and sets a signal to reflect the fact that it is no longer managed by the pid watcher. At this point, we see the hook client completing its work (signals are handled before pipes, but in this case, the signal is dispatched after the signal handling has been done [so it gets caught on the next pump of DaemonCore::Driver()). Instead of the pipes being cleaned up at this point, we see a call to ReadPipeEnd::io_ready(), wich returns true since by this point all reading is complete. Unfortunately, at this point in the code this return value is interpreted as if to mean that the pipe is also ready to be read from. (The semantics of this seem broken in this case, as it seems this call now has a double meaning: i.e. that no, there is no outstanding i/o or an error, and that yes, this pipe can continue to be read from [even if the pipe has signaled to pid watcher and told it that there is nothing left to read.].) Since the state of the ReadPipeEnd object contains no error (because the ReadPipeEnd::post_wait(), called above, succeeds), another call to the pipe handler is performed, due to the ReadPipeEnd::io_ready() returning the affirmative. After the pipe handler is called in DaemonCore::Driver() the pipe is once again added to the pid watcher, since the pipe has not been closed by its handler. Finally, the process reaper calls the pipe handler one last time and tries to close the pipe. This close attempt calls pipeHandler(), then DaemonCore::Close_Pipe(), then DaemonCore::Cancel_Pipe(), which hangs on PipeEnd::cancel() because it is still being watched by the pid watcher thread. 2009-May-14 12:31:15 by burnett: To reproduce the problem, add the following condor_config entries: STARTD_JOB_HOOK_KEYWORD = BROKEN BROKEN_HOOK_DIR = c:/condor/hooks BROKEN_HOOK_FETCH_WORK = $(BROKEN_HOOK_DIR)/fetch.bat FETCHWORKDELAY = 0 Where fetch.bat contains one line: @exit 0 Restart Condor and tail the startd log file. 2009-Aug-14 12:31:15 by rrati: The [14601] changes breaks job hooks in the startd/starter for hooks that are started, but not really cared about (reply & status hooks). The startd/starter fires off those hooks but doesn't care about the output of the hook. With [14601], the stdin pipe is being closed when the HookClient is deleted which prevents the data actually making it to the hook's stdin. Should we should roll back the changes from this commit? 2009-Aug-14 17:09:29 by tannenba: Hi Rob! Couple quick questions w/o fully context switching to look at the code involved and swapping back in all the context needed to be authoritative, so sorry if these questions are ignorant: Without looking closely at the code, if we revert [14601], aren't handles/descriptors being leaked? How does data not making it to the stdin of the hook "break" the hook? Shouldn't the hook just go away if stdin is closed out on it before it can read what it needs? 2009-Aug-17 08:51:55 by rrati: 1) As I was looking into what was happening with the hooks, I was noticing that without the changes in #422 it looked like fds were being leaked in the reply hook case. It's likely the same story with the status hook as well. I also need to dig into the fd situation more in these cases. 2) Data not making it to the hook "breaks" the hook from the usability perspective. If no data makes it to the hook stdin, then any hook that relies on that data will no longer work. The documentation calls out the data that should be available to the hooks in their stdins and without that data, there's really no way to tell which job a hook is being called for. 2009-Aug-17 09:00:36 by tannenba: While I am sympathetic to the hook usability factor, I guess the leaking of resources by daemons/services worries me more. Seems like we need to dig a bit deeper before simply reverting [14601]. Thanks. 2009-Aug-17 10:01:12 by rrati: File descriptors are not being leaked. pipeFullWrite will close the stdin pipe when all data has been written to the stdin pipe or there is an error writing to the pipe. All job hooks have data passed to the stdin, so there is no need to close the stdin pipe in any other place. All the changes for #422 should be reverted. 2009-Aug-17 10:17:20 by tannenba: Right then. [14601] reverted. 2009-Sep-04 09:51:20 by ichesal: Bump. Any updates on this guys? I've got about 1 more week where I can hold out and then...well...I'm looking at a full system re-architect. We bet the farm on hooks working in 7.2.x. Thanks. 2009-Sep-15 14:51:13 by pmackinn: Reproducibility notes: Multi-core seems more immune to problems (I have an 8-way box) to the point where my test hook will randomly render the expected output. In other words, pipes can get closed (not just stdin) before the fetched hook job is completed. title: Ticket #4615: Removed jobs go back to running
description: The CMS pool is having issues with jobs running after they have been "condor_rm"'d - causing many user complaints and inconsistent monitoring issues. Jaime and I did some detective work, and the sequence is like this: User kills task schedd sends SIGUSR1 to condor_dagman, indicating it should kill all jobs and exit condor_dagman does "condor_rm -const $STUFF" which matches all the jobs in the task Job starts staging out files, gets a glexec error. Job goes on hold. After a few minutes, glexec error is automatically cleared by PeriodicRelease. Job is now idle. Job goes back to executing. title: Ticket #6628: Customize new START expression when draining starts
description: Currently, when condor_drain or condor_defrag cause a startd to drain, that startd unconditionally but temporarily sets its START expression to the hard-coded constant FALSE. It would be nice if, when the startd was told to drain, it could also be given a START expression to use while draining. This expression would only apply to "graceful" draining (the default), where both MaxJobRetirementTime and MachineMaxVacateTime are honored; it doesn't seem to make sense for the other types of draining ("quick" and "fast"), where we don't expect there to be a useful amount of time to "backfill" into. Obviously, condor_defrag will require a new knob, and condor_drain a new command-line option, to activate this new feature. Once we allow new jobs to start while we're draining, we need to consider how to exit draining state, since the current implementation just sets MaxJobRetirementTime and vacates every slot. The obvious extension would be to do the same thing for each new job we accept, adjusting MaxJobRetirementTime to hit the deadline (that is, drain start time + max job retirement time) as we go, but this has a serious drawback: new jobs would then exit, and draining therefore complete, at the original deadline, regardless of when the last original job exits. You could try to mitigate this by only accepting short jobs, but that forces the admin to choose between "backfill" efficiency (potentially creating a lot of churn as jobs continually restart) and draining efficiency (the longer the "backfill" jobs can run, the longer you have to wait past the end of the last "original" job). Instead, we will have the startd preempt every slot when the last of the "original" jobs exits. (In addition to seeming 'natural', this solution has the advantage that it allows the regression test for this to avoid some race conditions.) Naturally, we need to provide for a different MaxJobRetirementTime for this preemption, or else we've effectively doubled the max draining time. For the initial release of this feature, we're hard-coding that time to 0 (but not changing MaxJobVacateTime, so self-checkpointing jobs will still work). Likewise, once we enter this preempting phase, we need to unconditionally set the START expression to FALSE. Finally, we also need to invalidate all claim IDs to avoid potential race conditions with the negotiator giving out claims based on an out-of-date ad (which could refragment the startd). (Arguably, we should invalidate all claim IDs whenever the START expression changes, and that may be the easiest way to implement this.) Hopefully, we won't have to change anything for the "automatically resume normal operation after a drain" code to work, although it would also need to reset MaxJobVacateTime to its normal value. For the convenience of administrators, the startd will set a new attribute, AcceptedWhileDraining, appropriately for each slot.
remarks: 2018-Apr-03 16:02:53 by tlmiller: Previous remarks removed as they were incorporated into the description. Current remarks: We hope at some point want to change the default START expression during drain from FALSE to 'MaxJobRetirementTime == 0'. The defragd may need a little help dealing with resources claimed by preemptible jobs when deciding how many machines to drain. This may require advertising Drained{CPUs,Memory,Disk,<custom machine resources>} in the pslot ad, where a "Drained" resource is either unclaimed or claimed by a preemptible job. 2018-Apr-10 16:32:39 by tlmiller: Regression testing assigned to another ticket. 2018-Apr-14 19:55:16 by tlmiller: I found 41 stack dumps (containing the string ZN6Reqexp7unavailEPN7classad8ExprTreeE; there may have been others) in the logs of the tests in April (whichever ones hadn't been purged by the 14th). These crashes started April 10, when this ticket, which changed Reqexp::unavail(), was merged in. Distressingly, this also appears to be as far back as our test logs go. Analysis indicates the problem is that ResMgr::walk() is calling Resource::shutdownAllClaims() on a Resource that has been delete()d. The initial approach will be to alter ResMgr::walk() to avoid doing so; a patch to do so is under testing. title: Ticket #1378: force-auth commands broken when security negotiation off
description: When SEC_DEFAULT_NEGOTIATION=NEVER or anything equivalent that causes security negotiation not to happen, DaemonCore rejects commands that are registered with force_authentication=true. The fix that Zach and I agreed on is to make DaemonCore do the authentication for the incoming connection. This means that we can eventually remove all of the server-side code that does authentication in the command-handler of commands that are registered with force_authentication=true. It would be nice to also remove the client-side code that does the authentication in the command protocol and instead have it done inside of startCommand(). This would either require passing an argument to startCommand() or having built-in knowledge about which commands always require authentication.

title: Ticket #1728: cmd_q_shows-sub-1 does not wait for schedd to update collector
description: The test 'cmd_q_shows-sub-1' fails when run against a newly-created personal Condor. (Long story below.) See http://nmi-s004.cs.wisc.edu/rundir/nmi-devel/2010/10/nmi-devel_nmi-s004.cs.wisc.edu_1287584045_20324/userdir/nmi:x86_deb_5.0/cmd_q_shows-sub-1.out for the exact error message(s), but the problem appears to be that the submit hook doesn't give the schedd any time to update the collector before running the 'condor_q -sub ...' command that fails. I don't know why this succeeds when the personal condor has existed for a while, although I suspect, since the submitter doesn't change from test to test, it's getting back old information for this particular check, and it happens to work. As far as I can tell, this is a race condition that would be easy to trigger in other circumstances, but I don't know if this has shown up in this test intermittently failing. (Long story abbreviation: I'm trying to add the ability to run tests concurrently to Metronome, using a DAG running on the execute node. Condor always cleans up after jobs -- including remote_pre, which deliberately leaves a personal condor running for the tests to share. While this improves test isolation, it does lead to some problems. (Including discovering a bug in detecting whether or not the personal condor is actually runinng.))

title: Ticket #3715: Network-aware matchmaking
description: As a part of the Lark project, Andrew is working on making matchmaking network-aware (design document to follow). The first idea is relatively straightforward - reject matches where the transfer queue is longer than X bytes. Due to the fact that the transfer queue can include match expressions, this rejection must be done in the context of a potential machine ad - and hence in the negotiator. As a first step, we'll need to advertise the TRANSFER_QUEUE_USER_EXPR in the schedd ad so the negotiator can access it. For an example of a non-trivial TRANSFER_QUEUE_USER_EXPR: TRANSFER_QUEUE_USER_EXPR = strcat("Owner_", Owner, "-", ifThenElse(MATCH_EXP_JOBGLIDEIN_ResourceName isnt null, MATCH_EXP_JOBGLIDEIN_ResourceName, "Unknown"))

title: Ticket #2807: Have DAGMan use a single node job user log file
description: We could avoid all of our problems with file descriptor throttles/macros not allowed in log file names/etc by changing the schedd to allow a job to have more than one user log file. So the use could specify whatever log file they wanted in their submit file, but DAGMan wouldn't pay any attention to that file. It would force the job to also log to the default node job log file, and just read that file. That way, DAGMan would only need to read a single log file, and we could solve a bunch of problems at one shot. This would also avoid "polluting" the per-job user logs with POST SCRIPT TERMINATED events. Note that we should probably have a configuration macro to turn on the old log file mode, in case someone needed to use a newer DAGMan with an older schedd. See also #2428, #2759, #2772, #445, #831, #965, #1428, #2053, #2645, #2702, #659. This work is on V7_9-gittrac_2807-branch [done] Added DAGManNodesLog attribute; schedd, shadow, and submit use this attribute to name the default node log. [done] Added dagman_log to submit file [done] DAGman uses default node log to read events [done] Added configuration option to enable old behavior of only one log per job. [done] Add a mask to attenuate the volume of events written to the DAGMan log.

title: Ticket #7756: startd runs scripts for excluded machine resources
description: Right now, if you have MACHINE_RESOURCE_NAMES = foo MACHINE_RESOURCE_INVENTORY_bar = some/path The startd will execute some/path on start-up, which at best violates the principle of least astonishment. Instead, we should pull the list of names on which to call init_machine_resource() from MACHINE_RESOURCE_NAMES, and only use the regex code to generate that list if MACHINE_RESOURCE_NAMES is unset (according to the code's current definition).
creator: tlmiller

remarks: 2011-Apr-27 14:43:36 by bbockelm: At Burt's suggestion (I contributed this patch), I looked into this: Globus mapping is done when the connection is established; the condor mapfile is done later. Based on the results of the mapfile, it determines whether it wants to keep the Globus mapping. Globus is always initialized, even in cases when it will never be used. Judging from the trace, I think the first item was fatal for glidein. 2011-Apr-27 15:08:37 by zmiller: Quick note: Observations 1 and 2 are correct. The code should be refactored so it only calls globus when needed. At one point in time it was quicker (i.e. a quick hack) to do it the way it is currently implemented. Would love to see it redone for 7.7.X. 2012-Aug-27 13:48:46 by zmiller: CODE REVIEW by zmiller: brian's attached patch looks good 2012-Aug-27 16:41:06 by danb: Perhaps I am misreading this patch. By my reading, it causes the following semantic change: if global_map_file==NULL (i.e. CERTIFICATE_MAPFILE is not defined), then GSI-authenticated users are always mapped to the generic "gsi@unmapped" rather than to whatever is in the gridmap file, if anything. 2012-Aug-27 16:47:36 by zmiller: dan: good catch. we definitely want to fall back to using gss_assist_gridmap in the case where there is no CERTIFICATE_MAPFILE defined.
