description: When I try to use condor_submit -i, or condor_ssh_to_job into a job running using singularity containers, it fails with: [khurtado@camlnd ~]$ condor_ssh_to_job -debug 60.0 04/22/20 10:37:01 SharedPortClient: sent connection request to schedd at <x.x.x.x:9618> for shared port id 1679808_2562_3 04/22/20 10:37:01 SharedPortClient: sent connection request to local schedd for shared port id 1679808_2562_3 04/22/20 10:37:01 Response for GET_JOB_CONNECT_INFO: ServerTime = 1587566221 Result = true StarterIpAddr = "<10.32.89.25:9618?addrs=10.32.89.25-9618&noUDP&sock=27245_512d_41>" RemoteHost = "slot1_2@qa-rtx6k-026.crc.nd.edu" CondorVersion = "$CondorVersion: 8.8.8 Feb 17 2020 BuildID: 496171 $" 04/22/20 10:37:01 Got connect info for starter <x.x.x.x:9618?addrs=x.x.x.x-9618&noUDP&sock=27245_512d_41> 04/22/20 10:37:01 SharedPortClient: sent connection request to starter at <10.32.89.25:9618> for shared port id 27245_512d_41 04/22/20 10:37:01 Executing ssh command: ssh -oUser=khurtado -oIdentityFile=/tmp/khurtado.condor_ssh_to_job_ebeeac57/ssh_key -oStrictHostKeyChecking=yes -oUserKnownHostsFile=/tmp/khurtado.condor_ssh_to_job_ebeeac57/known_hosts -oGlobalKnownHostsFile=/tmp/khurtado.condor_ssh_to_job_ebeeac57/known_hosts -oProxyCommand="condor_ssh_to_job"' '"-debug"' '"-proxy"' '"/tmp/khurtado.condor_ssh_to_job_ebeeac57/fdpass" condor-job.xx.crc.nd.edu 04/22/20 10:37:01 Passed ssh connection to ssh proxy. 04/22/20 10:37:01 Setting up ssh proxy on file descriptor 4 Welcome to slot1_2@xx.nd.edu! Your condor job is running with pid(s) 63160. /opt/condor/RedHat7/libexec/condor_ssh_to_job_shell_setup: line 50: /usr/bin/condor_docker_enter: No such file or directory Connection to condor-job.x.x.x.crc.nd.edu closed. This is because in the workers, we have the condor binaries located somewhere else and added to the environment via PATH. Specifically: /opt/condor/RedHat7/bin/condor_docker_enter Condor seems to expect this binary in /usr/bin only: https://github.com/htcondor/htcondor/blob/e9fa217ada022108e5403092adfd9790f2ad0c5b/src/condor_starter.V6.1/condor_ssh_to_job_shell_setup#L50 I think there should some logic that tries to find condor_docker_enter in the environment if it is not found inside /usr/bin, to better deal with this case. For now, we are just creating a symlink to /usr/bin for this binary.

title: Ticket #5784: Set NEGOTIATOR_CONSIDER_PREEMPTION intelligently
description: NEGOTIATOR_CONSIDER_PREEMPTION significantly improves negotiator performance, at the cost disabling preemption. The current default is false. We should change this knob from true or false to true/false/auto, where auto intelligently sets N_C_P to the right value based on PREEMPTION_REQUIREMENTS, startd RANK and pslot preemption.
creator: gthain

title: Ticket #2041: Cream status commands timing out

title: Ticket #4896: Make spool permissions more restrictive

title: Ticket #7243: classad function regexpMember should not error if list element undef
description: Classad function regexpMember takes a regexp string and a list of elements. Today it evaluates each element of the list, and if any element does not evaluate to a string, it returns false. We will change this so that if an element evaluates to undefined, regexpMember will continue to evaluate each member, and if the regexp is true, the whole function will return true. If at least one member is undefined, and the rest of the members evaluate to a string which doesn't match the regexp, it will return undefined. If any member evaluates to a type which is neither a string nor undefined, it will return error.

title: Ticket #3200: condor_submit -spool can return failure and still leave jobs submitted
description: Problem When doing a condor_submit with the -spool option, condor_submit first submits all the jobs on hold in one transaction, and then it starts a second transaction to transmit the input files. If there is an error sending the input files, condor_submit will exit with a nonzero exit status (this is good), BUT a pile of jobs will be left behind in the queue still sitting on hold (this is bad). If condor_submit returns failure, the job queue should be left in a state as if nothing happened - aka the entire submission should be rolled back. Suggested Fix The schedd already knows if the transmission of input files succeeds or fails. If the staging of the input files failed, schedd in method Scheduler::spoolJobFilesReaper() should remove all the jobs involved (this same method is already releasing all the involved jobs from hold if the transfer succeeds). In addition, in the rare event that condor_submit dies right after submitting the jobs but before it starts transferring the input files, the schedd should periodically remove (garbage collect) jobs that are in hold state due to file transfer for a long period of time, or for a short period of time if there are no file worker threads active (i.e. spoolJobFileWorkers hash table is empty). To keep Condor-C happy, in Scheduler::spoolJobFiles(), alongside the code where we look at ATTR_STAGE_IN_FINISH to be certain we do not allow stagein to happen more than once, we should also confirm that the job is in held state for stagein reasons - this will keep Condor-C from attempting to restage files to a job in X state after the changes suggested above are implemented.

title: Ticket #6452: Fix hard link security problems with public HTTP transfers
description: Our current implementation of public HTTP transfers uses hard links to target files. We need to safe_fopen these target files before creating the hard links, to make sure they do not contain soft links in their paths which could be changed later for nefarious purposes. Also update code to follow ToddT's 9/22/17 email suggestions, i.e.: I think you should a) impersonate the user and open the file using safe_open(), b) create the hard link as root, c) open the file using safe_open as user apache, d) fstat() the two open file handles and compare the inodes. The idea here is we want to be certain the file is accessible by the end user, and no shenanigans occurred between the time when we tested accessibility and created the hard link.

Ticket #988: Grand unified param() system: Phase 2
description: What is phase 2? This ticket describes the second phase of the new param() system. We have learned much since checking in phase 1 as described in #123 and #767. Phase 2 builds upon that knowledge and will possibly provide a different underlying implementation than the previous, but one that models our needs more precisely. The specification in the ticket is a work in progress, but it is 99% solidified. Milestones Work order is bottom to top. 1 Week Change each difficult param invocation to use the new/fixed API. 1-2 Weeks Fill in the holes in the API our param conversion to the table discovered. Write generator code to convert default table into non-naive memory optimized C++ API code. 2 Weeks Tag the master for reference purposes when inspecting code. Create default table representation for all known parameters. Change each easy param invocation to use the new API. This involes manually inspecting each invocation. Note any params which can't be modeled by our API and why. 1 Week Get familiar with the New Classad C++ API. Write generator codes to check/convert default table into naive C++ API code. 04/06/2010 [DONE] Figure out what default table actually looks like, add in real examples. 03/05/2010 [DONE] Present current ideas to FW, get feedback [DONE] 1/21/2010 [DONE] Meet with willb to remember what we have to do with this task. [DONE] Write up what we remembered from the previous meetings we've had. [DONE] What is the theory of operation? All parameter values are evaluable expressions which must result in a known and expected type. All option names which are known a priori will have a compile time interface. All options are built up, following a well-known order of definitions where later definitions overwrite previous ones, into a canonical evaluation expression. We shall strive to minimize the heap usage of the param system within reasonable cost bounds. Evaluation of a parameter's expression will occur with respect to an "environment" classad which fills in details like subsystem, full hostname--or any "instant value" needed directly at evaluation time. These "instant values" are to be documented as in the namespace of the param language. Such examples are Opsys, Arch, Subsys, Local, Now. There is an options object which contains everything about the association of names and values. C and C++ interfaces will be provided or C code will be converted to compile with C++ in cases where providing an interface is too difficult. What is the API? Options which have an a priori name at compile time Each of these parameters uses a default classad environment to evaluate the expression. This interface is algorithmically generated and will return the correct type of the parameter in question. Possibilities include returning STL Lists for collections of values, like FOO = A, B, C, D would result in an STL List containing the right types for A, B, C, D in lexical analysis order. Getting an option Value options.X.value() options.X.value(env) Setting an option Value options.X.set_value() options.X.set_value(env) Checking to see of an option has a defined value options.X.is_defined() options.X.is_defined(env) Existence checking is performed by the compiler at compile time for these a priori options. Options which have a name known only at runtime. Getting an option Value options.param_value(name) options.param_value(name,env) Setting an option Value options.param_set_value(name) options.param_set_value(name,env) Checking to see of an option has a defined value options.param_is_defined(name) options.param_is_defined(name,env) Checking to see of an option exists in the options table. options.param_exists(name) Consistency checks in the API TODO What is the well-known order of definition? Starting from lowest, going to highest definitional layer: unknown -> static default table -> simple runtime default table -> config files -> administrator settings with -rset -> environment variable -> complex runtime defaults Following the well-known order of definition, each scoping tree name (something like schedd.X or schedd.hawkeye.X) that directly matches a previous scoping tree name overwrites it until no more overwrites occur. At this point the finalized forest of scoping trees associated with an option are converted into the canonical expression and assigned to the option name for evaluation against the environmental classad. The scoping names used in the scope portion of the name become environmental attributes in the environment classad against which the expression is evaluated. The scoping names are somewhat hard coded to be classified under the correct attribute in the environmental classad. For example, schedd.haykeye in the above examples means that in the canonical form, (Subsys == "schedd" && Local == "hawkeye") will appear as a conditional selector for that value, and so on. How do we write down entries into the default table? XXX This code needs markup. Strawman default table layout. A main problem one must consider is that the elements and types of the config file language are not necessarily the same elements and types of the representation language, in this case new classads. This means that config file elements must be explicitly represented as values in new classads. Of particular note, and one that isn't fully solved, is the use of is* functions in the type domain equations. The full specification of a trivial config parameter: [ // The name of the attribute Name = "USE_VISIBLE_DESKTOP"; // What is the current viewpoint of this param in accordance to being // supported by the current revision of Condor? // Can be "supported", "deprecated", "obselete", "abort". // Defaults to "supported"; Status = "supported"; // what type the evaluator should expect the definition to be Type = "bool"; // Once we've computed the value, does it fall into the domain we are // expecting? Evaled in context of ENV ad. // If specified, the expression denoted is the one actually used. // If not specified, then it'll be something like below, derived from the // Type attribute. Domain = IsBool(val) // After I evaluate the parameter in whatever definitional layer that ended // up being the final version, this expression converts it into some // transform of itself. In this example, it is identity. We would use it to // implement clamping of a value or other transforms. // Evaled in context of ENV ad. // If specified, the expression denoted is the one actually used. // If not specified, it'll be what is below. Transform = val; // Once we finish the transform, we validate the operation to ensure it is // what we expect it to be: // If not specified it'll be what is below, derived from Type. Validate = isBool(val); // There are two concerns with the evaluation of a variable: // 1. When is the definition updated: RedefineWhen // 2. How often is it evaluated (per definition change): EvalWhen // Valid values are: "never", "startup", "reconfig", "full-reconfig" // defaults to reconfig if not specified RedefineWhen = "reconfig"; // Valid values are: // "once" -> memoize the value // "always" -> re-eval expression each time // defaults to once if not specified. EvalWhen = "once"; // There is always a default role, others can be specified. // This is the *full* specification. // There is a shortcut described later... Role = [ Default = [ // If we were to restrict (via conjuction with the master domain // function) the general domain to only be false, I can do this. The memory becomes owned by the config layer. Definition = [ call = "get_my_pid" ]; ]; What does the canonical form of a param value expression look like? Expressions are built up from "scoping trees" into a final form. A scoping tree is written like this for an option called OPTION, and is considered in order from specific to general: SUBSYS.LOCAL.OPTION, LOCAL.OPTION, SUBSYS.OPTION, OPTION. A default for an option named FOO might be: STARTD.HAWKEYE.FOO = 40 HAWKEYE.FOO = 41 CRONDOR.FOO = 42 STARTD.FOO = 43 SHADOW.FOO = 44 SCHEDD.FOO = 45 STARTER.HAWKEYE.FOO = 46 FOO = 10 This is converted into a canonical form like this: FOO = /* these are really specific, they come first */ IfThenElse(SUBSYS == "STARTD" && LOCAL == "HAWKEYE", 40 IfThenElse(SUBSYS == "STARTER" && LOCAL == "HAWKEYE", 46 /* local is more specific than subsys */ IfThenElse(LOCAL == "HAWKEYE", 41, IfThenElse(LOCAL == "CRONDOR", 42, /* next comes subsys stuff */ IfThenElse(SUBSYS == "STARTD", 43, IfThenElse(SUBSYS == "SHADOW", 44, IfThenElse(SUBSYS == "SCHEDD", 45, /* and the default */ 10))))))) We use the IfThenElse to make it much easier to have the result of its evaluation be an object of the correct value and type. Doing the above in boolean logic is very painful. We specifically mean, by "considered in order from specific to general" that we specify the most specific scoping tree first in the IfThenElse construct moving towards the least specific one. Then FOO is evaluated in the context of this classad (suppose in a regular schedd): ENV = [SUBSYS = "SCHEDD", OPSYS = "LINUX", ARCH = "INTEL", LOCAL = "", NOW = 12345678] To produce the answer. How do we handle param expansion in definitions? Consider the following example definitions: SBIN = /path/to/somewhere SCHEDD = $(SBIN)/condor_schedd Here SCHEDD depends on the value of SBIN. We can encode this dependence in several different ways, all of which are conceptually straightforward since we disallow circular definitions. Here are sketches of two possibilities: Dependence lifting. We can determine a priori what params some param P depends on by examining all of the clauses in which P is defined. We could then lift these params to the environment in which the definition of P is evaluated. Macro expansion. We could simply replace a reference to P1 on the right-hand side of the definition of P with the definition of P1. In simple cases, such as the one above, this would be a literal value. In more complex cases, it would be an expression. This approach would increase the size of definitions, although it would be straightforward to distribute the clauses of P1 over the clauses of P in order to prune contradictory or redundant clauses. Eager Evaluation Param expansion in definitions introduces a potential backdoor around the type constraint system. This happens because the actual value of the param is a string and may be expanded into other expressions before having its constraint system invoked upon it. We try to catch these violations before any Condor code uses the options object by eagerly evaluating the params after the final definition is calculated. If we lazily evaluated, say at runtime, then there would be means by which a constraint violation could happen and noone could know. Due to the practice of eager evaluation, a larger set than necessary might be flagged as an error due to cascading errors. An example is this: Suppose we have this in the default table: [ Name = "FOO"; Type = "integer"; Validator = val != 140; Definition = "100"; ] [ Name = "BAR"; Type = "integer"; Validator = val != 1400 Definition = "10 * $(FOO)"; ] And the user puts this into their config file: FOO = 140 or, more pathologically, FOO = 4 FOO = $(FOO)0 FOO = 1$(FOO) What happens? What are the values of FOO and BAR? All definitional layers are resolved first using the present macro expansion codes to produce the final definitions for FOO and BAR. This would make FOO = "140" and BAR = "10 * 140". All attributes are now eagerly evaluated and their results stored in the options object. This will eventually cause FOO and BAR to both be flagged as having failed their Validator functions. Unless we keep track of the expansion history of a parameter, there is no way to know that BAR was only made illegal because FOO was illegal. We can't narrow down the true source of the error precisely. The problem with lazy evaluation shows up in this example: [ Name = "FOO"; Type = "integer"; Validator = val != 140; Definition = "100"; ] [ Name = "BAR"; Type = "integer"; // notice no validator Definition = "10 * $(FOO)"; ] And the user puts this into their config file: FOO = 140 At this point, if the Condor code happens not to ask for options.FOO() for a very long time, but quickly asks for options.BAR(), options.BAR() will return 1400 as a value, even though it had been incorrect to do so since the dataflow had gone through an invalid parameter! We missed an error we should have caught! The other problem with lazy evaluation is that we'd likely need to keep track of the ExprTree of the parsed expression in order to evaluate it later, which means much more heap utilization--a thing we're trying to minimize.

title: Ticket #5157: isStillRunnable should examine job lease
description: When a busy schedd is restarted, we sometimes run out lease durations. This means there may sometimes be thousands of timed-out jobs. However, the schedd never checks to see if the lease duration has expired: only the shadow does this. Our busiest schedds have 1s duty cycles - hence if there are 5k lease-expired jobs, we spend upward of an hour spawning shadows that ultimately do nothing except immediately exit with a lease-duration-expired. During that time, we have thousands new matches that go unused. By time the schedd launches those shadows, the glidein is sometimes gone.
remarks: 2015-Jul-21 16:12:23 by jfrey: After a restart, the schedd does check the job lease before adding each job its list of jobs to attempt reconnecting to. But it doesn't check the lease when it's ready to spawn the shadow. 2015-Jul-21 20:32:37 by bbockelm: Yeah - I think that's precisely the problem. It does not take an extremely busy schedd (or a very large JOB_START_DELAY) for the shadow launch queue to exceed the default job lease.

This class will have two methods drainJobs(drain_type, resume_on_completion, check) returns drain_id drain_type optional, must be a member of the htcondor.DrainTypes enum: Fast, Graceful, or Quick. default: Graceful resume_on_completion option, if true exit draining state when draining completes. default: false check optional, an expression that must evaluate to true on all slots or the drain request will abort. drain_id is a string ID assigned to the drain request when the drain command is accepted. Startd's prior to 8.4.6 or 8.5.4, will always return the empty string as the drain_id even though a non-empty drain id was actually assigned. cancelDrainJobs(drain_id) drain_id optional, the drain request id assigned by the prior drain command. if no drain id is given, all drain commands are cancelled. Here's a sample script using the new drain binding. drain_fast_all_jobs.py #!/usr/bin/python # Drain all startds import htcondor collector = htcondor.Collector() addrs = set() for startd_ad in collector.locateAll(htcondor.DaemonTypes.Startd): # collector will return all of the slot (machine) ads, but we really only want the # address. addr = startd_ad['myaddress'] if addr in addrs: continue addrs.add(addr) print "Draining (Fast)", startd_ad['machine'], addr startd = htcondor.Startd(startd_ad) drain_id = startd.drainJobs(htcondor.DrainTypes.Fast, True) print "Drain id is", drain_id 2016-Jun-01 10:46:47 by tim: Pushing this to the 8.5.6 release. We need a design review before making this public. 2016-Jun-27 10:00:14 by tim: Brian Bockelmann says that this is OK. 2016-Jul-27 13:07:36 by wenger: I want to add an example to the docs for this, but I want to finish off some other tickets first...

title: Ticket #822: gt2 jobs with GridJobId crash gridmanager on startup
description: This bug was introduced in 7.3.2 with the GRAM5 code. In the constructor for GlobusJob, if the job ad has a valid GridJobId attribute, SetRemoteJobId() is called, which tries to invoke a method on myResource, which is still NULL at this point, resulting in a crash. The call to myResource is to determine whether the resource is gt2 or gt5. Since the constructor knows the answer, the short-term fix is to add an optional argument to SetRemoteJobId(), which is used if myResource is NULL. Part of the problem is that we have some circular reasoning going on. SetRemoteJobId() sets GridJobId in the job ad and updates some related data members. But the constructor is calling it with the value from GridJobId to just initialize the data members. We're not going to worry about that for now.

description: Currently (8.7.1 and earlier) the Starter sets JobStartDate to the time that it called create_process to begin the job's executable. title: Ticket #1544: Classad printing problem with INT_MIN valued attribute
description: On my 64 bit machine, if I set a value to INT_MIN, condor_status -l display it oddly. condor_status -format "%d" seems to be ok, though: $ grep GGT ResAttributes.cpp cp->Assign( "GGT", INT_MIN); bash-3.2$ condor_status -l | grep GGT GGT = - --2147483648 On a 32-bit machine, the value is -2147483647 (without the extra minus signs). The problem is that the new ClassAds parser parses -1 as '-' '1'. That is, the unary minus operator followed by the integer 1. This works ok for most integer and real values, as when the expression is evaluated, the correct value is reconstructed. INT_MIN (aka -2147483648) is an exception, since the negated value (2147483648) can't be represented in signed 32-bits. The parser calls strtol() on the string representing the number (without the minus), then casts the result to an int. On a 32-bit machine, strtol() detects overflow and returns LONG_MAX (which is the same as INT_MAX, 2147483647). On a 64-bit machine, 2147483648 is returned in 64 bits, which is then truncated to 32 bits by the cast, resulting in the value -2147483648. When this is unparsed, an extra minus sign ends up in front (for the unary minus operator). If the resulting string is parsed and unparsed again, another minus sign appears. The parsing code needs to be modified to treat -1 as a negative number, not the negation of a positive number. It also must take extra care with values returned by strtol() on 64-bit platforms, reducing large values to INT_MIN and INT_MAX, rather than truncating to 32 bits. The compat ClassAd layer provides methods to insert unsigned and long values into an ad, which just cast the values to int. We should consider removing these.

title: Ticket #7869: Debian and Ubuntu should have distinct version numbers across distros
description: The Debian and Ubuntu packages should have unique version numbers across distros within a single build. Then we can follow Debian and Ubuntu standard practices and have packages for all the distros in a single repository. Also, htcondor would get updated when doing a version updated
remarks: 2020-Oct-13 10:30:12 by matyas: It feels like there are multiple changes in this commit -- what's the difference between a 'full' build and a 'binary' build, why you're using dch for one but not the other, etc. Could you explain? 2020-Oct-19 08:27:15 by tim: So, Debian and Ubuntu have all versions in a repository. So, the version number must be different between stretch and buster and xenial, bionic, and focal. The convention is to add a +b1, +b2 to binary rebuilds and to increment the release modifier 8.8.11-1.1, 8.8.11-1.2 for rebuilds which include Debian source package changes. So, for the code, the dch in the block of code before the changes sets the base changelog entry for the build. If you are just doing a binary rebuild with no changes to Debian spec files, you use dch to bump the version in the changelog. If there are spec file changes, then you have to do a build including the sources. So, a binary build just produces the binary packages. No source packages are produced, because they are already available. A full build creates binary and source packages. Every build uses dch to set the changelog. However, dch is used to bump the version number when neeeded. 2020-Oct-19 13:04:38 by matyas: Makes sense. OK, looks good. Review passed.

title: Ticket #1114: Improve methods to add/remove Target scope in expressions
description: The ClassAds compatibility layer has a method that takes an ad and modifies all attribute references which don't resolve to a local attribute, adding a 'target' scope. The method is called AddExplicitTargetRefs(). That method creates a new ad that's a copy of the original ad, but with the modifications to the expressions. We want this method to modify the existing ad, rather than creating a new one. Also, we'd like to have a version that can modify an ExprTree that's not in an ad. We also want a companion method that will remove all 'target' scopes from an expression or entire ad. Milestones Change public version of compat_classad::ClassAd::AddExplicitTargetRefs() to modify the current ad in-place Make the private version of compat_classad::ClassAd::AddExplicitTargetRefs() into a free-standing function Create a wrapper for the free-standing AddExplicitTargetRefs() that takes a ClassAd*, creates a set of attribute names, and calls the real AddExplicitTargetRefs() Create a parallel set of functions named RemoveExplicitTargetRefs() Details The private version of compat_classad::ClassAd::AddExplicitTargetRefs() should be turned into a free-standing function. That will allow it to be used on ExprTrees that aren't in an ad. Having a second version of the free-standing function which takes a ClassAd* makes it easy for callers to use on a lone ExprTree. There will be places where we want to remove 'target.' from attribute references, which the RemoveExplicitTargetRefs() functions will do. They won't need a list of defined attributes, so we will only need one free-standing function, with no second argument.

It does the real work of modifying an expression. classad::ExprTree *AddExplicitTargetRefs(classad::ExprTree*, classad::ClassAd*) - A convenience function that builds a set of all attribute names in the given ad and calls the function immediately above. The first function looks good to go, but should be tested to make sure the iterator isn't thrown off by the Insert() that's replacing the current item. 2010-Jan-19 14:50:37 by jfrey: And here are the signatures for the removal functions: void compat_classad::ClassAd::RemoveExplicitTargetRefs() - Call the function below for each of the ad's attributes, inserting the returned ExprTree into the ad. classad::ExprTree *RemoveExplicitTargetRefs(classad::ExprTree*) - Create and return a new ExprTree based on the given one, but without any Target. scoping.

title: Ticket #5911: Invalid security session use by schedd
description: CMS noticed many many p-slots that were unnecessarily idling. Investigation showed that negotiation was fine, but, when the schedd attempted to claim the p-slot, it unexpectedly had the socket closed by the remote end. On the worker node, the corresponding lines were as follows: 09/20/16 14:28:57 (pid:5482) DC_AUTHENTICATE: attempt to open invalid session <WORKERIP:33277>#1474378538#1, failing; this session was requested by SCHEDD <SCHEDDIP:4080?addrs=SCHEDDIP-4080+[--1]-4080&noUDP&sock=79603_edf1_35> on <SCHEDDIP:64714> with return address <SCHEDDIP:4080?addrs=SCHEDDIP-4080+[--1]-4080&noUDP&sock=79603_edf1_35> 09/20/16 14:28:57 (pid:5482) Failed to send DC_INVALIDATE_KEY to daemon at <SCHEDDIP:4080>: SECMAN:2009:DENIED authorization of server 'unauthenticated@unmapped/SCHEDDIP' (I am acting as the client): reason: CLIENT authorization policy contains no matching ALLOW entry for this request; identifiers used for this host: SCHEDDIP,SCHEDD.example.com, hostname size = 1, original ip address = SCHEDDIP. Note that the timestamp in the session key is 1474378538, which is 09/20/16 13:35:38 (about the time the startd daemon started up). Looking through the StartdLog, this was the first time the schedd had contacted this worker node. It seems that the DC_INVALIDATE_KEY issue is a glideinWMS misconfiguration: should it even be possible for ALLOW_CLIENT to prevent session invalidation? CMS uses the knobs that allow the secondary collectors to skip the forwarding of updates to the parent collector if it does not think the update is "significant": COLLECTOR_FORWARD_FILTERING = TRUE COLLECTOR_FORWARD_INTERVAL = 600 Additionally, there were network connectivity issues throughout the day, but none logged between the startd startup and the error message at 14:28.. Current working theory is that "somehow" a private ad update is being missed, causing an invalid match-based session to be used for authentication. It's not clear how a public ad update would occur without a private ad update.

title: Ticket #4603: DAEMON_SOCKET_DIR=auto breaks partial use of shared port
description: The new DAEMON_SOCKET_DIR=auto setting breaks configurations where shared port is used by children of the master, but not the master itself. Each child daemon ends up with a different CONDOR_PRIVATE_SHARED_PORT_COOKIE value, meaning the shared port daemon uses the wrong name for the daemon's abstract socket and can't connect.
remarks: 2014-Sep-18 16:38:32 by jfrey: Having a set of daemons where only some use shared port is inadvisable. If they're configured to use shared port, they can fall back to using the daemon socket directory. This provides the same behavior as 8.2.x.

title: Ticket #4253: DAGMan abort-dag-on test improvement
description: We should improve one of the DAGMan abort-dag-on tests to make sure that the DAG abort removes running node jobs.
remarks: 2014-Mar-17 17:22:03 by wenger: Okay, today's modification of the job_dagman_abort-B test hits this case. (Note that the test currently fails, because DAGMan's notion of the status of the nodes doesn't get updated properly after they're removed from the queue.) Also, for this test, at the end of the DAG, FinishedRunning(true), DoneSuccess(true), DoneFailed(true), and DoneCycle(true) all return false! (Because the node counts still think node D is queued.) One way to deal with this could be for DAGMan to wait around for the events resulting from removing all of the node jobs, before it exits. I guess we could do this by removing all of the jobs and then going into halt mode or something like that...

title: Ticket #6794: HTCondor should start up after nfs and automounter
description: I have a pool configuration system which uses a shared configuration directory in an NFS-mounted /home/condor path. When HTCondor is started by systemd before the automounter and nfs-client units are online, it fails to read most of its configuration and starts up in a disconnected state. Adding the nfs.client.target and autofs.service to the "after" list for the condor.service unit file will provide the necessary ordering for sites which need it without having any effect on sites which don't. The autofs.service does not reference the nfs-client target, since it doesn't necessarily need an NFS filesystem to automount something, so both of them are needed in the after list. If you can recommend any configuration approaches that might achieve the same thing without needing a unit file change - maybe an include pipe? - then I'd appreciate that as well. Thanks! -Michael Pelletier.

remarks: 2015-Dec-15 16:56:57 by tlmiller: A possible explanation for the grid manager's behavior follows. The grid manager deliberately creates its pipes to the GAHP with the read side O_NONBLOCK; see condor_gridmanager/gahp-client.cpp:800. In GahpServer::read_argv(), the grid manager calls GahpServer::buffered_read() on the stdout pipe, which in turn calls GahpServer::err_pipe_ready(), which in turn calls DaemonCore::Read_Pipe() on the stderr pipe, which (because of the above) can return EAGAIN. This is one of the two FDs in the strace loop. After calling err_pipe_ready(), buffered_read() then calls Read_Pipe() on the stdout pipe. Again, this can return EAGAIN, and is the second of the FDs in the strace loop. read_argv() surrounds its call to buffered_read() with the following code: for (;;) { ASSERT(ibuf < buf_size); //result = daemonCore->Read_Pipe(m_gahp_readfd, &(buf[ibuf]), 1 ); result = buffered_read(m_gahp_readfd, &(buf[ibuf]), 1 ); /* Check return value from read() */ if ( result < 0 ) { /* Error - try reading again */ continue; } which of course busy-loops forever, waiting for the GAHP to reply. This function is, among other places, called from GahpServer::poll() (which, despite the name, is used is asynch mode) to wait for the results of the RESULTS command. 2015-Dec-15 17:16:52 by tlmiller: The above scenario would be consistent with the GAHP being hung. It could also be consistent with the GAHP being overworked, except the length of the gap in the log after "Setting CA path", which is normally more-or-less immediately followed by "Response was". In the log, there's a seventeen minute gap before the GAHP is restarted. Even in the unlikely event that the GAHP were busy for that long before it got to the RESULTS command (or whatever the grid manager was waiting for), the log would record what the GAHP was doing, rather than nothing. Between "Setting CA path" and "Response was" there is a lock release, a blocking call into libcurl, and a lock acquisition (among other things). 2015-Dec-15 17:36:40 by tlmiller: This suggests that we actually have two problems: first, that the grid manager can hang because of bad behavior on the GAHP's part; and second, the specific bad behavior of the EC2 GAHP. 2015-Dec-16 15:10:58 by jfrey: A badly behaved GAHP can cause the gridmanager to hang or EXCEPT(). This is a conscious decision made when these daemons were first developed. It simplifies the error handling in the gridmanager. Think of the GAHP protocol as a weird form of RPC. As ToddM suggested out-of-band, we could have the gridmanager EXCEPT() if the GAHP doesn't respond in a timely manner (say several seconds). That would us to recover from this type bad GAHP behavior. 2015-Dec-22 13:41:45 by tlmiller: Today we confirmed (thanks, Burt!), by attaching the processes, that the analysis above is correct -- the EC2 GAHP's stack traces don't change at all when taken around process continue/pause pairs (and match the core dumps); and the grid manager's stack traces alternate between buffered_read()/Read_Pipe() and buffered_read()/err_pipe_ready()/Read_Pipe(). I made a patch (last week) for the grid manager to EXCEPT if it takes more than five seconds for the GAHP to reply during the read_argv() function. This should work around the EC2 GAHP's problem. I also made a patch (last week) for the EC2 GAHP to perform many fewer allocations when reading commands off the pipe. (If we decide we need to spawn a new worker thread, we still perform many allocations; changing to a thread pool model could be done in a future patch.) Having confirmed the analysis that led to those patches, I've provided the patched binaries to Fermi, who will be testing them in the near future. If the GAHP patches are effective in reducing the frequency of the problem, we should examine the other GAHPs and determine if they could benefit from the same change(s). (Perhaps even formalize a "GAHPCore".) Burt also confirmed that Fermi's tests were able to proceed if the GRIDMANAGER_NOT_RESPONDING_TIMEOUT were set low enough. 2016-Feb-02 15:39:45 by tlmiller: Merged to 8.4 after successful Fermi testing. 2016-Feb-03 14:26:27 by jfrey: Code Review The idea of glibc's memory allocation not being thread-safe is scary. Since the change to avoid calling the default new/delete helps the problem, I won't object to it. The timeout code in the gridmanager for reading a response from the GAHP doesn't handle initial banner the GAHP prints on startup. 2016-Feb-03 14:40:13 by tlmiller: Created ticket #5502. 2016-Feb-03 14:43:46 by tlmiller: It's possible that some wacky combination of the presence or absence of the -pthreads flag when compiling the ec2_gahp, or when OpenSSL and/or libcurl were compiled, is causing this problem and that it's therefore technically a usage error; but since I haven't been able to reproduce it, I think we just have to leave well enough alone for now.

title: Ticket #96: NFS check in schedd done as wrong user
description: When a job completes, the schedd checks whether its IWD is on NFS. If it is, then the schedd creates and unlinks a file in the directory. This forces the NFS client to sync with the server, ensuring any files created or modified on the execute machine appear when the schedd scans the directory. The schedd does its check of the directory being on NFS as user condor. Thus, if any parent directory doesn’t have any global permissions enabled, the check will fail, even if the directory is on NFS. The schedd does switch uids to the job owner to do the file create/unlink. This patch moves the uid switch to before the NFS check.

title: Ticket #1952: the accountant is inconsistent about case sensitivity
description: If I submit a job with AccountingGroup="DAN", accounting records for both "DAN" and "dan" get created. All usage gets attributed to "dan", so the priority of "DAN" never degrades. condor_userprio can independently manipulate these two records, so the tool and much of the protocol is still case sensitive. The problem is that Accountant::AddMatch() writes records using the lower-case version of the username, but functions which look up accounting records, such as Accountant::GetPriority() do not lowercase the username. Even if the lookup routines were modified, there are further issues caused by AddMatch() lowercasing the username: There may be existing accounting records with the same name but different case. These would need to be detected at startup and handled appropriately (e.g. merge them together or abort or whatever). condor_userprio operations that take a username are currently case-sensitive. These would need to be checked to make sure they are consistent with the new way of doing things. The release notes would need to mention this important change in behavior. In CHTC, our daily reports were slightly messed up by it, because suddenly all the people who had previously showed up with uppercase letters in their names showed up in all lowercase, so the observed per-user difference in usage between one day and the next was messed up. Others could experience similar problems. How to reproduce the problem Submit a job using the following submit file: executable = /bin/sleep arguments = 3600 notification = never +AccountingGroup = "DAN" queue Observe that the accountant has records for both "DAN" and "dan" and has charged the latter rather than the former. $ condor_userprio -allusers -all Last Priority Update: 3/7 15:22 Effective Real Priority Res Total Usage Usage Last User Name Priority Priority Factor Used (wghted-hrs) Start Time Usage Time ------------------------------ --------- -------- ------------ ---- ----------- ---------------- ---------------- DAN@wireless70.cs.wisc.edu 0.50 0.50 1.00 0 0.00 12/31/1969 18:00 ??? <none> 0.50 0.50 1.00 1 0.05 3/07/2011 15:20 3/07/2011 15:22 dan@wireless70.cs.wisc.edu 0.50 0.50 1.00 1 0.05 3/07/2011 15:20 3/07/2011 15:22 ------------------------------ --------- -------- ------------ ---- ----------- ---------------- ---------------- Number of users: 2 1 0.05 3/07/2011 15:20 ??? In the negotiator log, with D_FULLDEBUG turned on, whenever a new round of negotiation starts, you can see that it is getting the priority for "DAN" from the accounting record for "DAN" rather than "dan", so the fair-share priority degradation is not applied. This effect can be magnified by using condor_userprio to give "dan" a large priority factor. Proposed Solution Preserve case in the accountant for display purposes, but do all lookups and comparisons of accounting names case-insensitively. At startup, the accountant must detect any records that differ only in case and it must merge them together. Ideally, condor_userprio should provide a way to rename an accounting record. This would permit changing the case of an accounting record, which may be desirable for readability. The schedd may require some modification, since it groups jobs by owner/group.

If anyone wants to make the rest of the accountant case-insensitive, that work can be done in 7.7. 2011-Mar-09 17:21:03 by eje: Current commit does not work quite right with multi-cased accounting groups. title: Ticket #5696: add knob to allow CCB reconnections from any ip address
description: When a daemon contacts a CCB server and requests a listen port, the CCB server returns a CCB ID and a cookie (capability string) to the daemon. In the event that TCP socket to the CCB server is closed, the daemon can send a reconnect request to the CCB server in order to keep the same CCB ID. The reconnect request must contain a copy of the cookie that was generated by the server during the original request, and also originate from the same IP address. To help facilitate the placement of HTCondor daemons inside of virtual machines that hibernate and subsequently restart with a different public IP address (think CMS@Home type volunteer computing, where the execute node may be a laptop that moves from a work network to a home network), we want a patch to relax the CCB server requirement that the reconnect request must come from the same public IP. Propose a patch to introduce CCB server knob CCB_RECONNECT_ALLOWED_FROM_ANY_IP, which defaults to false. If true, then the reconnect request can come from any IP address that can still produce the cookie. At this point, we do not want to document this knob, because it may go away; at this point we want it just for testing purposes. Ideally, eventually each individual CCB connection will be able to state if a reconnect is allowed from a different address instead of a single knob that impacts them all.

title: Ticket #7351: Add priority to yum repos
description: The YUM "priorities" plugin allows packages from one repo to be preferred over packages from other repos. Without the plugin, or between repos of equal priority, the highest version of an RPM gets picked when installing. With the plugin, the highest version of an RPM from the repo with the best priority gets picked when installing. Repos that don't have a priority defined have an effective priority of 100. At OSG, we use priorities to make sure our RPMs get picked over OS RPMs of the same name, to ensure users get our patches. Unfortunately, because the HTCondor YUM repos don't have priorities defined, the OSG packages get picked instead of the UW HTCondor RPMs when installing condor. This is not what users want: when they explicitly install the UW HTCondor repos, they expect the UW HTCondor packages to be picked. This can also cause weird installation failures. Users generally solve this by hand-editing their htcondor repo files to define the priority for them. It would be nice if the UW HTCondor repos had a priority in them that was better than the OSG priority. To do this, add the line priority=90 to each repo definition in the htcondor repo files. (OSG's priority is 98 and lower is better.)

title: Ticket #3742: Jobs creating Unix domain sockets too long in scratch
description: Unix domain sockets can be up to 108 characters long. They also need to be real filenames. It's common to put them in $TMP/$TEMP/$TMPDIR. Typically $TMP will be "pretty short", so it succeeds assuming the filename appended is "pretty short". HTCondor sets $TMP to the execute directory $_CONDOR_SCRATCH_DIR to ensure we can clean up temporary files. Unfortunately it's entirely possible for the execute directory to be moderately long to start. That, plus the filename the job adds, might break the 108 character limit. There is good news! If USE_FS_NAMESPACES=TRUE and the system supports it /tmp will be remapped to $_CONDOR_SCRATCH_DIR (See #2015). This solves the problem for any jobs that (erroneously) assume /tmp is a good place for temporary files However, I think we still set $TMP to $_CONDOR_SCRATCH_DIR, so well behaved programs don't get the benefit. (This also bites condor_ssh_to_job, see #3739. Note that this will improve #3739 even if #3739 is already "resolved.") Proposed: If USE_FS_NAMESPACES=TRUE, then set $TMP/$TEMP/$TMPDIR to /tmp instead of $_CONDOR_SCRATCH_DIR

title: Ticket #3312: Accumulated idle time (aka wait time, ?time to start?) attribute
description: The ability to tell how long a job is queued and runnable before running is a highly desired feature, as is its aggregate across jobs. An aggregate is provided via scheduler statistics on the condor_schedd's ad. It is based on QDate - JobStartDate. JobStartDate is the first time a job started. For comparison, JobCurrentStartDate is the most recent time a job started. No such attribute exists for a job, presumably because QDate - JobStartDate is available. However, QDate - JobStartDate only provides the wait time from submission until the first time the job starts, it does not factor in time the job spent when it was not runnable, e.g. on hold, and it does not factor in multiple starts of a job. For example, job transitions over time - I(5)->R->I(5)->R->C, has waited idle for 10 seconds I(5)->R->X, has waited idle for 5 seconds I(5)->H(10)->I(3)->R, has waited idle for 8 seconds The current statistics for these jobs will report wait time of 5 seconds for the first two jobs and 20 seconds for the last. An attribute capturing the amount of time spent idle should be added to jobs and aggregated across jobs in a schedd.
remarks: 2012-Nov-09 09:04:17 by johnkn: the schedd stats are aggregated each time Scheduler::jobExitCode is called, this is basically when a shadow exits, so I believe that accumulated wait time is captured because a shadow exit occurs whenever we leave the R state. (shadows pretend to exit on shadow re-use) For instance, if you have an I(5)->R->I(4)->R->C set of job transitions, the (5) is captured on the first R->I transition, and the (4) is captured on the R->C transition. The accumulated idle is not stored in the job in any case. 2012-Nov-13 08:33:13 by matt: https://github.com/htcondor/htcondor/blob/master/src/condor_schedd.V6/schedd.cpp#L8030 It looks like the JobsAccumTimeToStart++ is predicated on first run.

title: Ticket #6110: link and unlink afs token keyrings when switching priv state
description: Currently, we create a new session keyring and link a user's AFS tokens into that keyring every time we set_user_priv. This ends up creating more sessions than is really needed. Really, what we need is one session per process, where we link and unlink the token keyring into that session when changing priv state. This is not a security issue, and while not technically a bug it could lead us to running out of keyrings (limited by kernel per-user) so we're doing this in the stable series.
remarks: 2017-Mar-01 10:43:19 by tim: No documentation needed 2017-Mar-02 09:41:13 by tannenba: CODE REVIEW Looks like there are some problems with this code... as this is security related, we need to be very very careful.... Order of operations seems incorrect to me; specifically, we should be checking to see if the pid changed and creating a new session keyring earlier in the sequence of events. For one example of how this appears broken, consider a daemon is in user_priv state and then forks: i) the daemon will lose AFS access as soon as the child process leaves user_priv state, and ii) the child will lose AFS access as soon as the parent leaves user_priv state. Both problems occur because the parent and child are still sharing the same session keyring. This algorithm seems like it is becoming complex enough it should fully written out, ideally in a comment block in uids.cpp. Looks like uninitialized memory reads were introduced, which could, if we are unlucky, cause incorrect keyrings to be accessed. For example, variable PreviousSessionKeyringUID is compared to UserUid before it is ever initialized. Leaving PRIV_USER and entering PRIV_UNKNOWN state leaks root access. This was not the case before this patch. Commit [50063] has no comments and it is completely non-obvious why this special code in the event log implementation is required. I happen to know it has to do with the fact that AFS checks token authorization at every file write() while non-AFS file systems only check authorization at file open(), but never in 100 years could anyone figure that out from the patch itself. Not even the commit message helps. Good commenting for non-obvious code, esp security code, is a must. On Linux uid_t is unsigned, so in theory a value of -99 is a valid uid (although a very large one). Thus seems like using -99 for the value of KEY_SPEC_INVALID_UID is questionable. I'd suggest using -1 instead, as setreuid() man page claims that value is not allowed. Also, do we need an explicit cast to be sure to correctly/safely compare a literal like "-99" to a uid_t? Knobs, like USE_SESSION_KEYRING and friends, should be in the param table. 2017-Mar-07 16:08:29 by zmiller: To address the problem of what to do when forking and then potentially unlinking another process' credentials, we decided to return to creating a new session every time we switch priv state. Before committing, I wrote a test program that agressively creates new sessions. It takes about 3 seconds to create 1 million new sessions, and they are agressively garbage collected by the kernel, so the overhead of session creation was deemed negligible. 2017-Apr-21 14:29:19 by tannenba: CODE REVIEW PART 2 The issues identified in the initial code review look to be fixed, thanks. Documentation is still pending until such time that we make general AFS support available (currently it is still just for CERN's setup). Resolving this ticket.

title: Ticket #3607: Have HTCondor do CPU-level performance monitoring
description: Modern CPUs all can provide detailed accounting about what your jobs did with the CPU time they were given. A simple example is that the CPU can tell you how many instructions were run, or the cache hit ratio. At least in CMS, we care deeply about these metrics (and their trending over time) but have only ad-hoc measurements by the devs. We'd like to see HTCondor automatically report these for us. Linux provides a syscall to read these counters from user processes without any additional privileges. Alternately, a root user can monitor all processes in a cgroup. Branch posted: https://github.com/bbockelm/htcondor/tree/V7_9-perf-branch Design doc pending, but the basics are outlined here: http://research.cs.wisc.edu/htcondor/HTCondorWeek2013/presentations/BockelmanB_Containers.pdf
remarks: 2016-May-16 11:36:47 by tannenba: I think the major decision to make here is do we want to merge this code which is implemented via syscall(), or alternatively should we have HTCondor fork/exec the Linux perf command-line tool. Ticket #1790: Allow for policy adjustment via qedit/chirp for running jobs
description: Using condor_qedit to edit a job updates the classad within the schedd, but it doesn't send that update through to the startd running the job. This makes is impossible to update job policy for a running job.
remarks: 2010-Dec-03 12:36:47 by matt: Ticket #1598: using qedit to update periodic* exprs on running jobs. It would be advantageous to be able to update the periodic* expressions using qedit, currently it is not allowed. A couple ideas have been passed around, one possible solution is to allow for an explicit push schedd->shadows of elements which have +UpdateExprs in their submission file. 2010-Dec-20 11:49:06 by jfrey: Here are my comments on the proposed patch: I'd rather avoid adding the JobDirty attribute to the job ad. It's not useful to the user and the daemons don't need it to be stored persistently on disk. Instead of having the gridmanager query for jobs with JobDirty==true, how about having a GetAllDirtyAttributesByConstraint() call, similar to GetAllJobsByConstraint(), that iterates over the DirtyJobIDs list? That would be much more efficient and not require a new job attribute. DCSchedd::clearDirtyAttrs() should take a list of job ids. Otherwise, the gridmanager can end up making a lot of separate connections to the schedd needlessly. Better yet, roll it into DCSChedd::actOnJobs() as a new type of action. In the CLEAR_DIRTY_JOB_ATTRS command protocol, there's no acknowledgement sent to the client. This isn't a problem if you roll this command into actOnJobs(). In SetAttribute(), notification of the shadow/gridmanager is triggered only if SETDIRTY is set and the job is RUNNING. The gridmanager also handles idle jobs, and should be notified for those jobs as well. In GetDirtyAttributes(), you end up unparsing and reparsing each ExprTree when you add it to the udpate ad. It would be a little more efficient to make a deep copy of the tree and insert that into the new ad. In the send/receive stubs for GetDirtyAttributes(), you unparse the ClassAd and send it as a single string. Why not use ClassAd::put() and ClassAd::initFromStream(), as the other stubs do? qedit.cpp always uses the new CONDOR_SetAttributeByConstraint2 queue-management command. Thus, it can't talk to older schedds. Some kind of backwards-compatibility check should be there. That can be as simple as retrying without SETDIRTY if the first attempt fails. The commented-out code in schedd.cpp should be removed.

title: Ticket #7214: Signal handler can create daemon log owned by root
description: The code to write to the daemon's log file safely from a signal handler can end up creating the file with root ownership. This will prevent any new instances of the daemon from writing to the file. Due to a short-circuiting OR operator, a call to seteuid() is likely to be skipped in safe_async_log_open(). We saw this occur in CHTC under the following circumstances: The starter's log was moved to another directory (by third-party log rotation software) while the daemon was running. The starter called EXCEPT() while in root privilege (in the docker_proc job reaper). ABORT_ON_EXCEPTION was set to True in the Condor config files.

title: Ticket #2016: uncommenting PREEN no longer disables it
description: Burt made the following observation: We normally leave PREEN unset/commented out for glideins. According to the manual, this is the right thing to do: PREEN In addition to the daemons defined in $(DAEMON_LIST), the condor_master also starts up a special process, condor_preen to clean out junk files that have been left laying around by Condor. This macro determines where the condor_master finds the condor_preen binary. Comment out this macro, and condor_preen will not run. and yet I see the first preen kicking off after an hour under Condor 7.5.5. Looking just a little bit deeper on a Condor 7.5.5 install: [root@cms-xen37 ~]# condor_version $CondorVersion: 7.5.5 Jan 26 2011 BuildID: 308936 $ $CondorPlatform: I686-LINUX_x86_rhap_5 $ [root@cms-xen37 ~]# condor_config_val -verbose PREEN PREEN: /usr/sbin/condor_preen Defined in '<Internal>'. As opposed to 7.4.1 (which I had lying around): [root@cmslpc11 burt]# condor_version $CondorVersion: 7.4.1 Dec 18 2009 BuildID: 204351 $ $CondorPlatform: X86_64-LINUX_RHEL3 $ [root@cmslpc11 burt]# condor_config_val -verbose PREEN Not defined: PREEN How to Fix I think we should stick with the new behavior, which is to have a default value for PREEN in the param table, hard-coded into Condor. If we do that, we need to update the docs to correctly indicate that to disable PREEN, one must explicitly unset it rather than just uncomment it.

title: Ticket #6956: "Match password auth" for schedds
description: Once #6947 is completed, the schedd will be able to generate a token that can be used as part of PASSWORD2 authentication. Specifically, this allows a sort of "match password authentication" for the negotiator to authenticate with the schedd. That is, the schedd can generate a token that (a) maps as user condor, (b) only is usable for the NEGOTIATOR authorization, and (c) expires in 20 minutes. This match password can be embedded into the ad sent to the collector as a private attribute. When the negotiator retrieves the ads from the collector, it now has a valid PASSWORD2 token to perform negotiation with the schedd. This significantly simplifies a flocking setup: the schedd only needs to be able to advertise to the collector, enable PASSWORD2, and the remote negotiator will automatically be able to authenticate with the schedd.

title: Ticket #5383: The %cmake macro includes extra undesired CFLAGS for RPM builds
description: In HTCondor v8.2, we build all binaries posted on the web by invoking cmake, including the RPM packages. In HTCondor v8.4, we build the RPM packages using rpmbuild. However, the %cmake macro in the condor.spec file ends up setting in extra compiler flags (like FORTIFY and/or stack-protector) onto each and every source module; this breaks standard universe and potentially other things (see #5382, #5240). In addition, we now have the undesirable situation where the binaries tested in our regression test suite, and the binaries released in the tarball and/or DEB packages, are fundamentally different than the binaries contained in the RPM packages because they are built with different compiler flags. We should modify the condor.spec file so rpmbuild uses the same compiler flags that our regular cmake (tarball) build does.

description: condor_startd.V6/vmuniverse_mgr.cpp: vmtmp = param( "VM_MEMORY" ); condor_vm-gahp/vmgahp_config.cpp: int tmp_config_value = param_integer("VM_MEMORY", 0); VM_MEMORY is not evaluated when param'd by the Startd, which means VM_MEMORY = 1 + 1 is different when looked up in the vm-gahp vs the startd. Both should use param_integer.
remarks: 2010-Jan-26 21:53:37 by matt: There is no reason to param for VM_MEMORY in the Startd. It just causes inconsistent behavior. It should be removed.
check_ins: 2010-Jan-26 22:02 Check-in [16984]: Removed inconsistent handling of VM_MEMORY from the Startd (#1143) (By Matthew Farrellee )
creator: matt

title: Ticket #6686: HTCondor View: add sed script to rewrite <base> tag
description: We need a sed script to rewrite the <base> tag in already-rendered HTCondor View HTML. This will let users change where the site is being served from without re-rendering the HTML, which requires running a Python script. The sed script needs to be written in a way that the HTCondor config file can interact with it.
check_ins: 2018-May-16 09:46 Check-in [54938]: add a simple sed script to rewrite <base> tags in already-rendered HTML (#6686) (By JoshKarpel )
creator: karpel

title: Ticket #4711: Delayed bind() result causes slow client tools on Windows
description: When run rapidly in succession (or while under load), it's possible for HTCondor tools on Windows to fail to connect() with WSA error 10048, WSAEADDRINUSE. (This has been demonstrated to affect condor_submit and condor_q, although the latter tends to require fewer trials to reproduce.) On Windows, this can happen as a result of a connect() call if (and only if?) if bind() is called with a wildcard address. Theory: The test suite sets (or inherits from the BaTLab machines) a LOWPORT and HIGHPORT range of 1024-65535. The existence of this range causes us to call Sock::bindWithin() and set a particular port number. If, as by default, BIND_ALL_INTERFACES is true, Sock::bindWithin() will bind a wildcard address. Windows may then delay the error until the connect() call (when it chooses a specific interface to use). Since every tool (and every outbound daemon connection) will be using the same particular port number, the chance of a collision is quite high (especially since a closed socket may not become available immediately). Testing: Removing LOWPORT and HIGHPORT from the config file and the environment appears to work around the problem. Adding setting _CONDOR_HIGHPORT and _CONDOR_LOWPORT in the environment reintroduces it. Oddly, setting BIND_ALL_INTERFACES to false (and NETWORK_INTERFACE to suit) does NOT work around the problem. This may be a problem in my theory, or in my code analysis.

I have attached a master log with trials, the first without HIGHPORT/LOWPORT set and the second with them set. 2015-Nov-05 14:29:12 by johnkn: Clearly on Windows we believe that we have bound to the same port multiple times. fragment of master log with D_NETWORK:2 11/05/15 14:20:49 get_port_range - (LOWPORT,HIGHPORT) is (1000,50000). 11/05/15 14:20:49 Sock::bindWithin - bound to 17085... 11/05/15 14:20:49 CONNECT bound to <128.105.136.34:17085> fd=1380 peer=<128.105.136.34:7107> 11/05/15 14:20:49 condor_write(fd=1380 daemon at <128.105.136.34:7107>,,size=120,timeout=20,flags=0,non_blocking=0) 11/05/15 14:20:49 condor_write(fd=1380 daemon at <128.105.136.34:7107>,,size=645,timeout=20,flags=0,non_blocking=0) 11/05/15 14:20:49 condor_write(fd=1380 daemon at <128.105.136.34:7107>,,size=13,timeout=20,flags=0,non_blocking=0) 11/05/15 14:20:49 CLOSE TCP <128.105.136.34:17085> fd=1380 11/05/15 14:20:49 Sent signal 15 to COLLECTOR (pid 6500) 11/05/15 14:20:49 get_port_range - (LOWPORT,HIGHPORT) is (1000,50000). 11/05/15 14:20:49 Sock::bindWithin - bound to 17085... 11/05/15 14:20:49 SEND [648] <128.105.136.34:17085> <128.105.136.34:7108> 11/05/15 14:20:49 CLOSE UDP <128.105.136.34:17085> fd=1380 11/05/15 14:20:49 Sent signal 15 to NEGOTIATOR (pid 6892) 11/05/15 14:20:49 get_port_range - (LOWPORT,HIGHPORT) is (1000,50000). 11/05/15 14:20:49 Sock::bindWithin - bound to 17085... 11/05/15 14:20:49 get_port_range - (LOWPORT,HIGHPORT) is (1000,50000). 11/05/15 14:20:49 Sock::bindWithin - bound to 17085... 11/05/15 14:20:49 attempt to connect to <128.105.136.34:7107> failed: connect errno = 10048. If users really want the broken behavior on Windows, they can specify OUT_LOWPORT and OUT_HIGHPORT. This assumes that most people don't actually care about the outbound port range. I prefer this to tying the definition of HIGHPORT and LOWPORT to the setting of USE_SHARED_PORT (because we see the problem occur most frequently when shared port is active). Another option is to disable outbound port range limiting for Windows entirely, but since that's included as the default in the first proposal, its only advantage would be if we don't think that most don't people care about outbound port ranges, but the opposite for Windows, or that it's better to work more reliably than support a feature that occasionally breaks things. We could also check for -10048 on Windows and if OUT_LOWPORT and OUT_HIGHPORT are set, speculate to the user that the connection failed because of this problem, and not because of a connection problem. title: Ticket #2295: default job stack size bloats vsize
description: Checkin [20867] sets the stack size rlimit for jobs to 500MB. When CHTC was upgraded to a pre-release of 7.7.0, CMS jobs failed on CHTC because their vsize was 10 times bigger than it used to be. These jobs set their own vsize rlimit to a reasonable upper bound to avoid bugs causing problems. Apparently, they do not set their own stack limit to a reasonable value. It seems that they just use the max provided by the system. The workaround is to have the jobs specify a smaller stack size at submit time. However, it is a little worrisome that for this application, running the job by hand causes it to use 10x less virtual memory than when it runs under Condor using default settings. It took me a while to consider the possibility that running a job under Condor could significantly impact the amount of memory it allocates. What should we do? title: Ticket #875: DAGMan should support 'heredocs' for job submit files
description: Dagman should support a 'heredoc' syntax to make certain types of autogeneration of dagfiles easier to do. The heredoc would be the contents of the submit file. JOB JobName SubmitDescriptionFileName [DIR directory] [DONE]<<END # The lines of the submit file. universe = scheduler executable = /bin/true notification = Never output = $NAME.out error = $NAME.err # no log file means use the default log END # later in the dag file: VARS JobName "$NAME=$JOB" When dagman encounters this job, it will write a temporary submit file, then submit it. This will preserve the ability of VARS interpolants to work. The SubmitDescriptionFileName would either have to be a known keyword, or left out and the parser figures out that DIR wasn't the job name, but the directory directive if the << was found. There probably needs to be more thought on the syntax of the JOB directive to make it parser friendly. If we decided to add whole dag variables, then we'd have to reason about the name spaces of the dag variables versus the VARS variables in terms of the submit file. I believe we'd have to do this any way even in the case of a non-heredoc job, but I mention it here so it isn't forgotten.

title: Ticket #930: QMGMT_CMD is registered at READ access level
description: As discussed with Todd and Cathrin just now, here's a proposed item for her to try out. The QMGMT_CMD is a command that is sent to the schedd. All job queue operations such as submitting jobs, modifying jobs, and listing the jobs are done through this command. The command is registered as a READ command, so security negotiation happens according to the READ policy (e.g. SEC_READ_AUTHENTICATION, etc.). However, internally in the protocol of this command are some operations that require authentication (all operations that modify the job queue). This is handled by making authentication part of the command protocol rather than part of the initial security negotiation. This happens in qmgmt_receivers.cpp:do_Q_request(). There are two different calls made by the client: InitializeConnection and InitializeReadOnlyConnection. The problem with this is that condor_shadow periodically connects to the schedd and updates the job. If the READ policy is not to require authentication, then this means the shadow and schedd will create an unauthenticated security session. Then every time the shadow connects to the schedd and tries to update the job, it will have to authenticate inside InitializeConnection. If the READ policy requires authentication, then the shadow will get an authenticated security session the first time it connects and from then on it will not have to reauthenticate (until the security session expires). What I think needs to be done about this is to register two commands: QMGMT_READ and QMGMT_WRITE. These could both still have the same command handler that the current QMGMT command has. They would just be registered at different authorization levels so that the initial security negotiation phase would be more appropriate. The clients would then need to be changed to send the right command based on whether they are doing a read or write operation. Presumably this is already known at a fairly early stage, because the client sends InitializeConnection or InitializeReadOnlyConnection at the beginning of the qmgmt command. Old clients that send QMGMT should probably be treated as though they sent QMGMT_READ. (QMGMT_READ could be the same integer as the old QMGMT command.) The next bit is for "extra credit". Digging further, it would be nice if QMGMT_WRITE were not just registered at the WRITE authorization level. The problem with WRITE is that it doesn't necessarily require authentication. Many pools are configured with WRITE just requiring host-based authorization and no further authentication. In InitializeConnection, QMGMT will force authentication, even if WRITE doesn't require it. This means that if WRITE doesn't require authentication then we will still be in a situation where the shadow has to authenticate every time it updates the job ad, because the cached security session would be unauthenticated. One solution is to add a new authorization level (SUBMIT?) that always requires authentication. Another would be to allow commands to be registered with a boolean flag that indicates whether they should always require authentication (requires changing which commands are allowed for a given security session). Before doing that, we would want to get input from more people (like Zach and Todd).
remarks: I grabbed this ticket and resolved it for 7.5.0. There are now two QMGMT commands: one for read and one for write. When registering commands, it is now possible to pass force_authentication=true to force authentication in the security negotiation phase. This avoids the problem of using an anonymous cached security session for a command that forces authentication in the command handler. I have set force_authentication for all commands in the schedd that should have it.

title: Ticket #7582: SINful mangled when flocking
description: We have a schedd that has a separate public IP than private IP -- we created a private network with PRIVATE_NETWORK_INTERFACE set to the private IP, and used the public IP for TCP_FORWARDING_HOST. This schedd flocks and advertises itself to the flocking collector with the following SINful: <192.170.236.216:9618?PrivAddr=%3c192.168.35.156:9618%3fsock%3dschedd_568_2de2_3%3e&PrivNet=open-science-ce-ce1-5bd796976b-drplh&addrs=192.170.236.216-9618&alias=open-science-ce-ce1-5bd796976b-drplh&noUDP&sock=schedd_568_2de2_3> In the above, 192.170.236.216 is the public IP, 192.168.35.156 was the private IP, and open-science-ce-ce1-5bd796976b-drplh was the FULL_HOSTNAME (not in DNS). Somewhere along the line, the SINful was getting mangled, and the negotiator was responding to the schedd using <192.170.236.216:9618?addrs=192.170.236.216-9618&alias=open-science-ce-ce1-5bd796976b-drplh&noUDP&sock=schedd_568_2de2_3> This caused the security session to be invalid, and the negotiator had to reauthenticate. What caused this?
remarks: 2020-Apr-28 19:31:23 by tlmiller: Mat, I think it's still worthwhile for you to try to confirm using a less-unrealistic set-up, but I found one for which the master branch fails to run a job but this patch succeeds: use role : personal SCHEDD_DEBUG = D_SECURITY:2 # Speed the test up. NEGOTIATOR_INTERVAL = 5 # Allow condor_submit and condor_q to authenticate. SEC_DEFAULT_METHODS = FS # Grant them permission to submit jobs and read the queue user-specifically. ALLOW_WRITE = *@azaphrael.org/* # This allows all daemons in a single personal condor to talk to each other.. # (it's also the default, but we're trying to be clear about what's going on) SEC_USE_FAMILY_SESSION = TRUE # .. so make sure that the negotiator _must_ use the match password # (which is also on by default, but I forgot to be explicit about it) NEGOTIATOR.SEC_USE_FAMILY_SESSION = FALSE # Allows the negotiator to query private ads. COLLECTOR.ALLOW_NEGOTIATOR = 184.60.25.78 # Force only the schedd to use CCB. We must disable shared port for the schedd # because otherwise the shared port, and thus all its daemons, uses or doesn't # use CCB, which will cause problems (because one side must be public). SCHEDD.USE_SHARED_PORT = FALSE SCHEDD.PRIVATE_NETWORK_NAME = mish-mash SCHEDD.PRIVATE_NETWORK_ADDRESS = 10.10.2.20 COLLECTOR_HOST = 184.60.25.78:9618 SCHEDD.CCB_ADDRESS = $(COLLECTOR_HOST) # Give the schedd permission to register with CCB. COLLECTOR.ALLOW_DAEMON = 184.60.25.78 2020-May-11 15:20:03 by tlmiller: See also #7223. 2020-May-11 15:23:29 by tlmiller: The code review is against the stable-version patch. My previous testing was against the identical patch for v8.9. 2020-Jul-02 13:06:15 by johnkn: CODE_REVIEW : looks good. 2020-Jul-02 15:54:27 by zmiller: I just saw this ticket and I vaguely remember discussing it a while ago. I just wanted to throw a really general question out there, but I haven't thought about this AT ALL so maybe it doesn't make sense and we can disregard this comment. But anyhow: The problem was a mismatch of what was used for identifying session: the session was being stored under a different key than was being used to look it up (stored with private network info, lookup without). This latest code change keeps the private network name to store them and also to look them up. This makes the sesion ids match, and is the most specific, so this will certainly work. Did we consider the just the opposite, which is to remove the private info for both storing and retrieving? This might allow better session reuse and/or cut down on unnecessary information being transmitted. On the other hand it might create a conflict by having two distinct entities trying to use the same identifier. Like I said, I haven't thought about it and don't want to switch contexts so if someone who actually looked at it and understood can chime in please do. 2020-Jul-02 16:29:40 by tlmiller: IIRC, we didn't consider making the identifier less specific because this problem happened when we started including the whole Sinful in the identifier, which we did for some good reason which I don't presently recall. (It may have just been that the old <ip:port> style wasn't enough and it seems safer to use all of the indentifier bits that we have.)

title: Ticket #5946: MAX_JOBS_PER_OWNER broken if job specifies an accounting_group
description: The config knob MAX_JOBS_PER_OWNER works great at specifying a limit per owner unless the job specifies an accounting_group, in which case it is possible to exceed the limit. To reproduce, simply continuously submit jobs that specify an accounting_group. The schedd will refuse to accept jobs above the limit until the schedd performs count_jobs() (typically within a minute or less), at which point jobs will incorrectly be accepted again. The problem appears to be that the code introduced in #4641 uses the submitter name (eg accounting principle) for past submits, and the owner name for recent submits that have occurred since the last count_jobs(). Credit to INFN for reporting this bug; see this thread in htcondor-users.

title: Ticket #4654: Non-awful hold messages for VM Universe
description: The HoldReason for VM universe jobs which failed to launch is pretty terrible. A rough draft of suggestions follows. One possibility for implementation is to use the param table infrastructure to create an "error table" or "hold reason table" in which condor_q will look the short-form hold reasons to print out the long-form hold reasons below. Similar code would be welcomed / required for the (user) job log. (The instructions for VMGAHP_ERR_JOBCLASSAD_NO_VMWARE_VMX_PARAM are a little different than the others; it's not clear if it's better or not.) VMGAHP_ERR_JOBCLASSAD_NO_VM_MEMORY_PARAM The attribute ${ATTR_JOB_VM_MEMORY} was not set in the job ad sent to the VM GAHP. HTCondor will usually prevent you from submitting a VM universe job without ${ATTR_JOB_VM_MEMORY} set, so this may not be your fault. Examine your job (condor_q -l $(CLUSTER_ID).$(PROC_ID)) and verify that ${ATTR_JOB_VM_MEMORY} is set. If it is, please contact your administrator. HTCondor will usually set this attribute when you submit a valid VMWare job (it is derived from vmware_dir). If you used condor_submit to submit this job, contact your administrator. remarks: 2015-Jan-06 12:14:14 by bbockelm: Hold up on this one -- I'm not entirely sure about the approach here. If I understand right the approach here is, condor_q itself does some simple string matching on hold reason and substitutes strings from a lookup table. I worry about this because: This means that different condor CLI versions would have different outputs for "condor_q -held" Different clients (HTCondor-C, python bindings) would get different versions of the hold message. "condor_q -af:h ClusterID HoldReason" would have different hold reasons than "condor_q -held" I worry about using string mangling for the substitution (seems brittle) instead of hold sub-codes. You start to get inconsistencies between CLI output and the contents of the classad, which results in things like #4808 which look like a scary maintenance nightmare to me. As string constants are collapsed into a single object by ClassAds, the memory savings of having shorter strings in the schedd are going to be miniscule. On first blush, this approach seems to be problematic versus having the startd set a more reasonable hold reason in the first place. Is there a design doc here? Who did the code review? I think this warrants further attention, or at least recording previous discussions onto the ticket... 2015-Jan-06 14:02:35 by tlmiller: (Made verbatim to make the quotes readable on the web.) > This means that different condor CLI versions would have different outputs > for "condor_q -held" Why is that a problem? I don't think we make any promises about output stability. What would be better? A new flag to condor_q that nobody knows about? Printing the explanations beneath the output? > Different clients (HTCondor-C, python bindings) would get different versions > of the hold message. The hold message is the one in the job ad; everybody /except/ condor_q -hold sees the same message. > "condor_q -af:h ClusterID HoldReason" would have different hold reasons than > "condor_q -held" This is entirely deliberate; I'm assuming that 'condor_q -hold' is used primarily by users (rather than scripts). > I worry about using string mangling for the substitution (seems brittle) > instead of hold sub-codes. This is true. I suppose hold reason codes and sub-codes are cheap enough to add to the projection. > You start to get inconsistencies between CLI output and the contents of the > classad, which results in things like #4808 which look like a scary > maintenance nightmare to me.
