title: Ticket #4443: Allow sysadmins to enable PR_SET_NO_NEW_PRIVS
description: prctl(PR_SET_NO_NEW_PRIVS, ...) can be invoked by the forked starter (no root privs required) before it exec's to the user's job. This prctl flag prevents any processes launched by the job from gaining any capabilities (for example, by executing a setuid binary). This may not actually be a desired thing at all sites - for example, CMS relies on glexec which is setuid - but it is likely going to cover the majority of cases.

I'm thinking about a pool of mixed distro pool. 2014-Jul-10 19:53:02 by bbockelm: Hi Greg, That's a bit surprising - do you know what would be wrong with ssh_to_job? I didn't think that would be setuid... I would indeed like to make things Big Loud and Fatal if NO_NEW_PRIVS is enabled but the distro doesn't support it - if a site depends on it for security, I don't like to fail silently. Since the machine ad is available when it is evaluated, sysadmins can conditionally disable it on a mixed distro pool. Brian 2014-Jul-11 08:20:29 by gthain: No idea what is wrong -- it was a bit of a surprise to me, too. We don't start sshd as root, and it isn't setuid/setgid, nor is ssh-keygen.

title: Ticket #6184: Default annex should be restricted-use.
description: There's no default mechanism to restrict an annex to the user who's paying for it, and the optional one is clumsy (requiring a partially-constructed config.d). Since the "personal annex" is a major use case (and of particular interest to Frank Wuerthwein), we should make this easy. Add a command-line option to restrict the annex to a given (list of )user(s). (e.g., START = Owner == ${USER} or START = isMemberOf( Owner, $(USER_LIST) ).) Make the current user's Owner value the default for this attribute. This may be trivial (getpwnam() or whatever HTCondor already does) or it could be complicated (which HTCondor daemon do we ask what our authenticated Owner attribute is?). Once we've done the above, add an option to avoid restricting the START expression for the (infrastructural) capability and capacity use-cases.

title: Ticket #4910: Restore gnu linker option to wrap exit()
description: For unix, we define our own exit() function that can either call _exit() or exec() a program when the current process wants to exit. This is important for daemons in certain situations. We used to use a feature of the gnu linker to have our exit() alternative replace exit() for all callsites, and allow it to call the real exit() when appropriate. We lost the use of this gnu linker option when the build system was switched to cmake. As a consequence, we always terminate daemons and tools with a call to _exit() on unix, which bypasses exit-time cleanup code like global destructors. This can confuse run-time code analysis tools, leave FILE buffers unwritten, and bypass other cleanup code.

title: Ticket #7280: 8.7 to 8.9 upgrade caused VM universe jobs to stop matching
description: When the SWAMP upgraded from 8.7 to 8.9, VM universe jobs stopped matching. Those jobs' submit files included lines much like the following: swamp.submit +JobVMNetworking = true +JobVMNetworkingType = swampinabox Because of the leading +, the right-hand side is interpreted as a ClassAd, which makes the value of the attribute JobVMNetworkingType a reference to the attribute swampinabox. This attribute does not exist, so the value of JobVMNetworkingType is undefined. In 8.7, this didn't matter because the job's Requirements expression did not include JobVMNetworkingType for this job; in 8.9 it does. Since all startds in a SWAMP-in-a-Box actually had the 'swampinabox' network, this did not cause problems. I assume that either (a) the default network worked or (b) the awk script used to generate the libvirt XML files just assumed that all of the job-ad attributes that were supposed to be strings were strings, and used the value of JobVMNetworkingType without checking (maybe after stripping some non-existing double quotes). The intent in 8.7 was clearly to include a networking-type requirement if the user specified a networking type. I don't know if using the issue is that 8.7 and 8.9 are treating absent attributes and undefined attribute references differently, or if that in 8.9, the VM universe requirements-writing is done against the job ad (as modified by the +) instead of the submit file. The immediate fix for SWAMP was to (a) add "swampinabox" to the list of vm networking types in the startd config swamp-modified.config VM_Networking_Types = "nat,swampinabox" and (b) quote "swampinabox" in their submit file template(s). swamp-modified1.submit +JobVMNetworking = true +JobVMNetworkingType = "swampinabox" The work for us is to determine if (a) 8.8 and 8.9 are consistent in this behavior and (b) if we thinkg the 8.7 or 8.9 behavior is correct. SWAMP may also benefit from switching from the syntax above to using the equivalent submit language commands, although I haven't verified that the second one actually works. swamp-modified2.submit vm_networking = true vm_networking_type = swampinabox
remarks: 2019-Sep-24 14:33:45 by johnkn: Todd's analysis is correct here. In 8.8 requirements generation is done by looking at submit commands, which are not being set. In 8.9 requirements generation is done using job attributes, which are being set here, but set incorrectly, so that the generated requirements will only work if swampinabox is a string-valued job or machine attribute that is one of the advertised VM networking types. Essentially, the switch to 8.9 exposed a bug in the submit files. Also, it is bad form to bypass the submit keywords in 8.8 because that also bypasses requirements generation.
creator: tlmiller

title: Ticket #2082: IPv6: SafeSock includes ipv4 addr in header
description: SafeSock reassembles a stream of packets from UDP. Inbound streams of packets may come from multiple multiple daemons, multiple machines, or some combination. Conceivably multiple streams may even come from a single source daemon. For reassembly it's necessary to identify which stream a given packet is for. To do this, SafeSock adds an identifying header. The header is written in _condorPacket::makeHeader (/src/condor_io/SafeMsg.cpp line 532). It's read in _condorPacket::getHeader (src/condor_io/SafeMsg.cpp line 214) and used to identify the correct stream in SafeSock::handle_incoming_packet (/src/condor_io/safe_sock.cpp line 625). To determine if two identifiers are from the same, SafeSock::same is used (/src/condor_includes/safe_sock.h line 142). The identifier is a _condorMsgID struct (/src/condor_includes/SafeMsg.h line 28). The members are: Name Type Bytes on wire Meaning How created ip_addr long 4 Source IPv4 address my_ip_addr() pid int 2 Source PID getpid() time long 4 Time source SafeSock created time(NULL) msgNo int 2 Random number, incremented Windows: rand(); Elsewhere: lrand48() To verify: these are only used to identify streams, and are treated strictly opaquely. Problem 1: Two different machines with the same IP address (because they're using private network addresses behind two different NATs) can theoretically collide today. As pools scale up, the chances increase. Problem 2: An IPv6 address won't fit in ip_addr. Potential problems to investigate You may be able to denial of service a Condor daemon by sending a stream of UDP packets purportedly from actual daemons in the pool with bogus sequence numbers, causing Can make a bit harder by adding the source IP address (as seen in recvfrom or equivalent) to the hash/identifier for the message (meaning you'd need to start spoofing IP packets). Current plan Hijack ip_addr, pid, and time (10 bytes). They're just used as opaque integers anyway. Generate 10 reasonably random bytes of data. Maybe md5(concatenate(ipv4/6_addr, pid, time to the microsecond, weak random number))? Maybe just 10 bytes from /dev/random? Shove those 10 bytes into ip_addr, pid, and time. This should drop out chances of collision on any given pair of packets down to 1 in 2^80. Note that using MD5 or SHA1 might require OpenSSL, which is not(?) currently a requirement for building Condor. If we go down that route, we might as well just use OpenSSL's ability to generate cryptographically secure random numbers. Another option would be to drag in a small hash implementation. Another option is to have some platform specific code to acquire a random number is a suitable way (/dev/urandom on many Unixes, /dev/random where that doesn't work. Something unknown on Windows.) Assume a collector serving 1,000,000 nodes. Each node has 10 daemons. Each daemon is sending an update (and thus a message) once per minute. So every minute, there are about 10,000,000 messages received. Assume that we're worried about re-assembling only 10,000,000 potential streams at a time (true if a given stream is 6 or fewer packets given the 10-second timeout in /src/condor_includes/safe_sock.h line 37 "SAFE_SOCK_MAX_BTW_PKT_ARVL".). Given those assumptions, the chances at a collision are 0.00000000004135902731 in any given window. If we consider a 1 in a 1,000,000 chance of collision acceptable, we can be reassembling up to about 1,554,944,645 streams at once. Given that UDP streams are lossy to start, I believe that level of risk is acceptable. (Math behind the above calculations is attached as collision_probability.xls.) Idea brainstorming Set it to 0x00000000 in all cases: highly likely to cause UDP streams to erroneously mix. Set it to a subset of the IPv6 address: chance of collisions, possibly a large chance depending on how we pick the subset. Set it to a hash of the IPv6 address: chance of collisions. Extend it 16-bytes: breaks backward compatibility Modify code to ignore it and use the source of the UDP packet. May collide things if a NAT is forwarding UDP packets for several machines behind it. Modify code to ignore it and extend protocol with "real" information. Can this be done in a backward compatible way? Hash the IPv6 address, but stuff the hash across all of ip_addr, pid, and time. Maybe msgNo except 1 bit. Gives us 10 or more bytes to distinguish connections. Needs investigation for safety. Still some risk of collision. Have two code paths: IPv4 and IPv6, where if the socket is from an IPv6 source, we use a variant supporting 16-bit addresses. Risk: what about IPv6 <-> IPv4 gateways? Can we end up in the wrong code path. Also, duplicate code paths are a recipe for unintentional future divergence. Also, necessitates teaching this layer about the source of a packet; something it doesn't currently do. Note that in all cases where we put an invalid/fake value in ip_addr field, we could pick a "safe" or "invalid" area of the address space. That loses bits to distinguish sources (increase collision chance) at the benefit of eliminating the possibility of a collision with an IPv4 address. The traditional private network (especially 10.x.x.x) is problematic since we have using using such spaces, but invalid or nonsensical addresses might work. Note that Random notes Is there a risk today of collisions? What if two different NATted, private networks both have a 192.168.0.1 machine, and both such machines contact us. We could have SafeSock know if it's dealing with IPv4 or IPv6 and have different code paths. Essentially the IPv6 path would be a new revision of the protocol. Down side: duplicated code paths to keep in sync, not obvious what to do when IPv9 comes out or if we use non-TCP protocols with SafeSock. Status Decision made. Minjae will be implementing. Talking with Minjae to ensure we've handled all necessary cases.

title: Ticket #4506: condor_master crashes if LOCAL_CONFIG_DIR has unreadable files
description: If one has LOCAL_CONFIG_DIR set and creates a new file in that directory with ownership of root, group ownership of root, and mode 0600, then the condor_master will crash upon execution of condor_reconfig. On a full restart, you see something like this in the MasterLog: 07/21/14 18:23:55 Using config source: /etc/condor/condor_config 07/21/14 18:23:55 Using local config sources: 07/21/14 18:23:55 /etc/condor/config.d/facter 07/21/14 18:23:55 /etc/condor/condor_config.local
remarks: 2015-Sep-22 15:50:26 by gthain: Proposed solution -- condor_reconfig should not send the reconfig if the config files aren't readable. 2015-Sep-22 15:51:20 by tpdownes: Consider addition of "parsing test" in addition to file permission testing. 2015-Sep-23 16:06:26 by tannenba: OSG also reported the same issue in #5254. Here is the wisdom from that ticket: If /etc/condor/config.d contains a configuration file that is not readable by the condor user, then the master starts up normally, but a reconfig will cause it to exit without a log message or killing its daemons. Looks like the master is acting as root when it reads the config files on initial startup, but is acting as the condor user when doing a reconfig. This inconsistency can keep admins from discovering the error in their config files in the first place. The master prints the error message to stderr instead of logging it, and exits without shutting down any of its children. These should probably both be fixed. The logging is most important to me, though I think that from an admin's point of view, the ideal behavior is that if a reconfig fails due to broken files (or any other reason), that Condor should keep running with the old config. I have no idea how feasible that is with the Condor codebase. Given this is an issue for both OSG and LIGO, I'd like to target it for early in the v8.4 series. 2015-Sep-23 16:17:42 by tpdownes: So prioritize it as a 2? 2015-Sep-23 16:48:18 by tannenba: Hi Tom, you can keep the priority at whatever makes sense for LIGO. I already edited the target fixed version field in the ticket. 2015-Sep-23 16:53:08 by johnkn: Keeping in mind that the config files have to parse as valid in order for condor_reconfig to actually send any messages to any daemons, I think we can reasonably assume that this problem is always permissions. (That is unless there are people changing config files and then rebooting the machines, etc). So The quick-and-dirty solution is to have condor_reconfig check to see that all of the config files that IT reads are group & world readable before sending the reconfig message. The better solution would be to change the behavior of the master on reconfig so that it first parses the new config files, and only if they are valid does it actually reconfigure and send the reconfig message on to its children 2015-Sep-23 17:29:03 by johnkn: I propose that if condor_reconfig is running as root, it should change it's uid to condor and then do an access check on each of the config files. if any fail the access check it will print out an error message and then exit without sending the reconfig. 2015-Oct-06 16:06:48 by johnkn: I have a patch that changes condor_reconfig/on/off/restart to check to see if the config files are readable by the condor user if the tool is run as root. If any of the files are not readable by condor, it will print: ERROR: The following configuration files cannot be read by user 'condor'. Aborting command /scratch/rootly/condor841/local.localhost/config/00stuff 2015-Oct-20 13:06:40 by adesmet: Code Review: Approved. Should generate a few new tickets for: Daemons should be able to re-read their config files, but back up to old configuration on an error. (The only way to know you're looking at all of the configuration files is to read them, since any given file might add some more.) Various tools, especially reconfig, restart, and off, should block until the daemon replies "Yes!" If not yes, should return something useful ("Unable to re-read configuration." "Permission denied.")

title: Ticket #1354: Report network traffic for daemons
description: Ken Hahn notes that he would occasionally find it useful to know how much bandwidth Condor is using. After a brief discussion, some ideas: Track total bytes read and written over the network, dividing them into data to and from localhost and remote hosts. (As local traffic is "cheap".) So we'll end up with four totals: localhost_bytes_written, localhost_bytes_read, remote_bytes_written, remote_bytes_read. Make this available conveniently available to the sysadmin: Report this in the daemon's ClassAd. Handy for polling via condor_status and feeding to tools like rrdtool. This one seems like a solid win. Report in logs at regular intervals. More questionable value, but shouldn't be too hard. Perhaps at D_DAEMONCORE or D_FULLDEBUG level? Feed to a hook or plugin. Specialized, but allows for instantaneously updates. Of course, we probably don't want to be calling this for ever read and write. The ability to ask questions like, "What is the bandwidth over the last X seconds" would be nice, but turns four simple bigints into a queue of values, chewing up memory and adding lots of complexity. Many routers have similar limitations, so this isn't particularly mean. You can get 99% of the benefit by simply feeding the current cumulative total to a system like rrdtool which is prepared to figure out values over time automatically and at whatever interval the admin likes.

title: Ticket #6491: Report late materialization hold, resume and failure in the user log
description: When a job factory fails to load on restart of the schedd, or when materialization fails, the Job Factory should be placed into a non-resumable pause state. when condor_hold is used and the cluster object matches the constraint expression for the hold, the factory should be placed into a resumeable pause state. In both of these cases, the change to a paused state should be reported in the user event log, along with the reason for the pause. When condor_release is use and the cluster object matches the constraint expression, the factory should be unpaused provided that it was paused because of a hold and not because of materialization failure. This should also be reported in the user event log. Two new event types will be added to the condor event module, one for factory pause and one for factory release. The factory pause event will include an optional reason, an optional pause code and an optional hold code. In addition, the existing factory remove event will be expanded to report how many jobs had been materialized at the time of removal, whether the materialization was known to be complete or incomplete. If the factory was paused at the time of removal, the pause reason will be reported. Thus if a factory fails to re-load, when it is removed on completion of all of the existing jobs, the reason for the failure will be reported. title: Ticket #361: Export failover functionality in HDFS datanode as plugin
description: This has two parts (a) To let data-nodes of Hadoop fail-over if they loose connection with the name server (b) We want to have a plug-in that is invoked and kind of tell data-node what it should do if it looses connection with a name server. We would be able to use this plug-in to query our collector to know the network address of redundant name server (if first one fails) and have data-node reconnect. So, once the connection via this proxy is broken, we probably need to create a new proxy object as these objects are tied to network address. The plug-in code is invoked once the 'sendHeartbeat' fails and this plug-in updates the local configuration object (passed to it as argument when notifying it about lost connection). One comment about using HADOOP-5257's plug-in modules is that those are specific to starting and stopping daemons along with name/data node startup/shutdown. Although we can add a generic changeState(state_info, Object) method to surf other purposes like ours but still in our case we probably need at one time only one plug-in to handle fail-over and only that plug-in should be notified when a connection is broken. I will try to attach a patch by tomorrow after doing some cleanup in the code. I still need to test the full effects of these changes on Hadoop. title: Ticket #1587: Problems with semantics of failed file transfer
description: Number 1 should be in V7_4-branch, all other stuff in master branch. it is a flat out bug that the ExitStatus, ExitSignal, and ExitedBySignal attributes are not set when file transfer fails. these attributes must be propagated into the job ad so the user can see them and make policy decisions using on_exit_hold and on_exit_remove. [DONE] the behavior of transfer_output_files will change so that a failure does not put the job on hold. (if the user desires this, they will be able to implement it using the on_exit_hold expression in the submit file... see items 3 and 4) each file that is successfully transferred is added to a list of "Good Files" in the job ad. each file that fails to transfer will be added to the list of "Bad Files" in the job ad. using these lists, users can specify what should happen when errors occur. if a file fails to be transferred for any reason other than not existing, the job will still go on hold as this is a system failure, not a problem with the job. in this case condor should increment NumSystemHolds for the job, which it currently does not. to recreate the behavior we have today, you would simply add a line like this to the submit file: on_exit_hold == (BadFilesList != "") (that is, if there are any files in the bad files list, put the job on hold, which is what happens now) Additional: The output files should be brought back smallest to largest first. If it is easy to specify an arbitrary ordering as well, then do it.
remarks: 2010-Aug-19 16:27:02 by psilord: Ok, implementing number 1 in 7.4 correctly is a non-backwards compatible rathole. To implement it incorrectly would require a terrible hack that would be a nasty surprise for someone in the future and difficult to maintain. The reason is that in JICShadow::transferOutput() when the file transfer fails (and it doesn't know if it is a critical error or recoverable error!), we call notifyStarterError() passing in the hold reason, hold code, hold subcode and enforcing that it is a critical error. This call ends up calling REMOTE_CONDOR_ulog() in the starter with the hold information. When the shadow sees the critical hold request via the pseudo op ulog, it updates the job ad with the hold information from the network packet, updates the schedd with the new ad, then immediately exits with the JOB_SHOULD_HOLD code for the schedd. At this point there is no opportunity to inject the exit information of the job into the job ad. One would think the correct way to fix this would be to implement a new pseudo call which simply updates whatever attributes in the sent ad into the job ad and commits it. Then I could call this just before notifyStarterError() and things would be happy. HOWEVER Doing this allows a race condition that if after the update from the starter to the shadow about the job exit status, then if the file transfer fails and both daemons are taken down, the schedd thinks the job completed successfully. Bad. But, if this is in the stable series, then I can't change the protocol between the starter and the shadow. So, the nasty hack would be to encode the exit status of the job into the hold reason string, and decode it on the shadow side, if present, and insert the attributes into the job ad along with the hold attributes and continue. This probably still suffers from the race condition mentioned above if the shadow manages to update the jobad in the schedd and die badly before exiting with JOB_SHOULD_HOLD. 2010-Aug-19 16:29:54 by psilord: Another bad idea would be to touch all of the output files at the job completion so the file transfer couldn't fail at all due to nonexistence. This is bad because if the job core dumped, we touch all of its files, then it would leave the queue totally. This is different behavior that what 1 implies. Which is the job still goes on hold, but the exit information is still injected into the ad. 2010-Aug-19 16:31:32 by psilord: I'm going to explore making the file transfer failure a non-critical error and see what happens. 2010-Aug-19 16:42:32 by psilord: I tried it and it won't work. ANY hold event from the starter to the shadow results in the shadow exiting ASAP. 2010-Aug-20 10:36:57 by psilord: Ok, new tactic. I'm going to expand the interface to RemoteErrorEvent to include the exit information. Then, an updated starter and shadow can correctly serialize the exit information across the ulog pseduo call. For updated starters and old shadows, the old shadow will simply ignore the new information in the serialized classad instance of the RemoteErrorEvent and work as usual. This allows backwards compatibility in the stable series. 2010-Aug-20 14:11:22 by psilord: Ok, expanding the interface wasn't a good idea. I found REMOTE_CONDOR_set_job_attr() as a method of the starter setting job attrs in the jobad of the shadow. So I'm exploring that now. 2010-Aug-24 13:30:33 by psilord: Ok, I have a different method, this one looks far better: In JICShadow::transferOutput(), decouple the handling of the failed transfer from the transfer itself. Put the handling of the failed transfer in to a new function called JICShadow::transferOutputMopUp(). Add a new remote system call in NTsenders.cpp which transmits the exit status of the job over to the shadow which calls updateJob(U_TERMINATE) with the information. This sets the process specific termination attributes in the job ad, but this code path will not treat the job as having exited wrt terminate events in the job log, etc, etc, etc. In if JICShadow::transferOutput() fails, then if the shadow is of 7.4.4 or later, then send the new remote system call if the transfer failed due to the job having exited and not produced the whole of the transfer_output_files set. Then call JICShadow::transferOutputMopUp() which will notify the shadow of the failure and cause the shadow to drop the connection to the starter. 2010-Aug-26 11:26:42 by psilord: Ok, the last proposal seems to be the right method. I've implemented the starter side, and am now just implementing the shadow side of what to do when it gets this termination information from the job. Other than a nagging question of how to handle the list of jobs under the starter (like how do I know I picked the right job's exit status?) I think I'm on the downhill slide to completion. 2010-Aug-30 16:05:06 by psilord: I can pick the right job out of the list by looking for the published ad from the user proc which contains ATTR_JOB_PID. All other jobs which are not the main job, like the pre/post scripts or condor_ssh, will name mangle that attribute name. A bit circuitous, but sufficient. 2010-Aug-30 16:32:13 by psilord: I had a little bit of a crappy merge with the master code. Hopefully it is all fixed up. 2010-Oct-20 16:03:30 by jfrey: Bulk change of target version from v070504 to v070505 using ./ticket-target-mover. 2010-Nov-01 15:34:26 by danb: I think that the changes in commit b3ef6289 [18897] to improve handling of file transfer failures have somewhat broken disconnected shadow/starter handling. The changes were intended to improve handling of the case where file transfer fails and wants to put the job on hold. However, there are other types of failures (such as network disconnect) where file transfer can fail without trying to put the job on hold. These cases used to be handled by the shadow/starter disconnect behavior. Now, the starter just blows up in an assert: 11/01 14:58:57 Sandbox transfer failed. 11/01 14:58:57 ERROR "Assertion ERROR on (m_ft_info.hold_code != 0)" at line 435 in file jic_shadow.cpp I see the following responsible code: if(!m_ft_info.success) { ASSERT(m_ft_info.hold_code != 0); } One way to test this code path is to SIGSTOP the shadow while the job is running. Then when the job finishes and the starter is blocked waiting for a response to its file transfer request, do condor_off -schedd. The desired behavior is that the starter sees the connection to the shadow go bad and enters disconnected mode. Turning the schedd back on should cause a new shadow to connect to the starter and successfully finish the file transfer. I have verified that this worked in 7.4.2. I have made a child ticket #1750 for the disconnect bug. 2011-Jan-27 14:46:04 by danb: Bulk change of target version from v070505 to v070506 using ./ticket-target-mover. 2011-Feb-01 16:19:13 by tannenba: Bulk change of target version from v070506 to NULL using ./ticket-target-mover. 2011-Mar-31 17:10:20 by zmiller: reviewed. was committed long ago. resolving ticket.

title: Ticket #6242: Debian jessie upstream package named htcondor
description: Debian has renamed its OS-provided package to htcondor. This means that adding the UW-managed repo and running "apt-get install condor" runs into conflicts and that "apt-get upgrade" doesn't see a reason to upgrade the package. One solution is for the UW-managed package to set "Provides: htcondor" in its package settings. Alternative you could rename your package and set "Provides: condor" for backwards compatibility. Either option allows "apt-get install condor" to behave as it currently does.

description: LIGO reports the following problem: We upgraded the Caltech LIGO Condor pool from version 7.8.0 to 7.8.1 today and this has resulted in the following potentially serious +problem. In particular, it appears that a user's dag was lost without a rescue dag being generated. Of particular interest is the user +dag.lib.err file, [root@ldas-grid condor]# cat +/home/dtalukder/Projects/ringdown/S5/finalihoperuns/mo_17_18/857232370-862070770/s5_ring_mo_1-24.dag.lib.err condor_scheduniv_exec.99293315.0: error while loading shared libraries: libcondor_utils_7_8_0.so: cannot open shared object file: No +such file or directory Is there a problem with the condor_dagman binary being unable to survive a Condor upgrade due to its use of shared libraries? title: Ticket #7845: schedd doesn't send available jobs to negotiator
description: When you release a job that was on hold, the schedd doesn't immediately update the priorec array; that's sensible, it's an expensive task and who knows how many other changes will happen before we need it again. However, if you release a job that was on hold, at least in some cases, the schedd won't send it to the negotiator the next time the negotiator asks for jobs. The particular scenario I encountered was easy to see because the released job was the only idle job in the queue. The immediate cause was that the negotiator contacted the schedd before the schedd's update interval had expired, so count_jobs() hadn't been called since the job was released. What made this particularly frustrating is that their appear to code to recompute the priorec array when the negotiator contacts the schedd, but it wasn't firing. To quote the schedd log: Reusing prioritized runnable job list because nothing has changed. Shouldn't we be marking the priorec array dirty when a held job is released?
creator: tlmiller

title: Ticket #1092: Git update hook to disallow development code in stable branches
description: On two recent occasions (#1089, #1091), a significant amount of development code on the master branch was merged into V7_4-branch. This is bad for several reasons. To help prevent this from happening in the future, we should add an update hook in our main git repository that rejects pushes that introduce commits from the master branch into any stable branch. Cherry-picking of individual commits should still be allowed. The update hook can work as follows. If a branch head is being moved (not created or deleted) and the branch name indicates it's a stable branch (i.e. '=Vx_y...=' where x and y are numbers and y is even), then perform the following check: Produce a list of SHA1s that are on master but not on the stable branch, and a list of SHA1s that the push is adding to the stable branch. If these two lists contain any common elements, reject the push. Cherry-picking commits from master to a stable branch would be allowed, since the new commits have new SHA1s. Branch creation is always allowed, so creating a new stable series branch off of master would work fine.

title: Ticket #1568: Shadow doesn't notice dead connection until remote machine rebooted
description: This is a report from Rob Lahaye on condor-users. During input file transfer, the startd's SUSPEND expression evaluates to True. It tries to send a DC_SIGSUSPEND to the starter. The OS is Windows, so this is a CEDAR message. The startd times out after 20 seconds because the starter doesn't return to daemon-core during file transfer. The startd immediately hard-kills the starter. It then tries to send a DC_SIGCONTINUE and a SIGTERM to the dead starter. The shadow notices the file transfer connection close when the starter is killed. But it doesn't notice the claim connection close, so it continues to hang around. The startd now considers the job and claim dead, but the schedd and shadow think they're still going. The schedd sends periodic keep-alives on the claim, which the startd ignores. This continues for three days until the execute machine is rebooted, at which time the shadow notices the claim connection close, so it exits, returning the job to idle status. The job is subsequently rematched and run successfully. The submit machine is linux and the execute machine is Windows. Both are running Condor 7.4.2. We don't know why the shadow wasn't informed of the closed claim connection for 3 days. The fact that the shadow saw the connection close when the execute machine was rebooted implies the OS on the execute machine was retaining state for the connection. We don't know how a process on the execute machine could be keeping the connection open, or how the OS would hold the connection open without a process having a handle to it. An immediate solution (more of a band-aid) for this problem is to set STARTD_SENDS_ALIVES to True. The startd would stop sending keep-alives, and the schedd would kill the shadow. We should consider making this the default in Condor 7.6.x. See #671 and #1420. This problem is similar to #1272, where the shadow didn't notice its connection with the starter dying for 2 hours. The solution suggested there of having the starter send regular job update messages and shadow going into disconnected mode when several messages are missed could be used here as well. The initial cause of this problem is that the starter cannot receive messages from the startd while in file transfer. The same is true of the shadow. In this case, it's Windows-specific as DC_SIGSUSPEND is delivered as an OS signal on unix. We should consider how to make both daemons able to respond to CEDAR commands during file transfer.
remarks: 2014-Jan-27 11:33:37 by tannenba: Resolving this ticket because 1) the suggested work-around, aka to enable startd sends alives, is now the default operation, and 2) likely #4122 will result in the shadow noticing the dead connection within 6 minutes (by default)

title: Ticket #7668: Make Python bindings Schedd constructor location_ad argument optional
description: The Schedd constructor is an overloaded function with two signatures, __init__(_object* self) __init__(_object* self, ClassAdWrapper location_ad) The intent is that in the first form, it finds the local schedd, and in the other form, it contacts a remote schedd. This works, but because the location ad is required, if you're writing a wrapper function where someone may or may not pass in a location ad, you have to do something like this: def get_schedd(location_ad = None): if location_ad is None: return Schedd() else: return Schedd(location_ad) instead of the more convenient def get_schedd(location_ad = None): return Schedd(location_ad) which right now emits an error like Boost.Python.ArgumentError: Python argument types in Schedd.__init__(Schedd, NoneType) did not match C++ signature: __init__(_object* self) __init__(_object* self, ClassAdWrapper location_ad) I checked another constructor for consistency, Startd, and found a similar problem: $ python -c "import htcondor; htcondor.Startd(None)" Traceback (most recent call last): File "<string>", line 1, in <module> File "/home/jkarpel/.python/lib/python3.7/site-packages/htcondor/_lock.py", line 77, in wrapper rv = func(*args, **kwargs) TypeError: No registered converter was able to produce a C++ rvalue of type ClassAdWrapper from this Python object of type NoneType which is confusing because the C++ declaration implies that it can take a None as its argument. It must be failing internally, once the None has already been passed through Boost into our code. In all these cases, passing the location ad as None should work identically to not passing it at all (and it should always be called either ad or location_ad; they are mixed right now (maybe we save that for a later date...)).

title: This attachment is private.
Ticket #6583: VM Universe jobs and use policy : hold_if_memory_exceeded
description: CHTC had a problem with VM universe jobs immediately going on hold when they used the hold-if-memory-exceeded policy. This was caused by #6577, and that change solved the problem. However, during the investigation, we noticed that the slot ad's ImageSize was way too small. This is of potential concern as a reporting issue rather than a policy (because VM universe jobs can't go over JobVMMemory). I eventually determined that the slot running a VM universe job reports the "default" ImageSize, that is, the size of the starter and all of its children. This, of course, includes the VM GAHP but not (at least for KVM) the hypervisor. I discussed this with Moate. We agreed that "over memory" is not meaningful for VM universe jobs, and the that hold-if-memory-exceeded policy should therefore ignore VM universe jobs. We agreed that the memory usage reported to the user would ideally be the peak "memory used" reported by the hypervisor, in the hopes that some hypervisors in some configurations would actually be able to tell. We agreed that the slot reporting the sum of the starter and VM GAHP sizes as the 'ImageSize' was at best rather deceptive, but that knowing that number would be useful for setting the VM_MEMORY config knob. Our thought was to either document what the slot's ImageSize reports, or to change it so the VM universe slots report the same number but in an attribute called 'MemoryOverhead' or something similar. We also agreed based on current sizes, that a good nonzero value for the VM_MEMORY config knob would be detected memory minus reserved memory minus 1 GB per four cores (assuming one-core VMs) or fraction thereof for the overhead. This should also be documented somewhere. Action items: The hold-if-memory-exceeded policy should ignore VM universe jobs. Document the meaning of a slot ad's ImageSize attribute in the VM universe, or rename it to MemoryOverhead (or something similar). Document our recommendation for the VM_MEMORY config knob (possibly as a metaknob).
remarks: 2018-Feb-27 17:35:15 by tlmiller: Standard universe jobs suffer from a similar problem. A standard universe job's MemoryUsage is set by the shadow, some long time after the job starts. The startd evaluates policy expressions in the context of its (the original) copy of the job and the slot ad. In the vanilla universe, the starter sends updates for the job ad to the startd, and the ImageSize attribute is updated. In the standard universe, the starter does not send updates to the startd, only the shadow. However, the startd (for all starters) update things like ImageSize on its own. (This is why the ImageSize for VM universe jobs is so wacky.) Thus, evaluating '((TARGET.ImageSize + 1023)/1024) > Memory' in the PREEMPT expression will get the correct memory usage (because the standard universe shadow unconditionally set MemoryUsage to ((ImageSize + 1023)/1024). Thus, MEMORY_EXCEEDED should have three clauses: one for VM universe (which means 'always ignore'), one for standard universe with the expression above, and one for everything else (the current value). However, standard universe jobs can't (presently) be put on hold from the startd; they will be evicted instead. This can be addressed in the START expression if necessary, or perhaps by adding another requirement by default (in condor_submit), that ImageSize < Memory. Additionally, each schedd can help by adding the equivalent clause to its system_periodic_hold. 2018-Mar-01 11:56:18 by johnkn: CODE_REVIEW change looks good. 2018-Mar-09 11:18:17 by tim: DOC REVIEW: Looks good.
check_ins: 2018-Mar-01 10:05 Check-in [54399]: (#6583) Fix typo in HOLD_IF_MEMORY_EXCEEDED policy. (By Todd L Miller ) 2018-Feb-28 15:57 Check-in [54390]: (#6583) WANT_HOLD_IF() no longer evicts (instead of hold) standard universe jobs; it ignores them, instead. The *_MEMORY_EXCEEDED policy metaknobs now ignore VM universe, since those jobs /can't/ exceed their allocation. (By Todd L Miller )

title: Ticket #6096: Fix systemctl config to perform a fast shutdown when stopping
description: On Linux systems using init, doing a service condor stop command is the equivalent of doing a condor_off -master -fast. This is exactly what we want. Unfortunately, currently on systems using systemd, doing a systemctl stop condor is the equivalent of sending SIGKILL to all the condor daemons. This means the HTCondor daemons do not have a chance to do any clean-up, such as removing their classads from the central manager. This has frustrated folks several times, as reported in htcondor-users. To get the desired behavior under systemd, we need to tell systemd to send a SIGQUIT signal to just the condor_master process when stopping the service. Note that we cannot use the systemd ExecStop directive accomplish this, because condor_off is asynchronous and systemd assumes synchronous -- as soon as the ExecStop command returns, systemd immediately kills all daemons with SIGKILL. So instead, we need to not specify ExecStop and instead use KillMode and KillSignal to instruct systemd to send SIGQUIT to the condor_master.

Then as root run systemctl daemon-reload to re-read the systemd config change. or Option 2: Instead of doing systemctl stop condor, do condor_off -master -fast. 2017-Oct-23 08:42:06 by tim: Code Review: Good job. title: Ticket #5340: Controlling daemon startup dependencies and delay for ready
description: We need a way to delay starting up some HTCondor daemons until other daemons are not just created, but also ready to go. This will be configured by adding knobs to list the dependencies and readiness conditions. <DAEMON>_STARTUP_DEPENDS_ON = <DAEMON2>[:condition] [<DAEMON3>[:condition] ...] So, for instance the standard dependencies if the collector depends on the shared port daemon, and the other daemons depend on the collector you could have COLLECTOR_STARTUP_DEPENDS_ON = SHARED_PORT:alive NEGOTIATOR_STARTUP_DEPENDS_ON = COLLECTOR:ready STARTD_STARTUP_DEPENDS_ON = COLLECTOR:ready SCHEDD_STARTUP_DEPENDS_ON = COLLECTOR:ready on the right hand side, the : and the text after it will be optional, with the 'alive' state being the default if non the :<state> is not specified. the possible state values will be arbitrary strings. A new command handler will be added to the master so that daemons can send a command to the master to indicate their readiness. The master will also set an environment variable for daemons that it creates that will encode the sinful address of the master and a capability that identifies who is sending the command and a provides a secret to prevent spoofing of the command. The new command will be DC_SET_READY The command payload will be a ClassAd. The initial version of this command will have a single string value that indicates the readiness state. As indicated above that state string can be optionally used in the *_DEPENDS_ON configuration to wait for a specific state. There will also be a condor tool that can be used to send this command for non-deamoncore daemons. condor_set_ready -state "ready" The tool will pick up the environment variable that has the masters sinful and the capability and use that to send the command. This will allow the master to be sure that the command is coming from the correct instance of the correct daemon. There may also be a tool that can send a command to the master to query the readiness of the various daemons. This command will be DC_QUERY_READY This will return the current readiness state of the daemons, and will have a optional argument that will make it wait to respond until the daemons have achieved the desired state. This will be very useful for the test suite.

title: Ticket #7687: Use stable GPU identifiers
description: (As discussed originally in Slack) Whenever a GPU device dies - or, really, the CUDA library decides relative GPU speeds have changed - the CUDA library will reorder the CUDA devices (so CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=1 actually indicates a different physical device than it did before). HTCondor will not notice this change; this behavior is especially problematic when a GPU disappears as HTCondor will continue to try and schedule a GPU job on a non-existent device (e.g., if a GPU dies on an 8-GPU host then, according to CUDA, device 7 no longer exists; further attempts to use it will blackhole GPU jobs). Since we already enumerate the UUID of existing devices, we can set CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=GPU-8932f937-d72c-4106-c12f-20bd9faed9f6 where GPU-8932f937-d72c-4106-c12f-20bd9faed9f6 refers to the detected UUID of the device. This provides a stable sorting for GPUs in the system. When combined with the ability to mark GPUs as offline, this would allow us to work around problematic nodes (such as those in CHTC currently). HTCondor would no longer try to start on these GPUs and we can blacklist them in the nvidia driver which fixes corresponding Docker problems.

title: Ticket #3017: Parallel Universe jobs with ParallelSchedulingGroups can stay idle
description: Parallel universe jobs that specify they want parallel scheduling groups can stay idle when there are available machines in a group they could match to. This is because of the two phase matching in the dedicated scheduling. When PSG is on, the job is tentatively matched in the schedd, and if a match is found, the dedicated scheduler asks the negotiator for machines. However, it does not ask for any particular machines, so the machines given out by the matchmaker may be from arbitrary parallel scheduling groups. To fix this, when the dedicated scheduler matches to a particular parallel scheduling group, it will amend the requirements of that match to add in the PSG, so that the negotiator will be forced to give it machines from that group.

Additionally, it looks like PSGs may need to have a condor restart instead of doing a condor_reconfig in order to have PSGs initialize (at least on a slot-by-slot basis). 2012-Nov-12 17:45:38 by samf: So it looks like the code does what it's supposed to do. title: Ticket #2256: Multiple vars definitions go into the vars list
description: If you define the same macro name twice for the same node, e.g.: Vars job1 a="foo" Vars job1 a="bar" both definitions go into the table of vars values for the node, and both get passed to condor_submit. (Within condor_submit, the last one takes effect.) Anyhow, there's no reason for both values to get stuffed into the vars data structure within DAGMan. (And fixing this would be a good chance to clean up that data structure in general.)
remarks: 2011-Jun-20 11:21:24 by nwp: I do not understand this ticket. I think the behavior after #2090 and #2255 makes sense: If you submit the same variable twice, then warn the user and if the STRICT warning triggers, abort the DAG. But this ticket asks us to divine the mind of the user, in that we cannot really know whether she means to use the new value or that it is a mistake. If she means to use the new value, the only cost is an additional, albeit ignored, line in a submit file. 2011-Jun-20 12:10:56 by wenger: Hmm, I guess my initial explanation here wasn't very clear. What I'm saying is this: if you do the following: Vars job1 a="foo" Vars job1 a="bar" "bar" should overwrite "foo" within DAGMan's internal data structures. The way things are right now, you end up with two values of a for job1, instead of "bar" overwriting "foo". And then both values of a get passed on the condor_submit command line; but it seems like any reference to $(a) within the submit file can't access the first value of a. Basically, I think having both values for a within DAGMan's data structures is wasteful and unclear. Hopefully that makes sense... 2011-Jun-20 14:18:56 by nwp: I implemented this, tested it in a personal condor, am pushing it (onto master), and resolving this ticket. 2011-Jun-21 13:40:17 by nwp: V7.7.0 is not really broken here, because #2090 is not in 7.7.0

title: Ticket #859: startd does not correctly do claim cleanup
description: I observed a number of machines in the CS pool that have been rejecting claim requests for over 2 weeks without ever successfully running a job during that time. The startd reports: 10/15 12:39:41 (fd:7) (pid:2164) slot1: Request to claim resource refused. The claim requests are rejected because there are left over attributes in the slot ad from some previous job that ran and was booted off due to using too much memory. These left over attributes are not visible via condor_status, even when using -direct. This is because the startd generates ads from scratch when publishing or responding to queries. The extra attributes are visible when using D_MACHINE at the time the claim request is made. There is no longer evidence for exactly how the startd got into this state. However, I have reproduced essentially the same behavior by finding several problematic code paths in the startd where proper claim cleanup is not done. These do not appear to be new problems. The bad code paths that I found all happened to be related to what we do after failing to send signals to the starter. These code paths either bypassed the preempting state altogether or failed to call leave_preempting_state(). The consequences of this could include other bad things in addition to not cleaning out job attributes from the slot ad. Assuming the problem was caused by the code paths I found, this does not appear to be a new problem in 7.3.2. However, it is puzzling why so many machines in the CS pool are in this bad state (about 7% of the p cluster). Perhaps there is another bad code path that I have not found yet.

title: Ticket #7541: S3 uploads result in files unmodifiable by bucket owner
description: Ian has an AWS account with permission to upload files to another account's S3 bucket. When he does so using HTCondor, the other account has no permissions on those files -- it can't even delete them, despite owning the containing bucket. This is apparently a feature of S3, rather than a bug: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/dev/example-bucket-policies.html#example-bucket-policies-use-case-8 https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/dev/amazon-s3-policy-keys.html#grant-putobject-conditionally-1 (where the second bullet point in the second link seems like the better way). However, even if the bucket's owner re-configures their permissions for Ian's account, HTCondor will need to be modified to upload files to the bucket with the required ACL (that is, granting permissions to the bucket owner). In the short term, we should instead investigate the possibility of creating an IAM user under the bucket owner's account and having Ian use those credentials to do the upload.

title: Ticket #7812: Fix test_concurrency_limits.py
description: This Ornithological test is currently disabled; fix it and enable it. The fundamental problem for this test is that there's a race condition in the negotiator's implementation of concurrency limits: it depends on startds reporting their concurrency token usage before the beginning of the next negotiation cycle; this is the reason for the NEGOTIATOR_CYCLE_DELAY knob. The problem is fundamentally intractable: in a distributed system, we have to have a lease on the token and the lease has to time out to prevent failures from draining all of the tokens out of the system. To make the test deterministic, we have to either control when the negotiator begins a new negotiation cycle or ensure that there are no more jobs in the queue than the concurrency limit until all of those jobs have started. It's not clear if we can do the former (does condor_reschedule interrupt NEGOTIATOR_CYCLE_DELAY), but the former should not be too difficult to arrange. So the plan is for a concurrency limit of k, submit k jobs, and wait for k slots to be reported as busy and using the concurrency token in the collector. Then submit another job and wait to see the beginning and then then end of a negotiation cycles; this should cause the negotiator to log a concurrency limit exceeded event. To make sure the negotiator can handle job completion and token re-use, put one of the running jobs on hold, and then wait for the new job's slot to be reported as busy in the collector. Then feed another job in, and wait for a complete new negotiation cycle, which should also cause the negotiator to log a concurrency limit exceeded event.

title: Ticket #6700: min & max job run times as explicit timers (ints)
description: Miron gave us what sounded to me like pretty explicit instructions during our discussion (regarding #6664, #6697, and the issues discovered during the testing thereof) on Friday: add minimum and maximum job run times as simple (integer) first-class /matchable/ constants. The assumption appears to have been that these knobs will be exclusive of PREEMPT in practice (although this may be because we're assuming that a new, non-PREEMPT knob will be used to deal with the misbehaving jobs for which max job retirement time should be ignored). I'm opening this ticket so we don't forget about this; it doesn't seem directly related to the issue of adding a sematic for ignoring max job retirement time (although it may depend on it, see parenthetical remark above). Implementing this ticket should also obviate the need to rename MAXJOBRETIREMENTTIME (and MaxJobRetirementTime), because everyone should stop using it (them). We would also like to have users be able to specify required minimum and expected maximum durations in their jobs, and have those automatically be included in the requirements expression, like the request_* attributes. We should think hard about the actual names for everything mentioned here.
creator: tlmiller

title: Ticket #5985: x509UserProxyExpiration job attribute is unreliable
description: x509UserProxyExpiration does not always match the expiration date of the current proxy and the HTCondor-CE uses this attribute to determine whether or not the job has a valid proxy. In 8.4.9 this resulted in an issue where a factory was releasing a held job with a renewed proxy whose x509UserProxyExpiration attribute was not updated. Jaime says this specific issue is fixed in 8.5.7 but there are other instances where the expiration attribute does not reflect reality.
remarks: 2016-Nov-02 15:33:48 by tannenba: Some action items on this ticket: Jaime will write down (as a remark on this ticket) what attributes the job router will forward from a CE job to the routed job. Currently the shadow will update the x509UserProxyExpiration attribute when it forwards a refreshed proxy, but the gridmanager will not. We think, for consistency, the gridmanager should also update this attribute. 2016-Nov-02 16:05:51 by jfrey: The problem fixed in 8.5.7 was the following: At the GlideinWMS factory, a Condor-C job is submitted destined for the CE schedd. The job is held for a long period of time, during which its original proxy expires, but the file is replaced with a fresh proxy. Once the job is released, it is submitted to the CE. The proxy expiration time in Condor-C job's ad is never updated, and the old value is propagated to the job ad in the CE schedd. This causes problems at the site, where they see a job whose proxy appears to have expired before the job was submitted. This is fixed by #5064. Now, the CE schedd will set the proxy expiration time in its job ad based on the proxy it receives over the wire. 2016-Nov-02 16:17:53 by jfrey: Once the routed job exists, no updated attribute values are forwarded from the CE job ad to the routed job ad. title: Ticket #1495: Condor on Windows unable to run jobs in 64-bit mode
description: We currently provide the Windows Condor as a 32-bit application. If run on a 64-bit Windows environment, Condor will be executed via the Windows-32-on-Windows-64 (WOW64) subsystem. One of the advantages of 64-bit applications over 32-bit applications on Windows is that they are able to use more than 4GB of RAM. However, it seems if we spawn a Condor job, the executable is always run in 32-bit mode and can therefore not benefit from the 64-bit OS and suffers from the 4GB memory limit. Condor should be able to run a job in 64-bit mode - if supported by the running Windows. All information collected so far indicates that it is possible to fork off a 64-bit process from a 32-bit program. Relevant read: http://stackoverflow.com/questions/509989/how-to-allow-32-bit-apps-on-64-bit-windows-to-execute-64-bit-apps-provided-in-win
creator: cweiss

title: Ticket #635: Job ClassAd should absorb arbitrary Machine ad fields on user request
description: A Job ClassAd should be able to specify a list of attributes from a Machine ClassAd. When the job is matched to a given machine, the attributes so named are copied from the Machine ClassAd and inserted into the Job ClassAd. Use cases: A user is doing their own checkpointing in the vanilla universe. Once they start running, future matches must be to a machine with similar attributes, perhaps Arch, or perhaps a custom attribute indicating a particular shared filesystem's presense (SharedFS). A user might want to collect information about the machines his jobs ran on. For example, he might collect Memory, KFlops, and perhaps some custom attributes (NetworkSpeed) and compare against run times to tune Requirements and Rank for future submissions. Strawman syntax: A use puts in his submit file: PullFromMachine = Arch, SharedFS, Memory, KFlops, NetworkSpeed The Job ClassAd ends up with: PullFromMachine = "Arch, SharedFS, Memory, KFlops, NetworkSpeed" Once matched to a machine, the job add would have something like the following added: LastRemoteArch = "INTEL" LastRemoteSharedFS = "/nfs/cluster-1-shared" LastRemoteMemory = 1023 LastRemoteKFlops = 1569267 LastRemoteNetworkSpeed = 1000

title: Ticket #4402: Improve directory execute permission check in access_euid()
description: The Condor utility library provides access_euid() (and helper access_euid_dir()), which acts like access(), but uses the current effective uid of the process, rather than the real uid. To test execute permission on a directory, we check whether the current euid or egid matches the owner or group of the directory and whether the corresponding execute bit is set. This doesn't take into account supplemental groups or POSIX ACLs, which can make Condor conclude the euid doesn't have permission when, in fact, it does. Instead of manually examining the ownership and permissions of the directory, we could just try an operation that requires the permission that we want to check. That's what we do for read and write permissions on a directory. If we can chdir() to the directory, then we have the necessary execute permission.

title: Ticket #1600: make BOINC via fetch-work more convenient
description: Plan To make it easier for users to run BOINC as a backfill task using Condor's fetch-work hooks, the following things need to be done: Create a fetch-work tool for generating boinc jobs. The tool must work on windows as well as unix, so a shell script is probably not acceptable. The boinc job should be made with a working directory equal to boinc/slotX inside the slot execute directory. The hook must create this directory if it does not exist (using the privsep switchboard if necessary). The startd and preen must be made to avoid deleting the boinc execute directory, because boinc needs this directory to be persistent. Condor should automatically generate the boinc global_prefs_override.xml file in the working directory. One possible solution is to have a template for this file, modifiable by the administrator, which is turned into the working file by replacing macros in the file with values configured/computed by condor. It is important that this file be configured correctly to limit how many cpus boinc tries to use so that this matches the number of cpus associated with the slot. This is done via max_cpus (I believe older versions used max_ncpus_pct, which is less convenient for our purposes, because it is not a fixed scale). Optional but nice: The state of the machine should appear as "Backfill" rather than "Claimed" in order to make it easy for admins to see what is going on. The administrator will need to configure the following: STARTD_JOB_HOOK_KEYWORD = BOINC BOINC_EXECUTABLE - path to the boinc executable BOINC_PROJECT_URL - e.g. http://einstein.phys.uwm.edu BOINC_PROJECT_KEY - e.g. 23451132 The admin will also need to create a 'boinc' account and will need to install boinc. The following settings should have reasonable defaults that do not typically need to be edited: BOINC_IdleTime = 900 BOINC_REQUIREMENTS = (State == "Unclaimed" && $(StateTimer) > $(BOINC_IdleTime)) BOINC_ACCOUNT = boinc BOINC_ACCOUNTING_GROUP = BOINC BOINC_ARGS = -no_gui_rpc -attach_project $(BOINC_PROJECT_URL) $(BOINC_PROJECT_KEY) BOINC_HOOK_FETCH_WORK = $(LIBEXEC)/fetch_work_boinc BOINC_MaxJobRetirementTime = 0 RANK = -MY.IsBackfillJob Notice that the default RANK expression needs to rank BOINC jobs below all others. The semantics of RANK are a pretty good fit for expressing when backfill should run. However, this is somewhat fragile. Is there a better way? If the admin has overridden the RANK expression and forgotten to preserve the term for backfill jobs, then backfill jobs may run when they should not. The admin must also be careful about assigning jobs a rank <= boinc jobs. In summary, the generality of RANK gives the admin flexibility, but this comes at the cost of making it possible for the admin to change the meaning of "backfill" without realizing it.

title: Ticket #4052: RecentDaemonCoreDutyCycle is sometimes negative
description: RecentDaemonCoreDutyCycle for machines that are not spending a lot of time in select is sometimes reported as a negative number. This happens because the two values that are used to calculate the duty cycle are both subject to independent quantization and error accumulation. the duty cycle is calculated as 1.0 - (RecentSelectWaitTime / RecentDCPumpCycleSum); When RecentSelectWaitTime is greater than RecentDCPumpCycleSum then the calculated value for duty cycle will be negative. This can happen when nearly all of the pump cycle time is spent waiting in select, (i.e. the daemon is not busy). It also appears to be the case that the select wait time is over-reported because of accumulated errors in summing the wait times for each select call. The proposed fix is to add code to increase the accuracy of the select wait calculation, and also to suppress the publication of negative values when they occur. 0.0 will be published instead.

title: Ticket #5213: Allow more flexible dependencies between splices
description: As per yesterday's phone conversation with John Calley. Basically he would like to do something like this: * A.dag: job A1 ... job A2 ... ... * B.dag: job B1 ... job B2 ... ... * top.dag: splice A A.dag splice B B.dag (B1 depends on A1, B2 depends on A2, etc.) Currently this is not possible -- if splice A is a parent of splice B, every node in B depends on every node in A. And it turns out it's not possible to "manually" add dependencies between the individual nodes. The rough idea that we have so far is that splices could be defined with a set of input and output nodes (which could be DAG-level NOOPs). Then you'd say: connect A to B and this would mean that each output node in A would be the parent of the corresponding input node in B. (It would be a fatal parse error if the input and output nodes didn't match exactly.)
remarks: 2015-Aug-14 14:41:21 by wenger: (I'm just adding this note here because I haven't created a design doc yet.) Anyhow, one question is how to identify the nodes that we use to connect the splices. It seems that there are fundamentally two options: Special keywords instead of "JOB". Special node names. I'm inclined to go with number two, partly because it will definitely be easier to implement, and partly because I think it might be less confusing. My initial thought is that the nodes would be named something like PININ.1, PININ.2, ... and PINOUT.1, PINOUT.2... (continuing Miron's hardware analogy). The main disadvantage of this is that if someone happened to already have conflicting node names, they couldn't use the connect feature. But I don't think this is a big problem, because it won't break any existing DAGs (they'd have to use the connect feature for it to be a problem). Continuing the hardware analogy, it would be possible to have "impedance matching" splices that would do something like connect 10 inputs to one output -- it would be possible to have a splice that was nothing but noop nodes, just to do the "impedance matching". 2015-Aug-17 11:23:12 by wenger: Also, we talked about whether to use PARENT/CHILD for this type of connection, or add a new keyword. We pretty much decided in favor of a new keyword, partly because you might still want to have a "normal" PARENT/CHILD dependency between splices, and partly to avoid a chance of goofing up existing DAGs. 2015-Aug-19 13:30:28 by wenger: Design doc here: https://docs.google.com/document/d/1ayE8hGkFPud8WhIiXEEqa2m-E4_ikMdkAzzeg0_ZSHA/edit 2015-Nov-20 16:12:32 by wenger: Updated the design doc as per email discussions with Miron. 2015-Dec-17 12:50:29 by wenger: Just had another discussion about this with Miron. He wants some changes to the design: Split off specifying pin in and pin out from the node names. Just use numbers to identify which pins get connected to which. Possibly allow separate files that would be included in a splice that specify pin ins and pin outs (longer-term). Possibly allow regexs or ClassAd expressions for node names (and maybe pin numbers) (longer-term). Specifically Miron is looking for something like this: JOB foo foo.cmd PIN_IN foo 1 One thing I have to think about is allowing multiple pin in and pin out connections for a single node (or multiple nodes for a single pin). Anyhow, I need to update the design document accordingly... 2015-Dec-18 14:33:22 by wenger: Something else I was just thinking about this -- if we allow many-to-many relationships among nodes and pins, should pin in and pin out be attributes of Job objects (my first thought)? Or should they be their own objects, with the pin objects having a list of the relevant nodes, instead of the nodes having lists of pins? One advantage of having pin objects is that we could delete the pin objects once we've fully parsed our whole workflow. On the other hand, if we just allow numbers to identify the pins, that would be a very compact representation in the Job objects... 2015-Dec-22 10:24:55 by wenger: Finished updating design document as per discussion with Miron a few days ago. 2016-Jan-16 11:31:15 by wenger: Created V8_5-gittrac_5213-branch for this. 2016-Jan-26 13:29:24 by wenger: Some of the tests we should have for this: Tests where the DAG should succeed: Simple Many-to-many pin/node connections. title: Ticket #7384: Support job-id's as element type in ranger class
description: TJ requested we make the element type a template parameter to the ranger class to allow ranges of job-ids to be used, in addition to the current behavior, which typedefs element_type to int. This means adding a couple required methods to the JOB_ID_KEY class in proc.h, templatizing everything in the ranger class, and specializing the part of the load/persist functions that read/write each supported element type.
remarks: 2019-Nov-29 17:58:56 by edquist: This is all ready to go. There are plenty of unit tests in src/condor_unit_tests/OTEST_ranger.cpp, and hopefully the interface in ranger.h explains itself alright, but I'll provide some discussion & examples here for reference & getting started. --- The basic idea is a ranger<T> is a container of T elements, like a std::set<T>, but internally they are stored as ranges, and can be inserted/erased as such (as well as element-wise). The container is searchable to test if it contains a particular element within any of its ranges. Currently the supported element types are int and JOB_ID_KEY, though we can add any type that is comparable (<, ==) and incrementable/decrementable (++, --, and +/- int) - details are in the commit message for [58491]. The internal ranger<T>::range objects are a [start,end) pair of T elements, with the end element being one-past the last element in the range (as is the standard pattern for STL containers & algorithms). Sub-ranges can be inserted/erased either by specifying a [start,end) range, or by using the *_slice versions, which take a start and a back element, for specifying inclusive [start,back]. (These are just wrappers that set the end of the range to back+1.) A ranger<T> object is iterable over the ordered set of ranges it contains, and each range (that is, ranger<T>::range) is iterable over the elements in that range. Iterable element-wise access to the entire container is also provided with ranger<T>::get_elements(). front_element() and back_element() members provide a reference to the first and final elements in the entire ranger set. It is invalid to call either of these if the ranger container is empty(). load() and persist() member functions are provided for inserting a C-string representation of ranges, or storing that representation to a std::string, in a format per discussion with TJ. (Semicolon-separated sub-ranges, where each sub-range is either START-BACK (with inclusive BACK), or just START for a single-element range. Eg, "2", "5-10", "4;7;10-20;44;50-60". JOB_ID_KEY elements are stored as the obvious CLUSTER.PROC. More generally, any new type to be supported has to implement a read_element() and write_element() in ranger.cpp. persist_range() and persist_slice() are also provided for storing only a subset of the full container. load() can be called multiple times against persisted subsets (ie, partitions) to reproduce the original full container. The ranger<T> template class, along with ranger<T>::range, are basically agnostic to the details of the type T. The only requirement is that each range have start < end (that is, start <= back). Thus, for a ranger<JOB_ID_KEY>, a range like [7.11, 8.4) will contain 7.100 and 8.1, but not 7.9 or 8.10. While [7.11, 8.4) is a valid range (since 7.11 < 8.4), it is not possible to iterate across all the elements in that range, since there is no way to reach the end (8.4) from the beginning (7.9) by incrementing the .PROC part. Thus, if you want to be able to list / iterate over every element in your ranger<JOB_ID_KEY>, you should ensure that within each range inserted, the CLUSTER components match. (Eg, "7.11-7.100;8.1-8.3") Likewise, there is no special treatment of a job-id element with a PROC of -1. It just falls in line according to the job-id element class's own sorting, which puts 4.-1 after all 3.x but before 4.0. So a range representing all 3.x elements (for non-negative x) would be [3.0, 4.0), or equivalently, for the slice versions, [3.0, 4.-1]. --- Ok! Some examples. // initialize empty int ranger ranger<int> r; // initialize with list of elements ranger<int> r2 = {1, 2, 3, 5, 10}; // initialize with list of ranges ranger<int> r3 = {{20,30}, {40,50}, {60,80}}; // insert elements r.insert(77); r.insert(88); // insert [start,end) ranges r.insert({100, 150}); ranger<int>::range rr(200, 300); r.insert(rr); // insert slice with [start,back] elements r.insert_slice(302, 310); // erase methods work the same as insert r.erase(120); r.erase({125, 130}); r.erase_slice(133, 139); // test element membership if (r.contains(131)) /* true */ { ... } if (r.contains(135)) /* false */ { ... } // get min and max elements if (!r.empty()) { int min_elt = r.front_element(); int max_elt = r.back_element(); ... } // save string representation std::string s; r.persist(s); // save string representation in [start,end) range partitions std::string s0, s1, s2, s3; r.persist_range(s0, { 0, 100}); r.persist_range(s1, {100, 200}); r.persist_range(s2, {200, 300}); r.persist_range(s3, {300, 400}); // same thing, but save in [start,back] slice partitions r.persist_slice(s0, 0, 99); r.persist_slice(s1, 100, 199); r.persist_slice(s2, 200, 299); r.persist_slice(s3, 300, 399); // clear and reload from saved buffer r.clear(); r.load(s.c_str()); // clear and reload from partitions r.clear(); r.load(s0.c_str()); r.load(s1.c_str()); r.load(s2.c_str()); // iterate over each sub-range for (auto &subrange : r) for (int i : subrange) process_int(i); // same thing, but iterate over all elements directly for (int i : r.get_elements()) process_int(i); That's pretty much the tour. Everything for JOB_ID_KEY elements follows the same pattern, which I'll enclude just to provide explicit examples. // initialize empty job-id ranger ranger<JOB_ID_KEY> r; // initialize with list of elements ranger<JOB_ID_KEY> r2 = {{1,1}, {1,2}, {1,3}, {5,5}, {10,10}}; // initialize with list of ranges ranger<JOB_ID_KEY> r3 = {{{1,20},{1,30}}, {{2,40},{2,50}}, {{3,60},{3,80}}}; // insert elements r.insert({1,77}); r.insert({2,88}); // insert [start,end) ranges r.insert({{1,100}, {1,150}}); ranger<JOB_ID_KEY>::range rr({1,200}, {1,300}); r.insert(rr); // insert slice with [start,back] elements r.insert_slice({1,302}, {1,310}); // erase methods work the same as insert r.erase({1,120}); r.erase({{1,125}, {1,130}}); r.erase_slice({1,133}, {1,139}); // test element membership if (r.contains({1,131})) /* true */ { ... } if (r.contains({1,135})) /* false */ { ... } // get min and max elements if (!r.empty()) { JOB_ID_KEY min_elt = r.front_element(); JOB_ID_KEY max_elt = r.back_element(); ... } // save string representation std::string s; r.persist(s); // save string representation in [start,end) range partitions std::string s0, s1, s2, s3; r.persist_range(s0, {{0,0}, {3,0}}); r.persist_range(s1, {{3,0}, {6,0}}); r.persist_range(s2, {{6,0}, {9,0}}); r.persist_range(s3, {{9,0}, {12,0}}); // same thing, but save in [start,back] slice partitions r.persist_slice(s0, {0,0}, {3,-1}); r.persist_slice(s1, {3,0}, {6,-1}); r.persist_slice(s2, {6,0}, {9,-1}); r.persist_slice(s3, {9,0}, {12,-1}); // clear and reload from saved buffer r.clear(); r.load(s.c_str()); // clear and reload from partitions r.clear(); r.load(s0.c_str()); r.load(s1.c_str()); r.load(s2.c_str()); // iterate over each sub-range for (auto &subrange : r) for (JOB_ID_KEY id : subrange) process_jobid(id); // same thing, but iterate over all elements directly for (JOB_ID_KEY id : r.get_elements()) process_jobid(id); 2019-Dec-02 14:46:30 by tim: Internal code. No user visible changes. No documentation.

description: when sites use glexec, it is possible that glexec will fail for a number of reasons and the job will not be started. at the moment, this causes that individual job to go on hold. however, if that user has submitted thousands of jobs, condor needs to do something more intelligent so we do not attempt to launch more jobs at the same site with the same proxy. possibilities could include rate limiting (exponential backoff?) or blacklisting (with a timeout). a major challenge seems to be knowing ahead of time that glexec will fail, and i think we need to be careful here. i posit that a single glexec failure should not cause blacklisting of a site. also, how do we know which machines are grouped together in a single "site" from the glexec perspective?

title: Ticket #2539: Alter rpath to support multiple Condor installations
description: Now that we're dynamically linking most of the libraries that Condor uses, we're encountered some situations where the Condor binaries find the wrong version of shared libraries. Specifically, this can happen when there are multiple installations of Condor on a system, one of which is a native package. Glideins and the BaTLab are two particular instances. In a native package installation, the ClassAds library is installed in /usr/lib[64]. In a non-native installation, /usr/lib[64] appears in the RPATH before the installation's lib directory. Thus, the non-native package Condor binaries can end up using the ClassAds library from the native package installation. Shared library versioning is a partial, but incomplete solution. Setting LD_LIBRARY_PATH isn't a solution, as it doesn't preempt searching of directories in the RPATH. We want to keep /lib and /usr/lib in the RPATH so that it's easy for users to use Condor on a different flavor of linux than it was compiled for, while still getting updated security libraries where available. We propose making two changes to minimize the chance of using the wrong libraries within the constraints above: Set RUNPATH instead of RPATH in the binaries. This allows LD_LIBRARY_PATH to over-ride the default search path. Move $ORIGIN/../lib to the front of the RUNPATH. This will cause binaries to prefer the local copy of libclassad, but still prefer the OS copy of normal system libraries (openssl, krb5, etc).

title: Ticket #4814: tools that -format should support an un-evaluated value format tag
description: In some cases when using -format or -autoformat, it is desired that the value be printed without first being evaluated. This is usually the case for Requirements, for instance. With the current code "%s" will sometimes print unevaluated raw, but can't be relied on to do this in all cases. The only way to get this format is to use -long or to pass unparse(attr) as the attribute name to format. We should have a new format tag %r (for raw or round-trip), that prints out the same thing for the value as -long would. When using -autoformat, -af:r will use the %r format for all printing, instead of %v or %V that it currently uses.

title: Ticket #6080: Supporting MOUNT_UNDER_SCRATCH for Docker universe jobs
description: One of the last few nags for Docker on red is the location of /tmp for jobs. The attached patch adds support for MOUNT_UNDER_SCRATCH to Docker jobs. With EL6, MOUNT_UNDER_SCRATCH mounted job /tmp and /var/tmp under /var/lib/condor/execute. The nodes were partitioned to provide a large amount of space for /var. With EL7+Docker, /tmp and /var/tmp remain inside the container. Jobs writing to /tmp end up using the Docker LVM pool. The pool is fairly small on red and it Docker jobs hang when it fills up. The attached patch takes the directories from MOUNT_UNDER_SCRATCH and converts them to "--volume" arguments for docker run, bind mounting them inside the job directory.
