description: condor_submit - no longer ends up meaning read config file from stdin. this ends up breaking condor_qsub which depends on this behavior. The following patch will fix condor_qsub. It would be fantastic if this was incorporated in the next release. --- /usr/bin/condor_qsub 2013-07-24 12:45:27.000000000 +0200 +++ /home/raid3/gorgolewski/bin/condor_qsub 2013-09-09 11:06:12.865587821 +0200 @@ -1100,7 +1100,7 @@ if [ -n "$job_deps" ]; then sentinel_file="$(mktemp --tmpdir cluster${cluster_id}_sentinel.XXXXXXXXXXXXX)" create_dep_sentinel $sentinel_file "$job_deps" "$cluster_id" - condor_submit - < $sentinel_file.submit > /dev/null + condor_submit < $sentinel_file.submit > /dev/null [ $condor_keep_files -eq 0 ] && rm $sentinel_file.submit || true fi else

title: Ticket #2240: RFE: secondary submitter sort using starvation in negotiateWithGroup
description: From Jon Thomas: // ----- Sort the schedd list in decreasing priority order dprintf( D_ALWAYS, "Phase 3: Sorting submitter ads by priority ...\n" ); scheddAds.Sort( (lessThanFunc)comparisonFunction, this ); Currently the code sorts on prio. Comments indicate it does a random secondary sort of names, but it looks like it doesn't really. The sort needs to be changed to either 1) based on starvation 2) based on prio and then a true secondary sort on starvation. I think option (2) is reasonable, since the primary sort on submitter priority is a longstanding behavior.
remarks: 2011-Jun-15 12:30:58 by eje: The analog of #2186 here would be sorting by (submitter_usage/submitter_limit). Currently, the sorting of submitters occurs before submitter limits are computed. Also, those limits are currently computed on the fly, not attached to the submitter structure. To do the above, there would have to be a new loop assigning submitter limits (perhaps just the submitter limit of spin-1 could be used for convenience) to the submitter ads, prior to the sort. Another lower-impact option might be to sort by some surrogate like submitter_usage / (idle+running). That does not take into account the negotiator's view of the submitter's limit or group quota, but it is a reasonable measure of starvation and could be accomplished without moving the logic for submitter limit computations around. 2011-Jun-24 11:23:34 by eje: repro/test Using the following configuration, which sets a very large PRIORITY_HALFLIFE so that user priorities all remain equal at 0.5: CLAIM_WORKLIFE = 0 NEGOTIATOR_CONSIDER_PREEMPTION = FALSE NEGOTIATOR_DEBUG = D_FULLDEBUG NEGOTIATOR_USE_SLOT_WEIGHTS = FALSE GROUP_QUOTA_MAX_ALLOCATION_ROUNDS = 1 NEGOTIATOR_INTERVAL = 30 SCHEDD_INTERVAL = 15 PRIORITY_HALFLIFE = 1e100 NUM_CPUS = 20 GROUP_NAMES = a GROUP_QUOTA_a = 20 GROUP_ACCEPT_SURPLUS = FALSE The following three job submissions are used in a sequence (submission 2 will be used twice). title: Ticket #7042: Allow files to be checkpointed via plugins
description: Our friendly gravitational wave enthusiasts at Syracuse have an interesting challenge -- they'd like to use the self-checkpointing job features but their checkpoints are too large to bring back to the schedd without overwhelming it. Instead, they'd like to use the power of the file transfer plugins to manage the data movement for them. However, on the worker node, we only invoke stageout plugins when it is the "final transfer" - the job has completed successfully. It's pretty trivial (I think) to enable file transfer plugins for all stageouts. It's even straightforward to only enable this behavior behind a job attribute. However, is it the complete solution? What happens when the job starts up again? Unlike the case where we are restoring from spool, we don't keep a record of which stageout files should be staged back in. Duncan will have his checkpoints on his webserver - but HTCondor won't know to pull them back. I suppose it's possible to put the same file on the transfer_input_files list (pre-creating an empty checkpoint), but that seems unnecessarily user-unfriendly. Anyhow, we promised Duncan we would allow him to invoke the plugins on all stageouts. I'll do that for now -- but it's not entirely clear that it solves the problem.
remarks: 2019-May-14 14:12:27 by tlmiller: The user-friendlier solutions seems like #5238 (an explicit list of checkpoint file(s)); the obvious implementation would be to assume that the file transfer uploads go to unique directories. (This also allows the checkpoint transfer list to include directories.) It also assumes symmetric file transfer plug-ins, but I don't know how big of a problem that really is. The former restriction may be relaxable when we implement manifest files. 2019-May-14 14:24:34 by tlmiller: Code Review It seems like it would be clearer to go bool tmp; bool should_invoke_output_​plugins = m_final_transfer_flag; if( jobAd.​EvaluateAttrBool("Out​putPluginsOnlyOnExit"​,​ tmp ) ) { InitDownloadFilenameR​emaps(&jobAd)​;​ should_invoke_output_plugins = !tmp; } especially if EvaluateAttrBool() does the right thing and doesn't set (or unset) tmp if OutputPluginsOnlyOnExit is undefined. However, I'm not sure why you invoke InitDownloadFilenameRemaps() only if file transfer using output plugins -- why do the two have anything to do with each other? According to the commentary: // The case where we want to apply them is when we are the shadow // or anybody else who is writing the files to their final // location. which is certainly not what's happening if we're checkpointing. 2019-May-30 13:21:51 by tim: Not documenting this for now. Let the Syracuse folks kick the tires first. 2019-May-30 14:06:40 by tlmiller: Brian remarks that InitDownloadFilenameRemaps() is just really terribly named.

title: Ticket #6653: Fix build on Mac OS 10.13 High Sierra
description: In macOS 10.13 (High Sierra), the default version of libssl and libcrypto was changed from OpenSSL 0.9.8zh to LibreSSL 2.2.7. The older libraries are still available, but still no header files. The main effect on HTCondor is that VOMS uses some old ssleay functions that have been removed from LibreSSL (ASN1_verify(), ASN1_sign(), ASN1_digest()). Oddly, the VOMS and HTCondor code still builds and links, and the HTCondor binaries run fine. But the Python bindings fail when dlopen()ing libcondor_utils, due to the missing symbols. The newest VOMS code still uses these old functions that aren't in LibreSSL, and VOMS doesn't appear to be under active development anymore. These old functions should be replaceable by newer functions in the API, but I'm having trouble finding documentation. For example, EVP_Digest() appears to be suitable replacement for ASN1_digest(), but the parameters are different. A few options: Continuing using the crusty OpenSSL 0.9.8 on macOS. Drop VOMS support on macOS. Figure out how to patch VOMS to replace the old ssl functions.
remarks: 2018-Apr-17 15:55:52 by jfrey: I figured out why the linking and running succeed when the openssl functions are missing. The voms build script passes -undefined dynamic_lookup to the linker when creating the voms dynamic library. So everything compiles and runs without the symbols. But the process will explode if it tries to call one of them. 2018-May-03 10:59:24 by jfrey: All versions of macOS will continue to use OpenSSL 0.9.8 in the 8.6.x series. On macOS 10.13 and above, we will directly link with the "out-of-date" 0.9.8 libraries in /usr/lib. A switch to LibreSSL may happen in 8.7 (#6668). 2018-May-04 13:24:24 by tim: CODE REVIEW: Changes look good and are concise. 2018-May-04 13:24:48 by tim: DOC REVIEW: No docs needed

title: Ticket #6346: condor_store_cred won't accept registration of dedicated user cred.
description: Problem description I'm using a setup of HTCondor on Windows which executes jobs using a dedicated user account (SLOT_USER). I can't use the standard "transient" accounts as the user account used for the jobs needs special privileges which I configured for the dedicated account. I used to register the dedicated account credentials on execution machines using condor_store_cred. This worked fine in Condor version 8.4.x and earlier. When switching from HTCondor version 8.4.7 to 8.6.4 the setup stopped working though and the condor_store_cred failed to store the credentials of the dedicated account and printed its standard error message: "Operation failed. Make sure your ALLOW_WRITE setting includes this host." Digging through the source I found a part which was introduced in the 8.6 series as it seems: condor-8.6.4/src/condor_utils/store_cred.cpp (line 725): // We don't allow one user to set another user's credential The code part which follows leads to the failure. As this breaks the existing feature of having a dedicated user account on Windows to run the jobs I think that this should be considered as a bug. One may argue that the setup still works and one has to log in using the dedicated account but this makes the setup really cumbersome. Proposed fix To address the above, we can add a configuration knob that would allow the admin to say who, if anyone, is allowed to run condor_store_cred for other users. So after this change, to get the behavior you used to have in v8.4, you would put into your condor_config something like: CRED_SUPER_USERS = * Or to only allow specific users - CRED_SUPER_USERS = mike, todd

title: Ticket #6716: Prioritize Condor-C GAHP commands
description: The gridmanager throttles the number of requests it will issue to each GAHP at a time, with a default of 100. Additional requests are queued until previous requests complete. This can result in time-critical requests being delayed by a large number of older lower-priority requests. In #958, we added a priority queue with three levels of priority, but we only prioritized CREAM and GRAM requests. For other grid types, the queueing of GAHP requests is strict FIFO. Recently, this caused a problem for CMS with Condor-C (grid-type condor) jobs. When a large number of jobs (e.g. 6000) are submitted at once, all of those jobs must be submitted to the remote schedd (100 at a time) before the input files for any of them are staged. The jobs are Held in the remote queue waiting for their input files. If we set the submit request to a low priority, then the early jobs could get their input file staged sooner and the remote schedd could start running them. Delay of job lease renewal is another problem that would be avoided.

title: Ticket #3847: Freezer controller triggers kernel crash when freezing SIGSTOP'd proce
description: While we can't reproduce the exact conditions, it seems HTCondor triggers a kernel crash when: A job has already been suspended (likely, when any processes in the job are suspended). The freezer controller is used to freeze the set of processes. While the freezer controller provides atomic signal delivery to jobs - very important for killing jobs - it's probably more important to not trigger a kernel crash. Proposal: have the procd track whether the process family is currently suspended; if it is, don't use the freezer-based methods for signal delivery. This has a slight security risk - we re-introduce the possibility of a fork-bomb escaping signal delivery. I believe this is acceptable because: We can track which processes still exist post-SIGTERM, and if the freezer did the SIGSTOP, we can assume all processes are already stopped - there's nothing alive to forkbomb.

title: Ticket #7107: Wrong semantics for Python bindings ExprTree equality
description: While trying to write some tests for htcondor-jobs, I ran into the following weirdness: In [1]: import classad In [2]: a = classad.ExprTree('a') In [3]: a_again = classad.ExprTree('a') In [5]: expr = (a == a_again) In [6]: expr Out[6]: a == a In [7]: type(expr) Out[7]: classad._classad.ExprTree In [9]: bool(expr) Out[9]: False In [10]: a < a_again Out[10]: a < a While this is quite sensible from the perspective of the actual ClassAd language, it's total gibberish in Python. Equality operators must return booleans, by contract. For example, the semantics of == should be the same as In [8]: str(a) == str(a_again) Out[8]: True This will make ExprTree and therefore ClassAd play much more nicely with standard Python. For example, right now, even if two ClassAd contain all the same keys and values, if any of those values are expressions, dict(classad) will not compare equal to each other because of the bool(expr) example above. Proposal: __eq__ should check whether two expressions are literally the same expression. The other overloaded boolean operators should be removed. Add a new set of ExprTree methods which express the various ClassAd comparisons. ClassAd.__eq__ should behave exactly like dict.__eq__ (equal if and only if all keys and values compare equal). This is unfortunate, because the operator overloading on ExprTree is very clever, but ultimately it's very confusing for doing anything other than building ExprTree. Is there a compelling reason to break the boolean comparison contract here?
remarks: 2019-Jun-13 08:16:34 by bbockelm: I disagree. This is where the semantics of ClassAds are different than python and relevant. ExprTree('a == a') Evaluates to undefined; in terms of if statements, it evaluates to false. That is, if ExprTree('a == a'): print("foo") will not print foo. This is how the ClassAd language works. The only questionable matter in this case is whether undefined should map to False or throw an exception. Possibly an exception is better, but the die is cast... To quote the python data model: By convention, False and True are returned for a successful comparison. However, these methods can return any value, so if the comparison operator is used in a Boolean context (e.g., in the condition of an if statement), Python will call bool() on the value to determine if the result is true or false. Even if ExprTree('a').__eq__(ExprTree('a')) returns a boolean, I'd still argue the correct boolean is False (or throwing an undefined comparison exception). Long story short, I think this is correct behavior: >>> {"1": classad.ExprTree('1')} == {"1": classad.ExprTree('1')} True >>> {"1": classad.ExprTree('a')} == {"1": classad.ExprTree('a')} False It's just unfortunate that ClassAds makes a distinction between equality and the sameAs operator. The three different ClassAd concepts of "equality" are always going to be tough to map to Python Now, one thing that is really just wacky is that the Undefined bool operator is not overloaded resulting in the integer __bool__ being used. Look at this nonsense: >>> if classad.ExprTree("undefined"): ... print "foo" ... >>> if classad.ExprTree("undefined").eval(): ... print "foo" ... foo >>> if classad.ExprTree("error"): ... print "foo" ... Traceback (most recent call last): File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module> RuntimeError: Unable to evaluate expression. >>> if classad.ExprTree("error").eval(): ... print "foo" ... foo That seems worth fixing.

Histogram of autocluster sizes, up to size 50. Here is the CDF of autocluster sizes. We see that most are of size 1, or small: 2011-Jul-28 13:52:10 by eje: Thoughts about MatchList memory requirements: As a straw-man, consider a large-scale pool with 40,000 slots, and where there are around 5000 unique autoclusters in a given neg-cycle (which is what I'm seeing from the above, correctly accounting for scoping autoclusters by scheduler id) Each AdListEntry is 40 bytes (assuming 4-byte pointers). Currently the MatchList just brute-force allocates an entry for each slot (the maximum possible match-list length), so in a pool with 40K slots the MatchList uses 1.6 megabytes. In a hypothetical enhancement to keeping match-lists around for the duration of the neg-cycle, the worst case would be all 5000 cluster-ids X 1.6e6, or 8 gigabytes. As-is, that would be a non-starter. Clearly there is some low-hanging fruit. For openers, use vector<AdListEntry>, which grows adaptively. It doesn't prevent the worst-case, but the worst case of all slots matching all autoclusters is probably very unlikely. match-list length is likely to be zipfian in the same way that autocluster size is, although it would be interesting to get some real measures on it. Additionally, the histograms above show that we can straight-up ignore a large fraction of autoclusters, as their size is 1 -- they cannot provide any cost-savings to the negotiation loop. Heuristically, one might also choose to ignore autoclusters of size < N, for some N > 1. (There might also be a similar heuristic on match-list length, although by the time you know that length you've sunk the cost of building the list, so any motivation for dumping it would be for memory reasons only) Ignoring autoclusters by size implies that we compute that size on the schedd side. I noted a couple places that could be done above. It would add some computation to the schedd, although it should be at worst nlogn on job ads. One impact of storing multiple match-lists is that a slot ad may appear in multiple lists, and so when a slot is matched that ad may need to be annotated to prevent re-use in some other autocluster. That should be easy as long as slot ads are re-used via pointer: just set a flag-attribute.

title: Ticket #4906: Add DAG node job timeout
description: Mats Rynge at ISI just ran into a bug in which a job exited the queue without a terminated event getting written for that job. (Solving the problem of the event not getting written is obviously outside the scope of DAGMan). Anyhow, Mats would like DAGMan to deal with this case in a better way, the proposal being something like that you define (at the DAG level) a timeout, and if DAGMan hasn't seen any events for a job for more than the timeout, the job is considered failed (and, probably, condor_rm'ed). There are a number of issues to consider, such as: Should the user also be able to define different timeouts for specific jobs? Should there be different timeouts for different states? (E.g., should we wait longer between a submit event and an execute event than between an execute event and a terminated event?) Probably some more that I haven't thought of yet. Something else to think about is how to implement this. The obvious way is to add a "last event time" field to the Job object. On the other hand, we only care about that for jobs that are actually in the queue, so maybe it would be better off having some separate data structure so that we don't increase the size of the Job object. Another issue is what to do about multi-proc clusters -- would we need to keep track of "last event time" individually for each proc, or could we just do it for the cluster as a whole?

title: Ticket #7629: figure out how to conclusively determine which credd we should use
description: For storing and querying credentials such as Kerberos and OAuth, we assume that there is a CredD colocated with the SchedD we will be using to submit jobs. Knowing how to contact the CredD is straightforward if we are talking to a local SchedD and CredD. However, it's less clear what it means to contact "The CredD" when daemons are remote. For Krb/OAuth, there is probably one CredD associated with each SchedD. Do they need to have the same name? Does the SchedD advertise its associated CredD? How would a condor_submit client know who to store creds with to do a remote submit. Etc. However, in non-Krb/OAuth cases, we might have one CredD for the whole pool. How is this communicated to condor_submit? How is it specified in the config file? This ticket is a broad umbrella to list different modes of operation we support, what assumptions are making for each, and proposals for making this easy for admins to configure.
creator: zmiller

title: Ticket #6891: job ads do not specify which tokens should be transferred
description: When a user submits a job that requires (or is provided) tokens, nothing is added to the job ad that says what (1) tokens the job requested and/or (2) what tokens the starter should request from the shadow. This is a problem because: a user may want to query or edit jobs based on their token requests, and the shadow sends all of a user's tokens to the starter from the submit machine because there is no way for the starter and/or shadow to know which tokens a job needs. We should limit the tokens a user's job has access to to only those tokens the job needs. title: Ticket #7783: remove existing nice-user mechanism because it pollutes User attribute
description: The ancient nice-user mechanism in the schedd involves prefixing the User attribute with "nice-user" and then passing that on to the Negotiator as the submitter name. This produces a second accounting principal, which can be given a very low priority and accounted for separately from the normal user. Now that the User attribute of the job is to be the username of record for the job, in part replacing Owner in many places in the code, we can no longer afford to mutate the User attribute for jobs that have nice_user set. This ticket is for the removal of that mechanism. There will be a separate ticket for introduction of a new mechanism for allowing users to opt-in to running low-priority jobs that do not impact their fair share.

title: Ticket #5244: Improve security UX
description: The default security settings should be improved to make it easier for our administrators to use higher-security methods. In particular, if we changed the (param table) default for the HTCondor map file to a particular value, we could create a file for the corresponding location (and use the packaging to install it) which does what the hard-coded defaults do (if there's no map file at all). After adding support for comments in the map file, we could then explain the options there. This seems like a best practice. Additionally, if we preserve the GSS_ASSIST_GRIDMAP (?) default for GSI in the HTCondor map file, we could (more?) easily add a metaknob 'use security : gsi' for administrators which already have GSI configured. A detail for Zach to consider is what to do if an entry in the map file is missing. Presently, security rejects, but this allows abuse of the mapfile as a whitelist, and changing those semantics would be Bad(TM). Perhaps we could map to unmapped@method instead, and add 'unmapped@*' to the default DENY list(s), instead? [This may have been prompted by Brian Lin.]
creator: tlmiller

title: Ticket #7279: Late materialization from mismatched bindings version fails silently
description: Due to bad config, I ended up in a situation where I tried to submit late materialization jobs from 8.9 Python bindings into a 8.8 schedd. The submit returned successfully, but no jobs ever entered the queue. TJ believes the basic problem is that the schedd doesn't try to materialize until after it has already returned. The late materialization digest is effectively malformed because the schedd doesn't know how to read the 8.9 version of the digest. Also relevant for remote submit, or simply mismatched tools/daemons versions on the same machine. Fix: the schedd should be able to report which versions of the digest it supports, and submit should fail if it can't produce a digest of that version.

title: Ticket #6192: Collector should queue queries when it can no longer fork
description: Currently when the number of forked children processing Collector queries surpasses the maximum set by config knob COLLECTOR_QUERY_WORKERS, the Collector handles all new incoming queries in-processes (i.e. without forking). As processing a query and sending out the result to the network could take a long time, the result of servicing such queries in-process is the Collector is likely to drop a lot of updates. To avoid this, currently the only recourse is to set COLLECTOR_QUERY_WORKERS very high, which results in forking a lot of child processes that can exhaust memory on a central manager handling a very large pool. The following enhancements are proposed: Instead handling queries in-process, the patches in this ticket will have the Collector queue up query requests. As children exit, new queries will be forked. (Done) Config knob COLLECTOR_QUERY_WORKERS_PENDING defines the maximum number of fork requests that can be pending (i.e. queued). Queries that would exceed this maximum pending are aborted. Defaults to 50. (Done) Queries coming from the condor_negotiator should be considered high priority, and be serviced ahead of all other queries. (Done) Queries coming from from "condor_sos condor_status" should be considered high priority. (Done) Config knob COLLECTOR_QUERY_WORKERS_RESERVE_FOR_HIGH_PRIO is the number of COLLECTOR_QUERY_WORKERS slots that will be held in reserve to only service high priority requests. Defaults to 1. Also, the default for COLLECTOR_QUERY_WORKERS should increase from 2 to 4. (Done) When a query request is pulled from the queue, the Collector should confirm that the client has not closed the TCP socket (because it was tired of waiting) before going through all the work of actually forking a child and starting to service the query. (Done) Config knob COLLECTOR_QUERY_MAX_WORKTIME should define the maximum amount of time in seconds that a query should be in the system. Queries that wait in the pending queue longer than this period of time will be aborted before forking. Queries that have already forked will also abort after the worktime has expired - this protects against clients on a very slow network connection. If set to 0, then there is no timeout. The default is 0. (Done) There should be statistical attributes available in the collector set of stats (i.e. visible by using "-collector -statistics collector" flags to condor_status) (Done): ActiveQueryWorkers - current number of forked workers ActiveQueryWorkersPeak - peak number of forked workers since startup or stat reset PendingQueries - number of queries pending (waiting to fork) PendingQueriesPeak - peak number of queries pending (waiting to fork) DroppedQueries - number of queries aborted because COLLECTOR_QUERY_WORKERS_PENDING exceeded, or COLLECTOR_QUERY_MAX_WORKTIME exceeded, or client closed TCP socket while request was pending RecentDroppedQueries - number of queries aborted in the recent time window (20 min by default) Add an undocumented config knob COLLECTOR_TRACK_QUERY_BY_SUBSYS which, when set to True (the default), will instruct the Collector to publish counts on the number of queries grouped by subsystem (e.g. TOOL, NEGOTIATOR, STARTD, etc) of the client. This knob can remain undocumented, as support for this will be conditionally compiled, and we anticipate removing this feature after we have a better understanding of what daemons perform queries. The metrics published will take the following form, where SUBSYSTEM will be replaced by the subsystem name of the client: ForkQueriesFromSUBSYSTEM - counter of the number of queries handled by forking from SUBSYSTEM InProcQueriesFromSUBSYSTEM - counter of the number of queries handled in-process from SUBSYSTEM RecentForkQueriesFromSUBSYSTEM - counter of the number of queries in the recent time window (20 min) handled by forking from SUBSYSTEM RecentInProcQueriesFromSUBSYSTEM - counter of the number of queries in the recent time window (20 min) handled in-process from SUBSYSTEM When the collector aborts a query request due to load, in the initial implementation it will simply close the socket. In a future refinement, it would be nice if a specific error was give back to the client (aka 'Server too busy').

title: Ticket #662: Create a SOAP-based command-line tool execution service
description: Primarily to help out the BatLab w/ some collaborative work w/ ETICS, we need to create a daemonCore service that accepts a SOAP request, executes a command-line tool (in the specific case of ETICs, it will be nmi_submit), and then returns the results. We are calling this service the condor_soapshell. Some pithy documentation on the initial pass at this service exists here. Some known deficiencies of this initial pass as of 8/12/09: No user priv switching yet (!). Ideally it should switch UIDs based upon SSL authentication. Doesn't take advantage of the procd for privledge separation support. Doesn't take advantage of procfamily to clean up the entire process tree when a command complete. It can only handle one request at a time. In other words, when a command is launched, the service will block until it completes. The difficulty arises because gsoap assumes a threaded model, not a daemoncore-style callback model. No Win32 support --- currently just Unix/Linux only.

title: Ticket #6468: Memory handling issues in python bindings when using projections
description: This ticket cleans up memory management bugs in the Python bindings with respect to STL vectors. These bugs result in ASSERTS being thrown by the standard C library on Windows when using query functions with projections, and I suppose could result in the memory of the Python process being trashed. The problem was in several places in the Python binding implementation, the following idiom was used: std::vector<xxx> array; array.reserve(max); for (x=0; x<max; x++) { array[x] = .... } In the above code, the reserve() method was used instead of the resize() method. This is a problem because reserve() alone is not sufficient to start referencing vectors by index, as no vector entries were actually created. Turns out the patch to fix these incidents does not bother with calling resize(), because in most cases the use of an STL vector wasn't required and thus the errant code was simply removed. In other cases, push_back() was used.

title: Ticket #3390: MPI Parallel Universe jobs fail when USE_NFS=True - Developer Series
description: This is the developer series version of Ticket #3361. We already have a quick fix for the stable series. From Todd in #3361 The problem is a protocol mismatch: the remote I/O client in the vanilla starter does not understand all the potential file mappings that the remote I/O server in the shadow may return. Behold from /src/condor_starter.V6.1/io_proxy_handler.cpp: result = REMOTE_CONDOR_get_file_info_new(path,url); if(result==0) { dprintf(D_SYSCALLS,"Directed to use url %s\n",url); ASSERT( strlen(url) < CHIRP_LINE_MAX ); if(!strncmp(url,"remote:",7)) { strncpy(path,url+7,CHIRP_LINE_MAX); } else if(!strncmp(url,"buffer:remote:",14)) { strncpy(path,url+14,CHIRP_LINE_MAX); } else { EXCEPT("File %s maps to url %s, which I don't know how to open.\n",path,url); } So if USE_NFS=True, the remote I/O server in the shadow will return a mapping URL that starts with local:, and the remote I/O client in the starter only understands remote: and buffer:remote. Plan for developer series fix: For the development branch moving forward, we should either teach the remote I/O client how to handle all the possible server responses such as local:, or rip out the possibility for local: responses from the server.

title: Ticket #4455: Let chirp set/read private job ad attributes
description: A parallel universe job might be using chirp to transfer private information between nodes. For example, node 0 might set up a server for other nodes to connect to, and need to transmit a dynamically created security key. While you could bake a hard coded key in, a dynamic key ensures that someone who gains read access to the executable can't connect to the running server. To aid in this, it would be nice for chirp to be able to read and set private attributes in the job ad. Some additional security would be warranted, perhaps similar to https://htcondor-wiki.cs.wisc.edu/index.cgi/tktview?tn=3353

title: Ticket #727: VOMS support not documented
description: VOMS does not appear to be documented in the main manual.
remarks: 2009-Dec-08 12:58:35 by smoler: As of Dec 8, 2009: The 7.4.0 manual has a version history item identifying that VOMS does not work in 7.4.0, and that it should be disabled. 2010-Jan-28 14:38:35 by zmiller: Wrote first pass, assigned to karen in review state. 2010-Jan-28 15:24:33 by smoler: Zach's documentation: There are two new uses of VOMS in Condor. The first is that VOMS attributes now appear in the Job Ad when x509userproxy is specified in the submit file. These attributes can then be used for matchmaking or for accounting. x509UserProxySubject: This attribute contains only the Distinguished Name (DN) of the credential used to submit the job. This was already present and the VOMS work does not change the meaning of this attribute. x509UserProxyVOName: This attribute contains the name of the VO that the user's credential is part of. x509UserProxyFirstFQAN: This attribute is equal to only the primary role of the credential. A credential may have multiple roles defined, but by convention the one listed first is the primary role. x509UserProxyFQAN: This is a serialized list of the DN and all FQAN. A comma is used as a separator, and any existing commas in the DN or FQAN are replaced with the string ','. Likewise, any ampersands in the DN or FQAN are replaced with '&'. It should be noted that these attributes are placed into the Job Ad but they are NOT verified, and can be modified using condor_qedit after the job is submitted. Therefore, you should not rely on their authenticity. The other area of Condor that is enhanced by the recent VOMS work is the mapping of users using the CERTIFICATE_MAPFILE. Normally, rules for the GSI method are executed using the DN of the credential used for authentication. Now, with the integration of VOMS, the rules are first interpreted using the full serialized DN and FQAN (quoted if needed in the same way as x509UserProxyFQAN was above). If no matching rules can be found using the full DN and FQAN, the DN is then used on its own without the FQAN. Using the regular expression capabilities of the CERTIFICATE_MAPFILE, you can then extract roles or usernames from the VOMS attributes to be used as the target for mapping. In this case, the FQAN are verified, and you can rely on their authenticity.

title: Ticket #4510: Separate query handler for schedd
description: There's interest for an external query handler for the schedd. Envisioned use cases: Isolate query activity from other schedd activity. Don't allow the launching of shadows impede queries (and vice versa). For example, if we know a certain user tends to flood the schedd with tons of condor_qs, we may want to handle this gracefully without slowing down the main process. Provide a quick response time for a subset of queries. For example, in CMS, we have busy schedds (20k running, 40k pending) that get queried by the web interface to get the status of specific DAG tasks (so there's only one classad in the response). We often see the response take >5s. We would like to have the query handler follow only DAGMan jobs. The idea is we have a separately-launched daemon that tails the schedd's job_queue.log and responds to client requests. The schedd should pass the client queries to the query handler process which then responds with the normal protocol. Further, the query handler should be able to filter and project the classads it tails. Design doc to follow. A few items to think about: How does the query handler get the client query? Does it become part of the schedd ad (client talks to query_handler, getting the coordinates from the collector)? Does the schedd handle the request, handing it off to the appropriate query handler? Does a third-party-daemon (shared_port or something new?) handle the request and route it appropriately? If the query handler can filter out jobs, what are the semantics? What if I change a job didn't pass the filter at submit time but passes it later (and vice versa)? For projections, how do we determine an attribute should be kept (what if an attribute A whitelisted in the projection refers to attribute B but we see B before A in the submit)? What are the semantics of the response? Is it simply a mirror of the schedd job_queue.log, delayed by up to N seconds? Or is the response guaranteed to be up-to-date with the latest commit (meaning we need to check the job_queue.log for each query handled)?

title: Ticket #5751: add a userMap function to condor ClassAds
description: For use in the job router and in the future submit transforms - a function is needed in classads that will take a username as input and look it up in a mapfile (like the security mapfile) and return an accounting group or list of groups. the list of userMaps to load is configured on a per-daemon basis. We do this to avoid having a naieve configuration causing the tools and shadows/starters to parse a userMap file that they will never use. The knobs are: <subsystem>_CLASSAD_USER_MAP_NAMES = name1 name2 etc CLASSAD_USER_MAPFILE_<name1> initalize userMap <name1> by parsing this file CLASSAD_USER_MAPDATA_<name1> initialze userMap <name1> by parsing the value of this knob. If both CLASSAD_USER_MAPFILE_<name1> and CLASSAD_USER_MAPDATA_<name1> are specified the MAPFILE will be read and the MAPDATA ignored. The format of the MAPFILE or MAPDATA will be the same as security Canonicalization files. The first field must be * (or a subset name - see below), the second field is a regex that we will match against the input, and the third field will be the output if the regex matches, the 3 and 4 argument form of userMap expect that the third field will be a comma separated list of values. for example groups.mapdata * John chemistry,physics,glassblowing * Juan physics,chemistry * Bob security * Alice security,math The classad userMap function takes 2 to 4 arguments. In all forms the mapping table indicated by mapname is scanned until field2 of a row matches the input. If a match is found, the return value is based on the other args and the value of field3 from that row. If there is no matching row, then the return value is undefined (or arg4 if using the 4 argument form). The various forms of userMap are: userMap(mapname,input) -> returns field3 of the mapdata or undefined userMap(mapname,input,preference) -> returns the value from field3 of the map data that matches preference. returns undefined if no field3 or it does not match the preference. userMap(mapname,input,undefined) -> returns the first value from field3 of the map data. returns undefined if there is no field3 userMap(mapname,input,preference,default) -> returns default if no row matches the input, or if field3 doesn't contain the preference. otherwise behaves the same as the 3 argument form. userMap(mapname,input,undefined,default) -> returns default if no row matches the input, or if field3 is empty, otherwise returns the first item from field3 Optional submaps If the first field of the mapfile contains something other than *, then a submap is defined. To select a submap for lookup, the first argument for userMap should be "mapname.submap". for example mapdata 'groups' with submaps * Bob security * Alice security,math alt Alice math,hacking Using the above mapfile. the following lookups will result userMap("groups","Alice") -> returns security,math userMap("groups.alt","Alice") -> returns math,hacking

title: Ticket #5301: Shared Port and HAD don't work together
description: The HAD daemons don't work properly when Shared Port is enabled. The standard configuration for them to listen on their own well-known port, but they believe their primary address is behind the shared port daemon. For an immediate fix, we can force the HAD daemons to always ignore shared port. One way to do this is to add daemon-specific entries in the param defaults table, like this: HAD.USE_SHARED_PORT = False REPLICATION.USE_SHARED_PORT = False Another way to do this is to modify SharedPortEndpoint::UseSharedPort() to always return False inside the HAD and REPLICATION daemons, like it does inside the SHARED_PORT daemon. Long term, we should investigate how to have the HAD daemons work with shared port. This could mean allowing shared port ids to be specified in the current HAD configuration. Or it could mean developing a new way for the HAD daemons to find each other, say via ads in the collectors.

title: Ticket #4639: Help CMS with group-based scheduling policy questions
description: James at CMS would like to discuss group-based scheduling mechanisms in HTCondor.
remarks: Statement of the Problem: In general in CMS we would like to have a 50%/50% fair-share between the production and analysis accounting groups. In this way grid resources will be shared equally between Monte Carlo production and analysis users as a group. However, we have a certain class of resources (Tier-1 sites) where we want to have a different fair-share, 95%/5% between production and analysis. Can HTCondor provide us with a way to have different fair-shares by accounting group on different classes of resources? Currently we have worked around this problem by adding a resource group in the glideinWMS fronted which sends pilots with a special VOMS role to the Tier-1 sites, and the fair-share is enforced at the site level in the CE. Ideally we would like to be able to control this fair-share centrally and not delegate setting it to the Tier-1 sites. Related Problem: Some sites provide CMS opportunistic access to resources that are not part of their pledge to the experiment, but are accessible by the normal HTCondor/glideinWMS infrastructure in CMS. The sites would like to be able to give a preferential access to certain classes of local users before the cycles are delivered to non-local users. These local users can be identified either individually (list of users) or as members of a VOMS group, i.e. their grid DNs have a special VOMS role identifying them as members of a group such as the Spanish national group. Currently we have worked around this problem by adding a resource group in the glideinWMS fronted which sends pilots with a special VOMS role to a class of sites, and the fair-share is enforced at the site level in the CE. While we do not wish to control this fair-share centrally, rather leaving it to the sites themselves to manage, we do not want the significant overhead of having to introduce a new glideinWMS frontend group for every site that wants to deliver low-priority opportunistic cycles to CMS. Can HTCondor provide us with a way to have different priorities for classes of users even more finely-grained than accounting group (site-maintained list, VOMS role based) on different classes of resources? 2015-Feb-05 15:04:18 by jfrey: Here is a proposed solution for the different production/analysis split for Tier-1 vs non-Tier-1 sites. Run two negotiators, each matching a subset of machine ads in the global CMS glidein collector. The first negotiator will match all glide-ins at Tier-1 sites. It will have dynamic group quotas of 95% for production and 5% for analysis, with surplus enabled for production. The second negotiator will match all glide-ins at non-Tier-1 sites and Tier-1 glide-ins that have been Unclaimed for more than 5 minutes. It will have dynamic group quotes of 50% with surplus enabled for both production and analysis. If there are insufficient analysis jobs, then production jobs will take over more than their guaranteed share of both Tier-1 and non-Tier-1 machines. If there are insufficient production jobs, then analysis jobs will take over more than their guaranteed share of non-Tier-1 machines. The first negotiator will only give 5% of Tier-1 machines to analysis jobs. Any glide-ins that go unmatched due to insufficient production jobs will soon be picked up by the second negotiator, which will match them to analysis jobs. Fair share between analysis users will be enforced by the second negotiator, except for 5% of Tier-1 glide-ins; the first negotiator will enforce fair share for those glide-ins. This bifurcation of fair-share should be close to the stated requirement of fair-share across all glide-ins running analysis jobs. 2015-Feb-05 19:27:53 by bbockelm: Hi Jaime, I think that would work (long term, I'm still interested in remote accountants!). We'll lose some percentage of glideins due to the idle minutes and negotiation time. It'll probably be acceptable. Any ideas of how we can measure that? Brian

title: Ticket #2647: Schedd's job evaluation timer can become unregistered
description: In the schedd, it's possible for the daemon-core timer for Scheduler::timeout() to become unregistered. If this happens, the schedd will no longer examine the job queue for idle jobs or send its ads to the collector. Once the schedd enters this state, only a reconfig or restart can revive it. We have observed occasional instances of this happening in Metronome, in the form of a personal schedd that has one dagman job that remains idle forever. We've identified one codepath that can lead to this situation, and possibilities for other codepaths. The simplest solution is to never cancel the timer and also keep it as a periodic timer
remarks: 2011-Nov-21 16:21:35 by tannenba: CODE REVIEW of timer patch attached to this ticket. Looks good, except change the code fragment in RegisterTimers() from if (timeoutid < 0) { timeoutid = daemonCore->Register_Timer(10, (TimerHandlercpp)&Scheduler::timeout,"timeout",this); } to be instead if (timeoutid < 0) { timeoutid = daemonCore->Register_Timer(10, 10, (TimerHandlercpp)&Scheduler::timeout,"timeout",this); } Note the difference is the second version registers the timer as periodic, as a defensive measure against the timer not being reset (which is after all, part of the goal of the patch in the first place). 2011-Nov-21 17:34:25 by jfrey: I've incorporated your comments into my patch.

title: Ticket #1968: Making flocking the general case, even for "local" pool. FLOCK_TO
description: Currently flocking is a special case: If there are jobs that can't get slots locally, try the first entry in the FLOCK_TO list. Still jobs without slots, try the second entry, and so on until you run out of sites. Problem 1: Special cases add complexity. Problem 2: You can't dynamically change the flocking rules, perhaps based on the job ad. Problem 3: If you have a mix of jobs that desire different flocking rules, you need multiple schedds. Proposal: "Flocking" becomes the default state. A schedd doesn't automatically advertise to the local collector, it's a side effect of the "local" collector being the first entry in the FLOCK_TO list. We'll probably want to rename FLOCK_TO and friends. Furthermore, make FLOCK_TO and friends expressions that are evaluated in the context of a job ad. Concrete example, based on a real CHTC use case: There are two pools, the local pool and a glide-in pool. The administrator wants to be able to control where jobs go: local overflowing to glide-in, glide-in overflowing to local, just local, or just glide-in. The flow will vary on a job-by-job, user-by-user basis. Most jobs only run locally, but Octave jobs should run glide-in overflowing to local, while user Xavier's GNU-R jobs should run locally overflowing to glide-in. We want to be able to change these assignments, including for queued, but not yet running, jobs. For example, we might discover that a particular user's Octave jobs don't work on the glide-ins, so we want to exclude him from using the glide-in pool. Another user of GNU-R might discover that he can use the glide-in pool and we want to add him to the flocking. IS_OCTAVE=(regexp("/octave$",CMD)) IS_XR=(USER=="xavier" && regexp("/R$",CMD)) FLOCK_TO= \ ifThenElse(IS_OCTAVE, "glidein.example.com,local.example.com", \ ifThenElse(IS_XR, "local.example.com,glidein.example.com", \ "local.example.com" \ ) \ )
remarks: 2011-Mar-15 16:09:00 by adesmet: Implementation note: We'll need to know which jobs are interested in which flocking lists when a) building an ad to send to each collector and b) when the collector wanders by looking for jobs. Rebuilding those lists every time we care could be expensive for a large queue. We may need to cache and only update occasionally. Perhaps every 5 minutes, or on a rolling basis, or on job state transitions. 2011-Mar-15 16:54:47 by bbockelm: Hi Alan, One thing I've been wanting for awhile is the ability to have dynamic FLOCK_TO lists. I.e., if I had an "uber-collector" which contained other several collector ads, it would be nice if the schedd was smart enough to take its list of collectors to flock to from there. When looking at the ticket, I think how unmanageable a job ad would be at Purdue where there are 10-15 levels of flocking. Anyhow, if it's not possible to actually execute this idea, if we're redesigning this code, it would be beneficial to make sure the framework is there for further improvements. In general, a great idea. Brian 2011-Mar-16 14:14:23 by adesmet: Further thoughts after a discussion with psilord, inspired by bbockelm's thoughts above. Take the above proposal, then add a ClassAd function something like this: String QueryCollector(String collector_name_and_port, String constraint_expr, String rank_expr, String attr_to_extract, String concatenation_character) Query collector_name_and_port (e.g. condor-cm.example.com:3472) for classads that satisfy constraint_expr. Ads are queried from all available ads, equivalent to the -any option to condor_status. The ads are then sorted by rank_expr. For each ad, extract the attribute named attr_to_extract as a string. Join the list of extracted attributes with concatenation_character Given this, you might say something like: FLOCK_TO=QueryCollector("condor-cm.example.com", "MyType==\"Collector\"", "Machine==\"condor-cm.example.com\"", "CollectorIpAddr", ",") That sets the flocking list to all collectors reporting to condor-cm.example.com, with a preference for condor-cm.example.com. We could design the entire system around pulling collectors from the collector. Instead of FLOCK_TO, we would have FLOCK_CONSTRAINT and FLOCK_RANK, which evaluate pairs of Job ads and Collector ads. It would look something like: FLOCK_CONSTRAINT = TRUE FLOCK_RANK = Machine=="condor-cm.example.com" You could have more clever things, like letting a job be picky (This assumes that the collector is MY and the job is TARGET): FLOCK_CONSTRAINT = ifThenElse(TARGET.OnlyRunLocal, Machine=="condor-cm.example.com", TRUE) The default would be: FLOCK_CONSTRAINT = TRUE FLOCK_RANK = Since the local collector advertises itself locally, this would Just Work for the non-flocking case. Either of these solutions will be making a large number of queries, so some kind of caching would likely help. We could to a sort of autoclustering on attributes specified in FLOCK_TO to identify a smaller number of queries we might reuse. We could query all collectors, then do the constraint filtering on the schedd side where it should be cheaper (even with a huge number of potential flocking sites, say 100, a constraint and rank operation should be relatively cheap).

remarks: 2009-Jan-20 15:51:04 by tannenba: Ian Alderman ( mailto:ialderman@cyclecomputing.com ) conjectures on condor-users: The addition of the function getWindowsEnvironmentString (in env.cpp, called from daemon_core.cpp) may have a role. This function reorders the environment variables; could reordering be sufficient to result in the funky behavior? 2009-Jan-22 14:21:29 by gquinn: This appears to be a bug that has always existed. It must have surfaced in 7.2.0 for some users as a result of the getWindowsEnvironmentString work I did earlier. In other words, I fixed a bug without fixing its anti-bug ;) The problem is that onn Windows, environment variable names are case insensitive, but our Env object is case sensitive. Fixing this is more subtle than it may seem, because of our ability to cross-submit. I decided to keep the hash table in the Env object case-sensitive, but on Windows we additionally maintain an STL set that ignores case. With this additional data structure, when Env::getWindowsEnvironmentString is called, we can produce an environment that: is sorted, as Windows requires does not contain any duplicate variable names when case is ignored When multiple variable names that differ only in case exist in the Env object's hash table, the set ensures that the last one to be inserted "wins".

title: Ticket #7150: Sinful alias and daemon name inconsistencies
description: For SSL/X.509, it's unreliable at best, at a security hole at worst, to assume that reverse DNS maps to the subject name of a given host. (For instance, foo.org may be a CNAME to bar.org, which means reverse DNS would return bar.org, which is not the site to which you're trying to connect.) HTCondor deals with this by including the 'alias' attribute in its Sinful strings. Brian Bockelman observed two problems: The flock collector list's daemon (client) objects return Sinfuls without aliases. The collector list's Sinfuls have aliases, but Daemon (client) objects constructed from those Sinfuls have no name(). The former is almost certainly wrong. The latter could be defended by arguing that Sinfuls have a getAlias() member function. It's unclear why the Daemon (client) object has no name(), and it's unclear if it should always correspond to the alias attribute. Straw-man proposal is for the latter is to make name() return the Sinful alias if the Daemon object wasn't constructed from a name. The obvious thing to do for the former is to set the Sinful alias to the string used in the config file (which we'd just call name if that weren't potentially confusing), which I think is always passed as the name parameter in the constructor. The potential issue is here is the existence and meaning of the HOST_ALIAS knob. However, I believe that knob is intended for precisely this purpose (so that the daemons on a given host will advertise Sinfuls with an alias which matches their certificate), so this is likely fine. (If specified, HOST_ALIAS should set the Sinful alias rather than the daemon's name; otherwise, the Sinful's alias attribute and the daemon's name() should always be the same.)
remarks: 2019-Jul-19 17:27:03 by tlmiller: I can't reproduce the first problem. I'll have to ask BrianB for more details. 2019-Jul-26 14:51:10 by tlmiller: Even checking where [57429] changed from ->addr() to ->name() reveals no problems with the Sinful aliases. However, I verified that constructing a Daemon (client) object from a Sinful with an alias does not set the Daemon object's name(). This shouldn't matter (since its Sinful has the alias), since the only place _alias is used is to set the Daemon object Sinful's alias property. The branch contains a bunch of debug code for if we ever decide to pick this up again. The changes include a patch that sets Daemon object's name() to the Sinful's alias if it's available and name() is otherwise not set. (And a patch to set _alias, although it never matters, and a bunch of debug code.)

title: Ticket #2702: Document DAGMan file descriptor issues
description: We should document the issues DAGMan currently has with the number of file descriptors that it may need (depending on the structure of the DAG, etc.). If you have a very wide DAG, and each node job has a separate log file, this will cause DAGMan to have many file descriptors open at once (e.g., 10,000 or more if your DAG is wide enough). I think the default limit for file descriptors for a process on Linux is 10k, but the limit on Windows is currently 512. Z is planning to raise this to 2048 (the most we can have using the C runtime). A workaround is to have the node jobs share the same log file (an easy way is by not specifying a log file at all in your submit files -- DAGMan will supply a default).

title: Ticket #1084: Undo merge of V7_5-cream_hardening-branch into V7_4-branch
description: The changes documented below involve versions of Condor that were never released. Customers do not need to worry about them. V7_5-cream_hardening-branch was merged into V7_4-branch in commit 80fc0a87a790657756aed97dd3d4bdc852e50081. This is probably wrong. Notably, V7_5-cream_hardening-branch has repeatedly had master merged into it, so V7_4-branch now contains all of the master (7.5.x) work! This has been undone, but it has ramifications for anyone working with out Git repository. All developers will need to check to make sure they don't have the bad merge lurking in their repositories. If you haven't done a "git pull" or fetch since December 20th, you're probably okay, but check anyway. To check, on any local branch you have that is based on V7_4-branch, do the following, replacing V7_4-branch with your local branch name. Note that this only applies to branches based on or intended to merge to V7_4-branch. Branches based on or intended to merge with 7.5.something (AKA "master") are fine and do not need changes. Check if you have the bad merge on the branch: git rev-list V7_4-branch | grep 80fc0a87a790657756aed97dd3d4bdc852e50081 Check the output and return code ("echo $?") of the previous command: If there is no output and a non-zero return code, all is well. This branch is safe. Go back to the start and repeat for other branches based on V7_4-branch. If you're out of branches, you're done! If the return code is 0 and the output is "80fc0a87a790657756aed97dd3d4bdc852e50081", then you have the bad merge. If this is the case, you must destroy and recreate the branch, otherwise you could reinfect the central repository. Continue: You'll need to delete your infected V7_4-branch and recreate it. Do you have committed changes to V7_4-branch that you haven't pushed? No un-pushed changes: Just run the following to delete and recreate the local branch: git checkout master git branch -D V7_4-branch git branch V7_4-branch origin/V7_4-branch Un-pushed changes: You will want to store your good changes away and reapply them. Be careful to not accidentally drag in the bad merge! You can not use git stash for this, as git stash will just stash away the bad merge. You can do this by hand, or you can use "git format-patch" and "git am" to store them away and re-apply them. Use "gitk" or similar to find the ranges of SHAs that contain your changes. Be sure to not include 80fc0a87a790657756aed97dd3d4bdc852e50081 in the range! If you have multiple ranges, simply call "git format-patch" repeatedly, appending to the same file. Once you have your ranges, use the following, or something similar: git format-patch --stdout EARLIEST_GOOD_SHA1..CURRENT_GOOD_SHA1 > v7.4-rescue git checkout master git branch -D V7_4-branch git branch V7_4-branch origin/V7_4-branch git checkout V7_4-branch git am v7.4-rescue How the revert was done This is old notes on how the revert was done. It is not necessary reading for a developer just wanting to fix their local repository. Reverting a merge is Hard. Here's the official reason why and how to do it. The official way to do it assumes that you'll want to redo the merge at some later date, or will never want to do the merge. We will never do the merge, but will may cherry pick some stuff over. Doing a straight revert would leave us with a landmine if any developer later tries to cherry pick stuff from master to V7_4-branch. Furthermore, it would leave Git with a confused view of the world; if you ask "is this commit part of this branch?" Git will unhelpfully say "yes", when in fact it was part of the reverted merge. So instead we're going to "git reset" to cause the commit to never have happened at all. The plan: # Save good work on V7_4-branch. Check the second version number is the head. git-format-patch --stdout 80fc0a87a790657756aed97dd3d4bdc852e50081..63964181bbe027cfead32e3a6886349dbfab61a7 > v7.4-rescue # Back V7_4-branch to the commit immediately before the bad merge. 584e2bb18f4e038066e44b53cddd9945e0b9dbbb git reset --hard 584e2bb18f4e038066e44b53cddd9945e0b9dbbb # Reapply the good work git am v7.4-rescue # Push it up git push --force That didn't work. Our main respository is a "bare" repository; it lacks a working directory. We can't "git push --force" to stomp over the old versions. We need to delete the branch ("git push origin :V7_4-branch"), then recreate it ("git push origin +V7_4-branch"). So, what actually happened: # Save good work on V7_4-branch. Check the second version number is the head. git-format-patch --stdout 80fc0a87a790657756aed97dd3d4bdc852e50081..63964181bbe027cfead32e3a6886349dbfab61a7 > v7.4-rescue # Back V7_4-branch to the commit immediately before the bad merge. 584e2bb18f4e038066e44b53cddd9945e0b9dbbb git reset --hard 584e2bb18f4e038066e44b53cddd9945e0b9dbbb # Reapply the good work git am v7.4-rescue # Delete upstream version git push origin :V7_4-branch # Push corrected version git push origin +V7_4-branch

title: Ticket #7853: python submit method on schedd object should take a Submit object
description: As a part of fixing #7655, and transitioning to a stable and usable python submit API. We plan to change the arguments of the schedd.submit method, deprecating some, and replacing them with others. Currently, schedd.submit takes a classad as it's first argument, that will be deprecated but still allowed, and the new argument type will be htcondor.Submit In all cases, count and spool will be unchanged. But other arguments will depend on what is passed as the first argument. If the first argument it a classad, a deprecation warning will fire, but the existing submission mechanism will still work, the submitted job ad(s) will optionally be returned in the result_ads list, and the return value will be the ClusterId as an integer. If The first argument is not a classad it must be a htcondor.Submit object. The return value will be a htcondor.SubmitResult object instead of an integer. count and the new itemdata arguments will behave as they do with Submit.queue method the spool argument will cause jobs to be submitted on spooling hold and the passed in htcondor.Submit object will be changed so that the jobs needed to spool can be accessed via the htcondor.Submit.jobs iterator method. A new method on the schedd object: Schedd.insert_jobs will be added as a non-deprecated way to submit raw job classads to the schedd. This will replace both Schedd.submit and Schedd.submitMany and it will do the absolute minimum amount of mutation of the classads (ClusterId, and ProcId will be set to agree with the newly allocated cluster / proc. nothing else will change. In the future we may allow ProcId to pass through unmodified if is set in the incoming job classad. In keeping with the way condor_submit works, the jobs passed to Schedd.insert_jobs, will undergo attribute de-duplication so that there is a cluster classad, and a sequence of proc classads that contain only the differences.

title: Ticket #6605: Revised regression testing milestones.
description: While the overall and final goals of the testing program haven't changed, the fact that we added PEAK metrics before finishing the SUM metrics tests means we're doing things in a different order. This ticket supersedes #6543, #6569, and #6554. I'll commit test improvements on this ticket number until the next point release, at which point I may have to create another ticket for the changes to the next point release. The existing tests are: cmr-monitor-basic and cmr-monitor-basic-partitionable cmr-monitor-memory and cmr-monitor-memory-partitionable cmr-monitor-both and cmr-monitor-both-partitionable The first tests one SUM metric, the second one PEAK metric, and the third running both at the same time. All three tests test one resource per slot of a single resource type. To address the comments on the previous tickets: The -partitionable tests check dynamic slots. The cmr-*-ad.cmd files submit eight jobs to a configuration known to have only four resources and check all eight jobs; this checks slot reuse. The next test will build on cmr-monitor-both. The first step is to run the cmr-monitor-both tests in the presence of another active monitor (also with one resource instance per slot, but now with two resource types). If these pass, the test should be extended to add tests of the second resource's reporting. Once that's done, we can consider how to structure our answer to the next section. We also need to have a test for multiple SUM and multiple PEAK metrics per monitor. (Although it might make sense to develop a test for each type of metric independently, since we need to test both simultaneously, that may be the only test we actually have/run.) We would then have to test those monitors in the presence of other monitors (resource types) like them (that is, with multiple SUM and PEAK metrics), as well as test multiple resource instances per slot for each resource type.

title: Ticket #4638: Disk space machine attributes on Windows are incorrect
description: Disk attributes in the startd ad (aka Disk,TotalDisk,TotalSlotDisk) on Windows are incorrectly being reported in bytes. They should be reported in kilobytes. Note they are correctly in kbytes on Linux. Furthermore, although we have not been able to reproduce it, Nate reported an instance where TotalDisk is being incorrectly reported with a value capped at 2^31 (2147483647). title: Ticket #1590: delegation of rfc proxies fails in file transfer
description: The GSI function globus_gsi_proxy_handle_set_is_limited() contains a bug that causes delegation of rfc proxies to fail. This causes attempts to delegate a proxy in Condor's file transfer object to fail. Delegations only fail when using GSI from Globus 5.x, thus Condor 7.4 is unaffected. A bug report with patch has been submitted to the Globus team. It can be found at http://bugzilla.globus.org/globus/show_bug.cgi?id=7093. The patch should be applied to the version of Globus built for Condor. A work-around is to set DELEGATE_JOB_GSI_CREDENTIALS to false, causing proxies to be copied rather than delegated. This is insecure if encryption isn't enabled.

title: Ticket #4268: Some DAGMan tests are non-deterministic
description: Some tests, for example job_dagman_halt-A are not 100% deterministic in that they rely on things like doing sleeps to order certain aspects of the test. It seems like there are two basic approaches to this: Make the actual test execution totally deterministic Make the test checking tolerant of certain variations in execution order To do option 1 we'd have to replace the sleeps with some kind of explicit waits that would only stop waiting once they verified that a certain condition was true. title: Ticket #4792: simple option to condor_q to query the negotiator's autocluster
description: To perform matching (to determine what pilots are needed), glideinWMS currently queries the schedd for all jobs matching a certain constraint, returning several significant attributes. We've found that this query is prohibitively expensive - on a test with 500k idle jobs in queue, this took over 40 minutes to return However, glideinWMS takes the result of the query and counts the number of jobs with identical significant attributes (the total count is then used to gauge demand). In other words - it performs auto-clustering! If the schedd could provide the auto-clusters (and job count per auto-cluster) as a query protocol, then we could greatly reduce the cost of the query. There is no immediate need to query anything other than the autocluster information currently built by the schedd. note: this ticket is the former #4613, since the scope of that task was substantially reduced after that ticket already had several commits (that no longer apply.)

/var/lib/condor/execute/spool/job_queue.log The condor_master tried to start the condor_schedd several more times with the same result. I contacted Christina and notified her that the SPOOL filesystem had filled up. After looking around a bit we discovered that the culprit was a single user's job that had a multitude of output files that had a maximum size of about 50MB. Christina suggested that we backup and remove the directory representing the files of the user's largest cluster to get the condor_schedd back online. I tar'ed the directory to another server, removed the directory in SPOOL, and started the condor_schedd. It came back up just fine. Christina put the user's jobs on hold and contacted him; He removed his jobs from the queue not long after. The SPOOL filesystem currently has 206GB of space available. The user seemed to think that the backed-up data was not particularly useful (after the fact) and only asked for a small sample of what was backed up. This has started a conversation on what HTCondor should do, if anything, to keep this from happening. Note that the condor_schedd's shutdown was due to the job queue log being on the same filesystem as the rest of the SPOOL when the filesystem filled up. In the future infrastructure plans on putting the job queue long on it's own filesystem on a solid state drive. Theoretically, this would keep the condor_schedd from crashing in such a situation. I learned today from Todd Tannenbaum that there's a "SpoolOnEvict" knob in the submit file that, if set to false, will keep job output from being written to the spool on eviction (it instead gets written to the directory the job was submitted from, I think?). Due to an error in the documentation code this knob is not currently documented. I'm not sure how the engagement team feels about this, but it's there. The SPOOLed output files are owned by the unix account of the submitting user. Using GNU/Linux quotas in SPOOL filesystem may be an option. However, I don't trust GNU/Linux filesystem quotas (I've seen them become inaccurate a few times), and Todd and I agree that a user hitting their SPOOL quota may lead to strange and unforeseen consequences. I'm not crazy about this idea. Since the job queue log goes in the SPOOL directory by default, perhaps HTCondor should have some logic for refusing to SPOOL output files after a certain threshold is reached? -Moate
remarks: 2016-Aug-31 15:03:26 by tlmiller: FWIW, I would guess that SpoolOnEvict transfers to wherever the user specified the output files should go.

title: Ticket #5029: Documentation of ClassAds new vs. old syntax is incorrect/misleading
description: The documentation for Classads implies that there is a distinction between new and old classad syntax. This is no longer true. HTCondor instead uses the new classad library with a compatibility layer that adds on HTCondor specific behavior. There is no plan to ever move fully to 'new' classad syntax, we should strike that word entirely from our documentation.
remarks: 2015-Apr-29 08:38:03 by bbockelm: To my knowledge, there's no difference between the old/new language. However, HTCondor loads many functions at runtime that are not present in the classads library.

title: Ticket #7014: Vanila universe checkpoint on eviction by default
description: Vanilla Universe checking pointing for job eviction should be enabled by default and leave it to users to opt out if so desired. Our proposal is to (a) make vanilla universe check pointing first-class in the submit language and (b) simplify the interface. Specifically, all the user will have to set is CheckpointExitCode (name subject to change); HTCondor will take care of the details. This will not by default set when_to_transfer_files to ON_EXIT_OR_EVICT; the vanilla universe check pointing implementation will be changed so that this is not necessary. If we did make transferring the checkpoint on eviction the default, then the default would be to require checkpoint updates to be atomic, which seems like a good way to cause problems. Implementation-wise, we presently anticipate the following: changing the submit utils to transform CheckpointExitCode into SuccessCheckpointExitCode and WantFTOnCheckpoint; changing the starter so that WantFTOnCheckpoint being set will force intermediate file transfer regardless of the setting of when_to_transfer_files; (optionally) changing the starter so that the presence of SuccessCheckpointExitCode implies WantFTOnCheckpoint; changing the startd to advertise the ability to transfer files on checkpoint, and changing submit utils to add that requirement to the job. See #7031.
remarks: 2019-Apr-24 13:48:47 by tlmiller: I think this means, specifically, that setting CheckpointSig does not set or override KillSig. 2019-Apr-24 13:51:45 by tlmiller: Once we actually remove standard universe for good, we can switch 'ckpt or syscalls' to 'checkpointing' (and short name to 'ckpt', not 'std'). [Referring to string constants in gittrac.] 2019-May-01 13:21:30 by pfc: We will defer this until Todd Miller's application-level checkpointing HOWTO is complete, and then re-asses how much this trips up users. 2019-May-01 13:25:18 by tlmiller: This may be a lower priority once #7022 is done. 2019-May-02 15:48:49 by tlmiller: Sorry -- I've lost context on this ticket, and I'm no longer sure what my first comment meant. Is this ticket referring to requiring the user to set when_to_transfer_files to ON_EXIT_OR_EVICT when setting +WantFTOnCheckpoint? If so, see #7031 -- we think that the user shouldn't have to specify it, but that it shouldn't be enable by default (because it relaxes the requirement for atomic checkpoints). 2019-May-08 13:34:45 by tannenba: The idea here is if the user specifies a checkpoint exit status, then we know they want to transfer ON_EXIT_OR_EVIT. Why make the user set both? Also, if they set the knobs in conflict with each other, submit should throw an error. 2019-May-08 14:06:45 by tlmiller: > The idea here is if the user specifies a checkpoint exit status, then we know > they want to transfer ON_EXIT_OR_EVICT. If we adopt the proposal that ON_EXIT_OR_EVICT should be orthogonal to vanilla-universe checkpointing -- which would allow vanilla-universe checkpoints to be update non-atomically -- then I would expect many users would not want to set ON_EXIT_OR_EVICT, because atomic updates may be hard or tedious to arrange. 2019-Jun-14 17:11:20 by tlmiller: See #7031.

title: Ticket #5479: Allow user to define failure for DAG node jobs
description: Miron wants users to be able to define (at the DAG level) what constitutes failure for a DAG node job (as opposed to the current semantics that any non-zero exit code is a failure). The user should be able to specify a ClassAd expression (first globally, then with the capability to override it for individual nodes). One other issue is how this should apply to PRE and POST scripts -- should the same expression apply to them, or do they each need their own expression? My initial thought is that there should just be a single expression that applies to the PRE script, HTCondor job, and POST script. Also, another question (just syntactic) is whether this should be defined in terms of failure or success. Part of the motivation for this is to make it explicit if a non-zero exit code constitutes "success", as opposed to "hiding" that semantic in the POST script.

title: Ticket #5183: schedds RESCHEDULE handler needs faster check for idle local jobs
description: The SCHEDD can melt down when it has lots of jobs in the queue and new submit requests are happening frequently because each submit sends a RESCHEDULE command; and the handler for that command will walk the job queue looking for idle local jobs. We've seen this walk take .25 seconds or more on a large schedd with many jobs ine the queue. Not only does this limit the submit rate to 4/sec. But it effectively also limits that job completion rate to 4/sec because of the way the self draining queues work (only one job can be removed from the queue per pump cycle). Currently the schedd's RESCHEDULE command handler calls WalkJobQueue(find_idle_local_jobs);. We should either fix that code to iterate faster (which we can easily do). or change the code so that it doesn't walk the entire job queue.

title: Ticket #7151: Improve usability of StartCommandRequest
description: SecMan::StartCommandRequest is a structure used to condense ten parameters of Daemon::startCommand_internal into one. Presently, each member of the structure is initialized explicitly, on its own line. There should be a way to improve both the usability of the interface and the readability of code using it. One further possibility is to analyze patterns in the usage and write a few well-name factory functions (but not constructors, because we can't change the names of those). Another (suggest by GregT), is to arrange the interface as function calls describing what you want to do. title: Ticket #3811: Jobs can leave queue without writing relevant event to user job log
description: Many job management tools that submit jobs to HTCondor use the user job log to monitor the status of those jobs, particularly to detect when jobs leave the queue (whether because they complete or are removed). Thus, it's very important that an "abort" or "terminate" event be written to the job log before the schedd removes the job from the queue. Unfortunately, there are several situations where writing to the job log fails but the schedd still lets the job leave the queue. We have seen this happen several times in the past month in the BaTLab, where the disk holding the job logs filled up but the disk holding the spool directory still had room. Numerous Metronome jobs left the queue, but DAGMan thought they were still queued. This problem applies to both the regular user job log and the DAGMan job log. Failure to write to the global event log was previously deemed to be unimportant (#2858). Here are some cases where this can happen: In the schedd, if opening or writing to the job log fails, completed scheduler and noop jobs are still allowed to leave the queue. Scheduler::InitializeUserLog() returns NULL when no logging required and when opening a log file fails. Scheduler::scheduler_univ_job_leave_queue() and count() ignore the return value of Scheduler::WriteTerminateToUserLog(). In the schedd, if opening or writing to the job log fails, any removed job is still allowed to leave the queue. Scheduler::InitializeUserLog() returns NULL when no logging required and when opening a log file fails. All callers of Scheduler::WriteAbortToUserLog() ignore its return value. In the gridmanager, if opening or writing to the job log fails, any completed or removed job is still allowed to leave the queue. InitializeUserLog() ignores any failure returned by WriteUserLog::initialize(). Any subsequent calls to WriteUserLog::writeEvent() will return success without trying to write anything. BaseJob::DoneWithJob() ignores any failures returned by WriteTerminateEventToUserLog() or WriteAbortEventToUserLog(). There are also some problems with writing the submit event: In condor_submit, when talking to an old schedd, if opening or writing to the job log fails, the job is still submitted and can run. When a logging failure is detected in log_submit(), all that's done is to print an error to stderr. In the schedd, if opening or writing to the job log fails, the job is still submitted and can run. Scheduler::InitializeUserLog() returns NULL when no logging required and when opening a log file fails. The return value of Scheduler::WriteSubmitToUserLog() is ignored. Code to properly initialize a WriteUserLog object based on information from a job ad is replicated in 5 or 6 locations with different behavior. These should be consolidated. (This is the topic of #5329)
