title: Ticket #819: Parse() too forgiving in what it accepts
description: Parse() is too lax in what it considers valid expressions. It will parse both assignment and non-assignment expressions. It will also allow an arbitrary non-assignment expression on the left-hand side of an assignment. Here are some expressions it will accept: 3 = a 2 + 2 = 5 2 + 3 The first two forms should cause Parse() to return failure. Any caller to Parse() is expecting only a non-assignment expression or only an assignment expression. Callers expecting a non-assignment expression should call ParseClassAdRvalExpr() instead. Callers expecting an assignment expression need a function that fails on non-assignment expressions. Parse() can be turned into that function, or a new function created and Parse() deprecated.

title: Ticket #7501: Add new Python-based test framework
description: Yes, we already have a Python-based test framework: #6613 . Confusingly, it is named pytest. No relation to the pytest mentioned later. However, we keep running into problems with it for (in my opinion) one main reason: it is not backed by a real Python test framework, so we keep needing to reinvent the wheel to deal with problems like #7451 To address this core problem, I've been prototyping a new test framework at https://github.com/JoshKarpel/pytest-condor which is backed by pytest, a venerable Python test framework (https://docs.pytest.org/en/latest/). It handles test execution, reporting, output capture, and provides a convenient way to specify test setup and dependencies, including ways to parameterize tests. The new framework has two main components: ornithology, a Python library for managing the lifecycle of a personal Condor executing HTCondor command-line programs (and parsing their results into Python data structures where appropriate) inspecting the state of the personal Condor via the job queue log, daemon log files, and job event logs providing "assertion helpers" that abstract away common conditions we need to test, like "are these things in the right order?". A conftest.py file (a pytest configuration file) that uses ornithology to provide basic building blocks for writing HTCondor tests with pytest. ornithology should not be aware of pytest, such that ornithology could (in principle) be re-used with some other test runner or for entirely different purposes. Goals: The control flow of the test should be clear from reading the test file itself (i.e., you should not have to follow a mess of callbacks to figure out what the test does). We should focus on building re-usable components and factoring common code out into the framework itself (assertion helpers, for example). We should document how the test framework itself works, possibly even with a full Read the Docs website. You shouldn't need to know Python deeply to "read" a test, and hopefully as little as possible to write a test. This is doubly true for test output on failure: you may need to know Condor-isms to interpret it, but you shouldn't need to know Python-isms. Milestones: Get the new framework running in nightly builds (teach run_test.pl to run them; add them to the list of tests to run; make sure Metronome understands their output). Teach the team to use the new framework and start writing new tests using it. Convert old tests, especially ones we don't trust, to the new framework. Another good target would be the Python bindings tests. (Optional) Flip the script: make pytest the overall test runner (it would use run_test.pl to run any leftover old tests). We can argue about this in the future :) This is a tracking ticket for the overall effort; extra dependent tickets may be spawned off for discrete tasks.

title: Ticket #7852: Remove old concurrency limit tests.
description: Following up #7812, we should have plenty of data by the release of 9.0.0 on that new test. Assuming it's behaving as well as expected, remove each of the old concurrency limit tests.
remarks: 2020-Oct-02 13:59:04 by tlmiller: This will resolve #4530 (concurrency test failure) and #5036 (unstable concurrency tests). I believe that #4503 and #4504 are symptoms of the same underlying design problem -- the negotiator has no memory of the concurrency tokens it's assigned. (A memory of the assignments isn't a perfect solution, because the corresponding job may never start. But it's almost certainly better, and less surprising, to schedule fewer jobs too many.) I'm content to continue ignoring #5669 (concurrency incident report). However, AFAIK, #4121 (reusing a claim retains the concurrency token) is still unresolved and needs fixing. It is not currently tested for. 2020-Dec-08 15:43:17 by tlmiller: No documentation necessary for this strictly-internal change.

title: Ticket #3112: Path to main class/jar file of java job broken in condor_submit
description: When a relative path is used for the executable attribute for a java universe job, the path is treated is relative to the CWD and the job's initialdir in different parts of condor_submit. This causes condor_submit to fail if these are different directories. Condor_submit first checks that the executable is readable, resolving relative paths based on the CWD. Then, for java universe jobs, the executable is added to the list of input files to be transferred. This list is passed to process_input_file_list(), which checks that they are readable, and resolves all relative paths based on the job's initialdir.
creator: jfrey

title: Ticket #6310: Some audit-related messages missing from normal schedd log
description: As part of the schedd audit log code, several dprintf() statements were added or modified to have a debug level of D_AUDIT|D_FAILURE. The intention was for these messages to always be written to the primary schedd log, and also be written to a D_AUDIT-only log (if configured). In reality, they are only written if the D_AUDIT level is enabled.
creator: jfrey

title: Ticket #4907: Accept ClassAd expression as constraints for the python bindings
description: The constraint argument passed to the Schedd.query and Collector.query functions has been a wart on the API design - reflecting the HTCondor internals, it only accepts a string (which is internally parsed as a ClassAd expression). We should allow ExprTree objects to be used directly; we should also accept simple casts (python 'True' to classad 'true'). To maintain backward compatibility, strings passed to as constraints should not be converted to a ClassAd string value - instead, they should be parsed as a ClassAd expression.
remarks: 2015-Feb-21 11:16:44 by bbockelm: For example, the following are broken: schedd.query(False) schedd.query(classad.ExprTree('Owner=?="osg"')) but this is acceptable: schedd.query("false") schedd.query('Owner=?="osg"') Both mechanisms should be fine. 2015-Feb-21 11:25:14 by bbockelm: Pushed fix, including version history. No changes to the manual as the reference for these functions already claimed this worked!

title: Ticket #7782: Fix prioritization of commands in condor_c-gahp
description: Commands in the c-gahp that involve file transfer with the remote schedd can block faster, higher priority commands (like querying the status of the remote jobs). Since file transfer commands can take a long time and they don't block the remote schedd (it services them in a child process), we should make them lower priority in the c-gahp. We already have two worker processes in the c-gahp, one dedicated to stage-in commands. We should use that dedicated worker for stage-out and proxy refresh commands as well. Also, we should limit the number of file transfer commands that we batch into a single request to the remote schedd, so that the worker can come up for air on a regular basis. This is particularly important to the CMS glidein factor at UCSD. They are having problems when their jobs' x509 proxy is refreshed. Pushing the new proxy to the remote schedd could tie up the c-gahp for 40+ minutes. Making the proxy refresh request more efficient is the subject of another ticket (#4693).
remarks: 2020-Oct-13 16:42:16 by tlmiller: Code Review This all looks good to me. You'll need to document the new knobs, in addition to writing a release note; in documenting C_GAHP_MAX_FILE_REQUESTS, it seems like you need to be clear that it limits each different command (kind of file request) individually, to minimize confusion for anyone checking their logs. Maybe something like "When executing low-priority commands, HTCondor will do no more than this value of each command before checking for new high-priority commands. Lowering this number should improve the responsiveness of high-priority commands, at the cost of some throughput."?

title: Ticket #4141: Add support for non-fungible user-defined slot resources
description: Certain kinds of slot resources are not fungable - a specific instance of the resource must be assigned to a specific slot in order to things to work correctly. HTCondor should support this by allowing user defined resources to be enumerated (rather than just having a total number available). By enumerating the resource, HTCondor is instructed to assign specific members of the enumeration when allocating resources of that type. So, for instance to use enumerated GPUs, you would configure MACHINE_RESOURCE_GPU = A, B, C, D This would declare that there are 4 resources of type GPU, and the specific instances have the names A, B, C and D. When resources are divided into slots, slots that are allocated a GPU will also be assigned a specific one. So a slot that was assigned 2 GPUs would not only have the attribute GPU = 2 It would also have AssignedGPU = A,B

title: Ticket #376: remote_ attributes disappearing from Condor-C job ads
description: If a Condor-C job ad contains remote_foo and remote_remote_foo attributes, the ad submitted to the next schedd may not have a remote_foo attribute (which should be copied from remote_remote_foo). This is a bug in how the CondorJob class in the the gridmanager translates the local job ad into an ad for remote submission. The original ad is first copied wholesale to form the new ad. Then, the original ad is searched for remote_* attributes. For each one, a new attribute is inserted in the new ad with the 'remote_' stripped off and the original attribute name is deleted from the new ad. If the original ad has both remote_foo and remote_remote_foo, and remote_remote_foo is found first, then the translated remote_foo will be deleted when remote_foo from the original ad is processed.
remarks: 2009-Apr-13 12:22:09 by jfrey: The solution I'm using is to delete all remote_* attributes from the new ad before translating remote_* attributes from the original ad. 2009-Apr-13 12:27:23 by jfrey: This same code is in INFNBatchJob, but it doesn't delete any remote_* attributes from the new ad. Now it does in the same way as CondorJob.

title: Ticket #7413: GPU attribute improvements
description: Jettison the CUDA runtime version attribute. Add better-named attribute (duplicating DriverVersion) for the max version of the CUDA runtime supported by the driver. Add a submit command, something like but not actually request_cuda_version, which edits the requirements expression appropriately. Talk to ????, our GPU-jobs-on-SLURM friends, to check our assumptions, and see if they have anything useful to say about our proposed solution. Maybe require_cuda_version, or require_at_least_cuda_version?
remarks: 2020-Feb-18 13:37:25 by tlmiller: Implemented points 1 and 2 on master. It seems like we shouldn't release point 3 until we're sure we have a good name for it, so that I pushed off into a branch. 2020-Feb-18 14:09:27 by tlmiller: Currently implemented as "required_cuda_version". Mat suggests "CUDAVersion" (or CUDA_Version, really, I guess), which has the benefit of being nice and simple, as well as descriptive; I wonder if it would be more or less confusing to mention the 'RT' part of what's actually going on, especially considering how we don't want to get into providing the libraries. 2020-Feb-19 15:47:43 by tlmiller: Consensus after polling is "cuda_version": We'd like a submit-file command to deal with CUDAMaxSupportedVersion rather than explain the conversion from the string '8.1' to the integer 8001 (or, worse, why floating-point comparison don't always work). Having a submit-file command will allow us to enforce the convention that the job have attribute which is used in the requirements expression; this allows things like job transforms to be constructed much more easily. If NVidia's drivers ever drop support for older version of the CUDA runtime, we can adjust the constructed requirements expression to match (rather than have the user change their jobs). This point also argues against being specific about which comparison will be used to do match-making. "cuda_version" is nice and short, and although it's maybe a little vague, that's sometimes helpful in these situations; it also sounds more like a description of the job rather than a description of its requirements, which I think is something we want. 2020-Feb-19 15:48:04 by tlmiller: Also, cuda_version should accept both the x.y format and the x000y format. 2020-Apr-10 07:46:37 by tim: Bulk change of target version from v080906 to v080907 using ticket-target-mover.

The user should be able to pass this value to the Condor job of the node, and also to the PRE and POST scripts. 2011-Mar-31 09:07:05 by wenger: I'm also thinking that we should have a config knob for whether the final node is run if DAGMan is condor_rm'ed. 2011-Mar-31 13:01:29 by psilord: I'd rather specify the aforementioned config knob in the job description line for that specific job.... by default it is always run. 2011-Mar-31 13:05:13 by wenger: Another issue is, what if a splice, and the upper-level DAG both have final nodes? But it should be illegal to specify any parent or child relationships for it. Another question is, if everything in the DAG works, except that the final node fails, is the DAG considered failed? My initial thought is that in that case the DAG should be considered failed. On the other hand, if other stuff fails, but the final node succeeds, I think the DAG should probably still be considered failed. 2011-Apr-05 13:46:02 by nwp: This is probably a dumb question, but can a subdag be a final node? 2011-Apr-05 13:59:47 by wenger: Hmm, that's actually kind of an interesting question. Anyhow, my reaction comes from two things: 1) I just kind of don't like the idea of encouraging people to do something too complex for the final node -- especially if they set things up so that the final node will be run on condor_rm of DAGMan. 2) It would be more syntactically complex. title: Ticket #6717: Memory leak when SSL authentication fails
description: When using the SSL authentication method in CEDAR, memory is leaked if a failure occurs during the procedure. Specifically, in Condor_Auth_SSL::authenticate(), several data structures are dynamically allocated at the top of the method and deallocated at the end. If a failure occurs in the middle, the method returns immediately without deallocating the memory. Failures that can trigger this memory leak include the peer having an expired certificate. We observed this in CHTC when the host certificate for annex-cm.chtc.wisc.edu expired.

title: Ticket #7805: starter should set HOME correctly when running docker CLI
description: When the starter runs the docker cli, it generally runs it as the unprivileged "condor" user. It does the by setting the real uid and effective uid to condor, then spawning the appropriate docker program, and inheriting all environment variables from the starter, which come indirectly from whatever started the condor_master. One of these environment variables is $HOME. docker looks in $HOME to find some configuration files. If HOME is set to /root (common if an interactive shell user started condor), docker will complain with a warning that it can't read the file /root/.docker/config, which it can't, as it is running as the non-root condor user. This warning comes back in the docker_stderr file, which confuses users. We want some of the environment to percolate down to the docker cli, for example, the DOCKER_HOST variable tells the docker cli where the server is. So, in this ticket, when we run docker commands, we will set the HOME directory correctly in the docker cli (note -- NONE OF THIS APPLIES TO THE JOB IN THE CONTAINER!) to remove this error.

title: Ticket #3515: Ganglia Integration
description: Within the OSG context, Ganglia is an extremely common monitoring package in use. We should make it straightforward for sysadmins to push the basic statistics HTCondor provides (DaemonCore, Schedd) into Ganglia.
remarks: 2013-Feb-25 12:53:31 by bbockelm: Proof-of-concept is pushed to V7_9-ganglia-branch. Design document to come. 2013-Mar-04 13:59:53 by bbockelm: Design doc attached. There are a few fundamental questions here: Should the monitoring be a hook vs plugin? Should the monitoring be centralized (all within / at the collector) or decentralized? The design doc describes a decentralized, hook-based architecture. There are definite advantages to the approach in terms of maintenance and completeness of the statistics. However, there are disadvantages of not reusing existing work and requiring changes on every node in the pool. 2013-Mar-05 08:42:07 by tstclair: So the typical model we've take here has been plugin and offload. So the plugin's can do anything we desire with the classads and shuffle them off if needed, provided they are non-blocking (which in our cases they are). So forking based on hook is an option, but hooks are only triggered on "events", unless your thinking of some cron approach. Provided your overhead is low, registering a timer in a plugin is a very simple option and works well. 2013-Mar-05 08:42:51 by tstclair: Adding TJ b/c he has expressed interest. 2013-Mar-05 08:48:26 by bbockelm: In the proof-of-concept, the ganglia callouts are based on a cron (DaemonCore Timer, actually) and enabled on each daemon. I'm interested in forking out of paranoia - I'd prefer it if libgmond couldn't crash the daemon itself. libgmond simply sends out a UDP packet, so it's more-or-less non-blocking. 2013-Mar-05 09:01:07 by tstclair: You could still keep your separate daemon, with the plugin simply signaling the process that now is a good time to consume. It also sounds like what you want is the "would be" master-cron which doesn't exist yet. 2013-Mar-05 10:42:29 by johnkn: I don't like the way the genric_stats code "knows" about ganglia in the proof of concept. That level of interconnectedness seems unnecessary to me. Instead the ganglia publish timer should create a classad and call StatsPool.Publish() into the Classad hand that Classad off to a hook/plugin Neither the stats code nor daemon_core should know that the plugin is going to push the stats into ganglia (or anywhere else). The only changes to daemon core/stats should be enough configuration to tell it what stats to publish and what plugin/hook to publish it to. 2013-Apr-02 12:16:42 by danb: I'm interested in seeing the ganglia integration get released. Here is a summary of my understanding of the current state of the prototype: There is no forking. The Ganglia library is explicitly linked into condor daemons. i.e. it's not a hook or a plugin. The ganglia rpm is a prerequisite of the condor rpm. I assume we don't want this to be true in the version of the ganglia integration that gets released. The condor statistics pool knows about the ganglia integration, and the ganglia integration knows about internals of the statistics pool. Some of the latter interdependency is to filter out stuff that isn't needed in ganglia such as histograms and recent values. Only attributes that are in statistics pools are published, because we aren't using the same code path that generates the published daemon ad. As Tim pointed out, there is already a plugin interface that gets called when the daemon ad is published. I can think of two issues with using this for the ganglia integration: The timing of updates to ganglia would be tied to the timing of updates to the collector. It might be nice to control them independently. The set of stats that are published would be tied to the set that is published to the collector. It might be nice to control them independently. Proposal Redo the ganglia integration as a plugin using the existing plugin mechanism for capturing published ads. The plugin would be released in a separate rpm. It may contain some "hacks" to filter out undesired attributes (like recent values) based on patterns in the names of attributes. Similar hacks could be used to set appropriate units such as "Megabytes". Once that is working, think about how to make it more flexible. One idea would be to allow for the configuration of an independent probe with its own timer and verbosity level. It would use the same code path as condor_status -statistics "verbosity" -direct to generate the ad that is passed to the plugin. 2013-Apr-11 12:14:31 by danb: I talked to Todd and Becky about this. They argued for a collector plugin rather than a plugin in each of the individual daemons. This would make it easier to deploy in pools where the execute and submit nodes are not all easily modifiable by the pool administrator. 2013-Apr-11 12:26:06 by johnkn: A plugin in the collector means we have to send statistics values to the collector before we can send them to the plugin. But we don't send most SCHEDD stats values to the collector because the bloat the SCHEDD ad for everyone. So unless we go to the trouble to make a separate ad in the collector for SCHEDD statistics, having the ganglia integration in the collector seems like a bad idea. Or, to put it another way. the ganglia plugin needs to be able to able to have independent control over statistics verbosity level, which is something that you can't get if you put the plugin in the collector. 2013-Apr-11 12:33:23 by danb: Agreed, TJ. Longer term, Todd said he wants to have a separate collector for statistics. 2013-Apr-11 13:42:49 by bbockelm: Hi all, We've been spinning on determining the correct approach here for some time. Can we do a group phone call tomorrow to speed things up? In particular, I'm available tomorrow 9-10 and 11-1 tomorrow. I can send phone details out-of-band to those interested. Brian 2013-Apr-12 11:45:42 by danb: Here's a summary of our conclusions in the meeting about ganglia integration: Phase 0: Becky's scripts that query the collector and push stats to ganglia. Phase 1: Create a new daemon (condor_statd?) that does basically what Becky's scripts do. It could get ads by querying or by having ads forwarded to it by the collector. It should dlopen the ganglia library so as not to create an explicit dependency on ganglia. Phase 2: Add Todd's stat aggregation stuff into condor_statd and have it publish to the new Condor View. (No immediate plans for this, but it's where we imagine things going.) Features of Phase 1 that we prefer over a plugin in the schedd or collector: The ganglia code runs in a separate process. condor_statd is free to query for additional information if it needs to (e.g. a direct query to the schedd at higher verbosity). title: Ticket #2754: File transfer fails for local universe
description: The Pegasus people want file transfer for local universe to work just like it does for vanilla universe. The motivation is that, for Pegasus, they want to be able to change between vanilla and local universe, make no other changes in the submit file, and have things including file-transfers work.
remarks: 2012-Apr-05 11:36:14 by tannenba: Our current plan to have local universe jobs run under a startd running on the same machine as the schedd. In Condor, typically the condor_shadow (shadow) process is responsible for managing a running job. With local universe, there is no shadow process, only a starter that is launched as a child process directly under the schedd - as a result, there are many semantic differences -vs- vanilla universe, including the file transfer issues you are experiencing. So we are thinking of making local universe jobs exactly like vanilla universe jobs, except for the fact that local universe jobs will only be scheduled to run on the same machine where the schedd resides. To accomplish this, we would have a startd running alongside the schedd on the submit machine that would launch local universe jobs. Of course, you could effectively do this today by simply adding a startd to the DAEMON_LIST on your submit machine, and then submitting your local universe jobs as vanilla universe with requirements = Machine == "name.of.your.submit.host" and in the config file have the following to tell the startd to only run your local universe jobs Start = User == "vahi@name.of.your.submit.host" But ultimately we are thinking of making this startd-that-runs-local-universe jobs a first-class citizen, e.g. perhaps the startd would be launched automatically as needed, it would automatically register itself with the local schedd so that no waiting for a negotiation cycle would be required (just like local universe today), etc. Besides helping out with this problem of having the same file transfer semantics, there are other advantages to this approach, such as the additional resource management opportunities the startd can bring to local universe jobs. 2013-May-23 11:23:35 by gthain: dup of #3019

title: Ticket #3846: Round trip per attribute for remote condor_submit
description: CERN testers reported that remote condor_submit had unexpectedly poor performance. Looking into things, it appears remote condor_submit does a ACK after each SetAttribute. We removed this in HTCondor-C; I think it's time to remove this for submits too. CERN reported a 3x performance increase in remote-submits-per-second. Pushed as branch V8_1-submit-no-ack; needs review.
remarks: 2014-Mar-22 21:57:49 by bbockelm: Seems to have gotten lost in the noise. Pinging ticket. 2014-Jun-10 15:43:27 by tannenba: The V8_1-submit-no-ack did not get rid of all the ack round trips, and it also left misleading error messages (without an ack, submit cannot actually tell the user which specific setattribute had a failure because with no ack roundtrip the schedd will simply close the tcp socket which may not be detected right away), so I rewrote the patch. The patch pushed below handles the issues mentioned above. It can also be disabled at runtime via condor_config setting SUBMIT_NOACK_ON_SETATTRIBUTE = False (the default value is True). There is no need to document this knob, end-users should never care to change it. It is just there to aid in any debugging by developers. Failure to parse an attribute expression would be the primary culprit for setattribute to fail. Because condor_submit already checks that input from the user parses before sending anything to the schedd, it is not clear when a setattribute would actually ever fail. Thus there is really no disadvantage to the user of the default of SUBMIT_NOACK_ON_SETATTRIBUTE = True. Note we still check the return code from the schedd on a transaction commit (via DisconnectQ()), so ultimately the return code from condor_submit will still be the same as before the patch. On my own laptop (Windows 7, SSD drive) with a personal condor, before the patch it took 4.02 seconds to submit 200 job clusters (about 15k setattribute calls). After the patch it took 2.97 seconds, or an ~25% improvement even when submitting to a local schedd. Obviously with a remote submit, the improvement would be substantially better. 2014-Jun-11 09:23:26 by johnkn: CODE_REVIEW: code patch and version history both look good!

title: Ticket #4403: Job rank may not always work as documented - autoclustering bug
description: There is a bug in how HTCondor performs autoclustering of job ads. All jobs that get assigned the same AutoClusterID job ad attribute by HTCondor are supposed to be identical for purposes of matchmaking. For background, see the autoclustering design document. In the design document, it states "...the schedd augments the significant attributes received from the negotiator by adding the job’s Requirements and Rank attributes, as well as any job ClassAd attribute that is referenced by the job’s own Requirements or Rank expression." Unfortunately, the autoclustering implementation fails to inspect the job's rank expression. This bug has existed since autoclustering was initially implemented back in the summer of the year 2006! Demonstrating the Problem Here is how I reproduced the issue - just in a personal v8.1.5 HTCondor on my Windows 7 laptop, here is what i added to my condor_config.local : NUM_CPUS = 5 STARTD_EXPRS = $(STARTD_EXPRS) MachineDataSet SLOT1_MachineDataSet = "S00" SLOT2_MachineDataSet = "S01" SLOT3_MachineDataSet = "S02" SLOT4_MachineDataSet = "S03" SLOT5_MachineDataSet = "S04" The above gives my test setup fives slots, were each slots advertises a unique MachineDataSet attribute Next I submitted the following with condor_submit: executable = c:\utils\sleep.exe transfer_executable = false arguments = 6000 # For easy monitoring, take the MachineDataSet attribute from # the slot we match with and add it into # the job classad as attribute MachineAttrMachineDataSet0 job_machine_attrs = MachineDataSet # Prefer slots where MachineDataSet attribute in the slot # is equal to the JobDataSet attribute in the job rank = JobDataSet =?= MachineDataSet # Set JobDataSet to be S00, S01, S02, etc. +JobDataSet = "S0$(Process)" queue 5 And behold, jobs did not match up as expected based on the job rank expression: C:\condor\test>condor_submit lsst.sub Submitting job(s)..... 5 job(s) submitted to cluster 6971. C:\condor\test>condor_q -af ProcId RemoteHost JobDataSet MachineAttrMachineDataSet0 AutoClusterId 0 slot1@ToddsThinkpad S00 S00 44 1 slot5@ToddsThinkpad S01 S04 44 2 slot4@ToddsThinkpad S02 S03 44 3 slot2@ToddsThinkpad S03 S01 44 4 slot3@ToddsThinkpad S04 S02 44 A key thing to note in the above is all the jobs ended up with the same autoclusterid... Immediate Workaround Add a clause to the job requirements expression that will reference all attributes used in the job rank expression; an easy/foolproof way to do this is a clause like requirements = Rank =!= UNDEFINED And indeed, behold that when I add this requirements expression to the submit file above, jobs matched up on slots as expected: C:\condor\test>type lsst.sub executable = c:\utils\sleep.exe transfer_executable = false arguments = 6000 job_machine_attrs = MachineDataSet rank = JobDataSet =?= MachineDataSet requirements = Rank =!= UNDEFINED +JobDataSet = "S0$(Process)" queue 5 C:\condor\test>condor_submit lsst.sub Submitting job(s)..... 5 job(s) submitted to cluster 6972. C:\condor\test>condor_q -af ProcId RemoteHost JobDataSet MachineAttrMachineDataSet0 AutoClusterId 0 slot1@ToddsThinkpad S00 S00 52 1 slot2@ToddsThinkpad S01 S01 53 2 slot3@ToddsThinkpad S02 S02 54 3 slot4@ToddsThinkpad S03 S03 55 4 slot5@ToddsThinkpad S04 S04 56 Note each job is in a different autoclusterid...

title: Ticket #634: Java maxheap initial setting should be correct
description: We've had a problem for a long time: when installing Condor, we try to guess the maximum heap size for Java jobs. When using the Sun JVM on a 32-bit machine with more than 2GB of memory, we select a heap size that is too big and the Java universe doesn't work. There are two workarounds for this: 1) The user can specifically set the heap size 2) The user can clear the option to set the heap size. (But then it might be too small.) I argue that both of these are bad options. By default, the Java universe should work without user intervention. I recently met a Condor user who installs on Windows. He can do distributed installations, but right now he only knows how to customize the installation through the MSI installer and not by automatically editing the configuration files. The MSI installer doesn't have an option to set the Java heap size and his computers are 32-bit with more than 2GB of memory. So by default, Java universe is broken for him. And he uses the Java universe, so this is a pain. Two ideas: 1) We should do a better job of setting the Java universe heap size. We should never set a bad value, that just sucks. 2) We could simply not set the Java universe heap size, and expect users to use "java_vm_args" in their submit files. This would require clear documentation of this change. I don't have a strong opinion between these two options, but I really think we should make one of the choices before we ship Condor 7.4.0. Our install shouldn't result in an unusable Java universe when it's possible to have a usable Java universe.
remarks: 2009-Jul-21 09:34:25 by matt: (2) sounds quite reasonable. This was surely not an issue back in 2002 when Doug first wrote the code, see 25a7c0c3d. 2009-Dec-14 10:29:20 by cweiss: code submitted to branch V7_5-java_Xmx-branch 2010-Feb-23 14:40:02 by matt: Cathrin, please provide an executive summary of how you went about solving the problem, and why. Thanks. It looks like you went to some elaborate measures. 2010-Jun-22 09:24:45 by tannenba: Results from a code review of [16653] - a few items: Important! This patch breaks error propagation for method java_config(). Previously, this methods returned 0 on failure and non-zero on success. In some places, the patch returns -1 on failure - this failure will not be detected by several call sites that still think non-zero means success. Instead of changing all the call sites, I think the patched code should be made consistent to always return 0 on failure. In the patch, max_memory is initialized to 90% of (physical memory / physical num of cores). Why shouldn't max memory be initialized to 90% of the advertised Memory in the machine/slot classad ? IIRC, this ad can be easily fetched from inside the starter by invoking Starter->jic->machClassAd() - if this call returns NULL, then fallback to the patch's current algorithm using physical memory. The patch's handling of JAVA_MAXHEAP_ARGUMENT is weak. I see what you are trying to do [although a comment would be nice ;)], but we can do better than hard-coded logic of "if arg string length is greater than 4 than the user specified an actual head value". Instead, I'd suggest simply scanning the string with isdigit(), and if all the trailing characters are digits than assume the string contains the actual heap size. In java_detect.cpp:76, the while (rc!=0) loop could use a dprintf in the common case that shows iterative tries of new values - currently looks like only dprintfs happen during errors. Since a new job ad attribute was added (JAVA_MAX_HEAP), seems like condor_submit should be patched so users can specify this without neededing to use the "+" operator. And then of course condor_submit man page must be updated. title: Ticket #4950: Consumption policy should disable claim partitionable leftovers
description: Consumption policies (enabled by CONSUMPTION_POLICY) allow the negotiator to make multiple matches to a single partitionable slot. Claim Partitionable Leftovers (enabled by CLAIM_PARTITIONABLE_LEFTOVERS) allows the schedd to make multiple claim requests to a single partitionable slot. If both are enabled for the same partitionable slot, then the negotiator and schedd will conflict in their attempts to efficiently match the slot to multiple jobs. This will waste time, as the slower party to attempt to claim the slot will fail, and will need to search for another match. To avoid this problem, if a slot has Consumption Policies enabled, the startd should not give a claim for the partitionable leftovers to a claiming schedd (essentially disabling CLAIM_PARTITIONABLE_LEFTOVERS for that slot).

title: Ticket #5642: Provide a stop constraint for history queries
description: In CMS, we use the python binding's remote history query functionality to centralize all our job ads. Unfortunately, it's fairly expensive to ask for a subset of the ads. For example, if we want to query for all jobs completed since noon, HTCondor will still parse the last 10,000 jobs by default - even though we know we can stop parsing once we found a single job with completion date prior to noon. Hence, we should add the concept of a "stop expression" to the API. If a parsed ad matches the given expression, do not return it and immediately stop processing. The python API would look something like this: import htcondor sd = htcondor.Schedd() iter = sd.history(requirements='VO=?="CMS"', stop_requirements='CompletionDate < 1460815361') for job in iter: # Do stuff with our wonderful job ads. print job['ClusterId']
remarks: 2016-May-04 16:00:23 by jfrey: The only useful stop requirements I can think of are CompletionDate less than a given value, and job id (cluster and proc) matching a given value. Can you think of any others? If not, wouldn't it be better to support these two cases specifically rather than a general expression? 2016-May-04 16:04:07 by bbockelm: Ah - my original plan was to just hardcode the date (as that's my narrow use case). TJ suggested to turn it into an expression. Can you chat with him on what other items he had in mind? Honestly, given this is a programmatic-only interface, I would lean toward the more generic. 2016-Jun-01 17:09:37 by johnkn: We should do this by enhancing condor_history to that it has a stop condition, and also so that it knows how to write into a socket. Then change the schedd to just use condor_history as the history helper application. I propose adding the following arguments to condor_history -since-job <job.id> stops when this job is seen and does not return it. -sock <inherited-socket-info> act as a history helper, writing into the given sock. -since-job is the only way to do perfect periodic updates without ever risking missing a job or reading the same job twice. We might also want to have a bit of cleverness in the argument parsing and support this. -since <time>|<job.id>|<expr> where the argument is parsed as a classad expression, and if the result is an int literal, treat that as a time, if it's a float literal, treat that as a job id, and if it's anything else, treat it as an expression. We might also have a special case here for delta times, eg. 2hr, 1day, 1week, etc. On the reading side, we could look at the attribute references for the -since expression, and if it looks only at cluster, proc, completiondate and/or owner, we could skip parsing the job ad entirely and just evaluate the stop expression against those 4 bits of information. 2016-Jun-06 14:41:03 by johnkn: commit [48496] adds -since and -completed since to condor_history. also -scanlimit, -inherit and -attributes arguments. title: Ticket #7385: Wrong CUDA runtime library name on Linux
description: In #6883, we switched from getting version information from the runtime library to getting this from the driver itself. That works fine and well for driver information we gather - but the runtime information from the cudaGetRuntimeVersion symbol is not in the driver. Hence, the code falls back to querying a runtime library named libnvcuda.so. To the best of my digging via Google, that library name has never existed on Linux (there is an equivalent nvcuda.dll on Linux?) and the name of the runtime library should be libcudart.so. Prior to the patch in #6883, we pulled the symbol from that library (although fell back to libnvcuda.so); you can see this on the V8_6-branch for reference. If I manually copy libcudart.so and rename it libnvcuda.so, then condor_gpu_discovery properly sets CUDARuntimeVersion.
remarks: 2019-Nov-18 11:58:29 by bbockelm: Edit: Had the prior ticket reference incorrect in the original description of the ticket. It is now the correct #6883 and not #4339. 2019-Nov-18 12:00:14 by johnkn: libcudart.co is also the wrong name, although it was right for cuda 8.0 (or maybe 7.0? i'm not sure when it stopped being a thing) The fallback codepath using libnvcuda.so was always wrong on Linux, but it used to be unreachable because we used to use libcudart.so for all detection. In current versions of CUDA however (9 and 10?), there is no name we can use for the runtime library. you have to know the runtime version to find the library. So we switched to using the driver library for detection. The problem here is that Nvidia gave up on backward compatibility at the runtime layer. They have backward compatibility only at the driver layer - thus there is no libcudart.so for cuda9 or cuda10. The driver does tell us the highest supported runtime version, although it calls this the DriverVersion, and we report it by that name. (the actual driver version cannot be queried as far as I can tell) 2019-Nov-18 12:21:08 by bbockelm: > libcudart.co is also the wrong name, although it was right for cuda 8.0 (or maybe 7.0? i'm not sure when it stopped being a thing) I'm not sure I'm following this. On Linux, if you install CUDA-10.1, then libcudart.so is installed as well and is available to the linker in a default environment (that is, no LD_LIBRARY_PATH set -- thanks to ld.so.cache). Further, it identifies itself correctly as 10.10. Now, that said, this is only a minimally useful attribute as it simply tells you one CUDA runtime version that is installed on the host. Arguably, one would want to know all CUDA versions if you want to use this in matchmaking! 2019-Nov-18 15:59:43 by johnkn: For reference in this discussion: condor_gpu_discovery currently uses libcuda.so, which is the CUDA driver API by default. Only if that does not load, or if the -rl command line option is used does it try to load libcudart.so. When libcuda.so does load successfully, there is currently a bug where we never load the runtime library to get its version number on non-Windows platforms, even if that library does exist (which it probably will not) When gpu discovery loads the driver library, it uses cuDriverGetVersion to get the the attribute it publishes as CUDADriverVersion. In older versions of the API docs this was described as the "driver version", but in fact it is not that and never has been. Newer versions of the docs indicate (correctly) that it is the highest supported runtime version for that driver API. 2019-Nov-18 16:02:48 by johnkn: > On Linux, if you install CUDA-10.1, then libcudart.so is installed as well and is available to the linker in a default environment (that is, no LD_LIBRARY_PATH set -- thanks to ld.so.cache). Further, it identifies itself correctly as 10.10. If that were true, then we have not received bug reports about GPU detection failing and switched to using the driver API instead. I'm not sure what the condition is, but it is not guaranteed that you get a libcudart.so when you install the CUDA runtime.

title: Ticket #6982: Oddities in job event logging evictions
description: Josh reports that evicting jobs via the Python wrapper does not (always?) result in a job log eviction event. My analysis follows: actOnJobs( JA_VACATE_JOBS ) in the schedd eventually calls abort_job_myself( JA_VACATE_JOBS ), which calls daemonCore->Send_Signal_nonblocking() with a DCShadowKillMsg constructed from the shadow's PID and the SIGTERM constant. This will (eventually) calls kill() with the same pair of arguments. When the shadow receives a SIGTERM, daemon core redirects it to main_shutdown_graceful(), which calls gracefulShutDown(). This function has two problems: (1) If the job lease has any time remaining, the shadow will immediately exit (without killing the starter and without writing to the job event log). It appears that the job lease duration variable is only set while we're attempting to reconnect, so I guess the thinking here is that if the shadow is going away and it hasn't reconnected yet, it's OK to let the starter die of old age. (2) Otherwise, the shadow attempts to deactivate (and maybe release) the claim... without writing to the job event log. TJ and I speculate that much of this handling was written for the case where the schedd is shutting down for an upgrade, and that we didn't want to log events (like the shadow exiting and restarting) that were implementation details, and the eviction case got lost in the wash. TODO: (1) Reproduce the problem with small test case. (2) It seems like we should log an event when the user evicts a job; otherwise, the log has the job being started twice before exiting once. Can we reliably distinguish this case from other SIGTERMs? Should we write some sort of ambiguous job event instead of nothing?

title: Ticket #4815: ace leak in Starter when USE_VISIBLE_DESKTOP is true
description: Via RUST, a customer reports: We've been experiencing a problem where after "some time" we start seeing the message: Create_Process: Unable to use visible desktop In our StarterLog.slotN files. The process is created, but not on the "visible desktop". This causes the application that we are running to fail since it needs to be associated with the desktop. It turns out that it takes about 2300 condor_starter.exe invocations after a reboot for this to occur. I've downloaded condor source, built it and added additional debugging output in order to track down the problem. I found the problem in condor_utils\access_desktop.WINDOWS.cpp. The last function in the file is RemoveTheAceDesktop(HDESK hdesk, PSID psid) which includes a call to AddAccessAllowedAce. Well, this is the very Ace it is meaning to remove! The loop above the call copies all the other ACEs skipping the one added by AddTheAceDesktop; this call then adds it back in! It looks like a simple copy/paste error from AddTheAceDesktop since most of the code is nearly identical. The simple fix is to remove the call to AddAccessAllowedAce from RemoveTheAceDesktop. This seems to affect only condor_starter since that is the only call to RevokeDesktopAccess which is the only call to RemoveTheAceDesktop. This causes me a little concern since GrantDesktopAccess is called from the daemon_core code which is I think used by all daemons, but only if USE_VISIBLE_DESKTOP is set.

title: Ticket #771: Schedd updates in gridmanager causes extra load
description: In the gridmanager, whenever changes to job ad are pushed to the schedd, the relevant job object is notified after the push completes. The job object may be waiting for the push to finish before performing certain operations (such as waiting for a job id to be saved before finishing a submission to a remote system). But there are many changes to the job ad for which the job object isn't waiting. When there are 10,000s of of jobs, unnecessary signaling of the job objects can cause a lot of load. For gt2 jobs, each new grid monitor status report causes LastRemoteStatusUpdate to be changed in all related jobs submitted. These reports arrive every couple minutes, resulting in many schedd updates and signaling of job objects. When a job ad change needs to be pushed to the schedd, the caller needs to identify whether job object is waiting for the push to complete. If it's not waiting, then it doesn't need to be signaled.

title: Ticket #1314: matches in M_STARTD_CONTACT_LIMBO are not removed as soon as desired
description: When all jobs that could have run on a match have been removed and that match is still waiting for the response to REQUEST_CLAIM (i.e. the match is in M_STARTD_CONTACT_LIMBO), the schedd holds onto the match until the startd responds. It would be better to remove the match, which would cancel the REQUEST_CLAIM operation, allowing the startd to back out of retirement if it is in retirement, or at least allowing it to offer the slot to someone else.
remarks: 2010-Oct-20 16:03:30 by jfrey: Bulk change of target version from v070504 to v070505 using ./ticket-target-mover. 2011-Jan-27 14:46:04 by danb: Bulk change of target version from v070505 to v070506 using ./ticket-target-mover. 2011-Feb-01 16:01:00 by tannenba: Bulk change of target version from v070506 to NULL using ./ticket-target-mover. 2011-Jul-11 14:47:45 by danb: I fixed this for the non-dedicated scheduler case, which is the case that originally spawned this ticket. The dedicated scheduler is a very different case, because the scheduler may want to hold onto the claim even if no existing job can immediately make use of it. In general, the dedicated scheduler has not been optimized to quickly yield unneeded claims, not just in this case but in others as well. Therefore, I think we should consider this problem closed, without attempting an optimization to the dedicated scheduler for job removal during startd contact limbo.

title: Ticket #1181: 32-bit procapi (procd) fails to see some processes on 64-bit systems
description: When condor is compiled 32-bit, procapi cannot see entries in /proc when those entries happen to have inodes that do not fit in the 32-bit ino_t. This is because readdir() skips over such entries. We found two possible workarounds. One is to use readdir64(). The other is to use glob(), which probably internally uses readdir64(). The former seems the better choice, since it is a smaller code change and more explicitly addresses the problem. The environment in which we happened to notice this had /proc/sys/kernel/pid_max set to a big number (4 million) rather than the default 32768. This led us to believe that the problem had something to do with large PID values. However, we do not know of any reason why small PIDs would be protected from having 64-bit ino values. The failure mode we observed is that if the procd does not see its own parent PID, then it exits immediately with the message "ERROR: master has exited". This caused condor to accept jobs but to fail when trying to launch the starter. The environment where this problem was observed: SL5.3 x86_64 system with kernel 2.6.18-164.9.1.el5.

title: Ticket #4679: Make SpoolOnEvict more useful
description: Hm - it looks like #4292 was less useful than we had originally envisioned. While the patch does work, it doesn't work in the case we had targeted - periodic_remove. So "condor_vacate_job" will bring back the output we want; "condor_rm" or running afoul one of the "periodic_remove" expressions will not. title: Ticket #3446: DEFAULT_PRIO_FACTOR should be much higher
description: I think we shouldn't have the default value of DEFAULT_PRIO_FACTOR the same as the minimum priority factor, because then there's no way you can give a user a better priority than the default. A support user just ran into a case where they wanted to give a few of their users higher priority -- but instead of decreasing the priority factor for those users, they have to increase the priority factor for all their other users, plus set a new, higher values of DEFAULT_PRIO_FACTOR in case any new users come along. If the default for DEFAULT_PRIO_FACTOR had been, say, 1000, all they would have had to do was set a new priority factor for the few "special" users. I guess the main argument I can see against this is that, for people upgrading existing HTCondor installations, things could get mixed up between existing and new users. I guess one way to deal with that would be to put "DEFAULT_PRIO_FACTOR = 1000" into the config files, along with some explanation -- I assume that most people pretty much keep their existing config files when they upgrade.
remarks: 2013-Jan-16 17:33:38 by wenger: Hmm, now that I think about it, a better fix would be to just allow fractional priority factors. I don't know enough about how things work internally to know if that would be a big problem in terms of implementation. One possibility would be to just internally multiply the priority factors by 1000, say, and allow 0.001 as the minimum. (Although it would clearly be less confusing to simply allow fractions, if that isn't too hard to implement.) 2018-Sep-21 10:45:19 by jfrey: The default user priority factor was changed to 1000 in #4282.

title: Ticket #6214: Have option to not run POST script if node job fails?
description: On htcondor-users today, someone requested a way to not run a POST script if their node job fails, and have DAGMan consider the overall node failed. This seems like a fairly reasonable request, and not too hard to do. My initial thought is that it should be a DAG command rather than another config knob, especially since we now have the "ALL_NODES" option. We could have something like this: NO_POST_ON_FAIL <node name> or RUN_POST_ON_FAIL <node name> true|false (I don't know if I like those command names, but you get the idea...)
remarks: 2017-Apr-05 09:16:37 by wenger: On the other hand, doing this in configuration would make it easier to do it across splices or sub-DAGs with a single command... I guess we should think about which way is better (I don't want to do both!). 2017-May-01 11:31:00 by coatsworth: I've checked in an update. Code is in the following branch waiting for review: remotes/origin/V8_7-gt6214-no-post-on-fail I decided to take the NO_POST_ON_FAIL approach because I think it's intuitive. This commit includes a full implementation and a couple simple tests. 2017-May-23 14:25:51 by wenger: CODE REVIEW There's a problem with the NO_POST_ON_FAIL code in that it short-circuits node retries, which it should not do. I think that you can just change if ( failed && job->_scriptPost == NULL ) { to if ( failed && ( job->_scriptPost == NULL || job->GetNoPostOnFail() ) ) { and eliminate the whole new block of code below that. The job_dagman_no_post_on_fail test needs to be added to Test_Requirements; after that you should be able to do a build/test on all platforms. You should be sure to check whether the test works on Windows. The version history item links to the wrong gittrac ticket. NO_POST_ON_FAIL should have the \MacroNI{...} format in the version history. Comments in job_dagman_no_post_on_fail.run refer to PRE_SKIP -- I assume you copied the .run file and forgot to change the comment. I wonder if it might be worthwhile to have the syntax of the command be something like: NO_POST_ON_FAIL true|false <node_name>|ALL_NODES then a user could do something like NO_POST_ON_FAIL true ALL_NODES NO_POST_ON FAIL false nodeX if they wanted to skip the post script on failure for all but one node. This would also be good if we ever decide to make not running the POST script on failure the default in the future. 2017-May-31 15:34:15 by coatsworth: I've fixed the code problem, fixed the errors in the version history, and updated the comments in the test code. The one thing I didn't do is implement the true|false value selection. I found this to be really confusing, on top of the fact that NO_POST_ON_FAIL is already confusing. If people ask for it I'll implement at a later date.

title: Ticket #3016: blahp canceling of completed job causes a failure
description: I managed to screwup a proxy, which caused the gridmanager to attempt to cancel the job after a failed renewal. The job had already completed before the cancellation was attempted. In such a case, qdel has the following output: Request invalid for state of job MSG=invalid state for job - COMPLETE 19.brian-test.unl.edu This causes the job to go on hold; see below. I propose the gridmanager should either screen-scrape this particular error message or check the status after a failed cancel. [bbockelm@brian-test ~]$ condor_q -held -- Submitter: brian-test.unl.edu : <129.93.239.174:45320> : brian-test.unl.edu ID OWNER HELD_SINCE HOLD_REASON [... removing other jobs ...] 25246.0 bbockelm 5/29 09:02 qdel: Request invalid for state of job MSG=invalid state for job - COMPLETE 19.brian-test.unl.edu 5 jobs; 0 completed, 0 removed, 0 idle, 0 running, 5 held, 0 suspended
remarks: 2012-Jun-28 16:51:43 by jfrey: Another possibility is to have the blahp's pbs_cancel.sh script detect the error message and report a successful removal. 2012-Jul-03 15:25:06 by tannenba: Also important for Bosco work.
attachments: pbs_qdel.patch 808 bytes added by jfrey on 2012-Jun-28 22:02:44 UTC. Patch to blahp's pbs_cancel.sh that treats qdel errors about completed and non-existent jobs as successes.

These failures should be treated as a success. (By Jaime Frey )

title: Ticket #7055: overly large parallel jobs disrupt the SchedD
description: If a user "accidentally" queues a parallel universe jobs with a large number of machines, the schedd suffers. We should prevent that from happening. I propose a knob along the lines of "PARALLEL_UNIVERSE_MAX_SIZE" and param-table default it to 1024. Submit should fail if over the limit, but the admin can adjust it upward if needed.
remarks: 2019-May-17 14:35:30 by gthain: I've pushed code that just prevents attempting to schedule any parallel job that requests more cpus than exist in the pool. No new knobs! 2019-May-17 14:50:45 by zmiller: Even better. Down with knobs! Plus then in approximately 12 years when a 2,222,226 node pool is as common as an 8,680 node pool is today, we'll be in good shape! :) 2019-Jun-19 14:04:53 by zmiller: CODE REVIEW: Spoke with Greg about a possible off-by-one error when counting p-slots. Greg will take another look to see if it's a problem.

title: Ticket #5068: Multiple keys for the remote_gahp
description: Currently, we can only use a single SSH pubkey with remote_gahp. This is a fairly annoying limitation. Here's a proposal to allow multiple keys: For remote_gahp, change the default hashing function so a unique remote_gahp is started per-user per-key (where the pubkey is specified as a job attribute). When the remote_gahp is started, it will preferentially use the pubkey specified in the job attribute (defaulting to the current one). This should preserve backward compatibility while allowing a per-job key to be specified. Thoughts?
creator: bbockelm

title: Ticket #5592: Application-level vanilla universe checkpointing needs attr, reqs.
description: In a mixed-version pool, a job trying to use the experimental support for application-level vanilla universe checkpointing might run on a version which doesn't have that support and not really run at all as it was intended. We need to add a startd attribute (HasALCVU?) and an automatically-inserted requirement for it, if condor_submit detects any of the ALCVU-specific attributes.
creator: tlmiller

title: Ticket #7405: document security implications of condor_chirp
description: We would like a clear understanding of the security issues relating to use of chirp for job classad updates and/or file xfer between the submit and execute hosts.
remarks: 2019-Dec-03 13:42:38 by gthain: Today, if a job has access to chirp, it can read and write any file on the submitting machine as the submitting user. That is, if anyone on the execute machine steals the chirp token (which is in a file), they can read an write any file on the submit machine as the user. We have talked about ways to limit this to a particular directory tree or the submitting directory, but have not implemented this. 2019-Dec-03 22:19:33 by pfc: Help me understand how many of these vulnerabilities exist anyway in a hypothetically compromised execute machine (sans Chirp), given the attacker's ability to communicate with the shadow (and maybe schedd) using the starter's stolen credentials. Does Chirp really add new vulnerabilities, or just make them easier to exploit? 2019-Dec-03 22:26:27 by pfc: And in another direction, how much work (i.e., days, weeks, or months) would it be to add the directory constraint you mention above -- and would that fully address the Chirp-specific vulnerability? 2019-Dec-17 11:22:47 by gthain: If chirp is off, then the shadow blocks these requests, so it is a bit of a new vulnerability. Implementing a fix is a couple days work. 2020-Mar-10 10:10:42 by pfc: Closing since Greg T. says #7482 is the only security issue we need to worry about.

title: Ticket #3850: condor should publish live job i/o statistics
description: Modern linux kernels accurately track the total io (read_bytes and write_bytes) of a process, as documented here: http://git.kernel.org/cgit/linux/kernel/git/torvalds/linux.git/tree/Documentation/filesystems/proc.txt?id=HEAD#n1491 It would be nice if Condor updated and published this data for each job periodically. E.g., I want to know the i/o rate (e.g., KB/s over the last 60s) for each job, so I can identify i/o-heavy jobs in my pool -- or maybe for longer periods like 1h, stuck jobs. I am simulating this now with a very very hacky startd cron script which scrapes the process table to identify all condor_starters, then scrapes their command-line arguments to associate each one with its slotid, then identifies each starter's children, and then runs pidstat (which just looks in /proc/pid/io) on each child, and then sums the info and stuff it into a slotid_ prefixed machine ad attribute. But this is ugly and doesn't get saved into the job's history.
remarks: 2013-Aug-12 21:53:38 by bbockelm: To chime in - This should be a fairly straightforward improvement. We already have the attributes defined from the cgroups work; we just need to read in the statistics in a different way. Would be about 6 hours of work for someone interested in learning the procd code. 2013-Nov-04 16:53:37 by eje: Something that operates similar to ImageSize today, but that records ClassAds maybe something like: JobBytesRead JobBytesWritten JobReadSysCalls JobWriteSysCalls ...and ideally also... JobReadOpsPerSecond JobWriteOpsPerSecond Where you could develop throttling policies at a DAGMan management level around concurrency limiting or potentially evicting jobs based on stats like number-of-jobs * writes-per-second. 2014-Mar-07 12:50:25 by eje: An observation about tracking rate information: this information is compiled by the starter, which updates at a default frequency of 5 min, and then passes through the shadow, whose default update rate is 15 minutes. This double-layered latency, combined with large-ish default update intervals, has a possible impact on semantics for rate info. To wit: it doesn't mean much to compile rates over last 60 seconds, unless you (re)configure startd update interval to <= 60s. And all stat updates to the wider universe are subsequently rate limited by the shadow's update interval. My current plan is to define rates as being "change in reported cgroup i/o metrics since last update, divided by the seconds since last update." A possible alternative is to use the stats lib, however imo that seems somewhat heavy-weight for rate stats where sampling resolution is limited by typical update times in the >= minute range. 2014-Mar-07 18:22:00 by eje: topic branch on V8_1-gt3850-job-io-stats 2014-Mar-09 10:41:14 by eje: Actually, some notion of 'recent' i/o activity is probably useful, which would warrant stats lib support. 2014-Mar-17 11:49:02 by eje: proposed attributes are: BlockReadKbytes # these 1st two already exist BlockWriteKbytes BlockReads BlockWrites The above are maintained via the generic_stats lib, and so analogous to the scheduler stats, you can also turn on: RecentBlockReadKbytes RecentBlockWriteKbytes RecentBlockReads RecentBlockWrites Also like the schedd, the 'recent' windowing is controlled by: STATISTICS_WINDOW_SECONDS_STARTER = 60 STATISTICS_WINDOW_QUANTUM_STARTER = 15 I think this would also work: STARTER.STATISTICS_WINDOW_SECONDS STARTER.STATISTICS_WINDOW_QUANTUM There will be no direct 'rate attributes'. To get reads/sec or bytes/sec, the user can divide 'Recent*' by RecentWindowMaxStarter The following may be advertised if configured: StatsLastUpdateTimeStarter StatsLifetimeStarter RecentStatsLifetimeStarter RecentWindowMaxStarter RecentStatsTickTimeStarter turning "all of the above" on happens by configuring: STATISTICS_TO_PUBLISH = STARTER:2ALL 2014-Mar-17 11:51:53 by eje: See also: #4259 2014-Mar-17 18:24:23 by eje: I've been discussing file i/o with customer in the background. They've got a definite interest in tracking NFS related i/o, which is also not covered by the blkio controller. Traversing /proc/<pid>/io to obtain /proc's version of io stats and advertise those is a reasonable option. That's a bit more work, and has the problem of being able to miss process sub-trees that fall between sampling intervals, but it can serve as a complementary source of i/o stats. If we did that, it might be useful to make it optional. Maybe 'verbose-only', or something like it. Might also deserve its own separate ticket. 2014-Mar-19 17:44:57 by johnkn: CODE_REVIEW: partial. I'm still looking, but one thing I see is that I think m_previous_usage isn't needed in vanilla_proc.cpp. The stats_entry_recent<> template has a class override for += which you are currently using. but it also has an override for = which I think you should be using. have a look at generic_stats.h line 926. the stats_entry_recent<> will let you just set the absolute value and it will calculate the recent change in value automatically. Also, I think if you stored BlockReadBytes instead of KBytes, an int64_t would be plenty big enough and you would never need to worry about error accumulation. This would be better than using double because doubles have their own form of error accumulation once the base value you are adding to gets large, a double will begin to accumulate error sooner than an int64_t would. 2014-Mar-20 15:09:40 by eje: I excised the m_previous_usage since it's redundant, just used '=' instead of '+=' Consensus to keep BlockReadKbytes and BlockWriteKbytes as-is, on the grounds of preserving legacy behavior. 2014-Mar-21 13:07:27 by johnkn: I don't see a commit for this change? It occurred to me that we could track bytes in the statistics using int64_t, but set the publication level of those longs to IF_VERBOSEPUB and the publish name BlockReadBytes. Then add code to ..Stats::Publish class to generate the Kbytes values ... Pool.Publish(ad, flags); if ((flags & IF_PUBLEVEL) > 0) { ad.Assign("BlockReadKBytes", this->BlockReadBytes.value / 1024); ad.Assign("RecentBlockReadKBytes", this->BlockReadBytes.recent / 1024); } 2014-Mar-21 16:28:02 by johnkn: CODE_REVIEW: stats stuff looks good to me. I'm not qualified to judge the cgroups code, so I'm transferring this ticket to gthain. 2014-Mar-25 15:10:37 by gthain: CODE REVIEW cgroup block I/O looks good to me. 2014-Mar-30 13:08:54 by eje: In my downstream testing, the publication of the new BlockReadBytes and BlockWriteBytes was getting corrupted by downcasting to 4-byte integer somewhere in the path from the Starter to the Job ads in the scheduler. Downstream I changed the publication flags of those to IF_NEVER, as the "KBytes" versions stay small enough to work at larger i/o values. I haven't yet tested whether this same problem happens on the newer 8.1 code.

title: Ticket #7540: Rename TOKENS to IDTOKENS
description: In discussions with Miron, he suggested the name of the TOKEN auth method is confusing. Why? There's a second method called SCITOKENS. It is not immediately clear the difference between TOKEN and SCITOKENS. SCITOKENS is plural while TOKEN is singular. Miron's input is that, given TOKEN auth provides an identity, we should call these IDTOKENS. As we already have many configs saying TOKEN, we should just add an alias mapping the word IDTOKENS to TOKEN at the configuration file level instead of changing the wire protocol. Also fixing confusion about singular or plural, we end up with the following mappings from user-provided name to internal name: TOKENS -> TOKEN TOKEN -> TOKEN IDTOKENS -> TOKEN IDTOKEN -> TOKEN SCITOKENS -> SCITOKENS SCITOKEN -> SCITOKENS The preferred names we put into the documentation will be IDTOKENS and SCITOKENS.

title: Ticket #5654: Implement "shadow" DAGMan
description: As per discussion today with Miron: have the capability to have a "shadow" DAGMan that reads the jobstate.log file produced by the "real" DAGMan running a given workflow. The shadow DAGMan should maintain the same internal state as the "real" DAGMan, so that eventually we can query the shadow DAGMan instead of having to query the real DAGMan. My initial thoughts on this: Have something like a -shadow flag to condor_submit_dag and condor_dagman that puts DAGMan into shadow mode. I think we can get most of what we need with recovery mode -- the shadow DAGMan would have to permanently stay in recovery mode, instead of switching into "normal" mode, so it doesn't start submitting jobs. The shadow DAGMan would have to ignore lock files. We would need to write a jobstate.log parser, which should be pretty easy because the format is so simple. My thought is that the parser should probably emit ULogEvent objects, to integrate as easily as possible into the existing DAGMan code. One question is what to do about things in the jobstate.log that don't correspond to existing events -- like starting and ending recovery mode. I guess if we need to deal with those things in the shadow, we could use ULOG_GENERIC events. I think we could do a lot of the initial implementation with the shadow DAGMan reading the regular workflow log, and then write the jobstate.log parser and substitute that for the "regular" log file parser. Make sure the shadow DAGMan can deal with restarts of both itself and the "real" DAGMan. The shadow DAGMan should not write a node status file or jobstate.log file, even if these files are specified in the DAG.

title: Ticket #7669: Add configuration template to generate a secure personal condor
description: It seems like the existing use ROLE: PERSONAL doesn't quite generate the right security configuration for an out-of-the-box-secure personal condor. In particular, it does things like set ALLOW_ADMINISTRATOR to $(authuser)@$(CONDOR_HOST), but doesn't set CONDOR_HOST, so it's very easy for someone who doesn't know anything (like me) to set CONDOR_HOST to a bad value (or just not set it at all) and be confused. There is probably some right combination of existing roles to make this work correctly, but it should be easier than it is: a single macro that just does the right thing. At the very least, we should settle on a correct, uniform group of settings that should work on most systems and document them in the manual. An extra layer of complexity here is that I'd like to use this macro to set up a personal condor with a new config file on a system that has a bare HTCondor install on it, with a default existing system condor_config file that I need to inherit from (by running condor_config_val -write:up or condor_config_val -summary). So this macro should be able to "overlay" on an existing config using the default use SECURITY: HOST_BASED. If someone is feeling brave: the reason I need to inherit the system config like this is because there are platform-specific config macros I need, namely the kind of things in this block: RELEASE_DIR = /usr LIB = $(RELEASE_DIR)/lib/condor INCLUDE = $(RELEASE_DIR)/include/condor LIBEXEC = $(RELEASE_DIR)/lib/condor/libexec SHARE = $(RELEASE_DIR)/share/condor MAIL = /usr/bin/mail AUTH_SSL_SERVER_CAFILE = /etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt AUTH_SSL_CLIENT_CAFILE = /etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt AUTH_SSL_SERVER_CERTFILE = /etc/ssl/certs/localhost.crt AUTH_SSL_SERVER_KEYFILE = /etc/ssl/private/localhost.key ... so if I didn't need to do that, we wouldn't need the overlay behavior.

title: Ticket #5204: Make processing of periodic exprs in schedd more efficient
description: The handling of Periodic expression evaluations in the SCHEDD can use a significant amount of time. It can be 5 seconds or so each time the queue is walked to check expressions even if all most of the expressions are trivial and false and none of them fire. This slowness is because the code that actually does the evaluation isn't careful about how many attributes are fetched for each job. Because trivial Expr=false expressions are inserted into the job ad and thus cannot be quickly skipped, and because the system periodic expressions are repeatedly param'd and parsed. two of these things can be easily fixed, and should help the CERN schedd deal with 100's of thousands of jobs.

title: Ticket #7239: support for more usable selection+binding of GPU devices by user
description: Users want to be able to require a specific GPU model. For Nvidia GPUs, Currently that information is published in the CUDADeviceName attribute for single-GPU machines, however for multi-GPU machines it's published in CUDA1DeviceName, CUDA2DeviceName, CUDA3DeviceName, etc. So users must cobble together something like: Requirements = (CUDADeviceName == "Tesla K10.G2.8GB" || CUDA1DeviceName == "Tesla K10.G2.8GB" || CUDA2DeviceName == "Tesla K10.G2.8GB" || CUDA3DeviceName == "Tesla K10.G2.8GB") Condor should support a better attribute scheme that enables users to select specific GPU models without all this... workaround - multiple p-slots If Multiple p-slots are configured, such that each p-slot contains only one type of GPU, then the job's requirements can be use to select the slot with the GPU that is needed without a lot of complexity in the job. This could be something like Assume that the machine has 4 GPUs like this partial output of condor_gpu_discovery DetectedGPUs="CUDA0, CUDA1, CUDA2, CUDA3" CUDA0DeviceName = "Tesla K10.G2.8GB" CUDA1DeviceName = "Tesla K10.G2.8GB" CUDA2DeviceName = "TITAN RTX" CUDA3DeviceName = "TITAN RTX" The 4 gpus can be split into 2 p-slots, each with 2 gpus like this configuration fragment # configure SLOT_TYPE_1 with 70% of resources and the first 2 gpus use Feature:PartitionableSlot(1,70%, Gpus=2) # configure SLOT_TYPE_2 with 30% of resources and the second 2 gpus use Feature:PartitionableSlot(2,30%, Gpus=2) # advertise CUDADeviceName in each p-slot using the name of the first gpu in that slot STARTD_ATTRS = $(STARTD_ATTRS) CUDADeviceName SLOT_TYPE_1_CUDADeviceName = CUDA0DeviceName SLOT_TYPE_2_CUDADeviceName = CUDA2DeviceName Since GPUs are assigned to slots in order, we know that the first 2 GPUs, which are both DeviceName "Tesla K10.G2.8GB" will be assign to the first p-slot. If the output of condor_gpu_discovery indicates that the devices are interleaved (CUDA0 and CUDA2 have the same device name) then a wrapper script around condor_gpu_discovery is needed that re-arranges the order of devices in DetectedGPUS. This wrapper script also also need to oversubscribe GPUs, so LIGO very likely already has a wrapper script. This wrapper can be made simpler and more robust by making use of stable GPU ids, which are introduced in 8.9.8, see #7696

title: Ticket #6582: ReadUserLog class fails to detect file overwrites
description: The ReadUserLog class is responsible for tracking log files and retrieving information from them. This is used by DAGMan to track the .nodes.log file which coordinates DAG events with the schedd. ReadUserLog uses a file descriptor to reference whichever file it is tracking. If that file gets overwritten, however, the file descriptor continues pointing to the old file (which doesn't actually get deleted until the last handle is closed). So we never notice that the file has been overwritten or its size has changed. We need to find a reliable method to detect file overwrites. I'm not sure what that looks like at the moment, will update this ticket later. If anybody has suggestions I'd love to hear them!
remarks: We can detect file overwrites by looking at the number of hard links on the open file descriptor. There should be exactly one link (the file itself) to the open descriptor; if the file gets erased or overwritten, this number drops to 0. 2018-Mar-12 16:53:22 by zmiller: CODE REVIEW: Looks good.

title: Ticket #6078: Fix recovery of GCE jobs after failure during submission
description: Recovery of a Google Compute Engine (GCE) job after a failure during submission is flawed. When the GridJobId job attribute contains the HTCondor-assigned name for the job but not the GCE-assigned id, the gridmanager retries the submission to GCE. This assumes that a second submission of an instance with the same client-chosen name will return the id from the first submission. This is true for EC2, but not GCE. With the latter, the second submission will fail. The fix is to do a query of all instances and look for one with a matching HTCondor-assigned name. The gridmanager always does this if the job status is Removed. It should do so regardless of the job status.

title: Ticket #2892: Shadow, spool_version file approach don't work with multi-schedd setup
description: I've run in to an issue with the condor_shadow, spool_version file and a multi-schedd setup. My shadows are failing to run with the error: 03/15/12 11:00:55 ERROR "According to /mnt/condor_data/spool/spool_version, the SPOOL directory is written in spool version 0, but I only support versions back to 1. " at line 67 in file /home/condor/execute/dir_2782/userdir/src/condor_utils/spool_version.cpp The condor_config file is vanilla from 7.6.6 save for RELEASE_DIR and LOCAL_DIR being set to my specific locations. The condor_config.local file looks as such: DAEMON_LIST = MASTER MASTER.USE_PROCD = True SHADOW_LOG = $(LOG)/ShadowLog.$(PID) # Define the first SCHEDD on this machine SCHEDD1 = $(SCHEDD) SCHEDD1_ARGS = -f -local-name Q1 SCHEDD1_LOG = $(LOG)/ScheddLog.1 SCHEDD1_SPOOL = $(SPOOL)/1 SCHEDD.Q1.SCHEDD_NAME = Q1@$(HOSTNAME) SCHEDD.Q1.SPOOL = $(SCHEDD1_SPOOL) SCHEDD.Q1.SCHEDD_LOG = $(SCHEDD1_LOG) SCHEDD.Q1.SCHEDD_ADDRESS_FILE = $(SCHEDD1_SPOOL)/.schedd_address SCHEDD.Q1.SCHEDD_DAEMON_AD_FILE = $(SCHEDD1_SPOOL)/.schedd_classad SCHEDD.Q1.HISTORY = $(SCHEDD1_SPOOL)/history DAEMON_LIST = $(DAEMON_LIST), SCHEDD1 VALID_SPOOL_FILES = $(VALID_SPOOL_FILES), 1 # Make the q1@<hostname> schedd the default if the user doesn't use a -name option SCHEDD_HOST = Q1@$(HOSTNAME) # Define the second SCHEDD on this machine SCHEDD2 = $(SCHEDD) SCHEDD2_ARGS = -f -local-name Q2 SCHEDD2_LOG = $(LOG)/ScheddLog.2 SCHEDD2_SPOOL = $(SPOOL)/2 SCHEDD.Q2.SCHEDD_NAME = Q2@$(HOSTNAME) SCHEDD.Q2.SPOOL = $(SCHEDD2_SPOOL) SCHEDD.Q2.SCHEDD_LOG = $(SCHEDD2_LOG) SCHEDD.Q2.SCHEDD_ADDRESS_FILE = $(SCHEDD2_SPOOL)/.schedd_address SCHEDD.Q2.SCHEDD_DAEMON_AD_FILE = $(SCHEDD2_SPOOL)/.schedd_classad SCHEDD.Q2.HISTORY = $(SCHEDD2_SPOOL)/history DAEMON_LIST = $(DAEMON_LIST), SCHEDD2 VALID_SPOOL_FILES = $(VALID_SPOOL_FILES), 2 My LOCAL_DIR layout is: spool/ 1/ .schedd_address .schedd_classad job_queue.log local_univ_execute spool_version 2/ .schedd_address .schedd_classad job_queue.log local_univ_execute spool_version log/ lock/ config/ condor_config.local If I copy one of those spool_version files to the $(LOCAL_DIR)/spool directory everything works as expected. Why isn't the SPOOL setting from the multi-schedd propagated to the condor_shadow daemons on startup? They seem to be taking their settings directly from the condor_config/condor_config.local files instead of inheriting the environment the condor_schedd that spawned them. Does the schedd not rewrite the SCHEDD.<name>.SPOOL setting to SPOOL in the environment of sub-processes so they see that specific scheduler's settings at not the (wrong) global settings? Is there a way to make this happen using the named config syntax?

title: Ticket #622: DAGMan does not check node state consistency in recovery mode
description: I just checked, and in recovery mode DAGMan does not detect any problem if it sees an event marking a node as terminated, if the node's parent is not yet terminated. In, fact, it happily runs the parent after recovery mode is done, and also doesn't complain that when the parent finishes its children are already marked as done! I suspect that LIGO's problem referenced in the RUST ticket was caused by something like stale NFS handles temporarily rendering some log files unreadable, and therefore getting the internal state of the DAG into an incorrect state.
