title: Ticket #6428: store credentials in the SEC_CREDENTIAL_DIRECTORY as Owner
description: Currently, credentials are stored using the username the job will run as. When running as owner, this is correct, but when using slot users, pilots, or running as 'nobody' this causes collisions among the running jobs. So, two things to do here: In the shadow, already return the credential for the owner of the job, regardless of the username requested. In the starter, ask for the owner of the job, rather then the username the starter/job will run as.

title: Ticket #4415: Relative proxy path doesn't work in submit file
description: A relative path in x509userproxy attribute is handled inconsistently by condor_submit. When condor_submit checks the proxy's validity, it resolves the path relative to the current working directory. But when it sets x509userproxy in the job ad, it constructs a full path using the initialdir attribute. Condor_submit should consistently treat the proxy path in x509userproxy as relative to the initialdir.

title: Ticket #1302: config-file macro expansion doesn't see param table defaults
description: Macro expansion in the config file only works for configuration values defined in the config file (or environment). It doesn't work for values that only have a default value from the param table. Instead, it replaces the macro reference with an empty string. Example: LOCK = /var/condor/log MY_LOCK_FILE = $(LOCK)/MyLockFile The above case will result in MY_LOCK_FILE being /var/condor/log/MyLockFile. However, if LOCK is not defined in the config file, MY_LOCK_FILE will be /MyLockFile, even if LOCK has a default value in the param table. One potential issue is how to treat "empty assignment" of configuration values. Example: LOCK= MY_LOCK_FILE = $(LOCK)/MyLockFile Should the empty assignment override the default from the param table or should it effectively erase any previous assignment of LOCK and reset its value back to the default? I propose that it should be the former, not the latter. So in the above example, MY_LOCK_FILE will be /MyLockFile, even if LOCK has some default in the param table.
remarks: 2010-Mar-22 16:36:31 by matt: +1 to LOCK= setting LOCK to nothing, not resetting. This maintains the current semantics.
check_ins: 2010-Apr-09 16:32 Check-in [25417]: Documented change to macro expansion of defaults. #1302 (By Dan Bradley ) 2010-Mar-29 10:07 Check-in [17720]: Macro expansion now sees defaults from the param table. #1302 Previously, macro expansion only saw values explicitly set in the config file. (By Dan Bradley )

title: Ticket #767: Updating some of 7.4 parameter defaults to modern machines
description: Out of the ~1500 or so parameters available in the condor configuration, we are to update around ~620 of them to be current for modern machines, if applicable. This means changing: The code location(s) where the default is often hard coded The default table specified in param_info.in The condor_config.generic configuration file I have a tool which will dig around in the Condor source and map each entry to the locations in the source code which deals with it. This tool is not fool proof, however I did try and make it catch 99% of the cases. Changes to 7.5 defaults All changes should be made as early as possible in the 7.5 series. Changes to 7.4 defaults We will perform a small number of changes to the default parameters for 7.4. They are: MAX_JOBS_RUNNING START_LOCAL_UNIVERSE START_SCHEDULER_UNIVERSE SHADOW_SIZE_ESTIMATE RESERVED_SWAP NEGOTIATOR_INTERVAL Convert HOSTALLOW/DENY to be ALLOW/DENY ENABLE_GRID_MONITOR GRIDMANAGER_MAX_SUBMITTED_JOBS_PER_RESOURCE Please inspect their proposed defaults in the table. Higher Level Tasks Create a $(TMP) macro which has the correct value in it for any arch. Maybe instrument param to shove into a database the parameters it looks up so we can determine what it is doing at a more fine grained level. Remove the *_EXPRS format and replace wholesale with *_ATTRS. Unify VMWARE_ and VM_ namespaces. Rethink MAX_JOBS_RUNNING as instead an expression which using things like available virtual & physical memory, number of available bindable ports, amount of disk space available in spool, knowledge if a job is a remotely or locally executed entity, decides on an amount of jobs, which could simply be 0 or 1 initially) that can be run in an iteration of the schedd trying to run jobs. remarks: 2009-Oct-08 20:07:27 by matt: ENABLE_SOAP does indeed control if SOAP connections are enabled, a default of true is good though. The SOAP params came into existence before the SUBSYS. notation and thus have a SUBSYS_ notion. All that code should be simplified. [15997] If FILE_LOCK_VIA_MUTEX indeed does what it suggests and avoids advisory locks on file then it should be promoted and documented. It could be very useful in environments where fcntl is unreliable. Don't remove GLOBAL_JOB_ID_WITH_TIME. Do we know if the GRIDSHELL still works, if not it should be removed instead of documented. There are a number of different UPDATE_INTERVAL params, they should be unified, and specialized using the SUBSYS. functionality if necessary. The HA_LOCK_HOLD_TIME is insanely long. We should recognize that HA via the Master is primarily there for HA Schedds and change the HOLD_TIME to a fraction of the default claim lease duration to avoid as much bad put as possible. LOCAL_UNIV_EXECUTE -> LOCAL_UNIVERSE_EXECUTE for consistency. Note on HAD_ namespace, HAD is a SUBSYS, consider HAD. . MPI_ namespace should become PARALLEL_? Or be removed? NEGOTIATOR_STATE_FILE and STATE_FILE should be removed in favor of NEGOTIATOR.SPOOL, for when relocating the Accountantnew.log is desired. We should remove QUILL_ and isolate it in a plugin. RELEASE_DIR should not be param'd for, fix the code that does. HDFS_DATANODE_DIR should not be /scratch/tmp. HDFS_HOME should use $(LIBEXEC). STARTD_SENDS_ALIVES has had some discussion and may have downsides, please explore before switching this. USE_AFS and USE_NFS are Standard Universe specific and should be identified as such, they confuse people. VM_MAX_MEMORY, VM_MAX_NUMBER and VM_MEMORY should go the way of the dodo. Merge the XEN_ namespace with VM_ and VMWARE_. 2009-Oct-09 07:52:08 by danb: Our proposed expression for MAX_JOBS_RUNNING references SHADOW_SIZE_ESTIMATE. Without the default param table, this reference will give back nothing, unless this variable is explicitly set in the config file. The unfortunate thing about setting it in the config file is that if somebody upgrades from 7.4 without upgrading their default config file, whatever default we put in the param table will not take effect, because it will be explicitly set in the config file. To make matters worse, this variable was explicitly set in the default config file prior to 7.4. It was set to 1800, which seems rather high. I chose to simply insert a number (800k) directly into the MAX_JOBS_RUNNING expression, rather than reference SHADOW_SIZE_ESTIMATE. 2009-Oct-09 07:59:48 by danb: Greg T was wondering if we could provide a script for converting old config files (e.g. for doing the HOSTALLOW --> ALLOW switch). A naive script would mess things up in the following case: ALLOW_WRITE = blah1 HOSTALLOW_WRITE = blah2 --> ALLOW_WRITE = blah1 ALLOW_WRITE = blah2 That's wrong, because in the first config, the allow list is "blah1 blah2" whereas in the second it is "blah2". 2009-Oct-09 09:27:08 by jfrey: FILE_LOCK_VIA_MUTEX only works on Windows. It turns out USE_NFS and USE_AFS are used in the new shadow/starter for the I/O proxy. 2009-Oct-19 20:35:31 by matt: USE_NFS and USE_AFS should be renamed to more clearly express what they do in which context. As for their use in the new shadow, a quick looks suggests it is a little suspect. 2009-Nov-03 23:28:35 by matt: Simplification of SETTABLE_ATTRS, see #903 2009-Nov-04 16:03:19 by psilord: In the context of 7.4, this ticket is pretty much done since the new param system was turned off for 7.4, and only the recommended changes happened, documentation included. I'm not sure what to mark this ticket as since it clearly isn't active, but shouldn't be resolved. title: Ticket #3295: condor_glexec_run executes target user's .bashrc
description: When condor invokes condor_glexec_run to launch a job under glexec, the target user's ~/.bashrc is executed if /bin/sh is a symlink to /bin/bash. Depending on what happens in .bashrc, this can cause a failure to launch the job. By some miracle, Brian Bockelman managed to debug one such case, which is how we found out about this problem. Why does bash source ~/.bashrc, even though it is being used in non-interactive mode? It turns out that this happens, because bash wrongly guesses that it is the top level shell under rshd. The following bash code is responsible /* If we were run by sshd or we think we were run by rshd, execute ~/.bashrc if we are a top-level shell. */ if ((run_by_ssh || isnetconn (fileno (stdin))) && shell_level < 2) Since SHLVL is cleared by glexec and stdin is a socket, the above code causes ~/.bashrc to be executed. If we were invoking /bin/sh rather than /bin/bash, it would not read ~/.bashrc (even if /bin/sh is a symlink to /bin/bash). So why are we invoking /bin/bash rather than /bin/sh? The reason is that older versions of glexec refused to run symlinks. Modern versions allow execution of symlinks by default but can be configured not to with prohibit_exec_via_symlink = yes. Here are two possible solutions: 1. Run /bin/sh directly, and require that sites use a compatible glexec. 2. Hide the invocation of /bin/sh from glexec: glexec /usr/bin/env /bin/sh -c ... This should work with all versions and configurations of glexec (assuming /usr/bin/env is not a symlink itself). Igor prefers option 1.

title: Ticket #4803: Allow tools to contact starter when CCB and shared port are in use
description: Some client tools need to contact the starter (condor_ssh_to_job and condor_tail). However, this may be impossible if the following two conditions are true: Startd uses CCB. This means the starter must connect to the client tool. Client host uses shared_port. This means the client must be able to write to the shared port directory (or the shared_port otherwise leaks the secret cookie). This fact is the remaining reason (known to me, at least) that shared_port is not default. I propose that, when the DCSched::getJobConnectInfo is invoked (and we're in the above situation), the schedd will send back a socket already connected to the starter.
remarks: 2014-Dec-30 22:01:23 by bbockelm: Note to reviewers - branch V8_3-gt4803 includes branch V8_3-gt4800; however, probably only [42042] is needed. 2015-Jan-13 10:45:50 by tlmiller: Design Review These patches implement the following algorithm: 1) If HTCondor is configured to use shared port, but the ssh-to-job client can not, request socket forwarding when connecting to the schedd to get the starter's security session. 2) If the schedd sees a request for socket forwarding, it connects to the starter itself, and then passes that connection's FD to the client. This pass is accomplished by using an abstract unix domain socket. ("Abstract" means that it does not appear in the file system, which neatly avoids the permission problem which prevents the client from using registering with the shared port daemon itself.) The schedd adds the domain socket's name (address) and a random number, used as a capability, to the usual reply. 3) The client connects to the named unix domain socket and writes the capability; if it matches what the schedd sent, the schedd will reply by sending the FD of the connection it previously established to the starter. I have a number of questions about this design. A) We only care about shared port if the target starter uses CCB. Why don't we check the target address to see if it uses CCB? B) Do abstract domain sockets exist on any of our platforms other than Linux? (The autogenerated "address" may also be Linux-specific.) It's still worthwhile to do this even if they don't, we just need to be careful with our #ifdefs. C) The schedd and the ssh-to-job process are not necessarily on the same machine. We believe this configuration would normally work, but if shared port is configured on the ssh-to-job process's machine, we can't possibly pass it an FD. We should probably warn the user, or automatically try something else. 2015-Jan-13 11:07:57 by bbockelm: Hi ToddM, Thanks for the review! To address a few of your items: (a) We actually do check for CCB use in the target address. When the schedd returns the starter's address, there's another round-trip in the protocol where the client informs the server whether it wants the socket. Look for the following line: bool still_want_socket = rsock && sin.getCCBContact() && cant_use_shared_port; NOTE - this is only done by the client if the schedd appears to support FD passing. So, in cases where the client can use the shared port - or the target does not use CCB - the client tool is responsible for connecting. (b) Abstract name sockets are Linux-specific. It's actually important to note we use two Linux-specific features: abstract domain sockets and auto-bind sockets. This allows us to create a new listener socket without worrying about race conditions or otherwise stomping on pre-existing sockets. Autobind is what guarantees this (kind of like a mkstemp for domain sockets). (c) Yup - that's a limitation of this approach. I don't see any way around this without a whole lot of complexity. I'm willing to simply state this is a limitation we can't work around. 2015-Jan-13 11:22:52 by tlmiller: (A) Ah, OK. I'd missed that. Sorry. (B) I guess that simplifies the #ifdefs? (C) I might, but it requires a totally different approach to the problem. For this approach, we (HTCondor) will just have to think about how to warn/help users who try to do this. 2015-Jan-13 13:54:14 by tlmiller: Design doc draft here, which includes a brief section about the different approach: https://docs.google.com/a/wisc.edu/document/d/1rJpKNl-ack0F_Y_lfAEWi46Yml7aj9DcH34TDb5Yb4Q Brian notes that even if this approach fails (like his and ToddT's previous attempts), the problems should be recorded for posterity (especially since AFAIK, we haven't retrodesign-doc'd shared port). 2015-Jan-22 21:02:44 by bbockelm: Hi Todd, What's the next step here? This ticket ready to roll? Brian 2015-Jan-23 11:09:26 by tlmiller: It's still in design review. I have another (new) proposal that I haven't gotten a chance to write up yet. 2015-Feb-12 14:54:34 by tlmiller: I wrote up two new ideas: "Known-Connection Forwarding" and "Trusted Broker." Both assume that an administrator is willing to allow inbound connections to processes on their machine if they come from daemons they already trust, e.g., the startd/starter. The first proposal does this directly, the second via the trust relationship already established in the CCB. 2015-Mar-12 16:32:04 by tannenba: How about this idea: Client tools that may need to accept a reversed CCB connection are installed setgid to some group (perhaps just group condor?), and that group has write permission to the DAEMON_SOCKET_DIR. This solution is simple to code/understand, no special handling required if ssh-to-job and schedd are not co-located, and is not specific to ssh-to-job (i.e. it would work for condor_config_val, condor_fetchlog, etc). I think it is also as secure or more secure than any other idea we've had, assuming we audit each tool to make certain tools do not fork/exec a pathname provided by the user and/or always drop setgid upon fork/exec. This would be a good exercise regardless of this ticket. We could easily proceed one tool at a time, and only setgid the tools we anticipate requiring a reverse connection (e.g. condor_who would not need to be setgid). Thoughts? 2015-May-29 11:39:16 by tlmiller: Current plan is for Linux: We know that connections forwarded via an abstract domain socket are safe, because we control the (secret, random) name required to find/use them; only the daemons can use the abstract domain socket. Therefore, only tools will need to use the "daemon" socket directory. We think, then, that it will suffice to (audit) log connections made via the "daemon" socket directory; this won't prevent abuse, but it will make the guilty party clear(er). 2015-Jun-04 10:38:23 by tlmiller: Auditing code should be reviewed, since it's a little more sensitive than normal for a new feature. Also, we'll need to edit the shared port section of the manual, and talk about possible consequences from allowing users to write to the daemon socket directory, maybe suggest alternatives (group writable). 2015-Jun-25 16:17:28 by jfrey: I made a minor change to the audit calls. title: Ticket #5341: When cgroup OOM killer holds job, no final update or file xfer happens
description: When cgroups are enabled, and a job exceeds the memory limits, the per-cgroup OOM killer fires, and the starter puts the job on hold. However, it doesn't do a final job ad update, so the memory and cpu usage information are not up to date, and it looks like the job shouldn't have been OOM-killed. Also, file xfer doesn't happen if ON_EXIT_OR_EVICT is set, so releasing the job with a larger request_memory will cause self-checkpointing jobs to start from scratch.

title: Ticket #7686: Enforce per-submitter limits
description: From Stuart: I would like to discuss the possibility of adding a pool-level limit on the maximum amount of resources that can be claimed by a specific user at any given point in time. I am primarily concerned with cpu jobs, but if this is wroth doing it is probably worth considering generalizing to also be able to limit GPU devices, cpu-cores, jobs, ... The problems that a new or naive user can cause are legion, and I think such a knob would be a helpful throttle until a user has graduated condor flight school. We have made due for a long time with submit time throttles (and administrative scripts to dynamically query/hold/release jobs in individual schedd queues), but I would like to reconsider doing this centrally at the Negotiator. For example, * condor_clip gregory.thain@ligo.org 10cpu - Greg is hoping to pass flight school next year, but until then the negotiator will not match any jobs beyond a total of 10 cpu-cores * condor_clip james.clark@ligo.org 100gpu - Rift GPU code is working well, but James isn't ready to take over the whole cluster yet * condor_clip joshua.willis@ligo.org 200gpu - GPU version of PyCBC is working well and everything in Texas should be bigger or the one I really want to run right now at CIT, * condor_clip eric.howell@ligo.org 1000job - This user has multiple DAGs running but at somewhere around 2000 concurrent jobs running they overload a backend filesystem that impacts other users, and has lost opportunity costs while the jobs are blocked on I/O rather than flipping CPU transistors. P.S. condor_limit might be a more intuitive name than codor_clip. And it would be nice if 0 really meant 0, i.e., a pool-level block on claiming any such pool resources, and "unlimited" (ala ulimit) meant no limit (presumably the default for backward compatibility).

title: Ticket #7002: Fix ClassAds lexer to not read unneeded characters
description: The ClassAds lexer always reads one character beyond the last token consumed, even though it often doesn't need to. It frequently pushes these characters back into the input source, then usually re-consumes them when the next token is requested. When a ClassAd is parsed, the character after the end of the ad is pushed back but not re-consumed before the parse method returns. We'd like to avoid pushing back characters when possible, especially when it happens on the return of a successful parse. Here are two concrete problems that can result: When a FILE is open in text mode, the file position is undefined until a pushed-back character is re-consumed. In the Python 3 bindings, each parse call creates a temporary FILE around the file descriptor obtained from Python. If a parse operation finishes with a character pushed back into the stream via ungetc(), it will be lost in subsequent I/O, including another parse call. In particular, if a stream contains two ClassAds with no intervening whitespace, parsing the second one will fail: [ A=3 ][ B=true ]

title: Ticket #4784: User history file
description: Currently, the post-job for CMS CRAB3 has to parse all of the user log to find some simple statistics for the job that just ended (the alternate is to use condor_history, but that's similarly expensive). This has gotten increasingly expensive as users run a few thousand nodes per DAG. All of the information we need is in the final ClassAd dropped in the $PER_JOB_HISTORY_DIR; unfortunately, we need all the jobs associated with a node, meaning this approach isn't really going to work. Instead, I'd like to see a top-level submit command: history = /path/to/file This file gets the final job classad appended by the schedd at the same time it writes the final terminate event (so it's always available to the postjob).

If we want a classad available to the postjob script, we must write to this file immediately before updating the user log. However, the job has not yet exited the queue when this occurs - hence, it's not really the same as the ad in condor_history! A pithy example - when the shadow writes the terminate event (meaning that the postjob may fire up 1ms later), the job ad still lists itself as JobStatus = 2 (running). This is sufficient for our use case (even with the "wrong" JobStatus), but possibly shouldn't be named the "history" file. title: Ticket #3411: What does the chtcjobwrapper do?
description: Identify exactly what functionality the chtcjobwrapper is providing, with the goal of identifying features that Condor currently provides and features Condor should provide. Summary Updates itself - Users never update things; can be good for admin to do for them. Varies download source by execute node - User may know better sources for downloads. Logs progress - Useful for debugging, analysis Logs local environment - Useful for debugging Detects OS/Distribution version - For platform specific binaries Identify HTTP cache - For download speed, bandwidth savings Puts . in PATH - Simplify user's life Puts current working directory in $HOME - Simplifies running R and Matlab Downloads files - So we don't crush the submit point with input files Sets up prerequisites (R/Matlab/DMTCP) - Fiddly! Runs program/script correctly - R jobs need non-obvious command line Checks checksums for prerequisites - Can we trust network/disk? Selects appropriate build of prerequisites for the platform - Second part of detecting OS/Distro version Delete/don't send back unneeded files - Save bandwidth, disk space Sets requested environment variables - Absolute paths to scratch dir and appending to PATH are hard now Runs a pre-program and post-program - Execute side setup and teardown prior to real job Changes to another directory - ? benefit unknown Ensures the "real" job is executable - Wrappers means easy to get permissions wrong. Captures job standard output to another file - To separate from wrapper's noise Acts as a simple scripting language - Essentially execute-side DAGs for fast chains of programs Removes standard output and error - ? benefit unknown Details Updates itself Specifics: the job wrapper is actually a relatively thin script that exists to download the "real" script (chtcinnerwrapper) from our web site. This was a user can have a single static copy that they submit as part of their jobs and never have to update, but they get the benefits of bugfixes and changes made by CHTC. Broader applicability: A user might want to make a broad statement ("I need R version 2.15.X") and want to be never change their submit file again. They may want to delegate worrying about new builds for new operating systems, or bug-fixes, to someone else, presumably a system administrator. Actual experience supports this, if you ask users to change their functioning systems, they resist. Varies download source by execute node Specifics: The URLs used to download additional files changes depending on where the script is running. Specifically, if it detects it's running on a machine with IsEuclid set, it downloads from a local mirror instead of the public site. Broader applicability: A clueful user (or possibly administrator) may know that jobs running at site X have access to a fast local mirror of desired shared files. The local mirror's location varies from site to site. I could certainly see this being true from high energy physics data, or gene sequence databases. This might be useful functionality to put in the users hands, or in the administrators hands. But, it raises the possibility of being wrong, "Oops, the local mirror is missing this file, or has an out of date file," in which case you either need to download from the public mirror, or you need to declare failure. Logs progress Specifics: A log of downloads and runtime is maintained and returned to the user. The file is designed to be easy to parse. Broader applicability: What was downloaded, that it was or wasn't successful, and how long it took should certainly be logged. (We use download durations as a crude tool for measuring effectiveness of local caches.) But where? Especially if setting up a job environment is more user facing, this shouldn't be hiding in a StarterLog on a machine they may not be able to log into. Currently it ends up in a file called AuditLog.[something]. The information could certainly be dumped into supplemental messages in the user log. The runtime is an interesting question. Time spent downloading and setting up an environment, and time spend actually running the job are both potentially useful to someone managing the system. Notably, if setup time is dwarfing productive time, it's a clue there is a problem. Simply lumping the two together is probably the wrong answer, and making download and setup "free" is similarly wrong. If we consider keeping an installed environment on an execute node and sharing it between jobs, the idea of the cost of setting up a job is even weirder. Should later jobs hear what it originally cost, if only so they can easily see how much they saved? Logs local environment Specifics: The script logs information about the executing system: hostname, current environment, free disk space, current working directory, Linux distribution version, contents of scratch directory and potentially other directories, total size of the scratch directory. The contents and size of the scratch directory may be reported multiple times, before and after various steps run. This information has been found to be useful when diagnosing problems. Broader applicability: When a user is debugging a failed job, there is a pile of potentially useful information about the executing system they might like to have. Some is available in the machine's classad (OpSys and Arch), although if the machine is down the information may be gone, some information (Disk) is probably no longer accurate, and nearly anything may change if hardware or software is upgraded. Other information was never present in the machine's classad (environment, current working directory, distribution version). Either way, once the job has failed, your chance to collect useful information is gone. Maybe you can instrument your program and rerun it and see the same or a similar failure, but if failures are unusual this can be difficult. Perhaps Condor should identify a list of "common causes of failure for a program" (not enough disk, incorrect environment, etc), collect data about those, and store it somewhere convenient for the user. The user log is the most obvious spot, but a user might specify condor_diagnostic_file=diagnostics.txt in their submit file. The contents of the scratch directory at various stages (at the start, after unpacking any binaries or data, at the end) can also be useful. Detects OS/Distribution version Specifics: The script crudely determines if it's on Scientific Linux 5 or 6. It needs this information to make decisions about what binaries to download. Broader applicability: Condor is much better about providing this information (OpSysAndVer, OpSysVer, OpSysShortName, OpSysLongName, OpSysMajorVer, OpSysName). We might be done here. Potential future areas for consideration: More robust detection - Currently the Linux solution assumes /etc/issue's first line is something reasonable and easy to parse. Appears to work well in practice. Identification of equivalent versions - Currently there is no clue that SL6 and CentOS6 are nearly equivalent to RedHat6 Identification of other relevant aspects - Major library versions, in particular. Identify HTTP cache Specifics: OSG sites don't necessarily set HTTP_PROXY or http_proxy; we can only rely on OSG_SQUID_LOCATION. So the script ensures that HTTP_PROXY and http_proxy, basing them on http_proxy, HTTP_PROXY, or OSG_SQUID_LOCATION as it can be found. The specific value cannot be known in advance; it's site specific. Broader applicability: We may need up elements in the environment based on what we detect about the local site. We might be able to get the information from the machine ad (in which case it's a simple matter of "environment=HTTP_PROXY=$$(SQUID_LOCATION)"), but we might be stuck with nosing around in the environment as we do here. Puts . in PATH Specifics: . is put at the front of the path list. While a bad idea in the general case for security reasons, for a job running in a sandbox, probably safe? Probably in place to help people who insecurely put . in their path for their terminal. Broader applicability: Potentially dangerous if the job is prone to chdiring to weird places, but probably generally safe, and it eliminates a common problem in writing a shell script to drive your other programs. Puts current working directory in $HOME Specifics: the environment variable HOME is set to the scratch directory. This is useful because Matlab and R assume they can put dot files in your home directory. An HTCondor job's user may not have a home directory or that they have access and if they do we probably don't want to put files there. Broader applicability: This seems like pure win for dedicated execute nodes; it helps in a small way with job isolation. It's bad, however, if the job might really have access to your home directory (NFS?) and you want that. Perhaps we should automatically do it if slot users are being used (not clear how widely true this is for OSG) Downloads files Specifics: Prerequisite packages and data files are downloaded via HTTP. This is done to minimize load/bandwidth on the submit point. Through the use of a local HTTP cache (identified earlier), we can eve minimize load/bandwidth on the webserver. Broader applicability: Bandwidth is a challenge for any job with large binaries or data sets. Offering a ways to offload this is a win. The obvious answer is file transfer hooks, and that may solve the problem for most people. One challenge is that file transfer hooks are provided by the administrator, which leaves the user out of luck if the administrator hasn't or won't set up a hook for the desired protocol, be it HTTP, BitTorrent, or something else. Sets up prerequisites (R/Matlab/DMTCP) Specifics: The script ensures prerequisites are ready to go. Most of these steps are optional, but they're all available. Packages include: Matlab, R, DMTCP, "sharefiles.tar.gz" (user defined), SLIBS.tar.gz or SLIBS1.tar.gz (user defined libraries, should contain directory "SS"), RLIBS.tar.gz (user defined R libraries), SITEPACKS.tar.gz (user defined Python libraries? Unsure.) Download the package. - Doesn't use Condor's built in file transfer so we can potentially get benefits from local caches and multiple mirrors. Relies on the HTTP cache having been properly identified and set up properly. Pretty much guaranteed to be .tar.gz Unpack the package. - tar xzf filename.tar.gz Set up the environment - The varies from prerequisite to prerequisite, although setting the PATH and LD_LIBRARY_PATH are common. In addition, R sets RHOME, Matlab sets XAPPLRESDIR, DISPLAY, MATLAB_PREF, and MCR_CACHE_ROOT. R also rewrites the (official) R wrapper script itself to set a path (probably could be worked around by shipping a modified R wrapper script.) It's possible to use multiple prerequisites. Notably, a user might have a custom library they need for their R or Matlab program Broader applicability: This is the meat of what we're interested in. Download the package. - See "Downloads files" above. Unpack the package. - No current support beyond "teach your job to do it." If the job requires the package to even start, this means in practice "write a wrapper to do it." Might be part of the download hook (httpandunpack://url/foo.tar.gz). Set up the environment - If the job requires the package to even start, this means in practice "write a wrapper to do it." Slightly challenging because many of these settings should be absolute paths into the scratch directory, so they can't be simply set in the environment setting in the submit file. Runs program/script correctly Specifics: As far as HTCondor is concerned, the executable is always the wrapper script. But as far as the user is concerned, the executable is something else, and there are additional arguments to pass in. For Matlab, it's an actual executable, but for R it's a script. Instead of running "./myprogram arguments", you invoke "R-install-dir/bin/Rscript --no-save ./myprogram arguments". Broader applicability: If we're running a script, and we're bringing the interpreter along with us (from a shared location), what is logically our executable (the script) actually isn't, it's the interpreter, and we may need to have a complex command line for the interpreter. Maybe this should be in the user's hands (allows additional options to the interpreter), or maybe HTCondor should handle everything for simplicity. Checks checksums for prerequisites Specifics: In addition to downloading a prerequisite package, the wrapper also downloads a SHA1 checksum file and compares it to the sha1sum of the downloaded package. If the checksums don't match, it's a failure. Both the package and the checksum come from the same source, so this is a weak defense against active attack, but it can potentially detect accidental corruption. TODO: Check with bt to see if it's ever actually paid off. Maybe detected stale copies from cache? Broader applicability: Our file transfer mechanism (HTTP) is basically unsecured, and could conceivably be corrupted in transit, in memory, or on disk. The actual risk seems likely to be low. We could teach Condor to checksum transferred files easily, although it's not clear what they would be checked against, especially if the file's identity was decided at runtime (ex. "executable=my-program.$$(OpSysAndVer)"). Selects appropriate build of prerequisites for the platform Specifics: Appears to download both the SL5 and SL6 binaries and unpacks the appropriate one. Some prerequisites may have both sets of binaries inside of them, with each .so file prefixed with sl5- or sl6-; the appropriate one will be symlinked to. Broader applicability: seems like this is better solved with $$(OpSysAndVer) to download the appropriate version. But, if you might download Matlab-RedHat6.tar.gz or Matlab-Redhat5.tar.gz or even Matlab-Debian10.tar.gz, we need to handle unpacking correctly. Delete/don't send back unneeded files Specifics: To minimize bandwidth and submit-machine disk usage, the wrapper ensures that a list of files is automatically deleted, or at least not sent back. It's important to catch them when the job finishes or if the job is evicted and when_to_transfer_output=ON_EXIT_OR_REMOVE. Prerequisite packages - Sometimes added to deletion list and deleted at the end, sometimes deleted as soon as it's unpacked. Prerequisite installations - We rely on them being in a subdirectory, and that HTCondor ignores subdirectories when transferring files back. This may not be a safe assumption in the future. User specified files - Deleted when we finish. These are (typically) temporary working files that the user's job fails to clean up, but that we don't care about. Specified in a list in the file REMOVE. Broader applicability: Very relevant, for much the reasons given above. 1 can be avoided by doing downloads into another location (perhaps ./tmp?), or the window reduced by deleting the file as soon as it's unpacked. 2 works for now if everything is in a subdirectory. Sets requested environment variables Specifics: The user can provide an ENV file which contains instructions for environment variables to set. Obviously this can be handled with the environment setting in the submit file, but this file allows for some special cases, all revolving around handling of paths and the current working directory. These are useful because we might desire absolute paths, but can't predict the name of our scratch directory. Prepend something to an environment variable, specifically PATH. It may be useful to keep the system provided path, but to add another directory relative to our scratch directory. Set an environment variable (especially PATH, but also others) to an absolute path relative to the scratch directory. Broader applicability: The two cases above apply to many other situations. If you're installing libraries and applications in our scratch directory, there are plenty of possible reasons to set environment variables pointing at subdirectories or the scratch directory itself. Relative paths aren't what we want; sometimes they won't be accepted, more commonly they'll break if the program changes directories. We might special case a search and replace for [SCRATCH_DIR] in the environment variables to put in the absolute path to the scratch directory. Or maybe allow any environment variable (PERL5LIB=[PERL5LIB]:[SCRATCH_DIR]/myperl). The later also allows for appending/prepending. Runs a pre-program and post-program Specifics: Runs a user provided pre-program ("pre-script") prior to running the real job. The same is done for a post-program ("post-script") The program is run blindly and the wrapper continues without regard to the result. TODO: Who and or what is this for? Perhaps to allow a bit of simple setup before running a "real" Matlab/R program without need to add an entire shell script wrapper? Broader applicability: Unknown. PreCmd and PostCmd may fit the bill, although they lack the ability to take command line arguments like the wrapper. Need to also consider behavior if a given command fails: does a failed PreCmd mean we shouldn't run the actual job (and what do we return); do we return the job's exit code or PostCmds? Changes to another directory Specifics: Prior to running the job (but after downloading and unpacking various packages!), simply chdirs to a new directory specified by the user, presumably a relative path. Use case is unknown (TODO). Broader applicability: initialdir does the right thing for standard universe, or vanilla universe with a shared filesystem, but not otherwise. But I'm dubious as to actual need for this. Ensures the "real" job is executable Specifics: chmod 755 $real_executable. Since the executable isn't the executable Condor recognizes, and may have come from transfer_input_files, or from a download and unpackage earlier, it's possible that the execute bit isn't set. Broader applicability: If we move toward having Condor do the work of the wrapper script, the executable really will be the executable, largely eliminating the problem. It can come up in other cases (multiple executables), but the wrapper script doesn't worry about those at all. Captures job standard output to another file Specifics: The real executable's standard output can be redirected to a specified file, keeping it distinct from output generated by the wrapper script, programs called by the wrapper script (wget/curl/tar), and the PRE and POST scripts. Standard error is not similarly captured. Broader applicability: Not relevant. First, it's arguably backward; the wrapper script should put it's off-topic noise into a separate file and keep the "real" standard output and error clean for the real executable. Second, if we move a bunch of this functionality into Condor, the information will naturally end up elsewhere, not in the job's stdout/stderr. Acts as a simple scripting language Specifics: Instead of a simple executable to run, the user can specify, in a file named CONTROL, a list of executables to run. This essentially forms an incredibly simple scripting language, where each executable is run serially; any step returning non-zero terminates the run. The benefit of knowing how to re-write a job to run under R is preserved, so this can be used to easily run several R jobs one-after another Broader applicability: The fundamental problem: I have several programs that chained in a DAG, but there is no need to pull temporary results back (say, because many steps are really fast). This seems like a real issue. Solvable today with a shell script (but maybe not so easy to write, especially for R whose command line gets rewritten). Also solvable with execute-side DAGs, but support for that in Condor is weak. Removes standard output and error Specifics: At user request, removes/stops transfer of the standard output or error. This will include output from the wrapper script and potentially output from the real executable. Broader applicability: No idea. Perhaps saving bandwidth/disk for large scale DAGs? Kills ones ability to investigate problems. TODO

Depending on how many files are transferred, per-file stats might be a bit verbose (especially as we can recursively transfer a directory!). However, per-protocol (HTCondor file transfer, file transfer plugin protocol A, protocol B) statistics would be useful.

title: Ticket #3104: Crash during file spooling results in schedd releasing job
description: When spooling input files for a job, the schedd creates a child process to do the actual transfer. If the child's exit status is anything other than a normal exit code of 0, the schedd considers the transfer a success and releases the job. This includes if the child process crashes. The schedd should only consider the transfer a success if the child process's exit status is a normal exit code of 1 (the child's indication of success). In particular, generalJobFilesWorkerThread() returns TRUE for success and FALSE for failure. These values become the child process's exit code. The check of the exit status in spoolJobFilesReaper() and transferJobFilesReaper() needs to be changed.

title: Ticket #1093: condor_status default sorting broken in 7.4
description: condor_status is now sorting output based on the "Name" attribute, not the "machine" attribute. So, output can look like this: $ condor_status | egrep chevre\|charlie slot1@charlie.cs.w LINUX X86_64 Claimed Idle 0.000 1965 0+00:03:01 slot1@chevre.cs.wi LINUX X86_64 Owner Idle 0.000 1945 0+01:20:28 slot2@charlie.cs.w LINUX X86_64 Claimed Idle 0.000 1965 0+00:00:05 slot2@chevre.cs.wi LINUX X86_64 Owner Idle 0.000 1945 0+01:20:29 slot3@charlie.cs.w LINUX X86_64 Claimed Busy 0.160 1965 0+00:00:06 slot3@chevre.cs.wi LINUX X86_64 Owner Idle 0.070 1945 0+01:20:30 slot4@charlie.cs.w LINUX X86_64 Claimed Idle 0.000 1965 0+00:00:03 slot4@chevre.cs.wi LINUX X86_64 Owner Idle 0.000 1945 0+01:20:31 which is infelicitous. The problem is that the server-side classad attribute projection is only sending to the client the "Name" attribute, which is what condor_status displays, but condor_status sorts based on "Machine", if available. Forcing the projection code to also send the "Machine" attribute will fix the problem.

title: Ticket #4291: Overlayed I/O with dedicated transfer slots
description: User-visible information available on the wiki here: ExperimentalOverlayedFileTransfer The latest approach for overlaying execution of jobs with the transferring of the output sandbox. Full details in Design Doc Have the following in your condor_config: $EXPERIMENTAL : ASYNC_STAGEOUT which is equivalent to # append cluster ID to StarterLog, may be: Cluster, JobId, false or true. true gives 8.0 compatible behavior. ALLOW_SLOT_PAIRING=true STARTER_LOG_NAME_APPEND=false # create a type2 xfer slot for every type1 slot NUM_SLOTS_TYPE_1 = $(NUM_CPUS) NUM_SLOTS_TYPE_2 = $(NUM_SLOTS_TYPE_1) SLOT_TYPE_2 = minimal cpus=0.1 memory=100 disk=auto SLOT_TYPE_2_NAME_PREFIX = xfer SLOT_TYPE_2_PAIRED_WITH = SLOT_TYPE_1 SLOT_TYPE_2_HIDDEN = true SLOT_TYPE_2_START = TARGET.JobTransferringOutput && splitslotname(TARGET.RemoteHost)[1] == splitslotname(MY.Name)[1] STARTD_SLOT_ATTRS = $(STARTD_SLOT_ATTRS) State Activity EnteredCurrentActivity JobId GlobalJobId For testing I modified this slightly, and changed a few things to make HTCondor more "interactive": NUM_SLOTS_TYPE_1 = 1 SLOT_TYPE_2_HIDDEN = false SCHEDD_INTERVAL = 5 UPDATE_INTERVAL = 5 Here's the submit file I'm using for testing async.sub: universe = vanilla executable = async.sh should_transfer_files = ALWAYS when_to_transfer_output = ON_EXIT_OR_EVICT +wantioproxy = True output = a.$(Cluster).$(Process).out error = a.$(Cluster).$(Process).err log = a.log notification = never requirements = (CPUS >= 1) queue 4 You can use streaming out and error if you want, but be warned that reconnect won't work: stream_output = True stream_error = True And here is the script async.sh: #!/bin/sh echo "I AM:" whoami hostname uname -a echo "ENV:" env echo "executing for 120 seconds..." touch executing sleep 120 echo /scratch.1/zmiller/build/release_dir//libexec/condor_chirp phase output /scratch.1/zmiller/build/release_dir//libexec/condor_chirp phase output echo "transferring for 120 seconds..." touch transferring sleep 120 rm executing transferring echo THAT IS ALL! exit 0 Here is a template you can use to run "condor_status -pr pairs.pr": # condor_status query for slot pairs, use with condor_status -direct to see hidden pairs. SELECT # Machine WIDTH AUTO splitslotname(Name)[0] AS SlotName WIDTH -8 IfThenElse(SlotPairName isnt undefined,splitslotname(SlotPairName)[0],"-") AS Paired Strcat(Arch,"_",IfThenElse(OpSys=="WINDOWS",OpSysShortName,OpSysAndVer)) AS Platform Cpus AS Cpus PRINTF "%.3f" # IfThenElse(GPUs isnt undefined,GPUs,0) AS GPUs PRINTF "%4d" Memory WIDTH 6 Disk WIDTH 8 EnteredCurrentActivity AS " StatusTime" PRINTAS ACTIVITY_TIME NOPREFIX Strcat(State,"/",Activity) AS Status WIDTH -14 TRUNCATE ifthenelse(JobId isnt undefined, JobId, "") AS JobID

title: Ticket #1990: Performing a condor_qedit should use a separate authorization
description: A sysadmin should be able to block a user from editing his or her job: this can be done if there's a separate EDIT authorization level for the schedd. While this may not make sense for an interactive submit node, this would be useful for Condor-C or SOAP. It may be that the admins wants to enforce a policy on remote users via the job_router. Hence, the user would be able to submit jobs, but only the router would have edit permissions for their jobs. I believe doing this at the "authorization level" (as opposed to the individual attribute level) would provide sufficient granularity for the described use case. I wouldn't be surprised if the more flexible, finer-grained has a use case; just can't think of one for now.
remarks: 2011-Mar-21 14:20:53 by matt: Don't forget about chirp. It may be problematic in the case of a Condor integrated application. 2011-Mar-21 14:48:38 by bbockelm: Yeah, there's a bit of a philosophical question here: is the case where the "admin knows best" valid? In the case of the condor_job_router, the admin changes the job around so hopefully it has a better chance of running. However, the user can always change this back. With this ticket will strengthen the situation such that the user cannot override the admin. Is this something Condor wants to do? Is there anything inherently dangerous in the ClassAd?

title: Ticket #2345: gahp_server consumes 100% CPU
description: gahp_server.cpp contains the following at around line 1981: for (;;) { globus_poll_blocking(); } In old globus versions, this would be somewhat equivalent to "sleep": the main thread would go off and handle whatever asynchronous event is in the queue. title: Ticket #675: Support for GRAM5 in Condor-G
description: Globus GRAM5 is in development. It's a modification of GRAM2 and attempts to address most of the deficiencies of GRAM2. It's meant to interoperate with GRAM2 clients, but some changes need to be made in Condor-G to work well with it. Condor-G should automatically detect whether a server is GRAM2 or GRAM5. User can give a hint to Condor-G whether a server is GRAM2 or GRAM5. Grid monitor should be disabled for GRAM5 servers. Jobmanager limit shouldn't apply to GRAM5 servers. Jobmanagers on GRAM5 servers shouldn't be stopped or restarted.
remarks: 2009-Aug-19 16:14:05 by jfrey: Just pushed code for 7.3.2 to do everything outlined in this ticket other than automatically detecting whether a server is GRAM2 or GRAM5. Currently, we rely on the user to tell us by using 'gt2' or 'gt5' in the GridResource job attribute. The Globus team plans to add something to the GRAM API to allow clients to query to the version of the server. Once that's in place, the gridmanager can automatically distinguish between GRAM2 and GRAM5.

title: Ticket #4442: Enable PR_SET_CHILD_SUBREAPER in the starter if available
description: prctl(PR_SET_CHILD_SUBREAPER, ...) instructs the kernel to re-parent all child (and all subsequent children) processes to the current one instead of to init. This should greatly help the procd determine process trees (even in the lack of things like PID namespaces or cgroups) if processes are unable to re-parent to init.

title: Ticket #3387: Can't remove EC2 jobs with invalid authentication.
description: Attempts to remove a job with invalid authentication will fail, as the job will go back on hold when RunInstances() or DescribeInstances() is called during recovery. Jaime suggests recording in the resource object, which can already tell if a ping failed because of an authentication failure, when such has happened, and, in the EC2 job object, checking before even entering the state machine [or at least before creating the client token] (but after waiting for the first ping to complete) if an authentication failure has occurred. If so, by never calling RunInstances() (and never creating a client token), we know that no instance could have been started, and it's safe not to record anything about the job -- allowing the schedd to remove it on its own.
remarks: 2013-Jan-10 14:01:01 by jfrey: Code Review Whether or not the first ping for a resource is done is already available to job objects via BaseJob::resourceStateKnown. We could replace resourceStateKnown with didFirstPing(), which is more space-efficient and easier to understand. You don't need to set HoldReason in the job ad in the GM_INIT state. In GM_HOLD, the HoldReason will be taken from errorString if it's non-empty. In the GM_INIT state, I don't believe you can go to GM_DELETE for all REMOVED jobs. We can end up orphaning instances and ssh keypairs.

title: Ticket #5253: Blahp thread limit can kill gridmanager
description: The blahp has a limit on the number of non-trivial commands that can be in active at a time. The limit is set via the parameter blah_max_threaded_cmds in the blah config file. The default is 500. The gridmanager has a limit on the number of commands it will issue to the blahp at a time. This limit is set via the parameter GRIDMANAGER_MAX_PENDING_REQUESTS in the HTCondor config file. The default is 50. If the blahp's limit is set lower than the gridmanager's limit, then a command to the blahp can fail with the message "Threads limit reached". The failure occurs in the immediate response to the command, not the eventual result line. This is a fatal error in the gridmanager, which immediately exits. The system needs to deal with conflicting values for these limits more gracefully. When the gridmanager receives the "Threads limit reached" error, it could retry the command some time later. When the blahp receives a command that would exceed its limit, it could queue up the additional command(s) in memory until some active commands complete.

title: Ticket #7281: Exchange a SCITOKEN for a TOKEN
description: A SciToken is a bearer token, issued by a third party, that describes allowed capabilities. Two downsides of this authentication method are: In order to utilize it with HTCondor as part of a new security session, the server needs to have a SSL certificate. The server must download the SciToken issuer's public keys to verify the token's authenticity; this can potentially fail. TOKEN auth, on the other hand, does not require a host cert and, because the token is issued by HTCondor, doesn't rely on access to a third party. If we allow a SciToken to be exchanged for an equivalent-or-more-restricted TOKEN, then subsequent security sessions from the client can be established with the more robust TOKEN method. Further, the token exchange can be combined with the impersonation token in #7262 to allow the HTCondor-CE to run completely without a host certificate in the following setup: Sysadmin of HTCondor CE acquires a token allowing the CE to advertise to the OSG collector. Pilot factory registers its identity with the OSG collector. Pilot factory uses its identity to obtain an impersonation token as in #7262. Pilot factory contacts the HTCondor-CE, authenticating with its impersonation token, and exchanges the VO's SciToken for an equivalent TOKEN using the VO's identity at the CE. Pilot factory creates a new authenticated security session with the remote CE using the VO's TOKEN and can start to submit jobs. Finally, because the HTCondor-CE doesn't need a host certificate for any of its authentication methods, it also doesn't need a public IP or hostname -- the CE itself can (I think) be run behind a NAT.

title: Ticket #6869: scitokens: Abandon ZKM_QUERY_CREDS
description: Looking at the RPC protocol (ZKM_QUERY_CREDS) between condor_submit and the condor_credd for token submission, I have come to the conclusion it is unfixable: There is no mechanism for an error message to be passed or for the credd to otherwise indicate an error has occurred. It's named ZKM_QUERY_CREDS. It's narrowly limited to the web workflow, which is not necessarily always going to be the case. The code is 90% salvageable, however, as we simply just need to tweak the protocol to make it more flexible. I propose we instead: Create a new command int that is not literally named after the developer. In the new command int, we have it respond with a ClassAd instead of a string. This should allow for error messages, among other things. Do the normal protocol evolution based on the version of the remote condor_credd. By responding with a ClassAd, we can indicate that condor_submit should respond to missing credentials by having the job start off on hold -- and we can record which credentials are missing! Once we evolve this protocol slightly, we have more flexibility to do things like make OAuth tokens compatible with Pegasus and provide a reasonable Python binding to the credd.

It was essential for OSG builds; the glibc builds were the bulk of their build time and doing parallel builds was a huge improvement. I've tried to preserve existing behavior when using Makefiles while supporting other systems by providing a reasonable "make -jX" (where X is the number of processors). This is commit [43223]. I've asked Carl to review it. 2015-Feb-09 12:34:58 by adesmet: CODE REVIEW: (Copied from an email from Carl to Alan) +################################################################################ +# Various externals rely on make, even if we're not using +# Make. Ensure we have a usable, reasonable default for them. +if(${CMAKE_GENERATOR} STREQUAL "Unix Makefiles") + set( MAKE $(MAKE) ) +else () + include (ProcessorCount) + ProcessorCount(NUM_PROCESSORS) + set( MAKE make -j${NUM_PROCESSORS} ) +endif() + (1) I think you should actually be able to omit the "if" block entirely. Make lets you specify its variables either as $(x) or as ${x} (although the first is more common), so your other changes from $(MAKE) to ${MAKE} should work in a Makefile without needing to set the MAKE environment variable explicitly. (2) I think you have to omit the "if" block entirely. If you put MAKE='$(MAKE)' into make's environment, I think it explodes, since make's variables are actually recursively-expanding, kind of like condor's config system. For instance: [edquist@monza ~/foo/rmake]$ cat Makefile zoo: ${MAKE} -f zoo.mk [edquist@monza ~/foo/rmake]$ cat zoo.mk zoo: echo hi > zoo [edquist@monza ~/foo/rmake]$ make make -f zoo.mk make[1]: Entering directory `/afs/cs.wisc.edu/u/e/d/edquist/foo/rmake' echo hi > zoo make[1]: Leaving directory `/afs/cs.wisc.edu/u/e/d/edquist/foo/rmake' [edquist@monza ~/foo/rmake]$ rm zoo [edquist@monza ~/foo/rmake]$ MAKE='$(MAKE)' make Makefile:3: *** Recursive variable `MAKE' references itself (eventually). Stop. (3) for the "else" block ... so, setting MAKE="make -j${NUM_PROCESSORS}" for ninja (or whatever), I imagine, there is the same fundamental problem as putting 'make -j2' in when the outer build system is make -- namely that the outer build system can't manage the parallelism of the inner make. What I'm imagining is, for instance, Ninja thinks, OK, I can do 57 things at once (because you ran ninja -j57, or whatever). But then the glibc build steps, to ninja, each count as a single task. So then ninja kicks off "make -j${NUM_PROCESSORS}" for glibc, plus 56 other tasks. (And note that NUM_PROCESSORS in this case might be 57, or 64, or 2, or whatever.) In contrast, the way "make -j57" works when a sub-make is run with $(MAKE) (or ${MAKE}) is actually not to pass -j57 to the sub-make, but to set up a jobserver with pipes to make the original 57 jobs sharable between the top-level make and all sub-makes, recursively. Which is pretty cool. But I don't expect that Ninja is able to interoperate with make to share jobs this way... So anyway, I don't know what the right solution is for the "else" block. Part of me thinks, "ah, why not, use -j${NUM_PROCESSORS}, what's the worst that could happen?" -- but the rest of me thinks it might be better to be more conservative and keep a hard coded -j2 or something. So yeah, I guess I'd recommend something like one of these instead: +##############################################################################$ +# Various externals rely on make, even if we're not using +# Make. Ensure we have a usable, reasonable default for them. +if(NOT ${CMAKE_GENERATOR} STREQUAL "Unix Makefiles") + set( MAKE make -j2 ) +endif() + +##############################################################################$ +# Various externals rely on make, even if we're not using +# Make. Ensure we have a usable, reasonable default for them. +if(NOT ${CMAKE_GENERATOR} STREQUAL "Unix Makefiles") + include (ProcessorCount) + ProcessorCount(NUM_PROCESSORS) + set( MAKE make -j${NUM_PROCESSORS} ) +endif() 2015-Feb-09 12:40:33 by adesmet: After discussion with Carl, we confirmed that (1) and (2) are not necessary. There was a misunderstanding about which layers were evaluating $(MAKE)vs ${MAKE}. (CMake only evaluates the second; GNU Make evaluates both) (3) is harder; there really isn't a good answer. Possibilities discussed: -j1 - Slow but safe, shouldn't conflict with other things built in parallel. glibc is the slowest part of our builds, so this will likely make glibc the chokepoint. -j2 - Arbitrarily chosen. Probably faster but will slightly slow things down while other things build in parallel. -j$({NUM_PROCESSORS} - Maybe faster? Almost certain to slow down during parallel builds with other things. Optimal if glibc is building on its own. This is the current default. If we can convince Ninja "this rule must run all by itself", this might be optimal. All of this is irrelevant when using Make; but it will apply to other build systems, notably Ninja. As best I can tell, it's not feasible to get the sub-Make to play nicely with Ninja in the way that sub-Makes can interact with the parent Make. Also, there is no way to tell Ninja "this rule must run all by itself" (I think, need to query mailing list.). 2015-Feb-09 13:37:44 by edquist: Additional comments from email thread last week: --- Re #2: I think I'm okay because I believe it will never produce MAKE=$(MAKE) or any variant. If I didn't screw up it should just plot $(MAKE) into the Makefile where it was before. Ah, in that case you're probably fine then. I don't know enough about cmake, and i was assuming set( var value... ) would effectively put var='value...' into the environment ... But if it fills in "value..." for ${var} when it writes the makefile (or ninja) output, then i guess that changes things. (And so your original is probably fine.) ... I can also try doing a scratch build with your changes in our koji, just to make sure nothing explodes for the make-based build. Carl --- Yeah, fwiw, a scratch build in koji with your changes worked fine. 2015-Feb-09 16:14:35 by adesmet: My plan: stick with "-j$({NUM_PROCESSORS}". It's not a terrible choice, building glibc is rare enough that some inefficiency isn't a big deal, and it's simple. I've got a query out to the Ninja community, but I'm not optimistic. 2015-Feb-10 10:06:32 by adesmet: Merged into master.

title: Ticket #4507: Improve threading of the HTCondor python module
description: CMS noticed that the current python bindings don't play well with threading. That is, when a call to the HTCondor python library is made, we hold on to the GIL (global interpreter lock) that means no other python thread can make progress while the HTCondor call is made. We can improve this: We can have a module-level lock in the htcondor module. This would allow other threads to proceed as long as they aren't also making HTCondor library calls. Because libclassads should be threadsafe with caching turned off, we don't need to coordinate across the two modules. We can invert control for schedd queries by using the non-blocking read interface. That is, start the query, release the GIL when things would block, call select() the fd and reacquire the lock when there's network data to read. We would need a object-level lock to prevent two concurrent queries from happening on the same schedd object.

title: Ticket #3368: Red Hat linuxes fail to stop the condor service on shutdown
description: The beginning of /src/condor_examples/condor.init has the lines # The program being managed prog=condor_master lockfile=/var/lock/subsys/$prog The end result is that any redhattish linux will not stop HTCondor with the shutdown script, because the name of the lock file /var/lock/subsys/condor_master does not match the /var/lock/subsys/condor that the /etc/rc.d/rc script is looking for on shutdown. The rc script concludes that HTCondor is not running because the lock file isn't there and thus never runs the shutdown script. An unpleasant consequence of the above is when a sysadmin does a fast shutdown of the machine, they may get tons of emails from the master claiming "/usr/sbin/condor_startd" on "fnpc2024.fnal.gov" died due to signal 6 (Aborted). resulting from the hard kill coming from the system at the very end of shutdown.

title: Ticket #1355: Reset_Timer/ResetTimer one-off timer to periodic should be illegal
description: Hypothesis: Converting a one-off timer (timer with a period of 0) into a periodic timer (period > 0), is deeply suspicious. A one-off timer is always either truly one-off ("Go do this task") or is automatically resubmitting itself. Redoing that would range from incorrect and harmless through incorrect and crippling (#1337). I can't think of any non-insane reasons to use DaemonCore::Reset_Timer or TimerManager::ResetTimer to convert a one-off timer into a periodic one. Proposal: As such, doing so should trigger an EXCEPTion. This would catch bugs like #1337 quickly instead of creating hard to debug bugs. To do: Check our various one-off timers. Do we ever intentionally convert them to periodic timers?

title: Ticket #360: Each regression test should link to a wiki page talking about it
description: There should be a small additional link next to each test name on the test results page which points to a unique page in the gittrac wiki for that logical test. The page will be free form and in general have within it delineations for different branches, if need be. This feature is to allow us to keep track of test issues across branches, across discoverers, and over time. If a problem arises with a test, then a ticket should be made and referenced on the tests page. Something to consider is that the page name must be some unique and algorithmically generated camel case name that follows the rules of the wiki. I recommend whatever mapping we choose the prefix RegTest be placed before it so when we look at all of the nodes on the wiki, it is easily discernable. There are problems with automating wiki word generation from our test names in that gittrac's camel case can't have multiple capitals in a row, or digits in it. The rules we must abide by are here. So, we may have to be very careful in how we map a test name to a wiki page. Once we figure out a good mapping, we should implement the linkage between the php pages and gittrac.

title: Ticket #4157: Daemons on Mac OS X busy-loop accepting bogus connections
description: On the BaTLab macs, we observed large numbers of Condor daemons in a tight loop printing this: DaemonCommandProtocol: TCP connection to failed. This was caused by setting TCP_KEEPALIVE and friends on listening sockets (part of #4122). On OS X, once the modified keepalive interval elapses, the listen socket becomes closed. select() will then always say the fd is ready for reading, but calls to accept() will fail. The fix is to never set the keepalive socket options on a socket that will be used for listening.

title: Ticket #2980: RFC: Unify SPLICE and SUBDAG EXTERNAL in DAGman
description: This is from #2649. I want to solicit some commentary from more knowledgeable sources than I. Could we just get rid of SUBDAG EXTERNAL and SPLICE, and just have SUBDAG? Are people wedded to this notion of having an external DAGman? Idea is to combine the best of both SPLICE and SUBDAG EXTERNAL: Category throttles work across the whole DAGman job When subdag completes, the DAGman contracts the subdag by releasing the memory associated with the nodes. SUBDAGs can have FINAL nodes SUBDAGs can ABORT, etc. SUBDAGS can be lazily created Instead of having many DAGmans to query, we guarantee that there is exactly one DAGman to query. (This is for the oft stated request to have tools that can monitor DAGman status) At least one issue comes up immediately: Do people use a job_status file in a nested dag, without one for the "nesting" dag?
remarks: See also #2166. 2017-May-16 12:40:48 by wenger: Another big thing: sub-DAGs can have retries, and splices can't. 2017-May-16 12:41:54 by wenger: I don't think we should get rid of sub-DAGs entirely, because they can always have scaling benefits if used properly. But I think we should, as much as possible, add features that are currently sub-DAG-only (PRE/POST scripts, retries, etc.) to splices.

title: Ticket #5802: Job Router's JOB_FINALIZE hook has wrong name
description: The hook in the Job Router that's invoked when the routed job completes has different names in the code and the manual. In the code, it's JOB_EXIT. In the manual, it's JOB_FINALIZE. The behavior in the manual appears to be accurate. JOB_EXIT is also a starter hook, though the behavior is different between the two versions. We will make JOB_FINALIZE the official name of the hook. That will minimize confusion about two hooks with the same name but different interfaces. If JOB_FINALIZE isn't set in the config file, we'll look for JOB_EXIT as a fallback, in case any users are relying on the undocumented name from previous versions. This fallback should be removed in a future release.

title: Ticket #5551: Improve classad ingestion performance by presizing hash table
description: When we read a classad off the wire, the first thing we read is how many attributes it will have. The classad implementation stores the set of name-value pairs in a hash table. By default, this hash table is born small, and is resized as attributes are inserted. This resizing can be expensive. By exposing a rehash method, we can tell the classad at birth how many attributes to expect (as least initially). Tests show this improves the speed of classad ingestions almost 10%.

title: Ticket #2294: Schedd crash while asynchronously negotiating or claiming
description: These days the schedd does a host of activities related to a job in the queue asynchronously, such as claiming of startds and negotiating with the central manager. So during the process of claiming or negotiating, the schedd will return to daemon core - what happens if the job being processed is removed while these asynch activities are still in progress? To deal with this possibility, the schedd will typically make a copy of the job classad. Unfortunately, the classad copy constructor and assignment operator does not do a deep copy of chained classads. As a result, if the job is removed from the job queue, any copies of the job ad laying about in various objects dealing w/ asynchronous operations now have an invalid pointer to the deleted cluster ad. Proposed fixes In the v7.6 stable series, invoke ClassAd::ChainCollapse on the copied job ads we stick into these asynch opereation objects. This method copies all the attributes from the chained ad into the ad itself. DONE In the v7.7 developer series, always collapse chained ads into a copy of a job ad (aka in the copy ctor and assignment operator). In other words, make a deep copy of a classad instead of doing a deep copy of most things and a shallow copy of the chained ad. Hopefully this will prevent bugs like the below from being introduced in the future. SEE DERIVED TICKET(S) BELOW Down the road, consider if we ever want to make a copy of job classads in the schedd, or if all of these objects should only have a handle (aka the job id) to the ad. Another idea is take advantage of counted_ptr at either the classad or the qmgmt layers. title: Ticket #1841: Flocking broken under certain conditions post async-schedd merge
description: I found a condition where flocking stops working. It used to be the condition for decreasing the flocking level was this: ( JobsStarted < jobs || JobsRejected > 0 ) This has changed to: satisfied = getNumJobsRejected() == 0 We found that there's at least one condition where getNumJobsRejected() == 0 and flocking should increase: if the negotiator has zero resources: 01/06/11 20:30:52 Phase 4.1: Negotiating with schedds ... 01/06/11 20:30:52 Negotiating with bbockelm@glidein.unl.edu at <129.93.239.145:59940> 01/06/11 20:30:52 0 seconds so far 01/06/11 20:30:52 Reached submitter resource limit: 0.000000 ... stopping I think the original condition should be restored. In our case, the negotiator with 0 resources for the user is at flock level 0; so, whenever that negotiator talks to this schedd, the flock level resets to 0.

title: Ticket #5101: Infinite loop in non-blocking authentication
description: When doing non-blocking authentication, a daemon can go into an infinite loop retrying and failing the same method, quickly eating up all memory with an ever-growing error stack object. The problem occurs in Authentication::authenticate_continue() on the server side of the connection in non-blocking mode. To trigger, a call to handshake() returns "would block" and the subsequent call to the chosen authentication method's authenticate() call returns failure. The next time (and all future times) through the while loop in authenticate_continue(), we don't call handshake() and retry the previous authentication method, which fails because the two sides are now out-of-sync. As the server spins in the loop, it devours memory adding errors to the CondorError object. It appears the infinite loop can be broken if SEC_x_AUTHENTICATION_TIMEOUT is set to something other than "unlimited". The manual states that the default value of SEC_DEFAULT_AUTHENTICATION_TIMEOUT is 20, but the actual default is "unlimited" for both 8.2 and 8.3.

title: Ticket #1904: qedit JobLeaseDuration doesn't work on running jobs.
description: If you change JobLeaseDuration on a running job, the execute side never learns about the update and continues respecting the old JobLeaseDuration. If a user wants to extend leases to cover a scheduled outage, he's out of luck for running jobs. If the submit side ends up with a longer JobLeaseDuration, the job may remain "running" long after the execute side has abandoned it. If the submit side ends up with a shorter JobLeaseDuration, the submit side may return a job to idle and restart it while the execute side keeps running it, violating Condor's promise of only running a job once. Expected behavior: when I qedit the JobLeaseDuration for a job, the execute side should learn about it reasonably promptly. This functionality will help #1903.
creator: adesmet

title: Ticket #1007: cluster optimization (ad chaining) corrupts job ad semantics
description:
The way ad chaining is used during submission is the first job (first queue) in the submit file becomes the cluster and all other jobs are diffs against it. This means attributes only present in the first ad will appear in all others. For instance, $ condor_version $CondorVersion: 7.4.0 Nov 1 2009 BuildID: 193173 $ $CondorPlatform: I386-LINUX_RHEL5 $ $ echo "executable = /bin/sleep
arguments = 150
hold = true
queue
hold = false
queue
" | condor_submitSubmitting job(s).. 2 job(s) submitted to cluster 338. $ condor_q -- Submitter: chopin.cs.wisc.edu : <128.105.121.21:40246> : chopin.cs.wisc.edu ID OWNER SUBMITTED RUN_TIME ST PRI SIZE CMD 338.0 matt 11/30 11:05 0+00:00:00 H 0 97.7 sleep 150 338.1 matt 11/30 11:05 0+00:00:00 I 0 97.7 sleep 150 2 jobs; 1 idle, 0 running, 1 held $ condor_q -l 338.1 | grep Hold NumSystemHolds = 0 HoldReason = "submitted on hold at user's request" HoldReasonCode = 15 PeriodicHold = FALSE OnExitHold = FALSE

title: Ticket #462: upon removal, condor_dagman leaves orphaned jobs

exit and then be removed from the job queue while child jobs are still in the 'X' state. dagman should NEVER leave jobs behind in any state. the reason this is bad is because it is possible for jobs to go from 'X' state to 'H'eld if the removal fails (especially grid universe jobs), thus leaving the orphan job in the queue with no dagman overseeing it. i was able to reproduce this by submitting a dag with 1000 vanilla sleep jobs. run condor_rm on the dag, and then run condor_q in a tight loop and capture the output. you will (maybe) see that dagman has left the queue while child jobs remain in 'X' state. i was able to do this more than once, so it's fairly reproducible. see below. dagman should not exit until all jobs are actually gone. i believe it should do this by watching the job logs and verifying that the remove events (or complete events, since there may be a race here) are written for all jobs before exiting. a separate but related issue is when the remove events actually get written -- when the job goes TO 'X' state or when it actually leaves the queue, but i'm making a separate ticket for that. in any case, waiting for the remove events to be written will help ensure title: Ticket #4655: $(IP_ADDRESS) should [bracket] IPv6 addresses
description: When $(IP_ADDRESS) is expanded, if the address is an IPv6 address, it should have [square brackets] around it, ie [::1]. Anywhere in our configuration file where we might want an automatically determined IP address is a place where it should have square brackets if IPv6 but not is IPv4. For example: COLLECTOR_HOST = $(IP_ADDRESS):0 On an IPv4 machine, COLLECTOR_HOST should look something like "192.168.0.123:0", but on an IPv6 machine it should be something like "[fe80::250:56ff:fec0:1]:0" Currently, the latter is "fe80::250:56ff:fec0:1:0" which is definitely wrong.
