title: Ticket #2152: Introduce multiple concurrent claim activations
description: Motivation Condor needs a way to deal with multiple concurrent claim activations: as things currently stand, we are able to have one Shadow/Starter per claim at a given time. Being able to support more concurrent Shadow/Starter pairs per claim would allow for streamlining input/output transfers, overlapping I/O and execution (see sandbox manager project), or even to run multiple, low-resource jobs at once. Various changes in Startd and Schedd are needed in order to accomodate this. Involved objects Match A match is created by the negotiator between a user's job and a Startd's resource ("slot"). The negotiator informs both the startd and the schedd about the match. In Condor's current startd implementation, the match is manifested as a state ("matched state") in a resource's claim object. The lifetime of a match ends with the expiration of a claim (if a claim takes place), or times out. The scope of this work will not actually affect or modify the matching protocols or data structures. Claim A claim represents a provisioned resource. When a schedd is notified about a match, it typically proceeds to claim the resource. A claim object is maintained by the Schedd and the Startd. It contains information including the claim ID that was generated by the startd and passed to the schedd via the negotiator, and claim lease - a claim expires after a period of time if the lease is not renewed. A startd slot enters the Claimed/Idle state/activity upon being completion of the claiming protocol between the schedd and the startd. Claim activation Once a match has been made and a resource is marked as claimed (aka provisioned), the claim is activated to indicate the instantiation of an activity on the resource. The claim activation protocol is typically initiated by the shadow contacting the startd; upon completion the startd slot is said to be Claimed/Active and the startd spawns a starter to manage the activation. Deactivation of a claim places the startd slot back into Claimed/Idle state. A Startd can still reject the activation if circumstances changed. This would lead to the Schedd relinquishing the claim. In order to make claim activation more explicit (and to allow multiple activations per claim), we propose to implement an activation object containing an activation ID, which will be scoped within a claim ID. An activation without a claim is meaningless. A more detailed description of what is needed within an explicit activation object can be found in the "design" part of this document. Current claim activation protocol The Startd side maintains interleaved claim and resource objects. Each claim object contains a Starter object if the claim is activated. The schedd side maintains a match record for each claim, managing information such as the current state of the claim, a shadow record if the claim is active containing information about a spawned shadow, a copy of the resource ad as sent from the negotiator at match time, address of a matched startd, and a claim id. Relevant for this work is what happens after a resource has been claimed by the Schedd; in other words, we do not propose any changes to the code that manages matching or claiming. Given that the schedd already has a claimed resource and has identified a job it wants to launch on the resource, an the schedd initiates activation as follows: Schedd spawns a Shadow, and passes to the shadow a copy of the job ad augmented with some additional attributes that includes the startd address and the claim ID. Shadow sends a claim activate command to Startd, passing to the startd the claim ID and a copy of the job classad. The startd re-evaluates its policy expressions within the context of the job classad from the shadow and an updated machine ad; if policy decides the resource is no longer available, the Startd rejects the activation request, the Shadow shuts down, and Schedd relinquishes the claim. If Startd is will to activate the claim, it forks off a Starter to run the job, and passes the tcp socket initiated by the shadow to the starter. Thus the starter is born with a tcp socket connected back to the shadow. Once the jobs's execution and output data transfer are completed, the Starter sends the final update to the Shadow. The shadow then updates the final information in the job queue, and sends a deactivate command to the startd, resulting in the startd telling the starter to shutdown. While the job is running, the starter is sending update classads containing run-time information to both the shadow (for job policy enforcement) and the startd (so machine policy can refer to updated job attributes such as ImageSize). Starter exit triggers the Startd to change claim/resource state into CLAIMED/IDLE Shadow exit triggers match record update in Schedd Schedd tries to find next matching job for claim and spawns the next Shadow (which leads to the next activation) If no new job for claim can be found, the schedd tells the startd that the claim is relinquished, match record in Schedd deleted, and claim object in Startd destroyed. Proposed Design In this section we describe the proposed design changes in Startd and Schedd with associated objects to facilitate concurrent claim activations. The overall high-level change is the introduction of an explicit activation object, scoped and owned by the claim object. As before, there will be one shadow/starter instance pair per activation - but now a single claim may have X simultaneous shadow/starter pairs. With regards to startd policy, all policy expressions will continue to operate at the claim level, not at the individual activation level. However, we propose one circuit breaker startd enforced limit on the number of activations allowed per claim as a property that can be set per slot. Activation object The activation object needs to contain a unique ID (only needs to be unique within claim) and a field for a Starter sinful string, which is currently maintained by the claim object. We propose the activation ID will be the current public-part of the claim ID with an additional field appended - this will minimize code disruption and assist in backwards compatibility. Changes to the Startd While in state CLAIMED/RUNNING, the Startd must be able to accept further activations on a claim. In the startd, a Resource Claim object contains a Starter object and is responsible for activating a claim, managing a condor_starter, etc. Therefore, the Claim object needs to maintain a set of Activation objects. When a shadow is spawned, the schedd will generate an activation ID and pass it along to the shadow in the same manner as the claim ID. Requests from the shadow to the startd for activation (job launch) and deactivation (e.g. job held, removed, completed) need to include an activation ID, such that the appropriate Starter can be addressed. Activation does not necessarily imply spawning of a Starter but can and in the common case will. The activation object therefore maintains the activation ID and a Starter sinful string (may be NULL) Functions that address Starter object (such as Claim::setStarter or Claim::spawnStarter) will need to accept the activation ID as an additional argument - should default to 0 for backwards compatibility It may make sense to introduce a new startd RPC to deactivate all activations associated with a claim: this would be an iteration over all activations. Note that the process of vacating, suspending, continuing jobs would become an iteration over all activations, as startd policy expression always operate at the claim level. Starters advertise information back to both the shadow and the Startd. For update ads sent back to the startd, it will be the Startd's responsibility to aggregate that information across all starters associated with the same claim. Optionally, we may consider the startd advertising non-aggregated activation-specific information as well, perhaps by leveraging nested classads. Open issue: startd job hooks... we should allow job hooks to have multiple activations, but in terms of development milestones, we hope to postpone exposure of multi-activations to job hooks as future work. Part of our concern is we do not want to perturb the existing job hook API, as changing the API could cause hardship for clients. Advantage: Starter remains unchanged, no new object is introduced Disadvantage: Claim object needs to be extended by a list of activation objects, Startd behavior on claim activation/deactivation needs to be adjusted Other possible approaches and motivation for chosen design 1) Modify the startd to support an array of starters. In this case, the starter changes very little if at all, and the startd changes only to support managing and signalling multiple starters. There is exactly one activation per starter, but potentially multiple starters per claim. 2) Modify the starter to support an array of activations. Here, there would be one starter per claim, and it would track the activations internally. There already exists this concept in the starter, but none of the existing code uses it. 3) Introduce a new daemon between the startd and starter(s) that manages the activations for a given claim. Here there would again be one starter per activation, all under the new daemon which represents a claim to the startd. This daemon would manage and the starters. in all options, changes are needed to the startd (or more specifically, the Claim object) to accomodate multiple activations, reconnect, signalling all and/or specific activations, and combining the resources used into one set of resources so that policy enforcement can be applied at the claim level. in option 2, more changes are needed to the starter in addition to the above, and in option 3 an entirely new daemon would be created. given that, it seems that option 1 requires changing fewer components in the condor system as a whole and leaves the starter largely untouched.

title: Ticket #2502: condor_startd doesn't start in old batlab
description: After 7.7.2 was installed in old batlab the master couldn't start the startd with error code 127. strace didn't show any interesting output, and hung in the "T" state . Here's what is going one. 1) strace -ff doesn't work with our clone usage. set the condor_config knob USE_CLONE_TO_CREATE_PROCESSES= false to allow strace to follow the master's children. 2) After that, we see that the start can't find the shared library libclassad.so.2. Interesting, the token '$ORIGIN' is unexpanded in the open calls in the strace output 3) The ld.so docs say that $ORIGIN isn't expanded for setuid binaries. But, I hear you cry, neither the startd nor the master is setuid. In turns out that what determines it was "setuid", is if the euid != ruid. What the docs don't mention is that the program is also considered setuid if the egid != rgid. Note that this problem does not manifest in the test suite, because that's not run as root. Nor does it manifest in new batlab or CHTC, because they use native packages, and the shared libraries get plonked down in /usr/lib64, the default path. 4) Running a test program under the master shows that binaries spawned by the master have ruid == euid == 0, but rgid = 0 and egid = condor. 5) After further review, set_priv(PRIV_ROOT) inexplicably doen't set the gid. In this ticket, I'm going to have set_priv(PRIV_ROOT) also setegid(root). Note this is a pretty fundamental change, and I'm somewhat worried that some other code (NFS root squash?) may depend on this, but we just don't know.
remarks: 2011-Sep-26 17:18:53 by bbockelm: Hi Greg, There's already some specializations of set_priv for Create_Process. Is there a harm in doing further abuse there? This way, the changes only apply to post-fork and pre-exec. Or, at least, only do this for PRIV_ROOT_FINAL? Note about the CLONE issue: there's a patch floating around in gittrac to make Condor's clone usage compatible with gdb. I'd be curious if it works for strace also. Unfortunately, I never got it committed. Brian 2011-Sep-26 23:41:09 by gthain: Is there a PRIV_ROOT_FINAL? What would that mean? I think this is the right place, otherwise, switching to PRIV_ROOT leaves the egid in some random state. 2011-Sep-30 14:39:56 by gthain: Todd: should we cherry-pick this back to 7.6? 2011-Oct-12 10:29:31 by jfrey: This bug is caused by changes for tickets #1135, #2389 and #2390 and is only a problem for tarball releases of Condor. Even with this fix, upgrading from pre-7.7.2 to 7.7.2+ by replacing the binaries will lead to the master exiting, as it fails to re-exec itself. There's no good solution to this problem. We need to put a note in the version history. This argues strongly for back-porting this fix to 7.6. Then, people upgrading from 7.6 to 7.8 won't have the disappearing master problem. 2011-Oct-17 14:48:16 by jfrey: I've looked over the places we call set_root_priv() and believe there's very little risk of things failing if the egid changes to 0. dprintf() always changes to condor priv to access the daemon logs. For other files that are accessed, the code is switching to root so that it can access them securely (i.e. the files should be restricted to root-only write and possibly root-only read). 2011-Oct-17 16:10:37 by jfrey: I've cherry-picked this fix back to V7_6_4-branch. Thus, users upgrading from 7.6.4+ to 7.7.2+ or 7.8.x won't suffer the disappearing master problem.

title: Ticket #7700: NETWORK_INTERFACE=* should choose reverse DNS
description: A user contacted us to report problems is their dual-NIC machines left NETWORK_INTERFACES set to its default value of '*'. Their machines have interfaces bond0, bond1, and lo0, where bond0 and bond1 are both private network addresses. Between two private network addresses, HTCondor always chooses the first one listed. This caused problems for match password authentication, where the starter and the shadow were communicating over the second NIC; it's not clear why. While in general we can't choose between private addresses, in this case, the machines' names resolve to the bond1, and this problem could have been avoided. This heuristic should probably only be used to break ties.

title: Ticket #3743: condor_q -dag doesn't use a projection to query job ads

title: Ticket #4439: $$ macros don't work in transfer_input_files
description: Using $$ macros in transfer_input_files (e.g. transfer_input_files = x_$$(OpSys).zip) fails, because condor_submit tries to open the input file to check that it exists at submit time (obviously before the macro substitution happens). It looks like you can work around this by having a file literally named "x_$$(OpSys).zip" (or whatever) that exists at submit time, but I don't think you should have to do that.
remarks: 2014-Jul-10 15:22:14 by wenger: This also applies somewhat to log files, output files, etc. -- condor_submit creates them without resolving the macro, and then they get re-created with the "real" filename.
creator: wenger

title: Ticket #3606: Batch VM requests.
description: Tony Tiradani writes: Could we add the ability to request N number of VMs in one request for the EC2 universe? Currently, if I want 100 VMs, HTCondor will iterate through and make 100 requests. Additionally, if I understand things correctly, it will then perform 100 EC2DescribeInstances calls. If HTCondor will make one call for 100 VMs, then only make one EC2DescribeInstances call, this will dramatically reduce the load on OpenStack Cloud controllers.
remarks: 2013-May-02 09:14:15 by tlmiller: The 100 status requests occur because we still ask about a job individually when its state changes. There are two potential work-arounds: first, set the state of the job when we create it to its initial state ('pending', IIRC; possibly 'pending evaluation' for Spot); or second, adjusting the batch update code so that we can obtain and distribute all the information we would obtain via our single-instance query, thereby obviating the need for single-intance queries (and removing them entirely, rather than avoiding making them). 2013-May-02 09:32:58 by tlmiller: I need to investigate how multiple-instance requests interact with idempotence and recovery, especially since requesting 100 VMs may get you any number of them, up to 100. (If we crash after sending a multiple-instance request but before cramming the instance IDs into the queue, how do we know how many there are supposed to be?) Also, to preserve our usual semantics, we may end up needing to implement this an optimization within the EC2 GAHP and/or the grid manager (e.g., one submit per cluster); recognizing this opportunity is its own problem. (Also, if we require a minimum of 100 VMs as well as a maximum, the queue won't be behaving properly if fewer than that are available.) 2014-Feb-18 11:25:18 by tlmiller: One implementation possibility is to handle client token creation and RunInstances() batching in the resource. Thus: - Instead of unconditionally generating a new client token, each job object asks its resource for a client token, passing the same set of arguments along that it would to the GAHP to run its instance. - We treat this call as if it were a GAHP client call -- we come back some time later and call it again to find out if the resource has generated a client token for us. - The resource pauses for a few seconds to wait for identical instance requests to enter the queue and ask for a client token. Identical requests all get the same client token, and the resource records how many did. Once every job has called back (and reduced the outstanding total to 0), the resource will issue a batched command with the appropriate number. - Jobs which get a client token back will then block in GM_START, waiting for a batch status update. Otherwise, they will create their own client token (in the appropriate state) and proceed normally. - When RunInstances() returns, the resource will hand out instance IDs in an arbitrary order. If it didn't get enough, it will assign NULL instance IDs. If a job blocked in GM_START gets a NULL instance ID, it returns to GM_SAVE_CLIENT_TOKEN. This allows for a second batch request to be issued; it may instead be preferable to set a flag which forces it to generate a new client token immediately (or block in GM_SAVE_CLIENT_TOKEN instead of GM_START, although that has odd semantics). - Recovery is the tricky problem here. We will have n jobs sharing a single client token, some j of which will not have instance IDs, some k of which will not be getting instance IDs. However, I think the same process as the previous point will suffice: jobs with instance IDs will retain them, and some j arbitrary job in the set will get instance IDs, and the other k will issue new requests. Because the VMs are identical and we have no other information about them, it's OK for the job ID to "change" during recovery, because we don't remember anything about it. 2016-May-26 14:37:51 by tlmiller: See ticket #5691.

title: Ticket #7491: Interactive negotiator in CHTC slower than expected
description: In CHTC, we wanted interactive and build jobs to start executing quickly. We have a set of execute machines dedicated to these jobs, but the normal negotiation process was taking much longer than desired (multiple minutes instead of ~5 seconds). To improve this, we tried adding a second, "interactive", negotiator that only matches interactive/build jobs to their dedicate slots. Details can be read in RT #99072. Issues With the new negotiator, it still took over a minute for interactive jobs to start executing. Investigation revealed several problems: The Spalding lab's schedd was firewalled, causing repeated 30-second failed attempts to connect. This affected both negotiators. The interactive negotiator often didn't receive a RESCHEDULE command when new jobs were submitted. Thus, it often waited the standard 60 seconds between negotiation cycles. This is due to code in the schedd that sends the RESCHEDULE to one negotiator, not expecting that there could be multiple negotiators. Improvements The following changes in configuration and code may be considered to improve the performance of the interactive negotiator. Ban the Spalding submit machine until firewall issues can be resolved. DONE Configure a separate collector for the interactive negotiator and have only CHTC schedds flock to it. IN PROGRESS Add new option in the negotiator to constrain the submitter ads it fetches. #7490 Once #7490 is deployed, have interactive negotiator only pull submitter ads from CHTC schedds. Maybe implement way for submitter ads to indicate that they have interactive jobs, for further filtering. Change NEGOTIATOR_CYCLE_DELAY and possibly NEGOTIATOR_INTERVAL to 5 seconds. Change negotiator to do non-blocking connections to schedds during the prefetch phase.
creator: jfrey

title: Ticket #3981: Job running with PID namespace don't get SIGQUIT, reaping
description: When USE_PID_NAMESPACES=true, the job because pid 1, and starts to behave like init. In particular, if it doesn't install a signal handler for SIGQUIT, no process, regardless of uid, can send it the SIGQUIT signal. As a result, most jobs condor_rm'd will wait until the killing timeout to actually timeout. Also, the job will become the parent of any descendant processes who lose their parents, and this pseudo init must also reap them, or them become zombies. To fix this problem, we will put a mini-init wrapper between the job and the starter that handles signals and reaps needed children, but only when USE_PID_NAMESPACES = true

title: Ticket #2739: condor_chirp closes the same FD twice - Asserts on Windows
description: When condor_chirp opens a socket to the starter, it then uses fdopen twice on the same socket handle to get a "r" and "w" stream. This works, but after the command completes it tries to fclose() each stream. The windows version of the c-runtime treats the seconds fclose() as an error because the underlying socket handle was closed by the first fclose, thus condor_chirp always returns a non-zero error code on Windows. This seems to be a case of wrong code that is relatively harmless, which Linux ignores and Windows treats as an error.

title: Ticket #5506: More efficient updates of parent collector in a collector tree
description: The CMS global pool central manager consists of a collector tree. In Feb 2016, we observed the parent in the collector tree was unable to ingest ClassAds forwarded from the child collectors at a fast enough rate; the receive UDP buffer on the parent collector was full and the thus the parent collector is dropping ads. Traditionally, whenever an ad was updated in a child collector, it would be immediately forwarded to the parent collector. As a quick interim measure, this patch introduces two knobs to limit when a child collector will forward Startd ads to a parent collector to just two conditions: FORWARD_INTERVAL an integer representing seconds; if an update for an ad arrives at a child collector and this ad has not been forwarded to the parent collector for more than FORWARD_INTERVAL seconds, the ad is forwarded. If you set this knob to 0, you should get the same behavior as before this patch (i.e. every update gets immediately forwaded). FORWARD_WATCH_LIST a string list of classad attributes. If an update arriving at a child collector changes the value of any of the attributes listed in this knob, then the ad is forwarded to the parent collector. Defaults to State,Cpus,Memory. Note that all other ads besides startd ads (e.g. startdprivate ads, submitter ads, etc) are still always immediately forwarded. By only forwarding startd ads periodically or that only change their State, Cpus, or Memory value, we should reduce the number of ads sent to the parent collector. For instance, the startd sends an update for all slot ads whenever the Activity changes, which means without this patch the parent collector could be flooded with startd ads if a user were to submit a large batch of short running jobs.

title: Ticket #1545: Grid-type amazon can't submit to Eucalyptus
description: Eucalyptus provides an EC2 interface. Thus, Condor-G should be able to interact with it via the amazon grid-type. However, several minor issues prevent this from working. We're working with Brian Bockelman and others to get Condor to interact with the Magellan cluster at ANL (which uses Eucalyptus). Tasks Make SSL hostname check optional [DONE] Update to newer EC2 WSDL [DONE] Remove assumptions about image and instance names [DONE] Fix SSL token names [DONE] GSOAP SSL changes The service credential for Magellan is a self-signed host certificate with a hostname of 'localhost'. This causes authentication to fail, as that doesn't match the name used by the amazon_gahp to connect to the server. This appears to be a default setup for Eucalyptus. To make interacting with such systems easier, we're adding a config parameter, SOAP_SSL_SKIP_HOST_CHECK. If set to True, then the amazon_gahp will instruct gsoap to skip the server hostname check. The default is False. Brian Bockelman informs us that one of the security tokens in our soap messages has the wrong value. He suggests changing the call soap_wsse_add_BinarySecurityTokenX509(m_soap, "BinarySecurityToken", m_cert)) to soap_wsse_add_BinarySecurityTokenX509(m_soap, "X509Token", m_cert)). WSDL Update Condor is using an old revision of the EC2 WSDL, dated 2007-08-29. Brian Bockelman found that using that version doesn't work with Eucalyptus, but using the version from 2008-12-01 does. The differences are minor for the portions that Condor uses. Naming Assumptions The amazon_gahp checks whether image and instance ids match a particular pattern that Amazon's EC2 service is known to adhere to. Specifically, that image ids start with "ami-" and instance ids start with "i-". These patterns aren't part of the EC2 specificatoin, and Eucalyptus doesn't follow them. The checks should be removed.

title: Ticket #6280: starter incorrectly sets JobStartDate to the current job start time
description: G-RESEARCH was trying to calculate the time a job spent waiting in the queue before it first began to run, and was using the expression JobstartDate - QDate. This should work, since JobStartDate is documented to be the time the job first starts (set by the Schedd to the shadow birthdate when the job doesn't yet have a JobStartDate). But the Starter is sending a value for JobStartDate with each update ad to the shadow, and it is setting the value to the time that it called create_process, and not paying any attention to the current value. The result is that sometime after the job begins running, or when the job is placed on hold, the value of JobStartDate changes. This is clearly wrong, but it is likely that there are users that have Startd policy expressions that depend on having JobStartDate be the start time of the current run. So the fix for the stable series is to have the shadow filter JobStartDate out of the update ad before procesing it. This will result in the Schedd and the user seeing what it expects to see. In the development version, we should also change the Starter to set JobCurrentStartDate or even some new attribute where is now tries to set JobStartDate

title: Ticket #5855: Move decision about shared port endpoint creation into daemon core.
description: Right now, daemon core daemons will create shared port endpoints if USE_SHARED_PORT is set, even if the master decided not to let them inherit a shared point endpoint. Ticket #5769 changed the shared point endpoint code to check <SUBSYS>_USE_SHARED_PORT before USE_SHARED_PORT, but this doesn't really address the problem, which is that the daemon itself should know if it needs special shared-port handling, and unless it's special, should respect what the master has decided its command sockets should be. This logic will be complicated by our support for running the daemons without a master. At any rate, while it might make sense to further modify the master to also support <SUBSYS>_USE_SHARED_PORT (or maybe <DAEMON_NAME>_USE_SHARED_PORT?), it seems like we'd be better off letting the HAD and REPLICATION daemons declare as a special exception to the general rule, that they will respect [HAD|REPLICATION]_USE_SHARED_PORT instead of USE_SHARED_PORT (because their configuration changes quite a bit when they use shared port).

title: Ticket #3082: memory leak in classad functions returing lists
description: Brian observed that his custom classad function that evaluates to a newly allocated ExprList leaks memory, because the caller does not free the list. We believe this problem affects the existing classad functions splitUserName and splitSlotName.
remarks: 2012-Jun-22 15:17:07 by danb: I confirmed that splitSlotName leaks memory. Example: valgrind --leak-check=full condor_status -f "%d\n" 'isList(splitSlotName(Name))' ==9519== 192 (48 direct, 144 indirect) bytes in 1 blocks are definitely lost in loss record 1,109 of 1,209 ==9519== at 0x10003C679: malloc (vg_replace_malloc.c:266) ==9519== by 0x1012C0F04: operator new(unsigned long) (in /usr/lib/libstdc++.6.0.9.dylib) ==9519== by 0x1000B4859: compat_classad::splitAt_func(char const*, std::vector<classad::ExprTree*, std::allocator<classad::ExprTree*> > const&, classad::EvalState&, classad::Value&) (in /Users/danb/condor/CONDOR_SRC/release_dir/lib/libcondor_utils_7_9_0.dylib) ==9519== by 0x10077426D: classad::FunctionCall::_Evaluate(classad::EvalState&, classad::Value&) const (in /Users/danb/condor/CONDOR_SRC/release_dir/lib/libclassad.7.9.0.dylib) 2012-Jun-29 16:11:33 by danb: I believe the way the classad library was intended to work is that functions generating new lists would insert them into the EvalState object's list of things to delete. In Value::_Clear() I see this comment: case LIST_VALUE: // list values live in the evaluation environment, so they must // never be explicitly destroyed However, the EvalState class has a comment-out member variable cache_to_delete, so apparently this is not completely implemented. It is also wouldn't work in the general case without changing the classad Evaluate() interface. Currently, the EvalState object is created in the local scope within Evaluate(). Having it clean up before returning to the caller would be appropriate for deleting temporary lists, but it would not be appropriate if the list itself is being returned to the caller. In other words, it would be fine for matchmaking (where only boolean values are returned to the caller), but not for the general case. Everything that we have discovered about lists is also probably true for classad values. A new classad generated by a classad function would be leaked. 2012-Jul-12 13:58:01 by danb: I decided to fix this problem by using a shared_ptr<ExprList> in the classad Value object so that the Value object can share ownership of a list. There were two options in how to do this. I chose the second one: All lists in Value objects are set via a shared_ptr. Lists may be set via a raw pointer or a shared_ptr. In case of a raw pointer, the old semantics are retained: the Value object does not own the list. The problem with the first option is that it escalates into requiring all ExprTree objects within classad data structures to be owned via shared_ptr. This also impacts the public interface of the classad library. It could impact memory usage and performance as well. I did not want to make such a big change without more careful examination and a better motivation. Such a sweeping change is certainly not warranted just to fix this obscure memory leak. A similar patch could be made to handle dynamic ClassAd values in Value objects. I did not do this, because there is currently no need for it. If the need arises, it should be obvious what to do. 2012-Jul-13 15:17:52 by danb: I removed two methods from the public classad interface: EvaluateAttrList() and EvaluateAttrClassAd(). These both return a raw pointer to the caller but do not pass ownership to the caller. This is problematic for values that are dynamically allocated during the expression evaluation. When the Value that has a shared_ptr to the object goes out of scope, the dynamically allocated object gets deleted, and a pointer to deleted memory is returned to the caller. One reasonable solution would be to return a shared_ptr as obtained, for example, by Value::IsSListValue(). In the current implementation of classads, if the value contains a raw pointer to a list, this causes a copy of the list to be made, so that ownership can be given to the shared_ptr. In the future, it may be that all values contain shared_ptrs, so no copying would be required. Since the interface is not used in Condor (not sure about outside Condor), I chose to comment it out rather than upgrade it to a shared_ptr. EvaluateAttr() can be used instead. This avoids the need for copying the underlying object in order to fit it into a shared_ptr, because the Value lives in the caller's scope.

title: Ticket #1115: Remove Target scope from EvalBool() in new ClassAds
description: The free-standing function EvalBool() takes a ClassAd and an unparsed expression string, and returns true if the parsed expression evaluates to True. One of its oddities is that it uses the ClassAd as the target scope of the evaluation and no ad for for the local scope. Most callers use expressions with no 'Target' scope for the attribute references, which works fine in old ClassAds, but not new ClassAds. In the new ClassAds compatibility layer, we will change EvalBool() to use the provided ClassAd as the local evaluation scope and have no target scope. For the few cases where an expression may have a 'Target' scope (older condor_q querying a newer schedd), EvalBool() will call the new RemoveExplicitTargetRefs() to strip off the 'Target' scoping. The old ClassAds version of EvalBool should be left alone.

title: Ticket #120: Crondor jobs spam ScheddLog with "Requirements attribute...evaluated"
description: The "Crondor" functionality works, in part, by manipulating the Requirements expression for a job. So you might end up with something like this: Requirements = (Arch == "INTEL") && (OpSys == "LINUX") && (Disk >= DiskUsage) && ((Memory * 1024) >= ImageSize) && (((CurrentTime + ScheddInterval) >= (DeferralTime - DeferralPrepTime)) && (CurrentTime < (DeferralTime + DeferralWindow))) If the job is a local universe job, these will be periodically evaluated. When the job doesn't run (because its time hasn't come yet), you'll get log messages like this: 10/22 17:47:01 (pid:29249) The Requirements attribute for job 706.0 evaluated to false. Unable to start job If you've got a few dozen Crondor jobs, each spraying this message every few minutes, your ScheddLog because hard to read, is full of scary things that you should ignore, and causes teh log to rotate unnecessarily. Expected behavior: No log messages by default. Proposed change: schedd.C lin 5967, change D_ALWAYS to D_FULLDEBUG. Possible complications: This code handles all local universe jobs, not just Crondor. For "normal" local universe jobs, having Requirements evaluate to false may be problematic and worth logging; there is no other obvious place where the information is captured. (Imported from 1698 (backup) 1698 (public))

title: Ticket #5910: GSI credential map callout caching problem
description: CERN has encountered a problem whereby one HTCondor-CE server that is setup to use a GSI credential map callout cache via config knob GSS_ASSIST_GRIDMAP_CACHE_EXPIRATION (see #4138) is occasionally returning the wrong values from the cache. The result is GSI cert DN's get mapped to the wrong user! Very strangely, is this is only happening on one of three CE servers; doing a dump between the misbehaving CE and the other two behaving CEs show no config diffs barring the obvious hostname ones. Even setting the cache expiration to just 10 minutes results in faulty mapping on this one CE; disabling it completely (setting the expiration time to 0) eliminates the problem. BrianB at one point suggested that there could be a stuck sec session grid-manager side. I know they've had their condor restarted when the selection exprs change was made. Even though this is happening on just one CE and cannot be reproduced at this time, with the increasing deployments and interest in HTCondor-CE and the fact the result is an incorrect credential mapping, we should understand what is going on.
remarks: 2016-Sep-20 21:55:45 by bbockelm: Poking through the code: I can confirm that the hash key is based on the credential used for the GSI auth. The hash key is formed from the concatenation of the DN and the VOMS attributes, provided USE_VOMS_ATTRIBUTES is set to true (default). I don't see USE_VOMS_ATTRIBUTES being overridden anywhere at CERN. The code used to form the hash key (in extract_VOMS_info) is extremely scary-looking pointer arithmetic. I'm unable to determine its correctness without much more time spent. One theory is that the same condor_c_worker_thread process is being used to submit two jobs that have different VOMS roles. The theory doesn't seem very likely: we are pretty sure we got the submit side to make that change. Further, it doesn't explain why only one CE is affected. Another theory is that VOMS validation is failing on the "broken CE". This would cause the VOMS library to return zero attributes, then causing both jobs to be mapped to the same hash key, hence the same user. A third theory is there's some incorrect usage of the hash map that is only "slightly wrong" - memory management issues that only hit one CE. Rare, but not implausible. 2016-Sep-20 22:02:12 by bbockelm: Oh! Indeed - one of the three CEs has an empty /etc/grid-security/vomsdir. That means the VOMS role isn't validated, hence it's not included in the hash key for the credential cache. So any credential with the same DN - regardless of the VOMS role - will get mapped to the same username.

title: Ticket #7887: Questions about condor 8.9.8 and Token Authentication
description: On a test cluster at LIGO Hanford Observatory with a condor host, submit host, and a node (xcondor, xpcdev1, and xnode1 respectively) we are running condor 8.9.8 and I am testing Token Authentication. While I can get it to work, I'm having trouble setting up Authentication/Authorization to allow a user to submit from the submit host without a token. My hope is to allow a user logged onto xpcdev1 to use FS Authentication to run condor_submit. I also run into a few other questions while trying to set this up. 1. Here's what I've done: i. Based on the SEC settings for Token Authentication given here, https://htcondor.readthedocs.io/en/latest/admin-manual/security.html#token-authentication and the example ALLOW settings for user-based Authorization given here, https://htcondor.readthedocs.io/en/latest/admin-manual/security.html#example-of-authorization-security-configuration and the condor_token_request_auto_approve command given here, https://htcondor.readthedocs.io/en/latest/admin-manual/security.html#quick-configuration-of-security on the test cluster, xcondor, xpcdev1, and xnode1 at LIGO Hanford, I installed this config file: [root@xcondor ~]# cat /etc/condor/config.d/50-test-security SEC_NEGOTIATOR_AUTHENTICATION_METHODS = IDTOKENS SEC_COLLECTOR_AUTHENTICATION_METHODS = IDTOKENS SEC_DAEMON_AUTHENTICATION_METHODS = IDTOKENS SEC_DEFAULT_AUTHENTICATION_METHODS= IDTOKENS SEC_CLIENT_AUTHENTICATION_METHODS = IDTOKENS ALLOW_READ = *@dcs.ligo-wa.caltech.edu/* ALLOW_WRITE = *@dcs.ligo-wa.caltech.edu/*.dcs.ligo-wa.caltech.edu ALLOW_ADMINISTRATOR = condor@dcs.ligo-wa.caltech.edu/xcondor.dcs.ligo-wa.caltech.edu ALLOW_CONFIG = condor@dcs.ligo-wa.caltech.edu/xcondor.dcs.ligo-wa.caltech.edu ALLOW_NEGOTIATOR = condor@dcs.ligo-wa.caltech.edu/xcondor.dcs.ligo-wa.caltech.edu ALLOW_DAEMON = condor@dcs.ligo-wa.caltech.edu/*.dcs.ligo-wa.caltech.edu #ALL_DEBUG = D_CAT D_ALL:2 D_SECURITY ALL_DEBUG = D_SECURITY ii. However, probably not surprisingly, this failed on xcondor: [root@xcondor ~]# condor_token_request_auto_approve -netblock 10.21.199.0/24 -lifetime 3600 iii. If I create a token: [root@xcondor ~]# condor_token_create -identity root@dcs.ligo-wa.caltech.edu and install it in, ~/.condor/tokens.d/token then it still fails, [root@xcondor ~]# condor_token_request_auto_approve -netblock 10.21.199.0/24 -lifetime 3600 Failed to create new auto-approval rule: SECMAN:2010:Received "DENIED" from server for user condor_pool@ using method IDTOKENS. iv. However, in /etc/condor/config.d/50-test-security, if I change, SEC_CLIENT_AUTHENTICATION_METHODS = IDTOKENS to SEC_CLIENT_AUTHENTICATION_METHODS = FS, IDTOKENS then it works, [root@xcondor ~]# condor_token_request_auto_approve -netblock 10.21.199.0/24 -lifetime 3600 Successfully installed auto-approval rule for netblock 10.21.199.0/24 with lifetime of 1.00 hours Remote daemon reports no un-approved requests pending. Cool! I wanted to use FS to Authenticate in any case, when running condor admin commands as root on a host. v. But on xpcdev1 as root, if I change, SEC_CLIENT_AUTHENTICATION_METHODS = IDTOKENS to SEC_CLIENT_AUTHENTICATION_METHODS = FS, IDTOKENS and become user gregory.mendell, then these fail: -bash-4.2$ condor_q -debug 10/13/20 16:33:26 Can't open directory "/etc/condor/passwords.d" as PRIV_UNKNOWN, errno: 13 (Permission denied) 10/13/20 16:33:26 SECMAN: required authentication with schedd at <10.21.199.11:9618> failed, so aborting command QUERY_JOB_ADS_WITH_AUTH. -- Failed to fetch ads from: <10.21.199.11:9618?addrs=10.21.199.11-9618&alias=xpcdev1.dcs.ligo-wa.caltech.edu&noUDP&sock=schedd_576483_f778> : xpcdev1.dcs.ligo-wa.caltech.edu AUTHENTICATE:1003:Failed to authenticate with any method -bash-4.2$ cd public_html/testosg/localtest/ -bash-4.2$ condor_submit localhelloworld.sub Submitting job(s) ERROR: Failed to connect to local queue manager AUTHENTICATE:1003:Failed to authenticate with any method However, if I create a token for myself, [root@xcondor ~]# condor_token_create -identity gregory.mendell@xcondor and install it in ~/.condor/tokens.d/token under my home directory on xpcdev1 then condor_q and condor_submit work! That's nice. But here's my question: How can I get condor_q and condor_submit to work for myself (or any user) who in on the submit host (xpcdev1 for this test) without having to issue a token for user? 2. After trying the above I also changed, SEC_DEFAULT_AUTHENTICATION_METHODS= IDTOKENS to SEC_DEFAULT_AUTHENTICATION_METHODS= FS, IDTOKENS This seemed to allow condor submit as user gregory.mendell on xpcdev1 to work without a token. But two things still didn't work: i. Without a token, condor_status fails: -bash-4.2$ condor_status Error: communication error AUTHENTICATE:1003:Failed to authenticate with any method AUTHENTICATE:1004:Failed to authenticate using FS This probably makes sense, since authentication with the Collector on xcondor will fail without a token. ii. While condor_submit did work without a token, using FS authentication, the job never ran. So far I have been unsuccessful in finding authentication setting that allow user gregory.mendell on xpcdev1 submit jobs and have them run, without a token. 3. A couple of other things I've noticed, i. When condor was installed it created this file, [root@xcondor ~]# ls -l /etc/condor/passwords.d/POOL -rw------- 1 root root 64 Sep 30 10:06 /etc/condor/passwords.d/POOL It belongs to root, and when things fail, as above, one sees: Can't open directory "/etc/condor/passwords.d" as PRIV_UNKNOWN, errno: 13 (Permission denied) ii. Also, I had to copy /etc/condor/passwords.d/POOL from xcondor to xpcdev1 and xnode1 to get things to work. iii. Finally, this directory, which belongs to condor, [root@xpcdev1 ~]# ls -ld /etc/condor/tokens.d/ drwx------ 2 condor condor 6 Jul 30 17:01 /etc/condor/tokens.d/ [root@xpcdev1 ~]# ls -l /etc/condor/tokens.d/ total 0 is always empty. I'm not sure if i-iii above are expected or not. I thought tokens would show up in /etc/condor/tokens.d/ for daemon to daemon authentication. But maybe I misunderstood the documentation. Thanks for your help!

title: Ticket #6795: "FROM INSTANCE" credentials should be cached
description: We don't currently cache the security credentials obtained from the instance meta-data server. This is particularly egregious because we're already fetching the expiration for these temporary credentials but not actually using it for anything. (AWS recommends renewing the credentials >15 minutes before the expire.) For simplicity (and probably, correctness), the cache should be in memory and per-GAHP; if a GAHP terminates from idleness before the cache expires, we're clearly not issuing so many commands that fetching the credentials again will be a problem.
creator: tlmiller

title: Ticket #1050: Add details to dynamic startd provisioning documentation
description: http://www.cs.wisc.edu/condor/manual/v7.4/2_5Submitting_Job.html#2762 request_memory = <quantity> For pools that enable dynamic condor_startd provisioning (see section 3.13.9), the amount of memory space requested for this job. It should be noted that the units are MB.
remarks: Add links from section 3.13.9.9 to Appendix A for machine attributes PartitionableSlot and DynamicSlot. (merged in from ticket #1051). It should be mentioned that the default for request_cpu is 1, the default for request_disk is the attribute DiskUsage, and the default for request_memory is based on ImageSize or JobVMMemory. (merged in from ticket #1053). 2009-Dec-14 12:43:47 by smoler: request_disk is done in Kbytes. If dynamic provisioning is enabled for the slot, and this submit command is not specified, then for non-vm-universe jobs, it defaults (for the initial value of the job attribute DiskUsage) to the size of the executable plus the sum of input file sizes. For vm-universe, it defaults to the size of the disk image. 2009-Dec-14 13:18:16 by smoler: request_memory is in Mbytes. It sets an intial value for ImageSize if specified (for non-vm-universe jobs). If not specified, initial value of ImageSize is the size of the executable. For vm universe jobs, ImageSize is set by the submit cmd vm_memory, and if not specified ImageSize is initialized to 0. For the case of a vm universe job that (incorrectly) has both request_memory and vm_memory set, the value given by vm_memory is used.

title: Ticket #5013: SHARED_PORT_PORT = 0 doesn't work.
description: The following configuration doesn't start this-machine's shared port daemon on a randomly-chosen port. Instead, the schedd dies immediately when trying to send its keepalive to the master, which continuously restarts it. COLLECTOR_HOST = some-other-machine USE_SHARED_PORT = TRUE SHARED_PORT_PORT = 0 The problem is that port 0 is interpreted by CreateProcess() as meaning "no command port" (port 1 or -1 means choose randomly), and if the port is configured via SHARED_PORT_PORT (or COLLECTOR_PORT), this conversion is not performed. This probably doesn't matter for other daemons; I think their default port number is already 0.

title: Ticket #4481: Add a STARTD authorization for the schedd
description: When MATCH auth fails (reasons not yet determined) for the startd's RELEASE_CLAIM, the CMS pool is currently seeing startds fall back to GSI. However, this is not configured to work (and we don't want GSI used for any reason between schedd and startd). We would remove GSI from the list of allowable READ authentication methods; however, CMS actually needs this for secure queries from the frontend. I think the underlying issue is that the authorization needed for the STARTD is conflated with READ authorization (probably just convenient for the original implementation). We should separate the two. Without this, there's no obvious way to prevent the startd from using GSI on our schedds. We cannot remove GSI from the startd itself because it is used to talk to the collector.
creator: bbockelm

title: Ticket #2555: master sends UDP collector updates when collector doesn't accept UDP
description: In the personal condor used by the new batlab to run the user's tasks, it was observed that the shared port daemon received unregistered commands: 10/14/11 11:30:21 Received UDP command (2) (UNREGISTERED COMMAND!) from <128.104.103.16:29282> This is because the master was trying to use UDP to send updates to the collector, even though the collector had a shared-port address, which means it does not support UDP. Why didn't the master automatically switch to using TCP, like all other daemons? Because the collector's port is configured as 0 in the config file. This has the special meaning that the address should be looked up in the collector address file. The first time the master does this, the address file doesn't exist yet. The next time it does this, the reading of the address file is done by a different piece of code. This other code does not check to see if the address supports UDP, so the default setting is used. Since the collector is using a shared port, when the master incorrectly tries to send UDP messages to the collector, it actually ends up sending them to the shared port server, which doesn't recognize the commands.

title: Ticket #2105: Shadow will treat closed socket as an error after claim is deactivated
description: When a job completes and the shadow deactivates the claim. If the shadow then fails to notify the schedd of claim deactivation, it will set a timer to try the notify again later, then return the the daemon core pump. The shadow will then try and read from the socket to the execute machine and treat the fact that the socket has been closed as an error. Thus when the submit machine is loaded, and the schedd is slow to respond to shadow notifications, some jobs will be run again even when they completed successfully. The job log will show 022 (086.799.000) 04/27 12:39:03 Job disconnected, attempting to reconnect Socket between submit and execute hosts closed unexpectedly Trying to reconnect to slot7@e080.chtc.wisc.edu <128.104.58.90:59182> ... 024 (086.799.000) 04/27 12:39:04 Job reconnection failed Job not found at execution machine Can not reconnect to slot7@e080.chtc.wisc.edu, rescheduling job While the logs on the execute machine will show that the job completed successfully and the claim was deactivated normally. The fix is for the the shadow to NOT treat the closed socked as an error if the claim has been deactivated.
remarks: 2011-Nov-22 13:38:47 by tannenba: CODE REVIEW was performed by tannenba.
attachments: 2105.diff 3096 bytes added by johnkn on 2011-Apr-27 22:03:51 UTC. adds a method in the remote resource class to access the claim deactivated flags, and uses that method in baseshadow to test for claim deactivation when the socket read fails. This patch also adds a test param SHADOW_TEST_JOB_CLEANUP_RETRY which will force the condition that causes this bug to be triggered.

So a busy SCHEDD could result in the job being re-run. (By John (TJ) Knoeller )

title: Ticket #5785: Disable negotiator cross-slot user priority advertising by default
description: Much to the surprise of the entire condor team, the negotiator, when preemption is enabled, injects into the machine ad not only the current RemoteUser, RemoteGroup, and RemoteUserPrio for the current slot, but also for all other slots in that ad. This gets to be very expensive for startds with a lot of slots. In an unrelated test of a personal condor with 10,000 slots, the negotiation was taking over two minutes just to insert all these attributes. We have no known users of this feature, so this ticket will add a knob, false by default to enable this behaviour. The knob will be called NEGOTIATOR_CROSS_SLOT_PRIOS

Meanwhile, the work-around for people running v8.5.7 who desire priority preemption is add the following to condor_config: NEGOTIATOR_CROSS_SLOT_PRIOS=True

title: Ticket #209: Create a service to publish Condor events via JMS
description: Working with Purdue and Indiana, we would like to create a Condor daemon core service that reads the Event Log and publishes the events via Java JMS messaging. Note this ticket is somewhat related to #125.
remarks: 2009-Feb-26 13:21:52 by wooj: meeting note Plan (1) Merge JNI code : We first need to merge two different code of Faisal and Jungha. I will have a look at java_config.cpp and java_config.h (2) Developing Event API which parses event log. Three possible ways exist (a) JNI (b) Pure Java version. We think this will be the best way finally. Might want to use Java New IO(NIO) (c) Shared memory. David will find some example code to refer (d) use named pipe between master daemon and Java thread (3) Next stage is to connect with JMS \\ (a) Intefaces to jms client (b) Test server We will have next conference call between March 16th and 20th. Please upload Faisal's code after review and let me know how to check in my code to trac. We aim to have working version by mid April. 2009-Mar-08 01:11:40 by wooj: Log Event Parser architecture <Entity definition> Java thread Java Thread periodically probes event log file(ex, condor/log/EventLog) and reads new events if any change has been made to that file since last probe. These new events will be consumed by JMS. C++ shared library Java thread has to read event information stored in event log file. However, it actually cannot parse the log file directly because it does not know the log format of each type of event. Only C++ classes that aware of condor_event.h can correctly parse event information written in log file. We think reusing the condor event log parsing code will be the best solution since the authors of the code know best about the format and the way to parse. When C++ class needs to return newly parsed events to Java, JNI will play a role. With JNI, native C++ program can read/write to/from a buffer that was allocated from Java application.It will be good if C++ program serializes event class and Java program rebuilds the same sequence of bytes, which enables Java to read interesting fields of event class. However, Java application is not compatible with C++ Event class or not be able to invoke C++ class methods. ( Remark: I found Cedar can do this. so my argument is not correct any longer. For the same reason, Cedar should be considered if it provides better performance) So we have to use Java Language type object to exchange event information between Java and C++. Basically, C++ classes need to compose parse-able string which includes eventType, JobId, cluser Id, and so on. This string will be received and then parsed by Java to reconstruct original Job event information. We do this by overriding serialization routine. Every C++ event class, defined in condor_event.h such as ExecuteEvent, TerminatedEvent and so on, would have its corresponding Java class.(remark: I changed "should" to "would" since this is not the only way to obtain goal) The java class will be more like "struct" in C language since it will not have any member function but accessors. Some methods of ULogEvent are protected, and these protected method in C++ cannot be accessed from Java unless a class is derived from it or friends class. For example, strToRusage() method in ULogEvent should be called so as to get proper string information before C++ shared library sends it. The serialized event object would be a char string delimited by some delimiters.(remark: We do not used serialization for delivering an event object between C++ and Java. Java garbage collector will allocate and free memory frequently just for one time use of each event message. To prevent this from happening, we suggest the much more efficient way to minimize memory allocation/deallocation.That is to manage memory by ourselves. It will minimize the work of garbage collector.We gradually increase the memory buffer size up to threshold point but reuse an event which is consumed by JMS. Managing queue size manually will gradually increase the heap size used by queue and at a certain point, memory usage will saturate and stay the same if events are created with almost constant speed. title: Ticket #6453: Garbage collection for public HTTP transfer
description: Public HTTP transfers currently have no garbage collection; the hard links they create stay in the webroot folder indefinitely. When creating hard links, let's create an additional empty file with the same hash name and .access extension. We can look at these .access files later to determine when the hard link was created, and if it's older than a certain time period (we'll set this in a knob) then delete it.
remarks: 2017-Oct-26 15:52:57 by coatsworth: One thing we need to deal with here is a race condition between condor_preen trying to delete an old link, at the same time the shadow is trying to update it. I think the simplest solution is to treat .access files like locks. The very first thing the shadow will do when creating/updating a link is delete the .access file. This is the equivalent of grabbing the lock, since preen cannot delete a hard link without the .access file. Don't even check if exists, since that would break atomicity. Just unlink it and move on. The last thing the shadow will do when creating/updating a link is create a new .access file (with new timestamp). Thoughts? 2017-Dec-4 15:37:57 by coatsworth: It turns out my suggestion above did not eliminate all race conditions. We ended up implementing this using file locks on the access file. 2017-Dec-06 11:06:33 by coatsworth: Duplicate of #6452
creator: coatsworth

description: Note: I was manually running a large DAG test with a 20,000 x 5 node DAG, and this failed because of running out of file descriptors when it went into recovery mode. What I have in mind is that there would be some way to tell the lazy log file code to only have n file descriptors open at any given time, and it would open and close files as necessary to maintain that. One simple (but non-optimal) way to reduce the FD use in a DAG with lots of parallel nodes would be to just open and close each log file each time we look at it.
remarks: 2009-Aug-10 13:35:32 by matt: It's better to have a limit. Open and close on each event/read is a performance killer. It is currently making the EVENT_LOG quite slow. Can the immediate problem of the large dag test be changed to use fewer log files? 2009-Aug-10 13:59:57 by wenger: The problem is not really that I got the large DAG test to fail -- the problem is that a real user might conceivable generate a DAG that would require a similar number of log files to be read. I don't think this is real urgent, because we're at least no worse off with the new "lazy log file" code than with the old code. title: Ticket #4751: Detect authorization denied errors
description: Everyone freakin' hates this sort of issue when you screw up authorization: $ condor_ce_q -pool ce1.accre.vanderbilt.edu -name ce1.accre.vanderbilt.edu -- Failed to fetch ads from: <129.59.197.223:9620?sock=33630_8b33_4> : ce1.accre.vanderbilt.edu (to replicate, set ALLOW_READ=noone@nowhere and reconfig) It's impossible to distinguish a network / unknown error from an authorization error. I know that many folks have lost hours and hours chasing network issues that were actually security issues in the end. I think we can detect this situation, however. The security post-auth ad includes the list of ValidCommands (a string list of integers). If we are trying to execute command int X and it's not in this list, we should at least hint to the sysadmin that the problem is security. Brian
remarks: 2014-Dec-04 11:17:38 by bbockelm: Is this just a crazy idea? I know there may be some intricate issues here - but it seems like if we see a CEDAR error while executing a command not in the valid commands, we can at least put a hint into the error message. 2015-Mar-11 14:57:21 by tannenba: Bump.... Zach, your comments? 2015-Mar-11 16:34:26 by zmiller: It's actually easier to detect than what Brian is suggesting... there is no ClassAd returned when authorization fails, so there is no ValidCommands to examine. However, it's a fairly safe assumption that if the connection was closed after succesfully authenticating but before receiving the auth_info classad, that the server hung up on us because we were denied. In fact, the start command code already detects when this happens, and pushes an extremely unhelpful (to everyone but me :) message onto the ErrStack. Two things need to happen: Change the startCommand code to put a more friendly error message onto the ErrStack Find the call sites for startCommand in the various tools and make sure that if it fails, it dumps the errStack to stderr. Right now, this is not happening, so the error isn't fully propagated to the user. This is fairly trivial, and Todd says I can spend a couple hours on it, which should be enough. 2015-Apr-08 15:19:00 by bbockelm: Per the OSG / HTCondor call today, goal is to commit to gittrac by April 10. This ticket basically has boiled down to making sure all the tools push this to the errstack. Question from BrianB - what about python bindings? 2015-Apr-22 15:14:12 by bbockelm: Per OSG / HTCondor call: zmiller thinks this will take another week. 2015-May-06 15:14:08 by bbockelm: Any updates on this? Target delivery date was 1 week ago. 2015-May-06 16:29:36 by zmiller: Yes, it is done and working. I'm just testing extra thoroughly (different combinations of Auth/Crypto enabled) because the change was quite large. It'll all be committed before the code freeze friday. 2015-Jun-11 15:27:45 by tannenba: FYI, here is an example of how things now look when a tool has an authorization failure: % condor_off ERROR SECMAN:2010:Received "DENIED" from server for user zmiller@cs.wisc.edu using method FS. title: Ticket #3094: DMTCP doesn't work in 7.8; SIGINT ignored
description: Report from Gene Cooperman, made by phone: DMTCP/condor_dmtcp works in 7.2. It no longer worked in 7.8(?). Investigation suggests that SIGINT is being ignored, and SIGINT is what shim_dmtcp is using to detect a request to checkpoint and exit. This has been identified by both condor_ssh_to_job and "kill -2 PID" as well as looking in /proc/$PID/status at SigIgn. (Easy expansion of SigIgn: echo 0000000000384004 | xxd -r -p | xxd -b Doing initial triage. - adesmet 2012-06-28
remarks: 2012-Jun-28 15:08:24 by adesmet: Cannot reproduce. Only PIPE is blocked. Tested on Red Hat 5.8/Condor 7.8.1 and Red Hat 5.7/Condor 7.7.6. New hypothesis: init scripts on remote site are setting ignore INT? 2012-Jun-28 15:09:01 by adesmet: Because I couldn't find a tool to easily list the ignored signals, I quick wrote one. it's attached as "describe signals". 2012-Jun-28 17:20:16 by adesmet: Reported to work fine on Debian Squeeze/6.0 stable. 2012-Jun-29 17:23:40 by adesmet: Current status: it looks like the job is just inheriting the ignoring of SIGINT from Condor. Why is Condor ignoring it? Not sure, but I suspect that it was set that way by the process that itself started Condor. On the problematic machines, when Condor is started by init on boot, all is well. When stopped and restarted using the init script tool, all is well. But sometimes, none-the-less, it ends up blocked. They're looking into what's going on. 2012-Jul-02 14:36:01 by gene: This has now been diagnosed as a Debian bug (present in Debian 6.0/squeeze). The Debian bug report is at http://bugs.debian.org/cgi-bin/bugreport.cgi?bug=679630 The short story is that if Debian squeeze uses the dependency-based booting, then some of the early daemons in the boot process will block SIGINT. If you suspect this on your machine, test it with: cat /proc/*/status | grep "\(SigIgn\|Name\)" |egrep -B1 "[0-9a-f][0-9a-f]+2$" and look to see if many daemons (especially condor) have SigIgn ending in 2. The workaround is to kill condor and restart it again as root: /etc/init.d/condor restart For additional bugs in Condor/DMTCP integration, please also send a bug report to http://dmtcp.sourceforge.net to reach the DMTCP developers. Thank you. -- the DMTCP developers. 2012-Jul-03 17:24:27 by adesmet: Resolved as Debian specific bug. The idea that Condor should reset signal handling as a workaround for this and potentially other bugs is #3107: Should Condor reset signal handling to defaults?

title: Ticket #835: Make ExprTree handling in old ClassAds more like new ClassAds
description: One of the difficulties in writing a compatibility layer over new ClassAds is that ExprTrees are handled differently between old and new ClassAds. In old ClassAds, for each attribute in an ad, the assignment operator and attribute name are included in the ExprTree. When a user retrieves an attribute's ExprTree, that full tree is returned, including assignment operator and attribute name. In new ClassAds, ExprTree has no assignment operator. The tree contains only the value of each attribute, and the name is stored separately as a string. We can ease the transition from old to new ClassAds by having users of old ClassAds handle ExprTrees like with new ClassAds. While the internal handling of ExprTrees will remain the same, the API can be changed to only expose the attribute value portion of the ExprTree and provide the attribute name as a separate string. By also adding a free-standing function for unparsing an ExprTree into a string, we can eliminate most calls on ExprTree methods that don't have a transparent equivalent in new ClassAds.

title: Ticket #1800: NETWORK_INTERFACE should accept wildcards
description: Ben Cotton and Preston Smith at Purdue have requested that there be a way to specify which IP address to use as something like 128.210.*, because in some cases, it is awkward to have to specify an exact IP address. Also, it seems odd that NETWORK_INTERFACE cannot accept the name of an interface rather than an IP address. Previously, we relied on DNS to tell us the IP addresses associated with our hostname. This makes Condor more dependent on DNS than it needs to be and has been a source of trouble in many cases. To address the items above, I propose that the IP address be determined by iterating through the network devices. If there are multiple options, the algorithm for choosing one will be similar to the one used before: prefer public IPs over private IPs and private IPs over loopback. In case of a tie, choose the first one in the list. The default should be NETWORK_INTERFACE=*. When BIND_ALL_INTERFACES is true and NETWORK_INTERFACE matches more than one IP address, the existing mechanism that rewrites the published IP address to match the IP address used to talk to the collector will still be used (providing that the latter IP address matches NETWORK_INTERFACE). On platforms where we don't know how to iterate through the network devices, we could rely on the old method of doing a DNS lookup of the hostname. This ticket is somewhat related to #386, but I'm not proposing any change to how BIND_ALL_INTERFACES works in this ticket. That can be done separately if desired.

title: Ticket #7192: better submit_utils Requirements generation for custom resources
description: Requirements generation for submit_utils will be changed, in part because of #6936 (request for 0 of a custom resource should not alter Requirements), since the fix for this bug does not apply to the 8.9 submit_utils code. In 8.9, requirements generation will refer to job attributes rather than to submit keywords. This means that MY.RequestGPUs affect the generated requirements in the same way that request_gpus does. The fix for #6936 will be refined. custom resource requests will affect requirements generation by If the resource request is an expression that evaluates to a number at submit time, and the number is > 0, then requirements will be altered. If the resource request is an expression that evaluates to undefined at submit time, requirements will be altered as if it were a number > 0 If the resource request is an expression that evaluates to a string, requirements will be altered if the string is non-empty Always, requirements will not be altered if they already refer to the custom resource. i.e. if the requirements already refers to GPUs, then RequestGPUs will not result a change to the requirements. Furthermore, if the submit hash has MY.Requirements or "+Requirements", requirements generation will be entirely disabled. This will also disable the side effects of requirements generation, since these side effects exist to insure that attributes referred to by generated requirements will exist. Crondor jobs will not have a ScheddInterval attribute inserted into the job. VM universe jobs that use VMWare transfer will not have a FileSystemDomain attribute inserted.

title: Ticket #589: Condor security manual updates
description: In general, the security section of the manual should be improved, and some explicit examples/recipes should be provided (probably on the HOWTO section of the wiki, and the Manual could refer to them). Currently much of this explicit HOWTO wisdom only lives in Zach's powerpoint files. Other thoughts - ANONYMOUS causes the user to be identified as "CONDOR_ANONYMOUS_USER" This is completely insecure, but may be suitable for limited purposes. For example, ANONYMOUS access could be used to allow public read-only access to a collector or schedd. A bunch of stuff that might be appropriate to add somewhere: - FS - Very secure. Easy to set up. Only works for communications on a single computer. I recommend always using this. - PASSWORD - Very secure. Moderate complexity to set up. Only works for authenticating daemon-to-daemon communications. - SSL - Very secure. Complex to set up. Suitable for all purposes. - GSI - Very secure. Very complex to set up. Suitable for all purposes. This is really just SSL with additional functionality to support the Globus Security Infrastructure. If you are not already using Globus for other purposes, I recommend against this. May not be available for Windows. - KERBEROS - Very secure. Very complex to set up. Suitable for all purposes. If you are not already using Kerberos for other purposes, I recommend against this. May not be available for Windows. - FS_REMOTE - Variable security. Moderate complexity to set up. Relies on the security of your network filesystem for security. I recommend NOT using. - NTSSPI - Low security. Easy to set up. Microsoft Windows authentication. Only works on Windows. Authentication is security, but encryption and integrity checks are not. - CLAIMTOBE - Insecure. Easy to set up. If enabled, anyone can claim to be anyone! It's really just for debugging. I recommend NOT using. - ANONYMOUS - Insecure. Easy to set up. While insecure, it does limit users to the "CONDOR_ANONYMOUS_USER", a rough equivalent to unix's "nobody" account or Window's "guest". it can be useful if you want to allow read-only public access to parts of the system. You can use more than one, and I recommend that you do so. My general recommendation is: 1. Use FS. It's simple and secure. In a typical configuration users run condor_submit on the same computer that the condor_schedd is running on. In this case, FS is easy for both administrators and users. 2. Users frequently ant read-only access to at least the condor_collector. This makes it easier for them to check the state of the pool, and is required to "condor_q -analyze" or "-better-analyze" to work. If your collector information is public, you can use ANONYMOUS to accomplish this easily. If this isn't public, use the same option described in #3 below. 3. If users want to be able to use "condor_submit -remote", "condor_q -name" or other remote access, you'll need another system beyond FS. If you are already using GSI for other purposes, I recommend GSI. If you are already using Kerberos for other purposes, I recommend KERBEROS. Otherwise SSL is the easiest secure option. 4. Condor daemons need to authenticate as well. If you're using SSL, GSI, or KERBEROS, you can probably also use it for the daemons. Otherwise I recommend PASSWORD as the easiest secure option.
remarks: 2012-Aug-17 10:04:20 by smoler: From Todd T: In the security section of the manual, we list the available authentication methods, but we do not point out that not all methods are supported on all platforms. See the below post to condor-users. Todd On 8/16/2012 9:01 PM, Jewell, Chris wrote: > Hi, > > I've just downloaded the Windows binaries for Condor 7.8.2, and am trying to configure GSI security. I get messages such as: > > *** Last 20 line(s) of file C:\condor/log/NegotiatorLog: > 08/17/12 13:42:24 SECMAN: new session, doing initial authentication. > 08/17/12 13:42:24 SECMAN: Auth methods: GSI > 08/17/12 13:42:24 HANDSHAKE: in handshake(my_methods = 'GSI') > 08/17/12 13:42:24 HANDSHAKE: handshake() - i am the client > 08/17/12 13:42:24 HANDSHAKE: sending (methods == 32) to server > 08/17/12 13:42:24 HANDSHAKE: server replied (method = 32) > 08/17/12 13:42:24 AUTHENTICATE: unsupported method: 32, failing. > > Does this mean that the Windows version is not GSI capable? > Correct. GSI has never been ported to Windows. If you want something similar on Windows, consider SSL, which also uses public key certificates (but doesn't do the limited proxy delegation that GSI does). These Condor authentication methods work on Condor for Windows: SSL KERBEROS PASSWORD NTSSPI CLAIMTOBE ANONYMOUS and these Condor authentication methods do not work on Windows: GSI FS FS_REMOTE 2013-Aug-26 15:09:23 by bbockelm: Zach - for PASSWORD security, we should make a note that this is based on shared secret (right?) - one credential compromise on any node means all nodes could be compromised. title: Ticket #1046: Performance: job removal fsync for each job
description:
Job removal is exceedingly slow, especially when removing tens of thousands of jobs. A quick review of the Schedd code suggests that a single condor_rm should result in a single transaction and fsync, but that is not the case. Generate some Schedd traffic: $ echo "cmd=/bin/sleep
args=1h
notification=never
queue 29" | condor_submit Submitting job(s)............................. $ condor_rm -a While watching the Schedd: $ strace -c -efsync -p $(pidof condor_schedd) % time seconds usecs/call calls errors syscall ------ ----------- ----------- --------- --------- ---------------- 100.00 0.002000 65 31 fsync ------ ----------- ----------- --------- --------- ---------------- 100.00 0.002000 31 total The job_queue.log: 105 103 0.0 NextClusterNum 8 101 07.-1 Job Machine 101 7.0 Job Machine 103 7.0 GlobalJobId "robin.local#7.0#1260542935" 103 07.-1 ClusterId 7 ... 103 7.1 GlobalJobId "robin.local#7.1#1260542935" 103 7.1 ProcId 1 103 7.1 LastJobStatus 0 103 7.1 JobStatus 1 101 7.2 Job Machine 103 7.2 GlobalJobId "robin.local#7.2#1260542935" 103 7.2 ProcId 2 103 7.2 LastJobStatus 0 103 7.2 JobStatus 1 101 7.3 Job Machine ... 101 7.28 Job Machine 103 7.28 GlobalJobId "robin.local#7.28#1260542936" 103 7.28 ProcId 28 103 7.28 LastJobStatus 0 103 7.28 JobStatus 1 103 7.28 EnteredCurrentStatus 1260542936 106 105 103 7.10 LastJobStatus 1 103 7.10 JobStatus 3 103 7.10 RemoveReason "via condor_rm (by user matt)" 103 7.10 EnteredCurrentStatus 1260542937 104 7.10 JobStatusOnRelease 103 7.11 LastJobStatus 1 103 7.11 JobStatus 3 103 7.11 RemoveReason "via condor_rm (by user matt)" 103 7.11 EnteredCurrentStatus 1260542937 104 7.11 JobStatusOnRelease ... 104 7.27 JobStatusOnRelease 103 7.28 LastJobStatus 1 103 7.28 JobStatus 3 103 7.28 RemoveReason "via condor_rm (by user matt)" 103 7.28 EnteredCurrentStatus 1260542937 104 7.28 JobStatusOnRelease 106 103 7.10 JobFinishedHookDone 1260542937 105 102 7.10 106 103 7.11 JobFinishedHookDone 1260542937 105 102 7.11 106 ... 105 102 7.28 102 07.-1 106 105 is BeginTransaction, 106 is EndTransaction, 102 is DestroyClassAd We are getting one transaction, and thus one fsync, for the submit (good), one for the removal (good), and one for each job to destroy it (bad). Suggestion: Batch the job ad deletion.
remarks: I have made a 7.5-branch patch [17276] that resolves this issue by simply converting the transaction in DestroyProc to be NONDURABLE. I would like a second opinion (or maybe a group opinion during the next fw meeting) that this is an acceptable solution. The commit message and a comment in the code describes my reasoning for why NONDURABLE is ok here. The alternative solution of batching together deletes is complicated by the worry that batching together the job cleanup tasks for a lot of jobs could make the schedd less responsive to other events. title: Ticket #4244: allow StarterLog.JobId instead of StarterLog.slotN
description: It would be more meaningful to admins, and would facilitate the moving of jobs from slot to slot if the starter log extension was the job id rather than the slot name. A new param will be added STARTER_LOG_NAME_APPEND, it will have a string expression relative to the slot ad that defines the extension for the StartLog. The value for this expression that will be compatible with 8.0.x behavior is STARTER_LOG_NAME_APPEND = true Permitted values for STARTER_LOG_NAME_APPEND are true - same behavior as 8.0 false - append nothing, this is what 8.0 does for single slot machines Slot - append slot name (this is what 8.0 does) Cluster - append cluster id Jobid - append job id These are all case-insensitive keywords. title: Ticket #5286: condor_install for personal condor should set NETWORK_INTERFACE
description: when condor_install is not told to set a specific role, it will set use role:personal. Then it will override the CONDOR_HOST set by the personal role to be what it determines is the full hostname. This is arguably the correct behavior when condor_install is not given any arguments, but it is the wrong behavior when it is passed the --make-personal-condor argument. Additionally, when --make-personal-condor is passed, condor_install should set NETWORK_INTERFACE to $(CONDOR_HOST) to force the the right interface to be published by the daemon ads.

title: Ticket #2543: Failed job start causes starter to shutdown w/o completing exit hook
description: If the starter has a problem running the executable for the job, it will perform a shutdown fast. Part of this process invokes the exit hook as it should, but it shuts down without waiting for the exit hook to exit. Anything using the job hooks that runs into this case will likely not be notified the job has exited and been evicted. This could mean a job that is injected with the hooks (fetch hook) will lose track of what has happened to the job.

The starter will wait <keyword>_HOOK_<hook_type>_TIMEOUT seconds, defaults to 30 for the exit hook, before the starter determines the hook is hung and continues with shutdown.
