In many cases, like stochastic modeling and simulation, it is not required that all nodes at a given step complete. Additionally, we have noted that there can be significant variability in run times that often create a 'long tail' of run times. For example, 85% of nodes at a given level may complete in 20 minutes, while the remaining 15% may take up to 60 minutes. In these cases, significant workflow step speedups can be attained if the requirement that all parents complete before a child starts executing would be relaxed. It would be advantageous to enable a user to specify the condition upon which a child can begin processing. For example a user may specify that a certain number or percentage of parent nodes complete, or that parents are only allowed to run for a given amount of (wall clock) time. While we leave it to the Condor developers to determine the best implementation path, we suggest that this feature may best be implemented by providing the user with two tools: 1) a tool that lets a user query the number of completed parents for a given child and 2) a tool that let's a user say "I want child X to begin processing =97 do the right thing to clean up any still running parents, etc.). In these cases, it would be helpful to 'signal' the parent workflow step that it has been marked as 'no longer required' so that the post script could behave accordingly (perhaps by returning or outputting some default value). 2013-Jun-10 14:58:47 by nwp: abandoning as we are now post-7.9

title: Ticket #3702: Cannot preempt recently started jobs?
description: The logic for #3539 looks incorrect. RetirementTimeRemaining is always advertised by the starter, regardless of the state. When the job has just started, this is set to: MAX_JOB_RETIREMENT_TIME - (Job Age) If this attribute is positive, then the job will not be preempted. So, if MAX_JOB_RETIREMENT_TIME is 1 hour, it is not possible to preempt jobs within the first hour of running. Looking at #3539, this doesn't seem to be the desired behavior.
remarks: 2013-Jun-17 15:11:55 by danb: Hi Brian, If MAX_JOB_RETIREMENT_TIME is 1 hour, it has always been the case that you could not preempt the job in the first hour of running. You could preempt the claim during that time, which would allow you to sit in line on the startd until the job finished or the retirement time expired. What has changed is that the negotiator no longer will even let you preempt the claim by default. This can be overridden by setting NEGOTIATOR_CONSIDER_EARLY_PREEMPTION=True. Are you seeing some broken behavior that does not agree with my statements above? --Dan 2013-Jun-17 17:02:58 by bbockelm: Nope - just that it's all very hard to grok. So, what happens at 1 hour, 1 minute? The job can be preempted, and then has another hour of MAX JOB RETIREMENT TIME? 2013-Jun-17 17:14:11 by danb: After 1 hour, the job may be preempted at any time for the rest of its life. Perhaps a point of confusion is that MaxJobRetirementTime starts counting from the start of the job, not from the start of preemption. It is the amount of time a job is promised to be able to run. MachineMaxVacateTime, on the other hand, starts counting from the moment the job is sent a kill signal. 2013-Jun-17 19:54:26 by bbockelm: Oh. I guess I never figured that one out. From the startd policy page: An expression giving the maximum time in seconds that the startd will wait for the job to finish before kicking it off if it needs to do so. This is evaluated in the context of the job ClassAd, so it may refer to job attributes as well as machine attributes. Can we improve this? Maybe "Jobs will not be preempted if they have been running for less than MaxJobRetirementTime." To me, "wait for the job to finish" implies after it has gone into retirement state. 2013-Jun-18 09:48:36 by danb: Thanks for pointing that out. I was not aware of the inconsistencies in the various descriptions of MaxJobRetirementTime in the manual. Some of them were more misleading than others. I've checked in an improvement.

title: Ticket #6500: startd should retry deletion of sandbox until it succeeds
description: We have reports from the field from users of Windows pools that sometimes the job sandbox on the execute nodes is never cleaned up. We know that this is possible when some process that is not tracked by HTCondor (antivirus?) is holding files or the sandbox directory itself open. To mitigate this, the STARTD should remember sandboxes that it failed to delete and retry periodically until it succeeds. The retry should use exponential backoff, trying frequently for the first few minutes and more infrequently as failures mount. At some point in the future, this new cleanup retry mechanism should be expanded to retry cleanup of temporary user accounts and the registry/profile associated with them.

title: Ticket #3647: init.d script improvements for condor rpm
description: Currently some users (notably Fermilab) customize their init.d script for HTCondor. These customizations get blown away on upgrades because the script is not marked as a config file in the RPM. One option was to mark the script as %config(noreplace), but this was turned down in favor of fixing the limitations of the init.d script and providing a proper place for customizations. In particular, we would like to provide for the following: add a ulimit statement to boost the number of allowed file descriptors add a new command to the init script, service condor drain, which sends a condor_off -peaceful to the condor_master on the node fix the /var/lock/subsys file so it is the correct name. Otherwise the redhat shutdown script doesn't even attempt to shut down condor at system shutdown, which can lead to a virtual machine hang if you are running condor in a VM.

title: Ticket #4881: Eliminate or expand addrinfo_iterator::ipv6
description: addrinfo_iterator (/src/condor_includes/ipv6_addrinfo.h and /src/condor_utils/ipv6_addrinfo.cpp) has a member variable "ipv6", which identifies if ENABLE_IPV6=TRUE. If present, IPv6 addresses will be returned; otherwise they'll be skipped. (We can't just filter using getaddrinfo; at least OS we support has a buggy implementation.) But, the filtering should not be necessary! Currently if ENABLE_IPV4=FALSE, ENABLE_IPV6=TRUE, any code walking addrinfo_iterator will get IPv4 addresses, despite IPv4 being disabled. As far as we know, it works just fine. This suggests we can just get rid of addrinfo_iterator::ipv6 and all code paths where it is false. However, it's possible that it's actually broken, in which case addrinfo_iterator probably needs a member variables ipv4 and to do similar filtering. Plan: Are there any problems when ENABLE_IPV4=FALSE, ENABLE_IPV6=TRUE Yes: Add addrinfo_iterator::ipv4 with parallel logic. (Actually, you might want to generalize. set of ints representing ai_familys that we accept?) No: Remove the addrinfo_iterator::ipv6 code. Now does ENABLE_IPV4=TRUE, ENABLE_IPV6=FALSE work? Yes: Huzzah! No: Revert the previous step, be baffled, documented bafflement here, close ticket.
remarks: 2017-Dec-21 13:30:04 by jfrey: There are problems with ENABLE_IPV4=FALSE, ENABLE_IPV6=TRUE. When the collector is given as a hostname that resolves to both IPv4 and IPv6 addresses, the Daemon client object will happily try to use the IPv4 address, which may not work. In the getaddrinfo() bug described in #4838, the second record returned was complete garbage, including ai_family. I propose we eliminate addrinfo_iterator::ipv6 and restore filtering based on the family in the hint argument to getaddrinfo(). Add in filtering out IPv4 records if ENABLE_IPV4=False. Keep the code from #4838 that skips records with unknown ai_family values.

title: Ticket #5793: Problem with default JOB_DEFAULT_REQUESTMEMORY
description: Reported by Stuart via Tom to Condor ticket system. The default setting of JOB_DEFAULT_REQUESTMEMORY, ifThenElse(MemoryUsage ! UNDEFINED,MemoryUsage,(ImageSize+1023)/1024) appears to be problematic for jobs submitted without RequestMemory under HTCondor 8.4.7 and Partitionable slots if they are preempted and need to match/run again. In particular, I noticed that a number of jobs in the LIGO CIT SL7.2 pool that where relying on this default where being rejected by partitionable slot STARTD’s with, 07/09/16 15:07:44 slot1_3: New machine resource of type -1 allocated 07/09/16 15:07:44 Setting up slot pairings 07/09/16 15:07:44 slot1_3: Slot requirements not satisfied. 07/09/16 15:07:44 slot1_3: Job ad was ============================ However, if I condor_qedit RequestMemory to be quantize(ImageSize/1024,1) then jobs are not rejected and start in a dynamic slot. I believe there are a few problems: 0) Sec 3.5.1.19 states a different default default value, http://research.cs.wisc.edu/htcondor/manual/v8.4/3_5Policy_Configuration.html#37135 JOB_DEFAULT_REQUESTMEMORY = ifThenElse(MemoryUsage =!= UNDEFINED, MemoryUsage, 1) then what I observe and what is stated in Sec 3.3.13, http://research.cs.wisc.edu/htcondor/manual/v8.4/3_3Configuration.html#25623 ifThenElse(MemoryUsage =!= UNDEFINED,MemoryUsage,(ImageSize+1023)/1024) 1) It looks like RequestMemory must be an integer to be effective. I first tried manually calculating a reasonable RequestMemory value for a test job and entered that via condor_qedit as a real number. However, even when I seriously inflated the value STARTD for the partitionable slot would still reject the job until I rounded that to an integer. 2) Even with STARTD_DEBUG = D_ALL I was unable to find a mention in StartLog of what “Slot requirements” where not satisfied. I think it would be very helpful to log this and make it easy to access, e.g., from a submit machine I would love to see “condor_q -better-analyze JobId” report details on the last failed attempt to start a job (if there was a match that was rejected). 3) Attempting to use the ResidentSetSize directly (or via MemoryUsage) in RequestMemory did not work (even after rounding to an integer). I did not investigate this very much, but I believe startd is not happy if RequestMemory is less than ImageSize. At any rate, the following was successful in getting a number of otherwise idle jobs running, A) Make a list of idle jobs requesting less memory than ImageSize before and after running qedit, condor_q -constraint "(jobstatus == 1) && (RequestMemory < ImageSize/1024)" -af globaljobid RequestMemory ImageSize/1024 B) Set all of those jobs to track their ImageSize, condor_qedit -constraint "(jobstatus == 1) && (RequestMemory < ImageSize/1024)" RequestMemory "quantize(ImageSize/1024,1)" C) Change the default setting for new user jobs being submitted, [root@ldas-pcdev2 ~]# cat /etc/condor/config.d/memory JOB_DEFAULT_REQUESTMEMORY = quantize(ImageSize/1024,1)

title: Ticket #6916: CREAM update for OpenSSL 1.1.0 causes crashes

title: Ticket #2406: Input files are transferred with output when job is spooled
description: If a job's files are stored in the spool directory, then when output files are transferred from the starter to the shadow, all input files are transferred. Normally, unmodified input files are not transferred as part of the job's output. The normal ways a job's files end up in the spool directory are when it's submitted by Condor-C or by condor_submit with the -spool or -remote argument. Milestones Determine why input files are transferred as output only when a job is spooled. [DONE] Fix it. [DONE] Code review.
remarks: 2011-Aug-25 13:16:05 by jfrey: This is happening because the shadow adds all files in the job spool directory to TransferIntermediate in the job ad that it sends to the starter. Since the FileTransfer's file catalog isn't stored persistently, we need to change how the shadow consults it. 2011-Aug-25 15:14:28 by jfrey: I have a patch that fixes this bug by having the shadow tell the FileTransfer object to create a file catalog if the job's files are spooled. This will cause the FileTransfer to not add unmodified input files to the TransferIntermediate attribute. 2011-Sep-23 15:19:49 by danb: Code review: I don't see how this works, but I'm probably just not understanding things due to the complexity of the file transfer object. The transfer object in the shadow builds a file catalog of all the spooled files. Then it generates a list of intermediate files, excluding those in the catalog. Doesn't that mean it excludes everything in the spool, including both the input files (good) and the intermediate files (bad)? --Dan 2012-Jun-14 15:40:11 by jfrey: When the job's input files are spooled, it should be ok to treat intermediate files as input files in the shadow. They should be sent to the starter and they don't have to be transferred back to the shadow if they're not modified. Their final location is the spool directory as far as the shadow is concerned. 2012-Jun-14 15:44:38 by jfrey: There's a possible security problem due to this bug. If the job has an x509 proxy, it may be transferred in the clear along with the output files. 2012-Jun-20 16:35:37 by jfrey: The file named in the X509UserProxy job attribute is explicitly not transferred as an output file in the file transfer object. If a proxy is listed as an ordinary input file, then it will be transferred in both directions, but not delegated. If Condor is going treat such input files specially, it will need assistance identifying them from the user. 2012-Aug-23 14:09:08 by zmiller: Bulk change of target version from v070802 to v070803 using ./ticket-target-mover.

title: Ticket #2778: ProcAPI on windows should stop tracking a pid once it gets err=87
description: While investigating the cause of schedd crash/exits in a windows pool, ToddT and I noticed in the log that the ProcAPI will attempt to keep tracking a PID even after OpenProcess() return error 87 which means "PID does not exist". It seems likely that this could lead to confusion once the PID is re-used. If this flaw was combined with a failure to get the process birthdate (something we also saw in the log), then condor could potentially kill processes that it should not be tracking, or even possibly kill itself.

title: Ticket #7080: Auto-approve token rules
description: Now that we have the ability to request tokens in #7006, we should allow the sysadmin to install auto-approval rules: These rules should be time-limited (i.e., admin needs to specify that they are only valid for 1 hour). To allow for pools coming up quickly, requests predating the rule's installation (say, by 30 seconds) should be approved once the rule is installed. The admin should be able to specify a netblock (e.g., 192.168.0.0/24) the rule is valid for. The rule should only allow a very narrow set of fixed authorizations and identities. That is, this should only be allowed for token requests with the identity condor and requesting the authorization for ADVERTISE_SCHEDD or ADVERTISE_STARTD.
remarks: 2019-May-30 14:37:19 by tlmiller: BrianB and I had a discussion and we agree that: The CLI should have a default lifetime, but not a default netmask, unless (bonus feature) PRIVATE_NETWORK_NAME is set, in which case the default is the private network . Otherwise, we just have to ask (and not do anything). The CLI should tell the user what we're doing (e.g., confirm lifetime with time units and netmask). Instead of trying to guess a good time-out for historical auto-approval, the CLI should list all of the requests from that time period (just like the list tokens command) and say "to approve all these requests, run the following command." It should also mention, if there are any requests older than that, how to get a list of them (e..g, condor_list_tokens <num... num>). We should always log autoapprovals, but the first autoapproval for each rule should also log the rule in question (like security rejections). condor_reconfig should flush (delete) the autoapproval rules (and the collector should log that they're gone). This may be a little surprising, but we can argue that since the rules aren't in the config files, they shouldn't be in the configuration after a reconfig. Likewise, condor_config should flush (delete) pending requests. 2019-Jun-10 08:59:04 by bbockelm: The PR https://github.com/htcondor/htcondor/pull/50 should have all the above addressed except for the PRIVATE_NETWORK_NAME pieces; that's a good idea, but isn't really how that particular knob works. 2019-Jun-21 08:26:43 by bbockelm: Merged master back into the branch and updated GitHub. ctest run looks good on RHEL7. Ready for review. 2019-Jun-28 17:24:35 by tlmiller: Code Review I hoisted two of the checks out the per-rule loop in TokenRequest::ShouldAutoApprove(), because they didn't depend on the rule. Let me know if you had meant to be inefficient there for the sake of the logging. I moved the unimplemented features from the commentary to #7137. This is bad and wrong: $ condor_token_request_auto_approve -netblock 192.168.0.0/36 -lifetime 3700 Successfully installed auto-approval rule for netblock 192.168.0.0/36 with lifetime of 1.03 hours So is this: condor_token_request_auto_approve -netblock 192::168.0.0/36 -lifetime -3700 Successfully installed auto-approval rule for netblock 192::168.0.0/36 with lifetime of -1.03 hours Remote daemon reports no un-approved requests pending. I don't know that we need to have the CLI do any particular filtering, but it seems like the server should. 2019-Jun-28 17:26:59 by tlmiller: Changes pushed to v8_9-gt7080-branch in the UW repository. 2019-Jul-05 17:19:35 by tlmiller: Merged.

title: Ticket #3539: change recommended configuration for disabling preemption
description: There are several known problems with use of MaxJobRetirementTime: Jobs wait to run on a busy slot and only periodically try getting a new match. This can make it difficult to understand why things happen --- the order in which jobs start running, and which machines they run on. While jobs are waiting to run, a TCP connection exists between the schedd and the startd. This consumes a file descriptor in the schedd. If the schedd runs low on file descriptors, this can cause communication failures that result in unexpected behavior. For example, I have seen a case where the schedd was unable to authenticate to the collector, so it could not advertise submitters. A job that is matched and waiting to run on a busy slot becomes unavailable for being matched to flocked pools. While a claim is in the Claimed/Retiring or Preempting state, the resource is not counted as belonging to the preempting user. Preempting claims therefore do not subtract from the calculated share of the pool that should be given to the preempting user. This can result in the preempting user being given claims to more and more machines across multiple negotiation cycles. #2270 Proposed Change We considered two possible solutions. One is simply to stop recommending use of MaxJobRetirementTime in the section in the manual on disabling preemption. The default CLAIM_WORKLIFE is non-zero these days, so setting PREEMPTION_REQUIREMENTS=False and Rank=0 is not such a bad thing as it used to be. The other option is to change things so that when MaxJobRetirementTime would cause delayed preemption, the default negotiation policy will avoid matching jobs to the slot. Assuming we go with the second option, here is a plan for what would need to be done: Make the startd advertise the time when retirement of the current job would end: RetirementTimeRemaining. Currently, only the MaxJobRetirementTime expression is advertised. This is not enough information for the negotiator to compute when retirement of the current running job would end. Add a new option in the negotiator: NEGOTIATOR_CONSIDER_EARLY_PREEMPTION. The default will be FALSE, which causes slots that still have retirement time to be excluded from consideration during matchmaking. Remaining Issues Suspension does not count towards a job's retirement time, so RetirementEndTime could get extended when suspension happens. A race condition could result in a job getting sent to a machine where the negotiator thought retirement should have ended but which extended retirement due to suspension. Currently, the semantics of MaxJobRetirementTime are such that changes in the result of evaluating the expression take effect during retirement. This can produce similar effects to suspension: the advertised RetirementEndTime may change, and this could result in a race condition affecting our policy of avoiding preemption during retirement. One way to solve the race condition would be to modify the job/machine requirements to require that RetirementEndTime be in the past. The proposed policy addresses lengthy retirement times but not lengthy preemption times, which could result from a large MachineMaxVacateTime and jobs that take a long time to go away. Many of the problems associated with long retirement also apply to long preemption. I don't propose changing the default policy, but I do think it would be prudent to advertise VacateEndTime.

description: LIGO reports after they upgraded to RHEL7, whenever they reboot a submit machine, the first few jobs the schedd attempts to either reconnect or restart end up on hold. title: Ticket #7829: Hardening of TOKEN support before next stable release
description: Several misc issues to be addressed before token support in HTCondor goes in production in a stable series: Issues to resolve DONE Our JWT parsing code needs a copyright DONE Tokens with CRLF line endings, or any whitespace at all other than a single newline character, cannot be parsed. Prolly happened with commit [56470]. Daemons will read system tokens with PRIV_CONDOR (see findTokens() in condor_auth_passwd.cpp)... should it use PRIV_ROOT instead? condor_token_fetch should temporarily set SEC_DEFAULT_AUTHENTICATION=Required to prevent it from failing in typical configurations, even when a user can successfully authenticate to the schded. Either get this tested/working on Windows / Mac or document that it is Linux only Documentation: actual format of a token file sitting in tokens.d is not discussed; for instance, unclear that a single file in tokens.d can contain multiple tokens, or that a token file can have comments, or that a token follows the JWT standard. Documentation: No SCITOKEN authentication method documentation (why was #7281 resolved?) Documentation: No documentation for knob TRUST_DOMAIN Extra Credit Perhaps it would be really nice if a token entry in a token file could end with a comment (a space followed by a pound-sign then comment)? Like an ssh key? Currently comments are only allowed on their own line.

title: Ticket #1154: Tests should know / report own description and classes
description: Currently the description for a test is in the Imakefile, along with which classes the test is in. Further documentation is sometimes present in testmethods.txt. This is clumsy. A test should be more self contained. Perhaps each test (that is, .run file) should understand "--describe" which will return something like this: brief=Condor-C AB test long=This test verifies a basic condor-c job can be submitted to A and run on B and complete. implementation=Two condor pools are set up with dynamic address and predefined locations to read the port. Then the one configured as the A sends the job off to the B side. Expected result: job completion on the A side. classes=condorc,quick,full,quicknolink To generate the list_*s, you'd run --describe on each script to get the classes. To generate the *.desc files (are those used for anything?), you'd do the same. We cuold also use it to generate documentation if the urge struck us.

title: Ticket #4643: knobs to throttle remote condor_history queries never documented
description: In ticket #3897 we added remotely queryable condor_history, but somehow the config knobs associated with this mechanism were never added into the manual. The following schedd config knobs should be documented (and perhaps referenced in the condor_history docs): HISTORY_HELPER_MAX_CONCURRENCY - This specifies the maximum number of concurrent remote condor_history queries allowed at a time (defaults to 2). When there are more than HISTORY_HELPER_MAX_CONCURRENCY clients, further queries will be queued in a non-blocking manner. Setting this option to 0 disables remote history access. HISTORY_HELPER_MAX_HISTORY - This specifies the maximum number of ads to parse on behalf of remote history clients. The default is 10,000. This allows the system administrator to indirectly manage the maximum amount of CPU time spent on each client. Setting this option to 0 disables remote history access.

title: Ticket #474: BNL pilot job disaster when Condor-G started submitted to many sites
description: We are having a problem on BNL condor-g submit host. We have seen slowness of pilot job submission to BNL T1 site after reconfiguring the PANDA autopilot to submit from just BNL to BNL, US T2, and a few overseas sites. title: Ticket #1441: Move write of submit event from condor_submit to schedd
description: The schedd writes every EventLog/UserLog event except for the submit event. The UserLog submit event is written by condor_submit. This can cause synchronization problems, such as having execute/terminate events written first (see, for example, #1422 ). If we have the schedd also write the UserLog submit event, problems like that should vanish.
remarks: 2010-Jun-10 09:03:27 by tannenba: If implemented correctly, this should require very little code change because the schedd already writes the submit event at the proper time into the schedd's event log. So it should just be a matter of getting rid of the code that writes the submit event condor_submit and having the schedd always write the submit event into the job event log (if a job log is requested) whenever it writes it into the schedd event log. 2010-Jun-10 09:58:20 by cweiss: The change is essentially done. The only difference of the schedd submit event is that it is lacking the submit host information (which is included if condor_submit writes it). Is it crucial to have this information? 2010-Jun-22 14:23:43 by matt: Can that information be cribbed from the connection the job is coming in on? 2010-Jul-01 17:34:36 by cweiss: A slight semantic difference introduced by the attached patch: Now the submit event does not say anymore "submitted from host: <sinful string>" but "submitted to host: <sinful string>", since the schedd we submit to isn't necessarily the same machine from which we call "condor_submit". 2010-Jul-01 17:55:30 by gthain: It looks like with the new code, we now fsync the user log for every proc for every cluster that's submitted. In the old code, we only fsync'd in submit once, at the end. Is there a way to do this in the schedd? 2010-Jul-02 16:43:40 by cweiss: As of our previous discussion: I now included the fsync-per-cluster change. However, you can have a submit file like ... log = log1.log queue log = log2.log queue etc... In this scenario we have a separate log file for every single job in a cluster (which wouldn't be fsynced and currently aren't by condor_submit!) Thus, we should maybe include a check whether the log filename changed and act accordingly. 2010-Jul-06 11:51:37 by gthain: Doesn't this bug exist today? 2010-Jul-06 12:24:18 by cweiss: Correct. As condor_submit is doing it to date, it does only one fsync per cluster, no matter whether there are several different log files to be written to or not. 2010-Jul-06 13:21:23 by gthain: OK, let's commit this then, as it is no worse than before, and then fix the multiple log problem. 2010-Aug-11 09:01:21 by cweiss: Some remarks as identified in yesterday's FW meeting: - The change of the submit event text ".. submitted from host... " to ".. submitted to host..." breaks backwards compatibility. Either we stick with the old version (which would semantically be incorrect), or add a compatibility check. The later only works if a newer version of Condor has to deal with an old UserLog. It won't work the other way round. Therefore I propose to accept the slightly incorrect semantics and just leave the old phrasing. - A newer submit should still be able to write the submit event in case it is communicating with an older schedd (version check!) - A newer schedd should omit the writing if it is already written by an older submit. - Last but not least: exhaustive testing needed whether things work as expected in case we are submitting to a remote schedd (e.g. could we end up with an overwritten UserLog due to transfer or none) 2010-Aug-17 16:59:01 by jfrey: The host mentioned in the submit event when condor_submit writes it is the sinful string of the schedd. Even for a remote submit, it's the schedd's address. So there's no problem of that value changing. 2010-Aug-18 17:23:41 by jfrey: Pushed changes to master for 7.5.4. This reworked patch includes backward compatibility checks. 2010-Oct-20 14:29:46 by jfrey: #924 is identical to this ticket.

description: If a test using CondorTest.pm drops a core file, the code to handle and report that fails. The code emits a misleading error and terminates prematurely, possibly leading to failure to archive the core file. To reproduce: Modify /src/condor_tests/job_core_leaveinqueue_van.run, inserting the following at the top: my $logdir = `condor_config_val LOG`; chomp($logdir); system("touch", "$logdir/core.fake"); Now run the test "./job_core_leaveinqueue_van.run". (You'll need to have run "make tests" first, and you'll need to do an in-source build, not an out-of-source build.) The output ends: 12/02/27 13:41:20: CT:Job not in queue as expected ok + END STDOUT + BEGIN STDERR Can not count</scratch/adesmet/CONDOR_SRC_TEST/src/condor_tests/Cores/core_error_trace>:No such file or directory + END STDERR +------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Expectation Failed on cmd <./job_core_leaveinqueue-false_van.pl> The "Can not count" line is the best clue you get that the actual error is "A core file was created." The message is emitted in CondorTest.pm in CountFileTrace(), called from MoveCoreFile(), called from CoreCheck(). CoreCheck has detected a core file. MoveCoreFile wants to rename the core file by appending _$entries. $entries is returned by CountFileTrace, and is the number of lines in "core_error_trace". I believe it's being used to generate a unique identifiers to avoid collisions, essentially numbering the core files starting from 1. Theory: the problem is bootstrapping. The code is checking to verify that the file exists before doing any work on it. However, no one ever actually creates the file in the first place. MoveCoreFile should be modified to create the file if necessary.

title: Ticket #4090: Cleaner param_* interface
description: Based on a discussion between knoeller and adesmet: The current param_* system... ...is error prone; if you typo the name, it will "work", but not as you expect. ...requires passing in a default, which is redundant and potentially error prone for parameters in param_info.in. ...has silly names. param_boolean returns a bool, not a boolean. param_integer returns an int, not an integer. ...should remain valid C, so no function name overloading. Proposed: Add new functions. They should use the type actually returned (param_bool, param_int). They should not take a default. Instead of taking a typo-prone char*, it should take param_id, an enum from param_info_tables.h (the enum already exists, but is currently unnamed). Using the enum provides some type safety. If an out-of-range value is passed it, it should be a fatal error, as it represents either memory corruption or a serious programming error. For example, where today we have // These omit some specialized arguments bool param_boolean( const char *name, bool default_value); int param_integer( const char *name, int default_value = 0); we would also have bool param_bool(param_id id); int param_int(param_id id); These new functions can't replace all cases, but they can replace a large number, probably the vast majority.

title: Ticket #7346: Docker universe jobs should pull latest version of image
description: Currently, for Docker universe jobs, the startd does not check that the local image is the latest version of that image. This can be frustrating for users who aren't aware of this behavior and instead expect the execution image to be updated when they push to the same tag (i.e., latest) on DockerHub. Instead, the startd should do one of these two things: Run docker pull <image> before it creates the job container, which will update the local image to the latest version if it needs to. Run docker create with the --pull tag which will be introduced in Docker 19.09, which has not been released at the time of writing this ticket.

title: Ticket #5681: DAGMan fails to detect that node jobs have left the queue
description: I just talked to Karan Vahi, and he reports that Pegasus has seen some cases where DAGMan has failed to recognize that node jobs have left the queue. Interestingly, he says that in these cases there is no terminated event in the workflow log file, but condor_q reports the job as no longer being in the queue. That means that there's clearly a problem outside of DAGMan itself. However, Karan suggests that if we go too long without getting any events, DAGMan should directly query the schedd about jobs it still thinks are in the queue. If the job is no longer in the queue, DAGMan would consider the job failed (and initiate a retry, if one is defined). Hmm -- if we do this, we need to think about how it will interact with recovery mode. Maybe DAGMan should write a fake terminated event to the workflow log if we declare one of these nodes failed.

title: Ticket #2451: printf() in standard universe changes errno in violation of POSIX
description: When condor_compile is used it seems the value of errno is changed to 0 in the printf() call, which is not in keeping with standard C. While library functions are allowed to change the value of errno, even if there is no error, they must not change it to the value 0. $ uname -a Linux marlin.phys.uwm.edu 2.6.18-238.9.1.el5 #1 SMP Tue Apr 12 18:10:13 EDT 2011 x86_64 x86_64 x86_64 GNU/Linux $ condor_version $CondorVersion: 7.4.2 Mar 29 2010 BuildID: 227044 $ $CondorPlatform: X86_64-LINUX_RHEL5 $ $ cat hello.c #include <errno.h> #include <stdio.h> int main(void) { errno = 1; printf("hello, world\n"); printf("errno = %d\n", errno); return errno; } $ gcc -o hello hello.c $ ./hello hello, world errno = 1 $ echo $? 1 $ condor_compile gcc -o hello hello.c [... various condor_compile warnings suppressed ...] $ ./hello Condor: Notice: Will checkpoint to ./hello.ckpt Condor: Notice: Remote system calls disabled. hello, world errno = 0 $ echo $? 0 Specifically: in Section 7.5 of ISO/IEC 9899:1999 3 The value of errno is zero at program startup, but is never set to zero by any library function.172) The value of errno may be set to nonzero by a library function call whether or not there is an error, provided the use of errno is not documented in the description of the function in this International Standard. BTW, footnote 172 reads: 172) Thus, a program that uses errno for error checking should set it to zero before a library function call, then inspect it before a subsequent library function call. Of course, a library function can save the value of errno on entry and then set it to zero, as long as the original value is restored if errno’s value is still zero just before the return. POSIX is in alignment with the C standard on this point: http://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/009695399/functions/xsh_chap02_03.html contains (note the second sentence): The value of errno should only be examined when it is indicated to be valid by a function's return value. No function in this volume of IEEE Std 1003.1-2001 shall set errno to zero. For each thread of a process, the value of errno shall not be affected by function calls or assignments to errno by other threads.
creator: pfc

In the 8.9 series, we plan to change the compile time default to UTC,ISO_DATE and at that time, an admin can go back to the older date/time format by configuring !UTC,!ISO_DATE or by configuration LEGACY 2019-May-30 11:43:44 by johnkn: Currently, there is no way for the user to opt in to these formatting options for their own logs. the options can only be set by the schedd/shadow configuration. title: Ticket #7653: condor_wait should read all before deciding to exit
description: when condor_wait is not told a specific number of jobs to wait for, it currently stops reading the log file and exits as soon as the number of jobs that it is tracking goes to 0. This means that you cannot use the same .log file for more than a single test run, because a subsequent call to condor_wait will never see submit events that happen after the first set of jobs finishes. What condor_wait should do instead is read all of the events that currently exist, and then go into a read/poll loop waiting for any incomplete jobs to exit.

title: Ticket #248: Job Hooks leave starter in wrong privstate
description: (This ticket was once 1628 (backup) 1628 (public) and was copied over. The original submitter was psilord.) Submitted by psilord on Mon, 2008-08-11 13:42. Reproduction: Install condor 7.1.2 prerelease (as of 2008-9-10) as root, use the job hooks feature. After running the initial job hooks, one gets an error like this: 8/8 09:03:57 in VanillaProc::StartJob() 8/8 09:03:57 in OsProc::StartJob() 8/8 09:03:57 IWD: /autohome/u100/rherban/condortest 8/8 09:03:57 passwd_cache: setgroups( rherban ) failed. 8/8 09:03:57 set_user_egid - ERROR: initgroups(rherban, 6751) failed, errno: Operation not permitted 8/8 09:03:57 Input file: /autohome/u100/rherban/condortest/in.blast 8/8 09:03:57 Failed to open '/autohome/u100/rherban/condortest/out.blast' as standard output: Permission denied (errno 13) 8/8 09:03:57 Failed to open '/autohome/u100/rherban/condortest/err.blast' as standard error: Permission denied (errno 13) 8/8 09:03:57 Failed to open some/all of the std files... 8/8 09:03:57 Aborting OsProc::StartJob. 8/8 09:03:57 Failed to start job, exiting Expected behaviour: The job should execute under the correct permissions. The above error does not happen in 7.1.0. Additional notes: See admin 18237 which was the rust user that found the problem.
remarks: Submitted by rrati on Tue, 2008-08-12 10:18. Assigned to: Anonymous >> rrati Status: active >> patch (code needs review) This should fix the issue, but the windows code changes in DaemonCore::Create_Process need to be closely reviewed since I'm not sure I handled it correctly. The problem was that before condor was forking to create a process to run the hooks, it was doing checks on the executable/command as the priv mode specified. For the conodr_final priv, it was changing to ruid condor instead of changing to euid condor for the checks so the starter ended up permanently as the condor user and thus wasn't able to access files not world readable. (adesmet: this is attachment job-hooks-starter-condor-uid-fix.1.patch) Submitted by gquinn on Tue, 2008-08-12 13:59. Status: patch (code needs review) >> patch (code needs work) The change to uids.C and the UNIX path of DaemonCore::Create_Process() look good. On the Windows side, use of CreateProcessAsUser and the CREATE_NEW_CONSOLE flag are specific to launching stuff as the user and don't apply to PRIV_CONDOR_FINAL. So you can simply remove all changes to the Window-specific path of DaemonCore::Create_Process() from the diff. Submitted by gquinn on Tue, 2008-08-12 14:07. When I reviewed the original patch for CONDOR_PRIV_FINAL, I suggested running the test suite against a root-running Condor install. I guess that didn't catch this bug because there are no job hook tests :( I'm guessing that additionally Rob does his job hook development / testing using a personal Condor, otherwise he probably would have seen this right away. Before committing this patch, I suggest at least some quick testing of job hooks running under a root Condor. Submitted by rrati on Tue, 2008-08-12 15:18. Status: patch (code needs work) >> patch (code needs review) Here's the updated patch with the windows code removed. When I originally tested the change to the PRIV_CONDOR_FINAL, I didn't use a job that wrote/used any files that didn't have world readable permissions. I did run the test on a personal Condor as well as a root Condor, and I ran the list_quick test suite with batch_test.pl as well. Obviously a complication job would've been a good idea when running this test, and it would've shown this issue. TO test this fix, I ran with a root Condor using the following job: Cmd = "/bin/date" Out = "/home/rsquared/date.output" Err = "/home/rsquared/date.err" Iwd = "/home/rsquared" Owner = "rsquared" This job caused failures in the starter when trying to access the output files before the fix, but did not after the fix. (adesmet: this is attachment job-hooks-starter-condor-uid-fix.2.patch) Submitted by gquinn on Tue, 2008-08-12 15:59. Status: patch (code needs review) >> patch (ready to commit) Patch looks ready for 7.1.2. Thanks for the additional testing. Submitted by psilord on Tue, 2008-08-12 16:20. Robert, are you able to put this patch into V7_1_2-branch, or do you need someone else to do it? Submitted by rrati on Tue, 2008-08-12 16:56. Matt pushed the commits a little while ago. Submitted by gquinn on Wed, 2009-01-14 11:32. Status: patch (ready to commit) >> fixed The above comment seems to indicate this is fixed, so I'm marking it as such. adesmet: The above comments were all copied over from 1628 (backup) 1628 (public) 2009-Feb-25 15:23:29 by adesmet: It looks like the first patch, the one rejected by gquinn, was pushed to V7_1_2-branch in [12499] /89b7ed194a2e1416c4fd1a3b62cc847046561e25. It was never merged to any other branches. So it was in the 7.1.2 release, but nothing else. Even if it had been merged, it's the wrong patch. support 7788 has observed the same bug. 2009-Feb-27 18:58:49 by adesmet: Fixed in 7.2 in [14048]. Fixed in master in [14050].

title: Ticket #618: VM Universe support for helper scripts to generate libvirt XML
description: This patch adds support for helper scripts to generate XML configurations for libvirt in the VM Universe. It includes an example condor_config for using such scripts, and a simple example script that reproduces the existing behavior of the VM universe.
remarks: 2009-Jul-15 20:39:32 by bkreuter: Uploaded new patch based on Matt's comments. 2009-Aug-03 12:32:00 by jfrey: General: Why not use the code that already exists for calling out to a script to write the VM's control file (config param USE_SCRIPT_TO_CREATE_CONFIG)? Why add a condor_config.vm_xml_helper file? Config file parameter names should be in all-caps (XML_COMMAND, XML_COMMAND_DEBUG) Need better names for XML_COMMAND and XML_COMMAND_DEBUG config params. vmgahp.cpp: VMGahp:executeStart(): If XML_COMMAND is set, then a VirshType is always created. This parameter should be ignored if the VM type isn't virsh-based. vmgahp_common.cpp: systemCommand(): Don't change execvp() to execv(). The VMware code needs it to find perl. Do stdout and stderr need to be available separately? This introduces new deadlocking possibilities. All callers of systemCommand() used to have stderr merged with stdout. Now they lose stderr. If a caller wants stderr, the behavior is different between unix and windows. On unix, it's separate from stdout. On windows, it's merged with stdout, but the caller must provide a dummy StringList for stderr that's always empty. xen_type.cpp: VirshType::CreateVirshConfigFile(): Why is XML_COMMAND_DEBUG necessary? Can't the helper script write its debug information to its stdout or stderr? Will the file be appended to or overwritten each time the script is run? Why is the script's stderr logged, but not its stdout? You should call error_strings.rewind() before trying to loop over error_strings' entries. You log the contents of error_strings twice in a row. Was there a reason you used a socket in systemCommand() instead of a pair of pipes? With pipes, you wouldn't have the problem of being unable to close stdin and stdout separately. 2009-Aug-10 22:52:41 by bkreuter: The exist code will not pass classad attributes that do not have the JobVM or VMPARAM prefix. I did not want to break compatibility with existing scripts by changing this behavior. The condor_config.vm_xml_helper was created as part of an example of how to use this feature; it has two functional lines, and several lines of comments. I changed the names of the two parameters; it is now LIBVIRT_XML_SCRIPT and LIBVIRT_XML_SCRIPT_DEBUG. The second parameter is needed to allow extra debugging information; this was the simplest way to signal to a script that extra debugging information should be provided. How this file is opened -- whether it is overwritten or appended -- is at the discretion of the script writer. I updated systemCommand so that there is a final parameter, which allows callers to merge stderr and stdout. It does not appear that any current code in the vmgahp directory does so, but it is now possible nonetheless. The behavior on Windows and Unix will be the same now when the outputs are supposed to be merged. The purpose of separating stdout and stderr was to allow the XML generator scripts to write the XML to their stdout; stderr can then be used for warnings instead of just errors. The stderr is not actually logged twice; it is logged once, but a second copy of the logging code was included for the case when the execution failed. The rest of your comments should be corrected in this new patch. 2009-Aug-13 11:35:34 by jfrey: Comments on the latest patch... src/condor_examples/Imakefile: Why is the make target for condor_limits_wrapper.sh removed? I have no idea what it does and it isn't referenced anywhere else in the code, but it doesn't appear to be related. src/condor_examples/condor_config.generic: Remove changed value of STARTER_DEBUG. I see the new config code (#123) lists D_NODATE as the new default value, but that setting doesn't exist. I'll talk to Pete about that. src/condor_examples/condor_config.vm_xml_helper: This file should be removed and the sample usage of LIBVIRT_XML_SCRIPT and LIBVIRT_XML_SCRIPT_DEBUG placed in condor_config.generic, but commented out. There's no reason to have a separate file, whose other contents have already diverged from condor_config.generic. src/condor_examples/generic_xml.yacc, src/condor_examples/generic_xml.yy, src/condor_examples/mkqcow.sh: What do these do? They don't appear to be used by anything else in the code. vmgahp_common.cpp: systemCommand(): The parent process's handling of stdin_pipes and stdout_pipes is reversed. childerr is never closed. The patch still changes the default handling of stderr from being merged with stdout to being discarded. This will cause most errors messages to be lost, whereas currently they are logged. xen_type.cpp: VirshType::CreateVirshConfigFile(): With systemCommand() using pipes, the blank line after the classad shouldn't be necessary, and the interface is a little cleaner without it. When calling simple_helper.awk, you pass a filename on the command-line that the script writes the XML file into. After the script finishes, you then overwrite that file with the script's stdout, which it appears would be empty. One error print line in the script is missing a redirect. Here's an alternative to LIBVIRT_XML_SCRIPT_DEBUG which I think is more flexible: The script writes the XML to it stdout, which the gahp then writes to the desired file. The command-line arguments to the script are set by a config knob LIBVIRT_XML_SCRIPT_ARGS. The filename for the XML file doesn't have to be passed to the script, since the gahp writes the file. Then, all arguments to the script are at the discretion of the script's writer, who can set them as desired via the new config knob. 2009-Aug-13 13:09:29 by bkreuter: Some of the issues your brought up were a result of me creating the patch against the wrong commit; I have fixed that. The yacc script is just another example of a script that could be used with this new feature; I can remove it if you do not want to merge it in. I uploaded a new patch addressing the other concerns. 2009-Aug-13 14:22:07 by jfrey: Comments on patch.4. I missed a couple of these on the previous round. src/condor_examples/Imakefile: Remove condor_config.vm_xml_helper from FILES list. src/condor_vm-gahp/simple_helper.awk: Change script name to include 'libvirt'. src/condor_vm-gahp/vmgahp.cpp: param("xml_command") should be param("LIBVIRT_XML_SCRIPT") src/condor_vm-gahp/vmgahp_common.cpp: stdin_pipes and stdout_pipes are reversed in fdopen() calls. Use args.AppendArgsV1RawOrV2Quoted() instead of args.AppendArg() for LIBVIRT_XML_SCRIPT_ARGS. That allows multiple arguments to be given. 2009-Aug-13 14:31:03 by jfrey: One more comment on patch.4: CreateVirshConfigFile() is no longer sticking an extra newline after the classad in the script's stdin, but the awk script still has a comment about expecting a blank line. I don't know awk well enough to tell if the script needs the blank line. 2009-Aug-13 15:08:50 by bkreuter: Uploaded a new patch. 2009-Aug-13 15:49:57 by jfrey: Comments on patch.5 (almost there!): Patch isn't made against current master branch. src/condor_vm-gahp/Imakefile: Change name of awk script in all_target(). 2009-Aug-13 16:35:35 by bkreuter: This should do it. 2009-Aug-13 16:59:44 by jfrey: patch.6 doesn't include the awk script. 2009-Aug-13 17:08:10 by bkreuter: Thanks for catching that. 2009-Aug-14 09:46:11 by jfrey: Patch.7 is missing generic_xml.yacc, generic_xml.yy, and mkqcow.sh, as was patch.6 it turns out. 2009-Aug-14 10:02:43 by bkreuter: Ok, now everything should be good. 2009-Aug-14 10:27:00 by jfrey: In patch.8, src/condor_examples/Imakefile is missing the make target for lex.yy.c. 2009-Aug-14 10:36:14 by bkreuter: Fixed. 2009-Aug-14 11:00:00 by jfrey: It looks like you hand-edited the patch to add the Imakefile target, but forgot to update the line numbers. With a little tweak, I applied the last patch and pushed it.

title: Ticket #395: EventLog.lock fd leak and submission events are bogus
description: https://bugzilla.redhat.com/show_bug.cgi?id=496432 All the gory details are in the BZ above. The general issue is when the EVENT_LOG is configured in the condor_schedd, the schedd leaks fds to the event log's lock file whenever a cluster is submitted. The result is the schedd runs out of fds and EXCEPTs. The workaround for this is to not use the EVENT_LOG.

The NFS log shows FDs 11,13,14,15 being leaked. It appears that the lock is opened as fd 11, then the log is opened as fd 12. The header is written to fd 12. Then for each job in the cluster I submitted, queue 5, the lock is reopened though it exists, and that new fd is leaked. Finally at the end of the submission the last lock fd is closed, 16, and the fd to the log, 12, is closed. In the non-NFS case, the trace looks pretty similar, except the opens on the lock file fail, and thus can't be leaked. It seems the qmgmt.cpp::CloseConnection doesn't properly clean up the UserLog usr_log. It initializes it multiple times, and each initialization would leak the fd. This raises another question, do the events get written if a job is submitted via SOAP? 2009-Apr-27 07:52:03 by matt: With my last commit, c2cfbff08, I think this is resolved. The issue was qmgmt.cpp's CloseConnection would call UserLog::initialize for each proc in the submitted cluster. It did so purely (or so it seemed) to change the cluster/proc id held by the UserLog. However, because of a change back in May '08, the initialize call would also initialize lock fds. The result of init+init+init... meant that only the last init's fds were cleaned up when the UserLog was deleted. The fix I implemented for this was to init the UserLog once and then call setGlobalCluster/Proc to set the cluster/proc. The reason this did not leak on a local fs was because opening the lock file was failing with EACCESS, and the lock fd was never recorded on the UserLog. This is kinda scary because it means the lock wasn't really acquired and yet writing to the log went ahead. On NFS the open succeeded and subsequent inits would overwrite it. A separate issue here is why the open was failing on a local fs and if locking is happening properly on NFS, but that's another ticket that should be filed - likely by Nick.

title: Ticket #3237: Negotiator writes malformed Accountnew.log
description: Due to changes in ticket #3221, the 7.8.4 negotiator writes malformed entries in the Accountantlog.new. that problem has been corrected (checkins in parent ticket) but this ticket is here to deal with the fallout. The 7.8.5 negotiator must be able to repair a corrupt log generated by a 7.8.4 negotiator to make upgrading easy for users. The current proposal is to write C++ code that does the equivalent of: sed -i -e 's/< /</g' -e 's/ , /,/g' -e 's/ >/>/g' Accountantnew.log And have the 7.8.5 negotiator invoke this code when it detects the log is corrupt.

title: Ticket #5249: OOM killer score adjustment isn't low enough
description: The starter lowers the /proc/pid/oom_adj or /proc/pid/oom_score_adj for jobs, so that the OOM killer is biased to be more likely to chose a job instead of a condor daemon or other user process on the machine. Unfortunately, chrome also does this for its tabs, and at a larger level than condor. For systems with /proc/pid/oom_score_adj, set the value to 800 instead of 16, so that condor jobs will be chosen over chrome tabs, which are at 300.

title: Ticket #6936: job event log timestamps have no year, can appear to go backwards
description: A bug was reported to RT that the timestamps in the job event log don't work for users that care about the event times and have logs with events in them that were not written in the current year. In particular, there is no year or timezone information in the log, and the event reader c++ classes reconstruct the full timestamp assuming localtime and all that all event are from the current year. For example Worker and Scheduler both have the correct RTC time: 2019-01-01 04:00:00Z Worker's timezone is PST, Scheduler's timezone is UTC Worker localtime = 2018-12-31 20:00:00 -> writes 12/31 20:00:00 Reader localtime = 2019-01-01 04:00:00 -> tm_year = 119 + 12/31 20:00:00 :. EventTime = 2019-12-31 20:00:00 python code to reproduce the problem import htcondor data = """ 028 (1234.000.000) 12/31 23:59:59 Job ad information event triggered. EventTime = "2016-12-31T23:59:59" Cluster = 1234 Proc = 0 SubmitHost = "<xxx>" MyType = "SubmitEvent" TriggerEventTypeNumber = 0 EventTypeNumber = 28 Subproc = 0 TriggerEventTypeName = "ULOG_SUBMIT" ... 028 (1234.000.000) 01/01 00:00:00 Job ad information event triggered. EventTime = "2017-01-01T00:00:00" Cluster = 1235 Proc = 0 SubmitHost = "<xxx>" MyType = "SubmitEvent" TriggerEventTypeNumber = 0 EventTypeNumber = 28 Subproc = 0 TriggerEventTypeName = "ULOG_SUBMIT" ... """ TEST_FILE = "/tmp/condor.sampledata.txt" with open(TEST_FILE, "w") as outf: outf.write(data) with open(TEST_FILE, "r") as inf: for event in htcondor.read_events(inf): print(event['EventTime']) Run the script: note that both dates have the current year, but note that the first date is incorrect by an additional year. The bug reporter goes on to suggest that we could fix this bug by adding the year and possibly timezone information to the header of each event, or adding an EventTime field to the body of every event. Both of these suggestions would break backward compatibility. The first is much less work for us. The second suggestion seems like it might not break backward compatibility, but not all events would tolerate the inclusion of new fields, so it actually would break backward compatibility. We should fix this by changing the log reader so that either the current date/time format or an ISO 8601 time of the form yyyy-mm-dd hh:mm+hh or hh:mmZ is allowed. We should then add a configuration knob for the Schedd and Shadow that allows administrators to opt in to the ISO 8601 date/time format. This new configuration knob should default to off for the 8.8 series, and to on for the 8.9 series. We might also want to allow the Administrator to opt in to UTC timestamps. We could also optionally provide a tool - perhaps a python script, that would intelligently convert a completed user event log to one with ISO 8601 timestamps. Fixes In 8.8.2, the c++ event log reader will be changed to that it will read either the current date format or an ISO 8601 date including the year from the event header. It will also correctly parse a time with a fractional seconds value, and/or an optional trailing Z to indicate UTC. It will also parse but ignore a trailing timezone field in ISO 8601 form. So HTCondor 8.8.2 will be able to consume log files with either 8.8.1 or earlier event headers, or ISO 8601 compatible headers. It may not report the time correctly if a timezone other than Z is used, but it will not choke on the format. Two knobs will be added, but not documented that allows a system administrator to opt in to ISO 8601 dates and/or UTC for all user job logs and for the global event log. These knobs will be config fragment # this controls format of the EventLog EVENT_LOG_FORMAT_OPTIONS=UTC,ISO_DATE # this sets default format options for job's Log and DagmanLog DEFAULT_USERLOG_FORMAT_OPTIONS=UTC,ISO_DATE permitted values for these two knobs will be zero or more of the case-insensitive options UTC - print the date and time as UTC with a trailing Z as the timezone ISO_DATE - print the date as YYYY-MM-DD SUB_SECOND - (future) print a fractional seconds value These options may be prefixed by a ! to turn the option off, although at present there is no need to do this because all options are set to off by default in the code. In the the 8.9 series, we plan to change the compile time default to UTC,ISO_DATE and at that time, an admin can go back to the older date/time format by configuring !UTC,!ISO_DATE

title: Ticket #7624: clean up client to CredD interface for user impersonation
description: Credential Management *** THIS BRANCH HAS BEEN MERGED AND IS NOW CLOSED *** All changes went into the V8_9_7-gt7624-cred-branch, now merged to V8_9_7-branch NOTE: Documentation work to be done in ticket #7646 Summary There are a couple places in the code where users interface with the CredD. One is during job submission when they specify in the submit file that they need certain OAuth tokens. Another is when they use the condor_store_cred command to manipulate their credentials. Currently, condor_submit, condor_store_cred and python use the username that is running the process as the username argument when talking the Credd. This is passed to the Credd as a simple string in some cases, and in the ClassAd token requests that it sends to the CredD when submitting a job. This circumvents the credential mapping that the CredD and SchedD would normally employ. As such, it is possible to have a mismatch between who the CredD will store credentials for and who the SchedD will run the job as. Or to have the CredD refuse to store the credential because the mapped authenticated name does not match the supplied name. We propose to change this so that the CredD interprets a missing or empty username as a request to manage credentials for that mapped authenticated user. And the tools supply no username, counting on the CredD to fill that information in. The exception to this will be when managing passwords, since the wire protocol for managing passwords goes back many years and new tools may need to talk to an older CredD and V.V. Code changes [ZKM] Changes to the CredD: if no Username is supplied or it is the empty string, then then the CredD will store tokens for the authenticated user. If a Username is supplied and the authenticated user matches it or is a member of CRED_SUPER_USERS then the CredD will look at Username and do the operation on their behalf. These changes go into store_cred_handler() in store_cred.cpp, and in CredDaemon::check_creds_handler() in credd.cpp [ZKM] Change for submit: Pass an empty string for the Username argument to do_store_cred() for Kerberos creds Stop sending the Username attribute in token request ads, and always let the CredD fill it in. [TJ] Change for python bindings pass an empty string for Username argument when python passes None as the username for all of the methods on the CredD object that take a username except those that call do_store_cred() and pass a password. [TJ] Changes for condor_store_cred If the invoker does not provide a username, and is not storing a password, pass an empty string to the Username field of do_store_cred() Work Plan [DONE] There is a branch: V8_9_7-gt7624-cred-branch [DONE] Zach will modify submit.cpp and credd.cpp [DONE] TJ will modify all other client tools [DONE] Zach will merge to V8_9_7-branch (when code complete) [DONE] TimT will work with Moate to install on CHTC [DONE] Zach will test Kerberos functionality (submit and store/query/delete cred) [DONE] Jason will test OAuth functionality (submit and store/query/delete cred) [ ] TJ will test Password functionality (user and pool passwords, linux and windows, submit and store/query/delete cred)

title: Ticket #2563: bug in startd alive protocol when there are communication failures
description: Communication failure during the startd->schedd alive protocol can cause the startd to kill the job, because it incorrectly determines that the claim is no longer recognized by the schedd. I have observed this actually happen to jobs in the Wisconsin CMS T2. startd log: 10/19/11 12:07:20 Calling Handler <Alive to schedd <128.104.29.235:54791>> (3) 10/19/11 12:07:20 slot1: Received Alive response of -1 from schedd <128.104.29.235:54791> job 1.0 10/19/11 12:07:20 slot1: State change: claim no longer recognized by the schedd - removing claim schedd log, showing a timeout when reading a message from the startd: 10/19/11 12:07:15 (pid:93969) Received TCP command 441 (ALIVE) from unauthenticated@unmapped <128.104.29.235:55161>, access level READ 10/19/11 12:07:15 (pid:93969) Calling HandleReq <receive_startd_alive> (0) for command 441 (ALIVE) from unauthenticated@unmapped <128.104.29. 235:55161> 10/19/11 12:07:16 (pid:93969) condor_read(): timeout reading 5 bytes from <128.104.29.235:55161>. 10/19/11 12:07:16 (pid:93969) IO: Failed to read packet header 10/19/11 12:07:16 (pid:93969) Received startd keepalive for unknown claimid #... 10/19/11 12:07:16 (pid:93969) Return from HandleReq <receive_startd_alive> (handler: 1.000s, sec: 0.001s, payload: 0.000s) The schedd command handler receive_startd_alive is not correctly detecting the error. It is going ahead and processing the command with claim_id=NULL. It therefore sends back a negative response to the startd, indicating that the claim is no longer recognized by the schedd. How can this be? Why does the following code not detect the communication failure? s->get_secret(claim_id); // must free this; CEDAR will malloc cuz claimid=NULL if ( !s->end_of_message() ) { if (claim_id) free(claim_id); return FALSE; } The answer is that end_of_message() is returning true, because of the following code in end_of_message(): if ( allow_empty_message_flag ) { allow_empty_message_flag = FALSE; return TRUE; } allow_empty_message_flag hides the error! It basically makes the first end_of_message() after receipt of a command an unreliable indicator of success. A fix for this specific case would be to check the return value of s->get_secret(). I am making that change for 7.6. But can we do better? I think so. If any attempt to read from the socket automatically cleared the allow_empty_message_flag, then the schedd code would have correctly detected the error. I think this change should be made in 7.7, but, arguably, it could go into 7.6 instead. Another issue raised by this incident is that the receive_startd_alive command handler is getting called without doing a non-blocking wait for the command payload to arrive. In 7.7, commands can be registered so that DaemonCore does a non-blocking wait, so in 7.7, I will use that mechanism for this command. In addition, we should probably not set allow_empty_message_flag for commands that are registered in this way, because we know that they expect to receive data.

title: Ticket #6873: Starter RPC stubs handle disconnection poorly
description: The stubs in the starter for RPCs to the shadow handle network problems (including disconnection from the shadow) poorly. Some of the stubs will ASSERT(), killing the starter and the job. Others will return 0, which is a valid value for a successful invocation for some RPCs. A job can easily kill the starter by doing a chirp call while the starter and shadow are disconnected. The send stubs in NTSenders.cpp need to be cleaned up so that a network error is always distinguishable from a successful invocation. An ASSERT() or EXCEPT() in the stubs due to disconnection should be rare or non-existent. The callers should make that decision. The chirp code in the starter and the chirp client should also be reviewed to ensure good handling of errors. Currently, a failure of the get_job_attr chirp command can result in the condor_chirp client printing '(null)' and exit with status 0.

title: Ticket #3688: Remove hard-coded policies on how schedd can reuse claims
description: Currently, the Claim that is given out by the Negotiator to the Schedd is very open ended. As long as it matches the Startd requirements, the only additional restrictions on the Claim are hard-coded : it cannot be used for a different user, and it must be used for a job with the same set of concurrency limits. This situation has shown to be a problem when implementing the “Global Priority” feature. While the Negotiator will pick the globally higher priority job for a user, all bets are off once that job finishes, since the Schedd will pick the next job using local criteria. Other policies based on the global state of the system would equally be impossible to implement. The proposal is thus to remove the hard-coded claim reuse logic and for the negotiator to explicitly embed the restrictions on jobs that can reuse the claim in the requirements that are sent back to the Schedd.

title: Ticket #4321: Enable use of larger UDP (safesock) fragment size
description: Very large pools using a multi-tier collector setup, such as US CMS, can observe problems where the top-level parent collector cannot keep-up with incoming updates from child collectors. A significant contributor to this problem was the fragmentation of UDP datagrams, as SafeSock was hard-coded to always fragment into 1000 byte packets. As a result, when the kernel incoming UDP buffer started to fill up, complete messages would rarely make it because one or more fragments would not make it into the buffer. To demonstrate this phenomenon, see the graph below with results from an experiment where an increasing number of streams each sent 40 updates per second. UDP with 1k fragments peaks at 22 streams at 850 hertz, then the hertz nose dives rapidly once the incoming UDP receive buffer does not have enough free space to hold the incoming fragments. The collector does a lot of work but rarely is able to reassemble a complete message. TCP and UDP w/ 16k MTU perform about the same - most importantly, they do not self-destruct when overloaded. Instead, they continue to perform at their peak of ~1000 hertz. One solution would be to use TCP updates, but that could cause the child collectors to block sending updates to the parent (which is a concern esp if the child collectors are acting as CCB brokers). Thus for this ticket we will remove the hard-coded 1000-byte fragmentation size and introduce two new knobs: UDP_LOOPBACK_FRAGMENT_SIZE is used when connecting to the loopback interface (i.e. IPv4 address 127.0.0.1 or the IPv6 equal) and defaults to the largest allowable safesock message size, which is currently ~60k UDP_NETWORK_FRAGMENT_SIZE is used when connecting to an address other than the loopback, and defaults to 1000

title: Ticket #5863: Procd crash at Purdue
description: Steve Clark at Purdue reports regular crashes of the condor_procd, and sometimes the master and schedd. After a crash and restart of the procd, idle jobs don't start running (until the schedd is restarted). Investigation turned up a 3-layer cake of bugs: Procapi crash in reading a process's environment out of /proc. Procd clients don't recover for a procd restart discovered in Create_Process() Schedd doesn't handle cleanup after failure to start a local universe job Procapi Crash When building the process family tree on linux, procapi will look at each process's environment for special variables. This is done in ProcAPI::fillProcInfoEnv() by reading /proc/<pid>/environ. It calls read() with a 1MB buffer, and sometimes the result is a value around 1,000,000,000. The function then tries to examine that amount of data in its 1MB buffer, which quickly runs into unallocated memory space. This primarily affects the procd, but other daemons could run this procapi code directly (when USE_PROCD=False). This is under investigation. Procd Restart Recovery in Clients When the procd dies and restarts, it unlinks the old named pipes used for clients to communicate and creates new ones. When existing clients get a communication error on an open pipe, they normally close and reopen, thereby connecting with the new procd. But this doesn't happen with calls to the procd that happen in Create_Process() (used to register a new child process with the procd), because the recovery code may need to call Create_Process() to spawn the new procd. Thus, all calls to Create_Process() will fail until the daemon does a different call to the procd. Create_Process() knows when communication with the procd fails in the child process. In this situation, the parent could register a one-time timer to trigger a command to the procd that would happen after Create_Process() returns. Schedd Cleanup After Local Universe Spawn Failure When the schedd fails to launch the starter for a local universe job, it leaks a shadow_rec. There's an 11-year-old command saying this needs to be fixed ASAP. Also, LocalUniverseJobsRunning ends up being inaccurate, which can cause the schedd to not shutdown until the next run count_jobs() runs.
remarks: 2016-Aug-29 16:28:19 by jfrey: We've attempted adding retries when a read() of /proc/<pid>/environ returns a bogus value much larger than the requested read size. Doing an lseek() to the start of the file and then doing a read() gives the same result. Reopening the file and then doing a read() also gives the same result. I have failed to reproduce the behavior on a machine at UW with the same linux distribution (Debian 7). I attempted to recreate race conditions between reading the file and the target process exiting. The result was always a documented behavior of read(): read() returns an expected size read() returns 0 (empty file) read() returns -1 (No such process) We logged data about the affected processes that procapi had already gathered. They were all command-line tools, both HTCondor-related and unrelated, owned by several users, including root. Several google searches turned up no mention of this behavior. 2016-Sep-29 10:30:39 by johnkn: CODE_REVIEW : changes look good.

title: Ticket #5530: condor_q does not respect QUEUE_SUPER_USERS from CERTIFICATE_MAPFILE
description: With the change in condor_q (8.5.2) to default to only showing each user their jobs, running condor_q as root against an HTCondor-CE does not show any jobs. Jobs are shown when running condor_q -allusers. HTCondor-CE makes extensive use of the CERTIFICATE_MAPFILE and TJ mentioned that the new condor_q behavior does not play well with mapfiles: GSI "^\/DC\=com\/DC\=DigiCert-Grid\/O=Open Science Grid\/OU\=Services\/CN\=(host\/)?([A-Za-z0-9.\-]*)$" \2@daemon.opensciencegrid.org GSI "^\/DC\=DigiCert-Grid\/DC\=com\/O=Open Science Grid\/OU\=Services\/CN\=(host\/)?([A-Za-z0-9.\-]*)$" \2@daemon.opensciencegrid.org GSI "^\/DC\=org\/DC\=opensciencegrid\/O=Open Science Grid\/OU\=Services\/CN\=(host\/)?([A-Za-z0-9.\-]*)$" \2@daemon.opensciencegrid.org GSI "^\/DC\=ch\/DC\=cern\/OU\=computers\/CN\=(host\/)?([A-Za-z0-9.\-]*)$" \2@cern.ch GSI (.*) GSS_ASSIST_GRIDMAP GSI "(/CN=[-.A-Za-z0-9/= ]+)" \1@unmapped.opensciencegrid.org CLAIMTOBE .* anonymous@claimtobe FS (.*) \1 root appears to be a queue super user: I can qedit and remove any job as root. We set QUEUE_SUPER_USERS in our config, overriding the default: QUEUE_SUPER_USERS = $(FULL_HOSTNAME). We use GSI auth as our default auth method (SEC_DEFAULT_AUTHENTICATION_METHODS = GSI), so the root user gets mapped via the hostcert (GSI_DAEMON_CERT = /etc/grid-security/hostcert.pem). When I set QUEUE_SUPER_USERS to a non-root user, I'm still able to remove jobs as root. Does that mean root is always a queue super user? Adding 'root' to the list of QUEUE_SUPER_USERS results in condor_q showing all jobs. So root is being treated as a queue super user except for the condor_q case? I'm opening this as a support ticket for now because the items listed above are not clear to me and so this could all just be a configuration error.

title: Ticket #7389: Expose Data Reuse to the ClassAd
description: The current data reuse code slated for 8.9.5 includes some scaffolding to simply test the data reuse feature - but it's far from what we want. The existing scaffolding allows us to specify a SHA256 checksum for the executable and allow the shadow to try to invoke data reuse when the checksum is available. What we really want to allow is a data reuse manifest. That is, a file which, when provided by the user, contains a mapping from filename to checksum for reusable files. If specified, all files referenced inside the data reuse manifest should be transferred to the job sandbox using the reuse mechanism. Example: $ cat reuse_manifest.txt aba8412e2834958e70ca328ee2b9fbf75e6c22670a119903d0f78be56c1baf8e CMakeCache.txt 0f62f30ce1d39cfe61e5f89aa05d0ef3f62ff597e01d41ba56d150195949cfa0 hello_world2.txt 40ab846d061bff2ad228325eab9918a16155ebf0d373861f48f143b1a085d28d hello_world.txt b8bace8e943202fbd0c45f3156010414f6a2f9b0455d8ce094081c331dcb6567 install_manifest.txt This file would be referenced in the submit description as such: +DataReuseManifestSHA256 = "reuse_manifest.txt" and would cause the startd-side copy of CMakeCache.txt, hello_world2.txt, hello_world.txt, and install_manifest.txt to be reused if they are in the data reuse directory (and the checksum / sizes match). Note that the reuse mechanism needs both the SHA256 hash and the file size. If it's not provided (and the transfer file is not a URL), then we can use the stat() syscall to determine the size.

title: Ticket #7223: CCB interferes with new negotiator auth sessions
description: When we create a pre-negotiated security session in the negotiator from the schedd's capability -- and the CCB is used -- the negotiator creates a security session with this key. <192.168.2.85:9618?CCBID=XYZ.XYZ.XYZ.XYZ:9618%3faddrs%3dXYZ.XYZ.XYZ.XYZ-9618%26alias%3dflock.example.com#25188186212331&PrivNet=condor-login-56c47bcc47-8vr5n&addrs=192.168.2.85-9618&alias=condor-login-56c47bcc47-8vr5n&noUDP&sock=schedd_35_95e7_2> A second later, the negotiator tries to contact the schedd. The daemon client code causes the SecMan code to look for a session named this: <192.168.2.85:9618?CCBID=XYZ.XYZ.XYZ.XYZ:9618%3faddrs%3dXYZ.XYZ.XYZ.XYZ-9618%26alias%3dflock.example.com#25188186212331&addrs=192.168.2.85-9618&alias=condor-login-56c47bcc47-8vr5n&noUDP&sock=schedd_35_95e7_2> (Note that the PrivNet portion is missing) Since the key is different, the cache lookup fails. An authorization handshake is tried and - in this case - fails. I think this is a sinful string issue, so assigning to Todd Miller.

title: Ticket #6598: CUMULATIVE_SLOT_TIME sometimes not updated
description: CMS reports that rarely, but consistently, the CumulativeWallClockTime for a job that has been preempted and restarted more than once is clearly missing wall clock for a run. The CumulativeCpu time appears correct, but the CumulativeWallClock is missing an entire run's worth of updates. This is happening perhaps one job per hour, across all the thousands CMS runs. The Schedd updates cpu times on every update, but the Wall time only on shadow exit. We cannot reproduce this at UW, and a quick code inspection has not turned up anything. We have asked CMS to send us the Shadow Log file for a job where this has happened. title: Ticket #6062: Fix blatant idiocies in Resource::update()
description: By general acclaim, Resource::update() does a bunch of dumb things. First, the commented as "Send[ing] no more than 16 ClassAds per second to minimize the odds of overwhelming the collector" can in fact send more than 16 ClassAds per second (when more 64 slots are present). It also (a) gratuitously spreads an eight-core update out over eight seconds and (b) gratuitously updates the slots out of order (8, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7). Replacing if ( r_id > 0 ) { timeout += r_id % 8; } with if( r_id > 0 ) { timeout += (r_id + 1)/8; } would eliminate both problems. Second, we're more than a little suspicious of the idea of "overwhelming" the collector in this way in the first place. Our proposal is to replace this code with a rate limiting knob (implemented as above) that defaults to off if USE_TCP_UPDATES is enabled, and to eight (public/private) pairs per second otherwise. (The rate limit came from the UDP updates era, so we figure it was trying to avoid UDP buffer overflow drops.) Third: although the initial delay of three seconds appears to be blatantly stupid, it (and the check for an existing timer) is actually there to force update batching. That should probably be done at a higher level (don't send any updates until we're done with all of the updating we're doing), but we probably shouldn't change it until then. Action item: add this comment to the codebase. In the longer term, we should consider fixing the wire protocol so we can send chained ads efficiently, and do that so we can get all of a startd's updates done in a single efficient transaction.
remarks: 2016-Dec-21 15:22:47 by tlmiller: Revised, more-conservative proposal, but for 8.6.0: Add a knob, UPDATE_SPREAD_TIME (default value USE_TCP_UPDATES ? 0 : 8), where any positive number uses the old (broken and not actually rate-limiting) code. The old code will only be modified to fix its off-by-one error. This allows us to test fast updates in 8.6.0 (since USE_TCP_UPDATES is on by default) but also allows us to turn off the change if it proves problematic with only a configuration change. 2016-Dec-21 15:50:52 by tlmiller: ToddT thought this sounded OK. 2017-Jan-23 16:35:21 by johnkn: CODE_REVIEW : looks good to me.
