title: Ticket #2922: 64-bit guest OSes can't run in vmware for vm universe
description: On some (and probably all) versions of VMWare, the default ethernet driver, vlance, doesn't work with 64-bit guest OSes. They require the alternate e1000 ethernet device, which can be specified in the .vmx file like so: ethernet0.virtualDev = "e1000" When the vm gahp munges the .vmx file before starting starting a vmware vm, it removes all lines starting with 'ethernet' and replaces them with settings that enforce the networking options given in the job ad. This will cause 64-bit OSes to fail to start. As a quick fix for Condor 7.7.6, the vm gahp should keep 'ethernet0.virtualDev' settings in the .vmx file. For future consideration, the vm gahp has a white-list of .vmx settings to keep and strips out all others. We should rethink this setup, as other settings that should be kept are probably being dropped.

Kenwood Blvd/O=University of Wisconsin-Milwaukee/OU=Physics/CN=pcdev2.ligo.uwm.edu), but the host name in the certificate does not match any DNS name associated with the host to which we are connecting (host name is 'pcdev2.nemo.uwm.edu', IP is '172.20.1.34', Condor connection address is '<172.20.1.34:9618?addrs=172.20.1.34-9618&noUDP&sock=3068_490e_3>'). Check that DNS is correctly configured. If the certificate is for a DNS alias, configure HOST_ALIAS in the daemon's configuration. If you wish to use a daemon certificate that does not match the daemon's host name, make GSI_SKIP_HOST_CHECK_CERT_REGEX match the DN, or disable all host name checks by setting GSI_SKIP_HOST_CHECK=true or by defining GSI_DAEMON_NAME. It should further be noted that the error message is advising the use of GSI_DAEMON_NAME which the manual (even in recent 8.5) advises is retired. 2017-Feb-02 12:24:57 by tpdownes: It may be lost in the noise, but the way you read certificates and validate their hostnames is, very literally, not what the specification tells you to do. remarks: 2017-Feb-03 12:29:43 by tannenba: Section 3.1 of RFC 2818 likely has relevant information 2017-Feb-03 20:12:01 by bbockelm: (note - from the MyAddress Tom copied above, this looks like HOST_ALIAS wasn't setup right on pcdev2: we should revisit that after I record my piece below...) It's quite possible I'm the institutional memory on this part of the authentication infrastructure? RFC 2818 certainly existed when we did the original implementation, but the key difficulty is the fact that HTCondor internally doesn't necessarily use host names but whatever string is evaluated in the Name attribute. We can also use the IP address from MyAddress, but that then relies on reverse DNS. The HOST_ALIAS allows the HTCondor pool administrator to provide a mechanism that better aligns with certificates that might be on the host. Ok, where are our opportunities to make this better? We should probably utilize the Name attribute in the ad, possibly even to populate the host alias if it's not set by default. This is closest we have to the "name the user types into the URL bar" that RFC2818 suggests using -- but not guaranteed to work if you name your schedd "Brian is great!". We should outright drop populating the hostname based reverse DNS. It was only an OK-ish decision a few years back when we utilized it but generally understood to be a Really Bad Idea now. Do the normal deprecation period, add hidden knob, etc, etc. Once the user's desired hostname is established (via Name, via HOST_ALIAS, or preferably not reverse DNS), we should utilize OpenSSL's APIs to compare the name versus the certificate. OpenSSL understands SANs, wildcards, etc. Right now, we use Globus's gss_compare_name: this is more oriented toward the kerberos heritage of Globus than the X509 certificate state-of-the-art. Fixing this is the most "bang for the buck" and likely to fix most of the cases, including Tom's. 2017-Feb-03 20:19:16 by bbockelm: Whoops - stand correct on gss_compare_name. It actually should handle subjectAltNames like Tom is expecting. Not clear if HTCondor is failing to invoke it correctly or we're hitting a very subtle bug. 2017-Feb-03 20:34:13 by bbockelm: Two other comments after reading through the ticket again: When you skipped the host check, the error message you post looks like it might be hitting a failure somewhere else, not necessarily in the GSI hostname checks. What precise HTCondor version and compilation are you using? The Globus libraries have evolved rapidly in their support for RFC 2818 over the last few years. I'd really hate to chase down a solved bug by looking at a different Globus version. 2017-Feb-08 15:44:30 by tannenba: Note: I broke out the specific issue of supporting subject alternative names in x509 into a separate ticket, #6135, at the request of OSG. 2017-Feb-10 15:30:59 by tpdownes: It is indeed the case that I'm hitting a different error after I set GSI_SKIP_HOST_CHECK. I think it's the new 8.6 normal for condor_q requiring authentication, which I have not setup. I also note this: I've unset GSI_SKIP_HOST_CHECK and ensured that all of my head nodes have certificates which include the private DNS name as a subject alternative name. Now I only get that 2nd error: [pcdev3:~] condor_q -global -- Failed to fetch ads from: <172.20.1.34:9618?addrs=172.20.1.34-9618&noUDP&sock=435444_4204_3> : pcdev2.nemo.uwm.edu SECMAN:2007:Failed to received post-auth ClassAd AUTHENTICATE:1004:Failed to authenticate using KERBEROS AUTHENTICATE:1004:Failed to authenticate using FS -- Failed to fetch ads from: <172.20.1.35:9618?addrs=172.20.1.35-9618&noUDP&sock=2463625_ba1e_3> : pcdev1.nemo.uwm.edu SECMAN:2007:Failed to received post-auth ClassAd AUTHENTICATE:1004:Failed to authenticate using KERBEROS AUTHENTICATE:1004:Failed to authenticate using FS This makes me think that the error message is misleading. Maybe it's a result of the client's copy of /etc/grid-secuirty/hostcert.pem (which I may not have updated at the time) not including the client's hostname, even though the error message was printing certificate information about the server. Looking at the code, is that possible? I'm using HTCondor 8.5.8 and the globus libraries from Debian Jessie. https://packages.debian.org/search?keywords=globus&searchon=names&suite=stable&section=all I believe these are GT6 and comply with the Subject Alternative Names. So it's possible this is a non-issue, but the error message misled me into believing that it is. 2017-Dec-13 16:43:01 by jfrey: My testing indicates that GSI hostname checks in Condor 8.6 respect DNS type Subject Alternative Names as described in RFC 2818. Condor is not in full compliance with RFC 2818, as the CEDAR GSI code takes the server's IP address, determines the hostname via reverse- then forward-DNS lookups, and looks for that hostname in the server's certificate. But making Condor adhere fully to RFC 2818 would cause it to reject most of our users' certificates, as they lack IpAddress SAN items. We believe our current setup is sufficiently secure.

title: Ticket #3325: Shared port service breaks address re-writing
description: One of our OSG User School users reports a problem with private networks and the shared port service. He has one machine which is a central manager and a submit point. This machine is dual-homed, with one networking going to a physical network of dedicated machines, and a VPN connecting a set of HTCondor startds running inside of virtual machines. This all works without the shared port service, but when the shared port is enabled, then when jobs start on the VPN hosts, the startd tries to send the keepalives back to the schedd via the wrong interface, the public interface (which is not routed), then the jobs are killed after 20 minutes.
remarks: 2012-Nov-15 12:34:22 by nwp: Did he set PRIVATE_NETWORK_NAME and PRIVATE_NETWORK_INTERFACE in his config? 2012-Nov-19 14:40:27 by danb: I looked into this. To my surprise, I found that no address rewriting is ever done when the schedd sends its address to the startd in the claim request protocol. This is because the address is sent as a CEDAR string rather than as a classad attribute, where address rewriting is automatic. I am preparing a patch for that. (See #3330) The question remains, why did this user see things working without shared port and not working with shared port? Somehow, it must have been working without address rewriting, since whether or not shared port is used, the schedd address is not rewritten to match the network interface used to talk to the startd. It is not obvious to me how enabling/disabling shared port made any difference. It would be helpful to know what schedd address was printed in the StartLog with D_FULLDEBUG turned on in both cases. The line with the schedd address contains the string "Schedd addr =". 2012-Nov-19 14:54:32 by tannenba: Thanks Dan... since you are preparing the patch, I assigned the ticket over to you... 2012-Nov-19 16:06:06 by danb: Until we get more information specifically related to shared port causing problems on multi-homed submit nodes, I'll just leave this ticket as is. The problem that I found with address rewriting has nothing to do with shared port, and is thus now in its own separate ticket (#3330). 2012-Nov-21 11:13:44 by danb: Hermann reports that when shared port was removed from the configuration, private network settings were added at the same time. Therefore, in hindsight, it seems plausible that shared port was not the cause of trouble. I'm closing this ticket until new evidence suggests otherwise.

title: Ticket #1318: Have DAGMan be a server or daemon
description: Just yimmed with Igor S about this -- he's interested in a scenario along the lines of having DAGMan be a daemon that would run multiple DAGs -- so he can run a lot of DAGs (independently) without having the overhead of a separate DAGMan for each one. (And Miron has proposed this idea in the past, too.) I think the idea is that you'd have a DAGMan daemon, kind of like the schedd, and condor_submit_dag would communicate with that daemon, instead of submitting a Condor job. There's an awful lot to think about, though: * Just having multiple DAG objects inside DAGMan would take a lot of surgery. * Establishing a protocol for communicating with the daemon. * What happens when you want to condor_rm one DAG? * And I suspect that there are a ton of little gotchas waiting... Anyhow, I told Igor that I'd make a ticket for this, but I really think it can't get worked on without a push from Miron, because it will be a big job.

title: Ticket #6824: Update processing of ALLOW lists
description: In conjunction with #6788, we need to change the default processing of ALLOW_* lists. If there are no configuration files, the default is for HTCondor to DENY all requests. The previous default was to DENY configuration requests, but ALLOW all others. In addition, if ALLOW_DAEMON was not specified, then the ALLOW_WRITE permission was used. To return to the previous behavior, the following to your configuration will work in most cases: ALLOW_READ = * ALLOW_DAEMON = $(ALLOW_WRITE) The metaknob use SECURITY:HOST_BASED applies these two changes. title: Ticket #4819: "queue" for multiple files
description: One of the most common user questions we get is "how do I process a directory of files?" Sadly, there's no answer that doesn't involve a perl script. We should introduce some new semantics for the "queue" command in condor_submit files. Currently, queue N Means to queue N jobs, with $(Process) expanding to values 0 through N-1. The expanded queue syntax will be one of the following queue [<int-expr>] [<v>] in <itemlist> queue [<int-expr>] [<v>] matching <globlist> queue [<int-expr>] [<v1>,<v2>,...] from <itemfile> where [] indicates optional parts of the syntax. <int-expr> is an expression evaluating to an integer <v> is a submit variable name to be used as the loop variable <itemlist> is a list of comma and/or spaces separated literals <globlist> is a list of comma and/or space separated glob patterns. <itemfile> is the name of a file, - indicates stdin. each line of the file will be tokenized and used to set values for loop variables <v1>,<v2>,etc if <itemlist> or <globlist> begins with '(' then the list continues until ')' even if the closing ')' is on another line. For multi-line lists, a leading '#' can be used to comment out lines, and line continuation using '\' is supported. (i.e. these lines follow the same rules as other lines in the submit file.) if <itemfile> begins with '(' then the content of the itemfile is read from the submit file until the closing '). (this behavior is sometimes called a herefile). if <itemfile> ends with '|', then it run as a command and it's stdout taken as the file content. design doc here: https://docs.google.com/a/wisc.edu/document/d/10UKaiu1BkirXP6qUmx9DyEOPPSNqKqmS-2foztKi_zU/edit# note: bbockelm's original ticket prose move to remarks section.
remarks: 2015-Feb-01 00:00:01 by bbockelm: [Proposed this to tannenba last year at CERN, but I believe I failed to capture it in a ticket until now - please let me know if it's a dup.] queue for FILE matching file1, file2, dir1, dir2, glob1, ... Here, we queue a job for matching files, with $(FILE) expanding to the filename that will be copied into the job's working directory. The file is added to the transfer_input_files. I propose the following semantics: For a filename, we create one job specifically for that file. For a directory, we create on job and transfer the whole directory. Trailing slash semantics are identical to those for transfer_input_files. For a glob, we create a job for all matching files and directories. Second: queue for FILE in dir1, dir2, dir3 This is similar to "matching" above, except that we recurse into directories and create a job for each file in a given directory (including sub-directories). As with LOCAL_CONFIG_DIR_EXCLUDE_REGEXP, we could have SUBMIT_FILE_EXCLUDE_REGEXP that would default to ignoring any vim / emacs temporary files and hidden files. For each job, we also expand $(Process) to be the proc id; however, we make no guarantees on the ordering - we do not sort files (ALTERNATE: sort according to filename). 2015-Mar-31 09:56:56 by johnkn: Note: in 8.3.5 on Windows the globbing does not support globbing of both file and directory at the same time - so Queue matching */*.dat does not work.

title: Ticket #1031: condor_kbdd is unable to write to the log file and excepting
description: All of the daemons currently write to the log folder in C:\condor, which actually requires elevated privileges to do as that location does not belong to a regular user account. Since condor_kbdd is a daemon, it tries to do the same. Unfortunately, since it's starting up as a regular user account, this means the daemon core code will actually except from what I've seen because it can't access the file in that directory. Thus idle checking on Vista and higher is broken again. It's actually also broken on XP, but there's a quickie fix that involves having master start up condor_kbdd, which will get Condor back to doing the same incorrect thing it does previously, but it's better than nothing. Current fix involves redirecting the kbdd log location to the temp directory. The attempt to do this with environment variables failed and is described in ticket #1120. A way around the issue would be to get the path to the temp directory and pass it dc_main as an argument, thereby forcefully setting the path we want the kbdd to use.

Even if they're injected, they're now running under that user's security context, so they still can't write to the logs. Short of elevating and running condor_kbdd with administrative privileges, which quite frankly isn't good practice, we need to either route the log writing to the user's temporary file or disable the logging. 2009-Dec-10 23:31:23 by zmiller: we definitely don't want to throw away the log, so keeping it in a user-writable tmp dir seems like the better bet. title: Ticket #19: Loop when killing process families
description: In both the ProcD and the older process-tracking code (still used in the Master by default), when killing all processes that are part of a family, we use do the following: Take a snapshot to get everything up to date Send a SIGKILL to each process in the family (as determined in step 1) This of course leads to a race condition where processes can be created in between these two steps which are then "leaked". Instead of executing these two steps once, we should loop until step 1 determines that there are no longer any processes in the family.
remarks: 2009-Jan-15 10:40:30 by gquinn: This applies to suspending a family as well. 2012-May-18 08:31:05 by bbockelm: Closing this ticket, as #1831 takes care of this in a generic, non-race-prone way. If people want better killing semantics, they should enable cgroups.
creator: gquinn

title: Ticket #2758: Enforce profile loading for Windows machines with dedicated user(s).
description: [Assigned to ToddT for a priority decision. I think this could be completed very quickly, easily in time for 7.7.5, which would make us happy.] Short version: Add a knob, probably named LOAD_PROFILE, that acts exactly like the submit-file attribute LoadProfile, but is machine- instead of job- specific. Long version: I just wasted an hour discovering that doing builds in the new Lab rather requires this. I don't want any of my users having to go through the same trouble; instead, I'd like to be able, as the administrator, to make LoadProfile true. I can do this by changing Metronome or tweaking SUBMIT_EXPRS. The former doesn't help other Condor users and the latter won't work for anyone who permits remote submissions.
remarks: 2012-Jan-13 12:54:02 by tannenba: I am all about making BaTLab happy :) Thoughts: TJ, what would be the downside(s) of running w/ Load Profile always on? If the user actually specifies a load profile preference in the job classad, we want that to have precedent over whatever some machine owner claims, right? Still not sure I want to special case load profile - essentially this is just an instance of a broader problem where we want to be able to specify default values for job classad attributes for any job that lands in our pool. Moreover, I am not sure I like the idea that this is at the startd level - seems like it should be more at the central manager level. What about the idea of a knob that is like the already existing NEGOTIATOR_MATCH_EXPRS knob, but instead of inserting attrs w/ a prefix, it inserts un-prefixed attrs into the job ads iff those attrs are not already specified? Maybe named something like NEGOTIATOR_DEFAULT_MATCH_EXPRS ?
creator: tlmiller

title: Ticket #1877: A job can use DACLs to deny condor the ability to clean up execute dir
description: If a job denies delete permission to SYSTEM for a file or folder that it creates in its execute directory, and the path is longer than 255 characters, condor will not delete that file or folder after the job exits. Condor should be modified to take ownership of files and folders in the execute directory when it cleans up after the job. It might be a good idea to write a recursive directory delete program for windows that automatically takes ownership and modifies ACLs as necessary. Alternatively, if there is a windows command line tool to recursively set ACLs that is available in all versions of windows, we could call that before calling "rd /s/q".
remarks: The problem turns out to be a combination of very deep paths (greater than 260 chars) and ACLs in the directories. The ACLs prevent rd /s/q from working, and the deep paths prevent the directory object from removing the ACLs. It would be better to fix directory object to handle deep paths rather than using the condor_rmdir.exe to delete the directory. although condor_rmdir is more efficient at modifying ACLs than the directory object would be because it knows that the goal is deletion.

title: Ticket #4376: VM Universe should advertise when the user job decided it has started.
description: One common problem for users of the virtual machine universe is that their VMs fail to boot or otherwise fail to start the user's application. This is particularly troublesome because this kind of badput can be hard to detect. We should therefore provide a facility with which a user can notify HTCondor that their application has, in fact, started. Once notified, HTCondor should advertise that fact, both for informative purposes and for possible use in policy decisions. (E.g., if my job doesn't start in twenty minutes, it's not going to, please try it again somewhere else.)

title: Ticket #3626: Make default file descriptor limit larger for schedd and collector.
description: For improved scalability-by-default, up the defaults for COLLECTOR_MAX_FILE_DESCRIPTORS and SCHEDD_MAX_FILE_DESCRIPTORS to 10240 and 4096, respectively. Add these defaults to the param table. The idea of upping in the collector is for CCB and/or TCP updates, and the idea of upping the schedd is for many simultaneous startd claims (i.e. startd claiming is non blocking, and the socket used for claiming may be kept open until MaxVacateTime expires) and also because each shadow waiting in the file transfer queue will have a connection to the schedd. To quote DanB about schedd FD limits: There are other things in the schedd that are affected by the FD limit. The file transfer queue consumes FDs. Each shadow waiting to do transfers maintains a TCP connection to the file transfer queue manager, which currently resides in the schedd. When DaemonCore accepts connections and registers them for a non-blocking read, this can also chew up FDs. When the schedd connects to collectors and does a non-blocking security handshake, this requires registering a socket. Registering a socket will fail if the schedd is low on FDs, due to the file descriptor "safety level" logic in DaemonCore. I have seen this result in submitters not being advertised during long periods of time when many claim requests were pending. Speaking of pending claim requests, keep in mind that when claims take a while to be requested (e.g. because of MaxJobRetirementTime), quite a lot of these request-to-claim connections can exist for long periods of time. We're planning to tweak the defaults so this situation doesn't happen, but we're not yet making it impossible.
remarks: 2013-May-15 13:32:24 by tlmiller: Is the following change significant? - limit(RLIMIT_NOFILE,max_fds,CONDOR_REQUIRED_LIMIT,"MAX_FILE_DESCRIPTORS"); + limit(RLIMIT_NOFILE,max_fds,CONDOR_HARD_LIMIT,"MAX_FILE_DESCRIPTORS"); Consensus seems to be yes, that despite the name, MAX_FILE_DESCRIPTORS when set is also sort of a minimum -- that there's no point in starting HTCondor if you you not sure you have enough file descriptors. To preserve this semantic without requiring all personal Condors to change these knobs, only require the limit when running as root. 2013-May-16 14:05:04 by tlmiller: This seems to do the job. 2013-May-16 15:55:05 by tannenba: CODE REVIEW Initial patch will not work correctly. The problem is the change in daemon core. The patch has: priv_state priv = set_root_priv(); if( priv == PRIV_ROOT ) { limit(RLIMIT_NOFILE,max_fds,CONDOR_REQUIRED_LIMIT,"MAX_FILE_DESCRIPTORS"); } else { limit(RLIMIT_NOFILE,max_fds,CONDOR_HARD_LIMIT,"MAX_FILE_DESCRIPTORS"); } set_priv(priv); The problem is 1) set_root_priv() returns the previous priv state, not the current one, and 2) set_root_priv() will still "succeed" even with a personal condor. remarks: 2012-Apr-12 17:18:46 by eje: A note on testing for parsing failures/corruption in classad log files. Certain kinds of corruption are not currently detectable. For example, the 'key' field (the 2nd field) is somewhat arbitrary, and so a corruption that only alters a key will not be detected. Similarly, a corruption that only alters an attribute name will not be detected. Any corruption that results in parse failure for a RHS classad expression (log op-code 103: set-attribute) is detectable. title: Ticket #3276: Improve blahp file handling
description: We need to reduce the number of orphaned files the blahp can leave behind. Work Plan We know from user reports that the blahp can leave behind orphaned files and directories that are never cleaned up. We looked over the user reports and audited the blahp's file usage to identify cases affecting the Condor-CE that we can fix. We identified two cases that required addressing. They can be handled with changes primarily to the condor_gridmanager, with minimal changes to the blahp. First case: For most batch systems, the blahp wraps the job with a script that manages the job's execution environment. The script creates a directory under the user's home directory in which to run the job. Once the job completes, it moves output files out of the directory and deletes it. Under the right circumstances, this directory may not be removed. When the user's home directory is shared (common for PBS, LSF and SGE clusters), the gridmanager can check for the existence of this directory and remove it after job completion. This requires that the gridmanager know the name of the directory. Currently, the directory's name is choosen at random by the blahp's submit script. We can add an optional attribute to the job description given to the blahp that dictates the name of the directory. Second case: When a job has an X.509 proxy, the blahp creates a limited proxy from the given one, using the same filename with ".lmt" appended. It then creates a symlink under $(HOME)/.blah_jobproxy_dir/ to the limited proxy. The name of the symlink is based on the blahp's job id. For some batch systems, the status script removes the symlink when returning a job status of 3 (REMOVED) or 4 (COMPLETED). In many situations, the symlink can get left behind. We can remove the symlink in the gridmanager after the job completes. If the limited proxy resides in the Condor spool directory, the gridmanager can also remove the limited proxy. We can't remove the limited proxy if it's outside the spool directory, as it could be shared by multiple jobs, some of which may still be running.

title: Ticket #5658: userlog 020 event still says "Globus" instead of "Grid"
description: This is loooow priority, but I noticed during some OSG debugging that one of the userlog events (020) still says "Globus" instead of having been converted to the "Grid" terminology that the other events have used ever since Globus code hasn't necessarily been involved in every grid transaction. Here's a snippet: 020 (242060.000.000) 05/03 19:13:35 Detected Down Globus Resource RM-Contact: ldas-grid.ligo.la.caltech.edu ... 026 (242060.000.000) 05/03 19:13:35 Detected Down Grid Resource GridResource: condor ldas-grid.ligo.la.caltech.edu ldas-grid.ligo.la.caltech.edu:9619 Aside from removing the misleading Globus name, it would make the events consistent with one another. Or is there some way in which the 020 event is in fact most accurately associated with a "Globus" resource? This is all Condor CE (and not GRAM) infrastructure, I believe.
remarks: 2017-Jan-20 13:44:38 by jfrey: The Globus log events are meant to be retired, in favor of the Grid log events. Changing the text in the events would mess up existing log reading code. I propose we stop writing the Globus events entirely in 8.7, possibly with a knob to re-enable in case some users need it. 2017-Jan-21 10:16:12 by pfc: Re, "Changing the text in the events would mess up existing log reading code" -- are you sure? Log reading code should be using the event number, not the text, and anything that isn't doing so is totally broken by design. Do you know of any examples of code that reads this specific log event text? I don't... 2017-Jan-23 10:13:05 by jfrey: The log reading code that ships with HTCondor (and used by DAGMan) reads the event text, and will fail to read the given event if the text were to change. While completely static text like the first line of the Globus events could be ignored by the reader, most events do have dynamic information that some consumers will want to recover. I suppose the HTCondor log reader code could return a partial parse failure that essentially said "Saw event 20 but failed to parse the details". But that's not how it currently works. 2017-Jan-23 10:22:53 by pfc: Thanks -- I stand corrected!

title: Ticket #2467: getdirentries is broken in stduniv
description: the getdirentries() system call was discovered to be fragile and broken. Also, the test program was discovered to be broken. Everything relating to this call and the requisite call to getdents() that getdirentries() make, is, in fact, broken. It appears to have been passing our test suite as a fluke and, in fact, didn't work in standalone mode.
remarks: 2011-Sep-15 14:37:19 by psilord: I found one problem in that we extract getdirentries from glibc and call it. This call then calls our getdents() call. The problem is that BOTH of them perform the unmapping of the fd through the file table. The second unmap is incorrect and causes failure. It turns out, that it is even worse. We need to unmap the fd when going to the shadow, but not when doing it locally, and there is no means to specify that. 2011-Sep-15 14:38:02 by psilord: Another problem I found was the test program for getdirentries(). It was simply wrong and worked as a fluke. I have a new test program which fixes this mess. 2011-Sep-19 11:11:12 by psilord: One major problem, and the reason why getdirentries went red in the first place after my initial commit to fix type correctness in the stub generator, was that when I refactored the stub generator to be type correct for return values of system calls, I missed the handling of the 'code_bytes_bool' expression in the syscall.tmpl file. That expression names the variable symbol in the generated source which holds a length quantity for the coding of a binary array. I had changed some aspects of the stub generator to hold the returned value in a symbol called "ret_val". However, "rval" was a symbol that was still valid in the scope of all of the calls in receivers.cpp. So I ended up choosing the wrong symbol and only wrote a tiny fraction of the bytes in an array back to the job. This fix makes ALL handling of the return valus of system calls use the "ret_val" symbol so it shouldn't happen anymore. I never saw the error from the compiler because it turned out, unluckily, that "rval" and "ret_val" were of the same type in the calls that were failing. 2011-Sep-19 11:22:28 by psilord: To summarize. The test program for this call actually found an error that I introduced when doing #2337. However, the test and system call emulation were so screwed up, that it took me a while to realize that this happened. Once I fixed the system call and the test, which were both wrong, I discovered the problem with #2337. 2011-Sep-19 14:18:46 by psilord: Ok, I'm waiting for a green (or green enough, at any rate) test through NMI and then I'll check in my fixes. 2011-Sep-21 10:25:24 by psilord: Ok, the tests pass. I'm committing this today, but I need to document the bugfix still. 2011-Oct-03 16:41:02 by psilord: Documented and checked in.

title: Ticket #7370: ClassAd.setdefault default argument doesn't work
description: ClassAd nominally supports the setdefault method of Python mutable mappings (https://docs.python.org/3/library/stdtypes.html#dict.setdefault). It works as expected when default is given and is not None. However, when default is not given, or is given as None (which are supposed to be equivalent), we get an error: c = classad.ClassAd() sd = c.setdefault('key') TypeError: Unable to convert Python object to a ClassAd expression. The obvious problem is that None doesn't have a ClassAd expression equivalent. If we can decide on one, that should be the default argument. If we can't, then the default argument of this method should be changed to whatever we think is most reasonable (Undefined?).

title: Ticket #2488: Parsing bugs in condor_submit.
description: Metronome uses the submit file 'environment' variable to pass data from the machine ad to the running job. We don't want to require these attributes to be set in the machine ad; they're (semantically) optional. So we end up with job ads that look like this: env = "NMI_INITIAL_PATH=$$(nmi_initial_path:NMI_PLACEHOLDER_DEFAULT_VALUE) NMI_FRAMEWORK_PATH=$$(nmi_framework_path:NMI_PLACEHOLDER_DEFAULT_VALUE)" The particular problem I'm seeing occurs on a Windows machine, but could occur on any machine with a space in a ClassAd attribute's value. In particular, $(nmi_initial_path) includes a space. The job goes on hold with the reason: Failed to convert environment to target syntax for starter (opsys=WINNT61): ERROR: Missing '=' after environment variable 'Files\Microsoft'. After expanding $(nmi_initial_path), of course, the space in "Program Files" starts a new environment variable. Feature request: we would like to be able to specify in a variable substitution that Condor should properly quote the result. Trying to do that by hand is a losing proposition. (Failing that, could we maybe gain a syntax that lets us use variable names directly, rather than having to worry about quoting rules?) However, as long as the paths don't contain single quotes, we can fix this problem by enclosing the variable subsitution in single quotes, right? Bug the First: Wrong. condor_submit strips the single quotes from the following: env = "NMI_INITIAL_PATH='$$(nmi_initial_path:NMI_PLACEHOLDER_DEFAULT_VALUE)' NMI_FRAMEWORK_PATH='$$(nmi_framework_path:NMI_PLACEHOLDER_DEFAULT_VALUE)'" Dan implies this is because condor_submit parses the whole thing and then puts it back together again, discarding any quoting characters it considers superflous. Bug the Second: Dan tried to help work around bug the first with strcat(): env = "NMI_INITIAL_PATH=$$([strcat(""'"",ifThenElse(isUndefined(nmi_initial_path),""NMI_PLACEHOLDER_DEFAULT_VALUE"",nmi_initial_path),""'"")])" This didn't work, but a close reading of the (bizarre) quoting rules indicated that using four single quotes in a row would generate a single single quote. Even this, however, did not work. It appears that single quotes are applied before, rather than after, variable expansion.
remarks: 2011-Sep-21 13:02:04 by tlmiller: In the short term, I'll try to work around this by using Windows short paths, which won't have spaces (or single or double quotes) in them, but this is more than a little clumsy. 2011-Sep-21 14:12:55 by danb: Creating an expression inside $$([]) that produces the desired quoting is problematic, because condor_submit parses the environment string, modifies it (e.g. adds in environment from getenv=true), and regenerates it. The problem is that when it regenerates the environment string, it assumes all single quotes in the string are for the benefit of the environment string parser. Changes made to single quotes by condor_submit may mess up the $$([]) expression. A workaround is to put the expression in its own classad attribute. Example: environment = "NMI_INITIAL_PATH=$$([nmi_initial_path_quoted])" +nmi_initial_path_quoted = strcat("'", ifThenElse(isUndefined(nmi_initial_path),"NMI_PLACEHOLDER_DEFAULT_VALUE",nmi_initial_path), "'")

title: Ticket #6832: Small bugs in curl_plugin
description: I came across some small bugs in curl_plugin while generating data for load-balanced HTTP file transfer. These don't have any serious impact on users but we should fix them. I'll let this sit for a while in case I find any other problems in the next few weeks. When a HTTP transfer fails and is retried, ConnectionTimeSeconds only reports the duration of the last connection. This should instead should the cumulative duration of all connections. In some cases, file transfers fail and go on hold with the following error: "FILETRANSFER:1:non-zero exit (4608) from /usr/libexec/condor/curl_plugin. Error: transfer closed with 5149571386 bytes remaining to read". When this happens the retry mechanism should kick in and just try the transfer again. Error reporting is generally not very good. We don't do a great job of distinguishing between transient and non-transient errors. Some failures result in generic non-descriptive messages showing up in the hold message. This generally needs to be overhauled and improved.

title: Ticket #291: Consistent Execute Directories
description: Some software packages build with absolute paths in their binaries, e.g., /home/condor/execute/dir_577/install. When that binary is retrieved by a later build or test, that directory may not exist, which could cause problems. It would convenient to be able to specify a token in the submit file used to create the directory instead of the PID. For instance, for the bigComplicatedTest token, Condor could create /home/condor/execute/token_bigComplicatedTest/, or /home/condor/execute/<username>/bigComplicatedTest/; whatever, as long as it was consistent. Initially, concurrency could be ignored (user beware), or maybe the execute node could just reject a job if its token directory is already in use. (In the same way it would if, for whatever reason, it couldn't create dir_<pid>, or ran out of disk space, whatever.). These directories would be identical to dir_<pid> directories in all ways, and the user (Metronome, really) responsible for populating them.
remarks: 2009-Mar-03 07:08:29 by matt: What are the problems that are caused? 2009-Mar-03 10:05:07 by tlmiller: Generally, the software won't work. For dynamic library dependencies, of course, setting LD_LIBRARY_PATH (or its equivalent) will probably get the job done, but other issues -- reading the configuration file, one binary executing another -- can't be handled by at the system level. Granted, not being able to work around problems like these really means that the software should be changed to avoid the problem, but this request sounds simple enough and would help people who depend on software they don't control. 2009-Mar-03 10:53:03 by matt: Are the dynamic library issues related to rpaths? Are people hoping to put their dynamic libs in a non-standard location (most sane systems have defaults search paths for dyn libs and provide a means to extend the paths) and not use LD_LIB_PATH type options? If the software is tied to /home/condor/execute/dir_<pid> or .../token (let's hope two pieces of software don't use the same token) then that path needs to exist on all machines where the software is to be run and it must be properly populated (installed)? 2009-Mar-03 11:29:09 by tlmiller: As I said, this generally isn't a problem for dynamic libraries. VDT may elect to disagree with me, but they distribute the generate binaries; this is strictly intended to allow software to be built and tested across multiple runs in the same pool. (So that the absolute path of the Condor execute directory is the same. Naturally, if it isn't, this technique won't work, but that's something we can fix as the admin. At present, we can't change how Condor names the per-job temporary directories.) If Condor names the execute directory in a predictable and repeatable way, the user (or Metronome, acting on the user's behalf) can populate it appropriately. 2009-Mar-03 21:31:13 by matt: Then what's a concrete, example of a, problem that you're trying to solve here? It sounds like you want a defined directory where your program is built under EXECUTE and then later some process, other than Condor, would control that directory. Would it be simpler/better to wrap the build process so that it is setup in a chroot. That might allow for a more consistent view of the world wrt the build, additionally assisting in rpath issues (incase there still are some). Since the builds should only be dependent on prereqs you even have the information needed to help populate a chroot. Thoughts? 2009-Mar-04 12:08:55 by tlmiller: > Then what's a concrete, example of a, problem that you're trying to solve here? For instance, we just received a user request to install nscd on some of our execute nodes, because a user needs to test against it. As it happens, nscd does let you specify the location of its configuration file on the command-line, but it's easy to imagine one that doesn't. (A widely-used daemon that has a hard-coded path to its configuration file(s) is 'cron'. I don't know why you'd be running tests of or with cron, but the problem is by no means hypothetical.) If you tried to do the right thing, you would build '=hardcodedpathd=' with --prefix=/some/condor/execute/directory, and then use that binary over and over for subsequent runs. However, since you have no way of ensuring that /some/condor/execute/directory exists, hardcodedpathd would fail. The simplest way around this problem is to find a safe way to allow users to request that their runs happen in a given directory. My suggestion is to allow the user to supply a name that gets used instead dir_<pid>. > It sounds like you want a defined directory where your program is built under > EXECUTE and then later some process, other than Condor, would control that > directory. Not in the slightest. If the Condor job in question happens to be Metronome, than Metronome can automatically populate the directory before running the user's tests, as a convienence for set user. > Would it be simpler/better to wrap the build process so that it is setup in a > chroot. Absolutely not. If we have to go the route of creating throw-away environments for our users' builds, we're better encapsulating them in virtual machines. This feature request could solve a user problem with far less effort and far greater efficiency. If the priority should be (even) lower, that's fine; Zach asked me to drop this idea here, presumably so if wouldn't be forgotten. The priority can just be bumped when a user actually trips on this.

remarks: 2012-Dec-06 07:53:24 by bbockelm: Per discussion with Dan in person on Wednesday: The proposed round-robin transfer mechanism isn't very fair as it gives the next transfer to the queue with the least-recently-started transfer. Consider the case where there are two users; User A has transfers which last 1s and User B has transfers which last 1hr. If the transfer limit is 10 transfers, then after 10s, User B will have all the transfer slots and User A will be starved. We proposed the following tweak: the next available transfer is given to the queue which has the least number of active transfers and the least-recently-started transfer. This way, in the steady state, no user starves. This does not solve startup issues (in the above example, if User A submits well after User B, they may have to wait an hour for the next transfer slot). 2012-Dec-06 07:59:41 by bbockelm: Another deviation from the design document: TRANSFER_QUEUE_USER_EXPR was added to determine how to configure the queue. TRANSFER_QUEUE_USER_EXPR = User; (default) this will round-robin transfers across users. TRANSFER_QUEUE_USER_EXPR = User,GLIDEIN_Site; this will round-robin transfers per-site, per-user for glideinWMS systems. 2012-Dec-06 09:42:18 by danb: TRANSFER_QUEUE_USER_EXPR should evaluate to a string, so I'd just modify your examples like so: TRANSFER_QUEUE_USER_EXPR = "FIFO"; this will keep the older FIFO behavior. title: Ticket #6131: Location of corrupted log is unclear
description: One of our users encountered a corrupted job log due to disk filling up and found the following message in their SchedLog 02/07/17 10:55:49 WARNING: Encountered corrupt log record 95654 (byte offset 5046225) 02/07/17 10:55:49 103 1354325.0 PeriodicRemove ( StageInFinish > 0 ) 105 02/07/17 10:55:49 Lines following corrupt log record 95654 (up to 3): 02/07/17 10:55:49 103 1346101.0 RemoteWallClockTime 116668.000000 02/07/17 10:55:49 104 1346101.0 WallClockCheckpoint 02/07/17 10:55:49 104 1346101.0 ShadowBday 02/07/17 10:55:49 ERROR "Error: corrupt log record 95654 (byte offset 5046225) occurred inside closed transaction, recovery failed" at line 1080 in file /builddir/build/BUILD/condor-8.4.8/src/condor_utils/classad_log.cpp 02/07/17 10:55:49 Cron: Killing all jobs 02/07/17 10:55:49 CronJobList: Deleting all jobs 02/07/17 10:55:49 Cron: Killing all jobs 02/07/17 10:55:49 CronJobList: Deleting all jobs The location of the 'corrupted log" was not specified, making it difficult to troubleshoot, and extending their downtime due to a non-functioning Schedd.
remarks: 2017-Feb-08 15:21:23 by tannenba: Easy enough to improve the error message. More concerning is the idea that the schedd tries to abort when write() says the disk is full, but Linux does not always propagate a full disk error (fancy optimistic file systems, etc). The result is only partial records are written, the schedd keeps running, and "appends" another record. To better handle this, we should consider: the classad log and event log code could use the linux system call to pre-allocate (reserve) disk space for the log, say 32 MB at a time, and reserve another 32 MB when some low-water mark (5MB?) is reached. the schedd, upon restart, could truncate the log at the spot of corruption. in practice, this is what a sysadmin would end up doing 95% of the time anyhow, so we could save them the hassle. I.e. recover from the corruption the best we can instead of simply refusing to start the schedd. 2017-Feb-22 15:13:19 by tannenba: See #6153, which hopefully fixed the primary culprit of the log getting corrupted in the first place. And see #6154, which adds the filename to the error message as requested. As such, I am abandoning this ticket.

remarks: 2019-Dec-09 16:17:20 by jfrey: This is a bug in the gridmanager that affects Condor-C (a.k.a. grid-type condor) jobs. It can trigger when the job's proxy file disappears and the job lease expires. If the gridmanager subsequently resumes managing the job (say after the job is held and released, or the gridmanager restarts), this ASSERT() is hit. Most of the code in the CondorJob class assumes it has a valid GahpClient object. The ASSERT() in question enforces this. If the job's proxy file is missing, then we can't create the appropriate GahpClient object. There's a narrow code path to put the job on hold in this situation, which avoids the ASSERT(). The lease expiration handler pushes the CondorJob object out of this narrow code path. 2019-Dec-12 13:23:56 by tlmiller: Code Review Looks good.

title: Ticket #5064: Set x509 job attributes from authenticated socket
description: Currently, the X509 (and VOMS) job attributes are set by the condor_submit utility. There's no verification on the schedd side - hence, they are inappropriate for use in security-related situations. I propose that we should do at least one of these two alternates: If GSI security is used, then fill in the X509/VOMS attributes from the authenticated socket object. If a proxy is delegated (regardless of auth used), then fill in the attributes from the proxy. See the design document.

One question: If GSI is used for submission, AND x509userproxy is set in the job ad, which set of x509 attributes should prevail? My assumption is the attributes from the proxy file specified in the job ad. In fact, I'm a bit dubious about pulling them from the GSI auth at all, actually. If you could chime on how you envision this being used, that would help. 2016-Jan-27 20:40:37 by bbockelm: Hi Zach, In the case of both being available, I'd like the proxy file to take precedence (this should also be the easier case: proxy is uploaded after the job is submitted). Why should a proxy be required for x509 attributes? In the case of remote submission via GSI, I see no reason why we should require a proxy (maybe the job has an alternate method for authentication at runtime?). Brian 2016-Apr-21 15:24:46 by jfrey: Code Review I ran into several problems with this feature: The X509 attributes need to be updated when a proxy file is received, in Scheduler::updateGSICred() and Scheduler::generalJobFilesWorkerThread(). Maybe combine with the existing AuditLogJobProxy(). It appears AuditLogJobProxy() assumes the spool files will be owned by condor. Need to fix that. In SetAttribute(), the schedd reads the proxy as user condor, which is almost guaranteed to be wrong. To do this correctly, we need the job owner, which may not be set yet when a job is being submitted. In SetAttribute(), the schedd may need to consult the Iwd, in case the proxy path is relative. Iwd may not be set yet if the job is being submitted. In SetAttribute(), we need to enforce that the proxy filename attribute is a string literal. Otherwise, the user can change the proxy filename without the schedd noticing. 2016-Apr-21 15:32:18 by bbockelm: Rather than trying to put this in SetAttribute, wouldn't it make more sense to do this as a pre-commit hook? 2016-Apr-21 15:36:32 by jfrey: Yes, I was thinking the same thing. Keep the code that examines the sock used for submit and if GSI was used, place those attributes into the job ad (overwriting any user-supplied values) Comment out (for 8.5.4) all code in the Schedd that tries to extract attributes from the proxy file since it won't work in its current state and the semantics are not at all obvious. This is done ONLY ONCE and further updates to either the proxy location or the file itself are NOT reflected in the attributes. This is less than ideal but at least it is well-understood and consistent: These were the values when the job was submitted. Have submit (c-gahp, jobrouter) stop putting the attributes in. Change them back to "secure" attributes. Then, the future: Decide if we want to have the attributes updated "in real time" to reflect changes to either the location or the proxy itself. This requires the SchedD periodically checking the file for updates, etc. 2016-Apr-26 20:48:13 by tim: The revert in the commit log below only refers to the V8_5_4_1-branch. title: Ticket #4225: Python bindings should support transaction API
description: The schedd API calls exposed by the python bindings that alter jobs all perform their own transaction. For example, if one wants to submit multiple clusters or edit multiple attributes atomically (or a combination of the two), this is not possible. Currently, multiple API calls are made; an unlucky reader can could query the schedd halfway into the changes. I propose exposing transactions as a context manager. That is, something along these lines: with schedd.transaction() as txn: schedd.submit(...) schedd.edit(...) The variable txn will be destroyed at the end of the block. If an exception is thrown, the transaction is aborted; otherwise, it will be committed upon destruction. See http://legacy.python.org/dev/peps/pep-0343/ for a discussion of context managers in python. A few implementation details which may not be obvious: If __exit__ has an exception passed, abort the transaction. False will be returned by the method but an exception raised if aborting the transaction fails. If __enter__ is called twice, a RuntimeError is raised. The schedd object is not thread-safe. We do not allow multiple concurrent transaction; if a second transaction is started, we throw a RuntimeError. Because of python's GIL, we do not need to worry about concurrency; no mutexes will be used in the implementation. The transaction() method should take two argument, flags and continue. Flag can be any flag in the enum SetAttributeFlags_t; only NONDURABLE will be supported. If continue is set to true (default is false) and a transaction is ongoing, the current transaction object will be extend the ongoing transaction. No error will be thrown and any actions within the context will be appended to the current transaction. If an exception is thrown and the ongoing transaction was extended, then the ongoing transaction will be aborted. While this is a bit too "magic" for my taste, it seems to be the most straightforward way to nest transactions in the case of nested function calls. This will allow us to avoid having to add another method along the lines of "begin_or_update_transaction()". I'm wavering on whether an "in_transaction" method is needed. This is usually only implemented to implement race conditions ("if not schedd.in_transaction(): ...") and I think the continue flag mentioned above is sufficient.

description: LIGO desires a feature where a starter can set the hard ulimit of the job family it starts up based upon slot attributes in the machine ad. I propose a new machine classad attribute: JOB_FAMILY_HARD_MEMORY_LIMIT = expr which is an expression and evaluated in context of the machine's slot ad as MY and the job ad as TARGET. If the result of the evaluation produces a defined integer greater than zero, it will be interpreted as the megabytes in size to which the job family will be hardlimited with setrlimit(). If less than zero, zero, or undefined, it will have no effect.
remarks: 2011-Jan-24 14:39:23 by gthain: First, note this needs to be the virtual memory, not the physical memory, which could be a problem for some jobs. 2012-Feb-10 14:51:43 by pfc: More generally, we'd like to know if Condor can help use to OS to enforce cpu/memory/disk limits. If this if trickier that it seems to do comprehensively, we're still interesting in any low-hanging fruit that might help. Updated priority to match Todd's new scheme (1=fire, 2=soon, 3=time permitting, 4=not yet prioritized, 5=wishlist/ideas). 2012-Apr-06 13:59:00 by gthain: Which platforms do you need this for? With cgroups, which I think is available on deb6, we should be able to limit the physical memory used by a job, which is ideal. Or, would you like the ulimit stuff, which is universally available, but limits virtual memory? 2012-Apr-20 13:27:35 by pfc: LIGO only cares about x86_64 SL6 and Debian 6. 2012-Apr-20 13:37:09 by pfc: This may or may not relate to #2948 (GPU jobs report incorrect ImageSize). 2012-Jun-26 14:12:07 by pfc: Greg wrote in email: In 7.9.0, there's a new starter knob, STARTER_RLIMIT_AS whose value should be a classad expression evaluated in the context of the machine ad (my) and the job ad (target). If the result of this evaluation is an integer, it represents the number of megabytes the starter should setrlimit(RLIMIT_AS) to for each of the processes in the job. Greg adds on the phone that everyone agrees cgroups is a better way to do this, but cgroups support in Debian 6 is poor so we may have to wait. 2012-Jun-26 14:14:45 by pfc: Currently (7.8.0) for SL6, cgroups can more accurately measure your physical memory usage, and you can write a policy expression to preempt based on that. In 7.9.x there will be a high-level knob to tell Condor to do this for us. 2012-Jul-10 14:21:14 by pfc: #1663 implements this high-level knob.
creator: psilord

title: Ticket #5121: Starter unaware of Shadow exit when TransferOutput file doesn't exist
description: I looked at this issue with TJ today (2015-06-24). User sverchko was submitting jobs from submit-5.chtc.wisc.edu. Some of the jobs were running his executable successfully, but don't seem to be creating his TransferOutput file, apn_sample.mat. title: Ticket #7632: Enable transplanting of jobs to another schedd
description: We want to provide a new way to temporarily transplant a set of jobs from one schedd to another, and return them later. This is similar conceptually to Condor-C and the job router, but is different in some respects: The two schedds are not co-located (as with the job router). Jobs are not predetermined to be moved (as with Condor-C). One-time movement of jobs in each direction, with no on-going update of job status and no communication between the two schedds (or related processes).
creator: jfrey

title: Ticket #6920: Local universe jobs can't submit to schedd because MOUNT_UNDER_SCRATCH
description: LIGO reports that after upgrade to 8.8, their local universe jobs can't submit to the schedd. This is because in 8.8 we made MOUNT_UNDER_SCRATCH default to /tmp, /var/tmp, and filesystem authentication requires a shared /tmp between the condor_submit binary and the schedd. To fix this, we will disable MOUNT_UNDER_SCRATCH for local universe jobs. Seems like there may be other cases where local universe jobs may want to share files in /tmp with the outside world.

title: Ticket #7262: Provide ability for collector to receive impersonation tokens
description: The collector is a source of trust. When match sessions are enabled, The schedd trusts the set of startds in the collector. As of 8.9.3, the schedd trusts the set of negotiators in the collector. The startd trusts the set of schedds in the collector. I'd like to add one more concept -- that the collector is a trusted source of identities. That is, the schedd can rely on the attestation of the collector for user identities. The collector is trusted to generate identities (i.e., impersonate) on behalf of users. This way, if the user has a way to authenticate with a collector with a particular identity, the collector is trusted to turn around and get an identity token from the schedd. Applications of this would be running a central submit host at the collector - or, for the OSG, bootstrapping a trust relationship between a CE and the factory (without needing a host certificate). More on the latter later.
remarks: 2019-Sep-24 16:57:19 by tlmiller: Generally looks good to me, but I'd like Zach to think about the security implications if he hasn't already. 2019-Sep-24 16:57:59 by tlmiller: Also needs documentation. 2019-Nov-14 14:49:07 by zmiller: CODE REVIEW: The ticket says, "More on the latter later"... I believe later is now, and for me to really understand this to review the security implications, I would like more context. I also generally dislike the idea of running a schedd on the same machine as the collector. In a lot of existing pools, commands coming from the collector are authorized as ADMINSTRATOR-level commands based on IP alone. So someone submitting a local/scheduler universe job to said schedd could turn off the pool or wreak other havoc. Of course, proper configuration of security measures will prevent that, but I'd like to perhaps also add protective code to really restrict the trust relationship to the narrowest set of commands, or perhaps have some default submit_requirements to prevent any bad behavior. title: Ticket #383: Green Computing
description: The Green Computing enhance activity involves adding smarts into Condor regarding power management features provided by modern operating systems. Development time on Green Computing will occur each week all day Wednesday and Thursday. Developers will meet briefly at the beginning of each of these days for any needed synchronization. Developers on Green Computing include: Ben Burnett Nick LeRoy Some initial Green Computing work has been pushed to the master branch of the central Condor git repository. Further work will occur on the branch V7_3-green-branch before being merged for Condor 7.3. We are limiting our implementation efforts (at least for now) to Linux and Windows. Milestones The following list gives a description of each milestone for Green Computing, including where progress toward the milestone currently stands (if there's been any progress). Milestones 1 - 4 are essential for the most basic functionality. Further milestones will be worked on as time allows. 1. SLEEP Expression [done] The StartD will be given a new policy expression that, when evaluated to TRUE, will result in the machine hosting the StartD being put into a low-power state. The machine will stay this way until woken up via some external mechanism. 2. Wake-Up Requirements [done] The StartD will add to its slot ClassAds whatever information is necessary to wake up its host machine once it has been put into a low-power state. For Windows, only the MAC address appears to be needed, and thus the StartD has been modified to advertise it. It is likely that only the MAC will be needed on Linux as well, but this needs to be verified. 3. Wake-Up Tool [done] A tool and/or library will be developed that, given a slot ClassAds and assuming that its host machine is in a low-power state, will do whatever is necessary to bring the machine back up. Such a tool is complete. The tool is likely going to work on both Windows and Linux. 4. Collector Support [done] The Collector will be modified to allow for ClassAds it contains to enter an "off-line" state. An off-line ClassAds is one that logically exists, but whatever entity is responsible for updating the ad is not available to do so. This obviously applies easily to Green Computing, but could also be used for virtual machines or as a simple way of maintaining a roster of machines that should be in a pool. 5. User Defined Tools Support The user should be able to supply tools to change power states, in addition, users should also be allowed to set which power states are supported on a machine. This is especially important in cases where the methods Condor incorrectly detects the supported power states and/or the tools. 6. Negotiator Support Building on Milestone 4, the Negotiator will be modified to support waking up off-line machines. This ability can, for example, take into account demand for specific types of machines. 7. Negotiator Support - Continued Building on the existing Negotiator Support, this phase will add a number of Class Ad function to help in determining (or ranking) which machines should be woken. This way, for instance, machines that have recently been hibernated, will not imediatly be turned back on until some other machies that have been hibernating for longer have been worken. These functions could further help by waking machines that better match the queued jobs, rather than blindly waking enough machines to satisfy the request for slots. 8. Enhanced SLEEP Expression The StartD will be given a new per-slot policy expressions that, when evaluated to TRUE, will execute user defined tools to modify the slot's status. For instance, on a multi-processor machine, if the processors support a speed-step like mechanism, idle slots could be put in a low power state, or individually turned off, if supported. This would supplement the previous sleep expression, which puts the entire machine to sleep.
remarks: 2009-Apr-15 10:24:00 by burnett: In order to completely support Green Computing under Condor we need to make some changes to the Collector. At the moment there is only one change we need to concentrate on: a method for updating class-ads with an acknowledgment of the update. This is required so that when a machine's HIBERNATE expression has evaluated to an integer in the range [1..5] (i.e. entering a sleep state), the machine will still be accounted for (via the GC Collector Plug-in). Thus, for now, this method will only apply to StartD ads, but may be used in other areas in the future. [done] 2009-Apr-15 10:24:28 by burnett: As we saw with the Collector, to completely support Green Computing under Condor we need to make some minor changes to the StartD. For one, we will add a new StartD command, which will make it resume accepting jobs. Due, in part, to the nature of the hibernation commands on the Windows platform, there is a possibility that a machine entering a state of hibernation may be matched and accept a job in the time window between issuing the hibernation command on the machine and the the machine actually changing states. As such, there is the need to have an additional StartD command that will re-enable job matching, when the machine emerges from its den. Another minor change involves advertising all the attributes required to wake a machine remotely. This includes the machine's network adapter's hardware address (currently this is only advertised for the public IP, even if the machine is listening on all adapters); we also export the subnet mask for the aforementioned IP address; and, finally, the machine's hibernation state: the hibernation state will always be zero while the machine is running, but will be set to the proper level just before the machine enters hibernation. [done] 2009-Jul-14 13:54:11 by adesmet: Note from Flightworthy discussion: condor_q's -analyze and -better-analyze options need to learn at least a little about green computing. Probably a first step is to not include offline machines in the calculations (either filtering in the query to the collector with a constraint, or after the fact.). A possible second step would be to count the machines excluded and give a generic "23 machines are offline and were not considered." 2009-Aug-12 22:15:00 by nleroy: The interface between the startd and the new power program (tentatively named "power_state") is simple... The startd looks for it at "$(HIBERNATION_PLUG)", and falls back to "$(LIBEXEC)/power_state". At startup / reconfig, the startd invokes "power_state ad"; this program then spits out a ClassAd to standard out. The recognized attributes of this ad are: HibernationMethod optional HibernationSupportedStates required HibernationRawMask optional When attempting to put the machine to sleep, the startd invokes the same program, but this time as "power_state set <state name>". This program is responsible for putting the machine into the desired state. New configuration parameters: HIBERNATION_PLUGIN HIBERNATION_OVERRIDE_WOL

title: Ticket #6473: Python bindings confuse old and new ClassAds quoting rules
description: Most of the python bindings don't appear to be aware that the string quoting rules are different between the old and new ClassAds formats, and most Condor APIs that take a ClassAd value as a string expect the old format. Internal to the bindings, they unparse an ExprTree into new ClassAds format and then pass the string to a Condor API that expects the old ClassAds format. That's easy to fix. More troublesome, the differences leak into the bindings API. For some functions, the caller needs to pass a string with new ClassAds formatting, and for other functions, the caller needs to use old ClassAds formatting. The main difference between the old and new formats is how backslash and newline are escaped within a string value.

title: Ticket #679: Add unalterable field to unified param table record
description: If it doesn't already exist: In the record for each config knob in the grand param table, we need a field that flags a knob as unalterable. The idea is if a knob is flagged unalterable, the value for that knob will be the default as specified in the table and the value cannot be changed by the config file or environment variables. In other words, the value for the knob is hard-coded into the binary, and nothing a user can do can change it (short of binary editing the executable).

title: Ticket #7777: Monitor SPOOL space
description: The schedd currently only notices that it's running low on SPOOL space when it runs out. This isn't so bad for spooling new jobs -- if the job queue log and history file aren't on the same partition -- but can result in a lot of wasted computation and i/o as jobs hit their checkpoints, take them, and fail to transfer them back. If the job queue log and history file aren't on a different partition, keeping SPOOL space available becomes a more-serious issue. The first task is to monitor SPOOL space available. The second task is to take an action when available SPOOL space drops below a threshold (whose value may be partially computed from the knbos HISTORY, ENABLE_HISTORY_ROTATION, MAX_HISTORY_LOG, MAX_HISTORY_ROTATIONS, ROTATE_HISTORY_DAILY, and ROTATE_HISTORY_MONTHLY; SPOOL and ALTERNATE_JOB_SPOOL; and JOB_QUEUE_LOG, SCHEDD_BACKUP_SPOOL, and MAX_JOB_QUEUE_ROTATIONS, as well as the size of the queue). At Miron's request, the initial action will be for the schedd to gracefully shut down. (This will certainly prevent idle jobs from starting. It may not prevent new jobs from arriving, but we probably want to preemptively reject spooled job submissions, so we may need additional code here.) It seems clear that we should implement the mechanisms to allow other, less-drastic and better-focused policies. One goal would be to prevent problems with SPOOL from affecting jobs and/or users who aren't using SPOOL; the other would be to throttle SPOOL-using jobs as necessary to prevent SPOOL from filling up.
remarks: 2020-Aug-04 21:41:14 by tlmiller: We'll start with a timer. We start by recording the schedd's usage of SPOOL, but (a) the shadows also use SPOOL and (b) on many systems, SPOOL's partition isn't used exclusively by HTCondor, so we'd need a polling-based backup in any event. Because partition sizes and (schedd) usage vary so widely, the minimum spool space will not be a fraction, but an absolute number. Next up: [done] Add knob to configure the timer interval. Hopefully unnecessary, maybe don't document initially. do something less extreme than EXCEPT()ing when the timer trips. 2020-Aug-05 03:16:48 by tlmiller: Setting MAX_JOBS_SUBMITTED to 0 and re-configuring is how the manual recommends disabling job submission. What we probably want instead is to disable submitting jobs to SPOOL enable a configurable submit requirement (which by default rejects new jobs which use vanilla-universe checkpointing) We also want to stop starting new jobs, at least those jobs which use SPOOL. This is arguably more important than not accepting new jobs (barring the possibility that the new jobs use SPOOL space just by existing). However, it's not clear how to report to anyone (submitter or admin) that jobs aren't being started because of low SPOOL (especially if only a subset of jobs are like that). Naturally, jobs which aren't going to be started shouldn't be advertised to the negotiator. In the short term, we simply start shutting the schedd down after the 're-configure' step in the first paragraph. I don't know if that's reversible, however. It may be ideal for the schedd to switch in and out of not starting/accepting SPOOL-using jobs as often as every timer tick; it may be better to have job-starting throttles related to SPOOL space available. title: Ticket #2575: Limit c-gahp's time connected to the schedd
description: The c-gahp should not spend more than a couple seconds at a time connected to a schedd. When the c-gahp is used to submit and monitor thousands of jobs, it can end up being connected to the schedd for 10 seconds at a time or more. During this time, the schedd won't talk to other clients. If several c-gahps are talking to a schedd, some of them will start timing out trying to connect. See ticket #2279 for a concrete example of this occurring. Having the schedd support multiple client connections and transactions is the best long-term solution, but would be a fair amount of work. A faster short-term solution is to have the c-gahp limit how many operations it does per connection. This would reduce the time for clients to get a response from the schedd. Multiple c-gahps would effectively round-robin their interactions with the schedd at a coarse granularity. The additional connections will add some overhead, which may hurt the schedd's scalability. We'll need to measure this. Milestones Plan changes to c-gahp, including prevention of command starvation Reproduce OSG grid school Condor-C failures Add connection-time limiting code to c-gahp Measure effects of connection-time limiting code

With the one second sleep between connections, we could probably submit 50 jobs a minute from a single thread (but not really, because it'll mix in staging too). attachments: cgahp_scaling.patch 3775 bytes added by bbockelm on 2012-Jun-17 14:45:24 UTC. Here's a simple, minimal fix. Status updates and submits (which happen in a separate transaction regardless) are changed to set NoAck for attribute updates. If one attribute update fails, then the whole command will fail: this is the same behavior as before, except the failure isn't discovered until the commit is attempted (instead of when the attribute is set). I also implement a simple time-limiting mechanism: if it has been more than 5 seconds since the client started interacting with the schedd, it will break out of the loops and reconnect to the schedd 1 second later. Right now, the QMGMT_TIMEOUT is hard-coded to 15 seconds. I would propose making that a parameter and increasing it to 50 seconds: this would allow 10 active clients to actively interact at once. Commands are processed in a FIFO by command type (i.e., all staging requests are done before submit requests). I actually kind of like the prioritization as-is. Are file transfers non-blocking? If they aren't, I think the only place where we now block the schedd is in the submit and status updates. If they do block the schedd, we might be in Big Trouble.

title: Ticket #7327: transfer_output_remaps doesn't remap implicitly-listed files
description: test.submit universe = vanilla output = s3/output error = s3/error log = s3/log executable = /bin/sleep arguments = 1 transfer_executable = false should_transfer_files = always transfer_input_files = ../input transfer_output_files = input transfer_output_remaps = "input = output" queue The preceding submit file copies ../input to output on the submit node, but the following submit file does not. test2.submit universe = vanilla output = s3/output error = s3/error log = s3/log executable = /bin/sleep arguments = 1 transfer_executable = false should_transfer_files = always transfer_input_files = ../input transfer_output_remaps = "input = output" queue In fact, test2.submit doesn't produce any output at all, probably because HTCondor noticed that 'input' was unchanged. However, while the following copies back the whole sandbox, it does not rename 'input' to 'output': test3.submit universe = vanilla output = s3/output error = s3/error log = s3/log executable = /bin/sleep arguments = 1 transfer_executable = false should_transfer_files = always transfer_input_files = ../input transfer_output_files = . transfer_output_remaps = "input = output" queue Naming 'input' in transfer_output_files causes both 'input' and 'output' to appear on the submit node: test4.submit universe = vanilla output = s3/output error = s3/error log = s3/log executable = /bin/sleep arguments = 1 transfer_executable = false should_transfer_files = always transfer_input_files = ../input transfer_output_files = input, . transfer_output_remaps = "input = output" queue This strongly suggests we're either applying the remaps early (before we expand dirnames) or to the wrong list (transfer_output_files rather than the dirname expanded list). The manual says "Note that this remap function only works with files but not with directories," but that seems more like it means remapping directory 'a' to 'b' won't do anything, rather than 'you must explicitly specify all output files you want to remap'.

title: Ticket #5930: updateGSICred is blocking
description: We noticed that a CERN HTCondor-CE was getting sluggish under heavy load. It turns out that one of the remote schedds had decided to do a proxy re-delegation on thousands of jobs. Proxy delegation is currently a blocking (and CPU-intensive!) activity; this meant the schedd was relatively unresponsive as it had to do round trips with the remote host. The unresponsive schedd further meant the job router slowed down, periodically causing the job router to be restarted by the master. The restarted job router than had even more work to send to the schedd, etc. What saved our bacon in this case is the remote schedd was at least on the same continent. Looking at the code: the call stack for proxy delegation (starting at Schedd:updateGSICred) is not particularly deep. Further, there's only one round-trip: the schedd sends out a request, then waits for a response. Finally, there's not a ton of state associated with updates. It should be possible to make updateGSICred non-blocking.

title: Ticket #946: DaemonCore timers should return void, not int

Some code returned true and false, sometimes true during a failure. Some code returned 0 (success), -1 (failure) and a positive number on success. Some code had timers that returned int just to "keep DC happy". Sometimes a single file would define two timers, one that returned int and the other that returned void. Some code cast to TimerHandler[cpp] other code to Event[cpp]. Some code returns QUILL_* codes. Some returned pids. The casting is partially due to the fact that the Register_Timer interface is ambiguous. Register_Timer(unsigned, Event, const char*, Service* s=NULL) vs Register_Timer(unsigned, Eventcpp, const char*, Service*) in condor_daemon_core.h. The implementation allows for a Service* other than NULL when registering a non-cpp handler. That Service* is an argument to the handler. This is especially bad because many of the non-cpp handlers are void (\*)(void), meaning they expect no arguments. Some of the non-cpp handlers take no arguments purely to avoid having a dependency on Service, i.e. including dc_service. To resolve the ambiguity and continue to avoid the include dependencies, the non-cpp handler should take no arguments and passing a Service* on register should be removed. This is the removal of an unused feature - it is not possible to access a Service from the non-cpp handler. title: Ticket #7848: DaemonCore argument parser should be more explicit with -dynamic flag
description: DaemonCore's argument parser is designed to look for certain command-line arguments specific to DC functionality, and hijack them from the calling executable. However its matching logic is overly aggressive; in many cases it hijacks arguments not meant for it. One such argument is -dynamic. DaemonCore's parser only looks at the first letter. If it sees a lower-case 'd', it assumes this refers to the -dynamic argument, processes and removes it from the argument list. This means that any condor daemon calling an argument that begins with a lower-case d (ie. -dagfile, -dosomethinguseful, -dontprocessthis) will get hijacked. We should fix this so DaemonCore only looks for an exact match with -d or -dynamic. Any other argument beginning with a lower-case 'd' (or upper-case 'D') gets ignored and passed on to the calling executable. As an aside, DaemonCore exhibits the same over-aggressive parsing for many letters besides d. We should generally fix all of these. I may later expand on this ticket (or create a new one) to deal with the other letters.
