title: Ticket #1135: "Real" dynamic binary releases
description: The "dynamic" binaries we release today aren't really. Only libc is dynamically linked. Everything else is static. This tickets describes the motivations and challenges to make Condor dynamically linked: Motivations to Keep Condor Static (the status quo) Binary compatibility between distros is easier to implement. For example, we exclusively run the RHEL 3 binaries on RHEL 4. It looks like the RHEL 5 binaries will also run on RHEL 6. There are other examples and we encourage users to work in this mode. This also makes glidin into heterogenous pools easier to accomplish. We know exactly what versions of what externals are in the executable. We can explicitly know which feature of Condor are available in a release of Condor because we know what externals were compiled into it. Motivation to Make Condor Dynamically Linked Newer versions of some libraries won't statically link or only will do so with work. So we patch the libary or we use an out of date version. Kerberos is one problem library. If a widely available library has an important security fix, we need to issue a new Condor, possibly going several versions back. If we were dynamic and used the distribution's version, the administrator could simply update the system-wide version to fix Condor and every other program using it. OpenSSL is the obvious win here. Static linking makes our libraries big. This wastes some RAM, a modest amount of disk space, and a bunch of bandwidth when transferring binaries. After experimental attempts at making Condor dynamically linked, we've determined the savings are actually very significant--especially in the case of dynamically linking libraries internal to Condor in addition to the externals. Static linking eliminates certain debugging techniques that involve replacing or intercepting library calls. Brian Bockelman reports doing exactly this All Externals needed by Condor 7.6.x and 7.7.x blahp part of glite, with custom modifications need to continue building for now boost 1.39.0 available on rhel6 (1.41.0-11.el6) available on rhel5 (1.33.1-10.el5) not installed on nmi's rhel3 machines available on debian 5.0 (1.34.1-14 ) available on debian 6.0 (1.42.0-4) not available on mac os 10.5 not available on mac os 10.6 coredumper 2011.05.24-r31 not available on rhel6, rhel5 cream part of glite, not available on any official platforms maybe in future platforms curl 7.19.6 available on rhel6 (7.19.7-16.el6) available on rhel5 (7.15.5-9.el5_6.2) available on rhel3 (7.10.6) available on debian 5.0 (7.18.2) available on debian 6.0 (7.21.0) available on mac os 10.5 (7.16.3) available on mac os 10.6 (7.19.7) drmaa 1.6 probably need to continue building ourselves expat 2.0.1 available on rhel6 (2.0.1-9.1.el6) available on rhel5 (1.95.8-8.3.el5_5.3) available on rhel3 (1.95.???) available on debian 5.0 (2.0.1-4) available on debian 5.0 (2.0.1-7) available on mac os 10.5 (2.0.0) available on mac os 10.6 (2.0.1) glibc globus 5.0.1 available on rhel6, via epel available on rhel5, via epel available on debian 6.0 We make a couple modifications to Globus, which we should push upstream. Until then, we may probably need to keep building ourselves gsoap 2.7.10 available on rhel6 (2.7.16-2.el6), via epel available on rhel5 (2.7.13-3.el5), via epel available on debian 5.0 (2.7.9l-0.2) available on debian 6.0 (2.7.9l-0.2) not installed on nmi's rhel3 not available on mac os 10.5 not available on mac os 10.6 hadoop 0.21.0 krb5 1.4.3 available on all linux/mac, library versioning limits binary portability (specifically, rhel3->rhel4) available on rhel6 (1.8.2-3.el6, 1.9-9.el6) available on rhel5 (1.6.1-55.el5_6.1) libdeltacloud 0.8 not available on any offical platforms libvirt 0.6.2 available on rhel6 available on rhel5 (0.2.3-9) available on debian 5.0 (0.4.6-10) available on debian 6.0 (0.8.3-5) libxml2 2.7.3 available on all platforms we care about, except rhel3 (where it's too old) openssl 0.9.8h available on all linux/mac, library versioning limits binary portability pcre 7.6 available on rhel6 (7.8-3.1.el6) available on rhel5 (6.6-6.el5_6.1) not installed on nmi's rhel3 machine available on debian 5.0 (7.6-2.1 ) available on debian 6.0 (8.02-1.1) not available on mac os 10.5 libraries available on mac os 10.6, but no headers (7.9 2009-04-11) postgresql 8.2.3 available on rhel6, rhel5, deb5, deb6 now only used for a contrib module qpid 0.8-RC3 available on rhel6 not available on rhel5 unicoregahp not available anywhere, it's our code voms 1.9.10_4 available on rhel6 (1.9.19.2-2), via epel available on rhel5 (1.9.19.2-1.el5), via epel available in debian squeeze (unstable) part of glite wso2 2.1.0 not available on rhel6,rhel5 only used for a contrib module zlib 1.2.3 available on all linux/mac Proposal There exists two viewpoints concerning shared libraries and Condor. The first viewpoint is that the external dependencies of Condor, like kerberos, openssl, etc, should be shared libraries against which Condor links. The second viewpoint is that Condor's internal organization itself should consist of shared libraries, so there would be libdaemoncore.so, libcondor.so, etc, etc. The former will be known an External Shared Libraries, the latter as Internal Shared Libraries. Some challenges we face are common to both, and some unique to each. External Shared Libraries Default Proper Builds: For libraries which are pervasive and important such as kerberos, stop building them at all; instead build against the system-wide ones. RPATH: Set the RPATH in Condor to search $ORIGIN/../lib or possibly $ORIGIN/../lib/condor. Open question: Should our custom search path come before or after the system-wide libraries? Do we even get a choice? If before, libraries we trust to work are used by default, but they are more likely to be out of date or lack useful local system changes. If after, we're likely to be more up to date and have useful local system changes, but we can't be as confident in their stability. RPATH needs to be fully understood--especially the security and political ramifications of using it. LD_LIBRARY_PATH: Build libraries we use as shared libraries. Install them to lib/condor (relative to the root of a Condor install). We use lib/condor instead of just lib because some installs, say from RPM or deb, will make the root /, and our libraries may conflict with standard system-wide ones. Late Binding: We write a wrapper around the usage of the library and when we need it, we dlopen/dlsym/etc the function. We'd specify in the configration file the locations of the shared libraries specific to each external. Hybdrid Option: We could mix and match the above options per external depending upon our requirements. Internal Shared Libraries There are two ways we can spplit internal libraries: Into tiny little pieces like libcondorio.so, libcondorconfig.so, libcedar.so, etc Into daemoncore and nondaemoncore libraries. Proposal The internal architecture of Condor will be split into three pieces: New Classads Daemoncore Everything that isn't daemoncore The reason for this proposal is that it will be easier to maintain just three internal libraries. It turns out there is a hefty amount of work to detangle the internal libraries from each other which really isn't worth it in practice at this time. We propose the discovery method of the internal libraries should be RPATH, or LD_LIBRARY_PATH, depending upon use case. Down sides - Users repackaging or redistributing Condor's binaries will face additional complexity. This would include users making custom glide-in distributions. There will be additional files to consider for inclusion and the resulting package will include more files. Expected impact: minimal. In the event of problems, shared libraries can complicate debugging. It becomes necessary to identify which libraries are being used, which could vary for a variety of reasons. When libraries not packaged with Condor are used, it is not feasible for the Condor Team to test all possible permutations; we will end up debugging problems that prove to be in libraries versions we're unfamiliar with. Expected impact: some. Use Cases Basic Installation Via RPM Dependencies are handled for us automatically but we need good spec files. Rpath is forbidden by some distros in the executables. Distro external libraries are in the usual system paths. Non-distro specific external libraries must go into condor specific paths. Binaries will just know where to find them! Via tarball Installed in Root Context Distro external libraries are in usual system paths Non-distro libs are put into release_dir/lib System paths are preferred over condor specific paths to find libs. Installed in User Context A Condor release is split into two functions tarballs, but released as one package: A condor tarball containing the binaries and usual stuff A external library tarball containing shared libraries. condor_configure queries the system to figure out which externals are already installed or not. Then it copies just the needed external libs not already present on the system into a condor specific directory which the binaries know to look in via RPATH. Glide In This uses only a tarball, as opposed to RPM, solution. Must be cross platform, since glidin resources are heterogeneous. Question: How does Igor make his glidin tarballs? How many flavors of linux does he use? If we choose the RPATH solution to solve this, it might also work for the Basic Installation in a User Context. Unexplored Ideas/Tasks The breaking of binary compatibility [RPATH tarball releases might help]. Need to inspect each external to see which proposed method would best work for it. Maybe more clipped ports for linux distros? [Each supported one has a cost.] Upgrading Condor The recommended practices for upgrading Condor will have to change away from the current model of "just copy over the binaries". This is because if the daemons were running, we can't atomically copy over all of the binaries and internal shared lirbaries in such a manner as a Condor process being invoked sees a consistent view of its internal text segments. Also let it be known that it will be more difficult to provide custom built test binaries to people since the discovery method of the shared libraries might be different in different contexts. See also #374: dlopen Kerberos #501: Turn the Condor static libraries on Windows into DLLs #1136: Eliminate "static" releases of Condor User feedback Con Ian Chesal reports the existing dynamic libraries are less portable for him than the static ones. He encounters missing and mismatched libraries. He has a mixed pool of RHEL, CentOS, and SuSE. Here is one concrete example. The static binaries allow him to use the RHEL5 binaries on both CentOS4 and CentOS5. What if the library search path is slow? /usr/lib might be on a slow filesystem (say, NFS). LD_LIBRARY_PATH might be large and on NFS (a common case for VDT installs). If each dynamic library load is hitting slow filesystems, possibly multiple times, that could significantly slow down starting various Condor processes. If we're starting processes quickly (say, condor_shadows), this could be a problem. Perhaps it's not too bad once the libraries are in memory and shared, or maybe it is since the kernel may need to check NFS to see if it's changed. Steve Timm raised this concern. This Debian documentation suggests that RPATH is searched first, so as long as our libraries are present in the RPATH, it won't have a speed hit. However, that doesn't help us for libraries where we really want to use the system library like OpenSSL. Of course, we already pay this price when we search for libc. There are concerns that dynamic libraries might be slower, particularly for condor_shadow, for which a large number might be started very quickly. Since one shadow is already running, there is no additional shared text-segment benefit, and there is some additional non-shared data to track loaded libraries and a bit more startup time to locate the libraries. Dan's summary. Bob Ball is also concerned. Steve Timm would like to know what happens when OpenSSL 1.0 starts shipping with distributions. If we're relying on the distribution providing OpenSSL, major version upgrades represent barriers across which we lose binary compatibility. Possible solutions: 1. Some distributions may provide backward compatibility (old) versions for exactly this purpose; ask users to install them. 2. Be timely and support a reasonable subset of these distributions as they appear. Rely on similarity working for less common distributions. Possibly provide a known good shared library as a fallback (but this gets us back into the OpenSSL distribution business!) The VDT (Via Alain Roy) has several concerns The VDT repackages Condor as more native RPMs and .deb. We should avoid breaking that process. Linking against a system OpenSSL or other libraries reduces our portability. We'll need to retest a fair number of platforms we currently assume portability between and may need to add native ports for some that break. While it is nice that users can replace the dynamic libraries, in practice noone is likely to do so. We cannot rely on it as a fix for important problems. This isn't really a problem, but we need to keep it in mind. Pete Keller believes that RPATH may tie a binary to extremely specific versions of libraries, making updates functionally impossible. To take an example grabbed from /usr/lib at random, if we linked to libboost_iostreams.so, we might actually end up requiring libboost_iostreams.so.1.33.1, by that exact name and version. Upgrading to libboost_iostreams.so.1.33.2 would fail. This would also limit compatibility between distributions where only revision numbers had changed on an otherwise compatible library. Pete Keller also brought up Debian's arguments against RPATH. In short: RPATH makes it easier to pull in libraries with conflicting requirements for each other, whereby if the default system-wide libraries are consistently used, presumably those are all compatible with each other. For example, my binary A might need B.so and C.so. If I grab the system-wide versions, I'll get B.so.1 which requires C.so.1 as well as C.so.1. All is well. But if I pull my own B.so.2 from an RPATH that requires C.so.2, now I have potential conflicts. If other system-wide libraries require C.so.1, I may try loading two different versions of the same library, which is madness. The autotool developers disagree (search for "rpath") and think RPATH is wonderful. Of course, autotool's helpfulness with RPATHs means that if you build in /tmp or similar, then distribute binaries, you've created a handy path for injection attacks, a problem the VDT has actually faced. Pro Horst Severini is happy with the current dynamic RPMS Yu Fu is happy with the current dynamic binaries Bob Ball is happy with the current dynamic RPMs Brian Bockelman is happy with the current dynamic binaries and likes increased use of dynamic libraries. The VDT doesn't use the static versions. title: Ticket #317: Make CCB work with standard universe
description: CCB doesn't work at all with standard universe. Why? Because the sockets that the shadow opens to communicate with the starter are created by connecting to the startd. It doesn't connect to the startd's command port (or all would be well). Instead, the startd creates two new listen ports and the shadow connects to those. One solution would be to have the shadow create the connections by connecting (in advance of ACTIVATE_CLAIM) to the startd command port with some kind of command that indicates to the startd that it should just hold on to those connections until ACTIVATE_CLAIM happens. There are other possible solutions, but I think this one would be the simplest. If that problem were solved, it would be possible to run standard universe jobs on a private execute node from a public submit node. It would still not be possible to run on a public execute node from a private submit node (or with a private checkpoint server). The reason is that the checkpoint is sent to the shadow (or checkpoint server) by creating a new connection, but the shadow and checkpoint server are not daemonCore, so this connection cannot be reversed via CCB.

title: Ticket #1288: schedd StartJobs() called multiple times during single event loop
description: During debugging we had noticed that there are paths within the schedd where we can call StartJobs() multiple times within an event loop cycle. It may be better to create a generic function which updates the timer to StartJobs() to be called during the next cycle as it does not appear to scale on a fully loaded schedd.
remarks: StartJobs() is now managed via a timeslice timer. By default, the schedd will attempt to schedule this timer so that it spends no more than 5% of its time in StartJobs() but never less frequently than once every 5 minutes (controlled via the existing SCHEDD_INTERVAL_TIMESLICE and SCHEDD_INTERVAL config knobs). In addition, when a shadow exits for a job with a claim (i.e. not a local job), we no longer call StartJobs() at all. We call the more specific StartJob() function to get a new job for the specific claim we are dealing with. Therefore, the limit on how much of a timeslice StartJobs() is allowed to consume should really only affect how long it takes to start new local universe jobs.
check_ins: 2010-Apr-12 15:06 Check-in [25422]: Documented StartJobs() optimization in schedd. #1288 (By Dan Bradley ) 2010-Mar-18 15:21 Check-in [17667]: StartJobs() is now regulated by a timeslice timer. #1288 Since StartJobs() involves a full queue scan to start local jobs, the frequency of calls to it needs to be adapted to the size of the queue in order for the schedd to remain responsive to other tasks. (By Dan Bradley ) 2010-Mar-17 12:18 Check-in [17649]: In schedd's child_exit reaper, find new job for specific claim when we have one. #1288 Previously, we just called StartJobs() which cycles through all the claims and local jobs. This is more work than we need to do when we are just dealing with a specific claim (i.e. when not a local job). (By Dan Bradley )

title: Ticket #4570: Allow override of hostname
description: There is no way to control the hostname HTCondor uses. In the HTCondor-CE code, we use $(FULL_HOSTNAME) extensively (especially in security settings, where we want to make sure FULL_HOSTNAME matches the DN of the host certificate); however, at some sites, FULL_HOSTNAME resolves to the private hostname and IP address (set as the host's default name due to restrictions on the other batch system). So, we need a way to override the hostname detection (currently centralized in condor_gethostname). It seems this is already possible in NO_DNS mode. I'd propose that we add an environment variable, CONDOR_HOSTNAME, which does the override. Why an environment variable and not a config variable? Unfortunately, the config variable route can easily result in a non-convergent configuration - the final configuration is often a function of the value of FULL_HOSTNAME. We also expect this to be used seldom enough that the pain of editing /etc/sysconfig/condor should be justified. Per ToddT (and based on the OSG need), we can backport this to the 8.2 stable series.
remarks: 2014-Sep-08 14:49:57 by jfrey: I will add a new configuration parameter, NETWORK_HOSTNAME, which will parallel the existing NETWORK_INTERFACE. If NETWORK_HOSTNAME is set, then that value is used for the hostname, instead of calling condor_gethostname(). 2014-Sep-08 15:31:43 by tannenba: Note that NETWORK_HOSTNAME, just like NETWORK_INTERFACE, will need to be set either in the top-level config file or via an environment variable. Setting it anywhere else (i.e. some condor_config.local) will not work, same as NETWORK_INTERFACE. Docs should be sure to state this restriction for both of these config knobs.... 2014-Sep-08 20:27:53 by bbockelm: I'm worried a bit about this - I've seen many people mess up "config file specific parameters". It's really inconsistent with how the rest of the config system works. I'd much rather have less of these than more. Any changes in condor_config have serious implications to our ability to cleanly upgrade between versions when using RPMs. Can we ASSERT if NETWORK_HOSTNAME is set in the wrong config file? Why not an environment variable? 2014-Sep-10 11:12:17 by tannenba: It can be an environment variable. setenv _condor_NETWORK_HOSTNAME = foo. Also, Jaime says I am wrong above. NETWORK_HOSTNAME can appear in any config file. It is just if it appears in condor_config.local, then you could have troubles if your use $(HOSTNAME) in the LOCAL_CONFIG_FILE knob. 2014-Sep-10 11:13:02 by tannenba: Jaime will investigate if we can apply this patch into v8.0. 2014-Sep-15 10:18:29 by bbockelm: Hi @tannenba - I think you're wrong about this being set-able from other config files due to init_local_hostname. This gets called before any other config files are read. Things that could go wrong include: Anything that references $(HOSTNAME) in the configuration file - as this is expanded after the global config and before others. That is, $(HOSTNAME) and $(NETWORK_HOSTNAME) will agree or disagree depending on which file this placed in. This can include security settings if the admin wants to limit to localhost. As this affects the IP address selection, you'll get the wrong IP address in the advertised ClassAd (and possibly HTCondor will bind to the wrong interface). So, important things will or will not work depending on which configuration file this is set in - even if it does not change which configuration files are parsed! In fact, the pre. This is the same confusing mistake as was made with ENABLE_IPV6 and I consider it somewhat handing a user a loaded gun. Brian 2014-Sep-15 15:25:54 by jfrey: Have you tried this, Brian? I get the same behavior no matter which config file I set NETWORK_HOSTNAME in. init_local_hostname() is called a second time after all of the config files are read, and parameters HOSTNAME and FULL_HOSTNAME are reset after that call. So the only difference in whether you place NETWORK_HOSTNAME in the root config file or another config file, is when you use HOSTNAME or FULL_HOSTNAME to define where to find the secondary config files. All macro substitutions in config param values are done lazily, at the time the parameter's value is consulted. Any value that references HOSTNAME or FULL_HOSTNAME will get the final value of those parameters, after all config files have been read and processed. All references to HOSTNAME and FULL_HOSTNAME will agree (except when defining the locations of config files). This is the same as with the existing param NETWORK_INTERFACE. The hostname does not affect the selection of the IP address. There's code in init_local_hostname() that looks like it should, but it never takes effect. The IP address is always determined from NETWORK_INTERFACE, where the default value of * triggers a search of all of the network interfaces and the last most-public address is chosen. Selection of hostname and IP address are completely unrelated. I've made a new ticket about that (#4581). 2014-Sep-17 14:55:14 by bbockelm: Hi Jaime, No, this is just based on my previous readings of the code. If you're sure of it, I'll defer these things to you and we can move forward. Thanks for looking at this! Brian 2014-Sep-22 13:28:19 by zmiller: CODE REVIEW: Looks good!

title: Ticket #4966: Fix MAX_JOBS_RUNNING default value
description: The default value for config param MAX_JOBS_RUNNING is calculated based on the amount of physical memory on the machine. The calculation done in the schedd is an order of magnitude too large. Additionally, the calculation can overflow 32-bit signed integers and result in a negative value. I was able to track down one of the log files and found the following: 12/20/16 00:16:50 (pid:776322) Using wrapper /var/lib/condor/execute/dir_937213/glide_XuwA0N/condor_job_wrapper.sh to exec /var/lib/condor/execute/dir_937213/glide_XuwA0N/execute/dir_776322/condor_exec.exe pdmvserv_task_SMP-RunIISummer15wmLHEGS-00072__v1_T_161214_221009_1026-Sandbox.tar.bz2 4927461 12/20/16 00:16:50 (pid:776322) Running job via glexec 12/20/16 00:16:50 (pid:776322) Create_Process succeeded, pid=776349 12/20/16 02:13:40 (pid:776322) Connection to shadow may be lost, will test by sending whoami request. 12/20/16 02:13:40 (pid:776322) condor_write(): Socket closed when trying to write 37 bytes to <128.142.209.43:4080>, fd is 15 12/20/16 02:13:40 (pid:776322) Buf::write(): condor_write() failed 12/20/16 02:13:40 (pid:776322) i/o error result is 0, errno is 0 12/20/16 02:13:40 (pid:776322) Lost connection to shadow, waiting 1200 secs for reconnect 12/20/16 02:33:40 (pid:776322) No reconnect from shadow for 1200 seconds, aborting job execution! 12/20/16 02:33:40 (pid:776322) chmod(/var/lib/condor/execute/dir_937213/glide_XuwA0N/execute/dir_776322) failed: Operation not permitted (errno 1) 12/20/16 02:33:40 (pid:776322) Failed to chmod(0700) /var/lib/condor/execute/dir_937213/glide_XuwA0N/execute/dir_776322 and all subdirs 12/20/16 02:33:40 (pid:776322) Can't remove "/var/lib/condor/execute/dir_937213/glide_XuwA0N/execute/dir_776322" as Condor daemon user 'unknown' (0.0), giving up! These are jobs started via glexec. Seems that this particular error path for disconnects doesn't kill via glexec (actually, looks like it can't kill if it's non-root).
remarks: 2016-Dec-20 13:30:42 by jfrey: What version of HTCondor is this, and how are the GLEXEC parameters set? 2016-Dec-21 16:31:00 by jfrey: When the job lease expires, the starter calls CStarter::StarterExit(), which does very minimal cleanup and doesn't attempt to kill the running job. It does try to delete the job's execute directory, but doesn't invoke the glexec code path. As a result, the starter orphans both the job (true for all job types when the lease expires) and the sandbox. The startd acts as a back-stop for cleaning up resources orphaned by the starter. But it doesn't know how to invoke glexec to do proper cleanup. For the job process family, the procd does know how to use glexec to kill it. But the procd purges that knowledge when the starter exits, since the starter is the watcher of that process family. As a fix for the immediate problem that's suitable for the stable series, I plan to fix the starter to start a fast shutdown when the job lease expires. This will hit the normal code paths for quickly killing the job and cleaning up after it. 2017-Jan-20 16:35:03 by tannenba: Code Review Looks good.

description: Information about this checkpointer is found here: http://dmtcp.sourceforge.net/ http://arxiv.org/abs/cs.DC/0701037 Latest source: svn co https://dmtcp.svn.sourceforge.net/svnroot/dmtcp dmtcp You'll want tp cd into the dmtcp/trunk directory since we're working on the end of the development branch. Compiling it with debugging is done like this: ./configure --enable-debug CXXFLAGS="-g -O0" CFLAGS="-g -O0" Debugging a restart in GDB: gdb --args ./bin/dmtcp_restart ckpt_dmtcp1_416dbb83-20780-49265447.dmtcp > run Running the test suite: ./test/autotest.py To run a particular test: ./test/autotest.py --stress dmtcp1 Contacts (with courtesy accounts on north!): Gene Cooperman <gene@ccs.neu.edu> Jason Ansel <jansel@MIT.EDU> Artem Polyakov <artpol84@gmail.com> Milestones Integration of DMTCP into Condor Produce a many job run through condor and give statistics of failure. Integrate DMTCP with our test suite Determine which DMTCP files to have prefix or be nameable. DMTCP development Fix a bug relating to the turning off if randomize_va_space Implement ckpt_and_exit() and ckpt() in dmtcpaware.a. Don't leave copy of stack segment around. remarks: I'm deferring this ticket until I have more time. 2009-Feb-13 18:22:23 by psilord: This ticket had a flurry of activity today in regards to a lot of email back and forth with Gene Cooperman. I also read, thought about, and commented on his accepted IPDPS paper on DMPTCP. 2009-Feb-16 15:29:37 by psilord: I got some helpful information from Gene I've extraced out of an email conversation the both of us had: Gene wrote: a. One can create a coordinator manually. If a dmtcp_checkpoint or dmtcp_restart command finds no coordinator, it will create one automatically. The default location of the coordinator is: localhost (actually: 127.0.0.1), port 7779) b. One can issue commands to the coordinator by any of three methods: i. Manually type input to the coordinator process. ii. Use the command-line utility: dmtcp_command -c iii. Use the dmtcpaware program API. (If you use this, tell us. We have done rudimentary testing, but this API has not been heavily used out in the real world.) c. When the checkpoint command is issued by the coordinator, every process registered with the coordinator will create a checkpoint image: ckpt_PROCESS_NAME_*_ORIGINAL_PID_*.dmtcp The checkpoint image is created in the local directory (cwd) and local host of that process. d. There are two ways of doing restart: i. dmtcp_restart ckpt_*.dmtcp [ Make sure you deleted any old ckp_* files if you use this method. It's also possible to issue several dmtcp_restart commands, one per checkpoint image, but see the caveat below. ] ii. dmtcp_restart_script.sh [ If you use the dmtcp_restart_script.sh, you may want to modify it according to issues like if you have dmtcp_restart in your path already. Read the script for details. ] e. dmtcp_coordinator knows about sockets. If one process has been restarted, but it has a socket to another process that has not yet been restarted, the coordinator will wait until a restart command is given to start the other peer process. Once all peers have been registered, dmtcp_coordinator will resume the computation. f. If two process share a memory segment, then it's important that their checkpoint images appear on the same dmtcp_restart command line. g. We will soon (this weekend) have pid virtualization working. If two processes share a controlling terminal, it will then be necessary to start them with the same dmtcp_restart command line. h. As we've discussed, DMTCP currently has some limited spam that cannot be silenced except by redirecting stderr. We can fix that if it becomes a problem. i. There are other details. if anything looks strange, please write to the full DMTCP list, and whichever of us sees the e-mail first will answer your question. > Some questions I have are: can a job run under the checkpointer/restarter > process be told explicitly where the barrier daemon is? If I recall > correctly, there can be one barrier daemon serving an entire cluster, > right? I believe what you refer to as the barrier daemon is our dmtcp_coordinator. You are correct on all details. If you type: ./dmtcp_coordinator -h you'll see the options for specifying a different default ports, default directories, etc. dmtcp_checkpoint --help also exists, as does dmtcp_command -h . > Also, is there an existence test for a barrier daemon and if I > say had multiple ones running, I could choose to use an arbitrary one > for the restart? The simplest existence test for a coordinator is: pgrep dmtcp_coordinator To kill a coordinator (and its registered processes), do: dmtcp_command -q If there are multiple coordinators, you must specify a specific host and port to identify your desired coordinator. Options like --port, --dir, --host exist, as well as appropriate environment variables. Note the --join option of dmtcp_checkpoint if you want to start up two related processes with one coordinator. Note the --checkpoint-open-files (which is useful if you have a file that is not written to sequentially). If for all of your files, you just read or write sequentially, you don't need this. Restart will truncate an existing file back to its original size at the time of checkpoint. > And is the barrier daemon's life mandatory when the > checkpointable program is running--example, I have 400 checkpointable > programs on seperate machines running with one barrier server, if the > machine running the barrier server crashes, what will happen? If the barrier server (dmtcp_coordinator) crashes, then processes registered with that coordinator may eventually die, too. (They each have a permanent socket connected to the dmtcp_coordinator.) The simplest thing in this case is to run some script to guarantee that you have killed all processes associated with that coordinator. Then use the last dmtcp_restart_script.sh produced by the coordinator to start a new coordinator, and to restart all processes from the time of the previous checkpoint. Note that the script calls dmtcp_restart, and dmtcp_restart will automatically start a new coordinator if the default one cannot be found. So, you don't need to manually start a new coordinator. 2009-Mar-02 10:22:24 by psilord: Working on this from 03/02/2009 to 03/06/2009 since that is when the DMTCP team is on spring break and can answer questions for me and perform a lot of help. 2009-Mar-02 11:24:29 by psilord: I've begun the work of figuring out how to integrate DMTCP into Condor. 2009-Mar-03 16:37:00 by psilord: I had done some work, here is a write up which I sent to Gene and his team on monday: Integration of DMTCP into Condor -------------------------------- PHASE 1: I'm choosing for this phase for each job to use a communal coordinator process located on the execution machine simply due to it being easier to attempt the integration. I'm setting LD_LIBRARY_PATH, DMTCP_HIJACK_LIB, and DMTCP_CHECKPOINT_DIR to appropriate values of the execution directory on the execute machine in which the job wakes up. ------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Problem: Condor wants to send a signal to the user job to checkpoint it using the kill_sig mechanism. title: Ticket #7130: User requirements from submit file should get their own job attribute
description: When the user specifies Requirements in their submit file, this is merged with the automatically generated requirements that submit_utils detects and the result is written to the job as the singular Requirements attribute. This complicates submit transforms, and also can lead to incorrect behavior for late materialization when user requirements contains $() expansions. (because not all of the context of submit is still available at materialization time) To fix this, and to make things cleaner going forward, we should put the user specified requirements into a new job attribute, and reference that attribute in the generated Requirements expression. So for instance, if the user specifies submit fragment Requirements = OpSysAndVer == 6 The resulting job classad will be job classad fragment SpecialRequirements = OpSysAndVer == 6 Requirements = SpecialRequirements && (TARGET.Arch == "X86_64") && (TARGET.OpSys == "LINUX") && (TARGET.Disk >= RequestDisk) && (TARGET.Memory >= RequestMemory) && (TARGET.HasFileTransfer && stringListIMember("http",TARGET.HasFileTransferPluginMethods))

title: Ticket #878: Accountantnew.log locations, locating
description: Accountant.cpp: Accountant's log: $(SPOOL)/Accountantnew.log AbstractReplicatorStateMachine.cpp: Account log version file: $(SPOOL) + "/" VERSION_FILE_NAME (aka Version) Accountant's log: $(STATE_FILE) or $(NEGOTIATOR_STATE_FILE) or $(SPOOL)/Accountantnew.log What's wrong with this: Accountant assumes SPOOL is the best place to stuff state - SPOOL is not always local, it requires updating PREEN's whitelist HAD has 3 notions of where to find the Accountant's log - two of which the accountant doesn't use STATE_FILE is too general a param name A better approach would be to have the Accountant and HAD share code that identifies the location of the Accountant's state. That code should use NEGOTIATOR_STATE_FILE, which should default to $(SPOOL)/Accountantnew.log for backwards compatibility. The Version file should be constructed from the state file's name, e.g. Accountantnew.log.version.

title: Ticket #3523: RFE: implement new function firstDefined() for classad language
description: A common scenario with condor's use of classads is allowing values to override other values, when they are present. Currently, this is somewhat awkward, requiring expressions like this: ifThenElse(_condor_RequestCpus isnt undefined, _condor_RequestCpus <= Cpus, RequestCpus <= Cpus) Having a function such as firstDefined() would allow the same use case to be written like this: firstDefined(_condor_RequestCpus, RequestCpus) <= Cpus It would also scale nicely with larger priority hierarchies: firstDefined(_4th_override_RequestCpus, _3rd_override_RequestCpus, _condor_RequestCpus, RequestCpus) <= Cpus Proposed semantics: firstDefined() is proposed to accept an arbitrary number of arguments (zero or more) It will return the value of the first expression (left to right) that evaluates to a value that is neither 'undefined' nor 'error' short circuit: Once a non-error non-undefined value is encountered, subsequent expressions are not evaluated firstDefined(), with no arguments, evaluates to 'undefined' firstDefined({e1, e2, ...}) is equivalent to firstDefined(e1, e2, ...) if all expressions evaluate to either 'undefined' or 'error', the return value will be 'undefined' Proposed additional functions in suite: firstNumeric() firstValid() (first non-error?) perhaps a variation that accepts a type as a parameter:, so return first expression that has the given type (string, int, etc) Proposal for an additional operator with similar semantics: e1 <op> e2 <op> ... is equivalent to firstDefined(e1, e2, ...) suggestion - <op> = '?:'

title: Ticket #6721: Segfault by the ClassAd python-wrapper
description: A user on htcondor-users reports a segfault when using the python bindings with python 3 as follows: Python 3.6.5 | packaged by conda-forge | (default, Apr 6 2018, 13:39:56) [GCC 4.8.2 20140120 (Red Hat 4.8.2-15)] on linux >>> import htcondor, classad >>> coll = htcondor.Collector() >>> schedd= htcondor.Schedd(coll.locate(htcondor.DaemonTypes.Schedd)) >>> print([(k,v) for k,v in schedd.query()[0].items()]) Segmentation fault (core dumped) The user investigated the problem and passes on the following useful explanation and potential solution: The root of this SEGFAULT is that the `items` method of `ClassAdWrapper` returns invalid references to its child objects. A ClassAd object usually contains some objects of nontrivial type, such as `classad.ExprTree`, which are destroyed when their parent is garbage-collected by the python runtime. Therefore trying to access such objects results in memory access violation (SEGFAULT). Here is the code section responsible for it: https://github.com/htcondor/htcondor/blob/3c73f7c8bcb9d4b99793cd3bc97251639e18b99d/src/python-bindings/classad.cpp#L993 This is a python3-only problem because the `items` method of python 3 object returns an `iterator` instead of a list of tuples. The proposed solution is to properly transform any non-trivial child object of `ClassAdWrapper` into a python object (with its own reference counter) so that the runtime can garbage collected them correctly.

title: Ticket #481: Recovery fails on a DAG that has retried nodes
description: If a DAG goes into recovery mode, and has previously retried a node when running "normally", DAGMan fails. If a user tries to recover a dag which contains retired jobs, the recovery fails when dagman encounters the first retried node from the previous DAG. Here's a test case: [dbrown@sugar ~]$ cat jessica.dag JOB 1 sleep.sub RETRY 1 1 JOB 2 sleep.sub RETRY 2 1 PARENT 1 CHILD 2 [dbrown@sugar ~]$ cat sleep.sub universe = vanilla executable = /bin/sleep arguments = 300 log = /tmp/duncantest.log output = sleep.$(cluster).out error = sleep.$(cluster).err queue I started jessica.dag, logged into the node that was running the sleep job and sent it a kill -9 so it failed. dagman then re-tried the sleep job, as it is supposed to. I then triggered the recovery procedure in dagman by doing a condor_hold on the dagman job and then a condor_release once it exited. The new dagman proceeds started up in recovery mode, but failed with the error message 5/6 23:24:39 ERROR: node 1: job ID in userlog submit event (2847958.0) doesn't match ID reported earlier by submit command (2847957.0)! Aborting DAG; set DAGMAN_ABORT_ON_SCARY_SUBMIT to false if you are sure this shouldn't cause an abort. 5/6 23:24:39 Aborting DAG... 5/6 23:24:39 Writing Rescue DAG to jessica.dag.rescue001...
remarks: Okay, I've fixed the actual bug in DAGMan. I'm putting this ticket into the "Active" rather than "Resolved" state, though, because the test doesn't work correctly yet. title: Ticket #6371: filetransfer plugins w/ relative dynamic libraries fail if run as root
description: HTCondor has an option to run your filetransfer plugins as root. (This is not the default and should only be enabled if you need it and know what you are doing!) In that situation, the plugin is invoked with real uid 0 and effective uid of the user doing the transfer. If the plugin uses shared libraries that are specified in the binary's RUNPATH relative to $ORIGIN as opposed to absolute paths, the loader will refuse to load them for security reaons when the uid and euid do not match. There's isn't much HTCondor can do about this other than try to print a helpful message in the log. The sysadmin has the option of installing the necessary shared libraries in a system location such as /usr/lib[64]/. Setting LD_LIBRARY_PATH doesn't do the trick either. Check man page for ld.so, although it's fairly lacking. Search the web for "ld.so setuid shared library" or similar.

title: Ticket #897: CREAM Hardening
description: To date, Condor-G's support for submitting to the CREAM service has only been tested with a small number of jobs in ideal conditions. We need to do additional testing that approximates conditions that may be encountered in production use. This includes using thousands of jobs and inducing failures on both client and server. The following scenarios should be covered: Steady influx of new jobs at same rate that completed jobs leave the queue. Sudden influx of several thousand new jobs. Sudden removal of several thousand jobs. Failure of client machine (software hard-killed and restarted). Failure of server machine (software hard-killed and restarted). Code changes for this work should be committed to V7_5-cream_hardening-branch. Bug fixes may go to V7_4-branch on a case-by-base basis.
remarks: 2009-Nov-16 15:12:40 by jfrey: On Nov 13, I ran a test run that kept 1500 cream jobs in the queue, submitting new jobs as old ones completed. A total of 20600 jobs ran. Here are some issues that came up: #958 When the initial 1500 job entered the queue, all jobs had to finish the REGISTER command before any could complete their submission with the START command. This is due to the way the GAHP code in the gridmanager queues commands. We either need to reintroduce MAX_PENDING_SUBMITS or prioritize GAHP commands. Other grid types are affected by this. #954 Cream reported several jobs as failed, either due to a proxy expiring (which shouldn't have been true) or files contents changing unexpectedly. The gridmanager ended up putting the jobs on hold with 'Unspecified gridmanager error' as the reason. The gridmanager should use the failure message returned by Cream. If possible, we should also understand how these errors occurred. #955 A couple cream commands failed with a 'Connection timed out' error. If the REGISTER or START command failed, the job went on hold with the timeout as the hold reason. If another command failed, the gridmanager tried to cancel and purge the job. The purged failed (due to the known problem of CANCEL not working) and the job went on hold with a hold reason about the PURGE failing. The gridmanager should handle these failures more gracefully, possibly retrying the command that timed out. We could use try using a longer timeout. Currently, we use 60 seconds.

title: Ticket #2277: generalize GROUP_DYNAMIC_MACH_CONSTRAINT
description: Long ago, Dan Forrest patched the GLOW central manager to add a knob that duplicates the functionality of GROUP_DYNAMIC_MACH_CONSTRAINT but makes it apply more generally---not just to dynamic group quotas. He called this DYNAMIC_MACH_CONSTRAINT. I have attached the patch. It never made it into the Condor source, due to inertia: we expected some better solution to the "matching against a subset of the pool" problem to be implemented. Question to be answered: can this effectively replace GROUP_DYNAMIC_MACH_CONSTRAINT, or do we really need two knobs, one with general scope and one that only applies to dynamic quotas?
remarks: 2011-Jun-28 15:06:23 by bbockelm: Hi Dan, TJ and I just discussed this: I don't think there's "non-group-based" code in the negotiator anymore. If there's no accounting group, your job gets inserted into a group named "<none>". Brian 2011-Jun-28 15:10:42 by johnkn: I propose that we have two constraint params one to control which slots are never considered for matchmaking, and one to control which slots are ignored when calculating the poolsize. NEGOTIATOR_SLOT_CONSTRAINT NEGOTIATOR_SLOT_POOLSIZE_CONSTRAINT GROUP_DYNAMIC_MACH_CONSTRAINT will be retained as an alternate name for NEGOTIATOR_SLOT_POOLSIZE_CONSTRAINT, which gives us backward compatibility 2011-Jun-30 21:00:36 by eje: FYI, GROUP_DYNAMIC_MACH_CONSTRAINT applies to all slots, dynamic or otherwise (which does make it poorly named, if nothing else). e.g. see repro/test for #2232 2011-Jul-11 17:08:16 by danb: In the negotiator, there is still special handling of the non-group case: if (hgq_groups.size() <= 1) { // If there is only one group (the root group) we are in traditional non-HGQ mode. // It seems cleanest to take the traditional case separately for maximum backward-compatible behavior. // A possible future change would be to unify this into the HGQ code-path, as a "root-group-only" case. negotiateWithGroup(untrimmed_num_startds, untrimmedSlotWeightTotal, minSlotWeight, startdAds, claimIds, scheddAds); } The size of the pool that is passed into this function is not affected by GROUP_DYNAMIC_MACH_CONSTRAINT. This is the motivation for this ticket. 2011-Jul-13 12:00:30 by danb: I believe that the problem that Dan Forrest's DYNAMIC_MACH_CONSTRAINT was trying to solve is mostly addressed by the new GROUP_QUOTA_ROUND_ROBIN_RATE. When negotiating with groups, this knob can be used to hand out only a fraction of the pie per negotiation iteration. By handing out only a fraction of the pie per iteration, one can reduce starvation effects when submitters are vying for subsets of the pool. The tradeoff is that the smaller the fraction, the more iterations it may take to hand out all the resources, which may lengthen the negotiation cycle. Even if one is not really using groups, one can make use of this feature by defining one dummy group to flip the negotiator into group negotiation mode. Longer-term, (as stated in the comment in the code above), this distinction between group and non-group mode should probably go away to avoid this bifurcation of the feature-set. One gotcha: GROUP_QUOTA_ROUND_ROBIN_RATE does not reduce the number of slots per iteration that can be claimed by machine rank preemption. This means starvation effects may still result when submitters are vying for a subset of machines already claimed by lower-ranked users. The reason GROUP_QUOTA_ROUND_ROBIN_RATE does not limit rank preemption is that it operates by adjusting the effective quota of submitters. Quotas do not constrain machine rank preemption. I think it is desirable for the round robin rate to constrain machine rank preemption. This might be achieved by adjusting the effective size of the pie rather than (or in addition to) adjusting the effective quota in each iteration. In summary: The existing GROUP_QUOTA_ROUND_ROBIN_RATE can be used to achieve most of the goals of this ticket, but it requires that at least one group be defined in GROUP_NAMES. It is desirable to have a negotiation round robin rate that applies even when no groups are defined. It is also desirable that this round robin rate apply to machine rank preemption, which it currently does not. If these goals were achieved, I think it would be good to rename the knob NEGOTIATOR_ROUND_ROBIN_RATE. 2011-Aug-11 14:21:13 by danb: TJ, Thanks for your patch! Sorry for the delay in reviewing it. Comments: The new configuration variables NEGOTIATOR_SLOT_CONSTRAINT and NEGOTIATOR_SLOT_POOLSIZE_CONSTRAINT need to be added to param_info.in. Log messages still refer to GROUP_QUOTA_DYNAMIC_MACH_CONSTRAINT rather than the new NEGOTIATOR_SLOT_POOLSIZE_CONSTRAINT. Ideally, the log message would correspond to whichever one was actually used. But if it is just hard-coded to one or the other, the log message should at least mention the non-deprecated configuration value. You added unconstrained_slots to NegotiationCycleStats, but it is not published in publishNegotiationCycleStats(). If you did the optimization suggested in my next comment, then we would not be able to conveniently compute unconstrained_slots anyway, so it could just be removed altogether. You do the trimming before the call to accountant.CheckMatches(startdAds) and before untrimmedSlotWeightTotal is computed. I think that is fine. It means that the trimmed slots have no effect whatsoever in the negotiator other than being (almost) reported in NegotiationCycleStats. That being the case, I would suggest an optimization: perhaps the constraint could be applied in the query that is sent to the collector in obtainAdsFromCollector(). Then the trimmed ads would not consume any memory in the negotiator or consume any bandwidth in the query to the collector. 2011-Aug-18 15:30:14 by jrt: I think the ads should be trimmed after CheckMatches. An Ad could match in cycle 1, be matched, but then get removed in the following cycle before checkmatches. I think the params can co-exist. So we have something like: NEGOTIATOR_SLOT_CONSTRAINT NEGOTIATOR_SLOT_POOLSIZE_CONSTRAINT NEGOTIATOR_SLOT_POOLSIZE_CONSTRAINT_REMOVE NEGOTIATOR_SLOT_CONSTRAINT first removes startdAds and reduces untrimmed_num_startds. NEGOTIATOR_SLOT_POOLSIZE_CONSTRAINT reduces numDynGroupSlots. The question here is whether numDynGroupSlots should be used in the non group path in place of untrimmed_num_startds. I would think this would be fine. NEGOTIATOR_SLOT_POOLSIZE_CONSTRAINT_REMOVE behaves as NEGOTIATOR_STARTD_CONSTRAINT_REMOVE. This is essentially a performance tweak to avoid iterating across startdAds that will never match (or we don't want to match). It seems the ads could be removed by default, but in the interest of backward compat the new param was used. The original patch attached to https://condor-wiki.cs.wisc.edu/index.cgi/tktview?tn=2232 changed GROUP_DYNAMIC_MACH_CONSTRAINT language to NEGOTIATOR_STARTD_CONSTRAINT language. We could change it again to NEGOTIATOR_SLOT_POOLSIZE and add code for NEGOTIATOR_SLOT_CONSTRAINT. 2011-Sep-15 11:15:35 by danb: TJ, Version 2 of the patch looks improved to me. As you noted, the new params must still be added to param_info.in. I'm assuming you will clean out the #if 0 section. Would it be better to EXCEPT immediately when you discover that the constraint cannot be parsed? If that produces a negotiator obituary email that makes the cause of the problem more obvious than it would be otherwise, I'd say yes. The implementation of NEGOTIATOR_SLOT_POOLSIZE_CONSTRAINT looks to me like it only applies to dynamic group quotas. I thought the intention was for it to apply to all calculations of pool size. Specifically, it does not appear to affect this case: if (hgq_groups.size() <= 1) { // If there is only one group (the root group) we are in traditional non-HGQ mode. // It seems cleanest to take the traditional case separately for maximum backward-compatible behavior. // A possible future change would be to unify this into the HGQ code-path, as a "root-group-only" case. negotiateWithGroup(untrimmed_num_startds, untrimmedSlotWeightTotal, minSlotWeight, startdAds, claimIds, scheddAds); } 2011-Sep-15 11:36:05 by danb: jrt, I agree with your comment that the non-group case should use the trimmed number of slots. As for whether the slot constraint should be applied before or after CheckMatches(), I agree that we could try to support the case where the accountant keeps track of usage on slots that are excluded from matchmaking in some cycles. For example, that is what is achieved by NEGOTIATOR_CONSIDER_PREEMPTION=False. I still think it is useful to have an option that completely excludes slots from both the accountant and the matchmaking. In very large pools, doing the trimming in the query to the collector is much more efficient. Perhaps we need to make a list of use-cases so we can understand what is covered by TJ's patch and what isn't. I don't understand why you would want CONSTRAINT, POOLSIZE_CONSTRAINT and POOLSIZE_CONSTRAINT_REMOVE. POOLSIZE_CONSTRAINT_REMOVE seems more than an optimization to me, because it has a big side-effect that could change the outcome of matchmaking, not just make it faster. This makes the semantics of POOLSIZE_CONSTRAINT seem rather muddy. Your thoughts? 2011-Sep-23 15:55:25 by danb: Code review: Thanks, TJ! In the following (non-group matchmaking case), the constrained pool size is passed to the matchmaking algorithm, but the unconstrained weighted pool size is passed. I think the constrained weighted size should be passed. Currently, that is stored in a variable named hgq_total_quota. negotiateWithGroup(cPoolsize, untrimmedSlotWeightTotal, minSlotWeight, startdAds, claimIds, scheddAds); I also just noticed that in the group matchmaking case, we are calling negotiateWithGroup() with the unconstrained pool size (both weighted and unweighted). This means the poolsize constraint is only applied when calculating the dynamic quotas, not when carving up the resource pie. For consistency, I think the constrained pool size should be passed (unweighted and weighted). negotiateWithGroup(untrimmed_num_startds, untrimmedSlotWeightTotal, minSlotWeight, startdAds, claimIds, *(group->submitterAds), slots, group->name.c_str()); In the following log message, the text "for dynamic quotas" should be removed, since it is now more broadly applicable. dprintf(D_ALWAYS, "warning: 0 out of %d slots match " "NEGOTIATOR_SLOT_POOLSIZE_CONSTRAINT for dynamic quotas\n", cPoolsize);

title: Ticket #1908: Reintroduce TRANSFERRING_OUTPUT job status
description: When the TRANSFERRING_OUTPUT job status was first introduced (#1641), it had a bug where running jobs that were held would be removed from the queue (#1900). The short-term solution was to stop using TRANSFERRING_OUTPUT. We need to consider re-introducing use of this job status without the bug. This can be part of the overlapped output file transfer feature the status was added for. One option is for the schedd to change the job's status to TRANSFERRING_OUTPUT when the shadow exits. This would be the easiest to implement safely, but would mean the status is only used when output file transfer is overlapped with execution of a subsequent job. Alternatively, the shadow can do the status change once the job has finished executing. This would require a change in the communication between shadow and starter. Currently, the starter tells the shadow that the job is no longer running, but not why it's no longer running. Also, the shadow would need to check the job status in the schedd's copy of the ad before changing it, in case the status changes to HELD or REMOVED just before the shadow tries to change it to TRANSFERRING_OUTPUT.

title: Ticket #4874: Fine-grained filtering of collector ads
description: Use Case HTCondor-CE OSG currently has a central collector that allows registered OSG sites to advertise the presence of a HTCondor-CE (internally - the HTCondor-CE's collector forwards the schedd ad to a central OSG collector). The HTCondor-CE's DN is mapped to a HTCondor user name (i.e., /DC=com/DC=example/OU=Services/CN=example.site.com maps to example.site.com@sites.opensciencegrid.org); only authorized users are allowed to post schedd ads. Currently, the list of authorized users is set to the list of authorized CEs in our other information systems (OSG's OIM web service). Miron dislikes this; anyone with a HTCondor-CE & valid certificate should be able to advertise their CE. An explicit registration step should not be required. However, we need to enforce a few simple rules: for example, an authenticated user of "site.example.com@sites.opensciencegrid.org" should not be permitted to advertise a schedd named "cms.fnal.gov". Xrootd Caches We are starting to plan the deployment of Xrootd caches across the OSG. We'd like these caches to be able to self-register in the collector so we can see which pieces are alive and some simple monitoring statistics. Similar to the case above - we'd like to be able to accept any Xrootd server with a DN, as long as we can filter out maliciously bad ads. Proposal I'd like to see COLLECTOR_REQUIREMENTS implemented. That is: In the collector engine, have an expression evaluated on every classad update within the context of the updated ad; if it evaluates to FALSE, UNDEFINED, or ERROR, then drop the ClassAd. No changes to the existing protocol. This would still only be applied after authorizations. In the examples above, OSG's central collector would authorize *@sites.opensciencegrid.org. If the collector drops the ad because the requirement evaluates to FALSE or UNDEFINED, log the reason why at D_FULLDEBUG; if the classad evaluates to ERROR, log the reason why to D_ALWAYS. To complete the project for the Xrootd caches, OSG will probably need a separate authorization level for generic updates (as the xrootd cache is likely not master, schedd, or startd ad type). I'm not sold on the proposal and am willing to listen to other solutions for the use case above.

title: Ticket #3718: Detect invalid interpreter in script
description: It's not-so-uncommon for a user to specify a bad interpreter in a shell script they submit to condor: #!/bin/bsh When this happens, the user gets the following hold message: Error from slot3@hcc-briantest.unl.edu: Failed to execute '/tmp/foo': (errno=2: 'No such file or directory') This is incredibly misleading - anyone who hasn't memorized every HTCondor failure mode will immediately think /tmp/foo doesn't exist and look for filesystem issues. That's certainly what I do! I propose to adopt the error handling logic for this case from /bin/bash and properly detect the bad interpreter. Here's my proposed hold message: [bbockelm@hcc-briantest condor]$ condor_q -held -- Submitter: hcc-briantest.unl.edu : <129.93.244.208:44063> : hcc-briantest.unl.edu ID OWNER HELD_SINCE HOLD_REASON 23319.0 bbockelm 6/24 21:51 Error from slot3@hcc-briantest.unl.edu: Failed to execute '/tmp/foo': invalid interpreter (/bin/blah) specified on first line of script (errno=2: 'No such file or directory') 1 jobs; 0 completed, 0 removed, 0 idle, 0 running, 1 held, 0 suspended Patch on the V8_1-bad-interpreter branch.

Job runs fine. I'll fix the script_fd. I think putting things on hold is the most appropriate way forward - it mimics what happens with other exec errors. It's just an improvement in the error message, not a change in semantics. If you're OK with it, I propose fixing the fd leak and pushing. 2013-Jun-25 15:14:13 by gthain: AFter talking this over with todd, he'd really profer that this just go into the starter. 2013-Jun-25 16:47:56 by bbockelm: What's the thinking behind that? title: Ticket #1375: reuse shadow processes
description: When operating at high frequency, the schedd spends something like 1/3 of its time creating shadows. There is additional overhead managing security sessions for the new processes, receiving an initial heartbeat message, and so on. There is additional overhead to the rest of the system as each new shadow parses the configuration file and initializes DaemonCore. If the shadow processes were reused for running multiple jobs this overhead would be reduced. In some tests I have done, this allows the schedd to run jobs at roughly twice the rate.

title: Ticket #4177: Add a config knob to take a GPU or other user resource offline
description: Sometimes non-fungible resources (like GPUs) are detected, but are known by the administrator to not work correctly. There should be a way to set an instance of that resource aside to that it cannot be assigned to a slot during configuration or dynamic slot creation. the ICECUBE project (and likely others) would like to be able to do this while jobs are running without having to evict all of the jobs, so a solution that does not require restarting the STARTD is preferred. A new knob OFFLINE_MACHINE_RESOURCE_<tag> will control the list of offline custom resources, so if GPU resources use the GPUs tag like this: MACHINE_RESOURCE_INVENTORY_GPUs=$(LIBEXEC)/condor_gpu_discovery -properties OFFLINE_MACHINE_RESOURCE_GPUs=CUDA2 Where the first line above does GPU detection and will create report a set of resource ids for resource type GPUs. The second line indicates that if there is a resource of type GPUs with an resource id of CUDA2, that that resource is offline. This will result in the attribute OfflineGPUs="CUDA2" being reported in all of the slot ads on that startd.

title: Ticket #4462: Parent-child security sessions never expire
description: When a daemon spawns a child daemon, it creates a security session for the two to use. This security session has an infinite lifetime and isn't explicitly removed when the child exits. It also punches a hole in the authorization table for the child's identity, but never fills it back in. This is particularly troublesome for the schedd and startd, which spawn a new child process for each running job.

title: Ticket #205: realpath() on Win32
description: We'd like an implementation of realpath for Windows that meets the POSIX.1-2008 specification; this is used in the static web server code. realpath(path, NULL) should resolve all components in path to canonical names (e.g. resolving .. and . elements) and return a newly-allocated C string containing the canonical name for path, or NULL if path does not exist. On Windows, realpath should also convert every pathname component to the "long file name" version, resolve any substituted drive names, and resolve any reparse points. See http://bit.ly/4dh6wb for more details on realpath and the POSIX.1-2008 amendments. (CERT mentions that canonicalizing pathnames on Windows is complex, but their alternate solutions are not obviously applicable to our problem.)

title: Ticket #4931: Document PreJobPrioX and PostJobPrioX
description: Brian and Todd had a lovely conversation on Friday about how it would be great if we could have secondary sorting keys for resource requests after JobPrio but before QDate. This would allow CMS to cluster similar jobs that were submitted in the same hour or day - making the current resource request count (a bit too large on CMS's pools) closer to the auto cluster count (comfortable size). It is such a wonderful idea that it got implemented 4 years ago in #1992. Being that neither of us knew this existed (and I don't see any references in the manual), it's likely a little documentation would go a long way. Notes: These are all Job classad attributes that are evaluated when the tables are built. The sorts are done by: PreJobPrio1, PreJobPrio2, JobPrio, PostJobPrio1, PostJobPrio2. This is a topological sort function. Higher is better. The valid values are INT_MIN+1 through INT_MAX on the relevant platforms.

title: Ticket #6326: Python bindings core dump when used with Python 3
description: In ticket #4146 a first pass at compiling the Python bindings against python3 was done. However, there are reports of the resulting library failing to work (core dump), and perhaps not even passing our Python regression tests. Current guess is there is a problem where our bindings call out directly to the Python interpreter (i.e. something changed semantically in the python developer api, or perhaps our binding code is not as strictly typed as it should be and we are running into trouble passing void pointers). One sensible future-proofing approach to fix this issue would of going through Boost.Python for everything and thereby hopefully avoid calling the python api directly at all. First step is to reproduce the failing behavior (hopefully via the regression tests) with python3 by building on a recent version of Fedora (at least until #6327 is resolved), then create patches (hopefully by converting fully to Boost.Python) to fix the problems revealed. --- Current test status: tests/classad_tests.py: 40 tests, all pass tests/htcondor_version_tests.py: 5 tests, all pass tests/htcondor_tests.py: 23 tests, failures=1, errors=1 The couple remaining errors are not python3-specific.

For some reason, in Python 3, the python object's file pointer (.tell()) is always set to the end of the file, despite the underlying classad library doing fgetc calls advancing a character at a time. But as noted in convert_to_FILEptr, it's dubious that python3's file-like objects can be safely converted to a FILE * https://github.com/edquist/htcondor/blob/p3/src/python-bindings/classad_module.cpp#L66-L69 2017-Jul-20 17:05:13 by edquist: So perhaps to re-iterate, the situation is: - in Python 2, when parsing a classad file, the python file object's FILE pointer is used directly, which gets used by the parser from the classad library. Advancing the file position via calls to getc and ungetc then gets reflected in the python file object. - in Python 3, there is no FILE pointer available for file-like objects, but we access the underlying fd and with that we use fdopen to make a new FILE pointer. When getc and ungetc calls are made to the FILE pointer, the position reported by ftell() no longer corresponds to the actual fd's file position. One idea was to extend the ClassAdFileIterator class to contain the python file object also, and calls to next() would call seek on the python object to reset it to match ftell() on the FILE pointer ... But this feels messy. Another approach which looks to work is to make our FILE object from fdopen() unbuffered, so that getc calls do not advance the fd position beyond what ftell() would report, and replace ungetc calls with fseek(_file, -1, SEEK_CUR) (since ungetc does not actually update the fd position). This is a performance hit since it means one read system call per byte, but I'm not sure if there is a much better option... Open to ideas. 2017-Jul-20 17:28:07 by edquist: All classad tests now pass; on to the htcondor tests... 2017-Jul-21 15:47:57 by bbockelm: Hi, I am starting to fear this will be a nightmare to review. title: Ticket #3124: "pipeFullWrite: Unable to write to fd" If startd hooks ignore stdin
description: If the startd is feeding significant input to a hook, and the hook ignores it, the startd will complain with message like this: DaemonCore::PidEntry::pipeFullWrite: Unable to write to fd 65590 (errno = 32). Aborting write attempts. This is not good. It's noise in the log file. If one decided to investigate it, it's not obvious what the source is. You can't even determine what the read FD is. (The FD is obfuscated to discourage other sections of code from doing overly clever things with it. Subtract 65536 to find the real FD.) Should hooks be allowed to ignore, not even reading, stdin? If so, we shouldn't complain at all. (Or if we must, downgrade it to D_FULLDEBUG) If not we should document that it isn't allowed we should provide a more useful error message explaining the problem. To reproduce: Create a simple fetchwork hook: #! /usr/bin/perl -w use strict; print <<END; Cmd="/bin/sleep" Args="3600" Owner="adesmet" JobUniverse=5 Requirements=TRUE RequestCpus=1 RequestMemory=8 RequestDisk=1024 END exit 0; Add the following to your configuration file, changing the path as appropriate: STARTD_JOB_HOOK_KEYWORD = ALAN ALAN_HOOK_FETCH_WORK=/scratch/adesmet/V7_8-branch/release_dir/hooks/fetch-work-infinite FetchWorkDelay=1 Start up Condor. Check StartLog, observe regular complaints similar to: 07/11/12 15:53:17 DaemonCore::PidEntry::pipeFullWrite: Unable to write to fd 65537 (actually 1) (errno = 32). Aborting write attempts.

title: Ticket #5859: Speed negotiation by ignoring job ranks
description: Currently, when we match a job, we try to match it to every possible machine, in order to then sort all the matches by NEGOTIATOR_PRE_JOB_RANK, JOB_RANK, and NEGOTIATOR_POST_JOB_RANK. So, if there 1,000 slots available, and 20 submitters, we notionally attempt 20,000 matches, even if each submitter is only allowed 50 matches. This patch adds a new knob, NEGOTIATOR_IGNORE_JOB_RANKS, which assumes that job ranks are independent of the job, and sorts the machines once, and only attempts to make as many matches as the submitter limit allows. We believe this may make a significant improvement in negotiation speed for cms.
remarks: 2016-Sep-27 10:05:52 by gthain: Note that we aren't going to document this one just yet, until we can verify that there's a good speedup, and to see if we can automatically enable this, when appropriate.

title: Ticket #3574: Have schedd advertised weighted slot demand, for group quota code use
description: Currently, partitionable slots don't work with hierarchical groups for a number of reasons. One reason is that the surplus sharing code relies on the submitter ad to estimate how many extra idle jobs there are per submitter. Because the schedd doesn't know the slots weight, the units it advertises is in number of jobs. In this ticket, we will help the common case where slot weights is "cpus", and have the schedd advertise number of idle jobs in units of cpus * idle jobs, which the negotiator group quota code will use to measure demand and thus surplus. The schedd will advertise it unconditionally in the submitter ad, but the negotiator will only use it if NEGOTIATOR_USE_WEIGHTED_DEMAND is set to true. Otherwise, it will continue as today and use the raw numbers. Also see #4324

Where does the schedd get its measurement of cpus? 2013-Apr-15 14:09:26 by gthain: From request_cpus in the job ads from idle jobs. it's not generalized, and it is a short term workaround (hack). 2013-Apr-18 15:41:40 by eje: Can you attach a testing scenario with results that demonstrates the new behavior? 2013-Apr-18 15:53:28 by eje: Under the assumption that this is an interim hack on emergency footing, the new WeightedRunningJobs and WeightedIdleJobs ought to be advertised conditionally on NEGOT​IATOR_USE_WEIGHTED_DE​MAND as well

title: Ticket #1549: New Classads should not support octal integer literals
description: New Classads supports octal integer literals, indicated by a leading zero. Old classads did not support this. We have no way to print out octal literals. More importantly, this is bound to surprise some user who accidentally enters a classad value with a leading zero, perhaps for formatting reasons. New classads also supports hex literals, but this is less of a problem, as no one is going to accidentally type in a leading 0x, and expect a decimal value. Let's drop support for octal, sorry pdp-11 lovers.

title: Ticket #7167: Support multiple slurm clusters in the blahp
description: Slurm supports a multi-cluster configuration, where multiple clusters share a slurmDBD and submitters can target any of the clusters from any submit machine. We should have first-class support for this setup in HTCondor's grid universe. A user submitting a grid universe job (grid-type batch slurm) should be able to specify which Slurm cluster to use. We can do this fairly easily by extending the syntax of the existing batch_queue submit parameter. We'd allow an optional @ character followed by the cluster name, like so: # Submit to partition named debug on cluster2 batch_queue = debug@cluster2 # Submit to the default partition on cluster2 batch_queue = @cluster2 No changes would be required in the blahp, except in the slurm-specific shell scripts. When an alternate cluster name is specified, the job id generated by the submit script would the same @clustername suffix. This allows the other scripts to target the correct cluster.

title: Ticket #3962: Add file-transfer plugin for HDFS
description: HDFS might be a nice way to deal with large input files. We presently only "support" it if it's mounted (via FUSE) and the submitter knows where, and thinks to use file:// URLs. This is suboptimal, not least because Nate doesn't trust FUSE. It should not be difficult to write a file-transfer plugin which uses (or natively speaks) the HDFS protocol to copy from HDFS to the execute directory. This issue particularly affects VM universe, because it is not possible to provide a wrapper script to use HDFS natively, because there is no executable.

title: Ticket #7188: Bad warning about line endings
description: Episode 1 When your job’s executable has Windows line endings, (rather than holding with “exec format error” as in the past,) HTCondor now tells you to submit some other way ... which doesn’t fix the line endings and results in an even more confusing error message. To be specific, the message from condor_submit.V6/submit.cpp line 1431 is "Executable file %s is a script with CRLF (DOS/Win) line endings", followed by "Run with -allow-crlf-script if this is really what you want", if that flag wasn't set. The former is fine, but the latter is almost never what anybody actually wants. We should therefore not mention it. Instead, based on the CHTC's page, change the message to read "... line endings. This generally doesn't work, and you should probably run dos2unix <executable> -- or a similar tool -- before you resubmit." Although dos2unix is not installed everywhere, just using tr involves a complicated construction to do an in-place replacement. (We could certainly print the whole construction out, but I'm not sure about how user-friendly that is.) The in-place replacement for perl is pretty simple, but Perl is becoming less common. For now, we'll just go with dos2unix.

title: Ticket #439: DAGMan internal data structures need improvement
description: In dagman, there are two important objects: Job and Dag. The dag edge connection information, shoved into a _queues[] array of sets--one for parents, waiting, and children, is stored in the Job object. Of course, this is insanity. The Dag object should store the connection information as related to a node key on each node. At this time, the Dag object asks for references for the _queues array from the nodes, and futzes about with them. In addition the Job object has a delegation API for those queues which is used primarily by the Dag object. The Job object doesn't appear to care that it actually contains the edge information.... I propose removing the _queues variable from the Job object and storing that information exclusively into the Dag object, since that is where it should have been all along. A great benefit for this encapsulation change would be that the implementation for the Job objects can be altered to store its information into an ephemeral sqlite database on disk. This would probably allow dag structures into the 10 million node range. The storage of the connection information can remain in memory as part of the Dag object until it is deemed necessary to shove it out to a sqlite database as well--though I don't see that needing to happen any time soon since it doesn't take up all that much memory, really. After a tiny bit of code inspection, it would appear that the lifting of the splice algorithm would have to change slightly to honor transferal of the edge connection data from the splice dag into the enclosing dag.

title: Ticket #4161: further clarify PREEMPTION_RANK definition
description: From HTCondor-users: the definition of what MY and TARGET refer to is not crystal clear. Make it better. Here is the prose from the email: -----Original Message----- From: HTCondor-users [mailto:htcondor-users-bounces@cs.wisc.edu] On Behalf Of Todd Tannenbaum Sent: Wednesday, January 15, 2014 8:40 PM To: HTCondor-Users Mail List Subject: Re: [HTCondor-users] PREEMPTION_RANK Trouble Hi Uri, Welcome to HTCondor! Re the below, I think I see the issue. You have PREEMPTION_RANK = -TARGET.JobPrio but in PREEMPTION_RANK, TARGET.xxx refers to an attribute from the candidate queued (idle) job classad that is being considered to preempt the job running on a machine. So in context of your test setup, -TARGET.JobPrio is referencing the JobPrio of a given User B job. The PREEMPTION_{REQUIREMENTS|RANK} expressions are evaluated within the context of the candidate machine ClassAd and the candidate idle job ClassAd; the MY scope prefix refers to the machine ClassAd, and the TARGET scope prefix refers to the ClassAd of the idle (candidate) job. There is no direct access to attributes from the currently running job, but attributes of the currently running job that need to be accessed in PREEMPTION_REQUIREMENTS can be placed in the machine ClassAd using STARTD_JOB_EXPRS. So you want to rank by the JobPrio of the job that is running on a given machine, which normally would not appear in either the candidate job ad or in the machine classad. So to deal with this, you want to use STARD_JOB_EXPRS to tell the condor_startd to copy an attribute out of the job classad of the job running on a slot, and publish it into the machine classad. So to get what you want, I think you want the append the following in your condor_config.local (or edit the knobs directly in condor_config, whatever): # Publish JobPrio of running jobs into machine ad STARTD_JOB_EXPRS = $(STARTD_JOB_EXPRS) JobPrio # Preempt based on JobPrio of running job found in machine ad PREEMPTION_RANK = -MY.JobPrio Hope the above makes sense. Give the above a whirl. Note the STARTD_JOB_EXPRS change needs to be seen by all your execute nodes, and the PREEMPTION_RANK change needs to be seen by your central manager. Don't forget to issue a "condor_reconfig -all" for the settings to take effect.
remarks: 2015-Jan-21 15:08:37 by smoler: Looks like the definition was updated long ago, so resolving this ticket without a fixed version field.
