title: Ticket #356: Obtain job status from LDAP for nordugrid ARC grid-type
description: For nordugrid ARC jobs in the grid universe, Condor currently determines the remote job's status by reading a 'status' file via ARC's gridftp interface. This doesn't scale well (each job has a separate file) and the status file doesn't give enough information (whether the job is running). Nordugrid ARC includes an LDAP server that provides job status info. Querying the LDAP server solves both of these problems. In nordugrid ARC's gridftp interface, each job has a /proc-like directory that contains files with information about that job, including the job's status. While the job is in the back-end batch system, the only status provided is 'IN_LRMS'. There's no indication as to whether the job is running. Since each job has a separate information directory, querying the status of N jobs requires N gridftp read operations. This doesn't scale very well. ARC's LDAP service provides a more detailed job status, which includes whether the job is currently running. It will also return information about all jobs from a single query. Implementation: Is every ARC server guaranteed to have an LDAP service running on a well-known port? If not, is there a way to determine the appropriate LDAP service? What happens if Condor can't contact the LDAP service? It can fall back on the current method of determining job status. Tomas Linden can arrange access to an ARC server for testing.
creator: jfrey

title: Ticket #4531: configuration variables missing from manual
description: These variables are missing from the manual. These variables exist due to scaling issues: to reduce the time spent servicing already- connected clients. CCB_POLLING_TIMESLICE default: 0.05 (5%), of all the time CCB is running, defines the percent/max/target to poll/service/check on already connected clients. CCB_POLLING_INTERVAL default: 20 sec, smallest amount of time that would go by before we start another polling. The interval (the value of this configuration variable does not change) can be extended if the measured amount of time previously taken to poll/check on already connected clients exceeded the amount of time desired, as expressed with CCB_POLLING_TIMESLICE. CCB_POLLING_MAX_INTERVAL default: 600 sec, No matter what, poll every 600 seconds. CCB_SERVER_READ_BUFFER default: 2Kbytes, Size of the kernel TCP read buffer for all sockets used by CCB. CCB_SERVER_WRITE_BUFFER default: 2Kbytes, Size of the kernel TCP write buffer for all sockets used by CCB. CCB_SWEEP_INTERVAL default: 1200 seconds (20 minutes), Frequency at which the CCB server writes its info about open TCP connections to a file, such that crash recovery from the info can be done. CCB_RECONNECT_FILE default: $(SPOOL)/.ccb_reconnect, Path and name of the file into which we write this info.

title: Ticket #706: RELEASE_CLAIM & daemoncore reaper race condition
description: In KillFamily::currentfamily() if the family size is zero, we emit an ERROR into the log file about that fact and continue. This disrupts the test suite. In the scenario of: starter finishes waitpid() reaps the pid schedd sends RELEASE_CLAIM startd goes from Claimed/Busy to Preempting/Vacating startd sends SIGTERM to process, which is non existent, an "ERROR: ..." gets emitted to the logs. startd sends SIGKILL to process, which is non existant and a different error gets emitted with ambiguious output. startd calls the daemoncore reaper for the originally finished starter. The race is that apparently a lot of things can happen while a pid was reaped by waitpid() and not yet by daemoncore. So, I've change the ERROR message to a WARNING since I can't tell if this is situation normal or what. Ultimately it seems the startd ends up doing the right thing. so this needs review.
remarks: 2009-Sep-02 14:31:42 by psilord: There is a danger here, that if the startd manages to use an out of band method to signal the starter, say the Starter.cpp interface, instead of the daemon core signal interface, then it may be possible to send a signal as root to a process which isn't part of the condor family tree. This needs investigation. 2009-Oct-05 15:33:48 by psilord: Ok, I investigated this problem but not entirely to the depth that I would prefer. I had a patch which passed review on multiple people, but in the end I didn't put it in because it dawned upon me some extra twisty passages in the code and I didn't like how the patch interacted with it. I have a new patch which should be reviewed by dab on wed which should be closer to what we need. 2009-Oct-06 16:30:36 by psilord: Ok, I made a fix and it was reviewed by danb. I found some other problems in the code related to the codepath in Starter::reallykill() that will arise in another ticket. This ticket is resovled.

title: Ticket #7608: Explicitly list source file in condor_utils CMakeLists
description: The CMakeLIsts in condor_utils forms a list of source for libcondorutil by globbing all the files in the condor_utils directory, minus a blacklist. This requires developers to re-build cmake when a new file shows up, which they may not be aware of if it comes from someone else. CMake best practice is to explicitly list all source files. Also, all the source files in this directory are built twice -- once for the shared library version and once of the static version. Making things worse, many of the files are built four times -- static and shared for both libcondorutils and libcondorapi. This change will explicitly list the files that go in just condorapi, just condorutils or both, and compile each one just once. As we already turn on -fPIC for all files, this should not be a problem. Also, the same problem happens in the classad library, so we'll do the same trick there.

title: Ticket #4024: Problems with DAG node priority implementation
description: In Dag::SetDefaultPriorities(), we go through and change the individual priorities of nodes according to the overall DAG priority. I haven't experimentally verified this, but I'm 99% certain that that means than if we dump out an old-style rescue DAG the nodes in the rescue DAG won't have their original priority values. I think it would be a lot cleaner to just keep the individual node priorities unchanged, and then figure out at submit time the higher of the overall priority and the node's priority. (Hmm -- and for that matter, a node's priority value has already been adjusted according to its parents. So maybe we need something like an original priority value and an effective priority value.) Unless we just want to forget about old-style rescue DAGs... Although I see another issue: say you have a bunch of priority 5 nodes and a bunch of priority 10s. If your overall DAG has a priority of 10 or higher you will erase the differences between the priority 5 and 10 nodes within this DAG. Is that what we want?
remarks: 2013-Oct-31 13:41:34 by wenger: One more thing: I kind of don't like the code appending priority to the VARS list of a node, as opposed to explicitly passing it in condor_submit() in dagman_submit.cpp. 2013-Oct-31 13:56:14 by wenger: I'm not sure why priority is in SubmitDagDeepOptions -- it seems like the priority for a sub-DAG should be automatically taken care of by the normal priority stuff for a node -- and it seems like if you explicitly set the priority for a sub-DAG within the top-level DAG file, this might conflict with the priority in SubmitDagDeepOptions. 2013-Oct-31 14:16:26 by wenger: I wonder if the "effective" priority of a node should be the sum of its own priority and the overall DAG priority. I think that might remove some inconsistencies. 2013-Oct-31 15:27:11 by wenger: Igor and I have been going back and forth about this, and I'm wondering whether something simpler is the way to go: effective node prio = explicit node prio + DAG prio and the node's parents don't affect its priority. 2013-Oct-31 15:28:50 by wenger: I'm thinking that we should ask for feedback on htcondor-users about a potential change to how priorities work. I don't know how many people are actually using them... 2013-Oct-31 15:36:17 by wenger: Hmm -- effective node prio = explicit node prio + sum(parents' prios) + DAG prio would be more consistent between sub-DAGs and parent/child, though. That would also be another reason to implement socket nodes for splices -- that would make implementing priorities for splices way easier. On the other hand, this could get kind of out-of-control for very "long" DAGs. I guess one argument in favor of not having the parent nodes affect the priority is that a node can only have one DAG, but it can have any number of parents, so having the parent DAG's priority affect things is a lot simpler. 2013-Oct-31 16:43:22 by wenger: Here's kind of a summary: Right now a node's priority is determined as follows: effective node prio = max(explicit node prio, parents' effective prios, DAG prio) This is really a problem for eventually fixing/re-implementing the "respond to priority change" feature, because it makes things asymmetrical with regard to increasing/decreasing the DAG priority. The current scheme also causes a problem because a high DAG priority erases relative priority differences of nodes within the DAG, which Igor and I both dislike. So there are a bunch of possible alternatives we've thrown back and forth: 1) effective node prio = max(explicit node prio, parents' effective prios) + DAG prio 2) effective node prio = sum(explicit node prio, parents' effective prios, DAG prio) 3) effective node prio = explicit node prio + DAG prio Number 1 is the smallest change from the way things currently work. But Igor doesn't like the max() function, and I'm not wild about it, either. Number 2 is probably the most self-consistent -- parent DAGs and parent nodes have the same effect on priorities. But I'm worried that in "long" DAGs priorities will get ridiculously high. Number 3 is very simple to understand, and avoids the "priority explosion" problem of number 2. The only down side is that things are not consistent between parent nodes and parent DAGs. I'm currently leaning towards number 3, and Igor says he's okay with that. But I wanted to get some feedback (and probably run things past htcondor-users) before making changes... (BTW, I'm open to schemes other than the above 3, but I think we should go with something fairly simple. We actually had a more complex scheme that the current one for a while, and as I recall we went away from it because it was too hard to understand.) 2013-Nov-29 14:11:07 by wenger: I just sent an email about this to htcondor-users -- we'll have to see what the reaction is. 2013-Dec-02 14:48:48 by wenger: Here's another possibility: 4) effective node prio = average(explicit node prio, parents' effective prios, DAG prio) This treats parent nodes and parent DAGs the same, but should be at least somewhat better in terms of the priority "explosion" than number 2 above. 2016-Jul-20 12:18:28 by wenger: Note: I think the changes to implement #5749 will fix this, but I need to verify things. Therefore I'm going to set this ticket back to the active state. 2016-Jul-29 15:41:53 by wenger: Yes, the #5749 fix does fix this problem, so I'm going to resolve the ticket.

title: Ticket #2959: Autofs and MOUNT_UNDER_SCRATCH do not mix
description: The MOUNT_UNDER_SCRATCH feature comes with one drawback - automount in Linux doesn't understand namespaces. Hence, when automount triggers, it will mount the filesystem in the parent namespace and it's not available in the job. You end up with an error message like this when mixing autofs and MOUNT_UNDER_SCRATCH: [bbockelm@rcf-bockelman condor]$ condor_run ls /cvmfs/cms.cern.ch ls: cannot open directory /cvmfs/cms.cern.ch: Too many levels of symbolic links While this is technically a problem with automount, I think it'll be quite awhile before a fixed version is widely available. Hence, we should provide a workaround, such as upgrading autofs mountpoints to shared-subtrees.

title: Ticket #7521: p-slot child rollup should contain evaluated d-slot values
description: When a custom d-slot attribute is rolled up into the p-slot, if the attribute value is an expression, the code currently puts the expression into the Child<Attr> list. This will almost certainly result in those list members evaluating to undefined, since they will refer to attributes in the d-slot and not in the p-slot. To fix this, we should evaluate the d-slot attribute values, and put the resulting literal values into the p-slots Child<Attr> attribute.

title: Ticket #4618: Remove DAGMan code that condor_rms node jobs on condor_rm of DAGMan
description: When DAGMan gets condor_rm'ed, there's code in the schedd to condor_rm the corresponding node jobs. But there's still code in Dag::RemoveRunningJobs() to do this as well. We should take that code out of DAGMan and just let the schedd do its thing without putting extra load on it. (Need to test to make sure this works, but I'm 99+% sure it will.)
remarks: 2014-Sep-30 10:08:34 by wenger: I just realized this isn't as simple as I thought, because if a DAG has a final node, and the DAGMan job gets condor_rm'ed, we need to remove any running node jobs before we submit the final node. (I'm actually kind of wondering whether we should wait for all node jobs to terminate before we start the final node, but that would be a change to the existing behaviour). 2014-Sep-30 13:02:24 by tannenba: What is the desired semantic for a FINAL node - is it supposed to run only once all jobs in the dag are done, or can it run beforehand? 2014-Sep-30 13:20:26 by wenger: Unfortunately, that hasn't been clearly defined in the "condor_rm of the DAG" and "ABORT-DAG-ON" cases. In all other (I think) cases, the FINAL node would only get run when all other node jobs have finished. The currently-implemented semantics are that, when you condor_rm a DAG with a final node, DAGMan condor_rm's any queued node jobs, and then submits the FINAL node (without waiting for the condor_rm'ed jobs to exit the queue). I guess I potentially want to split this ticket into two parts -- part one is duplicating the existing functionality except that DAGMan doesn't condor_rm the node jobs unless there's a FINAL node; part two would be possibly waiting for all of the node jobs to exit the queue before submitting the FINAL node. (Also see #3995.) 2014-Oct-28 12:17:51 by wenger: Note: Some of the tests, such as job_dagman_abort-A, job_dagman_abort-B, job_dagman_abort-final-A, and job_dagman_abort-final-B (and probably others) should check that node jobs get properly removed. (See the job_dagman_rm test for a way to do this.) 2014-Oct-29 17:30:41 by wenger: Hmm -- maybe we should make a test that checks that DAGMan does not, in fact, do a condor_rm when it gets condor_rm'ed itself. (Or add this functionality to the existing job_dagman_rm test.) Maybe one way to do this would be to specify a non-standard "condor_rm" binary to DAGMan, which would cause the test to fail if it gets run... 2014-Oct-29 17:44:54 by wenger: Okay, the fix for this (including documentation and a test improvement that checks the functionality) is committed. Since this is on the devel branch, I went ahead and committed it and I'm going to assign it to Zach for retroactive review. 2015-May-01 16:10:17 by zmiller: CODE REVIEW: Looks good!

title: Ticket #7034: condor_off -peaceful broken
description: Look like condor_off -peaceful broke in v8.7.10 ticket #6697 commit [55260]. Specifically, -peaceful now acts just like -graceful if MAXJOBRETIREMENTTIME=0 in condor_config on the startd, which is the default setting. This means with the default configuration, upon sending a condor_off -peaceful jobs will incorrectly get sent a SIGTERM after their max vacate time expires. Immediate workaround Until this bug is patched, if a site currently does not customize MAXJOBRETIREMENTTIME, a suggested workaround would be to add the following into the condor_config used by execute nodes MAXJOBRETIREMENTTIME = 1 A side effect of this workaround is there will be a 1 second delay when/if HTCondor wants to preempt a job due to policy reasons. But it should enable -peaceful to work as expected.

title: Ticket #7464: condor_q -better-analyze drops "!"
description: Stuart Anderson reports: Is it a bug or a feature that condor_q -better-analyze (version 8.8.6) drops "!", e.g., Requirements = !regexp("Intel.*Gold 6254", TARGET.cpuinfo_model_name) Slots Step Matched Condition ----- -------- --------- [0] 48 regexp("Intel.*Gold 6254",TARGET.cpuinfo_model_name) [1] 17847 TARGET.Arch == "X86_64" [2] 17799 [0] && [1] [5] 16739 TARGET.Disk >= RequestDisk [6] 16729 [2] && [5] [7] 16769 TARGET.Memory >= RequestMemory [8] 15692 [6] && [7] Line [0] is strictly true for this pool, but not the Condition being used in line [2] (pun intended).
remarks: 2019-Dec-11 15:33:44 by johnkn: It's a kind of a printing bug. The ! is preserved in the analysis, but is getting lost when the analysis steps are labeled for output. It would be clearer to show [0] as ! regexp(...) and give it the correct count for that sub-expression, but that's a harder fix. What is actually happening in the code is that step [2] is evaluating the sub-expression !regexp("Intel.*Gold 6254", TARGET.cpuinfo_model_name) && TARGET.Arch == "X86_64" but (mis)labeling it as [0] && [1] (it should perhaps be labelled ![0] && [1] ?) 2020-Apr-10 07:43:03 by tim: Bulk change of target version from v080808 to v080809 using ticket-target-mover. 2021-Jul-13 10:15:18 by tim: Moved to JIRA: https://opensciencegrid.atlassian.net/browse/HTCONDOR-514

title: Ticket #3974: EC2 jobs don't notice new X.509 authentication tokens.
description: Fermi is seeing a problem where they refresh their X.509 user proxies, but the new proxies aren't used until they restart HTCondor. This is different from the usual for grid universe.
remarks: 2013-Oct-08 18:31:21 by tlmiller: This appears to be a bug in libcurl; it seems to get different results for the same file contents (and presence/absence) depending on if the EC2 GAHP was restarted after the change. For instance, I submit an EC2 job to Amazon to keep the EC2 GAHP alive. I then submit an x509 job which goes on hold because Amazon doesn't like my grid proxy. (This should happen.) I then remove the contents of the proxy and submit a second x509 job, identical to the first. It fails in the same way -- which it shouldn't -- and I kill the GAHP. I force the GAHP (and the grid manager) to restart by submitting another EC2 job. I then submit another x509 job. That job fails with an error in CURL (problem with local certificate), before it gets to Amazon. Releasing the held jobs from before causes them to fail like the new job. Replacing the cert and submitting a new job doesn't change the error message. Oddly enough, putting all the jobs on hold does. Further investigation is required. I don't think this has anything to do with the grid manager or EC2 GAHP code directly -- we don't even read the X.509 keys, much less cache them. 2013-Oct-09 14:42:57 by tlmiller: Further review reveals a different potential problem: if a resource suffers an authorization failure, new jobs for that resource will automatically go on hold until the GRIDMANAGER_EMPTY_RESOURCE_DELAY seconds pass without any (active) jobs in the queue or the EC2 GAHP is restarted. Parag, when you see this problem occurring, what does the HTCondor queue look like? If it's full of held jobs, I'd like you to try setting GRIDMANAGER_EMPTY_RESOURCE_DELAY to 0 in your config file. Then any new or released job should cause a new attempt to contact the service, which should use the new proxy. 2013-Oct-09 14:44:14 by tlmiller: I also wasn't able to reproduce this problem in a simple test case that should have revealed if libcurl was caching auth tokens. The code paths aren't identical, but I'd like to get a better test case using HTCondor before proceeding now. 2013-Oct-09 16:26:50 by tlmiller: Notes on testing -- I have a job running on Amazon using an https:// URL and normal authentication tokens; this keeps the EC2 GAHP alive. I submit a job with a valid (but expired) X.509 proxy; because Amazon doesn't do that sort of thing, it replies with an error that the EC2 protocol level authentication is wrong, and the job goes on hold. I then delete the contents of the proxy. I have GRIDMANAGER_EMPTY_RESOURCE_DELAY set 0, so I can immediately submit a new copy of the same job. This one dies because CURL doesn't like empty files as X.509 proxies. So far, so good. I put the second job on hold. I copy the proxy back into the file and submit a third job -- which dies like the second job, not the first. Short of restarting the EC2 GAHP, I haven't been able to get a job submitted after the second one to get the first one's error again. (I have verified that I can get multiple first-job errors if I don't change the proxy.) 2013-Oct-16 14:29:49 by tlmiller: This problem occurs in the simple test case, but only if you test with three requests (first one with real proxy, second with empty proxy, third with real proxy). strace verifies that open() and read() are being called appropriately. I wasn't able to track down the problem, but retesting with libcurl 7.33.0 seems to solve it. I'm going to recommend Parag try using a newer version of libcurl while I start getting my changeset into shape. 2014-Jan-09 13:45:03 by tlmiller: Parag writes: Good news! I switched to new curl 7.33.0 and now updates to the credentials are picked up correctly. 2014-Jan-15 10:18:23 by tlmiller: Confirmed with Parag that other system updates (probably to OpenSSL, although it's unclear) since 2013-10-16 resolve the problem without requiring a libcurl upgrade.

title: Ticket #2518: Child processes are inheriting log files on Windows
description: When a file is opened through C runtime functions like open, its inheritance flag is set to true by default. As such, on Windows when a daemon calls Create_Process, if the inherit flag for the Windows CreateProcess function is also set to true, the child process will inherit any open files. On Linux Condor will go and close all open files as part of the fork/exec process. On Windows this code was commented out with the intention of developing a proper fix that never materialized. As such, with the new ability to keep logs open between writes, the child processes suddenly have handles to their parent's. log file. When Condor attempts to rotate the log, it fails because it cannot rename a file that is held open by another process. There are effectively two problems right now on Windows. Files are being inherited by child processes by default. Log files are being inherited because they are kept open by default. This ticket is to address the second issue. Solution: Have the safefile library support the _O_NOINHERIT flag for open and the N option for fopen. These will allow opening a file and set the inherit option to false. - Done, needs testing. Change the calls to safe_fopen in dprintf to include the N option. This option will be ignored on Linux but will pass down the correct flags within the safefile library. - Done, needs testing. Future Work: Figure out how to keep Condor processes from inheriting files in general on Windows. One solution may be to always pass in the N option for safe_fopen and use _O_NOINHERIT for safe_open.
remarks: 2011-Oct-07 12:50:37 by ziliang: Fix for this resulted in problems when 'c' was passed into safe_fopen. Jim has spun another version of safefile to address the issue.
attachments: inherit.patch 60974 bytes added by ziliang on 2011-Oct-04 17:24:11 UTC. Patch that updates safefile and changes dprintf callsites to use the N option for fopen.

title: Ticket #6808: Removed jobs remain in queue forever with leave_in_queue
description: When a job enters the REMOVED status, if LeaveJobInQueue evaluates to True, then the job remains in the queue. If LeaveJobInQueue later evaluates to False, the job is not retired from the queue, like it should be. It will remain there until the schedd is restarted or condor_rm -forcex is used on it. This is a side effect of a bug fix to handle removal of problematic grid universe jobs. When a grid universe job was removed, if the gridmanager couldn't cancel the remote job, it would put the job in the HELD status. If the job was later released (back to REMOVED status), we wanted the gridmanager to have a chance to retry canceling the remote job before retiring the job from the queue.

title: Ticket #5727: memory leak in condor_q client, noticed w/ condor_q python binding
description: Scott in htcondor-users reports a memory leak that can be reproduced with the below snippet of python code; with no jobs running, he typically sees the memory use increase by 128kb once every 45 or so iterations of the loop. import resource import htcondor import gc schedd = htcondor.Schedd() while True: schedd.query() # explicitly run the garbage collector to free up mem not leaked gc.collect() print('mem use: %s (kb)' % resource.getrusage(resource.RUSAGE_SELF).ru_maxrss) A work-around for people using an earlier version of HTCondor is to use Schedd().xquery() instead of query(). Valgrind did find a problem with Schedd.query() but not with xquery(); explicitly calling the garbage collector in the test code confirms this theory.

title: Ticket #751: Expected run time for DeferralTime jobs should be user visible
description: (Based on a report by Scot Kronenfeld for the VDT.) I can't tell when my job is going to run next. I could probably muck around in the log file to figure out when it last exited, and then add my deferral time to that - possible, but obviously not very use friendly. In my case above, I use a random expression in my deferral time, so I really couldn't figure it out precisely either. It would be really nice to have a command line utility (whether it's added to condor_q or something else) that told me when my job will run next. This could be useful even for 'cron' style jobs (as opposed to 'deferral' style jobs), because the cron jobs could be held for some reason (or because I'm lazy, and I don't want to open up submission files and parse cron expressions) Proposed behavior by Alan De Smet: DeferralTime can be a calculated expression. The expression is calculated once and cached. This result isn't in the class ad, at least not the one shown to condor_q. It should be, perhaps as DeferralTimeCalculated. Once present, users can now use "condor_q -format '%d' DeferralTimeCalculated" to get the answer. For the answer in more human terms, you can use "condor_q -format '%s' 'formatTime(DeferralTimeCalculated)'". We might optionally consider a "condor_q -deferred" option that will generate a specialized report (like -run and -hold) listing the expected start times for deferred jobs.

title: Ticket #1158: Condor Daemon Log can't grow beyond 2GB
description: Condor daemon log files are limited to 2GB on 32/64-bit machines, or any machine where int is 4 bytes wide, due to the fact that the param() return type is int, and the value we read from the config file passes through atoi(). Some work was done to compensate for the 2GB boundary during log rotations as found in ticket #823, but it is not enough as described in the remarks on that ticket.
remarks: Resolved by adding the option to have more than just one rotated log file. Thus, files still won't grow beyond 2GB but one can specify arbitrarily many. description: Vanderbilt ran into errors with their CEs that would occur after the Gridmanager sent a GM_REFRESH_PROXY command [1] to the Blahp. The Blahp creates symlinks in the user's home directories that point to the location of the old proxy. These are needed when the blahp creates a new proxy file as part of job submission (when the blahp is configured to create a limited proxy for the job and when glexec is used). title: Ticket #3535: Fetching user priorities from negotiator takes a long time
description: Resolved/abandoned as user priorities are now fetched from the collector Fetching user priorities from negotiator takes a long time; at times it has appeared that the negotiator waits for the end of a (potentially long) negotiation cycle until responding to a request to fetch user priority information. The end result to the user is often condor_userprio or condor_q -analyze:priority commands take a really long time to respond, or on a busy pool could timeout. SamF will investigate what is going on here and report back to ToddT, since ToddT's recollection is at least at one point in the past the negotiator invoked daemon core's ServiceCommandSocket() method periodically while doing negotiation specifically to avoid the above situation. Please refrain from remarks/comments on this ticket for a few days until SamF's initial investigation is done. Thanks! -ToddT
remarks: 2013-Mar-21 14:01:12 by samf: condor_userprio (or possibly condor_q -analyze:priority) takes a long time to run. We found that it hangs when the listening socket corresponding to the initial command socket (initial_command_socket or DC Command Handler) finds that there is an incoming command, spawns a new socket to read data, and then there is no data to read on the new socket. When there is data to read from the new socket, the data is read and the initial command finishes. In the case where the command hangs, the command DaemonCommandProtocol::WaitForSocketData gets called, the socket gets registered, and the socket is not listened to by the negotiator until after the end of the negotiation cycle; therefore, the command will not be run until after the end of a negotiation cycle. Currently, DaemonCore::ServiceCommandSocket does not listen to any socket other than the initial command socket. If the command for some reason does not finish, it will not finish until after the negotiation cycle. I also have a design document that I will probably post soon. 2013-Mar-22 16:11:16 by samf: I've attached a patch. Some differences from the design doc are that I need to call CallSocketHandler_worker instead of calling HandleReq directly. This will then call the handlers for a registered socket. Also, if the socket needs to be removed from sockTable, CallSocketHandler_worker will do that. One caveat is that I also need to make sure to exit the do/while loop in ServiceCommandSocket prematurely if the socket has been removed as otherwise an EXCEPT will be thrown unnecessarily. 2013-Mar-22 23:38:53 by bbockelm: Hi, Did you ever get the chance to attached the design doc? Brian 2013-Mar-25 09:04:09 by samf: How I reproduced the problem. First, I submitted a larger number (10000) jobs to make the negotiator take a long time. Submit File: universe = vanilla executable = /bin/sleep getenv=true arguments = 30 should_transfer_files = yes when_to_transfer_output = on_exit_or_evict output = o error = e log = l +NEGOTIATE_ALL_JOBS_IN_CLUSTER = True queue 10000 I think +NEGOTIATE_ALL_JOBS_IN_CLUSTER = True in the submit file didn't do the trick. So I changed my local condor config file. Settings that I have in my condor_config.local file: ###################################################################### # Testing long times for fetching user priorities from negotiatior ###################################################################### NEGOTIATE_ALL_JOBS_IN_CLUSTER = True NEG_SLEEP = 0 MAX_NEGOTIATOR_LOG = 1000000000 I needed to up the size of my negotiator log for debugging purposes. NEG_SLEEP can be set to a non-zero integer to have the negotiator sleep for that many seconds after each negotiation. I found that when NEG_SLEEP = 1 caused the problem to sometimes go away, so I did my testing with NEG_SLEEP = 0. Initially, I just called condor_userprio many times from the command line. I did see that I would get codnor_userprio to hang doing this. This would happen during the negotiation cycle. When the cycle finished, condor_userprio would finish. In order to call condor_userprio more times and faster than I could do so manually, I created a shell script to call condor_userprio: #!/bin/sh while true do date +"%D %T:%N" condor_userprio done date will spit out the date and time with nanoseconds. I found I needed about 1/100th of a second resolution to distinguish clearly if condor_userprio was hanging. I would pipe the result of this script into a file and examine the output of that file continuously to see the freeze. Once the negotiation cycle finished, condor_userprio would not hanging again until another negotiation cycle started. 2013-Mar-25 09:28:18 by samf: Two problems I ran into when implementing my solution: Making sure that I didn't do an infinite loop with the do/while loop in ServiceCommandSocket. HandleReq can return a result not equal to KEEP_STREAM. With the original code when HandleReq ran working on the socket that had been waiting for data, it would set its variable always_keep_stream to false. Since the stream is supposed to close in this case and we don't close it, the Selector for that stream will keep indicating that there is data to be read. Consequently, selector.has_ready() always returns true and we get an infinite loop. My initial work around was to reset the selector when HandleReq returned a value not equal to KEEP_STREAM. That would cause the loop to break. As indicated in the previous point, the steam/socket should be closed under some circumstances. To reduced code duplication and also to use the handlers associated with WaitForSocketData, I switched from HandleReq to DaemonCore::CallSocketHandler_worker which calls both HandleReq and CheckPrivState. It also calls Cancel_Socket appropriately. I just need to give CallSocketHandler_worker the correct parameters to emulate the original call to HandleReq. In the case where a socket has been cancelled, I need a way to exit the loop so that an EXCEPT is called (causing the negotiator to crash) when evaluating selector.failed(). We do expect a failure to occur when select is called while examining the recently closed socket. To exit the loop, I used the conditions that Register_Socket uses to check to see if a slot is empty or available; if those conditions returned ture, then I call selector.execute() to change the state of the selector to exit the loop. 2013-Apr-10 14:16:13 by tannenba: Code Review Calling selector.execute() on a potentially undefined descriptor (or even worse, on a descriptor that has been reused) to break out of loop seems dangerous. Break out of the loop a different way, ie. use another variable. Doing a string compare on the handler.descrip as a string constant is not a great idea, since someone could change the descrip elsewhere in the code and surprisingly break something. Either make this string a constant defined in one place, or even better, add a data member to the sockTable entry that says if DC is waiting for data. Confirm that the socket is not waiting for an outgoing connect when deciding to select on it or not. I.e., make sure SockEnt is_connect_pending is false. Add a comment explaining why you are iterating with one socket being passed to select() vs placing lots of sockets into the select fd set and calling select once. Perhaps it is because the set of fds could change every time you call a handler? Why invoke CallSocketHandler_worker() vs CallSocketHandler() ? please place a comment telling future hackers why this choice was made. Perhaps because you want the handler to be called in this same thread? Add a knob (no need to document it) to disable ServiceCommandSocket() all together. By default, ServiceCommandSocket() should do its thing, but having this knob will give us a safety net in the field (since it is a bit dangerous thing at least until the Future Work happens). Test Plan Please confirm (via remarks with console captures in the ticket, or even better via regression test) by doing a before and after test for: Confirm condor_userprio waits until end of negotiation cycle before patch, and responds immediately after patch -- and negotiator continues to operate correctly afterwards :). Confirm that "condor_off -fast" waits until end of negotiation cycle before patch, and responds immediately after patch. Confirm that both issuing a "condor_reconfig" or sending a SIGHUP waits until end of negotiation cycle both before and after patch, because iirc RH added code to make this always true and we want to make sure we didn't muck that up. Future Work Would really like to see a list of daemon_core command ints passed to ServiceCommandSocket(). We know that it is unlikely for every command to be safe to be handled this way, so the idea is the caller pass an explicit whitelist of safe command ints. Probably would require adding a data member to the SockEnt which contains the command int (once it is discovered), and any socket with command that does not match the white list is simply registered and thus the handler is not invoked until going back to the main daemoncore driver loop. 2013-Apr-16 12:23:46 by samf: Responding to the code review. Sounds reasonable. Using break command to exit loop. Had to make class DaemonCommandProtocol have friend class DaemonCore; (in theory). Then, adding to SockEnt the parameter bool waiting_for_data. This already will get initialized to false. We then set this to true in the function Register_Socket. Adding another condition on the non-initial command socket. Easy. The original code in ServiceCommandSocket has a do-while loop that selects on the initial command socket. There is a comment in the code that says, "loop until no more commands waiting on socket". While we are servicing a socket, more data could have come in and need to be read. So at least for the initial command socket, we need to call select multiple times. In such a case, we would need to confirm after each time we find that the selector is ready to ready data if the current socket we are examining is ready to be read by using selector.fd_ready(i,Selector::IO_READ) where i is the current socket index. We know that we will have to do this in the case where we have the initial command socket having a new command and another socket waiting for data. selector.has_ready() will return true. I do not see how this results in any fewer system calls. I also see this making the code harder to read because the loop will need to contain code to ask if the particular socket still has data to read. CallSocketHandler() when called on the initial command socket will perform an accept on the socket, which seems to be the desired behavior during the main DaemonCore loop. I don't think we want this behavior in ServiceCommandSocket and so we need to call the worker version. However, CallSocketHandler() does have a way to control the maximum number of accepts per cycle. m_iMaxAcceptsPerCycle = param_integer("MAX_ACCEPTS_PER_CYCLE", 8); Added. 2013-Apr-16 15:14:09 by samf: Code Review Remark: Point 4: Actually, I DO expect the list of fds to change. When we call a command that had previously been waiting for socket data, the socket will be removed from the list of registered sockets. I then will be later on possibly still be performing select on that fd. In which case, to ensure that selector.execute() does not go into the FAILED state, I would need to remove the fd from the selector. In order to accommodate this and deal with the fact selector.fd_ready needs cannot accommodate a non ready state, I see more reason to iterate through each socket via the selector rather than use the fd_ready command. I cannot use FD_ISSET directly because I don't have access to the read filters, and nor do I want to be maintaining this filter either. 2013-Apr-16 15:56:43 by samf: Regarding Future Work: In the class DaemonCommandProtocol (defined in daemon_command.h), there are three integers in: m_req Comment says: the command that was sent m_real_cmd Comment says: for DC_AUTHENTICATE, the final command to execute m_auth_cmd Comment says: for DC_AUTHENTICATE, the command the security session will be used for daemonCore->CommandNumToTableIndex(m_real_cmd,&cmd_index) is how we get the command integer. We could use the commnad daemonCore::InServiceCommandSocket to determine if we're in ServiceCommandSocket. To create a whitelist, this would be in daemonCore::HandleReq just before doProtocol gets called or somewhere in DaemonCommandProtocol::ExecCommand(). We'd ask if we were indeed in ServceCommandSocket and if the cmd_index was on our white list, then we'd continue on. Otherwise, ExecCommand() should return CommandProtocolInProgress. It's not perfect, but it's a start down this path. 2013-Apr-16 16:39:38 by samf: In terms of the test plan, condor_userprio can wait until the end of the negotiation cycle without the patch and does not wait with the patch. There is a knob that controls the implementation status of the patch. condor_off -fast seems to finish before the negotiation cycle finishes even without the patch. This is good, yes? I suspect there is some condition I'm not properly testing. condor_reconfig and sending a SIGHUP both indeed wait until the end of the negotiation cycle. 2013-Apr-16 18:39:59 by samf: There's a lot more code to use when using multiple fds. Also, CallSocketHandler() actually seems to work, so we're using that now instead of CallSocketHandler_worker(). 2013-May-10 10:54:27 by tannenba: I noticed that v7.9.6 is now running on the UW CHTC central manager in beta testing, and condor_userprio still seems slow to respond; please investigate/explain. title: Ticket #35: condor_schedd: use hardlinks for executables in SPOOL whenever possibl
description: An idea for reducing disk space use in the SPOOL: whenever the condor_schedd is about to copy a binary/initial checkpoint/ickpt into SPOOL, it should look for an identical binary owned by the same user. If such a binary exists, simply hardlink the existing one to the new one’s name. Advantages: Saves disk space no matter how the jobs arrive, so long as they share a binary. Can save space on jobs submitted via Condor-C. Disadvantages: Starting with 6.9.1, the default for copy_to_spool FALSE, so the local submission benefit is minimal. This is new functionality, and would necessitate someone tracking file identities (probably using a hashing algorithm). Will this tracking information be held by the schedd and lost on restart? That would be safe, but would make it less effective. If it’s stored on disk, where? Perhaps squeezed into the ickpt’s filename? A tempting proposal, especially since it will benefit Condor-C users. We have a number of Condor-C users who are basically submitting the same binary or small number of binaries over and over again, so this would help them.

title: Ticket #2631: Livelocked Metronome jobs.
description: We got bit by this again at the tail end of last week. (2011-11-06.) Background: Metronome run consists of a minimum of four jobs. Three of them are persistent: one DAGMan to watch the monitor, the monitor itself, and the DAGMan managing the worflow of the Metronome job proper. All three of these run in the scheduler universe. The submit-side jobs in the workflow all run in the local universe. We split them up this way because we can't limit either type of job on what we'd like, which is I/O; instead, we limit by number, and have a much larger limit for scheduler universe jobs than local universe jobs, which tend to much heavier-weight. Of course, the remote tasks run in the vanilla universe. These last two types of job are (of course) transient, but are the actual work we're trying to get done. The problem: we can end up in a state where no progress can be made. This happens when the queue starts to get very large because machines are down. What we see are a large number of idle scheduler universe jobs and (eventually) nothing but idle vanilla universe jobs. With enough idle Metronome runs (at most one per idle vanilla universe jobs), there will be enough running jobs in the scheduler universe -- ones that aren't doing anything, because they're waiting for vanilla universe jobs that won't run until we bring the machine back up -- to prevent any new Metronome job from getting started. (Its DAGMans will be submitted and stay idle.) (One subtlety is that if the monitor and its DAG start, their presence as running scheduler jobs can prevent the corresponding run DAG from starting, leading to a more-formal kind of livelock. We would like to be able to group these jobs to make sure that doesn't happen.) We don't want to lose the jobs -- because once we get the machine back up, they can start running -- but we also don't want to waste time leaving execute nodes idle. I'm just thinking out loud here, but I think what we want as a solution -- aside from limiting scheduler universe jobs by load -- would be some way to put the scheduler universe jobs corresponding to a given vanilla universe job on hold when the vanilla universe job has been idle for long enough (for say, eight hours). That would give some other Metronome job "room" to start running and try to get some of its own vanilla universe jobs through. With a PeriodicRelease expression, the held jobs could reenter the queue to check if the machine has been repaired.
remarks: 2011-Nov-16 18:24:15 by tlmiller: ToddT, ToddM, and BeckyG discussed this for a while. We came up with two ideas that we like. One idea daddresses the problem by allowing us to remove the numeric limit on scheduler universe jobs by directly limiting I/O. We presently use DAGMan node classes to limit io-intensive parts of the run, but that only works withing the DAG. The proposal is to leverage the token-dispensing code already present in the schedd for limiting Condor sandbox transfer, having DAGMan act on behalf of each node (including pre- and post- scripts) whose class is concurrency-limited. (With some sort of declaration of which token each class tries to grab, if any.) Doing this in DAGMan means that we can get it right once, instead of all of our users trying to reimplement in shell script. Another option, that should be easy to implement, but could be very dangerous, would be to add ClassAd functions getJobAttribute( jobID, attribute ) and setJobAttribute( jobID, attribute, value ). We could then use some periodic attribute in the vanilla universe jobs to place the corresponding scheduler universe jobs on hold, and give some other job a chance to run. The first idea requires a little more work, but is much less dangerous and probably much easier to use.

title: Ticket #3923: OpenNebula doesn't like long EC2 user data
description: HTCondor can't successfully submit jobs to OpenNebula when the job supplies user data of more than ~2K. Comparison with the functioning euca-tools revealed that HTCondor was embedding newlines in the base64 encoding of the user data in the URI. It's not clear why this might be a size-dependent problem, but testing w/o the embedded newlines and 3.6KB of user data succeeded.
remarks: 2013-Sep-16 16:47:05 by tlmiller: The obvious approach -- asking OpenSSL to not emit newlines -- failed because it (somehow) broke signature generation. Instead, the code removes newlines from the base64-encoded user data string (before URL-encoding). 2013-Sep-16 17:03:29 by tlmiller: diff --git a/src/ec2_gahp/amazonCommands.cpp b/src/ec2_gahp/amazonCommands.cpp index 74c1362..0d13970 100644 --- a/src/ec2_gahp/amazonCommands.cpp +++ b/src/ec2_gahp/amazonCommands.cpp @@ -714,6 +714,7 @@ bool AmazonVMStart::workerFunction(char **argv, int argc, std::string &result_st // // Handle user data. + // (FIXME: Will this code have problems with embedded NULs?) // std::string buffer; if( strcasecmp( argv[7], NULLSTRING ) ) { @@ -730,7 +731,21 @@ bool AmazonVMStart::workerFunction(char **argv, int argc, std::string &result_st buffer += udFileContents; } if( ! buffer.empty() ) { char * base64Encoded = condor_base64_encode( (const unsigned char *)buffer.c_str(), buffer.length() ); + + // OpenNebula barfs on embedded newlines in this data. + char * read = base64Encoded; + char * write = base64Encoded; + for( ; * read != '\0'; ++read ) { + char tmp = * read; + if( tmp != '\n' ) { + * write = tmp; + ++write; + } + } + * write = '\0'; + vmStartRequest.query_parameters[ "UserData" ] = base64Encoded; free( base64Encoded ); } 2013-Sep-17 13:32:55 by jfrey: CODE REVIEW This code change looks good. Embedded NULs shouldn't be a problem for this new code, as they should be encoded after condor_base64_encode(). However, readShortFile() does have an issue with embedded NULs. That should be fixed, but that's a separate ticket.

title: Ticket #3889: Periodically dump rescue DAG while continuing to run
description: As per discussion in the LIGO phone conference today -- I think it would be a great idea for DAGMan to periodically dump out a rescue DAG while continuing to run. This would mean that, even if something went wrong with recovery mode (see #3882), you still wouldn't have to start over from scratch. I think that the frequency at which the rescue DAG is dumped should be configurable -- it could default to something pretty infrequent, like every 24 hours or something. Also, if the DAG succeeds, I think DAGMan should remove the rescue DAG, so it doesn't accidentally get run. (Or maybe we could dump a rescue DAG that has everything marked as done?) Design doc at: https://docs.google.com/a/wisc.edu/document/d/1bqP6fcEsSM9yciJ9NlVPP7u71YLbRGrFDc5ihOwqMSA
remarks: 2013-Oct-11 16:10:20 by wenger: Hmm -- I'm wondering now whether this rescue DAG should have a special name that doesn't cause it to get run automatically if the DAG is re-submitted. (The user would have to rename the rescue DAG file or something for it to actually get used.) 2013-Oct-11 16:11:06 by wenger: Oh, yeah -- especially for condor_hold/condor_release -- we wouldn't want to run the rescue DAG in that situation... 2013-Oct-18 14:04:42 by wenger: Hmm -- I wonder if maybe we'd be better off just making a copy of the workflow log file periodically instead of dumping a rescue DAG. (Also see #3993.) 2013-Oct-22 10:29:26 by wenger: Okay, after thinking about this, I've changed my mind back to dumping a rescue DAG instead of copying the workflow log. Here are the reasons: Simplicity/reliability (at the present time, rescue DAGs are probably still more reliable than recovery mode). Smaller files -- the rescue DAGs are a lot smaller than the log file. Ease/speed of implementation -- not as much actual work has to be done to deal with the rescue DAGs. The condor_submit_dag -recovery <file> option would result in node jobs whose DAGManJobId doesn't match the new parent DAGMan, unless DAGMan does a condor_qedit on all of the child jobs. 2015-Sep-22 11:07:19 by tpdownes: Upon discussion w/Kent, lower priority to 4 and remove LIGO tag as it's a more a general DAG reliability feature rather than a specific LIGO problem.

title: Ticket #3470: Allow old signal escalation semantics and to use remove_killI_sig
description: The semantics of signal escalation changed, requiring that jobs add job_wants_graceful_removal in the submit file if it wants to use a custom exit signal for removal. Additionally, it removed the usage of remove_kill_sig as an optional for defining a custom signal for removal. It would be nice to have the option of whether to require jobs to specify if they want to use a custom signal (new method) or to use a custom signal if it is defined (original method) as well as to allow remove_kill_sig to be used to define the signal. If both remove_kill_sig and kill_sig are defined, remove_kill_sig should be preferred (as it was before).
remarks: 2013-Jan-31 13:34:44 by tstclair: Initial inspection looks ok to me, I'll let Dan chime in on his verdict. 2013-Jan-31 15:32:11 by danb: This syntax looks wrong to me: MachineMaxVacateTime = $(KILLING_TIMEOUT-1) According to the following code, the meaning of JOBS_REQUEST_GRACEFUL_REMOVAL is not that it is the default for WANT_GRACEFUL_REMOVAL. if( param_boolean("JOBS_REQUEST_GRACEFUL_REMOVAL",false) ) thejobAd->LookupBool(ATTR_WANT_GRACEFUL_REMOVAL, job_wants_graceful_removal ); } else if( findSoftKillSig(thejobAd) != -1 || findRmKillSig(thejobA&d) != -1 ) { job_wants_graceful_removal = true; } Instead, it is a switch between the new and old behavior. This is confusing to anyone who isn't intimately familiar with the history of all this. If it is false (the default), then graceful removal is only used if a custom kill signal is defined. The job's definition of WANT_GRACEFUL_REMOVAL is ignored. If JOBS_REQUEST_GRACEFUL_REMOVAL is true, then graceful removal only happens if he job also sets WANT_GRACEFUL_REMOVAL to true. I would perfer that if the job sets WANT_GRACEFUL_REMOVAL to true or to false, then we honor that setting. Make sense? 2013-Jan-31 16:21:31 by danb: The new patch assumes that LookupBool() leaves the result value alone if the attribute is not defined. While that may be how it is currently implemented, I don't see anything in the header file that guarantees these semantics. I'll leave it up to you how paranoid to be. One solution would be to update the header file ;-) Other than that point, I see no issues with the new patch. 2013-Feb-01 08:41:15 by rrati: Added protection for LookupBool semantic change if the attribute isn't defined. Better safe than sorry. :) 2013-Feb-01 08:41:46 by rrati: Please consider this change for inclusion the stable release. 2013-Feb-18 16:18:06 by smoler: Documentation task to be completed: Add documentation of the GRACEFULLY_REMOVE_JOBS config knob. This is a schedd param that controls whether jobs are gracefully removed by default. It can be overridden by a job setting want_graceful_removal in the submit description file. The default value is TRUE. 2013-May-20 15:15:18 by tannenba: Looks like this changed semantics from v7.8 and v8.0 - do we need to warn users who are upgrading? 2013-May-20 16:38:02 by danb: Hi Todd, I think I overlooked the fact that GRACEFULLY_REMOVE_JOBS is true by default when I reviewed the update to this patch. It certainly is a surprise to me. If we want to keep that behavior, I agree that users should be warned. --Dan 2013-May-21 15:39:01 by tstclair: The documentation might go something like: "8.0 series signal escalation semantics have changed to better align with previous versions (7.6 & prior) when kill_sig is present. By default 'GRACEFULLY_REMOVE_JOBS = TRUE' replaces 'JOBS_REQUEST_GRACEFUL_REMOVAL=FALSE' from the 7.8 series. Should users depend on the 7.8 series signal escalation semantics, they can set 'GRACEFULLY_REMOVE_JOBS = FALSE'." I'm not exactly certain where this goes in the manual so I'm kicking back to TT. 2013-May-21 15:53:02 by danb: Hi Tim, I'm not sure I agree that the new behavior is more in line with 7.6 behavior. The new default is GRACEFULLY_REMOVE_JOBS=TRUE. This was never the default prior to 7.9. By default, removal was done via a fast shutdown of the starter, not a graceful one. This influences how the job is shut down and whether file transfer has an opportunity to save state. Maybe there is some other behavior you have in mind when you say it is more in line with 7.6? 2013-May-21 16:04:27 by tstclair: should append 'when kill_sig is present' [EDITED]. Also feel free to edit the notice.
